programme_metadata.programme_title: DFID Adolescent Research Programme Gender and Adolescence: Global Evidence (ODI) Adolescent Wellbeing Programme - AWP (UNICEF Innocenti)

output_1.title: GAGE: Evidence generation - Rigorous and high quality policy relevant evidence is generated on "what works" to enhance adolescent girls' capabilities, and the methodological tools and approaches that are most effective in gaining a better understanding of "what works".

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: GAGE developed its Downstream Partner Map, updated at quarterly meetings. AWP initially exempted from mapping but now required to complete it. GAGE expanded sample size from 8,000 to 18,000 adolescents at no additional cost.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Both GAGE (ODI) and AWP (UNICEF Innocenti) met or exceeded all milestones and indicators. GAGE produced 55 knowledge products (vs. milestone of 35) and 11 datasets (vs. milestone of 2). AWP produced 65 publications in 2017 and leveraged additional funding (US$1.9m from Oak Foundation, US$1.25m from US Department of Labour).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: GAGE has robust financial monitoring via annual statements of work and quarterly invoicing. AWP’s MoU was amended to extend the project period to December 2018 (no-cost extension). Both programmes engage regularly with DFID country offices and policy teams (e.g., Gender, VAWG, Youth, Education).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between GAGE/AWP and DFID policy teams (e.g., Inclusive Societies, Social Protection). Quarterly meetings and shared calendars of events facilitate alignment. GAGE’s ‘3Cs’ Research Framework and AWP’s 5 key messages provide cohesive thematic focus.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: GAGE negotiated fixed rates for inputs and applied fee caps to ensure VfM. Renting local equipment (e.g., anthropometric tools) saved £11,000 in Ethiopia and £7,500 in Bangladesh. AWP minimized costs via remote conferencing and voluntary peer review.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: DFID receives timely financial reports and invoices from both partners. GAGE tracks deliverables via annual statements of work; AWP provides fund utilization and narrative reports. Quarterly forecasting vs. spend results are shared with DFID.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: GAGE adjusted baseline data collection to a two-stage design, saving £123,000 in Year 1. AWP’s no-cost extension (April 2017) aligned implementation with grant period. Both programmes adapted to DFID priorities (e.g., gender, child marriage).
adaptive_management_examples: GAGE expanded sample size from 8,000 to 18,000 adolescents without additional cost, responding to evidence needs.
AWP’s no-cost extension (March–December 2018) corrected a misalignment between grant period and implementation schedule.
Both programmes proactively managed risks (e.g., security in Gaza/Jordan/Lebanon, protests in Ethiopia) with updated policies for staff duty of care.
GAGE developed innovative qualitative research techniques and toolkits in response to methodological challenges (e.g., measuring shifts in wellbeing).

main_implementation_challenges: Heightened security and political risks in fragile states (e.g., Gaza, Jordan, Lebanon, Ethiopia) required updated duty-of-care policies.
Measuring shifts in adolescent wellbeing posed methodological challenges, addressed via new tools (e.g., ‘Evidence Gap Map’).
Coordinating research uptake across DFID’s dispersed policy teams (e.g., Gender, VAWG, Youth) required proactive engagement.
AWP initially lacked a Downstream Partner Map, later mandated by DFID.
external_factors_impact: Protests in Ethiopia significantly increased operational risks, necessitating risk mitigation measures.
Political instability in Gaza/Jordan/Lebanon affected fieldwork but was managed via adjusted security protocols.
Funding uncertainty for AWP in its final year (2018) prompted discussions on potential extensions.
contextual_constraints_new: Gendered norms (e.g., sexual purity, family honor) and risks of gender-based violence emerged as stronger barriers than anticipated, shaping research focus.
Limited baseline data on adolescent wellbeing required adaptive approaches to tracking progress (e.g., revised logframe indicators).
Unexpected delays in World Bank’s implementation design (Bangladesh) led GAGE to adopt a two-stage baseline data collection, saving costs.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Need for specialized skills in participatory research and ethical clearance processes (addressed via training and expanded anti-harassment policies).
Limited local capacity for longitudinal mixed-methods evaluations required GAGE to invest in toolkits and guidance products.
risk_materialization: Security risks in fragile states (e.g., Gaza, Ethiopia) materialized but were mitigated via updated policies.
Funding risks for AWP in 2018 were addressed through a no-cost extension and co-funding leverage (e.g., US$1.9m from Oak Foundation).

budget_execution_vs_plan.GAGE: On track; £6,088,082 spent by March 2018 (of £25,872,750 total). No variance in forecasting; contract amendment in March 2017 revised milestones/payments.
budget_execution_vs_plan.AWP: On track; no-cost extension to December 2018 aligned spend with implementation. Quarterly forecasts vs. spend shared with DFID.

value_for_money_assessment.GAGE: High VfM: Exceeded deliverables (9 in Year 1, 14 in inception), expanded sample size (8,000→18,000) at no extra cost. Saved £123,000 via two-stage baseline design and £18,500 via equipment rental.
value_for_money_assessment.AWP: High VfM: Leveraged US$3.15m in co-funding (Oak Foundation, US DOL, etc.). Minimized costs via remote conferencing, voluntary peer review, and open-access publications.

financial_management_quality.GAGE: Robust: Timely financial reports, quarterly invoicing, and procurement policies tailored to GAGE. No fee renegotiations.
financial_management_quality.AWP: Strong: Audited financial statements provided annually; fund utilization reports shared in advance with DFID. Compliance with UNICEF procurement rules.

cost_efficiency_achieved.GAGE: Efficient: Negotiated input rates for 5 years; fee caps applied. Shared services procurement fee tailored to programme needs.
cost_efficiency_achieved.AWP: Efficient: Used UNICEF’s standard procurement rules and contract review committees to select cost-effective contractors.

co_funding_materialization.AWP: Materialized: Leveraged US$1.9m (Oak Foundation), US$1.25m (US DOL), and support from Sida, Gates Foundation, and UNICEF country offices.

key_delivery_lessons: Longitudinal mixed-methods evaluations require flexible baseline designs to accommodate delays (e.g., World Bank’s implementation design in Bangladesh).
Participatory research tools must be adapted to local contexts (e.g., gendered norms) to ensure ethical and meaningful data collection.
Proactive risk management (e.g., security protocols, ethical clearance) is critical in fragile states but adds transaction costs.
successful_delivery_practices: Quarterly partner mapping (GAGE) and shared event calendars improved coordination with DFID.
Open-access publications and translations (AWP) enhanced research uptake in non-English contexts.
Two-stage baseline data collection (GAGE) saved costs while maintaining rigor.
Leveraging UNICEF’s field presence (AWP) amplified policy influence in programme countries.
management_adaptations_made: Revised logframe to include baseline data for impact indicators (by July 2018).
Expanded sample size (GAGE) and extended project period (AWP) in response to evidence needs.
Developed ‘Research Brochure’ (GAGE) to improve transparency with academic stakeholders.
innovations_attempted: GAGE’s ‘3Cs’ Research Framework (capabilities, change strategies, contexts) provided a novel lens for tracking adolescent progress.
AWP’s ‘Evidence Gap Map’ synthesized impact evaluations to identify research priorities.
Trialed innovative qualitative techniques (e.g., participatory methods) to capture gendered adolescent realities.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: All recommendations from the 2016 Annual Review were addressed, including logframe revisions, policy team engagement, and research uptake plans.
forward_recommendations: Clarify distinctions between output-level and outcome-level indicators (e.g., ‘Stories of Change’) by May 2018.
Complete Downstream Partner Map (AWP) and align milestone targets with ARP logframe by March 2018.
Target national media outlets (GAGE) to amplify country-level research uptake.
Decide on potential AWP Phase 2 by March 2018 (proposal submitted by Innocenti).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Highly effective: Proactive responses to security risks (e.g., Gaza, Ethiopia) and funding uncertainties (AWP extension). Ethical safeguards (e.g., anti-harassment policies) were strengthened.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.GAGE: Expanded longitudinal study to 18,000 adolescents (vs. planned 8,000) across 9 countries.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.AWP: Research influenced UNICEF’s global policy (e.g., forthcoming 2018 flagship report on adolescence).

policy_influence_achieved: GAGE’s ‘3Cs’ Framework adopted by DFID country offices (e.g., Rwanda, Nepal) to inform gender and youth policies.
AWP’s findings shaped UNICEF’s Research Uptake Strategy and leveraged co-funding (e.g., US$3.15m).
Both programmes engaged with DFID policy teams (e.g., Gender, VAWG, Education) to integrate evidence into programming.
capacity_building_results: GAGE produced toolkits and guidance on participatory research methods, used by local partners.
AWP’s Evidence Gap Map and handbook on adolescent research strengthened global capacity.
Training on ethical clearance and safeguarding (e.g., anti-harassment policies) improved partner practices.
unintended_consequences: Positive: GAGE’s expanded sample size (18,000 adolescents) provided richer data than anticipated, enabling cross-country comparisons.
Positive: AWP’s leverage of US$3.15m in co-funding exceeded expectations, amplifying impact.
Negative: Security risks in fragile states (e.g., Gaza) limited fieldwork scope but were managed via remote methods.
scalability_evidence: GAGE’s ‘3Cs’ Framework and toolkits are designed for adaptation to other contexts (e.g., non-DFID programmes).
AWP’s Research Synthesis Report (2018) aims to set a global standard for adolescence-focused evidence, scalable via UNICEF’s network.
Both programmes’ open-access outputs (e.g., 55+ knowledge products) facilitate replication.

continuation_decision.AWP: Decision pending (proposal for Phase 2 submitted by March 2018)

continuation_rationale.GAGE: Strong performance (A+ scores), high policy relevance, and expanded evidence base justify continuation. No-cost extension for AWP suggests alignment with DFID priorities.
continuation_rationale.AWP: Potential Phase 2 depends on DFID’s assessment of leverage opportunities (e.g., US$3.15m co-funding) and policy influence.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tackling Maternal and Child Undernutrition in Zambia (Phase II)
programme_metadata.review_period: Transition phase (January to December 2018) and historical performance (2014-2017)

output_1.title: Priority interventions to improve maternal, infant & young child feeding practices to reduce stunting scaled up in at least 14 districts

output_2.title: Households (with pregnant women and children under 2) taught to grow, preserve and consume a diverse range of more nutritious foods

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from CARE-led consortium (Phase I) to UNICEF as interim SUN Fund Manager (2018 transition) due to procurement delays. Pooled fund arrangement continued but with implementation challenges during handover period.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF performed well as interim manager but faced delays in workplan approvals and fund disbursements. Line ministries had variable capacity - Health sector performed better than Agriculture/Fisheries in service delivery. Community-based volunteers (CBVs) exceeded targets in some areas despite funding constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: National Food and Nutrition Commission (NFNC) coordination worked but faced challenges in cross-sector convergence. Ward Nutrition Coordinating Committees (WNCCs) were underutilized for beneficiary targeting. District-level structures (DNCCs) performed better than provincial coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Multisectoral coordination improved nutrition's national profile but struggled with "household-level convergence" of interventions. Zonal vs. ward-level implementation created misalignment in targeting.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Significant delays in 2018 due to UK suspension of government funding (August 2018) and late appointment of new SUN Fund Manager. Only 14/22 implementing partners received 2018 funds by September.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to financial management concerns in Zambian social sectors. DFID increased monitoring of fund flows to community level.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by: 1) Extending UNICEF's interim role beyond original plan; 2) Shifting resources to community-led interventions; 3) Using non-monetary incentives for CBVs during funding gaps.
adaptive_management_examples: UNICEF's rapid deployment as interim manager to prevent implementation gap during transition
Revised logframe for transition period to accommodate delayed Phase II start
Shift from monetary to non-monetary incentives for community volunteers when GRZ funding stalled
Added Nchelenge district to programme coverage during transition phase

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed fund disbursements (only 14/22 partners funded by Sept 2018)
UK suspension of government funding (August 2018) due to financial management concerns
Late workplan approvals (finalized June 2018 for 2018 activities)
Limited capacity in Agriculture and Fisheries ministries compared to Health
Challenges in cross-sector beneficiary targeting and intervention convergence
Underperformance in nutrition-sensitive agriculture outputs (Output 2)
external_factors_impact: GRZ austerity measures delayed implementation of 400 kwacha/child nutrition commitment
Currency/exchange rate fluctuations not explicitly mentioned but implied in budget constraints
Political prioritization of nutrition improved (VP commitment at 2018 summits) but budget allocation lagged
Donor coordination challenges during transition from CARE to UNICEF management
contextual_constraints_new: Lower-than-expected GRZ budget allocations despite political commitments
District-level implementation revealed misalignment between zonal and ward-level targeting approaches
Community volunteer sustainability threatened by lack of permanent GRZ positions/incentives
Delayed MTEF processes prevented timely nutrition budgeting by line ministries
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions during handover from CARE to UNICEF management
Variable performance between line ministries (Health vs. Agriculture)
Challenges in aligning donor expectations (DFID, SIDA, Irish Aid) with GRZ systems
Delayed partner funding affected trust with implementing partners
capacity_constraints_emerged: Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries lacked capacity to deliver nutrition-sensitive interventions
District Nutrition Coordinators operated without permanent GRZ positions
Limited technical capacity for integrated workplanning across sectors
NFNC required additional support for financial management and beneficiary tracking
risk_materialization: Financial management risks in Zambian social sectors (triggered UK funding suspension)
Delayed procurement of SUN Fund Manager (required UNICEF interim solution)
Lower-than-planned GRZ co-funding for nutrition activities
Implementation gaps during transition between programme phases

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Significant under-execution in 2018 due to: 1) Late workplan approvals (June 2018); 2) UK funding suspension (August 2018); 3) Only 64% of implementing partners received funds by September 2018. Phase I (2013-2017) had better execution with CARE management.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Mixed - Phase I demonstrated good VFM with exceeded targets in direct nutrition interventions (Output 1), but Phase II transition showed reduced efficiency due to management costs during handover. Agriculture outputs (Output 2) showed poor cost-efficiency with targets only 45-57% met despite similar resource allocation.
financial_management_quality: CARE (Phase I): Generally strong with timely reporting
UNICEF (transition): Adequate but faced systemic GRZ delays
GRZ systems: Concerns led to UK funding suspension; NFNC required additional support
District level: Variable quality with some districts showing weak financial tracking
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High for direct nutrition interventions (£0.08-0.12 per child reached for GMP/Vitamin A) but low for agriculture components (£1.50-2.00 per household for food production support). Community-based delivery proved most cost-efficient channel.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: GRZ's committed 400 kwacha/child/year (~$40) not realized in 2019 budget despite political commitments. Other partners (SIDA, Irish Aid) maintained contributions but no new co-funding materialized during review period.

key_delivery_lessons: Pooled funds require stronger financial management support at district level
Multisectoral programmes need dedicated convergence mechanisms (WNCCs underutilized)
Community-based volunteers critical for outreach but require sustainable incentives
Transition periods between phases need 6-12 month overlap for continuity
successful_delivery_practices: Direct nutrition interventions (Output 1) consistently exceeded targets when properly funded
District-level coordination (DNCCs) worked better than provincial structures
UNICEF's rapid deployment prevented implementation gap during transition
Technical assistance to NFNC improved national coordination
management_adaptations_made: Shifted to community-led interventions to improve targeting
Developed revised logframe for transition period
Increased focus on tracking beneficiaries receiving multiple interventions
Added non-monetary incentives for CBVs during funding gaps
innovations_attempted: Ward-level beneficiary tracking system (piloted in 2018)
Integrated workplans across sectors (in development for Phase II)
Pass-on programmes for agricultural inputs (goats, fish fingerlings)
National Nutrition Summit as advocacy platform (April 2018)
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially implemented: Improved convergence mechanisms but still weak at household level
Not implemented: Permanent GRZ positions for nutrition coordinators (target Dec 2020)
Implemented: Increased focus on maternal/adolescent nutrition in Phase II
Partially implemented: VfM indicators revised but data quality remains inconsistent
forward_recommendations: Strengthen WNCCs for cross-sector beneficiary targeting by Oct 2019
Develop integrated workplans with USAID TA by inception phase end
Assess community-level funding mechanisms by Oct 2019
Advocate for GRZ to create permanent nutrition coordinator positions by Dec 2020
Finalize VfM indicators and logframe during inception phase
Extend UNICEF MoU to June 2019 to ensure continuity
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate - Some risks were well mitigated (e.g., UNICEF interim management) but financial management risks materialized (UK funding suspension). Risk of GRZ under-funding was identified but not fully addressed. Beneficiary tracking risks emerged as new concern.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: High (for direct nutrition interventions) / Medium (for nutrition-sensitive interventions)
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Medium - Strong quantitative data on outputs but limited attribution evidence for stunting reduction. Endline evaluation data from 2017 not yet fully analyzed.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium - High for community-level interventions (CBVs, direct nutrition) but low for agriculture components and government coordination structures without permanent funding.
policy_influence_achieved: GRZ committed to 400 kwacha/child nutrition allocation (though not yet budgeted)
Nutrition Summit (April 2018) elevated national policy dialogue
NFNC budget increased but implementation phased
District Nutrition Coordinators included in national plans (though not yet permanent positions)
capacity_building_results: 1,395 community volunteers trained (exceeding targets)
NFNC and line ministry staff received technical assistance

Limited capacity built in agriculture/fisheries ministries
unintended_consequences: Positive: Increased national attention to nutrition through SUN Fund mechanism
Positive: Community volunteer networks created potential for other health programmes
Negative: Delayed funding created implementation gaps in some districts
Negative: Over-reliance on external funding may have weakened GRZ ownership
scalability_evidence: Direct nutrition interventions (Output 1) demonstrated scalability across 15 districts
Community volunteer model proved adaptable to different contexts
Agriculture interventions showed limited scalability due to funding constraints
Coordination mechanisms (DNCCs) could be scaled with additional resources

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_decision: Continue (Phase II already launched in 2018 with adaptations)
programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong performance in direct nutrition interventions (Output 1) and national policy influence justify continuation. Phase II designed to address Phase I limitations with revised delivery model and increased focus on maternal/adolescent nutrition.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High for direct nutrition components; Medium for nutrition-sensitive components; Low for full GRZ cost-sharing without additional advocacy.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable - Community-level delivery and pooled fund mechanism work well but require continued donor support. GRZ ownership remains weak without permanent budget allocations.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Generally satisfied with direct nutrition results but concerned about: 1) Agriculture component underperformance; 2) GRZ funding delays; 3) Transition management challenges.
planned_adaptations_future: Increased focus on maternal and adolescent nutrition
Stronger beneficiary tracking systems
Revised VfM indicators and logframe
Enhanced convergence mechanisms at ward level
Advocacy for permanent GRZ nutrition positions
Non-monetary incentives for community volunteers
Phased approach to GRZ 400 kwacha commitment implementation

programme_metadata.programme_title: Investing in Human Capital through Partnerships Beyond Aid in the Social Sectors Programme

output_1.title: Improved governance capacity, systems and mechanisms within social sector ministries to organise and deliver high quality services for all (e.g., more efficient distribution of HR resources to meet needs of the population; strengthened quality assurance/supervision systems to improve quality)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme pivoted from original business case to address COVID-19 in first two years (2020–2021). In 2022, focus narrowed to strengthening social sector services for women and girls due to reduced FCDO budget. Partial reset aligned with FCDO Ghana’s 2022 Country Business Plan and FCDO’s 2022 International Development Strategy.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (e.g., CHAG, STAR-Ghana, WHO) delivered critical COVID-19 response and institutional capacity-building but faced delays in contract finalization (e.g., WHO agreement signed in December 2022). STAR-Ghana’s CSO grants for accountability were implemented late in the AR period (August 2022). EBA programme (Education Beyond Aid) extended to September 2023 for responsible transition to PBA.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme governance adapted to FCDO’s refreshed strategic priorities, with oversight intensified during COVID-19 pivot. Coordination with GoG ministries (MoH, MoE, MoGCSP) was maintained, but budget constraints limited donor partnership opportunities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved coordination of UK aid across HMG departments and multilaterals was achieved, but cross-government systems for shock resilience (e.g., zoonotic disease surveillance) remained underdeveloped. PBA supported alignment with centrally managed FCDO programmes (e.g., GALOP, GEOP).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays (e.g., WHO agreement finalized in December 2022; SGF agreement in August 2022), limiting implementation timeframes. Costed extensions were granted (e.g., CRIB project) to mitigate gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was high during COVID-19 response but adjusted post-pivot to focus on strategic alignment with FCDO’s 2022 priorities. Financial constraints reduced flexibility for real-time adaptations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was used to extend projects (e.g., CRIB’s 9-month extension) and reallocate funds to SRHR and women/girls-focused interventions, but budget cuts limited broader adaptive programming.
adaptive_management_examples: Pivot from COVID-19 response to SRHR/women’s services in 2022.
Costed extension of CRIB project to address vaccine hesitancy.
Sequencing of EBA’s social accountability components into PBA.
Frontloading of donor funds for Demographic and Health Surveys pending PBA contracts.

main_implementation_challenges: Budget constraints due to reduced FCDO country operating budget, limiting partnership opportunities and programme scope.
Delays in finalizing implementation agreements (e.g., WHO, SGF) shortened delivery timelines.
High inflation (peaking at 54%) and economic crisis in Ghana strained social protection systems and service delivery.
Complex transition from COVID-19 response to original programme objectives (SRHR, governance).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic required a 2-year pivot, delaying original objectives.
Ghana’s economic crisis (debt restructuring, IMF negotiations) pressured social sector budgets (e.g., LEAP, NHIS).
Global macroeconomic downturn reduced influx of new donors, slowing multi-stakeholder collaboration.
High transport/food inflation (59.7%) increased poverty, stressing social protection systems.
contextual_constraints_new: Need for shock-responsive social protection systems (e.g., LEAP reassessment) uncovered by COVID-19 and economic shocks.
Gaps in cross-government surveillance systems for zoonotic diseases and health shocks.
Limited GoG capacity to absorb donor funds efficiently amid fiscal constraints.
partner_relationship_issues: Late contract finalizations (WHO, SGF) strained partner relationships and implementation timelines.
CSOs faced political sensitivity in advocacy, requiring PBA support for evidence-based approaches.
Transition from EBA to PBA required careful coordination to avoid disruption in education sector reforms.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoG ministries struggled with budget execution amid economic crisis, affecting service delivery.
Delayed recruitment and onboarding of TA personnel hindered capacity-building efforts.
Limited PBA team bandwidth to manage multiple transitions (COVID-19 exit, SRHR focus, EBA handover).
risk_materialization: Economic downturn (risk: Major) materialized, impacting GoG’s ability to co-finance social sectors.
COVID-19 fatigue and vaccine hesitancy (risk: Moderate) slowed public health response.
Partner dependency risks (risk: Moderate) exposed by delays in agreement finalizations.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspent due to delayed partner agreements (WHO, SGF) and reduced FCDO budget envelope. Costed extensions (e.g., CRIB) mitigated some under-execution. Final audits for closing projects (CRIB, WACCBIP) planned by November 2023.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Medium. Innovative COVID-19 programming averted severe drops in human development indicators, but reduced funding limited scalability. CSO advocacy demonstrated boldness but required protection mechanisms. Efficiency gains in education (71% of 2022 reform targets met) and health (medium-term strategic plan published) offset some costs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Adequate. Delays in contract finalizations and budget constraints challenged timely disbursements, but extensions and frontloading of funds (e.g., for DHS surveys) ensured critical activities proceeded. Financial oversight was strengthened post-COVID pivot.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Partial. Efficiency improved in education (e.g., curriculum/assessment reforms) and health (SAFECARE accreditation for CHAG facilities), but economic crisis increased costs for social protection (e.g., LEAP reassessment).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Limited. New donors (e.g., World Bank) entered social sectors, but PBA’s reduced budget constrained co-funding opportunities. Philanthropic donor engagement in education remained exploratory.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly mentioned, but Ghana’s cedi depreciation likely increased programme costs (implied by economic crisis context).

key_delivery_lessons: Early contract finalization is critical to avoid implementation delays (e.g., WHO/SGF agreements).
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., costed extensions) can mitigate unforeseen shocks (COVID-19, economic crises).
Cross-government coordination (e.g., for zoonotic surveillance) requires dedicated resourcing.
Sustainability considerations must guide interventions from design (e.g., SAFECARE accreditation for CHAG facilities).
successful_delivery_practices: Partnership with CHAG/WACCBIP for COVID-19 response and variant surveillance.
Use of SAFECARE accreditation to strengthen health facility quality.
Alignment with FCDO’s central programmes (e.g., GALOP, GEOP) to amplify education reforms.
Evidence-based CSO advocacy to depoliticize accountability initiatives.
management_adaptations_made: Narrowed focus to women/girls and SRHR in response to budget cuts.
Extended CRIB project to address vaccine hesitancy.
Sequenced EBA’s social accountability components into PBA for continuity.
Planned reassessment of LEAP programme to improve targeting.
innovations_attempted: Border-town surveillance for COVID-19 variants (with Togo, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso).
Integration of NHIS data for family planning rollout.
Education Reform Secretariat co-funding model with other donors.
Use of 2022 Census/DHS data for CSO-led advocacy.

previous_recommendations_progress.programme_reset: Partially achieved. SRHR focus confirmed in 2022 Country Business Plan, but budget constraints delayed implementation (WHO/SGF agreements signed late).
previous_recommendations_progress.responsible_COVID_exit: Moderately underachieved. CRIB extension supported vaccination drive but fell short of planned 6-month timeline.
previous_recommendations_progress.existing_outputs_delivery: Met/exceeded expectations for defined outputs (e.g., CHAG’s CRIB project).

forward_recommendations: Finalize PBA strategic approach and logframe revision by May 2023 to reflect reduced funding and SRHR focus.
Develop data generation/analysis component with UK ONS by April 2023.
Assess and scale high-performing CSO interventions for social accountability.
Submit business case addendum by July 2023 to address gaps (e.g., Education Reform Secretariat).
Conduct final audits for closing projects (CRIB, WACCBIP) by November 2023.
Strengthen cross-government shock resilience systems (e.g., zoonotic surveillance).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate. Major risks (economic crisis, COVID-19) were partially mitigated through adaptive management (e.g., pivots, extensions), but delayed partner agreements and budget cuts exposed vulnerabilities. Proactive surveillance (WACCBIP) and CSO advocacy demonstrated effective risk responses.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Partial data. CHAG’s CRIB project supported underserved districts; 18 CSOs funded via STAR-Ghana for women/girls’ services. Exact numbers not specified, but interventions targeted vulnerable groups (e.g., LEAP beneficiaries, SRHR services).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: Medium. Progress in education reforms (71% of 2022 targets met) and health systems (SAFECARE accreditation, variant surveillance), but SRHR and governance outcomes lagged due to delays.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Medium. Strong evidence for COVID-19 response (e.g., variant surveillance, vaccine hesitancy mitigation) and education reforms, but weaker for SRHR/gender outcomes due to late implementation.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium. Systems strengthening (e.g., SAFECARE, NHIS data use) and GoG’s commitment to reforms (e.g., LEAP reassessment) improve sustainability, but economic crisis threatens long-term funding.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Moderate. PBA influenced GoG’s focus on SRHR and shock-responsive social protection (e.g., LEAP reforms). Advocacy supported NHIS/family planning integration, but policy uptake was slowed by fiscal constraints.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Mixed. TA to ministries (MoH, MoE, MoGCSP) built analytical capacity (e.g., DHS data use), but delayed recruitment limited deeper institutionalization. CHAG’s SAFECARE accreditation improved health facility governance.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Ghana’s COVID-19 variant surveillance (WACCBIP) became a regional model.
Negative: Budget cuts reduced CSO engagement, limiting grassroots accountability.
Positive: Cross-sectoral coordination (e.g., education-health) emerged from COVID-19 response.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Limited. Education reforms (via GALOP/GEOP) and health surveillance systems show scalability potential, but reduced PBA funding constrains expansion. CSO advocacy models could scale with additional resources.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates progress in education/health systems and aligns with FCDO’s strategic priorities (women/girls, SRHR). Economic crisis and IMF programme create opportunities to protect social sector funding, but require focused interventions.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium-High. Strong GoG commitment to reforms (e.g., LEAP, NHIS) and PBA’s adaptive management improve prospects, but fiscal constraints and delayed partner agreements pose risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Current model (TA + CSO grants) is viable but depends on GoG’s ability to absorb capacities post-PBA. Shock-responsive systems (e.g., surveillance) need long-term funding.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate. Satisfied with COVID-19 response and education progress, but concerned about SRHR delays and budget execution.
planned_adaptations_future: Revised logframe and strategic approach by May 2023 to reflect SRHR focus.
Scaling high-performing CSO interventions for social accountability.
Strengthening data systems (with UK ONS) for evidence-based advocacy.
Co-funding Education Reform Secretariat with other donors.
Responsible exit from COVID-19 support with knowledge transfer to GoG systems.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Anti-Corruption Evidence (ACE) Programme

output_1.title: High quality, policy relevant new evidence and methodologically advanced research produced on 'what works to reduce corruption' and 'anti-corruption in the private sector'

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended multiple times (original end: July 2021 → March 2022 → September 2022 → March 2027). Shift toward deeper cross-workstream collaboration (e.g., health sector corruption by SOAS, illicit finance by GI-ACE). Added synthesis role planned for next phase to maximize research uptake.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (SOAS, GI-ACE, SOC-ACE) exceeded output targets (e.g., 108 working papers vs. 96 milestone; 21 journal articles vs. 18). Local researchers in 10+ countries (Bangladesh, Nigeria, Kenya, etc.) delivered context-specific evidence. Gendered analysis strengthened across all streams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Decentralized coordination among three implementing partners (SOAS, GI-ACE, SOC-ACE) with limited programme-level synthesis. Directors lacked capacity for deeper joint analysis; recommendation to add a dedicated synthesis role remains pending.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Joint working occurred at organizational level and between specific research teams, but not systematically. New cross-ACE workstreams launched (e.g., health sector, illicit finance) with designated leads. Business case addendum proposed an insourced coordination role.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Cost savings achieved via outsourcing (e.g., £45k saved on graphic design; £32k on peer review). Partners leveraged existing networks (e.g., Uganda/Kenya research hubs) to reduce overheads. Pan-ACE video/events reduced onboarding costs for new creatives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to extend research into new areas (e.g., climate corruption, SOC in Russia/Eastern Europe) based on emerging evidence gaps. Extended timelines allowed for deeper policy engagement (e.g., ministerial briefings).
adaptive_management_examples: Extended 13 new SOC-ACE projects in FY22/23 based on pilot phase success, including 4 extended projects and 3 with additional Pathway to Impact funding.
Shifted focus to sectoral priorities (e.g., health, energy, infrastructure) in response to HMG’s Integrated Review and IDS.
Added gendered corruption analysis to all workstreams after identifying gaps in initial research design.
Piggybacked video production for MOOCs onto in-person events, saving £50k+ in travel/production costs.

main_implementation_challenges: Limited programme-level synthesis due to decentralized management structure.
Attribution challenges in measuring anti-corruption impact (e.g., SDG 16.5) given the programme’s broad geographic scope.
Balancing academic rigor with policy relevance, especially in politically sensitive contexts (e.g., kleptocratic regimes).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted fieldwork and in-person engagement, though partners adapted via digital outputs (e.g., 81 annual comms products in 2023).
Geopolitical shifts (e.g., Russia’s invasion of Ukraine) increased focus on SOC/illicit finance, aligning with ACE’s expanded research agenda.
Data leaks (Pandora Papers, FinCEN Files) validated ACE’s focus on transnational corruption but raised expectations for rapid policy responses.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging evidence on corruption in climate finance and energy sectors required rapid pivot in research priorities.
Increased scrutiny of UK ODA spending post-2021 cuts necessitated stronger VFM justification.
Partner safety risks in countries with authoritarian regimes (e.g., research on beneficial ownership in Nigeria).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity among directors to coordinate cross-workstream analysis (addressed via planned synthesis role).
Need to build next-generation researchers from Global South (recommendation R5: ACE to develop pipeline by Dec 2023).
risk_materialization: Major risk rating persisted due to political sensitivity of corruption research and attribution challenges.
No major reputational risks materialized; ACE’s prestige among academics/policymakers mitigated operational risks.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Partners operated within budget while exceeding output targets (e.g., 21 journal articles vs. 18 planned). Extended timeline (2023) allowed full utilization of funds.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. Achieved cost savings via outsourcing (e.g., £45k on graphics, £32k on peer review), economies of scale (e.g., pan-ACE events), and in-kind contributions (e.g., University of Birmingham’s free peer reviews). Outputs per £ spent exceeded Business Case projections.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Partners benchmarked local fees (e.g., Nigeria/Bangladesh) and prioritized open-access publishing. SOAS’s publication strategy maximized reach without additional costs. No audit findings reported.
cost_efficiency_achieved: SOAS: £5k saved via repurposing MOOC video footage for social media.
GI-ACE: £50k+ saved by combining video shoots during in-person events (travel: £15k; editing: £8k–£10k; production: £25k).
University of Birmingham: £32k saved on peer review costs via academic networks.

key_delivery_lessons: Decentralized delivery enabled agility but required stronger programme-level coordination to maximize impact.
Problem-led research design (vs. preconceived solutions) increased policy uptake (e.g., ethics training in Nepal/Bangladesh).
Gendered analysis added value but needs explicit resourcing in future phases.
successful_delivery_practices: Leveraging local research hubs (e.g., Uganda/Kenya) reduced costs and improved contextual relevance.
Multi-format outputs (e.g., podcasts, blogs) amplified reach beyond traditional academic audiences.
Partnerships with NGOs/governments (e.g., A2i in Bangladesh) bridged research-policy gaps.
management_adaptations_made: Added cross-ACE workstreams (health, illicit finance) to address joint working gaps (Recommendation R4 from AR 2020).
Extended programme timeline to align with FCDO’s Spending Review cycles.
Prioritized ‘Gold standard’ open-access publishing to meet FCDO’s transparency requirements.
innovations_attempted: Pathway to Impact funding for pilot projects (e.g., 3 SOC-ACE projects received additional funds).
Use of video/podcasts to disseminate research (e.g., 50 videos in 2023).
Pilot phase extensions for high-potential projects (e.g., 4 SOC-ACE projects).
previous_recommendations_progress: ✅ **R1 (AR 2021)**: Programme extended to March 2027 (aligned with Spending Review).
⏳ **R4 (AR 2020)**: Synthesis role pending budget approval for next phase.
✅ **R6 (AR 2021)**: Partners submitted new research areas to FCDO (e.g., climate corruption).
⏳ **R5 (AR 2022)**: Global South researcher pipeline under development (target: Dec 2023).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Add a programme-level synthesis role to maximize research uptake and ‘shape the field’ (rolled over from AR 2020).
Develop a pipeline for Global South researchers to sustain long-term impact (R5).
Strengthen impact measurement by defining ‘chains of attribution’ for anti-corruption outcomes.
Expand ministerial engagement to embed ACE evidence in FCDO programmes (R4).

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Major risk rating persisted due to inherent challenges in corruption research (political sensitivity, attribution). Mitigation strategies (e.g., flexible funding, policy engagement) prevented reputational risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 100+ researchers across 10+ countries (Bangladesh, Nigeria, Kenya, etc.); 19 GI-ACE grants; 29 SOC-ACE projects.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Policymakers in target countries (e.g., civil service ethics training in Nepal/Bangladesh); FCDO teams (evidence used in IDS/Integrated Review).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.targets_met: Exceeded (e.g., 64 cumulative policy products vs. 45 milestone).

policy_influence_achieved: Ethics training interventions adopted by Bangladesh’s A2i programme.
Evidence on gendered corruption informed cross-border trade policies in Kenya/Uganda.
SOC research influenced UK’s illicit finance strategy (per Integrated Review).
capacity_building_results: Trained 100+ researchers in advanced anti-corruption methodologies.
Strengthened local research hubs (e.g., SOAS’s Nigeria/Bangladesh partnerships).
ACE funding enhanced career prospects for Global South academics (e.g., publications in high-impact journals).

unintended_consequences.description: ACE’s prestige attracted additional co-funding opportunities (e.g., pilot phase extensions).
Political sensitivity of research led to self-censorship in some contexts (e.g., beneficial ownership studies).

scalability_evidence: Research methodologies (e.g., problem-led approach) adopted by other FCDO programmes.
SOC-ACE’s transnational focus (e.g., Russia/Eastern Europe) demonstrates adaptability to new regions.
Policy briefs translated into multiple languages for local uptake (e.g., Bangladesh, Nigeria).

continuation_rationale: Consistent **A/A+** performance ratings and high strategic alignment with HMG priorities (Integrated Review, IDS).
Growing demand for ACE’s evidence (e.g., uptake by FCDO teams, HoMs, and target country governments).
Unfinished research agendas (e.g., climate corruption, illicit finance) require continued investment.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (requires stronger coordination mechanisms in next phase).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by repeated extensions and positive AR findings).
planned_adaptations_future: Add a synthesis/coordination role to improve joint working.
Expand research into climate corruption and SOC in new regions (e.g., Eastern Europe).
Develop a formal impact measurement framework with ‘chains of attribution’.
Increase ministerial engagement to embed evidence in FCDO programmes.

output_1.title: Insights and learnings are generated, disseminated and promoted

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: GSMA Mobile for Development Foundation has demonstrated strong performance in research dissemination, stakeholder engagement, and thought leadership. The partnership exceeded targets for closed-door convenings (252 vs. 224) and high-level platform engagements (203 vs. 201), indicating robust partner execution beyond original expectations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-collaboration between M4D programmes and other GSMA initiatives (e.g., Climate Tech, Innovation Fund) maximized impact through shared expertise and resource leveraging. Example: Climate Tech contributions to reports like "Combatting forest fires with AI in Pakistan" and coordination with FCDO country offices for AI landscape studies in Ethiopia.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Robust procurement processes aligned with international good practice, as validated by EY’s due diligence audit for Sida. Procurement includes competitive selection for Innovation Fund grantees, with external technical experts ensuring rigor and independence.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Enhanced due diligence for sub-grantees, including risk assessment frameworks tailored to country-level risk. Two field visits per grantee project, systematic vetting for high-risk environments (via iSOS), and compliance with FCDO’s SEAH requirements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to emerging priorities (e.g., AI, climate resilience) by reallocating resources to new research areas (e.g., AI for Africa report, climate tech studies) and adjusting Innovation Fund focus to include frontier technologies like IoT and blockchain.
adaptive_management_examples: Shift toward AI and emerging tech: Published reports on AI use cases in Africa (Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa) and launched studies on AI applications in climate resilience (e.g., forest fire combatting in Pakistan).
Response to gender gap data: Leveraged the 2024 Mobile Gender Gap Report to engage MNOs and governments in targeted actions, including webinars with 4,600+ impressions and policy advocacy.
Smart city initiatives: Co-designed urban futures roadmaps for Rwandan cities (Kigali, Bugesera, Kayonza) in collaboration with UN Habitat, aligning with Rwanda’s Smart City Master Plan.

main_implementation_challenges: Digital divide persistence: 900 million fewer women than men use mobile internet in LMICs, with 60% of unconnected women in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.
Emerging tech barriers: Limited local skills, data availability, and ethical frameworks hinder AI and IoT scaling in LMICs (e.g., lack of contextual data for generative AI in African languages).
Funding ecosystem gaps: Nascent investment landscape for digital entrepreneurs, requiring targeted outreach (e.g., Innovation Fund’s partnerships with tech hubs/accelerators).
Regulatory and logistical hurdles: Weak implementation of digital payment legislation, low consumer confidence, and challenging logistics in target regions.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 legacy: Accelerated digital adoption but exacerbated inequalities in access (e.g., gender gaps in mobile internet use).
Geopolitical risks: Operating in complex environments (e.g., Rwanda, Pakistan) required adaptive travel policies and enhanced sub-grantee due diligence.
Economic pressures: Currency fluctuations and inflation affected cost efficiency, though mitigated by strict travel policies and procurement controls.
contextual_constraints_new: Generative AI limitations: Only 2% of AI use cases in Africa are generative due to high compute costs and lack of local-language data.
Climate-related disruptions: Extreme weather events (e.g., forest fires in Pakistan) necessitated adaptive programming (e.g., AI-driven climate resilience tools).
Policy fragmentation: Inconsistent national digital strategies required tailored advocacy (e.g., Smart City Rwanda roadmaps to align with national plans).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Local skills gaps: Insufficient AI/ML expertise in LMICs limited the development of advanced solutions (e.g., reliance on external consultants for AI reports).
MNO collaboration challenges: Varied engagement levels from mobile network operators in different regions affected scaling of digital services.
risk_materialization: Strategy and Context: Political instability in target regions (mitigated via real-time monitoring and travel restrictions).
Programme Delivery: Some Innovation Fund grantees faced lower-than-expected market demand (addressed through enhanced selection rigor and partnership-building support).
Reputational: Sub-grantee risks managed via pre-award due diligence and routine compliance checks.

budget_execution_vs_plan.actual_vs_planned: Budget execution aligned with plan; cost per beneficiary reduced from £1.43 (planned) to £0.22 (6.5x improvement).

routes_to_vfm: Cost per beneficiary: Achieved £0.22 vs. £1.43 target (exceeding efficiency goals).
Crowding-in resources: Leveraged cross-programme collaboration (e.g., Innovation Fund’s use of GSMA team expertise) and co-funding with other FCDO programmes.
Research uptake: High dissemination of reports (e.g., Mobile Gender Gap Report: 574 downloads in first month; 8,800+ views for 2023 edition).
Procurement savings: Economy-class travel policies and benchmarked HR costs maintained.
value_for_money_assessment.evidence: EY audit confirmed procurement compliance; cost-sharing with FCDO’s Agriculture Research Team for climate evaluations.

strengths: Robust procurement: Audited processes (EY/Sida) and risk-based due diligence for sub-grants.
Transparency: Systematic reporting of grantee spending issues to FCDO with mitigation plans.
Efficiency: Cross-programme resource sharing (e.g., Climate Tech and Innovation Fund synergies).

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: 6.5x reduction in cost per beneficiary (£0.22 vs. £1.43 planned), driven by economies of scale in research dissemination and grantee support.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding realized through partnerships (e.g., UN Habitat for Smart City Rwanda initiative) and alignment with FCDO’s broader digital inclusion agenda.

key_delivery_lessons: Impact measurement gaps: Need for deeper socio-economic profiling of beneficiaries to assess digital inclusion outcomes beyond access metrics.
Emerging tech potential: AI and IoT can drive scale (e.g., ATEC’s e-cook carbon credits) but require localized data and ethical frameworks.
Gender-focused design: Mobile services must explicitly address barriers for women (e.g., affordability, digital literacy) to close the 15% gender gap in mobile internet use.
successful_delivery_practices: Thought leadership: High-impact reports (e.g., Mobile Gender Gap, AI for Africa) positioned GSMA as a trusted advisor to governments/MNOs.
Adaptive funding: Innovation Fund’s targeted outreach (tech hubs, accelerators) improved grantee quality and market relevance.
Public-private collaboration: Smart City Rwanda roadmaps demonstrated effective alignment with national plans via multi-stakeholder engagement.
management_adaptations_made: Enhanced M&E: Strengthened due diligence frameworks for sub-grants and real-time risk monitoring (e.g., iSOS travel vetting).
Research focus shift: Prioritized emerging tech (AI, IoT) and climate resilience in response to FCDO’s updated Digital Development Strategy 2024–2030.
Grantee support: Added technical assistance for grantees to build MNO/investor partnerships (e.g., Dayaxa’s blockchain traceability).
innovations_attempted: AI for development: Piloted AI applications in agriculture (Crop2Cash’s linguistic tools), energy (remote sensing for forest fires), and financial inclusion (Orenda’s content automation).
Blockchain for traceability: Supported Dayaxa’s use of blockchain to verify supply chains and enable carbon credit generation.
Mobile Big Data: Leveraged anonymized mobile data for development insights (e.g., mobility patterns during COVID-19).
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: Risk assessment framework for sub-grants implemented; SEAH requirements integrated into grantee agreements.
Ongoing: Impact evaluations for Innovation Fund (poverty/livelihoods) and climate work in progress, with ToRs finalized.
forward_recommendations: Deepen impact evaluations: Conduct rigorous studies on Innovation Fund’s poverty reduction and climate action contributions by end-2025.
Expand AI focus: Develop localized AI tools (e.g., generative AI for African languages) with partners like FCDO’s Frontier Tech Hub.
Strengthen gender integration: Embed gender-responsive design principles in all grantee projects, with targets for women’s participation.
Scale successful models: Replicate Smart City Rwanda’s public-private collaboration in Kenya and other African intermediary cities.

strengths: Proactive mitigation: Country-risk frameworks and grantee monitoring reduced reputational/operational risks.
Transparency: Early reporting of sub-grantee issues to FCDO with corrective action plans.
Diversification: Geographic and sectoral spread of Innovation Fund portfolio mitigated concentration risks.
gaps: Residual moderate risk: Innovative nature of programme inherently carries execution risks in complex contexts.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.qualitative: Programme reached underserved populations (e.g., women in LMICs, rural entrepreneurs) via mobile-enabled services, with evidence of improved digital access (e.g., 15% reduction in mobile internet gender gap since 2020).

scalability_evidence: Innovation Fund models (e.g., PricePally’s AI-driven efficiency tools) replicated in multiple countries.

output_1.title: Global Parametrics commercially sustainable and crowds-in industry players

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Significant structural change in 2023 with the sale of Global Parametrics (GP) by UK/Germany to CelsiusPro AG, transitioning GP to private ownership while retaining FCDO/BMZ as limited partners in the Natural Disaster Funds (NDF UK/Deutschland). GP now operates under Mirabella Financial Services LLP via seconded staff.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Global Parametrics demonstrated strong performance in client renewal rates (75% in 2023, up from 10 in 2022 to 13 in 2023) and commercial sustainability (EBITDA turned positive to ~£597,745 in CHF terms). Played a catalytic role in reinsurance markets, though NDF UK incurred a loss due to the Morocco earthquake payout.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Post-sale, governance involves CelsiusPro as sole shareholder of GPHC, with FCDO/BMZ remaining as limited partners in NDF entities. Key personnel departures required restructuring, with ongoing negotiations on revised personnel arrangements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between GP, NDF UK/Deutschland, and technical assistance providers (BMZ/KfW). Challenges arose during the sale transition period, requiring normalization of new working relationships.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensified during the sale process and post-transition to ensure capital preservation and alignment with revised KPIs. FCDO programme team engaged closely with GP on reporting adjustments to reflect long-term financial targets and operational realities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to hardening reinsurance markets by leveraging Hannover Re’s capacity and exploring new risk capacity providers. Flexibility in deploying NDF capital between UK/Deutschland funds to manage exposure (e.g., earthquake risk isolated to NDF UK).
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid response to Morocco earthquake (2023): NDF UK contributed ~US$4M to the FSEC’s US$275M payout, demonstrating agility in disaster response.
Expansion of GP’s client base from 24 (2022) to 31 (2023) through horizontal geographic scaling and renewed partnerships.
Initiation of discussions with Lloyd’s of London to leverage their global licensing and credit rating for NDF expansion.

main_implementation_challenges: Time-consuming and labor-intensive sale process of Global Parametrics, creating staff uncertainty and requiring post-sale relationship normalization.
Hardening reinsurance market conditions, increasing costs and complexity for risk transfer deals.
Significant financial loss in NDF UK due to the Morocco earthquake payout (largest in NDF history), though aligned with the fund’s protective purpose.
Key personnel departures post-sale, necessitating restructuring of management and personnel arrangements.
external_factors_impact: Morocco earthquake (September 2023) triggered the largest NDF payout, stressing NDF UK’s capital but validating the programme’s disaster response mechanism.
Global reinsurance market hardening reduced availability of affordable risk capacity, requiring GP to act as a catalytic player in deals.
contextual_constraints_new: Post-sale, the UK’s isolated exposure to earthquake risk (excluded from NDF Deutschland’s climate-focused mandate) requires careful capital management.
Need to balance market-led deals with GP-originated sales to fulfill the programme’s unique value proposition in underserved markets.
partner_relationship_issues: Temporary strain during the sale transition, resolved post-acquisition by CelsiusPro.
Ongoing coordination challenges between GP (now privately owned) and FCDO/BMZ as limited partners in the NDFs.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited risk capacity in NDF UK post-Morocco payout, requiring recalibration of exposure levels.
Need for additional capital to scale NDF operations, prompting outreach to new bilateral donors.
risk_materialization: Morocco earthquake (2023) materialized as a high-impact risk, leading to the largest NDF payout to date.
Hardening reinsurance market (external risk) increased operational costs and reduced deal viability without GP’s catalytic role.

budget_execution_vs_plan: NDF UK missed its 3-year rolling return target (1.42%) due to the Morocco earthquake payout, resulting in a loss for 2023.
GP achieved profitability in 2023 (EBITDA of ~£597,745 in CHF terms), reversing prior-year losses (2022: -£308,917).
Client renewal rates remained strong (75% in 2023, up from 100% in 2022 but with an increased absolute number of clients from 10 to 13).
value_for_money_assessment: Positive VFM demonstrated through GP’s move to profitability and its catalytic role in enabling reinsurance deals in hardened markets.
NDF UK’s loss in 2023 was justified by its core purpose (disaster response), with the Morocco payout reaching ~US$4M of the total US$275M FSEC arrangement.
Leverage of private capital (e.g., Hannover Re, potential Lloyd’s partnership) enhances VFM by expanding risk capacity without proportional increases in public funding.
financial_management_quality: GP improved financial reporting to reflect long-term capital preservation alongside immediate drivers (deployment, impact, market development).
Dynamic capital management between NDF UK and NDF Deutschland to optimize exposure (e.g., isolating earthquake risk to NDF UK).
Transparency in tracking and reporting payout impacts (e.g., Morocco earthquake case study).
cost_efficiency_achieved: GP’s horizontal expansion (e.g., One Acre Fund partnership scaling from Tanzania to Malawi) improved cost efficiency by reusing existing partnerships.
Use of NDF capital to leverage larger reinsurance deals (e.g., FSEC Morocco) demonstrated efficient use of limited funds.

output_1.title: Increased number of private sector infrastructure projects in targeted sub-sectors in the eight LIS

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme evolved from a high-risk perception model to demonstrating sustainable commercial viability in low-income states, attracting follow-on investments. The Technical Assistance component was expanded to include climate advocacy and policy reform initiatives beyond original compliance-focused plans.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: SBICAP Ventures Limited (SVL) exceeded expectations in portfolio diversification (11 projects across 9 sub-sectors/8 states) and exits (2 completed, 2 partial with defined paths). Partners like SBI/SIDBI facilitated co-investment synergies, while investees (e.g., SunSource Energy) attracted £180m follow-on investment from SHV Energy.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Leadership transition was completed efficiently with ramped-up teams. A Board of Advisers was finalized for strategic oversight, enhancing UK investor connections. The fund manager proactively developed exit roadmaps aligned with programme lifecycle.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between FCDO, Neev Fund, and investees enabled systemic changes (e.g., biomass cremation policy adoption in 4 states). Cross-HMG engagement (e.g., British High Commission climate initiatives) amplified impact.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensified during exit phase with six-monthly reviews and external expert inputs for approvals. ESG standards were rigorously tracked, influencing institutional investor preferences.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was used to: (1) Support 18 pilot initiatives (e.g., biomass cremation, waste management plants); (2) Adapt gender inclusion policies mid-implementation; (3) Pivot Technical Assistance toward climate policy advocacy.
adaptive_management_examples: Pivoting Technical Assistance to support climate advocacy initiatives that led to policy reforms (e.g., biomass cremation adoption in Punjab/Haryana).
Expanding gender inclusion efforts after identifying a 136% increase in women employment since 2020, including targeted sessions to address unconscious bias.
Developing structured exit roadmaps 2 years before programme end to maximize capital returns (35% already returned to HMG).

main_implementation_challenges: Early-stage risk perception in low-income states required sustained demonstration of viability to attract commercial investors.
Balancing financial returns with deep development impact in geographically dispersed, high-poverty regions.
Managing exits in a way that preserves development gains while meeting HMG’s capital return targets.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted supply chains for investees (e.g., agri-logistics, healthcare) but also accelerated demand for digital/health infrastructure (e.g., Rahi Care’s dialysis centers).
Government of India’s LiFE mission (2022) created tailwinds for biomass cremation and waste management pilots.
Global energy crises (2022–23) increased investor interest in renewable energy projects (e.g., SunSource Energy’s £180m follow-on investment).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated state-level regulatory barriers for waste management projects (e.g., Blue Planet’s Noida plant required prolonged municipal approvals).
Inflationary pressures (2022–23) increased operational costs for investees, requiring adaptive financial structuring.
Limited local capacity for ESG compliance in smaller enterprises, addressed via Technical Assistance.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment with SBI/SIDBI on risk appetite for early-stage projects, resolved through joint investment committee reviews.
Some investees (e.g., micro-enterprises under Indian Angel Network) required additional handholding for ESG reporting, delaying exits.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Fund manager’s capacity was stretched during simultaneous exits (2023–24), addressed by hiring specialized transaction advisors.
Investor readiness gaps in climate-tech startups (e.g., Chakr Innovation) required tailored Technical Assistance for scaling.
risk_materialization: Market risk: Slower-than-expected exits in 2 investees due to macroeconomic downturns (mitigated via partial exits).
Operational risk: Delayed policy approvals for biomass cremation in Maharashtra (resolved via state-level advocacy).
Reputation risk: Early concerns about women’s representation in leadership (addressed via 60% portfolio-wide target and bias training).

budget_execution_vs_plan.details: £39.5m Financial Transaction fully deployed; £1.5m Technical Assistance utilized with 10% reallocated to climate advocacy. 35% of invested capital (£13.8m) returned to HMG via exits, exceeding projections.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Strong – Competitive management fees (partially performance-linked) and full capital repayment projected. 35% reflows already recycled into other initiatives.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: High – £178m private sector capital mobilized (4.3x HMG investment). Cost per beneficiary (~£41) below sector benchmarks.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Exceeds targets – 1m+ beneficiaries reached; assets (e.g., solar plants, waste management infrastructure) ensure long-term impact.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Progressing – 60% portfolio companies have women in decision-making roles; 136% increase in women employment since 2020.

strengths: Transparent reporting on exits (e.g., SunSource Energy’s 7x women employment growth post-investment).
Competitive fee structure with ESG-linked incentives for the fund manager.
Proactive currency hedging minimized INR volatility impacts on returns.
weaknesses: Initial delays in Technical Assistance disbursements for pilots (addressed via streamlined approvals).

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost per job created (~£1,200) and per tonne CO₂ reduced (~£8) are 20–30% below comparable funds. Co-investment leverage ratio (4.3x) exceeds the business case target of 3x.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: £178m private capital mobilized (vs. £150m target). Key examples: SHV Energy’s £180m investment in SunSource Energy; GIC’s funding for Leap India’s agri-silos.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: INR depreciation (2022–23) reduced sterling-value returns by ~5%, partially offset by hedging and higher local-currency exits.

key_delivery_lessons: Early engagement on exit planning (2+ years prior) maximizes returns and development impact preservation.
ESG performance directly correlates with ability to attract institutional investors (e.g., SunSource Energy’s 7x women employment growth facilitated SHV Energy’s £180m investment).
Policy advocacy by investees (e.g., biomass cremation) can create systemic change but requires sustained government engagement.
successful_delivery_practices: Linking management fees to ESG targets incentivized portfolio-wide improvements in gender and climate metrics.
Pilot initiatives (e.g., 18 pilots across waste management, rural entrepreneurship) served as proof-of-concept for scaling.
Cross-HMG collaboration (e.g., British High Commission climate initiatives) amplified programme visibility and investor confidence.
management_adaptations_made: Added exit roadmap indicators to the logframe (2024) to track capital returns.
Expanded Technical Assistance to include climate policy advocacy based on investee demand.
Instituted six-monthly reviews with external experts for exit approvals.
innovations_attempted: Biomass cremation pilots (saving 2,000+ trees/year in Aurangabad) now adopted by 4 state governments.
Gender inclusion policies at investees (e.g., Mahendra Education’s skilling for marginalized groups) led to 136% increase in women employment.
Climate-tech pilots (e.g., Chakr Innovation’s energy storage solutions) attracted follow-on funding from UK/India investors.

completed: Leadership transition within Neev Fund team (2023).
Finalization of Board of Advisers for UK investor connections.
Raising Neev’s profile via British Investment Partnership dashboard (2023).
ongoing: Periodic review of exit pathways (six-monthly since 2023).
Tracking gender representation indicators (new logframe targets added Feb 2024).

forward_recommendations.action: Showcase Fund performance at 2+ industry forums to attract follow-on investments in under-served sectors.
Develop structured engagement plan with x-HMG Investment team for UK-India climate collaborations (e.g., Green Hydrogen).
Update logframe with gender-specific indicators and capital return milestones.
Map policy engagement opportunities across Deputy High Commissions for joined-up advocacy.

strengths: Proactive exit planning mitigated market risk (e.g., partial exits for underperforming investees).
ESG standards reduced operational risks (e.g., no major compliance breaches reported).
Diversified portfolio (11 projects/9 sectors) minimized sector-specific shocks.
gaps: Limited contingency planning for state-level regulatory delays (e.g., waste management approvals).
Currency risk hedging could be expanded to cover Technical Assistance disbursements.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 1m+ (direct); additional 11m indirectly via agri-silos/renewable energy projects

policy_influence_achieved.impact: 70% adoption in Aurangabad; 2,000+ trees saved annually
136% increase since 2020; 60% companies with women in decision-making roles
Influenced inclusion of biomass fuels in sustainable lifestyle guidelines

capacity_building_results.outcome: All investees achieved ESG benchmarks; 3 received industry awards for sustainability.
60% portfolio companies adopted gender-sensitive policies; Mahendra Education’s skilling programme for marginalized groups scaled to 3 states.
18 pilots supported; 6 new initiatives in 2023 (e.g., energy storage, waste-to-value projects).

positive: Agri-silos (Leap India) improved food security for 11m people beyond direct beneficiaries.
Solar rooftop projects (SunSource Energy) reduced industrial energy costs, improving competitiveness.
IAN’s micro-enterprise exits created a secondary market for impact investments in LIS.
negative: Delayed waste management plant approvals in Noida caused short-term waste accumulation issues (resolved post-approval).

scalability_evidence.scalability: High – Adopted by 4 states; potential for national rollout via LiFE mission.
High – Replicated across 60% of portfolio; demand from new investees.
Medium – Requires additional Technical Assistance for commercialization.

continuation_rationale: Exceeds performance targets (A+ score; 35% capital returned; 1m+ beneficiaries).
Strong alignment with UK-India Roadmap 2030 (climate, trade, gender).
Demonstrated ability to attract follow-on investments (£178m private capital mobilized).
Policy influence (e.g., biomass cremation) creates systemic change beyond programme lifecycle.

evidence: Neev Fund’s exit roadmap ensures orderly transition; 2 exits completed with 2 more in progress.
Portfolio companies (e.g., SunSource Energy, Leap India) secured independent funding post-exit.
Technical Assistance models (e.g., ESG standards) institutionalized across investees.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expand climate-focused Technical Assistance to support India’s 2070 net-zero targets.
Deepen UK-India investor collaborations via British Investment Partnership.
Scale gender inclusion models to new geographies (e.g., Northeast India).
Document and disseminate exit lessons for FCDO’s blended finance portfolio.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adapted to political environment and unanticipated opportunities by engaging diverse delivery partners (World Bank, Asia Foundation, IMF) for technical assistance. delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank's in-country staff leadership justified; Asia Foundation produced robust analyses well-received by stakeholders but faced regional accessibility constraints. EITI secretariat transitioned successfully to MoPF but progress slowed due to political transition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: DFID Burma's SRO and programme manager received specific credit for effective execution. Embedded senior adviser in MoPF (Component 2) provided broader-than-planned PFM support, integrating fiscal transparency work into Component 1.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Strong collaboration with **Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU)** for programme delivery; **96% of mentoring programme participants (2021-2022) reported they would participate again**; **89% of Scholars (2022/23) rated CSC support as "excellent" or "good"**.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance aligns with **HM Treasury’s Corporate Governance Code** for small NDPBs; **annual Commissioner performance reviews** conducted by the Chair; **Audit and Risk Management Committee** reviews risks quarterly.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: **Alumni Community Engagement Fund (ACEF)** delivered 10 activities across 7 countries (2022-2023); **96% of ACEF attendees reported learning new knowledge** (participant feedback). **Mentoring Programme** supported **134 active pairs** (2022-2023).

operational_challenges_context.main_implementation_challenges: **Afghanistan**: Negotiating education access for girls with Taliban authorities; **Pakistan**: Social stigma and inaccessible infrastructure for people with disabilities (PWDs) in employment. **Financial constraints**: Reduced **DFE Grant-in-aid** (from £158K in 2021/22 to £0 in 2022/23).
operational_challenges_context.external_factors_impact: **COVID-19**: Likely contributed to **decline in cash balance** (closing balance fell from -£3,191K to -£3,424K). **Political instability**: Taliban restrictions in Afghanistan required adaptive delivery models (e.g., home-based learning trials).

operational_challenges_context.risk_materialization: **One severe risk** (unspecified) materialized in 2022/23 but was mitigated; monitored via **Risk Register**.

financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: **98% of Scholars/Fellows** would recommend the programme; **96% of ACEF/mentoring participants** reported positive outcomes. **No financial losses or irregularities** reported. **Administrative costs held at 5% of total expenditure** (consistent with 2021/22).
