financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: **Scholarship cost distribution**: PhD (32%), Agency Master’s (13%), Shared Scholarships (17%), Distance Learning (13%). **Programme Management Costs**: **£1.372M (5%)** (stable vs. 2021/22).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: **DFE Grant-in-aid** dropped to **£0** (from **£158K** in 2021/22). **BEIS Grant-in-aid** also **£0** (vs. **£80K** prior year).

learning_adaptation_recommendations.key_delivery_lessons: **Alumni engagement**: Small-scale community projects (e.g., ACEF) yield high impact (96% knowledge gain). **Mentoring**: Structured pairs (134 in 2022-23) drive **personal/professional growth** (96% satisfaction). **Flexible funding**: ACEF’s thematic focus (e.g., clean energy) aligns with global priorities.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.successful_delivery_practices: **Research uptake**: Winners of **CSC Research Impact Awards** (e.g., solar cell materials, CO2 monitoring) demonstrated **applied development solutions**. **Partnerships**: Collaboration with **NASRDA (Nigeria)** and **World Bank (Caribbean)** amplified impact. **Scholar surveys**: **89% rated support as "excellent/good"** (2022/23).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.management_adaptations_made: **Risk management**: Enhanced **Risk Register reviews** (3x/year) and **conservative risk appetite**. **Governance**: Implemented **annual Commissioner performance reviews** and **Board Effectiveness audits** (per FCDO IAID recommendations).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.innovations_attempted: **Spaceborne CO2 monitoring (SHACS instrument)** in Nigeria; **home-based learning pilots** for Afghan girls; **FinTech and eye healthcare partnerships** in Africa/Asia-Pacific.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: **Board Effectiveness**: Addressed FCDO IAID audit recommendations via **annual review process**. **Alumni Strategy**: Expanded **ACEF and mentoring programmes** based on prior feedback.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.forward_recommendations: **Sustain funding**: Mitigate loss of **DFE/BEIS grants** by diversifying partnerships. **Scale innovations**: Replicate **SHACS-like technologies** in other low-resource settings. **Policy influence**: Leverage **Scholar research** (e.g., disability employment barriers) for **CRPD implementation** in Pakistan.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: **Low-risk appetite** maintained; **one severe risk mitigated** in 2022/23. **Risk Framework** aligned with FCDO, with **quarterly Audit Committee reviews**.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: **60,000 students** in Afghanistan (literacy programme); **134 mentoring pairs** (2022-23); **10 ACEF activities** (7 countries). **95% of Scholars/Fellows** view programme as prestigious.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: **ACEF model** replicated across 7 countries; **SHACS technology** adaptable to other low-resource regions; **mentoring programme** expanded annually.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: **Strong demand**: 95% of Scholars/Fellows would recommend the programme. **High impact**: Evidence of **policy influence** (e.g., Afghanistan, Nigeria) and **scalable innovations**. **Stable governance**: Aligns with **FCDO priorities** and **Corporate Governance Code**.

output_1.title: Improved synergy between collaborative and thematic research

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to hybrid policy events (in-person + online) to extend reach; increased reliance on online training for MSc/PhD programmes to reduce costs. Original business case anticipated more in-person engagement and international travel for training.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: African Economic Research Consortium (AERC) demonstrated strong performance in research output generation (A score) and policy engagement (A score), but underperformed in MSc/PhD student engagement (C score) and sustainability initiatives (B score). Core funding mobilization from partners remains below pre-COVID levels, affecting capacity-building activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: AERC operates under a strategic plan with fixed milestones (not adjusted annually), governed by a Board with FCDO representation. The rigid target-setting has limited adaptability to changing funding contexts (e.g., post-COVID core funding shortages).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Common reporting framework used by multiple funders and AERC Board streamlines monitoring but reduces flexibility to revise targets. Coordination with universities and policy-makers remains strong, as evidenced by hybrid event attendance and alumni engagement in policy roles.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive procurement processes for research contracts are followed, with cost as one assessment criterion. Deloitte’s 2022 Salary and Benefits Survey led to a 6% salary scale adjustment, mitigated by currency depreciation (Kenyan shilling vs. USD).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintains Board-level oversight but relies on AERC’s internal M&E systems for day-to-day management. Quarterly and annual monitoring are conducted, though adaptive management is constrained by fixed strategic plan targets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Limited flexibility due to fixed milestones in the 2020–25 strategic plan. Budget cuts were identified to align with reduced funding, but prioritization of activities remains a challenge. Shift to online training was an adaptive response to cost pressures.
adaptive_management_examples: Transition to hybrid policy events to expand reach despite funding constraints.
Online delivery of MSc/PhD training to reduce unit costs (e.g., eliminating international travel).
Budget reallocation to prioritize core activities (e.g., research over elective courses) in response to underperformance in student engagement.

main_implementation_challenges: Declining core funding from partners post-COVID, particularly for university capacity-building (down from 13% to 10% African government/institution contributions).
Weaker-than-expected progress in MSc/PhD student engagement, with fewer electives taken and under-representation of marginalized groups (C score).
Fixed strategic plan milestones (set 4 years ago) misaligned with current funding realities, limiting adaptability.
Currency depreciation (Kenyan shilling) affecting salary adjustments and operational costs.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic reduced partner core funding, which has not recovered to pre-2020 levels.
Global funding climate shifts have made it harder to attract diversified funding for the 2020–25 strategic plan.
Exchange rate fluctuations (USD/KES) impacted budget execution, though partially offset by lower online training costs.

programme_metadata.programme_title: J-PAL Post-Primary Education Initiative

output_1.title: Increased quality and quantity of the evidence base around post-primary education

output_3.title: Effective management of research process to produce high quality and policy relevant evidence around what works in post-primary education

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from active research commissioning (Phase 1-2 completed) to finalization of ongoing projects. All 14 RFP rounds concluded by Summer 2020. Current focus on completing fieldwork and disseminating results for 41 full RCTs and 40 pilot projects by March 2023 deadline.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: J-PAL and IPA's global field office network performed well in implementing RCTs, though some projects experienced COVID-related delays. Partner Dream a Dream's "Happiness Curriculum" won 2021 WISE Award, demonstrating high-quality implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: J-PAL's twice-yearly peer review process (spring/autumn) with senior affiliates and donors maintained as planned. Governance remained robust with quarterly risk updates and adaptive COVID mitigation measures.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between J-PAL, IPA field offices, and policy experts. COVID-specific coordination included safety protocols for in-person research and approvals from multiple stakeholders (J-PAL, universities, IRBs, local authorities).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Research grants (max $300k for full RCTs, $75k for pilots) administered as planned. Cost extensions granted during COVID to prevent project shutdowns, using leftover PPE funds.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to COVID: required pause/resume approvals for fieldwork, additional safety reviews, and budget extensions. Quarterly risk reporting maintained.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to: 1) Grant cost extensions for COVID-affected projects; 2) Reallocate impact weightings (Output 1 increased to 45%); 3) Adjust milestones mid-implementation based on progress.
adaptive_management_examples: Added COVID-specific safety questions to RFP application forms and review criteria (2021 rounds).
Revised milestone targets upward for fieldwork completion (1.1, 1.2) and downward for publication outputs (1.5) based on 2020 progress.
Deprioritized Output 3 (research management) to focus on Output 1 (evidence production/dissemination) in final year.
Introduced individualized researcher outreach (emails to teams with overdue working papers) to accelerate publication.

main_implementation_challenges: Slow conversion of RCT results into peer-reviewed publications (consistently below target for Outputs 1.3-1.5).
COVID-19 disruptions: fieldwork pauses (March 2020), shifts to remote data collection, and ongoing delays for in-person activities.
Four FCDO-funded pilot projects and seven full studies remain incomplete as of 2022, with tight March 2023 deadline.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Caused fieldwork halts, required safety protocols (social distancing, PPE), and extended timelines. Led to addition of 'people risk' category in risk register.
Academic publishing delays: Journal submission backlogs and peer review slowdowns exacerbated by pandemic.
Policy environment: Increased demand for COVID-responsive education evidence (e.g., low-tech parent engagement interventions) created both opportunities and pressure.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for COVID-specific research rounds (e.g., Round 14 in 2020) to address pandemic-related education challenges.
Higher-than-expected proposal submissions for COVID-focused rounds (18 proposals) despite narrow scope, indicating unmet demand for rapid-response research funding.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited leverage over affiliated researchers to prioritize timely publication of working papers/journal submissions (incentive structure gap).
J-PAL staff bandwidth stretched by dual focus on completing Phase 2 projects while managing COVID-response rounds.
risk_materialization: Moderate: "Personal risk to researchers/participants" (COVID exposure during fieldwork). Mitigated via safety protocols.
Moderate: "Research projects going off track in timing" (COVID delays). Mitigated via cost extensions and deadline flexibility.
Low: "Research projects going over budget" – managed through contingent cost extensions.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Average cost per FCDO-funded RCT remained at £147k ($182k). Cost extensions granted for COVID-affected projects using leftover funds, with no overall budget overruns reported.
value_for_money_assessment: Adequate: Strong performance on evidence generation (41 RCTs/40 pilots completed) and policy influence (45% of citations in Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel).
Weakness: Slower-than-planned conversion of results into publications, reducing VfM for dissemination outputs.
Strength: High citation rates for PPE-funded studies suggest academic impact exceeds targets, indicating long-term VfM.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Quarterly risk updates, proactive budget reallocations for COVID, and transparent cost extension processes. No fiduciary issues reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Met planned levels. Average RCT cost stable; pilot projects capped at $75k. Cost extensions were contingent and targeted.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Exceeded expectations. FCDO's 44% share supplemented by Echidna Giving, Gates Foundation, Google.org, and others, enabling larger research portfolio.

key_delivery_lessons: Rigorous peer review processes (twice-yearly RFPs with senior affiliates) ensure high-quality research selection but may slow implementation.
Flexible funding mechanisms (cost extensions, add-on grants) critical for adapting to crises like COVID.
Disaggregating all data by sex (programme requirement) yielded unintended benefit of generating robust gender insights across all studies.
successful_delivery_practices: Low-tech interventions (e.g., SMS/phone-based parent engagement in Botswana) proved scalable and policy-relevant during COVID.
Partnership with IPA's global field offices enabled rapid adaptation to local contexts and safety protocols.
J-PAL's brand and Nobel Prize association (2019) amplified policy uptake of PPE findings (e.g., citations in UNICEF, World Bank reports).
management_adaptations_made: Reallocated impact weightings to prioritize evidence dissemination (Output 1: 30%→45%) in final year.
Introduced mid-year stocktakes (e.g., July 2022 working paper audit) to track publication progress.
Added COVID-specific review criteria to RFP processes for 2021 rounds.
innovations_attempted: COVID-response research rounds (e.g., Round 14) to fund rapid-turnaround studies on learning loss mitigation.
Happiness Curriculum evaluation (India) integrating mindfulness and mental health support into education.
FCDO-branded evidence review and tracker planned as legacy product for What Works Hub for Global Education.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial: Publication targets (1.3-1.5) remain unmet despite 2021 push (individualized researcher emails).
Achieved: All fieldwork completion milestones (1.1, 1.2) revised upward and on track for March 2023.
Pending: Incentive structure changes for researchers not yet implemented (planned post-July 2022 stocktake).
forward_recommendations: Complete all outstanding evaluation summaries (4 remaining) by March 2023, with 50% progress by July 2022.
Produce FCDO-branded Evidence Review Paper and tracker for dissemination via What Works Hub by March 2023.
Host PPE seminar for FCDO audience by December 2022 to showcase final evidence and policy recommendations.
Develop at least one new gender-focused policy brief/insight using disaggregated data by programme end.
Revise researcher incentive structures to accelerate journal submissions without compromising quality (proposal due post-July 2022).
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective: Proactive COVID risk mitigation (safety protocols, cost extensions) prevented project failures.
Gap: Limited tools to address publication delays (reliant on researcher goodwill; incentives needed).
Strength: Quarterly risk updates and adaptive responses (e.g., adding 'people risk' category) demonstrated agility.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 41 full RCTs and 40 pilot projects completed, all with sex-disaggregated data (reaching thousands of students across LMICs).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Policy influence extends to millions via citations in global reports (e.g., UNICEF, World Bank) and government adoption (e.g., Uttarakhand's Happiness Curriculum).

policy_influence_achieved: 45% of citations in Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel (2021) from J-PAL studies.
30% of citations in World Development Report 2018 (World Bank) from PPE-funded research.
Uptake of low-tech parent engagement model in Botswana by UNICEF for COVID response.
Government of Uttarakhand, India, scaled Happiness Curriculum to grades 1-8 in public schools.
capacity_building_results: Built researcher capacity in LMICs through RCT implementation and peer review processes.
Strengthened local partner capacity (e.g., Dream a Dream foundation in India) to design and evaluate education interventions.
Policy maker capacity enhanced via dissemination of evidence reviews and direct engagement (e.g., PPE seminars).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Mandatory sex-disaggregated data revealed gender-specific barriers/opportunities not initially targeted by all studies.
Positive: COVID forced innovation in low-tech solutions (e.g., SMS-based learning) now adopted beyond PPE.
Negative: Publication delays may reduce timely policy uptake for some studies.
scalability_evidence: Happiness Curriculum scaled to all grades 1-8 in Uttarakhand (India) with government partnership.
Low-tech parent engagement model replicated in multiple countries via UNICEF guidance.
RCT methodologies and peer review processes adopted by other education research initiatives.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme has achieved its core objectives: 1) Generated robust evidence base (41 RCTs/40 pilots completed); 2) Influenced global policy (high citation rates); 3) All FCDO funding allocated with projects to conclude by March 2023. No further RFP rounds planned.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (objectives largely met; remaining tasks are completion-focused).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. J-PAL's core model (RCTs + peer review) is sustainable via other funders, but FCDO-specific PPE structure will conclude. Legacy products (evidence review, tracker) aim to ensure long-term impact.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High. Consistent 'A' scores reflect strong performance, though publication delays noted as area for improvement in future programmes.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize all FCDO-funded projects and dissemination products by March 2023.
Transition PPE learnings into FCDO's What Works Hub for Global Education for continued uptake.
No new adaptations planned; focus on closure and legacy documentation.

programme_metadata.programme_title: DFID-ESRC Joint Research Fund on Raising Learning Outcomes (RLO) Programme

output_1.title: A portfolio of high quality, policy-relevant research on what works to deliver learning outcomes through effective, equitable education systems in low income countries is delivered

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme has successfully utilized ESRC’s rigorous systems for bid selection and management, leveraging their academic networks. The selection of a Strategic Research Lead ('Research Knowledge Broker') was deprioritized and remains pending for early 2016.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ESRC has met or exceeded expectations, particularly in grant commissioning, financial management, and partnership collaboration. Their peer-review processes and quality thresholds have ensured high-caliber research outputs. DFID has benefited from ESRC’s established systems and cross-sectoral lessons (e.g., from the ESRC/DFID Poverty Alleviation programme).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance is maintained through quarterly programme meetings and fortnightly progress calls between DFID and ESRC. The logframe and narrative reports from ESRC are used for monitoring, though the template is flexible and evolves with programme needs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination is evident through joint DFID-ESRC workshops (e.g., the September 2015 grantholder event), cross-programme collaboration (e.g., with the RISE programme), and the establishment of the Impact Initiative (REAL/IDS partnership) to enhance research uptake. Regular communication channels are effective.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for research grants has been timely and rigorous, with two of three calls completed (Call 1: 11 grants, ~£4.5m; Call 2: up to 8 grants, ~£4.3m). The Impact Initiative was successfully procured and is operational.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight is robust, with quarterly financial and narrative reporting, annual budget reconciliations, and DFID’s involvement in grant assessment panels. ESRC’s systems ensure compliance with contract terms (e.g., ResearchFish validation).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme has adapted its outreach strategies (e.g., leveraging DFID’s country networks and the British Academy seminar) to attract a wider disciplinary and geographic range of applicants. The conceptual framework for education systems was refined based on emerging learning.
adaptive_management_examples: Expanded outreach for Call 2 to diversify applicant pools, including engagement with policymakers at the Education World Forum.
Postponement of the Strategic Research Lead role to prioritize grant commissioning, with plans to recruit in 2016 based on grantholder feedback.
Establishment of the Impact Initiative to address research uptake challenges, fostering cross-programme collaboration.

main_implementation_challenges: Delay in recruiting the Strategic Research Lead ('Research Knowledge Broker'), which was deprioritized due to focus on grant commissioning.
Ensuring sustained policy relevance of research outputs amid evolving education priorities in target countries.
Balancing DFID’s reduced future research funding capacity (post-2015 spending review) with programme ambitions.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Potential reduction in DFID’s research funding capacity may require adjustments to future-year funding balances with ESRC.
Need to strengthen grantholder networking and cohort development to maximize research impact (addressed via planned Research Knowledge Broker role).
risk_materialization: Risk of underspending in Call 2 (full allocation not initially awarded) was mitigated through pre-planned options to redirect funds to high-quality projects.
Medium risk rating maintained due to dependency on ESRC’s systems and the need for continued alignment between DFID and ESRC priorities.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. DFID contributes £15m and ESRC £5m. Quarterly financial forecasts are provided by ESRC, with spend aligned to grant activation timelines. Projects typically complete at 97% of awarded budgets, with no overspending.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong. VfM is assessed at three stages: (1) application (cost drivers scrutinized by peer reviewers), (2) contract award (ESRC Secretariat removes unjustified costs), and (3) grant implementation (annual budget reconciliations). Average project completion cost is 97% of budget.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. ESRC’s Professional Support Unit Finance Team manages budget profiles and payments, with DFID payments made in arrears. ESRC is responsive to DFID’s reporting requirements and provides assurance on budget spend.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient. Direct costs (staff, travel, consumables) are justified and monitored. Host institutions bear financial responsibility for sub-contracts, reducing risk to DFID/ESRC.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: ESRC’s £5m contribution is fully materialized. Future co-funding balance may need adjustment due to DFID’s reduced capacity post-2015 spending review.

key_delivery_lessons: Leveraging ESRC’s peer-review systems ensures high-quality, policy-relevant research commissioning.
Outreach through DFID’s networks and high-profile events (e.g., British Academy seminar) effectively diversifies applicant pools.
Early grantholder engagement (e.g., workshops) fosters collaboration and aligns expectations on reporting/impact.
successful_delivery_practices: Quarterly programme meetings and fortnightly calls between DFID/ESRC enable agile monitoring and issue resolution.
The Impact Initiative (REAL/IDS) has strengthened research uptake and cross-programme synergy (e.g., with RISE).
Flexible logframe reporting allows adaptation to programme evolution (e.g., shifting focus from grant commissioning to research uptake).
management_adaptations_made: Deprioritized the Strategic Research Lead role to focus on grant commissioning, with plans to recruit in 2016 based on grantholder demand.
Adjusted Call 3 outreach strategies to build on Call 2’s disciplinary/geographic diversity successes.
Instituted annual grantholder events to build a community of practice and clarify ESRC/DFID expectations.
innovations_attempted: Impact Initiative: A dedicated partnership (REAL/IDS) to enhance research communication and policy uptake across DFID-ESRC programmes.
Three-pronged education systems framework to guide call themes and ensure conceptual coherence.
Alignment with RISE programme to create a shared ‘systems language’ and cohesive research community.
forward_recommendations: Recruit the Research Knowledge Broker in spring 2016 to address grantholder demand for networking and cohort development.
Assess the balance of future-year funding between DFID and ESRC to accommodate DFID’s reduced capacity.
Strengthen links between RLO and RISE programmes through aligned communications and shared learning events.
Evaluate the Impact Initiative’s effectiveness in enhancing research uptake and policy influence.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Risks (e.g., underspending in Call 2) were proactively managed through contingency options. The medium risk rating reflects managed dependencies on ESRC systems and partnership alignment.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: 11 grants awarded under Call 1 (£4.5m) and up to 8 under Call 2 (£4.3m), targeting researchers and policymakers in low-income countries. Initial findings expected in 2016.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Emerging. Evidence from one Call 1 grant (DRC teaching practices) is already informing policy discussions. The Impact Initiative aims to amplify this influence.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Grantholder workshops and the Impact Initiative are building researcher capacity in research uptake and policy engagement. Cross-programme collaboration (e.g., with RISE) enhances systemic learning.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.unintended_consequences: Positive: Stronger-than-anticipated cross-programme collaboration (e.g., DFID’s Governance and Education teams) and disciplinary diversity in Call 2 applicants.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: The programme’s conceptual framework and Impact Initiative model are designed for scalability across DFID-ESRC research programmes. Lessons are being shared with the RISE programme.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has achieved an A+ score for two consecutive years, with strong progress in grant commissioning, partnership effectiveness, and conceptual development. Initial research findings are expected in 2016, and the Impact Initiative is positioned to enhance policy uptake.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes. The DFID-ESRC partnership leverages ESRC’s robust systems, and the Impact Initiative ensures long-term research communication and uptake. Adjustments to funding balance may be needed post-2015 spending review.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Recruit the Research Knowledge Broker to support grantholder networking.
Adjust future-year funding allocations between DFID and ESRC if necessary.
Deepening collaboration with the RISE programme for shared learning and impact.
Conduct an external evaluation in 3–4 years to assess long-term outcomes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Sustainable Urban Economic Development (SUED) Programme

output_1.title: Improved capacity of selected secondary towns to plan and deliver market-driven urban economic planning

output_2.title: Facilitation of public-private financing of climate resilient infrastructure and value chain development projects

output_3.title: County level business environment reform interventions are undertaken

output_4.title: Increased knowledge and information on sustainable urban development

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The Private Sector Consortium contract was signed in August 2018 (12-month delay from original plan), with a 12-month inception phase starting in September 2018. Procurement delays forced reliance on short-term technical assistance mechanisms (e.g., DFID CMPs like ICED) to bridge gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IFC (strategic partner) performed on track (Output 3 scored "A"), while the Private Sector Consortium (Coffey International) faced protracted mobilization delays, impacting Output 1 (scored "C").
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Monthly performance monitoring meetings with Coffey International introduced to track inception milestones (town selection, urban plan development, subcontractor procurement). Quarterly updates to DFID Kenya Head of Office mandated.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: High-level stakeholder engagement (e.g., Principal Secretary for Housing, World Bank) initiated to align with GoK priorities, but county-level coordination was limited pending consortium mobilization. IFC and Private Sector Consortium collaboration planned but not yet operationalized.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of the Private Sector Consortium took over 12 months longer than planned due to DFID process changes, delaying programme start. IFC’s pre-feasibility assessments (e.g., Laikipia County’s Integrated Feedlot Scheme) proceeded on schedule.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight introduced post-delay: monthly supplier meetings, quarterly Head of Office updates, and revised milestone tracking. Original oversight plan was less intensive.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by redistributing Output 4’s 15% impact weighting equally to Outputs 1–3 (5% each) due to delayed implementation. Short-term technical assistance (e.g., ICED) used to deliver interim milestones.
adaptive_management_examples: Redistribution of impact weightings to reflect measurable outputs during the review period.
Engagement of technical experts via IFC to conduct pre-feasibility assessments (e.g., Laikipia County livestock PPP) ahead of consortium mobilization.
Planned no-cost extension to align programme and contract end-dates, ensuring VfM.

main_implementation_challenges: 12-month delay in Private Sector Consortium procurement, attributed to DFID procurement process changes.
Protracted mobilization phase for the consortium, impacting Output 1 milestones (urban development plans, stakeholder engagement).
Lack of clarity in town selection criteria, risking reputational damage.
external_factors_impact: Political economy risks in Kenya (e.g., alignment with GoK’s "Big Four" priorities) required continuous stakeholder management.
Rapid urbanization (7.3% annual growth in secondary towns) increased pressure to deliver timely interventions.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated delays in DFID’s procurement processes, requiring adaptive management.
Need for transparent county selection to mitigate perceived bias, not fully addressed in original design.
partner_relationship_issues: Coordination between IFC and the Private Sector Consortium not yet operationalized due to delayed consortium mobilization.
County-level engagement (e.g., Wajir, Isiolo) was preliminary and lacked formal selection criteria.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in selected counties to engage in urban planning without consortium support.
IFC highlighted need for strengthened capacity building (e.g., for PPP development) during pre-feasibility assessments.
risk_materialization: Major risk of fraud/bribery in high-value infrastructure projects (as per business case) remained untested but mitigated via output-based payment structures.
Political risks (e.g., changes in GoK priorities) monitored but not yet materialized.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £645,000 spent by July 2018 (11% of total £60m budget). Key cost driver: IFC advisory services (£400,000, or 63% of spend). Procurement delays reduced budget execution rate; no-cost extension planned to realign timelines.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Too early to assess VfM definitively. Potential VfM risks due to compressed timeline (4 years remaining instead of 5). Mitigation includes output-based payments, capped daily rates, and leveraging DFID’s Global Evaluation Framework for M&E discounts.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by IFC adhered to institutional Trust Fund rules. Private Sector Consortium and M&E contracts include VfM frameworks with economy/efficiency indicators (e.g., cost per town intervention, management cost ratios).
cost_efficiency_achieved: IFC advisory costs (£400k) deemed necessary for pre-feasibility work but high relative to early-stage spend.
Planned VfM indicators include unit costs for infrastructure delivery and time savings in PPP project cycles.

key_delivery_lessons: DFID procurement process changes can cause significant delays; lessons shared to refine future processes.
Short-term technical assistance (e.g., ICED) can bridge gaps during procurement delays.
Transparent, objective town selection criteria are critical to mitigate reputational risks.
successful_delivery_practices: IFC’s engagement with counties (e.g., Laikipia) demonstrated high appetite for reforms, validating SUED’s approach.
Monthly performance monitoring meetings with Coffey International improved milestone tracking post-delay.
management_adaptations_made: Impact weightings redistributed to reflect measurable outputs during the review period.
Quarterly updates to Head of Office introduced to escalate risks promptly.
Planned no-cost extension to recover lost time and ensure VfM.
innovations_attempted: Pre-feasibility assessments for PPP projects (e.g., Laikipia’s Integrated Feedlot Scheme) conducted ahead of consortium mobilization.
Collaboration with World Bank’s Kenya Urban Programme explored to leverage complementary investments.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Apply for a no-cost extension to adjust implementation timeline and ensure VfM.
Finalize transparent, objective town selection criteria to mitigate reputational risks.
Revise Output Indicator 1.2 to accurately reflect private sector input.
Disaggregate milestone indicators by implementing partner to track performance.
Strengthen collaboration between IFC and the Private Sector Consortium via an action plan.
Test and refine the Theory of Change against logframe during inception.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective: major risks (political economy, fraud) were identified but not yet materialized. Adaptive measures (e.g., no-cost extension, oversight intensification) introduced to mitigate procurement delays.

policy_influence_achieved: Alignment with GoK’s "Big Four" priorities (e.g., affordable housing, manufacturing) demonstrated through stakeholder engagement.
IFC’s pre-feasibility work (e.g., SEZs, PPPs) influenced county-level planning (e.g., Laikipia’s livestock value chain).
capacity_building_results: Limited to IFC’s technical assistance (e.g., Laikipia’s feedlot scheme); full capacity-building outcomes pending consortium mobilization.
scalability_evidence: Framework for scaling Naivasha prototype to other counties developed, but not yet tested.
IFC’s engagement with multiple counties (e.g., Nyeri, Uasin Gishu) suggests potential for replication.

continuation_rationale: Clear need for sustainable urban economic planning in Kenya’s secondary towns, aligned with GoK priorities.
IFC’s progress (Output 3 scored "A") and county demand (e.g., Laikipia) validate programme relevance.
Procurement delays are addressable via no-cost extension and adaptive management.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
planned_adaptations_future: No-cost extension to recover lost time and ensure VfM.
Stronger collaboration between IFC and Private Sector Consortium via formal action plan.
Revised town selection criteria and disaggregated milestone indicators.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Transform – enterprises for sustainable development: Transformative market-based solutions and behaviour change in low income households (Unilever partnership)

output_1.title: New evidence on delivering sustainable uptake of behaviour changes and access to technologies and services in WASH and clean energy through business models

output_2.title: New communications approaches and tools for delivering behaviour change programmes at mass scale

output_3.title: 10-20 Increased number of early stage transformative business models identified and piloted

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted from planned 2014 start to August 2015 actual start due to extended partnership negotiations and election-related delays. Added CGEP (Clinton Giustra Enterprise Partnership) as additional partner mid-design with potential £5m leverage.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Unilever performed as expected in formalizing partnership (collaboration agreement signed 10 Aug 2015) and responding to due diligence. CGEP engagement progressed faster than anticipated with "arrangement in principle" signed Sept 2015, though full agreement still pending.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Joint DFID-Unilever governance established via collaboration agreement. Inception phase management structures (activities/budget/timelines) agreed by Sept 2015. SRO-led oversight with Unilever core team handling day-to-day implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination during design phase despite election delays. UNGA launch (24 Sept 2015) successfully aligned DFID, Unilever, and potential partners. Webpage (foundry.unilever.com/brightfuture/transform) established as central coordination tool.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Initial procurement focused on due diligence consultants and legal setup. Competitive processes for third-party pilots/research not yet implemented (planned for post-inception).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight during inception due to partnership novelty and high risk rating. Monthly check-ins between DFID SRO and Unilever team reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by: 1) Accommodating election-related delays; 2) Incorporating CGEP as unplanned partner; 3) Extending design phase to address due diligence recommendations.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended partnership formalization timeline to address election disruptions and due diligence findings.
Proactively engaged CGEP mid-design after identifying alignment potential, securing "arrangement in principle" within 3 months.
Adjusted inception phase activities to include comprehensive response to independent due diligence report.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed start (18 months behind planned Jan 2014 launch) due to protracted partnership negotiations and national elections in target countries.
High complexity of multi-stakeholder governance (DFID + Unilever + emerging CGEP partnership).
Need to balance private sector (Unilever) commercial interests with development objectives during business model design.
external_factors_impact: National elections in target countries caused 6-month delay in partnership formalization.
Global corporate priorities at Unilever required alignment with their sustainability agenda (e.g., linkage to their "Bright Future" initiative).
contextual_constraints_new: Underestimation of time required for legal due diligence and partnership agreement negotiations (took 12+ months).
Limited pre-existing frameworks for DFID-private sector joint programme management in behaviour change/WASH sectors.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between DFID’s development metrics and Unilever’s commercial KPIs required negotiation (resolved via collaboration agreement).
CGEP’s potential role created temporary uncertainty about intellectual property rights and funding flows.
capacity_constraints_emerged: DFID programme team required upskilling on private sector partnership management.
Unilever team needed additional capacity to manage development-focused M&E requirements beyond their standard commercial metrics.
risk_materialization: High risk rating materialized as "partnership establishment risk" (delays in formalization).
Legal/compliance risks identified during due diligence (all addressed via action plan).
Reputation risk from novel public-private partnership structure (mitigated via UNGA launch visibility).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Limited expenditure in 2015 (inception phase only). DFID’s £5m commitment secured; Unilever’s £5m (£1.7m cash + £3.3m in-kind) mobilized. CGEP’s potential £5m not yet contracted. Budget underspend in Year 1 due to delayed start.

value_for_money_assessment.proposition_status: VFM proposition holds true per business case, though metrics not yet measured. Strengthened by CGEP’s potential £5m leverage (25% increase in resources).
planned_metrics: Cost per individual demonstrating improved WaSH behaviours (£) – [baseline TBC]
Average growth in customer base per £ spent – [benchmark TBC]
% of customers maintaining behaviour change X months post-intervention – [target TBC]
Proportion of third-party resources procured competitively – [target x% TBC]
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency_notes: In-kind contributions (Unilever staff time, existing research) improve cost efficiency. Economy achieved via shared DFID-Unilever oversight costs.

financial_management_quality.dfid: Strong – timely release of ARIES funds for due diligence/legal setup. Clear budget approval processes.
financial_management_quality.unilever: Adequate – financial systems adapted to accommodate development reporting requirements. Initial delays in aligning commercial and development financial tracking.
financial_management_quality.joint_issues: Currency risk management framework not yet tested (multi-country operations planned).

co_funding_materialization.status: Partial – Unilever’s £5m committed (100% of pledge). CGEP’s £5m potential co-funding identified but not yet contracted ("arrangement in principle" signed Sept 2015).
co_funding_materialization.leverage_ratio: 1:1 (DFID:Unilever) with potential to reach 1:2 if CGEP joins.

key_delivery_lessons: Public-private partnerships in behaviour change require 12+ months for governance design (vs. 6 months planned).
Due diligence for novel partnerships should begin during business case development, not post-approval.
In-kind contributions (e.g., Unilever’s staff time) must be valued and tracked as rigorously as cash flows.
successful_delivery_practices: UNGA launch created high-visibility momentum for partner engagement.
Phased inception approach (legal setup → due diligence → activity planning) managed risks effectively.
Joint DFID-Unilever working groups on M&E and research design bridged sectoral gaps.
management_adaptations_made: Extended inception phase to 6 months (from planned 3) to address due diligence findings.
Added quarterly risk review meetings between DFID SRO and Unilever leadership.
Developed shared "partnership principles" document to guide decision-making.
innovations_attempted: Hybrid commercial-development business model pilots (e.g., testing financial viability + social impact simultaneously).
Digital behaviour change tools integrated into Unilever’s existing consumer platforms (e.g., mobile engagement).
Cross-sectoral research teams (public health + marketing experts) co-designing interventions.

forward_recommendations.action: Finalize logframe with baselines, VFM indicators, and data sources by 31 Dec 2015.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Critical for measuring behaviour change outcomes and cost efficiency.

forward_recommendations.action: Complete CGEP agreement negotiation to secure additional £5m.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Expands programme reach and improves VFM.

forward_recommendations.action: Develop competitive procurement framework for third-party pilots/research by Q1 2016.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Ensures transparency and cost efficiency.

forward_recommendations.action: Conduct mid-inception review (Jan 2016) to assess partner roles and risk mitigation.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Validates governance structures before full implementation.

strengths: Proactive due diligence identified and addressed legal/compliance risks before scaling.
High-risk rating triggered additional oversight, preventing governance gaps.
Contingency built into timeline for partner negotiations.
gaps: No pre-existing risk matrix for DFID-private sector behaviour change programmes.
Currency risk management plan not yet operationalized.

sustainability_prospects.basis: Strong partnership foundation (DFID-Unilever-CGEP) and private sector engagement increase likelihood of sustainability, but business model viability not yet tested at scale.

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: UNGA launch and Unilever’s global platform (e.g., Bright Future initiative) position programme to influence corporate and NGO practices in WASH/behaviour change sectors.

capacity_building_results.dfid: Programme team gained experience in private sector partnership management.
capacity_building_results.unilever: Expanded capacity to measure social impact alongside commercial metrics.

positive: Accelerated Unilever’s internal sustainability strategy alignment with SDGs via programme linkage.
Created template for DFID-private sector behaviour change collaborations.

scalability_evidence.basis: Business model design includes scale assessment criteria, but pilot results pending. Unilever’s global distribution networks provide potential scaling pathways.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong partnership foundation established (DFID-Unilever-CGEP), inception phase on track, and high potential for leveraging private sector resources to achieve development outcomes in WASH/behaviour change.

likelihood_success_overall.basis: High partner commitment and innovative approach offset by untested delivery model and behaviour change complexity.

delivery_model_sustainability.basis: Unilever’s commercial incentives aligned with programme goals (e.g., expanding low-income consumer base). CGEP’s potential involvement adds financial sustainability.

fcdo_satisfaction_level.basis: Programme met all inception milestones (A score), secured additional partner (CGEP), and demonstrated adaptive management. Risk rating remains high but is actively managed.

planned_adaptations_future: Expand from WASH to household energy sector if pilots succeed (per business case flexibility).
Develop standardized tools for measuring behaviour change at scale (linked to Unilever’s digital platforms).
Explore replicating partnership model with other multinational corporations post-2020.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Strategic Partnership on Agriculture and Food Systems for Nutrition

output_1.title: New research investments and collaborations that enhance the evidence base on both technological and policy options in agriculture and food systems that improve nutrition and health

output_2.title: Strengthened technical collaboration between the DFID/BMGF and identification of new areas for collaboration

output_3.title: Commissioning of large scale studies of the impact of agricultural interventions on nutrition

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The partnership evolved to include additional scoping and consultation for new research priorities, including food safety, beyond the original three components. Methodology changes were made to one of the Agriculture-Nutrition Impact Studies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The University of South Carolina (USC) delivered ahead of expectations for Output 1 (Drivers of Food Choice), commissioning 8 sub-grants instead of the anticipated 3. BMGF’s administrative role led to higher visibility with grantees, requiring ongoing DFID follow-up to ensure proper attribution of funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Joint management by DFID and BMGF proved effective, with a Collaboration Framework signed in 2016 to formalize the partnership. Quarterly review meetings were recommended to systematize risk and financial monitoring.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The partnership strengthened technical collaboration, lowered transaction costs, and ensured complementarity between DFID and BMGF investments. A unified voice on research priorities influenced wider sector investments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Two calls for proposals were issued under Output 3, resulting in four large-scale impact studies and two smaller formative studies. One study required methodology adjustments during implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was adaptive, with recommendations to formalize quarterly reviews and improve trial registration (e.g., IFPRI’s RCT protocols to be published by March 2017).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme utilized flexibility to expand research priorities (e.g., food safety) and adjust methodologies in response to emerging needs. Additional scoping was conducted to identify new collaborative areas.
adaptive_management_examples: Launch of a second round of calls for the Drivers of Food Choice programme in February 2017 to fill the research pipeline with 15 high-quality studies.
Methodology changes to one Agriculture-Nutrition Impact Study to address implementation challenges.
Planned logframe review (February 2017) to align indicators with refreshed evidence gaps.

main_implementation_challenges: Ensuring consistent DFID branding and visibility alongside BMGF’s higher profile as the programme administrator.
Coordinating attribution of funding across grantees to reflect joint DFID-BMGF contributions.
Managing methodology adjustments in one of the impact studies without compromising quality.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: BMGF’s administrative role created an imbalance in grantee visibility, requiring proactive DFID engagement to ensure equal credit for funding. No major relationship conflicts were reported.
operational_challenges_context.risk_materialization: Minor risks materialized, primarily around branding attribution and trial registration delays, but were mitigated through adaptive management (e.g., quarterly reviews, written guidance on branding).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; no significant deviations reported. Financial monitoring was highlighted as an area for strengthened oversight via quarterly reviews.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. The partnership lowered transaction costs through joint design/management and leveraged complementary technical capacities. Co-funding arrangements (e.g., with HarvestPlus) maximized efficiency.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Effective, with recommendations to formalize forecasting and tracking through quarterly DFID-BMGF meetings. No major issues identified.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The programme increased the research supplier base and strengthened technical quality without proportional cost increases, achieving economies of scale.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding with BMGF and other partners (e.g., Global Panel) materialized as planned, enhancing the programme’s reach and impact.

key_delivery_lessons: Joint DFID-BMGF partnerships can successfully lower transaction costs and improve technical complementarity.
Proactive branding management is critical when one partner (BMGF) has higher grantee visibility.
Adaptive scoping (e.g., adding food safety research) can address emerging evidence gaps without disrupting core delivery.
successful_delivery_practices: The Technical Advisory Group (TAG) model for the Drivers of Food Choice programme ensured high-quality grant selection and technical support to grantees.
Informational webinars and accessible websites (e.g., driversoffoodchoice.org) improved global applicant reach.
Quarterly review meetings (planned) to track grants, risks, and finances.
management_adaptations_made: Added food safety as a new research priority under Output 3.
Planned logframe updates to reflect refreshed evidence gaps (February 2017).
Formalized trial registration requirements for IFPRI’s RCTs.
innovations_attempted: Collaborative research agenda-setting with BMGF to identify cross-cutting priorities (e.g., Nutritious Food Systems Initiative).
Use of IMMANA as a platform to host Agriculture-Nutrition study outputs, improving dissemination.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Improve DFID branding on grantee communications (e.g., Drivers of Choice website) by February 2017.
Use IMMANA to host Agriculture-Nutrition study outputs by March 2017.
Conduct a review of existing agriculture/nutrition research to inform round three of Impact Studies by March 2017.
Institute quarterly review meetings to track grants, risks, and finances.
Ensure IFPRI registers RCT protocols on a formal trial registry by March 2017.
Develop a dissemination plan for impact study outputs by March 2017.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Minor risks (e.g., branding, trial registration) were identified early and mitigated through adaptive measures. The risk rating remained "Minor" for both years.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to BMGF’s launch of a Nutritious Food Systems Initiative.
Informed national/regional policies on agriculture-nutrition linkages in Africa and South Asia through high-quality evidence generation.
Strengthened DFID’s global leadership on nutrition-sensitive agriculture.
capacity_building_results: Expanded the research supplier base for DFID and BMGF.
Built technical capacity among grantees through TAG support and interdisciplinary research.
Enhanced collaboration between DFID and BMGF on shared priorities (e.g., HarvestPlus, Global Panel).

unintended_consequences.description: The partnership model influenced BMGF to increase investments in nutrition-sensitive agriculture beyond the original programme scope (e.g., Nutritious Food Systems Initiative).

scalability_evidence: The Drivers of Food Choice programme’s diverse research portfolio (15 studies) demonstrated scalability of interdisciplinary approaches.
Impact studies provided cost-effectiveness data to support scaling of agricultural interventions in Africa/South Asia.
The Collaboration Framework signed in 2016 laid groundwork for replicating the model in other sectors.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme is on track to deliver high-quality evidence (Outputs 1 and 3) and has strengthened DFID-BMGF collaboration. Early outcomes (e.g., BMGF’s Nutritious Food Systems Initiative) demonstrate policy influence and scalability potential.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. The joint DFID-BMGF management structure and co-funding arrangements are proven effective and replicable.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expand research priorities to include food safety under Output 3.
Strengthen dissemination of outputs via IMMANA and other platforms.
Formalize quarterly reviews and risk tracking mechanisms.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Exiting Poverty in Rwanda (EPR) Programme

output_1.title: Programme mobilisation activities are completed in a timely manner

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme focused on mobilisation in Year 1 (NBSFA component and TA Facility procurement) rather than full implementation. Delivery model expanded beyond VUP to support broader social protection sector capacity-building (MINALOC, LODA).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Interim TA Facility delivered effective mobilisation support (e.g., Financial Management Assessment, Capacity Needs Assessment). Embedded TA in MINALOC/LODA provided "effective support" per review. GoR engagement was timely (MoU signed within 1 month of negotiation).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: BHC Kigali co-chairs Sector Working Group with MINALOC, coordinating with UNICEF, World Bank, WFP, and EU. Governance includes monthly progress meetings with GoR and quarterly risk discussions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with development partners (e.g., UNICEF co-chairs DP coordination group). Sector Working Group mechanism enabled policy alignment. COVID-19 required virtual coordination (e.g., MoU negotiated via email/virtual meetings).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Interim TA Facility procured on time; long-term TA Facility tender launched but delayed (due Dec 2020, 5–6 months after NBSFA start). Procurement processes followed planned steps but faced timing challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to COVID-19 and mobilisation phase. Monthly finance/progress meetings with LODA introduced to address capacity gaps. Spot checks and field visits planned but limited by operating context.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to COVID-19 by prioritising mobilisation and virtual engagement. NBSFA delivery started despite TA Facility delays. Workplan flexibility emphasised for long-term TA (e.g., policy engagement on graduation/shock-responsive SP).
adaptive_management_examples: Virtual MoU negotiation/approval process (April–May 2020) due to COVID-19 travel restrictions.
Interim TA Facility produced unplanned deliverables (e.g., preparatory note on graduation) to inform long-term TA ToRs.
Monthly risk discussions introduced to monitor emerging challenges (e.g., LODA financial capacity, audit requirements).

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed procurement of long-term TA Facility (impacted by COVID-19 and bidding process).
Limited capacity at LODA for financial/narrative reporting, requiring additional TA support.
Draft results framework not finalised by review period.
Testing district-level audit requirements pending (risk to expenditure tracking).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted in-person engagement (e.g., MoU signed virtually; field visits limited).
GoR priorities shifted to pandemic response, requiring programme flexibility (e.g., shock-responsive SP focus).
Exchange rate/currency impacts not explicitly mentioned.
contextual_constraints_new: LODA’s internal capacity gaps in financial management (identified via 2020 interim TA report).
Need for robust mechanisms to address 2019 Fiduciary Risk Assessment recommendations.
District-level audit compliance untested (potential transparency risk).
partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported; GoR engagement described as collaborative (e.g., timely MoU signing).
LODA’s capacity constraints required additional BHC Kigali oversight (e.g., monthly meetings).
capacity_constraints_emerged: LODA’s financial reporting capacity limited, requiring TA intervention.
MINALOC embedded advisors (e.g., Minister’s advisor) provided but needed ongoing support.
Long-term TA Facility’s inception phase critical to address gaps (planned by June 2021).
risk_materialization: COVID-19 materialized as a major risk, requiring adaptive management (e.g., virtual coordination).
Delayed TA procurement (moderate risk) impacted timeline but did not halt NBSFA delivery.
Financial management risks at LODA identified but not yet fully mitigated.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: NBSFA component (£50.5m) mobilised on time; initial disbursements for cash transfers/PW started. No over/under-spend reported, but full execution data pending results framework finalisation.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Positive trajectory in Year 1 despite challenges. VFM not quantitatively assessed but programme deemed "one of BHC Kigali’s most significant mechanisms" for COVID-19 response. Efficiency gains expected from scaled-up NSDS and climate-sensitive PW.
financial_management_quality: Interim TA Facility’s Financial Management Assessment informed MoU audit requirements.
LODA’s financial reporting required additional TA support (monthly meetings introduced).
No major fiduciary breaches reported; 2019 FRA recommendations pending long-term TA action.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Not quantified. Efficiency noted in mobilisation phase (e.g., virtual MoU process reduced costs). Long-term efficiency dependent on graduation/shock-responsive SP innovations.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not mentioned in review; assumed GoR contribution via NBSFA mechanism.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexibility is critical for adaptive management (e.g., COVID-19 response, policy engagement).
Embedded TA in ministries (MINALOC/LODA) effective but requires sustained capacity-building.
Virtual coordination tools (e.g., email negotiations, monthly meetings) can maintain progress during disruptions.
successful_delivery_practices: Interim TA Facility’s rapid deliverables (e.g., Capacity Needs Assessment) informed long-term TA design.
Monthly progress/finance meetings with GoR improved transparency and risk monitoring.
Co-chairing Sector Working Group with MINALOC strengthened policy alignment with DPs.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced monthly risk discussions with GoR to monitor significant risks.
Prioritised testing district-level audit requirements (action planned by next review).
Developed policy engagement plan for graduation/shock-responsive SP (by Dec 2020).
innovations_attempted: Nutrition-Sensitive Direct Support (NSDS) scale-up to improve nutrition outcomes.
Climate-sensitive Public Works targeting women with caring responsibilities.
Exploring multi-sectoral ‘graduation’ support models for poverty exit.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: First Annual Review; no prior recommendations to track.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Long-term TA Facility must ensure workplan flexibility by end of inception (June 2021).
Develop comprehensive policy engagement plan for graduation/shock-responsive SP by Dec 2020 (BHC) and Mar 2021 (TA).
Address LODA’s financial reporting capacity via TA support, monthly meetings, and audit testing (by next review).
Conduct institutional capacity assessment to address FRA recommendations (by June 2021).
Test district-level audit requirements using June 2019 reports (by next review).

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Risks identified (e.g., LODA capacity, TA delays) with mitigation plans, but some pending implementation (e.g., FRA recommendations). Monthly risk discussions improved monitoring.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: NBSFA delivery (cash transfers, PW) started but quantitative data not reported. Target groups: extremely poor households, PwDs, women with caring responsibilities.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: Low (early mobilisation phase; outcomes not yet measurable. Draft results framework under development).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Weak (no impact data reported; focus on inputs/outputs e.g., MoU signed, TA mobilised).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium (long-term TA and capacity-building at MINALOC/LODA aim to strengthen systems, but risks remain e.g., LODA financial management gaps).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Medium (BHC Kigali co-chairs Sector Working Group; policy engagement on graduation/shock-responsive SP planned but not yet realised).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Early stage. Interim TA delivered assessments/notes; long-term TA expected to address institutional gaps (e.g., LODA financial management).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Programme flexibility allowed COVID-19 response integration (e.g., shock-responsive SP).
Negative: None reported, but delays in TA procurement may affect long-term outcomes.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Limited. Graduation and climate-sensitive PW models are pilot-stage; scalability dependent on long-term TA findings (by 2021).

continuation_rationale: Positive trajectory in Year 1 despite challenges (COVID-19, TA delays).
NBSFA delivery started; mobilisation near completion.
Programme aligns with GoR priorities (social protection expansion, poverty graduation).
Potential to contribute significantly to COVID-19 recovery.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium-High (dependent on long-term TA effectiveness and GoR commitment; risks include LODA capacity and external shocks).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (NBSFA mechanism sustainable if GoR ownership maintained; TA-dependent components require transition planning).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (programme described as "maintaining positive trajectory" and "should continue").
planned_adaptations_future: Flexible workplan for long-term TA (by June 2021).
Enhanced policy engagement on graduation/shock-responsive SP.
Strengthened financial oversight at LODA (audit testing, capacity-building).
Monthly risk/progress meetings with GoR to monitor adaptations.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Aawaz II - Inclusion, Accountability, and Reducing Modern Slavery Programme

output_1.title: Strengthened government institutions with effective legislative frameworks, evidence-based policies, strategies and sustainable child protection system

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Hybrid delivery model maintained with UNJP (UNICEF/UNFPA) leading systems strengthening, British Council implementing community empowerment in 37 districts of Punjab/KP, and CARE International planned for 5 districts in Sindh (not yet started). Third-party monitoring transitioned from OPM to a new provider (procurement advanced stage, expected August 2024 start).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNJP (UNICEF/UNFPA) achieved legislative/policy milestones (e.g., Punjab Child Protection Policy approved June 2024) but faced delays in KP. British Council’s community empowerment faced MEL partner issues. Government partnerships strengthened (e.g., Aawaz seen as "trusted partner" with behaviour change videos adopted on Peshawar buses).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UNICEF as Convening Agency for UNJP component; British Council for community empowerment. Strategic Steering Committee (SSC) oversight implied but not detailed. Coordination supported by third-party monitors (transitioning providers).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective early warning/response mechanisms for conflict pre-emption, with leadership from marginalised communities improving conflict responses. District/Provincial forums escalate unresolved issues. Challenges in No Objection Certificates (NoCs) delayed activities (e.g., KAP survey).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in third-party monitor procurement (OPM contract ended March 2024; new provider not yet onboarded). MEL partner procurement for British Council prioritised for completion by October 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: High oversight for legislative reforms (e.g., direct support to Punjab/KP Child Protection Bureaus) but adaptive to political constraints (e.g., behind-the-scenes lobbying on Child Marriage Bill).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme refocused resources due to UK ODA budget constraints, reprioritising targets. Adaptive management in response to political instability (e.g., delayed elections, fragile post-election settlement).
adaptive_management_examples: Bottom-up policy briefs influenced by Village/District Forum issues (e.g., Hindu/Christian marriage rules escalated to provincial governments).
Creative communications co-created with communities (e.g., behaviour change videos tested by Aawaz communities before scaling).
Diplomatic lobbying on politically sensitive issues (e.g., Child Marriage Bill in Punjab).
Early warning system successfully identified conflict red flags (e.g., Jaranwala/Sargodha violence against Christian communities).

main_implementation_challenges: UK ODA budget constraints requiring reprioritisation of targets.
Political instability in Pakistan (dissolved assemblies until February 2024 elections; fragile post-election settlement).
Delays in No Objection Certificates (NoCs) blocking activities (e.g., KAP survey).
MEL partner issues with British Council component.
Slow procurement processes (e.g., third-party monitor transition).
Government caution on politically sensitive reforms (e.g., child marriage, disability rights).
external_factors_impact: Pakistan’s balance-of-payments crisis (temporarily averted by IMF).
Sectoral tensions: violence against Christian communities (Jaranwala/Sargodha), Shia Muslim protests in Gilgit over blasphemy laws.
COVID-19 legacy: exacerbated gender gaps (e.g., 26% women internet access vs. 47% men).
Global Gender Gap Report 2024 ranked Pakistan 145/146, highlighting systemic inequality.
contextual_constraints_new: Expansion to Sindh province added complexity (implementation not yet started).
Increased sectarian/religious tensions (e.g., forced religious conversions, child marriage persistence at 18% for girls under 18).
Government institutional changes post-elections required re-engagement on advocacy.
partner_relationship_issues: MEL partner underperformance for British Council component (procurement of replacement prioritised).
UNJP component faced delays in KP policy approvals despite technical support.
Government line departments’ low capacity in some districts (e.g., DCPU establishment in new locations).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited government capacity to absorb/implement reforms (e.g., SSWF strengthening plans finalised but rollout slow).
Low community knowledge of government services despite referral pathways.
Social Service Workforce (SSWF) gaps in training/quality assurance structures (action plans developed but implementation lagging).
risk_materialization: Political risks: delayed elections and fragile settlement hindered policy advocacy.
Operational risks: NoC delays and MEL partner issues disrupted monitoring.
Reputational risks: sectarian violence (e.g., Jaranwala) required sensitive programme responses.
Financial risks: ODA budget cuts necessitated reprioritisation.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution adapted to ODA constraints; resources reprioritised against updated targets. No specific underspend/overspend data provided, but procurement delays (e.g., third-party monitor) suggest potential underspend in monitoring/evaluation.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM maintained despite challenges: legislative reforms (e.g., Anti-Rape Crisis Cell in PIMS) and community empowerment (1.8M beneficiaries reached) demonstrate cost efficiency. Hybrid model leveraged UN/NGO strengths, though MEL issues impacted data-driven VFM assessments.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High for UNJP component (e.g., UNICEF/UNFPA financial systems); British Council faced MEL-related financial oversight gaps. No major financial irregularities reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of resources in legislative support (e.g., Punjab CP Policy approved with technical assistance) and community outreach (1.5M reached via radio/social media at low marginal cost).

key_delivery_lessons: Government trust is critical: Aawaz’s collaboration with line departments amplified messages (e.g., Peshawar bus videos).
Bottom-up policy influence works: Village/District Forums effectively escalated issues (e.g., Hindu/Christian marriage rules).
Community co-creation improves targeting: communications tested by beneficiaries ensured relevance.
Political sensitivity requires adaptive advocacy: behind-the-scenes lobbying advanced contested reforms (e.g., Child Marriage Bill).
Early warning systems need leadership from marginalised groups to identify context-specific conflict triggers.
successful_delivery_practices: Hybrid delivery model balancing UN-led systemic reforms with NGO community engagement.
Conflict pre-emption mechanisms with youth volunteers/local leaders.
Referral pathways integrating government services (e.g., CP-CMRS scale-up plan for 10 districts by 2026).
Behaviour change campaigns using local media (e.g., buses in Peshawar).
management_adaptations_made: Refocused resources due to ODA cuts.
Shifted advocacy strategies in response to political instability (e.g., diplomatic lobbying).
Prioritised MEL partner procurement to address data gaps.
Escalated NoC delays to FCDO Development Director for resolution by October 2024.
innovations_attempted: Community-led communications creation (e.g., videos tested by Aawaz communities).
Policy briefs driven by forum discussions (bottom-up approach).
Digital birth registration focus on marginalised groups (girl child, religious minorities).
Early warning system integrating marginalised community leadership.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on MEL: new procurement advanced but not yet completed.
Policy advocacy adapted to political constraints (e.g., Child Marriage Bill lobbying).
Government relationships strengthened (e.g., trusted partner status).
Sindh expansion planned but not yet operational.
forward_recommendations: Complete MEL partner procurement by October 2024.
FCDO to raise NoC delays with Economic Affairs Division (EAD) by October 2024.
Scale successful communications strategies (e.g., community co-creation).
Strengthen government capacity for SSWF rollout (e.g., DCPU training plans).
Monitor sectarian tensions and adapt conflict pre-emption strategies.
Leverage Aawaz’s trusted partner status for advocacy on pending reforms (e.g., KP Child Protection Policy).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: early warning system worked well for conflict pre-emption, but political/operational risks (e.g., NoCs, MEL) required reactive adaptations. Risk of policy delays mitigated via diplomatic lobbying, but systemic risks (e.g., ODA cuts) remained outside programme control.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: 1.8M reached (272,681 direct; 1.5M via radio/social media) against 13M target by 2027.

policy_influence_achieved: Punjab Child Protection Policy approved (June 2024).
Anti-Rape Crisis Cell (ARCC) launched at PIMS (Islamabad).
Momentum on child marriage legislation: Punjab cabinet agreed to equalise marriage age to 18; National Assembly bill pending.
Hindu/Christian marriage legislation advanced in KP/Punjab.
CP-CMRS scale-up plan for 10 districts by 2026.
capacity_building_results: SSWF strengthening action plans finalised for Punjab/KP (training underway in Chitral).
District Child Protection Units (DCPUs) established/expanded (e.g., 3 new in Punjab: DG Khan, Hafizabad, Sargodha).
Community-based child protection committees’ TORs finalised (KP).
Government adoption of Aawaz referral pathways (e.g., behaviour change videos on public transport).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Government trust in Aawaz amplified state-led referral systems.
Negative: Political sensitivity around contested issues (e.g., child marriage) slowed public advocacy, requiring behind-the-scenes lobbying.
scalability_evidence: CP-CMRS scale-up plan demonstrates potential for replication across 10+ districts.
Early warning system model adaptable to other conflict-prone regions.
Community empowerment approaches (e.g., Village Forums) scalable with local government buy-in.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates resilience in challenging context (political instability, ODA cuts) with strong government partnerships and adaptive delivery. Legislative/policy achievements (e.g., Punjab CP Policy) and community reach (1.8M beneficiaries) justify continuation, though Sindh expansion and MEL improvements are critical for future phases.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable: UNJP component (UNICEF/UNFPA) has strong systems, but NGO components (British Council/CARE) face MEL and NoC challenges. Government ownership of referral pathways (e.g., CP-CMRS) improves long-term sustainability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (based on "A" overall score and trusted partner status, despite risks).
planned_adaptations_future: Operationalise Sindh component with CARE International.
Complete MEL partner procurement and strengthen monitoring.
Scale conflict pre-emption mechanisms based on early warning system lessons.
Expand DCPU coverage and SSWF training as per action plans.
Leverage government trust to advance pending reforms (e.g., KP Child Protection Policy).
Address NoC delays through FCDO-EAD engagement.
