programme_metadata.programme_title: Sub-National Governance Programme II (SNG II)

output_1.title: Interim Support to the Punjab Government

output_2.title: Programme mobilisation and management

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Interim support phase introduced to bridge gap between SNG I and SNG II. Focus shifted to immediate technical assistance for new PTI governments in KP and Punjab while full programme procurement finalized.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: New PTI governments demonstrated high engagement and responsiveness to reform support, particularly in Punjab where Finance Department actively implemented MTBF and budget transparency measures. KP showed enthusiasm for PFM reforms but required more capacity-building support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: DFID team established strong relationships with Finance, Planning, Education, and Health Departments in both provinces. Governance relied on direct engagement with ministerial offices rather than formalized structures during interim phase.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination with provincial governments achieved through embedded technical advisors and reform champions. Cross-departmental engagement in Punjab was stronger than in KP due to varying institutional capacities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Open procurement process for main SNG II programme reached final stages with Cabinet Office approval of sourcing strategy and technical moderation completed. Interim procurement (Nov 2018–Jul 2019) ensured continuity of support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required during interim phase due to political transition and need to align support with new government priorities. DFID maintained close monitoring of PEFA and MTBF implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility by redesigning interim support packages post-election to address immediate government needs (e.g., short-term assistance to KP Finance Minister on fiscal space and planning).
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid redesign of interim support to align with PTI’s anti-corruption and local government reform agenda post-July 2018 elections.
Adjustment of PEFA assessment timelines to accommodate extensive data collection challenges and government validation processes.
Embedding MTBF features into Punjab’s budget processes through iterative engagement with Finance Department to sustain reform momentum.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed finalization of business case and results framework due to ongoing procurement processes.
Extensive data collection requirements for PEFA assessments caused timeline slippages.
Fluctuating government enthusiasm for MTBF reforms required consistent advocacy and capacity-building.
Rapid decentralization of powers to districts created coordination challenges between provincial and local governments.
external_factors_impact: Political transition following PTI’s election victory in 2018 required reprogramming of support to align with new government priorities (e.g., anti-corruption, local government reforms).
Unanticipated merger of FATA with KP in 2018 introduced new administrative and security challenges in formerly tribal areas, requiring potential programme expansion to address reconstruction needs.
Currency fluctuations and inflation in Pakistan affected budget execution rates, though specific impacts on SNG II were not quantified.
contextual_constraints_new: PTI’s decentralization agenda accelerated faster than anticipated, requiring adjustments to support provincial and local government capacity-building.
Security constraints in newly merged KP districts (former FATA) limited field operations and service delivery reforms.
Low budget execution rates and revenue generation in provinces constrained fiscal space for service delivery improvements.
partner_relationship_issues: Varying levels of institutional capacity between Punjab and KP governments required tailored support approaches.
Delays in government approval processes (e.g., Chief Minister’s approval for Punjab Growth Strategy) slowed implementation of some milestones.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited technical capacity in KP’s Finance Department to lead PFM reforms independently, requiring deeper DFID engagement.
Line ministries in both provinces struggled to integrate MTBF processes into annual budget cycles without sustained hand-holding.
risk_materialization: Political risk: PTI’s election and reform agenda created both opportunities (e.g., alignment with anti-corruption goals) and challenges (e.g., reprioritization of government focus).
Operational risk: PEFA assessment delays due to data validation issues, as predicted in risk registers.
Contextual risk: FATA merger introduced unplanned geographical scope and complexity.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Interim phase budget executed as planned (£37m full programme value not yet disbursed). No specific underspend/overspend reported for 2019, but low provincial budget execution rates noted as a systemic challenge.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indications suggest VFM is on track due to: (1) Leveraging existing SNG I reforms to avoid duplication; (2) Focus on high-impact areas like revenue generation and MTBF; (3) Use of embedded technical assistance to build sustainable capacity. However, full VFM assessment pending completion of procurement and baseline data.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: DFID’s financial management rated as strong, with robust oversight of interim expenditures. Provincial counterparts demonstrated improving financial management (e.g., timely issuance of Budget Call Circulars in Punjab) but required ongoing support for complex processes like MTBF.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency not quantitatively assessed in 2019. Qualitative evidence suggests efficient use of resources through: (1) Targeted interim support packages; (2) Shared learning between KP and Punjab; (3) Digital tools (e.g., e-procurement pilots) to reduce transaction costs.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: No co-funding materialized during interim phase. Potential co-funding opportunities identified with provincial governments for future phases, particularly for digital governance initiatives.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Pakistani Rupee depreciation against GBP noted as a potential risk for programme costs, but no specific impacts reported in 2019.

key_delivery_lessons: PEFA assessments require realistic timelines accounting for data collection challenges and government validation processes.
Sustained political engagement is critical for embedding reforms (e.g., MTBF) beyond initial enthusiasm.
Interim phases can effectively bridge gaps between programme cycles if designed flexibly to respond to context changes (e.g., elections).
Decentralization reforms necessitate parallel capacity-building at both provincial and local levels to avoid implementation bottlenecks.
successful_delivery_practices: Embedding technical advisors within government departments (e.g., Punjab Finance Department) accelerated reform adoption.
Aligning support with government priorities (e.g., PTI’s anti-corruption agenda) increased buy-in and ownership.
Pilot initiatives (e.g., e-procurement) demonstrated potential for scalability and cost savings.
Cross-province learning (KP-Punjab) facilitated knowledge exchange on PFM reforms.
management_adaptations_made: Redesigned interim support packages post-election to focus on immediate government needs (e.g., fiscal space analysis in KP).
Increased advocacy for MTBF through formal roadmaps and informal champion engagement.
Accelerated procurement processes to minimize gaps between SNG I and SNG II.
innovations_attempted: PEFA methodology applied to develop targeted PFM reform strategies.
Digital tools (e-procurement, e-governance) piloted to improve transparency and efficiency.
MTBF implementation tailored to provincial contexts (e.g., Punjab’s multi-year budget planning).
previous_recommendations_progress: SNG I’s PCR recommendations partially addressed through interim support (e.g., continued PFM reforms in Punjab).
Gaps remained in local government strengthening and service delivery for marginalized groups, deferred to main SNG II phase.
forward_recommendations: Develop a refreshed PFM Reform Strategy for Punjab incorporating PEFA findings and KP lessons.
Establish PFM roadmaps with Finance Ministers in both provinces to ensure long-term reform sustainability.
Expand MTBF support to KP, with Finance Department leadership and line ministry engagement.
Conduct a PEFA assessment for KP to baseline reforms and inform strategy.
Plan for longer-term programming to maintain reform momentum and avoid implementation gaps.
Integrate FATA merger implications into programme design, including support for administrative reforms in merged districts.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was proactive in addressing political transition risks (e.g., rapid reprogramming post-election) but less effective in anticipating the scale of FATA merger impacts. PEFA delays were mitigated through revised timelines and steering committees.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Indirect reach to 140 million people in KP and Punjab through systemic PFM and planning reforms. Direct beneficiaries included government officials (Finance, Planning departments) and marginalized groups targeted through equitable budgeting (e.g., women, PWD). Quantitative targets not reported for 2019.
policy_influence_achieved: Punjab Growth Strategy 2018–23 developed and awaiting approval, incorporating inclusive planning principles.
MTBF adopted by Punjab Finance Department, with potential for KP replication.
PEFA assessment findings influenced Punjab’s PFM reform priorities.
capacity_building_results: Technical capacity of Punjab Finance Department improved through MTBF implementation and PEFA training.
KP Finance Ministry received targeted support on fiscal space analysis and planning manual revisions.
Limited evidence of sustained capacity at district level due to early phase of decentralization.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Increased government demand for reform support beyond initial scope (e.g., KP requested assistance on revenue mobilization).
Negative: PEFA delays created temporary data gaps for evidence-based planning.
scalability_evidence: MTBF and e-procurement pilots demonstrated potential for scaling to other provinces/sectors.
Punjab’s PFM reforms could serve as a model for KP with adaptations for contextual differences.
Digital governance tools (e.g., data collection systems) identified for broader application.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong government ownership in Punjab and emerging commitment in KP justify continuation. Interim phase demonstrated programme relevance to PTI’s reform agenda and potential to address systemic PFM challenges. FATA merger presents new opportunities for impact in marginalized regions.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-term sustainable with embedded technical assistance, but long-term sustainability depends on: (1) Provincial government ownership of reforms; (2) Capacity-building at local levels; (3) Alignment with decentralization policies.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (based on interim phase performance and government feedback)
planned_adaptations_future: Expand support to KP merged districts (former FATA) to address post-merger administrative challenges.
Deepened focus on revenue generation and digital governance in next phase.
Stronger integration of gender and social inclusion into PFM reforms (e.g., gender-responsive budgeting).
Development of a monitoring framework to track decentralization impacts on service delivery.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Zimbabwe Economic Stability and Transformation (ZEST) Programme

output_1.title: Contribution to ZIMREF trust fund - technical assistance under pillar 1: 'Stability and Economic Growth'

output_2.title: Contribution to ZIMREF trust fund - technical assistance under pillar 2: 'Effective and Transparent Public Sector'

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from mixed bilateral/multilateral delivery to exclusive focus on ZIMREF (World Bank-managed trust fund) after cancellation of bilateral dialogue component due to contextual changes. Original plan included direct engagement with BMOs/private sector.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (ZIMREF) performed well in policy/regulatory change delivery (13 laws/12 regulations enacted) but faced data availability challenges (EODB/BCI surveys unavailable). Strategic Initiatives fund enabled flexible contracting for energy/public sector reforms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme Oversight Committee (POC) meetings guided transition to new ZISET trust fund structure. More flexible donor earmarking introduced, though humanitarian crisis support was deprioritized due to existing donor programs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination with 7 other ZIMREF donors (EU, Norway, etc.) and World Bank secretariat. FCDO actively shaped ZISET restructuring discussions, though UK profile visibility remains a challenge.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Flexible Strategic Initiatives fund enabled rapid contracting of technical assistance (e.g., energy/public sector reforms). No major procurement delays reported, though budget constraints limited new bilateral procurements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to: (1) frequent POC meetings to manage ZIMREF→ZISET transition; (2) active FCDO engagement in results framework revisions; (3) close monitoring of policy reform milestones.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted from bilateral delivery to ZIMREF focus; adapted to COVID-19 via virtual expert engagement; restructured logframe in 2021 to align with ZISET’s new pillar framework.
adaptive_management_examples: Restructured logframe in 2021 to reflect ZIMREF→ZISET transition and new pillar-based results framework.
Reallocated budget from cancelled bilateral dialogue component to ZIMREF contributions and Strategic Initiatives fund.
Adjusted Output 2 to focus exclusively on public sector reform after deprioritizing private sector support due to budget constraints.
Used virtual delivery to involve senior experts during COVID-19, maintaining high-level technical assistance.

main_implementation_challenges: Cancellation of bilateral dialogue component due to deteriorating operating context in Zimbabwe.
Unavailability of key data sources (Ease of Doing Business survey discontinued globally; CZI Business Confidence Index not measured in 2021).
Delays in FINSCOPE survey fieldwork, preventing measurement of financial inclusion targets.
Budget constraints limiting new bilateral procurements (e.g., private sector support program).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic disrupted fieldwork (e.g., FINSCOPE surveys) and required shift to virtual delivery.
Global discontinuation of Ease of Doing Business survey by World Bank (unrelated to Zimbabwe) removed a key metric.
Zimbabwe’s economic volatility affected reform momentum, though 2021 saw partial recovery.
Political context changes led to cancellation of government-BMO dialogue component.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging humanitarian crises competed with economic reform priorities, though ZISET was not used for humanitarian support.
Currency instability (not quantified in review) likely affected programme costs/value for money.
partner_relationship_issues: World Bank’s transition to new ZISET framework created temporary alignment challenges with legacy ZIMREF activities.
UK’s contribution visibility was perceived as low relative to other ZIMREF donors, prompting discussions on profile enhancement.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited local capacity to measure business confidence (CZI did not conduct 2021 BCI survey).
Government of Zimbabwe’s absorption capacity for technical assistance varied across ministries.
risk_materialization: ‘Severe’/‘Major’ risk ratings materialized as political/economic instability (e.g., cancellation of bilateral component).
Data availability risks realized (EODB/BCI surveys unavailable), complicating results measurement.

budget_execution_vs_plan: £19.9m full-life budget on track; majority (~£12.2m) allocated to ZIMREF contributions (£6m 2015–2018 + £6.2m 2018–2022).
Strategic Initiatives fund enabled flexible spending on energy/public sector reforms outside ZIMREF.
Budget constraints prevented new bilateral procurements (e.g., private sector support program).
value_for_money_assessment: High VFM confirmed by 2019 ZIMREF mid-term review, citing: (1) 10% admin costs (below sector average); (2) policy impacts (e.g., Green Climate Fund accreditation); (3) flexibility to pivot priorities.
Efficiency gains from virtual delivery and mixed national/international expert teams.
Effectiveness partially limited by data gaps (EODB/BCI), though qualitative evidence (e.g., business optimism surveys) showed progress.
financial_management_quality: World Bank’s financial management rated satisfactory (e.g., timely disbursements, transparent reporting).
FCDO’s oversight ensured alignment with UK priorities (e.g., COP26-linked NDC revisions).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Admin costs at 10% of budget (below typical 15–20% for multilateral funds).
Leveraged £6.2m UK contribution to unlock $60m multi-donor ZIMREF fund.
co_funding_materialization: ZIMREF secured $60m in pledges ($51.6m received) from 7 other donors, exceeding co-funding targets.

key_delivery_lessons: Multilateral trust funds (e.g., ZIMREF) offer flexibility but require active donor coordination to align with bilateral priorities.
Virtual delivery can maintain expert engagement during crises but may limit local stakeholder participation.
Results frameworks must account for data volatility (e.g., survey discontinuations).
successful_delivery_practices: ZIMREF’s pillar-based structure enabled focused technical assistance (e.g., 13 laws/12 regulations enacted under Pillar 1).
Strategic Initiatives fund allowed rapid response to emerging priorities (e.g., energy reforms).
Mixed expert teams (national/international) balanced contextual knowledge with global best practices.
management_adaptations_made: Logframe overhauled in 2021 to reflect ZISET’s new pillars and deprioritize private sector support.
POC meetings expanded to include ZIMREF evaluation follow-up and ZISET transition planning.
Lessons from Public Sector EFO shared across FCDO portfolio via structured briefings.
innovations_attempted: Virtual delivery models for technical assistance during COVID-19.
Flexible earmarking under ZISET to adapt to donor priorities.

Completed: Logframe restructuring to focus Output 2 on public sector reform (Rec 2).
Inclusion of ZIMREF evaluation follow-up in POC agendas (Rec 4).
Not Completed: Design of bilateral private sector program (Rec 1) – blocked by budget constraints.
Increased targets for indicators 3.1–3.3 (Rec 6) – not actioned.

forward_recommendations: Enhance UK profile in ZISET communications to reflect contribution level.
Monitor ZISET’s flexibility in addressing emerging crises (e.g., food security).
Explore options for legacy sustainability as ZEST closes in 2023 (e.g., transitioning technical assistance to local institutions).
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating operational risks (e.g., pivot to ZIMREF after bilateral component cancellation).
Less effective in anticipating data availability risks (EODB/BCI discontinuations).

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Indirect: Policy/regulatory changes (13 laws, 12 regulations) benefit businesses/private sector.
Direct: Technical assistance reached government ministries (e.g., Infrastructure Development Bank’s Green Climate Fund accreditation).
Financial inclusion projects targeted youth, women, and people with disabilities (early signs of inclusive access).
policy_influence_achieved: Zimbabwe’s NDC revisions ahead of COP26 increased climate mitigation/adaptation ambition.
13 laws/12 regulations enacted under 2015 Doing Business Reform Memo (covering 9 DB indicators).
Infrastructure Development Bank of Zimbabwe accredited to Green Climate Fund.
capacity_building_results: Technical assistance strengthened public sector capacity (e.g., public financial management reforms).
World Bank’s FINSCOPE MSME survey will inform National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS II).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Virtual delivery enabled broader expert participation (including senior levels).
Negative: Reduced direct engagement with private sector after bilateral component cancellation.
scalability_evidence: ZIMREF→ZISET transition demonstrates scalability of trust fund model for other donors/contexts.
Policy reforms (e.g., EODB-related laws) provide templates for other sectors.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme designed as time-bound (2018–2023) to catalyze reforms; ZISET trust fund will continue post-ZEST with other donors.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High (ZISET’s multi-donor structure ensures continuity; World Bank management provides stability).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (programme met expectations with ‘A’ score in 2022, despite challenges).
planned_adaptations_future: Final year (2022–2023) will focus on: (1) completing ZISET transition; (2) documenting lessons for FCDO’s future economic governance programs; (3) ensuring sustainability of policy reforms (e.g., NDC implementation).
Explore options for handing over technical assistance roles to local institutions.

output_1.title: Essential economic development projects completed in time, within budget and to required standards

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from original focus on private sector/tourism to prioritizing basic infrastructure (hospital, schools, sewage, roads) due to unmet needs. PMO role expanded to include capacity-building across GoM ministries, though staffing gaps limited this function.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: GoM proposed projects were reviewed/approved by Programme Board but faced delays in procurement (e.g., asphalt plant components, hospital design tendering) and execution. PMO under-resourced despite approved ToRs for Project Managers (August 2022).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Steering Committee and Programme Board active but oversight intensity increased due to delays. PMO established but struggled with staffing (original model envisaged Team Leader + multiple officers; gaps persisted).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong FCDO-GoM dialogue but coordination challenges in procurement (e.g., cement shortages, shipping delays) and timeline updates. Monthly meetings introduced to track progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Significant delays in procurement (e.g., asphalt plant mechanical parts, hospital detailed design) and cost escalations (e.g., +$395K for shipping, 50% contingency used for airport tower doors). COVID and Ukraine conflict exacerbated supply chain issues.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to delays; FCDO increased oversight of PMO and project timelines. Steering Committee focus shifted to mitigating risks rather than strategic alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Budget reallocations within contingencies (e.g., airport tower, asphalt plant) and timeline extensions (e.g., hospital to 2025) approved. Scope adjustments for school blocks due to structural assessments.
adaptive_management_examples: Updated timelines for airport control tower (Oct 2022) and asphalt plant (Nov 2022) to reflect delays.
PMO ToRs revised and Project Manager roles approved (Aug 2022) to address capacity gaps.
Hospital budget increased from £15.4m to £19.4m with detailed design timeline extended to April 2023.
Use of contingency for cost escalations (e.g., shipping, inflation) rather than scope reduction.

main_implementation_challenges: Procurement delays (e.g., asphalt plant components, hospital design tendering) and supply chain disruptions (cement shortages, shipping logistics).
Cost escalations due to inflation (COVID, Ukraine conflict) exceeding contingencies (e.g., asphalt plant +$395K).
Capacity constraints in GoM’s Public Works Department (PWD) and PMO staffing gaps.
Structural assessment findings requiring scope changes (e.g., school blocks).
Coordinating multiple ministries and contractors with varying capacities.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Delayed shipments, increased costs, and reduced workforce availability.
Ukraine conflict: Further inflation in material/transport costs (e.g., fuel, steel).
Regional logistics challenges (e.g., port delays in Caribbean).
Natural disaster risks (hurricanes) requiring resilient design adjustments.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need to prioritize basic infrastructure (e.g., hospital, sewage) over economic growth/tourism projects.
GoM’s limited absorption capacity for large-scale capital projects simultaneously.
Higher-than-expected maintenance needs for existing assets (e.g., geothermal wells).
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between GoM’s project proposals and FCDO’s risk appetite (e.g., hospital cost increases).
Delays in GoM’s approval processes (e.g., tendering, contract sign-offs).
PMO’s dual reporting lines (FCDO and GoM) creating occasional conflicts in priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: PMO understaffed despite approved roles (Project Managers recruited late).
PWD lacked capacity for parallel projects (e.g., school blocks and road works).
Ministries required more hands-on support for project management than anticipated.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (high likelihood, high impact) – materialized for most projects.
Cost overruns (medium likelihood) – materialized for asphalt plant, hospital.
Supply chain disruptions (high likelihood) – materialized due to COVID/Ukraine.
Capacity gaps in GoM (high likelihood) – materialized in PMO and PWD.
Exchange rate fluctuations (low likelihood) – not explicitly mentioned as materialized.

budget_execution_vs_plan: £27m infrastructure budget largely committed; £3m TA budget used for PMO and capacity-building.
Underspend on airport runway ($9.275m vs $10.086m allocated) due to contingency use for COVID costs.
Overspend risks: asphalt plant (+$395K), hospital (£15.4m → £19.4m), airport tower (contingency exhausted).
Overall budget on track but contingencies heavily utilized for inflation/shipping costs.
value_for_money_assessment: VFM demonstrated for completed projects (e.g., runway resurfacing, sewage works) with lower life-cycle costs.
Challenges in quantifying VFM for delayed projects (e.g., hospital, asphalt plant) due to cost escalations.
PMO’s upskilling efforts for GoM ministries fell short of targets, reducing long-term VFM.
Business Case assumptions on private sector leverage not yet realized due to shift in focus.
financial_management_quality: GoM’s financial reporting improved but still faces delays in reconciliations (e.g., airport runway).
FCDO’s enhanced oversight (monthly meetings, updated delivery plans) improved transparency.
Contingency management reactive rather than proactive (e.g., used for unplanned cost increases).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient delivery for smaller projects (e.g., sewage works completed on time/budget).
Inefficiencies in large projects (e.g., hospital design delays, asphalt plant shipping costs).
Economies of scale not fully realized due to staggered project timelines.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: No evidence of planned co-funding materializing; all costs borne by FCDO.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly quantified, but global inflation (USD/GBP) likely affected procurement costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Need for realistic procurement timelines accounting for external shocks (COVID, conflicts).
Importance of front-loading capacity-building (PMO staffing delays hindered progress).
Critical to design contracts with KPIs incentivizing timely delivery (e.g., penalties for delays).
Monthly progress tracking essential for early issue escalation.
successful_delivery_practices: Strong FCDO-GoM partnership in revising timelines collaboratively.
Effective use of contingencies to absorb cost shocks without scope reduction.
PMO’s role in standardizing project documentation (e.g., ToRs, delivery plans).
Steering Committee’s approval of revised hospital budget/design timeline.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced monthly progress meetings to replace quarterly reviews.
PMO ToRs revised to clarify Project Manager roles/responsibilities.
FCDO increased direct oversight of high-risk projects (e.g., hospital, asphalt plant).
Business Case addendum planned to reflect hospital cost increases.
innovations_attempted: Embedding PMO Project Managers into ministries as part of Public Service Reform.
Consolidated lesson-learning register to track mitigating actions.
Use of MUL (Montserrat UK Office) for urgent procurements (e.g., sewage works).
previous_recommendations_progress: PMO staffing gaps partially addressed (ToRs approved, recruitment pending).
Risk register updated but mitigating actions not consistently tracked.
Results framework review initiated but not yet completed.
Theory of Change update planned but not implemented.
forward_recommendations: Recruit PMO roles urgently; escalate delays to FCDO leadership.
Enhance GoM’s oversight via regular Cabinet updates (reduce Steering Committee burden).
Submit documents to Programme Board 3 days in advance (per ToRs).
Comprehensively revise results framework (outcome/impact indicators) and Theory of Change.
Prepare costed Business Case addendum for hospital cost increases.
Develop consolidated lesson-learning register with tracked mitigating actions.
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk identification robust (e.g., procurement delays, cost escalations) but mitigation reactive.
Contingency planning insufficient for compounded risks (COVID + Ukraine conflict).
Risk ownership unclear between FCDO/GoM for some issues (e.g., PMO staffing).
Annual Review recommendations not systematically integrated into delivery plans.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Airport runway/resurfacing: Completed; benefits all air travelers (safety, lower maintenance costs).
Sewage works: Completed; benefits ~X households (environmental/health improvements).

PMO model adopted for other programmes (e.g., Technical Cooperation programme).
Limited evidence of private sector policy changes (geothermal maintenance may attract future investment).
capacity_building_results: PMO established but capacity-building for ministries incomplete due to staffing gaps.
PWD gained experience in managing large projects (e.g., school blocks, roads).
Steering Committee’s oversight capacity strengthened through revised processes.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Improved coordination between ministries via PMO.
Negative: Delayed economic growth projects (tourism/private sector) due to infrastructure focus.
Negative: Contingency use for cost overruns reduced funds for other activities.
scalability_evidence: PMO model scalable to other GoM programmes (already partially adopted).
Infrastructure designs (e.g., resilient hospital, sewage systems) replicable for other Caribbean islands.
Procurement lessons (e.g., KPIs in contracts) applicable to future FCDO programmes.

continuation_rationale: Programme has delivered critical infrastructure (runway, sewage) with tangible benefits.
Hospital and asphalt plant, though delayed, remain high-priority for Montserrat.
Shift from original Business Case justified by unmet basic needs.
FCDO and GoM committed to mitigating risks (e.g., PMO staffing, revised timelines).
delivery_model_sustainability: PMO model sustainable if fully staffed and embedded in GoM systems.
Current reliance on FCDO oversight not sustainable long-term; GoM ownership needs strengthening.
Procurement/contract management practices require further improvement for scalability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied with progress but concerned about delays and cost overruns; supports continuation with stricter oversight.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize PMO recruitment and embed Project Managers in ministries.
Implement consolidated lesson-learning register and track mitigating actions.
Revise results framework/Theory of Change to reflect shifted focus (basic infrastructure).
Prepare Business Case addendum for hospital cost increases.
Strengthen GoM’s procurement capacity to reduce future delays.
Explore phased handover of PMO functions to GoM by programme end (2024).

partner_performance_reality.world_bank_efo: Delivered well (A+), with efficient use of £175,000 to expand PSPR 2018 analysis and support IARIW conference planning.
partner_performance_reality.world_bank_tf: Behind schedule due to staffing/workload constraints on both DFID and World Bank sides, but now progressing with an ambitious Concept Note.
partner_performance_reality.rpc_bidding_process: Attracted 5 stage-1 bids from leading poverty research institutes, indicating strong technical and commercial competition.

management_structure_actual.governance_planned: Programme Management Group (PMG) will convene DFID, RPC, and World Bank twice yearly for coordination.
management_structure_actual.oversight_mechanisms: Twice-yearly reviews with RPC and World Bank; risk profile to be developed during inception.

coordination_effectiveness.internal_coordination: Consultations with 6 DFID country offices and 3 policy teams to align research with operational needs.
coordination_effectiveness.external_coordination: RPC will coordinate with World Bank TF during inception to ensure thematic coherence.

programme_metadata.programme_title: BRILHO – Energy Africa Mozambique Programme

output_1.title: Businesses have access to finance and technical assistance (TA) to offer off-grid energy products and related services for rural households and businesses. Supported businesses have improved sustainability and have a wider impact on the local economy.

output_2.title: Demand activation: Awareness and education of rural consumers on the benefits of modern energy solutions (e.g., Smoke-Free Village campaign).

output_3.title: Research and information: Market-relevant data and reports to fill evidence gaps in the Mozambique context.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended by 2 years (to Dec 2026) with £6.3M cost extension; expanded Results-Based Financing (RBF) limits to enable rural expansion. Original business case did not anticipate the need for diplomatic engagement to unblock regulatory barriers (e.g., mini-grid concessions).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: SNV delivery team performed strongly, with high responsiveness to market needs. Private sector partners (e.g., BURN) credited BRILHO’s RBF as "critical" for market entry and affordability. However, one subgrantee (SolarWorks!) liquidated, absorbing significant funds and requiring adaptive reallocation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Contract with SNV managed via competitive tender; Crown Agents Bank manages Swedish Sida’s £8.9M contribution. Oversight intensified for RBF disbursements and regulatory blockages (e.g., mini-grid concessions).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with Government of Mozambique (GoM) on policy reforms (e.g., off-grid electrification plan approved in 2023), but delays in concession issuance highlight gaps in inter-agency alignment. Synergies pursued with WB ProEnergia and potential new FCDO energy transition programme.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive procurement process ensured VfM; fees realigned during extension to comply with FCDO rules. Market Development Fund (MDF) absorbed largest budget share (£2.2M in FY 2023–2024).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to regulatory blockages (e.g., import tariffs, mini-grid concessions) and liquidation of SolarWorks!. Milestone-based payments for staff/running costs (£250K) introduced to mitigate risks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to: (1) Expand RBF limits for rural expansion; (2) Reallocate funds post-SolarWorks! liquidation; (3) Adapt demand activation strategies (e.g., targeted Smoke-Free Village campaign). Catalytic Grants and RBF tools were tailored to firm-specific needs (e.g., BURN’s Pay-as-you-Cook hotplates).
adaptive_management_examples: Expanded RBF limits to counter carbon financing revenue drops affecting ICS/SHS affordability.
Shifted demand activation from broad mass communication to targeted geographical campaigns (e.g., Niassa province).
Developed analytical note on RBF role to inform 2-year extension strategy for market sustainability.
Engaged diplomatically (via High Commissioner) to unblock mini-grid concession approvals.

main_implementation_challenges: Regulatory blockages: (1) Pending mini-grid concessions despite 2023 off-grid electrification plan approval; (2) Inconsistent import tariff exemptions for energy equipment, reducing RBF impact.
Market volatility: Drop in carbon financing revenues constrained ICS portfolio expansion and retail pricing.
Partner liquidation: SolarWorks! absorption of funds required reallocation and risk management.
Capacity gaps: Delays in GoM’s implementation of approved off-grid regulations slowed mini-grid sector startup.
external_factors_impact: Economic: Currency fluctuations and import tariffs increased costs for private sector partners (e.g., SHS working capital loans).
Political: Slow GoM approval processes for concessions and tariff exemptions, despite high-level commitments under the Energy Africa Compact.
Market: Competition and crowded donor landscape created risks of overlap (e.g., multiple energy access programmes targeting same regions).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for diplomatic intervention to resolve regulatory blockages (e.g., mini-grid concessions stuck at ministerial level).
Limited geographical reach of demand activation campaigns due to resource constraints, despite high performance in targeted areas (e.g., Niassa).
Emerging need for higher-tier energy solutions (e.g., electric induction hotplates) not fully addressed in original design.
partner_relationship_issues: SolarWorks! liquidation disrupted fund flows and required adaptive management.
Some firms pivoted to higher-income segments due to lack of RBF, creating tension with programme’s rural focus.
GoM institutions (e.g., energy ministry) slow to operationalize approved regulations, despite technical assistance from SNV.
capacity_constraints_emerged: SNV team stretched by need to manage both delivery and regulatory advocacy (e.g., mini-grid concessions).
Private sector partners (especially SHS firms) faced working capital constraints, limiting expansion into remote areas.
GoM’s limited capacity to process unsolicited mini-grid requests delayed project approvals.
risk_materialization: Regulatory risks: Mini-grid concession delays and tariff exemption inconsistencies (as identified in business case).
Market risks: Carbon financing revenue drops and SolarWorks! liquidation (partially mitigated by RBF flexibility).
Partner risks: Some firms stopped expansion without RBF, requiring programme intervention.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall_execution_rate: 63% of total approved budget spent as of March 2024.
budget_execution_vs_plan.deviations: Minor deviations due to: (1) RBF limits reached with top-performing subgrantees; (2) SolarWorks! liquidation absorbing funds.
budget_execution_vs_plan.spending_confidence: Supplier confident in ability to spend remaining budget within forecasts.

value_for_money_assessment.economic_level: Competitive procurement and fee realignment during extension ensured compliance with FCDO rules.

cost_per_unit.ics_shs: £34.68 per household (vs. African average of £41/year per IRENA 2016).
cost_per_unit.jobs: Not specified (but 25,024 MSME jobs created vs. 20,000 target).

efficiency_level.leverage_ratio: £36M private sector investment leveraged against £23.8M disbursed (1.5x leverage).

value_for_money_assessment.vfm_risks: Import tariffs and regulatory delays reduced RBF effectiveness by counteracting affordability gains.

financial_management_quality.supplier_performance: Excellent track record; milestone-based payments and budget reallocations managed proactively.
financial_management_quality.co_funding_materialization: Swedish Sida’s £8.9M fully materialized (managed via Crown Agents Bank).
financial_management_quality.cost_control: Cost extension (£6.3M) approved in Aug 2024 to cover 2-year extension; fees realigned to FCDO principles.

cost_efficiency_achieved.vs_plan: Better than planned (e.g., cost per SHS household below regional benchmarks).
cost_efficiency_achieved.drivers: RBF incentives reduced product costs for end-consumers; Catalytic Grants enabled market entry at lower setup costs.
cost_efficiency_achieved.inefficiencies: Import tariffs and regulatory delays offset ~20% of RBF’s affordability impact.

key_delivery_lessons: Catalytic Grants + RBF were critical for market entry and expansion, but RBF availability is a "make-or-break" factor for private sector viability in rural areas.
Flexible instruments (e.g., tailored grants, milestone-based payments) enabled responsiveness to firm-specific needs (e.g., BURN’s hotplates).
Regulatory advocacy requires both technical and diplomatic engagement (e.g., High Commissioner involvement for mini-grid concessions).
Demand activation works best when geographically targeted (e.g., Niassa province) rather than mass campaigns.
successful_delivery_practices: SNV’s proximity to market allowed rapid adaptation (e.g., shifting RBF limits, reallocating post-SolarWorks! liquidation).
Results-Based Financing directly linked to affordability (e.g., reduced product costs by ~30% for end-consumers).
Policy technical assistance (e.g., off-grid regulation drafts) created demand for GoM investments.
Partnership with Crown Agents Bank ensured smooth co-funding management (Swedish Sida).
management_adaptations_made: Expanded RBF limits to counter carbon financing drops.
Developed analytical note on RBF role to guide 2-year extension strategy.
Intensified oversight on mini-grid concessions via diplomatic channels.
Shifted demand activation to targeted campaigns (e.g., Smoke-Free Village).
innovations_attempted: Pay-as-you-Cook electric induction hotplates (BURN) as higher-tier energy solution.
Market Development Fund (MDF) used to pilot new business models in remote areas (e.g., Niassa province).
Synergies with WB ProEnergia explored for long-term market sustainability.
previous_recommendations_progress: RBF expansion implemented (addressing prior calls for greater flexibility).
Regulatory advocacy ongoing but delayed (mini-grid concessions still pending).
Geographical targeting improved (e.g., Niassa SHS deployment).
forward_recommendations: Pursue diplomatic escalation for mini-grid concessions and tariff exemptions (Recommendation 5).
Use 2-year extension to pilot transition from RBF to commercial financing (e.g., blended finance).
Strengthen GoM capacity for regulation implementation (e.g., unsolicited mini-grid requests).
Document BRILHO’s "Ayrton Demonstrator" lessons for broader UK energy access programmes (e.g., Just Energy Transition Partnerships).

risk_management_effectiveness.proactive: Strong adaptive responses to SolarWorks! liquidation and carbon financing drops.
risk_management_effectiveness.reactive: Slow to escalate regulatory blockages to diplomatic level (only addressed in 2024).
risk_management_effectiveness.gaps: Limited contingency for GoM’s slow regulatory implementation; import tariffs not fully mitigated.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 2.5 million people with access to clean energy (vs. original targets).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 25,024 MSME jobs created (vs. 20,000 target); 86,029 SHS units delivered in 2023 (20% of national electrification results).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.geographical: 6,600 SHS deployed in Niassa province (remote/low-income); first privately owned mini-grid operational (concession pending).

policy_influence_achieved: Off-grid electrification plan approved by GoM in 2023 (directly linked to BRILHO’s technical assistance).
Mini-grid regulation drafted but implementation delayed; import tariff exemptions partially secured.
Programme cited as model for UK’s £1bn Ayrton commitment and Just Energy Transition Partnerships.
capacity_building_results: Private sector: 1016 businesses supported (operational 12 months post-intervention); firms reported RBF as critical for viability.
Government: Off-grid regulation capacity built, but implementation gaps remain (e.g., concession approvals).
SNV team: Enhanced adaptive management skills (e.g., post-SolarWorks! reallocation).
unintended_consequences: Positive: RBF incentives accelerated market entry for firms like BURN, creating spillover effects in adjacent sectors (e.g., clean cooking).
Negative: Some firms pivoted to higher-income segments without RBF, reducing rural reach; import tariffs offset affordability gains.
scalability_evidence: Model replicated in other Energy Africa programmes (e.g., Ayrton Demonstrators).
Lessons informed WB ProEnergia and potential new FCDO energy transition programme.
Challenges in mini-grid scalability due to regulatory delays highlight need for systemic reforms.

continuation_rationale: Outputs exceed targets (A+ score) with outcomes beyond end-of-programme projections (e.g., 2.5M beneficiaries, £36M private leverage).
Regulatory blockages (e.g., mini-grid concessions) require continued support to unlock full impact.
2-year extension (to Dec 2026) provides runway to pilot market sustainability mechanisms (e.g., blended finance).
Alignment with UK’s Ayrton commitment and Just Energy Transition Partnerships justifies continued investment.

delivery_model_sustainability.strengths: SNV’s market-proximate approach and flexible instruments (RBF, Catalytic Grants) are effective.
delivery_model_sustainability.risks: Dependence on RBF may limit long-term commercial viability; GoM’s slow regulatory implementation could hinder scalability.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (A+ score, strong VfM, and policy influence)
planned_adaptations_future: Phase out RBF gradually in favor of commercial financing (e.g., blended funds).
Intensify diplomatic engagement to resolve mini-grid concessions and tariff exemptions.
Expand geographical targeting (e.g., Gaza, Tete provinces) for mini-grid projects.
Document and disseminate lessons as "Ayrton Demonstrator" for broader UK energy programmes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Impact Evaluations on Urban transport, transport corridors and road safety across multilateral development banks and bilateral programmes (ieConnect)

output_1.title: Increased quantity, quality and relevance of transport evidence available to improve policy design and implementation

output_2.title: Increased capacity of transport policymakers, implementers, researchers, and partners to incorporate rigorous evidence/tools into policy making

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted focus to data systems/data collection rather than completing full impact evaluations within original timeframe, with World Bank committing to long-term completion. Extension approved to expand research and integrate previous FCDO-funded work into new mobility projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (DIME/Transport Global Practice) met all financial/operational standards per central agreements. Quarterly meetings maintained, though extension negotiations took longer than planned. Co-financing exceeded targets (FCDO share now 36% vs planned <40%).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Dual management by FCDO and World Bank teams with clear division of roles. Standard World Bank fiduciary processes followed, with FCDO reviewing all fund disbursements (no advance payments).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with SuM4All partnership (FCDO holds Steering Committee seat) and operational-level engagement with 5 MDBs and 6 bilateral donors. Cross-cutting themes (gender, FCAS, climate) integrated through collaborative design.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: World Bank’s standard procurement policies applied without issues. Financial reports submitted bi-annually to FCDO as agreed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to capacity constraints in partner countries. FCDO conducts ad-hoc requests beyond scheduled reports, with World Bank responding promptly.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to include COVID-19 response (2020) and extended scope for policy dissemination. Logframe targets revised upward in 2024/25 to reflect over-performance.
adaptive_management_examples: Real-time impact evaluations (e.g., Liberia Road Safety IE) informed ongoing project design changes during implementation, not just post-completion.
Added Female Economic Empowerment (FEE) disaggregation mid-programme after identifying data gaps (now 52% of IEs disaggregated by sex/age).
Tanzania Gender-Based Violence study introduced mobile app-based reporting to address underreporting challenges.

main_implementation_challenges: Capacity constraints in partner countries delayed IE implementation, requiring intensive technical assistance.
Logframe milestones were incorrectly recorded in 2023 AR, complicating performance assessment (e.g., 2022 targets exceeded but not reflected).
Partner government delays in underlying transport projects (e.g., Ethiopia TRANSIP) risked IE timelines.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Digital Access Programme (DAP)

output_1.title: Increased digital inclusion of excluded or underserved communities in partner countries, through the support of systemic enablers and scalable models for affordable last-mile connectivity, digital literacy and skills, and locally-relevant digital content and services

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Rapid pivot to COVID-19 adaptation via virtual delivery models (e.g., digital skills training, policy dialogues). Budget reductions (25% in FY2020/21, 50% in FY2021/22) offset by lower virtual delivery costs. Maintained alignment with Theory of Change despite shifts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners in Brazil, Indonesia, Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa delivered 56 projects under Pillar 1, exceeding targets for policy/regulatory reforms (18 vs. 12 planned) and scalable models (73 vs. 60). Stakeholder engagement (884 vs. 480 planned) demonstrated strong local ownership.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Cross-government (FCDO-DCMS) X-HMG team with central advisory support and five in-country teams. Governance via Senior Governance Committee (SGC) and Programme Management Committee (PMC) remained effective despite institutional mergers (FCO-DFID → FCDO).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Successful cross-country peer learning events (2020, 2021) and mid-year results stock-takes improved knowledge sharing. Challenges in harmonizing pillar-specific Theories of Change (ToCs) post-Prosperity Fund closure.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement adapted to virtual modalities, enabling continued delivery during pandemic. No major delays reported, though budget cuts required reprioritization of contracts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight due to COVID-19 risks and ODA reductions. Central teams provided intensive advisory support to country teams, particularly for cybersecurity (Pillar 2) and digital inclusion (Pillar 1).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to reallocate funds across pillars/countries (e.g., repurposing connectivity projects for telemedicine in Indonesia). Adaptive management enabled response to external shocks (pandemic, ODA cuts).
adaptive_management_examples: Shift to virtual delivery for digital literacy training (all countries) within 3 months of COVID-19 onset.
Reprioritization of Pillar 1 projects in Kenya to focus on TV White Spaces (TVWS) regulation and community networks licensing, aligning with pandemic-era connectivity needs.
Development of a **National Framework for COVID-19 Adaptation Digital Innovations** (Kenya) to address emerging health-system gaps.
Accelerated policy dialogues via online platforms, increasing stakeholder engagement by 84% (884 vs. 480 planned).

main_implementation_challenges: 25% budget reduction in FY2020/21 and 50% in FY2021/22 due to FCDO ODA prioritization, requiring reprioritization of activities.
Closure of the Prosperity Fund necessitated refresh of secondary benefits strategy and non-ODA funding pursuit.
Institutional merger (FCO-DFID → FCDO) created temporary governance uncertainties.
Virtual delivery limitations in low-connectivity areas (e.g., rural Nigeria, Brazil) hindered inclusive reach.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Accelerated digital adoption but exposed digital divides; programme pivoted to pandemic-response models (e.g., telemedicine strategies in Indonesia, remote learning in Nigeria).
ODA cuts: Reduced scope for secondary benefits (UK trade/investment linkages) but focused resources on primary digital inclusion goals.
Political transitions in partner countries (e.g., Nigeria, Brazil) delayed some policy reforms but also opened windows for advocacy (e.g., digital gender gap policies).
contextual_constraints_new: Unexpected regulatory barriers to spectrum sharing (Kenya, Brazil) required additional advocacy.
Currency fluctuations in Nigeria and Brazil increased local implementation costs by ~12%.
Limited in-person engagement reduced trust-building with marginalized groups (e.g., people with disabilities in South Africa).
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in MoU sign-offs with government agencies in South Africa due to bureaucratic turnover.
Mismatched expectations with private-sector partners on last-mile connectivity sustainability (e.g., Kenya’s TVWS pilots).
Civil society partners in Indonesia required additional capacity support to adapt to virtual monitoring tools.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Country teams lacked specialized cybersecurity expertise (Pillar 2), addressed via central FCDO advisory support.
Local implementing partners needed upskilling in digital safeguarding for vulnerable groups (e.g., children in Brazil).
Reduced in-country presence due to travel restrictions limited hands-on technical assistance.
risk_materialization: **Budget cuts**: Materialized as planned (25% in FY2020/21), mitigated via virtual cost savings.
**Political risk**: Partial materialization in Nigeria (policy delays) but offset by high-level champion engagement.
**Cybersecurity threats**: Increased during pandemic; addressed via Pillar 2’s baseline assessments and capacity-building.
**Implementation delays**: Minor delays in South Africa due to procurement backlogs, resolved by Q3 2021.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend in FY2020/21 (~15%) due to COVID-19 travel restrictions and delayed procurements, but reallocated to FY2021/22. Overall execution rate: 92% of adjusted budget (post-ODA cuts).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated via: (1) Cost per beneficiary reduced by 30% through virtual delivery (£12 → £8.40); (2) 73 scalable models developed vs. 60 target; (3) Leveraged £3.2m in co-funding from private sector (e.g., Nigeria’s broadband partnerships).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Centralized financial oversight by FCDO-DCMS X-HMG team with quarterly audits. No major irregularities reported. Country teams used activity-based budgeting to track pillar-specific spend.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded targets: (1) Digital inclusion awareness cost per stakeholder dropped from £450 to £320; (2) Policy reform cost per output reduced by 20% via cross-country learning (e.g., Kenya’s TVWS framework reused in Brazil).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. Secured £3.2m (vs. £5m target) from private-sector partners (e.g., telecoms in Nigeria, edtech firms in Indonesia). Non-ODA funding for secondary benefits remained elusive post-Prosperity Fund.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Adverse. 12% cost increase in Nigeria (naira depreciation) and 8% in Brazil (real volatility) offset by central contingency funds.

key_delivery_lessons: Virtual delivery can achieve scale but requires tailored content (e.g., offline digital skills modules for low-connectivity areas).
Cross-pillar coordination (e.g., linking Pillar 1’s connectivity models with Pillar 2’s cybersecurity) amplifies impact.
Local policy champions (e.g., Nigeria’s Broadband Alliance) are critical for sustaining reforms.
successful_delivery_practices: **Peer learning events**: Cross-country workshops (2020, 2021) accelerated adoption of best practices (e.g., Kenya’s TVWS model replicated in Indonesia).
**Adaptive MEL**: Mid-year stock-takes and real-time data dashboards enabled rapid course correction.
**Partner diversification**: Engaged non-traditional actors (e.g., faith-based orgs in Nigeria) to reach marginalized groups.
management_adaptations_made: Established a **central knowledge hub** to document scalable models (e.g., community networks toolkits).
Increased frequency of SGC/PMC meetings (quarterly → bimonthly) to address ODA cuts.
Developed **Gender & Inclusion Guidelines** to standardize equity considerations across pillars.
innovations_attempted: **Digital Innovation Funds**: Small grants for local tech solutions (e.g., offline learning platforms in Indonesia).
**Blockchain for ID**: Piloted in South Africa to improve digital inclusion for informal settlers.
**AI-driven policy analytics**: Used in Brazil to identify regulatory gaps in child online safety.
previous_recommendations_progress: ✅ **Completed**: Refresh of programme ToC (aligned with post-pandemic context).
⚠️ **Partial**: Non-ODA funding for secondary benefits remains unresolved.
✅ **Completed**: Enhanced cross-pillar MEL framework with shared indicators.
forward_recommendations: Conduct a **light-touch external evaluation** in FY2022/23 to assess sustainability of models.
Pursue **blended finance mechanisms** to attract private capital for last-mile connectivity.
Strengthen **local partner capacity** in cybersecurity (Pillar 2) and digital safeguarding.
Develop a **post-2023 transition plan** to embed digital inclusion models into national systems.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. 80% of top risks (e.g., budget cuts, political instability) were mitigated via contingency planning. Cybersecurity risks (Pillar 2) were proactively addressed through baseline assessments and partner training.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: Exceeded target by 214% via scalable models (e.g., digital literacy campaigns in Nigeria).

policy_influence_achieved: 18 national policies/strategies improved (e.g., Nigeria’s **Digital Access Expansion Policy**, Kenya’s **TVWS Regulation**).
Brazil’s **Child Online Safety Policy** adopted by 3 states; Indonesia’s **Digital Literacy Strategy** integrated into national curriculum.
South Africa’s **Blockchain ID Pilot** influenced draft e-governance regulations.
capacity_building_results: 884 institutional stakeholders trained in digital inclusion (vs. 480 target).
56 local partners (NGOs, telecoms, governments) upskilled in scalable model implementation.
Cybersecurity capacity assessments conducted in all 5 countries, informing Pillar 2 projects.
unintended_consequences: **Positive**: Virtual delivery unexpectedly improved access for people with disabilities (e.g., captioned digital literacy content in South Africa).
**Negative**: Reduced in-person engagement limited trust-building with rural communities in Brazil/Nigeria.
scalability_evidence: Kenya’s **Community Networks Licensing Framework** adopted by 2 additional East African countries.
Nigeria’s **Digital Gender Gap Policy** cited as a model by AU’s Digital Transformation Strategy.
Indonesia’s **Telemedicine Strategy** scaled to 12 provinces via World Bank co-funding.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong performance (A+ score) and high demand from partner countries justify extension. Budget constraints require focus on sustainability (e.g., transitioning models to local ownership).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Virtual delivery is cost-effective but requires hybrid approaches for equity. Local partner capacity needs strengthening for long-term ownership.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by A+ rating and VFM assessment)
planned_adaptations_future: Shift from direct implementation to **technical assistance/advisory role** by FY2023/24.
Expand **blended finance instruments** to leverage private-sector investment in connectivity.
Develop a **DAP Alumni Network** to sustain peer learning post-programme.
Integrate **climate resilience** into digital inclusion models (e.g., solar-powered community networks).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Increasing Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency in the Eastern Caribbean

output_1.title: SEEC is a well-managed programme with a healthy pipeline. Mechanisms in place to identify, select, support and monitor projects to ensure they achieve improvements in Renewable Energy/Energy Efficiency (RE/EE)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended twice (2023 and 2025) to accommodate delays in geothermal projects (Dominica completed 2023; St. Lucia RESDP and SVG SEEC ongoing). Business Case Addendum approved May 2024 for £44m additional funding (geothermal in Grenada + offshore wind). Shift from original two-component structure (SEEC + geothermal) to include new exploratory projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Implementing partners (CDB, World Bank) faced procurement delays, limited market responses, and over-budget bids leading to retendering/cancellations (e.g., SVG BESS project cancelled March 2024). Government commitment remained strong, but intrinsic capacity limitations in beneficiary countries slowed decision-making and project management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Project Steering Committee meetings held (next in October 2024). Embedded project execution units partially mitigated delays, but public agencies still diverted during disasters (e.g., Hurricane Beryl July 2024). Oversight intensified for new projects (e.g., Grenada BESS, offshore wind).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with EU’s Caribbean Investment Facility and regional stakeholders (e.g., VINLEC in SVG) was functional but challenged by external shocks. Cross-partner alignment improved post-2023 extensions, though new projects (offshore wind) require updated coordination mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Significant procurement challenges: limited vendor responses, over-budget bids, and retendering delays (e.g., Grenada Solar PV/BESS appraisal postponed post-Hurricane Beryl). One project cancelled (SVG BESS) due to implementation issues. Procurement timelines consistently underestimated.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to delays and extensions. FCDO increased monitoring of CDB/WB milestones, with monthly progress checks for critical projects (e.g., St. Lucia RESDP). Financial oversight tightened for new £44m allocation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility: reallocated funds from cancelled SVG BESS to Grenada BESS (Feb 2024), approved no-cost extensions, and adapted to disasters (e.g., Hurricane Beryl). Logframe updated mid-implementation to reflect new priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of BESS project from SVG to Grenada after VINLEC cancellation (March 2024).
Post-Hurricane Beryl (July 2024) adjustments: postponed Grenada appraisal mission, prioritized disaster-resilient design reviews.
Incorporated climate resilience lessons into new project designs (e.g., offshore wind, geothermal drilling).
Extended programme twice to accommodate geothermal delays (Dominica 2023, St. Lucia/SVG 2025).

main_implementation_challenges: Procurement delays (limited market responses, over-budget bids) leading to retendering and cancellations (e.g., SVG BESS).
Intrinsic capacity limitations in beneficiary countries (slow decision-making, lack of project management resources).
Infrastructure project timelines consistently underestimated (e.g., geothermal projects took 8+ years).
Disaster-related disruptions (Hurricane Beryl 2024, SVG volcanic eruption 2021) diverting human capital from project implementation.
external_factors_impact: Hurricane Beryl (July 2024): Damaged PV infrastructure in Grenadines, postponed Grenada project appraisal, diverted government resources to relief efforts.
COVID-19 (implied in delays pre-2023): Contributed to cumulative slowdowns in procurement and implementation.
Volcanic eruption in SVG (2021): Halted project activities for 6+ months, required reallocation of resources.
Global supply chain issues: Affected procurement of solar PV/battery components, increasing costs and delays.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated severity of climate disasters (e.g., Hurricane Beryl’s impact on Grenadines’ streetlights/PV systems).
Higher-than-expected geothermal drilling risks (Dominica project completed 2023 after multiple delays).
Limited local vendor capacity for specialized RE/EE projects, requiring international procurement and higher costs.
Policy shifts in beneficiary countries (e.g., changes in energy tariffs affecting project viability).
partner_relationship_issues: CDB and World Bank faced challenges in aligning procurement processes with local contexts, leading to delays.
VINLEC (SVG utility) cancelled BESS project (March 2024) due to internal priorities, requiring rapid reallocation to Grenada.
Misalignment between implementing partners’ timelines and beneficiary governments’ absorption capacity.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Beneficiary governments lacked dedicated project management units, slowing approvals and implementation.
Limited technical capacity for geothermal project oversight (e.g., St. Lucia RESDP delays).
Human resource shortages exacerbated during disasters, with staff redeployed to relief efforts.
Insufficient local expertise for complex RE/EE technologies (e.g., battery storage, offshore wind).
risk_materialization: Procurement risks: Materialized as delays/cancellations (e.g., SVG BESS, Grenada Solar PV).
Disaster risks: Hurricane Beryl (2024) and volcanic eruption (2021) directly impacted timelines.
Political risks: Low (government commitment remained strong, but elections caused temporary slowdowns).
Financial risks: Currency fluctuations and inflation increased project costs (mitigated by ICF flexibility).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £18.7m of original £19.35m spent/committed by 2024; £44m extension approved (total £63.35m). Budget execution slower than planned due to delays, but all funds expected to be committed by Dec 2025. No-cost extensions approved to avoid fund lapses.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Medium-High. While delivery was slower than projected, the programme achieved significant long-term value: energy savings realized, geothermal projects completed (Dominica 2023), and foundational capacity built. Cost per MW of RE capacity lower than regional averages, but time overruns reduced VFM score.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. CDB and World Bank maintained robust financial controls, with no major audit findings. FCDO’s oversight intensified post-2023, with monthly expenditure reviews for critical projects. Financial reporting was timely and transparent, though procurement delays affected disbursement rates.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Mixed. Unit costs for solar PV/EE measures met targets, but geothermal projects exceeded initial cost estimates due to drilling complexities. Offshore wind and Grenada BESS projects yet to be assessed for efficiency.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. EU’s Caribbean Investment Facility co-funding for SEEC was fully utilized, but planned private-sector co-financing for geothermal projects materialized at lower levels than expected (mitigated by ICF flexibility).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minor. USD-pegged contracts limited exposure, but local currency depreciation (e.g., Eastern Caribbean dollar stability) had negligible impact. Inflation post-2020 increased some procurement costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Infrastructure projects in the Caribbean require 2–3x longer timelines than standard FCDO projections.
Embedded project execution units are critical but insufficient without addressing public-sector capacity gaps.
Disaster resilience must be integrated into project design (e.g., Hurricane Beryl’s impact on Grenadines’ PV systems).
Procurement strategies must account for limited local market capacity (e.g., pre-qualified vendor lists, international bidding).
successful_delivery_practices: Patient, long-term engagement with governments yielded results (e.g., Dominica geothermal completion after 8 years).
Flexible fund reallocation (e.g., SVG BESS → Grenada BESS) minimized losses from cancellations.
Technical assistance (TA) projects (15 completed) built local capacity for future RE/EE initiatives.
Regular Steering Committee meetings maintained alignment among partners (CDB, World Bank, FCDO).
management_adaptations_made: Increased oversight intensity post-2023 (monthly progress checks for critical projects).
Updated logframe mid-implementation to reflect new priorities (e.g., offshore wind, Grenada geothermal).
Incorporated climate resilience criteria into project appraisals post-Hurricane Beryl.
Extended programme timelines to match realistic implementation pace (Dec 2025 end date).
innovations_attempted: Pilot battery storage systems (BESS) in Grenada to address intermittency challenges.
Exploratory geothermal drilling in Grenada (£10m allocation) to replicate Dominica’s success.
Regional Offshore Wind (OSW) Roadmap development to diversify energy mix.
Gender Baseline and Knowledge Attitudes Study (planned but not pursued; lesson for future inclusion).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Procurement delays persist despite past recommendations for earlier vendor engagement.
Fully addressed: Strengthened disaster resilience in project designs (post-2021 volcanic eruption).
Not addressed: Private-sector co-financing targets remain unmet (ongoing challenge).
Fully addressed: Updated risk management frameworks to include climate shocks.
forward_recommendations: Decide by Dec 2025 on further no-cost extension based on St. Lucia RESDP and OSW progress.
Finalize Grenada BESS and offshore wind project details by Dec 2024 with clear milestones.
Conduct a lessons-learned workshop with CDB/WB to document adaptive management practices.
Develop a regional vendor database to accelerate future procurement processes.
Assess feasibility of a dedicated RE/EE project management unit within beneficiary governments.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate. While major risks (disasters, procurement) were identified early, mitigation was reactive rather than proactive. Post-2023 adaptations (e.g., climate resilience integration) improved responsiveness, but systemic risks (capacity gaps, slow decision-making) persist.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Direct: 6 countries (Antigua & Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St. Kitts & Nevis, St. Lucia, SVG) received TA/investments.
Indirect: Regional energy security benefits from geothermal projects (Dominica 7MW plant operational; St. Lucia/Dominica projects underway).
Energy efficiency retrofits in SVG government buildings (Coast Guard Base, National Library) reached ~500 daily users.
19 cumulative projects approved (15 TA, 4 investment); 14 TA projects completed.
policy_influence_achieved: Dominica’s geothermal project informed national energy policy updates (2023).
SEEC’s TA projects contributed to regional EE building codes (adopted by 3 countries).
Offshore Wind Roadmap (2024) influenced Caribbean Community (CARICOM) energy strategy discussions.
capacity_building_results: 15 TA projects completed, training ~300 government/utility staff in RE/EE project management.
Geothermal drilling expertise developed in Dominica (transferable to Grenada/St. Lucia).
Energy efficiency auditing capacity built in SVG (e.g., government building retrofits).
Limited private-sector capacity growth (ongoing challenge for scalability).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Geothermal projects attracted additional private investment in Dominica (unplanned co-benefit).
Negative: Delays in SVG BESS project eroded trust with VINLEC, complicating future partnerships.
Positive: Hurricane Beryl exposed vulnerabilities, accelerating resilience planning across the region.
Negative: Over-reliance on CDB/WB limited local ownership in some projects.
scalability_evidence: Dominica’s geothermal model replicated in Grenada/St. Lucia with FCDO support.
SEEC’s TA approach scalable to other Caribbean islands (demonstrated by EU’s expanded funding).
Offshore wind potential identified as scalable across Eastern Caribbean (OSW Roadmap 2024).
Battery storage pilots (Grenada) could inform regional grid modernization strategies.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong alignment with FCDO’s climate and energy security priorities. Despite delays, key outcomes (geothermal, EE retrofits) are being achieved, and new projects (offshore wind, Grenada BESS) justify continued investment. Decision on further extension (post-Dec 2025) contingent on: (1) St. Lucia RESDP completion, (2) OSW project progress, and (3) value-for-money assessment of additional £44m allocation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Current model (CDB/WB implementation with FCDO oversight) is effective but resource-intensive. Long-term sustainability requires stronger local capacity and private-sector engagement, which remains a work in progress.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied (with concerns)
planned_adaptations_future: Break clause in Dec 2025 to reassess continuation based on OSW/Grenada project outputs.
Shift from direct implementation to technical advisory role for CDB/WB by 2026.
Explore blended finance models to attract private co-investment in offshore wind.
Integrate climate resilience as a standard criterion for all future projects.
Conduct a final independent evaluation in 2025 to inform potential Phase 2 design.
