programme_metadata.programme_title: Central Asia – South Asia Power Transmission Project (CASA-1000)

output_1.title: FCDO contribution closes enough of the financial gap to enable timely implementation of overall programme

output_2.title: Construction of Tajikistan converter station is completed to satisfactory standard

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme management responsibility shifted from Indo-Pacific Regional Department to the Central Asia Development Programme Team (CADPT) on 1 September 2022 to improve partner engagement, communication, and risk management. Programme was extended by 3 years (completion now December 2025).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (MDTF administrator) has delivered as expected, with FCDO funds fully disbursed. Joint Working Group meetings were actively utilized for monitoring, though Afghanistan-related activities remain paused since August 2021 due to political instability.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Transition to CADPT enabled more comprehensive partner engagement and improved risk management. Dial-in meetings and Joint Working Groups were used effectively for coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Active participation in CASA-1000 Joint Working Group meetings in 2022, though no Inter-Governmental Council meetings were held. Coordination with World Bank on master schedule updates (e.g., Nowshera sub-station progress) was effective.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: HVDC Sangtuda converter station contract secured via International Competitive Bidding, with prices significantly lower than competitors. CSP contracts followed Local Competitive Bidding procedures per Project Operating Manual.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight post-transition to CADPT, with focus on risk management and partner engagement. Field visits were recommended but not detailed in the review.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme extension by 3 years (to 2025) demonstrates flexibility in response to delays. Adaptive management included log frame reviews and risk mitigation planning for Afghanistan-related uncertainties.
adaptive_management_examples: Extension of programme timeline by 3 years to accommodate delays.
Shift in management responsibility to CADPT for improved regional focus.
Active monitoring of Nowshera sub-station (critical but not FCDO-funded) via Joint Working Groups.
Planned review of log frame to remove redundant milestones and reassign outputs/outcomes.

main_implementation_challenges: Pause of all Afghanistan-related activities since August 2021 due to Taliban takeover, creating uncertainty about resumption and impacting transmission infrastructure completion.
Cost increases in non-FCDO-funded critical components (e.g., transmission lines) posing risks to overall project outcomes.
Dependence on World Bank-led components (e.g., Nowshera sub-station in Pakistan) for full project functionality, with delays reported (completion now June 2024).
Extreme weather events (e.g., flooding at Sangtuda and Pakistan 2022 floods) testing climate resilience of infrastructure.
external_factors_impact: Political instability in Afghanistan (post-Taliban seizure) halted all CASA-1000 activities in the country, directly threatening the project’s transmission corridor.
Global supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures contributed to cost overruns in non-FCDO-funded components.
Climate-related events (flooding) disrupted construction timelines and highlighted vulnerabilities in infrastructure design.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated long-term pause in Afghanistan engagement, with no clear timeline for resumption.
Increased costs for non-FCDO-funded infrastructure (e.g., transmission lines) not accounted for in original plans.
Regional geopolitical tensions affecting cross-border coordination (e.g., Pakistan-Afghanistan relations).
partner_relationship_issues: Limited engagement with Afghan stakeholders post-2021, reducing ability to align on transmission infrastructure completion.
World Bank’s role as MDTF administrator required additional coordination to address cost overruns and delays in non-FCDO-funded components.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Local capacity in Tajikistan/Kyrgyzstan/Pakistan for CSP implementation was adequate, but NGO staff costs required validation against World Bank benchmarks.
Need for enhanced climate resilience expertise in infrastructure design post-flooding events.
risk_materialization: Major: Afghanistan political risk (halted activities since 2021).
Moderate: Cost overruns in non-FCDO-funded components (e.g., transmission lines).
Moderate: Delays in Nowshera sub-station (critical for HVDC operation).
Minor: Extreme weather impacts on construction timelines.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: All FCDO funds (£31m) fully disbursed to the World Bank MDTF as planned. No additional FCDO funds required; cost overruns for non-FCDO components to be absorbed via tariff adjustments or IFI loan restructuring.
value_for_money_assessment: Economic rate of return remained attractive (21.4% in 2017 reassessment, down from 27.5% at appraisal) despite cost increases and delays.
Stress tests confirmed positive NPV (12.5% EIRR) even under worst-case scenarios (162% cost increase, 7-year delay).
World Bank fees (2% per instalment) and procurement costs (e.g., HVDC converter station) were competitive and aligned with business case expectations.
CSP costs (NGO staff, materials) were benchmarked against World Bank databases and local market prices.
financial_management_quality: World Bank’s administration of MDTF met FCDO expectations, with transparent reporting on disbursements.
Local Competitive Bidding for CSP contracts ensured cost-effectiveness.
No major deviations from original financial plans; additional financing needs were addressed without FCDO contributions.
cost_efficiency_achieved: HVDC converter station contract prices were significantly lower than competitors via International Competitive Bidding.
CSP material/equipment costs were controlled through World Bank-approved Local Competitive Bidding.
No evidence of inefficiencies in FCDO-funded components; delays/cost overruns were external to FCDO’s scope.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: FCDO’s £31m leveraged additional funding from EBRD and other donors (milestone achieved in 2019), though no updates on new co-funding in 2022.

key_delivery_lessons: Successful resolution of land procurement issues (documented in prior reviews) highlights the value of early stakeholder engagement.
Inclusive, community-driven CSPs demonstrated effectiveness in building local ownership and delivering tangible benefits.
Climate resilience must be integrated into infrastructure design (e.g., flooding at Sangtuda).
Flexibility in programme timelines (e.g., 3-year extension) was critical to adapting to external shocks.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of International Competitive Bidding for major contracts (e.g., HVDC converter station) secured cost savings.
Active participation in Joint Working Groups enabled real-time monitoring of non-FCDO-funded critical components (e.g., Nowshera sub-station).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Operations in Uganda were phased out in July 2021 due to UK ODA reductions. Added "on-demand" technical assistance for FCDO posts in Ghana, Indonesia, and Vietnam as a pilot. Component C expanded to include policy-related grants and evidence-building activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: NIRAS/Swisscontact (Component A) delivered inclusive market structures (Output 1: Score A) and improved SME pipelines (Output 2: Score A+). TechnoServe (Component B) adapted to include FCDO-post demand-driven TA, though coordination with existing investor-portfolio projects created divergence risks. CABI (Component C) expanded to policy grants and FCDO-post responsive research (e.g., agro-industrial parks for Nepal).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Retained minimum viable management staff during budget cuts to sustain TA origination, resulting in higher-than-planned management costs (reducing over time as project portfolio grows). Governance adapted to include FCDO-post coordination for "on-demand" TA.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with FCDO posts (e.g., Ghana) improved through tailored TA workstreams, but posts were not always fully aware of all TAF projects/investor relations. Cross-component learning occurred via annual portfolio reviews (e.g., CAPR 2020).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in milestone approvals caused underspend (e.g., Q1 2022-23 projects paused pending FCDO budget confirmation). Procurement flexibility allowed rapid adaptation to COVID-19 and ODA cuts (e.g., Uganda phase-out).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher oversight intensity during budget uncertainty to minimize disruption. Management costs exceeded targets but declined as TA portfolio expanded. Equity targets (women: 30% vs 50% goal; poorer households: 33% vs 20% minimum) showed mixed progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme reprioritized geographies (exited Uganda) and added FCDO-post demand-driven TA. Adapted to COVID-19 by shifting to virtual investor engagement (11 SME-investor meetings in 2021). Budget cuts triggered cost efficiencies (e.g., reduced in-country presence).
adaptive_management_examples: Phased out Uganda operations in response to ODA cuts, reallocating resources to Nepal/Malawi.
Piloted "on-demand" TA for FCDO posts (Ghana, Indonesia, Vietnam) to align with UK government priorities.
Expanded Component C to include policy grants (e.g., IIED for smallholder-investor engagement) and responsive research (e.g., agro-industrial parks for FCDO Nepal).
Adjusted TA project origination to focus on higher-potential Inclusive Business Plans (IBPs) after learning that even non-follow-on IBPs provided value to businesses.

main_implementation_challenges: UK ODA reductions (2020-21) forced geographic reprioritization (exit from Uganda) and budget constraints.
COVID-19 restrictions delayed investor engagement (e.g., face-to-face meetings) and project momentum.
FCDO budget uncertainty (2022-24 Spending Review) paused new project starts in Q1 2022-23.
Divergence between original TAF model (investor-portfolio driven) and new FCDO-post "on-demand" TA objectives.
Slower-than-planned smallholder reach increased cost per beneficiary (£152 vs £70 target).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted supply chains, investor engagement, and field activities (e.g., Uganda phase-out).
Climate change and conflict exacerbated agri-food market disruptions, increasing need for resilient supply chains.
Global fertilizer/food price crises (2022) required potential programme adaptations to address input shortages.
Political decisions (e.g., Ministerial reprioritization) led to Uganda exit and resource reallocation.
contextual_constraints_new: FCDO posts lacked full awareness of TAF projects/investor relations, limiting exploitation of technical assistance.
Carbon finance study revealed boundary conditions (e.g., scale, credit prices) for climate-resilient smallholder models not initially anticipated.
Gender inclusion targets (50% women) proved harder to achieve (current: 30%) than poverty targets (33% vs 20% minimum).
partner_relationship_issues: Coordination gaps between TNS (Component B) and FCDO posts on TA project visibility/alignment.
Investor engagement (e.g., FMO’s Niche Cocoa in Ghana) required independent evaluations to demonstrate smallholder impact, adding complexity.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Reduced in-country presence (post-Uganda exit) strained capacity for field-level TA delivery.
Management costs exceeded targets during budget cuts, requiring retention of "minimum viable" staff.
Delays in milestone approvals (e.g., concept notes) slowed project implementation and spend.
risk_materialization: ODA reductions ("Major" risk) materialized, forcing Uganda exit and budget reallocations.
COVID-19 ("Major" risk) disrupted implementation, though virtual adaptations mitigated some impacts.
Slower smallholder reach (equity risk) increased cost per beneficiary, though poverty inclusion exceeded targets.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend in FY 2021-22 (92% of forecast: £330,990 actual vs £360,977 planned) due to delayed milestone approvals and budget cuts. Geographic reprioritization (Uganda exit) reduced in-country costs but required reallocation to Nepal/Malawi.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM maintained despite budget cuts through adaptive management (e.g., repurposing TA for FCDO posts, focusing on high-potential IBPs). Cost per beneficiary remained above target (£152 vs £70) but declining as portfolio grows. Programme serves as FCDO’s flagship for inclusive agri-investment, leveraging knowledge-sharing and investor partnerships.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls during uncertainty, though management costs exceeded targets temporarily. Transparent reallocation of funds post-Uganda exit. Independent evaluations (e.g., Niche Cocoa baseline) added rigor to impact tracking.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficiency improved over time as TA portfolio expanded, reducing management cost proportion. "On-demand" TA for FCDO posts optimized use of existing resources. However, slower smallholder reach and budget cuts limited planned cost efficiencies.

key_delivery_lessons: Inclusive Business Plans (IBPs) provide value even without follow-on TA, improving business decision-making.
FCDO-post "on-demand" TA can diverge from original TAF model; requires clear reconciliation mechanisms.
Smallholder reach lags require targeted interventions (e.g., gender inclusion strategies) to meet equity goals.
Budget uncertainty necessitates flexible milestone planning and minimum viable staffing models.
successful_delivery_practices: Cross-component coordination (e.g., CABI’s CAPR 2020) strengthened evidence-based learning.
Pilot "on-demand" TA for FCDO posts (Ghana, Indonesia, Vietnam) demonstrated responsiveness to UK government priorities.
Independent evaluations (e.g., Niche Cocoa baseline) improved investor confidence and impact tracking.
Adaptive management during COVID-19 (virtual engagement, reprioritization) maintained programme continuity.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from geographic focus (Uganda exit) to deeper engagement in Nepal/Malawi.
Expanded TA portfolio beyond original 35 IBPs to increase smallholder engagement opportunities.
Increased coordination with FCDO posts to align TA with country-specific agri-food strategies.
Adjusted oversight intensity during budget cuts to balance cost control and delivery continuity.
innovations_attempted: Carbon finance study exploring climate-resilient smallholder models (e.g., cocoa in Ghana).
Agro-industrial park research for FCDO Nepal to inform policy on smallholder-linked infrastructure.
Demand-driven TA model for FCDO posts, testing responsiveness to UK government development priorities.
previous_recommendations_progress: Expanded IBP portfolio beyond original 35 target to address smallholder engagement risks (partially implemented; pending FCDO budget confirmation).
Improved information-sharing with FCDO posts (e.g., Ghana case study) but gaps remain in TA project visibility.
Enhanced equity tracking (gender, poverty) through disaggregated data collection (e.g., 60% women in Output 1).
forward_recommendations: Launch additional IBPs to diversify smallholder engagement opportunities (pending budget confirmation).
Strengthen FCDO-post coordination to maximize use of TAF projects/investor relations.
Scale successful pilots (e.g., Ghana’s carbon finance study) to other regions/crop sectors.
Address gender inclusion gaps (30% vs 50% target) through targeted TA designs.
Prepare for potential adaptations to fertilizer/food price crises (e.g., input subsidies, climate-resilient practices).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating COVID-19 and ODA cut impacts through adaptive management (e.g., Uganda exit, virtual engagement). However, persistent "Major" risk rating reflects ongoing budget uncertainty and equity challenges. Proactive adjustments (e.g., minimum staffing, TA reprioritization) demonstrated responsiveness.

policy_influence_achieved: EPIC grant strengthened smallholder associations’ (e.g., Nsuwadzi in Malawi) negotiation power with tea estates and local government.
CABI’s evidence-building (e.g., CAPR 2020) influenced FCDO’s agri-portfolio strategies.
Ghana pilot provided FCDO with actionable insights for catalyzing agri-SME investment (25 high-potential SMEs identified).
Carbon finance study findings shared with policy makers in Ghana and other jurisdictions.
capacity_building_results: Nsuwadzi Association (Malawi) developed gender-mainstreaming handbooks, strategic plans, and beekeeping initiatives to diversify income.
142,682 smallholders reported improved market access (54% perceived CASA support as useful).
11 SMEs engaged with new investors in 2021, demonstrating improved governance/financial management post-TA.
EPIC Nepal (CSRC/NACCFL) built smallholder agency through rights awareness and leadership training.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Beekeeping initiative (Nsuwadzi) created alternative income streams beyond tea farming.
Positive: Carbon finance study uncovered new climate-resilient funding mechanisms for smallholders.
Negative: Uganda exit disrupted local agribusinesses/smallholders reliant on CASA support (mitigated by phased transition).
Negative: "On-demand" TA for FCDO posts risked diluting focus on core smallholder-investor linkages.
scalability_evidence: TAF model (investor-linked TA) replicated in Ghana and scalable to other FCDO priority countries.
EPIC’s smallholder empowerment approaches (e.g., rights training, association-building) adaptable to other crops/regions.
Carbon finance study identified scalable archetypes (e.g., cocoa) for climate-resilient smallholder models.
DevTracker and annual portfolio reviews provide templates for monitoring scalable agri-investment programmes.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong performance (consistent "A" scores) and alignment with FCDO’s commercial agriculture priorities. Adaptive management during COVID-19/ODA cuts proved resilience. Serves as flagship for British Investment Partnerships’ inclusive growth agenda. However, budget uncertainty and equity gaps require attention.

planned_adaptations_future: Expand TA portfolio (pending budget confirmation) to deepen smallholder/investor linkages.
Strengthen FCDO-post coordination to align TA with country-specific agri-food strategies.
Scale successful pilots (e.g., Ghana’s carbon finance study) to other regions.
Address gender inclusion gaps through targeted TA and monitoring.
Prepare for potential food/fertilizer price crisis adaptations (e.g., climate-resilient practices).
Phase out management cost overruns as TA portfolio matures.

output_1.title: Water and sanitation infrastructure provided

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between FCDO/CDB, though COVID-19 disrupted stakeholder consultations. British High Commissioners engaged to resolve political bottlenecks (e.g., procurement delays).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in 2020 due to COVID-19 (design, stakeholder consultations, construction). Shift to e-procurement in some countries improved efficiency. Major procurements underway/beginning in several countries as of Dec 2020.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to COVID-19 (more frequent virtual meetings, adjusted supervision). FCDO/CDB adapted to virtual working arrangements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme timeline extended to 2024. Reconstruction Window added (2018) for hurricane response. Milestones rebased for water/sanitation projects due to delays.

Programmatic approach for Dominica water sector to determine funding post-feasibility study.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tackling Serious and Organised Corruption (TSOC) in Malawi

output_1.title: Legal and regulatory framework enhanced

output_2.title: An increase in the capacity of Malawian law enforcement agencies to investigate and prosecute corruption and money laundering cases

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme introduced a "Strategic Fund" for tactical needs and an "Opportunity Fund" for civil society/media support, both of which were not fully detailed in the original business case. The Strategic Fund has been used flexibly to respond to emerging needs, such as supporting urgent investigations and enhancing technical infrastructure.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ICAR has exceeded expectations in delivering technical assistance, particularly in embedding plea bargaining, digital evidence use, and inter-agency cooperation. The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB), Financial Intelligence Authority (FIA), and Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) have shown improved capacity and ownership, with evidence of skill transfer (e.g., cases handled with minimal ICAR involvement).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme is managed through a combination of ICAR-led technical assistance and direct DFID administration of the Opportunity Fund. Governance includes regular coordination with Malawian agencies (ACB, FIA, DPP) and international partners (e.g., UK’s National Crime Agency, South Africa’s Asset Forfeiture Unit).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective inter-agency coordination has been achieved through the establishment of Financial Investigations and Sanctions Teams (FISTs), which include representatives from ACB, DPP, FIA, Malawi Revenue Authority, and police. A draft inter-agency communication protocol has been developed to address historical silos and mistrust.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement has been responsive to needs, with the Strategic Fund allowing timely support for operational requirements (e.g., forensic digital data units, training). Irish Aid’s co-funding for analytical devices was linked to demonstrated strategic need, showing alignment with programme priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has been adaptive, with ICAR providing hands-on support during early stages (e.g., plea bargaining pilot cases) and gradually reducing involvement as local capacity improved. DFID’s direct management of the Opportunity Fund ensured alignment with civil society priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The Strategic Fund’s problem-driven approach allowed rapid responses to emerging needs, such as supporting the National Risk Assessment (NRA) for FATF evaluation and funding urgent investigations. The Opportunity Fund’s design enabled innovative proposals (e.g., CSO consortium for collective action).
adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of plea bargaining and digital evidence use in Malawian courts, informed by real-time case feedback.
Establishment of Financial Investigation Units (FIUs) at FIA in response to identified gaps in financial crime investigations.
Use of Strategic Fund to support the National Audit Office in uncovering economic crimes, which fed into law enforcement cases.
Adjustment of training programs based on skills gap analyses (e.g., ACAMS certification for FIA staff).

main_implementation_challenges: Historical silos and mistrust among Malawian law enforcement agencies, requiring targeted interventions (e.g., FISTs, communication protocols).
Limited initial capacity for financial investigations and asset recovery, addressed through the establishment of dedicated units (e.g., FIA’s Financial Investigation Unit).
Need for coordination between civil (FIA) and criminal (DPP) asset forfeiture approaches to avoid duplication and maximize deterrence.
external_factors_impact: The programme leveraged external partnerships (e.g., UK’s National Crime Agency, South Africa’s Asset Forfeiture Unit) to strengthen international cooperation on transnational corruption cases.
No significant negative external shocks (e.g., political instability, COVID-19) were reported during this review period.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging need for clearer methodologies to coordinate asset forfeiture between FIA (civil proceedings) and DPP (post-conviction confiscation).
Increased demand for support to non-state actors (media, civil society) to counter legal threats (e.g., libel laws) and amplify anti-corruption messaging.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial resistance from judiciary and legal community to plea bargaining required extensive awareness-raising (e.g., national/regional consultations).
Some tension between agencies over case ownership was mitigated through FISTs and joint training.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Gaps in forensic digital investigation capacity were identified and addressed through ICAR support (e.g., ACB’s digital data unit, training for FIA staff).
Limited bandwidth for international cooperation required targeted facilitation (e.g., NCA-Malawi case collaborations).
risk_materialization: The "Major" risk rating reflects persistent challenges in sustaining inter-agency trust and embedding reforms beyond the programme’s lifetime.
Delays in finalizing the National Risk Assessment (NRA) for FATF evaluation were mitigated through TSOC’s technical assistance.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme is on track financially, with no reported underspends or overspends. The Strategic Fund’s increased utilization in 2018 reflects higher demand for operational support (e.g., investigations, infrastructure).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High value for money (VFM) is evidenced by: (1) Leveraging small investments (e.g., Strategic Fund) to achieve outsized impacts (e.g., 22 cases advanced on ICAR’s progress chart); (2) Co-funding from Irish Aid for forensic equipment, reducing FCDO costs; (3) Deterrent effects of asset recovery (e.g., plea bargaining, forfeitures) expected to yield long-term benefits.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by ICAR and DFID has been strong, with transparent use of funds and alignment with programme priorities. The Government of Malawi’s increased budgetary commitments to ACB/DPP indicate growing local ownership.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency exceeded expectations due to: (1) Shared use of forensic facilities (e.g., ACB’s digital unit supporting police cases); (2) Problem-driven Strategic Fund allocations avoiding waste; (3) Pro bono support (e.g., NYU law students researching plea bargaining).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Irish Aid provided co-funding for forensic analytical devices, contingent on demonstrated need. No other co-funding sources were mentioned.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., Strategic Fund) are critical for responding to dynamic anti-corruption needs.
Embedding reforms requires sustained engagement with judicial and legal communities (e.g., plea bargaining consultations).
Inter-agency coordination platforms (e.g., FISTs) are essential to overcome silos in corruption investigations.
successful_delivery_practices: Problem-driven iterative learning (e.g., adjusting training based on skills gap analyses).
Leveraging international partnerships (e.g., NCA, South Africa) to strengthen transnational casework.
Using pilot cases (e.g., plea bargaining) to demonstrate proof-of-concept before scaling.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from direct ICAR implementation to capacity-building (e.g., ACB handling cases with minimal ICAR input).
Increased focus on sustainability (e.g., drafting SOPs for ACB/FIA, advocating for government budget increases).
innovations_attempted: CSO consortium proposal to test collective action models for corruption reduction.
Media Institute for Southern Africa (MISA) support to counter libel threats against journalists.
Use of pro bono legal research (e.g., NYU students) to inform plea bargaining rules.
previous_recommendations_progress: Fully implemented: Embedding plea bargaining and digital evidence systems.
Partially implemented: Inter-agency communication protocols (draft completed, full adoption pending).
Ongoing: Strategic coordination of asset forfeiture between FIA and DPP.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Develop a strategic approach for FIA-DPP coordination on asset forfeiture by December 2018.
forward_recommendations.rationale: To avoid duplication and maximize deterrence by aligning civil and criminal forfeiture processes.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Strengthen UK-Malawi international cooperation on specific cases using diplomatic channels by August 2018.
forward_recommendations.rationale: To operationalize NCA support and achieve tangible results in transnational corruption cases.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Support MISA’s strategic litigation fund via the Opportunity Fund to protect media freedom.
forward_recommendations.rationale: To counter legal threats (libel) against investigative journalists exposing corruption.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Develop a communications strategy for high-profile cases to amplify deterrent effects.
forward_recommendations.rationale: To maximize public awareness of successful prosecutions and asset recoveries.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management has been proactive, with most planned risks (e.g., inter-agency mistrust, capacity gaps) addressed through adaptive measures (e.g., FISTs, Strategic Fund). However, the persistent "Major" risk rating highlights ongoing challenges in sustaining reforms post-TSOC.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Primary beneficiaries include ACB, FIA, DPP, and Malawian Police Service (e.g., 10+ agencies using ACB’s forensic unit; 7 FIA staff trained for ACAMS certification).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Civil society (via Opportunity Fund), media (MISA), and the broader Malawian public through deterrent effects of high-profile cases.

policy_influence_achieved: Draft National Risk Assessment (NRA) for FATF evaluation, led by FIA with TSOC support.
Plea bargaining rules advanced through judicial consultations and pilot cases.
Inter-agency communication protocols drafted to institutionalize cooperation.
capacity_building_results: ACB’s forensic digital unit now supports cases beyond the Bureau (e.g., police investigations).
FIA’s Financial Investigation Unit established, with staff trained in financial crime analysis.
DPP’s office strengthened in asset recovery and case prosecution (e.g., 22 cases advanced).

unintended_consequences.description: ACB’s forensic unit unexpectedly benefited other agencies (e.g., police), fostering cross-agency collaboration.
Risk of over-reliance on TSOC’s Strategic Fund for operational needs, potentially undermining long-term budgetary commitments by the Government of Malawi.

scalability_evidence: Plea bargaining and digital evidence models are replicable in other jurisdictions with similar legal systems.
FISTs and inter-agency protocols could be adapted for regional anti-corruption initiatives (e.g., ESAAMLG).
CSO consortium approach may inform collective action programs elsewhere in Africa.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong progress (A+ score) and high potential for achieving its objective of deterring high-level corruption through enhanced sanctions. Key outputs (e.g., legal frameworks, inter-agency cooperation) are on track, but require continued support to ensure sustainability and address remaining risks (e.g., asset forfeiture coordination).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium – while local capacity has improved (e.g., ACB, FIA), long-term sustainability depends on: (1) Government of Malawi’s continued budgetary support; (2) Institutionalization of inter-agency protocols; (3) Effective handover of Strategic Fund-like mechanisms.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High – the programme has exceeded expectations in delivery and adaptation, with clear evidence of impact (e.g., cases advanced, FATF preparation).
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize FIA-DPP asset forfeiture coordination strategy by December 2018.
Scale up international cooperation with UK/NCA on specific cases.
Test CSO consortium and media support models for broader application.
Transition Strategic Fund usage to focus on embedding systems (e.g., SOPs) rather than operational support.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Humanitarian Emergency Response Operations and Stabilisation (HEROS) Programme

output_1.title: DFID and HMG's Humanitarian planning, preparedness and capacity to respond to humanitarian events is strengthened

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transition from Crown Agents' long-standing agent contract to Palladium's supplier contract introduced both advantages and challenges. The new model emphasizes continuity of service while requiring adaptation to supplier-based accountability mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Palladium demonstrated resilience and responsiveness (e.g., flexibility in procurement/logistics, compliance with UK legislation, proactive safeguarding) but faced challenges in internal communication, milestone finalization, and financial forecasting. SRM scores improved to 'good performance' by June 2018, though Value for Money remained an area for improvement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Core team of Palladium staff manages a database of experts for surge support. Governance relies on monthly SMT issue logs and collaborative planning with DFID/SU, though coordination gaps (e.g., delayed milestone agreements) persisted.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UK EMT working groups and online platforms (e.g., Google Drive for SOPs) were established successfully, but cross-team communication (Palladium-DFID-SU) required urgent improvement. Peer learning sessions (e.g., HSOT-protracted crises team) were organized ad-hoc.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Pharma licenses obtained and Type 1 simulation exercises conducted, but procurement systems (e.g., personnel management modules) faced delays. Forecasting inaccuracies impacted invoicing and budget oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: DFID/SU conducted quarterly KPI assessments and SRM reviews, with a formal financial review planned for Q3 2018. Oversight intensified around risk mitigation (e.g., safeguarding, compliance) but was reactive to emerging issues like communication gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to unplanned crises (e.g., Rohingya, Caribbean, Venezuela) and adjusted milestones (e.g., preparedness offer redesign). Innovative partnerships (e.g., Humanity and Inclusion) were formed to address niche expertise needs.
adaptive_management_examples: Redesigned preparedness offer after DFID feedback to include country office engagement and maturity modeling.
Established virtual platforms for EMT SOPs and site configurations to improve coordination.
Negotiated extended deadlines for training needs assessments and personnel management systems in response to implementation challenges.

main_implementation_challenges: Poor internal communication within Palladium and between Palladium-DFID-SU, leading to unclear deliverables and delayed milestones.
Financial management weaknesses (e.g., forecasting inaccuracies, invoicing delays) affecting Value for Money.
Delayed finalization of critical systems (e.g., personnel management modules, database enhancements).
Ambitious initial indicators (e.g., preparedness milestones) required mid-year adjustments.
external_factors_impact: Unanticipated surge responses (e.g., Rohingya crisis, Caribbean hurricanes) diverted resources from planned activities.
HSOT restructuring required proactive adaptation to maintain service quality.
contextual_constraints_new: Transition from agent to supplier contract model created teething issues in accountability and service expectations.
Increased demand for niche expertise (e.g., outbreak specialist cells) not fully anticipated in original design.
partner_relationship_issues: DFID and Palladium initially misaligned on preparedness offer design, requiring iterative revisions.
SU’s evolving vetting/visa support needs led to renegotiated timelines.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Palladium’s core team struggled with workload peaks during simultaneous crises, highlighting roster management gaps.
DFID country offices had varying capacities to engage with preparedness initiatives, affecting rollout.
risk_materialization: Procurement/logistics risks (e.g., licensing delays) were mitigated but impacted timelines.
Safeguarding risks prompted proactive policy training (e.g., Code of Conduct, Child Protection) for all staff.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was on track, but financial management quality (e.g., forecasting accuracy) was flagged as a critical area for improvement. Invoicing delays and KPI scores for Value for Money fell below expectations.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Mixed: While continuity of service was maintained, the anticipated ‘step-change’ in efficiency (e.g., HERMIS implementation, Grand Bargain objectives) was not yet realized. Cost savings from innovative partnerships (e.g., Humanity and Inclusion) offset some inefficiencies.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Adequate but requiring improvement: SRM scores showed progress, but persistent issues in forecasting and milestone tracking. Quarterly reviews were introduced to monitor corrections.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Partial: Efficiency gains in surge deployments (e.g., tailored country support) were counterbalanced by overheads from delayed system implementations (e.g., personnel management modules).

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible milestone adjustments (e.g., preparedness offer redesign) are critical to balancing ambition with feasibility.
Supplier contracts require clearer communication protocols than agent models to avoid deliverable misunderstandings.
Early engagement with country offices improves buy-in for global initiatives (e.g., preparedness maturity models).
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid deployment of niche expertise (e.g., medical teams, outbreak specialists) through ad-hoc partnerships.
Virtual collaboration platforms (e.g., Google Drive for EMT documents) enhanced transparency and coordination.
Monthly SMT issue logs facilitated timely resolution of operational bottlenecks.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced quarterly KPI reviews to track financial and milestone progress.
Prioritized finalization of 12-month workplans to align DFID-SU-Palladium expectations.
Established working groups (e.g., UKEMT Training, Medical Supplies) to address specific capability gaps.
innovations_attempted: Partnership with Humanity and Inclusion to provide specialized expertise on demand.
Development of a preparedness maturity model to tailor country office support.
Pilot of online HEAT training modules to scale capacity building.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress: Communication improvements were initiated but not fully resolved; financial management remains a work in progress.
Personnel management system modules were re-phased with new deadlines (e.g., PMS completion by May 2019).
forward_recommendations: Implement a structured communication plan by November 2018 to address internal and external coordination gaps.
Accelerate rollout of HERMIS and supply-chain strategies to achieve ‘bigger, better, faster’ service goals.
Conduct a mid-term review of Grand Bargain alignment to refine VFM approaches.
Strengthen SU vetting/visa support systems by December 2018 to meet increasing demand.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Reactive but improving: Safeguarding and compliance risks were proactively addressed (e.g., mandatory training), but financial and coordination risks required more systematic mitigation. The Issues Log helped track emerging risks.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Surge support deployed to 10+ contexts (e.g., Caribbean, Lebanon, Yemen, Nepal, Ethiopia, Philippines, Rohingya crisis, Venezuela). UK EMT achieved deployment readiness through simulation exercises (e.g., Simex Portsmouth).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to DFID’s humanitarian reform agenda and SU’s CSSF objectives. Advisory recommendations on outbreak specialist cells were submitted for EDT review.
capacity_building_results: DFID staff included in HEAT training and peer learning sessions.
Palladium extended HR Compass modules to HEROS staff for policy training (e.g., Centrality of Protection).
Country-specific preparedness support (e.g., Bangladesh, Lebanon) built local response capacities.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Ad-hoc partnerships (e.g., Humanity and Inclusion) created models for future niche expertise collaborations.
Negative: Delayed system implementations (e.g., PMS) temporarily reduced operational efficiency.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Moderate: The roster-based surge model demonstrated scalability across multiple crises, but database enhancements are needed to fully realize global reach. Preparedness maturity model has potential for wider DFID adoption.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has maintained continuity of critical humanitarian/stabilisation services and shown adaptability to emerging needs. While financial management and communication require improvement, the core model aligns with DFID/SU strategic objectives and has demonstrated value in rapid response.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: The supplier contract model is viable but depends on resolving systemic issues (e.g., financial forecasting, partner coordination). Long-term sustainability hinges on achieving the ‘step-change’ in efficiency and scaling innovations like HERMIS.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfactory but with significant room for improvement, particularly in VFM and communication. SRM scores reflect progress, but expectations for Year 2 are higher.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize and implement HERMIS and database enhancements by 2019.
Strengthen SU support systems (vetting, visas, personnel management) per agreed timelines.
Conduct a lessons-learned review of Year 1 to inform Year 2 workplans and risk management.
Explore co-funding opportunities to leverage the £330m contract ceiling for expanded reach.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Increasing Access to Electricity in Sierra Leone

output_1.title: Establishment of project management and procurement systems

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The original schedule for appointing a construction firm by the end of Year 1 proved unrealistic due to lengthy procurement processes. The timeline was revised, with construction now expected to start in late 2018. A Resident Engineer was appointed by AfDB to directly manage the project and provide additional oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: EDSA’s procurement performance was poor, leading to delays. The African Development Bank (AfDB) was responsive to delays but required increased monitoring. The Ministry of Energy acknowledged EDSA’s shortcomings and pledged to mitigate further delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: A Project Implementation Unit (PIU) was established within EDSA to manage the project. AfDB appointed a Resident Engineer to provide direct oversight, and supervision missions were increased from twice a year to quarterly.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between DFID, AfDB, and EDSA was initially challenged by procurement delays. Improved oversight mechanisms (e.g., monthly progress updates, quarterly supervision missions) were introduced to address this.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement timelines were significantly delayed due to underestimation of the time required for loan/grant effectiveness, design preparation, and tender documentation. The Design and Supervision consultancy contract was awarded 6 months behind schedule (December 2017 instead of June 2017).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified beyond the original plan, with AfDB increasing supervision missions from twice a year to quarterly and appointing a Resident Engineer for direct project management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted by revising procurement schedules and work plans to reflect realistic timelines, particularly ahead of Sierra Leone’s 2018 Presidential Elections. DFID deferred funding to the next financial year to align with revised timelines.
adaptive_management_examples: Appointment of a Resident Engineer by AfDB to mitigate delays and provide direct oversight.
Revision of procurement schedules and annual work plans to account for election-related disruptions.
Deferral of DFID funding to the next financial year to accommodate delays.
Introduction of monthly progress updates from EDSA to AfDB to track procurement.

main_implementation_challenges: Lengthy procurement processes caused significant delays in appointing consultants and contractors.
Underestimation of the time required for loan/grant effectiveness, design preparation, and tender documentation.
EDSA’s limited capacity to manage complex procurement processes within original timelines.
Potential disruptions due to Sierra Leone’s 2018 Presidential Elections.
external_factors_impact: Political context: Upcoming Presidential Elections (March 2018) required adjustments to the work plan to avoid disruptions during the election period.
Post-Ebola recovery: The project was designed as part of Sierra Leone’s Ebola recovery plan, aiming to boost economic growth and livelihoods.
contextual_constraints_new: EDSA’s procurement and project management capacity was weaker than anticipated, leading to delays.
The need for additional oversight (e.g., Resident Engineer) was not fully foreseen in the original business case.
partner_relationship_issues: EDSA’s poor procurement performance required intervention from the Ministry of Energy and AfDB.
DFID deferred signing an agreement with AfDB pending progress on key milestones (EPC contract and capacity-building plan).
capacity_constraints_emerged: EDSA’s Project Implementation Unit (PIU) lacked the capacity to manage procurement processes efficiently, leading to delays in contract awards.
The need for a capacity-building needs assessment was identified mid-implementation, delaying training initiatives.
risk_materialization: Delays in procurement and construction start dates materialized due to underestimation of timelines and EDSA’s capacity constraints.
Risk of further slippage due to election-related disruptions was mitigated through revised scheduling.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The project is currently 6 months behind the original schedule due to procurement delays. However, the revised timeline anticipates compensating for some delays by aligning construction with the dry season (September/October 2018). No funds have been disbursed yet, as DFID deferred commitments pending progress on key milestones.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Early indications of value for money are positive, as demonstrated by the competitive tender for Project Design and Engineering Services, which resulted in a winning bid 15% (£204,000) lower than the highest bidder. However, a comprehensive VfM assessment will only be possible once bids for the main infrastructure work are received (expected by June 2018).
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Not yet assessable, as efficiency gains (e.g., reduced power outages, technical losses, improved revenue collection) will only materialize after infrastructure improvements are completed in Year 3.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Not yet assessable, as the project is still in the preparatory phase with no construction activity to date.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management is overseen by EDSA’s Financial Controller, with additional support from AfDB’s robust systems. Procurement payments are made directly from AfDB to suppliers, reducing fraud risks. Quarterly interim financial reports are submitted to AfDB, though no assets or disbursements have occurred yet.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The tender for Project Design and Engineering Services achieved cost savings (15% below the highest bid). However, overall cost efficiency cannot be fully assessed until the main infrastructure contracts are awarded.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: The African Development Bank (AfDB) is co-financing the project as planned. No issues with co-funding materialization have been reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Procurement timelines in complex infrastructure projects must account for realistic preparation periods, including loan effectiveness, design finalization, and tender documentation.
Local implementing partners (e.g., EDSA) may require more capacity-building support than initially anticipated, particularly in procurement and financial management.
Political contexts (e.g., elections) can significantly impact implementation and must be factored into scheduling.
successful_delivery_practices: Appointment of a Resident Engineer by AfDB to provide direct oversight and mitigate delays.
Increased supervision frequency (quarterly missions) to monitor progress and address slippages.
Use of AfDB’s financial management systems to reduce fraud risks in procurement.
management_adaptations_made: Revised procurement schedules and work plans to reflect realistic timelines.
Introduction of monthly progress updates from EDSA to AfDB.
Deferral of DFID funding to align with revised milestones.
innovations_attempted: Conducting a capacity-building needs assessment mid-implementation to inform training programs (though this caused delays in training initiation).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: Not applicable – this is the first annual review.
forward_recommendations: DFID and AfDB should agree on measurable actions to accelerate progress, including clear and realistic timeframes for course correction.
AfDB should maintain quarterly supervision missions to ensure adherence to revised schedules.
EDSA should provide monthly progress updates to AfDB against the agreed work programme.
The project work programme and procurement schedule should be updated by January 2018 to reflect realistic activity and expenditure forecasts.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective. While risks related to procurement delays and election disruptions were identified, mitigation measures (e.g., Resident Engineer, revised schedules) were implemented reactively rather than proactively. The risk of fraud was effectively mitigated through AfDB’s financial systems.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: No beneficiaries have been reached yet, as the project is in the preparatory phase. The target is to improve electricity access for 316,000 people (56% access rate in project areas by 2020, up from 20%).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Limited progress: A capacity-building plan was finalized by December 2017, but implementation has not yet started due to prioritization of procurement activities. Training for EDSA staff in procurement and financial management was provided, but broader capacity-building is pending.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: The project is designed to link Bo and Kenema to the West African Power Pool, which could facilitate regional scalability. However, evidence of scalability is not yet available.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Despite delays, the project has laid critical foundations (e.g., Parliamentary approval, PIU establishment, procurement progress) and remains feasible within the revised timeline. The expected impact (increased electricity access for 316,000 people) justifies continuation, provided that mitigation measures (e.g., increased oversight, revised schedules) are implemented.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium – The current model relies heavily on AfDB’s oversight and EDSA’s capacity, which has proven limited. Sustainability will depend on EDSA’s ability to improve procurement and management practices with continued support.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate – DFID acknowledges the delays but is satisfied with the corrective actions (e.g., Resident Engineer appointment, revised schedules) and the project’s potential impact.
planned_adaptations_future: Update the project work programme and procurement schedule by January 2018.
Increase AfDB supervision missions to quarterly.
Appoint a procurement specialist to support EDSA.
Monitor progress monthly against the revised procurement schedule.
Conduct capacity-building needs assessment to inform training for EDSA staff.

programme_metadata.programme_title: GREAT for Partnership Programme

output_1.title: High quality practitioner-to-practitioner partnerships in the Health, Extractives and Financial Accountability and Anti-Corruption sectors delivered.

output_2.title: Well-managed and coordinated partnerships.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from original CMU procurement plan to exploring alternative models: (i) HMG civil servants taking strategic decisions, (ii) strong in-country presence for coordination. Focus on feasibility testing and financial implications of new options by December 2017.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Early partnerships (BGS, NCA, OPF) showed positive engagement with developing country counterparts (e.g., Rwanda’s MINEACOM, Sierra Leone’s Ministry of Health). Legal Fellows received strong feedback for high-quality outputs and capacity-building support. However, no formal CMU was in place to manage partnerships systematically.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: No CMU established due to procurement delays. Interim management by DFID advisers and programme managers provided ad-hoc support for early partnerships. Governance relied on existing DFID structures rather than the planned centralized model.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Limited by lack of CMU. Early partnerships progressed through bilateral arrangements (e.g., OPF’s 2-year Legal Fellow placements). Separate initiatives (e.g., NSGI’s Civil Service Partnerships Programme, OECD Learning Exchange discussions) were launched to fill coordination gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Formal procurement for CMU halted in December 2016 due to misaligned Terms of Reference (included out-of-scope health partnerships). Commercial advice required restarting the process, causing significant delays. No contractor selected by review date.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to CMU delays. DFID directly oversaw early partnerships and strategic revisions, diverting resources from original oversight plans.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Funds reallocated from CMU establishment to support 15 early partnerships (BGS, NCA, OPF) and exploratory initiatives (NSGI, OECD). Programme paused to revise delivery models and sectoral strategies.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised CMU design criteria to include HMG-led decision-making and in-country coordination.
Shift from short-term assignments to longer-term strategic partnerships (e.g., OPF’s 2-year Legal Fellow placements).
Initiated separate NSGI programme to build partnership practitioner networks and MEL capacity.
Explored OECD Learning Exchange for anti-corruption knowledge-sharing.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed CMU establishment due to procurement issues (ToR misalignment, restart requirement).
Lack of formal coordination mechanisms for UK-HMG partnerships, leading to ad-hoc progress.
Underestimated complexity of brokering cross-sectoral partnerships (extractives, anti-corruption, financial accountability).
contextual_constraints_new: Realization that UK practitioners often lack contextual knowledge for effective partnerships in developing countries.
Need for stronger in-country presence to assess local political economy and demand.
partner_relationship_issues: Early partnerships (e.g., Legal Fellows) succeeded due to direct ministry engagement, but scalability challenged by lack of centralized support.
UK institutions (e.g., BGS, NCA) required additional guidance on international partnership management.
capacity_constraints_emerged: DFID advisers stretched by interim management of partnerships without CMU.
Developing country partners needed capacity-building to maximize partnership benefits (e.g., systems training post-Fellow placements).
risk_materialization: Procurement risk: ToR errors halted CMU contracting, delaying programme mobilization.
Strategic risk: Lack of CMU undermined partnership coordination and MEL functions.
Reputational risk: Slow progress threatened programme credibility as a "central element of UK aid."

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend on CMU establishment due to procurement delays. Funds reallocated to early partnerships (15 initiatives) and exploratory activities (NSGI, OECD). No detailed expenditure breakdown provided.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Not assessable due to lack of CMU and limited partnership scale. Potential VFM identified in longer-term strategic partnerships (e.g., OPF’s 2-year Fellows) vs. short-term assignments. Centralized MEL and brokering functions expected to improve VFM post-CMU.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: DFID’s interim oversight ensured compliance, but ad-hoc arrangements increased transaction costs. No formal financial management structure in place for partnerships.

key_delivery_lessons: Centralized coordination (CMU) is critical for scaling partnerships; ad-hoc management is unsustainable.
Strategic sectoral focus (extractives, anti-corruption) requires tailored brokering and MEL systems.
UK institutions need capacity-building to design effective international partnerships.
successful_delivery_practices: Longer-term placements (e.g., 2-year Legal Fellows) generated stronger institutional impact than short-term assignments.
Direct ministry engagement (Rwanda, Sierra Leone) ensured local ownership and sustainability.
Separate NSGI programme effectively built MEL capacity for less experienced UK partners.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from CMU procurement to testing alternative delivery models with HMG leadership.
Revised logframe to prioritize sustainable partnerships over individual assignments.
Developed sectoral strategies (anti-corruption, extractives) to guide future partnerships.
innovations_attempted: OECD Learning Exchange proposal for anti-corruption knowledge-sharing.
NSGI’s Civil Service Partnerships Programme to create practitioner networks.
Exploration of in-country coordination hubs for demand assessment.
forward_recommendations: Finalize CMU alternative by December 2017 with HMG-led governance and in-country presence.
Revise business case and logframe to reflect new delivery model and sectoral strategies.
Develop detailed mobilization plan by March 2018 to recover implementation delays.
Pause new early partnerships to focus resources on CMU establishment.
Seek HoD approval to continue/restructure programme following ‘C’ score (per SmartRule27).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Procurement risks were identified but not mitigated in time. Strategic risks (lack of CMU) triggered adaptive responses (e.g., model revision, sectoral strategies).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: 15 early partnerships initiated (BGS, NCA, OPF) with in-country beneficiaries (e.g., Rwanda’s MINEACOM, Sierra Leone’s Ministry of Health). Exact numbers not quantified; focus on institutional capacity-building.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Limited. Potential for future influence through sectoral strategies (anti-corruption, extractives) and OECD Learning Exchange, but no policy changes reported yet.
capacity_building_results: Legal Fellows in Rwanda/Sierra Leone produced draft ordinances and training systems adopted by ministries.
UK institutions (e.g., BGS) developed multi-year partnership proposals for strategic engagement.
NSGI programme began building MEL capacity among UK partners.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Early partnerships demonstrated demand for UK expertise, informing CMU design.
Negative: Procurement delays eroded stakeholder confidence in programme timeline.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Limited. Early partnerships showed potential for replication (e.g., OPF’s Fellow model), but lack of CMU constrained systematic scaling. Sectoral strategies aim to address this.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme scored ‘C’ (substantially below expectations) due to CMU delays, but early partnerships demonstrated potential. Continuation contingent on: (1) approving a revised delivery model by December 2017, (2) HoD approval per SmartRule27, and (3) pausing new partnerships to focus on CMU establishment.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium (improved with CMU establishment but high risk of further delays)
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Low (current ad-hoc model unsustainable; revised CMU model untested)
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Low (concerns over slow mobilization and lack of coordination)
planned_adaptations_future: Establish HMG-led CMU with in-country coordination by 2018.
Transition from individual assignments to strategic, multi-year partnerships.
Integrate NSGI’s Civil Service Partnerships Programme into GREAT for Partnership.
Develop sectoral strategies for anti-corruption, extractives, and financial accountability.
Strengthen MEL systems to capture partnership impacts systematically.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Jordan Compact Economic Opportunities Programme (JCEOP)

output_1.title: World Bank Programme for Results implemented to schedule

output_2.title: EBRD solid waste and waste-water management investments are implemented to schedule

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme evolved from original £110m/2-year plan to £216.5m/9-year implementation with two cost extensions (2017, 2019). Delivery shifted to accommodate protracted refugee crisis and macroeconomic reforms. Partnerships with WB and EBRD expanded beyond initial scope.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (WB) delivered 95% of DLIs for Output 1, exceeding expectations despite external demand challenges (e.g., work permits). EBRD faced delays in Output 2 (wastewater pipeline at 75% completion; solid waste workshop completed late). Government of Jordan (GoJ) demonstrated commitment through policy reforms (e.g., flexible work permits, vocational licensing laws) but struggled with demand-side issues (e.g., employer preferences for informal hiring).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme Management Unit (PMU) and Reform Secretariat (RS) played central roles in coordination. Monthly oversight meetings introduced between JCEOP SRO/PRO, WAJ, and EBRD to address infrastructure delays. Adaptive management required for YTJ project restructuring and DLI adjustments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between FCDO, WB, EBRD, and GoJ ministries (MoPIC, MoIN, MoF) on macroeconomic and reform agendas. Challenges in wastewater pipeline coordination due to land permit issues and contractor disputes, requiring ministerial escalation. Cross-donor alignment under Jordan Compact framework facilitated systemic reforms (e.g., work permits, business licensing).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement savings in Output 2 (solid waste) were reinvested into expanded activities, but budget clarity remained an issue. EBRD faced contractor claims and land permit delays for Ain Ghazal pipeline, requiring revised timelines and budget submissions. WB procurement for P4R was largely on track, with all funds disbursed by 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required for infrastructure components (e.g., monthly progress meetings for wastewater pipeline). Light-touch oversight for Output 1 (P4R) due to WB’s strong performance, shifting to ex-post evaluation. FCDO increased scrutiny of YTJ’s wage subsidy component due to VFM concerns.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to external shocks (e.g., COVID-19, refugee dynamics) through flexible work permits and extended fee waivers. Output 2’s underspend was reallocated to address emerging needs (e.g., Ghabawi workshop equipment). YTJ project restructured to focus on market access and tech sector growth, adjusting DLIs accordingly.
adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of flexible work permits and fee waivers (extended to June 2024) to boost Syrian refugee employment, despite initial shortfalls in targets.
Restructuring of YTJ project to prioritize tech sector jobs and home-based business registration (3,980 registered; 3M e-wallets opened).
Reallocation of EBRD savings to expand solid waste management activities, though Ain Ghazal pipeline delays persisted.
Adjustment of DLIs for P4R to reflect realistic demand-side constraints (e.g., childcare facility e-licensing).
Escalation of land permit issues to Jordanian ministers (MoWI, MoPW) to unblock wastewater pipeline progress.

main_implementation_challenges: Persistent delays in Ain Ghazal wastewater pipeline (75% complete as of Oct 2024) due to contractor disputes, land permits, and budget uncertainties.
Demand-side constraints for work permits (e.g., employer preference for informal hiring, refugee misinformation about cash assistance loss).
Capacity gaps in GoJ ministries (e.g., MoSD’s childcare facility e-licensing; WAJ’s contractor management).
Procurement and budget clarity issues in EBRD-led infrastructure projects, leading to underspends and timeline revisions.
Policy sustainability risks post-JCEOP, particularly for refugee-focused interventions (e.g., work permit fee waivers ended June 2024).
external_factors_impact: Protracted Syrian refugee crisis created both the programme’s rationale and ongoing demand-side challenges (e.g., refugee employment barriers).
COVID-19 disrupted economic activities and service delivery, though flexible permits mitigated some impacts.
Regional economic instability (e.g., inflation, currency fluctuations) affected private sector engagement and investment climate.
ODA budget constraints (post-Compact) limited UK’s ability to extend or scale interventions, shifting focus to targeted programmes.
Global evidence on wage subsidies (YTJ) raised VFM concerns, prompting closer monitoring of job retention post-subsidy.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated resistance from employers to cover work permit fees (475 JOD/year) post-waiver, threatening refugee employment targets.
Land permit bottlenecks for wastewater pipeline, requiring high-level ministerial intervention.
GoJ’s budgetary pressures reduced appetite for refugee-inclusive loans, limiting future P4R models.
Misinformation among refugees about work permit consequences (e.g., perceived loss of cash assistance) hindered uptake.
Contractor claims and disputes in EBRD projects (e.g., Ain Ghazal) created budget overruns and delays.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between EBRD and WAJ over contractor claim settlements and project timelines, requiring FCDO mediation.
GoJ ministries (e.g., MoSD) struggled to meet DLI targets (e.g., childcare e-licensing) due to administrative capacity limits.
WB and FCDO aligned on P4R reforms, but demand-side DLIs (e.g., home-based businesses) depended on factors beyond partner control.
Private sector partners in AMRTC cost-sharing showed variable commitment, affecting training centre sustainability.
YTJ’s PMU faced challenges in monitoring wage subsidy outcomes, requiring WB to strengthen M&E systems.
capacity_constraints_emerged: WAJ lacked technical capacity to manage contractor disputes and land permits for wastewater pipeline.
MoSD’s limited digital infrastructure delayed childcare facility e-licensing, missing DLI targets.
GAM’s procurement savings created opportunities but also required additional oversight to ensure VFM in reinvestments.
YTJ’s PMU needed strengthened M&E to track post-subsidy job retention, highlighting gaps in labour market data.
FCDO’s reduced staffing in later phases limited hands-on programme management, relying more on partners.
risk_materialization: Demand risks for work permits and home-based businesses materialized as predicted, though mitigated by flexible policies.
Infrastructure delays (Ain Ghazal pipeline) were anticipated but worsened by contractor performance and land issues.
Currency/exchange rate risks did not significantly impact budget, but global inflation affected private sector participation.
Political risks (e.g., GoJ’s reluctance to take on new refugee-inclusive loans) emerged as a constraint for future programming.
Sustainability risks for AMRTC and YTJ interventions became evident as programme closure approached.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: All funds (£216.5m) disbursed by 2024, but budget execution varied by component: Output 1 (P4R) fully spent with 95% DLI achievement; Output 2 (EBRD) faced underspends (solid waste savings reinvested) and cost overruns (wastewater pipeline). Infrastructure delays led to revised timelines and budget submissions (due Dec 2024).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Output 1 (P4R) demonstrated strong VFM with 95% DLI achievement and systemic reforms (e.g., work permits, business licensing). Output 2’s VFM was mixed: solid waste management met expectations with cost savings, but wastewater pipeline delays reduced efficiency. YTJ’s wage subsidies raised VFM concerns; post-subsidy job retention studies are pending. Overall VFM assessment deferred to forthcoming WB completion report (2025).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: WB’s financial management for P4R was robust, with transparent DLI tracking and full disbursement. EBRD faced challenges in contractor cost control (Ain Ghazal claims) and budget revisions, requiring FCDO oversight. GoJ ministries (e.g., GAM) managed savings effectively but needed support for procurement compliance. FCDO’s financial monitoring intensified for high-risk components (e.g., YTJ subsidies).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Output 1 exceeded cost efficiency targets (95% DLIs met with full disbursement). Output 2’s solid waste component achieved savings (e.g., Ghabawi workshop completed under budget), but wastewater pipeline inefficiencies offset gains. YTJ’s cost per job created (~£X) will be assessed post-closure; early indicators suggest subsidies may not be cost-efficient long-term. AMRTC’s cost-sharing model improved sustainability but required private sector buy-in.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding from GoJ and partners (e.g., EBRD loans) materialized as planned, though GoJ’s budgetary pressures limited additional contributions. GCFF and other donors aligned funding for refugee-focused components, but no new co-funding was secured in 2023/24. Private sector co-funding for AMRTC was partial, requiring programme adjustments.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: No significant adverse impacts reported; JOD stability mitigated exchange rate risks. Global inflation affected procurement costs (e.g., construction materials for wastewater pipeline) but was managed within contingencies.

key_delivery_lessons: P4R model proved effective for incentivizing GoJ reforms but required realistic demand-side DLIs (e.g., work permits dependent on employer behaviour).
Infrastructure projects in complex contexts (e.g., wastewater pipeline) need built-in contingencies for land permits and contractor risks.
Flexible policy instruments (e.g., work permit fee waivers) can boost short-term uptake but require exit strategies to avoid cliff-edge effects.
Private sector partnerships (e.g., AMRTC cost-sharing) need clear value propositions to ensure sustained engagement.
Adaptive management is critical for refugee-focused programmes, where external factors (e.g., misinformation, cash assistance policies) heavily influence outcomes.
successful_delivery_practices: Monthly oversight meetings between FCDO, EBRD, and WAJ improved accountability for infrastructure delays.
Restructuring YTJ to focus on tech sector and home-based businesses aligned with Jordan’s economic priorities and refugee skills.
Reallocating EBRD savings to expand solid waste activities demonstrated agile budget management.
GoJ’s introduction of flexible work permits and vocational licensing laws created systemic enablers for refugee employment.
Cross-donor coordination under Jordan Compact amplified impact (e.g., aligned work permit policies with EU and WB programmes).
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from annual to monthly progress reviews for high-risk components (e.g., wastewater pipeline).
Adjusted DLIs mid-implementation to reflect realistic demand (e.g., childcare e-licensing targets).
Strengthened M&E for YTJ’s wage subsidies to track post-subsidy job retention, addressing VFM concerns.
Escalated land permit issues to ministerial level (MoWI, MoPW) to unblock infrastructure progress.
Commissioned a synthesis study (due May 2025) to assess JCEOP’s contribution to Jordan Compact and ToC validity.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective: anticipated risks (e.g., work permit demand, infrastructure delays) were identified early but required adaptive responses. Unanticipated risks (e.g., contractor disputes, land permits) highlighted gaps in mitigation strategies. The programme’s ability to escalate issues (e.g., to ministers) and reallocate budgets demonstrated resilience, but systemic risks (e.g., GoJ’s budget pressures) limited long-term solutions. Lessons: future programmes should include contingency buffers for land/permit risks and deeper demand-side analysis.

policy_influence_achieved: GoJ adopted flexible work permits and vocational licensing laws as national policy, influenced by JCEOP.
P4R model informed Jordan’s approach to results-based financing, though GoJ reluctant to repeat due to budget pressures.

capacity_building_results: Strengthened GoJ’s Reform Secretariat capacity to manage P4R DLIs and monitor reforms.

positive: Work permit fee waivers (2017–2024) unintentionally created a "rush" effect in 2023, with refugees applying before deadline, followed by sharp drop in 2024.
Home-based business registration formalized informal economic activities, improving tax base potential.
E-wallet adoption improved financial inclusion for refugees, enabling access to digital payments and services.
YTJ’s tech training attracted higher-skilled refugees, creating a talent pool for Jordan’s digital sector.
negative: Employer dependence on fee waivers reduced willingness to pay post-2024, threatening refugee employment sustainability.
Wastewater pipeline delays exacerbated water scarcity in Ain Ghazal, increasing community tensions.
Focus on Syrian refugees in some components (e.g., work permits) led to perceptions of favouritism among Jordanian job seekers.
Wage subsidies in YTJ risked creating short-term jobs without long-term market integration.

scalability_evidence: P4R model is scalable but requires demand-side adjustments; GoJ’s reluctance to repeat suggests limited political appetite.
YTJ’s tech sector approach is scalable, with potential for regional replication (e.g., Lebanon, Iraq).
Solid waste management innovations (e.g., Ghabawi workshop) can be scaled to other Jordanian municipalities.
E-wallet/bank account model is highly scalable; 3M accounts demonstrate feasibility for national rollout.
Wastewater pipeline delays highlight need for improved land acquisition frameworks before scaling infrastructure projects.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: JCEOP will close as planned in June 2025, as the programme has achieved most objectives and FCDO Jordan is shifting to more targeted interventions under constrained ODA budgets. The strategic importance of the Jordan Compact remains, but future UK support will focus on narrower, high-impact areas (e.g., tech sector, water security) rather than broad economic opportunity programmes. Infrastructure components (e.g., Ain Ghazal pipeline) will be monitored post-closure via GCFF.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partial: Some components (e.g., P4R reforms, AMRTC cost-sharing) have strong sustainability prospects due to GoJ adoption, while others (e.g., wage subsidies, wastewater pipeline) face risks without continued donor support. The P4R model’s sustainability is limited by GoJ’s budget constraints and reluctance to take on new loans.

Integrate successful YTJ tech training modules into national TVET systems via MoIN partnerships.
Document and disseminate lessons from JCEOP’s P4R and infrastructure components to inform future FCDO programmes in Jordan and regionally (e.g., Lebanon, Turkey).
Advocate for GoJ to sustain refugee-inclusive policies (e.g., flexible permits) through diplomatic engagement and donor coordination.
