programme_metadata.programme_title: Building Resilience and an Effective Emergency Refugee Response (BRAER) Programme

output_1.title: Deliver more efficient emergency, life saving response to humanitarian crises in Uganda

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme demonstrated flexibility beyond original business case by: (1) Rapidly responding to Karamoja drought and Ebola outbreak through UNICEF/WFP partnerships; (2) Reintroducing Karamoja as implementation area for food/nutrition/child protection; (3) Using Internal Risk Facility (£45m) for emergency responses not originally planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (WFP, UNICEF, WHO) performed well despite budget cuts, with UNICEF leveraging BRAER funds to reach 39,821 SAM admissions (vs 8,000 target) through co-funding. WFP effectively deployed logistics (5 trucks, 3,369m³ medical supplies) for Ebola response. Coordination with Government of Uganda remained strong.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance adapted to crises through: (1) Quarterly risk reviews with partners; (2) UK's co-chair role in Risk Assessment Group (RAG) to address accountability issues (e.g., refugee registration fraud); (3) ULEARN consortium for learning/accountability.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination demonstrated by: (1) Aligning with Government of Uganda priorities for Ebola/Karamoja responses; (2) Leveraging UK's diplomatic role (e.g., RAG co-chair) to address systemic issues; (3) Cross-partner collaboration (WFP/UNICEF/WHO) for integrated responses.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement performed well under pressure: (1) Timely activation of Internal Risk Facility funds for emergencies; (2) Digital cash transfer infrastructure scaled successfully; (3) Logistics support (e.g., oxygen cylinders, medical supplies) deployed within weeks of Ebola outbreak.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensified due to risks: (1) Quarterly engagement meetings with partners to review risks/finances; (2) Close monitoring of fraud cases (3 new cases reported by WFP); (3) OPM/UNHCR/WFP collaboration on refugee registration irregularities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility critically utilized for: (1) Reallocating funds to Karamoja drought response; (2) Activating Ebola outbreak funding within 30 days; (3) Adjusting food assistance prioritization (vulnerability-based vs status-based).
adaptive_management_examples: Scaled digital cash transfers during COVID-19, later adapted for Ebola/Karamoja responses.
Reintroduced Karamoja as implementation area mid-programme due to drought.
Shifted from status-based to vulnerability-based food assistance prioritization (Phase 3 rollout July 2023).
Used ULEARN consortium to document lessons on food assistance prioritization for global adaptation.

main_implementation_challenges: Shrinking donor resources for refugee response due to UK ODA budget cuts.
Irregular refugee registration fraud cases (ongoing investigation).
Inflation compounding vulnerability of refugees/host communities.
Capacity constraints in Ugandan systems for CRRF reforms and World Bank funding absorption.
external_factors_impact: Ebola outbreak (Oct 2022) required rapid reallocation of £X million and deployment of epidemiologists/surveillance teams.
Karamoja drought (2022–23) necessitated reintroduction of food/nutrition assistance in non-refugee areas.
South Sudan/DRC instability caused 17,400+ new refugee arrivals in 2023, straining resources.
UK ODA budget reductions limited response scale despite increasing needs.
contextual_constraints_new: Need to respond to non-refugee crises (e.g., Karamoja drought) stretched programme scope.
Currency inflation reduced purchasing power of cash transfers by ~15%.
Delays in World Bank protracted crisis funding due to Ugandan institutional capacity gaps.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions with WFP over vulnerability-based prioritization rollout delays (Phase 3 not implemented until July 2023).
Accountability challenges in refugee response coordination (e.g., RAG meetings irregularity).
Fraud cases reported by WFP’s Office of Inspections required joint investigations.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Ugandan government capacity gaps in CRRF implementation and World Bank funding absorption.
ULEARN consortium required additional VfM training/capacity building (identified in 2023).
Limited Ugandan lab/epidemiological capacity for Ebola response (addressed via UK-funded WHO deployments).
risk_materialization: Financial/fiduciary risk: Irregular refugee registration fraud cases materialized (under investigation by OPM/UNHCR/WFP).
Operational risk: Ebola outbreak temporarily increased risk rating; managed via rapid funding activation.
Reputational risk: Delays in vulnerability-based food prioritization (Phase 3) risked perceptions of inequity.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget executed as planned despite reductions: (1) Full allocation of Internal Risk Facility (£45m) for emergencies; (2) Cost savings achieved through digital cash transfers; (3) Under-spend in some areas (e.g., CRRF reforms) due to Ugandan capacity constraints.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM rated as "good" with innovations like digital cash transfers reducing costs by ~20% vs in-kind food aid. Mobile money introduction (2023) expected to further reduce CBT costs. VfM gaps identified in ULEARN consortium (addressed via planned training).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High quality: (1) Quarterly financial reviews with partners; (2) Transparent reporting on Ebola/Karamoja reallocations; (3) No major audit findings despite complex multi-partner structure.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency demonstrated by: (1) Digital cash transfers (lower overheads than in-kind aid); (2) Leveraging £8,000 FCDO SAM treatment funds to enable 39,821 admissions via co-funding; (3) Shared logistics (e.g., WFP trucks for Ebola response).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding partially materialized: UNICEF leveraged BRAER funds to secure additional resources for 39,821 SAM admissions (vs 8,000 target). World Bank protracted crisis funding delayed due to Ugandan capacity issues.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Currency inflation reduced real value of cash transfers by ~15%, partially offset by digital delivery efficiencies.

key_delivery_lessons: Digital cash transfers are more cost-effective and resilient than in-kind aid (scaled during COVID-19, adapted for Ebola).
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., Internal Risk Facility) enable rapid emergency response but require robust oversight.
Blending humanitarian/development objectives (e.g., CRRF reforms) is viable but requires long-term partner capacity building.
successful_delivery_practices: Quarterly risk reviews with partners improved transparency and early issue detection.
ULEARN consortium effectively documented lessons (e.g., food prioritization model).
UK’s diplomatic leverage (e.g., RAG co-chair) addressed systemic accountability issues.
management_adaptations_made: Added Karamoja as implementation area mid-programme in response to drought.
Accelerated vulnerability-based food prioritization (Phase 3) due to equity concerns.
Strengthened VfM monitoring after gaps identified in ULEARN consortium.
innovations_attempted: Digital cash transfers linked to financial literacy training (scaled to 704,321+ beneficiaries).
Mobile money introduction (2023) for refugee CBTs to reduce costs.
Ebola response coordination model (WHO epidemiologists + WFP logistics) adopted as best practice.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2022 recommendation to document food prioritization lessons: Completed via ULEARN (dissemination planned Dec 2023).
2021 VfM strategy gap: Partially addressed via quarterly VfM reviews (full strategy still pending).
2020 CRRF reform delays: Ongoing; Ugandan capacity constraints persist.
forward_recommendations: Design post-BRAER humanitarian programme by July 2024 (Humanitarian Adviser).
Disseminate food prioritization model globally via ULEARN (Dec 2023).
Strengthen Ugandan pandemic preparedness via Pandemic Fund application support (BHC).
Advocate for FSP-led financial literacy training for CBT beneficiaries (Dec 2023).
Plan for ULEARN’s future post-BRAER (Jan 2024).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective: (1) Major risks (Ebola, fraud) managed via rapid funding/oversight; (2) Quarterly reviews enabled early action on emerging risks (e.g., Karamoja drought); (3) UK’s RAG co-chair role addressed accountability gaps. Risk rating remained "Major" due to context, not management failures.

policy_influence_achieved: Influenced Government of Uganda’s Ebola response priorities.
Advocated for vulnerability-based food assistance prioritization (adopted in 2 settlements, scaling to all by July 2023).
Strengthened CRRF implementation via World Bank TA (though delays persist).
capacity_building_results: Trained 795,336+ beneficiaries in financial literacy via digital CBTs.
Supported deployment of 11 epidemiologists/5 surveillance teams for Ebola (WHO).
ULEARN consortium built M&E capacity among 20+ Ugandan NGOs.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Digital CBTs stimulated local economies in refugee-hosting districts (evidence from WFP market analyses).
Negative: Vulnerability-based food prioritization created tensions among non-prioritized refugees (mitigated via communication campaigns).
scalability_evidence: Cash transfer model adopted by other donors in Uganda (e.g., EU, US).
Food prioritization lessons shared with Kenya/Ethiopia via ULEARN (2023).
Ebola response coordination model cited in WHO regional guidelines.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme remains critical for refugee response but requires adaptation due to: (1) UK ODA budget reductions; (2) Need to transition from humanitarian to developmental focus (e.g., CRRF reforms); (3) Lessons on digital CBTs/food prioritization warrant scaling.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable: Digital CBTs and vulnerability-based prioritization are scalable, but Ugandan institutional capacity for CRRF/World Bank funding remains a constraint.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by consistent "A" scores and flexibility in crisis response).
planned_adaptations_future: Design post-BRAER programme with blended humanitarian-development focus (2024).
Scale mobile money for CBTs to reduce costs (WFP-led, 2023–24).
Transition ULEARN into standalone learning platform (Jan 2024).
Advocate for Pandemic Fund support to address health system gaps (BHC-led).

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Strong supply of researchers (387 proposals in 2020 call); **new climate/health economics experts** engaged

programme_metadata.programme_title: International Growth Centre Phase 3
programme_metadata.review_period: April 2019 – March 2020 (+ some COVID-19 work in April 2020 captured for information only)

output_1.title: IGC influences policy discussion in resident countries, non-resident countries and with regional and global stakeholders

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme demonstrated flexibility in adapting to COVID-19 by pivoting research focus and developing timely communications/products outside original logframe targets. This highlighted the value of built-in adaptability mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: LSE and University of Oxford (delivery partners) performed strongly in Phase 3 inception, meeting/exceeding early targets. Their ability to rapidly respond to COVID-19 (e.g., commissioning 387 research proposals from 42 countries) demonstrated effective partnership.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Existing governance structures (IGC Board, Hub-country team coordination) functioned effectively during transition between phases. Quarterly FCDO/IGC catch-ups were established for monitoring recommendations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between London Hub and 10 country offices worked well, enabling identification of cross-country growth issues. The Responsive Policy Function (RPF) teams achieved strategic objectives through consultative processes with country teams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Phase 3 procurement (competitive bidding) was completed successfully, with the winning bid demonstrating strong VFM understanding. Over £1.8m in savings were identified in Year 1 via a new VFM Register.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive during Phase 3 inception due to transition risks. FCDO conducted an Operations Review and introduced SPEAR (project/knowledge management system) to improve financial and project oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme utilized flexibility to: 1) Respond to COVID-19 with unplanned research/communications; 2) Adapt logframe indicators collaboratively with FCDO; 3) Reallocate resources to high-priority areas like climate research (planned for future).
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid commissioning of COVID-19-related research (387 proposals received within months).
Development of a Learning Framework to institutionalize adaptive management.
Introduction of an intermediate outcome tier (Level 4 policy changes) in the logframe to better capture transformational impact.
Planned integration of climate/environmental sustainability into ToC and logframe post-review.

main_implementation_challenges: Transition between Phase 2 and Phase 3 created temporary alignment challenges for logframe indicators.
COVID-19 disrupted in-person engagements (e.g., conferences, field research), requiring digital alternatives.
Need to strengthen inclusion of marginalized groups (e.g., people with disabilities) in research and policy advice.
Limited baseline data for Phase 3 outcome indicators due to early stage of implementation.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Forced rapid adaptation (e.g., virtual policy engagements, remote research commissioning). Generated unplanned outputs not captured in scoring but demonstrated programme resilience.
FCDO merger: Potential strategic shifts requiring IGC to develop a new organizational strategy by March 2021.
Global economic uncertainty: Increased demand for IGC’s policy advice on inclusive growth but also raised risks for partner countries’ policy implementation.
contextual_constraints_new: Restrictions on in-person academic conferences hindered dissemination of research (Indicator 2.1).
Emerging need to address low-carbon growth in research portfolios, previously not a core focus.
Safeguarding risks in expanded delivery chains (e.g., new partners for COVID-19 response) required enhanced due diligence.
partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported; however, the review recommended updating the delivery chain map to assess fraud/safeguarding risks by December 2020.
Coordination between LSE/Oxford and country teams required ongoing attention to align strategic objectives (e.g., RPF teams).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in some country offices to fully implement new Phase 3 strategic objectives in Year 1.
Need for additional expertise in climate economics to address new FCDO priorities (identified for future recruitment).
risk_materialization: COVID-19 (escalated to major risk; mitigation measures implemented).
Delay in finalizing organizational learning indicators (Output 4) due to logframe refinements.
Slower-than-planned progress on disability inclusion strategy (target: December 2020).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Programme met all financial targets for Year 1, with £1.8m in savings identified via efficiency measures (e.g., competitive commissioning, process automation).

value_for_money_assessment.evidence: £1.8m savings captured in VFM Register; competitive fee rates maintained.
SPEAR system automated payment/claim processes, reducing administrative costs. Operations Review streamlined project approvals.
Phase 2 evaluations showed strong past performance; Phase 3 logframe refinements (e.g., intermediate outcome tier) expected to improve impact measurement.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. SPEAR system provided robust financial tracking, and no significant issues were reported. The VFM strategy was actively developed, with savings reinvested into programme activities.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Costs were 5–10% below planned levels due to efficiency gains (e.g., digital tools reducing travel expenses). No specific efficiency ratio provided.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible programmes can effectively respond to shocks (e.g., COVID-19) when logframes, budgets, and workplans allow for adaptation in collaboration with FCDO.
Early-phase programmes benefit from intermediate outcome tiers to demonstrate progress toward transformational change.
Digital tools (e.g., SPEAR) enhance efficiency but require upfront investment in training and system integration.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid research commissioning (387 proposals in response to COVID-19).
Country-office-led strategy setting (e.g., RPF teams achieving 2+ strategic objectives).
Use of VFM Register to transparently track and reinvest savings.
Quarterly FCDO/IGC catch-ups to monitor recommendations.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced intermediate outcome tier (Level 4 policy changes) in logframe.
Developed Learning Framework to institutionalize organizational learning (Output 4).
Escalated COVID-19 as a major risk with quarterly mitigation monitoring.
Planned updates to delivery chain map for safeguarding/fraud assessment (Dec 2020).
innovations_attempted: SPEAR system for integrated project/financial management.
Digital dissemination strategies to replace in-person conferences (e.g., virtual policy briefings).
Cross-country research synthesis to identify regional growth patterns.
previous_recommendations_progress: Phase 2 evaluation recommendations were largely addressed (e.g., logframe refinements, stronger outcome measurement).
Organizational learning (Output 4) remained a work in progress, with a Learning Framework under development.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Develop new organizational strategy to address FCDO merger impacts (March 2021).
Finalize methodology for academic research dissemination (Indicator 2.1) and disability inclusion strategy (Dec 2020).
Strengthen climate/resilient growth focus in research portfolio (March 2021).
Establish independent monitoring function (Dec 2020).

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective for known risks (e.g., COVID-19 response). Emerging risks (e.g., climate integration, disability inclusion) required proactive management. Risk matrix updates were responsive but dependent on FCDO quarterly oversight.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Policy engagements reached senior/influential policymakers in 10 resident countries + non-resident countries (175 instances of research leading to policy change recorded).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Research outputs (e.g., 201 P2-funded projects) continued to influence policy discussions in Phase 3.

policy_influence_achieved: 175 cases of IGC research contributing to policy changes (Level 3/4 engagements).
89% of Level 3 engagements ranked as High/Medium impact.
Policy briefs and synthesis products used by governments in resident countries (e.g., 24 Level 3/4 instances in P3 vs. 16 target).
capacity_building_results: Country teams achieved 2+ strategic objectives annually, demonstrating improved policy engagement skills.
SPEAR system enhanced staff capacity for project/financial management.

unintended_consequences.description: COVID-19 response accelerated digital transformation (e.g., virtual policy engagements), which may improve long-term accessibility.
Reduced in-person interactions may limit depth of policy maker relationships in some contexts.

scalability_evidence: IGC model (Hub + country offices) successfully scaled from Phase 2 to Phase 3 with expanded geographic focus.
Research commissioning process (387 proposals from 42 countries) demonstrated ability to attract global expertise.
Policy influencing approaches (e.g., RPF teams) were replicable across new countries.

continuation_rationale: Strong Phase 3 inception performance (Overall Score: A) with all output targets met/exceeded.
Proven ability to adapt to shocks (COVID-19) and deliver unplanned high-value outputs.
High potential for sustained policy influence (175+ policy change instances in Year 1).
Alignment with FCDO priorities (e.g., inclusive growth, climate resilience).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. The Hub-country office model is well-established, with SPEAR system improving operational efficiency. Risk of partner fatigue mitigated by competitive procurement and performance incentives.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by Overall Score A and positive narrative in review).
planned_adaptations_future: Integrate climate/resilient growth into research portfolio (by March 2021).
Finalize disability inclusion strategy and organizational learning framework.
Develop digital dissemination strategies for academic research.
Expand use of data analytics in SPEAR to track outcome-level progress.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Contract-led consortium with embedded FCDO oversight)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £100m over 10 years (£70m core consortium contract + £30m flexible components)
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Annual budget allocations with performance-based release (PbR) mechanisms; consortium-led delivery with FCDO approval gates
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: High (designed with 50% climate finance target and adaptive TA components)

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Hybrid: Light-touch FCDO HQ oversight + intensive in-country advisory teams (regional advisers model)
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly performance reviews with annual deep dives; PbR-linked approvals
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Joint FCDO-McKinsey Consortium (MC) decision-making via Support Approval Committees (SACs); FCDO retained veto on high-value deals (>£5m)

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single consortium lead (McKinsey Development Partners) with 4 sub-contracted partners (BDO, Reformatics, Steward Redqueen, Technoserve)
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Private sector consultants (70% budget) + technical NGOs (30% for TA work)

partner_roles_planned.Technoserve: SME supplier linkages & local market development

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Restricted competition (pre-qualified consortium bid)

consortium_baseline.consortium_structure_planned: Hierarchical: McKinsey as prime contractor with fixed sub-contracts to 4 partners; 7-year term
consortium_baseline.consortium_governance_planned: Formal SACs for deal approvals; quarterly consortium governance meetings; FCDO-chaired steering committee

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Mixed (Contract-led consortium with reduced TA components)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £70m+ confirmed (original £100m reduced by ~30% due to FCDO budget cuts; annual delays in confirmations)
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Performance-based releases maintained but with tighter FCDO scrutiny; shift to prioritize Transaction Facilitation (TF) over Technical Assistance (TA) due to budget constraints
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Medium (climate finance target increased to 54% but TA budget reduced; PbR mechanisms retained)

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Hybrid retained but with reduced in-country advisory capacity (remote oversight increased post-COVID)
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Monthly check-ins added for forecast accuracy; quarterly reviews maintained but with deeper FCDO involvement in SACs
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: FCDO veto expanded to deals >£3m (from >£5m); MC’s autonomy reduced for high-risk markets (e.g., Ethiopia)

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Consortium structure unchanged but partner roles adjusted (e.g., Technoserve’s supplier linkage work reduced)
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Same partners but with shifted budget allocations (e.g., 80% to TF, 20% to TA in 2022/23 vs. original 70/30 split)

partner_roles_actual.McKinsey: Expanded to cover GESI screening (originally Steward Redqueen’s role)
partner_roles_actual.BDO: Role unchanged but reduced deal flow due to budget cuts
partner_roles_actual.Reformatics: Policy work deprioritized; focus shifted to investor climate analysis
partner_roles_actual.Steward Redqueen: Impact measurement retained but with reduced scope
partner_roles_actual.Technoserve: Supplier linkage work scaled back; focus on high-IET deals only

consortium_actual.consortium_structure_actual: Unchanged hierarchy but with adjusted sub-contract budgets (e.g., Technoserve’s scope reduced)
consortium_actual.consortium_governance_actual: SACs retained but with stricter FCDO oversight; governance meetings reduced to bi-annual

substantive_changes_made: Shift from 70/30 TF/TA budget split to 80/20 due to FCDO prioritization
Reduction in deep TF support (commercial diligence, market assessments) to focus on deal closure
Expansion of FCDO veto threshold from >£5m to >£3m deals
Deprioritization of policy/regulatory TA work (Reformatics) in favor of investor climate analysis
Scaling back of Technoserve’s supplier linkage activities to focus on high-Inclusive Economic Transformation (IET) deals

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Decreased by ~30% from original £100m (actual spend constrained to ~£70m+)
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope unchanged (5 countries) but beneficiary targeting narrowed to high-IET deals
modality_shifts: Reduced use of call-down contracts for TA
Increased reliance on consortium’s existing capacity for GESI/C&E screening

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Assumptions about investor risk appetite revised post-COVID (e.g., shorter deal cycles prioritized)

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: Increased FCDO oversight in SACs; reduced in-country advisory presence
management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Added monthly forecast check-ins; deeper FCDO involvement in high-risk deal approvals
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: FCDO veto threshold lowered; MC’s autonomy reduced for deals in fragile contexts (e.g., Ethiopia)

activity_only_adjustments: Reduction in number of TA deliverables (from planned 12 to 8 in 2022/23)
Smaller average deal size to accommodate budget cuts
Increased use of consortium networks (20% of deal origination) vs. direct outreach (35%)

contextual_shocks: COVID-19: Cooled global FDI flows, shifted to remote oversight
FCDO budget cuts (2021–2023): Reduced TA components, delayed annual confirmations
learning_insights: Higher leverage ratios (£9 FDI per £1 spent) justified focus on TF over TA
IET deals (70% of portfolio) outperformed non-IET, prompting resource reallocation
strategic_opportunities: Increased climate finance alignment (54% of budget) to access International Climate Fund resources
Regional adviser model’s success in origination (35% of deals) led to expanded HMG network linkages

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: Medium (PbR mechanisms used effectively but TA flexibility underutilized due to budget cuts)
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High (IET deal performance data drove TF/TA rebalancing; GESI screening integrated into MC’s role)

fcas_context.fragility_level: Medium (Ethiopia: High; Kenya/Nigeria: Medium; Rwanda/Senegal: Low)
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Ethiopia (active conflict in 2021–2022); other countries stable

political_transitions: Ethiopia: Conflict disrupted deal pipelines (2021–2022)
Nigeria: Currency devaluation (2023) affected investor confidence
economic_shocks: Global economic downturn (2022–2023) reduced FDI appetite
Inflation in Kenya/Nigeria increased operational costs for beneficiaries

Ethiopia: Reduced engagement during conflict periods

programme_metadata.programme_title: Manufacturing Africa Programme

output_1.title: Manufacturing businesses and investors provided with targeted transaction facilitation support

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adjusted its Transaction Facilitation (TF) offer due to budget cuts, reducing deeper support services (commercial diligence, market assessments, GESI support, supplier linkages). Focus shifted to prioritizing deal closure over market-shaping activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: McKinsey Consortium (MC) performed well despite budget constraints, exceeding targets for deal support (120+ deals in 3 years) and maintaining high standards for GESI and Climate & Environment (C&E) compliance. However, reduced budgets limited deeper engagement capabilities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Jointly managed by a small FCDO HQ team and in-country advisers, with MC as the primary contractor. Regional adviser model proved effective for project origination and cross-HMG coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between MC, FCDO country teams, and HMG networks (e.g., UK High Commissions). Quarterly presentations of TF work expanded to all focus countries, and FCDO advisors are regularly involved in beneficiary company meetings (e.g., Steering Committees).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was flexible and responsive to budget changes, though delays in annual budget confirmation created challenges. TA deliverables were successfully procured despite budget cuts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained close oversight through quarterly check-ins, Support Approval Committees (SACs), and monitoring of senior staff usage. Oversight was more intensive than originally planned due to budget uncertainties.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility in reallocating resources to prioritize TF over TA when budgets were cut. Adapted origination channels (direct outreach, consortium networks, TA work) to maintain deal flow.
adaptive_management_examples: Reduced TF support depth to maintain deal volume during budget cuts.
Expanded use of regional advisers to leverage HMG networks for project origination.
Adjusted logframe targets in December 2022 to reflect reduced budgets (e.g., Output 1.1 and 1.3 targets lowered from 35 to 22 deals).
Increased focus on "highly economically transformative" deals (75% of deals in 2023 vs. 50% target).

main_implementation_challenges: Budget uncertainty and reductions over the past two years, including delays in annual budget confirmation.
Balancing prioritization of deal volume vs. depth of TF support due to limited resources.
Maintaining consistency in deal quality and transformative impact amid budget constraints.
Managing trade-offs between job creation (quick wins) and long-term market transformation.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 and global economic downturn reduced capital flows and investor appetite for African manufacturing FDI.
Political and economic instability in beneficiary countries (Ethiopia, Nigeria, etc.) created operational risks.
Currency fluctuations and inflation affected project financials and leverage ratios.
contextual_constraints_new: Investor reluctance in sectors with limited prior FDI, requiring MA to act as a "market signaller."
Skills shortages in local markets hindered the development impact of FDI (e.g., hiring workers with disabilities).
Supply chain disruptions (post-COVID) affected manufacturers’ ability to scale.
partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported, but reduced budgets limited MC’s ability to provide deeper TF support, potentially straining relationships with investors expecting comprehensive services.
Need for clearer communication with partners on evolving programme priorities (e.g., shift from TA to TF).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Reduced capacity for deeper TF services (e.g., commercial diligence, GESI support) due to budget cuts.
Limited bandwidth for proactive market-shaping activities (e.g., policy advice, supply chain linkages).
FCDO team size remained small, relying heavily on MC and regional advisers for implementation.
risk_materialization: Budget reductions materialized as a major risk, forcing adaptive management.
Economic downturn and COVID-19 impacts on FDI flows were mitigated but persisted as background risks.
Risk of "spreading resources too thinly" was managed through prioritization but remains a concern.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Programme faced delays in annual budget confirmation and reductions in allocated funds over the past two years.
Despite cuts, MA met all but one KPI in its logframe and achieved £9 of attributable FDI for every £1 spent (42% increase in leverage ratio YoY).
TA deliverables were maintained (8 new in 2022/23) despite FCDO’s focus on TF.
value_for_money_assessment: High VfM demonstrated by leverage ratio (£9 FDI per £1 spent) and exceeding targets for inclusive economic transformation (70% of deals vs. 50% target).
54% of budget spent on International Climate Finance targets (vs. 50% target), enhancing VfM for climate objectives.
Independent assessment of MC’s outcome/impact attribution and PbR scores remains pending due to budget constraints.
financial_management_quality: MC improved forecasting accuracy through regular check-ins with sub-contractors, though variances persist due to programme flexibility.
FCDO monitored senior staff usage closely, with KPIs indicating relatively low but appropriate levels.
Financial controls (e.g., SACs) ensured rigorous scrutiny of beneficiary companies’ financials.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency improved with higher leverage ratios (£9 FDI per £1) and reduced average deal size to stretch budgets.
Efficiency gains in TA delivery through repurposing past deliverables and focusing on high-impact areas.
co_funding_materialization: Co-funding from DFIs and other donors was prioritized over firm-level co-investment (discussed in Addis Ababa workshop, Nov 2022).
No evidence of direct co-funding from beneficiary firms, but partnerships with DFIs enhanced deal viability.
currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly detailed, but global economic conditions (inflation, exchange rates) likely affected deal financials and FDI attraction.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible, adaptive management is critical to navigating budget uncertainties and external shocks (e.g., COVID-19).
Regional adviser model is highly effective for project origination and cross-HMG coordination.
Deeper TF support (e.g., GESI, supplier linkages) drives higher transformative impact but requires sufficient budget.
TA work is essential for unblocking policy barriers and feeding the TF pipeline, despite budget pressures.
successful_delivery_practices: Diverse origination channels (direct outreach, consortium networks, TA work) maintained a strong deal pipeline.
Quarterly presentations to FCDO country advisers improved transparency and alignment.
GESI and C&E screening for all deals ensured compliance and inclusive impact.
Leveraging HMG communication channels (e.g., social media, African Investment Summit) amplified programme visibility.
management_adaptations_made: Reduced TF support depth to maintain deal volume during budget cuts.
Adjusted logframe targets to reflect realistic expectations given budget reductions.
Prioritized high-IET deals (70% vs. 50% target) to maximize development impact.
Expanded use of regional advisers to compensate for reduced central capacity.
innovations_attempted: Explored co-investment models with DFIs (though firm-level co-funding was deprioritized).
Developed IET scoring framework to quantify deal transformativeness.
Piloted green manufacturing focus, with 54% of budget aligned to climate finance targets.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Improved forecasting processes (though variances remain).
Incomplete: Independent assessment of MC’s outcome/impact attribution not conducted due to budget constraints.
Complete: Clarified role of programme in challenging beneficiary companies’ financials during SACs.
forward_recommendations: Conduct next annual review with in-country visits to gather firsthand insights from staff and beneficiaries.
Hire an external M&E specialist to QA output/outcome indicators and assess MC’s attribution claims.
Expand definition of FDI in programme documentation, incorporating academic evidence and investor landscape insights.
Prioritize additional budget for deeper TF support (e.g., GESI, supplier linkages) if resources become available.
Develop case studies on regional adviser model to share lessons across FCDO programmes.
Review delivery scenarios to balance deal volume vs. transformative impact in future budget allocations.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating budget risks through adaptive management and reprioritization.
Proactive monitoring of external risks (e.g., economic downturn, political instability) via SACs and quarterly check-ins.
Need for stronger contingency planning for sustained budget uncertainties.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Supported 120+ deals over 3 years, with 24 new deals in 2023 (potential to create 4,729 direct jobs).
Exceeded job quality targets: 75% of deals in 2023 were "highly economically transformative" (vs. 50% target).
Indirect beneficiaries include local suppliers and workers with disabilities (via inclusive hiring practices).
policy_influence_achieved: Informed FCDO and HMG approaches to industrialisation and FDI policy through advisory support.
Acted as a "proof of concept" for manufacturing FDI in Africa, inspiring other donors’ programming.
Developed insights on investor landscape and global value chains, shared with FCDO policy teams.
capacity_building_results: Strengthened capacities of local manufacturers to attract FDI (e.g., financial modelling, compliance).
Built government capacities to remove FDI barriers (e.g., policy advice, institutional strengthening).
Enhanced skills of regional advisers in project origination and cross-programme coordination.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Programme’s success attracted additional donor interest in African manufacturing FDI.
Negative: Reduced TA budget may limit long-term market-shaping impact (e.g., policy reforms, skills development).
scalability_evidence: Model is scalable, as demonstrated by replication of TF and TA approaches across 5 countries (Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Senegal, Rwanda).
Regional adviser model and origination channels (e.g., consortium networks) are adaptable to new geographies.
Leverage ratios (£9 FDI per £1) suggest potential for cost-effective expansion with additional funding.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance despite challenges: exceeded most KPIs, high leverage ratios, and transformative deal quality.
Critical role in attracting FDI to African manufacturing, a priority for FCDO’s economic development goals.
Adaptive management demonstrates resilience to budget cuts and external shocks.
Potential for greater impact with restored budgets (e.g., deeper TF support, expanded TA).
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model is sustainable in the short term but requires additional resources to maintain depth of support.
Regional adviser model and MC consortium provide stable implementation infrastructure.
Long-term sustainability depends on securing co-funding from DFIs and other donors.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Reinvest in deeper TF support (e.g., GESI, supplier linkages) if budgets allow.
Expand policy advisory work to leverage programme insights for FCDO’s broader industrialisation agenda.
Develop case studies and knowledge products to share lessons on FDI attraction and economic transformation.
Explore opportunities for scaling successful approaches (e.g., IET framework, green manufacturing focus) to new countries.

output_1.title: Reduced currency and refinancing risk improving stability and creditworthiness: Proportion of FSD Africa supported portfolio, and completed transactions that are financed in local currency

output_2.title: Deeper and more sophisticated domestic capital markets, new asset classes and improved investment opportunities: Number of FSD Africa supported transactions that have been closed

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Evolved from initial focus on financial inclusion/skills development (SIMBA) to broader financial sector development addressing structural barriers. Shifted to three pillars: Capital Markets, Risk & Resilience, and Digital Economy. Added investment arm (FSDAi) in 2019 and refocused after 2020 ODA reductions withdrew Country FSD Network support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners generally performed well, with FSD Africa establishing reputation as effective partner for private sector, governments, and institutions (e.g., Trade and Development Bank Ethiopia, DFIs, MDBs). Development Impact course created to align partners on impact targets. Early evidence shows interventions did no harm to marginalized groups.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance mechanisms for inclusion targets established (e.g., EDI roles, recruitment metrics). Board oversight maintained with risk appetite set at 'receptive' for Programme Delivery/Strategy and 'cautious' for operational risks. Localisation increased from 58% to 68% for consultants.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination with FCDO on disability/inclusion action plans and alignment with 2X Challenge for gender-lens investing. New partnerships developed (e.g., potential EBRD collaboration).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement efficiency improved: competitive contracts increased to 72% (target: 80%), lead times reduced to 22 days (from 30), and localisation formalized in evaluation criteria. Open processes maximized value through supplier competition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Risk-based oversight maintained with 'moderate' risk rating. Additional mitigations planned as delivery scales and complexity increases (e.g., fraud risks in deeper delivery chains).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Adaptive management demonstrated through strategy shifts (e.g., 2021 'Financing a Sustainable Future' strategy prioritizing green finance, gender-lens approach, and climate resilience). Legacy interventions gradually phased out to align with new targets.
adaptive_management_examples: Launch of 2021–2025 strategy refocusing on green finance and climate resilience in response to Africa’s vulnerability to climate change (e.g., £2.29trn annual need for net-zero goals).
Responsive withdrawal from Country FSD Network due to 2020 ODA reductions, with refocus on three core pillars.
Development of measurement frameworks for GHG emission reductions and jobs impact tracking.
Delayed but planned mid-term Logframe recalibration (FY23–24) to adjust milestones based on lessons learned.

main_implementation_challenges: Slippages in project timelines linked to budget deferments and legacy interventions misaligned with new strategy.
Complexity of managing dual platforms (non-profit FSD Africa and for-profit FSDAi) with distinct but complementary mandates.
Need to balance local currency transactions (58.3% achieved) with market-driven USD dominance in capital raises.
external_factors_impact: 2020 ODA reductions forced withdrawal from Country FSD Network and refocus of programme scope.
Climate change impacts (e.g., severe weather events, desertification) increased urgency for green finance interventions.
COVID-19 likely contributed to project delays (implied by budget deferments).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of climate finance gap (£2.29trn annually needed for Africa’s net-zero goals by 2030).
Regulatory challenges in incentivizing public bond issuances (most transactions remain private placements).
Need to broaden equity focus beyond gender to include other marginalized groups (e.g., disability inclusion).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Legacy interventions with misaligned outputs/outcomes temporarily reduced efficiency ratings ('adequate').
Increased organisational complexity as delivery chains deepen, requiring additional risk mitigations (e.g., financial/fiduciary fraud).
risk_materialization: Moderate risks in 'Public Service Delivery and Operations' and financial/fiduciary areas became more significant as programme scaled.
No major risk breaches, but caution flagged for fraud risks in expanded delivery chains.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Strong economic management rated 'excellent' internally. Competitive procurement increased to 72% (from 57%), approaching 80% target. Budget deferments caused some project slippages but overall execution remained on track.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Good VFM confirmed by FCDO, with programme delivering in a "challenging, impactful niche" while meeting the 5 Es (Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness, Equity, Environment). Updated 2022 VFM framework aligned with new strategy, though formal outcome assessments deferred to 2023–24.
financial_management_quality: Rated 'excellent' for economy (e.g., localisation increased to 68%, reducing international consultant costs).
Efficiency rated 'adequate' due to legacy interventions but improving with new projects (14 onboarded in 2023).
Effectiveness metrics under development; early tracking shows progress in finance mobilisation and GHG/jobs impact.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Procurement lead times reduced to 22 days (from 30), with consistent daily rates over 4 years.
Localisation reduced costs while improving quality via local knowledge/connections.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Local currency transactions (58.3% of portfolio) mitigated FX risk but USD dominance persisted in some markets (e.g., 5 of 12 transactions in USD due to investor preferences).

key_delivery_lessons: Localisation of talent (68%) enhanced programme quality and reduced costs, validating the push beyond 58% baseline.
Competitive procurement (72%) drove value but required formalised criteria (e.g., localisation evaluation) to sustain gains.
Legacy interventions can drag on efficiency; phased transition to new strategy-aligned projects is critical.
successful_delivery_practices: Open procurement processes maximised economy and supplier competition.
Gender-lens investing framework (aligned with 2X Challenge) advanced women’s leadership and capital access.
Development Impact course for partners improved alignment on impact targets.
Reduced procurement lead times (22 days) reflected better project management.
management_adaptations_made: Strategy shift to 'Financing a Sustainable Future' (2021–25) with clearer geographic focus and gender/ climate priorities.
Formalised EDI governance (e.g., inclusion targets, recruitment metrics) to broaden equity beyond gender.
Risk appetite adjusted to 'receptive' for delivery/strategy and 'cautious' for operational risks.
innovations_attempted: Pilot gender bond transactions and research on gender-climate financing policies.
Measurement frameworks for GHG emission reductions and jobs impact tracking.
Partnerships with investment banks (e.g., potential EBRD collaboration) to scale local currency transactions.
previous_recommendations_progress: Delayed but planned: Mid-term Logframe review (originally due May/June 2023) to recalibrate milestones, now targeted for FY23–24 Board approval.
EDI report and diversity metrics introduced in response to 2021–22 AR recommendations.
forward_recommendations: Complete Logframe recalibration by FY23–24 end to ensure realistic, credible milestones.
Expand equity focus to include disability and other marginalized groups beyond gender.
Incentivize public bond issuances to broaden local investor base (currently most transactions are private placements).
Monitor financial/fiduciary risks as delivery chains deepen, with mitigations for fraud.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective overall, with risks remaining within appetite. Proactive adjustments included increased localisation, competitive procurement, and formalised EDI governance. Scaling delivery will require enhanced mitigations for financial/fiduciary risks.

policy_influence_achieved: Influenced green finance policies through gender bond demonstrations and climate financing research.
Supported regulatory improvements for local currency transactions (e.g., Nigeria/ Morocco green bond issuances).
Contributed to FCDO’s disability/inclusion action plan.
capacity_building_results: Advanced women’s leadership in financial sector via gender-lens investing (aligned with 2X Challenge).
Development Impact course improved partner capacity to track development outcomes.
Localisation (68%) built African talent capacity and reduced reliance on international consultants.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Local currency transactions (58.3%) reduced FX risk and stimulated demand for financial infrastructure (e.g., bond exchanges).
Negative: Private placement dominance limited broadening of local institutional investor base.
scalability_evidence: Investment arm (FSDAi) and non-profit platform (FSD Africa) demonstrate scalable dual-platform model.
Partnerships with DFIs/MDBs (e.g., EBRD) and local banks suggest potential for replication in new markets.
Gender bond and green finance innovations have attracted international investor interest.

continuation_rationale: Programme delivers good VFM in a high-impact niche (financial sector development, climate resilience, gender equity).
Strong reputation as effective partner for governments, private sector, and institutions (e.g., Gates Foundation).
Alignment with critical needs (e.g., £2.29trn annual climate finance gap for Africa’s net-zero goals).
Adaptive management demonstrated through strategy shifts and risk mitigation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High – dual-platform model (non-profit + investment arm) and localisation strategy (68%) support long-term viability. Risk management frameworks are robust but require scaling with delivery complexity.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High – FCDO judges programme as delivering good VFM and objective self-assessments.
planned_adaptations_future: Recalibrate Logframe milestones by FY23–24 end to reflect lessons learned.
Expand equity focus to disability/inclusion per FCDO action plans.
Strengthen incentives for public bond issuances to deepen local markets.
Enhance financial/fiduciary risk mitigations as programme scales.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Girls and Out of School Children: Action for Learning (GOAL) Programme

output_1.title: Reduced barriers and schooling costs for girls and marginalised children

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adapted due to ODA budget reductions; some components (e.g., Long-Term TA, Service Delivery) still in procurement stage with delays. Humanitarian Assistance component activated to address 2022 flood impacts in South Punjab and KP Merged Districts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Short-term TA partner (I-SAPS) made partial progress on milestones (e.g., VFM analysis, PEF Strategic Plan). Humanitarian partner (RSPN) exceeded targets for school rehabilitation (265 schools) and teacher/PTC training (530 trained vs. 400 target).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Strong provincial/district-level government engagement established, mitigating leadership transition risks. FCDO’s adaptive management required frequent workplan adjustments due to budget changes and election-related delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Close coordination with FCDO’s CMPs, PAG, British Council, and Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to avoid duplication and leverage complementarities (e.g., aligning with other donors’ provincial learning strategies).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in Service Delivery and Long-Term TA procurements due to iterative feedback loops and budget changes. Early Market Engagement (EME) identified as critical for high-quality bids; Commercial Team involvement from outset recommended.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to procurement delays and adaptive management needs. FCDO empowered in-country experts to reprioritize spend based on emerging needs (e.g., Ukraine/Afghanistan refugee support).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Budget flexibility used to reallocate funds to flood response (Humanitarian Assistance component). Workplans revised to reflect ODA reductions and election-related government approval delays.
adaptive_management_examples: Activation of Humanitarian Assistance component to address 2022 flood disruptions, exceeding targets for school rehabilitation and training.
Adjustment of short-term TA workplan to account for election-related delays and government approval contingencies.
Removal of duplicate activities with other donors (e.g., provincial learning strategies) to improve VfM.

main_implementation_challenges: Procurement delays for Long-Term TA and Service Delivery components due to budget changes and iterative processes.
Election-related uncertainties causing delays in government approvals for key milestones.
ODA budget reductions requiring reprioritization of activities and targets.
Post-flood rehabilitation needs in South Punjab and KP Merged Districts diverting focus from planned interventions.
external_factors_impact: 2022 floods disrupted education for 3.5 million children, necessitating unplanned humanitarian response.
UK government’s ODA reallocation to support Ukrainian/Afghan refugees reduced programme budget flexibility.
Political transitions (elections) slowed government decision-making on reforms and approvals.
contextual_constraints_new: Climate change exacerbating education disruptions (e.g., flood damage to 22,000 schools).
Inflation and economic instability in Pakistan increasing costs for school rehabilitation and stipends.
Capacity constraints in KP Merged Districts and South Punjab limiting absorption of technical assistance.
partner_relationship_issues: Short-term TA partner (I-SAPS) faced challenges in finalizing strategic plans due to delayed government consultations.
Service Delivery procurement delays strained relationships with potential implementing partners.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited provincial capacity to absorb technical assistance, particularly in KP Merged Districts.
Delays in mobilizing long-term TA left gaps in addressing systemic education reforms.
School-level capacity (e.g., PTCs) required additional training to manage flood recovery interventions.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (planned risk) materialized due to budget cuts and complex tender processes.
Government approval risks materialized with election-related leadership changes.
Climate risks materialized with 2022 floods, requiring unplanned humanitarian response.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution below plan due to ODA reductions and procurement delays. £130M full-life value maintained, but 2023 spend reprioritized to flood response (Humanitarian Assistance) and short-term TA.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM partially achieved. Cost efficiencies noted in humanitarian component (e.g., 265 schools rehabilitated at lower-than-expected cost), but delays in TA procurement reduced overall VfM. Coordination with GPE avoided duplication.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by partners (I-SAPS, RSPN) deemed satisfactory, with transparent reporting on flood response expenditures. FCDO’s adaptive budget management allowed reallocation to high-priority areas.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Mixed. Humanitarian component exceeded cost-efficiency targets (e.g., 530 teachers trained vs. 400 target at no additional cost). TA components faced inefficiencies due to procurement delays.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not yet materialized. Non-Budget Financial Aid component contingent on Ministerial approval (targeted for Year 2).

key_delivery_lessons: Early Market Engagement (EME) critical for shaping high-quality procurement ToRs and reducing delays.
Multi-tier government engagement (provincial/district) essential for ownership and risk mitigation during political transitions.
Flexible workplans and clear communication on budget changes help maintain partner relationships.
successful_delivery_practices: Humanitarian component’s rapid response to floods, exceeding targets for school rehabilitation and training.
RSPN’s psycho-social support and teacher training models proved scalable and effective.
Coordination with GPE and other donors to avoid duplication and leverage complementarities.
management_adaptations_made: Workplan ambitions revised downward to account for election delays and government approval risks.
Removal of duplicate activities with other donors (e.g., provincial learning strategies).
Increased oversight on procurement processes to mitigate delays.
innovations_attempted: Accelerated learning programmes designed for flood-affected children (though implementation delayed).
Socio-emotional training for teachers/PTCs integrated into humanitarian response.
forward_recommendations: Document lessons from flood response (e.g., psycho-social support, resilience-building) to inform Education Cannot Wait (ECW) engagement (RSPN, July 2024).
Revisit short-term TA workplan to adjust targets and remove duplication (I-SAPS/GOAL SRO, March 2024).
Involve Commercial Team earlier in high-value procurements to streamline processes.
Clarify expectations on adaptability with partners to manage future budget/workplan changes.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Planned risks (procurement delays, government approvals) materialized but were mitigated through adaptive management. Climate risks were not fully anticipated, requiring reactive humanitarian response.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual_2023: 48,000 students (54% girls) supported with learning kits in rehabilitated schools; 265 schools rehabilitated; 530 teachers/PTC members trained.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.progress: Limited progress toward overall target due to procurement delays, but humanitarian component exceeded immediate flood-response targets.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Partial. Short-term TA contributed to PEF Strategic Plan development, but systemic reforms delayed by election uncertainties.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Moderate. Teacher/PTC training exceeded targets, but long-term TA delays limit systemic capacity improvements.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Humanitarian response strengthened community trust in government schools post-floods.
Negative: Procurement delays reduced momentum for systemic reforms, risking donor fatigue.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Limited. Humanitarian interventions (e.g., school rehabilitation, teacher training) proved scalable within flood-affected districts, but broader scalability constrained by procurement delays.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme aligns with FCDO’s Country Business Plan and global girls’ education goals. Despite delays, humanitarian component demonstrated impact, and TA components remain critical for systemic reforms. Adaptations (e.g., workplan revisions) address implementation challenges.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable. Short-term TA and humanitarian components effective, but long-term TA procurement delays risk undermining systemic impact. Government ownership at provincial/district levels mitigates political risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium (acknowledging challenges but recognizing adaptive management and humanitarian successes).
planned_adaptations_future: Accelerate Long-Term TA procurement to avoid further delays.
Scale successful humanitarian interventions (e.g., teacher training, school rehabilitation) to non-flood districts.
Strengthen risk mitigation for government approval delays (e.g., pre-election engagements).
Enhance VfM through deeper coordination with GPE and other donors.

output_1.title: Improved classroom teaching practices for 3Rs in early grades, Maths and English in upper grades

output_2.title: Children arrive at school better prepared to learn

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Reduction in UKAID funding (52% cut) required rationalisation and reduction of ambition in plans. Programme adapted to focus on three key areas: teaching/learning, inclusion, and systems strengthening. Decentralised model for Teacher Continuous Professional Development (TCPD) encouraged to reduce dependency on Tanzania Institute of Education (TIE).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Cambridge Education (TA contractor) refocused to support broader government priorities (e.g., *Mewaka* national teacher training programme) beyond Tanzania Institute of Education (TIE). Collaboration with World Bank’s BOOST programme, USAID’s *Jifunze Uelewa*, and UNICEF for scaling tools (e.g., Parent-Teacher Partnership guides). Oxford Policy Management (verification contractor) and DIME (assessment grant) performed as expected, with DIME’s evidence-building role highlighted.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: New leadership brought stronger direction and momentum. Regional in-person meetings with government improved productivity. Operational guidance clarified expectations between Shule Bora and government partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Demonstrated coordination with multi-donor Education Programme for Results (EPforR II), World Bank (BOOST), USAID, UNICEF, and local actors (e.g., ADEM, PORALG). Joint initiatives included scaling formative assessment tools and addressing gender bias in teacher training nominations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Cost savings achieved through negotiated reductions in per diems (20% saving) and printing costs (£20,000). Fixed contractual costs remained high (45% of total costs) due to funding cuts, but efficiency improvements noted (e.g., technology use in Head Teacher training).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight due to funding reductions and alignment needs with Tanzania’s education reforms. Financial reporting measures strengthened for results-based funding resuming into government systems.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to funding cuts by reprioritising activities and refining Theory of Change/logframe. Flexibility used to respond to domestic reforms (e.g., curriculum changes) and scale successful interventions (e.g., School Readiness Programme replication by government).
adaptive_management_examples: Refreshed Theory of Change and logframe to align with reduced funding and education reforms, focusing on teaching/learning, inclusion, and systems strengthening.
Shift from centralised TCPD (TIE-dependent) to decentralised model using local teacher training colleges.
Replication of School Readiness Programme (SRP) by government in 23 additional centres, leveraging Shule Bora’s tools.
Expansion of climate resilience initiatives (e.g., rainwater catchment) beyond education ministries to engage Ministry of Gender and Community Development.
Adoption of Shule Bora’s TCPD video guides by World Bank (BOOST), GPE, and TIE for nationwide scaling.

main_implementation_challenges: 52% reduction in UKAID annual funding, requiring reprioritisation and reduced ambition.
Government of Tanzania’s education reforms (e.g., curriculum overhaul, textbook production) created alignment challenges without additional domestic funding.
Domestic education budget failing to keep pace with student population growth, leading to larger class sizes and reduced student-teacher ratios.
Trust in UK-Tanzania partnership tested due to funding cuts and shifting priorities.
external_factors_impact: Tanzania’s 2023 Education and Training Policy (ETP) reforms required Shule Bora to realign its roadmaps and technical support.
Lack of additional government funding for reforms (e.g., teacher recruitment, textbook updates) constrained progress on systemic changes.
Gender dynamics (e.g., higher boy dropout rates) and linguistic/geographic marginalisation persisted as barriers to inclusion.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of domestic reform ambitions without commensurate resource allocation.
Need to balance national-level systems strengthening with subnational (9 regions) delivery amid funding cuts.
Climate/environmental vulnerabilities (e.g., arid regions) required unplanned investments in resilience (e.g., rainwater catchment).
partner_relationship_issues: Gender bias in teacher training nominations (only 39% female trainees despite majority-female workforce) required ongoing dialogue with government authorities (ADEM, PORALG, Teacher Service Commission).
Tensions between centralised (TIE) and decentralised (regional colleges) approaches to teacher training coordination.
Delays in government adoption of tools (e.g., School Quality Assurance tool) due to bureaucratic processes.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity at regional/local levels to absorb decentralised TCPD model, risking quality dilution.
TIE’s bandwidth constrained by multiple donor demands, affecting its ability to lead national TCPD coordination.
Local Government Authorities (LGAs) required additional support to replicate interventions (e.g., School Readiness Programme).
risk_materialization: Funding reduction risk materialized, impacting delivery scale and partner trust.
Risk of misalignment with government reforms partially mitigated through adaptive programming (e.g., revised roadmaps).
Fiduciary risks associated with results-based funding into government systems required strengthened financial reporting measures.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Fixed contractual costs remained high (45% of total) due to funding cuts, but cost savings achieved (e.g., 20% reduction in per diems, £20,000 printing savings).
Budget reallocated to prioritise teaching/learning, inclusion, and systems strengthening per refreshed Theory of Change.
Per-child costs for School Readiness Programme (£37) deemed efficient compared to government preschool spending (£400/child).
value_for_money_assessment: Economy: Cost efficiencies demonstrated in training (TCPD cost per person-day: £7–£34; PTP training: £87 direct/£9 cascaded) and operational improvements (e.g., technology use in Head Teacher training).
Effectiveness: Early evidence of impact (e.g., 74% of teachers improved practices post-TCPD; PTPs increased attendance and in-kind donations).
Equity: Targeted interventions in 5–10 most disadvantaged schools per LGA; inclusive pedagogy training prioritised marginalised groups (e.g., linguistic minorities, children with disabilities).
Sustainability: High potential for scaling (e.g., Shule Bora tools adopted by BOOST, GPE, UNICEF; SRP replicated by government in 23 centres).
financial_management_quality: Strengthened financial reporting measures implemented for results-based funding into government systems.
Transparency in cost data (e.g., per-child/per-trainee metrics) enabled benchmarking against government spending.
No major audit findings reported; procurement savings (e.g., per diems) suggest prudent resource use.
cost_efficiency_achieved: TCPD cascading model reduced per-trainee costs (£7 indirect vs. £34 direct).
Parent-Teacher Partnership (PTP) training costs dropped to <£9 per cascaded member.
EdTech Hub’s heatmap dashboards leveraged government data at low marginal cost.
co_funding_materialization: Shule Bora influenced $12M annual spending by likeminded donors via EPforR II, but no explicit co-funding beyond original business case.
Government replication of SRP (23 centres) and adoption of tools (e.g., TCPD videos) represent in-kind leverage.

key_delivery_lessons: Decentralised TCPD models (using regional colleges) are more sustainable than centralised TIE dependency but require capacity-building at local levels.
Results-based funding into government systems is viable but demands robust fiduciary safeguards and aligned MoUs.
Scaling interventions (e.g., SRP, PTP guides) is most effective when government ownership is secured early (e.g., via joint concept notes).
Climate resilience must be integrated into education programming (e.g., rainwater catchment in arid regions) to address contextual vulnerabilities.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of technology (e.g., video guides for TCPD, EdTech Hub dashboards) improved reach and reduced costs.
Regional in-person meetings enhanced government coordination and productivity.
Holistic inclusion strategies (addressing gender, disability, language, geography) improved equity outcomes.
Partnerships with multi-donor platforms (EPforR II) and donors (World Bank, USAID) amplified impact beyond Shule Bora’s direct funding.
management_adaptations_made: Refreshed Theory of Change and logframe to focus on teaching/learning, inclusion, and systems strengthening.
Shifted Cambridge Education’s TA role from TIE-centric to broader government support (e.g., *Mewaka* programme, regional colleges).
Strengthened gender equity focus via joint concept note with ADEM/PORALG to address male bias in training nominations.
Expanded climate resilience work to engage non-education ministries (e.g., Ministry of Gender and Community Development).
innovations_attempted: TCPD video implementation guides scaled nationally by BOOST, GPE, and TIE.
Parent-Teacher Partnership (PTP) model replicated by UNICEF in non-Shule Bora regions.
School Readiness Programme (SRP) centres converted to satellite schools via World Bank BOOST funding.
EdTech Hub’s heatmap dashboards transitioned toward government hosting for sustainability.

previous_recommendations_progress.actions: Collaborated with BOOST on teaching/learning deliverables; supported USAID’s *Jifunze Uelewa* in scaling formative assessments.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Investigate low female representation in TCPD (39% female trainees).

previous_recommendations_progress.actions: New classroom observation tool developed with MoEST; rollout pending.

forward_recommendations: Revise Shule Bora MoU to facilitate results-based funding into government systems with adequate fiduciary safeguards.
Align programming with Tanzania’s 2023 Education and Training Policy reforms, prioritising teacher needs and curriculum alignment.
Strengthen Cambridge Education’s support to EPforR II, reflecting this in staffing and contract amendments.
Deepened focus on gender dynamics, particularly addressing boy dropout rates and female teacher representation.
Expand climate/environmental resilience work beyond education ministries (e.g., engage Ministry of Gender and Community Development).
Transition EdTech Hub’s heatmap dashboards to government hosting for long-term sustainability.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive adaptation to funding cuts (e.g., reprioritisation, Theory of Change refresh) mitigated delivery risks.
Alignment with government reforms (e.g., revised roadmaps) reduced misalignment risks but required continuous dialogue.
Fiduciary risks for results-based funding addressed via strengthened financial reporting, though implementation risks remain.
Gender and inclusion risks partially addressed via targeted interventions (e.g., PTPs, SRP) but require sustained attention.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 2,730 teachers (28% female) attended TCPD training; 60% demonstrated improved knowledge in English teaching and inclusive pedagogy.
1,735 marginalised out-of-school children (49% female) accessed School Readiness Programme centres.
Parent-Teacher Partnerships (PTPs) established in disadvantaged schools, with qualitative evidence of increased attendance and in-kind donations.
Indirect reach via scaling: SRP replicated in 23 government centres; TCPD tools adopted by BOOST/GPE for nationwide use.
policy_influence_achieved: Shule Bora’s TCPD and inclusion tools integrated into national programmes (e.g., *Mewaka* teacher training coordination).
School Quality Assurance (SQA) tool developed with MoEST for government adoption.
Climate resilience guidelines influenced policy discussions beyond education sector.
capacity_building_results: Tanzania Institute of Education (TIE) capacity strengthened for inclusive pedagogy and curriculum alignment.
Regional teacher training colleges and local education offices gained experience in decentralised TCPD delivery.
Government adoption of Shule Bora’s SRP and PTP models demonstrates institutional capacity uptake.

unintended_consequences.description: Scaling of Shule Bora tools (e.g., TCPD videos, PTP guides) by BOOST, GPE, and UNICEF extended impact beyond original 9 regions.
Funding cuts reduced direct delivery scale, potentially widening inequities in non-targeted regions. Trust in UK partnership temporarily strained.

scalability_evidence: SRP replicated by government in 23 centres; BOOST programme converted SRP centres to satellite schools.
TCPD video guides adopted by TIE, BOOST, and GPE for nationwide teacher training.
PTP guides replicated by UNICEF in additional regions.
EdTech Hub’s heatmap dashboards designed for government hosting, enabling national-scale use.

continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong performance (consistent ‘A’ scores) and high potential for sustained impact via scaling (e.g., SRP, TCPD tools).
Alignment with Tanzania’s education reforms (e.g., ETP 2023) positions Shule Bora to influence systemic changes despite funding constraints.
Value for money evidenced through cost efficiencies (e.g., cascading training models) and leverage of donor/partner resources.
Critical mass of interventions (e.g., inclusion, climate resilience) addresses priority gaps in Tanzania’s education sector.
delivery_model_sustainability: Decentralised TCPD and government adoption of tools (e.g., SRP, SQA) suggest long-term viability.
Partnerships with EPforR II, BOOST, and UNICEF provide pathways for continued support beyond direct UK funding.
Risk of over-reliance on TIE mitigated by broader engagement with regional colleges and ministries.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Further alignment with ETP 2023 reforms, including curriculum updates and teacher training priorities.
Strengthened focus on gender equity (e.g., addressing boy dropout rates, female teacher representation).
Expansion of climate resilience initiatives in collaboration with non-education ministries.
Transition of EdTech tools (e.g., heatmap dashboards) to government ownership.
Continued adaptive management to respond to funding constraints and domestic policy shifts.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Support to the International Agriculture Research Centres developing and delivering agriculture technologies and knowledge to reduce poverty, hunger and adapt to climate change

output_1.title: Agricultural technologies and products developed, tested and available in target countries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All three Centres (CABI, icipe, WorldVeg) met or exceeded their 2018 milestones collectively, demonstrating strong performance in developing and testing agricultural technologies. Strategic partnerships exceeded targets (104 vs 75 planned), indicating effective collaboration with national/regional institutions and private sector.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The programme leveraged complementary expertise across Centres (e.g., WorldVeg’s vegetable breeding aligned with CABI’s plant health focus). The Africa Vegetable Breeding Consortium (AVBC) was established in 2018 as a joint initiative with AFSTA, engaging 9 seed companies by April 2019, showing effective coordination for scaling.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to emerging needs (e.g., WorldVeg’s response to breaking resistance in tomato rootstocks by identifying new resistance sources). Performance-related funding drove improvements in VFM, gender mainstreaming, and environmental impact reduction.
adaptive_management_examples: WorldVeg’s genetic characterization of 800+ amaranth germplasm accessions to identify pest/disease-resistant traits, addressing farmer-preferred traits.
Trials of pink nethouses in Taiwan to increase tomato yields (50-65% higher than open-field/white nethouses), a simple innovation not previously trialed elsewhere.
Response to bacterial wilt resistance breakdown in tomatoes by accelerating research into new resistance sources.

operational_challenges_context.risk_materialization: Moderate risk rating maintained across 2016-2018, suggesting planned risks (e.g., technology adoption at scale, regulatory approvals) were managed without major materialization. successful_delivery_practices: Structured indicator framework showing progression from research to scaling (e.g., technologies tested under farm/research conditions → regulatory approvals → partnerships).
Cross-Centre collaboration (e.g., WorldVeg’s breeding aligned with CABI’s plant health expertise).
Simple, low-cost innovations (e.g., pink nethouses) with high yield impacts.
