programme_metadata.programme_title: Directorate for a Research and Innovation Hub on Technology for Education (EdTech Hub)

output_1.title: Robust research on using technology to improve governance, data management, equity and accountability within education systems

output_2.title: Robust research on using technology to improve teacher professional development, retention and attendance

output_3.title: Robust research on using technology to adapt to the diverse needs of learners (girls, disabilities, OOSC, PAL, TARL)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme pivoted significantly to support COVID-19 response, focusing on urgent evidence needs for policy makers. Shifted from planned 3-5 six-month studies per theme to producing 9 country briefs, 2 policy briefs, and the "EdTech and COVID-19: 10 Things to Know" publication. Leadership transitioned from ODI to R4D as operational lead in December 2020.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Consortium partners (BRINK, ODE, Jigsaw Consult, ODI, University of Cambridge, R4D) adapted well to COVID-19 demands. New Management Director role created and interim MD recruited to improve governance. In-country advisers strengthened connections with local stakeholders.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Original governance scored 'C' in previous AR due to weak leadership structures. Post-BMGF-funded organizational review, governance transformed with: 1) New Management Director role, 2) R4D taking operational lead, 3) Increased FCDO oversight (3 PFPs assigned), 4) Strengthened country-level coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Hub fostered 12+ cross-sector collaborations (e.g., Sierra Leone, Kenya, Malawi, UNHCR). Established Communities of Practice (CoP) with government/researcher/private-sector participation. 64 Helpdesk requests from FCDO/World Bank indicate strong demand for coordinated support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO dedicated significant management attention, including 3 Programme Funded Posts (PFPs) for oversight. Regular engagement with country advisers and government counterparts to align implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high adaptability by: 1) Reprioritizing research to COVID-19 response, 2) Accelerating sandbox deployments (7 active sandboxes in 2021 vs. original timeline), 3) Adjusting selection criteria for marginalized groups (e.g., learners with disabilities, refugees).
adaptive_management_examples: Pivot to COVID-19 evidence generation (9 country briefs, "10 Things to Know" publication launched by UK Special Envoy)
Sandbox methodology adapted for faster deployment (e.g., 6P model revisions, marginalized-group focus)
Leadership restructuring (R4D replacing ODI as operational lead, new Management Director role)
Helpdesk/Technical Assistance expanded to meet urgent policy demands (64 requests in 2020-21)

Currency/exchange rate impacts not explicitly mentioned.

value_for_money_assessment.assessment: High VFM demonstrated through: 1) Leveraging co-funding (e.g., Afghanistan sandbox supplemented by in-kind contributions), 2) Methodology adoption by external actors, 3) Focus on marginalized groups aligning with equity goals. Cost efficiency improved via iterative "learn and adapt" model.
Strong VFM: 64 requests fulfilled with existing resources, directly informing policy decisions (e.g., Madagascar hardware procurement, Zanzibar digital content strategy).
High impact per pound: "10 Things to Know" synthesized 50+ studies into accessible policy guidance, launched at ministerial level.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Public Finance Management Multi-Donor Trust Fund – Phase II

output_1.title: Execution rate of capital budget reaches 50% at the end of second trimester and 90% at the end of the year

output_2.title: PFM Reforms within a federal context developed supported with thorough analysis

output_4.title: Delivery of high-quality analysis of fiduciary and corruption risks in key sectors in Nepal and increase in capacity to support effective PFM systems

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned from WB MDTF (World Bank-implemented) to a bridging phase focused on foundational work for future reforms. PFM Facility shifted from DT Global to Alinea in August 2024, emphasizing strategic PFM support and fiduciary risk management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (WB MDTF) took a government-led, slow but inclusive approach, allowing GoN ownership but delaying strategy finalization. Alinea (PFM Facility) demonstrated agility in producing knowledge products and aligning with BEK priorities post-contract signing (July 2024).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: PFM Steering Committee structure revision to include Provincial/Local Governments (PLGs) remains pending Cabinet approval. MoF’s PFM Reform Unit creation awaits Cabinet decision, though O&M survey is complete.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Unified DP platform (WB MDTF) improved collaboration and leverage for PFM influencing. PFM Facility provided cross-cutting fiduciary risk analysis, reducing duplication and enhancing coherence across BEK’s portfolio.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: PFM Facility contract with Alinea was procured and signed in late July 2024, with workplan approved shortly after. No major procurement delays reported, though transitional period required rapid onboarding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight during transition due to WB MDTF closure and PFM Facility launch. BEK maintained close engagement to mitigate risks of slow reform progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme reprioritized to focus on foundational work (e.g., PFM Reform Strategy development, PEFA assessments) instead of direct reform implementation. PFM Facility provided on-demand support to adapt to emerging priorities (e.g., fiscal federalism synthesis, audit arrears management).
adaptive_management_examples: Refocused WB MDTF on process-oriented outputs (e.g., PFM Reform Strategy consultations) to bridge gap post-IPFMRP closure (2023).
PFM Facility quickly identified 7 fiduciary risk projects (e.g., public school audits, Karnali Province public finance analysis) in response to BEK’s evolving needs.
Adjusted capacity-building interventions to include subnational governments (e.g., Gandaki Province PEFA) after initial federal-level focus.

main_implementation_challenges: Slow progress in finalizing the 3–5-year PFM Reform Strategy due to consultative, government-led approach.
Limited subnational government participation in early strategy consultations (e.g., Madhesh, Gandaki provinces had mostly federal-level attendees).
Capacity gaps at subnational levels (e.g., local governments’ MTEF practices lack macroeconomic forecasting integration).
High staff turnover within GoN and delays in Cabinet approvals (e.g., PFM Reform Unit creation, Steering Committee revisions).
external_factors_impact: Economic slowdown in Nepal (federal revenue declined from 23.1% to 19.2% of GDP FY22–FY23), reducing fiscal space for reforms.
Post-pandemic recovery pressures diverted GoN attention from long-term PFM reforms.
Dependence on DP coordination (e.g., ADB, USAID funding for provincial PEFAs) introduced alignment challenges.
contextual_constraints_new: Legal framework barriers hindered subnational inclusion in PFM processes (e.g., IGFT system adjustments for NNRFC).
Political transitions at local/provincial levels disrupted continuity in reform engagement.
Unanticipated need for supplementary PEFA assessments (Gender-Responsive, Climate-Responsive) to address equity gaps.
partner_relationship_issues: Tension between GoN’s desire for ownership and DPs’ expectations for faster progress (e.g., PFM Strategy delays).
Limited alignment between WB MDTF’s process focus and BEK’s demand for catalytic technical assistance.
Transition from DT Global to Alinea required knowledge transfer and realignment of PFM Facility priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Subnational governments lacked capacity to contribute meaningfully to PFM Strategy consultations (e.g., limited representation in Madhesh/Gandaki workshops).
NNRFC’s technical/institutional capacity for Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (IGFT) remained insufficient despite CDNA action plans.
MoF’s PFM Reform Unit creation stalled due to Cabinet approval delays, limiting coordination.
risk_materialization: Moderate fiduciary risks materialized in school education sector (identified via Fiduciary Risk Assessments).
Delayed PFM Strategy approval risked misalignment with new WB MDTF phase (IPFMRP successor).
Currency/exchange rate fluctuations (not explicitly quantified) implied in cost management for international consultants.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: On track; provisional capital expenditure increased slightly in FY 2023/24 despite budget decrease. Average capital budget execution rate exceeded 60%.
budget_execution_vs_plan.wb_mdtf: Closed most components as planned, with residual funds focused on transitional activities (e.g., PEFA assessments).
budget_execution_vs_plan.pfm_facility: Budget reallocated to Alinea contract (post-July 2024) for knowledge products and fiduciary risk analyses.

value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Moderate. WB MDTF’s slow strategy finalization offset by unified DP platform reducing duplication. PFM Facility’s cross-sectoral approach improved cost efficiency.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High potential but not yet realized. Process-focused outputs (e.g., PEFA assessments, strategy consultations) laid groundwork for future impact. Effectiveness hinges on GoN’s political will to implement the PFM Strategy.
value_for_money_assessment.economy: Strong. Cross-cutting PFM Facility reduced costs by consolidating fiduciary risk analyses under one consultant. Mix of local/international experts optimized fees.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Improved. Supplementary PEFAs (Gender-Responsive, Climate-Responsive) and subnational consultations (e.g., Gandaki PEFA) addressed inclusivity gaps.
value_for_money_assessment.cost_efficiency: Achieved through: (1) Leveraging WB’s technical expertise for DP coordination; (2) PFM Facility’s portfolio-wide risk register reducing BEK’s oversight costs.

financial_management_quality.wb_mdtf: Sound. World Bank’s systems ensured transparent fund flows and compliance, though slower disbursement during transition.
financial_management_quality.pfm_facility: Alinea demonstrated rapid financial reporting and workplan adherence post-contract signing (July 2024).
financial_management_quality.government_systems: Challenges persisted in subnational financial management (e.g., audit arrears at local governments, identified via PFM Facility assessments).

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Higher than planned due to: (1) Reduced reliance on international consultants (local experts used for PEFAs); (2) Shared PFM Facility costs across BEK portfolio.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. ADB and EU provided budgetary support linked to PFM reforms, but co-funding for subnational PEFAs (e.g., Madhesh) required additional DP contributions (USAID, ADB).

key_delivery_lessons: Government-led reforms (e.g., PFM Strategy) enhance ownership but require prerequisites (e.g., PEFA-based indicators) to incentivize inclusivity.
Portfolio approach to fiduciary risk management (via PFM Facility) improves coherence and reduces BEK’s oversight burden.
Balancing process-oriented outputs (WB MDTF) with catalytic technical assistance (PFM Facility) mitigates risks of slow progress.
Subnational engagement must be prioritized earlier in reform cycles to avoid tokenistic inclusion (e.g., late consultations in Madhesh/Gandaki).
successful_delivery_practices: Unified DP platform (WB MDTF) strengthened advocacy for PLG inclusion in PFM reforms.
PFM Facility’s on-demand support (e.g., fiduciary risk assessments for NHSP, NREP) provided flexibility to address emerging priorities.
Collaborative PEFA assessments (e.g., Gandaki Province) built GoN capacity and transparency.
Mix of local/international consultants in PFM Facility reduced costs while maintaining expertise.
management_adaptations_made: Reprioritized WB MDTF to focus on foundational outputs (e.g., PFM Strategy development) post-IPFMRP closure.
Accelerated PFM Facility procurement (Alinea contract) to ensure continuity of technical assistance.
Introduced prerequisites for GoN in PFM Strategy development (e.g., PEFA-based indicators) to drive inclusivity.
innovations_attempted: Supplementary PEFA assessments (Gender-Responsive, Climate-Responsive) to mainstream equity in PFM reforms.
PFM Facility’s portfolio-level risk register to consolidate fiduciary risk management across BEK programmes.
Synthesis of existing evidence on fiscal federalism to inform subnational PFM interventions.

previous_recommendations_progress.2023_recommendation: Revise output descriptions to reflect outcome-level ambitions.
previous_recommendations_progress.status: Partially addressed. Output milestones were revised, but output descriptions remained unchanged. External factors (e.g., GoN delays) limited progress.
previous_recommendations_progress.justification: Focus shifted to adapting milestones to align with PFM Strategy development.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Update PFM MDTF II’s output indicators/milestones to align with the new PFM Reform Strategy (2025–2030) and WB MDTF’s next phase (IPFMRP successor).
forward_recommendations.action: PRO/lead adviser to revise log frame by September 2025, in consultation with WB and DPs.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Develop a robust M&E strategy for the PFM Reform Strategy, including subnational indicators and feedback loops.
forward_recommendations.action: PFM Facility to support MoF in designing M&E framework by March 2025.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Strengthen linkage between PFM MDTF II and BEK’s service delivery programmes (e.g., NHSP, NREP) by using PFM Facility for portfolio-wide fiduciary risk management.
forward_recommendations.action: PFM Facility to provide quarterly risk analyses to BEK programme teams by end-March 2025.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Enhance subnational inclusion in PFM reforms by: (1) Conducting at least two provincial consultations and one national workshop for the PFM Strategy; (2) Targeting capacity-building at SNGs (e.g., MTEF training).
forward_recommendations.action: MoF to finalize consultations by Q1 2025; PFM Facility to deliver SNG training by June 2025.

strengths: Proactive identification of fiduciary risks (e.g., school education sector, audit arrears) via PFM Facility assessments.
Use of prerequisites (e.g., PEFA-based indicators) in PFM Strategy development to mitigate implementation risks.
Portfolio-level risk register improved BEK’s ability to monitor cross-cutting risks.
weaknesses: Delayed Cabinet approvals (e.g., PFM Reform Unit) increased risk of reform stagnation.
Limited contingency planning for subnational capacity gaps (e.g., NNRFC’s IGFT role).
Over-reliance on DP coordination (e.g., ADB/USAID for provincial PEFAs) introduced alignment risks.
adaptations: PFM Facility’s on-demand support model allowed rapid response to emerging risks (e.g., fiscal federalism evidence synthesis).
WB MDTF’s prerequisites for GoN incentivized inclusive strategy development.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: GoN institutions (MoF, NNRFC, NPC), subnational governments (e.g., Gandaki Province PEFA), and DP programmes (NHSP, NREP) benefited from technical assistance and risk analyses.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Citizens of Nepal (potential long-term beneficiaries via improved PFM systems), though service delivery impacts are not yet measurable.

policy_influence_achieved: PFM Reform Strategy (2025–2030) development process influenced by PEFA assessments and DP coordination.
Subnational PEFAs (e.g., Gandaki) informed provincial PFM practices, with ADB/USAID adopting similar approaches.
NNRFC’s Fiscal Equalization Grant formula review incorporated PFM MDTF II inputs, though implementation awaits Cabinet approval.
capacity_building_results: GoN PEFA assessment team’s capacity strengthened through collaborative provincial PEFAs (e.g., Gandaki).
NNRFC’s capacity partially improved via CDNA and action plan, but institutionalization remains pending.
Local governments showed progress in MTEF adoption, though macroeconomic forecasting skills lag.

positive: Supplementary PEFAs (Gender/Climate-Responsive) created unintended momentum for equity-focused PFM reforms.
PFM Facility’s portfolio risk register improved BEK’s cross-programme risk awareness beyond PFM.
negative: Slow PFM Strategy finalization delayed donor alignment (e.g., WB MDTF successor project).
Focus on federal-level processes risked sidelining subnational priorities in early strategy drafts.

scalability_evidence: DP coordination model (WB MDTF) scalable to other sectors (e.g., health, education) via BEK’s PFM Facility.
Provincial PEFA approach (Gandaki) replicated in Madhesh with ADB/USAID funding, demonstrating scalability.
PFM Facility’s fiduciary risk tools (e.g., risk register) adaptable to other FCDO country programmes.

continuation_rationale.justification: PFM MDTF II remains the primary UK vehicle for PFM reforms in Nepal’s federal context. The transitional period successfully laid groundwork for the PFM Reform Strategy (2025–2030), with high potential for long-term impact if political will is sustained.
evidence: Improved DP coordination (e.g., ADB/EU budgetary support linked to PFM reforms).
GoN ownership of PFM Strategy development, despite delays.
PFM Facility’s agility in addressing emerging priorities (e.g., fiduciary risks in health/education sectors).
risks: GoN’s slow decision-making (e.g., Cabinet approvals) may hinder strategy implementation.
Subnational capacity gaps could limit reform scalability.
Dependence on DP funding (e.g., for provincial PEFAs) introduces sustainability risks.

programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium-High (contingent on GoN’s political commitment and DP alignment)

strengths: Unified DP platform (WB MDTF) reduces duplication and enhances leverage.
PFM Facility’s flexible, demand-driven model aligns with BEK’s evolving needs.
GoN-led reforms (e.g., PFM Strategy) ensure local ownership.
weaknesses: Over-reliance on Cabinet approvals for critical structures (e.g., PFM Reform Unit).
Limited subnational institutional capacity may undermine federalism objectives.
Transition risks between WB MDTF phases (e.g., IPFMRP successor delays).
delivery_model_sustainability.long_term_feasibility: Moderate. Sustainable if: (1) PFM Strategy is approved and resourced; (2) subnational capacity-building is prioritized; (3) DP coordination persists.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied (with caveats)
planned_adaptations_future: Align PFM MDTF II outputs with the new PFM Reform Strategy (2025–2030) and WB MDTF’s next phase (post-IPFMRP).
Expand PFM Facility’s role to provide M&E support for the PFM Strategy and portfolio-wide fiduciary risk management.
Increase subnational engagement via targeted consultations (e.g., Koshi Province) and capacity-building (e.g., MTEF training for local governments).
Integrate PFM MDTF II into the broader Sahakarya programme to enhance coherence with UK’s Nepal portfolio.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Transparency and Accountability to improve economic development and service delivery (TRACTION)

output_1.title: PEAs completed, IBPs identified, selected and designed, advice on media and advocacy provided

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Extension of MEIP programme due to post-election challenges; no-cost extension for UNDP MECS project pending court case resolution; adaptive management in response to political instability and violence.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: MEIP (NDI/IFES) delivered post-election analysis and conflict resolution support but faced delays due to violence; UNDP MECS had limited activity due to court case delays; Palladium's inception phase completed but with team capability challenges and slower-than-expected startup.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme Advisory Committee (PAC) established with DFID advisors, Palladium leadership, and Malawian experts; fortnightly progress reviews between DFID SRO/lead advisor and Palladium senior management; quarterly meetings with Palladium Project Director to review supplier indicators.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Multiparty Liaison Committees (MPLCs) effectively mediated election-related violence in some by-elections (e.g., Matenje Ward), though Lilongwe South by-election was postponed. Coordination with USAID/NDI on electoral reforms was strong, but UNDP coordination stalled due to legal uncertainties.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Palladium renegotiated milestone costings for greater transparency; DFID donated a vehicle to reduce Palladium’s operational costs (saving £300/month). Hotel rate negotiations saved £44/night per person.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to team capability issues and political context; DFID engaged closely with Palladium to address setup challenges and milestone alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to post-election violence by extending MEIP and reallocating resources to conflict resolution; Palladium’s issue-based approach (e.g., seeds certification pilot) reflects adaptive learning from other DFID programmes (e.g., I4ID in Tanzania).
adaptive_management_examples: Extension of MEIP to address post-election violence and reform gaps, including early warning/conflict resolution mechanisms.
Palladium’s use of evidence from DFID’s I4ID programme (Tanzania) to design issue selection criteria.
No-cost extension for UNDP MECS to align with court case timeline, with revised workplan to follow judgment.
Revised milestone costing approach for Year 2 to improve transparency and value for money.

main_implementation_challenges: Post-election violence and protests (destruction of property, deaths, alleged rapes) disrupted activities, particularly in Karonga and Msundwe.
Delayed court judgment on electoral disputes stalled UNDP MECS activities and institutional capacity-building.
Team capability gaps and slow startup in Palladium’s Issues-Based Accountability component, including unfilled positions and milestone quality issues.
Political uncertainty and mixed signals from parties regarding acceptance of court judgments, complicating reform advocacy.
external_factors_impact: Election-related violence (May 2019) created security risks and delayed by-elections (e.g., Lilongwe South postponement).
Constitutional court case (ongoing) froze UNDP’s electoral support activities, requiring a no-cost extension.
Political polarization hindered consensus on electoral reforms, requiring additional mediation efforts.
contextual_constraints_new: Need for early warning/conflict resolution mechanisms not anticipated in original design.
Legal delays exposed lack of contingency planning for prolonged judicial processes.
Gender and social inclusion requirements (e.g., 46% women trained as LTOs/STOs) added implementation complexity.
partner_relationship_issues: UNDP’s limited activity due to court case created tension with donors over basket fund utilization.
Palladium’s team capability issues required DFID intervention to realign milestones and costs.
USAID/NDI collaboration on MEIP was effective, but power analysis gaps (e.g., stakeholder interests in reforms) were identified as a weakness.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Palladium’s core team had gaps in political economy analysis (PEA) expertise, delaying issue-based project design.
MEC’s institutional capacity (e.g., financial management) required additional UNDP support beyond original scope.
Civil society partners lacked resources for sustained electoral reform advocacy post-MEIP extension.
risk_materialization: Political violence risk (high) materialized, requiring MEIP extensions and conflict mitigation strategies.
Legal/regulatory risk (moderate) materialized via court case delays, stalling UNDP activities.
Implementation capacity risk (moderate) materialized in Palladium’s team, necessitating DFID oversight.

budget_execution_vs_plan: MEIP: Extended with focused scope; costs tightly controlled but required additional DFID-USAID coordination.
UNDP MECS: Under-spent due to court delays; no-cost extension approved to realign spending with revised timeline.
Palladium: Inception phase costs higher than planned due to team gaps; Year 2 milestone costs renegotiated for transparency.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Achieved via MEIP extension’s targeted scope and UNDP no-cost extension; Palladium saved £300/month (vehicle) and £44/night (hotels).
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Improved through milestone renegotiation and reduced upfront costs; DFID’s close engagement enhanced cost transparency.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Partial—MEIP delivered conflict resolution and reform analysis, but UNDP’s stalled activities and Palladium’s slow startup reduced overall efficiency.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Gender inclusion met (46% women LTOs/STOs; 23% women MPs in training); social inclusion analysis underway for future phases.
value_for_money_assessment.evidence_use: Strong—Palladium incorporated lessons from DFID’s I4ID programme (Tanzania) into issue selection.

financial_management_quality: Palladium: Initially weak (delays in financial manuals/asset registers) but improved with DFID oversight; VfM indicators to be finalized by January 2020.
UNDP: Adequate but limited activity due to court case; financial management for CMD (Centre for Multiparty Democracy) strengthened.
USAID/NDI: No major issues reported; MEIP extension costs justified by post-election needs.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Palladium: £300/month saved via vehicle donation; £44/night saved on hotels; milestone costs reduced through renegotiation.
UNDP: No-cost extension avoided fund loss but delayed results.
MEIP: Cost-effective due to delegated cooperation with USAID, leveraging existing NDI/IFES structures.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not explicitly mentioned; UNDP basket fund relies on multiple donors, but no new co-funding secured during this period.

key_delivery_lessons: Adaptive management is critical in politically volatile contexts (e.g., MEIP’s conflict resolution role post-elections).
Delegated cooperation (USAID/NDI) can accelerate delivery but requires clear power analysis to avoid reform stalls.
No-cost extensions are useful for legal delays but require explicit contingency planning for stalled activities.
Team capability gaps must be addressed early to avoid milestone slippage (e.g., Palladium’s PEA expertise).
successful_delivery_practices: Multiparty Liaison Committees (MPLCs) effectively mediated election violence in some by-elections.
DFID’s close oversight of Palladium improved milestone alignment and cost transparency.
Use of existing evidence (e.g., I4ID Tanzania) to design issue selection criteria saved time and resources.
Gender inclusion targets (46% women LTOs/STOs) demonstrated commitment to equity.
management_adaptations_made: Added quarterly DFID-Palladium meetings to monitor supplier indicators.
Revised milestone costing approach for Year 2 to link payments to results and level of effort.
Extended MEIP and UNDP MECS timelines to align with political/legal realities.
Established PAC with Malawian experts to guide adaptive programming.
innovations_attempted: Pilot issue-based approach (e.g., seeds certification) to test methodology before scaling.
Early warning/conflict resolution mechanisms integrated into MEIP post-violence.
Power analysis tool proposed for NDI to map stakeholder interests in electoral reforms.
previous_recommendations_progress: MEIP extended as recommended, but follow-on Constitutional Review process remains unfunded.
Palladium’s team gaps partially addressed, but capability concerns persist.
UNDP MECS no-cost extension approved, but post-judgment workplan pending.
forward_recommendations: DFID to finalize VfM indicators with Palladium by January 2020 and revise logframe by February 2020.
Secure additional funding or partner support for post-MEIP Constitutional Review process.
Strengthen Palladium’s team capacity, particularly in PEA and issue-based project design.
Intensify mediation efforts with political parties to ensure peaceful acceptance of court judgments.
Develop a strategy for electoral reform advocacy beyond MEIP’s extension period, engaging other donors if needed.
Conduct a Gender and Social Inclusion analysis to inform future project design.
risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective—political violence and legal risks were mitigated via extensions and adaptive programming, but team capacity risks required reactive management.
Risk of stalled UNDP activities was addressed with no-cost extension, but proactive contingency planning was lacking.
Electoral reform risks (e.g., stakeholder resistance) were identified but not fully resolved due to limited power analysis.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.MEIP: Trained 46% women among LTOs/STOs; 23% women MPs in orientation sessions (44/192).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.UNDP MECS: Limited direct beneficiaries due to court delays; institutional support to Centre for Multiparty Democracy ongoing.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.Palladium: Inception phase only; no direct beneficiaries yet, but Social Accountability and PEA approaches designed.

policy_influence_achieved: MEIP’s review of 2014–2017 electoral reform failures informed strategy for post-2019 advocacy.
MPLCs’ role in mediating by-election violence recognized by Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC).
Palladium’s pilot (seeds certification) may influence agricultural governance if successful.
capacity_building_results: MEIP: Trained LTOs/STOs on election observation; supported MEC’s conflict resolution via MPLCs.
UNDP: Strengthened financial governance at Centre for Multiparty Democracy.
Palladium: Developed Social Accountability and PEA frameworks for future capacity-building.
unintended_consequences: Positive: MPLCs’ conflict mediation gained unexpected credibility with MEC, potentially strengthening future election security.
Negative: Post-election violence delayed by-elections and reform processes, eroding trust in institutions.
scalability_evidence: MEIP’s conflict resolution mechanisms (MPLCs) could scale to other high-risk elections with additional funding.
Palladium’s issue-based approach (if successful in seeds certification pilot) may be replicable in other sectors.
Limited evidence for UNDP MECS scalability due to stalled activities.

continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates potential for transformative change in accountability and service delivery despite challenges.
MEIP’s conflict resolution and reform advocacy remain critical post-election.
Palladium’s adaptive approach (e.g., pilots, PEA) aligns with FCDO’s politically informed programming.
UNDP MECS extension ensures electoral cycle support continues pending court resolution.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium—high for MEIP (due to adaptive management), medium for Palladium (dependent on team capacity improvements), low for UNDP MECS (pending court outcome).
delivery_model_sustainability: MEIP’s delegated cooperation with USAID is sustainable but requires continued donor coordination.
Palladium’s model is sustainable if team gaps are filled and VfM indicators met.
UNDP basket fund model is at risk if court delays persist or co-funding declines.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate—concerns about Palladium’s startup delays and UNDP’s stalled activities, but MEIP’s performance and adaptive responses are positively viewed.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize revised logframe and theory of change by February 2020.
Implement Palladium’s seeds certification pilot and expand if successful.
Develop a post-MEIP electoral reform strategy with Malawian stakeholders and other donors.
Strengthen UNDP MECS workplan post-court judgment, focusing on institutional capacity.
Conduct Gender and Social Inclusion analysis to inform future phases.
Explore additional funding for Constitutional Review process beyond MEIP extension.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Support to the Palestinian Authority to Deliver Basic Services, Build Stability and Promote Reform in the Occupied Palestinian Territories

output_1.title: Front-line education and health workers supported through salary provision by DFID

output_2.title: Service delivery supported by DFID

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme initially planned as an integrated package of financial aid, technical assistance, and monitoring/evaluation, but only financial aid component is operational due to delays in launching other components. Financial aid is delivered through the EU PEGASE mechanism rather than direct budget support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: European Union Representative Office (EUREP) has performed robustly in vetting beneficiary civil servant salaries through monthly eligibility checks, global payroll audits every 18-24 months, and field visits based on risk assessment. Independent auditors conduct ex-ante and ex-post audits to ensure compliance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Management is led by DFID’s Conflict Security and Justice Group, with oversight from an economic adviser, policy manager, Senior Responsible Owner (SRO), and programme manager. First annual review was conducted with limited prior institutional knowledge of the programme.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Donor coordination on Public Financial Management (PFM) reform priorities is identified as a gap; multiple organizations (e.g., World Bank) are providing financial contributions to the PA with potentially misaligned incentives. DFID is urged to commit advisory time to align donor incentives with PA priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components has experienced delays, with both components planned for launch in 2018. Two financial aid disbursements were successfully made (£25m in February 2017 and £20m in November 2017).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight is intensive due to the "Severe" risk rating. Strong safeguards and controls are in place, including monthly payroll eligibility scrutiny, global audits, and field visits by EUREP, complemented by independent audits.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme flexibility has been limited by the delay in launching technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components. Financial aid tranches are conditional on PA meeting KPI milestones, allowing some adaptability in response to reform progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: The programme adapted to the PA’s fiscal constraints and external shocks (e.g., Gaza administrative control costs) by maintaining financial aid while preparing to integrate technical assistance. KPIs are currently set on a 6-month basis, though the review recommends shifting to annual milestones linked to long-term structural reforms.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in launching technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components, limiting the programme’s ability to drive institutional reform and measure impact effectively.
Complex political and economic context in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (OPTs), including fiscal crisis, uncertain economic outlook, and vulnerability to external shocks.
Emerging challenge of the PA resuming administrative control in Gaza, increasing financial pressure on the PA’s budget.
Limited data availability for education sector outcomes due to the Palestinian school year reporting format, hindering progress monitoring.
external_factors_impact: Political instability and fiscal crisis in the OPTs have constrained the PA’s ability to implement reforms and sustain service delivery.
External shocks (e.g., changes in donor funding, regional conflicts) pose risks to the PA’s fiscal stability and programme sustainability.
The cost of resuming administrative control in Gaza has diverted PA resources, increasing reliance on external financial assistance.
contextual_constraints_new: The need for the PA to balance service delivery in the West Bank with new financial obligations in Gaza, which was not fully anticipated in the programme design.
Greater-than-expected challenges in aligning donor incentives (e.g., World Bank, other donors) with the PA’s PFM reform priorities, leading to potential fragmentation of efforts.
partner_relationship_issues: No significant partner relationship issues reported with EUREP, which has effectively managed the PEGASE mechanism. However, coordination with other donors (e.g., World Bank) on PFM reforms requires improvement to avoid misaligned incentives.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited PA capacity to disaggregate education data (primary vs. lower secondary) for reporting, requiring programme adaptations to combine indicators temporarily.
Delayed launch of technical assistance has limited the programme’s ability to build PA institutional capacity in PFM and education sectors.
risk_materialization: The "Severe" risk rating reflects the high-stakes political and fiscal environment in the OPTs, which has materialized as anticipated. Strong safeguards (e.g., EUREP audits, KPI-linked disbursements) have mitigated but not eliminated risks associated with financial aid delivery.
The risk of misaligned donor priorities has materialized, requiring DFID to invest in coordination efforts to harmonize incentives with the PA’s reform agenda.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Financial aid component (£125m allocated) has executed as planned, with two disbursements made: £25m in February 2017 and £20m in November 2017. Technical assistance (£12.5m) and monitoring/evaluation (£0.5m) components have not yet been disbursed due to delays.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: The programme is judged to represent "good" Value for Money (VfM), with the strongest evidence for *economy* (cost-effective delivery through PEGASE mechanism). Evidence for *efficiency* and *effectiveness* is less articulated. VfM could be improved by refining logframe indicators to better capture PA performance and DFID’s contribution to results.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by implementers (EUREP) is robust, with monthly payroll vetting, global audits every 18-24 months, field visits, and independent ex-ante/ex-post audits ensuring compliance with DFID rules. No significant financial management issues reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The use of the PEGASE mechanism (shared with other donors) has achieved cost efficiencies in disbursing financial aid. However, the fixed nature of DFID’s financial contribution means that rising PA salary costs (without corresponding increases in DFID funding) could reduce DFID’s attributable impact over time.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding through the PEGASE mechanism (multi-donor platform) is functioning as planned, with DFID’s funds earmarked specifically for health and education salaries in the West Bank. No issues reported with co-funding materialization.

key_delivery_lessons: Financial aid alone is insufficient to drive sustained reform; technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation are critical to maximizing impact and ensuring accountability.

Conditionality linked to KPI milestones is effective in incentivizing PA reform progress, but short-term (6-month) KPIs may not align well with long-term structural reforms. Annual milestones are recommended.
Donor coordination is essential to avoid fragmented incentives and ensure alignment with PA priorities, particularly in PFM reforms.
successful_delivery_practices: The PEGASE mechanism has proven effective for transparent and auditable disbursement of financial aid, with strong safeguards (e.g., monthly vetting, global audits, field visits).

Linking financial aid tranches to KPI milestones has successfully driven PA progress in PFM and education reforms, as evidenced by the achievement of all 2017 KPIs and finalization of the National Policy Agenda (NPA).
The programme’s focus on salary support for frontline health and education workers has directly contributed to service delivery continuity (e.g., 39,500 workers and 24,000 pupils supported).
management_adaptations_made: The review highlights the need to shift from 6-month to annual KPI milestones to better align with long-term reform objectives.
Plans to prioritize procurement of technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components in 2018 to address current gaps in institutional reform and impact measurement.
Recommendation to update the logframe to include indicators that measure both PA’s overall performance and DFID’s specific contribution, improving VfM articulation.
innovations_attempted: The integrated design of financial aid, technical assistance, and monitoring/evaluation (though not yet fully operational) represents an innovative approach to linking service delivery with institutional reform.
Use of independent auditors for ex-ante/ex-post audits and field visits adds rigor to the financial aid disbursement process.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: This is the first annual review; no previous recommendations exist.
forward_recommendations: Prioritize the launch of technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components to drive institutional reform and measure impact.
Develop long-term KPIs with annual milestones to replace the current 6-month cycle, ensuring alignment with sustainable structural reforms.
Enhance donor coordination on PFM reform priorities to avoid misaligned incentives and fragmentations.
Refine the logframe to include indicators that capture both PA performance and DFID’s attribution, improving VfM reporting.
Task the monitoring and evaluation supplier with developing a robust VfM strategy that balances economy, efficiency, and effectiveness.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management has been effective in mitigating financial and compliance risks through robust safeguards (e.g., EUREP audits, KPI-linked disbursements). However, the "Severe" risk rating persists due to the volatile political and fiscal context. Risk management could be strengthened by addressing donor coordination gaps and integrating technical assistance to build PA resilience.

pupils_supported.disaggregation: Combined primary (Grades 1-6) and lower secondary (Grades 7-10) due to data limitations

policy_influence_achieved: The programme contributed to the finalization of the PA’s National Policy Agenda (NPA) and credible sector strategies, particularly in PFM and education.
All 2017 KPI milestones for PFM and education reforms were met, indicating progress in policy implementation.
The programme’s financial aid is conditional on reform progress, incentivizing policy changes (e.g., reduced recurrent deficit despite fiscal constraints).
capacity_building_results: Limited capacity building results to date due to delays in launching the technical assistance component. Financial aid has supported service delivery continuity but has not yet driven institutional capacity gains.
The programme’s design includes plans for technical assistance to strengthen PA core state systems (e.g., PFM, education), but these are not yet operational.
unintended_consequences: Positive: The programme’s salary support has helped maintain stability in the West Bank by ensuring continuity of basic services (health and education) during fiscal crises.

Negative: The fixed financial aid amount may reduce DFID’s attributable impact over time if PA salaries rise without corresponding increases in DFID funding. Additionally, the focus on the West Bank excludes Gaza, where service delivery needs are also acute.
scalability_evidence: The PEGASE mechanism demonstrates scalability as a multi-donor platform for financial aid disbursement, though its effectiveness depends on the PA’s reform commitment and donor coordination.
The integrated model of financial aid + technical assistance (once operational) could be scalable to other sectors or regions if aligned with PA priorities and donor strategies.

continuation_rationale: The programme has achieved its financial aid objectives (e.g., salary support, KPI-linked reforms) and demonstrates progress toward stability and service delivery in the West Bank.
The PA remains reliant on external assistance to deliver basic services and implement reforms, particularly given emerging challenges (e.g., Gaza administrative costs).

The launch of technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components in 2018 is expected to address current gaps in institutional reform and impact measurement, unlocking the programme’s full potential.
The programme aligns with UK objectives to preserve the viability of the two-state solution by supporting PA effectiveness and fiscal stability.
delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model (financial aid via PEGASE) is sustainable in the short term but requires complementarity with technical assistance to drive long-term institutional reforms.
Sustainability is contingent on continued donor coordination, PA commitment to reforms, and adaptation to external shocks (e.g., fiscal crises, political instability).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (based on achievement of financial aid objectives and KPI milestones, though concerns remain about delayed technical assistance and VfM articulation).
planned_adaptations_future: Launch technical assistance and monitoring/evaluation components in 2018 to enhance institutional reform and impact measurement.
Shift from 6-month to annual KPI milestones to better align with long-term reform objectives.
Improve donor coordination on PFM reforms to harmonize incentives with PA priorities.
Refine the logframe and VfM strategy to better capture efficiency and effectiveness, not just economy.
Explore options to address data limitations in the education sector (e.g., disaggregation of primary vs. lower secondary outcomes).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Cross-Border: Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT)

output_1.title: Policy-relevant research, evidence and recommendations are generated and documented about conflict-affected borderlands, cross-border and regional conflict dynamics, drivers of violent and peaceful behaviour, and associated policy responses

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift toward more ambitious output targets for C2 and C3 in response to Annual Review feedback; mid-year budget/workplan adjustments for C1 partners. Introduction of thematic XRF Fellows to replace a single Research Director role.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (C1: TAF, RVI, Carnegie; C2: Chemonics, Chatham House, Conciliation Resources; C3: Chemonics, KCL) met or exceeded targets despite challenges. C1 partners adapted to significant mid-year budget/workplan changes. Demand from both delivery partners and HMG for more co-creation opportunities in research design and dissemination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Research Leadership Group (RLG) plays a central role in coordination. Cross-HMG Advisory Group (XHAG) under review for potential restructuring to align with XCEPT’s three thematic research areas. FCDO Project-Funded Post (PFP) links programme to HMG departments (Cabinet Office, MoD).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Good progress in cross-Component research dissemination (e.g., joint panels, briefings). Coordination with other FCDO RED-funded programmes (PeaceRep, SOC ACE, SPARC) identified as an area for improvement. RLG facilitates synthesis of cross-cutting findings.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in responding to crises (e.g., rapid briefings on Gaza, Niger, Sudan). Adaptive management seen in logframe revisions (e.g., separating journal articles/working papers/blogs for tracking) and thematic pivot toward XRF Fellows model.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised logframe indicators to clarify research uptake pathways (e.g., distinguishing dissemination vs. early-stage engagement in indicator 2.1).
Rapid response to emerging crises (Gaza, Niger, Sudan) with targeted briefings.
Transition from a single Research Director to thematic XRF Fellows to better align with research areas.
Adjustment of output weightings and introduction of new Outcome 2 indicator to reflect Theory of Change updates.

main_implementation_challenges: Ambiguity in logframe indicators (e.g., conflation of journal articles, working papers, blogs) leading to tracking difficulties.
Mid-year budget/workplan changes for C1 partners requiring adaptation.
Balancing ambitious output targets (doubled for C2/C3) with quality and stakeholder engagement.
Recruitment challenges for a programme-wide Research Director, resolved by shifting to thematic XRF Fellows.
external_factors_impact: Evolving crises (e.g., Gaza, Niger, Sudan) required rapid reprioritization of research outputs.
Increased demand for XCEPT’s research lens from HMG stakeholders due to geopolitical shifts (e.g., UK Integrated Review Refresh priorities on transnational security, SOC, terrorism).
contextual_constraints_new: Need for deeper engagement with local communities in conflict-affected contexts, requiring innovative methods (e.g., satellite data, big data, machine learning) to access hard-to-reach areas.
Expanding research uptake among practitioners while maintaining academic rigor.
partner_relationship_issues: HMG and partners expressed desire for more co-creation opportunities in research design and dissemination phases.

risk_materialization: Persistent "Major" risk rating reflects ongoing challenges in conflict-affected geographies and complexity of transnational research coordination.

successful_delivery_practices: Responsive research production (e.g., rapid briefings on emerging crises) strengthened HMG trust.

innovations_attempted: Use of big data and machine learning to analyze conflict dynamics in borderlands.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Productivity for Prosperity Programme

output_1.title: Aceli Africa. Mobilising investment for job-creating domestic agri-business ($15k-$1.75m ticket size), through (1) financial risk-sharing and (2) technical assistance to businesses and local/regional financial institutions.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme added a new component with ODI, requiring adjustments to impact weightings of existing components (reduced by 1-2% each). Aceli joined working groups with Tanzania Bankers Association (TBA) and Financial Sector Deepening Tanzania (FSDT) to address policy issues (loan classifications, collateral registry, leasing laws).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Aceli exceeded targets for technical assistance to businesses (46 vs. 34 planned, with 18 meeting 2x gender criteria) and loans approved (111 vs. 101 planned, with 72 meeting gender criteria). However, it moderately missed the target for active lending partners (9 vs. 10 planned). Manufacturing Africa (MA) onboarded local experts with strong networks, strengthening deal sourcing and contextual assessments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: A P4P coordination committee was established and met twice during the year, serving as an effective oversight platform for partner workstreams. The committee ensures alignment across Aceli, MA, GGF, and ODI.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Close coordination between P4P partners (Aceli, MA, GGF, ODI) was critical due to rapid onboarding of three new components. MA benefited from referrals from GGF partners, demonstrating cross-component synergy. The coordination committee helped mitigate risks of siloed implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO and partners maintained active oversight, particularly during the inception phase of new components (GGF, MA Tanzania expansion). Oversight included regular coordination meetings, political economy risk assessments, and alignment checks with Government of Tanzania priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: P4P’s flexible design allowed rapid response to emerging priorities, such as revising the investment target upward from £50mn to £100mn in 2023 based on partner forecasts. The programme also adapted to include climate resilience and food security focuses in MA’s Tanzania expansion.
adaptive_management_examples: Aceli joined policy working groups (TBA, FSDT) to address systemic barriers in agribusiness financing, expanding beyond its original technical assistance scope.
MA paused government engagement until GGF’s role was clearer, then realigned its logframe to the P4P Business Case.
GGF’s inception phase included scoping and relationship-building activities to tailor its technical assistance to Tanzania’s context, adjusting its initial workplan.

main_implementation_challenges: Navigating political economy constraints in Tanzania, particularly in sectors prone to interference (e.g., agribusiness value chains).
Ensuring additionality of private sector support amid risks of politically exposed persons or regulatory blocks.
Balancing rapid mobilisation of new components (MA, GGF, ODI) with limited inception periods (e.g., GGF had only 3 months of inception).
Meeting ambitious targets for job creation (10,000 jobs) and income support (125,000 people) while managing partner coordination.
external_factors_impact: The signing of the *Mutual Prosperity Partnership* (April 2024) between the UK and Tanzania provided a new framework for alignment but required partners to adjust workplans by October 2024.
Government of Tanzania policies (e.g., Vision 2050, Investment Act) influenced programme priorities, necessitating alignment via annual workplan agreements.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated delays in government engagement due to unclear roles between MA and GGF during inception.
Higher-than-expected political economy risks in manufacturing and agribusiness sectors, requiring strengthened analysis and mitigation strategies.
partner_relationship_issues: MA’s initial work with the Government of Tanzania was paused until GGF’s scope was defined, creating temporary coordination gaps.
Aceli faced challenges with one financial institution (Exim Bank) not yet active, despite signed agreements.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GGF’s lean team (admin-focused during inception) struggled to fully establish workstreams within the short 3-month inception phase.
MA’s reliance on a small pool of local consultants required careful management to avoid overburdening resources.
risk_materialization: The *Major* risk rating persisted due to political economy challenges, particularly in sectors like manufacturing and agribusiness where regulatory changes or political interference could disrupt private sector engagements.
Risks related to additionality and business integrity in private sector partnerships required active management, as noted in MA’s deal facilitation.

budget_execution_vs_plan.aceli: Spent 30% of total budget on management costs (including central staffing), deemed proportionate for a market-facilitation programme. Leveraged £4.5 in private investment for every £1 of UK funding (1:4.5 ratio).
budget_execution_vs_plan.ma: Maintained 88% of staff days charged at or below the £874 target rate (vs. 80% target). Achieved a regional leverage ratio of £22 for every £1 spent.
budget_execution_vs_plan.ggf: Reported 41% programme spend as a percentage of total spend in the first year, attributed to inception-phase activities (scoping, relationship-building). Expected to decline in subsequent years as workstreams mature.
budget_execution_vs_plan.odi: Too early to report; component commenced in August 2023.

value_for_money_assessment.aceli: High VfM: 69% of loans went to first-time borrowers, with repeat borrowers showing 26% average revenue growth. Leverage ratio (1:4.5) exceeds similar FCDO initiatives (e.g., Tanzania Agribusiness Window at 1:2).
value_for_money_assessment.ma: High VfM: Standardised templates and phased project delivery improved efficiency. Regional resource-sharing (e.g., consultants transferred between countries) reduced costs.
value_for_money_assessment.ggf: Moderate VfM: Early-stage costs were high due to inception activities, but expected to improve as technical assistance scales up.
value_for_money_assessment.overall: The programme’s VfM was rated positively, with most components meeting or exceeding leverage targets. Co-funding materialised as planned, with partners contributing to the revised £100mn investment target.

financial_management_quality.aceli: Lean structure (2 local staff + regional/US support) maintained cost efficiency. Financial incentives were effectively targeted to cover additional costs for partners (e.g., fuel, market studies).
financial_management_quality.ma: Strong cost management through balanced use of experienced team members and local consultants. Charge-out rates were kept within FCDO-agreed thresholds.
financial_management_quality.ggf: Administrative costs were high in Year 1 (41% of spend) but justified by inception needs. Financial systems were established to track Statement of Work expenditures.

cost_efficiency_achieved.aceli: Operated with a 30% management cost ratio, considered justifiable for its technical and market-development focus.
cost_efficiency_achieved.ma: Achieved cost savings by reusing commercial due diligence and TA studies across deals, and standardising deal-support templates.
cost_efficiency_achieved.ggf: Efficiency expected to improve post-inception as technical assistance delivery ramps up.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: The investment target was revised upward from £50mn to £100mn in 2023 due to stronger-than-expected co-funding commitments from onboarded partners. MA’s regional leverage (£22 per £1 spent) demonstrates significant co-funding mobilisation.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible programme design enabled rapid adaptation to emerging priorities (e.g., climate resilience, food security) and target revisions (e.g., investment goal increased to £100mn).
Coordination mechanisms (e.g., P4P committee) were critical to managing the complexity of multiple partners and new components.
Local expertise (e.g., MA’s Tanzanian consultants) accelerated contextual understanding and deal sourcing.
successful_delivery_practices: Aceli’s use of origination incentives to cover partners’ additional costs (e.g., fuel for SME visits) successfully expanded geographic coverage and product innovation (e.g., warehouse receipt loans).
MA’s standardised templates (e.g., Support Approval Committee forms) improved efficiency in deal facilitation and phased delivery reduced implementation risks.
GGF’s demand-driven technical assistance model (e.g., embedded advisers) aligned well with government and private sector needs.
management_adaptations_made: Impact weightings were adjusted to accommodate the new ODI component, ensuring continued focus on high-priority outputs.
Political economy analysis was strengthened across partners (especially MA) to mitigate risks in politically sensitive sectors.
Gender and geographic inclusion were identified as areas for improved mainstreaming in future workplans.
innovations_attempted: Aceli’s collaboration with ecosystem partners (e.g., AGRA, SAGCOT) to form a working group addressing policy barriers in agribusiness financing.
MA’s focus on climate-resilient and food-security-aligned investments in Tanzania, expanding its traditional FDI facilitation role.
GGF’s rapid, flexible technical assistance model, including embedded advisers to unlock systemic constraints.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: MA onboarded local experts and prioritised transaction facilitation pipeline development.
Ongoing: Alignment of MA’s logframe with the P4P Business Case and deeper engagement with Government of Tanzania.
Planned: Strengthened political economy analysis and risk management to be included in partners’ workplans by October 2024.
forward_recommendations: Align all partner workplans with the *Mutual Prosperity Partnership* and Government of Tanzania policies (e.g., Vision 2050) by October 2024.
Enhance political economy analysis, particularly for MA and GGF, to identify feasible intervention points and mitigate risks of regulatory blocks.
Improve gender mainstreaming and geographic inclusion, building on 2x Challenge progress to date.
Leverage GGF’s strengths in political economy to support risk management across P4P, including regular briefings to BHC.
Continue active coordination among partners to ensure the programme delivers more than the sum of its parts, particularly in business environment reforms.

strengths: Proactive identification of political economy risks (e.g., MA’s analysis of politically exposed sectors).
Cross-partner coordination (e.g., GGF sharing insights with MA and Aceli) improved collective risk awareness.
Flexible design allowed adjustments to mitigate risks (e.g., pausing MA’s government engagement until GGF’s role was clear).
weaknesses: Persistent *Major* risk rating indicates ongoing challenges in managing political and regulatory risks, particularly in agribusiness and manufacturing.
Some risks materialised (e.g., delays in government engagement due to unclear partner roles during inception).
adaptations: GGF will include risk management support (analysis, briefings) in its 2024 workplan.
Partners will strengthen additionality evidence to justify private sector subsidies and comply with FCDO policies.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.jobs: Progress toward 10,000 jobs target not quantified in this review; MA regionally generated 28,699 jobs (not Tanzania-specific).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.incomes: Progress toward 125,000 people with increased incomes not quantified; GGF targets 25,000 people.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.investment: Aceli facilitated USD13.4mn in loans to Tanzanian SMEs by March 2024 (vs. USD44mn forecast by 2025). MA regionally mobilised £989mn in investment (not Tanzania-specific).

policy_influence_achieved: Aceli’s participation in working groups (TBA, FSDT) contributed to policy discussions on loan classifications, collateral registries, and leasing laws.
GGF’s technical assistance supports Government of Tanzania’s economic planning (e.g., Tanzania Development Vision 2050).
The *Mutual Prosperity Partnership* (April 2024) provides a framework for aligning P4P with UK-Tanzania trade/investment priorities.
capacity_building_results: Aceli provided technical assistance to 46 businesses (18 meeting 2x gender criteria) and 1 financial institution (Tanzania Commercial Bank).
MA’s local expert recruitment strengthened deal-sourcing and contextual assessment capabilities in Tanzania.
GGF’s embedded advisers and policy research aim to build government and private sector capacity to unlock investments.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Aceli’s incentives enabled Tanzania Commercial Bank to expand into new geographic areas and develop innovative loan products (e.g., warehouse receipts).
Negative: None explicitly reported, though political economy risks could lead to unintended disruptions in private sector engagements.
scalability_evidence: Aceli’s model (loan guarantees + technical assistance) has demonstrated scalability, with plans to facilitate 200+ loans by 2025.
MA’s regional success (£22 leverage ratio) suggests potential for scaling its FDI facilitation approach in Tanzania.
GGF’s flexible, demand-driven technical assistance model is designed for replication in other sectors/geographies.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (consistent *A* ratings) and successful mobilisation of new components (MA, GGF, ODI).
Revised investment target (£100mn) reflects increased partner co-funding and alignment with UK climate finance commitments.
Flexible design allows adaptation to emerging priorities (e.g., climate resilience, food security).
Partners have demonstrated ability to leverage private investment (e.g., Aceli’s 1:4.5 ratio, MA’s £22:£1 regional leverage).

strengths: Coordination committee ensures cross-partner alignment and oversight.
Local expertise (e.g., MA’s Tanzanian consultants) enhances contextual relevance.
Demand-driven technical assistance (GGF) and flexible funding (Aceli) adapt to evolving needs.
risks: Persistent *Major* risk rating highlights ongoing political economy and regulatory challenges.
Sustainability of government engagement depends on alignment with Tanzania’s policy priorities (e.g., Vision 2050).
Long-term additionality of private sector support requires continued evidence and compliance with FCDO policies.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Align all partner workplans with the *Mutual Prosperity Partnership* and Government of Tanzania policies by October 2024.
Strengthen political economy analysis and risk management, with GGF taking a lead role in sharing insights.
Enhance gender and geographic inclusion strategies, building on 2x Challenge progress.
Expand MA’s engagement with Government of Tanzania to address systemic barriers in manufacturing and agribusiness.
Scale up GGF’s technical assistance to support business environment reforms and unlock private investment.
