programme_metadata.programme_title: Modern Energy Cooking Services (MECS) Programme

output_1.title: Understanding Transition Pathways to MECS

output_2.title: Research on driving increased choice of available MECS

output_3.title: Global Tracking: The Shift to Modern Energy Cooking Services

output_4.title: Research on the use of RBF, Climate and Carbon finance to improve choices of MECS

output_5.title: Research uptake, knowledge dissemination, consultation, and stakeholder coordination

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme expanded from £18.8m to £55.15m through two budget addendums (2019 and 2023). Shift towards country-specific "Ayrton Demonstrators" to scale national eCooking transitions, with funding channeled from FCDO Posts. Delivery model evolved to incorporate direct country engagement (Uganda, Tanzania, India) alongside original research/innovation focus.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Loughborough University and ESMAP performed according to expectations, with timely reporting and responsive engagement. Loughborough managed 61% of budget effectively, while ESMAP handled 12%. Over 190 sub-partners (innovators, academics, entrepreneurs) delivered activities across 20+ countries. WFP collaboration on school eCooking pilots (e.g., Namibia, Tanzania) exceeded initial plans.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Two-tier structure (Loughborough + ESMAP) maintained, but expanded to include direct country-level coordination for Demonstrators. Revised logframe (2023) better aligned with FCDO ICF indicators and theory of change. Governance adapted to accommodate GeCCo (Global Electric Cooking Coalition) launch at COP28, requiring cross-programme coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with Ayrton Fund partners and international bodies (e.g., SEforAll, IEA, WFP). Country-level coordination hubs (e.g., Uganda’s eCooking task force, Kenya’s eCAP programme) facilitated local stakeholder engagement. GeCCo framework enabled multi-stakeholder alignment, though required additional FCDO oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for country Demonstrators (£15m) still in progress as of 2023 review; details to be finalized. Existing contracts (Loughborough, ESMAP) managed efficiently with on-time invoicing and accurate forecasting. Independent evaluation (1% of budget) planned for final year.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required for GeCCo integration and country Demonstrators due to their strategic importance. Risk register updated to include strategic dependencies (e.g., alignment with national energy plans). FCDO SRO/PRO engagement increased for high-profile outputs (e.g., COP28 launch).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Budget flexibility enabled rapid response to country demand (e.g., Uganda’s tax waiver evidence, Kenya’s eCooking strategy). Adaptive management used to reallocate funds toward high-impact areas like RBF pilots and carbon finance methodologies. Pilot portfolio adjusted based on traction (e.g., scaling Kachione’s DC solar systems in Malawi).
adaptive_management_examples: Revised logframe (2023) to integrate ICF indicators and align with GeCCo.
Expanded WFP collaboration from 2 to 5+ countries for school eCooking pilots based on early success in Rwanda/Lesotho.
Pivoted from generic research to country-specific Demonstrators (Uganda, Tanzania, India) in response to policy traction.
Adjusted RBF and carbon finance tools (Output 4) to support Kenya Power’s eCAP programme and EnDev’s eCooking funding rounds.
Accelerated knowledge dissemination (Output 5) after identifying high demand for MECS tools (50,000+ downloads).

main_implementation_challenges: Balancing global research objectives with country-specific Demonstrator demands, requiring tailored approaches for Uganda, Kenya, and India.
Ensuring alignment between MECS’s technical innovations (e.g., EPCs, BioLPG) and national policy frameworks (e.g., NEPs, eCooking strategies).
Managing the complexity of 190+ sub-partners while maintaining quality control and attribution of results.
Scaling pilots (e.g., Kachione’s DC systems) to commercially viable models without distorting local markets.
Integrating MECS evidence into multilateral programmes (e.g., World Bank, EnDev) with differing priorities.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted field research and pilot implementations in 2020–2021, delaying some Output 1 milestones (e.g., country planning tool uptake).
Global energy crises (2022–2023) increased urgency for eCooking but also raised concerns about electricity grid reliability in target countries.
Political transitions in partner countries (e.g., Kenya’s 2022 elections) temporarily slowed policy adoption but later created opportunities (e.g., eCooking in presidential campaign pledges).
COP28 provided a platform to launch GeCCo, amplifying MECS’s global influence but requiring rapid scaling of coordination efforts.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for direct DC solar system innovations (e.g., Kachione’s 48-cell panels) to address off-grid cooking challenges in Malawi/Zambia.
Emerging demand for hybrid eCooking solutions (grid + solar) in areas with unreliable electricity access, not fully addressed in original business case.
Policy resistance from traditional cookstove industries (e.g., Kenya’s ICS producers) requiring targeted capacity-building to transition to eCooking.
Carbon credit methodologies for eCooking proved more complex to develop than anticipated, delaying Output 4 milestones.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between Loughborough’s research focus and ESMAP’s RBF tools, resolved through joint workshops and revised Output 2/4 indicators.
Delays in WFP’s school eCooking pilots due to procurement bottlenecks in some countries (e.g., Madagascar), addressed via FCDO mediation.
Tensions with local ICS manufacturers in Kenya/Uganda over market competition, mitigated by including them in eCooking Hub retraining programmes.
Challenges in attributing leverage from GeCCo to MECS, requiring new tracking mechanisms (action planned for Q1 2024).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited in-country technical capacity to implement eCooking policies (e.g., Uganda’s appliance certification criteria) necessitated MECS-led training.
FCDO Posts lacked dedicated clean cooking expertise, slowing Demonstrator design; addressed by embedding MECS advisors.
ESMAP’s bandwidth constrained by parallel World Bank energy programmes, leading to Output 4 delays in RBF tool development.
Loughborough’s team required upskilling on carbon finance to support Output 4, resolved via external consultant hire.
risk_materialization: Moderate risks around policy uptake (e.g., Rwanda’s Electrocook pilot slower than expected) partially mitigated by expanded country engagement.
Major risk of insufficient country ownership (2021–2022) addressed through co-development of Demonstrators with national governments.
Currency fluctuations in 2022 affected procurement of solar panels for Malawi pilots, managed via bulk purchasing.
Risk of over-reliance on Loughborough materialized; mitigated by diversifying to ESMAP and country-level partners for Output 4.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: £25m (45%) disbursed in first five years (2018–2023) against £55.15m total. On track for remaining £30m (55%) in 2024–2026, including £15m for Demonstrators. Annual spend aligned with revised logframe, though 2020 underspend due to COVID-19.

by_partner.Loughborough University: £33.45m (61% of total), with £4.5m in 2023/24. Consistent on-time invoicing and accurate forecasting.
by_partner.ESMAP: £6.35m (12% of total), with phased disbursements tied to RBF tool milestones.
by_partner.Country Demonstrators: £15m (27%) earmarked; contracts under negotiation as of 2023 review.

budget_execution_vs_plan.variances: 2020 underspend (~£1m) due to COVID-19 fieldwork delays. 2023 overspend on Output 5 (knowledge dissemination) due to unplanned GeCCo launch costs, offset by savings in Output 2 pilot adjustments.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Cost per output remained within business case projections (e.g., £1.2m/year for Loughborough’s research vs. £1.5m planned). Leveraged £15m in co-funding from FCDO Posts for Demonstrators, exceeding the 20% co-financing target.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Output 3 (Global Tracking) achieved A+ with minimal spend (included in Loughborough’s budget), delivering high-impact influence (e.g., SDG7 Review, IEA publications). Output 5’s knowledge products cost £0.1m but generated 50,000+ downloads (£0.002/download).
value_for_money_assessment.comparative_vfm: MECS’s cost per beneficiary (indirect) estimated at £5–10 vs. £20–50 for traditional improved cookstove programmes, based on pilot data from Uganda/Kenya.
value_for_money_assessment.challenges: VFM for country Demonstrators not yet assessable (implementation pending). Some pilots (e.g., BioLPG in Malawi) faced higher-than-planned costs due to supply chain issues.

financial_management_quality.Loughborough University: Strong: Timely financial reporting, accurate forecasts, and responsive to FCDO audits. No material findings in 2022/23 reviews.
financial_management_quality.ESMAP: Adequate: Met disbursement milestones but faced delays in RBF tool development, requiring budget reallocations.
financial_management_quality.FCDO: Effective oversight with quarterly reviews and risk register updates. Proactive management of currency risks (e.g., bulk purchasing for Malawi solar panels).
financial_management_quality.issues_identified: Minor delays in ESMAP’s 2022 invoicing due to World Bank internal processes. Resolved via revised payment schedules.

cost_efficiency_achieved.research_outputs: Output 1/2 delivered 11 research outputs at ~£200k/output (vs. £250k business case target).
cost_efficiency_achieved.pilot_programs: School eCooking pilots (WFP) cost £50–100k/country vs. £150k planned, due to leveraged WFP resources.
cost_efficiency_achieved.knowledge_dissemination: Output 5 achieved 2x download target at 60% of planned cost via digital platforms (e.g., MECS website, GeCCo portal).
cost_efficiency_achieved.inefficiencies: Carbon finance methodology development (Output 4) overran by £0.3m due to complex certification requirements.

co_funding_materialization.status: Partially materialized. £15m from FCDO Posts secured for Demonstrators (exceeding business case assumptions). Additional co-funding from WFP (school pilots) and EnDev (RBF tools) not formally tracked but estimated at £2–3m.
co_funding_materialization.gaps: Private sector co-funding (e.g., for BioLPG scale-up) slower than expected; MECS exploring blended finance models for 2024–2026.

currency_exchange_impacts.impact: GBP depreciation (2022–2023) increased costs for USD-denominated procurements (e.g., solar panels, EPCs) by ~10%. Mitigated via bulk purchasing and supplier renegotiations.
currency_exchange_impacts.examples: Malawi’s DC solar pilot faced 15% cost increase; absorbed via budget reallocation from Output 2 underspend.

key_delivery_lessons: Country ownership is critical: Demonstrators co-developed with governments (Uganda, Kenya) achieved faster policy uptake than top-down research dissemination.
Pilot design must balance innovation with scalability—small, bespoke projects (e.g., Kachione’s DC systems) struggled to attract follow-on funding without clear commercial pathways.
Cross-programme coordination (e.g., MECS + EnDev + WFP) amplifies impact but requires dedicated resources for alignment (e.g., GeCCo secretariat).
Carbon finance and RBF tools (Output 4) are effective levers for scaling but require early engagement with certification bodies to avoid delays.
Knowledge products (Output 5) have higher uptake when tailored to specific audiences (e.g., policymakers vs. entrepreneurs) and disseminated through trusted partners (e.g., SEforAll).
successful_delivery_practices: Challenge funds (e.g., SC2, COSMO) successfully identified scalable innovations (e.g., BURN’s eCooking pilots in Kenya).
Embedding MECS advisors in FCDO Posts accelerated Demonstrator design (e.g., Uganda’s tax waiver evidence).
Leveraging existing platforms (e.g., WFP’s school meals programmes) reduced pilot costs and expanded reach.
GeCCo’s launch at COP28 created a unified advocacy platform, increasing MECS’s global profile and attracting new partners.
Flexible budget reallocations (e.g., from Output 2 to Output 5) enabled responsive prioritization of high-impact activities.
management_adaptations_made: Revised logframe (2023) to integrate ICF indicators and GeCCo alignment, improving MEL (Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning) coherence.
Increased oversight of ESMAP’s RBF tools after 2022 delays, including joint planning workshops.
Established a country engagement team to manage Demonstrator relationships, reducing coordination bottlenecks.
Added carbon finance expertise to Loughborough’s team to address Output 4 gaps, accelerating methodology development.
Implemented quarterly risk review meetings with Tier 1 partners to proactively address emerging issues (e.g., currency risks).
innovations_attempted: Direct-DC solar cooking systems (Kachione, Malawi) to address off-grid challenges, with hybrid grid backup options.
BioLPG production models for Sub-Saharan Africa, combining agricultural waste with clean cooking.
eCooking Hubs in Kenya/Uganda to retrain traditional cookstove producers, creating local eCooking supply chains.
Integration of eCooking into National Energy Plans (NEPs) via policy toolkits and SEforAll collaboration.
Digital knowledge platforms (e.g., MECS website, GeCCo portal) to democratize access to research and tools.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2021 recommendation to strengthen country engagement: Addressed via Demonstrators and embedded advisors (e.g., Uganda MEMD collaboration).
2022 recommendation to improve RBF tool alignment: Partially addressed; ESMAP’s EnDev tools now linked to Kenya’s eCAP programme, but further integration needed for 2024.
2022 recommendation to track leverage: GeCCo attribution framework under development (action for Q1 2024).
2021 recommendation to diversify partners: Expanded from 150 to 190+ sub-partners, including WFP and EnDev.
2020 recommendation to address gender disparities: Integrated into all Demonstrators (e.g., Uganda’s women-led eCooking cooperatives).
forward_recommendations: Prioritize follow-through on country policy uptake (e.g., Uganda’s appliance certification, Kenya’s eCooking strategy) with timed Demonstrator support.
Develop a blended finance facility to attract private sector co-funding for scalable pilots (e.g., BioLPG, BURN’s eCookers).
Strengthen MEL systems to track GeCCo’s leverage and attribute outcomes to MECS, including a mid-term evaluation in 2025.
Expand capacity-building for local manufacturers (e.g., ICS producers) to transition to eCooking, reducing market resistance.
Conduct a cost-benefit analysis of Demonstrators to inform future ICF investments in clean cooking.
Explore partnerships with climate funds (e.g., Green Climate Fund) to sustain MECS innovations post-2026.

strengths: Proactive adjustment of risk register to include strategic dependencies (e.g., GeCCo, national energy plans).
Successful mitigation of currency risks via bulk procurement and supplier negotiations.
Early identification of carbon finance delays (Output 4) enabled corrective action (external expertise hire).
Country-specific risk assessments for Demonstrators (e.g., political transitions in Kenya) informed adaptive management.
weaknesses: Underestimation of partner coordination risks (e.g., ESMAP delays) in business case; required unplanned oversight.
Limited contingency for global shocks (e.g., COVID-19, energy crises), leading to 2020 underspend.
Risk of over-reliance on Loughborough only partially addressed; ESMAP’s capacity constraints persist.
Lack of formal risk-sharing mechanisms with co-financers (e.g., FCDO Posts) for Demonstrators.
improvements_needed: Develop a partner performance dashboard to track sub-partner risks in real time.
Integrate climate/energy price scenarios into financial planning to address volatility.
Formalize risk-sharing agreements with co-financers (e.g., WFP, EnDev) for joint activities.
Enhance political risk assessments for Demonstrator countries ahead of elections (e.g., 2024 in India).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Pilot programmes reached ~50,000 households (Uganda, Kenya, Malawi) and 200+ schools (via WFP partnerships).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Policy influence extended to ~100 million people in countries with eCooking strategies (Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, India). Knowledge products downloaded 50,000+ times by global audience.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Exceeded knowledge dissemination targets (Output 5) but lagged on direct household adoption due to pilot-scale constraints. Country Demonstrators (2024–2026) expected to close gap.

strong: Policy uptake: Uganda’s MEMD incorporated MECS evidence into tax waivers and appliance certification; Kenya’s National eCooking Strategy adopted MECS frameworks.
Global influence: MECS research cited in SDG7 Review, IEA reports, and GeCCo’s founding documents.
Pilot results: Kachione’s DC systems in Malawi reduced cooking costs by 30% vs. biomass; BURN’s eCookers in Kenya cut indoor air pollution by 70%.
Carbon finance: Methodology developed for eCooking carbon credits (Output 4), with Uganda pilot approved for certification.
medium: Household adoption rates in pilots (e.g., 60% in Uganda) not yet validated at scale.
Long-term health impacts (e.g., reduced respiratory disease) projected but not yet measured post-intervention.
Economic benefits (e.g., time savings for women) documented in case studies but lack rigorous counterfactual analysis.
weak: Sustainability of school eCooking programmes (WFP) dependent on continued donor funding.
Limited data on displacement of traditional cookstoves vs. additionality of eCooking solutions.
Attribution of GeCCo’s leverage to MECS not yet quantified.

high: Policy integration: eCooking embedded in national energy plans (Uganda, Kenya) with government ownership.
Market development: Private sector engagement (e.g., Kenya Power, BURN) creating commercial pathways for scaling.
Global momentum: GeCCo’s launch ensures continued advocacy and funding post-2026.
medium: Financial sustainability: Demonstrators require blended finance to transition from donor funding.
Institutional capacity: Local partners (e.g., Uganda’s MEMD) need continued support to implement certification systems.
Technology adoption: Off-grid solutions (e.g., DC solar) depend on supply chain maturation.
low: Grid reliability in target countries (e.g., Tanzania) may limit eCooking scalability without infrastructure investments.
Carbon finance markets for eCooking remain nascent; long-term revenue streams uncertain.

national: Uganda: MEMD adopted MECS evidence for tax waivers, appliance standards, and carbon credit eligibility.
Kenya: National eCooking Strategy (2023) aligned with MECS research; Kenya Power integrating eCooking into grid planning.
India: MECS inputs informed draft clean cooking policies under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency.
global: MECS research underpinned GeCCo’s formation, uniting 50+ organizations behind modern cooking.
SDG7 Review (2023) and IEA’s World Energy Outlook cited MECS data on eCooking transition pathways.
World Bank’s EnDev programme adopted MECS’s RBF tools for eCooking projects in Africa/Asia.
multilateral: SEforAll incorporated MECS’s planning tools into their Universal Energy Access frameworks.
African Development Bank referenced MECS in their 2023 Energy Transition Policy.

institutional: Trained 50+ government officials (Uganda, Kenya) on eCooking policy design and RBF mechanisms.
Established 3 regional testing facilities for eCooking appliances (Uganda, Kenya, India).
Developed eCooking curricula for 10+ universities (e.g., Makerere, Loughborough) via MECS partnerships.
private_sector: Retrained 200+ traditional cookstove producers (Kenya, Uganda) on eCooking technologies through County Hubs.
Supported 50+ entrepreneurs (e.g., Kachione, BURN) via challenge funds and accelerator programmes.
Enabled 10+ companies to access carbon finance for eCooking projects (e.g., Uganda’s pilot).
civil_society: Funded 30+ CSOs to conduct community outreach on eCooking benefits (e.g., health, gender).
Created women-led eCooking cooperatives in Uganda and Tanzania, reaching 5,000+ members.

positive: Accelerated electrification efforts in off-grid areas (e.g., Malawi) due to demand for eCooking solutions.
Spillover adoption of EPCs for non-cooking uses (e.g., water heating, small businesses) in Kenya.
Increased political prioritization of clean cooking in partner countries (e.g., Uganda PM’s COP28 speech).
Cross-sectoral collaboration (e.g., health ministries engaging on indoor air pollution) not anticipated in business case.
negative: Temporary market disruption for traditional cookstove producers in Kenya/Uganda, mitigated by retraining programmes.
Increased electricity demand from eCooking pilots strained local grids in Tanzania, requiring utility upgrades.
Some households adopted eCooking alongside (not instead of) biomass, limiting emission reductions.
neutral: Shift in donor focus toward eCooking reduced funding for improved biomass stoves, aligning with MECS’s theory of change.

demonstrated: WFP’s school eCooking pilots scaled from 2 to 5+ countries (2021–2023) with minimal additional MECS funding.
Kenya Power’s eCAP programme replicated MECS’s County Hub model in 12 regions.
Uganda’s tax waivers for eCooking appliances adopted by Rwanda and Tanzania post-MECS advocacy.
potential: BioLPG production models (Output 2) piloting in Malawi with potential for regional expansion (e.g., Zambia, Mozambique).
Direct-DC solar systems (Kachione) adaptable to other off-grid contexts (e.g., Sahel, island nations).
GeCCo’s global platform could standardize eCooking policies, reducing country-specific adaptation costs.
barriers: Upfront costs of eCooking appliances remain prohibitive for low-income households without subsidies/RBF.
Limited local manufacturing capacity for EPCs/solar panels in most target countries.
Policy fragmentation (e.g., conflicting energy and health ministry priorities) slows national rollouts.

achievements: Consistent high performance (A/A+ scores) with strong policy influence and global leadership (e.g., GeCCo).
Demonstrated demand from partner countries (Uganda, Kenya, India) for scaled-up support via Demonstrators.
Alignment with UK priorities: Clean cooking central to ICF and Ayrton Fund; MECS is flagship programme.
unfinished_business: Country Demonstrators (2024–2026) critical to translating research into scalable impact.
Need to solidify private sector engagement and blended finance models for post-2026 sustainability.
Ongoing policy gaps (e.g., India’s clean cooking strategy) require continued MECS input.
risks_of_closure: Loss of momentum in GeCCo and national eCooking transitions without MECS coordination.
Fragmentation of research/innovation pipeline, reducing VFM from prior investments.
Partner countries may deprioritize eCooking without sustained technical/financial support.

strengths: Diversified funding sources (FCDO core + Posts + co-financers) reduce dependency risks.
GeCCo provides a post-2026 platform for continued advocacy and knowledge-sharing.
Country ownership (e.g., Uganda’s MEMD, Kenya Power) ensures local institutionalization.
weaknesses: Demonstrators’ long-term funding relies on unsecured co-financing (e.g., private sector, climate funds).
ESMAP’s RBF tools require World Bank’s continued commitment, which may shift with energy priorities.
Loughborough’s central role creates key-person risk; succession planning needed.
adaptations_needed: Develop exit strategies for Demonstrators, including handover to national governments/private sector.
Formalize GeCCo’s governance to ensure MECS legacy is sustained post-programme.
Expand local partner capacity (e.g., African universities) to reduce reliance on UK-based expertise.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Shift focus from research to implementation support for Demonstrators, with 70% of 2024–2026 budget allocated to country-level activities.
Deepened engagement with climate funds (e.g., Green Climate Fund) to secure post-2026 financing.
Enhanced MEL systems to track GeCCo’s leverage and attribute outcomes to MECS for QCA purposes.
Pilot a results-based aid mechanism for Demonstrators to incentivize partner country contributions.
Expand gender-transformative approaches (e.g., women-led eCooking cooperatives) based on Uganda/Tanzania success.
Conduct a final independent evaluation (2025) to assess long-term impact and inform future ICF investments.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Sustainable Manufacturing and Environmental Pollution Programme

output_1.title: Improved knowledge and understanding of the environmental and health impacts of, and solutions for, pollution from manufacturing, including plastics.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme expanded into new sectors (Organic Waste and Textiles Portfolios) with 11 new grantee projects established. No fundamental changes to the core delivery model, but milestones were uplifted based on FY22/23 Annual Review recommendations. A GESI (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) lead was appointed to enhance cross-learning and engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (UNCTAD and PMA consortium of Pegasys and SouthSouthNorth) performed effectively, with close coordination across components and portfolios. Grantees generally met or exceeded milestones, though some (e.g., GESI-related outputs) required additional support. The PMA’s oversight mechanisms (quarterly reports, site visits, workshops) ensured alignment with programme objectives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The management structure remained consistent with the planned model: UNCTAD and the PMA (Pegasys/SSN consortium) worked collaboratively, with UNCTAD providing technical assistance and the PMA handling day-to-day programme management, grant oversight, and strategic coordination. The appointment of a GESI lead was an adaptive addition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination was effective, particularly through quarterly reporting, annual site visits, and workshops (e.g., the Q4 Organic Waste and Water grantee workshop in Nairobi). Cross-portfolio collaboration occurred, such as between RiverRecycle and FreshPPact in Ghana on plastic waste solutions. The PMA’s logframe reporting framework was revised to improve grantee alignment with programme-level outputs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was phased and flexible, allowing for the launch of new grant calls (e.g., Textiles and Tanneries) despite earlier COVID-19 delays. The PMA’s framework contract with FCDO (fixed fees) and UNCTAD’s in-kind contributions (staff time, conferences) supported cost efficiency. Savings were achieved by co-locating events (e.g., Strategy Workshop in Cape Town) and leveraging existing partnerships (e.g., Africa Legal Network).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than initially planned, with additional mechanisms introduced (e.g., GESI lead, quarterly progress meetings, and annual workshops) to address gaps in grantee performance (e.g., GESI and research output quality). Site visits and in-person engagements (e.g., Nairobi workshop) were prioritized for high-risk or high-potential projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was critical to adapting to delays (e.g., COVID-19, budget reductions) and expanding into new sectors. The two-year programme extension allowed for the launch of Textiles and Tanneries calls and realistic timelines for delivery. Milestones were adjusted mid-implementation based on performance (e.g., uplifting targets for Output 1.1 and 1.2 after exceeding expectations).
adaptive_management_examples: Appointment of a GESI lead to address underperformance in gender and social inclusion outputs (Output 1.2.ii).
Revision of logframe milestones mid-programme to reflect higher-than-expected progress in research outputs (Output 1.1 and 1.2.i).
Co-hosting workshops with external networks (e.g., Africa Legal Network) to reduce costs and enhance stakeholder engagement.
Pilot of a quarterly reporting mechanism to improve timely oversight, replacing less frequent reporting in the original plan.
Collaborative field trials between grantees (e.g., FreshPPact and RiverRecycle in Ghana) to share learnings on plastic waste solutions.
Adjustment of grant procurement timelines to accommodate COVID-19 delays, enabling the eventual launch of Textiles and Tanneries portfolios.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in launching new portfolios (Textiles and Tanneries) due to COVID-19 and associated budget reductions in earlier years.
Underperformance in Gender, Equality, and Social Inclusion (GESI) outputs (e.g., Output 1.2.ii), requiring targeted interventions.
Grantee overreporting of research outputs, necessitating clearer guidance and quality assurance by the PMA.
Logistical challenges in coordinating projects across geographically dispersed locations (SSA and South Asia), though mitigated by regional clustering (e.g., Organic Waste projects in Kenya).
Ensuring scalability and policy uptake of technology-based solutions, which required additional stakeholder engagement beyond initial plans.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 caused significant delays in the launch of new grant calls (Textiles and Tanneries) and reduced budgets, requiring a two-year programme extension.
Exchange rate fluctuations and inflation in some target countries (e.g., Nigeria, Pakistan) affected procurement costs, though mitigated by fixed-fee PMA contracts.
Political instability in certain regions (e.g., parts of South Asia) occasionally disrupted fieldwork but did not derail overall progress.
Global supply chain disruptions (e.g., for technology components) delayed some pilot projects but were managed through adaptive procurement.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated regulatory barriers to testing new technologies (e.g., biodegradable filaments in marine environments) required additional advocacy and stakeholder negotiations.
Limited local capacity in some countries to adopt technology-based solutions (e.g., pineapple waste extraction in Uganda) necessitated more intensive technical assistance from the PMA.
Unexpected resistance from informal sector actors (e.g., waste pickers in the Plastics portfolio) to formalized recycling systems, requiring inclusive design adjustments.
Climate-related disruptions (e.g., flooding in Pakistan) temporarily halted field trials but were addressed through flexible rescheduling.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between grantees and the PMA on what constituted a valid "research output," leading to overreporting. This was resolved through revised guidance and workshops.
Some grantees in the Plastics portfolio struggled with the commercialization readiness of their solutions, requiring additional PMA support (e.g., CSIR’s mulch film trials).
UNCTAD’s in-kind contributions (e.g., staff time) were occasionally delayed due to competing priorities, but this was managed through proactive coordination by the PMA.
Differences in risk appetite between the PMA and some grantees (e.g., GAIA Biomaterials’ marine pilots) required negotiated adjustments to trial designs.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited local technical capacity to operate and maintain new technologies (e.g., Mobile Harvester in the Organic Waste portfolio) led to additional training requirements.
Grantees in some countries (e.g., Zimbabwe) faced challenges in accessing international expertise due to travel restrictions, addressed through virtual technical assistance.
The PMA’s initial underestimation of the resources needed for GESI integration required the appointment of a dedicated lead and additional budget allocations.
Delays in hiring key personnel (e.g., for the Tanneries portfolio) slowed progress but were mitigated by interim support from existing staff.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 risks (delays, budget cuts) materialized as anticipated, leading to the programme extension and reprioritization of activities.
Grantee underperformance in GESI outputs (Output 1.2.ii) was a known risk that materialized, prompting the appointment of a GESI lead.
Currency fluctuations in some countries (e.g., Nigeria) affected procurement costs, though the fixed-fee PMA contract limited exposure.
Regulatory risks for technology trials (e.g., biodegradable filaments in Kenya) materialized but were managed through stakeholder engagement.
Partner capacity risks (e.g., grantee struggles with commercialization) were partially mitigated through PMA technical assistance.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: Budget execution was on track, with the two-year extension enabling full utilization of funds despite earlier COVID-19 delays. Savings of ~£13,600 were achieved through co-locating events (e.g., Strategy Workshop in Cape Town) and leveraging partnerships (e.g., Africa Legal Network).

by_category.programme_management: Staff time (PMA and UNCTAD) remained the largest cost driver, aligned with the business case. Fixed fees under the PMA’s FCDO framework contract controlled costs.
by_category.grants: Phased procurement of grants allowed for flexible allocation, with some reallocations to high-performing portfolios (e.g., Plastics).
by_category.technical_assistance: UNCTAD’s in-kind contributions (staff time, conferences) supplemented budgeted funds, improving cost efficiency.
by_category.monitoring_evaluation: Costs were slightly higher than planned due to additional oversight (e.g., GESI lead, workshops) but were offset by savings elsewhere.

economy.performance: Savings of ~£3,600 on flights (Cape Town workshop) and ~£10,000 through co-hosted events demonstrated strong economy. Fixed-fee PMA contract and UNCTAD in-kind contributions further reduced costs.
economy.vs_business_case: Better than projected, with actual costs per output lower due to efficiencies in procurement and oversight.

efficiency.performance: Quarterly reporting and logframe revisions improved grantee output conversion. All grantees submitted required reports on time, and site visits verified progress.
efficiency.vs_business_case: Efficiency was higher than planned, with faster-than-anticipated progress in some outputs (e.g., peer-reviewed papers) offsetting delays in others (e.g., GESI).

effectiveness.performance: Outputs were largely converted into outcomes, with strong stakeholder engagement (e.g., FAO Voluntary Code of Conduct on plastics, EAC policy briefs). Scalability pathways were identified for multiple technologies (e.g., CSIR’s mulch films, GAIA’s biodegradable filaments).
effectiveness.vs_business_case: Effectiveness exceeded projections in research and technology development but lagged slightly in policy uptake and GESI integration.

value_for_money_assessment.overall_vfm: High. The programme delivered more outputs than projected for the same or lower cost, with strong evidence of outcomes (e.g., policy influence, technology scalability). The extension period improved VfM by allowing delayed activities to reach fruition.

financial_management_quality.pma: The PMA demonstrated strong financial management, with timely reporting, auditable records, and proactive cost control (e.g., co-locating events). Fixed fees under the FCDO framework ensured transparency.
financial_management_quality.unctad: UNCTAD’s in-kind contributions were well-documented and aligned with programme needs, though occasional delays in staff availability required proactive coordination.
financial_management_quality.grantees: Grantees complied with financial reporting requirements, though some required additional support to align expenditures with logframe indicators. No major financial irregularities were reported.
financial_management_quality.fcdo_oversight: FCDO’s oversight was effective, with quarterly reviews and annual audits ensuring compliance. The flexible approach to grant procurement allowed for adaptive budget reallocations.

per_output.output_1: Costs were lower than planned due to higher-than-expected research output productivity (e.g., 19 peer-reviewed papers vs. 14 targeted).
per_output.output_3: Technology development costs were optimized through collaborative trials (e.g., FreshPPact and RiverRecycle sharing resources in Ghana).

cost_efficiency_achieved.overall: Cost efficiency was achieved through economies of scale (e.g., regional workshops), fixed-fee contracts, and phased grant procurement. The programme delivered ~10-15% more outputs than projected per pound spent.

co_funding_materialization.status: Partial. Some co-funding materialized (e.g., in-kind contributions from UNCTAD, grantee leverage of local resources), but planned cash co-funding from private sector partners was limited. This was offset by the programme’s flexibility in reallocating funds.
examples: UNCTAD’s staff time and conference support (in-kind).
Grantees leveraged local partnerships (e.g., Solidaridad Bangladesh’s textile industry collaborations).
Limited cash co-funding from private sector due to market uncertainties (e.g., tanneries sector).

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minor. While some grantees in Nigeria and Pakistan faced inflationary pressures, the PMA’s fixed-fee contract (denominated in GBP) and phased procurement mitigated major exchange rate risks. Local currency fluctuations were absorbed within grant budgets.

key_delivery_lessons: Phased, flexible grant procurement is critical for adapting to delays (e.g., COVID-19) and emerging opportunities (e.g., new portfolios).
Regional clustering of projects (e.g., Organic Waste in Kenya) enhances collaboration, reduces oversight costs, and improves learning.
Clear, granular guidance on output definitions (e.g., "research outputs") is essential to prevent overreporting and ensure quality.
Dedicated thematic leads (e.g., GESI) are effective for addressing cross-cutting underperformance but require early integration into programme design.
In-person workshops (e.g., Nairobi grantee event) are more effective than virtual engagements for troubleshooting and cross-learning.
successful_delivery_practices: Quarterly reporting with timebound indicators improved grantee accountability and enabled timely interventions.
Co-hosting events with external networks (e.g., Africa Legal Network) reduced costs and expanded stakeholder reach.
Pilot collaborations between grantees (e.g., FreshPPact and RiverRecycle) accelerated technology testing and shared learnings.
The PMA’s use of fixed-fee contracts (via FCDO framework) ensured cost control while allowing flexibility in service delivery.
UNCTAD’s technical assistance in policy engagement (e.g., EAC plastics regulations) amplified programme impact beyond direct grants.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced a GESI lead role to address underperformance in social inclusion outputs.
Revised logframe milestones mid-programme to reflect higher achievement in research outputs and realistic timelines for technology development.
Enhanced grantee reporting guidance (aligned with R4D and SMEP MERL Glossary) to improve data quality.
Increased frequency of progress meetings (quarterly) and added annual workshops for in-person troubleshooting.
Adjusted procurement timelines to accommodate delays, enabling the launch of Textiles and Tanneries portfolios.

innovations_attempted.outcome: Pilot showed promise in reducing labor costs and logistical challenges; further testing underway.

innovations_attempted.outcome: Demonstrated feasibility for textile industry adoption; scalability being explored.

innovations_attempted.outcome: Successful pilots in Kenya and French Polynesia; commercialization pathways identified.

innovations_attempted.innovation: Digital waste tracking module (UoW-GIVO, Plastics portfolio).
innovations_attempted.outcome: Enabled real-time data collection on recycling materials; integrated with financial incentives system.
Improved transparency and reduced administrative burden compared to annual reporting.

innovations_attempted.innovation: Cross-portfolio grantee workshops (e.g., Nairobi Organic Waste event).
innovations_attempted.outcome: Facilitated unexpected collaborations (e.g., FreshPPact and RiverRecycle) and reduced duplication.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Review and uplift logframe milestones to reflect achievements (FY22/23 AR).
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Partially implemented. Milestones for FY23/24 were revised, but outer-year adjustments are pending (target: Q2 FY24/25).

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Enhance grantee engagement on outward-facing research (FY22/23 AR).
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Fully implemented. Increased follow-ups and strategic framework alignment improved research quality and policy relevance.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Clarify research output definitions for grantees (FY22/23 AR).
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Ongoing. New guidance issued in Q1 FY24/25, but overreporting persists in some cases.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Develop a policy brief with FlipFlopi and UNCTAD (FY22/23 AR).
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Not yet completed. Draft in progress, delayed by stakeholder coordination challenges.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Strengthen GESI integration across portfolios (FY22/23 AR).
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Partially implemented. GESI lead appointed, but full integration requires further attention in new grants.

forward_recommendations: Complete the review of logframe milestones by Q2 FY24/25 to align with the programme extension and elevated ambitions, particularly for policy influence and GESI outputs.
Finalize and disseminate the FlipFlopi-UNCTAD policy brief on single-use plastics to strengthen regional policy engagement.
Conduct a lessons-learned workshop with grantees from the Textiles and Tanneries portfolios to capture insights from the delayed launch and inform future calls.
Develop a scalability roadmap for high-potential technologies (e.g., CSIR’s mulch films, GAIA’s filaments) in collaboration with private sector partners.
Enhance the PMA’s capacity to support grantees in commercialization readiness, particularly for technologies nearing market entry (e.g., FreshPPact’s waste tracking system).
Explore additional co-funding opportunities with multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank, UNDP) to supplement limited private sector co-investment.
Institutionalize the quarterly reporting and workshop model as a best practice for future FCDO programmes with similar structures.

covid_19.management: Effective. The two-year extension and phased procurement mitigated delays, allowing the programme to recover lost time.
covid_19.lessons: Flexible timelines and budget reallocations are critical for resilience to external shocks.

gesi_underperformance.management: Partially effective. The appointment of a GESI lead addressed immediate gaps, but systemic integration remains a challenge.
gesi_underperformance.lessons: Cross-cutting themes require dedicated resources from the outset, not just reactive measures.

technology_scalability.management: Effective for some technologies (e.g., CSIR’s mulch films), but others (e.g., Mobile Harvester) need further piloting.
technology_scalability.lessons: Early engagement with end-users and regulators accelerates scalability.

grantee_overreporting.management: Addressed through revised guidance and quality assurance, but required unplanned PMA resources.
grantee_overreporting.lessons: Clearer output definitions and grantee training upfront would reduce administrative burdens.

regulatory_barriers.management: Managed case-by-case (e.g., GAIA’s marine trials in Kenya), but delayed some pilots.
regulatory_barriers.lessons: Proactive regulatory mapping should be integrated into grant design.

risk_management_effectiveness.overall: Risk management was largely effective, with adaptive responses to both anticipated (COVID-19, GESI) and unplanned risks (overreporting, regulatory hurdles). The programme’s flexibility in procurement and oversight was a key strength, though some risks (e.g., GESI) required more resources than initially budgeted.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: The programme reached beneficiaries across 8 countries (Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Bangladesh, Pakistan), with additional coverage planned in Ethiopia. Over 50 grantee projects (including 11 new in FY23/24) engaged local manufacturers, policymakers, and communities. Exact numbers are not quantified in the review but exceed initial targets due to expanded portfolios.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Policy briefs and research outputs influenced regional stakeholders (e.g., East African Community plastics regulations, FAO Voluntary Code of Conduct). Indirect reach includes industry associations, regulators, and academic networks.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Exceeded direct beneficiary targets due to portfolio expansion; indirect reach was broader than anticipated but harder to quantify.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: High. Most milestones were met or exceeded, with significant progress in research outputs (Output 1), technology development (Output 3), and policy engagement. GESI and scalability outcomes lagged slightly but are on a positive trajectory.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Strong. Evidence includes peer-reviewed papers (19 vs. 14 targeted), policy briefs adopted by regional bodies (e.g., EAC), and pilot results (e.g., CSIR’s mulch films, GAIA’s filaments). Grantee case studies and third-party validations (e.g., FAO) further substantiate impact.

by_component.research: High. Research outputs (e.g., peer-reviewed papers, policy briefs) have enduring value and are disseminated through open-access channels.
by_component.technology: Medium-High. Technologies like CSIR’s mulch films and GAIA’s filaments have clear commercialization pathways, but long-term adoption depends on market conditions and regulatory support.
by_component.policy: High. Engagement with bodies like UNCTAD and FAO ensures policy recommendations are embedded in international frameworks (e.g., EAC plastics regulations).
by_component.capacity_building: Medium. Local capacity improvements (e.g., grantee training) are ongoing, but sustainability depends on continued PMA/UNCTAD support post-programme.

risks_to_sustainability: Market uptake of technologies may be slow without private sector co-investment.
Policy changes in target countries could affect scalability (e.g., tanneries regulations in Ethiopia).
Reduced oversight post-2026 may impact grantee performance without transition planning.

policy_influence_achieved.example: Contribution to the FAO’s ‘Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Sustainable Use of Plastics in Agriculture,’ informed by FreshPPact’s work.
UNCTAD’s policy brief on single-use plastics in the East African Community, adopted by regional policymakers.
University of Warwick’s case study on plastic waste policy in Nigeria, cited by national regulators.
Solidaridad Bangladesh’s zero liquid discharge unit influenced textile industry standards in Bangladesh.

capacity_building_results.grantees: Grantees demonstrated improved technical and reporting capacities, with many adopting the PMA’s logframe and MERL guidance. Cross-learning workshops (e.g., Nairobi event) enhanced collaborative problem-solving.
capacity_building_results.local_partners: Local manufacturers and waste processors gained technical skills through grantee projects (e.g., pineapple waste extraction in Uganda, plastic recycling in Ghana). However, capacity varies by country and sector.
capacity_building_results.pma_unctad: The PMA and UNCTAD strengthened their coordination mechanisms, with improved joint technical assistance and policy engagement strategies.
capacity_building_results.evidence: Capacity gains are documented in grantee reports and workshop outputs, though systematic tracking (e.g., pre/post assessments) was limited.

positive: Unexpected collaborations between grantees (e.g., FreshPPact and RiverRecycle in Ghana) led to shared solutions for plastic waste management.
Research on gender implications (Output 1.2.ii), though behind target, highlighted previously overlooked social dimensions of pollution, prompting adjustments in other programmes.
The programme’s flexibility in responding to COVID-19 set a precedent for adaptive management in other FCDO-funded initiatives.
negative: Some grantees focused narrowly on meeting output targets (e.g., research papers) at the expense of deeper stakeholder engagement, limiting immediate policy uptake.
The appointment of a GESI lead, while necessary, diverted PMA resources from other areas, causing minor delays in administrative processes.
Rapid expansion into new portfolios (Textiles, Tanneries) strained PMA oversight capacity, requiring temporary reallocations of staff time.
unintended_consequences.mitigation: Negative consequences were managed through adaptive oversight (e.g., additional workshops) and prioritization of high-impact activities.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Successful field trials in South Africa and Ghana; commercialization partnerships underway. Scalable to other crops/regions with minimal adaptation.
scalability_evidence.barriers: Regulatory approvals for new markets; cost competitiveness with conventional plastics.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Pilots in Kenya and French Polynesia demonstrated marine durability; interest from fishing industry. Potential for global scaling in net/rope applications.
scalability_evidence.barriers: High upfront costs for manufacturers; need for standardized testing protocols.

scalability_evidence.technology: Mobile Harvester for pineapple waste (Organic Waste portfolio).
scalability_evidence.evidence: Prototype reduced labor costs by 30% in Uganda; replicable for other fruit/vegetable waste streams.
scalability_evidence.barriers: Initial capital investment for smallholders; maintenance capacity in rural areas.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Adopted by other FCDO programmes for pollution-related challenges; UNCTAD integrating lessons into global trade/pollution initiatives.
scalability_evidence.barriers: Requires skilled programme management (e.g., PMA) and sustained donor flexibility.

scalability_evidence.policy: East African Community’s single-use plastics regulations.
scalability_evidence.evidence: Directly informed by SMEP research; being replicated in other regional blocs (e.g., SADC).
scalability_evidence.barriers: Enforcement capacity varies by country; industry resistance in some sectors.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong performance (consistent A scores, high VfM) and significant progress toward its objectives. The two-year extension (to 2026) is justified by: (1) delayed portfolios (Textiles, Tanneries) now on track; (2) high potential for scalability and policy influence; and (3) the need to consolidate gains in GESI and commercialization. Closure would risk losing momentum in critical areas (e.g., technology adoption, regional policy uptake).
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High. The programme is likely to achieve 80-90% of its original objectives by 2026, with some outputs (e.g., research, technology pilots) already exceeding targets. Policy influence and scalability outcomes are progressing well, though GESI integration remains a moderate risk.

delivery_model_sustainability.current_model: The current delivery model (PMA + UNCTAD) is sustainable for the remaining programme life, with fixed-fee contracts and in-kind contributions controlling costs. However, long-term sustainability post-2026 depends on:
post_2026_considerations: Securing follow-on funding or transitioning successful technologies to private sector/commercial partners.
Institutionalizing policy engagement mechanisms (e.g., UNCTAD’s role) to maintain influence.
Documenting and transferring PMA’s lessons to future programmes or local institutions.
risks: Loss of PMA/UNCTAD oversight could disrupt grantee performance without a handover plan.
Market or regulatory shifts could affect technology scalability (e.g., tanneries sector).

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High. FCDO’s satisfaction is evident from the consistent A scores, positive VfM assessments, and approval of the programme extension. The adaptive management, strong financial controls, and policy influence align with FCDO priorities on pollution and sustainable manufacturing. Minor concerns (e.g., GESI progress) are being addressed proactively.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize the review of logframe milestones by Q2 FY24/25 to align with the extension period and elevated ambitions for policy and scalability outcomes.
Strengthen grantee support for commercialization, including partnerships with investors and industry associations (e.g., for CSIR’s mulch films).
Conduct a sustainability planning workshop with grantees, UNCTAD, and local partners to identify post-2026 transition pathways.
Enhance monitoring of indirect beneficiaries (e.g., policymakers, industry actors) to better capture broader impact.
Pilot a "graduation" model for high-performing grantees to reduce oversight intensity and test self-sufficiency.
Explore opportunities to leverage the programme’s evidence base for new funding (e.g., Global Environment Facility, private sector partnerships).
Document and disseminate the adaptive management lessons (e.g., COVID-19 response, GESI integration) as a case study for FCDO and other donors.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Climate Adaptation and Resilience (CLARE) Programme

output_1.title: Collaborative partnerships of diverse cross-sectoral actors dedicated to gender-equitable and socially inclusive climate adaptation action are created and/or strengthened

output_2.title: Capacity strengthening of researchers, knowledge brokers, policy makers and practitioners for gender transformative and socially inclusive climate adaptation research and action is provided

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme has capitalized on strengthening existing partnerships rather than rapid expansion. Weighting of partnership growth indicators was reduced from 40% to 30% to reflect this strategic shift. The Met Office’s programme management team was restructured for better consistency and responsiveness in the Services Pillar.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong Southern leadership and diversity, but maintaining this requires continuous effort—particularly with Northern partners less accustomed to equitable collaboration models. The Adaptation Research Alliance (ARA) and other partnerships exceeded engagement targets (e.g., 336 organizations in Partnerships Pillar vs. 36 targeted).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Programme Management Unit (PMU) embedded within IDRC leverages their institutional capabilities, but FCDO’s advisory role has required unsustainable effort to fill gaps. Additional IDRC personnel were added to address coordination challenges, though structural risks remain due to over-reliance on a single Tier 1 partner (IDRC).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Working Groups (R4I, Capacity Strengthening, MEL, Gender/Inclusion) improved cross-programme learning, but coordination across Pillars and activities remains strained by portfolio scale. The R4I and CS Hubs expanded their remits to better integrate projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive procurement processes were followed for outsourced components, with IDRC’s day rates and expense policies aligned with FCDO standards. Due diligence checks and payment schedules were adjusted based on risk evaluations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO’s oversight was more intensive than planned, particularly in advisory roles to fill management gaps. This is flagged as unsustainable and will be addressed in the upcoming Business Case addendum.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted by refocusing the Services Pillar (e.g., Met Office training for Start Network and Save the Children) and introducing new projects like MECHANICS and BAOBAB to address emerging capacity needs. The ‘Threads’ approach was introduced to weave common research questions across projects.
adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of ‘Threads’ to synthesize findings across projects and demonstrate systemic impacts.
Restructuring of Met Office’s management team to improve Services Pillar delivery.
Expansion of R4I and CS Hubs to enhance cross-project support.
Reduction of partnership growth indicator weighting to reflect strategic focus on depth over expansion.

main_implementation_challenges: Over-reliance on a single Tier 1 partner (IDRC) for ~70% of budget and research delivery, creating capacity strains.
Scaling coordination across a large, growing portfolio of projects and Pillars (Research, Services, Partnerships).
Balancing Southern leadership with Northern partners’ differing expectations and working cultures.
Ensuring consistent quality and depth of support to a high number of diverse projects.
external_factors_impact: Climate change impacts (e.g., floods, droughts) increasing urgency for adaptation research, as highlighted by IPCC AR6.
Underfunding of adaptation research globally (e.g., only 3.8% of climate research funding to Africa, 78% of which went to EU/NA institutions).
Political prioritization of climate action by FCDO and UK government, aligning with CLARE’s goals but raising expectations for rapid results.
contextual_constraints_new: Institutional and scientific capacity gaps in target countries to implement evidence-based adaptation solutions.
Need for long-term resilience-building amid short-term pressures (e.g., anticipatory action for climate disasters).
Complexity of integrating gender equality and social inclusion (GESI) into all activities without tokenism.
partner_relationship_issues: Northern partners required additional support to adopt Southern-led, transdisciplinary approaches.
Tensions between rapid delivery demands and the time needed to build equitable partnerships.
capacity_constraints_emerged: IDRC’s capacity strained by portfolio growth, requiring additional personnel and expanded Hub remits.
Limited technical skills in certain areas (e.g., high-resolution climate modeling for adaptation planning).
FCDO’s advisory role created unsustainable workloads, highlighting gaps in the original management model.
risk_materialization: Risk of over-dependence on IDRC materialized, requiring mitigation through structural adjustments.
Coordination risks across Pillars and Working Groups partially addressed but persist due to scale.
Delays in reporting against ICF indicators (KPI1 and KPI15) due to partner capacity constraints.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Cost drivers aligned with the business case, with research staff salaries and associated costs as the largest expenditure. Travel and subsistence costs were proportionate and scrutinized by the PMU.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Achieved through competitive procurement, IDRC’s benchmarked day rates, and scrutiny of grant budgets. IDRC funds ~15% of research costs against ~16% personnel/overhead, providing VFM for FCDO.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Leveraged IDRC’s institutional capabilities for timely technical/financial management. FCDO’s advisory role filled gaps but was not sustainable (to be addressed in 2024/25).
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Robust processes for selecting technical experts and aligning outputs with outcomes. The ‘Threads’ approach enhanced systemic impact across projects.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Southern-led research and capacity strengthening (e.g., 23 Global South countries in Output 2) ensured equitable distribution of benefits.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. IDRC’s financial systems and FCDO’s oversight ensured compliance with policies. Payment schedules were risk-adjusted, and due diligence checks were conducted pre-contract.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Met or exceeded targets. IDRC’s management costs were effectively absorbed, and competitive procurement ensured market-aligned pricing.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Canada’s IDRC co-funded as planned (~10% of total programme value). No major gaps in co-funding reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Equitable partnerships require continuous effort to maintain Southern leadership and diversity, particularly with Northern partners.
Cross-Pillar coordination is critical but resource-intensive; dedicated personnel (e.g., expanded Hubs) are necessary.
Flexibility in project design (e.g., ‘Threads’) enables systemic impacts beyond individual outputs.
successful_delivery_practices: Embedded PMU within IDRC leveraged institutional strengths for efficient management.
Capacity strengthening through Hubs (R4I, CS) and micro-grants (e.g., 2049 participants in Partnerships Pillar).
Met Office’s training sessions (e.g., for Start Network, Save the Children) improved uptake of climate services.
Transdisciplinary approaches (e.g., BAOBAB, Tuwe Pamoja) enhanced local ownership and actionable research.
management_adaptations_made: Reduced weighting of partnership growth indicators to reflect strategic focus on depth.
Expanded R4I and CS Hubs to integrate projects and address coordination gaps.
Restructured Met Office’s management team for better Services Pillar delivery.
Introduced ‘Threads’ to synthesize findings across projects.
innovations_attempted: ‘Threads’ approach to weave common research questions across projects.
Micro-grants and delivery partner networks to broaden capacity strengthening (e.g., 82 organizations via ARA).
Co-learning events (e.g., Met Office’s training for NGOs) to bridge science-action gaps.
previous_recommendations_progress: Logframe fully embedded with GESI disaggregation.
Systems for reporting against RED and ICF KPIs operationalized (targeting March 2025 compliance).
GESI mainstreamed into core programme aims rather than treated as standalone activities.
Business Case addendum in development to address Services Pillar refocusing.
forward_recommendations: Address structural risks from over-reliance on IDRC by diversifying Tier 1 partners or adjusting management models.
Strengthen capacity for rapid commissioning/contracting to meet flexible response needs.
Finalize Business Case addendum to clarify Services Pillar refocusing and sustainable FCDO oversight.
Enhance MEL systems to better capture systemic impacts (e.g., ‘Threads’ outcomes).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Planned risks (e.g., coordination challenges) were identified early, but mitigation required reactive adjustments (e.g., additional IDRC personnel). Proactive risk management (e.g., payment schedule adjustments) worked well for financial risks.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributions to IPCC AR6 and other global assessments (e.g., highlighting adaptation funding gaps).
Support for FCDO’s £11.5bn International Climate Finance commitment and UK’s $100bn climate finance target.
Influence on strategic alliances like Adaptation Research Alliance (ARA) and CREWS.
capacity_building_results: 2049 participants in capacity strengthening activities (Partnerships Pillar).
135 organizations in Research Pillar (73% in Africa/Asia) with enhanced transdisciplinary skills.
New projects (e.g., MECHANICS, BAOBAB) built local capacity for high-resolution climate adaptation planning.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Strengthened South-South collaboration (e.g., African-led synthesis research via BAOBAB).
Negative: Risk of overburdening Southern partners with reporting requirements (partially mitigated by Hub support).
scalability_evidence: Approaches like ‘Threads’ and micro-grants demonstrate potential for replication in other climate research programmes.
Partnership models (e.g., ARA) are being adopted by other FCDO-funded initiatives.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: CLARE is FCDO’s flagship climate adaptation research programme, delivering high-quality, Southern-led research with strong policy alignment (e.g., IPCC, UK climate finance targets). The programme has demonstrated adaptability and high impact, though structural adjustments are needed for long-term sustainability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Moderate. Current model is effective but faces risks from over-reliance on IDRC and unsustainable FCDO advisory workloads. Adjustments (e.g., diversifying partners, refining oversight) are planned.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (with noted concerns about management sustainability)
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize Business Case addendum to address Services Pillar refocusing and FCDO’s oversight role.
Diversify Tier 1 partners to reduce IDRC dependency risks.
Strengthen MEL systems to better capture systemic impacts and GESI outcomes.
Enhance coordination mechanisms (e.g., Working Groups) to manage portfolio growth.

programme_metadata.programme_title: ASEAN CATALYTIC GREEN FINANCE FACILITY (ACGF)

output_1.title: Provision of loans for de-risking green infrastructure projects

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme expanded beyond the original business case by allocating additional technical assistance to seed fund a new Nature Solutions Finance Hub. The UK-ACGF Trust Fund became operational in March 2023, later than the MOU signing (July 2022), highlighting a need to align operational start dates with Trust Fund establishment in future partnerships.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ADB has demonstrated strong performance in project pipeline development and technical assistance delivery, exceeding targets for UK financing allocation. The embedded FCDO Infrastructure Adviser has successfully integrated into ADB’s systems, facilitating stronger coordination and earlier engagement on UK priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme is managed through a dedicated UK-ACGF Trust Fund within ADB, with an FCDO secondee embedded in the ACGF Projects Team. Governance arrangements were finalized in March 2023, including Implementation Guidelines agreed in December 2023. A Trust Fund Coordinator role is being recruited (as of 2024) to enhance oversight and communication.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO (including regional posts) and ADB has been effective, particularly through the secondee’s role in facilitating introductions and aligning workplans. The "no-objection" process for projects has strengthened connections between FCDO’s center and posts, amplifying programme visibility.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The first UK-funded project ($250m loan with $10m from UK-ACGF) was approved in December 2023, with allocations to two additional projects in Indonesia and the Philippines. Procurement for technical assistance (e.g., gender specialist, ACT TA platform) has proceeded as planned, though recruitment for the Trust Fund Coordinator was deliberately slowed to align with donor resources.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has been more hands-on than initially planned, with FCDO actively screening workplan activities and Project Information Memorandums (PIMs) alongside Climate and Environment advisers. The embedded secondee has enabled deeper engagement with ADB’s project origination processes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by reallocating £1.5m of RDEL to the ACT TA platform and seeding the unplanned Nature Solutions Finance Hub. Additional technical assistance was deployed to support project preparation (e.g., Lao PDR agri-food systems project).
adaptive_management_examples: Allocation of unplanned funds to the Nature Solutions Finance Hub in response to emerging opportunities in nature-based solutions.
Adjustment of the Theory of Change to align outputs with the programme logframe, as recommended in the 2023 Annual Review.
Replacement of the Climate and Development Impact Grid with simplified targets (e.g., 45% share for ‘priority green’ projects) to streamline monitoring.
Delay in Trust Fund Coordinator recruitment to ensure alignment with other donor resources and demand.

main_implementation_challenges: Organizing knowledge-sharing events required significant effort due to tight timelines, leading to advanced planning for 2024.
Difficulty in assessing the "bankability" of projects due to exceptions granted for UK-funded projects, complicating pivotal role assessments.
Inflation and debt pressures in some ASEAN countries affected co-financing distribution and project affordability.
external_factors_impact: Easing inflation in ASEAN improved the operating environment, though rising debt levels in some countries (e.g., Laos, Myanmar) may limit co-financing options.
Post-COP26 climate commitments increased demand for green finance, accelerating pipeline development but also raising expectations for project impacts.
contextual_constraints_new: The need to balance concessional loans with technical assistance grants to avoid exacerbating debt burdens in high-debt countries.
Unanticipated demand for nature-based solutions (e.g., flood management in Indonesia) required rapid adaptation of technical assistance focus.
capacity_constraints_emerged: ADB’s capacity to administer short-notice knowledge events was initially underestimated, requiring upfront planning for 2024.
Delays in recruiting the Trust Fund Coordinator highlighted capacity gaps in fund oversight, though this was mitigated by the FCDO secondee’s role.
risk_materialization: Moderate risk ratings persisted due to regional debt pressures and the need to demonstrate additionality in project interventions.
The "bankability" metric proved difficult to apply uniformly, requiring exceptions for UK-funded projects.

committed.status: Exceeded target of £100m allocation (note: target likely refers to cumulative multi-year goal; £15m was the 2023/24 milestone).

cost_effectiveness.current_value: N/A (Indonesia Flood Project is 100% adaptation, not mitigation).

leverage_ratio.indicator: Ratio of ACGF loans to co-financing
leverage_ratio.current_value: 1:32 (vs. target of 1:6 for Indonesia Flood Project).

value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: ADB trust fund fees remained as projected. Salaries/accommodation costs in Manila increased in line with expectations. Inflation pressures eased, but regional debt levels may limit future co-financing options. The programme’s counter-cyclical role (de-risking infrastructure) was highlighted as a VfM strength.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. ADB’s financial management met FCDO requirements, with transparent reporting on allocations (e.g., $10m to Indonesia Flood Project, $20m to two other projects). The Implementation Guidelines finalized in December 2023 clarified financial procedures.

efficiency_gains: Leverage ratio of 1:32 for the Indonesia project significantly exceeded the 1:6 target, indicating high efficiency in catalyzing co-financing.
Technical assistance grants (e.g., $500k for green buildings initiative) were used strategically to generate pipeline without increasing debt.
inefficiencies: Exceptions to bankability metrics complicated VfM assessments for some projects.
Delays in Trust Fund operationalization (March 2023 vs. MOU signing in July 2022) reduced implementation time.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialized. The programme attracted parallel co-financing (e.g., $250m ADB loan for Indonesia Flood Project with $10m UK-ACGF contribution), but regional debt constraints may limit future co-funding in some countries.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly mentioned, though the programme reports values in both GBP and USD, suggesting exchange rates are monitored. No significant adverse impacts noted.

key_delivery_lessons: Embedding an FCDO secondee within ADB’s team significantly improved coordination, trust, and early engagement on UK priorities.
Country-level engagement with FCDO posts (e.g., through "no-objection" processes) amplified programme visibility and alignment with regional climate goals.
Advanced planning for knowledge events is critical to balance administrative effort with pipeline generation.
successful_delivery_practices: The secondee’s role in originating projects (e.g., green buildings initiative) and facilitating ADB-FCDO connections.
Use of technical assistance to "de-risk" projects (e.g., Lao PDR agri-food systems) and attract private capital.
Flexible reallocation of funds to emerging priorities (e.g., Nature Solutions Finance Hub).
management_adaptations_made: Simplified monitoring by replacing the Climate and Development Impact Grid with two targets (priority green share and GESIAP updates).
Alignment of the Theory of Change with the logframe outputs, as recommended in the 2023 Annual Review.
Development of a pre-planned 2024 events pipeline to reduce last-minute organizational burdens.
innovations_attempted: Nature Solutions Finance Hub (unplanned in the original business case).
Green, Social, and Sustainable (GSS+) bonds initiative to build capacity in thematic bond frameworks.
ACGF Innovative Finance Clinic on Green and Resilient Buildings (September 2023).
previous_recommendations_progress: Theory of Change was amended to align outputs with the logframe (2023 recommendation).
Trust Fund operationalization was completed (March 2023), though later than ideal.
Gender and Social Inclusion Action Plan (GESIAP) is under review to incorporate trust fund partner requirements.
forward_recommendations: Recruit the Trust Fund Coordinator in 2024 with a mandate to enhance partner visibility.
Set a higher target for Output Indicator 3c (exceeded current target).
Develop qualitative milestones for Indicator 3d to assess FCDO network engagement.
Consider dedicated Climate and Environment adviser resourcing to formalize ad-hoc screening processes.
Align future partnership agreements’ operational start dates with Trust Fund establishment (not MOU signing).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderately effective. While the programme maintained a "Moderate" risk rating, adaptive measures (e.g., flexibility in technical assistance, exceptions for bankability) mitigated key risks. The GESIAP review and secondee’s role strengthened risk oversight.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 485,000 people (Indonesia Flood Management Project).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Exceeded (specific targets not provided in excerpt).

policy_influence_achieved: Contributes to UK COP26 commitments and ICF targets (Outcomes 1 & 12).
Influenced ADB’s focus on green buildings and demand-side energy through the ACGF-PSOD initiative.
Supported policy dialogue on climate-resilient infrastructure in Indonesia (e.g., flood management).
capacity_building_results: Trained government officials in innovative finance, strengthening pipeline development.
Technical assistance to Lao PDR improved access to climate-resilient agri-food financing.
GSS+ bonds initiative built capacity among financial institutions on thematic bond frameworks.
unintended_consequences: Positive: The programme’s flexibility enabled unplanned investments in nature-based solutions, expanding its impact beyond the original scope.
Negative: None explicitly reported, though debt constraints in some ASEAN countries may limit future project scalability.
scalability_evidence: The 1:32 leverage ratio for the Indonesia project demonstrates potential for scaling co-financing.
Replicability of green finance models (e.g., GSS+ bonds) is being tested through regional knowledge-sharing events.
The Nature Solutions Finance Hub could serve as a model for other regions if successful.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has exceeded performance targets (e.g., financing allocation, leverage ratios) and demonstrated strong alignment with UK climate and development priorities. The embedded delivery model (FCDO-ADB partnership) is effective, and emerging opportunities (e.g., nature-based solutions) justify continued investment.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. The ADB-managed Trust Fund structure is robust, and the secondee’s integration into ADB systems ensures long-term coordination. The planned recruitment of a Trust Fund Coordinator will further strengthen oversight.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expand technical assistance to new areas (e.g., Nature Solutions Finance Hub).
Enhance visibility and coordination through the Trust Fund Coordinator role.
Adjust monitoring indicators (e.g., higher target for Output 3c, qualitative milestones for FCDO engagement).
Explore further innovations in green finance models (e.g., GSS+ bonds, green buildings).
