programme_metadata.programme_title: Sustainable Energy and Economic Development (SEED) Programme

output_1.title: Enhanced public-sector capacity for public investment planning and management

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to demand-led technical assistance (TA) with embedded specialists (e.g., PPP experts housed within Planning & Development Department). Component 4 (impact evaluation) was dropped due to limited market interest, procurement delays, and ODA reductions. Programme now relies on partner-led effectiveness tracking with potential evaluations in 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Adam Smith International (Component 1) exceeded expectations in capacity-building (e.g., PIM tools adoption, data portal launch). Karandaz (Component 2) unlocked significant receivables (PKR 1.27B for Daral Khawar HPP) and secured favorable tariff decisions. NRSP (Component 3) progressed climate resource coordination cell setup, though early-stage.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Embedded technical specialists (e.g., PPP units within P&DD) replaced original standalone advisory model. Oversight intensified due to political instability and ODA reductions, with quarterly milestone tracking introduced.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with GoKP departments (e.g., PEDO, P&DD) and multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank-SEED collaboration on climate roadmap). Cross-component alignment improved via joint workplans (e.g., Output 1’s PIM tools informed Output 2’s project pipeline).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in Component 4 procurement led to its cancellation. Other components used flexible contracts (e.g., project-specific TA for high-priority investments like hydro projects). Corporate finance facility (PKR 7.2B) for PEDO established via streamlined procurement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to political risks (e.g., upcoming elections) and ODA cuts. Introduced Fast-Track Action Plans and 6-month implementation reviews to mitigate delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Reprioritized activities to focus on high-return interventions (e.g., Green Hydrogen Plant LOI, Khanpur Sustainable City). Adapted to rising capital costs by locking in reforms early and targeting transactions with clear timelines.
adaptive_management_examples: Developed bridge code design tools with end-user consultation, making their use mandatory for new projects to ensure sustainability.
Embedded PPP specialists in P&DD to build institutional ownership of reforms.
Shifted from broad capacity-building to targeted trainings (e.g., 35 GoKP officials from 12 departments on data portal use).
Created corporate finance facility for PEDO to enable self-sustaining project financing.

main_implementation_challenges: Political instability and upcoming elections causing delays in reform approvals.
Rising capital costs and project financing expenses due to global economic conditions.
ODA reductions requiring reprioritization and exit from lower-impact activities.
Limited market interest in Component 4 (impact evaluation) leading to its cancellation.
Early-stage nature of some investments (e.g., Green Hydrogen Plant LOIs) creating uncertainty in timelines.
external_factors_impact: Post-pandemic economic recovery exceeded forecasts (higher GDP growth than anticipated), but inflation and currency fluctuations (PKR depreciation) increased project costs.
Global energy crisis heightened demand for SEED’s renewable energy solutions (e.g., hydro project tariff modifications).
Pakistan’s energy sector reforms (e.g., NEPRA decisions) directly influenced by SEED’s TA but faced bureaucratic delays.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for climate adaptation tools (e.g., night light data for GDP estimation, air quality monitoring in Peshawar).
Increased competition for private-sector co-financing due to economic downturn.
Regulatory bottlenecks in energy wheeling agreements for hydro projects.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial resistance to PIM tools overcome through co-design and mandatory adoption policies.
Delays in GoKP’s approval processes (e.g., PPP pipeline projects) due to election-related caution.
NRSP’s climate resource cell faced coordination challenges with federal ministries.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoKP’s limited absorptive capacity for complex financial instruments (e.g., VGF guidelines required iterative revisions).
Shortage of skilled personnel in PEDO to manage corporate finance facility independently.
Need for additional training on data portal use beyond initial targets (expanded from 4 to 8 departments).
risk_materialization: Political risk: Election delays stalled key reforms (e.g., Pehur/Ranolia tariff decisions pending).
Financial risk: Currency depreciation increased project costs (e.g., $1B FDI targets now require higher PKR equivalents).
Operational risk: Component 4 cancellation due to procurement failures.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track overall, with underspends in Component 4 offset by higher-than-planned disbursements in Components 1–2. PKR 1.27B ($48.3M) in sales receivables unlocked for hydro projects, exceeding targets. Corporate finance facility (PKR 7.2B/£27.4M) established ahead of schedule.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Assessed as ‘B’ (satisfactory). Cost per output varied: Output 1 achieved high VFM (e.g., PIM tools applied to £365M projects vs. £1.9M target). Output 4’s green finance instruments leveraged £26.6M in private co-financing. ICF KPI 12 (private finance mobilized) requires revision by March 2023 to align with new guidance.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong for Components 1–2 (e.g., Adam Smith International’s transparent reporting on data portal costs). Karandaz’s financial tracking for energy efficiency loans improved but faced delays in disbursement audits. GoKP’s absorption of VGF/PDF guidelines slowed by capacity gaps.
cost_efficiency_achieved: PIM tools reduced project design costs by standardizing bridge/road designs (avoided £1.9M in overruns).
Energy wheeling agreements unlocked PKR 3.5B ($13.3M) in stranded assets with minimal SEED investment.
Corporate finance facility reduced PEDO’s reliance on ad-hoc grants, projecting £27.4M in self-sustaining funds.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. Private-sector LOIs signed for $1B in Green Hydrogen/Khanpur City investments, but actual disbursements pending feasibility studies. Commercial bank finance for renewable energy (ICF KPI 12) below target due to risk aversion.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: PKR depreciation increased project costs by ~15% (e.g., $1B FDI targets now require PKR 220B vs. PKR 160B at inception). Mitigated via early-stage currency hedging for hydro project tariffs.

key_delivery_lessons: User co-design is critical for tool adoption (e.g., PIM tools mandated after line department input).
Embedded TA (e.g., PPP specialists in P&DD) builds ownership better than standalone advisory.
Flexible financing instruments (e.g., corporate finance facility) outperform rigid grant structures.
Political economy analysis must precede reform timelines (e.g., election delays stalled NEPRA decisions).
successful_delivery_practices: Demand-led TA model (e.g., Output 1’s responsive support to PEDO’s tariff petitions).
Cross-component synergy (e.g., Output 1’s data portal informed Output 2’s investment pipeline).
Iterative capacity-building (e.g., expanding data portal training from 4 to 12 departments).
Risk-sharing mechanisms (e.g., VGF guidelines attracted £26.6M in private co-financing).
management_adaptations_made: Introduced Fast-Track Action Plans to accelerate high-priority reforms.
Shifted from annual to quarterly milestone tracking to monitor ODA-related reprioritization.
Dropped Component 4 to focus resources on core outputs (Components 1–3).
Developed 6-month implementation plans with clear exit strategies for non-critical activities.
innovations_attempted: Bridge code design standardization to reduce construction costs/overruns.
Night light data integration into KP’s GDP estimation methodology.
Energy wheeling agreements to monetize stranded hydro assets.
Climate resource coordination cell (CRCC) to streamline international climate finance access.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2021 recommendation to embed TA: Fully implemented (e.g., PPP specialists in P&DD).
2021 call for stronger MEL: Partially addressed via partner-led impact tracking; full evaluation deferred to 2024.
2021 risk mitigation for elections: Partially effective (some reforms locked in, but NEPRA delays persisted).
forward_recommendations: Finalize revised workplans by September 2022 to align with ODA reductions.
Conduct ICF KPI 12 review by March 2023 to ensure compliance with new guidance.
Prioritize feasibility studies for Green Hydrogen/Khanpur City LOIs to firm up FDI commitments.
Strengthen PEDO’s capacity to manage corporate finance facility independently by 2024.
Develop responsible exit strategies for tools/processes (e.g., data portal, PIM tools) by 2023.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate. Proactive in financial risks (e.g., currency hedging) and political risks (e.g., early reform lock-in). Less effective in procurement risks (Component 4 failure) and partner capacity gaps (e.g., VGF guideline delays).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 35 GoKP officials trained; 8 departments using data portal (vs. 4 targeted).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 45 projects (worth £365M) applying PIM tools; potential 1M+ beneficiaries from Green Hydrogen/Khanpur City investments (pending feasibility).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.targets_met: Exceeded for capacity-building (e.g., training); below for private-sector leverage (ICF KPI 12).

policy_influence_achieved: NEPRA tariff decisions for Daral Khawar/Machai HPPs adopted SEED’s recommendations (17% ROE).
KP’s PIM practices institutionalized via mandatory tool use and restructuring of Urban Planning Unit.
PDF/VGF guidelines (governing £45.6M) approved by GoKP, influencing future public investment processes.
Climate change integrated into provincial planning via ICF KPI 13 baseline and TA roadmap.
capacity_building_results: 8 departments now using data portal for planning (vs. 4 targeted); 35 officials trained on data management.
PPP framework strengthened via embedded specialists; PEDO’s corporate finance facility (£27.4M) operational.
Bridge code designs standardized across KP, reducing project preparation time by 30%.
Climate knowledge improved via workshops (KPI 14) and baseline assessments (KPI 13).
unintended_consequences: Positive: PIM tools adopted by non-targeted departments (e.g., Agriculture, Environment).
Positive: Data portal extensions (night light GDP estimation) attracted World Bank collaboration.
Negative: ODA reductions forced cancellation of Component 4, limiting impact evaluation.
Negative: Election delays stalled $13.3M in hydro project receivables (Pehur/Ranolia).
scalability_evidence: PIM tools and bridge codes scalable to other Pakistani provinces (e.g., Punjab expressed interest).
Energy wheeling model replicable for other stranded hydro assets nationally.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (consistent ‘A’ ratings, exceeded targets in Output 1).
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize 2024 evaluations to assess long-term impact of Components 1–3.
Transition CRCC to federal ownership by 2025 to ensure climate finance access post-SEED.
Develop exit strategies for embedded specialists (e.g., PPP unit handover to P&DD).
Explore blending SEED’s TA with other FCDO programmes (e.g., climate resilience) for scaled impact.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Umoyo Wathu Health System Strengthening Programme

output_1.title: Increased readiness of the primary health platform to deliver free quality essential health services to poor communities at facility and community level

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme had to refocus resources due to 0.5% ODA reduction, leading to new results targets and a transition phase. Original HSJF/UNJP funding scales were significantly impacted, requiring adaptation of delivery mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: HSJF management by MoH faced capacity constraints, leading to underutilization of funds and delays in governance processes (e.g., budget approvals, mid-year reviews). UNJP transition from inception to implementation was slower than planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: HSJF governance relied on a Fiscal Agent (FA) for fund management, but coordination among DPs (FCDO, Norway, Germany) and MoH was less effective than planned. UNJP used UN partners (UNICEF, WHO, UNFPA) under a Standard Administrative Arrangement, but embedding activities at district level was delayed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Sector-wide coordination was challenged by MoH’s limited capacity to align HSJF planning with national priorities (e.g., no Annual Implementation Plan developed). UNJP’s district-level coordination was hindered by pandemic disruptions and delayed inception.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement bottlenecks (e.g., construction delays, medical equipment distribution) persisted due to MoH capacity issues and pandemic-related supply chain disruptions. Only 377/420 planned HSJF supply chain deliveries were completed (Nov 2020–June 2021), with no data for July–Nov 2021.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than planned due to underperformance in HSJF fund utilization and governance. FCDO increased scrutiny of FA and Technical Implementation Consultant contracts, which now represent a larger share of reduced FCDO funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by reallocating resources to respond to COVID-19 (e.g., UNJP’s health shock preparedness component) and adapting to ODA reductions. However, rigid HSJF governance structures limited rapid reallocation.

adaptive_management_examples.1: Revised Theory of Change and M&E plans in 2022 to reflect COVID-19 and ODA reduction impacts.
adaptive_management_examples.2: Shifted focus to strengthening HSJF Results Framework to emphasize outcomes/VFM over inputs.
adaptive_management_examples.3: Triangulated routine DHIS data with ad-hoc surveys to compensate for poor data quality in Logframe reporting.

main_implementation_challenges: Reduction in UK ODA from 0.7% to 0.5% GNI, forcing programme budget cuts and reprioritization.
MoH’s limited capacity to manage HSJF funds efficiently, leading to underutilization (e.g., delayed budget approvals, mid-year reviews).
COVID-19 pandemic waves (2021) disrupted service delivery, particularly in rural areas and among vulnerable groups (e.g., pregnant women).
Poor alignment of HSJF planning with national priorities (e.g., no sector-wide Annual Implementation Plan).
Data quality issues in routine systems (e.g., DHIS) hindered progress tracking and gender/social inclusion disaggregation.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Recurrent waves (Jan–Nov 2021) strained health systems, with higher case fatality rates than regional averages. Vaccine rollout was slow due to global supply gaps and low uptake.
ODA cuts: Reduced FCDO funding increased the proportion of fixed costs (e.g., FA contracts) in HSJF, reducing flexibility.
HSSP-III transition: MoH’s preparation for the new Health Sector Strategic Plan (2022–2030) created uncertainty about future funding mechanisms (e.g., potential return to Sector Wide Approach).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated MoH staff time constraints due to pandemic response, limiting focus on HSJF/UNJP management.
Global vaccine inequity and supply chain disruptions delayed Malawi’s COVID-19 response.
Inflation/currency pressures (implied by budget utilization challenges) may have affected procurement.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between DPs (FCDO, Norway, Germany) and MoH over HSJF governance and fund utilization.
UNJP’s delayed implementation strained relationships with district-level partners (e.g., DHMTs).
Fiscal Agent’s role became contentious as fixed costs consumed a larger share of reduced FCDO funding.
capacity_constraints_emerged: MoH’s reduced capacity to manage HSJF budgets and coordinate with DPs.
Limited district-level capacity to absorb UNJP activities due to pandemic disruptions.
Poor data management skills at facility/district levels hindered DHIS-based reporting.
risk_materialization: HSJF underutilization (financial risk) due to MoH delays and pandemic disruptions.
Infrastructure output underachievement (e.g., construction bottlenecks).
Gender/social inclusion data gaps (programmatic risk) limited targeting of marginalized groups.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underutilization of HSJF funds during the review period, particularly for infrastructure outputs. UNJP faced delays in transitioning from inception to implementation, affecting expenditure.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM was compromised by: (1) High fixed costs for HSJF governance (FA/Technical Consultant contracts) as a % of reduced FCDO funding; (2) Input-focused HSJF spending with limited emphasis on outcomes; (3) Poor data quality increasing monitoring costs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: MoH’s financial management of HSJF was weak, with delayed budget approvals and mid-year reviews. FA’s role was critical but costly. UNJP financial management by UN agencies was more stable but slowed by inception delays.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was lower than planned due to: (1) Underutilized HSJF funds; (2) Duplication in HSJF/UNJP activities not fully leveraged; (3) Ad-hoc surveys required to compensate for poor routine data, increasing costs.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding from Norway (RNE) and Germany (KfW) continued, but additional DP contributions were not secured to offset FCDO reductions.

key_delivery_lessons: HSJF governance must shift from input tracking to outcome/VFM focus, especially with reduced funding.
MoH capacity is the critical bottleneck; without strengthening it, HSJF efficiency will remain low.
Routine data systems (e.g., DHIS) are unreliable for Logframe reporting; triangulation is essential but costly.
UNJP’s district-level approach is promising but requires longer lead times for embedding activities.
successful_delivery_practices: UNJP’s integration of COVID-19 preparedness into MNCH strengthening demonstrated adaptive capacity.
Use of SLAs (Service Level Agreements) with CHAM/IHAM facilities successfully expanded EHP service coverage (e.g., 170 facilities vs. 160 target).
Purposeful use of data feedback loops at district level (UNJP) improved local data quality over time.
management_adaptations_made: Revised HSJF management framework to address construction bottlenecks (partial success).
Increased FCDO oversight of FA contracts to improve VfM.
Planned 2022 review of Theory of Change and M&E frameworks to reflect ODA/COVID-19 context.
innovations_attempted: Triangulation of DHIS data with ad-hoc surveys to improve result tracking.
UNJP’s Work Improvement Teams (WITs) at facility level to enhance service quality.
Exploring synergies between HSJF (national) and UNJP (district) to reduce duplication.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on strengthening HSJF Results Framework (still input-focused).
Limited advancement in securing additional DP co-funding to offset FCDO cuts.
No significant improvement in MoH’s HSJF management capacity since last review.
forward_recommendations: Review HSJF governance to reduce fixed costs (e.g., FA contracts) and improve VfM.
Strengthen MoH capacity for budget execution and fund utilization through targeted TA.
Develop VfM indicators for both HSJF and UNJP components.
Enhance data disaggregation (sex, age, disability) to track equity in service delivery.
Accelerate UNJP implementation to embed district-level activities before 2025 AMP end.
Explore merging HSJF/UNJP reporting systems to reduce duplication and improve efficiency.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was reactive rather than proactive. While COVID-19 risks were partially mitigated (e.g., UNJP’s shock preparedness), financial risks (HSJF underutilization) and programmatic risks (data gaps) materialized due to weak contingency planning.

actual.facilities_providing_EHP: 170 CHAM + 5 IHAM (vs. 160 target; FCDO attribution: 77 vs. 73 target)

beneficiaries_reached_actual.gap: No data on total unique beneficiaries reached; OPD consultations exceed targets, but equity of access (e.g., marginalized groups) unclear due to poor disaggregation.

evidence: HSJF’s role in demonstrating efficiency of pooled funding may influence HSSP-III’s return to Sector Wide Approach (SWAp).
UNJP’s district-level MNCH strengthening aligns with MoH priorities but lacks documented policy uptake.
policy_influence_achieved.limitations: No explicit policy changes attributed to Umoyo Wathu in this review period.

positive: 170+ facilities received HSJF support (equipment, SLAs), improving service readiness.
UNJP’s district-level work improved data use/feedback loops (e.g., DHIS quality).
gaps: MoH’s HSJF management capacity remains weak.
Limited evidence of sustained capacity gains at facility level beyond SLA-covered services.

positive: Expanded EHP coverage through CHAM/IHAM SLAs reached more beneficiaries than targeted.
UNJP’s COVID-19 preparedness component strengthened health shock resilience.
negative: Reduced FCDO funding increased reliance on FA contracts, reducing funds available for direct service delivery.
Delayed UNJP implementation may limit long-term impact before 2025 AMP end.

potential: HSJF’s pooled funding model could scale if VfM improves and MoH capacity strengthens.
UNJP’s district-level MNCH approaches (e.g., WITs) are replicable but require more time to demonstrate scalability.
barriers: Current HSJF governance costs are unsustainable at reduced ODA levels.
MoH’s limited absorption capacity constrains rapid scaling.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Despite challenges, the programme remains aligned with UK/FCDO priorities (SDG3.8, UHC, global health security) and Malawi’s HSSP-III. The HSJF/UNJP components demonstrate potential for impact if governance and VfM issues are addressed. Closing the programme would risk disrupting essential health services for 2+ million beneficiaries.

strengths: HSJF’s pooled funding mechanism is preferred by MoH/DPs for future SWAp.
UNJP’s UN agency delivery model leverages existing systems (e.g., RCO support).
risks: Current HSJF governance costs are unsustainable without additional DP co-funding.
UNJP’s reliance on UN agencies may limit long-term MoH ownership.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium (concerns about VfM and MoH capacity, but recognition of adaptive responses to ODA/COVID-19 challenges)
planned_adaptations_future: Review HSJF governance to reduce fixed costs and improve efficiency.
Strengthen MoH capacity for budget execution through technical assistance.
Accelerate UNJP implementation to maximize impact before 2025.
Enhance data systems to better track equity and VfM.
Explore merging HSJF/UNJP reporting to reduce duplication.
Advocate for additional DP co-funding to restore original programme scale.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Climate Adaptation Water and Energy Programme (CAWEP)

output_1.title: Developed climate resilient multiple use water and energy infrastructure

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Component 1 (Adaptive & Flexible Water and Energy supply) was implemented through UNICEF with £2.5M budget, while Component 2 (Climate Adaptation) was led by UNDP with £12M budget. The programme adapted by revising output descriptions and adding five new indicators to track community management effectiveness.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNDP and UNICEF performed as expected, with UNICEF successfully completing 35 solar-powered piped water schemes in nine districts. Community engagement improved post-COVID-19 restrictions, allowing full implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme maintained its original governance structure but enhanced coordination with government entities (e.g., Rural Electrification Fund) to align with national climate priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between FCDO, UNDP, UNICEF, and Zimbabwean government (national/subnational) improved alignment with national policies (e.g., National Development Strategy 1). Multisectoral collaboration (education, health, agriculture) was achieved through the "multiple water use" approach.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for solar-powered infrastructure (e.g., piped water systems, mini-grids) was executed as planned, with 100% functionality reported for newly installed systems. Community-based insurance schemes for water infrastructure were piloted.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified to monitor the sustainability of community management structures and business models for water/energy infrastructure. Regular risk register updates were recommended.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by revising output milestones (e.g., adding indicators for community management effectiveness) and adapting to COVID-19 disruptions. Feasibility studies informed adjustments to Component 2’s scope.

adaptive_management_examples.example_1: Piloted community piped water insurance schemes to cover physical damage/mechanical breakdowns, ensuring long-term sustainability.
adaptive_management_examples.example_2: Revised Output 1’s description and indicators based on lessons from Component 1 (UNICEF-led) to improve measurability.
adaptive_management_examples.example_3: Aligned programme activities with Zimbabwe’s National Adaptation Plan and Rural Electrification Fund contributions (e.g., Hakwata solar project).

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 restrictions initially limited community engagement, delaying implementation.
Testing the sustainability of community-led business models for water/energy infrastructure (e.g., insurance schemes, tariff collection) remains a work in progress.
Upcoming elections in Zimbabwe (2023) may cause disruptions, requiring adaptive planning.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Lifting of restrictions in 2022 enabled full partner engagement with communities.
Political: Government buy-in was critical for co-funding (e.g., Rural Electrification Fund’s contribution to solar projects) and policy alignment.
Climate: Increased frequency of droughts/floods in target districts (e.g., Buhera, Chiredzi) validated the programme’s focus on resilient infrastructure.
contextual_constraints_new: Household affordability for water insurance premiums (US$2/year) requires long-term testing.
Capacity gaps in local government extension services to support community management of infrastructure.
Currency fluctuations (USD/ZWL) may impact cost efficiency for procurement and maintenance.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited technical capacity among community water management committees to maintain solar infrastructure (addressed via training).
Need for continuous support to local government to integrate CAWEP lessons into national climate policies.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 disruptions (mitigated by adaptive planning post-2021).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Component 1 (£2.5M) was fully executed by June 2022, and Component 2 (£12M) is progressing as planned. Co-funding from Zimbabwe’s Rural Electrification Fund supplemented CAWEP resources (e.g., Hakwata solar project).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. The programme leveraged government co-funding (e.g., REF’s 6.2km power line) and achieved 100% functionality for new water systems. Community contributions (e.g., US$2/household for insurance) enhance cost-sharing.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Financial oversight by UNDP/UNICEF ensured transparent use of funds, with regular risk register updates. No major audit findings reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient. Solar infrastructure costs were optimized through bulk procurement and government partnerships. Community gardens and livestock troughs added value beyond core targets.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Yes. Government of Zimbabwe contributed via REF and aligned CAWEP with national climate budgets (e.g., National Adaptation Plan).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: USD-denominated premiums for water insurance schemes were affordable for households (US$2/year), but ZWL depreciation may affect long-term maintenance costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Early government engagement (national/subnational) improves buy-in and co-funding opportunities (e.g., REF’s contribution to solar projects).
Multisectoral approaches (e.g., linking water access to education, health, and nutrition) amplify impact and value for money.
Pilot innovations (e.g., community water insurance) before scaling to test sustainability.
successful_delivery_practices: Community-based management structures with business models (e.g., tariffs, produce sales) improved infrastructure sustainability.
Climate-proofing designs (e.g., solar-powered systems, drip irrigation) enhanced resilience to droughts/floods.
Partnerships with UN agencies (UNDP/UNICEF) ensured technical expertise and alignment with global SDGs.
management_adaptations_made: Added five new indicators to Output 1 to track community management effectiveness.
Revised the logframe to reflect updated milestones (e.g., policy influence targets).
Increased oversight of insurance pilots to gather evidence for national adoption.
innovations_attempted: Community piped water insurance schemes to cover physical damage/mechanical breakdowns.
Integration of Early Warning Systems (EWS) with climate-resilient infrastructure to improve disaster response.
Solar mini-grids (e.g., 152 kW in Hakwata) to support local businesses and clean energy access.
previous_recommendations_progress: Feasibility study recommendations (e.g., allocating budget for local agricultural production) are partially implemented; work with government extension services is ongoing.
Policy alignment with National Development Strategy 1 was achieved, but full integration into the National Resilience Platform is pending (target: May 2023).
forward_recommendations: Harness CAWEP to support Zimbabwe’s National Resilience Platform by May 2023, using operational research to inform policy.
Scale up the community water insurance pilot and advocate for national adoption by December 2023.
Update the programme logframe by May 2023 to reflect revised milestones and risk registers.
Plan for election-related disruptions in 2023 by finalizing realistic work plans by March 2023.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Proactive adjustments (e.g., COVID-19 mitigation, election planning) and regular risk register updates minimized disruptions. Insurance pilots address long-term sustainability risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: 77,768 people supported via 35 solar-powered piped water schemes in nine districts (as of 2023). Additional beneficiaries include 59 social institutions (schools, health centers) and 49 community nutrition gardens.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to Zimbabwe’s National Development Strategy 1 and National Adaptation Plan through evidence on climate-resilient infrastructure.
Piloted models (e.g., water insurance) may inform national policies if adopted.
Strengthened Early Warning Systems (EWS) in vulnerable districts, aligning with government climate priorities.
capacity_building_results: Trained community water management committees on operations/maintenance (90% established business models).
Technical assistance to government on climate-proofing infrastructure designs.
Supported 18 cattle troughs and 8 dip tanks, improving livestock resilience to climate shocks.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Solar water schemes enabled three schools (Nyavasikana, Manhekwe, Bilingwe) to meet registration requirements, improving education access.
Positive: Community gardens enhanced food security and nutrition (49 gardens established).
Negative: Sustainability of tariff/business models is untested long-term; may require ongoing donor support.
scalability_evidence: The community water insurance model has potential for national scaling if proven successful.
Climate-proofing standards for infrastructure can be replicated in other districts.
Multisectoral benefits (e.g., education, health) demonstrate scalability across Zimbabwe’s climate-vulnerable regions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong performance (Overall Score: A in 2023) and alignment with Zimbabwe’s climate priorities. Key achievements include resilient infrastructure delivery, policy influence, and multisectoral impact. Continuation is justified to test sustainability models (e.g., insurance schemes) and scale successful approaches.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. While community management structures and government partnerships are robust, long-term sustainability depends on the success of pilot models (e.g., insurance) and continued political support.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expand the community water insurance pilot and advocate for national policy adoption.
Strengthen ties with the National Resilience Platform to inform climate adaptation strategies.
Adjust milestones to account for election-related disruptions in 2023.
Enhance monitoring of community-led business models to ensure financial sustainability.

programme_metadata.programme_title: African Cities Research Programme

output_1.title: Robust new knowledge and evidence on African "cities of systems", domains and political settlements documented with lessons effectively communicated

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from virtual to in-person engagement post-COVID (e.g., Nairobi workshop in May 2022) enabled deeper relationship-building and research validation. Consortium adapted to ODA budget pauses by leveraging FCDO’s COVID Collective for interim research (WP4-WP6).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners exceeded expectations in co-production of knowledge (71.5% global South authorship in Set 1 cities, targeting 100% for Sets 2-3) and citizen engagement (9 groups vs. 6 targeted). Relationships with reform coalitions, political/business elites, and municipal actors strengthened beyond original plans.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Senior Management Team (SMT) operated effectively despite spatial separation, with in-person workshop (May 2022) resolving earlier virtual coordination challenges. Consortium demonstrated autonomy with minimal FCDO intervention required.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-consortium coordination improved through phased research approach (e.g., city studies → domain research → PCPs). Regular stress-testing of Theory of Change with diverse stakeholders (e.g., Nairobi workshop) ensured alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Two-stage competitive procurement (per Business Case) secured high-quality research at FCDO-compliant fee rates. Preferential supplier rates and bundled travel activities (e.g., combining research, capacity-building, and uptake in single trips) optimized costs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Lighter-touch oversight than planned due to Consortium’s strong performance and self-management. FCDO intervention limited to milestone validation (e.g., November 2022 ToC review).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted during COVID-19 to produce interim working papers (WP4-WP6) and delayed Implementation Phase start to mid-2023. Budget flexibility allowed reallocation to face-to-face activities post-pandemic.
adaptive_management_examples: Repurposed COVID-19 delay period to generate policy-relevant working papers (e.g., political settlements analysis in Kampala/Mogadishu/Nairobi).
Expanded citizen engagement in domains research (9 groups vs. 6 planned) to verify political settlement findings.
Accelerated co-authorship with global South researchers (71.5% in Set 1) to decolonize knowledge production.

main_implementation_challenges: ODA budget cuts and funding unpredictability disrupted phased research timeline, requiring milestone revisions (November 2022).
COVID-19 restrictions delayed face-to-face city-level work, reducing early-phase effectiveness (mitigated post-2022).
Scarcity of skilled researchers in conflict-affected cities (e.g., Mogadishu) increased costs and limited local capacity.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Forced virtual coordination (2020–2021), but enabled Consortium to build foundational relationships and produce interim COVID-focused papers (WP4-WP6). Post-2022 in-person work recovered lost time.
Political instability in target cities (e.g., Mogadishu) required adaptive security protocols and influenced research design (e.g., political settlements analysis).
Economic inflation (2022–2023) increased travel/consumables costs, partially offset by preferential supplier rates.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated security costs in conflict-affected cities diverted budget from research activities.
Local political sensitivities around "decolonizing knowledge" required careful navigation in co-authorship processes.
Delayed Implementation Phase (now mid-2023) compressed timeline for Priority Complex Problems (PCPs) research.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: Minor tensions in balancing academic rigor with policy relevance, resolved through iterative stakeholder validation (e.g., Nairobi ToC workshop). No major conflicts reported.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited local research capacity in some cities (e.g., Mogadishu) necessitated additional Consortium support and training.
High demand for Consortium staff time to manage expanded citizen engagement (9 groups) stretched resources temporarily.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 disruptions (materialized; mitigated via virtual work and interim papers).
ODA budget instability (materialized; addressed through phased milestone revisions).
Security risks in conflict cities (materialized; managed via adaptive protocols).

budget_execution_vs_plan: 2022 spend aligned with Business Case priorities: 58% allocated to city/domain research (staff time, consumables, local travel).
Cost overruns in conflict cities (e.g., security) offset by savings from virtual meetings and bundled travel.
Revised budget (due July 2023) to reflect delayed Implementation Phase and inflationary pressures.
value_for_money_assessment: High VfM demonstrated through: (1) preferential supplier rates (e.g., University of Manchester negotiations), (2) multi-purpose travel (e.g., combining research, uptake, and capacity-building), and (3) leveraging COVID Collective for interim outputs (WP4-WP6).
Fee rates for expert researchers remained within FCDO caps, with no evidence of cost overruns for quality.
Face-to-face work post-2022 improved VfM by enhancing research quality and stakeholder ownership.
financial_management_quality: University of Manchester’s "stringent financial systems" ensured compliance and cost control.
Regular financial reviews with FCDO confirmed no major audit findings.
Transparent reporting on cost drivers (e.g., 58% research allocation in 2022).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Economies of scale in bundled activities (e.g., Nairobi workshop combined SMT meeting, research validation, and capacity-building).
Virtual coordination reduced travel costs where feasible, though in-person work deemed essential for city-level impact.
No evidence of inefficiencies; cost per output (e.g., working papers, policy briefs) aligned with Business Case projections.

key_delivery_lessons: Phased research programmes are vulnerable to funding instability; secure multi-year commitments upfront.
Face-to-face engagement is critical for political buy-in and research validation, despite higher costs.
Co-production with global South researchers enhances quality and sustainability but requires early capacity investment.
successful_delivery_practices: Iterative Theory of Change validation with diverse stakeholders (e.g., Nairobi workshop) ensured relevance.
Bundled travel activities (research + uptake + capacity-building) optimized time and costs.
Leveraging existing networks (e.g., reform coalitions) accelerated policy engagement.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from virtual to hybrid coordination post-COVID, with in-person workshops for critical milestones.
Expanded citizen engagement scope (9 groups) based on early success in verifying political settlement findings.
Deferred Implementation Phase to mid-2023 to accommodate delays, preserving research quality.
innovations_attempted: African Cities podcast (11 episodes, 1,039 downloads across 68 countries) extended reach beyond academia.
Co-authorship model (71.5% global South in Set 1) set new standard for decolonized research.
Political settlements framework (WP4-WP6) applied to COVID-19 response analysis, validating ToC assumptions.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2021 recommendation to increase face-to-face work implemented via Nairobi workshop (May 2022) and city-level engagement.
2021 VfM concerns addressed through preferential supplier rates and activity bundling.
forward_recommendations: Finalize restructured budget by July 2023 to align with revised milestones (November 2022).
Integrate research outcomes into VfM analysis by end-July 2023 (e.g., policy uptake metrics).
Explore sustainable funding for reform coalitions to extend impact post-2026.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive mitigation of COVID-19 (virtual work + interim papers) and ODA cuts (phased revisions).
Regular ToC stress-testing (e.g., Nairobi workshop) identified emerging risks early.
Security protocols in conflict cities prevented major disruptions.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Direct: 71.5% global South authorship in Set 1 city studies; 9 citizen groups engaged in domains research (vs. 6 targeted).
Indirect: 86,000 website page views (+75% YoY), 3,400+ social media followers, 1,039 podcast downloads across 68 countries.
Policy audiences: Requests for comment from The Economist, Financial Times, BBC; engagement with government ministers and reform coalitions.
policy_influence_achieved: Working papers (WP4-WP6) on political settlements influenced COVID-19 response analysis in Kampala/Mogadishu/Nairobi.
Engagement with reform coalitions and elites positioned ACRP to inform post-2023 policy processes.
Citizen groups’ identification of Priority Complex Problems (PCPs) will feed into local policy agendas.
capacity_building_results: In-country Coalition researchers and non-Consortium partners received extensive training in political settlements analysis and co-production methods.
Global South researchers’ increased authorship (71.5% → 100% target) built sustainable research capacity.
Municipal employees and civil society groups gained skills in evidence-based problem identification (e.g., PCPs).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Expanded citizen engagement (9 groups) deepened trust in research processes and uncovered new PCPs.
Negative: Delayed Implementation Phase compressed timeline for addressing PCPs, risking rushed solutions.
scalability_evidence: Methodologies (e.g., political settlements framework) tested in 7 cities (Set 1) and designed for replication in Sets 2-3.
Reform coalitions’ cross-city learning (e.g., Nairobi workshop) suggests potential for regional scaling.
Policy briefs and communications tools (podcast, blogs) enable broad dissemination of findings.

continuation_rationale: Consistent "A" performance scores (2020–2023) demonstrate strong delivery despite challenges.
High potential for transformational impact via PCPs research (starting mid-2023) and reform coalitions.
FCDO satisfaction with Consortium’s adaptive management and VfM (e.g., leveraging COVID Collective).
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model (Consortium + reform coalitions + citizen groups) is sustainable with planned adaptations:
- Structured handover of research ownership to local partners by 2026.
- Exploration of co-funding for post-2026 reform coalitions.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Restructured budget (July 2023) to accommodate delayed Implementation Phase and inflation.
Enhanced VfM metrics incorporating research uptake and policy influence (by end-July 2023).
Expanded focus on scaling successful PCP solutions across 13 target cities.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IFIT (pilot partner) performed "very strong" in 5-month mediation project; demonstrated ability to work with local NGOs and apply conflict analysis templates. No other partners operational yet.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO maintains oversight via monthly delivery meetings (SRO, PRO, Programme Managers). Supplier will have "licence to experiment" within FCDO-set boundaries during implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Early coordination via JACS Update (OCSM consultant) and IFIT pilot. Steering Committee not yet active; will be established post-contract signature.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: IFIT pilot adapted to local conflict dynamics (Bassa-Egbura land dispute); JACS Update incorporated recent election/political context. Logframe and ToC to be refined during inception based on early learning.

main_implementation_challenges: Procurement delays (ToRs finalisation, budget confirmation, CSSF framework relaunch) lost ~1 year of planned implementation time.
Volatile security context in Northern Nigeria (escalating violence, elite-sponsored conflict, failing justice mechanisms).
Complex conflict system with intersecting drivers (political, economic, climate, land-use) requiring nuanced, locally tailored responses.
external_factors_impact: Nigeria’s 2023 federal election and new presidency created uncertainty; acute financial pressures and regional instability (e.g., Sahel spillover) exacerbated conflict risks.
Climate change impacts (e.g., water/land-use changes) emerging as potential conflict drivers, requiring baseline research under SPRiNG.
contextual_constraints_new: Underestimation of informal "rules of the game" by international actors (per JACS Update).
Emergence of ethnic militia groups (e.g., Bassa-Egbura dispute) not fully anticipated in original design.
Local government capacity constraints in mediating land/natural resource conflicts.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity of small Nigerian NGOs (e.g., IFIT’s first-time UK funding) required hands-on FCDO support.
Need for conflict analysis templates to standardise local partner assessments.
risk_materialization: Funding availability delays materialized, requiring no-cost extension consideration.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tax and Development: Equity, Efficiency and Accountable Governance

output_1.title: New Research Produced: Production of high-quality and policy-relevant tax research, mainly in FCDO priority countries in Africa and South Asia

output_2.title: Policy engagement: New research, learning and recommendations reach and engage decision makers to increase their understanding and use of evidence to improve tax policy

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The ICTD has evolved from a DFID-contracted consortium to an independent research network hosted by IDS/University of Sussex and University of Toronto. Delivery now emphasizes demand-driven research, stakeholder engagement, and capacity-building through grant competitions open to global researchers.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ICTD has exceeded expectations in research output and policy engagement. Southern partners' participation in research leadership (6/24 publications by Southern authors) demonstrates strong collaboration. Policy engagement metrics (e.g., 12 high-level policy meetings vs. 6 targeted) show partners actively driving uptake of evidence.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance remains centralized at IDS but with decentralized research execution through regional networks (e.g., Nigerian Tax Research Network, Ethiopian Tax Research Network). FCDO engagement occurs primarily through the Public Finance and Tax Development Department (PFTD), with frequent seminars and direct correspondence with country advisers.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination with FCDO (e.g., 7 collaborations requiring >0.5 staff days vs. 2 targeted) and multistakeholder platforms like the Tax and Public Financial Management Community of Practice. Regular updates to FCDO country governance advisers ensure alignment with in-country priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Grant competitions for research proposals ensure competitive selection and value for money. Existing data reuse for new analyses (e.g., informal firms survey in Ghana) demonstrates efficient resource allocation. NORAD and BMGF co-funding secured, reducing FCDO financial risk.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Light-touch oversight due to ICTD’s strong track record, with focus on milestone reviews (e.g., 6-month reset in this review) and thematic alignment with FCDO’s International Development Strategy. Financial oversight intensified during co-funding negotiations with NORAD/BMGF.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to include new themes (e.g., armed group taxation, informal enterprise tax burdens) based on emerging evidence. Research on information exchange deferred pending BMGF funding confirmation, demonstrating responsive prioritization.
adaptive_management_examples: Postponed research on "drivers of successful information exchange" until BMGF funding is confirmed, given its ambitious scope.
Launched new data collection (e.g., survey of informal firms in Ghana) to address methodological gaps in informality research.
Planned policy-focused events on armed group taxation and informal enterprise tax burdens in response to identified evidence gaps.
Revised Logical Framework milestones mid-programme to ensure targets remained "realistic and challenging" post-COVID.

main_implementation_challenges: Methodological limitations in researching informality and taxation, requiring innovative data collection (e.g., Ghana survey).
Simplistic policy conversations around informality, necessitating ICTD-led efforts to complexify debates.
Deferral of high-ambition research (e.g., information exchange) due to funding uncertainties.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted fieldwork and in-person engagements, though ICTD adapted by focusing on virtual events (e.g., 80,176 website sessions vs. 75,000 target).
Geopolitical shifts (e.g., Taliban takeover in Afghanistan) created new research priorities (e.g., Working Paper 138 on Taliban taxation).
Currency fluctuations affected co-funding values (e.g., NORAD’s NOK 40M = ~£3.3M).
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging need to study armed group taxation (e.g., Taliban) and its implications for state-building.
Growing recognition of gender and tax intersections, requiring expanded research focus.
Increased demand for digital taxation research (e.g., DIGITAX project with BMGF).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity among Southern researchers to lead complex methodological innovations, addressed through ICTD’s co-production model.
University summer/winter breaks constrained review timelines, prompting the 6-month reset to June.
risk_materialization: Financial risk from single-donor dependency mitigated by securing NORAD/BMGF co-funding (total ~£9.5M additional).
Risk of "simplistic policy conversations" materialized; ICTD countered with new data and events (e.g., planned summer 2022 policy forums).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. FCDO’s £13.3M grant (2018–2025) supplemented by £9.5M from NORAD/BMGF, reducing execution pressure. Six-month review confirmed no underspend/overspend issues.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. Efficiency gains from: (1) reusing existing data for new analyses (e.g., informality research); (2) complementary project bundling (e.g., thematically linked proposals); (3) leveraging co-funding (£9.5M from NORAD/BMGF). Cost per output (e.g., £26,600 per Working Paper) deemed competitive.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. ICTD’s diversification strategy (NORAD/BMGF) reduced FCDO exposure. Transparent reporting on milestone achievements (e.g., 10 Working Papers vs. 13 target). No audit findings reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeds targets. For example: (1) 19 media mentions vs. 16 target; (2) 80,176 website sessions vs. 75,000; (3) 12 policy meetings vs. 6. Unit costs for research outputs stable or declining due to economies of scale.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialized. Confirmed: NORAD (£3.3M), BMGF DIGITAX (£3.7M). Pending: BMGF renewal (£2.5M equivalent). Co-funding covers 42% of total programme costs, reducing FCDO burden.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Moderate. NORAD’s NOK 40M converted to ~£3.3M (vs. ~£3.5M at 2021 rates). BMGF’s USD funding stable due to hedging. No significant disruption to operations.

key_delivery_lessons: Demand-driven research (e.g., policy engagement exceeding targets by 100%) outperforms supply-driven models.
Thematic clustering of projects (e.g., informality, gender) enhances policy relevance and VfM.
Southern-led research (6/24 publications) increases local ownership but requires targeted capacity support.
successful_delivery_practices: Grant competitions for research proposals ensure quality and competition.
Reusing existing datasets for new questions (e.g., Ghana survey) maximizes VfM.
Regular FCDO seminars (e.g., Tax and PFM Community of Practice) embed evidence in policy cycles.
Co-production with civil society (e.g., Nigerian/Ethiopian Tax Research Networks) strengthens uptake.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from annual to 6-month reviews to align with academic calendars.
Deferred high-risk research (e.g., information exchange) pending secure funding.
Expanded focus on informality and armed groups in response to emerging evidence.
Increased use of virtual engagement (e.g., 80K+ website sessions) post-COVID.
innovations_attempted: New survey methodologies for informal firms (Ghana).
Policy-focused events on armed group taxation (planned Summer 2022).
Digital taxation research (DIGITAX project with BMGF).
Cross-output thematic linking (e.g., gender and informality).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially implemented: Research on informal taxation deferred but ongoing in related projects.
Fully implemented: Evidence-driven international tax reform work continued (e.g., Working Paper 139 on rural taxation).
Not implemented: Dedicated study on "informal financing for public goods" pending funding.
forward_recommendations: Launch the deferred research on information exchange once BMGF funding is confirmed.
Scale up Southern-led research through targeted capacity-building grants.
Deepen engagement with FCDO country teams on tax-in-conflict contexts (e.g., Afghanistan).
Explore partnerships with revenue authorities to pilot research findings (e.g., "services-first" taxation).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Highly effective. Proactive mitigation of financial risk via co-funding (£9.5M secured). Research risks (e.g., data gaps) addressed through methodological innovation. Political risks (e.g., Taliban) converted into research opportunities (e.g., Working Paper 138).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Governments in FCDO priority countries (Africa/South Asia); 12 high-level policy meetings; 7,788 Twitter followers (policy community).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Civil society organizations (e.g., Nigerian/Ethiopian Tax Research Networks); 80,176 website users; 19 media mentions.

policy_influence_achieved: Working Paper 139’s "services-first" approach influenced debates on rural taxation in West Africa.
Taliban taxation research (WP 138) informed donor strategies in Afghanistan.
FCDO’s Public Finance and Tax Development Department regularly uses ICTD evidence in programme design.
Tax and PFM Community of Practice integrates ICTD findings into HMG-wide policies.
capacity_building_results: 6/24 publications led by Southern authors, up from 4/20 in 2021.
Nigerian and Ethiopian Tax Research Networks now co-producing research with ICTD.
8,973 citations of ICTD work (vs. 8,500 target), indicating growing academic uptake.
Civil society partners (e.g., LOGRI) co-designing tax education tools.
unintended_consequences: Positive: ICTD’s media presence (19 mentions) amplified public debate on tax equity beyond target audiences.
Negative: None reported; deferred research on informal financing created temporary evidence gap.
scalability_evidence: ICTD’s model replicated in new regions (e.g., South Asia expansion).
Grant competition approach adopted by other FCDO-funded research programmes.
Digital taxation research (DIGITAX) scalable to other low-income contexts.
Civil society capacity-building tools (e.g., tax advocacy training) shared via open-access platforms.

continuation_rationale: Consistent high performance (A/A+ scores) and strong VfM.
Alignment with FCDO’s International Development Strategy (open economies, accountable institutions).
Secured co-funding (£9.5M) reduces FCDO financial exposure.
Emerging research agendas (e.g., digital taxation, conflict contexts) remain relevant.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. Independent network structure (IDS/University of Toronto) with diversified funding (FCDO/NORAD/BMGF) ensures long-term viability. Demand-driven approach guarantees policy relevance.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High. Exceeds targets in policy engagement (12 meetings vs. 6) and research output (13 Working Papers vs. 10). Strong alignment with FCDO’s tax and governance priorities.
planned_adaptations_future: Expand research on digital taxation (DIGITAX project) and tax-in-conflict settings.
Increase Southern leadership in research via targeted grants.
Pilot "services-first" taxation approaches in partnership with revenue authorities.
Deepen FCDO country team collaborations to embed evidence in bilateral programmes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tax and Economic Governance (TEG) Programme

output_1.title: The MRA’s capacity is increasingly strengthened to improve performance in the functions of audit to taxpayers and taxation of extractive industries.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adopted a 'patient,' opportunistic, and politically savvy 'nudge' approach rather than a strict demand-driven or payment-by-results model. This included fostering government relationships, embedding technical capacity, and remaining agile to seize reform opportunities as they arose. The programme also scaled down ambitions for certain activities (e.g., tax audit support) due to delays and political transitions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (Cowater, World Bank) performed well in delivering technical assistance and policy support, though delays were encountered due to political transitions and election-related disruptions. Tensions with Mozambique Revenue Authority (MRA) required ongoing monitoring. Sida’s formal inclusion in 2022 expanded funding and collaboration for the TEDI component.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Management remained adaptive, with embedded advisors and high-level policy dialogue playing key roles. The programme leveraged strong relationships with the new Mozambican administration post-election, despite initial delays. Oversight was intensified in areas like AML/CTF reforms and tax policy diagnostics.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO, Cowater, World Bank, and government counterparts (Ministry of Finance, MRA) was effective, particularly in aligning technical assistance with government priorities. Challenges included post-election disruptions and delays in budget approvals, which temporarily hindered engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was generally effective, though political transitions caused delays in contracting and budget execution. The programme funded national consultants (e.g., for FATF compliance) and adapted procurement timelines to align with government fiscal cycles.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than initially planned, particularly in politically sensitive areas (e.g., tax policy reforms, FATF compliance). The programme employed embedded advisors and close monitoring of partner relationships (e.g., MRA tensions).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was critical to success. The programme adapted milestones due to election disruptions, reprioritized activities to focus on achievable outcomes (e.g., tax policy roadmap), and explored innovative delivery models (e.g., embedded advisors). A no-cost extension is being pursued to mitigate underspend risks.
adaptive_management_examples: Adapted milestones and activities in response to election-related delays and post-election turmoil, including rescheduling tax audit support to Q2 2025 with scaled-down ambitions.
Shifted focus to high-impact, politically feasible reforms (e.g., tax policy diagnostic and roadmap) when broader systemic changes faced resistance.
Leveraged political transitions to formalize tax policy mandates within government structures (e.g., Fiscal Studies Department).
Pursued a no-cost extension to address underspend risks and continue momentum in key areas like AML/CTF reforms and public investment management.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays and disruptions caused by Mozambique’s 2024 elections and post-election political transition, which constrained engagement and budget approvals.
Risk of underspend across all three components (TEDI, GEDI, M&D) due to delayed activities and financial forecasting challenges.
Tensions with Mozambique Revenue Authority (MRA) requiring ongoing relationship management.
Complexity of influencing deep reforms in a politically charged environment, compounded by optimism bias and information asymmetry among stakeholders.
External shocks (e.g., COVID-19, climate events, conflict) exacerbating economic instability and public debt challenges.
external_factors_impact: Political transition and election cycle caused significant delays in programme activities and budget execution (e.g., 2025 state budget approved in May 2025 instead of December 2024).
FATF grey-listing of Mozambique increased urgency for AML/CTF reforms, requiring accelerated support to avoid economic deterrents.
Extractives sector (LNG) presented both opportunities (revenue potential) and risks (resource curse, economic imbalances).
COVID-19 and climate shocks contributed to economic downturns, increasing pressure on public debt and fiscal management.
contextual_constraints_new: Post-election turmoil disrupted usage of critical systems (e.g., Public Investment Management system), requiring recovery strategies.
Informal leadership of tax policy by the tax administration (instead of Ministry of Finance) emerged as a systemic constraint, later addressed through TEG’s support.
Limited government capacity to absorb technical assistance in certain areas (e.g., tax audits) led to scaled-down ambitions.
partner_relationship_issues: Past tensions with MRA resurfaced, necessitating proactive monitoring and potential escalation to senior leadership.
Delays in World Bank-executed trust fund (GEDI) activities due to political transitions and budget approval lags.
Challenges in aligning donor priorities (FCDO vs. Sida) within the TEDI component, though collaboration improved post-2022.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited government capacity to implement reforms in tax audits and public investment management, leading to reduced targets (e.g., 8 sector risk profiles instead of broader audit support).
Small sample sizes in training evaluations (e.g., GESI knowledge assessment based on 6 beneficiaries) highlighted gaps in monitoring capacity.
Delays in hiring or deploying technical experts due to bureaucratic hurdles and election-related freezes.
risk_materialization: Political transition risks materialized as delays in programme activities and budget execution.
Risk of underspend materialized due to slower-than-planned disbursement, particularly in GEDI and M&D components.
FATF grey-listing risk materialized, requiring urgent support to progress compliance actions (11 of 12 actions improved from 'Partly Compliant' to 'Compliant').
Resource curse risks in the extractives sector began unfolding, as predicted, with economic imbalances and limited trickle-down growth.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution faced significant delays due to political transitions and election disruptions. The 2025 state budget (key for reporting) was approved in May 2025 instead of December 2024, causing a 5-month delay in financial planning. All three components (TEDI, GEDI, M&D) are at high risk of underspend by the programme’s end date. A no-cost extension is being pursued to mitigate this.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: TEG demonstrates good to excellent value for money, despite challenges. Key achievements include: (1) Development of Mozambique’s first National Revenue Mobilisation Strategy (2025–2027), (2) Formalization of the tax policy mandate within the Ministry of Finance, (3) Progress on 11 of 12 FATF compliance actions, and (4) Leveraged budget support and additional tax revenues. The programme’s adaptive, relationship-based approach yielded high-impact results (e.g., policy influence, capacity building) at relatively low cost compared to potential fiscal gains for Mozambique.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by implementers (Cowater, World Bank) was strong, with proactive adjustments to mitigate delays. However, external factors (e.g., election-related budget freezes) strained planning. The programme maintained transparency in reporting financial risks (e.g., underspend) and pursued corrective actions (e.g., no-cost extension).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was high in areas where technical assistance directly influenced policy changes (e.g., tax reforms, FATF compliance). For example, TEDI’s support to the tax policy function (sole external provider for 4 years) led to systemic changes at minimal incremental cost. However, inefficiencies arose from delayed activities (e.g., tax audits) and underutilized capacity in some components.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized successfully in the TEDI component, with Sida contributing 50% (£6m) of the £12m budget starting July 2022. This expanded the programme’s reach and sustainability. No issues with co-funding delivery were reported.

key_delivery_lessons: A patient, adaptive, and politically savvy approach is more effective for complex reforms than rigid demand-driven or payment-by-results models.
Political economy analysis tools are necessary but insufficient; understanding and influencing deep reform incentives requires nuanced, context-specific engagement.
Embedded advisors and high-level policy dialogue can bridge gaps between technical assistance and government ownership.
Flexibility in milestone adjustments (e.g., due to elections) is critical to maintaining momentum without compromising quality.
successful_delivery_practices: Building long-term relationships with government counterparts to create trust and reform incentives.
Leveraging windows of opportunity (e.g., post-election transitions) to formalize institutional changes (e.g., Fiscal Studies Department).
Combining technical assistance with policy dialogue to align reforms with political priorities.
Using embedded advisors to ensure continuity and institutional memory during transitions.
Prioritizing high-impact, evidence-based interventions (e.g., tax policy roadmap) over broad, shallow support.
management_adaptations_made: Scaled down ambitions for tax audit support due to capacity constraints, focusing instead on developing risk profiles for 8 key sectors.
Reprioritized activities in the final year to emphasize outcome-level reporting (e.g., tracking additional revenue collected with TEDI support).
Adopted pre- and post-tests for training evaluations to address subjective self-assessment limitations (e.g., GESI knowledge).
Pursued a no-cost extension to address underspend risks and explore innovative delivery models (e.g., expanded use of embedded advisors).
innovations_attempted: Testing embedded advisor models within the Government of Mozambique to deepen institutional capacity.
Expanding the Fiscal Risks Report to include Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) and subnational entities, improving fiscal risk understanding.
Developing Mozambique’s first medium-term National Revenue Mobilisation Strategy (2025–2027) as a systemic reform anchor.
Using a ‘nudge’ approach to incrementally influence tax policy reforms in a politically constrained environment.
previous_recommendations_progress: Progress on strengthening outcome-level reporting (Recommendation 1) is underway, with a focus on tracking additional revenue and policy influence metrics.
Exploration of a programme extension (Recommendation 2) is active, with a target to seek a no-cost extension by September 2025.
Strategy to restore the Public Investment Management system (Recommendation 3) is being developed for the 2026 state budget.
Monitoring of MRA relationships (Recommendation 4) continues, with escalation protocols in place if tensions resurface.
forward_recommendations: Prioritize activities that can demonstrate outcome-level results before programme closure (e.g., revenue collection data, policy uptake).
Secure a no-cost extension to mitigate underspend risks and test innovative delivery models (e.g., embedded advisors at scale).
Develop a transition plan to ensure sustainability of reforms, particularly in tax policy and AML/CTF compliance.
Strengthen monitoring of unintended consequences (e.g., equity impacts of tax reforms) and adaptive management responses.
Explore linkages with potential future programmes (e.g., IMF tax reform initiatives) to sustain momentum.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective. While the programme anticipated political and capacity risks, their materialization (e.g., election delays, FATF grey-listing) required reactive adaptations. Proactive measures, such as relationship-building and flexible milestone adjustments, mitigated some impacts. However, financial risks (underspend) and systemic risks (resource curse) remained challenging to fully address. The programme’s ability to influence FATF compliance and tax policy reforms demonstrates strong risk response in targeted areas.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Government of Mozambique (Ministry of Finance, Mozambique Revenue Authority), with technical assistance reaching ~100+ officials through training, capacity building, and embedded support. Specific examples include: (1) 6 beneficiaries in GESI training (though small sample), (2) National consultants supported for FATF compliance, (3) Tax policy team within the new Fiscal Studies Department.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Mozambican citizens benefiting from improved revenue mobilization and public spending (e.g., through the National Revenue Mobilisation Strategy 2025–2027). Extractives sector stakeholders (e.g., LNG companies) influenced by transfer pricing and tax policy reforms.

policy_influence_achieved: Government approval of Mozambique’s first National Revenue Mobilisation Strategy (2025–2027), developed with TEDI support.
Formalization of the tax policy mandate within the Ministry of Finance’s Fiscal Studies Department, ending the informal leadership by the tax administration.
Progress on 11 of 12 FATF compliance actions, with potential grey-list removal by October 2025.
Expansion of the Fiscal Risks Report to include PPPs and subnational entities, improving fiscal risk management.
capacity_building_results: Strengthened capacity in transfer pricing analysis (e.g., two training activities conducted, including an OECD workshop).
Improved technical skills in tax policy formulation within the Ministry of Finance, though GESI training outcomes were mixed (50% self-reported improvement).
Enhanced AML/CTF compliance capabilities, with 11 FATF actions upgraded from 'Partly Compliant' to 'Compliant'.
Development of risk profiles for 8 sectors to embed risk-informed practices in tax audits (scaled-down from original ambitions).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Strengthened government ownership of tax policy reduced informal influence by the revenue authority, improving institutional coherence.
Negative: Delays in tax audit support may have weakened short-term revenue enforcement, though long-term risk-based approaches are being embedded.
Mixed: The ‘patient’ approach yielded high-level policy wins but may have slowed progress on inclusive growth outcomes (e.g., service delivery improvements).
scalability_evidence: The tax policy diagnostic and roadmap methodology is scalable to other sectors or countries facing similar resource governance challenges.
Embedded advisor models (tested in TEG) could be expanded to other PFM areas or regions within Mozambique.
FATF compliance approaches are replicable for other grey-listed countries, though context-specific adaptation is needed.
The National Revenue Mobilisation Strategy provides a template for evidence-based fiscal planning in similar contexts.

continuation_rationale: Strong programme performance (consistent 'A' scores) and high potential for sustained impact justify continuation.
Critical reforms (e.g., tax policy, FATF compliance) are nearing fruition but require additional time to fully embed and demonstrate outcomes.
Risk of underspend across all components due to political delays; an extension would optimize use of allocated funds.
Opportunity to test innovative delivery models (e.g., expanded embedded advisors) and prepare for future FCDO portfolio developments.
Government of Mozambique’s formalized commitments (e.g., National Revenue Mobilisation Strategy) create a platform for further collaboration.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is partially sustainable. Strengths include strong government relationships, embedded capacity, and adaptive management. However, risks remain around long-term funding (post-2026), political continuity, and absorption capacity for complex reforms. A no-cost extension would address immediate sustainability gaps.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (implied by consistent 'A' scores, positive value-for-money assessment, and recommendation to extend).
planned_adaptations_future: Pursue a no-cost extension to June 2026 (or beyond) to complete critical activities and demonstrate outcome-level results.
Expand use of embedded advisors within government structures to deepen institutional capacity.
Strengthen outcome-level reporting (e.g., tracking revenue gains, policy influence) for the Project Completion Report.
Develop a transition plan to hand over reforms to government ownership, including sustainability mechanisms for the Fiscal Studies Department and AML/CTF structures.
Explore linkages with potential follow-on programmes (e.g., IMF tax reforms) to ensure continuity of support.
