output_1.title: Community & interpersonal engagement: girls, women and communities are empowered to discuss, challenge, and transform harmful social and gender norms in the target communities to end FGM and CM

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended to March 2026 due to conflict disruptions; increased focus on humanitarian response integration (e.g., mobile clinics, IDP camp services). Shift from federal to state/local-level system strengthening due to conflict-induced federal-level slowdowns. Expanded use of local partners (100+ entities in 2023 vs. 90 in 2022) to maintain access in conflict-affected areas.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UN agencies (UNICEF, UNFPA, WHO) demonstrated agility in adapting to conflict, though offices in conflict zones were closed and staff displaced. Local NGOs and grassroots organizations filled critical gaps in service delivery. Partners exceeded revised targets in Q4 2023 despite disruptions, leveraging existing community networks for continuity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Decentralized coordination due to conflict, with increased reliance on state-level task forces and local governance structures. Partnership Coordination Unit (PCU) played a pivotal role in adaptive planning. Regular workplan revisions (quarterly) to align with evolving context.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination among PUNOs (UNICEF, UNFPA, WHO) despite physical displacement, enabled by pre-existing relationships and digital platforms. Integration with humanitarian clusters (e.g., GBV, health) improved service reach. Challenges in federal-level coordination due to conflict, offset by subnational collaboration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Shift to international procurement channels (e.g., dignity kits via long-term agreements) to mitigate Sudanese pound depreciation and supply chain instability. Shared resources (e.g., office spaces in Port Sudan) reduced costs. Local procurement remained limited due to liquidity constraints and volatility.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight intensity in 2023 due to conflict risks, with more frequent partner check-ins (monthly vs. quarterly) and real-time monitoring of humanitarian adaptations. FCDO maintained remote oversight where in-person visits were infeasible.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme utilized flexibility to: 1) Reallocate funds to humanitarian response (e.g., mobile clinics, GBV services in IDP camps); 2) Extend timeline to March 2026; 3) Revise logframe to focus on critical indicators; 4) Integrate FGM/CM messaging into broader GBV/SRHR programming. adaptive_management_examples: Rapid scale-up of GBV services in 8 states via mobile clinics, reaching 100k+ women/girls despite conflict.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Teacher Effectiveness and Equitable Access for Children (TEACH) in Zimbabwe

output_1.title: Equitable access to schools for marginalised girls and boys, including Children with disabilities (CWDs)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned from two separate education programmes to one unified TEACH programme in 2023. Transferred school improvement grants and schoolgirls bursaries to the Global Programme for Education (GPE). Introduced two new components: Supporting Adolescent Girls Education (SAGE) via Plan Zimbabwe and an education innovation component via Think Equal. Consolidated from 5 to 6 active components with revised delivery partners (UNICEF, EDT, Plan Zimbabwe, Think Equal).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF and EDT performed as expected in delivering SIGs and TPD respectively. New partners (Plan Zimbabwe, Think Equal) were onboarded successfully post-election with no anticipated delays. Co-facilitation between MOPSE and EDT teams proved effective in balancing government priorities with innovation. Coordination challenges persisted in school leadership training due to multiple providers (UNICEF, EDT, British Council, NGOs) operating in parallel.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Direct implementation for monitoring/supervision (Component 103) alongside partner-led components. Monthly TEACH Implementation Committee meetings introduced to improve coordination. Adaptive management required extensive stakeholder engagement (MOPSE, FCDO, partners) to align with government systems.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved but inconsistent. School leadership coordination showed progress with unified training materials for FCDO-funded support, but gaps remain in districts with multiple providers. Sector-wide dialogue structures (e.g., October 2023 presentation) enhanced stakeholder awareness of changes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Amendments to UNICEF Standard Administrative Agreements and EDT contracts completed. New accountable grants for Plan Zimbabwe and Think Equal finalized without delays. Procurement processes adapted to Zimbabwe’s post-election context.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to hyperinflation and political transitions. Increased oversight of SIG disbursement to ensure timely delivery (91% of schools received SIGs by cutoff). Decentralized training models required additional monitoring to maintain quality.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility: adjusted SIG allocations (e.g., supplementary funds for remote schools/CWDs), revised TPD delivery to localised/IT-assisted approaches, and shifted ZELA task to GPE for 2024. Budget reallocations enabled by cost extensions (£39.84m → £55.54m).
adaptive_management_examples: Revised SIG criteria to harmonize with GPE funding, enabling transition of school financing to government systems.
Decentralized TPD training to provinces, increasing trainer capacity and reducing costs (from $21 to $19.99 per educator).
Introduced T-GROW coaching model for school leaders to shift from punitive to supportive supervision.
Adapted TPD materials to address gender barriers (e.g., mentorship for female teachers) based on research findings.
Postponed ZELA handover to GPE by one year to ensure smooth transition.

main_implementation_challenges: Hyperinflation (175.8% annualised) eroded purchasing power, requiring US$-denominated "Nostra" accounts for SIGs.
Political transitions (2023 elections) caused temporary delays in partner contracts and ministerial approvals.
Coordinating school leadership training across multiple providers (UNICEF, EDT, British Council, NGOs) led to uneven delivery quality.
Documentation gaps in SIG disbursement caused late/non-receipt for 9% of eligible schools.
Fuel price volatility (blend fuel increased from $1.33–$1.76/litre in 2021/22 to $1.61–$1.70/litre in 2022/23) raised school visit costs.
external_factors_impact: Zimbabwe’s economic crisis (hyperinflation, currency instability) necessitated US$-denominated transactions and frequent budget adjustments.
Post-election government restructuring delayed contract amendments and policy approvals (e.g., School Financing Policy).
COVID-19 legacy effects persisted in teacher capacity gaps (e.g., ICT skills, handling large class sizes).
Global Partnership for Education (GPE) funding shifts required alignment of TEACH components with GPE priorities.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for gender-specific interventions (e.g., barriers to female teacher promotion) identified through research (Indicator 3.3/3.5b).
School inspectors’ perverse incentives (rewarded for visit quantity over quality) hindered adoption of new supervision approaches.
Limited government capacity to absorb SIG mechanisms into domestic financing despite policy commitments.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial coordination gaps between UNICEF and EDT on school leadership training, later addressed through unified materials.
Delays in GPE-funded tasks (e.g., ZELA handover) due to misaligned timelines between TEACH and GPE workplans.
Differing priorities between MOPSE (policy alignment) and EDT (innovation) required extensive mediation.
capacity_constraints_emerged: MOPSE’s limited capacity to inspect resource units for Children with Disabilities (CWDs) despite indicator targets.
School leaders lacked training on using evidence for continuous improvement (e.g., inclusion, learning outcomes).
Teachers reported gaps in ICT skills and practical classroom management (e.g., large class sizes, diverse special needs).
District-level variability in implementing new coaching models (T-GROW) due to uneven trainer quality.
risk_materialization: Hyperinflation risk materialized, requiring US$ denominated transactions and VfM indicator adjustments.
Political transition risks materialized post-election, causing temporary implementation pauses.
Partner coordination risks materialized in school leadership training, addressed through monthly committee meetings.
Risk of low female teacher participation in leadership roles identified and mitigated via targeted mentorship programs.

Savings achieved in TPD training costs (reduced from $21 to $19.99 per educator) enabled training of additional participants.
SIG allocations adjusted downward (from $1,400 to $1,000 per school in 2023) with supplementary funds for remote schools/CWDs.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: No procurement issues reported. Existing MRC/Wellcome systems used for all calls, ensuring efficiency. Call 7 (2020) processed 185 proposals with 4 research grants and 7 foundation grants recommended for funding (subject to approval).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight maintained at planned levels despite COVID-19, with virtual monitoring replacing in-person meetings. No reduction in scrutiny quality reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Budget flexibility used to protect 2020/21 funding despite ODA cuts, with MRC covering deferred FCDO funds. Adaptive management included reducing foundation grant targets for 2021 and adjusting indicators to 3-year averages.
adaptive_management_examples: Transition to virtual Expert Panel meetings (March 2020 onward) without delaying funding decisions.
Adjustment of 2021 foundation grant targets and indicator methodologies in response to COVID-19 impacts.
MRC's agreement to cover deferred FCDO funds (2021/22) to protect ongoing research.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 pandemic disrupted workloads and priorities, diverting attention from follow-up on previous review recommendations.
Difficulty in measuring cross-portfolio impact due to limitations in ResearchFish data quality (e.g., lack of gender-disaggregated metrics, lag in 2019 data for 2020 reporting).
ODA budget reductions (2020/21) required protective measures to safeguard funding, affecting grant planning.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Economic impacts reduced FCDO's ODA budget, leading to a cut in HSRI contributions for 2020/21. Operational adaptation included virtual meetings and deferred funding coverage by MRC.
Global research priorities shifted temporarily, though HSRI's focus on health systems remained relevant (e.g., evidence used for WHO malaria guidelines and NCD policies).
contextual_constraints_new: ResearchFish data limitations (variable quality, outdated metrics) hindered comprehensive impact assessment.
Increased demand for policy-relevant research on pandemic response diverted some capacity from long-term health systems work.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: No significant issues reported. MRC/FCDO relationship remained strong, with MRC covering deferred funds. Minor challenge in aligning LMIC definitions across partners (to be resolved by June 2021).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity to follow up on 2019 review recommendations due to COVID-19 workloads.
Need for additional analysis to extract health systems improvement examples from ResearchFish data (planned for October 2021).
risk_materialization: Moderate risk of delayed outputs/outcomes due to COVID-19 (monitored but not yet materialized).
Budget risk materialized with ODA cuts, mitigated by MRC's deferred funding coverage.

budget_execution_vs_plan: 2020/21 FCDO contribution reduced due to ODA cuts, but total funding protected via MRC's deferred fund coverage.
£2.2m carried forward from previous phase used for ongoing projects. No underspend reported; all calls fully executed within adjusted budgets.
Call 7 (2020) held back some funding in anticipation of additional costs, affecting the number of new grants recommended.
value_for_money_assessment: High VfM achieved by leveraging MRC/Wellcome's existing systems (peer review, grant management), minimizing administrative costs.
Cost efficiency maintained despite COVID-19; no evidence of reduced quality in grant awards or oversight.
Potential future VfM risks if grant timelines extend due to pandemic delays (to be monitored).
financial_management_quality: MRC and Wellcome's financial management systems performed well, with rigorous monitoring frameworks in place.
No audit findings or financial irregularities reported. Transparent tracking via ResearchFish (though data quality issues noted).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Costs minimized by using partners' existing infrastructure (e.g., peer review panels, ResearchFish).
Staffing/overheads for research projects remained the primary cost drivers, as planned.
co_funding_materialization: Co-funding fully materialized: partners committed £28.5m total (including £8.5m FCDO), leveraging >2x FCDO's contribution.
No co-funding shortfalls reported; all partners honored commitments despite ODA cuts.

key_delivery_lessons: Virtual Expert Panel meetings (post-March 2020) were equally effective as in-person, reducing costs without compromising quality.
Leveraging existing partner systems (MRC/Wellcome) for grant management ensures efficiency and high standards.
Regular annual calls allow responsiveness to emerging issues (e.g., increased LMIC applications in Calls 6–7).
successful_delivery_practices: Use of ResearchFish for centralized output tracking, despite data limitations.
Collaborative funder governance (joint meetings, shared risk assessments) strengthened alignment.
Foundation grants (12–18 months) provided flexible funding for exploratory research, complementing longer-term grants.
management_adaptations_made: Reduced 2021 foundation grant targets to reflect COVID-19 constraints.
Adjusted indicators to measure 3-year averages (instead of annual) for more realistic benchmarking.
Increased focus on LMIC applicant monitoring and gender-disaggregated data collection (planned for June 2021).
innovations_attempted: Virtual grant review processes (successfully implemented in 2020).
ART Access app (Uganda) for HIV medication delivery, demonstrating research-to-practice innovation.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress: 2019 recommendations delayed due to COVID-19 workloads (e.g., impact measurement, gender data).
External review follow-up planned for October 2021 to address outstanding items.
forward_recommendations: By June 2021: Reduce foundation grant targets; confirm LMIC definition; improve gender-disaggregated data via ResearchFish.
By October 2021: Follow up external review recommendations; analyze ResearchFish data for health systems impact examples.
Ongoing: Monitor COVID-19/ODA budget impacts on MRC-FCDO relationship and grant awards.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective mitigation of budget risks (MRC covered deferred funds).
Moderate risk rating maintained despite COVID-19, with no major unmitigated risks materializing.
Need for stronger impact measurement tools (addressed via external review).

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 35 full research grants and 57 foundation grants awarded to date (6 calls).
48% of projects reported policy/practice impacts (e.g., Vietnam medical equipment policy, India's National Medical Commission Bill).
185 proposals submitted in Call 7 (2020), with increased LMIC representation.
policy_influence_achieved: National-level impacts: Vietnam (medical equipment policy), India (medical education regulation), Ethiopia (primary health care planning).
Global-level impacts: WHO technical brief on malaria RDTs; Caribbean NCD prevention policies.
79% of 2020 peer-reviewed publications had female first authors, indicating inclusive research leadership.
capacity_building_results: Strengthened research capacity in Southern institutions via grants and collaborations.
ART Access app (Uganda) demonstrates translational research impact.
Increased LMIC principal investigators in Calls 6–7 (e.g., 4/4 research grants in Call 7 led by female PIs).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Virtual meetings reduced costs and increased accessibility for LMIC participants.
Negative: COVID-19 delayed follow-up on some policy engagement activities (e.g., external review recommendations).
scalability_evidence: Research findings adopted in multiple countries (e.g., malaria RDT guidelines, NCD policies).
Grant mechanisms (foundation + full grants) proven adaptable to different contexts and scalable via annual calls.

continuation_rationale: Programme leverages >2x FCDO's contribution via partner funds, ensuring cost efficiency.
High demand for health systems research (185 proposals in Call 7) and strong policy uptake (48% projects report impacts).
Flexible annual calls allow responsiveness to emerging priorities (e.g., COVID-19, NCDs).
MRC/Wellcome systems ensure low administrative costs and high-quality oversight.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High (existing partner systems minimize costs; virtual adaptations reduce logistical burdens).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (consistent 'A' scores, strong VfM, and policy relevance).
planned_adaptations_future: Enhance ResearchFish data collection (gender, geography fields) by June 2021.
Monitor ODA budget impacts and adjust grant targets as needed.
Strengthen impact measurement via external review follow-up (October 2021).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Second phase of FCDO’s Support to the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG) Programme

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: PIDG underwent a 2018 restructure introducing the 'One PIDG' operating model, centralizing strategy and investment policy under PIDG Limited. This created stronger coordination across business lines (Upstream Technical Assistance, Developer-Investor, Credit Solutions). The 2022 review highlights continued adaptation through innovations like local currency guarantees and Credit Enhancement Facilities (CEFs).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong commitment despite market headwinds. GuarantCo diversified partnerships with insurance sector and corporate treasuries, while EAIF utilized PIDG facilities (e.g., VGF) to counter perceived risks in FCAS/low-income countries. InfraCo Africa and GuarantCo met/exceeded targets; EAIF and InfraCo Asia missed targets due to challenging conditions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The 'One PIDG' model with centralized PIDG Limited proved effective, enabling adaptive management. A new Group Head of CEFs was appointed in 2023 to scale Credit Enhancement Facilities. Board-approved revised targets (e.g., 18 projects for 'expected' performance, 20+ for 'excellent') provided clear benchmarks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Central coordination under PIDG Limited improved cross-company collaboration. Examples include joint work on the CLEAR Fund (climate resilience) and Kenya Credit Enhancement Facility launched at COP27. However, economic pressures required additional efforts to align partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: PIDG supported EVN Finance in Vietnam with a $50m partial credit guarantee for the first onshore local-currency green bond, demonstrating innovative procurement. Axian Telecom investment enabled access to international capital pools for SSA telecom infrastructure.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Active oversight was maintained, with Board reporting on Tier 1 KPIs (e.g., private sector mobilization ratios). The 2022 review notes increased focus on climate adaptation/resilience in investment decisions, requiring enhanced monitoring.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: PIDG's flexible structure allowed rapid adaptation to market shocks (COVID, Ukraine war, inflation). Examples include: 1) Diversifying funding sources (e.g., insurance sector partnerships), 2) Launching new instruments like CEFs, 3) Prioritizing climate-aligned projects despite reduced private capital flows.
adaptive_management_examples: Response to reduced private capital flows by using PIDG facilities (e.g., VGF) to bridge funding gaps in FCAS countries.
Launch of the CLEAR Fund (climate adaptation) in partnership with MOBILIST, addressing emerging priorities.
Support for EVN Finance’s green bond in Vietnam, demonstrating local-currency innovation.
Appointment of a Group Head of CEFs in 2023 to scale credit enhancement models.

main_implementation_challenges: Significant market headwinds from COVID-19 aftermath, inflation, and the Ukraine war led to reduced private sector investment in EMDEs.
Flight of capital from high-risk markets (FCAS/LDCs) to safer developed economies, increasing financing gaps.
Supply chain disruptions causing project delays, cost increases, and renegotiations.
Reduced funding availability for Technical Assistance (TA), critical for development impact.
Balancing climate ambition with financial sustainability in the new 2030 strategy.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Persistent operational disruptions and reduced investor appetite for risk.
Ukraine War: Inflationary pressures and capital flight from frontier markets.
Climate Change: Increased focus on adaptation/resilience required strategic shifts, e.g., prioritizing projects with lower emissions.
Macroeconomic Conditions: Higher interest rates and inflation reduced overall investment levels in PIDG markets.
contextual_constraints_new: Need to treat nature as an investment opportunity (not just a constraint) in infrastructure projects.
Emerging requirement to link infrastructure access metrics to adaptation/resilience principles.
Pressure to demonstrate additionality in a crowded DFI landscape with counter-cyclical investments.
partner_relationship_issues: EAIF and InfraCo Asia missed 2022 targets, highlighting challenges in aligning partner performance with ambitious goals.
Divergent risk appetites among PIDG companies required centralized coordination to maintain group-wide targets.
Fundraising for new CEFs required identifying strategic partners, an ongoing process in 2023.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Reduced TA funding constrained PIDG’s ability to enhance development impact in high-need areas.
Need for additional expertise in climate adaptation/resilience to meet new strategic ambitions.
Limited local institutional capacity in some FCAS markets slowed project implementation (e.g., first-of-a-kind green bonds).
risk_materialization: Market Risks: Inflation and capital flight materialized as predicted, requiring PIDG to act as a counter-cyclical investor.
Operational Risks: Supply chain disruptions and longer lead times for project completion.
Financial Risks: Reduced private sector mobilization (though still above targets) due to risk aversion.
Strategic Risks: Need for additional concessional capital to deliver the 2030 strategy became apparent.

budget_execution_vs_plan: PIDG supported projects mobilized $1.3bn in 2022 (vs. target of >$3.5bn ratio to PIDG commitments, achieving 4.2x).
$752m of the $1.3bn came from private sector investors, demonstrating continued (though reduced) private capital mobilization.
Budget execution was challenged by inflation and reduced investment flows, but PIDG met its mobilization ratio targets.
value_for_money_assessment: PIDG’s mobilization ratios (4.2x in 2022) exceeded the >3.5x target, indicating strong VFM.
Cost efficiency was maintained despite inflation, with PIDG acting as a catalyst for private investment in high-impact sectors (e.g., off-grid solar, climate resilience).
The shift toward smaller-scale projects (e.g., affordable housing, mini-grids) in 2022 reduced aggregate infrastructure access numbers but aligned with climate and inclusion goals.
financial_management_quality: Robust financial management enabled PIDG to exceed KPIs despite external shocks.
Centralized oversight under PIDG Limited ensured consistent reporting on Tier 1 KPIs (e.g., private sector mobilization).
Innovative financial instruments (e.g., local-currency guarantees, CEFs) were deployed effectively to mitigate risks.
cost_efficiency_achieved: PIDG’s lean structure and flexible capital deployment allowed cost-efficient operations.
The $50m partial credit guarantee for EVN Finance’s green bond in Vietnam demonstrated cost-effective risk mitigation.
However, inflation placed downward pressure on overall investment levels, requiring PIDG to prioritize higher-impact, smaller-scale projects.
co_funding_materialization: Several PIDG Owners (DGIS, SECO, DFAT) renewed funding commitments in 2022, reducing immediate uncertainty.
Additional funding is still required from other donors to fully deliver the 2030 strategy, particularly for TA and climate ambitions.
The CLEAR Fund was established in partnership with MOBILIST, showing successful co-funding for climate adaptation.
currency_exchange_impacts: Local-currency guarantees (e.g., EVN Finance bond in Vietnam) helped mitigate FX risks for investors.
Inflation and currency volatility in PIDG markets increased project costs but were partially offset by PIDG’s risk-sharing instruments.

key_delivery_lessons: PIDG’s counter-cyclical role is critical during economic downturns, but requires sufficient concessional capital to sustain impact.
Flexible instruments (e.g., CEFs, local-currency guarantees) are essential for mobilizing private capital in FCAS/LDCs.
Centralized coordination under 'One PIDG' improves adaptability but requires continuous alignment of diverse partner interests.
Climate adaptation/resilience must be integrated into core investment decisions, not treated as an add-on.
successful_delivery_practices: Diversifying funding sources (e.g., insurance sector partnerships, corporate treasuries) to maintain project pipelines.
Using PIDG facilities (e.g., VGF) to bridge gaps in high-risk markets during capital flight.
Launching innovative funds like CLEAR to address emerging priorities (climate adaptation).
Scaling successful models (e.g., InfraCredit) through dedicated leadership (e.g., Group Head of CEFs).
management_adaptations_made: Revised Board-approved targets for project financial closes (18 expected, 20+ excellent) to reflect market realities.
Elevated climate mitigation/adaptation/resilience as central to the 2030 strategy, requiring new KPIs and expertise.
Strengthened reporting on additionality and development impact to demonstrate VFM to Owners.
Enhanced coordination with FCDO to align with UK priorities (e.g., British Investment Partnerships, JETPs).
innovations_attempted: First onshore local-currency green bond in Vietnam (EVN Finance), attracting institutional investors.
Expansion of Credit Enhancement Facilities (CEFs) to de-risk projects in challenging markets.
CLEAR Fund for climate-aligned businesses in Africa, developed with MOBILIST.
Use of partial credit guarantees to crowd in private capital for green infrastructure (e.g., rooftop solar in Vietnam).
previous_recommendations_progress: 2021 recommendation to roll out InfraCredit model was integrated into the 2022 strategy refresh, with 8 new CEFs planned.
Funding uncertainties from 2021 were partially addressed by renewed commitments from DGIS, SECO, and DFAT in 2022.
Progress on climate KPIs was made, but full alignment with the new strategy requires further work in 2023.
forward_recommendations: Finalize the 2030 strategy with clear, ambitious Tier 1–3 KPIs reflecting climate and adaptation priorities.
Secure additional concessional capital from Owners to deliver the strategy, particularly for TA and climate goals.
Develop a robust evaluation framework to track climate adaptation/resilience impacts.
Strengthen FCDO-PIDG coordination to leverage UK government platforms (e.g., British Investment Partnerships).
Monitor and mitigate risks from continued inflation and private capital flight in 2023–2025.
risk_management_effectiveness: PIDG effectively managed market risks by acting as a counter-cyclical investor and diversifying funding sources.
Proactive adaptation to inflation and supply chain disruptions through flexible instruments (e.g., VGF, CEFs).
Climate risks were increasingly integrated into investment decisions, though full implementation of the new strategy is pending.
Centralized risk reporting to the Board ensured transparency, but external shocks (e.g., Ukraine war) required rapid adjustments.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 2022: 21 projects reached financial close, expected to provide >3 million people with new/improved infrastructure access (vs. 8.8m in 2021 and 14.4m in 2020).
43% of 2022 projects were in FCAS, and 76% in Least Developed Countries (LDCs).
1.5 million people gained *new* access to infrastructure (vs. improved access), driven by projects like Bboxx (897k new energy users) and Axian Telecom (400k new customers).
Cumulative results: 55% of projects in LDCs (vs. 50% target) and 53% in FCAS (vs. 45% target) since 2015.
policy_influence_achieved: PIDG’s climate strategy influenced investment decisions across the group, prioritizing lower-emission projects.
Launch of the CLEAR Fund and Kenya Credit Enhancement Facility at COP27 demonstrated thought leadership in climate adaptation.
Partnership with African Development Bank’s ‘Alliance for Green Infrastructure in Africa’ (AGIA) expanded policy reach.
PIDG’s role in the British Investment Partnerships toolkit aligns with UK government priorities on climate and infrastructure.
capacity_building_results: Technical Assistance (TA) supported project development in FCAS/LDCs, though funding constraints limited scale.
Local institutional capacity was strengthened through instruments like the EVN Finance green bond in Vietnam, attracting local investors.
PIDG companies (e.g., InfraCo Africa, GuarantCo) built partner capacity to navigate complex markets (e.g., first-of-a-kind projects in DRC, Madagascar).
unintended_consequences: Positive: PIDG’s counter-cyclical investments helped stabilize markets during capital flight, benefiting local economies.
Positive: Innovations like local-currency guarantees created precedents for other DFIs to follow (e.g., Vietnam green bond).
Negative: Reduced TA funding may have limited long-term capacity building in some markets.
Negative: Focus on climate-aligned projects may have diverted resources from other high-impact sectors (e.g., large-scale power plants).
scalability_evidence: Credit Enhancement Facilities (CEFs) and InfraCredit model are being scaled across new markets (8 additional CEFs planned).
Success of the CLEAR Fund suggests potential for replication in other regions beyond Africa.
Local-currency guarantee model (e.g., Vietnam) can be adapted to other FCAS markets with similar FX risks.
PIDG’s ‘One PIDG’ operating model demonstrates scalability for multi-donor infrastructure platforms.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (A+ ratings) and alignment with FCDO priorities (e.g., British Investment Partnerships, JETPs).
Critical role in mobilizing private capital in FCAS/LDCs, especially during economic downturns.
Successful adaptation to external shocks (COVID, inflation, Ukraine war) demonstrates resilience.
The 2030 strategy positions PIDG as a leader in climate adaptation/resilience, addressing emerging global priorities.
delivery_model_sustainability: The ‘One PIDG’ model has proven effective but requires continued centralized coordination.
Financial sustainability depends on securing additional concessional capital from Owners for the 2030 strategy.
Partner performance varies (e.g., EAIF/InfraCo Asia missed 2022 targets), requiring ongoing management.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize and implement the 2030 strategy with revised KPIs emphasizing climate and adaptation.
Scale innovative instruments (CEFs, local-currency guarantees) to new markets.
Strengthen monitoring of climate/resilience impacts through a robust evaluation framework.
Diversify funding sources further to reduce reliance on volatile private capital flows.
Enhance coordination with FCDO to leverage UK government platforms and policy influence.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Strengthening Public Finance Management in Tanzania Programme

output_1.title: Improved macroeconomic and macro-fiscal policy making, budget management, execution and scrutiny, and budget control and oversight

output_2.title: Improved Financial Accountability and Oversight and Audit

output_3.title: PFM systems and outcomes in Local Governments are improved

output_4.title: Improved research and analytical capacity on macroeconomics, PFM and business environment in Tanzania

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from financial aid to Government of Tanzania (GoT) to Alternative Delivery Arrangement (ADA) channeled through Ecorys (implemented from September 2021). Financial aid officially stopped in April 2021 due to disputed Tanzanian elections (November 2020). Budget reduced by 40% from £20M to £12.1M.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Ecorys performed well as ADA manager, leveraging embedded PFM advisors across regions. British Council successfully extended scholarships (6 additional master's + 2 short courses). REPOA faced 60% budget reduction and shortened duration (ended June 2022 instead of January 2023).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO took lead in procurement (e.g., Mid-Term Evaluation) and technical engagement (PFMRP V working groups). Ecorys contract amended to implement ADA. Governance adapted to ADA with high transaction costs (9 months setup).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: FCDO maintained participation in PFMRP V technical working groups (May/December 2021) despite funding withdrawal. Coordination with GoT (MoFP, PoRALG) remained strong, enabling ADA transition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: FCDO led procurement of Mid-Term Evaluation (OPM) and managed contractual amendments for ADA. British Council scholarships expanded successfully.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to ADA transition and reputational risk management. FCDO invested significant staff time to manage changes and stakeholder buy-in.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted entirely from financial aid to ADA within 9 months. Scholarship component expanded despite budget cuts. REPOA component scaled down but delivered within shortened timeline.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid design and implementation of ADA mechanism post-2021 Annual Review.
Extension of British Council scholarships to include PBO/MoFP cohorts and short courses.
Repurposing REPOA’s reduced budget to deliver core research outputs by June 2022.
FCDO’s proactive role in PFMRP V technical discussions despite funding withdrawal.

main_implementation_challenges: Discontinuation of financial aid to GoT (post-November 2020 elections) required complete delivery model redesign.
40% ODA budget cut (£20M → £12.1M) necessitated reprioritization of activities.
High transaction costs for ADA setup (9 months) delayed implementation.
REPOA’s 60% budget reduction and accelerated timeline (ended June 2022).
Balancing stakeholder expectations during transition (GoT, Ecorys, British Council).
external_factors_impact: Political disruption following Tanzanian elections (November 2020) led to financial aid suspension.
COVID-19 likely contributed to budget pressures (though not explicitly stated).
Donor coordination challenges (Norway/Denmark continued basket funding; FCDO exited).
contextual_constraints_new: GoT’s reduced engagement post-election required alternative influence channels (e.g., technical discussions).
Limited ICT system integration (planning, budgeting, accounting) emerged as a critical gap per MTR findings.
Need for independent PFM Communities of Practice (CoP) post-programme closure.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial resistance to ADA from GoT partners mitigated through leveraging existing relationships (MoFP, PoRALG).
British Council and Ecorys adapted well to changes; REPOA faced constraints due to budget cuts.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoT’s capacity to absorb ADA-funded activities was uncertain initially.
FCDO team required additional bandwidth to manage ADA transition and compliance risks.
Reduced capacity for Output 2 (Financial Accountability) due to funding shifts.
risk_materialization: Reputational risk from financial aid suspension managed through continued technical engagement.
Operational risk of ADA setup delays mitigated by Ecorys’ embedded advisors.
Financial risk of underspend due to transition managed via contract amendments.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend in 2021 due to ADA transition delays, but full £12.1M committed by 2022. REPOA component underspent due to 60% budget cut.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM maintained despite budget cuts: ADA reduced transaction costs vs. financial aid; scholarships delivered high impact per pound. MTR found progress in fiscal management (e.g., e-procurement) justified expenditures.
financial_management_quality: FCDO managed complex contractual amendments (Ecorys, British Council) effectively.
ADA financial controls implemented with Ecorys as fiscal agent, reducing GoT fiduciary risks.
Timely disbursement for scholarships and MTR despite budget reductions.
cost_efficiency_achieved: ADA reduced overheads compared to basket funding (no GoT financial management fees).
Scholarship unit costs optimized via British Council’s bulk procurement (6 master’s + 2 short courses).
REPOA’s shortened timeline reduced administrative costs.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: USAID provided £4.6M as planned; Norway/Denmark continued basket funding (PFMRP V) but FCDO exited.

key_delivery_lessons: ADA implementation is viable but requires 6–9 months setup and strong partner relationships.
Technical assistance (TAS) is more effective when embedded in government structures (Ecorys model).
Scholarships yield high impact but require flexible timelines for participant availability.
Mid-term evaluations (MTR) are critical for adaptive management in dynamic contexts.
successful_delivery_practices: Leveraging existing partner trust (MoFP, PoRALG) to navigate political disruptions.
Using accountable grants (British Council) for capacity-building with clear deliverables.
Ecorys’ regional PFM advisors enabled rapid ADA rollout.
Participation in PFMRP V technical working groups maintained influence post-financial aid exit.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from financial aid to ADA within 9 months.
Reprioritized outputs: reduced weighting for Outputs 1–2 (15% each) to reflect reduced effort.
Extended scholarships despite budget cuts by reallocating funds from other components.
Accelerated REPOA’s timeline to align with reduced budget.
innovations_attempted: ADA mechanism as alternative to financial aid in politically sensitive contexts.
PFM Communities of Practice (CoP) to sustain knowledge sharing post-programme.
Short-course scholarships added to address immediate capacity gaps.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2021 AR recommendation to stop financial aid implemented (April 2021).
ADA established as recommended, though with higher-than-expected transaction costs.
Scholarship expansion (Output 4) delivered as planned.
forward_recommendations: Close main programme by June 2022; use July–September for Ecorys contract closure and compliance.
Finalize British Council scholarships by December 2022 (scholars return October 2022).
Disseminate PFM CoP lessons and explore independence post-closure.
Complete final evaluation (OPM) by September 2022 and Programme Completion Report by December 2022.
Explore non-programme channels (e.g., BSAAT) for continued PFM support.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive management of reputational risks via technical engagement post-financial aid exit.
ADA mitigated fiduciary risks by bypassing GoT systems.
MTR identified emerging risks (e.g., ICT integration gaps) for future phases.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 6 additional master’s scholarships (PBO/MoFP) + 2 short courses delivered (target met).
PFMRP V technical working groups reached MoFP/PoRALG officials (indirect beneficiaries).
REPOA research disseminated to policy audiences despite budget cuts.
policy_influence_achieved: MTR findings on fiscal management (e.g., e-procurement, internal audit) influenced PFMRP V priorities.
PFM CoP established for long-term knowledge sharing.
Scholarship alumni positioned in PBO/MoFP to drive reforms.
capacity_building_results: Master’s/short-course scholars returned to key institutions (PBO, MoFP).
TAS advisors built local government PFM capacity (PoRALG, RS).
REPOA research strengthened analytical capacity despite reduced scope.
unintended_consequences: Positive: ADA model may be replicated for other FCDO programmes in sensitive contexts.
Negative: Reduced Output 2 (Financial Accountability) progress due to reprioritization.
scalability_evidence: ADA mechanism scalable for other donor programmes facing fiduciary risks.
PFM CoP model adaptable for other sectors/regions.
Scholarship approach replicable for targeted capacity-building.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme objectives largely met despite challenges; ADA transition successful. Remaining activities (scholarships, evaluations) will conclude by December 2022. Political context and budget constraints limit further extension.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (ADA model sustainable but requires donor commitment; PFM CoP independence uncertain).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (programme adapted well to disruptions and delivered key outputs).
planned_adaptations_future: Explore integrating PFM support into other FCDO programmes (e.g., BSAAT).
Disseminate ADA/PFM CoP lessons for broader application.
Monitor scholarship alumni impact in PBO/MoFP.

partner_roles_actual.New Actors: Climate/gender experts embedded in TA teams (reported in VfM metrics)

programme_metadata.programme_title: Supporting the International Monetary Fund (SIMF) Programme

output_1.title: Tax Administration Diagnostic Assessment Tool (TADAT) - Tax authorities in developing countries use TADAT tool to analyse tax administration

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme transitioned from separate thematic funds (TADAT, RMTF) to a consolidated Global Public Finance Partnership (GPFP) launched in 2024. The GPFP integrates previously separate external financing for IMF capacity development (CD) in taxation, spending, PFM, and macro-fiscal issues under a single fund with a more flexible, holistic approach.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The IMF delivered capacity development (CD) activities largely as planned, with positive beneficiary feedback. However, challenges persisted in IMF's monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems, particularly in tracking long-term impact and cost-effectiveness. The IMF's coordination with other donors remained uneven, with structured engagement lacking in some countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme operates under central IMF rules and processes, with a matrix management system for components like RMTF. Regional Technical Assistance Centres (RTACs/AFRITACs) function as collaborative ventures between the IMF, recipient countries, and development partners. No major deviations from the planned governance structure were noted, though political economy analysis (PEA) institutionalization remains incomplete.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination mechanisms showed gradual improvement, particularly in linking CD outcomes with IMF Article IV missions. However, feedback from FCDO offices indicated that IMF engagement with other development agencies (including FCDO) remains ad-hoc in certain countries. The IMF's lack of structured coordination risks misalignment between technical assistance (TA) and broader donor priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO oversight was maintained at planned levels, with timely and detailed information provided by the IMF for the annual review. The IMF's Value for Money (VFM) reporting expanded to include equity metrics (e.g., gender and regional diversity of short-term experts), reflecting FCDO's advocacy for transparency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by extending its duration by one year (to March 2025) to allow for the completion of ongoing phases and a meaningful evaluation. Adaptive management was also evident in the incorporation of climate change as a cross-cutting priority in the new GPFP fund, responding to emerging global priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Extension of the programme by one year to align with phase completions and evaluation needs.
Integration of climate change as a cross-cutting priority in the GPFP, with planned support for climate policies in 19 countries.
Expansion of VFM metrics to include gender and regional diversity of technical assistance teams, in response to FCDO recommendations.
Organisation of a joint learning event on Political Economy Analysis (PEA) with the IMF's Legal Department to improve contextual understanding.

main_implementation_challenges: Persistent gaps in the IMF's Results-Based Management (RBM) system, which failed to provide reliable data for monitoring. The transition to the new CD-MAP system has been slower than anticipated, requiring continued reliance on manual verification of trust fund annual reports.
Uneven progress in institutionalizing Political Economy Analysis (PEA) within the IMF's capacity development planning, despite workshops and FCDO advocacy.
Limited IMF engagement in disaster risk finance advisory support, despite its increased prominence in Fund programmes (e.g., Resilience and Sustainability Fund).
Challenges in measuring long-term impact and cost-effectiveness of CD activities, as highlighted in the Capacity Development Strategy Review.
external_factors_impact: Declining aid levels and competing ODA priorities posed risks to the fundraising efforts for the next phase of SIMF components, particularly as some trust funds transitioned to the new GPFP.

The COVID-19 pandemic (implied in contextual constraints) likely affected in-person technical assistance and training delivery, though the review period (2023–2024) showed recovery with 18 in-person TADAT assessments completed.
contextual_constraints_new: The need to integrate climate change considerations into public financial management (PFM) and revenue administration support, which required adaptive adjustments in AFRITACs' advisory services.
Increased demand for disaster risk finance advisory, which the IMF has not yet substantively addressed through technical assistance.
partner_relationship_issues: The IMF's reputation for weak coordination with other development agencies persisted, with FCDO offices reporting unstructured engagement in some countries. This risks misalignment between IMF TA and broader donor-supported reforms.
Feedback from beneficiary countries indicated that while IMF technical assistance was valued, there was limited medium-term support from other donors to sustain reforms initiated by the IMF.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Delays in the IMF's ability to implement the new CD-MAP system for monitoring and evaluation, prolonging reliance on manual data verification processes.
Limited IMF capacity to institutionalize PEA for wider use in CD planning, despite progress in diagnostics.
risk_materialization: The risk of "IMF failing to provide sufficient information for FCDO to monitor performance" materialized partially, as the RBM system proved unreliable, necessitating logframe revisions and manual verification of trust fund reports.

The risk of "other donors failing to sufficiently fund IMF CD" was mitigated by the IMF's overall strong donor support, though fundraising challenges emerged for specific components during the transition to GPFP.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme met or exceeded output targets, with no reported underspending or significant budget execution issues. The extension of the programme by one year (to March 2025) was funded within the existing £21.74M envelope.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: The programme was assessed as representing value for money (VFM), with significant improvements in VFM reporting. The inclusion of equity metrics (e.g., gender and regional diversity of short-term experts) enhanced transparency. However, further scope remains to improve results monitoring, particularly in tracking long-term impact and cost-effectiveness of different CD modalities.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: The IMF's financial management was deemed adequate, with timely and detailed information provided to FCDO for the annual review. The gradual improvement in VFM reporting reflected FCDO's advocacy, though the IMF only recently began sharing such information with other donors following an Independent Evaluation Office report.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: The GPFP aims to mobilize US$175–200 million in donor financing over its initial five-year phase, indicating strong co-funding prospects. However, the review noted risks from declining aid levels and competing ODA priorities, which could affect fundraising for specific components.

key_delivery_lessons: The IMF's centralised processes and rules can constrain adaptive management, but flexibility was demonstrated through the programme extension and integration of climate priorities into the GPFP.
Manual verification of trust fund annual reports proved necessary due to unreliable RBM data, highlighting the need for robust M&E systems in multilateral programmes.
Beneficiary feedback mechanisms (e.g., TADAT satisfaction surveys) provided valuable insights for assessing quality and impact, but broader stakeholder engagement could be strengthened.
successful_delivery_practices: The use of standardised diagnostic tools like TADAT enabled comparable assessments of tax administration systems across countries, with evidence of repeat assessments showing improvement over time.

Regional Technical Assistance Centres (RTACs/AFRITACs) effectively delivered context-specific advisory support, leveraging peer-learning and regional workshops (e.g., on climate-inclusive public investment management).
The gradual expansion of VFM metrics to include equity dimensions (gender and regional diversity) improved transparency and alignment with FCDO priorities.
management_adaptations_made: Revised the programme logframe to focus on real-life delivery monitoring after RBM data proved unreliable.
Extended the programme duration by one year to allow for phase completions and evaluation, in response to delays in transitioning to the GPFP.
Incorporated climate change as a cross-cutting priority in the GPFP, reflecting emerging global needs and FCDO recommendations.
innovations_attempted: Launch of the Global Public Finance Partnership (GPFP) as a consolidated fund, integrating previously separate thematic funds (TADAT, RMTF) to improve flexibility and holism in CD delivery.
Pilot efforts to mainstream Political Economy Analysis (PEA) in IMF CD planning, though institutionalization remains incomplete.
Introduction of equity metrics (gender and regional diversity) into VFM reporting, setting a precedent for other IMF trust funds.
previous_recommendations_progress: Progress was recorded across all headline recommendations from the 2022–2023 annual review, including improvements in VFM reporting and climate integration. However, challenges remained in institutionalizing PEA and enhancing long-term impact monitoring.
The IMF provided information for the annual review in a more timely and detailed manner, addressing past criticisms about data availability.
forward_recommendations: FCDO should continue advocating for the IMF to implement recommendations from the Capacity Development Strategy Review, including the development of strategic logframes for each trust fund and more outcome-focused reporting.
Explore opportunities to enhance the IMF's coordination with other donors, particularly in aligning TA with Article IV mission findings and medium-term reform priorities.
Consider supporting the IMF's efforts to institutionalize PEA for CD planning, potentially through a follow-up programme to SIMF.
Monitor the GPFP's performance closely during its initial phase, particularly its ability to deliver integrated support on climate change, gender/inclusion, and digitalization.
Assess the feasibility of scaling successful RTAC models (e.g., AFRITACs) to other regions or thematic areas, leveraging their collaborative governance structure.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective. While the overall risk rating remained "Minor," key risks materialized (e.g., unreliable RBM data, slow PEA institutionalization). FCDO's oversight and advocacy mitigated some risks (e.g., improved VFM reporting, programme extension), but challenges persist in monitoring long-term impact and donor coordination.

policy_influence_achieved: TADAT assessments directly informed reform plans in multiple countries (e.g., Mali), with repeat assessments showing average score improvements of ~0.3 points (on a 1–4 scale).
AFRITAC East's 20-year evaluation outlined significant lessons and impact on PFM and revenue administration in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Climate change was mainstreamed into public investment management frameworks in several countries through AFRITAC advisory support.
capacity_building_results: TADAT training achieved a 90% satisfaction rate among assessors, with 100% of reviewed countries satisfied with the assessment team's work.
RTACs provided technical assistance and training to government staff in beneficiary countries, though long-term capacity retention was not fully measured.
The IMF's matrix management system for RMTF enabled broad geographical coverage (38 country-specific/regional programmes), but coordination challenges persisted.
unintended_consequences: Positive: The TADAT framework's expansion into underrepresented regions (beyond Sub-Saharan Africa) increased its global footprint and standardised tax administration diagnostics.

Negative: Limited IMF engagement in disaster risk finance advisory created gaps in supporting countries vulnerable to climate-related fiscal shocks, despite the increased prominence of this issue in Fund programmes.
scalability_evidence: The TADAT tool has been successfully scaled to 107 countries, with repeat assessments demonstrating its adaptability to evolving good practices.
The RTAC model (e.g., AFRITACs) shows potential for scalability to other regions, given its collaborative governance and context-specific advisory approach.
The GPFP's consolidated structure aims to improve scalability by integrating previously fragmented CD funds, though its long-term effectiveness is yet to be evaluated.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme was extended by one year (to March 2025) to allow for the completion of ongoing phases (e.g., TADAT, RMTF transitions) and to conduct a meaningful evaluation of results before deciding on future support. The extension also provides time to assess the initial performance of the new GPFP fund.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The delivery model is assessed as sustainable in the medium term, particularly with the launch of the GPFP, which consolidates funding and improves flexibility. However, long-term sustainability depends on the IMF's ability to address persistent M&E challenges and strengthen donor coordination.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: FCDO's Public Finance and Tax Department (PFTD) is considering future support for IMF Capacity Development, with potential adaptations including:
- Greater focus on institutionalizing Political Economy Analysis (PEA) in CD planning.
- Enhanced monitoring of long-term impact and cost-effectiveness, leveraging lessons from the GPFP's initial phase.
- Strengthened coordination mechanisms between the IMF and other donors to align TA with broader reform priorities.
- Expansion of climate change and disaster risk finance advisory, building on the GPFP's cross-cutting priorities.
- Scaling of successful RTAC models (e.g., AFRITACs) to other regions or thematic areas, subject to evaluation results.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (core unearmarked funding to UNDP, UNICEF, UN Women, UNFPA) with limited earmarked components
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £531.5m total (2017-2021), with £510m core funding (£55m/year UNDP, £40m/year UNICEF, £12.5m/year UN Women, £20m/year UNFPA) and £21.5m earmarked (£6m gender data, £13.5m RC system, £2m M&E)
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: 30% of core funding tied to Payment by Results (PBR) against 3 output areas: Leadership & Collaboration, Organisational Effectiveness, Transparency/Accountability. Annual disbursements contingent on agency Strategic Plan (2018-2021) progress, verified by independent teams.
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: High (core unearmarked funding allows agencies to allocate based on strategic priorities, with PBR providing performance incentives)

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch oversight via Executive Boards (meeting 3x/year) with DFID representation. Annual Strategic Dialogues with agency heads and ministerial engagements (e.g., UNGA margins).
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Moderate: Quarterly performance reporting against 31 logframe indicators (10 PBR-linked), annual audits, and independent verification of PBR milestones.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Agency-led implementation with DFID influence through Executive Board votes, strategic dialogues, and PBR conditions. Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) signed with strengthened clauses on PSEAH, fraud, and corruption.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single multilateral partners (4 UN agencies) with no consortium structure. Earmarked components involved UN Women + WHO joint programme for gender data.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral (UNDP, UNICEF, UN Women, UNFPA) with secondary partnership with WHO for joint gender data programme.

partner_roles_planned.UNDP: Lead on procurement, HR, and financial services; joint procurement initiatives with UNFPA/UNOPS.
partner_roles_planned.UNICEF: Procurement of supplies/services ($3.49B in 2018); business operations strategies for field offices.
partner_roles_planned.UN Women: Gender data programmes (Making Every Woman and Girl Count) and VAWG data joint programme with WHO.
partner_roles_planned.UNFPA: Reproductive health/family planning; joint procurement with UNDP/UNOPS.
partner_roles_planned.DCO: Manage Resident Coordinator system reform (£13.5m earmarked).

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award to UN agencies based on mandate alignment with Agenda 2030/SDGs and UK priorities (women/girls’ rights, humanitarian-development nexus).

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (core unearmarked) with earmarked components unchanged. PBR mechanism retained but verification timelines extended due to "unaligned expectations."
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £531.5m total unchanged. Core funding disbursed as planned (£510m to 4 agencies; £21.5m earmarked). First RC system payment (£4.5m) made in Feb 2019; second gender data payment (£1.5m) in Nov 2018.
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: PBR disbursements proceeded but with delays in verification. Agencies met PBR milestones for Year 1 (e.g., 4/4 agencies contributed to RC performance appraisals; 94% UNCTs applied SOPs). Independent verification confirmed progress, but DFID noted concerns about "behaviour changes" for reform success.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High (core funding flexibility maintained). Agencies exceeded efficiency targets (e.g., UNICEF saved $351.2m via procurement in 2018, 45% of field offices adopted business operations strategies).

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Light-touch oversight retained. Executive Boards remained primary governance mechanism with DFID active participation (national statements, drafting decisions). Strategic Dialogues held in late 2018 (NYC) with agency heads; ministerial meetings at UNGA 2018.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Moderate-to-high: Quarterly reporting continued, but PBR verification took longer than planned. Independent monitoring (CHASE contract from Sept 2018) introduced for deeper performance assessment. Audits published on time with no significant issues.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Agency-led with enhanced DFID influence via: (1) Updated MOUs with strengthened PSEAH/anti-corruption clauses; (2) Performance Agreements; (3) Active role in Executive Board decisions (e.g., leading statements on PSEAH, SRHR).

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Single multilateral partners unchanged. No consortium formed, but UN Women + WHO joint programme implemented as planned.
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (UNDP, UNICEF, UN Women, UNFPA) + WHO (for gender data joint programme). No new partners added.

partner_roles_actual.UNDP: Procurement (51%→60% efficiency), HR (41%→42%), financial services (38%→48%). Transitioned RC system management to DCO by Jan 2019.
partner_roles_actual.UNICEF: Procurement savings ($351.2m in 2018; 91% efficiency). 45% field offices adopted business operations strategies (vs 40% target).
partner_roles_actual.UN Women: Gender data programme (A score); VAWG joint programme with WHO met expectations. Fraud prevention targets revised upward (80%→87%).
partner_roles_actual.UNFPA: Procurement (55%→72% efficiency), HR (44%→63%), financial services (73%→90%). Timeliness of IATI reporting improved (50→100).
partner_roles_actual.DCO: Assumed RC system management from UNDP; preparations for Jan 2019 launch completed.

Independent monitoring (CHASE) introduced to refine indicators for future years.
Agencies revised internal targets (e.g., UN Women increased fraud prevention target from 80% to 87%).

adaptation_triggers.performance_issues: PBR verification delays triggered addition of independent monitoring (CHASE) to streamline future assessments.
adaptation_triggers.learning_insights: Agencies’ exceeding efficiency targets (e.g., UNICEF’s $351.2m procurement savings) informed DFID’s continued support for core funding flexibility.
adaptation_triggers.strategic_opportunities: UN reform momentum (e.g., RC system transition to DCO) aligned with DFID priorities, reinforcing partnership.

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High: Proactive adjustments (e.g., CHASE contract, revised fraud targets) were evidence-based and aligned with programme goals.

adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High: Independent verification and agency reporting (e.g., IATI scores, procurement savings) directly informed minor adaptations.

political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: Agencies demonstrated capacity to exceed targets (e.g., UNICEF’s procurement savings) but DFID noted concerns about "behaviour changes" for long-term reform success.

programme_metadata.programme_title: DFID Investment in the UN Development System to Achieve Agenda 2030

output_1.title: Leadership and Collaboration: Effective UN Resident Coordinator system empowered to assess and coordinate UN country teams coherently and with corresponding accountability. UN agencies operating as a joint platform in country. Greater collaboration between UN development and humanitarian agencies, especially in fragile and conflict-affected states.

output_3.title: Organisational Transparency, Accountability and Efficiency: Progress across agencies on improving transparency, robust and accountable financial management, and management efficiency (e.g., IATI ratings, fraud prevention, procurement efficiency).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from four separate business cases to a **single consolidated business case** for core funding to UN agencies (UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UN Women). Introduction of **Payment by Results (PBR)** mechanism (30% of core funding tied to progress in Leadership/Collaboration, Organisational Effectiveness, and Transparency/Accountability). Earmarked funding streams added for **gender data initiatives** (£6m) and **Resident Coordinator system reform** (£13.5m).

strengths: Agencies met **all PBR milestones** for Year 1 and Year 2, securing full disbursement of results-linked funds.
**Strategic Dialogues** with agency heads (2018) strengthened alignment on UK priorities (e.g., UN reform, PSEAH).
Agencies demonstrated **improved coordination** (e.g., 94–96% of UN Country Teams applied Standard Operating Procedures).
**Timely publication** of audited financial statements with no significant issues identified.
challenges: Verification of PBR indicators took **longer than planned** due to misaligned expectations on timelines.
Concerns persist about **behavioral commitment to reform** at HQ and country levels (e.g., resistance to cultural changes needed for Resident Coordinator system).
UN Women **initially missed revised fraud prevention target** (87%) but later provided evidence of achievement.

governance: DFID leveraged **Executive Board membership** (3x/year meetings) to influence agency strategies and hold leaders accountable.
New **Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs)** signed with strengthened clauses on **PSEAH, fraud, and corruption**.
**Annual Strategic Dialogues** (New York, 2018) provided direct engagement with agency heads on performance and expectations.
oversight: Independent **verification team** used to assess PBR indicators, reducing DFID’s reliance on self-reporting.
**CHASE-led Monitoring & Evaluation contract** (from Sept 2018) introduced rigorous performance tracking.
DFID’s **country and SRO networks** used to cross-validate agency reports.

successes: **90% of UN Country Teams** (in conflict/humanitarian contexts) conducted joint needs assessments by Year 2 (up from 81% in Year 1).
Agencies **harmonized reporting** at country level and increased use of **common services** (e.g., procurement, HR).
UNDP/UNFPA/UNOPS **joint procurement initiatives** achieved **$351.2m savings** in 2018 (exceeding $260m target).
gaps: Joint **monitoring and evaluation** lagged behind planning (62% in Year 1 → 76% in Year 2).
Resident Coordinator system **transition from UNDP to DCO** faced initial delays but was completed by Jan 2019.

efficiency: UNICEF’s **strategic procurement** saved **$351.2m** in 2018 (38% above target).
Agencies exceeded **procurement efficiency targets** (e.g., UNICEF: 91% vs 85% planned; UN Women: 84% vs 63% planned).
Common facility services **cost-sharing increased** (e.g., UNFPA’s common services efficiency rose to 72%).
issues: UNDP’s **disaster risk reduction performance** remained weak despite mandate priorities.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to **PBR verification complexities** and need for independent validation. DFID increased **bilateral engagement** (e.g., country office checks) to supplement agency reporting.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Earmarked funds (e.g., **gender data, RC system**) allowed targeted adaptations. Core funding flexibility enabled agencies to **respond to emerging crises** (e.g., humanitarian scale-ups).
adaptive_management_examples: Revised **fraud prevention targets** for UN Women mid-year after initial underperformance.
Adjusted **PBR milestones** for 2019–2020 to ensure data sources were publicly accessible.
Accelerated **DCO transition** for Resident Coordinator system to meet Jan 2019 deadline.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in **PBR verification** due to misaligned timelines between DFID and agencies.
Resistance to **cultural/behavioral changes** required for UN reform (e.g., Resident Coordinator accountability).
Variable **fraud prevention performance** (e.g., UN Women initially missed targets).
Weak **disaster risk reduction outcomes** from UNDP despite core mandate.
external_factors_impact: Increasing **political threats to women’s rights** globally heightened pressure on UN agencies to deliver normative mandates.
Expansion of **humanitarian operations** strained agency capacity in fragile states.
contextual_constraints_new: Need for **greater ambition in reform milestones** to sustain ‘A’ scores in future years.
Emerging **data gaps** in tracking PSEAH and inclusion indicators.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions over **PBR verification burdens** (agencies viewed process as overly bureaucratic).
Divergent **priorities between HQ and country offices** slowed reform implementation.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited **DCO capacity** to manage Resident Coordinator system post-transition (2019).
Country offices struggled with **joint planning** in conflict contexts (e.g., 71% achieved vs 100% target).
risk_materialization: Moderate risks around **reform commitment** and **PBR verification delays** materialized but were mitigated through adaptive management.

budget_execution_vs_plan.core_funding: Fully disbursed as planned (£510m over 4 years).
budget_execution_vs_plan.earmarked_funding: £6m (gender data) and £13.5m (RC system) disbursed on schedule; £2m (M&E) utilized per plan.
budget_execution_vs_plan.pbr_tranche: 30% of core funding (£153m) released after agencies met Year 1 and Year 2 milestones.

evidence: UNICEF’s **procurement savings** ($351.2m in 2018) exceeded targets by 38%.
**Common services efficiency** improved (e.g., UNFPA’s financial management rose to 90%).
Agencies **harmonized reporting**, reducing duplication costs.
value_for_money_assessment.vfm_rationale: Core funding leverages **UK influence** via Executive Boards and strategic dialogues, ensuring alignment with SDGs. Multilateral reach enables **scale and legitimacy** unattainable through bilateral aid (e.g., global normative work on gender rights).

strengths: All agencies published **audited statements on time** with no major issues.
**IATI transparency ratings** improved (e.g., UNFPA’s timeliness score rose from 50 to 100).
Fraud prevention systems strengthened (e.g., UN Women hit 87% target for implemented recommendations).
weaknesses: UNDP’s **financial services efficiency** (48%) lagged behind other agencies (e.g., UNFPA at 90%).

cost_efficiency_achieved.procurement: Agencies exceeded **efficiency targets** (e.g., UNICEF: 91% vs 85% planned).
cost_efficiency_achieved.common_services: Cost-sharing for facilities/services improved (e.g., UN Women’s common services efficiency reached 76%).
cost_efficiency_achieved.overheads: Reduced through **harmonized reporting** and joint country-level operations.

key_delivery_lessons: PBR verification requires **clearer timelines and data sources** upfront to avoid delays.
**Strategic Dialogues** are critical for aligning agency priorities with UK goals.
Independent M&E (e.g., CHASE contract) **reduces reliance on self-reporting** and improves rigor.
successful_delivery_practices: Joint procurement initiatives (e.g., UNICEF’s $351.2m savings) demonstrate **economies of scale**.
**Payment by Results** incentivized performance but needed flexible milestones.
Earmarked funds (e.g., gender data) allowed **targeted impact** without bureaucratic overhead.
management_adaptations_made: Revised **PBR indicators** for 2019–2020 to ensure data accessibility and harmonization.
Increased **bilateral engagement** (e.g., country office checks) to validate agency reports.
Accelerated **DCO transition** to meet Resident Coordinator system deadline.
innovations_attempted: Consolidated **single business case** for core funding (replacing four separate cases).
**Independent verification teams** for PBR indicators to enhance objectivity.
Use of **CHASE-led M&E** to refine future indicators (e.g., PSEAH, inclusion).
previous_recommendations_progress: Agencies **met 2018 recommendations** on fraud prevention and IATI transparency.
UN Women **addressed gender data gaps** through earmarked programme funding.
forward_recommendations: Finalize **2019–2020 PBR/non-PBR indicators** by end-2019 with clear data sources.
Strengthen **behavioral commitment to reform** via Executive Board advocacy.
Expand **joint procurement** to other UN agencies (e.g., UNOPS) for greater savings.
Monitor **DCO’s capacity** to manage Resident Coordinator system post-transition.

strengths: PBR mechanism **mitigated performance risks** by tying funds to results.
Independent verification **reduced reporting risks**.
Strategic Dialogues **addressed emerging risks** (e.g., PSEAH) proactively.
gaps: Need for **earlier warning systems** to flag underperformance (e.g., UNDP’s disaster risk reduction).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Core funding supported **global delivery** of UN agency mandates (e.g., UNICEF’s $3.49bn procurement reached 175 countries).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Earmarked funds (e.g., gender data) benefited **50+ countries** through UN Women’s programmes.

policy_influence_achieved: UK priorities (e.g., **UN reform, PSEAH**) embedded in agency Strategic Plans via Executive Board advocacy.
Agencies adopted **joint reporting standards** and common services due to DFID pressure.
capacity_building_results: Resident Coordinator system **empowered 54 UN Country Teams** to improve coordination.
UN Women’s **gender data programme** built national capacities in 20+ countries.

positive: PBR mechanism **spurred broader UN reform momentum** beyond DFID-funded agencies.
Joint procurement savings **benefited non-DFID donors** via lower costs.
negative: Verification burdens **diverted agency resources** from programme delivery.

scalability_evidence: Joint procurement models **adopted by UNOPS**, demonstrating scalability.
Resident Coordinator system **rolled out globally** as a UN-wide reform.

continuation_rationale: Agencies **consistently met PBR milestones**, demonstrating accountability.
Core funding provides **unique leverage** for UK influence in multilateral spaces.
Progress on **UN reform** and **SDG delivery** aligns with FCDO priorities.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes – PBR and earmarked funds balance flexibility with accountability. Resident Coordinator system now institutionalized via DCO.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by ‘A’ scores and continued strategic engagement).
planned_adaptations_future: Refine **PBR indicators** to focus on **behavioral reform** (not just outputs).
Expand **joint procurement** to additional agencies/sectors.
Strengthen **DCO’s capacity** to manage Resident Coordinator system long-term.
