programme_metadata.programme_title: Disability Inclusive Development (DID) Programme

output_1.title: Expanded provision of disability-inclusive programmes in low- and middle-income countries

output_2.title: People with disabilities enjoy better access to education, health, and livelihoods services (all DIDIF indicators)

output_3.title: Strengthened global evidence base and research capacity for disability-inclusive development (PENDA indicators)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme was initially scheduled for six years with a £37m budget; a costed extension was approved in July 2023, increasing the duration to eight years and budget to £46m. DIDIF contract was amended in October 2023 to extend the end date from July 2024 to March 2026. PENDA contract was amended in November 2023 to extend the end date to June 2025, with a further extension to December 2026 under negotiation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: DIDIF consortium (led by Sightsavers) and PENDA consortium (led by LSHTM) both delivered as expected. PENDA is on track to achieve all targets, with strong collaboration between DIDIF and PENDA enhancing value for money. UNICEF engaged PENDA for co-leadership on the Global Disability Inclusion Report for the 2025 Global Disability Summit.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme is delivered through two separate contracts (DIDIF and PENDA) with coordinated governance. The extension aligned timelines between the two contracts to ensure evaluations (PENDA) match intervention delivery (DIDIF).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between DIDIF and PENDA, evidenced by joint learning products, aligned timelines, and collaborative dissemination (e.g., Women Deliver conference). The removal of Output Indicator 5.3 (measuring DIDIF-PENDA meetings) in 2023/24 reflects that collaboration is now embedded as a core strength.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Contract amendments for both DIDIF and PENDA were processed efficiently, with extensions approved by Ministers in July 2023. PENDA’s additional £3.5m extension is under negotiation to fully align with DIDIF’s timeline.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained active oversight, particularly during contract amendments and extensions. Risk management shifted from "Major" to "Moderate" in 2022, reflecting improved stability.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme utilized flexibility to extend contracts, realign timelines, and adapt to budget constraints (e.g., shifting workstreams from FY23/24 to FY24/25). Operational changes were made within interventions based on lessons learned (e.g., addressing poverty barriers to school attendance).
adaptive_management_examples: Extended DIDIF contract to March 2026 to complete final interventions, ensuring all scale projects started by end of 2023/24.
Adapted PENDA’s timeline to evaluate five DIDIF interventions, with negotiations for full alignment by December 2026.
Developed individualized home-support plans in Bangladesh for children with complex disabilities, achieving >50% school transition rate.
Modified a family-planning board game in Nigeria to include disability-specific scenarios, reaching 1,097 women directly and millions via radio.

Created the "six principles of disability-inclusive development" based on innovation-phase learning, influencing mainstream programmes (e.g., Kenya’s £1.8m commitment to inclusive early childhood centres).

main_implementation_challenges: Budget constraints in FY23/24 (£4.3m envelope) required deferring workstreams to FY24/25, risking delays in the penultimate contract year.
Low uptake of DIDIF learning products within other FCDO programmes despite increased dissemination efforts.
Need to balance rigorous research (PENDA) with timely intervention delivery (DIDIF) to ensure evaluations align with implementation.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 led to the addition of a dedicated research stream within PENDA to study pandemic impacts on disability inclusion.
Political and economic instability in target countries (e.g., Nigeria, Kenya) required adaptive implementation (e.g., community collaboration for social behavior change).
contextual_constraints_new: Poverty and low literacy rates emerged as significant barriers to disability-inclusive education, requiring linkages to social protection systems.
Cultural, religious, and political complexities in regions like Nigeria necessitated tailored approaches (e.g., involving OPDs, community leaders, and government officials in activity design).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity among Southern researchers with disabilities for disability-inclusive research, addressed through PENDA’s capacity-building streams.
Consortium partners initially overestimated budgets, leading to deferred spending and requiring mitigations for FY24/25.
risk_materialization: Budget risks materialized in FY23/24 due to low initial allocation, requiring workstream shifts.
Risk of misalignment between DIDIF interventions and PENDA evaluations was mitigated through contract extensions.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Original six-year budget was £37m; extended to £46m over eight years (approved July 2023).
FY23/24 budget constraints (£4.3m) led to deferred spending, with mitigations planned for FY24/25.
PENDA’s additional £3.5m extension is under negotiation to cover evaluation of five DIDIF interventions.
value_for_money_assessment: Strong VFM demonstrated through collaborative DIDIF-PENDA partnerships, reducing duplication and enhancing learning.
Cost efficiency achieved in livelihoods training: 80% of participants reported improved business skills, with 50% of female participants successful in procurement engagements (vs. 42% male).
Inclusive education interventions leveraged social protection systems to address poverty barriers, improving sustainability.
financial_management_quality: Consortium partners (Sightsavers, LSHTM) managed budgets effectively, though initial overestimates required adjustments.
FCDO’s oversight ensured realistic spending plans and risk mitigations for remaining contract periods.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Livelihoods interventions achieved higher success rates for women with disabilities (50%) compared to men (42%), indicating targeted efficiency.
Dissemination focused on mainstream conferences (e.g., Women Deliver) to maximize reach and policy influence.

key_delivery_lessons: Collaboration between implementation (DIDIF) and research (PENDA) consortiums enhances VFM and learning.
Dissemination at mainstream events (vs. disability-specific) increases policy uptake, though uptake within FCDO remains low.
Individualized support models (e.g., Bangladesh home-school transition) are effective for complex disabilities but resource-intensive.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of peer-to-peer support (e.g., Nigeria’s 60 "inclusion champions") for reproductive health outreach.
Adaptation of existing tools (e.g., board games, radio shows) to include disability-specific content, achieving broad reach.
Joint webinars and learning products (e.g., "six principles") to synthesize cross-portfolio insights.
management_adaptations_made: Extended contracts to align DIDIF interventions with PENDA evaluations, ensuring evidence generation.
Removed redundant indicators (e.g., Output 5.3 on DIDIF-PENDA meetings) to streamline monitoring.
Added COVID-19 research stream to PENDA to address emerging context.
innovations_attempted: Development of the "six principles of disability-inclusive development" framework for mainstream programme influence.
Integration of disability-inclusive scenarios into existing community tools (e.g., family-planning board games).
Targeted capacity-building for Southern researchers with disabilities through PENDA.
previous_recommendations_progress: No outstanding recommendations from prior reviews; all addressed (e.g., finalizing innovation portfolio, aligning DIDIF-PENDA timelines).
New recommendations focus on improving learning uptake within FCDO and managing budget risks.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: LSHTM and DIDIF FMT to consult FCDO advisers on "foundation" learning document formats for health/education by January 2025, with dissemination by March 2025.
forward_recommendations.purpose: Improve uptake of disability-inclusive evidence in FCDO programmes.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Develop a framework illustrating DIDIF-PENDA partnership model to guide future programmes by March 2025.
forward_recommendations.purpose: Enhance VFM through collaborative design and learning.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: FCDO and FMT to address budget deferral risks in FY24/25, requiring a realistic spending plan and mitigations by November 2024.
forward_recommendations.purpose: Avoid implementation delays in the penultimate contract year.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: PENDA to review the impact of its training programmes for the next Annual Review.
forward_recommendations.purpose: Assess capacity-building effectiveness for Southern researchers.

risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive risk management reduced overall risk rating from "Major" to "Moderate" by 2022.
Contract extensions mitigated risks of misalignment between interventions and evaluations.
Budget risks were identified early, with mitigations planned (e.g., spending plan adjustments).

education.notes: Includes 3,379 additional children with disabilities supported in FY23/24 (2,277 girls, 2,786 boys).

policy_influence_achieved: Local governments in Kenya committed £1.8m to create 250 inclusive early childhood development centres by 2027, directly influenced by DIDIF learning.
UNICEF engaged PENDA to co-lead the Global Disability Inclusion Report for the 2025 Global Disability Summit.
DIDIF’s "six principles" framework is being adopted by other FCDO programmes (e.g., health, education).
capacity_building_results: PENDA built capacity for 10+ Southern researchers with disabilities in disability-inclusive research methods.
150 children with complex disabilities in Bangladesh transitioned to school through individualized support plans.
60 "inclusion champions" trained in Nigeria to lead peer-to-peer reproductive health outreach.

unintended_consequences.description: Radio stories on reproductive health reached millions beyond direct beneficiaries, raising broader awareness.
Community collaboration models in Nigeria (involving OPDs, religious leaders) strengthened local ownership and trust.

scalability_evidence: DIDIF’s scale portfolio projects are designed for replication, with learning products (e.g., "six principles") intended for mainstream programme adoption.
PENDA’s evaluation tools and capacity-building models are being shared with other research institutions in the Global South.
Kenya’s £1.8m commitment demonstrates government willingness to scale inclusive interventions.

continuation_rationale: Programme is delivering strong results (A/A+ scores) with high likelihood of achieving long-term impact.
Extensions approved to complete interventions and evaluations, ensuring evidence generation for future disability-inclusive programmes.
Demonstrated policy influence (e.g., Kenya’s funding commitment) and scalability potential.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current two-contract model (DIDIF + PENDA) is effective but resource-intensive; future programmes may streamline governance.
Partnerships with local governments (e.g., Kenya) and OPDs enhance sustainability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize PENDA’s extension to December 2026 to align with DIDIF’s timeline.
Publish and disseminate "foundation" learning documents by March 2025 to maximize FCDO uptake.
Develop a partnership framework to guide future disability-inclusive programmes by March 2025.
Address budget risks for FY25/26 through realistic spending plans and mitigations (due November 2024).

output_1.title: Procurement of a research programme consortium to deliver Components 1 and 2

output_2.title: Sign the accountable grants for the delivery of Components 3 and 4

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Initial start-up was delayed by turnover in the ERICC programme team in early 2019. The tender launch was paused until late 2020 due to ODA prioritisation and the Spending Review. The programme resumed in May 2021 after Business Plan approval. The RPC will begin work in November 2021, later than originally planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The British Academy (Component 4) has demonstrated strong engagement and partnership, with an accountable grant signed in October 2020. The RPC supplier selection process was rigorous, with the preferred supplier ranked highest on technical and commercial criteria.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme has established closer links with FCDO's Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crisis team, including a shared work plan. Coordination with UK Research Councils and international actors (e.g., Education Cannot Wait, USAID) has been strengthened.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The programme has improved coordination through engagement with key stakeholders, including FCDO Country Offices, the Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies (INEE), and the Building Evidence in Education Global Group (BE2).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The tender for the RPC (Components 1 and 2) was launched in September 2020 and completed in May 2021, with a preferred supplier identified. Contracting is expected to finalise in September 2021. Delays were caused by the ODA prioritisation process and Spending Review.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: The FCDO maintained close oversight during the procurement process, including technical evaluation panels and moderation meetings. The Programme Team engaged extensively with the British Academy for Component 4.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted to delays by revising timelines and integrating lessons from other programmes (e.g., RISE, RLO). The RPC’s inception phase will focus on rapid research initiation and stakeholder engagement.
adaptive_management_examples: Pausing the tender process during the ODA prioritisation review and resuming post-Business Plan approval in May 2021.
Revising the log frame and Theory of Change based on lessons from RISE and RLO programmes.
Integrating Component 3 planning with RPC pre-launch discussions to ensure alignment.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in programme start-up due to turnover in the ERICC team (early 2019) and pauses during the ODA prioritisation process (2020).
Procurement delays for the RPC (Components 1 and 2) due to the Spending Review and reduced ODA budget (0.5% GNI target).
Dependence on external partners (e.g., British Academy, RPC supplier) for timely mobilisation.
external_factors_impact: The UK’s reduction in ODA spending to 0.5% of GNI in 2021 caused pauses in procurement and contracting.
COVID-19 implications (not explicitly stated but inferred from global context) may have contributed to delays in stakeholder engagement and mobilisation.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased importance of aligning with FCDO’s strategic priorities post-Spending Review, including SDG 4 and the Girls Education Action Plan (May 2021).
Need to integrate ERICC into the global education in emergencies architecture amid evolving donor landscapes (e.g., G7 Declaration on Girls’ Education).
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in signing the accountable grant for Component 3 due to RPC procurement timelines, pushing its start date to April 2022.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity within the ERICC Programme Team during early 2019 due to turnover, affecting initial start-up.
Need to build RPC capacity for safeguarding, data protection, and research ethics during inception.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays materialised as a major risk, reflected in the 2021 "Major" risk rating.
Turnover in the programme team early in implementation posed operational risks.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme experienced delays in disbursement due to procurement pauses, but Component 4 (British Academy) is active and on track. The RPC contract (Components 1 and 2) is expected to be finalised in September 2021, with mobilisation in November 2021. Component 3’s grant will be signed in early 2022.
value_for_money_assessment: The competitive tender process for the RPC demonstrated strong value for money, with high-quality proposals submitted.
Synergies between Component 4 (British Academy) and the RPC are expected to improve VFM by aligning research and capacity-strengthening efforts.

financial_management_quality: Close engagement between FCDO and the British Academy ensured effective financial management for Component 4.

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency is not explicitly quantified, but the competitive tender and market engagement activities suggest efforts to optimise spending. Delays may have increased transaction costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Extensive supplier engagement and market consultation improved the quality of RPC proposals and alignment with FCDO priorities.
Delays in procurement underscored the need for contingency planning in programme timelines.
successful_delivery_practices: Close collaboration with the British Academy (Component 4) ensured early progress despite broader delays.
Integration of RPC input into Component 3’s design is expected to improve coordination and VFM.
management_adaptations_made: Revised the log frame and Theory of Change to incorporate lessons from RISE and RLO programmes.
Prioritised stakeholder engagement (e.g., FCDO Country Offices, INEE, BE2) to strengthen programme relevance and uptake.
innovations_attempted: Planned establishment of Bilateral Research Chairs under Component 4 to strengthen local capacity and research uptake.
Development of a fellowship scheme for early career researchers on education and conflict (subject to funding).
previous_recommendations_progress: The 2020 Annual Review recommended accelerating RPC procurement, which was achieved by September 2021.
Component 4’s mobilisation aligned with prior recommendations to strengthen knowledge systems.
forward_recommendations: Develop a full log frame by February 2022, incorporating indicators across all components and lessons from RISE/RLO.
Organise pre-launch discussions with the RPC on research frameworks and country-level plans by April 2022.
Establish robust policies for safeguarding, data protection, and open access publication during inception.
Raise ERICC’s profile through engagement with global actors (e.g., INEE, BE2, UK Research Councils) and high-profile launch events.

policy_influence_achieved: The programme aligns with the Girls Education Action Plan (May 2021) and G7 Declaration on Girls’ Education, indicating potential future influence.
Planned engagement with FCDO Country Offices and global actors (e.g., Education Cannot Wait) may enhance policy uptake.
capacity_building_results: Component 4’s Bilateral Research Chairs and fellowship scheme aim to strengthen local research capacity, though results are not yet evident.

scalability_evidence: The programme’s design (e.g., RPC model, global stakeholder engagement) suggests potential for scalability, but evidence is not yet available.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift toward increased reliance on outreach services (especially MSI's expanded teams) due to underperformance of routine services. Extension of programme by 2 years (to Dec 2026) with adjusted targets.

UNFPA faced procurement delays but secured commodity savings. Government co-financing fell short of commitments.

Government's Medical Store Department (MSD) procedures created procurement bottlenecks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: UNFPA faced delays due to government procurement rules (non-WHO-prequalified suppliers) and funding gaps (USD $5m in 2023). MSI/Engender Health managed commercial contracts effectively despite ODA cuts, with clean audits.

Reallocated UNFPA’s USD $0.4m savings to support 2022 census data analysis (Output 4).
Introduced split outreach model (MSI) to serve 3+ locations/day, improving cost-efficiency.
Advocated for government to increase domestic FP funding despite procedural barriers.

main_implementation_challenges: Underperformance of routine family planning services (481,692 reached vs. 769,504 target) due to health worker shortages and non-functional facilities.
Over-reliance on donor-funded outreach services, raising sustainability concerns.

MSD’s uncompetitive procurement prices deterring government co-financing.

Inflationary pressures (e.g., fuel costs) increased outreach service costs by 4–11%.

Private sector’s limited role in FP service delivery despite potential (social marketing discouraged).
Remote facility constraints (non-functional theatres) limiting service provision.

Delays in government-UNFPA procurement alignment due to WHO prequalification requirements.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Skill gaps among primary healthcare workers in offering long-term FP methods.
Limited government capacity to absorb commodity procurement responsibilities.

Risk of reduced service sustainability post-donor exit due to weak routine service uptake.

Bridging intervention (KaLMA) implemented via British Council Accountable Grant to test Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) in Kano State as interim measure.

British Council performed as expected for KaLMA bridging intervention.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme managed through multiple components: OJEU contract (pending), Accountable Grants (e.g., British Council), MOUs (e.g., USAID), and Delegated Cooperation Agreements (e.g., IRC/UNICEF). Cross-cutting MEL and crisis-response elements added complexity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination mechanisms established but challenged by delayed contractor appointments and baseline data gaps. Federal-level policy influence remains aspirational; state-level implementation (KKJ/BY) progressed via bridging interventions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Two-stage OJEU tender process completed for main contractor (Window 1), with preferred bidder identified by March 2020. DELVe contract procurement delayed, affecting baseline establishment. Trust Fund negotiations with World Bank ongoing for Output 2 research.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to procurement delays and risk of contractor underperformance. Independent third-party monitoring (via DELVe) not yet operational.

adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of KaLMA (Kano Mathematics and Literacy Accelerator) as a bridging intervention to test TaRL while awaiting OJEU contractor.

Adjustments to World Bank research concept note to align with upcoming Global Partnership for Education (GPE) analysis.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed procurement of OJEU contractor (Window 1) and DELVe contract, impacting baseline establishment and programme inception.
Internal World Bank processes caused delays in research initiation (Output 2).
Complex multi-window structure (3 windows + DFID-managed component) required intensive coordination.
Logframe transition from transitional to programmatic version pending (due September 2020).

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK-India Tech Start-up Fund

output_1.title: Invest in a portfolio of impact focused fund managers to operationalise the DevCap (at fund level)

output_4.title: Mainstreaming Gender and inclusion in the investment portfolio and disseminate learnings

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: TSF received approval for an additional £100m FT budget in 2023, expanding the overall FT budget to £130m. This required initiating a process to identify prospective Fund Managers for implementation of the extended investment budget.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Fund Managers (e.g., Avaana, Neev II) exceeded expectations by mobilising £32m (vs. £20m target) during the review period, with cumulative mobilisation of £121m (vs. £100m target). Avaana secured £20m from the Green Climate Fund (GCF), demonstrating ability to attract high-profile co-investors. Neev II achieved its target corpus of ~£100m.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Presence of Fund Managers on Boards of investees helped drive inclusion in senior management. Regular engagement between TSF team and Fund Managers (e.g., quarterly tracking of gender/inclusion progress) facilitated adaptive management. Partnerships with x-HMG teams, BII, and GOI (e.g., via G20 Startup20 events) strengthened coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: TSF team conducted quarterly reviews with Fund Managers to track progress on gender inclusion, financial mobilisation, and climate impact. A development committee at the Fund Manager level screened all investments for alignment with development goals.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: TSF adapted to challenging market conditions (60% dip in start-up sector investments) by focusing on climate-tech sectors, which attracted 100% of funding (vs. 70% target). The programme also revised gender inclusion targets to reflect the pace of business growth.
adaptive_management_examples: Calibrated Gender Action Plan (GAP) targets to match the growth pace of small businesses, reducing risk of early mortality.
Leveraged Neev Fund’s seat on the Impact Investor Council (IIC) to strengthen the investor ecosystem and unlock new investments.
Initiated process to select new Fund Managers for the £100m extended budget, widening reach to pioneering sectors.

main_implementation_challenges: Market downturn in the tech start-up sector (60% drop in investments and 40% fewer transactions vs. previous year).
Balancing gender inclusion targets with the growth constraints of small businesses.
Attracting co-investors in high-risk, high-impact sectors (e.g., climate-tech) neglected by commercial investors.
external_factors_impact: Global economic slowdown reduced overall funding for tech start-ups, but TSF’s focus on climate-tech (with 100% alignment) mitigated risks by tapping into dedicated funds like the Green Climate Fund (GCF).
GOI’s match funding (via SIDBI) and policy support (e.g., DPIIT alignment) provided stability despite market volatility.
contextual_constraints_new: Funding gap in climate sectors (estimated at $170b annually) highlighted the need for public capital to crowd in private investment.
Policy barriers in emerging tech sectors (e.g., agri-tech, health-tech) required proactive engagement with GOI ministries (e.g., Ministry of Electronics, Niti Aayog).
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between GAP targets and the capacity of small investees to implement inclusion policies. Addressed by revising milestones and providing technical support.
Need for stronger collaboration with GOI counterparts (e.g., DPIIT, SIDBI) to streamline co-investment processes and reduce policy barriers.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Small investees required initial support to meet gender inclusion targets, prompting Fund Managers to provide tailored technical assistance.
Fund Managers needed capacity building on impact measurement standards (addressed via IIC sessions).
risk_materialization: Market risk: Decline in start-up investments (60%) materialized but was offset by TSF’s focus on climate-resilient sectors.
Partner risk: Delays in GOI match funding were mitigated by proactive engagement with SIDBI.

budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_justification: Extension justified by strong performance (1.6x mobilisation exceedance) and demand for climate-tech investments.

economy.description: Fees and costs of funds are competitive (agreed via competitive bidding and market benchmarking). FT structure enables capital recycling through financial returns.

efficiency.description: Leveraged private sector delivery partners (Fund Managers) to scale impact. Portfolio investees expanded footprint nationally, multiplying impact per £ invested.

effectiveness.description: Unlocked 7x co-investment for every £ of TSF capital (£121m mobilised vs. £100m target). Achieved 2.1x target on green jobs (2,400 jobs) and met beneficiary targets (600,000 people, including marginalised groups).

equity.description: 100% of investments focused on climate/environment (vs. 70% target), benefiting women and marginalised communities disproportionately affected by climate change. Fund Managers embedded inclusion and diversity at portfolio level.

financial_management_quality.description: Management fees charged by Fund Managers decreased post-commitment period, aligning with market standards. Rigorous due diligence and development committee oversight ensured compliance.

cost_efficiency_achieved.description: Co-investment ratio of 7:1 demonstrates high efficiency. Costs benchmarked against market rates for similar funds.

co_funding_materialization.description: GOI match funding (up to £30m via SIDBI) materialized as planned. Additional co-investors (e.g., Green Climate Fund, DFIs) exceeded targets.

key_delivery_lessons: Private sector Fund Managers can effectively crowd in co-investors (7x leverage) when aligned with development goals (e.g., climate-tech).
Gender inclusion targets must be calibrated to the growth stage of investees to avoid early mortality risks.
Policy engagement (e.g., via G20, IIC) is critical to reducing barriers in emerging sectors.
successful_delivery_practices: Presence of Fund Managers on investee Boards drove inclusion in senior management roles.
Quarterly tracking of gender/inclusion metrics enabled adaptive management.
Leveraging Neev Fund’s IIC seat to strengthen investor ecosystems and showcase opportunities.
management_adaptations_made: Revised GAP milestones to reflect business growth realities.
Initiated systemic engagement with GOI ministries (e.g., DPIIT, Niti Aayog) to align on co-investment priorities.
Added gender/inclusion milestones to the logframe for outer years (target: August 2024).
innovations_attempted: Curated advocacy initiatives (e.g., Climate Conference) to raise UK’s profile in tech sectors.
Piloted capacity-building sessions on impact measurement standards for Fund Managers via IIC.
Explored partnerships with SBI and other institutions to scale co-investment opportunities.

previous_recommendations_progress.technical_support_policy_barriers: Completed (ongoing collaboration with x-HMG teams and BII).
previous_recommendations_progress.startup20_events: Ongoing (e.g., Climate Conference partnerships with GOI).

forward_recommendations: Engage with GOI counterparts (Ministry of Electronics, Department of Economic Affairs) to sharpen co-investment approaches by July 2024.
Expand technical support to reduce policy barriers in new sectors (e.g., agri-tech, health-tech).
Scale gender inclusion initiatives by disseminating best practices across the portfolio.
Explore partnerships with SBI and other financial institutions to unlock additional co-investment.

risk_management_effectiveness.description: Proactive risk management (e.g., revising GAP targets, diversifying Fund Managers) mitigated market downturn impacts. Development committee oversight ensured alignment with climate and inclusion goals.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 600,000 women and men (including marginalised communities)
beneficiaries_reached_actual.variance: Met or exceeded (specific targets not stated)

policy_influence_achieved.description: TSF contributed to UK-India partnership priorities under the Climate and British Investment Partnership pillar. Engagement via G20 and GOI ministries (e.g., DPIIT) strengthened policy dialogue on tech investments.
policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Medium

capacity_building_results.description: Fund Managers and investees implemented Gender Action Plans, with 4 out of 11 investees achieving inclusion milestones. Capacity-building sessions on impact measurement were conducted via IIC.

positive: Attracted high-profile co-investors (e.g., Green Climate Fund) to India’s climate-tech sector, signalling market viability.
Strengthened UK-India linkages in tech innovation, raising the UK’s profile in India’s start-up ecosystem.

scalability_evidence.description: TSF’s model (public capital crowding in private investment) demonstrated scalability through the £100m extension and interest from additional DFIs. Avaana and Neev II funds serve as replicable examples for climate-focused investments.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (A+ score) with exceeded targets on mobilisation (1.6x), co-investment (7x), and job creation (2.1x).
Alignment with UK-India strategic priorities (climate, British Investment Partnership).
Demand for climate-tech investments remains high, with £100m extension approved to scale impact.

delivery_model_sustainability.description: The FT model (equity investments via Fund Managers) is sustainable, with potential for capital recycling. Technical Assistance (TA) supports systemic changes (e.g., gender inclusion, policy barriers).

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Onboard new Fund Managers for the £100m extended budget to diversify sectoral reach.
Deepened engagement with GOI ministries to reduce policy barriers in emerging tech sectors.
Scale gender inclusion initiatives and disseminate learnings across the portfolio.
Explore partnerships with SBI and other institutions to amplify co-investment.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Liberia Road Development Programme - Liberia South-eastern Corridor Road Asset Management Project (SECRAMP)

output_1.title: Increased paved road

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Original PPP model retained but facing delays due to National Road Fund (NRF) operationalization challenges; potential restructuring of financing arrangements under consideration if delays persist.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (WB) signed Grant Agreement with GoL in Oct 2019 (6+ months delayed). WB financial management not yet fully assessable as no funds disbursed. WB’s oversight and donor coordination criticized as insufficiently frequent (only 3 meetings in 2019).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Government of Liberia (GoL) established NRF in Apr 2019 but fund transfers were irregular until WB intervention in Sep 2019. Implementation Agreement between Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Public Works, and NRF remains pending for full effectiveness.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: LRTF donor coordination was reactive rather than proactive. British Embassy Monrovia/DFID had to lobby WB and IMF to unblock NRF funding delays. Recommendation made to increase frequency of Oversight Committee meetings.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Private sector concessionaire selection delayed to Apr 2020 (originally planned for 2019). Procurement hinges on NRF credibility and GoL’s ability to guarantee payments. IDA Guarantee mechanism in place but not yet utilized.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: DFID oversight was minimal due to one-off payment model, but increased engagement recommended for 2020. SRO visits every 6 months; Embassy attends Oversight Committees. WB’s internal reviews are quarterly with bi-annual expenditure assessments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme flexibility used to adapt to NRF delays (e.g., WB lobbying for fund transfers, restructuring discussions). No formal logframe updates yet, but recommendations made to include pre-construction milestones (e.g., private partner contracting).
adaptive_management_examples: WB and DFID pressured GoL to transfer $11m to NRF in Sep 2019 after identifying $17m arrears.
Minister of Finance instructed Central Bank to direct fuel levy collections to NRF weekly.
Consideration of alternative financing models if NRF risks persist (decision deadline: Mar 2020).
Planned VfM analysis of PPP model vs. traditional procurement due to macroeconomic challenges.

main_implementation_challenges: 6+ month delay in WB-GoL Grant Agreement signing (Oct 2019) due to NRF establishment.
Irregular NRF funding transfers by GoL, with $17m arrears accumulated before WB intervention.
Risk of NRF funds being diverted for non-road expenditures (e.g., $11m already withdrawn to close budget gaps).
Private sector concessionaire procurement delayed to Apr 2020, pushing construction start to late 2020 (missing 2019 dry season).
Macroeconomic instability: GDP growth fell to 0.4% (vs. 4.7% forecast), inflation doubled to 28%, and Liberian dollar depreciated 24.5%.
external_factors_impact: IMF austerity measures (2020) may further strain GoL’s budget, affecting NRF flows.
Corruption scandals and nepotism allegations led to street protests in Jun 2019, increasing political instability.
Volatile commodity prices and exchange rates heighten GoL’s counterpart funding risks.
COVID-19 not mentioned (review predates pandemic), but economic fragility exacerbates implementation risks.
contextual_constraints_new: GoL’s use of NRF for non-road expenditures was unanticipated and undermines PPP credibility.
Heightened private sector risk perceptions due to GoL’s repayment capacity doubts, despite WB partial risk guarantee.
Social unrest (protests) over transparency in government spending adds pressure on fiscal discipline.
partner_relationship_issues: WB’s slow response to NRF delays frustrated LRTF donors; more frequent updates recommended.
GoL’s commitment to infrastructure is high in rhetoric but constrained by fiscal mismanagement (e.g., wage bill prioritization).
DFID/WB coordination improved post-review but requires stronger collective lobbying (e.g., with IMF).
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoL’s weak capacity to manage NRF flows and contractual obligations (e.g., Implementation Agreement delays).
High staff turnover in Infrastructure Implementation Unit (IIU) risks institutional strengthening goals.
Limited GoL ability to handle environmental/social safeguards (e.g., resettlement, non-local labor conflicts).

risk_materialization.risk: Context: Reduced GoL commitment to infrastructure
risk_materialization.notes: GoL maintains high-level priority but fiscal constraints limit action.
GDP growth, inflation, and currency depreciation worse than forecast.

risk_materialization.risk: Delivery: Delays due to GoL capacity
risk_materialization.notes: NRF operationalization and Implementation Agreement delays.
NRF funds diverted for non-road expenditures; $17m arrears accumulated.
Minimal oversight required due to WB implementation.
Mitigation steps planned but not yet tested.

budget_execution_vs_plan.disbursement_status: £4.8m committed to WB but no funds disbursed to GoL or contractors as of Nov 2019.
budget_execution_vs_plan.spending_delay_justification: Construction not started; private sector procurement pending.

value_for_money_assessment.current_vfm_status: Not yet assessable (no construction costs incurred).
planned_vfm_actions: WB to conduct cost analysis vs. comparable road programmes in Liberia/region (requested by DFID).
Post-procurement, DFID/WB to agree on cost indicators for lifetime tracking.
Restructuring discussions may include VfM reassessment if PPP model is revised.
value_for_money_assessment.vfm_risk: High (due to macroeconomic volatility and NRF uncertainties).

financial_management_quality.wb_financial_oversight: Strong anti-corruption controls in place, but donor coordination criticized as insufficient. Quarterly internal reviews and bi-annual expenditure assessments planned.
financial_management_quality.gol_financial_management: Poor (NRF fund diversions, arrears, irregular transfers). Improved post-WB intervention but risks remain.
financial_management_quality.audit_findings: No audited statements available yet; WB to review external audit reports annually.

co_funding_materialization.details: NRF domestic revenues (fuel levy) now flowing but irregular; $11m transferred post-WB lobbying. IDA Credit and Guarantee pending full NRF effectiveness.

currency_exchange_impacts.liberian_dollar_depreciation: 24.5% against USD in 2019, increasing local costs for road materials/labor.
currency_exchange_impacts.mitigation: PPP model includes IDA Guarantee to mitigate GoL payment risks, but exchange rate volatility may affect private sector bids.

key_delivery_lessons: PPP models in fragile contexts require stronger safeguards for revenue streams (e.g., ring-fenced NRF accounts).
Multilateral partners (WB) must proactively coordinate donors to preempt delays (e.g., NRF funding blocks).
Macroeconomic shocks can derail infrastructure projects even with high-level government commitment.
One-off disbursement models limit oversight leverage; more frequent monitoring needed for high-risk programmes.
successful_delivery_practices: WB’s direct lobbying of GoL Minister of Finance successfully unblocked $11m NRF transfer.
Linking private sector payments to WB Performance Standards (e.g., safeguards compliance) reduces fiduciary risks.
SRO’s regular field visits (planned post-construction) and Embassy’s Oversight Committee participation provide critical oversight.
management_adaptations_made: Added pre-construction milestones to logframe (e.g., private partner contracting).
Increased Oversight Committee meeting frequency recommended for 2020.
DFID/WB to conduct comprehensive VfM analysis of PPP model vs. alternatives.
innovations_attempted: PPP financing model with IDA Guarantee is innovative for Liberia but faces credibility challenges.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Delivering Accelerated Family Planning in Pakistan Programme (DAFPAK)

output_1.title: Successful behaviour change programme implemented

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme pivoted to respond to 2022 floods, with partners setting up 4,000 free medical camps in 29 flood-affected districts. BCC campaign integrated flood-specific messaging while maintaining core objectives. Private sector partners (MSI, UNFPA, DKT, PSI) adapted service delivery models to emergency contexts, while Palladium provided technical assistance to provincial governments for emergency response.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All partners exceeded expectations despite challenges, with private sector partners demonstrating rapid adaptation to floods (e.g., MSI/PSI/DKT setting up 4,000 medical camps reaching 600,000 beneficiaries). Public sector partner (Palladium) effectively supported government emergency response. M&C Saatchi successfully integrated FP messages into flood relief communications.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Multi-partner coordination proved effective during crises, with partners aligning under a unified flood response strategy. Oversight was intensified during floods, though the programme maintained its decentralized implementation model across Punjab, Sindh, KP, and Baluchistan.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective during floods, with partners rapidly aligning activities (e.g., medical camps, TA to governments). Regular stakeholder consultations mitigated reputational risks (e.g., "Khairkhwah campaign" sensitivities). A DAFPAK learning event disseminated best practices to federal/provincial governments and donors.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Challenges included import restrictions on long-acting contraceptives and currency fluctuations increasing commodity costs. DKT’s local repackaging facility (awaiting government licensing) aims to address supply chain vulnerabilities. Partners adapted procurement to prioritize flood-affected areas.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased during floods, with TPV&M validating results and auditing financial adaptations. Safeguarding risks were actively managed, with incidents escalated via Reporting Concerns mechanisms. Financial oversight remained "cautious" per FCDO risk appetite.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility by repurposing activities for flood response (e.g., BCC campaign pivot, medical camps). Budget reallocations were approved to address emergency needs while maintaining core objectives.
adaptive_management_examples: Pivoting BCC campaign to include flood-specific health messages while retaining FP focus.
Establishing 4,000 free medical camps in 29 flood-affected districts within weeks of the disaster.
Palladium’s technical assistance to provincial governments for emergency health system strengthening.
M&C Saatchi’s integration of FP messaging into broader flood relief communications.
Alignment with World Bank and Gates Foundation to reduce aid fragmentation and improve sustainability.

main_implementation_challenges: Devastating 2022 floods disrupting 2,000+ health facilities and displacing 33 million people.
Import restrictions and currency fluctuations (PKR depreciation) increasing contraceptive commodity costs by ~30%.
Political uncertainties and high inflation (2022–23) straining partner budgets.
Safeguarding risks in a large, multi-partner programme with direct beneficiary interactions.
Reputational risks from conservative groups perceiving FP messaging as culturally sensitive (e.g., "Khairkhwah campaign").
Limited prioritization of SRHR in humanitarian response plans during floods.
external_factors_impact: Floods (June–August 2022) destroyed health infrastructure, displaced populations, and created urgent SRHR needs (e.g., 650,000 pregnant women in affected areas).
COVID-19 pandemic (ongoing in 2022) compounded health system strains, though less directly addressed in this review period.
Economic crisis (high inflation, PKR depreciation) increased operational costs, particularly for imported contraceptives.
Political instability in Pakistan affected government engagement on policy reforms (e.g., delayed reinstatement of population task forces).
contextual_constraints_new: Unprecedented scale of flood damage to health systems (only 30% of married women in flood zones reported contraceptive use post-flood).
Climate change impacts on reproductive health (e.g., heat effects on contraceptive efficacy, disaster-induced service disruptions).
Gender norms limiting women’s access to FP services in conservative areas, exacerbated by flood-induced displacement.
Supply chain breakdowns for FP commodities due to import bans and port disruptions.
partner_relationship_issues: No major conflicts reported, but coordination complexity increased during floods due to rapid reallocation of roles.
Delays in government approvals (e.g., licensing for DKT’s local repackaging facility) slowed supply chain adaptations.
Differing risk appetites among partners (e.g., private sector’s agility vs. public sector’s procedural constraints).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Shortage of female healthcare providers in flood relief camps, limiting SRHR service access.
Overstretched provincial health departments required additional TA from Palladium to manage emergency response.
Partners faced staff burnout due to extended flood response efforts alongside regular programming.
risk_materialization: Floods (high impact: disrupted services, increased needs).
Currency/exchange rate volatility (high impact: raised commodity costs).
Import restrictions (high impact: contraceptive stockouts).
Safeguarding incidents (managed via escalation protocols; no major breaches reported).
Reputational risks from conservative pushback (mitigated via stakeholder consultations).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Exceeded expectations despite challenges. Budget reallocations approved for flood response (e.g., medical camps, emergency TA) without compromising core outputs. Overall expenditure aligned with AMP, though currency fluctuations required adjustments.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Better than projected in the Business Case. Overachievement of targets (e.g., 9.5M FP users reached by June 2023) improved VfM, particularly in harder-to-reach and flood-affected areas. Equity gains noted via rural outreach and emergency response.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Partners maintained transparent financial reporting, with TPV&M validating expenditures. No major audit findings reported. Safeguarding financial controls were reassessed and strengthened during the review period.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Higher than planned due to economies of scale in flood response (e.g., shared medical camps) and leveraging existing partner infrastructure. Cost per FP user decreased in flood zones due to high-volume service delivery.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialized. Private sector partners (e.g., DKT, PSI) contributed in-kind resources for flood response, but planned government co-funding for sustainability remained limited. World Bank and Gates Foundation alignments reduced duplication.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Significant. PKR depreciation (~30% in 2022) increased contraceptive procurement costs. Mitigation included local repackaging (DKT) and bulk purchasing. Exchange rate losses were absorbed within contingency budgets.

key_delivery_lessons: Climate resilience must be integrated into health programmes (e.g., pre-positioning FP supplies, disaster-preparedness plans).
Multi-partner coordination is critical during crises but requires clear role delineation to avoid overlaps.
Local repackaging/production of commodities can mitigate import dependency risks.
BCC campaigns must balance cultural sensitivity with bold messaging to drive behaviour change.
Government TA should focus on institutionalizing FP services within emergency response frameworks.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid partner adaptation to floods (e.g., medical camps, TA to governments).
Integration of FP messaging into broader health communications during emergencies.
Use of quasi-experimental surveys (QES) to measure behaviour change impact.
Alignment with other donors (World Bank, Gates Foundation) to reduce fragmentation.
High-level advocacy (e.g., "5 Big Asks" script) to influence national population policy.
management_adaptations_made: Increased oversight during floods via TPV&M validations.
Budget reallocations approved within 4–6 weeks of flood onset.
Safeguarding policies reassessed and reporting mechanisms strengthened.
Delivery unit established in Punjab to monitor FP indicators.
Learning events held to disseminate flood response best practices.
innovations_attempted: Flood-pivoted BCC campaign combining FP and emergency health messages.
Local repackaging of contraceptives (DKT) to reduce import dependency.
Mobile medical camps in flood zones reaching 600,000 beneficiaries.
Use of boats to transport pregnant women to safe regions.
Climate-health evidence generation (e.g., studying heat impacts on reproductive health).
previous_recommendations_progress: Sustainability plans for private/public sector service delivery advanced, though extension proposed to fully realize goals.
Advocacy for population policy reforms initiated at federal/provincial levels (e.g., task force dialogues).
Partnerships with World Bank/Gates Foundation strengthened to reduce aid fragmentation.
Safeguarding risk management escalated to Development Director per prior recommendations.
forward_recommendations: Develop climate adaptation strategies aligned with FMoH’s Framework of Action on Climate Change and Health.
Advocate for reinstatement of Prime Minister/Chief Minister-led population task forces.
Scale up local production/repackaging of FP commodities to mitigate import risks.
Institutionalize FP services within provincial disaster management plans.
Conduct longitudinal studies on climate change impacts on SRHR (e.g., heat, floods).
Extend programme to 2025 with focus on sustainability of private/public sector models.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Generally effective. Proactive mitigation of flood risks (e.g., medical camps, TA) and reputational risks (e.g., stakeholder consultations). Safeguarding and financial risks were managed per FCDO protocols. Currency/exchange risks were partially mitigated but remain a challenge. Risk register was updated to include climate-related threats.

policy_influence_achieved: Initiated dialogues on reinstating population task forces at federal/provincial levels.
Advocated for revisions to National Finance Award to include FP funding.
Delivery unit established in Punjab to monitor FP indicators, institutionalizing data use.
Influenced inclusion of FP in climate adaptation plans via FMoH engagements.
capacity_building_results: Trained health workers in public sector (Palladium) to improve service integration and data quality.
Strengthened provincial governments’ emergency response capacities via TA during floods.
Built private sector partners’ (PSI, MSI, DKT) ability to pivot service delivery models for crises.
Enhanced M&C Saatchi’s capacity to design culturally sensitive BCC campaigns for conservative contexts.

positive: Increased visibility of SRHR needs during floods led to greater donor attention (e.g., World Bank alignment).
Medical camps improved trust in FP services among previously unreached populations.
Climate-FP linkages raised profile of reproductive health in climate adaptation discussions.
negative: Short-term diversion of resources from routine FP services to flood response.
Conservative pushback against FP messaging in some flood-affected areas.
Risk of beneficiary dependency on free medical camps post-emergency.

scalability_evidence: Private sector service delivery models (social franchising/marketing) demonstrated scalability in floods and can be expanded nationally.
BCC campaign approaches (multi-media, community outreach) proven effective in both routine and emergency contexts.
Public sector TA model (Palladium) replicable in other provinces with health system weaknesses.
Climate-resilient FP strategies (e.g., pre-positioned supplies) can be adopted by other health programmes in Pakistan.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme has exceeded targets despite challenges (floods, economic crisis) and demonstrates strong potential to achieve long-term objectives with additional focus on sustainability. Extension to 2025 proposed to consolidate private/public sector service delivery models and climate resilience.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (private sector requires 2–3 more years to fully sustain; public sector integration is progressing but needs continued TA).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (A+ performance in 2023, effective crisis response, and alignment with CBP Sub-objective 3.3).
planned_adaptations_future: Focus on sustainability of private sector service delivery (social franchising/marketing).
Institutionalize FP services within provincial disaster management frameworks.
Scale up local production of contraceptives to reduce import dependency.
Strengthen advocacy for domestic resource mobilization (e.g., National Finance Award revisions).
Expand climate-resilient health system interventions (e.g., heat-adapted service delivery).
Deepened partnerships with World Bank/Gates Foundation to leverage co-funding.

output_1.title: Governments, private sector and humanitarian organisations actively engage with GSMA M4H to implement programme activities

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Dedicated resources recruited for HCC and disaster preparedness. delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective, as demonstrated by regional HCC workshops that led to actionable partnerships (e.g., WFP-Digicel collaboration on business continuity plans, Globe Telecom’s adoption of Common Alerting Protocol in the Philippines).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Robust procurement processes aligned with international standards. Leveraged platforms like Peregrine and LinkedIn to broaden supplier base. Achieved £52k savings in market engagement and research contracts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Strengthened due diligence for Innovation Fund grantees, including risk assessment frameworks to align sub-grant monitoring with country-wide risk levels.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to emerging priorities (e.g., 'Connectivity in Crisis' research direction, EW4All alignment). Flexibility enabled rapid response to partner demands (e.g., HCC workshops, ETC Global Plenary hosting).
adaptive_management_examples: Reinvigorated HCC with dedicated strategy, microsite, and regional workshops, leading to UN OCHA-Digicel coordination in the Caribbean.
Expanded focus to include connectivity in conflict/crisis settings, aligning with ICRC for a holistic framework.
Launched GSMA Innovation Fund for Humanitarian Challenges, targeting startups/SMEs with 53% female-led applicants.

main_implementation_challenges: Sustaining multi-stakeholder engagement across diverse sectors (humanitarian, private, policy).
Balancing global thought leadership with localized, context-specific interventions.
Ensuring equitable access to digital services in low-connectivity or high-risk environments (e.g., conflict zones, disaster-prone regions).
external_factors_impact: Increased global recognition of digital humanitarian action (e.g., Refugee Connectivity, Early Warnings for All initiatives) created opportunities for alignment but also raised expectations for delivery.
Geopolitical and economic instability in some target regions affected partner engagement and operational continuity.
contextual_constraints_new: Demand for disaster preparedness solutions outpaced initial HCC capacity, requiring rapid scaling of convening activities.
Need to address digital divides (gender, disability, marginalized groups) in humanitarian cash/social protection systems.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial re-engagement of MNO signatories to the HCC required dedicated effort after a period of lower activity (2015–2022).
Coordinating between competitive private-sector actors (e.g., MNOs) and humanitarian organizations required neutral convening platforms.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited in-country presence required reliance on regional workshops and virtual engagement, which sometimes reduced depth of local partnerships.
High demand for technical assistance on mobile-enabled disaster response exceeded initial team capacity, prompting recruitment of dedicated HCC resource.
risk_materialization: Major risk rating persisted due to operational complexities in humanitarian contexts (e.g., network shutdowns, regulatory barriers).
Currency fluctuations and inflation impacted grant disbursements, mitigated by cost-saving measures (e.g., procurement savings).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Cost per person reached improved from £2.53 (business case) to ~£1.70, exceeding VfM targets.

efficiency_gains: Cross-collaboration with other GSMA programmes (e.g., M4D) reduced duplication.
Procurement savings of £52k through competitive sourcing and negotiation.
Leveraged existing GSMA platforms (e.g., Innovation Fund network) to reduce marketing costs.
effectiveness_gains: Follow-on funding for Innovation Fund grantees totaled £36.5m (9.7x initial M4H 1.0 portfolio).
Strengthened due diligence reduced financial risks for sub-grantees.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Robust processes included market-benchmarked HR policies, strict travel cost controls, and risk-aligned grant monitoring.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded targets. Cost per beneficiary reduced by 33% through economies of scale and efficient resource allocation.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialized. GSMA Innovation Fund leveraged additional applications (413 total, 53% female-led), but co-funding amounts not specified.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Mitigated through cost-saving measures; no significant disruptions reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Multi-stakeholder convenings (e.g., HCC workshops) are critical for catalyzing partnerships but require dedicated resources for follow-up.
Thought leadership must align with emerging global priorities (e.g., EW4All, Connectivity for Refugees) to maintain influence.
Digital humanitarian action requires both technical solutions (e.g., Common Alerting Protocol) and policy advocacy (e.g., network shutdown mitigation).
successful_delivery_practices: Regional HCC workshops created actionable outcomes (e.g., Philippines’ adoption of Common Alerting Protocol, WFP-Digicel coordination).
Cross-programme collaboration (e.g., with GSMA’s Digital Inclusion team) maximized impact and reduced costs.
Performance-based grant management (e.g., Innovation Fund) ensured accountability and high-quality outputs.
management_adaptations_made: Recruited dedicated HCC resource to rebuild disaster preparedness offerings.
Expanded research focus to 'Connectivity in Crisis' to address gaps in conflict/emergency contexts.
Strengthened risk assessment frameworks for sub-grantees to prevent fund misuse.
innovations_attempted: GSMA Innovation Fund for Humanitarian Challenges: Targeted startups/SMEs with gender-inclusive outreach (53% female-led applicants).
Adaptation of MISTT toolkit for humanitarian settings in collaboration with Digital Inclusion team.
Pilot partnerships with ICRC to integrate International Humanitarian Law perspectives into connectivity frameworks.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: Rebuilt HCC offer with strategy, microsite, and workshops; took leadership role in UN Emergency Telecommunications Cluster.
In Progress: Refreshing capacity-building content for governments with ITU partnership.
forward_recommendations: Deepening HCC’s role in national disaster preparedness plans, prioritizing in-person engagements in target geographies.
Scaling successful grantee projects (e.g., Anticipatory Humanitarian Action cohort) with follow-on funding.
Strengthening monitoring of gender and disability inclusion in digital humanitarian programmes.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Proactive measures (e.g., risk assessment frameworks, due diligence) mitigated financial and operational risks, though 'Major' risk rating persisted due to inherent humanitarian context challenges.

policy_influence_achieved: Influence on UN OCHA-Digicel disaster management coordination in the Caribbean.
Adoption of Common Alerting Protocol by Philippine government/MNOs for emergency alerts.
Contributions to global initiatives (EW4All, Connectivity for Refugees) and UK Digital Development Strategy.
capacity_building_results: HCC workshops strengthened multi-stakeholder coordination in disaster-prone regions (Caribbean, Asia-Pacific, Africa).
GSMA Innovation Fund built capacity of 413 applicant organizations (53% female-led).
Partnership with ITU to identify governments for National Emergency Telecommunications Plans.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Increased private-sector engagement (e.g., MNOs) in humanitarian response, normalizing cross-sector collaboration.
Negative: Risk of digital exclusion for non-mobile users or low-literacy populations in crisis settings (mitigated via inclusive design focus).
scalability_evidence: HCC model replicated across three regions with demand for further expansion.
Innovation Fund grantee projects (e.g., anticipatory action tools) show potential for scaling via follow-on funding.
Policy advocacy successes (e.g., network shutdown mitigation) adoptable by other humanitarian-tech programmes.

continuation_rationale: Consistent A+ performance and alignment with FCDO’s Digital Development Strategy priorities (e.g., digital humanitarian response, climate resilience).
Strong VfM (£1.70 per beneficiary vs. £2.53 planned) and scalable impact (12.6m reached).
Unique position as a global convener for digital humanitarian action, with demand from partners (e.g., UN, MNOs, governments).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. Cross-sector partnerships (e.g., HCC, EW4All) and GSMA’s institutional backing ensure long-term viability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expanding HCC’s role in national disaster preparedness plans with ITU and governments.
Deepening focus on 'Connectivity in Crisis' research and advocacy, including conflict settings.
Enhancing gender and disability inclusion in digital humanitarian programmes via targeted grantee support.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Girls’ Education South Sudan Programme Phase 2 (GESS2)

output_1.title: Communication to girls, boys, women, and men to shift attitudes and behaviour related to the education of girls and children with disabilities

output_2.title: Cash transfers to girls to improve enrolment, retention, transition, and completion rates

output_3.title: Capitation Grants to schools to improve learning environment for all learners

output_4.title: Quality of Education, Learning Groups & Resilience to contribute to improving learning outcomes

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted focus to access to education due to budget cuts, pausing some quality-focused activities (Output 4). Two new donors (USAID, EU) onboarded in 2021, requiring integration into decision-making. Logframe revised to prioritize access over quality temporarily.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Consortium partners (MM/CE, BBC MA, LC, Montrose, WTI) demonstrated adaptability to budget reductions and contextual challenges. Coordination with other donors (GAC, USAID, EU) was strong, with FCDO leading sector groups (Education Cluster, Education Coalition) to minimize duplication (e.g., ECW adjusted cash transfer plans in Western Equatoria).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO maintained leadership in donor coordination, influencing multilateral programmes (ECW, GPE) for complementarity. Joint lobbying lines developed through the Education Donor Group for MoGEI engagement. Oversight intensified due to budget constraints, with paused activities under Output 4.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination with donors and multilateral actors, avoiding duplication (e.g., ECW adjusted plans based on GESS coverage). FCDO’s leadership in sector groups facilitated alignment. However, budget cuts led to concerns about education quality among partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight due to budget reductions, with closer monitoring of paused/adjusted activities. FCDO worked to reinstate quality-focused activities (Output 4) by the end of the review period.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high adaptability: reprioritized logframe to focus on access, utilized family/school listening groups for behavior change, and adjusted to flooding/displacement by reaching affected communities in dry seasons. Cash transfer methodology improved for safeguarding and disability inclusion.
adaptive_management_examples: Reprioritized logframe to emphasize access over quality due to budget cuts, with plans to reinstate quality activities later.
Developed tracking templates for community mobilisation follow-up after identifying sustained engagement post-radio transfers.
Adjusted delivery in flood-affected areas (Northern Bahr-el-Ghazal, Unity, Jonglei) by targeting displaced populations during dry seasons.
Strengthened safeguarding practices in cash transfers, including disability-inclusive methodologies.

main_implementation_challenges: FCDO budget reductions (due to ODA cuts to 0.5% and reprioritization to COVID/Ukraine/Afghanistan crises) led to pausing of Output 4 (quality of education) and Output 5 (knowledge base).
GRSS failure to disburse primary school capitation grants and irregular teacher salaries, undermining programme impact.
Catastrophic flooding and climate shocks disrupted access to communities, particularly in Northern Bahr-el-Ghazal, Unity, and Jonglei states.
Volatile political/security context with humanitarian crises (displacement, food insecurity) limiting partner access.
High inflation and rising costs of goods/services reduced GRSS capacity to deliver essential services.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 residual effects compounded existing education barriers (retention, completion, learning levels).
FCDO’s ODA reduction to 0.5% and reprioritization to Afghanistan/Ukraine crises directly cut GESS budget, requiring logframe adjustments.
Climate-related flooding displaced populations, requiring adaptive delivery (e.g., dry-season mobilisation).
Economic deterioration (inflation, currency devaluation) increased operational costs and reduced GRSS service delivery.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of GRSS funding failures for capitation grants/teacher salaries, which were assumed to be partially addressed by programme influence.
Severity of flooding in 2021–2022 exceeded historical patterns, disrupting planned mobilisation in key states.
Rapid onset of FCDO budget cuts (2021/22) required immediate logframe revisions, limiting time for phased adaptations.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions arose among partners and donors over the shift from quality to access due to budget cuts, with concerns about long-term education outcomes.
GRSS (MoGEI) engagement remained challenging, with limited progress on capitation grant releases despite lobbying.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Reduced FCDO technical support (e.g., economists, conflict advisers) due to budget cuts, delaying formalized ToRs for internal expertise.
Partner capacity stretched by need to adapt to budget reductions while maintaining service delivery in volatile contexts.
risk_materialization: Budget reduction risk materialized fully, leading to paused outputs and revised logframe.
GRSS financial instability (unreleased capitation grants) materialized as a persistent risk, directly impacting Output 3 performance.
Climate risks (flooding) materialized more severely than anticipated, disrupting community access.

budget_execution_vs_plan: FCDO allocations reduced in Years 3–4 due to ODA cuts, with Year 5 funding unconfirmed at review time.
Total programme value pending final FCDO settlement; current confirmed funds: UK (£70m), GAC (£11.4m), USAID (£8m), EU (£15m).
Budget reductions led to pausing 6 indicators and amending 5, with a heavier focus on access (Outputs 1–3) over quality (Output 4).
value_for_money_assessment: VFM assessment remains positive: 4/5 outcome indicators achieved/exceeded despite budget cuts, with cost-effectiveness demonstrated by milestone achievements (e.g., gender parity progress, enrolment targets).
Economy reductions (budget cuts) did not proportionally reduce impact, as adaptive delivery (e.g., radio programmes, cash transfers) maintained reach.
Cash transfer methodology improvements (safeguarding, disability inclusion) enhanced VFM by reducing leakage and improving targeting.
financial_management_quality: Strong financial management by consortium, with transparent adjustments to logframe and donor reporting.
Effective mitigation of budget cuts through donor diversification (USAID, EU onboarding) and reprioritization.
Delays in GRSS capitation grant disbursements (outside programme control) were actively lobbied by GESS team.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency maintained through:
- Scaling radio programmes (2.3m reached at low marginal cost).
- Leveraging existing partner networks (e.g., BBC MA) for behaviour change.
- Pausing lower-priority outputs (e.g., knowledge base) to protect high-impact activities (cash transfers, mobilisation).
co_funding_materialization: New co-funding materialized from USAID (£8m) and EU (£15m) in FY 22/23, offsetting FCDO reductions.
GAC continued contribution (£11.4m) as planned, but total programme value remains uncertain pending FCDO Year 5 allocation.
currency_exchange_impacts: Inflation and currency devaluation in South Sudan increased operational costs, but programme mitigated through local procurement and donor coordination.

key_delivery_lessons: Family listening groups (not just school-based) are highly effective for behaviour change and should be scaled.
Radio programmes are a cost-efficient tool for reaching displaced/remote populations, especially when paired with community dialogues.
Adaptive logframe revisions are critical in volatile contexts but require clear criteria for pausing/resuming activities to avoid long-term trade-offs (e.g., access vs. quality).
Donor diversification (e.g., USAID, EU) can mitigate budget risks but requires early integration into governance structures.
successful_delivery_practices: Community mobilisation with solar/wind-up radios pre-loaded with content enabled sustained engagement even after direct programme support ended.
Cash transfer safeguarding improvements (disability inclusion, reporting quality) set a new standard for similar programmes in South Sudan.
Cross-donor coordination (e.g., Education Donor Group) minimized duplication and amplified lobbying power with MoGEI.
management_adaptations_made: Developed tracking templates for community mobilisation follow-up after identifying sustained post-intervention engagement.
Revised cash transfer methodology to include stronger safeguarding and disability-inclusive targeting.
Shifted oversight focus to monitor paused activities (Output 4) while maintaining delivery of high-performing outputs (1–3).
innovations_attempted: Family listening groups (beyond school-based groups) to deepen behaviour change.
Use of climate-resilient delivery timing (e.g., dry-season mobilisation in flood-affected areas).
Digital tracking tools for community follow-up post-radio distribution.

addressed: Partial progress on influencing GRSS for capitation grants/teacher salaries.
outstanding: Formalized internal technical support (e.g., economist, conflict adviser ToRs).
Logframe revisions (ongoing, delayed by budget uncertainty).
13 actions from 2020/21 review remain unaddressed due to budget constraints; programme to triage these based on current context.

forward_recommendations: Finalize and implement the education influencing strategy to systematize GRSS engagement.
Reinstate paused quality-focused activities (Output 4) as soon as funding allows, with clear sequencing to avoid further delays.
Formalize FCDO internal technical support (e.g., conflict advisers) to strengthen adaptive management.
Conduct a lessons-learned exercise on donor coordination to replicate successes (e.g., ECW alignment) in future programmes.
Develop a sustainability plan for community mobilisation activities, given evidence of post-programme engagement.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating budget cuts through donor diversification and logframe adaptations.
Less effective in influencing GRSS on capitation grants/teacher salaries, despite ongoing lobbying.
Climate risk responses (e.g., dry-season delivery) were adaptive but reactive; proactive climate resilience planning needed for future phases.

output_2_cash_transfers.indicator: Girls reached with cash transfers (review period)

beneficiaries_reached_actual.overall: Exceeded targets for behaviour change (Output 1) and cash transfers (Output 2); capitation grants (Output 3) underperformed due to GRSS delays.

policy_influence_achieved: Influenced ECW and GPE to adjust programme designs (e.g., cash transfers in Western Equatoria) to avoid duplication.
Joint donor lobbying lines developed for MoGEI engagement, though GRSS capitation grant releases remain unresolved.
Programme’s disability-inclusive approaches cited in national education sector discussions.
capacity_building_results: Improved capacity of school management officers and headteachers in safeguarding and disability inclusion through training linked to cash transfers and mobilisation.
Community dialogue groups demonstrated sustained engagement post-intervention, suggesting local ownership.
Limited progress on GRSS institutional capacity due to systemic financial constraints.

positive: Family listening groups emerged as a more effective behaviour change tool than initially planned, with broader reach than school-only groups.
Radio content on disability rights led to unanticipated demand for inclusive education in non-targeted communities.
negative: Pausing quality-focused activities (Output 4) risked long-term learning outcomes, though access gains were protected.
Budget cuts reduced capacity-building for MoGEI, limiting systemic impact.

scalability_evidence: Radio-based behaviour change models are highly scalable, as demonstrated by exceeding targets with minimal incremental cost.
Cash transfer methodologies (with safeguarding improvements) are being considered for replication by other donors in South Sudan.
Community mobilisation approaches are adaptable to other fragile contexts but require localised content and partner networks.

continuation_rationale: Programme is meeting expectations (Overall Score: A) despite significant challenges, with strong evidence of impact on enrolment, behaviour change, and gender parity.
New donors (USAID, EU) have mitigated budget risks, and there is potential to reinstate paused activities if funding stabilizes.
Critical role in South Sudan’s education sector, given GRSS constraints and high need (2.8m children out of school).
Lessons on adaptive delivery (e.g., climate-resilient mobilisation) are valuable for future phases.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (for access-focused outputs; medium for quality outcomes due to paused activities)
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium – Consortium model is effective but dependent on donor coordination and GRSS engagement, which remains unstable.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High – Programme demonstrates resilience, VFM, and alignment with FCDO priorities (girls’ education, disability inclusion).
planned_adaptations_future: Reinstate Output 4 (quality of education) activities as funding permits, with phased sequencing.
Finalize and implement the education influencing strategy to strengthen GRSS engagement.
Expand family listening groups based on evidence of sustained impact.
Develop a transition plan for community mobilisation activities to ensure post-programme sustainability.
Integrate climate resilience into delivery planning, given recurring flooding risks.
