programme_metadata.programme_title: Prosperity Fund Global Finance Programme

output_1.title: Promotion of Financial Technology: Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)

output_2.title: Promotion of Financial Technology: Cambridge Alternative Finance Collaboration Network (CAFCN)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme was transferred from Prosperity Fund to FCDO in March 2021. New initiatives paused due to 0.5% GNI ODA spending target; focus shifted to maximizing value from existing projects. Business case extended to 2045 to align with TCX investment maturity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IMF’s FSSF and Bank of England’s CCBS performed well in Financial Sector Stability pillar. TCX and IFC delivered on local currency financing objectives. FCA component concluded in March 2021; CAFCN exceeded expectations (A+ score).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Adapted to virtual delivery due to COVID-19, using digital tools for project management. Governance adjusted to FCDO’s new budget constraints and ODA priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with partners (IMF, BoE, TCX, IFC, CCAF) remained effective despite pandemic challenges. Cross-pillar collaboration maintained through virtual platforms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for TCX and IFC risk facility proceeded as planned. No major delays reported, though COVID-19 required flexible contracting approaches.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight on value-for-money due to budget cuts. More frequent monitoring of partner delivery rates (e.g., IMF’s FSSF technical assistance).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme reprioritized activities to focus on digital financial services (FinTech) due to COVID-19-induced demand. Budget reallocated to high-performing pillars (e.g., CAFCN).
adaptive_management_examples: Shift to virtual technical assistance delivery (e.g., BoE’s central bank training).
Combined SME Access to Finance and Investor Perception research into a single study (CAFCN).
Paused new initiatives to concentrate resources on existing high-impact projects (e.g., TCX, IFC risk facility).

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 disrupted in-person activities, requiring rapid transition to virtual delivery.
Budget reductions due to 0.5% GNI ODA target forced reprioritization and pause of new initiatives.
Geopolitical tensions (e.g., Russia-Ukraine conflict) added stress to target countries’ financial markets.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 accelerated demand for digital financial services, aligning with GFP’s FinTech pillar but straining implementation capacity.
Exchange rate volatility in frontier markets affected local currency financing (TCX/IFC pillars).
Supply chain disruptions delayed some technical assistance (e.g., BoE’s in-country missions).
contextual_constraints_new: Unexpected need for digital tools/support to partners lacking virtual infrastructure.
Increased competition for ODA funds within FCDO, requiring stronger justification for continued GFP funding.
Regulatory delays in some countries (e.g., Nigeria’s FinTech sandbox) due to pandemic-related backlogs.
partner_relationship_issues: Reduced service offerings to some central bank partners (BoE) risked reputational strain; managed through transparent communication.
TCX’s ambition to expand in Sub-Saharan Africa required realignment of logframe targets with FCDO priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Partners (e.g., CCAF) faced bandwidth limits due to increased demand for FinTech research post-COVID.
FCDO’s reduced staff capacity for oversight due to budget cuts.
risk_materialization: Moderate risks (as rated annually) materialized primarily around delivery delays (e.g., research outputs) and budget execution challenges.
No high-severity risks realized; adaptive management mitigated most operational disruptions.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track despite reprioritization. 2021/22 spending focused on existing commitments (TCX, IFC, CAFCN) with no over/under-expenditure reported. Budget extended to 2045 to match TCX investment horizon.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. CAFCN’s A+ score and TCX’s continued expansion demonstrate cost-efficiency. IMF/BoE technical assistance delivered within projected costs. FinTech pillar’s digital shift reduced travel expenses.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Partners (IMF, BoE, TCX) maintained transparent reporting. FCDO’s increased oversight post-2021 transfer ensured compliance with new ODA rules.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded in FinTech (CAFCN) and local currency financing (TCX) pillars. IMF/BoE costs stable; no significant variances from business case projections.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially realized. IFC’s cross-border risk facility leveraged additional private-sector funding, but some anticipated co-funding for new initiatives was paused.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal direct impact on GFP budget (GBP-denominated). However, TCX/IFC’s local currency work faced exchange rate volatility in target markets (e.g., Nigeria, Kenya), affecting borrower costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Virtual delivery can achieve high impact (e.g., CAFCN’s A+ score) but requires upfront investment in digital tools and partner capacity.
Flexible logframes (e.g., TCX’s updated targets) are critical for long-term programmes facing external shocks.
Pausing new initiatives to focus on existing projects can enhance value-for-money during budget constraints.
successful_delivery_practices: CAFCN’s integration of SME finance and investor perception research into a single study improved efficiency.
BoE’s virtual central bank training maintained engagement despite travel restrictions.
TCX’s focus on Sub-Saharan Africa aligned with FCDO’s geographic priorities, improving targeting.
management_adaptations_made: Increased monitoring of IMF’s technical assistance delivery rates.
Formalized VFM indicators for BoE’s services to manage reputational risks.
Updated TCX logframe to reflect impact report findings and regional targets.
innovations_attempted: Digital tools for FinTech regulatory research (CAFCN).
Cross-border risk facility with IFC to mitigate local currency risks.
Hybrid (virtual/in-person) technical assistance models (BoE/IMF).
previous_recommendations_progress: CAFCN expanded capacity-building tools as recommended in 2021 review.
BoE captured lessons for potential next-phase partnership (post-2022).
TCX logframe updated to include Sub-Saharan Africa targets (pending finalization).
forward_recommendations: Finalize IFC Cross-Border Risk Facility logframe with clear impact metrics.
Develop proposal for next-phase FCDO-BoE partnership (post-March 2022).
Scale CAFCN’s digital tools and education programmes to additional regions.
Monitor geopolitical risks (e.g., Ukraine conflict) on target countries’ financial stability.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Moderate risk ratings maintained despite external shocks. Proactive adjustments (e.g., virtual delivery, budget reprioritization) mitigated potential disruptions. Mid-term evaluations (e.g., IMF’s FSSF) planned to incorporate donor lessons.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Exceeded targets in FinTech (CAFCN) and local currency financing (TCX). IMF/BoE technical assistance reached planned central banks, though some in-person activities were delayed. No quantitative data provided for direct beneficiaries.
policy_influence_achieved: Nigeria’s Central Bank (CBN) applied to join Global Financial Innovation Network (GFIN) with FCA support.
TCX’s local currency financing model adopted by additional frontier market borrowers.
CAFCN’s regulatory research informed FinTech policies in SSA, MENA, and APAC regions.
capacity_building_results: BoE/IMF trained central bankers on crisis mitigation and monetary policy (virtual delivery).
CAFCN’s reports and tools strengthened regulators’ understanding of FinTech ecosystems.
TCX’s risk-sharing mechanisms built capacity of local financial institutions to access global markets.
unintended_consequences: Positive: COVID-19 accelerated digital financial service adoption, aligning with GFP’s FinTech goals.
Negative: Reduced in-person engagement limited relationship-building with some partners (e.g., central banks).
scalability_evidence: CAFCN’s research methodologies and digital tools are replicable in new regions.
TCX/IFC’s local currency models can be expanded to additional frontier markets.
BoE’s virtual training modules scalable to other central banks with minimal cost.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong performance (A+ score) and alignment with FCDO’s priorities on financial stability, digital finance, and climate-resilient growth. Extended business case to 2045 ensures long-term impact through TCX/IFC investments.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Sustainable. Virtual delivery and partner-led implementation (IMF, BoE, TCX) reduce FCDO’s operational burden. Risk facility with IFC ensures commercial viability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize logframes for IFC Cross-Border Risk Facility and TCX’s Sub-Saharan Africa targets.
Develop next-phase BoE partnership proposal (post-March 2022).
Expand CAFCN’s digital capacity-building tools to Latin America and South Asia.
Monitor and mitigate geopolitical/economic risks (e.g., inflation, Ukraine conflict) on target countries.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Modern Slavery – Supporting Global Action to End Modern Slavery
programme_metadata.programme_value_gbp: £22.2m (includes funding for the Independent MEL Unit)

output_1.title: New/improved tools and methodologies to assess scale and prevalence of modern slavery at sector level created and shared

output_2.title: Strengthened analysis identifies the structural drivers of modern slavery & learning from interventions is published through evaluations for use by key actors

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Delivery partners faced challenges in securing in-country operational permissions, impacting intervention timelines. GFEMS demonstrated capability in producing analytical outputs (e.g., prevalence studies, driver analyses) but required additional oversight for financial and risk management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with stakeholders (governments, private sector, civil society) was facilitated through stakeholder mapping and influence strategies, though operational delays affected full implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: DFID invested more staff time than proportionate for the programme size due to its strategic importance, with heightened oversight on financial management and risk mitigation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: GFEMS adapted by revising its risk register, Value for Money (VFM) framework, and theory of change based on early implementation lessons, with deadlines set for March 2020 submissions.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in securing in-country operational permissions for interventions, threatening viability of planned activities.
Financial sustainability concerns despite securing £9.1m from Norway, necessitating broader donor base diversification.
Evolving financial and risk management processes as programme scale increased, requiring stricter budget adherence (≤5% quarterly variance).
operational_challenges_context.capacity_constraints_emerged: GFEMS required strengthened financial management and risk register revisions to align with DFID’s expectations, indicating initial capacity gaps in these areas.
risk_materialization: Major risk rating due to operational delays and financial sustainability concerns.
Strategic risks around donor diversification and long-term funding stability.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Programme spent £1,715,639.20 during the 2019 review period. DFID mandated quarterly budget adherence (≤5% variance) starting April 2020 to address prior execution inconsistencies.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: A revised VFM framework, aligned with DFID guidance, was required by March 2020 due to insufficient initial clarity on delivery partner objectives and cost efficiency. Early outputs (e.g., prevalence studies) were delivered on time, but long-term VFM remained under review.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management required strengthening, with DFID imposing stricter quarterly budget controls and mandating a revised risk register to improve transparency and accountability.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Norway contributed ~£9.1m (100 million NOK) in December 2018, but additional co-funding was needed to meet GFEMS’s multi-donor fund ambitions.

key_delivery_lessons: Early engagement with in-country authorities is critical to avoid operational delays.
Robust financial and risk management systems must be established upfront to handle programme scale-up.
Stakeholder mapping and influence strategies (e.g., GFEMS’s Guidebook) are effective tools for aligning diverse actors.
successful_delivery_practices: Pilot prevalence studies and driver analyses produced actionable insights, demonstrating GFEMS’s technical capability.
Influence Strategy Guidebook successfully defined stakeholder engagement approaches.
management_adaptations_made: Revised risk register and VFM framework to be submitted by March 2020, with quarterly reporting.
Theory of change and logframe revisions planned to reflect updated delivery partner projects.
innovations_attempted: New methodologies for measuring modern slavery prevalence in targeted sectors (apparel, commercial sexual exploitation, labor migration).
Driver Analysis and Strategic Review studies to identify structural interventions.
forward_recommendations: Develop a resource mobilization strategy by March 2020 to diversify donor base.
Strengthen financial management to ensure ≤5% quarterly budget variance.
Submit revised risk register, VFM framework, and logframe by March 2020.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Initial risk management was inadequate (evidenced by ‘Major’ risk rating), prompting DFID to require a revised, multi-level risk register with quarterly reporting.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Influence Strategy Guidebook and stakeholder maps laid groundwork for policy engagement, but direct policy uptake was not yet documented in the review period.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Driver analyses and prevalence studies built technical capacity among partners, though long-term institutionalization of these approaches remained untested.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Pilot methodologies (e.g., prevalence measurement tools) showed potential for scalability, but broader adoption depended on future donor mobilization and implementation success.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrated strong alignment with UK priorities and produced high-quality analytical outputs (e.g., prevalence studies, driver analyses). Continued support was contingent on addressing financial management and donor diversification risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfactory, with caveats around financial oversight and risk management.
planned_adaptations_future: Resource mobilization strategy to secure additional donors.
Stricter financial controls and revised risk/VFM frameworks.
Updated theory of change and logframe to reflect partner projects.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Better Assistance in Crises (BASIC) Programme

output_1.title: High quality, policy relevant, inclusive research in different contexts generated and effectively disseminated

output_2.title: High quality technical assistance provided for the design and delivery of country plans, policies, programmes and systems

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned from Expert Advisory Call-Down Service (EACDS) managed by DAI Global UK (2018–June 2022) to the Social Protection Technical Assistance, Advice and Resources Facility (STAAR) procured in September 2021. Programme Funded Post (PFP) seconded to DAI for stakeholder engagement. Humanitarian expertise provided via HSOT (Palladium).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IDS (BASIC Research) faced delays in inception due to COVID-19 and budget uncertainty, requiring contract amendments for new partners. In-person engagement (e.g., Niger) improved partner alignment but budget instability strained relationships. STAAR’s demand-led model risked becoming reactive rather than strategic.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO SPT and IDS established clearer roles for review/sign-off processes (e.g., distinguishing FCDO SPT from advisers at post). Regular coordination with Programme Commercial Delivery (PCD) to mitigate contract amendment delays. Midline evaluation highlighted strong GESI mainstreaming but noted budget risks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: BASIC Research and STAAR developed uptake strategies (e.g., country stakeholder mapping, Nigeria Lead pilot) but faced challenges in aligning research dissemination with TA opportunities due to re-profiled budgets. Quarterly VfM updates and annual reports maintained.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Prolonged contract amendment processes (e.g., 3-month delay for BASIC Research amendments) impacted timelines. STAAR’s procurement for 24/25 demand-led assignments risks delays if not planned strategically. Competitive fee rates maintained via framework agreements (e.g., IMDP for IDS).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to budget uncertainty and contract management requirements. FCDO SPT increased engagement with BASIC Research/STAAR on workplan adjustments and risk mitigation (e.g., GESI monitoring, logframe reviews).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to COVID-19 via extensions (e.g., 1-month in 2021, 3-months in 2022) and re-profiled budgets (e.g., shifting STAAR spend to 24/25). Research focus adjusted based on partner input (e.g., Lebanon, Ethiopia contexts).
adaptive_management_examples: Granted two no-cost extensions for BASIC Research to accommodate COVID-19 and budget delays.
Revised research milestones post-inception to reflect slower country progress (e.g., Lebanon, Ethiopia).
STAAR adjusted workplans to prioritize strategic opportunities (e.g., Ukraine TA) over gap-filling.
Developed BASIC Research Uptake and Engagement Strategy to target policy influence despite budget constraints.

main_implementation_challenges: Prolonged inception phase (Oct 2020–Jan 2022) due to COVID-19 and budget uncertainty, delaying research implementation.
Contract amendment bottlenecks (e.g., 3-month approval delays) for adding new partners, impacting timelines.
Budget instability led to re-profiling of activities (e.g., STAAR spend shifted to 24/25), limiting dissemination and TA responsiveness.
High bounce rates (71.9%) on research webpages, missing the 40% target by 2024.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 caused a 4-month inception extension and disrupted in-country research (e.g., partner engagements in Niger).
Geopolitical crises (e.g., Ukraine) diverted TA resources (STAAR) to immediate humanitarian needs, delaying planned activities.
Currency/exchange rate fluctuations not explicitly mentioned, but global inflation may have indirectly affected cost efficiency.
contextual_constraints_new: Fragility in focus countries (Lebanon, Niger, Nigeria, Yemen) exacerbated by protracted conflicts, requiring adaptive research designs.
Limited capacity of national partners to absorb budget uncertainties, risking relationship continuity.
Humanitarian system’s short-term focus clashed with BASIC’s long-term social protection goals, complicating uptake.
partner_relationship_issues: Budget uncertainty strained trust with some partners, particularly where funding continuity was unclear.
Contract amendments for new partners created administrative burdens, delaying onset of collaborations.
Southern organizations’ ideas were incorporated into research design, but power imbalances in decision-making persisted.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s capacity to oversee the programme was stretched, risking strategic direction (noted as a "Moderate, ongoing risk").
Limited technical capacity among country partners to implement GESI mainstreaming without sustained support.
STAAR’s demand-led model required additional capacity to ensure assignments aligned with strategic (not just reactive) needs.
risk_materialization: Budget uncertainty ("Major, increased risk") materialized, causing delays and re-profiling of activities.
Contract management delays ("Major, new risk") impacted programme delivery, as seen in 3-month amendment approvals.
Limited evidence of diversified financing outcomes (per midline evaluation), risking long-term sustainability.
Failure to influence policy at scale ("Moderate, ongoing risk") persisted despite encouraging midline findings.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget uncertainty led to under-execution in 2022/23, with significant re-profiling of STAAR and BASIC Research funds to 24/25.
Two no-cost extensions granted for BASIC Research to align with revised budgets, but caused implementation delays.
Administrative costs for BASIC Research were initially in line with contract allowances, but later amendments reduced fee days to reallocate to expenses.
value_for_money_assessment: Mixed VfM performance: competitive procurement (IDS via IMDP framework, STAAR via EACDS) achieved economy, but prolonged inception and budget instability reduced efficiency.
STAAR demonstrated economy via travel savings (e.g., leveraging OCHA for Ukraine TA translation/local travel).
BASIC Research’s shift from fees to expenses in 2022 contract amendment maintained VfM but reduced flexibility.
Midline evaluation found VfM negatively impacted by delays, though strategic targeting (e.g., Research Uptake Strategy) partially mitigated this.
financial_management_quality: Suppliers (IDS, STAAR) established VfM frameworks with quarterly updates and annual reports, tracking economy/efficiency metrics.
FCDO SPT worked closely with partners to ensure contract amendments (e.g., fee reductions) did not undermine VfM propositions.
STAAR’s monitoring included fee cap compliance and budget adherence for TA assignments, but demand-led nature risked misalignment with strategic goals.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Fee rates remained competitive (no profit in IDS day rates; STAAR capped fees).
Cost savings realized in STAAR’s Ukraine TA via OCHA-provided translation/local travel.
However, cost efficiency was reduced by inception delays and the need for contract amendments (e.g., 3-month processing time).

key_delivery_lessons: In-person partner engagements (e.g., Niger) significantly improved research alignment with country contexts but were resource-intensive.
Early involvement of Programme Commercial Delivery (PCD) in contract amendments reduced later delays.
Budget uncertainty disproportionately affected research dissemination and GESI mainstreaming, requiring proactive risk management.
successful_delivery_practices: BASIC Research’s pre-development sharing of product contents with FCDO SPT aligned expectations and improved quality assurance.
STAAR’s six-monthly work planning process helped target TA strategically, though demand-led risks remained.
Collaboration between BASIC Research and STAAR (e.g., Nigeria Lead pilot) enhanced country-level uptake of research findings.
management_adaptations_made: Revised GESI mainstreaming approach post-budget revisions, with plans to develop a logframe indicator by Feb 2023.
Adjusted research milestones (Dec 2022) to reflect slower country progress and budget constraints.
Formalized check-ins on STAAR’s reach among non-FCDO users (planned June 2023) to address midline evaluation recommendations.
innovations_attempted: Piloted STAAR Nigeria Lead to integrate research uptake with TA delivery at country level.
Developed BASIC Knowledge, Evidence, Learning and Uptake (KELU) Strategy to foster collaboration between Research and STAAR.
Leveraged existing frameworks (e.g., OCHA support for Ukraine TA) to reduce costs and improve efficiency.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2021 Annual Review recommendations partially addressed: GESI mainstreaming was paused but is being revived with a logframe indicator (Feb 2023).
Midline evaluation’s call for clearer pathways to diversified financing outcomes led to a Theory of Change review (planned April 2023).
STAAR’s awareness among non-FCDO users remains limited; formal review planned for June 2023.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Review Theory of Change pathways for human/institutional capacity and financing outcomes by April 2023.
Develop a GESI indicator for the logframe and ensure STAAR’s GESI ambition is realized.
Conduct a formal STAAR service review to adjust to budget changes and longer timeframe, including midline evaluation recommendations.
Enhance collaboration between BASIC Research and STAAR via country stakeholder mapping and uptake strategies.
Review and adjust output milestones (1, 2, and 3) as part of the logframe update.

risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive mitigation of contract amendment delays via early PCD engagement, but risks persisted due to budget volatility.
GESI risks were identified (midline evaluation) and addressed via revised mainstreaming plans, though implementation was delayed.
Strategic targeting (e.g., Research Uptake Strategy) partially offset risks of limited policy influence, but scaling remains challenging.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Research communications reached 3,903 unique pageviews (Feb–Nov 2022), exceeding the 1,000 target but with high bounce rates (71.9%).
Policy recommendations on gender, age, disability, and intersecting vulnerabilities were mainstreamed across most research workstreams (cumulative milestone met).
Direct beneficiary data for TA (STAAR) not specified, but midline evaluation noted contributions to "more efficient, effective, and inclusive social assistance."
policy_influence_achieved: Midline evaluation found plausible contributions to improved social assistance efficiency/effectiveness, but limited evidence of capacity or financing outcomes.
Research outputs (e.g., 18 working papers, 12 briefs) engaged policy audiences, but uptake at scale remains constrained by humanitarian system’s short-term focus.
STAAR’s TA influenced country-level plans (e.g., Nigeria Lead pilot), but systemic policy change requires longer-term engagement.
capacity_building_results: Technical assistance (STAAR) supported country partners in designing social protection programmes, but midline evaluation noted limited progress on diversified financing.
BASIC Research’s GESI mainstreaming strengthened partner capacity on inclusion, though budget cuts risked backsliding.
Knowledge products (e.g., thematic briefs) aimed at capacity building, but dissemination was hindered by budget re-profiling.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Enhanced collaboration between humanitarian and social protection sectors in focus countries (e.g., Lebanon, Niger).
Negative: Budget uncertainty led to paused GESI activities and delayed research, potentially reducing long-term impact.
Demand-led TA (STAAR) risked diverting resources from strategic to reactive needs (e.g., Ukraine response).
scalability_evidence: Research findings (e.g., on social protection in crises) are designed for global applicability, but uptake depends on donor/policy appetite.
STAAR’s model is replicable for other FCDO programmes (e.g., Gender Responsive Social Protection), but requires stable funding.
Midline evaluation suggested BASIC’s approaches could scale if capacity and financing bottlenecks are addressed.

delivery_model_sustainability: Current model (STAAR + BASIC Research) is viable but faces risks from budget volatility and demand-led TA’s reactive tendencies.
Framework contracts (e.g., IMDP, EACDS) provide flexibility but require proactive contract management to avoid delays.
Long-term sustainability hinges on addressing midline evaluation findings (e.g., financing outcomes, capacity gaps).
fcdo_satisfaction_level: Encouraged by midline evaluation’s findings on social assistance improvements but concerned about limited progress on capacity/financing outcomes.
Satisfied with VfM frameworks and competitive procurement, but budget uncertainty has frustrated delivery.
GESI mainstreaming and adaptive management (e.g., COVID-19 extensions) were positively received, though implementation challenges remain.
planned_adaptations_future: Review Theory of Change pathways (April 2023) to clarify contributions to capacity and financing outcomes.
Adjust STAAR’s service model (June 2023) to better balance demand-led and strategic TA.
Strengthen collaboration between BASIC Research and STAAR via country uptake strategies (Dec 2022–Mar 2023).
Develop GESI logframe indicator (Feb 2023) and monitor mainstreaming in revised research designs.
Re-profile budgets to mitigate 24/25 spending risks, ensuring alignment with dissemination and TA opportunities.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Gender-Responsive Social Protection Programme

output_1.title: High quality and rigorous evidence on What Works to enhance results for women and girls from gender-responsive social protection

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Procurement of a new supplier for the Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) is ongoing due to delays from FCDO procurement pause (Nov 2020–Jul 2021). Original HEART consortium (via EACDS) was not designed for GSP’s complexity, requiring multidisciplinary teams for gender-social protection integration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF’s Office of Research (OoR) faced COVID-19 delays in primary data collection (e.g., Tanzania, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso). World Bank’s Gender Window in RSR MDTF was established but required catalytic grants to drive policy/practice changes. OPM/HEART consortium struggled with cross-cutting oversight of diverse call-downs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO’s Social Protection Team (SPT) lacked capacity to manage multiple TAF contracts. A Social Development Advisor was seconded to UNICEF’s Child Poverty Unit to strengthen coordination. Senior Gender Specialist co-funded at World Bank’s SPJ practice improved knowledge exchange.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Revised Theory of Change (ToC) introduced partner-specific pathways (UNICEF, WB, FCDO) and a thematic knowledge-exchange pathway, improving alignment but requiring more intensive coordination. Community of Practice pathway formalized lesson-sharing among partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: TAF procurement paused Nov 2020–Jul 2021 due to FCDO-wide freeze. Contract award expected post-July 2021. Weak market for gender-social protection consultants led to higher costs and management needs for multidisciplinary teams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to partner performance variability (e.g., COVID delays, TAF transition). FCDO increased monitoring of research quality and TA flexibility.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to COVID-19 by shifting to virtual knowledge-exchange (webinars, blogs) and reprioritizing research streams (e.g., delayed primary data collection). TAF’s on-demand model allowed responsive TA despite supplier transition.
adaptive_management_examples: UNICEF revised research timelines and methods (e.g., remote data collection in Burkina Faso, DRC) due to COVID-19.
FCDO approved programme extension consideration (decision pending Sept 2021) to accommodate delays.
KEL (Knowledge Exchange & Learning) group focused on thematic priorities (GBV, girls’ education) to streamline dissemination.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 restrictions delayed primary research (2020–2021), affecting Output 1 milestones (e.g., data collection in 4 countries postponed).
Procurement freeze (Nov 2020–Jul 2021) stalled TAF supplier transition, risking TA continuity.
Limited market for consultants with combined gender equality and social protection expertise, increasing costs and reducing response timeliness.
HEART consortium’s structure was misaligned with GSP’s need for cross-cutting gender TA oversight.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Halted field research, shifted events online, and delayed publications (e.g., 3 papers pushed to Q3/Q4 2021).
FCDO procurement pause: 8-month delay in TAF contract award, requiring interim TA solutions.
Multilateral shifts: World Bank’s RSR MDTF Gender Window required adaptive grant management to ensure gender-responsive design.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging evidence gaps in gender-responsive social protection during crises (e.g., care work, GBV) demanded rapid KEL pivots.
Partner capacity constraints (e.g., UNICEF’s OoR core costs vs. study costs imbalance) threatened evidence-generation quality.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between FCDO’s demand for rapid TA and HEART’s capacity to deliver cross-cutting gender-social protection advice.
World Bank’s bureaucratic processes slowed Gender Window grant disbursement, requiring FCDO advocacy.
capacity_constraints_emerged: UNICEF OoR: Underestimated core costs for high-quality research, risking output quality.
FCDO SPT: Lacked bandwidth to manage multiple TAF contracts, prompting supplier consolidation.
World Bank: Limited internal gender expertise in SPJ practice necessitated FCDO-co-funded Specialist role.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 operational risks (Score: Major in 2021) materialized as research delays and virtual engagement challenges.
Procurement risks: TAF supplier transition delay forced reliance on interim TA providers.
Partner dependency risks: Over-reliance on HEART consortium exposed gaps when demand exceeded capacity.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Overall spend on track, but UNICEF’s research stream faced cost pressures from extended timelines (COVID-19) and higher-than-planned study costs.
World Bank’s Gender Window grants disbursed slower than planned due to competitive selection processes.
TA facility underspent in 2020–2021 due to procurement delays, with carry-over expected post-TAF contract award.
value_for_money_assessment: Evidence generation (Output 1) scored B due to delayed outputs but high relevance of published work (e.g., 4 reports/journal articles in 2020–2021).
TA facility (Output 2) achieved B despite supplier issues; multidisciplinary teams improved gender integration but at higher cost.
World Bank influence (Output 3) and KEL (Output 4) scored A, with strong leverage of FCDO’s £8.5M investment in WB Specialist role and catalytic grants.
Independent evaluation noted "good" VFM for policy influence but "moderate" for research efficiency.
financial_management_quality: UNICEF: Transparent cost reporting but challenges in separating core vs. study costs for research streams.
World Bank: Robust financial systems for MDTF but slow grant processing affected timely disbursement.
OPM/HEART: Financial reporting met FCDO standards, but contract management was resource-intensive for FCDO SPT.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Research: Unit costs per publication increased due to COVID-19 extensions (e.g., data collection in 3 countries delayed).
TA: Multidisciplinary teams improved quality but raised per-assignment costs by ~20% vs. original HEART model.
KEL: Virtual events reduced travel costs but required higher investment in digital platforms.
co_funding_materialization: World Bank: FCDO’s £8.5M for Senior Gender Specialist leveraged WB’s MDTF contributions, but co-funding for Gender Window grants was competitive and slower than anticipated.
UNICEF: No additional co-funding secured for research; FCDO covered full £5M allocation.

key_delivery_lessons: Thematic focus (e.g., GBV, girls’ education) improved KEL impact; broad themes diluted engagement.
Multidisciplinary TA teams enhanced gender-social protection integration but required stronger FCDO contract management.
Partner-secondment model (e.g., UNICEF, WB) effectively drove institutional change but demanded long-term commitment.
successful_delivery_practices: Virtual KEL events (webinars, blogs) maintained engagement during COVID-19, reaching 2x more participants than in-person.
World Bank Gender Window’s small grants catalysed policy changes in 5 countries by Q2 2021.
UNICEF’s adaptive research methods (e.g., remote data tools) mitigated COVID-19 delays in 3/4 target countries.
management_adaptations_made: FCDO increased oversight of UNICEF’s research financial planning (Aug 2021 review).
Revised ToC (March 2021) introduced measurable interim outcomes, improving MEL alignment.
TAF procurement now includes gender-social protection expertise as a mandatory requirement.
innovations_attempted: Gender Window competitive grants: Tested catalytic funding to incentivize WB teams’ gender-responsive designs.
Cross-partner KEL working groups: Piloted joint FCDO-UNICEF-WB events on GBV/cash transfers.
Digital MEL tools: UNICEF adopted real-time data dashboards for research progress tracking.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2020 AR recommendation to address HEART’s oversight gaps: Partially implemented via new TAF procurement criteria (gender expertise mandatory).
Call for stronger UNICEF research risk management: Addressed via Aug 2021 financial review.
Demand for WB policy influence metrics: Achieved through Gender Window grant reporting templates.
forward_recommendations: Extend programme by 6–12 months to recover COVID-19 delays (FCDO decision pending Sept 2021).
Develop a partner performance scorecard to track TA quality and research outputs quarterly.
Increase co-funding for UNICEF’s core research costs to ensure evidence quality.
Scale World Bank Gender Window model to other multilaterals (e.g., UNDP, ILO).
risk_management_effectiveness: COVID-19 risks: Mitigated via adaptive research methods but required programme extension.
Procurement risks: TAF delay managed through interim TA, but caused 6-month service gap.
Partner risks: WB Specialist role improved gender integration; UNICEF secondment strengthened policy influence.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Indirect reach: World Bank Gender Window grants influenced social protection systems in 5 countries (1.2M+ beneficiaries, 60% women/girls).
Direct reach: UNICEF research engaged 1,500+ policymakers via webinars/KEL events (2020–2021).
TA facility supported 12 FCDO country teams, indirectly benefiting ~500,000 social protection recipients.
policy_influence_achieved: World Bank: Gender-responsive criteria integrated into RSR MDTF operations manual (adopted by 8 country teams).
FCDO: GSP evidence informed 3 bilateral social protection programmes’ gender strategies (e.g., Tanzania, Ethiopia).
UNICEF: Research on care work influenced 2 global policy briefs (2021).
capacity_building_results: World Bank: 15 WB staff trained on gender-social protection via Gender Window grants; 70% applied learnings in country programmes.
FCDO: 24 advisors completed GSP KEL modules; 80% reported improved gender analysis skills (2021 survey).
UNICEF: Seconded Social Development Advisor mentored 10 UNICEF country offices on gender-responsive design.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Virtual KEL events increased access for Global South participants (40% of attendees vs. 15% pre-COVID).
Negative: Procurement delays reduced TA availability for urgent country requests (e.g., Lebanon crisis response).
scalability_evidence: World Bank Gender Window model replicated in UNDP’s social protection portfolio (2021).
UNICEF’s research frameworks adopted by 3 regional offices (Africa, LAC) for gender analysis.
FCDO’s TA demand outstripped supply, indicating scalability potential for new TAF supplier.

continuation_rationale: Strong policy influence (WB, FCDO, UNICEF) justifies extension to consolidate gains.
COVID-19 delays require additional time to deliver research (Output 1) and TA (Output 2) milestones.
High demand for gender-social protection expertise (e.g., 12 pending FCDO country requests).
delivery_model_sustainability: UNICEF/WB partnerships are institutionalized (e.g., secondments, co-funded roles).
New TAF supplier (post-Sept 2021) will address HEART’s oversight gaps.
KEL structures (e.g., thematic working groups) are self-sustaining with minimal FCDO input.

planned_adaptations_future: Introduce quarterly partner performance reviews (from Q4 2021).
Pilot a results-based financing mechanism for WB Gender Window grants.
Expand KEL to include private-sector partners (e.g., digital financial services).
Develop a gender-social protection "toolkit" for FCDO country teams (2022).

output_1.title: Improved understanding of the type, scale and impact of attacks on healthcare (RIAH)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: FCDO re-did the log frame to reflect changes with the RIAH extension, JPAL coming on stream, and the new output 5 (Beyond Compliance). This included new output weighting. AHRC lessons on uptake were reflected in BCC design and implementation, e.g., Research Line support to FCDO and consortium composition mixing academic and practitioner agencies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners were receptive to feedback on documenting safeguarding risks and improving VfM assessments. RIAH demonstrated substantial progress despite delays in milestone achievement, with outputs reconfigured for better accessibility (e.g., splitting reports into practitioner-focused and academic versions).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with FCDO’s humanitarian protection policy team and other relevant teams (e.g., HFRD, UK IHL Committee) was maintained. Cross-programme learning was applied, such as adapting indicators and VfM metrics based on annual review feedback.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO provided additional guidance to partners on VfM assessments and risk documentation (e.g., safeguarding). Partners submitted improved narratives and examples for VfM themes, though further linkage to logframe outputs was recommended.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme extensions were granted (e.g., RIAH in 2024) to shift focus toward dissemination and advocacy. Adaptive management included shortening the RFP process for JPAL to address challenges in sourcing protection-related evaluations.
adaptive_management_examples: RIAH reconfigured its Impact Methodologies report into two audience-specific outputs (practitioner guide + academic manuscript) to improve uptake.
JPAL adjusted its RFP process to reduce time burdens on humanitarian agencies and cultivated strategic relationships for RCTs.
FCDO financed a 2024 RIAH extension with greater emphasis on engaging advocacy networks to drive normative change.

main_implementation_challenges: Complexity of linking research outputs to humanitarian protection outcomes, given the intangible nature of protection impacts (e.g., norm change, conceptual shifts).
Delays in milestone achievement (e.g., RIAH’s synthesis of case studies due to late Afghanistan data, publication delays for methodological reports).
Difficulty in designing protection-related RCTs, requiring more time and stakeholder engagement than anticipated.
contextual_constraints_new: Underestimation of the time required to build trust within large consortia (9 partners) and cultivate relationships for impact generation.
Duplicative or misaligned outcome/impact indicators that failed to capture key programme effects (e.g., normative change, network-building).
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: Initial challenges in the BCC Research Line’s engagement with FCDO country teams due to slow trust-building and unclear value proposition.
capacity_constraints_emerged: High demands on humanitarian agencies’ time/expertise for RCTs, necessitating JPAL’s increased support (e.g., training sessions, project design refinement).
Need for additional guidance to partners on VfM metrics and risk documentation (e.g., safeguarding).
risk_materialization: Safeguarding risks (e.g., sexual exploitation) required explicit inclusion in risk matrices, with mitigation processes documented in partner registers.
Delays in research outputs (e.g., RIAH’s case study synthesis) due to fieldwork challenges (e.g., Afghanistan access).

value_for_money_assessment: Partners conducted annual VfM assessments with improved metrics/narratives in 2024–25, though FCDO recommended stronger linkage to logframe outputs.
RIAH demonstrated efficiency by repurposing outputs (e.g., country literature reviews used for both fieldwork planning and future publications).
BCC leveraged complementary skills across work packages to maximize resource use (e.g., Research Line outputs informed IDC submissions).
financial_management_quality: Partners adhered to institutional financial regulations (e.g., MIT’s procedures for BCC), ensuring oversight while maintaining operational efficiency.
FCDO provided additional guidance to standardize VfM reporting, leading to more detailed partner submissions.
cost_efficiency_achieved: RIAH’s outputs (e.g., methodologies, case studies) contributed to cost-efficient data collection by other actors (e.g., Insecurity Insight’s 51,000-reach news briefs).
Shared resources across consortium partners (e.g., joint dissemination activities) reduced duplication.

key_delivery_lessons: Protection programming is inherently difficult to evaluate; current indicators often fail to capture normative or conceptual outcomes (e.g., changing humanitarian standards).
Demand for rigorous evidence exists, but translating it into RCTs requires significant stakeholder engagement and capacity-building.
Large consortia demand substantial upfront investment in trust-building to realize impact potential.
successful_delivery_practices: Adaptive dissemination strategies (e.g., RIAH’s audience-specific outputs) improved uptake of research findings.
Strategic relationship-building (e.g., JPAL’s training for humanitarian actors) facilitated successful RCTs.
Cross-programme learning (e.g., applying AHRC’s uptake lessons to BCC design).
management_adaptations_made: Extended RIAH’s timeline to focus on advocacy and norm change.
Shortened JPAL’s RFP process to reduce partner burdens.
Updated risk matrices to explicitly address safeguarding (e.g., power imbalances in research teams).
innovations_attempted: RIAH’s methodological innovations for measuring cumulative impacts of attacks on healthcare.
BCC’s dual-purpose country literature reviews (fieldwork planning + publication basis).
HPI’s standardized proposal evaluation criteria to ensure high-quality, policy-relevant research.
previous_recommendations_progress: Improved VfM assessments with clearer metrics linked to outcomes (though further refinement needed).
Enhanced safeguarding risk documentation across all partners.
forward_recommendations: Revise outcome indicators to better capture normative/conceptual impacts (e.g., shifts in humanitarian practices).
Strengthen partner capacity for VfM reporting by aligning metrics with logframe outputs.
Prioritize relationship-building in consortium management to accelerate impact generation.
Explore scalable dissemination channels (e.g., podcasts, policy briefs) to amplify research uptake.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive adjustments (e.g., programme extensions, RFP streamlining) mitigated delays and partner burdens.
Safeguarding risks were systematically addressed through updated risk registers and mitigation procedures.

policy_influence_achieved: RIAH’s methodologies informed data collection by 3 additional organizations in 2024.
82 academic/policy citations in 2024–25 demonstrate growing influence on protection discourse.
Engagement with advocacy networks (e.g., attacks on healthcare) positions BEPAC to shape humanitarian norms.
capacity_building_results: 90 humanitarian organizations attended HPI’s capacity-building activities.
JPAL’s training sessions improved stakeholders’ understanding of impact evaluations.
unintended_consequences: Positive: RIAH’s delayed outputs led to more accessible, audience-tailored products (e.g., practitioner guides + academic papers).
Negative: Normative focus of research may face resistance from actors prioritizing short-term operational needs.
scalability_evidence: BCC’s Research Line outputs were repurposed for multiple uses (e.g., fieldwork tools, policy submissions).
HPI’s standardized proposal evaluation process is replicable for other FCDO-funded research programmes.

continuation_rationale: Consistent "A" ratings for overall performance indicate strong delivery despite challenges.
Extension of RIAH (2024) and adaptive management demonstrate programme agility in responding to learning.
Growing policy influence (e.g., citations, advocacy engagement) aligns with FCDO’s humanitarian protection priorities.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Greater focus on dissemination and normative change (e.g., RIAH’s advocacy networks).
Refinement of outcome indicators to better capture conceptual/normative impacts.
Strengthened VfM frameworks with clearer links between outputs and humanitarian policy outcomes.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme maintained "thinking and working politically" approach with federal/state MDAs, using mutual accountability frameworks. New government (2023) brought policy agenda shifts, including appointment of Coordinating Minister for Health (Dr. Muhammad Pate) who is advancing Sector Wide Approach reforms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with complementary programmes (e.g., PERL governance programme, DHSC/UKHSA investments) and engagement in fora like HDPG, NDPG, and KPPG. Mutual Accountability Frameworks (MAFs) with states bolstered alignment. Missed opportunity noted in linking public health emergency preparedness with UKHSA’s IHR Strengthening project.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Active oversight required due to budget volatility and political transitions. Reputational risk management was prioritised, particularly during naira redesign and economic instability.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to respond to: 1) Budget reductions (reprioritising activities), 2) Political transitions (adapting to new ministerial priorities), 3) Economic shocks (naira redesign, fuel subsidy removal), and 4) Security constraints (adjusting travel and engagement in conflict-affected areas).
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid integration of reduced budget into partner plans while maintaining delivery.
Engagement with new Coordinating Minister for Health to align with Sector Wide Approach reforms.
Adjustment of activities in Borno/Yobe due to insecurity, including support to 83 health facilities via HeRON consortium.
Response to economic crisis (e.g., double-digit inflation, cash shortages) by reprioritising technical assistance.

main_implementation_challenges: Substantial budget reductions (FY22/23: £14.7m planned → £9.65m actual; FY23/24: £6m planned).
Volatile economic context: naira redesign, fuel shortages, 20-year-high inflation (July 2023), and exchange rate depreciation.
Political transition (2023 elections) with party changes in key states (e.g., Kano) and new federal ministers.
Widespread insecurity (terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, ISWAP/Boko Haram insurgency) limiting travel and direct engagement in North West/North East.
Multidimensional poverty (133 million Nigerians affected, per 2022 data) impacting health service access.
external_factors_impact: Economic reforms (fuel subsidy removal, exchange rate adjustments) increased programming costs and reduced household purchasing power for health services.
COVID-19 and cholera outbreaks diverted resources, though UN Basket Fund (UNDP) provided crisis support.
Humanitarian crises in North East (Borno/Yobe) strained service delivery, requiring adaptive support via HeRON consortium.
Global inflation and supply chain disruptions affected contraceptive procurement (UNFPA basket fund).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of naira redesign impacts (cash shortages, digital payment challenges).
Accelerated fuel subsidy removal created short-term economic hardship, affecting health worker mobility and patient access.
State-level political shifts (e.g., Kano) required rapid re-engagement with new administrations.
Overlap and potential duplication between RMNCAEH+N coordination platforms and NPHCDA’s SEMCHIC initiative at state level.
partner_relationship_issues: Budget uncertainty tested partner trust, requiring transparent communication to maintain collaboration.
Differing priorities between federal and state governments (e.g., Kano’s party change) created alignment challenges.
Capacity gaps in some LGAs (e.g., Borno’s PHC Advisory Committees) slowed progress on governance outputs.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in newly established Departments of Family Health (e.g., Yobe) to sustain RMNCAEH+N coordination platforms.
Health worker shortages in conflict-affected LGAs (Borno/Yobe) hindered service delivery.
Reduced FCDO direct engagement in insecure areas limited political influencing for health investment.
risk_materialization: Budget reduction risk materialized, requiring programme reprioritisation.
Political transition risk materialized with state/federal government changes.
Economic volatility risk materialized (inflation, currency depreciation).
Security risks persisted, particularly in North East, limiting access.

budget_execution_vs_plan: FY22/23: Planned £14.7m → Actual £9.65m (65% execution).
FY23/24: Planned £6m (subject to uncertainty).
Cumulative underspend due to budget reductions, partially offset by reprioritisation.
value_for_money_assessment: High VfM maintained despite budget cuts, leveraging: 1) Political relationships (health as top governor ask), 2) Coordination with complementary programmes (PERL, UKHSA), 3) Adaptive TA delivery.
Cost efficiency achieved through shared platforms (e.g., RMNCAEH+N coordination) and basket funds (UNFPA/UNDP).
Challenges in demonstrating VfM for demographic transition component post-World Bank EFO closure.
financial_management_quality: Strong financial management by implementers (Palladium, IRC) in adapting to budget cuts.
Transparent communication with partners on funding uncertainty mitigated reputational risks.
Early engagement enabled integration of budget shifts into partner plans.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of reduced funds through: 1) Focused TA on high-impact policy windows, 2) Leveraging existing government structures (e.g., MDAs), 3) Shared costs with USAID (HeRON).
Currency depreciation increased GBP costs of local activities, partially offset by reprioritisation.
co_funding_materialization: Co-funding via basket funds (UNFPA for contraceptives, UNDP for emergencies) materialized as planned.
Domestic co-funding (e.g., Basic Health Care Provision Fund) remains uncertain but is a focus of new Sector Wide Approach reforms.
currency_exchange_impacts: Naira depreciation increased local costs for GBP-denominated budget, requiring activity adjustments.
Exchange rate volatility contributed to inflation, affecting procurement (e.g., medical supplies).

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible, politically-informed TA delivery is critical in volatile contexts (e.g., responding to ministerial transitions).
Early partner engagement on budget changes preserves trust and delivery continuity.
Coordination platforms (RMNCAEH+N) must be institutionalised to avoid duplication with parallel initiatives (e.g., SEMCHIC).
Humanitarian-development nexus requires adaptive programming (e.g., HeRON in Borno/Yobe).
successful_delivery_practices: Demand-led TA aligned with government priorities (e.g., supporting Department of Family Health establishment).
Basket fund mechanisms (UNFPA/UNDP) enabled rapid response to crises (COVID-19, cholera).
Policy window exploitation (e.g., engaging new Coordinating Minister on Sector Wide Approach).
Cross-programme coordination (PERL, UKHSA) maximised UK influence.
management_adaptations_made: Revised log-frame and theory of change to reflect budget reductions and political shifts.
Increased oversight during economic volatility to manage reputational risks.
Adjusted monitoring focus to high-impact governance outputs (e.g., RMNCAEH+N platforms).
innovations_attempted: Mutual Accountability Frameworks (MAFs) with states to enhance alignment.
Integration of demographic transition analysis with National Population Council.
Engagement of religious/traditional leaders to promote family planning (World Bank component).
previous_recommendations_progress: Progress on institutionalising RMNCAEH+N platforms (now established in all 5 states).
Partial progress on aligning SEMCHIC and RMNCAEH+N platforms (ongoing challenge).
Limited progress on sustaining HeRON-supported nutrition services post-2024.
forward_recommendations: Secure domestic co-funding for Basic Health Care Provision Fund to ensure sustainability.
Strengthen state-level capacity to maintain RMNCAEH+N platforms post-Lafiya.
Develop transition plan for HeRON-supported services in Borno/Yobe.
Explore mechanisms to sustain demographic transition work post-World Bank EFO.
Enhance linkage between Lafiya’s emergency preparedness and UKHSA’s IHR Strengthening project.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating budget/reputational risks through transparent communication.
Less effective in anticipating scale of economic shocks (naira redesign, inflation).
Political risk management strengthened by rapid engagement with new government.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: RMNCAEH+N coordination platforms established in 128 LGAs across 5 states (vs. target of 138 LGAs).
Functional RMNCAH+N coordination committees in 93% of target LGAs (vs. 52% baseline).
100% of HeRON-supported ward development committees functional in Borno/Yobe.
Family planning services reached vulnerable women via UNFPA basket fund (specific numbers not stated).
Nutrition interventions reached children under 5 and pregnant women in HeRON sites (below expectations due to insecurity).
policy_influence_achieved: Catalysed establishment of Departments of Family Health in Kano, Jigawa, and Yobe.
Influenced development of Sector Wide Approach for health sector reform (led by new Coordinating Minister).
Supported institutionalisation of RMNCAEH+N platforms at state/LGA levels.
Contributed to Basic Health Care Provision Fund reforms (domestic financing mechanism).
capacity_building_results: Trained government counterparts on RMNCAEH+N coordination and PHC advisory committees.
Strengthened capacity of National Population Council on demographic transition analysis.
Built health worker skills in family planning service delivery (via UNFPA/IRC).
Limited sustainability of capacity gains in conflict-affected LGAs (e.g., Borno).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Strengthened UK-Nigeria bilateral relationship through health sector engagement.
Positive: RMNCAEH+N platforms created unintended synergies with SEMCHIC in some states.
Negative: Budget cuts reduced support to some LGAs, risking reversal of governance gains (e.g., Borno PHC committees).
Negative: Insecurity limited reach in North East, leaving gaps in nutrition service coverage.
scalability_evidence: RMNCAEH+N coordination model scalable to other states (demonstrated in 5 focus states).
Basket fund approach (UNFPA/UNDP) replicable for other health crises.
Demographic transition analysis methodology adoptable by National Population Council.
Challenges in scaling HeRON model due to insecurity and humanitarian dependencies.

continuation_rationale: Programme remains central to UK-Nigeria health partnership and aligns with government priorities.
Strong performance in governance outputs (RMNCAEH+N platforms, family health departments).
New policy windows (Sector Wide Approach) offer opportunities for sustained impact.
Critical role in supporting Basic Health Care Provision Fund reforms.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model is partially sustainable: 1) Political engagement remains strong, 2) Coordination platforms are institutionalised, but 3) Funding uncertainty and state-level capacity gaps pose risks.
Dependence on TA may limit long-term sustainability without domestic resource mobilisation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Align with Sector Wide Approach reforms to leverage domestic financing.
Develop transition plans for HeRON-supported services in Borno/Yobe by May 2024.
Strengthen state-level ownership of RMNCAEH+N platforms.
Explore mechanisms to sustain demographic transition work post-2026.
Enhance monitoring of policy influence (e.g., Basic Health Care Provision Fund uptake).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from planned MOU-based delivery to individual financing agreements with implementing agencies due to unresolved MOU with Government of Tanzania. This created limitations in initiating new partnerships or extending existing ones.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Mixed performance: EU partnership for OSIS project failed due to contractor bankruptcy and lack of direct oversight by TMEA. Strong relationships with Tanzania Ports Authority enabled completion of Dar Port lorry parking yard despite political economy challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Decentralized implementation through direct agreements with agencies rather than centralized MOU framework. Required intensive stakeholder engagement to maintain progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Proactive linkage creation between complementary projects (e.g., logistics platform and Tanzania Mercantile Exchange) but some workstreams remained siloed where cooperation could have yielded greater results.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Prolonged procurement processes for non-intrusive scanners (Tunduma) and TMX system equipment due to required government approvals and tax exemption delays. Achieved 85% expenditure rate (US$10.243M of US$12.073M budget).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to need for direct influence over partnered projects (e.g., contract involvement and supervision roles) to mitigate risks identified in previous reviews.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by reducing weighting of underperforming outputs (e.g., OSIS construction reduced from 14% to 6%) and reallocating resources to higher-performing areas like SWIFTs and ATMIS.
adaptive_management_examples: Reduction of OSIS output weighting from 14% to 6% after contractor failure and project suspension.
Rebuilding relationships with Tanzania Ports Authority to complete Dar Port infrastructure despite MOU delays.
Accelerated delivery of Single Window Interface for Trade (SWIFTs) across 12+ government agencies, reducing phytosanitary certificate issuance time from 2 days to 3-6 hours.

main_implementation_challenges: Two-year stalemate in signing MOU with Government of Tanzania, limiting new partnerships and causing delays (e.g., stalled work with EPZA).
Contractor bankruptcy for OSIS project (Manyoni/Nyakanazi stations) leading to 41-60% completion vs. 100% target.
Slow government implementation of regulatory reforms (e.g., Blueprint for Regulatory Reforms, Arrears Management Strategy) despite private sector support.
external_factors_impact: Deteriorating investment climate: Tanzania dropped 12 spots in World Bank Doing Business rankings (2017-2019), recovering slightly to 141st in 2020 but remaining below regional peers.
Political economy shifts under current administration created uncertainty, with GDP growth estimates disputed (official 6.7% vs. World Bank’s 5.6% in 2019).
Upcoming 2020 general election risked further delays in reform implementation.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for direct TMEA involvement in partnered contracts to ensure results, deviating from original hands-off partnership model.
Government’s lack of commitment to regional trade integration and tax exemption disputes blocked MOU finalization.
Varied adoption rates of digital systems (e.g., SWIFTs) across agencies required additional advocacy efforts.
partner_relationship_issues: EU partnership for OSIS project failed due to contractor’s inability to meet terms and lack of TMEA’s contractual influence.
Tanzania Chamber of Commerce (TCCIA) showed weak ownership of TMEA-supported initiatives, raising sustainability concerns.
Delays in financing agreements (e.g., with EPZA) stalled project components.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Government agencies lacked capacity to fully adopt and maintain new systems (e.g., ATMIS) without ongoing TMEA support.
Limited technical expertise in some partners (e.g., standards agencies) required additional TMEA training and handholding.
risk_materialization: Major risk of MOU non-signature materialized, forcing reliance on individual financing agreements.
Contractor default risk materialized in OSIS project, requiring output weighting adjustment.
Political risk to reform implementation materialized with slow progress on regulatory blueprints.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Achieved 85% expenditure (US$10.243M of US$12.073M revised budget) in 2018/19. Underspending due to prolonged procurement for Tunduma scanners and TMX equipment requiring government approvals/tax exemptions.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Positive VFM in high-performing outputs (e.g., SWIFTs, ATMIS) but concerns about risk aversion pushing programme toward easier-to-deliver interventions. Review recommends reassessing portfolio to avoid "going off course" in challenging operating environment.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial oversight with adaptive reallocation (e.g., reducing OSIS weighting) but procurement bottlenecks persisted due to government processes.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High efficiency in digital systems (e.g., ATMIS reduced phytosanitary certificate time from 2 days to 3-6 hours) but infrastructure projects (e.g., OSIS) faced cost inefficiencies due to contractor issues.

key_delivery_lessons: Direct contractual involvement in partnered projects is critical to mitigate risks (lesson from OSIS/EU partnership failure).
Political economy analysis must inform adaptive management, especially in volatile contexts like Tanzania.
Strong government relationships can overcome formal agreement delays (e.g., Dar Port completion despite MOU stalemate).
successful_delivery_practices: Proactive linkage between complementary projects (e.g., logistics platform + TMX) enhanced trade environment outcomes.
Digital systems (SWIFTs, ATMIS) achieved transformative efficiency gains (e.g., 90% reduction in phytosanitary certificate time).
Flexible output weighting adjustments (e.g., OSIS reduction) allowed resource focus on high-performing areas.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from MOU-dependent model to individual financing agreements with agencies.
Increased oversight role in partnered projects to ensure result delivery.
Reduced emphasis on underperforming infrastructure outputs in favor of digital/regulatory reforms.
innovations_attempted: Single Window Interface for Trade (SWIFTs) accelerated across 12+ agencies, revolutionizing license/permit access.
Agriculture Trade Management Information System (ATMIS) cut export certification time from days to hours.
Female trader transition programs supported formalization of informal cross-border trade.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: 2017/18 recommendation on risk-based partnership assessment was implemented but contractor risks still materialized (e.g., OSIS).
Ongoing: MOU resolution remains pending despite continued stakeholder engagement.
Completed: Logframe updates and political economy analysis initiated as recommended.
forward_recommendations: Finalize MOU with Government of Tanzania to unlock stalled partnerships (e.g., EPZA).
Conduct portfolio review with political economy analysis to align interventions with context.
Update logframe and Theory of Change to reflect adaptive delivery model and risk environment.
Assess value for money and additionality of interventions to avoid risk-averse drift.
Strengthen partner ownership plans (e.g., for TCCIA) to ensure sustainability post-TMEA.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Identified risks (e.g., MOU delays, contractor defaults) materialized but adaptive responses (e.g., output reweighting, relationship-building) mitigated some impacts. Continuous risk assessment needed.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to Cabinet endorsement of Blueprint for Regulatory Reforms (2018) and Arrears Management Strategy, though implementation remains slow.
Supported WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement implementation (score: A).
Influenced standards regulation frameworks (score: A+) and trade community information systems (score: A).
capacity_building_results: Strengthened capacity of standards agencies (e.g., TBS efficiency systems scored A).
Trained partners on prioritized standards (score: A+).
Mixed sustainability: Strong ownership in standards agencies but weak in TCCIA.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Digital systems (SWIFTs, ATMIS) created unintended efficiency spillovers across unrelated agencies.
Negative: MOU delays unintentionally shifted programme toward easier, less transformative interventions.
scalability_evidence: SWIFTs and ATMIS models demonstrate scalability potential across East African Community regions.
Freight Logistics Platform and TMX linkages offer replicable integration templates.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong output delivery (overall score: A) and critical role in Tanzania’s trade environment, despite challenging context. Adaptive management has mitigated major risks, and digital/regulatory reforms show high potential for impact.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable: Digital systems (e.g., SWIFTs) have strong ownership, but infrastructure projects and some partnerships (e.g., TCCIA) face sustainability risks without MOU resolution.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize MOU to stabilize partnerships and unlock stalled components (e.g., EPZA collaboration).
Revisit Theory of Change and logframe to align with political economy realities and avoid risk-averse drift.
Enhance partner ownership strategies (e.g., co-investment plans) for post-TMEA sustainability.
Scale successful digital models (SWIFTs, ATMIS) to additional agencies/regions.
