output_1.title: Outcomes Funds operating in priority SDG areas

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme did not initiate any financial commitments to new outcome funds due to budget constraints and team capacity gaps. Focus shifted to managing existing funds (GEOP, SLEIC) and exploring new opportunities (e.g., clean cooking) for 2024/25.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Existing outcome funds (GEOP, SLEIC) experienced expected first-year management challenges, including delays due to national elections and procurement issues. Partners like GPRBA paused fundraising pending internal World Bank changes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Managed by FCDO’s Impact Team in PSCMD, with additional support from Education and Gender Equality Department. A full-time Programme Responsible Officer (PRO) was hired late in 2023/24 to address capacity gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with thematic/country teams (e.g., FCDO Energy, Climate and Environment Directorate) improved after targeted outreach, but remains an area for strengthening in 2024/25.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement delays affected SLEIC and GEOP implementation, particularly in their first year. These are being addressed through enhanced governance and risk management plans for 2024/25.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was initially lighter than planned due to team capacity gaps but intensified after hiring the PRO. Governance reviews for GEOP are planned for Q1 2024/25.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme flexibility was used to reallocate focus from launching new funds to supporting existing ones and scoping future opportunities (e.g., clean cooking). Adaptive management included pausing GPRBA fundraising pending WB internal changes.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocated team efforts to support existing funds (GEOP, SLEIC) instead of launching new ones due to budget/team constraints.
Identified a new clean cooking opportunity for 2024/25 in partnership with FCDO Energy, Climate and Environment Directorate.
Paused GPRBA fundraising for GEOP pending World Bank internal process resolution.

main_implementation_challenges: Insufficient budget and team capacity to launch new outcome funds in 2023/24.
Management issues in the first year of GEOP and SLEIC implementation (e.g., procurement delays, election-related disruptions).
GPRBA’s pause on fundraising for GEOP due to World Bank internal changes.
Unpredictable funding availability for the Outcomes Accelerator.
external_factors_impact: Political disruption in Sierra Leone (national elections) caused delays in SLEIC implementation.
World Bank internal changes led to GPRBA pausing fundraising for GEOP, limiting co-funding opportunities.
contextual_constraints_new: Limited appetite from host governments and donors to co-fund new outcome funds, reducing opportunities for scaling.
Currency/exchange rate impacts not explicitly mentioned, but budget constraints suggest potential indirect effects.
partner_relationship_issues: EOF (Education Outcomes Fund) faced challenges in SLEIC’s first-year delivery, requiring enhanced oversight.
GPRBA’s fundraising pause created uncertainty for GEOP’s long-term sustainability.
capacity_constraints_emerged: POF team lacked sufficient human resources until a full-time PRO was hired late in 2023/24, limiting proactive opportunity exploration.
Partners (e.g., GEOP, SLEIC) required additional support to address governance and procurement delays.
risk_materialization: Management risks in outcome funds (GEOP, SLEIC) materialized as expected (e.g., procurement delays, election disruptions).
Budget risks materialized, preventing new fund launches in 2023/24.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget constraints prevented new fund launches in 2023/24. Existing funds (GEOP, SLEIC) were fully funded but faced cost pressures. Total committed funding: FCDO (£31.6m), host governments (£4.6m), donors (£0.8m), philanthropists (£1.6m).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: On track but requires stronger cost-effectiveness data collection in 2024/25. Early evidence from SLEIC and GEOP suggests VfM is achievable, but management issues must be resolved to maintain it.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by implementers (e.g., EOF, GPRBA) was adequate but highlighted gaps in procurement and risk management, particularly in the funds’ first year. Plans to enhance governance in 2024/25.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency is not yet fully measurable due to limited data on outcomes per pound spent. SLEIC and GEOP delivered results (e.g., 43,568 children reached in SLEIC) but require deeper analysis for efficiency benchmarks.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized partially: host governments (£4.6m vs. £5m target), donors (£0.8m vs. £0 target), philanthropists (£1.6m vs. £1m target). GPRBA’s paused fundraising limited additional donor contributions.

key_delivery_lessons: Outcome funds require intensive management support in their first year to address procurement and governance challenges.
Team capacity is critical for proactive opportunity exploration; gaps directly limited new fund launches.
Flexibility in delivery models (e.g., pausing fundraising, reallocating focus) is essential to adapt to external constraints.
successful_delivery_practices: Targeted outreach to FCDO thematic teams successfully identified new opportunities (e.g., clean cooking).
Partnership with Oxford GOLab generated valuable evidence on outcome-based finance, supporting wider FCDO uptake.
Seed funding through the Outcomes Accelerator demonstrated demand for small-scale, innovative projects.
management_adaptations_made: Hired a full-time PRO to address team capacity gaps.
Shifted focus from launching new funds to managing existing ones and scoping future opportunities.
Enhanced governance and risk management plans for GEOP/SLEIC in response to first-year challenges.
innovations_attempted: Outcomes Accelerator seed funding rounds tested demand for small-scale outcome-based projects.
Peer learning through the Outcome Finance Alliance conference (delivered by Levoca).
Exploration of clean cooking as a new SDG area for outcome-based financing.
previous_recommendations_progress: Logframe updates and VfM data collection remain works in progress, with plans to finalize in Q2–Q4 2024/25.
Equity improvements and learning agendas for GEOP/SLEIC are slated for Q1–Q3 2024/25.
forward_recommendations: Update logframe outputs/indicators to better track progress (Q2 2024/25).
Strengthen VfM data collection and cost-effectiveness analysis across all components (Q4 2024/25).
Improve equity in programme design with support from PSMCD (Q1 2024/25).
Develop learning agendas for GEOP/SLEIC to disseminate lessons (Q3 2024/25).
Enhance governance and risk management for GEOP (Q1 2024/25).
Align POF strategy with the 2023 FCDO International Development White Paper (Q1 2024/25).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was reactive in 2023/24, addressing issues as they arose (e.g., procurement delays, election disruptions). Proactive measures (e.g., governance reviews, enhanced oversight) are planned for 2024/25 to improve effectiveness.

policy_influence_achieved: POF’s work has contributed to broader FCDO policy discussions on outcome-based financing, with an internal review generating recommendations for strengthening capability across FCDO.
Evidence from GEOP/SLEIC is being used to inform host government commissioning practices (e.g., Sierra Leone, Ghana).
capacity_building_results: Host governments (Ghana, Sierra Leone) gained experience in commissioning outcome-based projects, with 3 agencies and 1 donor (KOICA) participating in co-funding.
Providers (e.g., EOF, GPRBA) developed capacity in managing outcome funds, though first-year challenges highlighted ongoing needs.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Seed funding through the Outcomes Accelerator attracted diverse philanthropic donors (e.g., Bank of America, Jacobs Foundation), broadening the funding base for outcome-based projects.
Negative: Budget constraints limited the programme’s ability to launch new funds, potentially slowing the scaling of outcome-based financing.
scalability_evidence: SLEIC and GEOP demonstrate scalability within education, but replication in other sectors (e.g., clean cooking) is still being tested.
The Outcomes Accelerator’s demand suggests potential for scaling small-scale outcome-based projects, though funding remains a constraint.

continuation_rationale: All programme components have completed at least one year of implementation with robust management structures now in place.
Alignment with FCDO’s 2023 International Development White Paper and broader outcome-based financing priorities.
Potential to address identified challenges (e.g., governance, VfM data) in 2024/25 with planned adaptations.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (dependent on resolving management issues in outcome funds and securing co-funding for new opportunities).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (programme is seen as a valuable test case for outcome-based financing, despite challenges).
planned_adaptations_future: Strengthen governance and risk management for existing outcome funds (GEOP, SLEIC).
Explore new sector opportunities (e.g., clean cooking) with FCDO thematic teams.
Improve VfM data collection and equity considerations across all components.
Align programme strategy with the 2023 FCDO White Paper and broader policy recommendations on outcome-based financing.

output_1.title: Improved relationships between customers (taxpayers) and government

output_2.title: A robust and high-functioning Tax and Customs system

output_4.title: The tax and customs systems are equitable, transparent and accountable

output_5.title: Tax Transformation Office (TTO) Delivery Mechanism enables Government of Ethiopia (GoE) to make progress on Tax and Customs reform priorities

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted from transformation-focused to stabilization-focused due to external shocks (COVID, conflict, macroeconomic instability) and budget cuts. Original competitive procurement of ITAS abandoned in favor of domestic in-house development.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Government of Ethiopia (GoE) capacity deteriorated significantly due to high staff turnover, real wage cuts, and shifting priorities. Tax Transformation Office (TTO) leadership departure after 5 years disrupted continuity. Partners (e.g., World Bank) acknowledged TSTP's critical role in stabilizing SIGTAS but noted reduced ambition due to context.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Embedded TTO within Ministry of Revenues (MoR) remained the primary delivery vehicle, but its effectiveness was hampered by leadership changes and capacity constraints. FCDO and suppliers engaged in frequent discussions to adapt to budget reductions and reprioritize activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with other donors (e.g., World Bank, IMF) improved in FY23/24, with TSTP positioning itself to complement future World Bank support. Donor coordination was identified as a priority for scaling impact.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Original plan to competitively procure ITAS was abandoned by GoE in favor of domestic in-house development, eliminating the need for UK procurement support. SIGTAS stabilization became the primary IT focus.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight increased due to the critical need to stabilize SIGTAS and adapt to shocks. Independent evaluators played a key role in assessing progress and recommending adjustments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility by refocusing on stabilization (e.g., SIGTAS maintenance, data cleaning) rather than transformation. Budget reallocations were made to prioritize critical IT support and advisory roles.
adaptive_management_examples: Reprioritized IT support to maintain SIGTAS functionality amid GoE capacity decline.
Shifted from ITAS procurement support to technical preparation (e.g., RFI/RFP drafting) before GoE's in-house decision.
Reduced scope to focus on Large Taxpayers Office (LTO), which collects 80% of revenue, due to budget constraints.
Explored e-based training to address high staff turnover and capacity gaps cost-effectively.

main_implementation_challenges: Extraordinary series of shocks: COVID-19, domestic conflict, macroeconomic instability (high inflation, misaligned exchange rate, import price shocks).
FCDO budget cuts and unpredictable in-year budgets, reducing financial predictability.
GoE's deteriorating capacity due to high staff turnover (e.g., TTO leadership departure) and falling real wages, exacerbating skills gaps.
Abandonment of competitive ITAS procurement in favor of domestic development, introducing timeline uncertainties.
Declining tax revenue collection (in real terms and as % of GDP) due to economic distress, reducing reform momentum.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted economic activity and tax collection, distorting investment incentives.
Domestic conflict in Ethiopia's largest regions further strained the operating environment.
Macroeconomic challenges (inflation, exchange rate misalignment) reduced GoE's fiscal space and prioritized crisis response over reforms.
Failed IMF macroeconomic stabilization program (2019) left Ethiopia without expected external support.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated reliance on TSTP to stabilize SIGTAS due to MoR IT department collapse (no backup/recovery plan, vacancies, skill erosion).
GoE's decision to develop ITAS in-house without competitive procurement, despite TSTP's preparatory work.
Shift in GoE priorities toward crisis management, stalling reform progress and reducing engagement with TSTP outputs.
partner_relationship_issues: High turnover in GoE counterparts (e.g., TTO leadership) disrupted long-term relationships and institutional memory.
Misalignment between TSTP's transformation goals and GoE's crisis-driven priorities, leading to reprioritization tensions.
Reduced absorption capacity in MoR for technical assistance due to staffing and wage constraints.
capacity_constraints_emerged: MoR IT department's capacity collapsed due to real wage cuts, vacancies, and skill erosion, increasing dependence on TSTP for SIGTAS stabilization.
Limited GoE ability to retain qualified personnel for tax administration, undermining sustainability of reforms.
Reduced bandwidth for policy engagement and reform implementation due to crisis management demands.
risk_materialization: Operational risk: SIGTAS near-collapse (as warned by 2018 WB diagnostic) materialized, requiring TSTP intervention to prevent system failure.
Political risk: Domestic conflict and economic shocks diverted GoE attention from tax reforms, stalling progress.
Financial risk: FCDO budget cuts and unpredictable funding disrupted planning and forced scope reductions.
Partner risk: GoE's in-house ITAS decision disrupted procurement plans and introduced implementation uncertainties.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Programme spent ~£3.9m annually in FY19/20 and FY20/21, but budget cuts and unpredictable in-year funding followed. Total spent to date: £13.9m (of £20.27m). Expenditure was reprioritized toward stabilization activities (e.g., SIGTAS support) due to reduced ambition.
value_for_money_assessment: Independent reviewers and partners (World Bank, IMF, MoR) attributed significant value to TSTP's role in preventing SIGTAS collapse, which would have severely disrupted Ethiopia's revenue system.
VFM achieved through stabilization (e.g., IT support, data cleaning) rather than transformation, given the context. Outputs met expectations despite challenges, justifying the 'A' score.
Cost efficiency was maintained by focusing on high-impact areas (e.g., LTO support, e-training) and reducing lower-priority activities (e.g., MTO/STO coverage).
However, original VFM projections (based on ~£4m/year spend and IMF stabilization) were not met due to external shocks.
financial_management_quality: Financial management adapted well to unpredictable budgets and reprioritization needs, though expenditure divisibility constraints limited flexibility.
Independent evaluators noted robust oversight of funds, particularly for critical IT support and advisory services.
Budget reductions were managed through close FCDO-supplier coordination, though some technical assistance (TA) was scaled back.
cost_efficiency_achieved: E-based training pilots introduced to address capacity gaps cost-effectively amid high staff turnover.
Focus on LTO (80% of revenue) improved resource allocation efficiency.
SIGTAS stabilization leveraged existing TSTP IT resources, avoiding higher costs of system failure.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Misaligned exchange rate and import price shocks (part of broader macroeconomic challenges) contributed to declining tax revenue and increased cost pressures, though direct impacts on TSTP budget were not specified.

key_delivery_lessons: In unstable contexts, stabilization (e.g., preventing system collapse) can deliver critical value even if transformation goals are off-track.
Flexibility in delivery models (e.g., shifting from ITAS procurement to SIGTAS stabilization) is essential to adapt to partner decisions and shocks.
Embedded advisory roles (e.g., TTO) are vulnerable to host government capacity fluctuations and require contingency planning.
Donor coordination (e.g., with World Bank) can amplify impact and reduce duplication, especially when new actors enter the space.
successful_delivery_practices: SIGTAS stabilization through IT support and data cleaning was universally recognized as a lifeline for Ethiopia's revenue system.
Focused technical assistance on high-revenue areas (e.g., LTO) maximized limited resources.
Adaptive management (e.g., reprioritizing workplans, revising logframes) helped maintain relevance amid shifting contexts.
Independent evaluations provided credible evidence for decision-making and external stakeholder engagement.
management_adaptations_made: Refocused programme goals from transformation to stabilization in response to shocks and budget cuts.
Reduced scope to prioritize critical IT support and LTO operations, deprioritizing MTO/STO activities.
Introduced e-based training to address capacity gaps sustainably amid high turnover.
Enhanced coordination with World Bank and other donors to align with emerging support priorities.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of e-based training for tax administration capacity building, aiming for cost-effective and scalable solutions.
Data cleaning and matching initiatives to improve SIGTAS functionality and reduce tax evasion/leakages.
Exploration of a strategic adviser role to the Minister to improve high-level engagement and reform prioritization.
previous_recommendations_progress: Logframe and Theory of Change revisions planned for Q1 2024/25 to better reflect stabilized (vs. transformational) ambitions.
Increased focus on SIGTAS stabilization and data quality, as recommended in prior reviews.
Reduced TA spread to concentrate resources on highest-impact areas (e.g., LTO).
forward_recommendations: Continue SIGTAS stabilization and data quality improvements to prevent system collapse and reduce leakages.
Appoint a strategic adviser to the Minister to enhance political engagement and reform ownership.
Deeply engage with GoE on the Medium Term Revenue Strategy to align TSTP support with national priorities.
Focus TA on LTO administrative functioning, audit processes, and transparency guidance to improve revenue collection.
Scale up e-based training to address capacity gaps sustainably and cost-effectively.
Establish a Donor Coordination Unit within MoR to improve alignment and reduce duplication.
Revise logframe and ToC to reflect stabilization (not transformation) goals and realistic impact pathways.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in identifying and mitigating operational risks (e.g., SIGTAS collapse) through adaptive management.
Less effective in anticipating political risks (e.g., GoE's in-house ITAS decision) and macroeconomic shocks (e.g., conflict, inflation).
Independent evaluations highlighted the need for contingency planning for host government capacity fluctuations.
Risk of withdrawal of TSTP support was flagged as potentially catastrophic for SIGTAS, justifying programme extension.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Indirect beneficiaries include Ethiopian taxpayers and the broader economy through stabilized tax systems. Direct support focused on MoR/GoE institutions.
E-filing usage varied by tax office: LTO (79-80%), MTO (81-82%), STO (62-75%), exceeding some targets but falling short for LTO.
E-payment adoption: LTO (80%), MTO (82%), STO (62%), with discrepancies between TTO and independent evaluator data.
policy_influence_achieved: TSTP-supported IT stabilization and data improvements influenced MoR's operational resilience, though policy reforms stalled due to crisis priorities.
Technical preparations (e.g., ITAS RFI/RFP) informed GoE's in-house system development, though timeline and quality remain uncertain.
Research on tax expenditures and compliance (e.g., risk-based approaches) was produced but absorption by GoE was limited by capacity constraints.
capacity_building_results: SIGTAS stabilization prevented system collapse, but MoR's IT capacity remains critically dependent on TSTP support.
E-based training pilots addressed immediate skills gaps, but high turnover undermines long-term retention.
Advisory support improved specific processes (e.g., audit functions, guidance notes) but broader institutional capacity gains were limited by context.
unintended_consequences: Positive: TSTP's stabilization role averted a potential revenue system collapse, which would have had severe economic consequences.
Negative: Reduced ambition due to stabilization focus may have delayed longer-term transformational reforms.
Dependence on TSTP for IT support risks creating a sustainability gap if/when programme exits.
scalability_evidence: SIGTAS stabilization approaches (e.g., data cleaning, IT support) are replicable but require sustained funding and capacity.
E-based training models show potential for scalability across MoR if institutionalized.
Coordination mechanisms (e.g., proposed Donor Coordination Unit) could scale impact if adopted by GoE and other partners.

continuation_rationale: TSTP's stabilization role is critical to preventing SIGTAS collapse, which would disrupt Ethiopia's revenue system and economic stability.
Independent evaluators and GoE partners (e.g., MoR) emphasized the programme's value in maintaining basic tax administration functions amid crises.
Withdrawal of support could jeopardize tax systems and country stability, given MoR's limited capacity to absorb functions independently.
Alignment with World Bank's emerging revenue support provides an opportunity for complementary donor coordination.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model (embedded TTO, IT support) is not sustainable long-term due to GoE capacity constraints and dependence on TSTP.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Major Partnerships component folded into Strategic Opportunities Fund for 2021/22 to reflect FCDO priority shifts and budget reductions. Short-term pause in CoST funding to focus on long-term sustainability (e.g., World Bank Trust Fund).
adaptive_management_examples: Introduced gender-disaggregated data indicators (Output 2.2) and developed gender inclusion guidance after identifying gaps in CoST Uganda’s procurement data.
Shifted from direct funding to policy support for CoST in 2021/22 to catalyze World Bank Trust Fund co-financing.
Adopted open-source tools (e.g., Honduras’ OC4IDS technology) for replicability by other FCDO partners.
Added interview stage to CoST member application process to preemptively address risks.

main_implementation_challenges: Aligning procurement timing with uncertain Spending Review cycles, risking delays to 2022/23 outputs.
Balancing ambitious programme scope (e.g., global CoST rollout) with reduced ODA budget and evolving FCDO priorities (climate, COVID-19 recovery).
Ensuring financial sustainability of partners (e.g., CoST) amid paused FCDO funding in 2021/22.
external_factors_impact: ODA budget reductions forced reprioritization (e.g., folding Major Partnerships into Strategic Opportunities Fund).
COVID-19 required adaptive transparency tools (e.g., CoST’s crisis-specific guidance on infrastructure accountability).
Political shifts (e.g., FCDO’s focus on trade/climate) necessitated realignment of programme components with HMG priorities.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for gender-inclusive approaches after CoST Uganda’s workshops revealed lack of disaggregated procurement data.
Sensitivity of infrastructure corruption issues in pilot countries (e.g., Honduras, Ukraine) delayed publication of learning papers.
Currency/exchange risks not explicitly mentioned, but global economic uncertainty implied in budget constraints.
partner_relationship_issues: CoST’s long-term funding uncertainty created tension with partners (e.g., World Bank Trust Fund dependency).
Diverse stakeholder objectives (e.g., Bogotá Mayor’s Office vs. UK Embassy) required enhanced application vetting.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited FCDO resources for engaging multiple partners led to consolidation under Strategic Opportunities Fund.
Need for specialized commercial advisers to manage complex procurement (unlike prior FCDO technical assistance programmes).
risk_materialization: Financial sustainability risks for CoST materialized, prompting shift to policy support and co-funding strategies.
Delays in publishing sensitive learning materials (e.g., PPP papers) due to political risks in partner countries.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for 2020/21. Costs minimized via outsourced International Secretariat (Engineers Against Poverty) and regional managers (lower fee rates). Short-term pause in CoST funding for 2021/22 to reallocate resources to Strategic Opportunities Fund.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VfM demonstrated through: (1) Economies of scale via partnerships (e.g., shared OCP helpdesk; World Bank PPP framework collaboration); (2) Decentralized operations reducing overheads; (3) Open-source tools (e.g., Honduras’ OC4IDS) enabling replication without additional costs. Input costs tracked (consultancy rates, travel, assurance unit costs).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. CoST monitored partner efficiency (e.g., Bogotá’s self-funding commitment) and tracked unit costs. World Bank Trust Fund progress indicates robust co-financing potential.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded targets: (1) CoST trained 6,789 government stakeholders (vs. 6,000 target) at lower per-unit cost via regional hubs; (2) Leveraged existing platforms (e.g., OCP’s helpdesk) to avoid duplication.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. World Bank Procurement for Development Umbrella Trust Fund secured as a co-funding route, but full materialization pending. Bogotá Mayor’s Office committed local funding for CoST membership.

key_delivery_lessons: Complex programmes require early commercial adviser engagement to mitigate procurement risks (e.g., Spending Review alignment).
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., Strategic Opportunities Fund) better accommodate shifting FCDO priorities than rigid partnerships.
Decentralized regional management (e.g., Singapore/Panama hubs) improves cost efficiency and local ownership.
successful_delivery_practices: Stakeholder co-design of procurement ToRs (e.g., IPA feedback loops) improved relevance and buy-in.
Strategic partnerships (e.g., OCP, World Bank) amplified impact through shared standards and co-funding.
Gender-inclusive indicators (Output 2.2) and guidance enhanced equity outcomes (e.g., CoST Uganda’s disability advocacy).
Open-source tools (e.g., OC4IDS) ensured scalability across FCDO programmes.
management_adaptations_made: Paused CoST funding in 2021/22 to prioritize long-term sustainability via World Bank Trust Fund.
Folded Major Partnerships into Strategic Opportunities Fund for greater alignment with FCDO’s climate/trade priorities.
Introduced application interviews for new CoST members to assess risk/alignment upfront.
innovations_attempted: OC4IDS real-time disclosure pilots in Honduras/Ukraine (digitizing infrastructure transparency).
Gender-disaggregated procurement data advocacy (CoST Uganda).
Joint World Bank PPP disclosure framework development.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: N/A (first Annual Review).
forward_recommendations: Continue aligning CRCI with FCDO Posts’ diplomatic priorities (e.g., climate, COVID-19 recovery) via cross-departmental engagement (DIT, BEIS, HMT).
Finalize World Bank Trust Fund to secure CoST’s financial sustainability post-FCDO funding pause.
Expand open-source tool adoption (e.g., OC4IDS) across FCDO infrastructure programmes.
Strengthen gender inclusion metrics in all outputs, building on CoST Uganda’s model.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate. Proactively addressed financial sustainability risks (e.g., Trust Fund, Bogotá co-funding) but faced challenges with external factors (ODA cuts, Spending Review delays). Sensitivity of corruption data in partner countries required adaptive disclosure strategies.

policy_influence_achieved: CoST tools integrated into Sustainable Infrastructure Foundation’s SOURCE platform (endorsed by World Bank, EBRD, EIB).
CoST Malawi case study included in UNEP’s Good Practice Principles for Sustainable Infrastructure.
World Bank adopted CoST’s PPP disclosure framework for global implementation.
Bogotá Mayor’s Office institutionalized CoST membership with local funding.
capacity_building_results: 5,773 civil society stakeholders trained in infrastructure transparency (exceeding target by 44%).
CoST Uganda developed gender-inclusion paper and advocated for disaggregated procurement data.
Regional managers in Singapore/Panama/Uganda built local capacity for CoST implementation.

unintended_consequences.description: CoST’s work in Afghanistan highlighted gender barriers (e.g., Foman Forough’s role as sole female MSG member), catalyzing broader FCDO focus on women’s inclusion in infrastructure.
Sensitivity of corruption findings in Honduras/Ukraine delayed publication of learning materials, limiting timely knowledge sharing.

scalability_evidence: ITI Manual adopted by 4 countries (Costa Rica, Ukraine, Afghanistan, Thailand) with potential for global rollout.
OC4IDS helpdesk model replicated across 5 countries (Honduras, Ukraine, Malawi, Afghanistan, Sekondi-Takoradi).
Open-source tools (e.g., Honduras’ OC4IDS technology) designed for adoption by any FCDO partner.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong 2020/21 performance (Overall Score: A) and alignment with FCDO priorities (climate-resilient infrastructure, trade). CoST’s policy influence (e.g., World Bank adoption) and financial sustainability progress (Trust Fund) justify continuation, albeit with adaptive delivery model (Strategic Opportunities Fund).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Current model (outsourced Secretariat, regional hubs) is cost-efficient but dependent on securing co-funding (e.g., World Bank Trust Fund) and navigating ODA budget constraints.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by Overall Score A and expansion of CoST’s global footprint).
planned_adaptations_future: Merge Major Partnerships into Strategic Opportunities Fund for greater flexibility.
Pause direct CoST funding in 2021/22 to focus on policy support and co-funding mobilization.
Deepened engagement with UK government agencies (IPA, Connected Places Catapult) to align with trade/climate priorities.
Scale open-source tools (OC4IDS) and gender-inclusive approaches across FCDO infrastructure programmes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Creating Hope in Conflict Humanitarian Grand Challenge (CHIC)

output_1.title: Innovative and relevant products or services selected for CHIC funding

output_3.title: Communication, engagement and outreach activities support CHIC outcomes

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Initial focus on launching the programme, selecting innovations for funding, and maximizing communication opportunities. Adaptations planned for Year 2 include: improving efficiency of innovation selection, clarifying technical expertise timelines, and enhancing geographical outreach (e.g., francophone countries).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Grand Challenges Canada (GCC) demonstrated ability to attract a diverse portfolio of relevant innovations, particularly at seed stage. Independent Scientific Advisory Board feedback was "overwhelmingly positive." One funding offer was withdrawn due to non-compliance during grant negotiations, a decision endorsed by all three donors.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: GCC managed the programme with input from DFID, USAID, and the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs. A RED Humanitarian Advisor was added to the CHIC Steering Committee (effective May 2019) to align innovations with DFID priorities. Decision-making processes were clarified via a matrix (planned by September 2019).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination among DFID, USAID, and the Netherlands was effective, as evidenced by joint announcements (e.g., UNGA 2018) and aligned funding commitments. GCC’s role as the implementing platform facilitated multi-donor collaboration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: First-round applications (615 total) surpassed expectations despite limited proactive communication. Seed grants (22 signed) and Transition-to-Scale (TTS) grants (3 approved) were awarded through a rigorous, multi-stage review process involving external experts and donor advisors.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Intensive due diligence and agreement negotiations were conducted for all grants. DFID advisors were involved at all selection stages. Whistleblowing policies were strengthened (planned by September 2019).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted to include francophone outreach (e.g., Sahel, DRC) and merged under DFID’s broader "Strengthening and Scaling Innovation in Emergencies" programme (planned by December 2019).
adaptive_management_examples: Withdrew funding from one applicant for non-compliance during negotiations (endorsed by all donors).
Added a RED Humanitarian Advisor to the Steering Committee to better align with DFID priorities.
Planned improvements to application processes (e.g., self-selection dropdowns, outsourcing innovation screening) for Round 2.
Expanded outreach to francophone regions and reviewed engagement strategies to increase geographical diversity.

main_implementation_challenges: Inefficiencies in the first-round application process (e.g., time-consuming reviews, lack of self-selection tools).
Limited proactive communication prior to the first call, though applications still exceeded expectations.
Need to improve sequencing for Transition-to-Scale (TTS) selections to allow sufficient time for expert input.
Geographical imbalance in applications, with underrepresentation from francophone priority regions (e.g., Sahel, DRC).
external_factors_impact: Additional funding commitments from the Netherlands (US$7.5M), USAID (US$4.9M), and DFID (£3.8M) at UNGA 2018 expanded the programme’s scope and budget.
Media coverage (e.g., Telegraph, Daily Mail) generated public interest but required active management.
contextual_constraints_new: Need to manage innovations in both English (official donor language) and French (for outreach) created operational complexity.
High demand for seed grants (615 applications) required scalable review processes.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited time for technical experts to engage with TTS applicants before Investment Committee presentations.
Need for clearer decision-making roles among partners (addressed via a decision matrix planned for September 2019).

value_for_money_assessment.status: Too early to assess fully, but the VfM proposition in the business case remains valid.
changes_since_business_case: DFID’s contribution increased from £5.5M to £9.2M over 5 years (39% of total funding, down from 50% initially).
USAID extended its timeline to 5 years (from 3), and the Netherlands joined as a third donor (21% of funding).
Indirect costs for GCC remain at 10%, aligned with similar programmes.
efficiency_notes: First-round application process was "mostly efficient" but identified areas for improvement (e.g., self-selection tools, outsourcing screening).
Cost drivers: GCC operational costs (grant management, due diligence), innovator support, and seed/TTS grants.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: GCC’s financial management was deemed effective, with transparent processes for grant reviews, due diligence, and budget tracking. DFID’s increased oversight (e.g., Steering Committee additions) further strengthened governance.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Additional co-funding materialized from the Netherlands (US$7.5M) and USAID (US$4.9M), exceeding initial expectations.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Exchange rate used for reporting: £0.77 to US$1 (as of 14 May 2019). No significant adverse impacts noted.

key_delivery_lessons: Open, competitive processes can attract high volumes of applications (615 in Round 1) but require efficient screening tools.
Early engagement of technical experts is critical for TTS selections to ensure rigorous probing before Investment Committee reviews.
Clear decision-making matrices improve partner coordination and accountability.
successful_delivery_practices: Multi-stage review process (external panels + donor advisors) ensured high-quality seed grant selections.
High-profile launches (e.g., ODI event with DFID Secretary of State) and media engagement (Telegraph, Daily Mail) boosted visibility.
Partnership with GCC leveraged existing innovation challenge expertise (e.g., Saving Lives at Birth).
management_adaptations_made: Added RED Humanitarian Advisor to Steering Committee to align with DFID priorities.
Planned improvements to application processes (e.g., dropdown menus, outsourcing screening) for Round 2.
Developed a decision-making matrix to clarify roles for partners (by September 2019).
Strengthened whistleblowing policies (by September 2019).
innovations_attempted: Soliciting applications in French to increase francophone participation (review by December 2019).
Incorporating unit cost tracking (cost per beneficiary/unit) into application and monitoring tools (by April 2020).
Expanding innovator support beyond TTS grantees to include seed innovators (recommended).
forward_recommendations: Improve efficiency of innovation selection by addressing Round 1 inefficiencies (by May 2019).
Clarify technical expertise timelines via a Gantt Chart (by May 2019).
Enhance TTS selection sequencing to allow deeper expert engagement (by January 2020).
Increase applications from francophone regions (Sahel, DRC) by soliciting French-language submissions (review by December 2019).
Merge CHIC under DFID’s broader "Strengthening and Scaling Innovation" programme (by December 2019).
Track innovation unit costs routinely to assess cost-effectiveness (by April 2020).
Add logframe indicators to measure innovator satisfaction with support (recommended).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was proactive, with donors endorsing the withdrawal of one non-compliant applicant. Planned improvements (e.g., whistleblowing policies, decision matrices) aim to further mitigate operational and reputational risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.status: Too early to report; seed grants (22) and TTS grants (3) were awarded in Year 1, but implementation is ongoing.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.targets: DFID committed to supporting ~25 seed grants and 7 TTS projects over the programme lifetime.

policy_influence_achieved: Programme launch and UNGA 2018 announcements amplified focus on conflict-driven humanitarian innovation.
Partnership with GCC and multi-donor funding model positioned CHIC as a reference point for humanitarian innovation policy.
capacity_building_results: Seed innovators received funding and technical support, though broader capacity-building outcomes are not yet measurable.
Planned expansion of innovator support (beyond TTS grantees) aims to accelerate scaling.
scalability_evidence: High application volume (615) suggests strong demand for innovative solutions in conflict settings.
First-round innovations focused on technology-driven approaches, which may have higher scalability potential (e.g., energy access, life-saving information).
TTS grants are designed to scale proven seed innovations.

continuation_rationale: Programme is "on track" against expectations, with strong first-year performance (Overall Score: A).
Successful attraction of diverse, relevant innovations and additional co-funding (Netherlands, USAID).
Alignment with DFID’s humanitarian priorities and broader innovation agenda (e.g., merger with "Strengthening and Scaling Innovation" programme).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Merge CHIC under DFID’s broader innovation programme (by December 2019).
Improve application processes and geographical outreach (francophone regions).
Enhance TTS selection processes and innovator support mechanisms.
Strengthen monitoring of innovation costs and effectiveness (e.g., cost per beneficiary).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Data and Research in Education (DARE) Programme

output_1.title: National education data systems are strengthened through improved data management processes and enhanced coordination. The regular and robust monitoring and evaluation of increased administrative and learning data informs decision making.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme sought an 18-month extension (to 31/12/2025) due to delays in Research Consortium procurement. Original delivery model relied on timely establishment of a research consortium, which has faced protracted delays due to "constraints beyond the programme team’s control," including non-compliant bids, HQ human resource constraints, and ODA-related organizational pauses.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank’s technical assistance (TA) delivery through Pakistan@100 Trust Fund has progressed with six contracted organizations supporting discrete outputs. However, the Pakistan Institute for Education (PIE) has demonstrated limited absorption capacity, requiring adjusted pacing of TA. ASER implementation by Idara e Taleem o Agahi (ITA) appears on track, though specific performance details are not provided.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Management has adapted to delays by extending timelines and reallocating oversight to monitor TA funds closely. The programme team is working with the World Bank to expedite PIE’s organogram approvals and hiring, leveraging diplomatic relations and the WB’s ASPIRE programme to create an enabling environment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO, World Bank, and PIE has been challenged by capacity constraints and procurement delays. Technical Working Groups (TWGs) are implied but not detailed. The programme highlights the need for stronger political buy-in to improve cross-stakeholder alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of the Research Consortium has been severely delayed (since August 2021), attributed to non-compliant bids, HQ resource constraints, and ODA spending pauses. This has cascading impacts on the programme’s research agenda and timeline.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has intensified to address delays, with closer monitoring of TA funds and a focus on ensuring PIE’s institutional capacity is built sustainably. The programme team is actively assessing the validity of the Theory of Change (ToC) due to procurement setbacks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme has utilized flexibility by securing an 18-month extension and considering restructuring options (e.g., removing the Research Consortium component) if delays persist. Adaptive measures include reallocating funds and revising the logframe.
adaptive_management_examples: Securing an 18-month extension to accommodate Research Consortium delays.
Adjusting TA pacing to match PIE’s absorption capacity.
Exploring diplomatic levers (e.g., BHC relations) to accelerate PIE hiring.
Planning for potential restructuring of the programme if Research Consortium procurement remains stalled by early 2023.

main_implementation_challenges: Protracted delays in Research Consortium procurement (since August 2021), threatening the programme’s research objectives.
Limited human resource and institutional capacity at the Pakistan Institute for Education (PIE), slowing TA absorption.
Lack of sufficient data access protocols and data protection laws in Pakistan, hindering data-sharing and use.
Mixed messaging from FCDO leadership in FY2022/23, affecting partner planning and execution.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated existing data gaps and highlighted the need for resilient education systems, which DARE aims to address.
Political and institutional demand for better data/evidence exists but is constrained by bureaucratic inertia and low accountability culture in Pakistan’s education sector.
ODA spending pauses and organizational changes within FCDO/WB have disrupted procurement and implementation timelines.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated delays in regulatory frameworks for data governance (e.g., data protection laws) emerged as a critical gap.
Low political appetite for bureaucratic reforms (e.g., organogram approvals) has slowed institutional strengthening efforts.
Currency/exchange rate impacts are not explicitly mentioned, but economic instability in Pakistan may indirectly affect programme delivery.
partner_relationship_issues: World Bank’s use of short-term consultants risks creating parallel, unsustainable systems if PIE’s capacity isn’t simultaneously strengthened.
Delays in Research Consortium procurement have strained relationships with potential research partners and universities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: PIE’s limited absorption capacity has required TA pacing adjustments and delayed outputs (e.g., National Assessment Test reports).
MoFEPT and provincial governments face chronic understaffing and skill gaps in data management and research utilization.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (Research Consortium) materialized as a high-risk issue, directly impacting the programme’s ability to generate research evidence.
Institutional capacity risks at PIE have manifested, requiring adaptive management to avoid parallel systems.
Data governance risks (lack of protocols/laws) were identified as a barrier to sustainable data use.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution has been affected by procurement delays, particularly for the Research Consortium. The programme secured approval to use capital expenditure funds (CDEL) to mitigate funding gaps, but overall spend is likely behind schedule due to implementation lags.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM is at risk due to delays in Research Consortium delivery, which may reduce the programme’s ability to generate timely, high-quality research. However, the extension to 2025 provides an opportunity to recover value if procurement issues are resolved. TA components (e.g., PIE capacity building) show progress but are constrained by absorption limits.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by implementers (WB/ITA) appears robust, but mixed messaging from FCDO in FY2022/23 has created planning uncertainties. TA funds are being closely monitored to ensure alignment with PIE’s capacity development.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency is compromised by procurement delays and the need for extensions. The programme’s adaptive use of CDEL funds aims to improve efficiency, but the full impact remains unclear pending Research Consortium progress.

key_delivery_lessons: TA pacing must align with partner absorption capacity (e.g., PIE’s limited HR) to avoid inefficiencies or parallel systems.
Procurement timelines for complex components (e.g., Research Consortium) require realistic buffer periods to account for external delays.
Political and diplomatic levers (e.g., BHC relations, WB’s ASPIRE programme) are critical to overcoming bureaucratic inertia in partner institutions.
Data governance frameworks (e.g., access protocols, protection laws) must be prioritized early to enable sustainable data use.
successful_delivery_practices: Engaging multiple consultancy firms to deliver discrete TA outputs has maintained momentum in data systems strengthening.
Leveraging existing platforms (e.g., ASER, Pakistan@100 Trust Fund) has facilitated efficient delivery of citizen-led data and federal TA.
Adaptive use of extensions (e.g., 18-month delay) and CDEL funds has provided flexibility to address unforeseen challenges.
management_adaptations_made: Slowed TA delivery to match PIE’s capacity, with closer fund monitoring.
Increased coordination with WB to expedite PIE hiring via organogram approvals.
Planned logframe revisions to incorporate long-term objectives (e.g., data demand-building).
Consideration of programme restructuring (e.g., removing Research Consortium) if delays persist.
innovations_attempted: Exploring partnerships with universities/think tanks to establish Master’s-level courses in education assessment (e.g., Psychometrics).
Targeted research dissemination to non-traditional stakeholders (e.g., journalists, parliamentarians) to build data literacy.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on PIE capacity building, but hiring delays persist.
Data governance reforms remain pending despite identified needs (e.g., access protocols).
Research Consortium procurement delays have stalled previous recommendations on evidence generation.
forward_recommendations: Conduct a ToC validity assessment by January 2023 to determine if programme objectives remain achievable.
Accelerate PIE hiring via diplomatic pressure and WB’s ASPIRE programme.
Develop a sustainability plan for PIE’s research wing, including transitioning successful interventions to government budgets.
Broaden stakeholder engagement to build demand for data/evidence beyond traditional government actors.
Reassess the Research Consortium’s feasibility by early 2023; restructure or close the component if delays continue.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management has been reactive rather than proactive. While procurement delays were anticipated as a risk, mitigation efforts (e.g., extensions, CDEL funds) were implemented late. The programme now faces a critical juncture to either resolve Research Consortium delays or restructure.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: The programme contributes to UK KPIs targeting 40 million more girls in school and 20 million more girls reading by 2026. Specific beneficiary numbers are not reported, but outputs (e.g., ASER data, PIE capacity building) aim to improve learning outcomes for marginalized groups (girls, minorities, children with disabilities).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Emerging evidence of influence: PIE’s publication of Pakistan Education Statistics (PES) 2018/19 and policy-focused research briefs (with WB) indicate gradual uptake. However, systemic use of data/evidence remains limited by institutional capacity and political will.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Partial progress in PIE’s capacity (e.g., PES publication, NAT tools development), but absorption constraints and hiring delays hinder long-term institutionalization. ASER’s citizen-led data model shows stronger sustainability.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Increased visibility of education data gaps has spurred demand for reforms (e.g., data protection laws).
Negative: Delays in Research Consortium risk eroding trust in FCDO/WB’s ability to deliver, potentially reducing partner engagement.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Limited scalability evidence to date. The Research Consortium, if successfully established, could generate scalable teaching/learning innovations, but current delays limit this potential. ASER’s model is inherently scalable but depends on sustained funding.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme’s core objectives remain valid and aligned with UK/FCDO priorities (e.g., girls’ education, system strengthening). However, continuation is contingent on resolving Research Consortium delays by early 2023 and demonstrating progress in PIE capacity building. Closure is not recommended at this stage, but restructuring (e.g., removing the Research Consortium) may be necessary if procurement issues persist.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Low
planned_adaptations_future: Reassess the Research Consortium’s viability by January 2023; explore alternative mechanisms if delays continue.
Strengthen PIE’s institutional capacity via accelerated hiring and organogram approvals, leveraging WB’s ASPIRE programme.
Revise the logframe to incorporate long-term sustainability indicators (e.g., data demand-building, transition plans).
Develop an exit strategy for TA components to ensure government ownership by 2025.
Expand stakeholder engagement to include non-government actors (e.g., media, parliamentarians) to build broader demand for evidence.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Regional and International Tax Initiatives (RITI) Programme

output_1.title: Improved coordination among international organisations in their support of improved DRM by developing countries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to online training delivery due to COVID-19, enabling broader geographical reach (e.g., OECD trained 16,000 officials). Technical assistance continued with tangible impacts (e.g., tax crime units in Colombia, financial crime tracking in Kenya).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All RITI partners exceeded expectations in capacity-building (7/9 targets met). ATAF surpassed milestones but faced challenges in setting realistic targets due to COVID-19 uncertainty. Gender imbalance in training participants improved (female participation rose from 32% in 2020 to 41% in 2021).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: PCT (Platform for Collaboration on Tax) strengthened coordination through fortnightly meetings, annual reports (e.g., Nigeria/Pakistan case studies), and a functional website (20,000+ unique visits). However, in-country coordination and quality of impact remain areas for improvement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to COVID-19 by expanding online training and revising targets mid-year. Partners like ATAF introduced flexible target ranges to account for pandemic-related uncertainties.
adaptive_management_examples: PCT Development Partners agreed to: i) produce more case studies, ii) facilitate peer-to-peer exchanges, iii) develop a toolkit for technical assistance coordination.
ATAF introduced a Women in Tax network, mentoring programs, and language-specific outreach (e.g., Lusophone/Francophone attendance rose from 25% to 49%).
GTP (Global Tax Programme) implemented a mid-term evaluation to refine project delivery.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 disrupted in-person training and technical assistance, requiring rapid shifts to virtual delivery.
Uncertainty in target-setting due to pandemic-related restrictions (e.g., ATAF milestones were initially unrealistic).
Gender imbalance in training participation (though improved from 32% to 41% female attendance).
Low engagement from some ATAF member states (<10% attendance in 2019–2020, later addressed via language-specific programs).
external_factors_impact: UK ODA budget reduction to 0.5% GNI (2021) forced programming adjustments.
COVID-19 accelerated demand for digital training and data analysis support, revealing gaps in initial targets.
Political/economic instability in partner countries (e.g., Kenya, Colombia) influenced reform adoption timelines.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased demand for support on international tax standards (e.g., OECD digital tax agreement) required reprioritization.
Need for in-country coordination to implement complex reforms (e.g., BEPS Action 4, digital economy taxation).
capacity_constraints_emerged: ATAF’s financial sustainability and planning framework required strengthening.
Limited capacity in some member states to engage with new tax rules (e.g., Pillar 1/Pillar 2 of OECD Inclusive Framework).
risk_materialization: Pandemic-related delays in in-person activities (training, technical assistance).
Budget reductions due to UK ODA cuts impacted programming scale.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget adjustments were made due to UK ODA reductions (0.5% GNI in 2021). Despite this, partners delivered results efficiently, with no reported underspending.
value_for_money_assessment: High VfM from multilateral partners (e.g., OECD, World Bank) due to their technical expertise, despite high salary costs.
ATAF’s use of African experts and secondments reduced consultant costs.
PCT improved coordination, reducing duplication across partners (e.g., joint events, regional workshops).
GTP’s strategic framework enhanced World Bank’s internal collaboration, amplifying VfM beyond direct RITI funding.
financial_management_quality: Partners submitted timely financial reports (e.g., WB GTP narrative report Jan 2021, OECD May 2022).
Audited statements were up-to-date (e.g., WB period ending 30/06/2021, OECD 30/12/2020).
No major financial irregularities reported.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Online training reduced travel/logistics costs while expanding reach (e.g., OECD trained 16,000 officials).
Shared platforms (e.g., PCT website) minimized redundant expenditures.

key_delivery_lessons: Virtual delivery can achieve broader reach but requires quality measurement frameworks.
Flexible target-setting (e.g., ranges instead of fixed numbers) improves accountability under uncertainty.
Gender-inclusive strategies (e.g., mentoring, Women in Tax networks) enhance participation equity.
successful_delivery_practices: PCT’s fortnightly meetings and case studies (Nigeria/Pakistan) improved cross-partner coordination.
ATAF’s language-specific programs (Lusophone/Francophone) increased engagement from 25% to 49%.
GTP’s mid-term evaluation identified opportunities for green recovery projects in LAC.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from quantitative to qualitative impact assessment (e.g., PCT’s focus on in-country coordination quality).
Dynamic target adjustments to reflect real-time challenges (e.g., COVID-19, ODA cuts).
innovations_attempted: Digital training platforms to scale capacity-building.
PCT toolkit development for technical assistance coordination.
ATAF’s gender course (planned for 2023) and mentoring programs.
previous_recommendations_progress: ATAF reviewed its results framework to align with its 2021–2025 Strategic Plan, addressing overambitious milestones.
Gender balance improved (41% female participation in 2021 vs. 32% in 2020).
PCT expanded in-country coordination efforts (e.g., Nigeria/Pakistan case studies).
forward_recommendations: Strengthen PCT’s role in facilitating OECD’s two-pillar digital tax agreement implementation.
Develop systematic approaches to measure intervention quality (beyond quantitative targets).
Enhance country-level reporting to avoid duplication and assess impact.
ATAF should finalize its gender course and monitor progress toward 50% female training participation.
risk_management_effectiveness: Pandemic risks were mitigated through rapid shifts to virtual delivery.
Financial risks (ODA cuts) were managed via reprioritization without compromising core outputs.
Ongoing challenge: Predicting in-person activity timelines in post-COVID environments.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: OECD trained 16,000 officials via online platforms (exceeding pre-pandemic reach).
ATAF’s training attendance rose, with 49% participation from Lusophone/Francophone countries in 2021.
GTP-supported reforms in Malaysia (personal income tax) and Kenya (financial crime units, BEPS Action 4).
policy_influence_achieved: Kenya: New interest limitation rules (BEPS Action 4) and MAAC for AEOI signed.
Malaysia: Proposed abolition of tax exemption on foreign-sourced income (Jan 2022).
Colombia: Establishment of a new tax crime unit via TIWB Criminal Investigations pilots.
PCT’s Annual Report (2021) advanced coordination at country level (Nigeria/Pakistan case studies).
capacity_building_results: 16,000 officials trained by OECD, with expanded geographical coverage.
ATAF’s mentoring programs and Women in Tax network addressed gender gaps.
IGF supported resource-rich countries on BEPS in mining issues.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Online training unexpectedly increased access for officials in remote/low-capacity regions.
Negative: Reduced in-person engagement may have limited hands-on technical assistance quality in some contexts.
scalability_evidence: PCT’s coordination model is replicable for other multilateral tax initiatives.
ATAF’s language-specific and gender-inclusive approaches can be scaled across regions.
GTP’s green recovery projects in LAC demonstrate potential for environmental tax expansion.

continuation_rationale: Consistent high performance (A+ scores in 2021–2022) with tangible policy impacts (e.g., Kenya, Malaysia, Colombia).
Strong VfM and adaptive management in response to COVID-19/ODA cuts.
Critical role in supporting developing countries navigate complex international tax reforms (e.g., digital economy taxation).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Enhance PCT’s in-country coordination for OECD’s two-pillar digital tax agreement.
Strengthen ATAF’s financial planning and gender inclusion strategies.
Expand country-level reporting to better demonstrate impact and avoid duplication.
Prioritize green recovery and environmental tax projects (e.g., via GTP).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tackling Deadly Diseases in Africa Programme 2 (TDDAP2)

output_1.title: Improved participation of communities and civil society in surveillance mechanisms and national health security governance

output_2.title: Stronger core public health functions and capacity in focus countries

output_3.title: Strategic partnerships with key African health institutions to strengthen capacity on emergency preparedness and response

output_4.title: Expertise, financial, logistical, and technical support for rapid containment and response to emerging outbreaks

output_5.title: Robust information is generated and used by government, communities and partners for evidence-based decisions, programme adaptation and lesson learning

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adopted a comprehensive Health Systems Strengthening and One Health approach, integrating climate change, gender equality (GEDSI), and social inclusion considerations. The ARRO component demonstrated flexibility by pivoting resources to mpox and Ebola responses in DRC and Uganda, though mobilisation delays limited full contribution.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Palladium-led consortium (including Resolve to Save Lives) was contracted for the national component, demonstrating strong technical capacity in health security but faced delays in DRC due to security concerns. Africa CDC and WHO AFRO showed effective collaboration through the Joint Emergency Action Plan (JEAP), raising $360m for health emergencies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Regional component (54% spend) led implementation, with ARRO (32% spend) providing rapid response. National component (10% spend) and MEL (1.2% spend) were newly contracted during the review period. Governance aligned with Lusaka Agenda principles, though coordination with Global Health Initiatives (GHIs) requires streamlining.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Joint working with WHO AFRO and Africa CDC was effective, particularly through JEAP. However, complementarity between ARRO (emergency response) and national component (long-term capacity building) needs improvement to avoid silos. Integration of community engagement structures post-outbreak was identified as a gap.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive bidding process for the national component contract (awarded to Palladium in September 2024) was rigorous. Delays in DRC launch due to security issues highlight the need for contingency planning in procurement timelines.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Intensified monitoring recommended for regional partners (e.g., Institut Pasteur de Dakar) as they scale up. Current oversight was sufficient for inception phases but requires strengthening for expanded portfolios.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated agility by reallocating ARRO funds to mpox and Ebola responses. However, delays in national component mobilisation limited adaptive capacity during outbreaks. Rapid pivoting mechanisms need formalisation for future threats.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of ARRO funds to address mpox and Ebola outbreaks in DRC/Uganda.
Integration of climate change and GEDSI considerations into National Action Plans for Health Security (NAPHS).
Planned Theory of Change (ToC) review workshop to reprioritise activities amid ODA reductions.

main_implementation_challenges: Security-related delays in DRC affecting community engagement and launch activities.
Limited integration between emergency response (ARRO) and long-term capacity-building components.
Newly contracted components (national, MEL) had minimal time to demonstrate outputs beyond inception.
external_factors_impact: UK decision to reduce ODA to 0.3% of GNI by 2027, requiring significant portfolio adjustments.
Shifts in global health security funding landscape, with bilateral donors reducing support.
Emerging disease threats (e.g., mpox, Marburg Virus Disease) tested programme adaptability.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for rapid response to mpox alongside existing Ebola/Cholera outbreaks stretched ARRO resources.
Political and security instability in DRC disrupted community-based surveillance (CBS) rollout.
Currency/exchange rate fluctuations (not explicitly detailed) may impact regional partner budgets.
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in DRC due to security concerns strained relationships with local stakeholders.
Coordination gaps between regional (Africa CDC/WHO AFRO) and national partners in aligning JEAP priorities with country-level NAPHS.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in newly contracted MEL component to demonstrate immediate impact (only 1.2% spend in Q4).
National component partners required additional time to recruit country leads and finalise workplans.
Africa CDC’s expanding portfolio risks diluting surveillance quality without intensified monitoring.
risk_materialization: Security risks in DRC materialised, delaying output 1 activities.
Funding uncertainty due to ODA cuts materialised as a major risk, requiring reprioritisation.
Partner capacity risks (e.g., Institut Pasteur de Dakar expansion) were identified but not yet fully materialised.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Fully spent allocated budget during the review period. Spend breakdown: Regional (54%), ARRO (32%), National (10%), MEL (1.2%), Africa CDC indirect (3.5%).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Assessed as meeting expectations. Early achievements in emergency response (e.g., Marburg, Cholera) and workforce development (AVoHC training) demonstrate cost-efficiency. However, long-term VFM depends on sustaining regional partnerships and integrating MEL findings.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High quality for regional/ARRO components, with transparent reporting through DevTracker. National component financial systems are nascent; risks identified in rapid scale-up require mitigation.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: ARRO component achieved high efficiency in rapid response (A+ score for output 4). Regional partnerships (e.g., JEAP) leveraged $360m in additional funding, amplifying FCDO’s £95m investment.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial materialisation: JEAP mobilised $360m from African governments/institutions for the Pandemic Fund, but planned co-funding from other GHIs (e.g., Gavi, CEPI) requires further alignment.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., ARRO) are critical for responding to emerging threats but require faster mobilisation.
Community engagement (output 1) needs deeper integration into all components, not just the national component.
Regional partnerships (e.g., Africa CDC/WHO AFRO) are force multipliers but require proactive coordination to avoid duplication.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid response through ARRO effectively contained Marburg and Cholera outbreaks while embedding community structures.
JEAP’s collaborative model (Africa CDC/WHO AFRO) successfully attracted additional funding and strengthened regional ownership.
Palladium’s locally led consortium approach balanced global expertise with country-level adaptation.
management_adaptations_made: Reprioritised activities in response to ODA cuts, focusing on high-impact regional partnerships.
Added mpox response to ARRO’s scope, demonstrating adaptive management.
Planned ToC review workshop to align activities with reduced funding and evolving health security needs.
innovations_attempted: Integration of One Health and climate change considerations into NAPHS.
Pilot of African Volunteers Health Corps (AVoHC) training to build surge capacity for outbreaks.
Use of MEL component to drive real-time programme adaptations (though early stage).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Community engagement (from TDDAP1) was included in ARRO responses but requires deeper institutionalisation.
JEAP collaboration (recommended in AR1) advanced significantly, raising $360m.
GEDSI integration remains a work in progress, with thematic assistance planned for NAPHS reviews.
forward_recommendations: Intensify monitoring of Africa CDC and WHO AFRO to ensure quality during scale-up.
Streamline joint working with GHIs (Gavi, Global Fund, CEPI) to avoid fragmentation.
Formalise rapid pivoting mechanisms for future outbreaks, building on mpox/Ebola experience.
Prioritise sustainability of community engagement structures post-outbreak via national component workplans.
Accelerate MEL component’s role in adaptive management, linking lessons to real-time decisions.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Security risks in DRC were anticipated but mitigation (e.g., delayed launch) impacted outputs. Funding risks (ODA cuts) were identified late; proactive reprioritisation is now underway. Partner capacity risks (e.g., Institut Pasteur) require preemptive action.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Early achievements in training African Volunteer Health Corps (AVoHC) and supporting Marburg/Cholera responses reached targeted communities, but quantitative data on beneficiaries is not specified. National component (10% spend) is in inception phase.
policy_influence_achieved: JEAP’s annual report, MEL plan, and Resource Mobilization Strategy influenced African governments’ contributions to the Pandemic Fund ($360m).
Support for Africa CDC’s new health financing strategy aligns with AU Roadmap to 2030.
Integration of community engagement into NAPHS advances Lusaka Agenda priorities.
capacity_building_results: AVoHC training strengthened regional outbreak response capacity.
Technical assistance to DRC, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, and Uganda (via Palladium) began but is not yet fully measurable.
Africa CDC’s expanded role in JEAP demonstrates institutional capacity growth.
unintended_consequences: Positive: ARRO’s emergency responses (e.g., Cholera) inadvertently strengthened cross-border coordination between countries.
Negative: Delays in DRC may have eroded trust with local communities, risking long-term engagement.
scalability_evidence: JEAP’s model for regional collaboration is scalable to other health security initiatives.
AVoHC’s volunteer network can be expanded to additional countries with further funding.
Community-based surveillance (CBS) approaches are adaptable but require deeper local ownership to scale.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme is meeting expectations (overall score A) with strong early achievements in emergency response and regional partnerships. Despite ODA cuts, TDDAP2’s adaptive approach and leverage of additional funding ($360m via JEAP) justify continuation, with reprioritisation to focus on high-impact areas.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Regional partnerships (Africa CDC/WHO AFRO) are sustainable, but national component’s long-term funding is uncertain due to ODA reductions. MEL and community engagement structures require deeper institutionalisation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Reprioritise activities to align with reduced ODA, focusing on regional leverage and policy influence.
Strengthen integration between ARRO (emergency) and national (long-term) components.
Expand MEL’s role in adaptive management to respond to real-time lessons.
Formalise rapid response mechanisms for future outbreaks, building on mpox/Ebola experience.
Intensify monitoring of Africa CDC’s expanding portfolio to ensure quality.
