programme_metadata.programme_title: Mozambique Demographic Transition – Waala Programme

output_1.title: District and community health services strengthened for the benefit of mother and child

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned from World Bank Health Systems Strengthening Programme Phase 1 to Phase 2 (District and Community Health Services Revitalization Programme). Output 1 indicators were refocused: 1.1 shifted to local capacity for service quality assessment, and 1.2 revised from "coverage of institutional births" to "training and integration of Community Health Workers (CHWs)."
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Multilateral partners (World Bank, UNFPA) delivered collectively through pooled funding (Multi-Donor Trust Fund), but UK’s direct attribution of results is limited. World Bank’s Disbursement-Linked Indicators (DLIs) were reported as achieved, though validity of some (e.g., internet connectivity) remains questionable. Partners faced disruptions due to political crises and U.S. funding cuts, diverting focus to staff security and mitigating SRHR intervention gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance involved multi-donor coordination via the World Bank’s MDTF, with UK playing a convening role. Oversight included active monitoring of the transition between programme phases, allowing for logframe revisions. However, slower decision-making and complex governance were noted as challenges in pooled funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UK’s convening power advanced donor alignment and prioritization, particularly during funding debates. Coordination with the Mozambican government improved decentralization of service delivery, though district-level engagement in programme design was insufficient to ensure local ownership.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in CHW subsidy payments and shortages of training materials (e.g., starter kits) were reported. Procurement of contraceptives via UNFPA faced accountability concerns due to lack of traceable mechanisms for Government of Mozambique’s domestic contributions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to transition risks between programme phases. Active monitoring of World Bank’s implementation completion report (ICR) and Value for Money (VfM) lessons informed adaptations. UK’s early engagement in the new MDTF operation helped safeguard its reputation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to political crises (e.g., elections) and funding cuts by reprioritizing activities. Flexibility in integrating new concepts (e.g., Women’s Economic Empowerment into cash transfers) was highlighted as critical but required trust-building with government partners.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised Output 1 indicators to reflect lessons from Phase 1 and align with Phase 2 of the World Bank programme.
Shifted focus from quantitative activity targets to output quality (e.g., CHW training deployment).
Developed a responsible exit strategy in response to ODA reductions, planning to scale up domestic-system-delivered initiatives.

main_implementation_challenges: Political crisis during Mozambican national elections disrupted partner activities.
Abrupt reduction in U.S. funding for health/social sectors created gaps in SRHR interventions, requiring mitigation efforts.
Poor internet connectivity in health facilities undermined electronic data management and scorecard submissions.
Delays in CHW subsidy payments and shortages of training materials (e.g., medicine starter kits).
Lack of district-level ownership in the World Bank programme design, limiting local problem-solving.
external_factors_impact: U.S. funding cuts reduced coverage/quality of health services, raising questions about long-term aid feasibility.
Global decline in ODA pressured the programme to optimize resources and prioritize interventions.
Political economy constraints (e.g., low statistical literacy, fragmented cross-sector coordination) hindered data-driven policymaking.
contextual_constraints_new: Government of Mozambique’s 5% domestic contribution target for contraceptive procurement was deemed too modest to impact health financing.
Weak subnational capacity and buy-in from key ministries limited embedding of demographic data into planning.
Fragmented donor coordination (despite UK’s convening efforts) slowed alignment on shared goals.
partner_relationship_issues: World Bank’s pooled funding model created visibility challenges for UK’s specific contributions.
UNFPA’s domestic contribution mechanism lacked transparency, risking misallocation of funds.
Distrust between government and partners when integrating new concepts (e.g., WEE) into existing programmes.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Low statistical literacy and capacity at subnational levels hindered data use for planning.
Health facilities lacked reliable internet for electronic systems, despite reported DLI achievements.
Limited government capacity to absorb and act on high-quality demographic analyses.
risk_materialization: Political instability (elections) materialized as a high-risk factor, disrupting implementation.
ODA cuts and U.S. funding reductions materialized, requiring adaptive resource allocation.
Governance risks in pooled funding (e.g., slower decisions, complex structures) were realized but managed via early MDTF engagement.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track, though disbursement delays in the first operation were linked to late ODA commitments and cuts. Early engagement in the MDTF mitigated risks to budget execution.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Pooled funding via the World Bank’s MDTF improved efficiency and cost-effectiveness but introduced challenges (e.g., slower decision-making, reduced donor visibility). VfM lessons from the previous phase informed the new programme’s design, with a focus on alignment toward shared goals.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Mixed. While the World Bank’s financial systems ensured collective accountability, UK-specific financial oversight was limited by the pooled model. Delays in CHW payments and procurement gaps (e.g., starter kits) signalled inefficiencies.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High in collective outputs (e.g., 9,507 CHWs trained at scale), but cost efficiency for UK’s direct contributions was difficult to isolate. Commodity accuracy improved (88% in spot checks), reducing stockouts significantly (e.g., from 63% to 20% in Nampula).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. Government of Mozambique’s 5% domestic contribution for contraceptives lacked traceable mechanisms, raising accountability concerns. UN matching mechanisms and World Bank payments-by-results were proposed to accelerate domestic resource mobilization.

key_delivery_lessons: Pooled funding boosts alignment and efficiency but requires proactive risk management (e.g., governance complexity, donor visibility).
Scorecards are effective for driving quality improvements in health facilities but need stronger follow-up on action plan implementation.
Early engagement in multi-donor programmes (e.g., MDTF) safeguards influence and reputation during transitions.
successful_delivery_practices: Leveraging UK’s convening power to advance donor coordination and policy dialogue.
Using data-driven tools (e.g., scorecards, demographic analyses) to inform national/provincial strategies.
Scaling self-injectable contraception across districts (e.g., Nampula) through adaptive implementation.
management_adaptations_made: Revised logframe indicators to reflect lessons from Phase 1 and align with Phase 2 priorities.
Shifted monitoring focus from activity volume to output quality (e.g., CHW deployment effectiveness).
Strengthened verification processes to improve evidence-based reporting.
innovations_attempted: Integration of Women’s Economic Empowerment (WEE) into social protection programmes (e.g., cash transfers).
Political Economy Analysis (PEA) to identify barriers to data use in policymaking.
Pilot initiatives in the education sector to improve girls’ retention and transition.

output_5.title: EIAF II is approved and operational by January 2020

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Switched to a **one-step procurement method** to accelerate contracting, replacing the originally planned two-stage process (Selection Questionnaire + Tender). This was necessitated by delays in finalizing the Terms of Reference (ToR).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Steering committee with government is actively used to capture and mitigate risks. No major deviations from planned governance reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation:
Procurement faced **significant delays** (9+ months) due to:
- Multiple iterations of the ToR (June 2018–May 2019), including a major revision in May 2019 to introduce **payment-by-results**.
- Competing priorities within DFID’s Procurement and Commercial Department (PCD) in late 2018/early 2019.
- Tender launched on **28 June 2019** (vs. original plan of October 2018), with bids received by **9 August 2019** and evaluation completed in September 2019.
- **TRAMP contract amendment** (transition from EIAF I to EIAF II) not finalized due to procurement delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: DFID remained closely engaged during procurement but **no supplier contracted yet** as of this review. Safeguarding spot-checks planned for the coming year.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The **£6m flexible facility** (DFID-managed grants) was considered during procurement but not yet operationalized. Logframe adjustments were made to reflect delayed implementation (e.g., dropping impact weighting from 100% to 5% in 2020).
adaptive_management_examples: Adopted **one-stage procurement** to shorten timelines after ToR delays.
Logframe revised in **November 2018** to remove early implementation outputs (1–4) and add Output 5 (mobilization/transition).
Planned to **review theories of change and results frameworks** during inception if delays persist.

main_implementation_challenges: **Procurement delays**: ToR finalization took 11 months (June 2018–May 2019), pushing contract award from June 2019 to November 2019.
**Contract amendment backlog**: TRAMP supplier transition not formalized due to EIAF II procurement delays.
**Logframe completion gaps**: Baseline data identified but full logframe finalization deferred to inception phase.
**Capacity constraints in DFID/PCD**: Competing priorities slowed ToR iterations and procurement approvals.
external_factors_impact: **Ethiopia’s economic reforms**: The **Homegrown Economic Reforms (September 2019)** aligned with EIAF II priorities (e.g., public investment efficiency, SOE governance, logistics reform), strengthening programme rationale.
**Political volatility**: Frequent shifts in government priorities (e.g., PM Abiy’s "100-day plans") risk misalignment with EIAF II support.
**Debt distress**: Reduced external borrowing increased GoE’s reliance on efficient public investment, heightening demand for EIAF II advice.
contextual_constraints_new: **National Logistics Council inactivity**: Despite logistics reform being a GoE priority, the Council has not met, potentially stalling cross-ministerial coordination.
**Hawassa Industrial Park risks**: Sub-standard dormitory construction (non-compliance with ILO standards) poses reputational risks for DFID/EIAF II.
capacity_constraints_emerged: DFID’s **Procurement and Commercial Department (PCD)** faced bandwidth issues, delaying ToR approvals.
**GoE capacity gaps**: Assumption that government has (or can develop) capacity to deliver reforms may be optimistic; EIAF II will need to provide deeper support.
risk_materialization: **Leadership commitment fluctuations**: Senior GoE turnover could reduce reform momentum (e.g., National Logistics Council inaction).
**Reputational risk**: If GoE ignores EIAF II advice (e.g., on Hawassa dormitories), DFID’s credibility could be undermined.
**Transition gap**: Delayed EIAF II start risks losing momentum from EIAF I, requiring rebuilding of political capital.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: **No expenditure in 2018/19** (all activities focused on procurement). Delays incurred **additional costs** (e.g., DFID staff time for ToR iterations, though not quantified).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment:
**Not assessable** (no implementation yet). Key VfM risks:
- **Economy**: Procurement delays likely increased internal DFID costs.
- **Effectiveness**: Gap between EIAF I and EIAF II could reduce public investment capacity in GoE institutions, requiring costly rebuilding of relationships.

key_delivery_lessons: **Procurement complexity**: Payment-by-results focus required major ToR revisions, highlighting need for earlier clarity on incentive structures.
**Flexibility trade-offs**: While the one-stage procurement saved time, it reduced opportunities for supplier feedback before final bids.
**Transition risks**: Contract gaps (e.g., TRAMP) create operational discontinuities; future programmes should plan overlapping transitions.
successful_delivery_practices: **Early market engagement**: 17 organizations attended London event (June 2018) and 9 in Addis Ababa (August 2018), informing ToR design.
**Steering committee use**: Effective for risk mitigation and GoE alignment (e.g., capturing Hawassa dormitory risks).
management_adaptations_made: Shifted to **one-stage procurement** to mitigate delays.
Added **Output 5** (mobilization/transition) to logframe to reflect realistic 2019 milestones.
Planned **safeguarding spot-checks** for 2020 to address emerging risks.
innovations_attempted: **Payment-by-results**: Introduced in May 2019 ToR revision to align supplier incentives with outcomes.
**Flexible facility**: £6m DFID-managed grants designed for responsive, complementary support (not yet operational).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: N/A (first annual review for EIAF II).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Complete EIAF II supplier contracting and ensure effective handover from EIAF I.
forward_recommendations.action: DFID Ethiopia to work with PCD to finalize contracting and handover processes.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Finalize TRAMP supplier contract amendment.
forward_recommendations.action: DFID to prioritize amendment to avoid service disruption post-December 2021.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Conduct robust inception phase aligned with **Homegrown Economic Reforms** and build GoE relationships.
forward_recommendations.action: DFID to engage closely during inception to assess theory of change/results framework adjustments (e.g., separate outputs for SOEs/PPPs).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Review procurement process lessons and share with other programmes.
forward_recommendations.action: SRO to document delays/causes and disseminate learnings.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Mitigate Hawassa dormitory risks by leveraging DFID’s influence to ensure ILO compliance.
forward_recommendations.action: Use programming/policy relationships to advocate for best practices.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: **Moderate**. Steering committee effectively captured risks (e.g., Hawassa dormitories), but **residual risks remain** (e.g., GoE non-compliance, transition gaps). Risk matrix (Figure 2) shows net risks as manageable but dependent on supplier contracting.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength:
**Medium** (theoretical basis strong but no implementation evidence yet).
- **Exports/growth**: Literature (IMF 2014/2015) supports public investment efficiency → growth, but Ethiopia’s export growth remains limited (e.g., garment exports growing but from low base).
- **Poverty reduction**: World Bank (2014) links manufacturing-led growth to poverty reduction, but EIAF II’s contribution is untested.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: **Medium**. Strong GoE commitment to reforms (Homegrown Economic Reforms) but **capacity and political will** are variable (e.g., National Logistics Council inaction).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: **Potential high**. EIAF II priorities (e.g., SOE reform, PPPs) directly align with GoE’s stated agenda, but influence depends on implementation quality.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.unintended_consequences: **Negative risk**: If GoE ignores EIAF II advice (e.g., on Hawassa dormitories), DFID’s reputation could suffer. **Positive potential**: Strengthened GoE systems could attract more FDI, but this is speculative.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: **Theoretical**. EIAF’s model (technical assistance + payment-by-results) could be replicated in other contexts, but scalability depends on supplier performance and GoE uptake.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: **Strategic alignment**: EIAF II supports UK Aid Strategy (trade/investment) and GoE’s Homegrown Economic Reforms. **Demand**: GoE’s increased focus on public investment efficiency (due to debt constraints) strengthens programme relevance. **VfM**: Business case rationale remains valid; delays are mitigable if supplier is contracted by early 2020.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: **Medium-High**. Assuming timely implementation, the programme’s theory of change is sound and aligned with GoE priorities. **Risks**: Political commitment fluctuations, capacity gaps, and procurement delays could undermine outcomes.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: **Moderate**. Payment-by-results and flexible facility (£6m) enhance adaptability, but **supplier performance** and GoE engagement are critical. Steering committee provides oversight but may not address deeper coordination issues (e.g., National Logistics Council).
planned_adaptations_future: Revise logframe post-inception if theories of change require adjustment.
Explore **separate outputs** for focal areas (e.g., SOEs, PPPs) currently bundled under PIM.
Assess need for **new TRAMP tender** in 2021 if current supplier’s contract expires.

output_1.title: Commonwealth Governments are supported to implement commitments to make trade related policies more gender responsive

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Pivoted from direct WOB support in 4 countries (Bangladesh, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria) to macro-level policy interventions via SheTrades Outlook due to budget reduction (£3.5M → £0.5M). Added 5 standalone WOB-focused projects in Q4 2021 after £255K supplemental funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ITC demonstrated strong capacity to onboard 10 governments (6 new, 4 ongoing) despite resource constraints. High demand required triaging requests. Partners (e.g., Gambia, Cameroon) actively committed resources to diagnostics and policy reforms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Centralized around ITC’s core team with lean oversight due to reduced budget. Quarterly risk/VFM discussions introduced as a new practice. Coordination with FCDO intensified for strategic alignment with UK priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective global coordination through SheTrades Outlook platform, enabling cross-country learning (e.g., Rwanda’s gender mainstreaming in "Made in Rwanda" policy informed by Cameroon’s National Development Plan). Regional workshops (9 delivered) facilitated knowledge exchange.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Efficient deployment of £284K for Outlook expansion (10 governments onboarded vs. target of 6). Spanish translation and SEO improvements enhanced accessibility. Technical assistance contracts (£159K) delivered offline BSO directories and policy briefs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight due to budget volatility (3-month no-cost extension followed by 9-month costed extension). FCDO required more frequent financial/performance reporting during transition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Rapid reallocation of £255K supplemental funding in Q4 2021 to launch 5 WOB-focused projects. Adaptive use of existing ITC partnerships to scale activities (e.g., leveraging SheTrades global portfolio for standalone projects).
adaptive_management_examples: Pivot to macro-level policy focus within 3 months of budget confirmation to avoid delivery cliff edge.
Development of offline BSO directory for Sub-Saharan Africa to address digital access barriers.
Global Summit on Gender-Responsive Public Procurement organized in response to country demand (Gambia, Bangladesh).
ISO IWA 34 adoption in Bangladesh secured through iterative policy dialogue.

main_implementation_challenges: 78% budget reduction (£3.5M → £0.5M) required complete delivery model overhaul mid-implementation.
Balancing demand from 10+ countries for Outlook onboarding with limited resources (only 6 officially counted in targets).
Short-term funding horizons (initial 3-month no-cost extension) disrupted long-term partner engagement.
Diverse country contexts (from Comoros to South Korea) complicated standardized support approaches.
external_factors_impact: FCDO merger (DFID → FCDO) caused budget delays and strategic realignment to UK’s International Development Strategy.
COVID-19 restricted in-person policy dialogues, shifting to virtual workshops (9 delivered vs. 6 planned).
Global economic pressures increased demand for gender-responsive trade tools (e.g., Outlook requests from Philippines, Ecuador).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated demand from high-income countries (South Korea, New Zealand) self-funding data collection, requiring coordination without ODA funds.
Need for Spanish-language tools to engage Latin American countries (Ecuador, Mexico, El Salvador).
Policy windows opened unexpectedly (e.g., Gambia’s Public Procurement Regulations review) requiring rapid ITC response.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial resistance from some Trade Ministries to gender data collection, overcome through peer-learning (e.g., Cameroon’s Trade and Gender Officer appointment).
Misalignment between ITC’s global SheTrades brand and FCDO’s country-specific priorities, resolved via quarterly alignment workshops.
Delayed MoU signings in 2 countries due to government turnover (resolved by leveraging existing ITC relationships).
capacity_constraints_emerged: ITC’s core team stretched by 50% increase in onboarding demand (10 countries vs. 6 target).

risk_materialization: Budget volatility risk materialized (initial no-cost extension, then 9-month costed extension with 86% reduction).

budget_execution_vs_plan.underspend_justification: Efficient onboarding (10 governments for £284K vs. £500K budgeted for 6) offset by £159K technical assistance and £255K supplemental WOB projects.

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK Action to support Developing Countries Fighting Corruption Programme

output_1.title: The sustained and increased level of investigation of grand corruption (the theft of significant public assets by senior foreign officials) and international bribery impacting lower income, lower middle-income countries (priority), middle-income and upper middle-income countries (lower priority), and with a connection to the UK. This includes the investigation of related activity by professional enablers and efforts to recover assets using civil powers.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Planned 25% expansion over five years was halted mid-year due to COVID-19 budget cuts (14.79% reduction in 2020/21). Proposed increases in NCA staff (ICU, BCIU, CRT) did not proceed. CRT team recruitment freeze led to paused work on Unexplained Wealth Orders (UWOs).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (NCA, CPS, UKCA) delivered targets despite budget cuts and pandemic constraints. ICU submitted 6 cases to CPS for charging (significant achievement). City of London Police (CoLP) partnership ending; learning capture recommended.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Core delivery through NCA’s ICU/BCIU and CPS’s PoCU remained stable. UKCA (Home Office) and legacy OACU (CoLP) roles continued as planned, though OACU is concluding. Governance adapted to budget uncertainties via log-frame adjustments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-HMG coordination (e.g., Ibori case asset return to Nigeria) demonstrated effectiveness. Inter-Ministerial Group on Anti-Corruption flagged as key coordination mechanism for court delay issues.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight maintained despite budget cuts, with regular log-frame reviews. Pandemic required adaptive oversight (e.g., remote monitoring).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Log-frame targets and indicators were adjusted mid-year to reflect budget cuts and pandemic impacts (e.g., removed UWO indicators, recalibrated case investigation targets).

Recalibrated targets for court delays (e.g., asset confiscation timelines extended).
Shifted to remote working and digital case management during pandemic.
Captured learning from CoLP partnership conclusion for future collaborations.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 pandemic: 14.79% budget cut mid-year, halting expansion plans; court delays (1–2 year backlogs) deprioritized corruption cases.
Court system constraints: Pre-pandemic backlogs worsened, delaying asset recovery and prosecutions (e.g., Ibori case took 10+ years).
Budget uncertainty: 2021/22 budget unconfirmed at review time, hindering planning.
Indicator design flaws: Investigation-stage targets (1.1b, 1.2b) missed due to cases progressing to charging/completion (a perverse incentive).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Reduced GNI led to ODA budget cuts; travel restrictions limited international cooperation; partner agencies (e.g., intelligence providers) scaled back activities.
Political/legal: Court prioritization of custodial cases over corruption delayed proceedings. Brexit impacts (if any) not mentioned.
Economic: Currency/exchange rate impacts not specified, but budget cuts directly reduced operational capacity.
contextual_constraints_new: Pandemic-induced court backlogs became a structural constraint (expected to persist "for several years").
Reduced intelligence flows from partner agencies due to their pandemic-related scale-backs.
Increased reputational risks for UK as a money-laundering hub (per ToC) required faster asset returns, but systemic delays undermined this.
partner_relationship_issues: CoLP partnership ending required knowledge transfer; no major issues reported but learning capture recommended.
UKCA (Home Office) and NCA coordination effective, but budget cuts strained capacity (e.g., CRT freeze).
capacity_constraints_emerged: CRT team (UWOs) unable to recruit due to budget cuts, pausing related workstreams.
ICU portfolio management stressed by case progression bottlenecks (court delays).
Reduced ability to initiate new investigations due to resource reallocation to live cases.
risk_materialization: Budget cuts ("Major" risk in 2020) materialized, reducing staffing and expansion plans.
Court delays (anticipated but worsened by pandemic) impacted asset recovery timelines (3.2b indicator missed).
Intelligence supply risks (4.2 indicator) materialized due to partner agency scale-backs.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Original 2020/21 budget cut by 14.79% mid-year due to ODA reductions, reverting to pre-expansion levels.
Planned 25% expansion over 5 years halted; no new NCA/CRT staff hired.
Budget uncertainty for 2021/22 persisted at review time, complicating financial planning.
value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated by £1.1B+ assets frozen/confiscated since 2006 (£741M in past 5 years).
£4.2M returned to Nigeria (Ibori case) highlighted symbolic and tangible impact despite decade-long timeline.
Cost efficiency maintained by leveraging existing law enforcement structures (NCA, CPS) with targeted ODA funding.
Budget cuts forced trade-offs (e.g., paused UWO work) but core outputs (cases, intelligence) delivered at "A" level.
financial_management_quality: Adaptive financial management: Log-frame and indicators adjusted mid-year to align with reduced budget.
Transparency in reallocating funds to priority areas (e.g., live cases over new investigations).
No evidence of mismanagement; partners (NCA, CPS) reported as delivering despite constraints.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficiency gains from consolidated ICU/BCIU model (since 2015) vs. previous fragmented police teams.
Intelligence output (901 packages vs. 500 target) achieved at lower cost due to remote working.
Asset recovery costs offset by returns (e.g., Ibori case), though timelines undermine immediate cost-benefit visibility.

key_delivery_lessons: Log-frame indicators must account for systemic delays (e.g., court backlogs) to avoid perverse incentives (e.g., 1.1b/1.2b targets).
Flexibility in budget reallocation (e.g., pausing UWOs to fund live cases) preserved core delivery.
Cross-HMG coordination (e.g., Ibori asset return) is critical for high-impact outcomes but requires senior-level advocacy.
successful_delivery_practices: ICU’s portfolio management approach (25 live cases) balanced long-term investigations with annual targets.
Intelligence-sharing mechanisms (901 packages in 2020/21) exceeded targets through digital collaboration.
Adaptive indicator adjustment (e.g., removing unachievable UWO targets) maintained realism.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from expansion to consolidation mode post-budget cuts.
Prioritized case progression over new investigations to align with reduced capacity.
Enhanced monitoring of court delays via Inter-Ministerial Group escalation.
innovations_attempted: Digital case management and remote intelligence-sharing during pandemic.
Cross-agency task forces (e.g., Ibori case) for high-profile asset returns.
Pilot indicators for mutual legal assistance (1.4) to track international cooperation.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2020 PCR recommendations partially addressed: Log-frame revised but budget cuts limited full implementation.
Theory of Change (2018) remained valid; no fundamental operational changes needed per 2021 review.

forward_recommendations.action: Review log-frame post-2021/22 budget confirmation, focusing on indicators 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, 4.1, 5.2.
Monitor and escalate court delay impacts via Inter-Ministerial Group on Anti-Corruption.
Capture and document lessons from CoLP partnership conclusion.
Recalibrate targets to reflect pandemic/court delay "new normal" and avoid perverse incentives.

risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive: Budget cut risks mitigated via log-frame adjustments and reprioritization.
Reactive: Court delays and intelligence shortages addressed via escalation and indicator pauses.
Gaps: No contingency for prolonged court backlogs; UWO risk materialized without backup plans.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Direct: Developing countries (e.g., Nigeria received £4.2M in Ibori case; Kenya supported via 5 mutual legal assistance requests).
Indirect: Global anti-corruption efforts benefited from 901 intelligence packages shared with UK/overseas authorities.
Quantitative: 49 money laundering + 86 bribery cases concluded since 2006; 25 live cases in ICU portfolio (2021).
policy_influence_achieved: Symbolic: Ibori case asset return reinforced UK’s anti-corruption commitments (aligned with 2016 Anti-Corruption Summit pledges).
Operational: ICU/BCIU model influenced NCA’s structural approach to economic crime.
Limited: Court delays undermined deterrence effect; no evidence of systemic policy changes in developing countries.
capacity_building_results: UKCA (Home Office) enhanced mutual legal assistance processing capacity (5 cases supported in 2020/21).
ICU’s intelligence-sharing built investigative capacity in partner agencies (e.g., 901 packages in 2020/21).
No direct capacity-building in developing countries reported; focus remained on UK enforcement.
unintended_consequences: Positive: High-profile cases (e.g., Ibori) raised UK’s profile as a leader in asset recovery, attracting more mutual legal assistance requests.
Negative: Court delays eroded public trust in timely justice; budget cuts reduced UK’s ability to initiate new cases, potentially emboldening corrupt actors.
scalability_evidence: Model scalability: ICU/BCIU structure demonstrated replicability within UK law enforcement (e.g., expansion plans pre-budget cuts).
Limits: Court system bottlenecks and budget dependency constrain scalability without systemic reforms.
International: Mutual legal assistance mechanisms (1.4) showed potential for scaling cross-border cooperation.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance ("A" score) despite challenges; core outputs (cases, intelligence) delivered effectively.
Alignment with HMG priorities: Anti-corruption remains a strategic focus (e.g., Ibori case return).
Unfinished business: 25 live ICU cases and pending asset returns (e.g., £1.1B+ frozen) require continuation.
Budget uncertainty is manageable with adaptive planning (per recommendations).
delivery_model_sustainability: Strengths: Leverages existing UK law enforcement infrastructure (NCA, CPS) with targeted ODA funding; proven track record since 2006.
Risks: Court delays and budget volatility threaten long-term sustainability; CoLP partnership conclusion requires knowledge transfer.
Adaptations needed: Secure multi-year budget commitments; advocate for court system reforms.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Invest Salone: Private Sector Development, Trade and Job Creation in Sierra Leone
programme_metadata.programme_status: In transition (adapting to ODA reductions and refocusing resources)

output_1.title: Market Development: Enterprises strengthened (improved productivity/competitiveness) to grow, become export ready and/or investment ready

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adapted to ODA reductions by refocusing resources on a new plan with revised results targets. Shift towards more adaptive management due to external shocks (COVID, Ukraine war, elections). Sector-strategy under review to focus more on high-impact areas like agribusiness.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Local partners (e.g., Innovation SL, Farrell Elliott) delivered technical support effectively, particularly in financial management training. Diaspora-led businesses showed high commitment. Public-Private Dialogues (PPD) became more challenging post-election but achieved some high-value advocacy results (e.g., influencing land rights legislation).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Core team primarily comprises national long-term consultants. Programme leveraged local expertise (e.g., Sierra Leonean nationals leading textiles/tourism interventions) but faced challenges in sourcing specialized skills (e.g., agronomy).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with DFIs (e.g., IFC, British International Investment) helped unlock £13.5m in additional investment since 2020. However, PPD coordination was strained post-election due to political tensions and funding squeezes. PPD survey methodology is under review for improved value.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: De-risking grants successfully financed due diligence, ESIAs, and documentation for 13 firms, enabling access to impact investor/DFI capital. Local procurement of expertise (e.g., financial training for SMEs) was effective but limited by skill gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to macroeconomic instability and political risks. Adaptive management intensified to reallocate resources to high-potential sectors (e.g., agribusiness).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme used flexibility to reallocate funds from underperforming sectors (e.g., tourism, textiles) to agribusiness and blue carbon credits. Adaptive responses included tailored support for firms like Sierra Bo (cassava) and Jolak (palm oil).
adaptive_management_examples: Revised sector strategy to focus on agribusiness based on performance data.
Facilitated B2B networks to pool expertise across supported businesses.
Partnered with BII to host the Africa Resilience Investment Accelerator (ARIA) mission to attract DFIs.
Adjusted financial training delivery after weak initial results, targeting female-owned companies.

main_implementation_challenges: Macroeconomic instability (inflation, food/fuel price shocks from Ukraine war).
Post-election political tensions (June 2023) disrupted Public-Private Dialogues and government engagement.
ODA budget reductions forced reprioritization of activities and targets.
Limited pool of "medium/large" firms in Sierra Leone constrained scalability.
Weak infrastructure and institutional capacity (e.g., corruption, rent-seeking) persisted as systemic barriers.
external_factors_impact: Ukraine war: Increased food/shipping costs, reduced investor confidence.
COVID-19: Lingering supply chain disruptions and economic contraction.
Elections (2023): Delayed policy reforms and created uncertainty for private sector.
Global inflation: Reduced purchasing power and increased operational costs for businesses.
contextual_constraints_new: Intensified public sector funding squeeze post-election.
Emerging climate risks (e.g., impact on agribusiness productivity).
Regional instability affecting trade and investment flows.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between development partners and new government post-election.
Some international partners (e.g., in tourism/textiles) underperformed relative to agribusiness-focused partners.
Local expertise gaps required additional capacity-building investments.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Scarcity of local agribusiness skills beyond smallholder farming.
Limited financial management capacity among SMEs (addressed via ISL training).
Government counterparts faced reduced bandwidth for PPD due to funding cuts.
risk_materialization: Major risks materialized: Macroeconomic instability ("Major" risk rating since 2020), political transition risks, and sector-specific underperformance (tourism/textiles).
Investment climate deterioration due to external shocks.
Currency depreciation (Leone) increased costs for imported inputs.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track despite ODA reductions; £13.5m in additional investment mobilized since 2020 (including £4.9m in Y4) through de-risking grants. Budget reallocated from low-performing sectors to agribusiness and blue carbon credits.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VfM in agribusiness (e.g., £4.9m leveraged in Y4) but weaker in tourism/textiles. Local expertise procurement improved VfM (e.g., regional agronomy experts proposed). Adaptive management protected VfM amid shocks.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls for grant disbursements (e.g., due diligence/ESIA documentation). Local financial training for SMEs (e.g., bookkeeping) addressed capacity gaps. No major audit findings reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost-efficient in agribusiness (e.g., tailored support to Sierra Bo/Jolak achieved expansion at lower cost than international consultants). Textiles/tourism interventions were less efficient due to lower demand.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized through DFI partnerships (e.g., IFC, BII). ISL’s due diligence support helped firms access DFI financing (e.g., cassava/palm oil projects).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Leone depreciation increased costs for imported inputs (e.g., agribusiness equipment), partially offset by local procurement.

key_delivery_lessons: Sector-agnostic approach was less effective; focusing on high-potential sectors (e.g., agribusiness) yields better results.
Local expertise is critical but requires upfront investment in capacity-building.
B2B networks and knowledge-sharing mitigate risks of individual firm failures.
PPD effectiveness depends on political stability; alternative advocacy channels needed during transitions.
successful_delivery_practices: De-risking grants successfully unlocked DFI capital (£13.5m mobilized).
Tailored technical support (e.g., cassava/palm oil mill rehabilitation) achieved measurable firm-level growth.
Local consultants (e.g., Innovation SL) delivered cost-effective financial training.
Diaspora-led businesses showed high commitment and co-investment.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted resources from tourism/textiles to agribusiness/blue carbon credits.
Intensified adaptive management post-ODA cuts and elections.
Reviewing PPD survey methodology for better stakeholder insights.
Exploring regional expertise pools (e.g., Senegalese agronomy experts).
innovations_attempted: Africa Resilience Investment Accelerator (ARIA) mission to attract DFIs.
Blue carbon credit activities as a new revenue stream for sustainability.
B2B networks to share expertise across sectors.
Localization of technical assistance (e.g., financial training for female-owned SMEs).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Sector refocusing initiated but not fully implemented.
PPD challenges persist; methodology review planned for 2024.
Local expertise utilization increased but gaps remain in specialized skills.
forward_recommendations: Finalize sector strategy to prioritize agribusiness and blue carbon credits.
Strengthen local expertise pipelines (e.g., regional knowledge networks).
Enhance DFI coordination to scale successful de-risking models.
Develop contingency plans for political/economic shocks.
Improve M&E to capture long-term job creation impacts.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Major risks (macroeconomic, political) were anticipated but mitigation was constrained by external shocks. Adaptive management helped reallocate resources, but systemic risks (e.g., corruption) persist.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 46 businesses supported in Y4 (11 women-owned), exceeding target of 36 (10 women-owned). 13 firms benefited from £13.5m mobilized since 2020.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Downstream supply chain partnerships reached 11 informal sector groups (farmers, fishermen, traders) in Y4, exceeding target of 8.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.targets_met: Most output targets met or exceeded (e.g., 1.1: 46 vs. 36 firms; 1.3: 11 vs. 8 partnerships).

policy_influence_achieved: Influenced Customary Land Rights and National Land Commission Acts via PPD advocacy.
Private sector feedback incorporated into draft land bills, though implementation remains uncertain post-election.
capacity_building_results: Financial management training improved SME capacity (e.g., bookkeeping, forecasting).
Firms like Sierra Bo/Jolak expanded operations with ISL technical support.
Local consultants (e.g., Innovation SL) built enduring training capacity.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Diaspora engagement strengthened local business networks.
Negative: Reduced support for tourism/textiles may have weakened nascent sectors.
scalability_evidence: Agribusiness models (e.g., cassava/palm oil) demonstrate scalability with DFI co-funding.
Blue carbon credits offer potential for regional replication.
B2B networks could be expanded nationally with minimal additional cost.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong results in agribusiness and investment mobilization despite challenges. Adaptive management has protected VfM, and refocused sectors (agribusiness/blue carbon) align with Sierra Leone’s economic priorities. However, political and macroeconomic risks require ongoing mitigation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable: Local expertise and DFI partnerships enhance long-term viability, but systemic issues (corruption, infrastructure) and ODA uncertainty pose risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied with adaptive performance but concerned about sectoral imbalances and political risks.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize sector strategy to exit low-performing areas (tourism/textiles).
Deepened DFI partnerships to scale agribusiness investments.
Enhanced localization (e.g., regional expertise, B2B networks).
Strengthened M&E to track job creation and policy influence.
Contingency planning for 2025 elections and potential ODA changes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK Trade Partnerships Programme (UKTP)

output_1.title: Firms and institutions are aware of how to use EPA preferences and potential benefits

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to remote coaching and expanded digital transformation offerings due to COVID-19; delayed implementation of Component 1 (EPA agreements) with focus planned for 2021/22; pilot of REACT methodology for BSO resilience assessments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ITC demonstrated flexibility and decisiveness in responding to COVID-19 and budget challenges, though Component 1 delivery was stalled. Quarterly/bi-annual check-ins with regional trade advisers were inconsistent due to staff absences, with improvements noted in Zimbabwe.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Regular FCDO/ITC meetings for spend forecasting and plan approvals were maintained, but governance for programme extension (1-year) remains pending due to FCDO structural changes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with ITC was effective in adapting to challenges (e.g., virtual trade fairs), but consistency in regional check-ins needs improvement. Stakeholder consultations lacked specificity in reporting (e.g., distinguishing between Trade Support Institutions, businesses, etc.).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: ITC’s procurement processes were rigorous with 19% of spend on global management (including 1% UN levy) and 81% on delivery. Travel costs were reduced to 1% of total spend due to COVID-19, improving cost efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was maintained through regular meetings, but adaptive management was required due to external factors (COVID-19, ODA cuts). Quarterly reports lacked detailed stakeholder consultation breakdowns.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted to virtual delivery (e.g., 16 webinars with 747 participants, virtual trade fairs) and reprioritized activities in response to COVID-19 and budget cuts. One-year extension planned to achieve gross targets.
adaptive_management_examples: Shift to remote coaching and digital tools (e.g., Market Analysis Tools webinars).
Pilot of REACT methodology for BSO resilience assessments.
Support for beneficiaries to participate in virtual trade fairs (e.g., Food Matters Live, Biofach 2021).
Delay of Component 1 implementation to 2021/22 due to COVID-19 and EPA signing delays.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 restrictions limiting in-person training and trade fairs.
UK ODA reprioritization (2020/21) and budget cuts (0.7% to 0.5% of GNI in 2021/22).
Delays in EPA signings (e.g., Ghana), creating uncertainty for Component 1.
Capacity constraints in partner countries (e.g., data collection delays in Ghana).
Inconsistent regional coordination due to staff absences.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Forced shift to virtual delivery, delayed trainings, and reduced travel.
ODA cuts: Reduced budget for 2020/21 and 2021/22, requiring reprioritization.
EPA signing delays: Protracted negotiations impacted Component 1 planning.
Global economic downturn: Weakened beneficiary business prospects, risking outcome achievement.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for virtual trade fair participation due to cancellations.
Geographic disparities in digital access for remote coaching.
Limited stakeholder engagement in Pacific region for feedback collection.
partner_relationship_issues: Inconsistent quarterly check-ins between FCDO regional advisers and ITC country teams.
Delays in ITC sharing data (e.g., Market Analysis Tool visits) for monitoring.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Delayed data collection in Ghana for market access information.
Limited institutional capacity to embed Market Analysis Tools in national websites (e.g., Caribbean OECS, Madagascar).
Challenges in reaching geographically disadvantaged SMEs despite inclusion efforts.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 disruptions (high impact).
ODA budget cuts (high impact).
EPA signing delays (moderate impact).
Weaker-than-expected beneficiary business resilience (emerging risk).

budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_reason: Rescheduled spending due to COVID-19 and programme extension to 2022/23; lower travel costs (1% of spend vs. planned higher allocation).
budget_execution_vs_plan.alignment_with_business_case: Deviated from original plan but aligned with revised extension-approved spending profile.

economy.evidence: ITC’s procurement processes were rigorous; 81% of spend on delivery vs. 19% management costs (including 1% UN levy). Potential for benchmarking competitiveness in future.

efficiency.evidence: Lower travel costs (1% of spend) improved efficiency, but external factors (COVID-19, ODA cuts) reduced cost-effectiveness of lifecycle outcomes. Staffing/consultancy costs dominated spend (aligned with business case).

effectiveness.evidence: Output 1 (score: B) faced delays, but adaptive delivery (e.g., virtual fairs, webinars) maintained progress. Risk of weaker outcomes due to beneficiary business struggles post-COVID.

value_for_money_assessment.overall_vfm: Moderate – Adaptive management mitigated risks, but external factors pressured lifecycle value.

financial_management_quality.evidence: Clear financial reporting; regular FCDO/ITC meetings for spend forecasting; no unapproved cost inefficiencies identified.

cost_efficiency_achieved.evidence: Travel costs reduced to 1% of spend (vs. higher planned allocation); more funds redirected to direct delivery (e.g., consultancy, digital tools).

key_delivery_lessons: Virtual delivery (e.g., webinars, trade fairs) can effectively replace in-person activities in crises.
Flexible procurement and financial management enable rapid adaptation to external shocks.
Regular stakeholder check-ins are critical but require enforcement to ensure consistency.
successful_delivery_practices: REACT methodology for BSO resilience assessments.
Digital transformation offerings (e.g., Market Analysis Tools webinars with 747 participants).
Gender-inclusive targeting (e.g., 298 women participants in webinars).
Pivot to virtual trade fairs (e.g., Food Matters Live, Biofach 2021).
management_adaptations_made: Reprioritized Component 1 to 2021/22 due to COVID-19/EPA delays.
Extended programme by 1 year (to 2022/23) to achieve gross targets.
Enhanced monitoring of gender equity impacts (e.g., gender assessment reports).
innovations_attempted: REACT methodology for institutional resilience.
Digital coaching and virtual trade fair participation.
Call for Feedback tool to assess EPA awareness and UK trade interest.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial: Equity impacts expanded to include gender but non-gender groups remain underaddressed (Recommendation 001).
Pending: Cost-per-beneficiary analysis to be implemented by March 2022 (Recommendation 002).
Pending: Logframe updates dependent on governance approval of programme extension (Recommendation 004).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Expand equity targets beyond gender (e.g., geographically disadvantaged SMEs) in logframe by October 2021.
Implement cost-per-beneficiary monitoring by March 2022 to direct resources to high-impact areas.
Use Call for Feedback results to appraise activities and redirect resources by October 2021.
Confirm 1-year extension approval and update logframe milestones by October 2021.
Improve consistency of quarterly check-ins with ITC country teams by Q2 2021/22.
Specify consulted stakeholders in quarterly reports to aid monitoring by August 2021.

risk_management_effectiveness.evidence: Proactive adaptation to COVID-19 and ODA cuts, but some risks materialized (e.g., EPA delays, weaker beneficiary resilience). Risk monitoring needs strengthening for emerging economic risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 747 participants (including 298 women) in Market Analysis Tools webinars; 14 companies supported in virtual trade fairs (7 in Food Matters Live, 5 in Fi Europe Connect, 2 in Biofach 2021).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Component 1 targets not yet addressed; Output 1 indicators (e.g., trainings, tool embedments) delayed.

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Limited direct policy influence reported; focus on capacity building for EPA implementation. Gender action plans adopted in partner countries.

capacity_building_results.evidence: Digital skills enhanced via webinars; BSO resilience assessed using REACT methodology; Market Analysis Tools introduced (though embedding delayed).

positive: Increased digital literacy among beneficiaries due to virtual pivot.
Stronger focus on gender inclusion (e.g., 40% women in webinars).
negative: Risk of marginalizing non-digital-ready SMEs/farmers.
Delayed EPA implementation may reduce long-term trade benefits.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Virtual delivery models (e.g., webinars, trade fairs) are scalable; REACT methodology adaptable to other regions. However, EPA-specific tools require country-level customization.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme has demonstrated adaptive capacity and aligns with UK EPA commitments, despite external challenges. Extension to 2022/23 is critical to achieve gross targets and justify ODA spend.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Moderate – High delivery capability but dependent on EPA progress and economic recovery of beneficiaries.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium – Virtual delivery is cost-effective but requires ongoing partner capacity (e.g., ITC) and digital infrastructure in ACP countries.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate – Satisfied with adaptive management but concerned about external risks (ODA cuts, EPA delays).
planned_adaptations_future: Focus on Component 1 (EPA implementation) in 2021/22.
Enhanced monitoring of cost-per-beneficiary and equity impacts.
Formalize programme extension and update logframe milestones.
Strengthen regional coordination (e.g., consistent check-ins).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Support to the International Security Sector Advisory Team (ISSAT) Programme

output_1.title: Advisory Field Support (AFS) for Members' missions

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Component 2 budget (£100k p.a. for external research) was reallocated to Component 1 (ISSAT core activities) during the financial year. Programme extended from 31/08/2024 to 31/12/2024 to align with ISSAT's financial year and complete deliverables.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ISSAT exceeded expectations in 2023, with 100% of International Partners Group Members (IPGMs) reporting that ISSAT's contributions met or exceeded expectations (vs. 80% target). Partners like the African Union (AU), UNDP, and ECOWAS provided formal appreciation for ISSAT's technical support and convening role.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Led by FCDO's Office for Conflict, Stabilisation and Mediation (OCSM). UK remains a Core Group member of ISSAT's pooled fund and participates in the International Partners Group (IPG). Governance aligns with the multi-donor structure, with no significant deviations from planned arrangements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination through ISSAT's three-pillar structure (Pillar 1: donor priorities; Pillar 2: multilateral support; Pillar 3: training/knowledge). The IPG meetings and joint mandates (e.g., AU 10-Year SSR Framework, ECOWAS lessons identification) demonstrate strong collaboration among bilateral/multilateral actors.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Pre-agreed rates for ISSAT staff/advisers and contracted expertise are used. Cost-sharing mechanisms with multilaterals (e.g., UNDP, UN OROLSI) reduce procurement burdens. No major procurement delays or issues reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintains regular oversight through progress reviews, risk reporting, and feedback from IPGMs. The 2023 Due Diligence Assessment (DDA) of DCAF (ISSAT's corporate platform) confirmed adequate controls and policies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by reallocating Component 2 funds to Component 1 and extending the timeline to complete deliverables. Adaptive management seen in responding to external changes (e.g., cancellation of Sudan mandate due to UNITAMS closure).
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of Component 2 budget to Component 1 to focus on core ISSAT activities.
Extension of programme timeline to 31/12/2024 to align with ISSAT's financial year and complete mandates.
Adjustment of mandates in response to geopolitical changes (e.g., Sudan, Ukraine).
Development of new training products (e.g., Climate Security and SSG/R stocktaking study) based on emerging priorities.

main_implementation_challenges: Difficulty in measuring direct impact of ISSAT's interventions due to reliance on partner feedback and indirect influence on policy/action.
Cancellation of mandates due to external factors (e.g., UNITAMS closure in Sudan).
Delays in utilizing Pillar 1 funding for OCSM's SSR policy/guidance development due to FCDO team capacity constraints.
external_factors_impact: Geopolitical shifts (e.g., Sudan coup, Ukraine war) disrupted planned mandates and required reprioritization.
UN Security Council decisions (e.g., closure of UNITAMS) led to cancellation of specific activities (e.g., Rural Courts assessment in Sudan).
Increased demand for SSR support in conflict-affected regions (e.g., Sahel, Moldova) stretched ISSAT's capacity.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging priority areas (e.g., climate security, AI in SSG/R) required rapid adaptation of ISSAT's knowledge products.
Limited capacity of some partner organizations (e.g., RECs, national governments) to act on ISSAT's recommendations.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: No significant issues reported. Strong appreciation from partners (AU, UNDP, ECOWAS) for ISSAT's neutral convening role and technical expertise.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO OCSM team capacity delays in leading Pillar 1 activities (SSR policy/guidance development).
ISSAT's roster of ~40-50 advisers occasionally stretched by high demand for mandates.
risk_materialization: Minor risks related to staff capacity and donor funding fluctuations were managed proactively.
No high-severity risks materialized; overall risk rating remained 'Minor' throughout the period.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Component 2 funds were reallocated to Component 1 due to underutilization, with no underspend reported. Extension to December 2024 allows full disbursement of allocated budget.
value_for_money_assessment: High VFM achieved through pooled funding model (economies of scale) and cost-sharing with multilaterals.
ISSAT's pay-for-service model (core team + on-demand advisers) optimizes costs.
Training and joint mandates amplify impact beyond UK's direct investment (e.g., AU SSR conference support).
Business case projections on donor influence and multilateral engagement were met or exceeded.
financial_management_quality: Adequate controls confirmed by 2023 DDA of DCAF (ISSAT's corporate platform).
Transparent reporting via IATI standards and regular financial updates to FCDO.
Pre-agreed rates for advisers and travel costs adhered to; no significant audit findings.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost-sharing with multilaterals (e.g., UNDP, UN OROLSI) reduced per-mandate costs.
Joint training events (e.g., SSR courses) leveraged economies of scale.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Multilateral cost-sharing arrangements (Pillar 2) performed as planned, with partners contributing to joint mandates (e.g., AU, ECOWAS).

key_delivery_lessons: Pooled multi-donor funds enable flexibility but require clear earmarking to avoid underutilization (e.g., Component 2 reallocation).
Neutral convening platforms (like ISSAT) are highly valued by partners for SSR coordination but face challenges in attributing direct impact.
Geopolitical volatility necessitates built-in flexibility for mandate adjustments.
successful_delivery_practices: ISSAT's three-pillar structure effectively balances donor priorities, multilateral support, and knowledge-sharing.
Feedback forms from IPGMs provide actionable data for performance assessment.
Cost-sharing with multilaterals enhances VFM and amplifies UK influence.
management_adaptations_made: Extended programme timeline to complete deliverables and align with ISSAT's financial year.
Increased focus on emerging priorities (e.g., climate security, AI) in training and research products.
Planned raise of awareness among FCDO country teams and MOD about ISSAT's support offerings.
innovations_attempted: Development of new knowledge products (e.g., Climate Security and SSG/R stocktaking study).
Participation in cross-cutting initiatives (e.g., C4SI challenge-setting, NATO Defence College lectures).
Advisory notes on youth engagement in SSR and SSG/R migration links.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Delay in maximizing ISSAT's direct value for OCSM/HMG due to FCDO team capacity constraints, but progress expected as OCSM SSR team expands.
Completed: Integration of lessons from field mandates (e.g., ECOWAS, AU) into training materials.
forward_recommendations: Explore a new UK mandate on SSR and peace processes aligned with OCSM priorities.
Strengthen monitoring of how ISSAT's outputs influence partner decision-making (beyond feedback forms).
Increase utilization of Pillar 1 for OCSM-led SSR policy/guidance development as team capacity grows.
Develop a strategy for sustaining ISSAT's role post-2024, given its unique convening function.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive risk reporting and minor risk rating maintained throughout the period.
DCAF's risk policy and safeguarding measures assessed as adequate in 2023 DDA.
No major risks materialized; adaptive management mitigated minor operational challenges.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 17 AFS mandates active in 2023, with 10 completed (excluding cancelled Sudan mandate).
30+ practitioners trained in SSR governance courses (e.g., UNTSI Ireland ESDC EAB).
Multilateral partners (AU, UNDP, ECOWAS, OSCE) directly supported through joint mandates.
Indirect reach through knowledge products (e.g., advisory notes, stocktaking studies) used by broader SSR community.
policy_influence_achieved: ISSAT's contributions shaped the AU 10-Year SSR Framework conference agenda and recommendations.
UNDP fully accepted all 8 recommendations from ISSAT's evaluation of the Rule of Law Global Programme in OPTs, leading to strategy adjustments.
Influence on multilateral SSR approaches (e.g., coordination mechanisms for AU/RECs) documented.
capacity_building_results: Enhanced capacity of IPGMs through training (e.g., SSR governance courses, masterclasses).
Strengthened AU and ECOWAS ability to coordinate SSR assistance via joint mandates and lessons identification.
Development of new guidance materials (e.g., People-Centered Approaches to SSG/R advisory note).
unintended_consequences: Positive: ISSAT's neutral platform facilitated unexpected collaborations (e.g., NATO Defence College lectures, OSCE Academy summer school).
Negative: Limited direct attribution of ISSAT's influence on partner actions due to indirect delivery model.
scalability_evidence: ISSAT's pooled fund model and cost-sharing mechanisms are replicable for other SSR initiatives.
Knowledge products (e.g., stocktaking studies) have been adopted by partners beyond the core programme (e.g., WB, UN).
Demand for ISSAT's services from new regions (e.g., Moldova, Georgia) suggests scalability potential.

continuation_rationale: ISSAT remains a unique and valued platform for SSR coordination, aligning with FCDO/OCSM priorities (SSR, stabilisation, peace processes).
Consistent 'A' performance ratings and minor risk levels demonstrate effective delivery.
Strong demand from international partners (AU, UNDP, ECOWAS) for continued support.
Extension to December 2024 allows completion of ongoing mandates and alignment with ISSAT's financial year.
delivery_model_sustainability: Pooled multi-donor fund model is sustainable with continued Core Group contributions.
Cost-sharing with multilaterals reduces dependency on single donors.
ISSAT's neutral convening role ensures ongoing relevance to the SSR community.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Increased focus on OCSM-led Pillar 1 activities as FCDO team capacity expands.
Exploration of new UK mandates on SSR and peace processes.
Enhanced monitoring of ISSAT's influence on partner decision-making.
Potential transition planning for post-2024 sustainability (e.g., reduced UK funding with increased multilateral contributions).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Strategic Impact Evaluation and Learning (SIEL) Programme

output_1.title: Increased quantity, quality and relevance of evidence available to improve policy design and implementation in SIEL's priority areas

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adapted to shifting FCDO priorities post-July 2024 election; introduced quarterly reflection sessions to sense-check logframe targets. First-time implementation of Expressions of Interest (EOI) process for impact evaluations, with 13 applications received across FCDO directorates and priority areas.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IPA and J-PAL demonstrated high engagement and collaboration with FCDO, evidenced by joint development of learning agendas, training sessions, and EOI processes. Subaward between IPA and J-PAL for learning agendas took longer than expected but was successfully finalized. Feedback from training sessions was positive, indicating strong demand and effective delivery.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Collegiate working partnership established among FCDO, IPA, and J-PAL, facilitated by in-person workshops (e.g., inception workshop, "Impact Evaluation 101" course). Adaptive management principles introduced, including quarterly reflection sessions to align with evolving FCDO priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: High engagement with FCDO staff and external experts in producing learning agendas, ensuring relevance and alignment with FCDO priorities. Coordination mechanisms (e.g., motivator sessions, conferences) successfully generated interest and participation in SIEL activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive grant procurement process completed in March 2024, marking the start of the inception period. Delays in subaward finalization between IPA and J-PAL were resolved, with improved understanding of FCDO’s project management requirements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was adaptive, with a focus on quarterly reflection sessions to refocus logframe targets. The programme team responded to delays (e.g., learning agenda reviews) by extending timelines and prioritizing alignment with FCDO’s evolving narrative (e.g., growth agenda).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in extending timelines (e.g., growth learning agenda) and modifying priorities to reflect shifting departmental aims. Adapted to budgetary uncertainties (e.g., ODA reductions) by promoting quicker, less expensive pilot studies.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended timeline for the growth learning agenda to align with FCDO’s post-election growth strategy.
Introduced quarterly reflection sessions to adjust logframe targets and maintain relevance.
Modified EOI process based on lessons learned (e.g., streamlining information collection for future rounds).
Pivoted to promote pilot and nimble studies in response to ODA budget reductions.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in finalizing learning agendas (e.g., Conflict, Growth) due to extended FCDO internal reviews and evolving departmental priorities post-election.
Longer-than-anticipated review process for the first EOI round, though it provided valuable learning for future rounds.
Reduction in ODA budgets (from 0.5% to 0.3% of GNI in February 2025) led to withdrawal of two EOI proposals and required reprioritization.
Administrative delays in IPA subawarding to J-PAL, impacting early-stage financial forecasting and reporting.
external_factors_impact: July 2024 UK election resulted in shifting FCDO priorities, requiring adjustments to learning agendas (e.g., growth agenda) and programme timelines.
ODA budget cuts (February 2025) reduced funding certainty for potential EOI applicants, leading to withdrawals and a need to promote lower-cost evaluation options.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated length of learning agendas (10–15 pages vs. original expectations), though FCDO supported the longer format due to high internal interest.
Need to clarify SIEL’s scope for EOI applicants, as some Round 1 questions were not addressable via SIEL’s quantitative evaluation methods.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Initial challenges in IPA’s understanding of FCDO’s project management requirements, resolved through experience and improved financial forecasting.
High demand for capacity-building activities (e.g., training sessions) required piloting new content and delivery methods, which were successfully received.
risk_materialization: Delays in learning agenda finalization due to FCDO’s internal review processes.
Budgetary uncertainty from ODA reductions materialized, affecting EOI proposal submissions.
Longer-than-planned procurement and subaward processes impacted early implementation.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Programme met most output milestones and over-performed on outcome indicators despite delays. Budget execution was on track, though administrative processes (e.g., IPA-J-PAL subaward) took longer than planned. Financial forecasting and reporting expected to improve in the next year.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: SIEL demonstrated strong value for money by exceeding outcome targets and delivering high-demand capacity-building activities (e.g., training sessions with positive feedback). The programme’s adaptive approach (e.g., promoting pilot studies) mitigated risks from ODA budget cuts, ensuring continued relevance.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Initial challenges in financial management (e.g., delays in subawarding) were addressed through improved understanding of FCDO requirements. The programme plans to enhance financial reporting by including outturn cost data by activity (e.g., learning agendas, EOI rounds).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was maintained through adaptive measures (e.g., extending timelines for learning agendas instead of rushing production). The EOI process, though time-consuming, provided learning to streamline future rounds.

key_delivery_lessons: Latent demand for impact evaluations exists within FCDO, as evidenced by 13 EOI applications, but budgetary uncertainty can hinder proposal submission.
Learning agendas require iterative development to align with evolving FCDO priorities, necessitating flexibility in timelines.
Pilot and nimble studies are valuable in budget-constrained environments and should be promoted more actively.
successful_delivery_practices: Quarterly reflection sessions to adjust logframe targets and maintain relevance.
High-engagement motivator activities (e.g., conferences, Nobel laureate launch event) successfully generated interest in SIEL’s work.
Collaborative development of learning agendas with FCDO staff and external experts ensured relevance and buy-in.
Positive feedback from capacity-building training sessions indicated effective delivery and high demand.
management_adaptations_made: Introduction of quarterly reflection sessions to sense-check logframe targets.
Extension of timelines for learning agendas to align with FCDO’s post-election priorities.
Modification of EOI outreach materials to clarify SIEL’s evaluation methods and scope.
innovations_attempted: First-time implementation of an EOI process tailored to FCDO-supported programmes.
Development of "learning agendas" as concise research question sets to guide evaluative work.
Piloting of new capacity-building content and delivery methods (e.g., "Impact Evaluation 101" course).
Evidence Use Diagnostic to assess evaluative capacity and barriers to evidence uptake in FCDO.
forward_recommendations: Review the logframe quarterly to ensure alignment with shifting FCDO priorities.
Promote quicker, less expensive pilot studies to mitigate budgetary uncertainties.
Explore evaluation opportunities in non-ODA areas (e.g., behavioural nudges, multilateral spend).
Continue nurturing the collegiate partnership with IPA and J-PAL through regular engagement activities.
Improve financial forecasting and reporting by including outturn cost data by activity.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective: planned risks (e.g., delays in learning agenda reviews) materialized but were mitigated through adaptive measures (e.g., timeline extensions). New risks (e.g., ODA budget cuts) were addressed by promoting flexible evaluation options. Quarterly reflection sessions will enhance proactive risk management.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: SIEL’s capacity-building activities (e.g., training sessions, conferences) reached a broad audience within FCDO and external stakeholders, with high engagement and positive feedback. The EOI process engaged 13 FCDO-supported programmes across priority areas, though two withdrew due to budgetary uncertainty.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Learning agendas (e.g., Humanitarian, Conflict) were developed in consultation with FCDO staff and are intended to directly inform policy design. The Evidence Use Diagnostic stimulated internal conversations on evaluative capacity, laying groundwork for Evidence Use Plans in 2025/6.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Training sessions and motivator activities (e.g., conferences, online drop-ins) generated strong demand and positive feedback, indicating effective capacity building.
