output_1.title: Investment activities: Impact investment facilities created and financed

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: FCDO established Prospero Zambia as a special purpose vehicle to implement PEPZ II. The Policy and Learning Support (PLS) function, originally planned to sit alongside Prospero, was delayed for a second year due to FCDO funding constraints. Prospero became the primary implementing partner, with TMEA supporting trade and logistics.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Prospero exceeded all adjusted output and outcome targets for the year, despite budget reductions and logframe revisions. The programme demonstrated strong performance in investment facilitation (8x target) and climate finance mobilization (507% over-achievement). However, gender targets for women-owned businesses were missed (369 vs. 456 target), reflecting structural challenges in Zambia’s SME sector.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Significant management attention was devoted to strengthening Prospero’s governance, internal policies, systems, and fraud risk mitigation, with FCDO providing additional funds for these improvements. Coordination with line ministries (Agriculture, Mining, Tourism, MSME, Green Economy) remained a work in progress, requiring further engagement to secure buy-in and alignment with government priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between Prospero, TMEA, and other UK-funded interventions (e.g., FSDZ, FSDA) was identified as needing improvement to maximize synergies and value for money (VFM). A review of UK-funded SME support in Zambia was recommended to ensure complementarity and alignment with the UK-Zambia Green Growth Compact.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO provided heightened oversight to Prospero, including funding for internal system improvements and fraud risk mitigation. Oversight was more intensive than originally planned due to budget constraints and external risks (e.g., COVID-19, currency volatility).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by adjusting targets downward mid-year due to budget reductions and revising the theory of change. Prospero also adapted to FCDO’s increased focus on climate change by building new partnerships and an investment pipeline for green businesses.
adaptive_management_examples: Adjusted output and outcome targets mid-year in response to budget cuts, while still over-achieving the revised targets.
Shifted focus to climate-smart investments, mobilizing £3.8m in private funds for climate change (507% over target).
Revised gender targets from 50% to 30% to reflect Zambia’s male-dominated SME sector while maintaining ambition.
Exited the Prospero Debt Facility (PDF) due to low uptake and reallocated resources to the International Climate Finance (ICF) facility.

main_implementation_challenges: Lower-than-expected budget from FCDO Zambia, limiting the number of activities undertaken.
Volatility and fluctuation of the Zambian kwacha, which constrained private and public sector investment.
Ongoing impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on SMEs and programme partners.
Delayed implementation of the Policy and Learning Support (PLS) facility due to FCDO funding constraints.
Structural challenges in reaching gender targets, given the male-dominated nature of Zambian SME ownership and employment.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic negatively impacted SMEs and investor confidence, though co-operating partners (EU, USAID, World Bank) scaled up relief investments, offsetting some commercial investment scarcity.
Currency volatility (kwacha fluctuation) limited investment and increased costs for businesses.
Political transition in August 2021 improved investor perceptions and expectations for regulatory reforms, creating a more favorable environment for PEPZ II.
contextual_constraints_new: The male-dominated structure of Zambian SMEs made it difficult to meet original gender targets (50% women-owned businesses), requiring a downward revision to 30%.
Limited uptake of the Prospero Debt Facility (PDF) by target enterprises, leading to an exit from the PDF portfolio.
Increased competition for SME support from other donors (e.g., EU, USAID) required Prospero to differentiate its value proposition.
partner_relationship_issues: Prospero faced challenges in securing buy-in from line ministries (e.g., Agriculture, Mining, Tourism) for its interventions, requiring more systematic engagement.
Coordination with TMEA and other UK-funded programmes (e.g., FSDZ, FSDA) was suboptimal, leading to recommendations for a cross-programme review to maximize synergies.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Prospero required additional FCDO funding to strengthen internal governance, systems, and fraud mitigation, indicating initial capacity gaps.
Limited capacity within Prospero to fully integrate gender and safeguarding targets, necessitating the hire of a social development consultant.
risk_materialization: Budget reductions materialized as a major risk, limiting activity levels and requiring target adjustments.
Currency volatility and COVID-19 impacts materialized as expected, though the political transition partially mitigated investor concerns.
Fraud risks were identified, prompting FCDO to fund improvements in Prospero’s internal controls.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme operated with a lower-than-planned budget from FCDO Zambia, which constrained activity levels. Despite this, Prospero over-achieved on revised financial targets, demonstrating efficient budget execution. For example, £1.011m was invested into financial facilities (101.1% of the £1m target), and £3.8m in private climate finance was mobilized (507% of the £750k target).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: The programme demonstrated strong VFM, with outputs and outcomes significantly exceeding conservative targets. Prospero facilitated £13m in investments (8x the £1.5m target), including £800k raised by Good Nature Agro, £7.8m by Prospero-supported SMEs, and £5m by Seba Foods. Cost efficiency was high, as evidenced by the over-achievement of targets despite budget cuts. However, a cross-programme review was recommended to ensure VFM is maximized across all UK-funded SME interventions in Zambia.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by Prospero was assessed as strong, with FCDO providing additional funds to enhance internal policies, systems, and fraud risk mitigation. The programme’s ability to over-achieve financial targets despite budget constraints suggests robust financial controls and adaptive management.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was high, as demonstrated by the programme’s ability to mobilize significantly more private finance than targeted (e.g., 573% over-achievement for investment facilitated and 507% for climate finance). The conservative initial targets, revised downward due to COVID-19, were easily surpassed, indicating that costs per outcome were lower than planned.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized from unexpected sources, including COVID-19 relief and investments from cooperating partners (e.g., EU, USAID, World Bank, SNV, Finland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs). This offset some of the scarcity of commercial investment and contributed to the programme’s over-achievement.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: The volatility of the Zambian kwacha against major currencies negatively impacted investment levels and increased costs for businesses, though the programme adapted by focusing on climate-smart and high-impact sectors.

key_delivery_lessons: Conservative target-setting can lead to significant over-achievement but may also indicate that targets could be more ambitious.
Flexibility in adjusting targets and delivery models (e.g., exiting the PDF, focusing on ICF) is critical for adapting to budget constraints and external shocks.
Strong coordination with government ministries and other UK-funded programmes is essential for maximizing impact and VFM, but requires dedicated effort and resources.
Gender and safeguarding targets must be realistic and contextually grounded, with adaptive strategies to address structural barriers in male-dominated sectors.
successful_delivery_practices: Prospero’s use of returnable capital facilities (e.g., ICF) to catalyze private investment in climate-smart SMEs was highly effective, mobilizing 507% of the targeted climate finance.
The programme’s ability to leverage co-funding from other donors (e.g., EU, USAID) to offset budget constraints and commercial investment scarcity.
Strengthening internal governance and fraud mitigation systems with FCDO support improved financial management and risk resilience.
Building partnerships with climate-focused investors and aligning with government priorities (e.g., Green Growth Compact) enhanced programme relevance and impact.
management_adaptations_made: Adjusted output and outcome targets mid-year in response to budget cuts, while still achieving strong results.
Revised gender targets from 50% to 30% to reflect the reality of Zambia’s SME sector, while maintaining ambition through targeted interventions.
Exited the underperforming Prospero Debt Facility (PDF) and reallocated resources to the higher-impact International Climate Finance (ICF) facility.
Increased focus on climate change alignment, building new partnerships and an investment pipeline for green businesses.
innovations_attempted: Development of climate-smart investment products, such as the ICF facility, which mobilized £3.8m in private funds for climate mitigation and adaptation.
Use of a social development consultant to improve gender integration and safeguarding, with revised targets and strategies.
Exploration of new interventions in the mining services and light manufacturing sectors, leveraging opportunities from FQM’s $1.35bn investment in Zambia.
previous_recommendations_progress: Progress was made on strengthening advocacy and influencing work, though further improvement is needed, particularly in engaging line ministries and aligning with government priorities.
The recommendation to establish the Policy and Learning Support (PLS) facility remained unfulfilled due to FCDO funding constraints, though it was reiterated as a priority for 2022.
Gender and safeguarding targets were adjusted and partially met, with ongoing efforts to improve performance in these areas.
forward_recommendations: FCDO should conduct a review of all UK-funded SME support in Zambia to ensure complementarity, maximize synergies, and align with the UK-Zambia Green Growth Compact by December 2022.
Fund and implement the Policy and Learning Support (PLS) facility by October 2022, as originally envisaged in the business case, to strengthen evidence-based interventions and M&E processes.
Refine the logframe to reflect greater ambition for Prospero, TMEA, and PLS contributions, and include new interventions funded under PEPZ II by September 2022.
Increase efforts to meet gender and safeguarding targets, including hiring a social development consultant and revising strategies to better serve women-owned businesses.
Strengthen advocacy and influencing work by building relationships with key ministries (Agriculture, Mining, Tourism, MSME, Green Economy) to secure buy-in and alignment with government priorities.
Explore new climate-smart interventions in the mining services and light manufacturing sectors, leveraging opportunities from recent investments (e.g., FQM’s $1.35bn commitment).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective. While some risks materialized (e.g., budget cuts, COVID-19, currency volatility), the programme adapted well by revising targets, focusing on high-impact areas (e.g., climate finance), and strengthening internal controls. However, the delayed implementation of the PLS facility and challenges in meeting gender targets highlight areas where risk mitigation could be improved. The programme’s ability to over-achieve despite risks suggests a resilient approach, though proactive risk management (e.g., earlier PLS funding) could have further enhanced performance.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: The programme facilitated investments supporting SMEs across food and agriculture, tourism, and mining services sectors. Specific examples include: 6 SMEs received £641,000 from the International Climate Finance (ICF) facility; 13 SMEs received £210,000 in debt relief financing; and 800+ jobs were created or sustained (623 created, 309 of which were women; 913 sustained, though women-held jobs fell short at 369 vs. 456 target). The programme reached fewer women-owned businesses than targeted, reflecting structural barriers in Zambia’s economy.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: The programme contributed to improving the investment environment in Zambia, particularly through its alignment with the UK-Zambia Green Growth Compact and engagement with line ministries (e.g., Agriculture, Green Economy). The election of a new government in August 2021 improved investor perceptions, and Prospero’s work supported this positive trajectory. However, policy influence remains a work in progress, with recommendations to strengthen advocacy and ministerial engagement.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Prospero strengthened the capacity of SMEs to access finance and adopt climate-smart practices. For example, Diamond Touch (a cashew processing SME) received funding to purchase a 1mt/day processing plant, which will boost incomes for smallholder farmers and contribute to afforestation (45,000 trees planted over 3 years). The programme also built the capacity of financial intermediaries (e.g., ZICB) to disburse climate finance. However, capacity-building efforts for women-owned businesses were limited by structural challenges.

unintended_consequences.description: The programme’s focus on climate-smart investments (e.g., ICF facility) unintentionally positioned Prospero as a leader in green finance in Zambia, attracting additional co-funding from donors like the EU and USAID. This enhanced the programme’s reputation and leverage.

The exit from the Prospero Debt Facility (PDF) due to low uptake may have left some SMEs without access to concessional debt, though resources were reallocated to higher-impact areas like climate finance. Additionally, the downward revision of gender targets, while realistic, risks normalizing lower ambition for women’s economic empowerment.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: The programme demonstrated scalable models in climate finance (e.g., ICF facility) and SME investment facilitation. The over-achievement of financial targets (e.g., £13m invested vs. £1.5m target) suggests that the approach can be replicated or expanded, particularly in high-potential sectors like agriculture and green manufacturing. However, scalability is constrained by Zambia’s broader economic challenges (e.g., currency volatility, male-dominated SME sector) and the need for continued donor coordination.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong performance in its second year, over-achieving on financial and investment targets despite budget constraints and external challenges. Prospero’s adaptive management, focus on climate-smart investments, and alignment with government priorities (e.g., Green Growth Compact) justify continuation. However, key improvements are needed, including funding the PLS facility, strengthening gender integration, and enhancing coordination with other UK-funded programmes. The political transition in Zambia has created a more favorable environment for private sector growth, further supporting the case for continuation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (implied by the "A" performance score and recommendations for continued funding, though explicit satisfaction levels are not stated)
planned_adaptations_future: Fund and implement the Policy and Learning Support (PLS) facility by October 2022 to strengthen evidence-based interventions and M&E.
Refine the logframe to reflect greater ambition, including contributions from TMEA, PLS, and other interventions under PEPZ II.
Adjust gender targets to 30% (from 50%) and implement targeted strategies to improve women’s access to finance and employment opportunities.
Conduct a review of UK-funded SME support in Zambia by December 2022 to ensure complementarity and maximize synergies.
Explore new climate-smart interventions in mining services and light manufacturing, leveraging opportunities like FQM’s $1.35bn investment.
Strengthen advocacy and influencing work by engaging key ministries (Agriculture, Mining, Tourism, MSME, Green Economy) to align with government priorities.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Kenya Devolution Programme

output_1.title: Intergovernmental relations support devolution

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The IGRTC (Inter-Governmental Relations Technical Committee) coordination framework was established with members appointed and inaugurated in July 2020. The Devolution Sector Working Group (DSWG) plan was implemented with technical assistance contracted by the World Bank within the State Department of Devolution.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted to COVID-19 challenges by supporting the development of a socio-economic recovery plan for counties, launched by the President in November 2020.
adaptive_management_examples: Support to the Council of Governors (CoG) in finalizing an assessment of COVID-19's impact on counties and developing a socio-economic recovery strategy, launched on 30 November 2020.
Utilization of existing IGRTC reports (e.g., on intergovernmental disputes and litigation costs) to inform current committee priorities.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 pandemic disrupted county operations, exposing gaps in health systems (infrastructure, financing, personnel) and reducing revenue generation due to lockdowns and curfews.
Legal disputes between national and county governments (e.g., 23 Acts of Parliament declared unconstitutional in October 2020 for bypassing Senate review).
Delays in disbursement of funds to counties due to parliamentary stalemates over revenue allocation bills.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 lockdowns (Nairobi, Mombasa, Kilifi, Kwale) and national curfews severely impacted county economies and service delivery.
School closures, business restrictions, and loss of livelihoods reduced county own-source revenue (OSR).
Judicial rulings (e.g., Supreme Court advisory on revenue bills) created both opportunities (clarity on devolution) and challenges (implementation delays).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for COVID-19 recovery planning at county level, requiring rapid programme adaptation.
Emergence of public interest litigation as a critical factor in devolution, necessitating programme support to the Senate and judiciary.
capacity_constraints_emerged: County health systems lacked capacity to respond to COVID-19 (infrastructure, financing, personnel).
Gaps in county coordination mechanisms (e.g., County Emergency Response Committees) required programme support.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 pandemic (unplanned risk) materialized, disrupting implementation and requiring reprioritization.
Political-legal risks materialized (e.g., unconstitutional acts, revenue disbursement delays).

key_delivery_lessons: COVID-19 recovery must be integrated into devolution support, with detailed milestones for 2021 (e.g., county socio-economic recovery plans).
Public interest litigation and judicial rulings are critical to resolving devolution disputes; programme should support the Senate and judiciary.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid adaptation to COVID-19 through support to the Council of Governors (CoG) and KIPPRA in developing a recovery strategy.
Leveraging existing IGRTC frameworks and reports to strengthen intergovernmental coordination.
management_adaptations_made: Inclusion of COVID-19 recovery milestones under Outputs 2 and 3 for 2021.
Planned support to the Senate (Output 1) to address legislative gaps exposed by judicial rulings.
innovations_attempted: Development of a socio-economic recovery strategy for counties, launched by the President in November 2020.
Use of County Emergency Response Committees (co-chaired by Governors and County Commissioners) as a coordination mechanism.
forward_recommendations: By March 2021, integrate COVID-19 recovery plans into Outputs 2 and 3 with specific milestones.
By March 2021, include Senate support activities under Output 1 to address devolution-related legal gaps.
Conduct Political Economy Analysis (PEA) to adapt to Kenya’s fast-changing political environment.

policy_influence_achieved: Judicial rulings (e.g., October 2020 declaration of 23 unconstitutional acts) clarified devolution frameworks, influenced by programme-supported IGRTC reports.
Presidential launch of the Counties Socio-Economic Re-engineering and Recovery Strategy (November 2020) demonstrates high-level uptake of programme outputs.
capacity_building_results: IGRTC secretariat supported to convene sessions and utilize technical reports (e.g., on intergovernmental disputes).
Council of Governors (CoG) coordination framework established, enabling COVID-19 impact assessment and recovery planning.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Judicial rulings (e.g., on Senate’s role) created unexpected momentum for devolution clarifications.
Negative: COVID-19 exposed systemic weaknesses in county health systems and revenue generation, requiring unplanned programme resources.

planned_adaptations_future: Integration of COVID-19 recovery milestones into 2021 workplans (Outputs 2 and 3).
Expanded support to the Senate and judiciary to address devolution-related legal challenges (Output 1).
Enhanced use of Political Economy Analysis (PEA) to guide adaptive management.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Innovative Methods and Metrics for Agriculture and Nutrition Actions Phase 2 (IMMANA 2)

output_1.title: IMMANA Competitive Research Grants to develop new and validate existing methods and metrics at the nexus of agriculture-food systems, nutrition, and health (ANH)

output_2.title: IMMANA Fellowships to support emerging leaders in ANH research

output_3.title: ANH Academy (synthesis and support centre, capacity strengthening, partnerships, and in-house research)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: LSHTM (lead) and Tufts University (fellowships) performed as expected; Gates Foundation co-funding partnership remained strong. ANH Academy grew to 9,600+ members across 145+ countries, exceeding engagement targets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Centralized management by LSHTM with Tufts University leading fellowships. Governance included annual ANH Academy Weeks, working groups, and synthesis activities. No major deviations from planned structure reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination through ANH Academy platform, which facilitated interdisciplinary collaboration, knowledge exchange (e.g., Learning Labs, Research Conferences), and policy uptake. Example: ANH2023 co-organized with Malawi government and LUANAR.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Quarterly financial monitoring and rigorous VfM criteria for sub-grants. Independent reviews conducted in Year 5 to assess integration of workstreams and MEL processes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to grantee feedback (e.g., demand for longer grant periods, post-grant uptake funds) and emerging priorities (e.g., plastics/circular economies research in response to global treaty negotiations).
adaptive_management_examples: Expanded ANH Academy activities (e.g., Training of Trainers for African/Asian lecturers, mentorship schemes for LMIC researchers) based on capacity-building needs.
Added research themes (e.g., mental health-nutrition links, plastics/health intersections) in response to stakeholder demands and global policy agendas.
Increased focus on equity and gender-transformative approaches in grant selection and working groups.

main_implementation_challenges: Integration of three workstreams (Grants, Fellowships, ANH Academy) into a cohesive network, particularly for capacity development.
Limited post-grant funds to support uptake/scaling of tools and methods by grantees.
Informal distribution of MEL responsibilities without a dedicated resource, leading to gaps in impact documentation.
contextual_constraints_new: Demand for longer grant periods (36 months) to allow sufficient time for dissemination and uptake.
Need for dedicated funds to bridge the gap between research completion and policy/practice adoption.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Overstretched staff managing MEL tasks without dedicated roles.
Grantees (especially in LMICs) required additional support for networking, data access, and capability building.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Administrative costs held steady over 5 years (Phase 1 and 2), with quarterly monitoring ensuring alignment with VfM criteria.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Costs for administering fellowships/grants minimized and stable. Sub-grant awards prioritize VfM.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Outputs maximized relative to budget: ANH Academy membership grew 25% YoY (7,700 to 9,600); 300+ publications in 8 years; 44 fellowships awarded. Digital engagement metrics (e.g., website users, social media followers) showed consistent growth.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: ANH Academy effectively connected donors with interdisciplinary research communities, fostering national communities of practice (e.g., Ag2Nut). Grantees produced policy-relevant outputs (e.g., 6 peer-reviewed publications in Year 5).

OQ’s diplomatic role proved critical for facilitating international engagement with Israel/PA.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: WB’s procurement for water/energy projects faced delays (e.g., Subcomponent 1.1 contracts signed March 2023 but works paused due to conflict). Emergency procurement (e.g., UNICEF-PWA fuel/hygiene kit contract) was accelerated. LSAPS (energy sector) disbursed $20m after PA endorsement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased from planned levels due to conflict. FCDO introduced quarterly progress checks and will update logframe in Q1 2025/26. Partners required to align 2025/26 workplans with revised ToC.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: High: £9m repurposed for Gaza relief; Tasdeer shifted to crisis-response lending; WB restructured energy/water projects. Flexibility enabled by pre-existing adaptive design but stretched by conflict scale.
adaptive_management_examples: WB’s March 2024 restructuring of water project to deliver emergency supplies via UNICEF-PWA contract (6,500 hygiene kits delivered by Nov 2024).
Tasdeer’s interest-free loan scheme for 700 displaced workers, launched in partnership with Palestinian Monetary Authority.
OQ’s development of technical non-papers endorsed by PA to facilitate international engagement on Gaza’s basic services resumption.
LSAPS disbursement ($20m) to incentivize private renewable energy investments in West Bank.
Pivot from long-term infrastructure (e.g., paused Subcomponents 1.1–1.4) to immediate relief while maintaining logframe milestones for post-conflict recovery.

main_implementation_challenges: Conflict in Gaza (86% GDP contraction in early 2024) and West Bank economic decline (35% GDP drop Q1 2024) disrupted all planned activities.
Breakdown of Israel-PA cooperation halted progress on movement/access reforms and joint infrastructure projects.
Supply chain disruptions (e.g., 5–10x price increases for basic commodities) impeded procurement and service delivery.
Data collection challenges due to inaccessible areas and partner capacity constraints in Gaza.
Restrictive Israeli policies (e.g., trade barriers, permit denials) limited trade facilitation and private sector interventions.
external_factors_impact: Gaza war (since Oct 2023) created humanitarian crisis, shifting focus from development to emergency relief.
West Bank economic contraction (22% GDP drop Q4 2023) reduced PA fiscal capacity and private sector resilience.
International donor fatigue and shifting priorities (e.g., Ukraine war) competed for attention/resources.
Climate change exacerbated water/energy stress, compounding conflict impacts on infrastructure.
contextual_constraints_new: Unprecedented scale of Gaza’s economic collapse (beyond original risk assessments).
PA’s fiscal crisis (public salary cuts, service reductions) undermined institutional capacity to implement reforms.
Emergence of new vulnerable groups (e.g., women-headed households, displaced workers) requiring targeted interventions.
Israeli restrictions on movement of goods/people blocked trade facilitation activities (e.g., Tasdeer’s cross-border initiatives).
Need for early recovery planning in Gaza (not anticipated in original design).
partner_relationship_issues: Initial lack of coordination between WB, OQ, and Tasdeer led to duplicated efforts (addressed in 2025 recommendations).
UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF) required rapid onboarding for emergency procurement, creating contractual delays.
PA’s reduced capacity strained partnerships (e.g., delayed approvals for WB’s water sector studies).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Local implementing partners (e.g., PWA, CMWU) overwhelmed by crisis response, delaying long-term projects.
FCDO’s limited in-country presence required reliance on partners for monitoring, reducing oversight quality.
Shortage of technical expertise (e.g., gender specialists, safeguards officers) to address conflict-induced vulnerabilities.
Tasdeer’s trade facilitation team redirected to crisis response, pausing planned customs reform activities.
risk_materialization: Political risk: Breakdown of Israel-PA cooperation (assumed in ToC as a medium-risk scenario).
Conflict risk: Gaza war exceeded "high" risk threshold, requiring full programme reprioritization.
Economic risk: PA fiscal collapse (2023–24) disrupted revenue-generation components (e.g., customs reforms).
Operational risk: Supply chain breakdowns (e.g., fuel shortages) halted infrastructure works.
Reputational risk: Perception of aid ineffectiveness due to limited access to Gaza.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Original budget: ~£60m (pre-extension). 2024 extension added £32m (total £91m) for 2.5 additional years.
2021: EBRD component closed early, reallocating funds to WB/OQ.
2024: £9m of WB water funds repurposed for Gaza emergency relief (UNICEF contract).
Disbursement rate accelerated for crisis response (e.g., $20m LSAPS released in 2024 vs. planned 2025).
Underspend in energy sector due to conflict-related contract delays (4 contracts worth $3.3m paused).
value_for_money_assessment: Adaptive design enabled VfM despite conflict: flexibility to reallocate resources to high-impact areas (e.g., Gaza relief).
WB water/energy projects: Restructuring maintained VfM by shifting from infrastructure to emergency supplies.
OQ: Judged "good VfM" due to unique diplomatic role and low-cost, high-impact facilitation (e.g., non-papers for basic services resumption).
Tasdeer: VfM demonstrated through job creation (359 workers hired) and trade barrier reductions (8 new solutions adopted).
Cost efficiency challenged by conflict premiums (e.g., 5–10x commodity price increases) but mitigated by bulk procurement (e.g., hygiene kits).
financial_management_quality: WB: Satisfactory safeguards compliance pre-conflict; emergency procurement (UNICEF contract) followed accelerated but audited processes.
OQ: Strong financial controls with transparent staffing costs (main cost driver).
Tasdeer: Robust tracking of job creation (359 workers) and customs revenue impacts (3 new PA functions adopted).
FCDO: Introduced quarterly financial reviews in 2024 to monitor repurposed funds.
Audit findings: No major issues reported, but 2024 conflict disrupted standard financial reporting cycles.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Emergency relief: £9m repurposed for Gaza reached 6,500+ households (hygiene kits) at ~£1,385/household (below regional benchmarks).
LSAPS: $20m leveraged ~$50m in private renewable energy investments (2.5x multiplier).
Tasdeer’s loan scheme: £1.2m created 700 jobs (~£1,714/job, competitive for crisis contexts).
OQ’s diplomatic outputs achieved at low cost (staffing-focused model).
Infrastructure delays (e.g., water networks) increased unit costs by 15–20% due to conflict-related pauses.
co_funding_materialization: KFAED co-funded water infrastructure (Subcomponents 1.1–1.2), but conflict delayed disbursements.
Planned PA co-financing for customs reforms (Tasdeer) reduced due to fiscal crisis (only 60% materialized in 2024).
Private sector co-funding for renewable energy (via LSAPS) exceeded targets by 30% ($50m vs. $38m planned).
International community contributions to basic services resumption (OQ-facilitated) supplemented SEED funds.
currency_exchange_impacts: Shekel depreciation (5% vs. GBP in 2023) reduced local purchasing power for PA salaries and imports.
WB’s $9m emergency procurement benefited from GBP/USD strength (1.25 exchange rate in Q4 2024).
Tasdeer’s trade facilitation activities faced volatility in customs revenue collections (denominated in shekels).

key_delivery_lessons: Adaptive programming is essential in fragile contexts: SEED’s pre-existing flexibility enabled rapid crisis response.
Local partnerships (e.g., PWA, CMWU) are critical for legitimacy but require capacity support during shocks.
Diplomatic leverage (OQ’s role) can unlock progress where technical programming stalls.
Data collection systems must be conflict-resilient (e.g., quarterly checks introduced in 2024).
Cross-partner coordination is not automatic; requires active FCDO facilitation (lesson from 2024 duplication).
successful_delivery_practices: WB’s use of MDTFs allowed rapid reallocation of funds to emergency needs.
Tasdeer’s partnership with Palestinian Monetary Authority enabled crisis-targeted financial products.
OQ’s technical non-papers provided neutral ground for Israel-PA dialogue.
UNICEF’s pre-existing frameworks accelerated procurement of relief supplies.
FCDO’s light-touch oversight balanced accountability with partner autonomy during crisis.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from annual to quarterly progress reviews (2024).
Introduction of logframe updates tied to ToC revisions (planned Q1 2025/26).
Partner workplans now require cross-referencing to avoid duplication (2025 requirement).
Risk management focus expanded from financial to include political/diplomatic risks.
Gender and safeguards monitoring integrated into emergency response (e.g., female-headed household targeting).
innovations_attempted: LSAPS mechanism to de-risk private renewable energy investments in West Bank.
Interest-free loan scheme for displaced workers (Tasdeer/Palestinian Monetary Authority).
Real-time trade flow monitoring (Tasdeer/FPCCIA) to inform crisis response.
Repurposing infrastructure funds for emergency relief while maintaining logframe milestones.
Use of OQ’s diplomatic convening power to align international community behind basic services resumption.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2023 recommendation to strengthen PA customs capacity: Partially achieved (3 new functions adopted, but fiscal crisis limited progress).
2022 call for gender mainstreaming: Advanced in energy sector (female engineers hired, solar for women-headed households).
2021 risk of over-reliance on WB: Mitigated by diversifying to OQ/Tasdeer for crisis response.
2020 trade facilitation targets: Exceeded in West Bank (8 new solutions) but stalled in Gaza due to access restrictions.
2019 safeguards compliance: Maintained pre-conflict; emergency procurement introduced new audit trails.

forward_recommendations.action: Update Theory of Change (ToC) by June 2025 to reflect conflict realities and extension scope.
Revise logframe in Q1 2025/26 with conflict-sensitive indicators and milestones.
Strengthen partner coordination via joint workplans and complementary activity mapping.
Develop early recovery plan for Gaza, conditional on access improvements.
Enhance data collection methods (e.g., remote monitoring, partner capacity building).
Advocate for Israel-PA policy dialogue on economic issues (e.g., trade, customs).
Pilot climate-resilient interventions (e.g., solar microgrids, water recycling) in West Bank.

risk_management_effectiveness: Strengths: Pre-existing adaptive design allowed rapid repurposing of funds. Political risks (Israel-PA breakdown) were partially mitigated by OQ’s diplomatic role.
Weaknesses: Original risk register underestimated conflict scale (e.g., Gaza’s 86% GDP contraction). Safeguards monitoring lagged during emergency phase.
Lessons: Risk management must include scenario planning for total collapse of operating environment. Partners need shared risk frameworks.
Adaptations: Risk register expanded to include "catastrophic" conflict scenarios; quarterly risk reviews introduced.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 6,500 households (hygiene kits) + ongoing fuel/water tank deliveries (contract extended to Dec 2025).
$20m LSAPS leveraged $50m private investments in renewables; solar expanded to female-headed households.
700 workers supported via loans; 359 new jobs created; 8 trade barriers reduced.
3 new revenue administration functions adopted; fiscal crisis limited broader reforms.

policy_influence_achieved: OQ-facilitated non-papers influenced international community’s engagement on Gaza basic services resumption.
Tasdeer’s trade monitoring reports adopted by PA Ministries for policy adjustments.
WB’s water sector studies (e.g., National Water Policy) endorsed by PA but implementation paused due to conflict.
LSAPS model cited in PA’s 2024 Energy Strategy as a template for private sector engagement.
capacity_building_results: PWA/CMWU: Strengthened bulk water management via BWSU-CMWU agreement (signed Aug 2024).
PA Customs: 3 new functions (VAT/excise administration) operationalized, but staff turnover remains high.
Private sector: 700 workers trained/employed via Tasdeer’s loan scheme; 150 women-headed households received solar support.
OQ: Enhanced PA’s analytical capacity on clearance revenues (used in 2024 budget negotiations with Israel).
Weaknesses: Capacity gains risk erosion without sustained PA fiscal stability.

unintended_consequences.description: Tasdeer’s loan scheme unintentionally supported informal sector businesses (e.g., home-based food production), boosting women’s economic participation.
OQ’s diplomatic role expanded beyond mandate, creating new channels for Israel-PA technical dialogue on water/energy.
Repurposing funds for Gaza relief delayed West Bank water infrastructure, exacerbating regional disparities.
Emergency focus reduced attention on long-term safeguards (e.g., environmental assessments for solar projects).

scalability_evidence.evidence: $20m pilot leveraged $50m private investment; model replicable in other fragile contexts with donor guarantees.
Successful for 700 workers but requires PA regulatory reforms to scale (e.g., collateral rules).
Adopted by EU and US for Gaza reconstruction planning; template for neutral technical dialogue.
Gaza-specific; requires political solutions for cross-border water management.

continuation_rationale: Conflict has exacerbated OPTs’ economic collapse (35% GDP decline in 2024), creating urgent need for stabilisation support.
SEED’s adaptive track record demonstrates ability to deliver in crisis (e.g., Gaza relief, West Bank job creation).
Partners (WB, OQ, Tasdeer) have strong local trust and technical capacity to navigate political constraints.
Extension aligns with UK’s two-state solution objectives by preserving PA institutions and economic viability.
Risk of programme closure would remove critical lifeline for Palestinians and undermine UK influence in OPTs.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium (conditional on ceasefire and improved access to Gaza).
delivery_model_sustainability: Strengths: Adaptive design, trusted partners, and diplomatic leverage (OQ) provide resilience.
Weaknesses: Over-reliance on WB/OQ for implementation; PA fiscal crisis threatens long-term ownership.
Risks: Further conflict escalation could halt operations; donor fatigue may limit co-funding.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (despite challenges, SEED is viewed as a "flagship" adaptive programme in FCDO’s OPTs portfolio).
planned_adaptations_future: Shift from emergency relief to early recovery in Gaza (conditional on access).
Expand climate-resilient interventions (e.g., solar microgrids, water recycling) in West Bank.
Deepened focus on marginalized groups (women, displaced workers) via targeted financial products.
Strengthened political economy analysis to inform programming in volatile context.
Pilot new partnerships (e.g., with Palestinian private sector associations) for job creation.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Low Carbon Development Initiative (LCDI) Phase 2

output_1.title: LCDI Technical Assistance (TA) products that support LCD adoption with national ministries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from planning (LCDI1) to practical implementation (LCDI2) with focus on institutional capacity building, policy innovation, and coalition development. Consortium partners (OPML, INDEF, ICLEI, etc.) were procured but underutilized in early implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: OPML demonstrated technical capabilities but consortium partners were not effectively integrated during initial period. Political economy analysis proved more critical than anticipated, requiring deeper operationalization.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Workplan, results framework, and Theory of Change required refinement. Middle management gaps during inception phase led to overstretch of team leader, delaying strategic leadership. New team leader recruited in September 2024 to address gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Formal bilateral cooperation established via Technical Agreement with Bappenas (October 2023). Coordination with provincial governments expanded but constrained by regional elections and bureaucratic timelines. Stakeholder alignment (Bappenas, MoHA, MoEF, MOF) requires strengthening.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Commercial procurement completed for Project Management Unit (OPML consortium, August 2023) and Evaluation & Monitoring Unit (NIRAS, operational <6 months). NIRAS-FCDO relationship established but monitoring/learning value-add remains underdeveloped.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO tracked recommendations closely but concerns persist about delayed team maturation and capability sourcing. Evaluation and Monitoring Unit (EMU) operational but limited time to demonstrate impact.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Adaptive management required due to political transitions (2024 elections) and provincial data delays. Programme adjusted timelines for draft outputs (e.g., 5/8 documents drafted by Sept 2024 vs. March 2025 targets).
adaptive_management_examples: Aligned technical assistance timelines with Indonesia’s planning bureaucracy (e.g., RPJMN 2025–2045 draft integration).
Paused activities in two provinces during regional elections to await new administrations.
Refined Theory of Change and results framework mid-implementation to improve outcome tracking.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed data provision from provinces, impacting draft output finalization.
Underutilization of consortium partners’ technical expertise and networks.
Over-reliance on short-term roles during inception, leading to weak Theory of Change and workplan deliverables.
Political transitions (2024 national/sub-national elections) disrupted provincial engagement.
Bureaucratic alignment with Indonesia’s planning cycles (e.g., RPJMN timelines) caused scheduling constraints.
external_factors_impact: Regional elections in pilot provinces halted activities until new administrations took office.
Need to align with Indonesia’s 5-year/20-year planning cycles (RPJMN/RPJPN) affected output timelines.
Collaboration with GIZ on Circular Economy Roadmap required coordination across donor-funded initiatives.
contextual_constraints_new: Greater-than-anticipated need for political economy analysis at sub-national level.
Provincial capacity limitations in data collection/analysis for Green Economy Index.
Slower-than-expected progress on enacting Ministerial Regulation for Green Economy Index.
partner_relationship_issues: Consortium partners (e.g., INDEF, ICLEI) were not fully integrated into core delivery, limiting their contribution.
Delays in provincial workplans due to election-related transitions and Bappenas’ prioritization shifts.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Lack of workstream leadership during inception weakened key deliverables (e.g., Theory of Change).
Team leader overstretch reduced time for strategic relationship-building with senior stakeholders.
GEDSI mainstreaming lagged despite technically rigorous analysis.
risk_materialization: Risk of delayed provincial engagement due to elections (materialized).
Risk of underutilized consortium expertise (materialized).
Risk of bureaucratic misalignment with planning cycles (materialized, mitigated via timeline adjustments).

budget_execution_vs_plan.inception_cost: 82% of contracted cost (actual expenses, no quality reduction).
budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: Consultancy fees 11.09% below initial benchmarks, indicating cost efficiency.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Achieved: Costs below benchmarks; inception phase delivered at 82% of budget without quality compromise.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Partial: Staffing gaps and short-term roles weakened inception deliverables (e.g., Theory of Change). Overstretch of team leader reduced strategic focus. Recent recruitment shows improvement.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Not yet assessable: VfM framework (4E model) under development by NIRAS. Technical output quality deemed adequate by Bappenas but lacks quantitative metrics.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Not yet assessable: GEDSI analysis completed but mainstreaming into delivery remains limited.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Adequate: Cost controls effective (e.g., 11.09% below benchmarks) but delays in VfM framework development raise concerns about long-term tracking.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High: Consultancy fees under benchmark; inception phase delivered efficiently. Efficiency risks persist due to staffing instability.

key_delivery_lessons: Political economy analysis must be routinely integrated, especially at sub-national level.
Consortium partners require clearer integration pathways to leverage their technical/network strengths.
Alignment with Indonesia’s planning cycles (RPJMN/RPJPN) is critical but requires flexible timelines.
Middle management roles are essential to prevent team leader overstretch and ensure strategic focus.
successful_delivery_practices: Systems dynamics modelling expertise enabled integration of Green Economy Index into RPJPN 2025–2045.
Collaboration with GIZ on Circular Economy Roadmap demonstrated effective donor coordination.
Technical Agreement with Bappenas (October 2023) formalized bilateral cooperation.
management_adaptations_made: Refined workplan and results framework to improve outcome tracking.
Recruited new team leader (September 2024) to address leadership gaps.
Adjusted provincial activity timelines to accommodate election transitions.
innovations_attempted: Pilot provinces workplan developed to test sub-national LCD integration approaches.
AKSARA platform roadmap initiated to improve data transparency for LCD monitoring.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Strengthen collaboration with provincial governments for Green Economy Index data quality.
previous_recommendations_progress.status: Partially implemented: TA provided but limited by elections and workplan delays.
previous_recommendations_progress.evidence: Data quality improved conditionally; training programs initiated.

forward_recommendations.action: Strengthen stakeholder coordination via formal technical committee meetings (Bappenas, MoHA, MoEF, MOF).
Enhance data quality through capacity-building for national/provincial governments (training workshops, TA).

Integrate GEDSI recommendations into core delivery mechanisms.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partial: Planned risks (e.g., political transitions, data delays) materialized but were mitigated via adaptive management. Proactive risk management weakened by delayed VfM framework and underutilized consortium expertise.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.national_level: Technical assistance contributed to 2 completed documents (Green Economy Index integrated into RPJPN 2025–2045; Circular Economy Roadmap launched at Green Economy Expo 2024 and integrated into draft RPJMN 2025–2029).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.provincial_level: 5 draft documents developed for 7 provinces (aligned with RPJMN targets) but finalization delayed by data/bureaucratic constraints.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Collaboration with GIZ and other donors expanded reach of circular economy analytics.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: Medium: Progress on national integration (e.g., RPJPN/RPJMN) is strong, but provincial implementation lags due to external constraints. Outputs remain largely in draft form.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Medium: Technical contributions to RPJPN/RPJMN are tangible but lack quantitative impact data. Bappenas’ qualitative endorsement suggests relevance.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium: National-level integration (e.g., Green Economy Index in RPJPN) has high potential for sustainability, but provincial adoption depends on post-election stability and capacity-building.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: High: Green Economy Index and Circular Economy Roadmap incorporated into national planning documents (RPJPN 2025–2045, RPJMN 2025–2029).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Partial: Technical assistance improved data analytics for national outputs, but provincial capacity remains limited. GEDSI analysis completed but not yet mainstreamed.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Collaboration with GIZ on Circular Economy Roadmap created synergies beyond original scope.
Negative: Election-related pauses in provinces delayed sub-national progress.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Potential: National integration of LCD targets (RPJPN/RPJMN) provides a model for other sectors, but provincial scalability hinges on data systems and political commitment.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme remains relevant to Indonesia’s NDC targets and Vision 2045. National-level achievements (e.g., RPJPN integration) demonstrate effectiveness, while provincial delays are addressable with adaptive management. Complements FCDO’s broader climate portfolio in Indonesia.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High: Strong national buy-in (Bappenas) and alignment with planning cycles, but success depends on resolving provincial implementation bottlenecks and consortium utilization.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Current model is viable but requires stronger consortium integration, VfM tracking, and sub-national political engagement to ensure long-term sustainability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate: Confident in national-level progress but concerned about provincial delays and team maturation. Satisfaction contingent on addressing AR recommendations.
planned_adaptations_future: Formalize stakeholder coordination mechanisms (e.g., technical committees).
Accelerate provincial capacity-building post-elections.
Operationalize VfM framework to track effectiveness/equity.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (African Development Bank - AfDB) via General Capital Increase (GCI-VII)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £110m paid-in capital + £1.7bn callable capital (contingent liability); intended to boost AfDB lending capacity from ~$8bn/year (2020) to >$11bn/year by 2030
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Shareholder capital contributions (paid-in + callable) to AfDB’s non-concessional window, enabling near-market-rate lending to middle-income African countries and private sector. UK shareholding originally planned to increase to **1.776%** via new share purchases (2020–2027).
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium – Contingent on AfDB’s capital adequacy framework and shareholder agreements, with callable capital as a backstop mechanism.

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch oversight via FCDO’s multilateral team, with governance embedded in AfDB’s existing Board/Shareholder structures. UK influence proportional to shareholding (originally 1.776%).
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Annual – Through AfDB’s Annual Development Effectiveness Review (ADER) and FCDO’s Annual Review process. Policy engagement during replenishment negotiations.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Collective shareholder decision-making via AfDB Board; UK votes aligned with shareholding. Strategic decisions (e.g., capital increases) require shareholder consensus.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single multilateral partner (AfDB) with no sub-contracted implementers. AfDB acts as sole delivery vehicle for UK’s capital contribution.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral Development Bank (AfDB)
partner_selection_baseline.partner_roles_planned: AfDB responsible for all lending operations, project implementation, and results delivery. FCDO’s role limited to capital contribution, policy dialogue, and performance monitoring.
partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award – UK’s contribution tied to AfDB’s GCI-VII replenishment agreement (2019).

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (AfDB) via GCI-VII (unchanged)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £110m paid-in capital + £1.7bn callable capital (unchanged nominal value), but **lending capacity revised downward** due to COVID-19 and credit rating constraints. Actual lending dropped from $7bn (2019) to $3.6bn (2020), recovering to $4.9bn (2022) – **below pre-pandemic projections of $7bn/year**. UK shareholding increased to **1.865%** (vs. planned 1.776%) via additional share purchases in 2022.
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Capital contributions flowed as planned, but AfDB **reoriented lending toward COVID-19 crisis response** (2020–2021) and later to food security post-Ukraine war. Callable capital remained uncalled but used as a credit rating backstop.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Medium – Utilized to adapt to crises (COVID-19, Ukraine war) but constrained by AfDB’s AAA credit rating requirements. Temporary callable capital sought from AAA shareholders to stabilize operations.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Light-touch oversight maintained, but **FCDO engagement intensified** to address underperformance in results frameworks and logframe revisions. UK’s increased shareholding (1.865%) slightly enhanced voting influence.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Annual (unchanged), but **ad-hoc policy dialogue increased** to address COVID-19 impacts, target realism, and capital adequacy reforms (e.g., G20 recommendations).
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Unchanged (shareholder consensus), but **FCDO pushed for logframe revisions** and more realistic target-setting in AfDB’s Results Measurement Framework (RMF).

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Single multilateral partner (AfDB) unchanged. No sub-partners added or removed.
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral Development Bank (AfDB) – no change.
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: AfDB’s role expanded to **crisis response lending** (COVID-19, Ukraine war food security) while maintaining core High-5 Agenda priorities. FCDO’s role evolved to include **more active performance monitoring and logframe challenges**.

substantive_changes_made: AfDB **reallocated lending priorities** from long-term development to crisis response (COVID-19 in 2020–2021; food security post-Ukraine war 2022).
UK **increased shareholding to 1.865%** (from planned 1.776%) via additional share purchases in 2022, enhancing influence.
Lending scale **reduced from projected $11bn/year (2030) to ~$7bn/year (2023)** due to credit rating constraints and external shocks.
FCDO **pushed for revisions to AfDB’s Results Measurement Framework (RMF)** to address overambitious targets, though formal changes were delayed until 2023.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Nominal budget unchanged (£110m + £1.7bn), but **effective lending capacity reduced by ~30%** (from $11bn to $7bn/year projections) due to external shocks.
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope unchanged, but **sectoral focus shifted** to crisis mitigation (health, food security) at the expense of long-term infrastructure/High-5 targets.
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: No shift in funding modality (remained multilateral via AfDB), but **temporary reliance on callable capital** to maintain credit rating.

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Informal updates to **assumptions about external shocks** (COVID-19, Ukraine war) and AfDB’s capacity to deliver under crisis conditions, but no formal ToC revision.

management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Oversight intensity **increased informally** via ad-hoc FCDO-AfDB dialogues on RMF revisions and crisis response, but no structural changes.

activity_only_adjustments: AfDB **streamlined projects** under High-5 Agenda to improve efficiency (e.g., energy, MSME support).
Increased focus on **knowledge-sharing events** to address human capital gaps.

contextual_shocks: **COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021)**: Led to lending reductions, remote operations, and crisis-response reorientation.
**Ukraine war (2022)**: Triggered food security focus and further strain on lending capacity.
**Credit rating constraints**: AfDB reduced lending to maintain AAA rating, requiring temporary callable capital.
performance_issues: Underperformance against **overambitious RMF targets** (e.g., electricity connections, MSME turnover) exposed need for logframe revisions.
IDEV evaluation (2022) flagged **misalignment between ambitions and resources**.
learning_insights: AfDB’s **mid-term review of New Deal on Energy for Africa (NDEA)** identified gaps in electricity access targets.
FCDO learned that **qualitative measures** (not just quantitative targets) were needed to assess AfDB’s performance.
strategic_opportunities: G20 **Capital Adequacy Framework reforms** provided opportunity to explore callable capital issuance and SDR channelling.

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: Medium – **Reactive adaptations** to crises (COVID-19, Ukraine war) were necessary but delayed formal RMF revisions. FCDO’s push for logframe updates was slow due to staff constraints.
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: Medium – Callable capital and shareholding adjustments were used effectively to stabilize operations, but lending flexibility was constrained by credit rating requirements.
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Medium – Lessons from IDEV and NDEA reviews **informed informal adjustments** (e.g., target realism), but formal ToC/RMF changes were pending as of 2023.

fcas_context.fragility_level: Medium – AfDB operates across Africa, including fragile states (e.g., Sahel, Horn of Africa), but GCI-VII focuses on **credit-worthy middle-income countries**.
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Indirect – No direct conflict in primary borrower countries, but **regional spillovers** (e.g., Sahel instability, Ukraine war food shocks) affected economic conditions.

major_external_shocks.covid_impact: **Severe disruption**: Lending dropped 50% in 2020 ($3.6bn vs. $7bn in 2019). Travel restrictions and health crises diverted resources. Recovery to $4.9bn in 2022 remained below projections.
economic_shocks: **Ukraine war (2022)**: Caused food/fuel price spikes, forcing AfDB to reprioritize lending to food security.
**Exchange rate volatility**: Weakened borrower currencies increased debt burdens, reducing lending capacity.
**Credit rating pressures**: AfDB reduced lending to maintain AAA rating, seeking temporary callable capital from shareholders.
major_external_shocks.conflict_escalation: Indirect – **Sahel conflicts** and global tensions (e.g., Ukraine) created economic instability in borrower countries.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: Stable – No major shifts in borrower country commitment, but **fiscal space tightened** post-COVID, reducing demand for non-concessional lending.
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: AfDB adopted **G20 Capital Adequacy Framework recommendations** to explore callable capital issuance and SDR channelling.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: **Mixed** – AfDB maintained strong institutional capacity (e.g., DBDM decentralization) but faced **bottlenecks in project approval times** (27.4 months vs. 15-month target) and cost overruns.

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Stable – AfDB’s multilateral model insulated from supplier market risks, but **private sector lending slowed** due to borrower credit downgrades.
market_conditions.cost_inflation_impacts: **Significant** – Project preparation costs rose to **$153,000** (from $118,000 in 2020), driven by staff time recording and post-pandemic mission resumption.
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: **High** – Currency depreciations in borrower countries (e.g., Nigeria, Egypt) increased debt servicing costs, reducing effective lending capacity.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Moderate – **1 substantive change** (funding scale/adaptation) with governance and partners stable.
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Funding adaptation – **Lending reprioritization and scale adjustments** in response to external shocks, with minor governance intensification.
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate – Multilateral modality proved resilient, but **overambitious RMF targets** and lack of contingency for global shocks (COVID-19, Ukraine war) exposed design limitations.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The Bank pivoted its lending programme to crisis response during COVID-19, moved staff to remote working, and reduced lending approvals from ~$7bn (2019) to $3.6bn (2020), recovering to $4.9bn in 2022. The Bank streamlined projects under the High-5 Agenda and adapted to capital constraints while maintaining organisational efficiency reforms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The AfDB maintained its AAA credit rating despite pandemic pressures, demonstrating resilience. However, lending targets were not met due to external shocks (COVID-19, shareholder downgrades, exchange rates), requiring adjustments to capital calls and lending projections.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Bank improved organisational efficiency (e.g., cross-cutting strategic alignment, decentralisation under the DBDM model) but faced challenges in business process speed and productivity. The FCDO’s planned logframe revisions were delayed due to staff constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The Bank’s High-5 Agenda and knowledge-sharing events improved human capital coordination, but pandemic disruptions hindered long-term development progress. FCDO-Bank coordination on logframe updates and RMF revisions remains a work in progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO oversight was constrained by staff limitations, delaying logframe consultations. The Bank’s independent evaluations (e.g., IDEV) highlighted the need for realistic target-setting, which management committed to address.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The Bank adapted lending priorities to COVID-19 response and capital constraints, with FCDO supporting trade-offs at the Board level. Flexibility in reallocating resources was critical to maintaining operations.
adaptive_management_examples: Reorientation of lending programs to pandemic response (2020–2021).
Adoption of remote working and cost-saving measures (e.g., reduced office seat costs).
Mid-term review of the New Deal on Energy for Africa (NDEA) to improve electricity access targets.
Commitment to revise the Results Measurement Framework (RMF) targets post-IDEV recommendations.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 disruptions (travel restrictions, lockdowns, resource diversion to health crisis).
Overambitious targets in the Results Measurement Framework (RMF) not adjusted for pandemic impacts.
Reduced lending capacity due to shareholder downgrades and exchange rate shifts, requiring temporary callable capital increases.
Delayed logframe revisions by FCDO due to staff constraints.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic reduced lending from $7bn (2019) to $3.6bn (2020), with partial recovery to $4.9bn (2022).
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (2022) exacerbated food insecurity and economic instability in African countries.
Currency/exchange rate fluctuations and borrower credit downgrades constrained lending projections.
contextual_constraints_new: Unprecedented demand for crisis-response lending diverted resources from long-term development goals.
Need for additional callable capital to maintain AAA credit rating, though no calls have been made historically.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO staff limitations delayed critical logframe consultations and adaptive management.
Bank’s project implementation support costs increased due to strengthened portfolio oversight, straining efficiency.
risk_materialization: Pandemic-related operational disruptions (Risk: Moderate, materialized).
Overoptimistic RMF targets leading to perceived underperformance (Risk: Moderate, materialized).
Exchange rate and borrower credit risks affecting lending capacity (Risk: Moderate, materialized).

budget_execution_vs_plan: Lending approvals dropped from ~$7bn (2019) to $3.6bn (2020), recovering to $4.9bn (2022) but remaining below pre-pandemic projections of $7bn.
Administrative costs per UA 1m disbursed increased to UA 91,500 (2021) from UA 65,000 (2020), within the UA 92,000 ceiling but above historical trends.
value_for_money_assessment: Mixed efficiency: Administrative costs rose due to declined transaction volumes, but remote work reduced office costs temporarily.

financial_management_quality: The Bank maintained its AAA credit rating through prudent capital management, including temporary callable capital increases.

cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficiency gains from remote work (e.g., reduced office costs) were partially offset by rising project-related expenses.
Decentralisation under the DBDM model improved client proximity but fell short of full productivity targets.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Exchange rate shifts and borrower downgrades reduced lending capacity, requiring adjustments to capital projections.

key_delivery_lessons: Overambitious RMF targets can undermine perceived performance; realism must balance with ambition.

Crisis response (e.g., COVID-19) necessitates flexible reprioritisation but may delay long-term goals.
successful_delivery_practices: Organisational efficiency reforms (e.g., DBDM model) enhanced strategic alignment and cross-cutting issue integration.
Adaptive lending reprioritisation during COVID-19 maintained operational continuity.

scalability_evidence: The Bank’s model (e.g., High-5 Agenda, cross-country infrastructure projects) is inherently scalable but constrained by capital limitations.

continuation_rationale: The AfDB remains a critical vehicle for large-scale development impact in Africa, with high country ownership and trust.

delivery_model_sustainability: The current model is sustainable in the medium term but requires addressing efficiency bottlenecks (e.g., project approval delays).

planned_adaptations_future: Finalise logframe and RMF updates by end-2023 to reflect post-pandemic realities.
