programme_metadata.programme_title: Accelerating Ethiopia’s Economic Transformation (ACCELERATE)

output_1.title: Worker support systems in the selected industrial clusters are improved

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme downsized from three original pillars to one (focused on Industrial Parks) due to UK ODA budget reductions. Budget reduced from £22M to £15.2M, with co-financing of €12.5M from BMZ. Secured 3-year no-cost extension until September 2027 with revised Theory of Change and logframe to focus on resilience of manufacturing companies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: GIZ maintains strong delivery performance, praised for collaborative intervention design, high-quality independent advice, and responsive communication. Strong relationships with Ethiopian government stakeholders, especially as other donors withdraw. Occasional delays in technical assistance and limited funding for trade events noted as challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination with government institutions and private sector stakeholders in Industrial Parks. Public-Private Dialogues (PPDs) and partnerships with entities like IPDC and EIC facilitate alignment, though budget constraints limit full participation in some activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: External annual review process with agreed recommendations between reviewer and FCDO team. Adaptive management demonstrated through revisions to ToC/logframe and responsiveness to prior review recommendations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by revising ToC/logframe mid-implementation to address macroeconomic challenges and focus on resilience. No-cost extension allowed continuation without additional funding, with adjusted milestones to reflect longer-term capacity-building needs.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised Theory of Change and logframe in response to 2024 annual review recommendations and macroeconomic reforms (e.g., birr devaluation).
Shift from three pillars to focused support for Industrial Parks due to budget cuts, with co-financing from BMZ.
Scaling up existing worker support interventions (e.g., STOP programme for harassment-free workplaces) rather than introducing new approaches during budget constraints.

main_implementation_challenges: Reduced UK ODA budget leading to downsizing from three pillars to one, with lower funding (£15.2M vs original £22M).
High demand for trade event participation exceeding available funds.
Delays in technical assistance deployment and expertise mobilization.
Macroeconomic volatility (e.g., birr devaluation, forex shortages) affecting private sector resilience.
Political sensitivities around issues like minimum wage discussions, which lost momentum due to reforms.
external_factors_impact: Ethiopian government’s macroeconomic reforms (e.g., exchange rate float in July 2024) improved forex availability but created short-term instability.
Global market shifts (e.g., reduced US orders for Ethiopian textiles) increased pressure on manufacturers to meet European social compliance standards.
Withdrawal of other development partners due to budget cuts, increasing reliance on GIZ’s role.
Rise in coffee exports outpacing textile/garment export growth, affecting impact indicators.
contextual_constraints_new: Need to accelerate private-sector-led growth due to reduced donor assistance.
Closure of call centres and limited capacity of Ethiopian Investment Commission (EIC) to sustain worker welfare support post-programme.
Emerging safeguarding risks (e.g., SEAH prevalence in Industrial Parks) requiring independent assessment.
partner_relationship_issues: Occasional tensions due to insufficient funds for all companies to access international trade opportunities.
Delays in technical assistance delivery impacting timely support to partners.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited government capacity (e.g., EIC) to maintain worker support systems after programme closure.
Loss of Social Development Advisor (SDA) role creating safeguarding oversight gaps.
risk_materialization: Budget reductions (UK/US ODA cuts) materialized, requiring programme downsizing.
Macroeconomic risks (e.g., birr devaluation) affected private sector stability, though mitigated by government reforms.
High staff turnover in Industrial Parks persisted, linked to wage/benefit issues.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: All output and outcome targets (6/6 outcomes, 7/7 outputs) met or exceeded for the reporting period. Two of three impact indicators met (export growth and job creation); one missed (textile/garment export share) due to external factors (coffee export growth). Budget flexibility allowed patient capacity-building support despite challenging context.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong VfM demonstrated by exceeding output/outcome targets despite reduced budget. Revised ToC/logframe aligned ambition with available funding (£15.2M + €12.5M co-financing) and economic realities. Efficiency savings approach (ESA) likely contributed to cost-effective delivery.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High quality, with GIZ adapting to revised financial frameworks and reporting requirements. Transparent milestone tracking, though some indicators set to zero for H2 2024–25 to reflect longer-term impact timelines.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency evident in scaling existing interventions (e.g., worker support services) rather than developing new approaches. Co-financing from BMZ leveraged to extend reach.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: BMZ provided €12.5M co-financing as planned, enabling continuation of core activities despite UK ODA reductions.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Birr devaluation in July 2024 improved forex availability but initially created cost pressures. Programme adapted by focusing on resilience-building activities less sensitive to exchange rate fluctuations.

key_delivery_lessons: Focused interventions in Industrial Parks yield higher impact than dispersed efforts across multiple sectors.
Co-financing (e.g., BMZ) is critical for sustainability amid donor budget cuts.
Adaptive management (e.g., ToC/logframe revisions) enables responsiveness to macroeconomic shocks.
successful_delivery_practices: Collaborative design of interventions with government/private sector stakeholders.
Scaling proven worker support models (e.g., STOP programme) rather than piloting untested approaches.
Leveraging GIZ’s strong reputation with Ethiopian government to maintain influence as other donors exit.
management_adaptations_made: Revised ToC/logframe to prioritize resilience over original growth-focused pillars.
Adjusted impact indicators to reflect realistic ambitions given budget constraints.
Increased focus on safeguarding (e.g., SEAH assessments) in response to emerging risks.
innovations_attempted: Pilot initiatives to link manufacturers with European buyers (higher compliance standards).
Exploration of national minimum wage discussions (though stalled due to political sensitivities).

Completed: Revision of ToC/logframe to link with adjacent programming (e.g., UK Trade Partnership).
Assessment of trade-offs between addressing multiple barriers vs. focused activities.
Ongoing: Minimum wage discussions (lost political backing but SIC continues stakeholder engagement).
GIZ assessment of staff turnover drivers in Industrial Parks (wage/benefits confirmed as key factors).

forward_recommendations: Strategically prioritize Output 3 activities to maximize manufacturing sector impact (by July 2025).
Review logframe target ambition given strong progress and government momentum (by December 2025).
Develop exit strategy with government to sustain worker welfare support post-programme (Section C).
Conduct independent SEAH prevalence survey in Industrial Parks (by March 2025).
Allocate new Social Development Advisor (SDA) or escalate risk if unfeasible (by August 2025).
Analyze manufacturer data from buyer matchmaking to target support effectively (by October 2025).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Proactive adaptations to budget cuts and macroeconomic risks (e.g., ToC revisions) mitigated some challenges, but emerging risks (e.g., SEAH, EIC capacity gaps) require stronger safeguarding measures. Political risks (e.g., minimum wage) proved difficult to manage.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to macroeconomic reform discussions (e.g., exchange rate float).
Informed government policies on Industrial Park resilience, though minimum wage advocacy stalled.
capacity_building_results: 1,288 female workers accessed support services, exceeding milestone targets.
697 workers (568 women) participated in trainings (though 295 in one-off nutrition sessions were excluded from core indicator).
Strengthened public-sector capacity in Industrial Parks (e.g., EIC, IPDC) through technical assistance.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Increased focus on European buyers raised social compliance standards, benefiting worker welfare.
Negative: Budget cuts reduced access to trade events for some manufacturers, limiting export opportunities.
scalability_evidence: Worker support models (e.g., STOP programme) scalable to other Industrial Parks with sustained funding.
Business resilience interventions adaptable to other Ethiopian manufacturing clusters.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong performance in output/outcome delivery (all targets met) despite external challenges. No-cost extension until 2027 provides runway to consolidate gains, though future UK budget cuts may require further adaptations. Co-financing from BMZ and government reforms (e.g., forex liberalization) create favorable conditions for private-sector-led growth.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Further refinement of Output 3 activities to align with government priorities.
Development of exit strategy to transition worker welfare support to government/EIC.
Enhanced safeguarding measures (e.g., SEAH surveys, SDA role).
Targeted support for manufacturers based on buyer matchmaking data analysis.

output_1.title: Diverse, active networks support meaningful connections and collaborative partnerships

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme evolved to include three main delivery routes: 1) KTN Global Alliance Africa (co-funded with Innovate UK), 2) RISA Fund (joint with FCDO's SRIA programme), and 3) Flexible funds managed by FCDO Africa Research and Innovation Hubs. This represents an expansion from the original business case to include more countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Ethiopia) and flexible country-responsive funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (KTN GAA, RISA Fund, UNDP) generally performed well, with KTN GAA achieving a network health score of 0.82 (vs RISA's 0.57) and demonstrating stronger outcomes in partnership formation (18 case examples vs RISA's 22). Chemonics (RISA Fund Manager) effectively leveraged internal resources and surge support for award-making.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Restructured MEL function with embedded MEL Manager delivered higher-quality outputs with similar investment. Programme uses continuous learning to revise Results Framework and Theory of Change, showing adaptive management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between UK and African innovation stakeholders through KTN GAA networks. Cross-country collaborations (e.g., GAA/RISA space agency visit) demonstrated effective knowledge exchange. However, some challenges remain in aligning diverse partner approaches across 6 countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: RISA Fund's detailed budget negotiations with awardees ensured market-rate costs. Chemonics mobilized surge support for concept development during peak periods (Dec 2023-Jan 2024), indicating responsive procurement practices.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to complex multi-country implementation and need for adaptive management. MEL restructuring increased oversight quality without proportional cost increases.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexible funds managed by FCDO Hubs allowed responsive support to country business plan priorities. Programme adapted to include additional countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Ethiopia) beyond original focus (Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa).

programme_metadata.programme_title: The Evidence Fund Programme

output_1.title: HUBS: Country office and regional research and evidence projects carried out are high quality and meet the objectives as set-out.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme pivoted to provide responsive COVID-19 support, demonstrating flexibility in its hybrid delivery model. A temporary delegation of the Responsive Policy Fund component was used to fund the COVID-19 Collective grant, which addressed urgent social science research needs. This shift was not originally planned in the business case but was enabled by the programme's adaptive design.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners such as the Institute of Development Studies (IDS) delivered the COVID Collective platform effectively, supporting rapid research across 26 countries. Commercial, non-profit, and academic partners performed well under challenging circumstances, with 27 grant/contract agreements signed totaling £6m in the first year.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Internal governance arrangements were quickly established to prioritize and implement COVID-19 response activities. The Evidence Fund working group and Director of Research Office played key roles in adaptive decision-making. The management structure proved responsive but was initially stretched due to the pandemic and procurement delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO’s Evidence and Capability Department, Evaluation Unit, and regional research teams was effective, enabling rapid pivoting to COVID-19 priorities. Engagement with country offices (e.g., South Asia, East Africa, MENA) ensured alignment with local needs, though some regions (e.g., WARIH) had limited activity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays due to COVID-19 and FCDO budget directives, reducing efficiency. However, the programme adapted by using existing FCDO routes and delegated authority to issue urgent grants (e.g., COVID-19 Collective). By July 2021, 27 agreements were signed, demonstrating progress despite initial setbacks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified during the COVID-19 pivot, with frequent internal governance meetings and prioritization matrices. The programme’s adaptive management required closer monitoring of rapid-response grants, though this was balanced against the need for speed in delivery.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme’s flexibility was critical to its success, allowing it to reallocate funds (e.g., Responsive Policy Fund) and expand geographic scope (e.g., including West and Southern Africa). The ability to commission unplanned but high-impact research (e.g., COVID-19 modelling in Bangladesh) demonstrated effective use of flexibility.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of the Responsive Policy Fund to establish the £3.2m COVID-19 Collective grant, supporting research in 26 countries.
Expansion of geographic focus to include West and Southern Africa beyond the original scope.
Rapid commissioning of COVID-19-related studies (e.g., pandemics and urban planning in India, COVID modelling in Bangladesh) to inform policy responses.
Adjustment of logframe targets mid-implementation to accommodate COVID-19 priorities.

main_implementation_challenges: Procurement and grant setup delays due to COVID-19 and FCDO budget directives, reducing the efficiency of early implementation.
Limited capacity in some regions (e.g., WARIH) to fully utilize the fund’s offerings.
Balancing the need for rapid research (e.g., COVID-19 response) with maintaining rigorous evidence standards.
Establishing new internal governance and prioritization processes under pandemic conditions.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted planned activities, requiring a shift to pandemic-related research and remote working arrangements.
FCDO’s broader budget reprioritization in 2020/21 delayed the programme’s procurement launch.
Increased demand for timely, policy-relevant evidence to inform COVID-19 responses across FCDO’s priority regions.
contextual_constraints_new: Unexpected need to support COVID-19 social science research, which was not anticipated in the original business case.
Regional disparities in engagement (e.g., lower uptake in WARIH compared to SARH or MENAH).
Capacity constraints in country offices to absorb and utilize research outputs effectively, particularly under pandemic conditions.
partner_relationship_issues: No significant partner performance issues were reported. However, the rapid setup of grants/contracts (27 in 9 months) may have strained some relationships due to compressed timelines.
Coordination with country offices required additional effort to ensure research aligned with local priorities, particularly in regions with less prior engagement (e.g., West Africa).
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO staff capacity to manage the fund was initially stretched due to the dual demands of COVID-19 response and normal programme setup.
Limited in-house capacity to handle the volume of grants/contracts during the interim period pre-supplier tender.
Country offices varied in their ability to engage with and utilize research outputs, highlighting gaps in evidence-uptake skills.
risk_materialization: Delays in procurement and grant setup (mitigated by adaptive use of existing FCDO routes).
Risk of reduced rigour in rapid-response research (addressed through quality assurance processes for COVID-19 studies).
Risk of misalignment with country priorities (mitigated by increased engagement with Heads of Mission and country teams).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme spent £6m in its first year (August 2020–July 2021), primarily on 27 grants/contracts. While this was below the annualized £9.67m target (based on £58m over 6 years), the underspend was attributed to procurement delays and the interim pre-tender phase. Budget execution is considered on track given the challenging context.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indications suggest good VFM, particularly for the COVID-19 Collective (£3.2m supporting 26 countries), which leveraged existing IDS expertise to deliver rapid, policy-relevant research. The programme’s flexibility to reallocate funds to high-impact areas (e.g., pandemic response) enhanced efficiency. However, full VFM assessment is pending as outcomes are not yet measurable.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management was robust, with clear tracking of grants/contracts and adaptive reallocation of funds. The temporary delegation of authority for the COVID-19 Collective demonstrated agile financial governance. No significant issues were reported, though the interim period required additional oversight.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was high for rapid-response mechanisms (e.g., COVID-19 Collective), which delivered research at scale with relatively low overheads. However, procurement delays reduced overall efficiency in the first year. The programme’s hybrid model (combining central and country-level funding) is expected to improve efficiency as implementation matures.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexibility in fund design is critical to responding to emerging priorities (e.g., COVID-19). The ability to reallocate resources rapidly enabled the programme to remain relevant.
Centralized funds must balance global priorities with country-specific needs. Engagement with country offices (e.g., through Heads of Mission) improved alignment but required dedicated effort.

Timeliness of evidence is as important as rigour for policy uptake. The programme’s rapid-response mechanisms (e.g., COVID-19 Collective) were more effective in influencing decisions than slower, traditional research processes.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of delegated authority to fast-track urgent grants (e.g., COVID-19 Collective).
Establishment of internal governance structures (e.g., prioritization matrices) to manage adaptive programming.
Leveraging existing partner networks (e.g., IDS) to deliver rapid, high-quality research.
Regular engagement with country offices to ensure research addressed local evidence gaps.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from planned procurement timeline to interim grant-making via existing FCDO routes.
Introduction of the COVID-19 Collective as a new output component mid-implementation.
Increased focus on training and capacity-building for FCDO staff to improve evidence uptake (e.g., in-person training on evidence use).
Adjustment of logframe targets to reflect COVID-19 priorities and expanded geographic scope.
innovations_attempted: The COVID-19 Collective platform, which tested a model for rapid, demand-driven research in crisis contexts.
Hybrid delivery model combining central fund management with country-office engagement.
Use of evidence brokering to connect research outputs with policy windows (e.g., COP26 priorities in India).
forward_recommendations: Finalize the supplier tender to transition from interim grant-making to a sustainable delivery model.
Strengthen capacity-building for country offices to improve evidence uptake and utilization.
Develop mechanisms to better anticipate and respond to "windows of opportunity" for policy influence.
Monitor the long-term impact of COVID-19 research to assess its contribution to programming and policy.
Explore ways to institutionalize the adaptive management practices piloted during the pandemic.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was effective in mitigating procurement delays and aligning research with emerging priorities. The programme’s ability to pivot to COVID-19 response demonstrated strong adaptive capacity. However, risks related to evidence uptake (e.g., country-office capacity) require ongoing attention.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 16 research projects commissioned (exceeding the target of 15), with outputs reaching FCDO country offices in East Africa, South Asia, MENA, and expanded regions (West and Southern Africa). The COVID-19 Collective supported research in 26 countries, indirectly benefiting policymakers and practitioners globally.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Research outputs (e.g., Nature-based Solutions in India, pandemic urban planning studies) influenced FCDO programmes and external stakeholders (e.g., Government of India’s National Disaster Management Authority).

policy_influence_achieved: Nature-based Solutions research informed FCDO India’s climate programmes and UK-India engagement on COP26 priorities.
Pandemics and urban planning study influenced policy discourse in India’s National Disaster Management Authority.
COVID-19 modelling in Bangladesh supported the development of a business case for government engagement.
COVID-19 Collective research informed FCDO’s pandemic response strategies across multiple countries.
capacity_building_results: Training and support provided to FCDO staff improved skills in evidence use for programme design and evaluation.
Country-office engagement enhanced local capacity to identify and commission context-specific research.
Brokering relationships between FCDO and research partners (e.g., IDS, universities) strengthened institutional capacity for evidence generation.
unintended_consequences: Positive: The programme’s flexibility allowed it to address unanticipated COVID-19 evidence needs, enhancing its relevance and impact.
Negative: Procurement delays reduced efficiency in the first year, potentially limiting the scope of non-COVID-19 research.
scalability_evidence: The COVID-19 Collective demonstrated scalability, supporting research in 26 countries with potential for replication in future crises.
The hybrid delivery model (central fund + country engagement) could be scaled to other FCDO priority regions or thematic areas.
Rapid evidence synthesis products proved adaptable to diverse contexts (e.g., East Africa, South Asia), suggesting potential for broader application.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong adaptive capacity, delivering high-quality research and influencing policy despite challenging circumstances. Its flexibility and relevance to FCDO’s strategic objectives (e.g., evidence-based programming, VFM) justify continuation. The interim delivery model has proven effective, and transitioning to a supplier-led tender is expected to enhance efficiency.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current hybrid model is sustainable in the short term but requires finalization of the supplier tender for long-term stability. The programme’s adaptive practices (e.g., rapid reallocation of funds) suggest it can maintain effectiveness under changing conditions.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Transition from interim grant-making to a supplier-managed fund to improve efficiency and scalability.
Strengthen monitoring and evaluation frameworks to better capture outcomes and impact, particularly for policy influence.
Expand capacity-building efforts to ensure country offices can effectively utilize research outputs.
Institutionalize adaptive management practices (e.g., rapid-response mechanisms) for future crises.
Enhance coordination with other FCDO research programmes to avoid duplication and maximize synergies.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Economic Development Investment Programme (EDIP) – St Helena

output_1.title: Social and economic development infrastructure investments and utilities delivered to meet short term and medium term needs with a justifiable return on investment

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Initial focus shifted to priority-setting and governance strengthening rather than immediate construction due to lack of upfront strategic products. Flexibility introduced to mitigate COVID-19 impacts (e.g., remote working, adjusted workplans for rockfall protection).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: SHG was eager to start construction immediately but faced challenges due to lack of agreed strategic vision/theory of change upfront. Relationship between SHG and DFID/FCDO was formative, with initial tensions around "shovel-ready" project expectations, business case standards, and review timelines. PMU developed strong managerial/technical capacity, but local representation gaps emerged after Resident Representative’s early departure (Feb 2020).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance mechanisms (High-Level Panel, Programme Review Group) were established but require strengthening. Technical reviews (PRG) need clearer delineation from strategic decisions (HLP). Roles/responsibilities of stakeholders (e.g., FCO, SHG, DFID) were not fully clarified, leading to process delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Collaboration mechanisms (e.g., monthly monitoring workbooks, joint reviews) were implemented but need refinement. Alignment between DFID and SHG risk registers was poor initially; improvements were initiated mid-year. Safeguarding remained a priority but was not formally logged in SHG’s risk registers.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Payments (£2.744m disbursed, 94.6% of Year 1 budget) were made in arrears per MOU, with no reported procurement delays. However, exchange rate risks (e.g., South African Rand fluctuations) and supply chain disruptions (monthly freight vessel delays, COVID-19) impacted procurement of goods/services.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than planned due to COVID-19 and merger of DFID/FCO. Quarterly risk updates were recommended but not yet institutionalized. DFID’s Social Development Adviser provided additional safeguarding support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted workplans (e.g., rockfall protection) and extended expert contracts to mitigate COVID-19. Proposed no-cost time extension (4 years instead of 3) to accommodate delays.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended consultant stays due to COVID-19 travel restrictions (e.g., strategic infrastructure plan development).
Adjusted Rupert’s Bay business case timeline to align with HLP approvals.
Shifted to remote monitoring and flexible project sequencing.

main_implementation_challenges: Delay in finalizing strategic vision, theory of change, and logframe indicators (first 12 months).
Misalignment between SHG’s urgency for construction and DFID’s requirements for strategic planning/business cases.
Local representation gap after Resident Representative’s departure (Feb 2020).
Supply chain vulnerabilities (monthly freight vessel, material/expertise shortages).
Reactive (vs. preventive) maintenance culture for infrastructure.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Border closures, halted tourism, supply chain disruptions, and shift to remote working.
DFID-FCO merger: Created institutional uncertainty and risk management gaps.
Exchange rate volatility: Affected procurement costs (e.g., South African Rand for materials).

Increased lead times for procurement (e.g., 1-month freight delays).
Limited local capacity for complex business case development (e.g., cost-benefit appraisals).
Public engagement gaps risking project delays (e.g., planning permissions).
partner_relationship_issues: Initial tensions over "shovel-ready" project expectations vs. DFID’s strategic planning requirements.
Differing views on public consultation adequacy (potential for later-stage delays).
SHG’s reactive maintenance approach conflicted with DFID’s sustainability goals.
capacity_constraints_emerged: PMU had strong technical capacity but lacked local representation post-Feb 2020.
Short-term expert contracts (12 months) proved insufficient for continuity (extended due to COVID-19).
SHG’s limited experience with UK Treasury 5-case business case templates.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 supply chain/health risks (mitigated via flexibility).
Resident Representative departure (operational risk for local monitoring).
Exchange rate risks (not initially in DFID’s risk register).
Construction safety risks (terrain challenges).

budget_execution_vs_plan.notes: 94.6% of Year 1 budget (£2.9m) disbursed via two payments (£769,814.70 and £1,981,300.22). Payments made in arrears per MOU.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Payments were processed efficiently per financial procedures, with no reported overruns.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Spend achieved 94.6% of target, but exchange rate risks (e.g., South African Rand) and supply chain delays (COVID-19) increased costs. Longer expert contracts recommended to reduce onboarding costs.

strengths: Timely payments with clear authorization (Financial Secretary sign-off).
Transparent expenditure tracking via spreadsheets.
No fraud or misprocurement reported.
weaknesses: Risk register alignment between DFID and SHG was initially poor.
O&M budget sustainability not assured (reliant on unspecified revenue sources).
Lack of formal safeguarding risks in SHG’s registers.

cost_efficiency_achieved.notes: Efficiency gains from remote working (COVID-19) offset by supply chain costs. No quantitative comparison provided.

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Fluctuations in South African Rand increased procurement costs for materials/services. Risk not initially captured in DFID’s register.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Unlocking Digital Impact for Development Programme

output_1.title: Digital development actors convene, partner and collaborate at global forums to increase alignment on digital transformation in developing countries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme funding was paused since April 2021 due to FCDO financial constraints (UK ODA reduction to 0.5% GNI). delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: DIAL's donor-coordination role (e.g., GovStack with Estonia/Germany/ITU, Digital Public Goods Charter with USAID/DPGA/Gates/Sida) demonstrated effective multi-stakeholder alignment despite funding pause.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Reduced oversight due to funding pause; programme kept open for policy engagement only.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to funding pause by maintaining policy dialogue and leveraging other donors' support for DIAL's continued operations (e.g., DIAL 2.0 transition).
adaptive_management_examples: Transition from DIAL 1.0 to DIAL 2.0 (Digital Beacons strategy) despite funding constraints.

Refocusing on high-level policy engagement during funding hiatus.

Global shift in donor priorities affecting digital development funding.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Water Resource Accountability in Pakistan Programme (WRAP)

output_1.title: Climate resilient reforms introduced, implemented and scaled up for efficient allocation of water at the federal level and in Punjab

output_2.title: Improved government and targeted communities’ capacity to plan, manage and sustain nature-based solutions

output_3.title: Water solutions tested by diverse stakeholders and a pipeline of projects developed through Catalytic Fund

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Mobilisation of Components 1 (IWMI) and 2 (WWF-UK) completed by December 2021; Component 3 (Catalytic Fund) procurement delayed until March 2023. Mixed delivery modalities used: Accountable Grants for Components 1-2 and planned commercial contract for Component 3.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IWMI and WWF-UK met inception phase expectations, establishing governance mechanisms (e.g., provincial steering committees) and delivering baseline work. Strong collaboration with government noted, but political instability risks future traction.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme steering committees established at provincial levels (e.g., Punjab committee notified and first meeting held May 2022). Advisory and governance mechanisms operationalised during inception.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Close coordination between BHC Islamabad, IWMI, and WWF-UK reported, with joint meetings to address cross-component risks (e.g., geographic silos between Punjab and KP/GB). Donor-government alignment described as "well-informed and coordinated."
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Components 1-2 contracts awarded on schedule. Component 3 (Catalytic Fund) Terms of Reference approved but contract delayed to March 2023 due to procurement framework (IMDP) timelines.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: BHC Islamabad maintained active oversight during inception, including Political Economy Analysis (PEA) validation and stakeholder consultations. Quarterly partner reporting and combined meetings planned for ongoing monitoring.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Adaptive management demonstrated in response to political shifts (e.g., revising milestones for Output 1 to engage new government stakeholders). Inception phase allowed for baseline adjustments based on PEA findings.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised Output 1 milestones to account for 2022 political transition (e.g., new Prime Minister Sharif’s administration).
Selection of Okara district for IWRM/IDM pilot via consensus-driven approach, validated by BHC Islamabad.
Expansion of federal reforms from planned 2-3 to 6, based on government support and PEA insights.

main_implementation_challenges: Political instability following April 2022 change in federal/provincial governments, risking delays in reform uptake (Output 1).
Geographic fragmentation: Components 1 (Punjab) and 2 (KP/GB) operate in different regions, risking siloed impact.
Delayed Component 3 procurement (Catalytic Fund) pushes innovation testing to late 2023.
external_factors_impact: 2022 Pakistani constitutional crisis and no-confidence vote against PM Imran Khan created uncertainty for government engagement.
Unclear election timeline (post-mid-2023) complicates long-term planning with public sector partners.
High economic/legal risks identified in PEA, with moderate political/social risks.
contextual_constraints_new: Government buy-in risk elevated due to leadership changes; initial interventions focused on "less sensitive" entry points to build trust.
Operating space may shrink if new policies reduce climate/water priorities (identified as a "Major" residual risk).
partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported; IWMI and WWF-UK collaborated effectively during inception, with joint steering committees.
Potential future challenges if government counterparts deprioritise WRAP due to political reshuffling.
capacity_constraints_emerged: No explicit capacity gaps noted, but sustainability depends on government’s ability to scale piloted solutions (e.g., IWRM in Okara).
Safeguarding capacity addressed via partner due diligence (IWMI/WWF developed policies and appointed focal points).
risk_materialization: Strategy/Context risk ("Severe" inherent, "Major" residual): Government buy-in remains uncertain.
Policy/Programme Delivery risk ("Major" inherent, "Moderate" residual): Political changes may alter operating environment.
Safeguarding risks (SEAH/GBV) mitigated to "Minor" residual via partner policies and FCDO due diligence.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; inception phase completed within budget. No underspends or overspends reported for 2021-22.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early stage to assess VFM fully, but inception activities (e.g., PEAs, baseline setting) delivered efficiently. Mixed modalities (grants + commercial contract) align with FCDO’s risk appetite.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Partners (IWMI/WWF) demonstrated compliance with FCDO financial requirements. Risk registers aligned with FCDO framework and integrated into programme-level monitoring.

key_delivery_lessons: Early stakeholder engagement (e.g., PEA validation with BHC Islamabad) critical for baseline credibility and government ownership.
Flexible milestone-setting essential in politically volatile contexts (e.g., revising Output 1 targets post-election).
Cross-component coordination (e.g., WRAP-BRAVE synergies) can mitigate geographic fragmentation risks.
successful_delivery_practices: Consensus-driven site selection (e.g., Okara district for IWRM pilot) enhanced local buy-in.
Joint steering committees at provincial level improved donor-government alignment.
Comprehensive risk registers (partner + programme level) enabled proactive mitigation.
management_adaptations_made: Added quarterly combined meetings with IWMI/WWF to monitor cross-component risks.
Expanded reform targets (e.g., 6 federal reforms vs. planned 2-3) based on government demand.
Increased political-level engagement in Output 1 to secure sustainability.
innovations_attempted: Catalytic Fund designed to test scalable water solutions (though not yet operational).
Use of PEA to tailor interventions to political economy realities (e.g., focusing on technical officials during transitions).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: IWMI to maintain close contact with government counterparts to sustain Output 1 traction amid political uncertainty.
Document partner responses to EAD’s broad recommendations in Q1 2022 reports.
Monitor delivery challenges across Components 1-2 to assess overall impact, given geographic separation.
Leverage synergies with BHC’s BRAVE programme to enhance climate resilience coherence.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in inception phase: risks identified via PEA/DDA were mitigated (e.g., safeguarding policies, steering committees). "Eager" risk appetite for strategy/context risks allowed adaptive responses to political changes.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.planned: Process-oriented Year 1 targets (e.g., inception reports, stakeholder consultations).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: All Year 1 milestones met: inception reports submitted, steering committees notified, and government engagements documented.

policy_influence_achieved: 6 provincial/federal reforms identified with government support (linked to Punjab Water Act 2018 and National Water Policy).
PEA findings used to baseline assumptions for policy uptake, though long-term influence depends on political stability.
capacity_building_results: Technical capacity of federal/provincial institutions (e.g., Irrigation Department, MoCC) strengthened via PEAs and reform identification.
Nature-based solutions capacity building planned but not yet implemented (Component 2).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Stronger-than-expected government collaboration in inception phase (e.g., 6 reforms vs. planned 2-3).
Negative: Risk of siloed impact due to geographic separation of components.
scalability_evidence: Okara district IWRM pilot designed for replicability; Catalytic Fund (Component 3) aims to upscale innovative solutions post-2023.
Scaling depends on government adoption of piloted reforms (e.g., climate-smart water allocation).

continuation_rationale: Strong inception phase delivery (all Year 1 milestones met) justifies continuation.
Programme aligns with FCDO’s climate resilience priorities and Pakistan’s National Water Policy.
Risk mitigation strategies (e.g., steering committees, adaptive management) address key challenges.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Mixed modalities (grants + commercial contract) are appropriate, but long-term sustainability hinges on government uptake of reforms and Catalytic Fund innovations.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by "A" score and positive narrative in review).
planned_adaptations_future: Revised milestones for Output 1 to account for political transitions.
Enhanced coordination between Components 1-2 to mitigate geographic fragmentation.
Operationalisation of Catalytic Fund (Component 3) by March 2023 to test scalable solutions.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Direct to Government of Mozambique via Joint Fund (PRONASAR) + Contracted Fund Manager + Capacity Building Agent + Independent Monitoring Partner)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £70 million over 2019-2026, targeting 4.6 million beneficiaries (women, girls, children) in rural Mozambique
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Performance-based funding via Joint Fund (FCDO + GoM + Austria + Switzerland + UNICEF) with Fund Manager overseeing disbursements tied to WASH service delivery milestones. Direct contracts for CBA and IMP.
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium - Performance-based disbursements allow reallocation based on results, but core Joint Fund structure and partner roles were fixed at design.

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch FCDO oversight with delegated implementation: (1) Joint Fund managed by contracted Fund Manager; (2) Capacity Building Agent (CBA) for government systems; (3) Independent Monitoring Partner (IMP) for verification. Aligned with GoM’s PRONASAR structure.
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly - Joint Fund performance reviews with GoM, plus annual independent verification by IMP. CBA progress reported semi-annually.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Decentralized: GoM districts/provinces implement WASH infrastructure; Fund Manager approves disbursements based on verified results; FCDO retains strategic oversight via IMP data.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Multi-partner consortium: (1) GoM (PRONASAR) as primary implementer; (2) Fund Manager (contracted); (3) CBA (contracted); (4) IMP (to be procured). Plus private contractors and community-based orgs for service delivery.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Government (GoM/PRONASAR), Multilateral (UNICEF), Private Sector (contractors), Civil Society (community-based orgs), Bilateral (Austria/Switzerland co-financing).

partner_roles_planned.GoM/PRONASAR: Lead implementer of rural WASH infrastructure via Joint Fund
partner_roles_planned.Fund Manager: Fiduciary oversight, disbursement management, and performance verification
partner_roles_planned.CBA: Government capacity building (multi-sectoral planning, budgeting, procurement)
partner_roles_planned.IMP: Independent results verification and monitoring framework strengthening
partner_roles_planned.Private Contractors: Construction of WASH infrastructure (boreholes, water systems)
partner_roles_planned.Community-Based Orgs: Local service delivery and behavior change activities

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Restricted (Fund Manager and CBA via FCDO procurement; GoM/PRONASAR as pre-selected government partner; private contractors via PRONASAR tendering processes).

consortium_baseline.consortium_structure_planned: No formal consortium. Loose multi-stakeholder collaboration centered on PRONASAR Joint Fund, with FCDO as anchor donor and separate contracts for CBA/IMP.
consortium_baseline.lead_partner_planned: Government of Mozambique (PRONASAR) as de facto lead for WASH delivery, with FCDO as lead donor.
consortium_baseline.consortium_governance_planned: Joint Fund Steering Committee (GoM + donors) for strategic decisions; Fund Manager for operational oversight; CBA/IMP report directly to FCDO.

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Mixed (Joint Fund expanded to include USAID co-financing; Fund Manager role strengthened; CBA scope expanded to include nutrition fund pilot; IMP procured in 2023).
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £70m budget maintained, but scope expanded: (1) Additional 9 water systems completed (carryover from T-WASH I); (2) 99 boreholes vs. planned 40; (3) USAID added £3.7m (2021) via UK/T-WASH II channel.
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Performance-based disbursements continued with revised indicators (co-designed with GoM). Fund Manager’s role expanded to include more rigorous quality assessments pre-payment. USAID funds channeled through existing Joint Fund mechanism.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High - Performance-based model allowed reallocation to overperform on boreholes/water systems; USAID co-financing absorbed without structural changes; nutrition fund pilot added via CBA.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Enhanced delegation: (1) Joint Fund Steering Committee now includes USAID; (2) Fund Manager’s verification role expanded to pre-payment quality checks; (3) IMP’s scope broadened to include targeted studies on monitoring gaps. FCDO oversight remains light-touch but more data-driven via IMP.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Quarterly + ad-hoc: Joint Fund reviews now monthly in some provinces (DNAAS request); IMP’s real-time data sharing enables faster course correction. CBA reporting remains semi-annual but with deeper field-level insights.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: More participatory: (1) Revised performance indicators co-designed with GoM; (2) DNAAS now co-leads scaling decisions (e.g., expanding performance-based approach nationwide); (3) IMP data directly informs disbursement decisions.

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Expanded multi-partner model: Original structure retained but with (1) USAID as new co-financer; (2) IMP formally added (2023); (3) Private contractors’ role grew (batch processing of boreholes reduced costs).
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Government (GoM/PRONASAR), Multilateral (UNICEF, USAID), Private Sector (contractors), Civil Society (community-based orgs), Bilateral (Austria/Switzerland/UK).

partner_roles_actual.GoM/PRONASAR: Lead implementer + now co-designing performance indicators and scaling decisions
partner_roles_actual.Fund Manager: Expanded to pre-payment quality verification and fiscal risk mitigation
partner_roles_actual.CBA: Added nutrition fund pilot (2023) and deeper field-level capacity building
partner_roles_actual.IMP: Independent verification + targeted studies to address monitoring gaps
partner_roles_actual.USAID: New co-financer (£3.7m) channeled via Joint Fund
partner_roles_actual.Private Contractors: Optimized batch processing for boreholes, reducing costs by ~30%
partner_roles_actual.Community-Based Orgs: Increased role in behavior change (e.g., SBC campaigns)

consortium_actual.consortium_structure_actual: Still no formal consortium, but tighter collaboration: (1) USAID integrated into Joint Fund governance; (2) IMP now links all partners via shared monitoring data; (3) CBA’s nutrition pilot bridges WASH-nutrition sectors.
consortium_actual.lead_partner_actual: GoM/PRONASAR remains lead implementer; FCDO’s role evolved to facilitator of donor coordination (e.g., USAID alignment).
consortium_actual.consortium_governance_actual: Joint Fund Steering Committee now includes USAID; IMP data used for collective decision-making; CBA’s cross-sectoral work (nutrition+WASH) creates de facto programmatic integration.

substantive_changes_made: Added USAID as co-financer (£3.7m) via existing Joint Fund mechanism, expanding donor pool without structural changes.
Expanded performance-based funding indicators co-designed with GoM, increasing local ownership.
Introduced Independent Monitoring Partner (IMP) in 2023 to address verification gaps, strengthening accountability.
Scaled up borehole/water system delivery (99 boreholes vs. planned 40; +9 water systems) via optimized contractor batching.
Added nutrition fund pilot (2023) under CBA, broadening multi-sectoral scope.
Enhanced Fund Manager’s pre-payment verification role to mitigate fiduciary risks.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Budget maintained at £70m, but co-financing increased by £3.7m (USAID 2021). No formal budget revision.
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic/beneficiary scope expanded via: (1) Additional 59 boreholes; (2) 9 extra water systems; (3) Nutrition pilot in selected districts. No contractions.
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: No shift in core modalities, but USAID funds channeled through UK’s Joint Fund mechanism, increasing multilateral coordination.

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Assumptions refined on: (1) Community willingness-to-pay for water systems (evidence from field visits); (2) Private sector’s role in sustainability (e.g., multi-system operators). No formal ToC revision.

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: Steering Committee expanded to include USAID; IMP added as cross-cutting oversight body. No formal restructuring, but roles deepened.
management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Oversight intensity increased via: (1) Monthly reviews in some provinces (DNAAS-led); (2) IMP’s real-time data sharing; (3) Fund Manager’s pre-payment checks.
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: More participatory: GoM now co-designs performance indicators; IMP data directly informs disbursements; DNAAS leads scaling decisions.

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: No locations removed. Additional resettlement areas included for humanitarian WASH rehabilitation (linked to natural disasters).
geographic_scope_changes.geographic_focus_shifted: No shift in urban/rural focus, but drought/flood-prone areas prioritized for climate-resilient technologies (e.g., desalination, solar pumps).

activity_only_adjustments: Pilot Social Behavior Change (SBC) campaign under CBA (no structural change).
Methodology refinements for household satisfaction surveys (no scope change).
Field visit protocols adjusted to increase beneficiary engagement time.

contextual_shocks: COVID-19: Delayed IMP procurement (now in 2023) and field visits, but no major delivery disruption.
Natural disasters: Added WASH rehabilitation in resettlement areas (within existing budget flexibility).
Climate risks: Prioritized drought/flood-resilient technologies in vulnerable areas.
performance_issues: Slow progress on satisfaction surveys → Methodology co-design with DNAAS to accelerate.
Fiduciary risks → Expanded Fund Manager’s verification role pre-payment.
learning_insights: Batch processing of boreholes reduced costs → Scaled up contractor batches.
Community feedback on MHM facilities → Adjusted inclusion approaches to reduce stigma.
Private operator sustainability lessons → Informed water system technology choices.
strategic_opportunities: USAID alignment → Absorbed co-financing via Joint Fund.
GoM’s interest in scaling performance-based funding → Co-designed revised indicators.
Donor recognition of T-WASH model → World Bank/USAID replicating capacity-building approaches.

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High - Adaptations were data-driven (IMP/field insights), participatory (GoM co-design), and leveraged existing flexibility (e.g., performance-based funding).
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: High - Baseline flexibility (performance-based disbursements) enabled scope expansion (boreholes, nutrition pilot) without budget increases.
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High - Field lessons (e.g., batching, climate resilience) directly informed adaptations; IMP’s targeted studies addressed monitoring gaps.

fcas_context.fragility_level: High - Mozambique faces chronic instability (e.g., insurgency in Cabo Delgado), climate shocks (cyclones/droughts), and weak subnational capacity.
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Active conflict in Cabo Delgado (though T-WASH II operates in Nampula/Zambezia/Inhambane, which are stable but disaster-prone).

major_external_shocks.covid_impact: Moderate - Delayed IMP procurement and fieldwork (2020–21), but no delivery halt. Remote monitoring mitigated risks.
major_external_shocks.economic_shocks: Inflation increased construction costs (e.g., water systems ranged 16–106M MZN), but batching and Fund Manager negotiations contained impacts.
major_external_shocks.climate_disasters: Severe - Cyclones Idai/Kenneth (2019) and ongoing droughts/floods triggered humanitarian WASH rehabilitation in resettlement areas.
major_external_shocks.conflict_escalation: Indirect - Cabo Delgado conflict diverted some GoM attention, but T-WASH II areas remained unaffected.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: Positive - GoM’s DNAAS now advocates scaling performance-based funding nationwide; PRONASAR alignment strengthened.
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: Stable - No major policy shifts, but T-WASH II’s model influenced World Bank/USAID WASH programs.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: Lower than expected - Subnational capacity gaps required deeper CBA engagement; Fund Manager filled fiduciary gaps.

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Adequate - Sufficient contractors for boreholes/water systems, but remote areas faced higher costs (logistics, materials).
market_conditions.cost_inflation_impacts: Moderate - Water system costs varied widely (£305k–£675k avg); boreholes stable at ~£7k. Batching and Fund Manager negotiations mitigated inflation.
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: Minimal - FCDO’s £70m budget in GBP; local costs in MZN managed via Fund Manager’s procurement oversight.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Moderate - 3/4 delivery mechanisms substantively adapted (funding, governance, partners), but core Joint Fund structure and GoM leadership remained stable.
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Comprehensive adaptation - Changes spanned funding (USAID co-financing, scope expansion), governance (IMP addition, participatory indicators), and partners (USAID, IMP, expanded contractor roles).
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate - Baseline’s performance-based funding and multi-stakeholder model proved resilient, but underestimated (1) subnational capacity gaps; (2) need for real-time monitoring (addressed via IMP); (3) climate resilience requirements.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Transforming Access to Water, Sanitation, Hygiene and Nutrition Services in Mozambique (T-WASH II)

output_1.title: Central, provincial and district government respond to demand for improved and inclusive WASH services, in target rural communities, by delivering agreed WASH infrastructure and services.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme aligned implementation closely with PRONASAR (GoM's national rural WASH programme) through a Joint Fund mechanism, which proved effective and was replicated by other donors (USAID, World Bank). Performance-based funding was introduced to incentivize service delivery, with revised indicators agreed participatively with GoM. USAID contributed additional funds (£3.7m in 2021) through T-WASH II, validating the model.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Government partners (DNAAS) demonstrated commitment to scaling the performance-based approach across Mozambique. Private contractors and community-based organizations delivered WASH infrastructure (15 water systems, 99 boreholes) with transparency, as verified by the Fund Manager. USAID's co-funding and adoption of T-WASH II's capacity-building approach by other donors (World Bank) indicate strong partner buy-in.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: A Fund Manager (FM) was contracted to reduce fiduciary risks, overseeing disbursements tied to performance indicators. The Independent Monitoring Partner (IMP), to be procured in 2023, will verify GoM reporting systems and field results, adding an additional layer of accountability. Provincial-level accountability mechanisms were established, requiring service providers to report progress to provincial leaders.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The Joint Fund mechanism facilitated coordination among multiple donors (FCDO, Austria, Switzerland, UNICEF, USAID) and alignment with GoM systems. The programme's multi-sectoral approach (WASH + nutrition) required coordination across government levels (national, provincial, district) and sectors (health, education). Donor replication of the model (e.g., World Bank, USAID) suggests effective coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement processes were transparent and accountable, with payments contingent on quality assessments by the Fund Manager. Batching borehole contracts reduced costs (average £7,000 per borehole). For water systems, costs varied (£16m–£106m MZN) due to technological adaptations (e.g., desalination, solar power) for climate resilience, but remained below historical averages (£481,036 vs. £675,000 in 2015 study).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified through performance-based disbursements, regular reporting to provincial leaders, and planned independent verification (IMP in 2023). Quarterly meetings with the Fund Manager and GoM ensured real-time monitoring. The programme's focus on vulnerable areas (e.g., drought-prone, flood-affected) required adaptive oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by: 1) Reallocating funds to humanitarian emergencies (e.g., rehabilitation of WASH infrastructure in resettlement areas); 2) Adapting technological solutions (e.g., desalination, solar power) for climate resilience; 3) Piloting new approaches (e.g., social behavior change campaigns, nutrition fund in 2023); 4) Responding to community feedback (e.g., avoiding stigmatizing dedicated MHM facilities).
adaptive_management_examples: Revised performance indicators for the Joint Fund were agreed participatively with GoM to reflect local priorities.
Technological adaptations (e.g., submersible pumps, solar power) were made for water systems in drought-prone or flood-affected areas, increasing costs but ensuring sustainability.
The programme paused dedicated MHM facilities after feedback that they stigmatized users, opting for mainstreamed inclusion instead.
A pilot nutrition fund (2023) was added to test integrated nutrition-sensitive activities in selected districts.
Survey methodologies for beneficiary satisfaction (Outputs 1.2–1.3) were iteratively developed with DNAAS based on pilot findings (e.g., 64% satisfaction in Nampula/Zambezia).

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in agreeing survey methodologies with DNAAS for beneficiary satisfaction indicators (Outputs 1.2–1.3) due to competing priorities, though pilots showed 64% satisfaction.

Logistical challenges in remote areas (e.g., poor roads, distance from towns) increased construction costs and complicated material transport, particularly for water systems in Vila Franca do Save (Inhambane).
Balancing climate resilience (e.g., flood/drought adaptations) with cost efficiency led to higher-than-planned expenditures for some water systems (up to £106m MZN vs. £38.5m average).
Social norms and stigma around dedicated MHM facilities required adaptive approaches to inclusion, risking dilution of women's roles in WASH decision-making.
Sustaining open defecation-free (ODF) status proved difficult with community-led total sanitation (CLTS) alone, necessitating climate-resilient latrine construction.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 (implied but not explicitly detailed) likely affected implementation timelines and community engagement, though the review focuses on 2021–2022 recovery.
Climate shocks (droughts, floods) required unplanned adaptations (e.g., desalination equipment, submersible pumps) and increased costs for resilient infrastructure.
Political stability in Mozambique enabled continued alignment with GoM systems, though no specific political risks are noted.
USAID's co-funding (£3.7m in 2021) and donor replication (World Bank, USAID) of T-WASH II's model created opportunities for scaling but also raised expectations for performance.
contextual_constraints_new: The need for climate-resilient WASH infrastructure (e.g., flood/drought adaptations) was underestimated in initial planning, leading to unplanned cost increases.
Community resistance to dedicated MHM facilities revealed unintended stigma, requiring a shift to mainstreamed inclusion strategies.
Variability in water system costs (£16m–£106m MZN) due to geographical and technological factors (e.g., energy sources, remoteness) was not fully anticipated.
The time lag in observing outcome-level results (4–5 years, per T-WASH I experience) necessitated adjustments to multi-year budgeting and expectations.
partner_relationship_issues: DNAAS's delayed agreement on survey methodologies (Outputs 1.2–1.3) slowed progress on beneficiary satisfaction metrics, though pilots proceeded.
Private operators of water systems faced challenges with affordability (e.g., high energy costs) and community willingness to pay, risking sustainability.
Some community-based organizations struggled with the technical capacity to maintain climate-resilient latrines, affecting ODF sustainability.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoM capacity at district/provincial levels required ongoing support (via the Capacity Building Agent) for multi-sectoral planning, budgeting, and monitoring.
Limited capacity of private water system operators to manage long-term maintenance (e.g., energy costs, repairs) threatened sustainability in remote areas.
The programme team's field visits often focused on official events rather than deep beneficiary engagement, limiting contextual understanding.
Need for anthropological expertise to navigate social norms (e.g., reusable sanitary pads, latrine stigma) was identified but not yet fully addressed.
risk_materialization: Fiduciary risks were mitigated by the Fund Manager and performance-based disbursements, with no major breaches reported.
Climate-related risks (droughts, floods) materialized, requiring adaptive technological solutions and increased costs.
Risk of stigmatizing vulnerable groups (e.g., PWD, menstruating girls) through dedicated facilities emerged, prompting a shift to mainstreamed inclusion.
Risk of unsustainable water systems due to high energy costs or low community payment willingness was partially addressed through piloting private operator models.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: The programme delivered more WASH infrastructure than planned (15 water systems + 99 boreholes vs. targets of 6 water systems + 40 boreholes), with a slight increase in costs for water systems due to climate adaptations. Budget execution was on track, with co-funding from USAID (£3.7m in 2021) supplementing FCDO funds.

by_component.Component_1_Joint_Fund: Performance-based disbursements ensured efficient use of funds, with payments tied to verified results (e.g., construction completion, reporting). The average cost per water system (£481,036) was 29% below the 2015 benchmark (£675,000) but 58% above the 2018 study (£305,000), reflecting climate-resilient adaptations.
by_component.Component_2_Capacity_Building: Budget was used to pilot new approaches (e.g., social behavior change campaigns, nutrition fund in 2023) and support GoM multi-sectoral planning. No major underspends or overspends reported.
by_component.Component_3_Independent_Monitoring: IMP procurement planned for 2023; budget reserved for verification activities and targeted studies.

value_for_money_assessment.vs_business_case: The programme achieved stronger-than-expected results (e.g., 9 additional water systems from T-WASH I) with marginal cost increases. Cost per person for drinking water (£106 average) was efficient compared to alternatives, though higher in remote areas (£120 in Inhambane). The performance-based funding model improved VFM by linking payments to outcomes.

Private operator models for water systems can improve sustainability but require support for affordability (e.g., energy costs) and community payment willingness.

policy_influence_achieved.government_adoption: GoM (DNAAS) plans to scale the performance-based Joint Fund model to all provinces. The approach was recognized as a "positive model" by GoM and replicated by USAID/World Bank in their WASH programmes.
policy_influence_achieved.donor_alignment: USAID channeled £3.7m through T-WASH II in 2021, and both USAID and World Bank adopted the programme's capacity-building approach at the provincial level.
policy_influence_achieved.sector_standards: The programme's climate-resilient WASH technologies (e.g., desalination, solar power) and private operator models are influencing sector practices in Mozambique.

capacity_building_results.government: Enhanced GoM capacity at district/provincial/national levels for multi-sectoral planning, budgeting, and monitoring. District development plans are now nutrition-sensitive, and integrated WASH-nutrition interventions are being piloted.
capacity_building_results.private_sector: Private contractors demonstrated improved transparency and accountability in procurement (e.g., batching boreholes). Private operators of water systems are being supported to build capacity for long-term maintenance.

positive: Climate-resilient latrines improved social status for households in some communities.
Private-operated water systems reduced travel time for water collection, particularly benefiting women and girls.
T-WASH II's model attracted additional donor funding (USAID) and replication by other programmes (World Bank, USAID), amplifying impact.
negative: Dedicated MHM facilities initially stigmatized users (PWD, menstruating girls), requiring a shift to mainstreamed inclusion.
Focus on water supply systems risked reducing women's roles in WASH decision-making forums (e.g., water committees).
High energy costs for private-operated water systems threatened affordability for some communities, risking sustainability.

scalability_evidence.within_mozambique: Strong: GoM (DNAAS) plans to scale the Joint Fund's performance-based model nationwide. USAID and World Bank are already replicating capacity-building approaches at the provincial level.
scalability_evidence.regional_global: Moderate: The climate-resilient WASH technologies and private operator models could be adapted to similar contexts (e.g., other drought/flood-prone regions), but require upfront investment.
lessons_for_scale: Performance-based funding is scalable but requires strong GoM buy-in and fiduciary safeguards (e.g., Fund Manager).
Climate adaptations increase costs but are essential for resilience; batching contracts can offset some expenses.
Mainstreamed inclusion (vs. dedicated facilities) reduces stigma and improves scalability.
Private operator models need support for affordability (e.g., energy subsidies) to ensure sustainability at scale.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: T-WASH II is pivotal to UK strategic objectives in Mozambique, with strong alignment to GoM priorities and donor coordination. The programme has demonstrated effective delivery (e.g., exceeding WASH infrastructure targets), innovation (e.g., climate-resilient technologies), and influence (e.g., donor replication of its model). Its focus on women/girls and climate change aligns with FCDO priorities, while the performance-based approach ensures accountability. The programme is positioned to transition responsibilities to GoM and private sector as other revenue streams (e.g., extractives) become available.

strengths: Joint Fund mechanism reduces fiduciary risks and aligns with GoM systems, improving long-term sustainability.
Performance-based funding creates incentives for continued service delivery post-FCDO support.
Private operator models and multi-system approaches aim to maximize economies of scale.

risks: Sustainability of private-operated water systems depends on resolving affordability challenges (e.g., energy costs).
GoM's ability to take over funding relies on future revenue streams (e.g., extractives) materializing as planned.
Climate shocks may continue to stress resilient infrastructure, requiring ongoing adaptation.
delivery_model_sustainability.overall: Likely sustainable with adaptations: The delivery model is robust and replicable, but long-term success hinges on addressing energy affordability, GoM revenue growth, and climate resilience.

programme_metadata.programme_title: ATscale – The Global Partnership for Assistive Technology (AT) Programme

output_1.title: An effective ATscale global partnership, with engaged partners, strong governance, a secretariat, a strategy, a well-functioning operational and financial model, and the ability to effectively implement interventions.

output_2.title: Comprehensive market shaping interventions on both supply and demand sides under a coordinated framework

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned from start-up phase to scale-up phase in 2023/24, with expanded country engagement (28 countries planned/underway) and increased funding diversification (new donors: UAE, Australia, EU). Operational Plan 2024 approved in November 2023 to formalize this shift.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (e.g., WHO, UNICEF, GDI Hub) performed well, with successful collaboration on country programmes and global public goods. Private sector engagement strengthened via board representation (e.g., Shonaquip Social Enterprise).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Board expanded with new members (Australia, private sector) and improved diversity (60% women, 53% Global South representation). Secretariat filled 15/17 posts, with adjustments to recruitment criteria to include AT users.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with national governments and local organizations in 28 countries was successful, though some country programmes faced delays (2/8 off-track). Global public goods portfolio required stronger strategic articulation to avoid fragmentation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Board oversight intensified during scale-up transition, with monthly monitoring of resource mobilization and operational plan implementation. UK (as donor) actively participated in Executive Board decisions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to budget reductions (UK ODA cuts) by pausing non-critical activities and reprioritizing resource mobilization. Operational Plan 2024 included contingency measures for delayed donor funding.
adaptive_management_examples: Pivoted from standalone AT Credit Facility (deemed unfeasible) to regional AT distribution hubs model, informed by lessons shared with GDI Hub.
Revised recruitment policies to accommodate AT users (e.g., replacing post-graduate degree requirements with work experience).
Updated Theory of Change (2022) to streamline country-led initiatives, market shaping, and advocacy strands for scale-up phase.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed and reduced UK ODA funding (2021 onwards) required budget reprioritization and pauses in some activities.
Resource mobilization diverted secretariat focus from core delivery, though successfully secured £25.3m by 2024/25 (up from £8.8m in 2023).
Fragmentation risk in global public goods portfolio due to broad scope; required stronger strategic narrative.
Two of eight country programmes faced delays, though managed via adaptive planning.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic disrupted initial implementation and exacerbated funding constraints due to UK ODA reductions to 0.5% GNI.
Geopolitical shifts (e.g., donor priorities) affected timely disbursement of funds, requiring contingency planning.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated difficulty in recruiting AT users for secretariat roles despite policy adjustments.
Need for stronger disability-inclusive event practices (e.g., prioritizing speakers with disabilities) identified during scale-up.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Secretariat capacity stretched by dual focus on resource mobilization and scale-up delivery, mitigated by board expansion and operational plan updates.
Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) systems required upgrades to handle increased country programme data and demonstrate outcomes (not just outputs).
risk_materialization: Budget reductions (UK ODA cuts) materialized as planned risk, managed via expenditure pauses and resource mobilization strategy.
AT Credit Facility feasibility risk realized; lesson shared with GDI Hub for alternative approaches.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution improved despite initial delays: 85% of available budget committed by end-2023 (target adjusted to 65% due to ODA cuts). Funding grew from £8.8m (start 2023/24) to £25.3m (start 2024/25) via new donors (UAE, Australia, EU).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Assessed as delivering against VfM statement in Business Case. Cost efficiency achieved through strategic engagement (e.g., leveraging £1.85m UK core funding to catalyze £25.3m total). Country programmes reached 167,769 people with AT services by June 2024, with scalable models in place.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Comprehensive Resource Mobilisation Strategy approved; financial commitments well-managed despite volatility. Board oversight ensured alignment with operational plan.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of reduced UK funding (£1.85m in 2023/24) to leverage 3x co-funding. Per-beneficiary cost not specified but scalability evidence strong (e.g., 28 countries engaged).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized significantly: new partnerships with UAE (Reaching The Last Mile), USA (Leahy War Victims Fund), and EU (DG INTPA) secured. Pipeline of additional donors in development.

key_delivery_lessons: Close collaboration with national governments improves efficacy and sustainability (e.g., policy buy-in, partnership agreements).
Resource mobilization requires dedicated secretariat focus but can crowd in significant co-funding (£25.3m secured).
Global public goods portfolio needs clearer strategic framing to avoid fragmentation and demonstrate impact.
successful_delivery_practices: Board diversification (e.g., private sector, programme countries) strengthened governance and regional representation.
Adaptive recruitment policies (e.g., flexibility for AT users) improved inclusivity, though challenges remain.
Country-led initiatives with local organizations proved effective in addressing AT ecosystem gaps.

Resource Mobilisation Strategy prioritized; leadership/board focus ensured donor pipeline growth.
AT Credit Facility lessons informed shift to regional distribution hubs model.
innovations_attempted: Regional AT distribution hubs proposed to address affordability/accessibility gaps (replacing unfeasible Credit Facility).
Disability-inclusive event practices (e.g., prioritizing speakers with disabilities) piloted.
