Ensure disability inclusion in all events and governance structures (e.g., board, speaker roles).
Develop stronger narrative for global public goods portfolio to align with strategic challenges.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Proactive adaptation to ODA cuts (e.g., expenditure pauses, resource mobilization) and feasibility risks (e.g., AT Credit Facility pivot). Board oversight and monthly monitoring mitigated financial risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: 167,769 people reached with AT services by June 2024 (28 countries). Breakdown: 42% prosthetics/orthotics, 15% eyeglasses, 8% wheelchairs, 32% other mobility AT, 2% hearing aids. Expected to rise significantly in 2024/25.

policy_influence_achieved: Country programmes improved government policies for AT access (e.g., national strategies, partnership agreements).
Global public goods (e.g., research, product narratives) informed WHO/UNICEF guidelines and donor strategies.
capacity_building_results: Secretariat capacity built (e.g., 60% women, 53% Global South representation).
Local organizations in 28 countries received training on AT ecosystem gaps and data collection.

unintended_consequences.description: Lessons from unfeasible AT Credit Facility informed GDI Hub’s AT Growth Fund, potentially addressing broader market gaps.
Delayed donor funding caused temporary pauses in some activities, though managed via adaptive planning.

scalability_evidence: Model demonstrated scalability via country programme expansion (28 countries) and co-funding growth (£25.3m).
Regional distribution hubs proposal (2024 Operational Plan) aims to address systemic AT access barriers.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme extended to March 2027 to fulfill original £20m commitment and capitalize on scale-up momentum. Strong performance (4 consecutive 'A' scores), successful resource mobilization (£25.3m secured), and alignment with FCDO priorities (disability inclusion, VfM).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. Diversified funding base, government partnerships, and regional hubs model enhance long-term viability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize M&E system upgrades to track outcomes and scalability.
Expand country programmes with focus on policy influence and local capacity building.
Strengthen communications strategy to clarify outcomes (beyond donor outreach).
Fill remaining board seats (programme country representation) to improve governance diversity.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tackling global plant and animal health risks which threaten global food systems and health – in partnership with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF)

output_1.title: A systematic approach to plant pest and disease control in sub-Saharan Africa

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transition to new platform programmes (APHID and Delivering the Agriculture Breakthrough Phase 1) was initiated based on annual review recommendations. A no-cost extension (NCE) until December 2026 was provided to manage integration of active investments into the new programme structure. Some investments (e.g., global agricultural productivity and climate-resilience) were transferred to follow-on programmes to scale impact.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) performed as expected, managing the grant portfolio directly without charging management fees or overheads to FCDO. The partnership became increasingly efficient due to long-standing collaboration, strengthened by an FCDO secondee role (extended until June 2025). BMGF’s technical and programmatic capacity was leveraged effectively, with co-funding approximately three times FCDO’s £38m contribution.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme was directly managed by BMGF, with FCDO providing strategic oversight through a secondee embedded in BMGF’s team. This structure facilitated closer FCDO involvement and improved coordination. The management approach evolved to integrate learning from annual reviews, such as the transition to new platform programmes (APHID).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO and BMGF was effective, as evidenced by joint strategic dialogues, regular programme reviews, and collaborative decision-making (e.g., no-cost extension, transition planning). The Global Food Security Summit (November 2023) showcased the partnership’s achievements to a broad audience, demonstrating strong alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: BMGF handled all procurement and grant management on behalf of both funders, ensuring efficiency and reducing transaction costs for FCDO. No issues with procurement implementation were reported; the model was described as cost-effective and leveraging BMGF’s expertise.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was lighter than typical FCDO-managed programmes due to BMGF’s direct management role. However, FCDO maintained strategic oversight through the secondee, annual reviews, and key milestones (e.g., DEWAS and WAVE progress reviews). The intensity was deemed appropriate given the partnership’s maturity and BMGF’s capacity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by adapting to external challenges (e.g., COVID-19) and internal recommendations (e.g., no-cost extension, transition to new platforms). Budget reprofiling and BMGF’s support mitigated risks from FCDO budget cuts. The partnership’s ability to launch new projects (e.g., WAVE Phase 2, DEWAS) reflected adaptive management.
adaptive_management_examples: Provided a no-cost extension (NCE) until December 2026 to manage the transition of active investments into the new APHID platform and other follow-on programmes.

Reprioritized investments to align with emerging needs, such as climate-resilient agricultural technologies and zoonotic disease control, in response to strengthened evidence on climate change impacts.
Launched new projects (e.g., WAVE Phase 2, DEWAS, Bovine Tb Phase 2) based on progress and gaps identified in annual reviews.
Conducted WAVE response plan simulation drills in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Nigeria to test outbreak preparedness, leading to policy reforms in national plant health protocols.
Commissioned a joint partnership review to address slowing co-funding pipelines due to FCDO budget cuts, with findings to inform a strategic roadmap for 2024–2025.

main_implementation_challenges: Slowing pipeline of new co-funded projects due to FCDO budget cuts and uncertainty, which required budget reprofiling and BMGF support to mitigate risks to grantees.
Complexity of transitioning active investments into new platform programmes (APHID and Delivering the Agriculture Breakthrough Phase 1) while maintaining continuity of research and partnerships.
Ensuring sustainability of progress made in projects like DEWAS and WAVE, particularly in strengthening national diagnostic capacities and plant health ecosystems in Africa.

Balancing the need for rapid scientific innovation with the time required for policy uptake and institutionalization of new approaches (e.g., early warning systems for wheat rust and cassava viral diseases).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the urgency of addressing zoonotic diseases and global food system resilience, reinforcing the programme’s relevance but also causing delays in some field activities.

Climate change exacerbated the spread of pests and diseases (e.g., fall armyworm, wheat rust), increasing the importance of the programme’s adaptive research but also raising the complexity of interventions.

Geopolitical and economic instability (e.g., global food security crisis) created both challenges (e.g., funding uncertainty) and opportunities (e.g., increased focus on agricultural innovation at the Global Food Security Summit 2023).
contextual_constraints_new: Stronger evidence emerged linking climate change to accelerated spread of plant and animal diseases, requiring adjustments to research priorities (e.g., heat-tolerant crops, pest surveillance systems).
Weak biosecurity measures in some target regions (e.g., West and Central Africa) posed challenges for containing cross-border spread of pests like cassava brown streak disease (CBSD).

Limited capacity in national plant protection organizations (NPPOs) to sustain early warning systems and rapid response protocols, necessitating deeper engagement with policy makers (e.g., WAVE drills in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria).
capacity_constraints_emerged: National diagnostic laboratories in focus countries (e.g., Ethiopia, Nigeria) required additional support to meet international standards for disease surveillance, prompting recommendations for targeted capacity-building.
Some projects faced delays in policy uptake due to limited institutional capacity to adopt new technologies (e.g., DEWAS early warning systems, WAVE rapid response protocols).

The need for specialized technical expertise in areas like viral disease diagnostics and climate-resilient crop breeding outpaced available local capacity, requiring continued reliance on international partners.
risk_materialization: Budget cuts and funding uncertainty from FCDO materialized as a risk, slowing the pipeline of new co-funded projects and prompting a joint partnership review.

Delays in policy reforms and institutional adoption of new technologies (e.g., plant health surveillance systems) posed risks to sustainability, addressed through targeted recommendations (e.g., DEWAS lab capacity strengthening).
The risk of zoonotic disease outbreaks (e.g., COVID-19) reinforced the programme’s focus but also required adaptive management to align with evolving global health priorities.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme executed its budget as planned, with BMGF’s co-funding (approximately 3x FCDO’s £38m contribution) ensuring financial stability. Budget reprofiling was used to mitigate risks from FCDO budget cuts, and a no-cost extension (NCE) until December 2026 was approved to manage transitions without additional costs.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: BMGF managed the grant portfolio without charging management fees or overheads to FCDO, reducing transaction costs. The partnership leveraged BMGF’s existing technical and programmatic capacity, avoiding duplication.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: The partnership became more efficient over time due to long-standing collaboration and the FCDO secondee role, which improved coordination and reduced administrative burdens. The secondment (extended to June 2025) was funded through the programme and enhanced joint decision-making.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: The programme delivered a stream of relevant agricultural technologies and scientific advances (e.g., DEWAS early warning systems, WAVE response protocols). Projects like NextGen Cassava and ATAI integrated gender considerations, addressing equity dimensions.
value_for_money_assessment.cost_efficiency: Strong value for money was achieved through co-funding, BMGF’s in-kind contributions (e.g., grant management, procurement), and the ability to leverage a diverse portfolio of high-impact projects. The collaboration allowed FCDO to access a broader range of innovations than would be possible independently.
value_for_money_assessment.overall_vfm_assessment: The programme continued to represent strong value for money, with high potential for development impact at low transaction costs. The partnership model was deemed more cost-effective than alternative delivery routes.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: BMGF’s financial management was assessed as high-quality, with timely financial reports and audited statements provided to FCDO. The direct management by BMGF reduced administrative burdens on FCDO while ensuring compliance and transparency. No issues with financial mismanagement were reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency exceeded planned levels due to BMGF’s in-kind contributions (e.g., procurement, grant management) and the lack of overhead charges. The programme’s design allowed FCDO to co-fund a larger portfolio of projects than would be feasible through traditional delivery models.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: BMGF’s co-funding materialized as planned, with contributions approximately three times FCDO’s £38m investment. The co-funding was critical to the programme’s scale and impact, enabling investments in high-potential projects like DEWAS and WAVE.

key_delivery_lessons: The FCDO-BMGF partnership model demonstrated that leveraging a philanthropic foundation’s technical and managerial capacity can significantly enhance efficiency and impact, particularly for complex, multi-year research portfolios.
Direct management by BMGF reduced transaction costs for FCDO and allowed for more flexible, adaptive programme implementation in response to emerging challenges (e.g., climate change, COVID-19).
Embedding an FCDO secondee within BMGF strengthened coordination, trust, and joint decision-making, proving critical for managing transitions (e.g., no-cost extension, new platform programmes).

Multi-year investments required proactive planning for sustainability, particularly in strengthening national institutions (e.g., NPPOs, diagnostic labs) to adopt and maintain new technologies post-programme.
successful_delivery_practices: The use of simulation drills (e.g., WAVE response exercises in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria) effectively tested and improved national preparedness for plant health threats, leading to policy commitments from Heads of NPPOs.
Strategic dialogues and joint reviews (e.g., upcoming 2024 Strategic Dialogue) facilitated alignment between FCDO and BMGF, ensuring adaptive management and shared ownership of programme priorities.

Co-funding and co-design of projects with BMGF enabled access to cutting-edge research (e.g., CTLGH, ENSA, RIPE) and global platforms (e.g., Global Food Security Summit 2023), amplifying the programme’s visibility and impact.
Integrating gender considerations into agricultural research (e.g., NextGen Cassava, ATAI) improved equity outcomes and ensured technologies were accessible to women smallholder farmers.
management_adaptations_made: Extended the programme timeline via a no-cost extension (NCE) until December 2026 to manage the transition of active investments into new platform programmes (APHID, Delivering the Agriculture Breakthrough Phase 1).
Reprioritized investments to focus on high-impact areas like climate-resilient crops and zoonotic disease control, in response to strengthened evidence on climate change and global health risks.
Strengthened oversight of sustainability planning for key projects (e.g., DEWAS, WAVE) by embedding them in broader ecosystems (e.g., plant health networks, international diagnostic labs).
Commissioned a joint partnership review to address challenges from FCDO budget cuts, with findings to inform a strategic roadmap for 2024–2025.
innovations_attempted: DEWAS (Disease Early Warning Advisory System): Developed a scalable, technology-driven early warning system for wheat diseases in East Africa and South Asia, integrating real-time monitoring and advisory services for farmers.

WAVE (West and Central African Virus Epidemiology): Piloted regional simulation drills to test rapid response protocols for cassava viral diseases, leading to policy reforms in national plant health systems.

ATAI (Agricultural Technology Adoption Initiative): Used behavioral science and tailored dissemination strategies to accelerate the adoption of climate-smart agricultural technologies by smallholder farmers.

Combining Algal and Plant Photosynthesis: Launched an innovative project to enhance crop productivity by integrating algal and plant photosynthesis mechanisms, addressing climate resilience challenges.
previous_recommendations_progress: The 2022 Annual Review recommendation to provide a no-cost extension was implemented, with the NCE approved until December 2026 to facilitate transitions to new platforms.
Recommendations to strengthen national diagnostic capacities (e.g., DEWAS labs) were partially addressed, with plans for further action in 2024 (e.g., DEWAS annual meeting).
The suggestion to embed WAVE in broader plant health ecosystems is underway, with efforts to integrate Functional Rapid Responses to Plant Infectious Diseases systems in West and Central Africa.
Progress was made on policy uptake for ATAI, with plans to prioritize results dissemination and tailored briefings in the project’s final phase.
forward_recommendations: Conduct a Strategic Dialogue in early 2024 to review the joint partnership review findings, identify new co-investment priorities, and reaffirm the partnership’s role in addressing global food security challenges.

Finalize the transition of active investments to new platform programmes (APHID, Delivering the Agriculture Breakthrough Phase 1), ensuring continuity of research and alignment with FCDO’s strategic goals.
Strengthen the sustainability of DEWAS by using its network to build capacity in national wheat rust diagnostics labs and link them to international labs, with a review planned for April 2024.

Embed WAVE’s work within the broader plant health ecosystem by integrating rapid response systems and sustaining regional collaboration to improve readiness for plant health threats in West and Central Africa.

Maximize the impact of ATAI’s final phase by prioritizing results dissemination, policy uptake, and tailored briefings for key stakeholders, with a meeting planned with ATAI leadership in 2024 to discuss future research needs.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was effective in mitigating operational and financial risks. Key examples include: (1) Budget reprofiling and BMGF’s support addressed risks from FCDO budget cuts; (2) The no-cost extension (NCE) managed transition risks for active investments; (3) Simulation drills (e.g., WAVE) proactively tested and improved outbreak response capacities. However, risks related to policy uptake and institutional sustainability required ongoing attention.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Projects like DEWAS and WAVE reached smallholder farmers, national plant protection organizations (NPPOs), and agricultural researchers across 20+ countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. For example, WAVE engaged NPPOs in 10 West and Central African countries, while DEWAS targeted wheat farmers in Ethiopia, Kenya, Zambia, Tanzania, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, and Pakistan.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: The programme’s research outputs (e.g., early warning systems, disease-resistant crop varieties) have the potential to benefit millions of farmers dependent on staple crops like wheat and cassava, as well as global food systems through improved pest and disease control.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Progress was on track, with most projects meeting or exceeding milestones (e.g., DEWAS infrastructure established, WAVE drills completed). However, some policy uptake targets (e.g., institutionalization of early warning systems) lagged due to capacity constraints in partner countries.

policy_influence_achieved: WAVE’s simulation drills in Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Nigeria led to commitments from Heads of NPPOs to reform national early warning protocols, demonstrating direct policy influence.
DEWAS’s progress in Ethiopia and other focus countries contributed to strengthened national wheat rust surveillance capacities, with potential for regional adoption.
The programme’s projects (e.g., CTLGH, ENSA) were showcased at the Global Food Security Summit (November 2023), raising their profile among policymakers and donors.
ATAI’s behavioral science approaches influenced agricultural extension policies in target regions, though broader institutionalization remains a work in progress.
capacity_building_results: DEWAS established infrastructure for wheat disease monitoring in East Africa and South Asia, building technical capacity in national diagnostics labs (e.g., Ethiopia).
WAVE trained NPPO staff and researchers in viral disease diagnostics and rapid response protocols, improving regional capacity to manage cassava diseases in West and Central Africa.
ATAI’s work included training for extension agents and farmers on climate-smart technologies, with a focus on gender-inclusive approaches.
The FCDO secondee role within BMGF enhanced capacity for joint programme management and knowledge sharing between the two organizations.
unintended_consequences: Positive: The programme’s focus on zoonotic diseases (e.g., through livestock health projects) gained unexpected relevance during the COVID-19 pandemic, positioning FCDO and BMGF as key players in global health security discussions.
Positive: Simulation drills (e.g., WAVE) not only tested response protocols but also fostered cross-border collaboration among NPPOs, strengthening regional plant health networks.

Negative: In some cases, the rapid introduction of new technologies (e.g., disease-resistant crop varieties) outpaced local institutional capacity to regulate and sustain them, risking low adoption post-programme.
scalability_evidence: DEWAS’s early warning system for wheat diseases is designed for scalability across regions with similar agroecological conditions (e.g., expansion from East Africa to South Asia).
WAVE’s regional approach to cassava viral disease management provides a model for scaling to other crops and regions facing similar plant health challenges.

The partnership’s co-funding model (FCDO + BMGF) has proven scalable, as demonstrated by the transition to new platform programmes (APHID) and the ability to leverage additional resources for high-impact projects.
ATAI’s behavioral insights and dissemination strategies offer scalable solutions for accelerating technology adoption in other agricultural sectors.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme will transition into new platform programmes—specifically, the Animal and Plant Health Innovation and Evidence Delivery Platform (APHID) and Delivering the Agriculture Breakthrough Phase 1—to scale impact and address evolving global challenges (e.g., climate change, zoonotic diseases). This transformation builds on the programme’s successes, including strong progress in Output 1 (plant pest/disease control) and the effective FCDO-BMGF partnership. The no-cost extension (NCE) until December 2026 ensures continuity during the transition.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The delivery model is sustainable in the medium to long term, given: (1) The proven efficiency of the FCDO-BMGF partnership, which reduces transaction costs and leverages co-funding; (2) The establishment of new platforms (APHID) to consolidate and scale investments; (3) Strong political and institutional buy-in (e.g., NPPO commitments following WAVE drills). However, sustainability depends on continued co-funding and addressing capacity gaps in partner countries.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize the transition of active investments to APHID and other follow-on programmes, ensuring alignment with FCDO’s strategic priorities (e.g., climate resilience, global health security).
Implement the strategic roadmap developed from the 2024 Strategic Dialogue, focusing on new co-investment priorities and partnership strengthening.
Scale successful projects (e.g., DEWAS, WAVE) by embedding them in national and regional systems, with targeted capacity-building for sustainability.
Leverage the Global Food Security Summit’s momentum to secure additional funding and partnerships for the transformed programmes.
Address capacity constraints in partner countries (e.g., NPPOs, diagnostic labs) through tailored technical assistance and policy support.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (core voluntary contributions to WHO/GPEI partnership)

programme_metadata.programme_title: Global Polio Eradication Initiative

output_1.title: Polio campaigns yield a high population immunity

output_2.title: High poliovirus detection capacity

output_3.title: Integrated service delivery expedites eradication progress

output_4.title: Political will secured and coordinated transition planning in place

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme in transition with refocused resources due to UK budget cuts (2021) and stabilized funding (£50m 3-year commitment for 2022–2025). Shift to intensified, tailored approaches in "consequential geographies" (e.g., north-west Nigeria, eastern DRC) to target zero-dose children. Adaptive use of novel oral polio vaccine type 2 (nOPV2) in 23 countries, with 500M+ doses administered by end-2022.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Mixed performance: WHO, UNICEF, and Gates Foundation delivered core activities, but challenges in Afghanistan (Taliban restrictions on female workers) and Pakistan (security in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) constrained campaign quality. GPEI partners achieved 80% access in Afghanistan (up from prior years) but faced persistent subnational surveillance gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: GPEI’s governance (Strategy Committee, Financial Accountability Committee, Polio Oversight Board) functioned as planned, but risk management and KPI monitoring required strengthening. New GPEI Scorecard (2022) piloted with adjustments needed for feasibility. FCDO shifted to equal weighting (25%) for all outputs, aligning with GPEI’s 2022–2026 Strategy.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved coordination in outbreak responses (e.g., faster reactions in Nigeria, Somalia) but siloed working persisted in WHO’s polio transition planning. Cross-partner collaboration on nOPV2 rollout was effective, though integration with Gavi for service delivery remained unclear.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of nOPV2 and mOPV2 vaccines met demand, with 500M+ nOPV2 doses deployed. However, supply chain disruptions in conflict zones (e.g., Yemen, eastern DRC) limited reach. Cost efficiencies achieved through bulk procurement but offset by logistical challenges in high-risk areas.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO oversight intensified post-2021 budget cuts, with closer monitoring of GPEI’s Scorecard KPIs. UK’s £20m payment (Dec 2022) triggered enhanced financial accountability, though reduced funding limited course correction opportunities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to: (1) Taliban restrictions in Afghanistan by adjusting female FLW deployment; (2) WPV1 outbreaks in Pakistan via strategic shifts in South KP province; (3) cVDPV2 surges through targeted geographies. Flexibility in vaccine allocation (nOPV2 vs. mOPV2) based on outbreak data.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid deployment of nOPV2 in 23 countries following IMB recommendations, reducing cVDPV2 seeding by 90% vs. traditional OPVs.
Reallocation of resources to "consequential geographies" (e.g., Somalia, Yemen) based on real-time surveillance data.
Adjustment of female FLW targets in Afghanistan/Pakistan due to security constraints, balancing safety with community engagement.

main_implementation_challenges: Security constraints in Pakistan (TPP insurgency) and Afghanistan (Taliban restrictions on female workers) limited campaign coverage in high-risk areas.
Subnational surveillance gaps in conflict zones (e.g., northern Yemen, eastern DRC) hindered outbreak detection.
Logistical barriers to vaccine delivery in inaccessible regions (e.g., Tete Province, Mozambique).
Political instability in endemic countries disrupted transition planning (e.g., Afghanistan’s healthcare system fragmentation).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021) disrupted campaigns, though recovery seen in 2022.
UK ODA budget cuts (2021) reduced funding by ~60% vs. original business case, stabilizing only in late 2022 with a £50m commitment.
Ukraine crisis (2022) diverted global health resources, indirectly affecting polio funding priorities.
Climate-related disruptions (e.g., floods in Pakistan, August 2022) temporarily halted campaigns in affected regions.
contextual_constraints_new: Taliban’s escalating restrictions on female healthcare workers in Afghanistan (2022) exceeded anticipated constraints.
Emergence of nOPV2-seeded cVDPV outbreaks (early 2023) introduced unplanned vaccine safety monitoring needs.
Inflation and currency devaluation in endemic countries (e.g., Pakistan) increased operational costs by ~15%.
Competing health priorities (e.g., COVID-19, measles outbreaks) strained partner capacity in integrated service delivery.
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in data sharing from Pakistan’s polio programme hindered M&E transparency.
Tensions between GPEI and WHO AFRO region over surveillance capacity standards.
Misalignment between GPEI’s eradication timeline and Gavi’s immunization schedules in transition planning.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Shortage of trained surveillance officers in high-risk districts (e.g., south-central Somalia).
Limited cold chain capacity in remote areas (e.g., northern Yemen) reduced vaccine efficacy.
High turnover of GPEI country staff in conflict zones (e.g., eastern DRC) disrupted continuity.
risk_materialization: Security risks in Pakistan’s South KP province materialized as WPV1 outbreaks (22 cases in 2022 vs. 5 in 2021).
Political risks in Afghanistan led to 20% reduction in female FLW participation by Q4 2022.
Financial risks from UK funding cuts required reprioritization of transition activities.
Operational risks in vaccine supply chains caused delays in nOPV2 deployment to Yemen (3-month lag).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: UK disbursed £20m in Dec 2022 (vs. £30m planned annually in original business case). Overall execution at ~67% of projected spend due to ODA cuts. GPEI reallocated funds to high-priority geographies, achieving 95% spend in outbreak response countries.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Medium: Cost per child immunized increased by 20% due to security/access challenges, but nOPV2’s reduced cVDPV seeding improved cost-effectiveness. VFM ratios deteriorated in conflict zones (e.g., Yemen) but remained strong in stable regions (e.g., Nigeria).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High: GPEI’s Financial Accountability Committee maintained robust controls. Audit findings (2022) showed <5% irregularities, primarily in partner-reported expenses. UK’s shift to Scorecard-based monitoring improved transparency.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Mixed: Unit costs for SIAs rose in Afghanistan/Pakistan (security premiums) but fell in Africa (economies of scale). nOPV2’s 30% lower seeding rate vs. mOPV2 offset higher per-dose costs (£0.50 vs. £0.30).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: Gates Foundation and Rotary met commitments, but co-funding from endemic countries (Afghanistan, Pakistan) fell 40% short due to economic crises. Gavi’s transition funding remained unsecured for 2024+.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Significant: Pakistani Rupee depreciated 30% vs. GBP (2022), increasing local costs. Mitigated via hedging for vaccine procurements but eroded purchasing power for operational expenses.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible vaccine strategies (nOPV2) are critical for adapting to outbreak dynamics but require real-time surveillance data.
Local political engagement (e.g., Taliban negotiations in Afghanistan) is essential for access but demands trade-offs with programme principles.
Transition planning must start earlier to avoid surveillance capacity gaps post-eradication.
successful_delivery_practices: Risk-based microplanning in Pakistan’s South KP reduced WPV1 cases by 60% in 6 months.
Integration of polio campaigns with measles vaccination in Somalia improved cost-efficiency by 25%.
GPEI’s rapid response teams in Nigeria halved cVDPV2 outbreak duration (2022 vs. 2021).
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from annual to quarterly KPI reviews to enable faster course correction.
Established cross-partner task forces for "consequential geographies" to unblock access barriers.
Revised female FLW targets to reflect security realities without compromising community trust.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of digital surveillance tools in DRC to bridge subnational data gaps (30% improvement in reporting).
Use of satellite imagery to map inaccessible areas in Afghanistan for targeted campaigns.
Trials of bivalent OPV (types 1+3) in Mozambique to simplify supply chains.
previous_recommendations_progress: ✅ Improved political engagement (e.g., POB meetings with Afghan authorities).
⚠️ Partial progress on surveillance gaps (persistent issues in Yemen, eastern DRC).
❌ Limited advancement in Gavi integration due to funding uncertainties.
forward_recommendations: Conduct a feasibility study for a hybrid eradication/control strategy for cVDPVs by Q1 2024.
Develop a transition funding mechanism with WHO to secure £50m for post-eradication surveillance.
Expand nOPV2 use to all cVDPV2-affected countries, pending safety data from 2023 outbreaks.
Strengthen GPEI’s risk management framework to escalate cross-cutting risks (e.g., transition, integration).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate: GPEI’s risk registers were comprehensive but lacked dynamic prioritization. The 2022 IMB report highlighted slow responses to cVDPV1 outbreaks. New EMU-led risk monitoring (2023) aims to address this.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 58% (global average); 71% in outbreak countries; <50% in Afghanistan/Pakistan’s high-risk regions
beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: 80% of Afghanistan’s population accessed (vs. 60% in 2021) but coverage in Taliban-controlled areas dropped to 30%.

policy_influence_achieved: GPEI’s advocacy led to polio eradication being included in WHO’s 2023–2025 Global Health Strategy.
UK’s polio transition funding influenced Gavi’s 2023 investment case to prioritize post-eradication surveillance.
Afghanistan’s Taliban approved limited female FLW participation after GPEI negotiations.
capacity_building_results: Trained 12,000+ surveillance officers across 20 countries (2022), but retention rates in conflict zones were <50%.
Established 5 regional polio labs in Africa (2021–2022) with WHO accreditation.
Integrated polio data systems with national health information platforms in Nigeria and Somalia.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Polio infrastructure supported COVID-19 vaccine delivery in 15 countries, reaching 5M+ additional children.
Negative: Focus on polio diverted resources from routine immunization in Pakistan, contributing to a 10% drop in measles vaccination coverage (2022).
Negative: nOPV2-seeded cVDPV outbreaks (2023) created vaccine hesitancy in Mozambique and Yemen.
scalability_evidence: nOPV2’s success in 23 countries demonstrates scalability for cVDPV2 response, but supply constraints limit global rollout.
Digital surveillance tools piloted in DRC are being adapted for measles and yellow fever programmes.
Transition models in Nigeria (polio assets repurposed for primary healthcare) show potential for replication in Somalia.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Despite challenges, GPEI remains the most viable path to polio eradication. WPV1 interruption in Afghanistan/Pakistan is feasible by end-2023 with current strategies, and cVDPV2 progress (via nOPV2) justifies continued investment. UK’s £50m commitment (2022–2025) aligns with FCDO’s global health security priorities.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High for WPV1 eradication; Medium for cVDPV2 elimination (timeline extended to 2026).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-term sustainable with adjustments: (1) Secure transition funding; (2) Resolve Taliban restrictions; (3) Scale nOPV2 production.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied with progress on WPV1 but concerned about cVDPV2 trajectory and transition risks. Scorecard improvements (2023) will be critical for maintaining support.
planned_adaptations_future: Expand nOPV2 use to all cVDPV2-affected countries by mid-2024, contingent on safety data.
Pilot hybrid eradication/control strategies in eastern DRC and Yemen if cVDPV2 persists.
Repurpose 30% of polio surveillance assets for broader disease monitoring in transition countries (e.g., Nigeria).
Advocate for a UN-led polio transition fund to bridge the £200m gap identified for 2026–2030.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Digital Identity as an Enabler for Development

output_1.title: Implement robust, applied and ambitious thought-leadership and analytics work on digital ID

output_3.title: Provide technical assistance to over 30 governments and regional institutions

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme contributes to a multi-donor trust fund (MDTF) governed by World Bank, with UK funds co-mingled (13% contribution). Delivery model leverages World Bank's ID4D initiative across three pillars: analytics/research, global platforms, and technical assistance (TA).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank's ID4D initiative has exceeded expectations in demand for TA (now supporting ~60 countries vs. original target of 30+) and knowledge products. Partner governments actively request and utilize ID4D's guidance, with evidence of uptake in policy and system design (e.g., Philippines' PhilSys ID, Cameroon's authentication reforms).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO participates in ID4D's steering committee, providing oversight and strategic direction alongside other donors. The World Bank manages day-to-day implementation, with FCDO conducting annual reviews to assess progress against UK-specific milestones.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination occurs through the MDTF structure, with ID4D serving as a global convener for digital ID stakeholders. Peer-to-peer exchanges and knowledge-sharing platforms (e.g., G20 working groups) enhance collaboration, though attribution of specific activities to UK funds remains limited due to co-mingled financing.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO conducts annual reviews and sits on the ID4D steering committee, but operational oversight is delegated to the World Bank. Oversight focuses on high-level performance (e.g., output scores, risk ratings) rather than granular activity tracking.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The MDTF model allows for adaptive allocation of funds based on country demand. For example, TA expanded from 15 to 59 countries, and new diagnostics were added in response to emerging needs (e.g., Eswatini, Lebanon). UK funds benefit from this flexibility as part of the pooled resource.
adaptive_management_examples: Expanded TA from 15 to 59 countries + 4 regional organizations based on demand.
Added 6 new country diagnostics in 2023 (Eswatini, Lebanon, Kiribati, Cameroon, Sao Tome and Principe, Colombia) in response to identified gaps.
Incorporated participant feedback from capacity-building events to refine knowledge-exchange designs.
Adjusted research priorities to address persistent gender gaps in ID coverage (e.g., focused studies in 13 of 15 countries with the largest gender disparities).

main_implementation_challenges: Data limitations in tracking the global ID gap over time (e.g., methodology changes in ID4D Global Dataset prevent time-series analysis).
Persistent gender disparities in ID coverage, particularly in Low-Income Countries (LICs), where 35% of women lack ID vs. 27% of men.
Difficulty attributing specific outputs/impacts to UK funds due to co-mingled MDTF financing.
Limited granular cost data for output-level Value for Money (VFM) assessments.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 accelerated demand for digital ID to enable emergency cash transfers and service delivery, increasing relevance of ID4D's TA (e.g., verification mechanisms for pandemic responses).
Geopolitical and economic instability in some partner countries (e.g., Somalia, Lebanon) created implementation delays for diagnostics and TA.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging needs for digital authentication infrastructure in countries with existing ID systems but no verification capabilities (e.g., Cameroon).
Increased focus on Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) in global forums (e.g., G20) requiring ID4D to expand its knowledge-partner role.
capacity_constraints_emerged: High demand for TA (now ~60 countries) strains ID4D's core team (9 FTEs) and consultant resources, though World Bank financing helps scale support.
Limited capacity in some partner governments to implement complex ID system reforms (e.g., digital authentication, gender-inclusive design).
risk_materialization: Moderate risk rating persisted due to challenges in closing the gender ID gap and data limitations for impact tracking.
No major risks fully materialized; ID4D's adaptive approach (e.g., expanded diagnostics, gender-focused TA) mitigated potential setbacks.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. UK contributions (~13% of ID4D MDTF) have been fully disbursed as planned. The World Bank reports $2 billion in approved/pipeline financing for ID/CR systems, with $283 million newly approved in FY2023.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong. UK funds are estimated to have contributed to ID improvements for ~247 million people at an average cost of £0.03 per person. While direct attribution is limited, ID4D's leverage of World Bank financing (supporting 1.9 billion people across partner countries) enhances VFM. Research products show high uptake (e.g., 606 downloads for "Federated Ecosystems for Digital ID").
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. World Bank's MDTF governance ensures robust financial management, though donor-specific reporting is restricted per trust fund policies. No issues flagged in financial oversight.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient. Pooled funding reduces transaction costs, and economies of scale are realized through shared TA/knowledge platforms. Cost per person reached (~£0.03) is significantly below typical development programme benchmarks.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Yes. ID4D's MDTF model attracts co-financing from multiple donors, leveraging UK contributions. World Bank financing ($2 billion approved/pipeline) further amplifies impact.

key_delivery_lessons: Multi-donor trust funds (MDTFs) are effective for scaling global public goods (e.g., digital ID) but limit donor-specific attribution. Clear milestones and proportional reporting (e.g., 13% UK contribution = ~13% of results) help assess value.
Demand-driven TA (vs. pre-planned interventions) enhances country ownership and impact, as seen in ID4D's expansion to 59 countries.
Peer learning and knowledge exchanges (e.g., G20 partnerships) amplify influence beyond direct funding.
successful_delivery_practices: Co-mingled financing reduces administrative burdens and enables flexible allocation to high-demand areas (e.g., gender-focused diagnostics).
Strategic use of global datasets (e.g., ID4D-Findex) to identify gaps and target TA (e.g., 13 of 15 countries with largest gender ID gaps).
Leveraging World Bank's convening power to attract co-financing ($2 billion) and scale impact.
Participant feedback loops for capacity-building events improved design of knowledge exchanges.
management_adaptations_made: Added new diagnostics (e.g., Kiribati, Sao Tome and Principe) in response to emerging country needs.
Increased focus on digital authentication TA (e.g., Cameroon, Philippines) based on implementation gaps identified.
Strengthened gender-disaggregated data collection in ID4D-Findex surveys to monitor equity progress.
innovations_attempted: Integration of ID4D data with Findex surveys to enable gender/Income-disaggregated analysis of ID coverage.
Development of "federated ecosystems" guidance for interoperable digital ID systems (606 downloads).
Pilot of participant feedback surveys for knowledge-exchange events to refine delivery.
previous_recommendations_progress: Implemented recommendation to collect participant feedback from capacity-building events (now standard practice).
Expanded gender-focused TA to 13 of 15 highest-gap countries, addressing prior concerns about equity.
forward_recommendations: Explore mechanisms to improve attribution of UK-specific contributions within the MDTF model, while retaining flexibility.
Deepened engagement with countries showing slow progress on gender gaps (e.g., LICs with 35% women unregistered).
Scale successful models like Philippines' PhilSys (80M enrolled, 8M new bank accounts) through South-South learning.
Strengthen post-TA monitoring to assess sustainability of ID system reforms.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. ID4D's proactive adjustments (e.g., expanded diagnostics, gender-targeted support) mitigated risks related to data gaps and equity. Steering committee oversight (including FCDO) ensured strategic alignment. Moderate risk rating reflects persistent but managed challenges (e.g., gender disparities).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: UK funds estimated to contribute to ~247M people gaining improved ID at £0.03/person. Total ID4D/WB financing supports systems covering 1.9B people.

policy_influence_achieved: ID4D's analytics and TA directly inform World Bank's $2B financing pipeline for ID/CR systems.
Principles on Identification for Development integrated into 16 country diagnostics and WB lending projects.
G20 adoption of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) agendas influenced by ID4D's knowledge partnership.
Philippines' PhilSys ID system (80M enrolled) and Cameroon's authentication reforms cite ID4D guidance.
capacity_building_results: 59 countries + 4 regional organizations received TA, strengthening institutional capacity for ID system design/implementation.
16 diagnostics completed (6 in 2023) to assess and address country-specific gaps (e.g., Eswatini, Lebanon).
Knowledge exchanges and peer learning platforms (e.g., G20) built capacity among 60+ countries.

unintended_consequences.description: Digital ID enabled 8M new bank accounts in the Philippines, predominantly for low-income individuals, exceeding financial inclusion targets.
Risk of exacerbating exclusion for marginalized groups (e.g., women in LICs) if gender gaps in ID coverage (35% vs. 27% men) are not addressed. ID4D has mitigated this through targeted TA.

scalability_evidence: ID4D's TA model has scaled from 15 to 59 countries, demonstrating adaptability to diverse contexts.
World Bank's $2B financing pipeline (leveraged by ID4D) indicates potential for further expansion.
Lessons from Philippines and Cameroon are being replicated in new diagnostics (e.g., Mali, Honduras).
Global platforms (e.g., ID4D-Findex) provide scalable data tools for monitoring ID coverage worldwide.

continuation_rationale: Consistent A+ performance and high demand for TA (now 60 countries) justify continuation.
Alignment with UK priorities on digital inclusion, SDG 16.9 (legal identity for all), and global leadership in digital development.
Strong VFM (£0.03/person) and leverage of World Bank co-financing ($2B) maximize impact.
Ongoing gaps in global ID coverage (850M unregistered) and gender disparities require sustained support.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes. The MDTF model is sustainable, with World Bank governance ensuring long-term viability. UK's steering committee role provides strategic influence.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Deepened focus on closing gender ID gaps through targeted TA and data collection.
Expansion of digital authentication support (e.g., Cameroon, Somalia) to enhance service delivery.
Strengthened post-TA monitoring to ensure sustainability of reforms.
Exploration of new partnerships (e.g., G20 DPI working groups) to amplify global influence.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Child Wasting Innovation Programme (CWIP), formerly PARSNIP

output_1.title: Effective financing and pre-positioning for RUTF

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended by 5 years (to 2030) with £30.7m additional funding to scale successful financing mechanisms (Child Nutrition Fund) and strengthen prevention evidence base. Original business case focused on 9-year timeline with £61.4m budget, now adjusted to £61.5m with extended scope.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF exceeded expectations in Output 1 (financing solutions), particularly through the Child Nutrition Fund's governance and donor mobilization ($46.1m committed, $40.3m received from 13 countries). However, global supply chain challenges (e.g., RUTF cost increases) impacted some operational targets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UK played a leading role in shaping the Child Nutrition Fund's steering committee and strategic framework, demonstrating stronger-than-planned governance influence. Monthly catch-ups with UNICEF and participation in WHO guideline groups enhanced coordination beyond original plans.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved coordination at global level (e.g., WHO guideline development, multi-donor Child Nutrition Fund) addressed earlier fragmentation. Country-level coordination varied, with conflicts (e.g., East DRC) disrupting logistics for landlocked regions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of 853,369 RUTF cartons (vs. 135,833 target) significantly exceeded plans, but landed costs increased due to global raw material price volatility. Regional production (Burkina Faso, Nigeria) improved delivery times for coastal countries but not landlocked ones.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight due to complex multi-country financing mechanisms and need to manage supply chain risks. FCDO's role in steering committees required more active engagement than initially anticipated.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to COVID-19 (£0.75m extension in 2020 for research) and food/nutrition crises by reprioritizing treatment scale-up over prevention innovation. Funding extension enabled redesign of logframe and weightings to reflect new priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Creation of Child Nutrition Fund in response to early success with financing pilots, now a multi-donor mechanism with 13 subscribed countries.
Shift in Output 1.4 delivery routes to leverage regional RUTF production (Burkina Faso, Nigeria), reducing coastal delivery times from 50 to 16 days.
Deprioritization of alternative RUTF formulations due to crisis-driven focus on treatment scale-up, with plans to revisit prevention innovation post-2024.

main_implementation_challenges: Volatility in global RUTF production costs (raw materials) reversing previous cost-reduction trends (Output 1.3: $55.20 vs. $48 target).
Logistical disruptions in landlocked countries (e.g., East DRC) due to conflict, increasing delivery times to 59 days (vs. 70-day target).
Balancing treatment scale-up (driven by US funding influx) with prevention innovation, leading to deprioritization of longer-term evidence-building.
Unstable donor funding cycles creating market inefficiencies for RUTF producers and supply chain partners.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 (2020): Required £0.75m extension for research on malnutrition treatment/prevention in pandemic context (contributed to Output 3).
Global food/nutrition crisis (2022–23): Increased treatment demand, shifting focus from prevention to emergency response.
Climate change: Exacerbated child wasting prevalence in target regions, requiring adaptive programming (e.g., climate-resilient supply chains).
Geopolitical conflicts: Disrupted RUTF delivery routes in East DRC and other landlocked areas.
contextual_constraints_new: Limited government capacity in some target countries to integrate wasting treatment into broader health financing (e.g., GFF investment cases).
Over-reliance on a few regional RUTF suppliers (Burkina Faso, Nigeria) creating vulnerability to production shocks.
Competing donor priorities (e.g., US focus on treatment) diverting attention from systemic prevention reforms.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between short-term treatment scale-up demands and long-term prevention goals among implementing partners.
Delays in some countries' subscription to the Child Nutrition Fund due to bureaucratic hurdles (e.g., Mauritania, Uganda renewals pending).
capacity_constraints_emerged: UNICEF's global coordination capacity stretched by expanded Child Nutrition Fund management roles.
Limited in-country technical expertise to operationalize climate-resilient wasting prevention strategies.
Supply chain partners' inability to maintain production levels during funding troughs, risking market instability.
risk_materialization: Supply chain risks (Output 2): Increased RUTF costs and landlocked delivery delays materialized as predicted in early risk registers.
Financial risks: Currency fluctuations and raw material price spikes (e.g., 2022–23) impacted VFM, though mitigated by regional production.
Political risks: Conflicts in East DRC disrupted logistics, as flagged in initial context analyses.
Programmatic risks: Prevention activities (Output 3) were deprioritized due to crisis response, aligning with risk scenarios around funding volatility.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution exceeded plans with £61.5m total (vs. original £61.4m) due to two extensions: £0.75m in 2020 for COVID-19 research and £30.7m in 2023 for scale-up. 2023 spend aligned with revised AMP, with no underspend reported.

value_for_money_assessment.assessment: High VFM achieved through bulk procurement (853,369 cartons vs. 135,833 target) and regional production, though cost per carton increased to $55.20 (vs. $48 target) due to global inflation. Savings from reduced delivery times (coastal: 16 vs. 50 days) partially offset cost increases.
Exceeds VFM projections: $15.1m leveraged $40.3m in donor contributions (1:2.67 match ratio), with governance costs lower than anticipated due to UNICEF's existing systems.
Lower VFM than planned due to reprioritization toward treatment, delaying returns on prevention investments (e.g., alternative RUTF formulations).

financial_management_quality: UNICEF's financial reporting met FCDO standards, with timely audits and transparent Child Nutrition Fund accounting.
No material findings in 2023 financial reviews, though minor delays in country-level fund disbursements were noted (e.g., Mauritania).
Strong donor coordination reduced transaction costs for multi-country financing mechanisms.

cost_efficiency_achieved.efficiency: Improved for coastal countries (16-day delivery vs. 50-day target) but deteriorated for landlocked (59 vs. 70 days). Net efficiency gain due to regional production scale.
Child Nutrition Fund administrative costs at 5% of total (vs. 8% projected), achieving economies of scale.
Lower than planned due to deprioritization; cost per output delayed by crisis response.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding exceeded expectations: Child Nutrition Fund secured $40.3m from 13 countries (vs. initial target of 4 GFF countries). Additional co-funding pipelines identified (e.g., Angola, Namibia).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minor adverse impacts from USD strength in 2023 increased RUTF production costs, partially offset by local currency procurement in regional hubs (e.g., Nigeria).

key_delivery_lessons: Multi-donor financing mechanisms (e.g., Child Nutrition Fund) can achieve scale and VFM but require intensive governance (e.g., UK's steering committee role).
Regional production hubs (e.g., Burkina Faso, Nigeria) reduce delivery times but need stable demand to sustain supplier viability.
Crisis-driven treatment scale-up can crowd out prevention innovation, requiring explicit safeguards for long-term goals.
Climate-resilient supply chains demand upfront investment in redundancy and local partnerships.
successful_delivery_practices: UNICEF's leadership in convening donors (13 countries in Child Nutrition Fund) and shaping global guidelines (WHO engagement).
Flexible funding extensions (e.g., COVID-19 research) enabled rapid adaptation to emerging needs.
Monthly catch-ups with implementers improved real-time problem-solving (e.g., DRC logistics).
Output 1's financing solutions (A+ score) demonstrate that pilot-to-scale transitions are feasible with donor alignment.
management_adaptations_made: Redesign of logframe and impact weightings planned post-2023 to reflect extended funding and prevention focus.
Increased oversight of supply chain partners to mitigate raw material cost risks (e.g., diversifying RUTF suppliers).
Shift from alternative RUTF formulations to standard products to meet immediate treatment demands, with prevention research deferred.

innovations_attempted.outcome: Successful scale-up from pilot to 13-country mechanism, exceeding co-funding targets.
Reduced coastal delivery times by 68% (16 vs. 50 days) but limited impact on landlocked routes.
Early-stage; evidence base for prevention in climate-vulnerable contexts remains weak.

The high volume of grant applications (1200+ concept notes) exceeded expectations, particularly from smaller local organisations, revealing both strong demand and eligibility gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The SMU has operationalised governance bodies (Steering Committee and Independent Technical Advisory Panel - ITAP) with diverse geographic, gender, and technical representation. These bodies are actively shaping grant calls and programme direction, exceeding the planned advisory role.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with FCDO Country Offices has been critical in sifting grant applications and aligning with local priorities. New partnerships (e.g., JICA ORI, NERC, DEFRA) have been established to maximise synergies, demonstrating stronger-than-planned cross-programme collaboration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The procurement of downstream partners (e.g., for JICA collaboration) and the launch of the Nature Facility were implemented efficiently. The online grants application platform was developed and deployed on schedule.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has been more intensive than originally planned due to the overwhelming response to Grant Call 1. The SMU has proactively managed this through additional engagement with FCDO Country Offices and adaptive resource allocation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme has demonstrated significant flexibility by: 1) Adjusting the REDAA Strategy based on scoping studies and stakeholder consultations; 2) Launching demonstrator projects to test approaches; 3) Responding to high grant demand by revisiting SMU resourcing and targeting future calls to match capacity.
adaptive_management_examples: Mitigated partner delays (ICLEI/UNU) by conducting internal scoping of sub-Saharan Africa priorities to keep strategy development on track.
Adjusted Grant Call 2 and 3 design to better target locally led initiatives and manage application volumes, incorporating lessons from Call 1.
Launched the Nature Facility in response to identified FCDO demand for technical support on nature-and-people issues, which was not part of the original plan.
Initiated an AI scoping study to assess its potential for locally led nature restoration, responding to emerging technological opportunities.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays from partners (ICLEI and UNU) in delivering sub-Saharan Africa scoping studies due to capacity constraints outside their control.
Overwhelming demand for Grant Call 1 (1200+ concept notes), far exceeding expectations and straining SMU sifting capacity.
Eligibility criteria for grants excluded many small, local organisations, creating tension between risk management and inclusivity goals.
High initial workload for the Nature Facility due to unanticipated FCDO demand, challenging existing SMU capacity.
external_factors_impact: Global uncertainties (unspecified) required adaptive management but did not derail milestones.
FCDO’s evolving priorities (e.g., focus on International Climate Finance reporting) necessitated alignment adjustments in grant design and monitoring.
contextual_constraints_new: Stronger-than-expected demand for locally led research funding revealed gaps in accessibility for smaller organisations, requiring policy adjustments.
The need for FCDO-wide technical support on nature-and-people issues (addressed via the Nature Facility) was not fully anticipated in the business case.
AI’s emerging role in nature restoration presented both opportunities (e.g., programme efficiency) and risks (e.g., equity in locally led action) that required unplanned assessment.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial delays with ICLEI and UNU due to capacity constraints, though mitigated through collaborative problem-solving.
Tension between FCDO’s financial eligibility requirements and the programme’s goal of supporting small, local organisations, requiring ongoing negotiation.
capacity_constraints_emerged: SMU’s capacity was stretched by the volume of Grant Call 1 applications, necessitating additional resources and process adjustments.
The Nature Facility’s popularity exceeded SMU’s capacity to respond to FCDO requests without additional resourcing.
Need for specialised expertise in AI and its applications for locally led nature restoration was not anticipated.
risk_materialization: Risk of partner delays (ICLEI/UNU) materialised but was mitigated through internal scoping work.
Risk of overwhelming grant demand materialised, requiring adaptive management to maintain quality and timeliness.
The "Moderate" risk rating was briefly revised to "Major" in Year 1 but returned to "Moderate" after mitigation measures.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. All set-up phase milestones were met within budget, and the programme is progressing toward disbursing grants to up to 21 initiatives by Q4 FY2023-24. The high demand for grants did not result in cost overruns but required reallocation of SMU resources.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. The programme has demonstrated strong VFM by: 1) Leveraging existing FCDO partnerships (e.g., NERC, DEFRA) to avoid duplication; 2) Attracting high-quality applications at a lower-than-expected cost per grant (due to competitive demand); 3) Designing the Nature Facility to serve multiple FCDO teams, maximising its impact per pound spent.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. The SMU has maintained robust financial controls, as evidenced by: 1) Timely establishment of governance and fiduciary risk systems; 2) Efficient procurement of downstream partners; 3) Transparent reporting on grant call processes. No significant financial irregularities were reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The cost efficiency exceeds expectations due to: 1) Higher-than-planned leverage of existing FCDO platforms (e.g., DevTracker); 2) Shared events with NERC and DEFRA reducing individual programme costs; 3) Digital tools (e.g., online grants platform) reducing administrative overhead.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. While the programme attracted interest from other funders (e.g., JICA ORI collaboration), planned co-funding has not yet fully materialised. Efforts are ongoing to secure co-funding for future grant calls, particularly for large-sized grants.

key_delivery_lessons: Locally led research-to-action is a highly relevant and underserved niche, as demonstrated by the overwhelming response to Grant Call 1.
Adaptive management is essential for responding to external uncertainties and partner constraints without compromising milestones.
Early investment in scoping studies and demonstrator projects provides critical evidence for refining programme strategy and grant design.
Coordination with FCDO Country Offices is vital for aligning grant selections with local priorities and managing application volumes.
successful_delivery_practices: Co-design workshops (e.g., in Bangkok and Kathmandu) ensured the REDAA Strategy responded to regional priorities.
The Nature Facility’s on-demand technical support model proved highly effective in influencing FCDO policy and programming decisions.
Demonstrator projects and seed funds (e.g., RAEng Frontiers Programme) provided low-risk opportunities to test innovative approaches.
Regular engagement with the Independent Technical Advisory Panel (ITAP) enhanced the scientific rigour and local relevance of grant calls.
management_adaptations_made: Revised the REDAA Strategy and logframe milestones based on scoping study findings and Grant Call 1 lessons (Recommendation 1a).
Planned to launch a REDAA Community and Learning Programme to strengthen grantee support and cross-project linkages (Recommendation 1b).
Adjusted future grant calls (Calls 2 and 3) to better target locally led initiatives and manage application volumes (Recommendation 2a).
Initiated a review of SMU resourcing to address capacity constraints from high grant demand (Recommendation 2b).
innovations_attempted: Pilot of the Nature Facility as an on-demand technical support mechanism for FCDO, with potential to scale to other UK government departments.
Exploration of AI applications for locally led nature restoration, including a planned scoping study to assess opportunities and risks (Recommendation 4).
Development of an ICF-aligned reporting methodology for grantees to meet FCDO’s climate finance monitoring requirements (Recommendation 2d).
Trialling of small catalytic grants in Grant Call 3 to improve accessibility for local organisations while managing risk.
previous_recommendations_progress: The 2022 Annual Review’s recommendation to strengthen local leadership was addressed through the co-designed REDAA Strategy and Grant Call 1’s focus on locally led projects.
The need for adaptive management (highlighted in earlier reviews) was institutionalised through the SMU’s responsive approach to partner delays and grant demand surges.
Recommendations to improve MEL systems were partially addressed through the development of an ICF-aligned reporting methodology (ongoing).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Review and update the REDAA Strategy, thematic priorities, and logframe milestones based on sub-Saharan Africa scoping findings and Grant Call 1 lessons (by April 2024).
Launch the REDAA Community and Learning Programme to support grantees and foster cross-project collaboration (by June 2024).
Adjust Grant Calls 2 and 3 to better target locally led initiatives and manage application volumes, drawing on scoping studies and in-country consultations (by June 2024).
Review SMU resourcing to address capacity constraints from high grant demand and Nature Facility workload (by January 2024).
Develop options to scale the Nature Facility, including potential expansion to other UK government departments (by June 2024).
Assess the prospects and pitfalls of AI for locally led nature-people-climate action and trial AI in programme management (by October 2024).
Develop an ICF-aligned reporting methodology for REDAA grantees to meet climate finance monitoring requirements (by August 2024).

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. The programme has proactively managed risks by: 1) Mitigating partner delays through internal scoping work; 2) Adjusting grant designs to balance demand with capacity; 3) Elevating risk ratings temporarily (e.g., Year 1 "Major" revision) when needed and successfully returning to "Moderate" through corrective actions. The Independent Technical Advisory Panel (ITAP) has played a key role in identifying and addressing emerging risks.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: The programme is on track to support up to 21 locally led initiatives through Grant Call 1 by Q4 FY2023-24, with over 1200 concept notes received, indicating strong potential reach. Three demonstrator projects were completed in FY22/23, and two more in FY23/24, directly engaging local communities in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. The Nature Facility has influenced FCDO policy decisions (e.g., Indonesia biomass strategy), indirectly benefiting broader populations.
policy_influence_achieved: The Nature Facility’s technical support has directly shaped FCDO’s understanding of biomass in Indonesia and influenced UK policy positions.
REDAA’s co-designed strategy and grant calls have aligned with FCDO Country Office priorities, increasing the likelihood of policy uptake at local and national levels.
Collaborations with NERC and DEFRA have strengthened the programme’s credibility and potential for joint policy advocacy.
capacity_building_results: Demonstrator projects have built local capacity in ecosystem restoration techniques and research-to-action methodologies.
The planned REDAA Community and Learning Programme aims to further strengthen grantee capabilities in project delivery, MEL, and communications.
The Nature Facility has enhanced FCDO staff capacity to integrate nature-and-people considerations into programming.

unintended_consequences.description: The overwhelming demand for grants revealed a previously under recognised appetite for locally led, interdisciplinary research funding in the target regions, prompting other funders (e.g., JICA) to explore similar models.

The eligibility criteria for grants inadvertently excluded many small, local organisations, creating a perception of inaccessibility among some target beneficiaries. This is being addressed in future grant calls.
The Nature Facility’s popularity within FCDO has led to interest from other UK government departments, potentially expanding its impact beyond the original scope.

scalability_evidence: The Nature Facility’s model has demonstrated scalability potential, with interest from other UK government departments in adopting or expanding the mechanism.
The locally led research-to-action approach has proven attractive to other funders (e.g., JICA collaboration), suggesting potential for replication in similar programmes.
The programme’s adaptive management practices and governance structures (e.g., ITAP) are designed to be scalable to larger or additional geographic regions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong performance (consistent "A" scores) and high relevance to FCDO priorities. Key achievements include: 1) Successful launch of Grant Call 1 with overwhelming demand; 2) Effective adaptive management in response to challenges; 3) Strong policy influence through the Nature Facility; 4) Progress toward locally led, interdisciplinary research goals. The programme is well-positioned to achieve its long-term objectives with continued SMU oversight and minor adjustments to grant accessibility and resourcing.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is sustainable long-term, with the following strengths: 1) The SMU’s adaptive management approach has proven resilient; 2) Governance structures (Steering Committee, ITAP) are functional and additive; 3) Partnerships with FCDO Country Offices and other UK government entities (e.g., NERC, DEFRA) enhance sustainability. Minor risks include SMU capacity constraints and the need for additional resourcing to meet demand.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Review and update the REDAA Strategy and logframe to reflect lessons from Grant Call 1 and sub-Saharan Africa scoping (by April 2024).
Launch the REDAA Community and Learning Programme to strengthen grantee support and cross-project collaboration (by June 2024).
Adjust Grant Calls 2 and 3 to better target locally led initiatives, incorporating capacity-building for smaller organisations.
Expand SMU resourcing to manage high demand for grants and Nature Facility support, including potential trial period extension for the Facility.
Develop and pilot AI applications for programme management and locally led research, with GESI considerations (by October 2024).
Finalise and implement an ICF-aligned reporting methodology for grantees to meet climate finance requirements (by August 2024).
