programme_metadata.programme_title: Getting children ready to learn and thrive – Research into implementing effective and quality Early Childhood Development at scale

output_1.title: Robust and rigorous research on effectiveness ('what works' to strengthen implementation of ECD service delivery at scale) and efficacy (innovative approaches to ECD)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme faced delays due to COVID-19 and ODA reductions, leading to an extension to 2026. Mobilisation phase prolonged due to FCDO pause in new programme procurement (2020-21), impacting THRIVE Research Partner Consortium (RPC) mobilisation and MRC grant processes. Delivery continued through World Bank Early Years Fellows and near-complete RPC procurement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: MRC partnership operated as expected for bid moderation, with FCDO Programme Funded Post (PFP) embedded in MRC’s Global Health Team managing peer review. UKRI ODA review suspended MRC AGHRB, delaying future milestones. PFP secondment to FCDO Sierra Leone office provided cost savings and contextual insights.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Prolonged mobilisation phase due to external delays. PFP played a key role in thought leadership (e.g., contributing to FCDO’s Gender Equity and Childhood Development Review) and stakeholder coordination (e.g., ECD Action Network, UNICEF submissions). RPC procurement nearing completion for FY 2022/23 start.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Emerging programme influence via PFP’s technical engagement across FCDO and external ECD initiatives (e.g., KEEP programme, BE2 ECD Special Interest Group). Coordination with New Zealand MFAT for Kiribati component remained on track despite delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: RPC procurement delayed by FCDO procurement pause but nearing completion. MRC grant processes paused due to UKRI ODA review, with calls expected to restart in Spring 2022. World Bank Early Years Fellows component leveraged £272,750 in new projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher oversight intensity during mobilisation phase due to delays. PFP’s dual role (MRC/FCDO Sierra Leone) provided cost efficiencies and deeper country-level engagement. External evaluation paused indefinitely due to budget constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to ODA reductions by extending timeline to 2026 and reallocating PFP resources (e.g., surge to Sierra Leone). Milestones revised to reflect delayed RPC mobilisation and MRC call timelines (2023–2026 for research outputs).
adaptive_management_examples: PFP secondment to FCDO Sierra Leone to cover advisory gaps, saving costs while building country-specific expertise.
Revised RPC mobilisation timelines and logframe indicators to align with delayed procurement, maintaining realistic targets.
Leveraged World Bank Fellows component to generate early results (£272,750 in new projects) despite broader delays.

main_implementation_challenges: Prolonged mobilisation phase due to FCDO procurement pause (2020–21) and ODA budget reductions (0.5% GNI target).
UKRI ODA review suspended MRC AGHRB, halting new research calls and delaying grant awards.
COVID-19 pandemic disrupted in-country activities and partner engagements, requiring timeline extensions.
Delayed RPC procurement pushed back research implementation and evidence generation to 2023–2026.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Caused procurement delays, reduced ODA budget, and limited in-country research activities.
UK ODA reduction to 0.5% GNI: Led to funding uncertainties and paused new programme procurements, directly impacting THRIVE’s mobilisation.
Global economic shifts: Affected partner organisations’ capacity and willingness to co-fund (e.g., New Zealand MFAT’s £975k contribution remained stable).
contextual_constraints_new: Difficulty in aligning in-country implementation research with at-scale ECD service delivery due to shifting political and economic contexts (e.g., Sierra Leone’s education system complexities).
Unanticipated pauses in MRC’s AGHRB required reprogramming of research call timelines, affecting indicator milestones.
Limited capacity in fragile contexts (e.g., South Sudan, Kiribati) to absorb research findings into policy during mobilisation phase.
partner_relationship_issues: MRC partnership faced operational disruptions due to UKRI ODA review, requiring THRIVE to adapt call management processes.
Delayed RPC procurement strained relationships with potential research consortia, risking partner engagement.
Co-funding partner (New Zealand MFAT) maintained commitment, but coordination required additional effort due to geographic and institutional distances.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited in-country capacity to conduct scoping activities for research design, exacerbated by COVID-19 travel restrictions.
FCDO’s reduced ODA budget constrained ability to hire additional technical staff for RPC mobilisation support.
PFP’s dual role (MRC/FCDO Sierra Leone) stretched thin, though mitigated by surge deployment.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (FCDO pause) materialised as a high risk, extending mobilisation phase.
ODA budget cuts materialised, requiring programme extension to 2026 and reprioritisation of activities.
MRC AGHRB suspension materialised, delaying research grant awards and publication timelines.
COVID-19 travel restrictions materialised, limiting in-country engagement and data collection.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Programme remained within budget despite delays, with cost savings achieved through PFP’s surge deployment to Sierra Leone (reduced MRC secondment costs).
ODA reductions led to indefinite pause of external evaluation, reallocating funds to core activities.
World Bank Fellows component demonstrated early leverage, generating £272,750 in new projects from UK-funded investments.
value_for_money_assessment: MRC’s AGHRB applied rigorous VFM criteria, rejecting poorly costed proposals and requesting revisions. Example: 5 out of 8 ECD proposals reviewed in January 2021 were deemed unfundable or required budget adjustments.
PFP’s dual role (MRC/Sierra Leone) improved efficiency by reducing redundancy and building country-specific knowledge without additional costs.
Delayed RPC mobilisation deferred expenditure to outer years (2023–2026), aligning with revised research output timelines.
financial_management_quality: Strong financial oversight maintained during mobilisation, with no reported mismanagement or audit findings.
FCDO’s financial controls ensured compliance with ODA reductions, though flexibility was limited for new commitments.
Co-funding from New Zealand MFAT (£975k) was managed transparently, with clear reporting on Kiribati-specific activities.
cost_efficiency_achieved: PFP surge deployment saved ~£50k (estimated) by reducing MRC secondment costs while filling FCDO Sierra Leone’s advisory gap.
Leverage ratio of £272,750 in new projects from World Bank Fellows component indicates efficient use of UK funds (input:output ratio not quantified).
Delayed RPC procurement avoided premature expenditure, preserving budget for extended timeline.
co_funding_materialization: New Zealand MFAT’s £975k contribution materialised as planned, supporting Kiribati component.
No additional co-funding materialised beyond MFAT’s commitment, with other partners (e.g., World Bank) contributing in-kind through Fellows programme.
Potential co-funding from other donors deferred due to global ODA reductions.

key_delivery_lessons: Timing of country scoping for research design is critical and vulnerable to external shocks (e.g., COVID-19, ODA cuts). Stress-testing country selection during inception is essential.
Embedded PFPs can provide high-value thought leadership and cost efficiencies when deployed flexibly (e.g., surge support to country offices).
Multi-sectoral research calls require continuous adaptation to align with FCDO’s evolving strategic priorities (e.g., girls’ education, Indo-Pacific tilt).
successful_delivery_practices: PFP’s dual role (MRC/FCDO Sierra Leone) successfully bridged global research priorities with country-level needs, generating early policy influence.
World Bank Early Years Fellows component demonstrated quick wins, leveraging UK funds to catalyse new ECD projects (£272,750).
Partnership with ECD Action Network (ECDAN) and BE2 amplified THRIVE’s visibility and facilitated knowledge sharing (e.g., CIES conference submission with UNICEF).
management_adaptations_made: Logframe milestones revised to reflect delayed RPC mobilisation, with uncompleted indicators carried forward to FY 2022/23.
PFP’s role expanded to include horizon scanning for evidence translation, addressing gaps in linking research to policy uptake.
MRC call texts were adapted to emphasise cross-sectoral research and scale, improving alignment with THRIVE’s objectives.
innovations_attempted: PFP surge deployment model: Temporary reallocation of technical staff to fill country-office gaps, combining cost savings with capacity building.
Integration of gender equity into ECD research design (e.g., contributions to KEEP’s Gender Equity and Childhood Development Review).
Leveraging existing networks (ECDAN, BE2) to disseminate findings and influence policy debates without additional funding.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2020 AR recommendation to articulate THRIVE’s ambition for national-level ECD scale-up was paused due to delays. Rolled over to 2022 with focus on RPC inception phase.
Recommendation to review MRC’s ECD grants portfolio for coherence with THRIVE priorities was completed (e.g., cross-sectoral bids in 2021 calls).
Recommendation to simplify logframe remains outstanding; planned for July 2022 alongside RPC results framework development.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: By July 2022, streamline THRIVE logframe to separate outputs by component (RPC, MRC, PFP) and clarify accountability for funding streams.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Current logframe lacks clarity on which activities align with which partners, hindering performance tracking.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: By September 2022, prioritise RPC-led landscape mapping to identify optimal FCDO ECD country programmes for research alignment, ensuring multi-sectoral focus.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Delayed scoping risks misalignment between research and in-country ECD priorities.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Embed horizon scanning in PFP’s role to systematically track and integrate emerging ECD evidence into THRIVE’s research and policy engagement.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Current ad-hoc engagement limits THRIVE’s ability to shape global ECD debates proactively.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: By September 2022, ensure RPC and PFP prioritise engagement with broader ECD networks (e.g., BE2, ECDAN) to enhance research uptake and policy influence.
forward_recommendations.rationale: THRIVE’s influence depends on visibility within key stakeholders beyond FCDO.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Update logframe to distinguish between peer-reviewed academic publications and policy-focused outputs (e.g., briefs), with separate milestones.
forward_recommendations.rationale: Current indicators conflate research and policy products, obscuring progress on evidence translation.

risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive: Extended programme timeline to 2026 mitigated risks from ODA cuts and procurement delays.
Reactive: PFP surge deployment addressed unexpected advisory gaps in Sierra Leone, demonstrating adaptive capacity.
Gaps: Limited contingency planning for MRC AGHRB suspension; future risks should include alternative research funding mechanisms.
Learning: Stress-testing country selection and scoping timelines during inception is now a priority to anticipate contextual shifts.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: Programme remains in mobilisation phase; no direct beneficiaries reached yet. World Bank Fellows component catalysed £272,750 in new projects, indirectly benefiting early years programmes.

policy_influence_achieved: PFP contributed to FCDO’s Gender Equity and Childhood Development Review, distributed to 100+ organisations via ECDAN and presented at BE2.
THRIVE’s engagement with UNICEF and CIES conference submission advanced gender-ECD linkages in global policy debates.
World Bank Fellows’ projects identified new ECD investment opportunities, though direct policy uptake is not yet measurable.
capacity_building_results: World Bank Early Years Fellows built capacity in 5 countries (including Sierra Leone, Tanzania) through project development and technical support.
PFP’s secondment to MRC and FCDO Sierra Leone strengthened cross-sectoral ECD expertise within both institutions.
No formal capacity-building outputs reported for RPC or country teams due to delayed mobilisation.
unintended_consequences: Positive: PFP’s surge to Sierra Leone unintentionally deepened FCDO’s in-country ECD expertise, informing broader education programmes (e.g., KEEP).
Negative: Delayed RPC procurement risked partner disengagement and lost momentum in country-level research planning.
Negative: ODA cuts reduced THRIVE’s ability to fund additional capacity-building activities, limiting scope in fragile contexts (e.g., South Sudan).
scalability_evidence: World Bank Fellows model demonstrates scalability potential, with £272,750 leveraged from initial UK investment.
MRC’s cross-sectoral ECD calls (e.g., 3 funded proposals in 2021) suggest demand for scalable research, though implementation is pending.
THRIVE’s partnership with New Zealand MFAT for Kiribati offers a template for replicating co-funded research in other Pacific islands.

continuation_rationale: THRIVE aligns with FCDO’s strategic priorities on girls’ education and women’s empowerment, addressing a critical global evidence gap in ECD scale-up.
Despite delays, the programme has demonstrated early influence (e.g., policy contributions via PFP, World Bank Fellows’ leverage) and maintains strong partnerships (MRC, New Zealand MFAT).
Extension to 2026 provides sufficient time to deliver research outputs (2023–2026) and achieve intended outcomes, given the prolonged mobilisation phase.
Co-funding from New Zealand MFAT and potential for further leverage (e.g., World Bank projects) enhances VFM and sustainability.
delivery_model_sustainability: Strengths: RPC procurement nearing completion; PFP’s flexible deployment model proven effective; strong partnerships with MRC and MFAT.
Risks: Prolonged mobilisation may erode partner engagement; ODA uncertainty could limit future flexibility; fragile contexts (e.g., South Sudan) pose implementation challenges.
Mitigations: Streamlined logframe and RPC results framework (2022) will improve clarity; stress-testing country selection during inception will address contextual risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium
planned_adaptations_future: Develop RPC results framework by July 2022 to align outputs with funding components and improve accountability.
Prioritise country scoping and landscape mapping by September 2022 to ensure research aligns with FCDO’s strategic priorities and in-country ECD programmes.
Enhance PFP’s role to include horizon scanning for evidence translation, linking THRIVE research to policy debates (e.g., BE2, ECDAN).
Explore additional co-funding opportunities post-2023 to supplement ODA constraints, leveraging THRIVE’s growing influence in ECD networks.
Simplify logframe to distinguish between academic and policy outputs, facilitating clearer QCA reporting.

output_2.title: Facilitated and de-risked investment opportunities supported, including green investments

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Procurement process for Component 1 (accountable grant) required adjustments mid-process based on FCDO commercial team recommendations. Component 3 was paused to prioritize mobilization of Components 1 and 2.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Component 1: Partner selection ongoing (due diligence underway). Component 2: World Bank performed satisfactorily—responsive, aligned with programme objectives, and delivered initial activities (e.g., EVS roadmap, training). Component 3: Not yet implemented.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Biweekly FCDO-World Bank meetings initially, transitioned to monthly as programme operationalized. Component 1 management structure not yet tested (partner not finalized).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Limited coordination among donors (Swiss Corporation, USAID, EU) and financial institutions identified as a gap. Programme plans to address this in Year 2 by aligning stakeholders around agriculture financing goals.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Component 1: Mini-competition for accountable grant faced delays (optimism bias in timelines). Three proposals received; preferred partner selected but grant agreement unsigned. Component 2: World Bank disbursement and work plan refinement proceeded smoothly.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight for Component 1 due to procurement complexities. Component 2 oversight aligned with plan (monthly progress meetings).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted procurement process mid-competition based on FCDO guidance. Component 3 paused to focus on Components 1–2 mobilization.
adaptive_management_examples: Adjusted mini-competition process for Component 1 based on real-time FCDO commercial team feedback.
Leveraged CASA Centre of Expertise for parallel market analysis on carbon credit financing, informing Component 1 design.
Postponed Component 3 to prioritize early-stage mobilization of core components.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in Component 1 partner selection (grant agreement unsigned, activities not initiated).
Optimism bias in procurement timelines (mini-competition took longer than anticipated).
Regulatory hurdles for establishing SPV under Mozambican framework (legal analysis required).
Limited alignment among donors and financial institutions in agriculture financing landscape.
external_factors_impact: Upcoming Mozambican general elections (October 2024) risk disrupting government relationships (potential change in MADER leadership).
Global donor landscape (e.g., Swiss Corporation, USAID, EU) operating separately, creating fragmentation.
contextual_constraints_new: Complexity of SPV establishment under existing Mozambican regulations (not fully anticipated).
Need for broader stakeholder coordination (e.g., CIFAM mechanism) to avoid duplicated efforts.
partner_relationship_issues: Component 1: Preferred partner’s due diligence ongoing; no performance issues yet identified.
Component 2: World Bank collaboration effective, but government turnover risk post-elections.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Programme team initially lacked clear guidance on running mini-competitions for accountable grants (vs. commercial contracts).
Government capacity gaps in climate-smart policy implementation (addressed via OECD training).
risk_materialization: Delays in Component 1 mobilization (as predicted in risk register).
Emerging risk: Political transition post-elections may require relationship rebuilding with new MADER officials.
Regulatory challenges for SPV setup (identified during partner selection).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £500,000 disbursed to World Bank (Component 2) as planned. Components 1 and 3 have minimal expenditure to date (mobilization delays).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Too early to assess; VfM proposition from business case remains valid. Cost drivers not yet analyzable (programme in early stages).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Component 2: World Bank demonstrated satisfactory financial management (aligned with work plan, responsive reporting). Components 1/3: Not yet applicable.

key_delivery_lessons: Accountable grant procurement requires clearer FCDO guidance (vs. commercial contracts).
Optimism bias in early-stage timelines can delay mobilization (realistic targeting needed).
Stakeholder coordination (donors, financial institutions) is critical but currently fragmented.
successful_delivery_practices: World Bank’s responsive collaboration (Component 2) and adaptive work planning.
Leveraging external expertise (e.g., CASA CoE for carbon credit analysis) to inform design.
Study visits (e.g., Kenya EVS) effectively built government capacity and cross-country learning.
management_adaptations_made: Adjusted procurement process for Component 1 mid-competition.
Paused Component 3 to focus on core mobilization.
Transitioned from biweekly to monthly World Bank meetings as programme stabilized.
innovations_attempted: Parallel market analysis on carbon credit financing (via CASA CoE) to pilot innovative climate-smart approaches.
Electronic Voucher System (EVS) roadmap development with Kenyan government collaboration.

forward_recommendations.text: Once Component 1 is mobilized, ensure stakeholder interventions (donors, financial institutions) are complementary to avoid duplication in agriculture financing.
Develop realistic annual targets and headline results for programme end (February 2025).
Define more realistic targets for Component 1, accounting for mobilization timelines (by February 2025).
Conduct legal analysis during Component 1 inception to address SPV regulatory hurdles.
Monitor post-election government transitions and proactively rebuild MADER relationships.
Finalize programme evaluation framework and baseline data collection.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk register updated to include new risks (e.g., political transition, SPV regulatory challenges). Mitigation measures defined but not yet tested.

policy_influence_achieved: EVS roadmap developed with MADER; Kenyan collaboration agreement signed for knowledge transfer.
OECD training improved 14 MADER officials’ capacity in policy monitoring (71% rated training as "very good").
Farmer organization diagnostic initiated to inform regulatory reforms.
capacity_building_results: 14 MADER officials trained in OECD methodology for agriculture policy evaluation.

scalability_evidence: EVS model (piloted in Kenya) shows potential for scalability in Mozambique.

Strong supplier expertise identified for Component 1 (despite delays).
World Bank partnership enhances potential for scaled impact.
Early progress (e.g., EVS roadmap, MADER training) validates programme approach.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Strengthening Research Institutions in Africa (SRIA) Programme

output_1.title: Delivery of a range of research system strengthening projects in FCDO priority countries in Africa, via a fund manager

output_2.title: Strategic Fund to support existing research system strengthening initiatives in Africa

output_3.title: Support to coherence and ODA funded research in SRIA priority countries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The RISA fund (40% SRIA-funded) was implemented through a competitively selected fund manager (Chemonics-led consortium) after delays due to COVID-19 and internal processes. The inception phase was extended to adapt to funding changes and improve long-term preparation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated resilience and creativity in adapting to COVID-19 constraints, though governance challenges at the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) led to grant termination and transition of AESA programmes to a third-party host.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The RISA fund manager (Chemonics) onboarded key personnel and established governance structures, though country-level technical leads were still being finalized. FCDO oversight was intensified to address coordination needs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with ATIP (complementary FCDO programme) and other UK funders (e.g., Wellcome) was leveraged for strategic alignment, though cross-programme coherence required refinement in the updated logframe.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive procurement for the RISA fund manager was delayed by COVID-19 but ultimately successful, with Chemonics selected. Contract revisions were needed to align with budget updates.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight was required during inception due to delays and COVID-19 adaptations, with FCDO actively reviewing governance and country engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme reprioritized activities in response to ODA budget cuts (0.7% to 0.5% GNI) and COVID-19, extending the inception phase and reallocating funds to high-priority areas like COVID-19 tele-convenings.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended RISA inception phase to incorporate lessons learned and improve implementation readiness.
Transitioned AESA programmes from AAS to a third-party host due to governance issues.
Repurposed Strategic Fund resources to support COVID-19 policy engagement and tele-convenings.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 restrictions disrupted travel, timelines, and in-person engagement, requiring virtual adaptations.
ODA budget reduction (0.7% to 0.5% GNI) necessitated reprioritization and flexibility in funding allocation.
Governance issues at the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) led to grant termination and programme transitions.
Delays in contracting the RISA fund manager due to COVID-19 and internal FCDO processes.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Prolonged travel restrictions, economic downturns in target countries, and shifts to virtual delivery (e.g., tele-convenings).
ODA cuts: Drove prioritization of value-for-money activities and closer scrutiny of partner performance.
Political/economic instability in priority countries (e.g., Nigeria, Kenya) affected local partner capacity.
contextual_constraints_new: Limited in-country presence due to COVID-19 hindered relationship-building with national research institutions.
Currency fluctuations and inflation in some target countries (e.g., Nigeria) impacted local procurement costs.
Increased competition for research funding due to ODA reductions across UK government programmes.
partner_relationship_issues: AAS governance challenges led to termination of grants and transition of AESA programmes.
Some local partners struggled with virtual collaboration tools, requiring additional capacity-building support.
Misalignment between FCDO’s strategic priorities and some partners’ institutional agendas in early implementation.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Fund manager (Chemonics) faced initial delays in onboarding country technical leads due to travel restrictions.
Local research institutions had limited bandwidth to engage in virtual workshops and reporting.
FCDO’s reduced staffing levels (due to ODA cuts) increased workload for remaining programme managers.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 disruptions (High impact: delayed contracting, reduced in-person engagement).
Partner governance failures (Medium impact: AAS grant termination).
ODA budget cuts (High impact: reprioritization of activities, reduced ambition in some areas).
Currency volatility (Low impact: managed through budget revisions).

budget_execution_vs_plan: Overall budget execution met expectations (score: A), with reprioritization to address ODA cuts.
Delays in RISA fund manager contracting led to underspend in 2020, later absorbed in 2021.
Strategic Fund and COVID-19 activities (e.g., tele-convenings) were fully disbursed as planned.
value_for_money_assessment: Achieved "gold rating" for financial grants practices, with efficient use of resources despite ODA reductions.
Leveraged partnerships (e.g., Wellcome, UKCDR) to co-fund activities, reducing duplication.
Cost per output remained within planned levels, though inception phase extensions increased overheads slightly.
financial_management_quality: Fund manager (Chemonics) demonstrated strong financial controls during inception, with transparent reporting.
FCDO’s financial oversight was intensified post-AAS issues, with monthly reviews of fund manager expenditures.
No significant audit findings or financial irregularities reported.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Virtual delivery (e.g., tele-convenings) reduced travel costs by ~40% compared to pre-COVID plans.
Shared costs with ATIP for RISA fund management improved efficiency (40:60 cost-sharing).
Strategic Fund grants achieved 15% higher output delivery per £ spent due to competitive selection processes.
co_funding_materialization: Co-funding from Wellcome (via DELTAS 2 MoU) materialized as planned, covering 20% of Output 2 activities.
Discussions with BMGF and other funders for COVID-19 work led to additional (unplanned) co-funding of £1.2M.
Some planned co-funding from African governments was delayed due to COVID-19 fiscal constraints.
currency_exchange_impacts: Naira devaluation in Nigeria increased local costs by ~10%, managed through budget reallocations.
South African Rand fluctuations were hedged via multi-year contracts, minimizing impact.
No major exchange rate disruptions reported in Ghana or Kenya.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexibility in funding allocation (e.g., repurposing Strategic Fund for COVID-19) was critical to maintaining delivery.
Virtual engagement (tele-convenings) proved effective for multi-country programmes, with high policy uptake (e.g., Africa CDC mental health strategy).
Partnerships with other UK funders (e.g., Wellcome, UKCDR) amplified impact and reduced duplication.
successful_delivery_practices: Competitive selection of the RISA fund manager ensured high-quality implementation despite delays.
Gender-balanced expert panels (49% women) in tele-convenings improved inclusivity and policy relevance.
Rapid Cochrane-style reviews for COVID-19 policy briefs enhanced credibility and uptake by Africa CDC/WHO.
management_adaptations_made: Extended RISA inception phase to incorporate lessons learned and strengthen implementation plans.
Intensified FCDO oversight of fund manager performance post-AAS issues, with monthly check-ins.
Updated logframe to track coherence across outputs and alignment with FCDO’s multi-year business planning.
innovations_attempted: COVID-19 tele-convenings: Virtual, consultative policy engagement with 1,400+ African scientists/policymakers.
Transdisciplinary research focus in Strategic Fund grants (e.g., SSH + climate + health intersections).
Digital dissemination of policy briefs via AAS Open/Twitter, achieving high engagement metrics.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2020 recommendation to improve partner coordination: Partially addressed via RISA fund manager’s governance structure, but country-level coordination remains a work in progress.
2020 call for stronger M&E: Implemented through IMC’s role in the RISA consortium, though data quality varies by country.
2020 suggestion to explore co-funding: Successfully advanced with Wellcome (DELTAS 2) and BMGF (COVID-19).
forward_recommendations: Refine programme theory of change and results framework post-business planning (Sep 2022), ensuring alignment with FCDO RED priorities.
Extend RISA inception phase to apply lessons learned before full implementation (by Mar 2022).
Strengthen country-level coherence by finalizing Country Technical Lead appointments and governance buy-in from FCDO posts.
Develop case studies to demonstrate SRIA’s impact at country level (Dec 2022).
Advance partnerships with UK funders (e.g., MoU with Wellcome) to support African-led research (Sep 2022).
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive adaptation to COVID-19 and ODA cuts mitigated major disruptions, though some risks (e.g., AAS governance) materialized despite mitigation efforts.
Risk of partner capacity gaps was partially addressed through virtual capacity-building but remains a challenge in some countries.
Currency risks were managed via hedging and budget flexibility, with minimal impact on delivery.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 1,400+ African scientists/policymakers engaged in COVID-19 tele-convenings (vs. target of 1,000).
49% women representation in expert panels (exceeding 40% target).
RISA fund awarded 10 projects (2 research ecosystem, 4 research+innovation, 4 innovation) in 4 countries (Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa).
AESA programme transition affected ~50 researchers, with mitigation plans in place.
policy_influence_achieved: COVID-19 tele-convening findings informed Africa CDC’s 5-year mental health strategy.
Policy briefs disseminated to Ministries of Health in Kenya and WHO Afro, with uptake in e-learning platforms.
Research management guidelines (GRMP) adopted by multiple African institutions, improving institutional practices.
capacity_building_results: Virtual workshops enhanced research management skills for 200+ African institution staff.
RISA fund manager’s inception phase included capacity-building for local partners on proposal development and M&E.
Transition of AESA programmes to a third-party host preserved research capacity despite AAS governance issues.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Virtual engagement models (tele-convenings) attracted interest from other funders (e.g., BMGF) and may be scaled beyond SRIA.
Positive: Gender-balanced panels set a precedent for inclusive policy dialogue in African research ecosystems.
Negative: Delayed RISA contracting reduced the timeframe for project implementation, compressing timelines for achieving outcomes.
scalability_evidence: Tele-convening model is being explored for replication by Africa CDC and WHO Afro.
RISA fund’s coordinated approach (research + innovation) could be expanded to additional African countries post-2025.
Partnerships with Wellcome/UKCDR demonstrate potential for joint funding models in other regions.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (consistent A scores) and high policy influence justify continuation.
Alignment with FCDO’s Africa Strategy and UK research/innovation priorities remains relevant.
Lessons from RISA inception phase position the programme for effective scale-up post-2022.
delivery_model_sustainability: The fund manager model (RISA) is sustainable with planned extensions and adaptive governance.
Co-funding partnerships (e.g., Wellcome) reduce FCDO’s financial burden and improve long-term viability.
Virtual delivery components (e.g., tele-convenings) lower costs and increase accessibility.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Refine theory of change and logframe to reflect multi-year business planning outcomes (Sep 2022).
Strengthen country-level engagement via finalized Country Technical Leads and FCDO post coordination.
Explore additional co-funding opportunities with African governments and private sector partners.
Develop a communications strategy to amplify country-level impact stories (Dec 2022).

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Contract (externally contracted due diligence via KPMG as the primary delivery partner)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £371,411 total budget with focus on "externally contracted due diligence" as the programme-funded element; original plan included 3 externally commissioned HQAs per year plus internally managed assessments
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Funding flowed to KPMG for Headquarters Assessments (HQAs) and Central Assurance Assessments (CAAs), with DD Hub providing oversight and internal capacity for complementary activities
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium - Original design allowed for balance between externally contracted (KPMG) and internally managed HQAs, with some flexibility to adjust based on demand

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch central governance: DD Hub as coordinator/oversight body with embedded technical skills, working alongside FCDO Commercial team as co-owner of due diligence policy (PrOF Rule 16). External provider (KPMG) managed via contract with DD Hub oversight.
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly monitoring of external provider deliverables (HQAs/CAAs) with annual review of internal processes. Policy ownership required periodic updates to PrOF rules.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Centralized decision-making for HQA partner selection and commissioning (DD Hub), with decentralized use of HQA outputs by FCDO programme teams. Escalation of major risks via FCDO risk management process.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single primary external provider (KPMG) for HQAs/CAAs, supplemented by internal DD Hub capacity for direct assessments. Collaborative relationships with FCDO programme teams as "users" of outputs.
partner_types_planned: FCDO Internal (DD Hub team as oversight/implementation support)

partner_roles_planned.KPMG: Primary deliverer of HQAs/CAAs under contract
partner_roles_planned.DD Hub: Oversight, quality assurance, internal assessments, and policy maintenance
partner_roles_planned.FCDO Programme Teams: End-users of HQA outputs for local due diligence

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award to KPMG (existing cross-government contract) for external assessments; internal DD Hub resources for complementary work

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Contract (KPMG remains primary external provider) + increased internal delivery by DD Hub team
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: Budget unchanged (£371,411) but **substantive shift in delivery mix**: Only 1 externally commissioned HQA (vs planned 3) in 2023/24; 3 internally managed HQAs (vs planned 2) plus 1 additional internal HQA planned for autumn 2024. Total HQAs in progress: 8 INGOs (6 ongoing + 2 new).
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Reduced flow to KPMG (only 1 HQA commissioned in 2023/24). Increased internal resource allocation for DD Hub-led assessments. Delayed action on Business Case addendum for programme-funded resources.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High - **Substantive reprioritization** from external to internal delivery due to capacity constraints and lessons learned. Flexibility used to shift balance of work.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: **Substantive change**: Increased internal delivery role for DD Hub (from oversight to direct implementation of HQAs). Governance remains light-touch but with **greater internal resource intensity** than planned. Cross-government contract for KPMG nearing end (Jan 2025), triggering urgent need to define future mechanisms.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: More frequent internal monitoring of HQA progress (monthly tracking of internally managed assessments). External oversight of KPMG reduced to ad-hoc due to limited commissions.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: **Shift to hybrid model**: DD Hub now makes decisions on both external commissions *and* internal prioritization of HQAs. Increased collaboration with FCDO programme teams to tailor HQA utility.

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: **Changed**: Reduced reliance on KPMG (single provider) to mixed model with **DD Hub as co-deliverer**. Stronger emphasis on internal capacity-building and direct engagement with FCDO programme teams.
partner_types_actual: FCDO Internal (DD Hub - expanded delivery role)
FCDO Programme Teams (increased collaboration as co-designers of HQA utility)

partner_roles_actual.KPMG: Reduced to 1 HQA in 2023/24 (from planned 3); CAA work excluded from programme outputs
partner_roles_actual.DD Hub: **Expanded**: Direct delivery of 3+ HQAs internally, policy maintenance, and performance improvement planning
partner_roles_actual.FCDO Programme Teams: More active feedback loop on HQA utility, pushing for tailored local DDA questions

partner_names_actual: International Rescue Committee (IRC) - subject of 1 completed HQA

substantive_changes_made: Shift from external to internal delivery of HQAs (3 internally managed vs 1 externally commissioned in 2023/24, reversing the original 2:3 ratio).
Expanded DD Hub role from oversight to direct implementation, including resource allocation for internal assessments.
Delayed formalization of programme-funded resources (Business Case addendum not progressed).
Increased emphasis on maintaining/updating existing HQAs (new resource requirement identified).

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: No change in total budget (£371,411), but **substantive reallocation** from external (KPMG) to internal (DD Hub) delivery.
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Scope maintained but **delivery mechanism shifted** (more internal, less external). Geographic scope unchanged (HQ-level focus).
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: Reduced contract-based delivery (KPMG) in favor of internal capacity utilization.

theory_of_change_revisions.pathway_changes: Added explicit recognition of **programme funding as required input** for external due diligence support (originally assumed ad-hoc). Emphasized **maintenance of HQA documents** as critical for long-term utility (not in original TOC).
theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Assumption that external providers would deliver majority of HQAs **revised** to reflect mixed internal/external model. Assumption about one-off nature of HQAs **challenged** (now recognized as requiring periodic updates).

management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Increased internal oversight frequency (monthly tracking of HQAs) with reduced external monitoring (fewer KPMG commissions).
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: DD Hub now makes **operational decisions** on internal vs external delivery mix, beyond original oversight role.

activity_only_adjustments: Minor updates to guidance documents and training sessions (non-substantive).
Ad-hoc support to FCDO programme teams on using HQA outputs (existing activity).

adaptation_triggers.performance_issues: Underperformance in external HQA delivery (1/3 commissioned in 2023/24) triggered internal capacity expansion.
adaptation_triggers.learning_insights: Recognition that internal delivery could leverage existing FCDO knowledge and reduce duplication (e.g., IRC case showed variable efficiency gains).
adaptation_triggers.strategic_opportunities: Opportunity to test internal HQA delivery as cross-government contract nears end (Jan 2025).

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: Medium - Adaptations were reactive (performance-driven) rather than proactive. Lack of formal evaluation limits evidence base.
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: High - Baseline flexibility clause enabled shift to internal delivery, but delayed action on resourcing.
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Medium - Lessons from IRC HQA utility informed internal delivery approach, but data gaps remain (e.g., no quality assurance of DDAs).

fcas_context.fragility_level: High - FCDO operates in fragile and conflict-affected states, though DD Hub itself is HQ-focused.
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Indirect - Programme supports due diligence for FCAS contexts but is not field-implemented.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: Stable - FCDO commitment to due diligence reform maintained, but **resource constraints** within DD Hub limit pace of change.
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: Minor - PrOF rules (Rule 16) embedded, but **no major policy shifts**. DD Hub now co-owner with Commercial team.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: **Lower than expected** - DD Hub capacity proved insufficient for both external oversight *and* internal delivery, requiring reprioritization.

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Limited - KPMG remained sole external provider under cross-government contract (expires Jan 2025). No evidence of alternative suppliers explored.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Low - **3+ substantive changes** (funding modality, governance role, partner mix).
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Comprehensive adaptation - Changes across **funding** (internal/external mix), **governance** (DD Hub role expansion), and **partners** (reduced KPMG reliance).
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate - Original design allowed for flexibility in delivery mix, but **underestimated resource requirements** for internal capacity and HQA maintenance. TOC assumptions about external delivery dominance were overly optimistic.

programme_metadata.programme_title: The Due Diligence Hub Programme

output_1.title: High quality, timely and accurate Headquarters Assessments (HQAs) of INGO delivery partners are produced by external provider, and accessible within FCDO

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from primarily externally contracted HQAs to a mix of internally and externally managed assessments due to capacity constraints and resource availability. The programme initially planned for 3 externally commissioned HQAs but only 1 was completed externally in the review period, with 3 managed internally.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: KPMG (external provider) demonstrated capability by finalizing two assessments (1 HQA and 1 CAA) and maintaining quality, though the CAA was not counted toward programme outputs. Programme teams showed variable efficiency in utilizing HQA findings, with some teams reducing document requests but others requiring pushback on non-tailored questions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The DD Hub retained oversight of externally managed assessments while increasing internal management of HQAs. Governance remained aligned with FCDO’s Programme Operating Framework (PrOF) and risk escalation processes, but resource constraints limited broader process improvements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Collaboration with FCDO programme teams and stakeholders (e.g., Commonwealth Unit) was effective for oversight but inconsistent in adoption. HQA findings were referenced in only 4 project-level DDAs, indicating uneven uptake.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of KPMG for HQAs was on track, but delays in commissioning new HQAs occurred due to internal prioritization. The cross-government contract for external expertise is set to expire in January 2025, requiring urgent action to secure future mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was maintained for externally managed assessments (e.g., KPMG’s CAA), but internal capacity limitations reduced the Hub’s ability to monitor broader due diligence processes across FCDO.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted by shifting to internal management of HQAs to meet targets, leveraging existing FCDO knowledge. However, this reduced bandwidth for wider process improvements.
adaptive_management_examples: Prioritized internal completion of 3 HQAs (exceeding the target of 2) when external commissioning fell short.
Engaged early with KPMG for a new HQA in Q4 2023/24, incorporating lessons from past delays.
Explored options for dedicated programme-funded resources (internal/external) to address capacity gaps.

main_implementation_challenges: Underachievement on externally commissioned HQAs (1 completed vs. 3 targeted), leading to a score of **C** for the review period.
Limited internal capacity to balance HQA production with broader due diligence process improvements.
Inconsistent utilization of HQA findings by programme teams, reducing intended efficiency gains.
Lack of a formal mechanism to track and update HQA recommendations, risking outdated documents.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased demand for maintaining/updating existing HQAs as the number of completed assessments grows, creating a resource burden.
Unanticipated complexity in tailoring HQA findings to programme-specific needs, requiring additional pushback from partners (e.g., IRC).
partner_relationship_issues: Programme teams often sent non-tailored due diligence questions to partners, requiring intervention from partners (e.g., IRC) to refine requests.
Variable engagement with HQA findings across FCDO teams, with some ignoring recommendations or failing to reference reports.
capacity_constraints_emerged: DD Hub’s limited bandwidth to manage both HQA production and internal process improvements (e.g., guidance updates, training).
No dedicated resource for monitoring/updating HQAs post-completion, risking reduced utility over time.
risk_materialization: Risk of **duplication of effort** materialized, as programme teams continued requesting documents already covered in HQAs.
Risk of **outdated HQAs** emerging due to lack of maintenance resources, potentially undermining their value.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was on track for completed activities, but under-spending occurred due to fewer externally commissioned HQAs than planned. The programme is prioritizing resource allocation for the remaining AMP period (until March 2025).
value_for_money_assessment: HQAs provide **some efficiency gains** (e.g., reduced document requests for IRC), but evidence of VFM is **limited** due to inconsistent uptake by programme teams.
The programme’s 0.5% investment of FCDO’s total spend is considered proportionate, but lack of data on DDA quality assurance hinders robust VFM evaluation.
Internally managed HQAs offer cost savings but reduce capacity for other improvements.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management was effective in monitoring expenditures, but procurement delays (e.g., late commissioning of HQAs) impacted delivery. The Hub is addressing this via a performance improvement plan.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost per HQA was not explicitly reported, but internal management reduced external contracting costs.
Efficiency gains from HQAs were **uneven**—some teams reported reduced workload (e.g., IRC), while others saw minimal impact.

key_delivery_lessons: Internally managed HQAs can leverage FCDO’s institutional knowledge but require **dedicated resources** to avoid trade-offs with other priorities.
**Early engagement** with external providers (e.g., KPMG) improves timeliness and quality of deliverables.
HQAs are **not a one-time exercise**—ongoing maintenance is critical to sustain their utility.
successful_delivery_practices: Pooling technical skills within the DD Hub improved consistency of due diligence standards.
Oversight of externally managed assessments (e.g., KPMG’s CAA) ensured alignment with FCDO requirements, even when not counted as programme outputs.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted focus to internal HQA management to meet targets when external commissioning lagged.
Developed a **performance improvement plan** to address underdelivery, including realistic target-setting and resource allocation.
innovations_attempted: Explored drawing assurance from assessments by other organizations/governments to reduce duplication.
Piloted internal HQA management to test feasibility and quality outcomes.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Internal HQAs exceeded the target (3 completed vs. 2 planned), but external commissioning fell short (1 vs. 3).
No progress on securing long-term resources for HQA maintenance or process improvements.
forward_recommendations: Secure a **dedicated programme-funded resource** (internal or external) for HQA production and maintenance.
Clarify the **balance between internal and external HQAs** to optimize quality and cost-efficiency.
Develop a **tracking mechanism** for HQA recommendations to ensure updates reflect organizational changes.
Enhance **training/guidance** for programme teams on utilizing HQA findings to improve uptake.
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk escalation processes (via PrOF Rule 16) functioned as planned, but **proactive risk mitigation** was limited by capacity constraints.
The materialization of duplication risks highlights the need for stronger enforcement of HQA utilization.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 2 fully completed HQAs (shared with FCDO teams), 1 CAA (oversight only), and 3 internally managed HQAs in progress.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 4 project-level DDAs referenced HQA findings, with variable efficiency gains reported by partners (e.g., IRC).

policy_influence_achieved: HQAs are embedded in FCDO’s Programme Operating Framework (PrOF) and due diligence policies, but **adoption is inconsistent**.
No evidence of broader policy changes beyond FCDO’s internal processes.
capacity_building_results: DD Hub team gained deeper understanding of HQA complexities and resource needs.
Limited capacity building for programme teams on utilizing HQAs effectively.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Some programme teams reduced document requests to partners (e.g., IRC) by using HQAs.
Negative: **Increased workload for DD Hub** due to unplanned internal management of HQAs, diverting resources from process improvements.
scalability_evidence: The HQA model is **theoretically scalable**, but current resource constraints and inconsistent uptake limit practical scalability.
Potential to expand to other HMG departments if capacity and demand align.

continuation_rationale: The DD Hub plays a **critical role** in FCDO’s risk management framework, supporting evidence-based decision-making.
Despite underdelivery in 2023/24, the programme has demonstrated **partial progress** toward efficiency and quality goals.
The **performance improvement plan** and planned resource allocations (e.g., dedicated post) aim to address current gaps.
Alignment with the Centre for Delivery’s mission to "inspire, empower and equip FCDO staff" justifies continuation.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model is **not fully sustainable** without additional resources for HQA maintenance and process improvements.
Dependence on internal capacity risks **burnout and inconsistent output quality**.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium (acknowledges strategic value but concerned about delivery delays and inconsistent uptake)
planned_adaptations_future: Implement the **performance improvement plan** to realign outputs with logframe targets.
Explore **hybrid internal-external resourcing models** for HQA production and maintenance.
Strengthen **monitoring of HQA utilization** by programme teams to demonstrate impact.
Finalize post-2025 contracting mechanisms for external expertise before the current agreement expires.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Ghana Revenue Programme (GRP)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adapted to delays in FCDO funding decisions and ODA budget reductions (£600k cut, offset by £520k from Public Finance and Tax Department). Logframe revised (approved 27 March 2023) to add Output 2.5 (enterprise/compliance risk management) and sharpen indicators, without reducing ambition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UK partners (HMRC, IFS, Cabinet Office) demonstrated flexibility and responsiveness, particularly in adapting to Ghana’s evolving economic context (e.g., IMF programme, domestic fiscal pressures). Embedded consultant model (4+ years) proved valuable for oversight and support within GRA.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme team maintained strong coordination despite personnel changes. Annual workplan priorities agreed with partners, though Theory of Change (ToC) workshop stalled due to staff transitions. ToC remains outdated (e.g., references defunct World Bank Doing Business index, unrealistic tax exemption targets).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination among UK providers (HMRC, IFS, Cabinet Office) and Ghanaian counterparts (MoFEP, GRA). Joint support aligned with Ghana’s Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) and Tax Administration Diagnostic Assessment Tool (TADAT) preparations. Political and Governance Team engagement recommended for election-year risks/opportunities (Dec 2024 elections).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensified in response to economic volatility (e.g., IMF conditions, debt crisis). Programme team proactively monitored progress and adapted to delays (e.g., DTRD restructuring pauses). Embedded advisors provided real-time support to GRA.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility: (1) Reallocated funds to mitigate ODA cuts; (2) Adjusted workstreams to address emerging priorities (e.g., HNW Office’s data-matching training, VAT compliance); (3) Revised DTRD restructuring phases to align with GRA’s changing needs.
adaptive_management_examples: Added Output 2.5 (risk management functions) mid-implementation to address gaps in GRA’s decision-making.
Shifted focus to HNW taxpayers and SME compliance after identifying undercontribution from these sectors.
Revised DTRD restructuring plan (Phase 2 delayed to June 2023, reprioritized Kinbu Department first).
Secured alternative access to Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI) data after initial plans stalled.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in FCDO funding decisions caused minor adjustments and postponements.
Institutional hurdles in GRA (e.g., DTRD restructuring pauses, slow adoption of VAT systems).
High Net Worth (HNW) sector remained under-scoped despite progress in profiling 467 new taxpayers.
Confrontational relationships between GRA and taxpayer communities (businesses, HNW individuals).
Capacity constraints in GRA’s ability to sustain reforms (e.g., CRM training for 200 staff not yet translating to structural changes).
external_factors_impact: IMF $3bn programme imposed conditions on domestic revenue mobilisation, increasing pressure for reforms.
Global economic shocks (COVID-19, Ukraine war) exacerbated Ghana’s fiscal/debt vulnerabilities, limiting social sector funding.
Currency depreciation and inflation (31.5% nominal tax revenue growth partly offset by inflation).
Upcoming 2024 elections introduce political uncertainty for tax policy continuity.
contextual_constraints_new: Tax Exemptions Act increased transparency but failed to reduce exemptions as anticipated.
GRA’s TADAT assessment (August 2023) may reveal unaddressed systemic weaknesses.
MTRS development (due October 2023) requires alignment with UK support, risking misalignment if delayed.
partner_relationship_issues: Strong trust built with MoFEP/GRA senior officials, but election-year politics may strain collaboration.
HMRC’s Long-Term Adviser (LTA) role needed redefinition to focus on strategic transformation (delayed replacement).
CSO engagement improved, but business/taxpayer relationships remained adversarial.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GRA’s ability to operationalize reforms (e.g., VAT system adoption at 20% vs. 50% target).
Limited sustainable access to third-party data sources (only 1/4 sources integrated via Data Warehouse).
Personnel changes disrupted ToC review and embedded advisor continuity.
risk_materialization: ODA budget cuts (£600k) materialized but were mitigated by Public Finance and Tax Department funds.
Economic downturn increased revenue collection urgency, aligning with programme goals but straining GRA capacity.
DTRD restructuring delays due to GRA leadership pauses (December 2022–June 2023).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Original £1.2m annual plan reduced by £600k due to ODA pressures, but £520k supplementary funding from Public Finance and Tax Department enabled 93% of planned activities. Minor delays occurred but no major disruptions to delivery.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated through: (1) Leveraging embedded UK advisors (HMRC/IFS) for cost-effective technical assistance; (2) Achieving 5% overperformance in tax revenue (GHS 75.54bn vs. GHS 71.94bn target); (3) Low-cost interventions (e.g., HNW Office’s GHS 214m collection from data-matching training).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial management by programme team, with proactive budget reallocations and transparent reporting. No significant audit findings or mismanagement noted.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost-efficient delivery via: (1) Shared UK-Ghana resources (e.g., joint MTRS/TADAT support); (2) Focus on high-impact areas (HNW taxpayers contributed disproportionate revenue); (3) Minimal overheads due to embedded advisor model.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Currency depreciation (GHS vs. GBP) increased local-cost delivery efficiency but reduced real value of fixed-GBP targets. Tax revenue growth (31.5% nominal) partially offset inflation.

key_delivery_lessons: Long-term, patient technical assistance yields breakthroughs (e.g., HNW Office’s 85% filing rate after years of capacity-building).
Embedded advisors enhance trust and real-time problem-solving but require clear role definitions (e.g., LTA strategic focus).
Flexible logframes (e.g., adding Output 2.5) allow responsiveness to emerging needs without reducing ambition.
Political economy analysis is critical—IMF conditions created both constraints and opportunities for reform.
successful_delivery_practices: Joint UK-Ghana workplanning (e.g., aligning with MTRS/TADAT) ensured ownership and relevance.
Data-driven interventions (e.g., HNW profiling using NIC/DVLA data) improved compliance.
Staged implementation (e.g., VAT system rollout) mitigated operational risks.
Cross-partner coordination (HMRC/IFS/Cabinet Office) provided holistic support to GRA.
management_adaptations_made: Revised DTRD restructuring phases to reflect GRA’s changing priorities.
Shifted focus to HNW/SME taxpayers after identifying gaps in contribution.
Streamlined reporting by rationalizing ‘enabler’ indicators (pending further review).
Enhanced gender mainstreaming (e.g., interviews with women taxpayers, safeguarding reviews).
innovations_attempted: Pilot of AEOI data access via embedded staff in secure perimeter.
Behavioural research to inform SME compliance interventions (planned for 2023–24).
Communication framework co-developed with Institute of Chartered Accountants Ghana for tax education.
previous_recommendations_progress: Logframe revised (March 2023) to address 2022 review recommendations (e.g., added Output 2.5).
ToC workshop initiated but stalled; prioritized for next review period.
Partner coordination improved (e.g., annual workplan alignment).
Gender and tax learning integrated into programme activities (e.g., women taxpayer interviews).
forward_recommendations: Finalize ToC update to reflect post-IMF/MTRS context and remove outdated assumptions (e.g., Doing Business index).
Accelerate LTA replacement with revised strategic focus.
Reprioritize activities post-TADAT assessment (August 2023) and MTRS publication (October 2023).
Develop SME compliance campaign with behavioural insights.
Strengthen GRA’s female staff support mechanisms (e.g., fair treatment reviews).
Monitor election-year risks (Dec 2024) and align with FCDO’s governance programme.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating ODA cuts and economic shocks but less proactive on institutional risks (e.g., DTRD delays, ToC stagnation). TADAT/MTRS processes will test adaptive capacity. Recommend stronger contingency planning for election-related disruptions.

direct: 467 new HNW taxpayers identified/profiled (vs. 500 target).
200 GRA staff trained in CRM (LTO, PSSTO, Excise, HNWO units).
600 women taxpayers (Ghana National Tailors and Dressmakers Association) engaged by GRA.
indirect: Tax revenue benefits reached all Ghanaian citizens via social sector funding (e.g., education, infrastructure).
SME taxpayers targeted for future compliance campaigns (planned 2023–24).

policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to 5% overperformance in tax revenue (GHS 75.54bn collected, 0.6% increase in tax-to-non-oil GDP ratio).
Supported draft Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) and TADAT assessment, influencing future tax administration reforms.
Tax Exemptions Act transparency improvements (though reduction targets unmet).
HNW Office’s operational manual adopted for voluntary filing procedures.
capacity_building_results: GRA’s HNW Office achieved 85% filing rate (vs. 80% target) and secured GHS 214m in collections.
VAT unit operationalized at 50% (backend staff trained, help desk established).
DTRD restructuring plan advanced (Phase 1 completed; Phase 2 revised for Kinbu Department).
Embedded UK advisors enhanced GRA’s risk management and compliance functions (Output 2.5).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Improved CSO engagement led to broader taxpayer education (e.g., tailors/dressmakers association).
Negative: Confrontational taxpayer-GRA relationships persisted, risking long-term compliance.
Negative: Delayed DTRD restructuring may have temporarily reduced efficiency in tax offices.
scalability_evidence: HNW Office’s data-matching model replicable for other taxpayer segments (e.g., SMEs).
VAT compliance tools (e.g., help desk, Technical Steering Committee) adaptable to other tax units.
Embedded advisor model proven scalable across GRA departments (e.g., LTO, Kinbu).
Limited by GRA’s institutional capacity to absorb rapid expansion.

continuation_rationale: Strong political commitment to revenue mobilisation (IMF conditions, Ghana Beyond Aid policy).
Proven impact on tax revenue (5% overperformance in 2022) and institutional reforms (HNW Office, DTRD).
Critical juncture with MTRS/TADAT processes (2023) offering opportunities for deeper engagement.
UK’s trusted advisor status with MoFEP/GRA provides unique influence for transformational change.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Reprioritize activities post-TADAT/MTRS to align with Ghana’s revised fiscal plans.
Expand focus on SME taxpayers and behavioural compliance interventions.
Strengthen GRA’s female staff support and gender-responsive tax policies.
Enhance election-year risk mitigation (Dec 2024) through political economy analysis.
Review embedded advisor model for long-term sustainability (4+ years in place).
Finalize ToC update to reflect post-IMF context and remove outdated metrics.

output_1.title: Effective Procurement and Programme Management to deliver a) Urban Planning and Green Urban Infrastructure b) Mobilising finance for Climate Resilience Urban Infrastructure c) Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme faced delays due to an internal FCDO strategic review and UK government change, which paused procurement and contracting. Only the £9.1m World Bank SURP-II component is currently at implementation stage, while other components (Implementing Partner and MEL contracts) remain stalled.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The World Bank component (SURP-II) is on track, with funds disbursed and implementation underway. Other partners (Implementing Partner and MEL supplier) have not yet been contracted due to delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme management team worked closely with UK Commercial teams to advance procurement, but internal reviews and approval layers caused setbacks. The World Bank agreement was successfully signed and disbursed, demonstrating effective coordination in that area.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with the World Bank was effective, with regular updates and FCDO participation in progress monitoring meetings. Internal FCDO coordination faced challenges due to strategic reviews and approval bottlenecks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for the Implementing Partner and MEL supplier was delayed due to internal reviews and additional documentation requirements from the UK Commercial team. The World Bank agreement was successfully executed, with funds disbursed in July 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified for the World Bank component, with regular monitoring. For other components, oversight was limited due to procurement delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by focusing on the World Bank component while other elements were paused. However, the lack of anticipatory planning for internal delays limited adaptive responses.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: The team prioritized the World Bank SURP-II component to ensure progress despite broader delays. Options for alternative delivery models (e.g., increased World Bank financing or knowledge-focused roles) were proposed in response to potential programme pauses.

main_implementation_challenges: Internal FCDO strategic review and UK government change led to procurement and contracting delays.
Pause in finalizing contracts for the Implementing Partner and MEL supplier due to portfolio rationalization.
Unanticipated need for additional documentation and approval layers in procurement processes.
external_factors_impact: Somalia’s rapid urbanization, driven by conflict, climate shocks, and economic pressures, increased the urgency for programme delivery but also complicated implementation due to weak municipal capacity.
Political and economic instability in Somalia created an unpredictable operating environment.
contextual_constraints_new: Weak municipal governance and lack of urban planning capacity in Somali cities posed challenges for programme rollout.
Limited access to finance for urban infrastructure investments constrained progress on Outcome 3 (mobilizing finance).
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in contracting risked damaging relationships with Somali stakeholders (federal/state governments, mayors) due to raised expectations during programme design.
Coordination with the World Bank remained strong, but other partnerships were not yet operational.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s internal capacity was stretched due to portfolio reviews and approval processes, slowing procurement.
Limited municipal capacity in Somalia required more intensive technical assistance than initially planned.
risk_materialization: Political risk (UK government change and FCDO portfolio review) materialized, causing delays.

cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency for the World Bank component met expectations.
Overall cost efficiency was reduced due to unplanned delays and additional procurement-related workload.

key_delivery_lessons: Early engagement with Commercial teams to clarify procurement requirements can prevent delays.
Managing stakeholder expectations is critical, especially in uncertain political environments.
Flexibility in delivery models (e.g., increased World Bank financing) can mitigate risks during transitions.
successful_delivery_practices: Close coordination with the World Bank enabled timely disbursement and implementation of the SURP-II component.
Proactive development of alternative delivery options (e.g., knowledge-focused roles) demonstrated adaptive planning.
management_adaptations_made: Prioritized the World Bank component to ensure progress despite broader delays.
Proposed options for alternative delivery models in response to potential programme pauses.
innovations_attempted: Explored integrating GUG with other FCDO programmes (e.g., Somali Land Development Fund) to reduce transaction costs and improve coherence.
Developed adaptive MEL frameworks to capture lessons at different stages, though implementation is delayed.
forward_recommendations: Finalize procurement for the Implementing Partner and MEL supplier to avoid further delays.
Strengthen stakeholder communication to manage expectations and reputational risks.
Develop detailed contingency plans for alternative delivery models if internal reviews disrupt implementation.
Leverage GUG’s role as a lead economic development programme to enhance UK influence on urban resilience in Somalia.
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective: political and procurement risks were identified but not fully mitigated.
The programme demonstrated resilience by adapting to delays (e.g., focusing on the World Bank component), but anticipatory planning for internal risks was insufficient.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: The World Bank SURP-II component is on track to reach beneficiaries in six target cities, but data on actual reach is not yet available.

policy_influence_achieved: GUG is positioned to influence Somalia’s urban resilience policies through its alignment with the World Bank and UK leadership on climate finance.
Potential for policy influence is high but not yet realized due to early-stage implementation.
capacity_building_results: Capacity building for municipal governments (Output 1) is planned but not yet implemented.
The World Bank component includes capacity-building elements, but results are not yet reported.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Increased focus on urban resilience in Somalia’s development discourse due to GUG’s design.
Negative: Delays in implementation may have eroded stakeholder trust and created reputational risks for FCDO.
scalability_evidence: The programme’s theory of change supports scalability, particularly through the World Bank’s Multi-Partner Fund mechanism.
Scalability depends on resolving procurement delays and demonstrating results in Year 2.

continuation_rationale: The programme’s objectives remain valid and aligned with UK and Somali priorities (climate resilience, urban economic development).
Delays in Year 1 were due to external factors (FCDO reviews, UK government change) rather than fundamental flaws in the programme design.
GUG is positioned to become FCDO’s lead economic development programme in Somalia, offering strategic value.
delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is sustainable if procurement delays are resolved and the Implementing Partner and MEL contracts are finalized.
Alternative models (e.g., increased World Bank financing) are viable if internal constraints persist.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize procurement for the Implementing Partner and MEL supplier to enable full implementation.
Develop contingency plans for alternative delivery models if internal reviews disrupt progress.
Strengthen coordination with Somali stakeholders to rebuild trust and manage expectations.
Leverage GUG’s role to enhance UK leadership on urban resilience and climate finance in Somalia.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift towards greater emphasis on partnerships and strategic alignment with evolving UK development priorities due to anticipated ODA reductions. delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Five of seven implementing partners met or exceeded 2024/25 targets. SEFA (A+) achieved record project approvals and electricity connections (5.7M since 2020). WISER (A) demonstrated strong institutional uptake (165+ institutions). CAFI (B) made progress on cleaner cooking (163,189 households) but faced challenges in Congo Basin forest protection. CIWA (A) influenced $6.4B in water investments but required governance strengthening.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved donor coordination (e.g., FCDO-led CAFI presidency in 2024–25) and cross-sector collaboration (joint humanitarian-climate missions). However, synergies between projects (e.g., WISER, FFF, CIWA) remain underutilized. Cross-programme joint learning is a priority for 2025/26.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to ODA cuts by reprioritizing investments (e.g., halted locally-led adaptation project). Flexibility used to scale successful initiatives like WISER’s weather/climate services and SEFA’s energy access projects.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of funds to high-performing projects (e.g., WISER scale-up planned for 2025).
Launch of $100M private sector investment facility under CAFI to address forest protection gaps.
Response to reduced ODA by focusing on African ownership and capacity-building (e.g., transformational change assessments by end-2025).

main_implementation_challenges: Sustaining impact amid reduced ODA funding (UK and other donors).
Mobilizing private sector finance due to worsening macroeconomic conditions in Africa (affecting SEFA, SRMI, AAAP).
Uneven implementation of MEL systems, limiting actionable evidence for programming.
Slow progress in Congo Basin forest protection despite UK leadership in reforms.
Dependence on donor financing/expertise for sustainability of outcomes.
external_factors_impact: 2025 Spending Review anticipating ODA reductions, forcing delivery model adaptations.
Global macroeconomic downturn reducing private sector investment in African climate/nature projects.
Reduced donor budgets (US, UK, others) increasing pressure on programme sustainability.
contextual_constraints_new: Difficulty in securing private sector co-financing (optimism bias in Business Case targets).

Policy environment shifts (e.g., UK development priority realignment) demanding strategic reprioritization.
partner_relationship_issues: Varied performance across partners (e.g., CAFI’s B score vs. SEFA’s A+).
GESI (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) targeting and reporting requires stronger partner accountability.
Fraud/safeguarding risks necessitated FCDO reminders to partners on obligations (e.g., PSEAH compliance).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Gaps in partner capacity for safeguarding, fraud reporting, and intersectional GEDSI approaches.
