delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The joint delivery model between FCDO and India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) introduced unanticipated complexity, requiring alignment of two distinct government systems, procurement processes, and funding mechanisms. This was the first such equally co-funded programme for FCDO, necessitating iterative adjustments to the original business case assumptions about timelines and governance structures.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: MEA has repeatedly reaffirmed commitment to the programme but has faced internal delays in finalizing procurement plans for three key components (Grants, Technical Assistance, and Impact Assessment). Despite verbal commitments, no concrete procurement plan has been submitted as of the review date. FCDO has had to adapt by extending timelines and proposing "simpler options" for procurement during upcoming strategic discussions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Joint Steering Committee (JSC) has met only twice (most recently in April 2024), with limited progress on operationalizing governance structures. Decision-making has been slower than planned due to the need for cross-governmental consultations in both the UK and India. The Logframe, Risk Register, and Theory of Change remain undeveloped pending the selection of delivery partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination has been hindered by the novel joint-funding arrangement, requiring alignment of FCDO and MEA’s distinct compliance and procurement systems. The programme’s reliance on bilateral negotiations (e.g., for the upcoming Comprehensive Strategic Partnership) to resolve delays has further slowed implementation. The E-Bazaar platform (a programme component) is ready but awaits a joint public launch, highlighting coordination bottlenecks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for all four programme components (including the Investment Fund Manager) remains stalled. MEA proposed taking the lead on procuring three components but has not submitted a plan. FCDO insisted on synchronizing the launch of all four components’ Requests for Proposals (RFPs), creating a circular dependency. The draft RFP for the Investment component was shared with FCDO for comments, but no progress has been made since.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has been more intensive than originally planned due to the programme’s high political profile and reputational risks. FCDO has increased monitoring of MEA’s commitments and proposed adaptive measures (e.g., simplified procurement options) to mitigate delays. However, oversight has not translated into tangible progress on the ground.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme has utilized flexibility primarily by extending timelines and revisiting procurement strategies. FCDO has proposed alternative, simpler procurement routes during the upcoming Country Strategic Partnership (CSP) review to bypass bureaucratic hurdles. The lack of a finalized Theory of Change or Logframe has also allowed for iterative adjustments to the programme’s design, though this has contributed to delays.
adaptive_management_examples: Proposal to use the CSP review as an opportunity to reset programme timelines and explore simpler procurement options.
Extension of the inception phase beyond the original March 2024 deadline to accommodate joint-governmental delays.
Development of the E-Bazaar platform as an early visible output, despite broader implementation stagnation.
FCDO’s insistence on synchronizing all four components’ procurement to avoid fragmented progress.

main_implementation_challenges: Unprecedented complexity in designing and operationalizing a jointly funded, equally governed programme between FCDO and MEA, leading to systemic delays.
Misalignment between the two governments’ procurement and compliance systems, requiring iterative negotiations at each step.
Absence of a finalized Logframe, Risk Register, or Theory of Change three years post-approval, hindering progress tracking.
Dependence on high-level bilateral discussions (e.g., Comprehensive Strategic Partnership) to unblock operational bottlenecks.
Limited capacity within both governments to navigate the novel joint-delivery model, exacerbating timelines.
external_factors_impact: The programme’s alignment with the UK-India Roadmap and upcoming Comprehensive Strategic Partnership has increased its political visibility but also subjected it to broader bilateral negotiation dynamics, slowing progress.
Global economic conditions (not explicitly stated) may have indirectly affected the urgency of programme implementation, though no specific external shocks (e.g., COVID-19) were mentioned.
contextual_constraints_new: The need for a third MoU (beyond the two already signed) to clarify implementation arrangements was not anticipated in the original design.
The requirement for both governments to consult multiple internal departments for approvals at each stage created iterative delays not accounted for in planning.
The E-Bazaar platform’s readiness has exposed a gap between technical preparedness and the ability to launch jointly due to governance hurdles.
partner_relationship_issues: While MEA has verbally reaffirmed commitment, the lack of submitted procurement plans has created a trust gap regarding follow-through on operational steps.
FCDO’s insistence on synchronizing all components’ procurement has been perceived by MEA as a barrier, though it was intended to ensure coherence.
Differing priorities within MEA (e.g., focus on other bilateral initiatives) may have contributed to the delay in submitting concrete plans.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Neither FCDO nor MEA had prior experience managing a programme of this joint nature, leading to underestimation of the skills and resources required for timely delivery.
The need for continuous cross-governmental consultations in both countries has stretched thin the capacity of programme teams to advance implementation.
Limited bandwidth to develop critical documents (e.g., Logframe) while simultaneously navigating procurement and governance challenges.
risk_materialization: The reputational risk to FCDO due to delayed progress has materialized, as the programme’s high profile contrasts with its lack of on-the-ground results.
The risk of "severe" programme failure (as upgraded in this review) has materialized due to the cumulative effect of governance and procurement delays.
The risk of misaligned expectations between partners has materialized, evident in the stalled procurement plans and differing approaches to problem-solving.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: No financial disbursements or budget execution have occurred to date, as the programme remains in an extended inception phase. The joint funding mechanism (£37.5M from FCDO and £37.5M from MEA) has not been operationalized due to procurement delays.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Not applicable (N/A) – No activities have been implemented to assess value for money against the business case. The prolonged inception phase has eroded potential VFM, as administrative costs (e.g., staff time for negotiations) have accumulated without corresponding outputs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Not applicable (N/A) – No financial management has been required beyond minimal administrative costs. However, the inability to establish joint funding mechanisms reflects poorly on the financial preparedness of both partners.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Not applicable (N/A) – No implementation has occurred to evaluate cost efficiency. The delays suggest inefficiency in the use of pre-implementation resources (e.g., staff time, consulting support).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: The co-funding commitment from MEA (£37.5M) remains formally intact, but the lack of progress on procurement raises questions about the practical materialization of these funds. No co-funding has been disbursed to date.

key_delivery_lessons: Jointly funded, equally governed programmes between two sovereign governments require significantly longer inception phases and more flexible planning assumptions than standard FCDO programmes.
The complexity of aligning two distinct public-sector systems (procurement, compliance, governance) must be explicitly accounted for in programme design, with contingency built into timelines.
High-level political commitment does not guarantee operational progress; mechanisms to translate commitment into actionable plans (e.g., binding procurement timelines) are essential.
For novel delivery models, upfront investment in dedicated programme management capacity (e.g., joint secretariat) may be necessary to navigate complexities.
successful_delivery_practices: The reiteration of commitment by both partners during Joint Steering Committee meetings has maintained programme momentum despite delays.
The development of the E-Bazaar platform as a tangible output demonstrates the programme’s potential to deliver visible results once governance hurdles are resolved.
FCDO’s adaptive approach to proposing simpler procurement options during the CSP review reflects responsive management.
management_adaptations_made: Extension of the inception phase timeline to accommodate joint-governmental delays.
Proposal to leverage the upcoming Country Strategic Partnership (CSP) review to reset programme expectations and unblock procurement.
Increased focus on visible milestones (e.g., E-Bazaar launch) to demonstrate progress amid broader stagnation.
innovations_attempted: The joint FCDO-MEA governance model itself is an innovation, though its implementation has exposed critical challenges.
The E-Bazaar platform represents an innovative approach to showcasing Indian climate-smart solutions, though its launch has been delayed by governance issues.
Exploration of simplified procurement routes to bypass bureaucratic bottlenecks.
previous_recommendations_progress: Recommendations from the prior annual review to finalize procurement plans and launch implementation remain unaddressed. No progress has been made on these fronts.
forward_recommendations: Use the CSP review to agree on a revised, simplified procurement strategy and reset realistic timelines for programme delivery.
Establish a joint FCDO-MEA working group with a mandate to resolve operational bottlenecks (e.g., procurement, funding mechanisms) within a defined timeframe.
Develop interim milestones (e.g., launch of E-Bazaar, selection of one delivery partner) to build momentum and demonstrate progress.
Conduct a lessons-learned exercise to document challenges in joint programme delivery for future FCDO initiatives of this nature.
Consider appointing an independent facilitator to mediate between FCDO and MEA on procurement and governance issues, if delays persist.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management has been ineffective in practice. While risks were identified (e.g., delays due to joint governance), the programme lacked contingency plans to address their materialization. The upgrade of risk to "severe" reflects the failure of mitigation strategies to date. Proactive risk management has been hindered by the absence of a finalized Risk Register and the programme’s reliance on high-level political processes to resolve operational issues.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: The programme is listed as a deliverable in the UK-India Roadmap and may influence bilateral climate innovation policy if successfully implemented. However, to date, its stagnation has limited any policy impact.
unintended_consequences: Negative: The programme’s delays have created skepticism among stakeholders about the feasibility of joint FCDO-India programmes, potentially discouraging future collaborations of this nature.
Negative: Prolonged inception has diverted FCDO and MEA resources from other priorities without tangible outputs, reducing overall efficiency.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme’s high political profile and alignment with the UK-India Comprehensive Strategic Partnership justify its continuation, despite poor progress to date. Both governments remain verbally committed, and the potential impact of the programme (scaling Indian climate-smart innovations) is deemed valuable. However, continuation is contingent on resolving procurement and governance bottlenecks during the upcoming CSP review.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is not sustainable in its present form. The joint governance structure has proven too cumbersome for timely implementation, and the lack of progress suggests that either the model must be simplified or additional resources (e.g., a joint secretariat) must be allocated to manage its complexity.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Low
planned_adaptations_future: Reset programme timelines and milestones during the CSP review to reflect realistic expectations.
Explore alternative procurement routes (e.g., FCDO-led procurement for some components) to bypass delays.
Develop interim outputs (e.g., launch E-Bazaar) to demonstrate progress and maintain stakeholder confidence.
Invest in dedicated programme management capacity to navigate the joint-delivery challenges.
Revisit the Theory of Change and Logframe once delivery partners are contracted, with a focus on achievable outcomes given the reduced timeline.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme transitioned from being part of 'Ideas to Impact' (I2I) to a standalone initiative in October 2019. Emphasis on flexibility to 'fail fast and scale successes' through iterative investments in new approaches/contexts/technologies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Consortium led by GDI Hub demonstrated strong performance, exceeding targets in AT product innovations (7 vs. 5 planned), ventures (5 delivered), and service delivery models (5 delivered). Partners like Humanity & Inclusion and Hope Tech showed tangible results (e.g., 1,200+ users reached via accelerator support).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance aligned with updated Logical Framework (Logframe) for close tracking of outputs/outcomes across partners. No changes to Theory of Change (ToC) or indicators proposed in Year 1.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-programme coordination evident through shared learning (e.g., 'life stories' for qualitative impact interpretation) and joint reporting. Recommendation to strengthen FCDO in-country engagement by March 2021.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Regular contact between GDI Hub, partners, and FCDO to manage COVID-19-related delays. Bi-weekly updates on pivots planned for COVID-19 response.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to exceed targets (e.g., 7 innovative ATs supported vs. 5 planned). Adaptive management included reprofiling resources based on emerging evidence of 'what works.'
adaptive_management_examples: Accelerated support for Hope Tech’s 'Sixth Sense' device following successful 'Fourth Eye' prototype.
Pilot of telerehabilitation + 3D printing for orthotic devices in Uganda (Humanity & Inclusion).

external_factors_impact: COVID-19 exacerbated health/economic vulnerabilities for people with disabilities, increasing programme relevance but complicating implementation.
Shrinking ODA budgets posed risks to long-term sustainability.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of indirect beneficiary reach (1.35M vs. original 6M target based solely on Paralympic broadcasts).
Emerging need for COVID-19-responsive AT innovations (e.g., remote service delivery models).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Gap in fund management expertise for the new AT Impact Fund (planned for future phases).
Need for venture-building support to ensure innovators/entrepreneurs can scale solutions.
risk_materialization: Moderate risk rating maintained; COVID-19 materialized as a significant external risk requiring programme pivots.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track despite COVID-19 disruptions. Adjustments to budget profile anticipated in next reporting year due to delayed activities (e.g., travel, events).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong VFM demonstrated through: (1) Exceeding output/outcome targets (e.g., 0.5M direct beneficiaries vs. plans); (2) 100% match funding target (ambitious but aligned with FCDO priorities).

key_delivery_lessons: Programme flexibility and iterative learning are critical to scaling 'what works' (e.g., rapid prototyping, pilot feedback loops).
Cross-sub-programme knowledge sharing enhances coherence (e.g., shared 'life stories' for qualitative impact assessment).
successful_delivery_practices: Accelerator model (Innovate Now) effectively supported innovators from prototype to market (e.g., Hope Tech’s 1,200+ users reached).

Integrate COVID-19 learning into AT service delivery models (e.g., remote assessments).

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in identifying COVID-19 as a material risk and adapting quickly (e.g., bi-weekly updates, budget reforecasting). Moderate risk rating reflects managed exposure to external shocks.

direct.progress: Exceeded early-stage expectations (0.5M direct vs. negligible target for Year 1).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The bridging phase (Jun 22–Dec 23) was more complex and slower than anticipated, delaying the delivery phase by six months. Governance structures (PMU, Leadership Group, Fund Administrator, IMEA) were established but took longer than planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF (Component 1) delivered essential medicines and governance setup but faced challenges in aligning with Government of Zimbabwe’s reduced budgets. Coordination with 1st-tier UN agencies was "sensitive, challenging, and complex."
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Established Health Resilience Fund Programme Management Unit (PMU), Leadership Group, Fund Administrator (UNICEF), and Independent Monitoring, Evaluation and Accountability (IMEA) function. FCDO’s Senior Health Expert post supports the PMU and engages with global funds.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination mechanisms (e.g., Leadership Group) were established but required sensitive negotiations with Government of Zimbabwe and donors. Political and diplomatic sensitivities slowed consensus-building.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Essential medicines (e.g., amoxicillin, benzylpenicillin) were procured, but some antibiotics (e.g., cotrimoxazole) were partially supported by the Global Fund, creating dependency risks. Procurement for the bridging phase was largely on track.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to delays in governance setup and need for close monitoring during the bridging phase. FCDO and UNICEF played active oversight roles.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The £5 million crisis reserve (Component 2) was earmarked for rapid response but not yet utilized. Technical Assistance and Strategic Research (Component 3, £1.5M) was designed for flexible deployment but not yet implemented.
adaptive_management_examples: Adjusted Indicator 1.5 (antibiotics availability) to focus only on HRF-controlled medicines after missing the 80% target (87.8% achieved).
Delayed delivery phase by six months to prioritize governance setup, recognizing the complexity of pooled fund establishment.
Proposed revision of output weightings (e.g., increasing from 15% to 20%) based on early implementation lessons.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed onset of the delivery phase by six months due to complex governance setup for the pooled fund.
Government of Zimbabwe’s struggles to honor co-financing commitments (a carryover issue from the Health Development Fund).
Reduced funding envelope (~$90M over 4 years vs. ~$350M for the predecessor Health Development Fund), requiring reprioritization.
Health worker attrition and reintroduction of user fees at facilities, undermining service continuity.
Political and diplomatic sensitivities in pooled fund design, requiring careful stakeholder management.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 response diverted resources and attention during the bridging phase.
Economic instability in Zimbabwe (e.g., inflation, currency fluctuations) affected procurement and partner operations.
Previous shocks (cholera, Cyclone Idai, doctors’ strikes) informed the need for a crisis reserve but also highlighted system fragility.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated delays in agreeing on technical priorities with reduced budgets, requiring sensitive negotiations.
Limited Government of Zimbabwe capacity to track and report on health facility financing, complicating results-based financing.
Supply-side data limitations (e.g., Vital Medicines Availability surveys) lacked demand-side validation, reducing evidence quality.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions with Government of Zimbabwe over unmet co-financing commitments and conflicting priorities.
Challenges in aligning UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF) with Government of Zimbabwe’s reduced budgets and political constraints.
Need for clearer communication on roles/responsibilities within the Leadership Group to avoid conflicts of interest.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Government of Zimbabwe’s Ministry of Health and Child Care lacked capacity to lead pooled fund governance independently.
Limited local capacity to manage and disburse crisis reserve funds rapidly (e.g., for future cholera/COVID-19 outbreaks).
Health facility staff attrition reduced the effectiveness of results-based financing and service delivery.
risk_materialization: Government co-financing risks materialized (as seen in the Health Development Fund exit).
Delayed governance setup increased reputational risks for donors.
Supply chain risks for Global Fund-procured antibiotics (e.g., cotrimoxazole) affected indicator performance.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Bridging phase (Component 1, £6.6M) was fully executed for governance setup and essential medicines.
Delivery phase (Component 2, £27.5M) was delayed by six months; no disbursements yet for core activities.
Technical Assistance/Research (Component 3, £1.5M) not yet disbursed; funds earmarked for future competitive tendering.
Overall, 2022 spending focused on bridging activities, with ~£6.6M of the £35.4M committed.
value_for_money_assessment: VFM not yet assessable for delivery phase due to delays. Bridging phase achieved continuity of essential services but at higher transaction costs (e.g., governance setup).
Lessons from Health Development Fund highlighted need for clearer tracking of Government of Zimbabwe commitments to improve VFM.
Pooled fund design aimed to reduce duplication but added complexity, potentially affecting efficiency.
financial_management_quality: UNICEF (Fund Administrator) demonstrated strong financial management for bridging phase procurements.
FCDO’s oversight was robust, but delays in governance setup created temporary bottlenecks.
Risk of inefficiency in crisis reserve management if rapid-disbursement mechanisms are not pre-agreed.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Bridging phase costs were higher than planned due to extended governance negotiations.
Results-based financing for health facilities showed cost efficiency in maintaining service continuity (e.g., 87.8% antibiotics availability vs. 95% target).
No data yet on cost efficiency for delivery phase (Component 2).
co_funding_materialization: Government of Zimbabwe’s co-financing commitments were partially unmet, mirroring challenges from the Health Development Fund.
EU, Ireland, and GAVI contributions were on track, but total pooled fund (~$90M) was significantly smaller than predecessor (~$350M).
currency_exchange_impacts: Zimbabwe’s economic instability (e.g., inflation, ZWL depreciation) increased procurement costs for medicines/equipment.
No explicit exchange rate hedging mentioned; risks managed through flexible fund administration.

key_delivery_lessons: Pooled funds in fragile contexts require simpler initial designs to build trust before tackling complex issues (e.g., Government co-financing).
Governance setup for multi-donor funds takes 6+ months longer than planned; buffer periods are critical.
Results-based financing is effective for maintaining service continuity but requires demand-side data validation.
Exit strategies must be designed at programme inception, not mid-term (a lesson from Health Development Fund).
successful_delivery_practices: Establishing the Leadership Group to track Government of Zimbabwe commitments improved accountability.
Flexible use of bridging funds to procure essential medicines prevented stockouts during transition.
FCDO’s Senior Health Expert post enhanced coordination with global health initiatives (e.g., Global Fund).
management_adaptations_made: Adjusted Indicator 1.5 to focus on HRF-controlled antibiotics after missing the 80% availability target.
Proposed increasing output weightings (e.g., from 15% to 20%) to reflect implementation realities.
Prioritized governance setup over delivery to avoid longer-term risks, accepting a six-month delay.
innovations_attempted: Strategic research funds (Component 3) designed for flexible deployment to policy opportunities (not yet implemented).
Crisis reserve (£5M) earmarked for rapid response to health threats (e.g., cholera, COVID-19).
Planned competitive tendering for research to improve transparency and innovation.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Government co-financing tracking improved via Leadership Group but commitments remain unmet.
Not addressed: Exit strategy still pending mid-term review (December 2023).
Addressed: Results-based financing continued but with data validation gaps.
forward_recommendations: Finalize and track Government of Zimbabwe’s specific financing commitments (e.g., health facility incentives).
Expedite health facility financing decisions to prevent service disruptions during economic crises.
Simplify pooled fund governance to reduce transaction costs and improve agility.
Develop a clear exit strategy by mid-term review (December 2023) to guide responsible transition.
Strengthen demand-side data collection (e.g., user fees, client satisfaction) to complement supply-side metrics.
risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate: Governance risks were mitigated through delayed delivery but created new implementation delays.
Financial risks (e.g., Government co-financing) were identified but not fully resolved; Leadership Group provides oversight.
Operational risks (e.g., medicine stockouts) were managed via bridging funds but require long-term solutions.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 87.8% of primary health facilities had ≥80% availability of selected antibiotics (vs. 95% target).
No data yet on beneficiaries reached for Outputs 2–5 (milestones set for 2023).
Bridging phase maintained continuity of essential services for mothers/newborns but without quantified reach.
policy_influence_achieved: Limited evidence in 2022; strategic research (Component 3) aims to influence policy but not yet implemented.
Engagement with Global Fund and other initiatives may yield future influence (e.g., on domestic financing).
capacity_building_results: Governance structures (PMU, Leadership Group) built capacity for pooled fund management but require long-term Government ownership.
Health facility staff received indirect capacity support through results-based financing, but attrition remains a challenge.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Bridging phase prevented complete disruption of essential services during transition.
Negative: Delays in delivery phase may have reduced trust among health workers and communities.
Negative: Over-reliance on Global Fund for certain antibiotics (e.g., cotrimoxazole) created dependency risks.
scalability_evidence: Pooled fund model is theoretically scalable but requires simpler governance for replication.
Results-based financing could be scaled but needs stronger demand-side validation.
Crisis reserve mechanism (£5M) is scalable for future health emergencies (e.g., cholera, COVID-19).

continuation_rationale: Programme aligns with Zimbabwe’s National Health Strategy 2021–2025 and UK global health priorities.
Bridging phase successfully established governance and maintained service continuity, justifying further investment.
Mid-term review (December 2023) will assess feasibility of exit or transformation based on delivery phase progress.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model is not fully sustainable without Government of Zimbabwe co-financing and donor coordination.
Pooled fund design is diplomatically sensitive; long-term sustainability depends on Government ownership.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate (score: B; risks: Moderate)
planned_adaptations_future: Adjust output indicators/milestones based on 2022 lessons (e.g., focus on HRF-controlled metrics).
Simplify governance structures to reduce delays in future phases.
Develop a clear exit strategy by December 2023, including options for gradual bilateral funding withdrawal.
Explore mechanisms to improve Government of Zimbabwe’s domestic financing contributions.

programme_metadata.programme_title: FCDO voluntary contributions to the DAC in 2023 and 2024

output_1.title: DAC demonstrates that it is fit for purpose in advancing policy, innovative instruments and its financing for development agenda

output_3.title: DAC peer review process considers new realities and challenges in the development landscape in order to promote, monitor and review members' efforts to deliver more inclusive and impactful development co-operation

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The DAC Secretariat demonstrated consistent progress on Paris Agreement alignment and financing for development, though some work (e.g., FfD4 contributions) remains ongoing. Peer exchanges (e.g., localisation data) and Development Country Profiles were successfully delivered, with strong collaboration between DAC subcommittees (e.g., WP-STAT and Environet).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The UK actively engaged in PWB 2025/6 negotiations and maintained oversight through UKDEL OECD, HQ, and DAC subsidiary bodies (e.g., gender, climate, SIDS working groups). Quarterly SRO-PRO risk discussions and adherence to OECD financial controls were implemented as planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination was demonstrated through joint subcommittee meetings (e.g., WP-STAT/Environet), cross-OECD collaboration (e.g., Responsible Business Conduct), and formal network updates to the DAC committee (3 updates reported). Outreach activities (Arab-DAC dialogue, AOSIS-DAC partnership) showed strong member engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The majority of UK VCs (£735k) funded DAC Secretariat technical/policy experts directly, with limited downstream partner expenditure. First instalment (£100k) was paid in March 2024; remaining £635k due by March 2025. No high-risk country expenditures were reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight matched planned intensity, with continuous engagement in OECD/DAC governance bodies, regular Secretariat interactions, and adherence to MoU financial reporting schedules. Risk management included quarterly SRO-PRO assessments and climate risk judged as low.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted to emerging priorities (e.g., biodiversity monitoring, coal transition discussions) and geopolitical shifts through proactive engagement in PWB negotiations and outreach activities (e.g., SIDS4, Arab-DAC dialogue).
adaptive_management_examples: Initiation of biodiversity monitoring work during the review period to address data gaps, funded via a separate UK VC.
DAC’s response to the 2023 High-Level Meeting commitments by embedding climate and financing priorities into the 2025-26 PWB, with UK advocacy for geopolitical responsiveness.
Development of an OECD-wide development strategy (announced at 2024 MCM) to enhance cross-organisational coherence, with DAC playing a central role.
Adjustment of Output 2’s TEC by +737 KEUR in Q4 2023 due to additional VC resources, enabling expanded activities.

main_implementation_challenges: Translating 2023 HLM communiqué commitments into concrete actions remains a work in progress, particularly for financing for development (FfD4) and climate alignment.
Ensuring the DAC’s responsiveness to the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape and partner expectations, as noted in the UK’s 2023 Mid-Term Review.
Balancing the DAC’s traditional donor-focused mandate with demands for greater inclusivity (e.g., non-member engagement, locally led development).
external_factors_impact: Geopolitical shifts required the DAC to adapt its outreach strategies (e.g., Arab-DAC dialogue, AOSIS-DAC partnership) and prioritise issues like coal transition and conflict sensitivity.
Increased global focus on climate change (e.g., COP29, Paris alignment) and biodiversity necessitated accelerated work on data monitoring and policy coherence.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated demand for DAC leadership on emerging issues (e.g., media/information environment principles, adopted March 2024) stretched Secretariat capacity.
Need to integrate non-traditional development challenges (e.g., trust deficit, economic crises) into DAC’s core workstreams without diluting focus on ODA effectiveness.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited Secretariat resources for implementing new recommendations (e.g., Gender Equality and SEAH) despite their adoption, requiring UK monitoring to ensure adequate resourcing.
Challenges in coordinating across DAC’s expanding subsidiary bodies (e.g., climate, fragility, SIDS) while maintaining coherence with OECD-wide strategies.
risk_materialization: Minor financial overrun risk (projected £3.8M/44.6M total for 2023-24 PWB) due to increased VC-funded activities, mitigated by OECD controls.
Delayed progress on some climate finance commitments (e.g., FfD4 contributions) due to complex member negotiations, though momentum remains positive.

actual_execution.budget_adjustments: +737 KEUR for Output 2 in Q4 2023 to accommodate expanded activities.

budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_justification: Increased VC resources led to higher-than-planned expenditure on technical experts and policy work, deemed justified by Secretariat to meet expanded priorities.

original_vfm_assumptions: ODA system adaptation to new challenges (climate, conflict, economic growth) would improve efficiency.
Stronger political engagement via Senior/High-Level Meetings would enhance DAC’s influence.
Reduced duplication through OECD-wide cooperation (e.g., Responsible Business Conduct).
actual_vfm_achieved: Good progress on peer reviews, Development Co-operation Profiles, and subcommittee collaboration (e.g., joint WP-STAT/Environet meetings) demonstrates efficient use of resources.
Outreach activities (Arab-DAC dialogue, AOSIS partnership) delivered cost-effective engagement with non-members, aligning with UK priorities.
DAC’s role in shaping global norms (e.g., Gender Equality Recommendation, May 2024) provides long-term VFM by influencing ODA standards.
vfm_gaps: Unclear final DAC offer for FfD4 may limit short-term VFM demonstration; longer-term impact depends on 2025 conference outcomes.
Limited evidence of cost savings from OECD-wide strategy (announced 2024 MCM) to date; benefits expected post-2025.

financial_management_quality.secretariat controls: DCD adheres to OECD-wide financial/corporate controls, with no high-risk expenditures. Downstream partner spending is minimal and monitored by SRO.
financial_management_quality.uk_oversight: Quarterly SRO-PRO risk discussions, participation in OECD/DAC governance bodies, and MoU-compliant financial reporting ensure robust management.
financial_management_quality.audit_findings: 2023 DCD risk profile assessed as ‘minor’ by FCDO, with no material findings reported.

efficiency_measures: Majority of UK VCs (£735k) allocated to in-house technical/policy experts, minimising transaction costs.
Leveraging existing OECD systems (e.g., Part I contributions, Central Priority Funds) reduced administrative overhead.
efficiency_gaps: Projected 3.8 MEUR overrun (9.4% of 40.4 MEUR budget) indicates pressure on cost control, though attributed to justified scope expansion.
No explicit cost-benefit analysis provided for new initiatives (e.g., media/information environment principles).

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: All planned UK VCs (£735k) were committed; no co-funding shortfalls reported. Additional VCs from other donors (e.g., Canada, EU) enabled expanded activities (e.g., biodiversity monitoring).

key_delivery_lessons: Proactive UK engagement in PWB negotiations is critical to aligning DAC priorities with UK objectives (e.g., climate, gender, SIDS).
Cross-subcommittee collaboration (e.g., WP-STAT/Environet) enhances policy coherence and reduces duplication.
Outreach to non-members (e.g., Arab-DAC dialogue, Croatia’s participant status) requires sustained senior-level advocacy to overcome institutional inertia.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of High-Level Meetings (e.g., 2023 HLM) to secure political buy-in for DAC commitments (e.g., Paris alignment, gender equality).
Leveraging OECD-wide mechanisms (e.g., 2024 development strategy) to amplify DAC’s influence and resource efficiency.
Regular progress updates from subcommittees to the DAC committee improved transparency and accountability.
management_adaptations_made: Increased UK monitoring of Secretariat resourcing for gender equality and SEAH recommendations post-adoption (May 2024).
Stronger emphasis on geopolitical responsiveness in PWB 2025-26, reflecting lessons from the 2023 Mid-Term Review.
Enhanced coordination between UKDEL OECD, HQ, and DAC working groups (e.g., climate, fragility) to streamline UK input.
innovations_attempted: Pilot work on biodiversity-related development finance statistics (joint ENVIRONET/WP-STAT meetings).
Adoption of Principles on Media/Information Environment Support (March 2024) to address emerging development challenges.
AOSIS-DAC Partnership (agreed at SIDS4) as a model for non-member engagement.

2020_peer_review_recommendations.follow_up: UK’s 2023 Mid-Term Review (published January 2024) provides a roadmap for outstanding actions, with continued Secretariat engagement prioritised.

forward_recommendations: Strengthen DAC’s monitoring of climate finance commitments (e.g., Paris alignment) ahead of COP29 and FfD4, with clear deliverables.
Advocate for greater Secretariat resourcing to implement new recommendations (e.g., Gender Equality, SEAH) in PWB 2025-26.
Enhance DAC’s agility to respond to geopolitical shifts (e.g., conflict, trust deficit) through more flexible PWB mechanisms.
Deepening collaboration with non-members (e.g., via AOSIS-DAC Partnership) to promote DAC standards globally.
Ensure OECD-wide development strategy (post-MCM 2025) aligns with DAC priorities to maximise policy coherence.

planned_risks_materialized: Minor financial overrun (projected 3.8 MEUR) was anticipated and managed via OECD controls.
Delayed progress on some climate commitments (e.g., FfD4) was mitigated through ongoing DAC sessions and UK advocacy.
unanticipated_risks: Rapid expansion of DAC’s mandate (e.g., media/information environment) stretched Secretariat capacity, requiring adaptive resourcing.
risk_mitigation_success: Quarterly SRO-PRO risk assessments and UKDEL engagement in DAC governance bodies ensured timely interventions.
Diversified funding sources (70% VCs) provided flexibility to address emerging priorities (e.g., biodiversity monitoring).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: DAC member states (including UK) and non-members engaged through outreach (e.g., Arab-DAC dialogue, AOSIS partnership).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Global development practitioners and policymakers influenced by DAC standards (e.g., ODA reporting, gender equality recommendations).

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: DAC’s leadership in aligning development cooperation with the Paris Agreement, reiterated at 2023 HLM and embedded in PWB 2025-26.
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Member commitments secured; ongoing work on ODA/climate metrics ahead of COP29.

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Adoption of DAC Recommendation on Gender Equality (May 2024) and SEAH implementation monitoring.
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: UK tracking Secretariat resourcing to ensure operationalisation; included in PWB 2025-26.

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Technical-level work with non-members and AOSIS-DAC Partnership (SIDS4) to promote inclusive standards.
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Outreach activities (e.g., Arab-DAC dialogue) demonstrate growing non-member engagement.

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Enhanced data on biodiversity-related finance (joint ENVIRONET/WP-STAT work) and Development Co-operation Profiles.
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Used by members to inform ODA reporting and SDG progress tracking.

capacity_building_results.results: DAC peer reviews and 2024 Development Co-operation Profiles provided members with actionable insights (e.g., UK’s Mid-Term Review progress).
UK-funded technical experts in DAC Secretariat supported policy shaping (e.g., financing for development, climate alignment).
Capacity of non-members (e.g., Croatia, AOSIS) to adopt DAC standards strengthened through dialogues and partnerships.

positive: DAC’s expanded role in media/information environment (March 2024 principles) addressed an unanticipated but critical development challenge.
Cross-OECD collaboration (e.g., Responsible Business Conduct) enhanced DAC’s influence beyond traditional ODA remits.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Adopted by non-members (e.g., Croatia’s participant status) and replicated in other OECD committees (e.g., gender, conflict).
AOSIS-DAC Partnership and Arab-DAC dialogue demonstrate adaptability to diverse regional contexts.
Integration into PWB 2025-26 and FfD4 preparations shows potential for global uptake.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (Overall Score: A; Risk: Low) with demonstrated progress on UK priorities (climate, gender, ODA effectiveness).
DAC’s unique role in shaping global development norms aligns with FCDO’s strategic objectives (SDGs, VFM, geopolitical responsiveness).
High likelihood of achieving long-term outcomes (e.g., Paris-aligned ODA, inclusive development standards) with sustained UK engagement.
Cost-effective leverage of UK VCs (£735k) to influence £44.6M DAC PWB and OECD-wide strategies.

strengths: Stable governance structure with UK representation in DAC decision-making bodies (e.g., PWB negotiations, High-Level Meetings).
Flexible funding model (70% VCs) allows adaptation to emerging priorities (e.g., biodiversity, media principles).
Strong Secretariat technical capacity, supplemented by UK-funded experts.
risks: Dependence on voluntary contributions (70% of PWB) may limit predictability; mitigated by UK’s G7-leading VC commitment.
Expanding mandate (e.g., geopolitical responsiveness) could strain Secretariat resources without additional core funding.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Increase UK advocacy for Secretariat resourcing to implement new recommendations (e.g., Gender Equality, SEAH) in PWB 2025-26.
Strengthen DAC’s monitoring framework for climate finance commitments (e.g., Paris alignment metrics) ahead of COP29/FfD4.
Deepening engagement with non-members (e.g., via AOSIS-DAC Partnership) to promote DAC standards in middle-income and fragile contexts.
Align DAC’s 2025-26 work plan with OECD-wide development strategy to maximise policy coherence and VFM.
Enhance UKDEL-HQ coordination to ensure DAC activities reflect evolving FCDO priorities (e.g., conflict sensitivity, economic resilience).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Support to Social Protection Programme (SSPP2)

output_1.title: A higher proportion of poor and vulnerable people receive more predictable social protection transfers

output_2.title: The national social protection system is strengthened to manage cash transfers more effectively and efficiently

output_3.title: The national social protection system is better prepared for shocks and faster and better targeted responses are delivered when needed

output_4.title: Social protection programs address gender gaps leading to improved agency and empowerment

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Budget reductions in FY2021-2022 led to cancellation of Outputs 4 and 5 and discontinuation of two components. Programme adjusted to focus on remaining outputs while maintaining original business case outcomes. Shift from MUVA-Assistentes to MUVA-Link model for Component 3 (employability).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF and INAS made good progress on Child Grant implementation despite delays. World Bank MDTF and UNJP coordination improved through BHC-facilitated meetings, reducing frictions. MUVA's employability models showed differential impacts (LINK model had higher job placement rates but lower education retention).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Regular coordination between UNJP and WB teams improved implementation synergy. UK technical advisory support provided directly to MGCAS for shock-responsive social protection dialogue. BHC played active role in facilitating partner coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: BHC-led coordination mechanisms between WB and UN teams were instrumental in operationalizing Child Grant expansion and reducing inter-partner frictions. However, limited dialogue between GoM and partners persisted, delaying bottleneck resolution.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in Standard Administrative Arrangement signing (e.g., BHC-UNICEF agreement signed November 2022) due to ODA budget reductions. Digital payment rollout exceeded expectations despite initial provincial resistance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to GoM decision-making delays and need for adaptive management. BHC increased technical advisory support to MGCAS to compensate for institutional capacity gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in reallocating funds after budget cuts (cancelling Outputs 4-5) and rapidly rolling out Child Grant in new provinces (Nampula, Cabo Delgado). Adaptive management used to adjust to inflation impacts on transfer values.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid Child Grant rollout in Nampula (first payments October 2022) and Cabo Delgado (March 2023) despite approval delays
Shift from MUVA-Assistentes to MUVA-Link model based on longitudinal impact evidence
Reallocation of budget to prioritize remaining outputs after FY2021-2022 reductions
Accelerated digital payment adoption in hard-to-reach areas

Capacity constraints in INAS/MGCAS affecting timely disbursements and reporting

Provincial authorities' initial resistance to digital payments (later overcome)
Macroeconomic pressures (inflation, currency devaluation) reduced purchasing power of transfers

Political economy constraints limiting GoM's fiscal space for social protection

Misalignment between GoM's ambitious targets (250k children by 2024) and realistic delivery capacity

Provincial-level capacity gaps in digital payment implementation

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was below plan due to FY2021-2022 reductions (£ adjustments not specified). Programme adapted by cancelling Outputs 4-5 to maintain focus on remaining components. Disbursement delays occurred due to GoM approval processes but were partially mitigated through adaptive management.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Moderate. Child Grant cost per child reduced from £79.50 (baseline) to £28.23 in pilot phase. MUVA-Link model cost £38/person but showed higher employment impacts (39% vs 23%).
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Low. Delays in GoM decision-making created inefficiencies in payment delivery, programme launches, and digital transitions. Cancellation of MUVA-Assistentes due to implementation delays.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Moderate-to-low. Transfer values (MzN540/£6.50) insufficient against inflation (11% consumption increase reported in 2021 evaluation). Poverty reduction impacts (10% reported) may diminish without value adjustments.
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: Original VfM proposition partially achieved. Cost efficiencies in Child Grant delivery but systemic inefficiencies persist due to external factors. Shock-responsive components slower to materialize than planned.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Mixed. UNJP and WB demonstrated strong financial management, but INAS/MGCAS required additional safeguards staff (hired per 2023 recommendation). Delays in Ministry of Finance approvals affected budget execution. Digital payment expansion improved fiduciary controls.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Child Grant delivery costs improved (62% reduction from baseline). MUVA models showed variable cost-efficiency (LINK more expensive but higher impact). Systemic costs increased due to need for additional oversight and technical support to GoM institutions.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. World Bank MDTF and UNJP contributed to reaching 110,000 beneficiaries (vs GoM's 250,000 target). No evidence of additional GoM co-funding materializing; reliance on donor funds persists.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Exchange rate fluctuations reduced purchasing power of transfers. MzN540 transfer value equivalent dropped to £6.50, affecting beneficiary consumption levels (Household Quintile 1: £3.1/month).

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (Central Emergency Response Fund - CERF as primary mechanism, with Disaster Response Emergency Fund - DREF, British Red Cross, and Integrated Food Security Phase Classification - IPC as secondary channels)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £400m total programme value over 4 years (2020-2024), with core funding to CERF as the dominant allocation
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Two-tranche disbursement: 70% upfront based on satisfactory progress, 30% contingent on Payment by Results (PbR) milestones. Direct transfers to UN-managed CERF and IFRC-managed DREF pooled funds.
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: High (pooled fund structure designed for rapid reallocation to crises as they emerge, with anticipatory action components)

governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Annual performance reviews with real-time monitoring via CERF/IFRC reporting systems. PbR milestones for 30% of funding tied to timeliness/quality metrics.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Decentralized to CERF Secretariat/IFRC for operational decisions; FCDO retains strategic approval for major adaptations (e.g., new components).

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Multi-partner (CERF as UN-wide mechanism + DREF/IFRC network + British Red Cross + IPC). No single implementer.

Technical Partner (IPC for food security classification)

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (CERF remains primary at ~95% of 2021 disbursements: £63.5m/£67m total). Secondary channels expanded to include FAO (£3m new component added Sept 2021).

funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Two-tranche PbR maintained, but 2021 saw: (1) Virtual grant approval processes (COVID adaptation); (2) Increased delegation of approval authority from UN leadership to CERF Secretariat; (3) Fast-track procedures for anticipatory action.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High (utilized for: (a) COVID-19 NGO allocations; (b) new FAO component; (c) anticipatory action scaling). No reduction in overall £400m ceiling, but ODA cuts (0.7%→0.5% GNI) affected forecasting.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Light-touch maintained, but with increased working-level engagement: (1) Quarterly FCDO-CERF/DREF meetings formalized; (2) Thematic webinars added (e.g., resource mobilization, external reviews); (3) Virtual Advisory Group meetings (May/Nov 2021).
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Enhanced monitoring via: (1) Real-time process tracking (11.25-day RR allocation average); (2) Task teams for Process Review recommendations (5 workstreams: Process, Templates, Accountability, etc.); (3) Fraud/safeguarding systems strengthened.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Further decentralized: (1) CERF Secretariat approval authority expanded; (2) FCDO strategic approval limited to new components (e.g., FAO addition). Operational decisions (e.g., RR allocations) fully delegated.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Enabling Predictable Quick and Effective Responses to Humanitarian Crises

output_1.title: CERF and DREF disburse targeted, principled and timely humanitarian funding

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme expanded to include additional components such as £3m funding to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in September 2021, aligning with the programme’s objectives on early action and anticipatory initiatives. The CERF secretariat transitioned to a fully virtual grant approval process, including paperless procedures and increased delegation of approval authority to improve efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: CERF demonstrated strong performance in timely disbursements (11.25 working days on average for Rapid Response allocations in 2021, slightly slower than 2020 but still the second-fastest on record). The FCDO noted improvements in CERF’s engagement with NGOs, including its first allocation to front-line NGOs for COVID-19 response. However, reporting on outlier analysis and evidence provision requires further improvement. DREF performed well against agreed indicators, though the absence of a full indicator set limited comprehensive assessment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: CERF maintained governance structures through virtual Advisory Group meetings (held in May and November 2021) and published recommendations transparently. The Secretary-General Bulletin (SGB) and Life-Saving Criteria (LSC) were updated in 2020–2021 to reflect operational improvements and evolving humanitarian contexts. The DREF Advisory Group continued to function as planned, though no specific milestones were set for 2021.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO, CERF, and DREF was strengthened through quarterly engagements and Advisory Group meetings. The High-Level Humanitarian Event on anticipatory action (co-hosted by the UK in September 2021) facilitated alignment among stakeholders. However, the FCDO recommended closer working-level engagement to improve forecasting and programme planning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained oversight through regular monitoring of CERF’s internal systems (e.g., fraud reporting, safeguarding) and DREF’s financial management. The UK’s 13% contribution to CERF in 2021 enabled robust accountability mechanisms, though the FCDO encouraged further improvements in partner reporting and fraud detection.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by adapting to COVID-19 constraints (e.g., virtual processes) and expanding to include new components (e.g., FAO funding). CERF’s ability to adjust allocation procedures (e.g., fast-track reviews) and DREF’s support for Forecast-based Action Funds (FbAF) showcased adaptive management.
adaptive_management_examples: Transition to virtual grant approval processes and paperless systems at CERF HQ, building on COVID-19 measures.
Increased delegation of approval authority from the Emergency Relief Coordinator (ERC) to the CERF secretariat to expedite decisions.
Expansion of anticipatory action initiatives, including UK co-hosting of the High-Level Humanitarian Event in September 2021.
Addition of a £3m component for FAO in 2021 to support early action and food security classification.
DREF’s implementation of Forecast-based Early Action Protocols (EAPs) in collaboration with National Societies (e.g., Namibia, Eswatini, Niger).

main_implementation_challenges: Balancing speed and quality in CERF’s Rapid Response allocations, with average processing times increasing slightly to 11.25 days in 2021 (from 10.7 days in 2020).
Limited comprehensive performance data for DREF due to the absence of a full set of agreed indicators.
Ensuring timely and transparent reporting from implementing partners, particularly on outlier analysis and fraud cases.
Adapting governance processes (e.g., virtual Advisory Group meetings) during the COVID-19 pandemic while maintaining engagement.
external_factors_impact: The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated global humanitarian needs, increasing demand for CERF/DREF funding and complicating in-person coordination.
Reduction in UK ODA funding from 0.7% to 0.5% of GNI disrupted original Theory of Change assumptions, requiring adjustments to funding forecasts.
Climate change and conflict drove a 40% increase in people needing humanitarian assistance (from 167.6m in 2020 to 235m in 2021), straining response capacity.
contextual_constraints_new: Unpredictable funding environments due to ODA budget cuts, necessitating proactive communication of UK funding levels to CERF/DREF for better planning.
Emerging needs for anticipatory action (e.g., forecast-based financing) required rapid adaptation of programme components and partner capacities.
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in partner reporting (e.g., CERF’s implementing agencies) affected the timeliness of qualitative data for programme assessments.
Challenges in ensuring all UN partners consistently reported fraud cases to CERF, limiting donor assurances.
capacity_constraints_emerged: CERF secretariat’s capacity to manage increased demand for Rapid Response allocations while maintaining quality standards.
DREF’s need to strengthen National Societies’ capacities (e.g., in Namibia, Eswatini) to access Forecast-based Action Funds (FbAF) effectively.
risk_materialization: Moderate risks related to funding unpredictability (due to ODA cuts) materialized, impacting programme forecasting.
Operational risks from COVID-19 (e.g., virtual processes, travel restrictions) were mitigated but required adaptive management.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The UK disbursed £63.5m to CERF (13% of total 2021 funding), £1.5m to DREF, £477,372 to the British Red Cross, and £1.5m to the IPC Global Strategic Programme, aligning with planned allocations. The programme remained on track despite ODA budget reductions, with no significant underspending reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: CERF demonstrated strong VFM by maintaining rapid response times (11.25 days for RR allocations) and expanding anticipatory action initiatives, which reduce long-term humanitarian costs. DREF’s unearmarked pooled fund model provided efficient start-up financing for National Societies, with loan/grant facilities tailored to disaster scale. The FCDO noted that CERF’s internal systems (e.g., fraud reporting, safeguarding) enhanced donor confidence in VFM.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: CERF’s financial management was rated highly, with transparent reporting through interim updates, field narratives, and HQ financial reports. The 2020–2021 updates to the Secretary-General Bulletin (SGB) and Life-Saving Criteria (LSC) improved procedural clarity. DREF’s administration by IFRC ensured accountable fund distribution to 192 National Societies, though the FCDO recommended stronger fraud reporting mechanisms.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The programme achieved cost efficiencies through: (1) CERF’s ability to pool funds for underfunded crises, reducing duplication; (2) DREF’s Forecast-based Action Fund (FbAF), which minimized response delays; and (3) UK funding leveraging CERF’s global reach to areas without FCDO bilateral programmes. Anticipatory action initiatives further lowered costs by mitigating crisis impacts preemptively.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized as planned, with CERF’s multi-donor model ensuring complementary contributions from other donors. The UK’s 13% share in 2021 was critical for CERF’s operational continuity. DREF’s loan facility (reimbursed via Emergency Appeals) also demonstrated effective co-funding coordination.

key_delivery_lessons: Clear, proactive funding forecasts from the UK are essential for CERF/DREF to programme effectively, given the UK’s significant contribution share.
Virtual processes (e.g., paperless grant approvals) adopted during COVID-19 improved efficiency and should be institutionalized.
Anticipatory action initiatives (e.g., FbAF) require continued evidence-building to demonstrate impact and secure donor buy-in.
successful_delivery_practices: CERF’s delegation of approval authority to the secretariat expedited decision-making without compromising quality.
DREF’s Forecast-based Early Action Protocols (EAPs) enabled timely responses to predictable hazards, reducing humanitarian costs.
Quarterly engagements between FCDO and partners (CERF/DREF) enhanced coordination and adaptive management.
Transparency in governance, such as publishing CERF Advisory Group recommendations, strengthened accountability.
management_adaptations_made: Transition to fully virtual Advisory Group meetings and grant processes in response to COVID-19.
Introduction of a gender/GBV expert secondment to the CERF secretariat to address cross-cutting issues.
Expansion of the programme to include FAO funding (£3m) in 2021 to support food security classification and early action.
innovations_attempted: CERF’s fast-track allocation procedures for Rapid Response windows, reducing processing times.
DREF’s Forecast-based Action Fund (FbAF), enabling preemptive disaster responses via National Societies.
British Red Cross’s capacity-building project to help National Societies (e.g., Namibia, Niger) develop Early Action Protocols (EAPs).
previous_recommendations_progress: CERF implemented 30% of the 2020 Process Review recommendations, including virtual approvals and updated templates.
DREF improved reporting practices but lacked a full indicator set for comprehensive assessment (addressed in 2022 planning).
FCDO’s push for SMART indicators was partially adopted, with further refinements planned for 2022.
forward_recommendations: Agree simplified, quantifiable SMART indicators with CERF for 2022 to better capture performance.
Ensure all milestones are pre-agreed with DREF to enable full performance assessment.
Strengthen fraud reporting systems in CERF and DREF, with timely updates from implementing partners.
Continue building evidence on anticipatory action impact, leveraging the momentum from the 2021 High-Level Event.
Enhance predictability of UK funding communications to CERF/DREF for annual programming.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was effective in mitigating operational disruptions (e.g., COVID-19 adaptations) and financial risks (e.g., ODA cuts). However, the FCDO recommended stronger mechanisms for fraud detection and partner accountability. The programme’s moderate risk rating remained stable, reflecting proactive adjustments to emerging challenges.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: In 2021, CERF supported millions affected by disasters, conflict, and displacement globally, with the UK’s £63.5m contribution enabling responses in underfunded crises. DREF reached 192 National Societies via its pooled fund, though exact beneficiary numbers were not quantified in the review. The programme’s anticipatory action components (e.g., FbAF) targeted vulnerable populations in Namibia, Eswatini, and Niger.
policy_influence_achieved: CERF’s updated Life-Saving Criteria (LSC) and Secretary-General Bulletin (SGB) influenced UN-wide humanitarian standards.
The UK’s co-hosting of the High-Level Humanitarian Event on anticipatory action (September 2021) advanced global policy dialogue.
DREF’s Forecast-based Action Fund (FbAF) model was adopted by multiple National Societies, demonstrating scalability.
capacity_building_results: British Red Cross’s project strengthened the capacity of four National Societies (Namibia, Eswatini, Niger, and a Sahelian country) to develop Early Action Protocols (EAPs).
CERF’s task teams improved internal capacities (e.g., virtual processes, accountability frameworks) based on the 2020 Process Review.
DREF’s advisory group engagement enhanced National Societies’ ability to respond to small/medium-scale disasters.
unintended_consequences: Positive: CERF’s first allocation to front-line NGOs during COVID-19 expanded partner diversity and local response capacity.
Negative: Limited comprehensive data on DREF’s performance due to indicator gaps, partially addressed in 2022 planning.
scalability_evidence: CERF’s model is highly scalable, with the UK’s funding enabling responses in 100+ countries annually. The programme’s expansion to include FAO in 2021 demonstrated adaptability.
DREF’s FbAF and EAPs were replicated by multiple National Societies, indicating potential for broader adoption.
Anticipatory action initiatives (e.g., forecast-based financing) gained traction globally, supported by the UK-hosted 2021 event.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has consistently achieved high performance (A+ ratings) and demonstrated adaptability to emerging challenges (e.g., COVID-19, ODA cuts). Its alignment with global humanitarian priorities (anticipatory action, underfunded crises) and strong VFM justify continuation. The FCDO’s recommendations focus on refining indicators and strengthening partner accountability, not fundamental changes.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The delivery model is sustainable long-term, given: (1) CERF’s established role as a UN global fund with multi-donor support; (2) DREF’s unearmarked pooled fund structure, which ensures flexibility; and (3) the programme’s ability to integrate new components (e.g., FAO funding) as needs evolve.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Adopt SMART indicators for CERF and pre-agreed milestones for DREF to improve performance tracking.
Enhance fraud reporting and partner accountability mechanisms in collaboration with CERF/DREF.
Expand anticipatory action initiatives, building on the 2021 High-Level Event’s outcomes.
Improve funding predictability through proactive UK-FCDO communication with partners.
Strengthen gender/GBV mainstreaming via the CERF secretariat’s new expert secondment.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Better Lives for Somali Women and Children (Health and Nutrition)

output_1.title: Humanitarian: Provide humanitarian services with a focus on reproductive, maternal, newborn, child health and nutrition delivery in priority health facilities / Development: Women of childbearing age access and utilize quality RMNCAH and nutrition services including family planning

output_2.title: Humanitarian: Promotion of a learning culture in Better Lives to inform the wider health sector / Development: Children under five have access to an essential package of health services to reduce morbidity and mortality from malnutrition and main childhood illnesses

output_3.title: Humanitarian: Promote an adaptive approach towards climate change and ensuring that the health sector is safer and more resilient / Development: Parents, caregivers, children, and pregnant women receive support intended to enhance healthcare practices

output_4.title: Development: The MOH and partners have enhanced capacity to deliver, monitor and report on services towards strengthening the quality of health systems

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from planned development phase (April 2022) to 18-month humanitarian phase due to ODA reductions and FGS delays in strategic prioritization. Transition to development phase began October 2023 with reduced scope (geographical, service packages, and HSS components). Technical Assistance Facility paused due to ODA cuts; ME&L component awarded to Oxford Policy Management (August 2023).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF (prime partner) performed well in humanitarian phase, leveraging additional funds (GFATM, Gavi) and procurement capacity. Downstream partners (Mercy USA, Save the Children, Action Against Hunger, Trócaire) delivered services but faced challenges in development phase transition. UNFPA collaboration on family planning was below target (35% vs 57% facilities).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance structure between FCDO, UNICEF, FMOH/MoHD still being formalized (MoU exists but operational governance pending). Oversight intensified through revamped partner meetings (monthly/quarterly) and bilateral engagements with downstream partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with health authorities (Somalia/Somaliland) improved but remains challenged by resource competition. Humanitarian Country Team membership facilitated alignment. Joint FCDO-UNICEF-Government communication plan partially implemented via MoU.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: UNICEF’s procurement capacity (tax-free commodities, bulk purchasing) delivered VfM, especially for vaccines and medical supplies. Delays in development phase procurement due to phased transition and ODA uncertainty.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to risk environment (Major rating). Monthly/quarterly partner meetings introduced, with risk data integration from UN risk management units.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted from development to humanitarian phase (April 2022–Sept 2023) and adapted to ODA reductions by reducing geographical scope and HSS components. Development phase design adjusted based on OPM’s ToC refresh.
adaptive_management_examples: Transition from humanitarian to development phase in Oct 2023 with revised ToC and reduced scope.
Leveraged UNICEF’s existing partnerships (GFATM, Gavi) to maintain service delivery despite funding cuts.
Introduced vulnerability criteria for targeting marginalized populations (urban/rural/hard-to-reach areas).
Strengthened social behavior change interventions to address ANC dropout rates (1st to 4th visit).

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed development phase start (18 months) due to ODA reductions and FGS prioritization delays.
Reduction in geographical scope, service packages, and HSS components due to budget cuts (£120m programme redesigned).
High partner turnover and capacity gaps in downstream NGOs (e.g., only 35% of facilities received FP commodities vs 57% target).
Low ANC4 attendance (18% of target) due to dropout between 1st and 4th visits, linked to behavioral and access barriers.
Skilled birth attendance below target (40% vs 48%) and immunisation coverage decline (58% vs 71% pentavalent3).
external_factors_impact: ODA reductions (2022) forced pivot to humanitarian phase and delayed development activities.
Political instability in Somalia/Somaliland affected government engagement and resource allocation decisions.
El Niño impacts (2023) strained health systems and required reprogramming of resources.
Global supply chain disruptions (e.g., vaccine/medical supplies) and inflation increased costs.
Conflict dynamics in target regions (e.g., Gedo, Mudug) limited access to some populations.
contextual_constraints_new: Steep competition for limited health resources among development partners in Somalia.
Government’s limited absorptive capacity for health system strengthening (HSS) components.
Hard-to-reach areas (e.g., Hobyo district) required tailored delivery models not fully anticipated in business case.
Behavioral barriers to service uptake (e.g., ANC4 dropout) more pronounced than expected.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between UNICEF and downstream partners over resource allocation during transition phases.
Delays in MoU operationalization between FCDO, UNICEF, and FMOH/MoHD created coordination gaps.
UNFPA’s complementary FP support was slower than planned due to alignment challenges.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited MOH capacity to absorb technical assistance (TA facility paused).
Downstream partners lacked experience in development-phase service delivery (vs humanitarian).
FCDO programme team stretched due to dual humanitarian/development phase management.
ME&L systems underdeveloped until OPM’s August 2023 contract award.
risk_materialization: Major risk of "Government delays in strategic prioritization" materialized (caused 18-month development phase delay).
"ODA reductions" risk materialized, leading to scope reductions and TA facility pause.
"Partner capacity gaps" risk partially materialized (e.g., FP commodity distribution delays).
"Conflict/political instability" risk affected implementation in Gedo and Mudug regions.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Overall underspend due to phased transition and ODA cuts. Humanitarian phase fully executed; development phase budget reallocated.
6-month humanitarian bridging phase (Apr–Sept 2023) constrained budget flexibility.
Medical supplies and nutrition commodities accounted for largest expenditures, aligned with humanitarian focus.
value_for_money_assessment: Humanitarian phase demonstrated VfM through UNICEF’s leverage of GFATM/Gavi funds and bulk procurement savings.
Development phase VfM constrained by reduced scope and delayed start; metrics not yet harmonized.
Equity: UNICEF’s vulnerability targeting reached marginalized populations (urban Banadir, rural Togdheer, hard-to-reach Hobyo).
Efficiency: Commodity procurement costs minimized via UNICEF’s tax exemptions and global supply chains.
Effectiveness: High SAM recovery rates (97%) but lower utilisation rates (0.68 vs 1.2 target) in development phase.
financial_management_quality: UNICEF’s financial systems robust (monthly/quarterly reporting, risk-informed adjustments).
Downstream partners required additional oversight to meet FCDO standards (e.g., Save the Children, Action Against Hunger).
Currency fluctuations managed via UNICEF’s hedging mechanisms; no significant exchange rate losses reported.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Pentavalent vaccine cost per dose: £X (below regional average due to UNICEF’s bulk purchasing).
SAM treatment cost per child: £Y (efficient due to integrated OTP/SC model).
Overhead costs higher than planned (12% vs 10%) due to additional oversight needs.
co_funding_materialization: GFATM and Gavi co-funding materialized for vaccines and immunisation campaigns.
UNFPA’s complementary FP funding partially materialized (35% facility coverage vs 57% target).
World Bank alignment discussions ongoing but no co-funding secured yet.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal direct impact reported; UNICEF’s procurement in USD mitigated Somali Shilling volatility.

key_delivery_lessons: Phased transitions between humanitarian/development phases require 12+ months of lead time to avoid implementation gaps.
Prime partners (e.g., UNICEF) must be included in government negotiations from the outset to align priorities.
Vulnerability-targeted approaches (e.g., UNICEF’s criteria) improve equity but require adaptive monitoring.
Behavioral barriers (e.g., ANC4 dropout) need dedicated SBCC resources, not just service provision.
successful_delivery_practices: UNICEF’s leverage of GFATM/Gavi funds to maintain service delivery despite FCDO cuts.
Integrated SAM treatment model (OTP + SC) achieved 97% recovery rates.
Monthly/quarterly partner meetings improved risk data flow and adaptive management.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme novated from UNOPS to IOM as fund manager; RSS pilot project transitioned to Integrated Security Fund; reduced scope due to HMG budget changes and narrower security/justice portfolio.
