programme_metadata.programme_title: Somalia Stability Fund III
programme_metadata.programme_value_gbp: Maximum BC value is £200m (UK commitment up to £60m, targeting to leverage £140m from other donors)

output_1.title: Political Settlement: Supporting political processes at multiple levels to effectively address contentious issues as part of transforming the political settlement to be more inclusive and sustainable

output_2.title: Conciliation

output_3.title: Democratisation and local governance

output_4.title: Social Contract

output_5.title: Research

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from Phase II's focus on government-led infrastructure projects to a more explicitly political mandate in Phase III, requiring greater donor coordination and political engagement. Transition involved reappraising objectives and methodologies with government partners, posing alignment challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Somalia Dialogue Platform (SDP) demonstrated strong analytical capacity and local credibility, producing 20+ policy papers, 20+ dialogues, and 8 Somali-language podcasts. However, its engagement with the National Consultative Council (NCC) secretariat was discontinued after 6 months due to concerns over inclusivity and feasibility of agreements. UN window activities were not fully integrated into workstream results during this period.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme governance structures (e.g., Joint Donor Committee coordination) were partially operationalized but required further alignment. Collaboration between Fund Manager (ASI consortium) and SDP showed promise (e.g., joint elections scenario papers) but needed calibration to balance cohesion with SDP’s autonomy as a locally trusted platform.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with FGS/FMS was strained by fluctuating relationships (e.g., Puntland’s disengagement, Somaliland-Ethiopia MOU). Donor alignment improved through SDP’s weekly updates and policy dialogues but required deeper integration with FCDO’s campaign goals. Cross-donor coordination was critical for addressing shared state-building vision gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement via Fund Manager (ASI) included framework/non-framework agreements (e.g., grants to local CSOs, MOUs with government). Challenges included delays in inception (4-month post-contracting period) and ensuring procurement aligned with adaptive political priorities (e.g., electoral support via UNDP IESG).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensive during inception but adapted to allow flexibility in political engagement (e.g., SDP’s autonomous dialogue facilitation). Financial oversight of UN window activities required strengthening to ensure alignment with SSF objectives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in responding to political crises (e.g., Puntland elections support, constitutional review engagement) and reallocating resources (e.g., discontinuing NCC secretariat support). Adaptive management was constrained by donor risk appetite and fluctuating government priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Discontinuation of NCC secretariat support after 6 months due to feasibility concerns, reallocating focus to higher-impact dialogues.
Rapid response to Puntland’s election cycle through UNDP IESG partnership ($548,847 for local council elections in 30 districts).
SDP’s pivot to sub-national political dialogue and Somali-language podcasts to address emerging crises (e.g., Al-Shabaab territorial gains).
Adjustment of MEL frameworks to measure SDP’s contribution to political trends (e.g., constitutional review, Somalia Transformation Plan) rather than input-based metrics.

main_implementation_challenges: Fluctuating FGS-FMS relationships (e.g., Puntland’s suspension of engagement, Somaliland-Ethiopia MOU tensions).
Al-Shabaab’s territorial recapture and attacks disrupting stability and programme access.
Delayed constitutional review progress despite parliamentary approval of initial chapters, due to internal criticism.
Donor coordination gaps in aligning state-building visions and risk tolerance.
Transition from infrastructure-focused Phase II to political Phase III created expectation misalignment with government partners.
external_factors_impact: Worsening security context (Al-Shabaab offensives) limited programme reach in contested areas and increased costs for secure implementation.
Regional geopolitical shifts (e.g., Ethiopia-Somaliland MOU) exacerbated federal-state tensions, complicating political settlement efforts.
Humanitarian crises (drought, displacement) diverted government and donor attention from long-term state-building.
International donor fatigue and shifting priorities (e.g., Ukraine war) affected co-funding mobilization for SSF III’s £140m leverage target.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated resistance to OPOV (One-Person One-Vote) commitments from political elites, delaying electoral reforms.
Emergence of parallel dialogue platforms (e.g., clan-based forums) competing with SSF-supported processes (e.g., SDP, PUNSAA).
Restrictions on civil society participation in high-level political processes, limiting inclusivity efforts.
Currency devaluation and inflation increasing operational costs (e.g., local partner contracts, election logistics).
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between FGS and FMS (e.g., Puntland) created implementation blockages for cross-government initiatives.
UN window partners (e.g., UNDP IESG) required closer integration into SSF results frameworks to avoid siloed activities.
Local CSO partners faced capacity gaps in adapting to SSF III’s political mandate, requiring additional mentoring.
SDP’s credibility with FGS was tested by its critical analysis of NCC processes, leading to temporary disengagement threats.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited FGS technical capacity to absorb advisory support (e.g., constitutional review, electoral preparations).
Fund Manager (ASI consortium) required additional political economy expertise to navigate Somalia’s fragmented governance.
Local partners (e.g., TPEC in Puntland) needed strengthened MEL systems to track political settlement indicators.
Donor representatives lacked consistent bandwidth for high-level political engagement, delaying strategic decisions.
risk_materialization: Severe political risks materialized: FGS-FMS relations deteriorated beyond baseline assumptions, requiring crisis-response adaptations.
Security risks: Al-Shabaab attacks disrupted field activities (e.g., election monitoring in Mogadishu).
Reputational risks: Criticism of constitutional review outcomes threatened donor confidence in SSF’s influence.
Financial risks: Exchange rate volatility (Somali Shilling depreciation) reduced purchasing power for local grants.
Operational risks: Delayed inception (4 months post-contracting) compressed implementation timelines.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was ~80% of plan for Year 1 (July 2023–June 2024), with underspends in UN window activities due to delayed integration into results frameworks.
Electoral support ($548,847 for Puntland local elections) was fully disbursed but required rapid reallocation from other outputs.
NCC secretariat support (6 months) was discontinued early, freeing ~£200k for redeployment to higher-priority dialogues.
Currency fluctuations increased costs by ~10% for local partner contracts, offset by donor flexibility in exchange rate adjustments.
value_for_money_assessment: VFM rated as ‘Amber’: SDP’s policy dialogues and analyses demonstrated donor utility (e.g., 20+ policy papers informed JDC decisions), but input-based metrics (e.g., number of workshops) lacked outcome linkage.
UN window activities underdelivered on VFM due to weak integration with SSF outputs; governance review recommended to align spending with strategic objectives.
Cost per beneficiary for electoral support (~$18k/district in Puntland) was deemed efficient compared to regional benchmarks, but sustainability of outcomes remains uncertain.
Donor coordination reduced duplication (e.g., joint elections scenario paper with Fund Manager), but overlapping advisory roles (e.g., FGS technical support) persisted.
financial_management_quality: Fund Manager (ASI) maintained robust financial controls, with no audit findings. However, sub-grant management for local CSOs required strengthened due diligence.
UN window financial reporting lagged SSF standards, complicating consolidated donor oversight.
Exchange rate hedging strategies were partially effective but failed to fully mitigate Somali Shilling depreciation impacts.
Co-funding mobilization fell short of the £140m target, with only ~£80m leveraged to date due to donor prioritization shifts.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Elections support achieved cost efficiencies through UNDP IESG’s existing infrastructure (e.g., shared logistics for 30 districts).
SDP’s use of digital tools (e.g., podcasts, virtual dialogues) reduced travel costs by ~30% while expanding reach.
Fund Manager’s consortium model (ASI + local partners) reduced overheads by 15% vs. Phase II, but transaction costs for small grants remained high.
Delayed NCC support termination avoided sunk costs, but early-stage investments in secretariat setup were not recoverable.
co_funding_materialization: Co-funding realized: ~£80m of £140m target (57% achievement). Shortfalls attributed to donor reprioritization (e.g., EU, Netherlands) and Somalia’s risk profile.
Denmark and Sweden fulfilled commitments, but USAID contributions were delayed pending congressional approval.
Leverage ratios varied by output: Political Settlement (Output 1) attracted 80% of planned co-funding, while Research (Output 5) secured only 40%.
Donor coordination mechanisms (e.g., JDC) improved alignment but could not fully offset global funding constraints.
currency_exchange_impacts: Somali Shilling depreciated by 12% against USD during the review period, increasing local costs for grants and partner contracts.
Fund Manager partially hedged exposure via forward contracts, but residual impacts reduced real value of £-denominated budgets by ~8%.
Electoral support costs in Puntland rose by ~$50k due to exchange rate movements, absorbed via programme contingencies.
Donors agreed to adjust exchange rates for reporting, but volatility complicated multi-year budgeting for local partners.

key_delivery_lessons: Strategic patience is essential in Somalia’s turbulent context; donors must accept prolonged debates and iterative progress toward political settlements.
Locally led platforms (e.g., SDP) require autonomy to maintain credibility, but need clearer linkages to programme outcomes to demonstrate VFM.
Donor coordination must transcend operational alignment to agree on a shared vision for state-building, including timelines and risk tolerance.
Infrastructure-focused approaches (Phase II) are insufficient for political transformation; Phase III’s shift to dialogue and governance requires sustained stakeholder buy-in.
Continuous investment in civic actors (beyond government) is critical for nation-building, as they shape public opinion and social contract dynamics.
successful_delivery_practices: SDP’s weekly political updates and policy dialogues provided actionable intelligence for donors, enhancing adaptive decision-making.
Joint Fund Manager-SDP products (e.g., elections scenario papers) improved coherence between technical and political workstreams.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., rapid-response grants for Puntland elections) enabled timely support during crises.
Somali-language podcasts and local CSO engagements expanded reach to marginalized groups, addressing inclusivity gaps.
Early termination of underperforming activities (e.g., NCC support) demonstrated agile resource management.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted MEL focus from input tracking (e.g., workshops) to outcome contribution (e.g., SDP’s influence on constitutional review).
Strengthened programme governance structures to integrate donor political representatives into strategic oversight.
Developed clearer criteria for UN window usage to ensure alignment with SSF’s political settlement objectives.
Increased FCDO Somalia network coordination to embed SSF activities into UK campaign goals (e.g., Freedom and Democracy pillar).
Introduced risk-sharing agreements with donors to enable faster adaptations to political shocks (e.g., Al-Shabaab offensives).
innovations_attempted: Pilot of ‘political economy light’ analyses to inform rapid-response grantmaking in volatile contexts.
Use of digital dialogue platforms (e.g., SDP podcasts) to circumvent physical access constraints in Al-Shabaab-controlled areas.
Joint donor-SDP missions to FMS capitals to test sub-national political settlement hypotheses.
Integration of clan mapping tools into SDP’s mediation support to address historic grievances.
Experimental funding for ‘track II’ dialogues (non-state actors) to complement traditional government engagements.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Governance structures were operationalized but required deeper donor integration (e.g., JDC role clarification).
Not addressed: UN window activities remained siloed from core workstreams due to bureaucratic delays.
Fully addressed: MEL frameworks were revised to measure contribution to political trends (e.g., constitutional review).
Partially addressed: Co-funding mobilization improved but fell short of targets due to external donor constraints.
Not addressed: Capacity-building for local CSOs in political analysis lagged behind demand.
forward_recommendations: Fully operationalize programme governance structures to ensure donor alignment on state-building vision and risk appetite.
Develop a clear FGS engagement policy to streamline government support and avoid ad-hoc responses to requests.
Strengthen MEL systems to attribute SSF’s contribution to high-level processes (e.g., constitutional review, elections).
Increase investment in civic actors and sub-national dialogues to balance executive-focused state-building.
Conduct a lessons-learned review on UN window integration to inform Phase III’s final years.
Explore multi-year funding commitments with key donors to mitigate exchange rate and co-funding risks.
Enhance SDP’s role as a ‘neutral convener’ while clarifying its accountability to SSF outcomes.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in crisis response (e.g., Puntland elections, Al-Shabaab attacks) but less so in anticipating political risks (e.g., NCC feasibility).
Donor risk appetite varied, creating tensions between adaptive management needs and compliance requirements.
Risk registers were updated quarterly but lacked scenario planning for severe FGS-FMS ruptures.
Currency risk mitigation was reactive; proactive hedging strategies are needed for Phase III’s remaining years.
Partner due diligence (e.g., for local CSOs) was robust but slowed implementation in fast-moving political contexts.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Puntland local elections: 30 districts, 7/9 political associations participated; ~500,000 voters (indirectly reached via awareness campaigns).
SDP dialogues: 20+ events with ~300 unique participants (government, clan leaders, civil society).
Constitutional review: Engagement with 150+ parliamentarians and stakeholders during approval of first four chapters.
Research outputs: 20 policy papers and 8 podcasts reached ~10,000 listeners/readers (Somali/international audiences).
Direct beneficiaries underperformed against targets due to access constraints in Al-Shabaab-controlled areas (e.g., only 60% of planned districts for social contract activities).
policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to parliamentary approval of first four constitutional chapters (including OPOV commitment), though implementation faces elite resistance.
SDP analyses influenced donor positions on Puntland elections and FGS-FMS mediation strategies (e.g., JDC briefings).
Elections scenario paper shaped international community’s contingency planning for Somalia’s 2024–25 electoral cycle.
Limited evidence of direct policy uptake by FGS due to capacity gaps and competing priorities (e.g., security crises).
capacity_building_results: TPEC (Puntland Electoral Commission) strengthened operational capacity for local elections but remains dependent on donor technical support.
SDP’s Somali-language podcasts improved civic awareness of political processes among ~8,000 listeners.
National Consultative Council secretariat received 6 months of support, but capacity gains were not sustained post-discontinuation.
Local CSOs engaged in dialogues showed improved advocacy skills but lacked resources for independent political analysis.
unintended_consequences: Positive: SDP’s neutral convening role enhanced its credibility with non-state actors, creating new entry points for mediation.
Positive: Puntland’s relatively peaceful power transition (post-elections) set a precedent for FMS-level democratic processes.
Negative: Elite criticism of constitutional review outcomes undermined public trust in SSF-backed processes.
Negative: Focus on high-level dialogues (e.g., NCC) diverted attention from grassroots reconciliation needs, exacerbating local grievances.
Negative: Donor coordination improvements inadvertently sidelined smaller donors (e.g., Sweden) in decision-making.
scalability_evidence: SDP’s dialogue model is scalable to other FMS (e.g., Hirshabelle, South West State) but requires tailored conflict sensitivity analyses.
Electoral support packages (e.g., Puntland) can be replicated for 2024–25 cycles if security permits, with adjusted timelines.
Constitutional review methodologies are transferable to other post-conflict contexts but depend on elite buy-in.
Limited scalability of social contract activities due to Al-Shabaab’s territorial control and clan-based resistance in central regions.
Research outputs (e.g., policy papers) have regional applicability but require localization for non-Somali contexts.

continuation_rationale: SSF III remains the primary multi-donor vehicle for addressing Somalia’s political settlement challenges, aligned with FCDO’s Freedom and Democracy pillar.
Phase III’s political mandate is gaining traction (e.g., Puntland elections, constitutional review) despite contextual setbacks.
Donor commitment (£80m co-funding secured) and FCDO’s lead role justify continued investment, pending adaptive management improvements.
Closure would risk losing momentum in critical areas (e.g., OPOV preparations, FGS-FMS dialogue spaces).
Transformational potential exists if governance structures are fully operationalized and delivery models better aligned with Somali-owned processes.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model (Fund Manager + UN window) is financially sustainable but requires stronger integration between workstreams.
SDP’s locally led approach is sustainable if donor coordination improves and its role in outcome measurement is clarified.
Long-term sustainability hinges on FGS capacity development, which remains nascent.
Risk of donor fatigue persists, particularly if co-funding targets remain unmet or political risks escalate.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize and implement a clear FGS engagement policy to depoliticize technical support.
Fully integrate UN window activities into SSF results frameworks with defined contribution pathways.
Expand sub-national focus (e.g., Hirshabelle, Jubaland) to address regional disparities in political settlement progress.
Develop a phased exit strategy for SDP, transitioning its convening role to Somali institutions by 2027.
Enhance MEL systems to better attribute SSF’s contribution to high-level processes (e.g., constitutional review, elections).
Pilot innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., challenge funds) to attract non-traditional donors and improve co-funding ratios.
Conduct a mid-term political economy analysis to reassess programme theory of change in light of evolving FGS-FMS dynamics.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Contract + Multilateral)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £60 million over 7 years (2023–2030), targeting 700,000 children across 4 components (Foundational Learning, Girls in School, Girls Out of School, Children with Disabilities) + cross-cutting TA/Advocacy
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: 1) Lead commercial supplier (Components 1, 3, 5 via open tender, £32.5m); 2) UNICEF (Components 2, 4, 5 via MoU); 3) Separate MERL supplier contract. Phased disbursement aligned with component milestones.
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium - Built-in adaptability for "test-learn-adapt" approaches, with contingency for procurement delays and scaling of cost-effective interventions.

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch FCDO oversight with delegated implementation to partners. Quarterly risk reviews and annual programme reviews. Steering Committee with MINEDUC representation planned *post-inception*.
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly monitoring (financial/technical) with annual deep-dive reviews. Risk-based audits as needed.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Partner-led operational decisions; FCDO approval for major design/adaptation changes. Joint decision-making on scaling interventions via Steering Committee.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Tripartite: 1 lead commercial supplier + UNICEF + MERL supplier. No consortium structure.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: 1) Commercial supplier (Foundational Learning/TA); 2) UNICEF (Girls in School/Inclusion); 3) MERL specialist (evaluation/learning).

partner_roles_planned.lead_supplier: Components 1, 3, 5 (Foundational Learning, Girls Out of School, TA/Advocacy)
partner_roles_planned.UNICEF: Components 2, 4, 5 (Girls in School, Children with Disabilities, TA/Advocacy)
partner_roles_planned.MERL_supplier: Independent monitoring, evaluation, research, and learning (quality assurance).

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: 1) Lead supplier: Open tender (£32.5m, 7-year contract); 2) UNICEF: Direct award via MoU; 3) MERL: Competitive procurement.

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Mixed (Contract + Multilateral) *with delays*
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £60m budget unchanged, but *phased rollout delayed*: UNICEF inception began Oct 2023; lead supplier contract signing delayed to Sept 2024 (originally April 2024); MERL supplier not yet onboarded. Scope (700,000 children/400+ schools) remains unchanged.
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: 1) Lead supplier: Open tender completed (4 bids received), contract signing delayed by 5 months; 2) UNICEF: MoU active, inception phase underway but underspend reported; 3) MERL: Procurement ongoing. *Actual flow*: UNICEF disbursements started; commercial supplier funds pending contract signature.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Medium-High - Flexibility leveraged to mitigate delays: UNICEF MoU allowed early activities; scenario planning for underspend. Contingency used for procurement extensions.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Light-touch *with enhanced oversight due to delays*: Weekly procurement tracking (Education Huddle); monthly risk meetings; ad-hoc escalations to leadership. Steering Committee with MINEDUC *not yet formalized* (planned for 2024/25). *New*: Insourced Education Adviser (Grade 7) added July 2024 for technical oversight.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased to *monthly* (from quarterly) for procurement/financial tracking; risk-based monitoring intensified. UNICEF now reports monthly to FCDO on implementation progress.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Partner-led operations continue, but FCDO now *more involved in troubleshooting* (e.g., procurement rewind decision March 2024). Joint decision-making on mitigation strategies (e.g., MoU flexibility).

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Tripartite *unchanged*, but *UNICEF role expanded* to compensate for commercial supplier delays (e.g., early school interventions). MERL supplier still pending.
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: 1) Commercial supplier: *Not yet active* (contract pending); 2) UNICEF: Active in 800 schools (vs. planned 400+); 3) MERL: *Not yet selected*.

partner_roles_actual.lead_supplier: *Delayed* - Components 1, 3, 5 not yet started (contract signing Sept 2024).
partner_roles_actual.UNICEF: *Expanded* - Delivering Components 2, 4, 5 + *temporary gap-filling* for Component 1 (e.g., remedial learning in 800 schools).

substantive_changes_made: Added *insourced Education Adviser* (Grade 7) for technical oversight and partner coordination (July 2024).
Intensified governance: *monthly* UNICEF-FCDO meetings (vs. quarterly planned) and weekly procurement tracking.
Leveraged UNICEF MoU flexibility to *start activities earlier* (800 schools vs. planned 400+) and mitigate commercial supplier delays.
Revised procurement timelines: Lead supplier contract deadline extended by 5 months (April → Sept 2024) due to regulatory compliance needs.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: No change to £60m budget, but *phased disbursement delayed* (underspend in 2024/25 due to procurement lag).
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: *Geographic scope expanded temporarily*: UNICEF working in 800 schools (vs. planned 400+) to compensate for supplier delays.
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: No shift in modalities, but *greater reliance on UNICEF* (multilateral) to cover gaps during commercial supplier onboarding.

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: No formal ToC revision, but *new evidence* (Education Statistical Yearbook 2022/23) highlighted worsening repetition rates (30% in primary), reinforcing need for remedial learning interventions (already in design).

management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: FCDO now *more proactive* in procurement troubleshooting (e.g., rewind decision March 2024) and risk mitigation (e.g., MoU flexibility).

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: *Temporary expansion*: UNICEF operating in 800 schools (vs. planned 400+) to maintain momentum.

activity_only_adjustments: UNICEF accelerated inception activities (e.g., safeguarding assessments) to offset commercial supplier delays.
MERL indicators to be amended *once supplier is in place* (no substantive change).

adaptation_triggers.performance_issues: Procurement delays (commercial supplier) and UNICEF underspend/implementation lags.
adaptation_triggers.learning_insights: Lessons from UNICEF’s early implementation (e.g., capacity limitations) prompted monthly check-ins and fast-tracking plans.
adaptation_triggers.strategic_opportunities: UNICEF’s existing relationships with MINEDUC enabled *faster school access* (800 schools).

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: Medium - *Reactive* adaptations to procurement delays (e.g., MoU flexibility) but *proactive* in governance intensification (monthly meetings, insourced adviser).
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: High - Baseline flexibility (test-learn-adapt) effectively used to mitigate delays via UNICEF expansion and scenario planning.
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Medium - Adaptations based on *implementation learning* (e.g., UNICEF capacity gaps) but no formal ToC revision.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: MINEDUC engagement *strengthened* post-inception: Ministerial representation on Steering Committee planned for 2024/25; regular meetings with Minister of Education initiated.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: UNICEF implementation revealed *capacity limitations* (underspend, reporting delays), prompting FCDO to fund additional programme management roles (e.g., GIRL Technical Lead).

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Strong market interest (120+ participants in Early Market Engagement; 4 bids for lead supplier). *Delay cause*: FCDO’s Global Development Delivery framework not ready, forcing open tender route.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Moderate (2 substantive changes: governance intensification + partner role adjustments)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Comprehensive adaptation (governance + partner roles + management restructuring to address procurement delays)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate - Flexibility clauses (test-learn-adapt, MoU) enabled effective crisis response, but procurement risks were underestimated.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Girls in Rwanda Learn (GIRL) Programme

output_1.title: GIRL Supplier: Foundational Learning, Innovation Fund, Technical Assistance and Advocacy

output_2.title: UNICEF: Improved learning outcomes and a safer and more inclusive school environment for girls and boys in upper primary, including children with disabilities and other marginalised groups

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Procurement delays led to revised timelines for supplier contracts. UNICEF began inception phase in October 2023 while commercial supplier procurement remained ongoing. Preferred procurement route changed from framework agreement (Global Development Delivery) to open tender due to framework unavailability and contract value/length requirements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF demonstrated commitment but faced capacity limitations leading to underspend and delayed reporting. Market engagement for commercial suppliers showed significant interest (120+ participants, 4 bids). Partnership with UNICEF helped mitigate underspend risks through flexible MoU arrangements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme team demonstrated agility in scenario planning. New insourced Education Adviser (Grade 7) role filled in July 2024 to provide technical oversight. Steering Committee establishment with MINEDUC representation remains pending.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Weekly Education Huddle meetings track procurement timelines. Monthly/quarterly risk meetings discuss mitigation actions. Coordination with MINEDUC facilitated through UNICEF's existing relationships but requires formalization.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in commercial supplier procurement due to: 1) Internal approval processes taking longer than expected for compliance, 2) Preferred framework agreement (Global Development Delivery) not being available, 3) Rewind decision on 25 March 2024 requiring timeline revisions. Contract signing now expected mid-September 2024 (original deadline: 17 April 2024).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Enhanced oversight through risk-based monitoring strategy and Delivery Chain risk mapping. FCDO maintains close tracking of procurement milestones and financial execution.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by: 1) Leveraging UNICEF's existing relationships to begin activities during procurement delays, 2) Revising contract signing deadlines based on market feedback, 3) Using scenario planning to manage underspend risks.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised procurement timeline after tender pack publication and rewind decision
Established monthly implementation tracking meetings with UNICEF to address capacity issues
Planned use of MERL supplier to develop VfM metrics once onboarded
Secured insourced Education Adviser role to strengthen technical oversight

main_implementation_challenges: Procurement delays for commercial suppliers impacting budget execution
UNICEF capacity limitations causing underspend and reporting delays
Slow programme start affecting FCDO's sector visibility
Increased repetition rates in Rwandan primary education (30% average, up from 25% in 2020/21) highlighting systemic challenges
operational_challenges_context.external_factors_impact: No major external shocks reported, but existing systemic issues in Rwanda's education sector (high repetition/dropout rates) create challenging implementation context. Political stability and government cooperation remain supportive.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-expected repetition rates in target schools (36% in P1, 33% in P5) not fully anticipated in programme design
Capacity constraints in UNICEF's programme management team emerged during implementation
Delays in establishing formal governance structures (e.g., Steering Committee with MINEDUC)
partner_relationship_issues: UNICEF's underspend and delayed reporting highlighted need for stronger implementation oversight
Commercial supplier procurement delays created tension with original implementation timelines
Need for clearer roles/responsibilities between FCDO, UNICEF, and future commercial suppliers
capacity_constraints_emerged: UNICEF's programme management capacity proved insufficient for timely implementation
Limited FCDO in-country capacity prior to Education Adviser recruitment (July 2024)
Delayed MERL supplier onboarding affecting evidence generation
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (severe risk) materialized, causing budget execution challenges
UNICEF capacity limitations (moderate risk) affected implementation pace
Underspend risk materialized due to delayed contract signings

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend due to procurement delays. UNICEF faced continuous underspend issues. Budget execution for 2024/25 fiscal year impacted by delayed contract signings, though scenario planning helped mitigate risks. UNICEF's inception phase activities began but with financial execution below plan.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Acceptable VfM demonstrated through: 1) UNICEF's leverage of existing relationships to save time/resources, 2) Strong VfM indicators in procurement processes, 3) Focus on cost-effectiveness in contract design. Areas needing improvement: 1) Establishing VfM metrics with UNICEF, 2) Accelerating implementation pace to meet spending targets.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: UNICEF showed strong commitment but needs improvement in: 1) Timely financial execution, 2) Reporting quality, 3) Utilization of budgeted programme management capacity. FCDO maintained robust oversight through risk-based monitoring and regular financial tracking.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency emphasized in procurements with clear expectations set. UNICEF's existing sector relationships helped fast-track some activities. However, delays in full implementation limit current cost-efficiency assessment. Efficiency gains expected once all partners are fully operational.

key_delivery_lessons: MoUs with multilaterals (e.g., UNICEF) can provide implementation flexibility during procurement delays

key_delivery_lessons: Co-creation phases are critical for aligning multi-country programmes with local priorities but require clear timelines to avoid delays in implementation.
Early Post engagement (even pre-business case) enhances country-level ownership, though funding uncertainties may limit this.
Indirect reach (e.g., campaigns) can rapidly scale impact but must be complemented by direct engagement for sustainability.
successful_delivery_practices: VSO’s adaptive use of VfD’s Volunteering for Development model to prioritise local capacity-building.
Collaborative logframe design with FCDO Posts improved strategic alignment.
Quarterly reviews supplemented by real-time monitoring (e.g., Q3 reach data) enabled proactive adjustments.

programme_metadata.programme_title: What Works Hub for Global Education (WWHGE)

output_1.title: Research synthesis and evidence translation outputs generated and disseminated globally and in project countries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted to a three-pillar model (synthesis/translation, institutionalizing evidence use, implementation science) with nested Theories of Change for each pillar. Added Strategic Partners (World Bank, LGI, British Council, UNICEF Innocenti, UNESCO IIEP, GEEAP/BE2) to complement the £30m BSG-led consortium. Three FCDO Implementation Roles (IRs) were introduced for coordination, country uptake, and buy-in from country offices.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: BSG exceeded milestones (e.g., 19/9 synthesis products, 37/33 dissemination events). LGI met tool development targets (Delivery Approach Toolkit piloted in 5 countries). World Bank underperformed on diagnostics (Pakistan dashboard delivered but limited engagement on Output 3). Strategic Partners demonstrated variable engagement, with some (e.g., British Council) meeting regional support targets while others (e.g., World Bank’s ISE/EPLE) lacked clear output tracking.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance includes: 1) Strategic Partnership Board (approved ToC in May 2024), 2) BSG-led consortium with 40 partners, 3) FCDO IRs for coordination, and 4) MEL team for adaptive management. Nested ToCs and pillar-specific oversight were added post-Business Case to improve alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Community of Practice (100+ orgs, 30 countries) and Policy Fellows network (Blavatnik School) enhanced cross-partner collaboration. However, duplication risks emerged (e.g., overlapping synthesis products by BSG/UNICEF Innocenti). BE2 donor group helped mitigate this but requires stronger integration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Contracts with Strategic Partners (e.g., World Bank £4.2m, LGI £2.5m) were signed between 2021–2025, with some delays (e.g., British Council MoU signed May 2024). Procurement for Pillar 3 research faced challenges due to ambiguous definitions of "research products" vs. synthesis outputs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to: 1) ToC revisions (May 2024/2025), 2) logframe indicator clarifications, and 3) MEL team’s expanded role in tracking output-outcome linkages. FCDO IRs increased country-level engagement but stretched capacity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by: 1) revising ToC to focus on implementation science, 2) adding nested ToCs for pillars, 3) reallocating Pillar 3 funds to large-scale studies, and 4) introducing rapid response mechanisms (though not yet formalized). EdLabs in 6 countries (Ghana, Rwanda, etc.) allowed context-specific adjustments.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised logframe to distinguish between research (3.1) and diagnostics (3.3) after World Bank’s ambiguous reporting.
Added "pathways to impact" protocols for 3–4 reform pathways per country (e.g., EMIS in Kenya, middle-tier reform in Tanzania).
Expanded MEL team’s role to surface "what works, for whom, and under what conditions" via programme learning agenda.
Paused World Bank’s diagnostic milestones pending shared conceptual vision (planned for 2025–26).

main_implementation_challenges: Ambiguous definitions for "research products" vs. synthesis outputs led to inconsistent partner reporting and milestone tracking (Output 3).
Weak linkage between high-volume outputs (e.g., 19 synthesis products) and policy uptake/institutionalization at country level.
Limited World Bank engagement on Output 3 (implementation science) despite signed contract, requiring FCDO/BSG intervention.
Capacity constraints in rapid response mechanisms, relying on ad-hoc availability rather than formalized processes.
Duplication risks among Strategic Partners (e.g., overlapping synthesis by BSG and UNICEF Innocenti) despite BE2 coordination efforts.
external_factors_impact: Post-COVID education system disruptions in focus countries (e.g., Pakistan, Rwanda) increased demand for evidence-based recovery strategies, accelerating uptake of WWHGE outputs.
Global economic pressures (e.g., currency fluctuations) affected partner budgets, though FCDO’s £39m CDEL/£16m RDEL allocation remained stable.
Political transitions in some countries (e.g., Pakistan) delayed EdLab embedment but also created opportunities for new reform champions.
contextual_constraints_new: Government middle-tier capacity gaps (e.g., in Tanzania, India) emerged as a bottleneck for evidence uptake, prompting UNESCO IIEP’s diagnostic tools.
Unanticipated demand for multilingual synthesis products (e.g., French/Spanish translations) to reach Francophone/Latin American stakeholders.
Need for disability-inclusive evidence (not fully anticipated in original ToC) required ad-hoc adjustments to Pillar 1 outputs.
partner_relationship_issues: World Bank’s limited engagement on Output 3 created tensions; BSG had to compensate by expanding its research portfolio.
Delays in British Council’s MoU signing (May 2024) caused initial gaps in regional coordination (India, Pakistan, Tanzania).
Divergent partner priorities (e.g., LGI’s focus on delivery tools vs. UNICEF Innocenti’s FLN Hub) required FCDO mediation to align with WWHGE’s ToC.
capacity_constraints_emerged: BSG’s consortium (40+ partners) stretched thin by expanded MEL demands and ToC revisions, risking burnout.
FCDO IRs lacked bandwidth to fully support country uptake, leading to uneven EdLab performance across regions.
Limited in-country MEL capacity hindered real-time tracking of output-outcome linkages (e.g., in Ghana, South Africa).
risk_materialization: World Bank’s underperformance on diagnostics (Output 3) materialized as a "Moderate" risk, addressed via paused milestones and joint FCDO/WB redefinition efforts.
Partner coordination risks (e.g., duplication) materialized as "Minor" but required BE2’s intervention to streamline activities.
Political risk in Pakistan (government transitions) materialized as "Minor", delaying EdLab integration but ultimately creating entry points for new reforms.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: Broadly aligned with the 60% strategic allocation for Pillar 3 (implementation science). Pillar 1 and 2 expenditures met or exceeded targets, though partner-level transparency remains limited.

pillar_specific.pillar_1: On track; synthesis outputs overdelivered (19/9 products) with efficient use of £39m CDEL funds.
pillar_specific.pillar_2: On track; EdLabs and CoP activities fully funded, though British Council’s £1.6m MoU faced initial delays.
pillar_specific.pillar_3: Underspent on diagnostics due to World Bank’s limited output; reallocated to large-scale implementation studies.

value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: High volume of outputs (e.g., 37 dissemination events) achieved cost-efficiently, but VFM for policy influence remains unproven due to weak output-outcome tracking.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Early signs of VFM in Pakistan/Rwanda where WWHGE outputs informed national reforms, but systemic impact is not yet demonstrable at scale.
value_for_money_assessment.economy: Strategic Partner contracts (e.g., LGI at £2.5m) delivered expected outputs, but World Bank’s £4.2m allocation underperformed on diagnostics.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Gender and disability inclusion were retrofitted into ToC/indicators, adding marginal costs but improving long-term VFM.

financial_management_quality.bsg_consortium: Strong; transparent reporting on £30m contract, with overdelivery on milestones (e.g., 19/9 synthesis products).
financial_management_quality.strategic_partners: Mixed. UNICEF Innocenti and LGI demonstrated robust tracking, while World Bank’s financial reporting lacked granularity on Output 3 expenditures.
financial_management_quality.fcdo_oversight: Effective in enforcing logframe revisions but struggled to harmonize partner financial systems (e.g., varying definitions of "research products").

positive_examples: LGI’s Delivery Approach Toolkit (1 tool) leveraged by 5 countries, achieving economies of scope.
Community of Practice (100+ orgs) operated at low marginal cost via digital platforms.
BSG’s synthesis products (19) produced at ~£2m/year, below sector benchmarks for similar outputs.
inefficiencies: World Bank’s underutilized £4.2m allocation for diagnostics (only Pakistan dashboard delivered).
Duplicative synthesis efforts (e.g., BSG and UNICEF Innocenti) incurred avoidable costs.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. The £16m RDEL (Girls’ Education) was fully utilized, but anticipated co-funding from multilateral partners (e.g., via BE2) materialized slower than planned, requiring FCDO bridge funding for 2024–25 activities.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal direct impact reported, though partners in South Asia/Africa noted indirect cost pressures from GBP volatility. Mitigated via FCDO’s multi-year funding commitments.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible, actor-driven ToC enabled rapid adjustments (e.g., adding nested ToCs for pillars) but required intensive MEL oversight.
Strategic Partners’ diverse strengths (e.g., LGI’s delivery tools vs. British Council’s regional networks) created complementarities but also coordination overhead.
EdLabs’ government-embedded model proved effective for evidence uptake but demanded high initial capacity-building investments.
successful_delivery_practices: Community of Practice (100+ orgs) facilitated cross-country learning (e.g., TaRL scaling insights shared from India to Rwanda).
Policy Fellows programme (Blavatnik School) enhanced mid-level government officials’ evidence-use skills, with measurable impact in Pakistan/Tanzania.
BSG’s synthesis "insight notes" (shorter, actionable formats) achieved higher policy uptake than traditional academic papers.
management_adaptations_made: Added "pathways to impact" protocols to clarify how outputs (e.g., diagnostics) link to reforms (e.g., Kenya’s EMIS).
Formalized MEL team’s role in tracking output-outcome linkages, including quarterly partner check-ins.
Paused World Bank’s diagnostic milestones until shared definitions/conceptual vision are agreed (target: 2025–26).
innovations_attempted: Delivery Approach Toolkit (LGI): Piloted in 5 countries to standardize evidence-based delivery, with interest from 3 additional countries.
Multilingual synthesis products: French/Spanish translations of key outputs to reach Francophone/Latin American audiences.
Rapid response mechanism (prototype): Tested in Rwanda to address urgent policy needs, though not yet institutionalized.

completed: Revised ToC and logframe to emphasize outcome-level change (May 2024/2025).
Developed nested ToCs for each pillar to improve MEL alignment.
ongoing: Clarifying research product definitions (Output 3) – target completion: Dec 2026.
Strengthening World Bank collaboration via joint diagnostics framework (2025–26).
stalled: Formal rapid response mechanism remains ad-hoc due to capacity constraints.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Revise logframe and ToC to set outcome-focused targets that track quality/relevance/influence of outputs (Owner: Simon Blower + BSG MEL team; Deadline: Dec 2026).
Conduct strategic review to strengthen output-outcome linkages, including risk mitigation for translation gaps (Owner: Rachel Hinton; Deadline: March 2026).
Define and operationalize diagnostics as strategic tools with minimum standards (Owner: FCDO + World Bank; Deadline: 2025–26).
Formalize rapid response mechanism to address emerging policy needs systematically (Owner: FCDO IRs; Deadline: June 2026).
Map partner activities against ToC to identify/reduce duplication (Owner: FCDO + OPM; Deadline: Feb 2026).
Expand disability-inclusive evidence generation and track gender/equity outcomes explicitly (Owner: MEL team; Deadline: Dec 2026).

strengths: Proactive pause of World Bank’s diagnostic milestones to address underperformance.
Nested ToCs improved risk visibility at pillar level (e.g., Pillar 3’s research-definition risks).
FCDO IRs’ country-level engagement mitigated political risks (e.g., in Pakistan).
weaknesses: Late identification of duplication risks (e.g., BSG/UNICEF synthesis overlap).
Limited contingency planning for currency fluctuations or partner budget shortfalls.
Ad-hoc rapid response relied on individual capacity rather than systemic processes.
adaptations: Added quarterly risk reviews with Strategic Partners to surface implementation bottlenecks.
Developed "champions and spoilers" analysis for reform pathways (e.g., in Kenya, Tanzania).

direct.policy_fellows: Mid-level government officials from 6+ countries (Pakistan, Tanzania, etc.) via Blavatnik School programme.
direct.edlabs: Government teams in 6 countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Tanzania, South Africa, Pakistan, India) embedded in education ministries.
direct.community_of_practice: 100+ organizations across 30 countries/6 continents engaged in technical dialogues.

indirect.synthesis_products: 19 evidence products disseminated globally (e.g., 222 stakeholders at WWHGE Annual Conference 2024).
indirect.diagnostic_tools: LGI’s Delivery Approach Toolkit piloted in 5 countries, with 3 additional expressions of interest.
indirect.policy_influence: Early uptake in Pakistan (national reform plans) and Rwanda (TaRL scaling).

high: EdLabs’ government embedment (e.g., Rwanda, Ghana) increases likelihood of institutionalized evidence use.
Community of Practice’s digital platform ensures low-cost knowledge sharing post-programme.
medium: Policy Fellows’ skills may fade without continued mentorship (risk in Pakistan, Tanzania).
Synthesis products’ uptake depends on sustained donor/partner demand (e.g., BE2’s long-term commitment unclear).
low: World Bank’s diagnostics face adoption risks without stronger government buy-in (e.g., Kenya’s EMIS reforms).

confirmed: Pakistan: WWHGE outputs informed national education reform priorities (e.g., structured pedagogy scaling).
Rwanda: TaRL evidence influenced Ministry of Education’s foundational learning strategy.
emerging: India: British Council’s national conference (150 participants) sparked dialogue on evidence use with NCERT/UNESCO.
Tanzania: Utafiti Elimu conference (Feb 2025) featured WWHGE tools, with potential for UPE policy integration.
mechanisms: EdLabs’ direct advisory role to ministries (e.g., Ghana’s curriculum reform).
GEEAP’s cost-effectiveness reports cited in donor coordination forums (e.g., BE2).

government_level.edlabs: Strengthened middle-tier capacity in 6 countries (e.g., Pakistan’s EMIS data use, Rwanda’s TaRL monitoring).
government_level.policy_fellows: 60+ officials trained in evidence-based policy analysis (Blavatnik School), with 80% reporting improved skills (self-assessment).

partner_level.strategic_partners: LGI/British Council enhanced delivery toolkits; UNICEF Innocenti improved FLN Hub integration.
partner_level.bsg_consortium: 40 partners upskilled in implementation science methodologies (e.g., mixed-methods studies).

systemic.community_of_practice: 100+ orgs shared best practices (e.g., structured pedagogy adaptations for children with disabilities).
systemic.global_public_goods: Tools like LGI’s Delivery Approach Toolkit adopted by non-WWHGE actors (e.g., Nigeria, Sierra Leone).

positive: Unanticipated demand for multilingual products (French/Spanish) improved accessibility in Francophone Africa/Latin America.
EdLabs’ embedded model created unintended cross-ministerial collaborations (e.g., Ghana’s education-finance ministry joint planning).
Policy Fellows network fostered South-South exchanges (e.g., Pakistan-Tanzania lesson sharing on girl’s education).
negative: Overlap in synthesis products (BSG/UNICEF) caused confusion among policymakers in Kenya.
Rapid response mechanisms’ ad-hoc nature led to inequitable support across countries (e.g., Rwanda received more attention than South Africa).
High volume of outputs (e.g., 37 events) risked partner fatigue, reducing engagement quality in later phases.
mitigation: Added MEL team’s "pathways to impact" reviews to identify/correct unintended overlaps.
FCDO IRs redistributed rapid response efforts to balance country coverage.

proven: TaRL scaling insights from India/Rwanda adopted by 3 additional countries via Community of Practice.
LGI’s Delivery Approach Toolkit piloted in 5 countries with 3 new adopters (Nigeria, Sierra Leone, +1).
potential: EdLab model replicable in new contexts (e.g., discussions with Nepal, Uganda).
Policy Fellows programme expandable to other sectors (e.g., health, climate) with FCDO support.
barriers: World Bank’s limited engagement on diagnostics hinders systemic scalability of implementation science.
Co-funding gaps (e.g., BE2’s slower-than-planned contributions) constrain expansion of CoP activities.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme is on track to achieve its objectives, with early signs of policy influence (Pakistan, Rwanda) and strong output delivery (A+ score). The flexible ToC and adaptive management (e.g., nested ToCs, paused milestones) demonstrate resilience. However, continuation is contingent on addressing output-outcome linkage gaps and formalizing rapid response mechanisms.

sustainable_elements: EdLabs’ government embedment ensures long-term evidence use (e.g., Rwanda’s TaRL institutionalization).
Community of Practice’s digital infrastructure requires minimal funding post-2029.
Strategic Partners (e.g., British Council, LGI) have independent funding streams to sustain activities.
risks: World Bank’s inconsistent engagement threatens Pillar 3’s scalability.
FCDO IRs’ capacity constraints may limit country-level support post-AMP.
Co-funding dependencies (e.g., BE2) create financial sustainability risks.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (with caveats)

planned_adaptations_future.adaptation: Revise ToC/logframe to emphasize outcome-level indicators (e.g., policy uptake metrics) by Dec 2026.
Formalize rapid response mechanism to address emerging policy needs equitably by June 2026.
Develop joint FCDO/World Bank diagnostics framework with 2+ country applications (2025–26).
Expand disability-inclusive and gender-responsive indicators across all pillars by Dec 2026.
Conduct annual partner activity mapping to reduce duplication (starting Feb 2026).
Pilot EdLab model in 1–2 new countries (e.g., Nepal, Uganda) to test scalability (2026–27).

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (contribution to Caribbean Development Bank’s Special Development Fund - SDF10)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £21,000,000 FCDO commitment over 2021–2024, with SDF10 total allocations including: Haiti £45mn; BNTF £40mn; environmental resilience £18mn; capacity building £12mn; private sector development £15mn; gender equality £2mn
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Concessional grants/low-interest loans/technical assistance channeled through CDB’s existing financial systems and governance structures, with FCDO funds pooled with other donors’ contributions
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium (funds earmarked for thematic areas but with some reallocation possible within CDB’s governance framework)

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch oversight via FCDO’s seat on CDB’s Board of Governors, with strategic influence exercised through board representation and periodic reviews
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Annual performance reviews (via CDB’s Results Monitoring Framework) with FCDO conducting independent annual reviews
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Decisions made by CDB’s governance bodies (Board of Governors/Executive Committee) with FCDO input as a major shareholder (second-largest at programme start)

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single multilateral partner (Caribbean Development Bank) as the sole implementing entity
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral Development Bank (CDB) with sub-contracts to Borrowing Member Countries (BMCs) and local implementing agencies
partner_selection_baseline.partner_roles_planned: CDB: financial intermediary and programme manager; BMCs: project implementation; FCDO: strategic oversight and priority-setting (e.g., climate, gender, private sector)
partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award to CDB based on historical partnership and alignment with UK priorities

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (unchanged, still channeled through CDB’s SDF10)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £21,000,000 commitment maintained, but *thematic allocations shifted in practice*: only 8% of 2022 programming supported renewable energy/climate (vs. 75% target), gender mainstreaming at 68% (vs. 80% target)
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Funds flowed through CDB’s systems as planned, but *disbursement delays* noted due to pandemic-related operational constraints and Haiti’s fragility
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Medium (utilized to reallocate between thematic areas, e.g., increased social protection spending in Haiti/Dominica/St. Lucia)

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Light-touch oversight maintained, but *increased FCDO engagement* via board to address underperformance in UK priority areas (climate, gender, PPPs)
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Annual reviews conducted; *additional ad-hoc monitoring* introduced for renewable energy and gender targets due to shortfalls
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: CDB governance unchanged, but FCDO *actively used board seat* to push for adjustments (e.g., revising social protection indicators, prioritizing climate financing)

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Single partner (CDB) unchanged, but *expanded sub-partnerships* with BMCs for social protection (e.g., cash transfers in Haiti, St. Lucia, Dominica)
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (CDB) + *increased direct engagement with BMC governments* for social protection and climate projects
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: CDB: unchanged; BMCs: *expanded role in social protection delivery*; FCDO: *more hands-on in addressing priority gaps* (e.g., climate, gender)
partner_names_actual: Governments of Haiti, St. Lucia, Dominica, St. Vincent and the Grenadines (for social protection)

substantive_changes_made: Reallocation of funds toward social protection in response to COVID-19/poverty increases (e.g., Haiti’s expenditure rose from 0.3% to 0.4% GDP)
Shift in oversight focus to address underperformance in climate (8% vs. 75% target) and gender (68% vs. 80% target) priorities
Revision of social protection indicators (Output Indicator 2) to align with UK priorities (previously linked to regional trade)
Target adjustments for education (classrooms) and agriculture (land improvement) due to pandemic delays

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: No change to FCDO’s £21mn commitment, but *internal reallocations* (e.g., more to social protection, less to climate)
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope unchanged, but *beneficiary focus shifted* toward vulnerable groups (e.g., BNTF communities, Haiti’s rural poor)
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: No shift in primary modality (remained multilateral), but *increased use of grants for social protection* vs. originally planned loan mix

theory_of_change_revisions.pathway_changes: Added emphasis on *social protection as a resilience pathway* (post-COVID); reduced focus on PPPs (Indicator 1.4 at 0% progress)
theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Revised assumptions about BMC capacity to implement climate projects (evidenced by 8% vs. 75% target)

activity_only_adjustments: Delay in renewable energy projects (e.g., Antigua and Barbuda solar PV) due to procurement/pandemic
Temporary pause in education facility upgrades due to school closures

contextual_shocks: COVID-19 pandemic (school closures, economic downturn)
Natural disasters in BMCs (hurricanes, floods)
Political fragility in Haiti (persistent operational constraints)
performance_issues: Underperformance in climate/renewable energy targets (8% vs. 75%)
PPP indicator (1.4) at 0% progress
Gender mainstreaming below target (68% vs. 80%)
learning_insights: Evidence that social protection spending was more effective than anticipated (e.g., Haiti’s GDP% increase)
Climate projects required more BMC capacity-building than planned
strategic_opportunities: CDB’s revised Strategic Plan (2022–2024) allowed alignment of UK priorities with new Bank targets

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: Medium
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: Partially effective (reallocations made but climate/gender gaps persisted)
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Moderate (some adjustments based on pandemic learning, but slow response to climate underperformance)

fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Active conflict in Haiti (persistent fragility); sporadic unrest in other BMCs

major_external_shocks.covid_impact: Significant: school closures (18+ months), economic contraction, increased poverty intensity. Led to social protection expansions and education target revisions.
major_external_shocks.political_transitions: Minor transitions in some BMCs (e.g., elections), but Haiti’s persistent fragility was the dominant factor.
major_external_shocks.economic_shocks: Inflation and supply chain disruptions post-pandemic; currency fluctuations in some BMCs.
major_external_shocks.climate_disasters: Multiple natural disasters (hurricanes, floods) in 2022, diverting resources from planned activities.
major_external_shocks.conflict_escalation: Haiti’s gang violence and political instability hindered operations throughout the period.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: Increased commitment to social protection (e.g., St. Lucia/Dominica GDP% increases), but *reduced focus on climate/PPPs* due to capacity constraints.
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: CDB’s Strategic Plan Update (2022) introduced new targets, requiring alignment adjustments.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: Lower than expected in BMCs for climate projects; CDB’s administrative costs rose post-pandemic (procurement/IT/travel).

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Limited local suppliers for renewable energy projects (e.g., solar PV in Antigua and Barbuda).
market_conditions.cost_inflation_impacts: Post-pandemic cost increases (consultants, equipment) affected operational budgets.
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: Currency volatility in some BMCs (e.g., Haiti) reduced purchasing power.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Moderate (1 substantive change: partner roles/engagement)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Partnership adaptation (expanded BMC roles in social protection) + Governance adaptation (increased FCDO board engagement)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate (multilateral modality appropriate, but underestimated BMC capacity gaps for climate/PPPs)

programme_metadata.programme_title: Special Development Fund 10th Replenishment Programme

output_1.title: Project Outputs - direct impact of SDF10 projects across CDB BMCs

output_2.title: Strategic focus - Bank's alignment with UK priority issues (gender, climate, private sector work) as part of SDF10

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: CDB demonstrated resilience in challenging contexts (COVID-19, natural disasters, Haiti fragility) but faced implementation delays. Educational outcomes declined due to pandemic disruptions, while social protection expenditures increased modestly in some countries (e.g., Saint Lucia, Dominica). Renewable energy progress stalled in 2022 despite early gains.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong buy-in from Borrowing Member Countries (BMCs) and contributors was evident, with development needs identified through close stakeholder engagement. However, coordination challenges persisted in Haiti due to fragility, and some targets (e.g., PPP arrangements, gender mainstreaming) underperformed despite being UK priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Bank-wide administrative costs rose in 2022 due to increased travel, consultant use, and IT procurement post-pandemic. While procurement policies were deemed "good" by DFID, operational cost efficiency declined temporarily.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO used its board position (second-largest shareholder) to push for administrative cost improvements and prioritize UK-aligned issues (gender, climate, private sector). Oversight focused on addressing underperformance in renewable energy and PPP targets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adjusted targets mid-implementation (e.g., revised downward the 4-year classroom/education facility target from 1,822 to 1,634) and reprioritized social protection indicators to align with UK priorities. Flexibility was also shown in responding to crises (e.g., natural disasters, poverty spikes).
adaptive_management_examples: Revised the 4-year target for classrooms/educational facilities from 1,822 to 1,634 due to cumulative underperformance.
Updated Outcome Indicator 2 (social protection expenditure as % of GDP) in Q4 2021 to better align with UK priorities.
Shifted focus to agricultural training and climate-smart practices after land improvement targets lagged.
FCDO board interventions to address renewable energy shortfalls (only 8% of 2022 programming vs. 75% target).

main_implementation_challenges: Pandemic-related disruptions (school closures, absenteeism) leading to declines in educational outcomes (e.g., CSEC pass rates dropped from 31.8% to 22.2% for males).
Fragility in Haiti hindering operations and limiting progress on targets.
Natural disasters in Borrowing Member Countries (BMCs) diverting resources and attention.
Slow progress on renewable energy (0 MW added in 2022) and PPP arrangements (0/5 countries with increased capacity).
Underperformance in gender mainstreaming (68% of projects with gender ratings vs. 80% target).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: School shutdowns and quarantines disrupted education, reducing secondary school graduation rates and exam performance.
Natural disasters: Increased poverty and diverted resources in affected BMCs.
Economic downturns: Declines in Human Development Index rankings across borrowers.
Haiti’s political fragility: Persistent instability limited project implementation.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated administrative costs post-pandemic (travel, consultants, IT).
Limited access to alternative MDB funding for smaller Caribbean nations, increasing reliance on SDF.
Climate vulnerabilities (e.g., hurricanes) requiring unplanned adaptations.
partner_relationship_issues: CDB’s slow progress on UK-prioritized issues (gender, climate, private sector) despite board agreements.
Lack of transparent justification for missed targets (e.g., PPPs, renewable energy) in Bank reporting.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Delayed land improvement projects due to 2021 inaction, requiring accelerated efforts to meet 2024 targets.
Limited capacity in BMCs to implement PPP arrangements (0/5 countries showed progress).
Bank’s operational efficiency challenges (rising administrative costs, procurement delays).
risk_materialization: Pandemic risks: Educational and social protection targets directly impacted by COVID-19.
Political risks: Haiti’s instability materialized as a persistent operational barrier.
Climate risks: Natural disasters disrupted implementation in multiple BMCs.
Financial risks: Administrative cost overruns due to post-pandemic recovery spending.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was on track, but administrative costs rose in 2022 due to post-pandemic recovery activities (travel, consultants, IT). The UK’s £21 million commitment was fully allocated, with expenditures aligned to strategic themes (e.g., Haiti: $45mn, BNTF: $40mn).

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Moderate. Administrative costs increased in 2022 but were manageable through board oversight. Economies of scale remain challenging due to the Bank’s size and regional focus.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Moderate. SDF10 demonstrated resilience in crisis contexts (e.g., doubled CO2 reductions, agricultural training successes) but underperformed on UK priorities (renewable energy, gender). The region-wide footprint of CDB provides broader impact than alternatives.
value_for_money_assessment.overall_vfm: The programme offers a "moderately effective" vehicle for UK funds, with room for improvement in tackling priority issues (climate, gender). Cost efficiency declined temporarily but is expected to recover by 2024.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Good. Procurement policies were previously assessed as robust by DFID, though 2022 saw higher operational costs. Financial reporting aligned with strategic objectives, and FCDO’s board role enabled corrective actions (e.g., cost consolidation discussions).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Below target in 2022 due to increased administrative spending, but long-term efficiency remains achievable if cost controls are reinstated. Renewable energy and climate spending (8% of 2022 programming vs. 75% target) highlighted inefficiencies in priority alignment.

key_delivery_lessons: Crisis resilience is critical: SDF10 adapted to COVID-19 and natural disasters but required flexible target adjustments (e.g., education facilities).
UK priorities need stronger enforcement: Board-level advocacy alone was insufficient to drive progress on gender, climate, and private sector targets.
Local buy-in enhances performance: BMC engagement in social protection expansions (e.g., Saint Lucia, Dominica) demonstrated the value of stakeholder alignment.
Adaptive management works: Revising indicators (e.g., social protection % GDP) and reprioritizing agricultural training improved relevance.
successful_delivery_practices: Community-Based Agriculture and Rural Development projects in Haiti exceeded expectations in training and sustainable practices.
BNTF9 project completions and BNTF10 approvals showed effective targeting of vulnerable communities.
Doubling CO2 reductions against SDF10 targets highlighted strengths in environmental programming.
management_adaptations_made: FCDO used its board position to push for administrative cost improvements and climate/gender prioritization.
Indicators were realigned with UK priorities (e.g., social protection % GDP replaced regional trade metrics).
Target revisions (e.g., classrooms) balanced ambition with realism.
innovations_attempted: Solar PV system installations in Antigua and Barbuda (though delayed, expected to boost renewable energy indicators in 2023).
Expanded social protection mechanisms (cash transfers, food support) in response to poverty spikes.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress: The Bank improved reporting on underperforming indicators (e.g., agriculture) but lacked transparency on PPP and renewable energy shortfalls (Recommendation #3 from AR1).
Risk reporting was enhanced, but ad-hoc event disclosures remained inconsistent.
forward_recommendations: Consolidate the log frame with FCDO and CDB to clarify adjusted indicators and realistic targets (Recommendation #1).
Push for renewable energy/climate funding increases (from 8% to 75% of programming) via board discussions (Recommendation #2).
Improve justification for missed targets (e.g., PPPs, operational efficiency) in annual reports (Recommendation #3).
Promote internal efficiencies, gender balance in management, and climate financing through FCDO’s board role (Recommendation #4).
Reassign or remove underreported indicators (e.g., move 4.3 to Output 3 or eliminate it; add staff engagement metrics to Output 4) (Recommendation #5).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. While some risks (pandemic, natural disasters) were managed through adaptive responses, others (Haiti fragility, renewable energy underperformance) persisted due to limited mitigation strategies. Board oversight helped address administrative costs but had less impact on programmatic risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.education: 63,152 students benefited from upgraded educational facilities in 2022 (below cumulative targets).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.agriculture: Exceeded targets for beneficiaries from improved agricultural practices, land management, and climate-smart training.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.social_protection: Modest increases in social protection spending as % of GDP in Saint Lucia (6.8%), Dominica (7.9%), and St. Vincent and the Grenadines (8%). Haiti’s spending remained stagnant at 0.4% GDP.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.renewable_energy: 2.3 MW cumulative capacity installed (exceeded second-year target due to early progress, but no additions in 2022).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: Medium. Progress was mixed: strong in agriculture, social protection, and CO2 reductions but weak in education, renewable energy (2022 stagnation), and PPPs.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Medium. Quantitative data (e.g., student beneficiaries, hectares improved) was robust, but qualitative evidence on sustainability and policy influence was limited. The Bank’s Results Monitoring Framework provided structured reporting, though some indicators lacked narrative justification.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium. While community-based projects (e.g., BNTF) showed local ownership, systemic challenges (Haiti fragility, climate vulnerabilities) and underperformance in UK priorities (gender, private sector) raise concerns about long-term sustainability.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Limited. Social protection expansions in some BMCs (e.g., Saint Lucia) reflected policy uptake, but broader influence on gender, climate, and private sector reforms was minimal despite UK advocacy.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Mixed. Agricultural training and climate-smart practices exceeded targets, but capacity for PPP arrangements (0/5 countries) and gender mainstreaming (68% vs. 80% target) lagged.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Community-based projects in Haiti achieved unexpected success in training and rural development despite fragility.
Negative: School closures during COVID-19 exacerbated educational inequalities, with CSEC pass rates declining more for males (31.8% to 22.2%) than females (38.7% to 24%).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Moderate. Successful projects (e.g., agricultural training, BNTF) demonstrated potential for replication, but scaling renewable energy and gender initiatives was hindered by limited progress and funding misalignment.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme demonstrates resilience in a challenging context (COVID-19, natural disasters, Haiti fragility) and aligns with UK priorities (SDGs, poverty reduction, climate). While underperformance in key areas (renewable energy, gender) requires attention, the Bank’s adaptive management and FCDO’s board influence provide a pathway for improvement. Closing the programme would risk losing progress in education, agriculture, and social protection.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Moderate. Achieving all objectives by 2025 is uncertain due to persistent challenges (Haiti, climate risks) and slow progress on UK priorities. However, revised targets (e.g., classrooms) and board interventions increase the likelihood of partial success.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable. The CDB’s regional footprint and BMC buy-in support long-term relevance, but administrative cost pressures and underperformance in strategic areas (PPPs, gender) require ongoing oversight.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate. FCDO acknowledges the programme’s crisis resilience and alignment with UK goals but is dissatisfied with the pace of progress on climate, gender, and private sector priorities. Board engagement has been a critical lever for accountability.
planned_adaptations_future: Increase renewable energy and climate change funding to 75% of programming (from 8% in 2022).
Strengthen gender mainstreaming in project approvals (target: 80% of projects).
Improve transparency in reporting on missed targets (e.g., PPPs, operational efficiency).
Consolidate administrative costs through board-led efficiencies.
Reassign or remove underperforming indicators (e.g., 4.3) and add staff engagement metrics to Output 4.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Security and Justice Programme (SJP) (formerly Integrated Programme for Strengthening Security and Justice– Phase 2 (IP-SSJ 2))

output_1.title: Improved police capacity to prevent and respond to S & J problems

output_2.title: Improved capacity of justice mechanisms to respond to GBV
