delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted from a 'Bridging Project' to a 'Launching Project' within existing UNOPS agreement parameters to accelerate SJP implementation. Added People in Need (PIN) as a sub-partner mid-implementation to strengthen GBV social norms work.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNOPS team was small and stretched, leading to parallel operation of partners (PIN, BBC Media Action, International Alert) with limited coordination. Some sub-partners (e.g., BBC MA and Nepal Police Spokesperson’s team) had misaligned expectations on custody management components.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance structures (Implementation Committee, National Steering Committee) not fully functional; key police leadership (IGP, RPDD DIG) not formally engaged despite repeated efforts. Provincial coordination committees exist but lack senior police participation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Limited by governance gaps and lack of senior police buy-in. Cross-programme coherence improved after PIN was integrated into UNOPS framework in October 2023, but coordination challenges persisted due to initial design limitations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Bridging/Launching Project constituted 100% of FY23-24 budget via sole-source agreement with UNOPS. Multi-year phase procurement approach revised mid-implementation to consider UNOPS proposal without competitive bidding, pending FCDO approval.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to governance delays and need for BEK to actively manage partner alignment. BEK took direct role in designing exposure visits (e.g., UK study tours for Nepal Police leadership) to compensate for weak governance structures.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted from bridging to launching phase, reallocated focus to GBV social norms research (via PIN), and accelerated design work for multi-year grants. Budget weightings were not formally adjusted despite misalignment with actual investments (70% to Output 1 vs. logframe’s 30%).
adaptive_management_examples: Repurposed Bridging Project into a Launching Project to align with SJP objectives post-signature of MoU.
Fast-tracked PIN’s inclusion as a sub-partner to address GBV social norms lag and prepare for multi-year direct grant.
Organized two UK exposure visits for Nepal Police leadership (October 2023, March 2024) to build strategic buy-in for reform priorities.
Revised commercial approach for multi-year phase to leverage UNOPS’s existing relationship with Nepal Police, avoiding new procurement.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed programme start (UK approval in late 2021, GoN approval in late 2022) created awkward transition from Bridging to Launching Project.
Governance structures (IC, NSC) remained non-functional due to lack of senior police participation (IGP, RPDD DIG), complicating reform alignment.
Nepal Police leadership prioritized infrastructure investments over systemic reforms (e.g., resistance to adopting PMS framework or inspection/QA systems).
Misalignment between UNOPS sub-partners (e.g., BBC MA and Nepal Police Spokesperson’s team) on custody management and media components.
Limited capacity of UNOPS team to manage expanded scope, leading to parallel partner operations and coordination gaps.
external_factors_impact: Political transitions in Nepal (e.g., new IGP appointed March 2024) required renewed engagement efforts to secure governance participation.
Post-COVID recovery in Nepal affected police bandwidth for reform activities, with some units deprioritizing SJP initiatives.
contextual_constraints_new: Sudurpaschim Province added as a fourth focus area (beyond original three provinces), increasing coordination complexity.
Federalism in Nepal created fragmented accountability for justice mechanisms, requiring additional provincial-level engagement.
partner_relationship_issues: UNOPS’s small team size and pre-existing sub-partner agreements constrained adaptive management during Launching Project.
PIN’s integration was delayed until October 2023, creating initial misalignment with policing components led by UNOPS.
BBC Media Action’s media training components progressed slowly due to limited buy-in from Nepal Police Spokesperson’s office.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Nepal Police’s capacity to absorb systemic reforms (e.g., PMS, QA systems) was overestimated; interest in hardware (e.g., infrastructure) outweighed software (e.g., training, processes).
Local government justice committees lacked institutionalized skills development pathways, requiring foundational work (e.g., PIN’s GIPEA analysis).
UNOPS team lacked bandwidth to manage expanded scope, leading to underperformance in custody management and media components.
risk_materialization: Major risk of weak governance participation materialized, with NSC/IC remaining non-functional and police leadership disengaged from reform priorities.
Risk of misaligned partner efforts materialized in custody management and media components due to lack of shared theory of change.
Risk of delayed social norms work was mitigated by proactive investment in PIN’s research during Launching Project.

budget_execution_vs_plan: 100% of FY23-24 budget (£35m programme value) allocated to UNOPS Bridging/Launching Project, exceeding original bridging scope.
Actual investments disproportionately focused on Output 1 (70% vs. logframe’s 30%), but overall score remained ‘A’ due to strong performance in other areas.
Seed funding for PIN’s GBV social norms work was accelerated, drawing from Launching Project budget to prepare for multi-year grant.
value_for_money_assessment: Moderate VFM due to governance delays and underutilized capacity investments (e.g., PMS framework, QA systems not adopted by Nepal Police).
UNOPS’s leverage of existing MIPP/IPSSJ relationships improved cost efficiency for policing components, but media and custody management components underdelivered.
PIN’s GIPEA analysis provided foundational evidence for GBV work, but VfM pathways for justice committee capacity development remain unclear.
financial_management_quality: BEK demonstrated agile financial management by repurposing Bridging Project funds and accelerating GBV research investments.
Lack of formal budget reweighting created misalignment between actual investments (70% Output 1) and logframe (30% Output 1).
UNOPS’s financial reporting was adequate, but limited transparency on sub-partner (BBC MA, International Alert) expenditures.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of existing UNOPS-MIPP relationships reduced transaction costs for policing components.
Exposure visits for Nepal Police leadership (UK, 2023/24) were cost-effective in building strategic buy-in but had limited immediate reform impact.
Custody management and media components incurred sunk costs due to misalignment between partners.

key_delivery_lessons: Governance engagement must be prioritized early; delayed police participation in NSC/IC created persistent alignment challenges.
Bridging projects should be designed with flexibility to pivot to full implementation, or clear exit strategies should be defined upfront.
Partner selection must account for capacity constraints; UNOPS’s small team size limited adaptive management during Launching Project.
Social norms work requires upfront investment in research/design to avoid lags in multi-year implementation.
successful_delivery_practices: BEK’s agile decision to reframe Bridging Project as Launching Project mitigated start-up delays.
Exposure visits for Nepal Police leadership (UK, 2023/24) built strategic relationships and demonstrated reform priorities.
Integration of PIN into UNOPS framework improved cross-programme coherence for GBV components.
Accelerated investment in PIN’s GIPEA analysis provided evidence base for multi-year GBV prevention work.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from competitive procurement to direct negotiation with UNOPS for multi-year phase to leverage existing relationships.
Reallocated Launching Project funds to prioritize GBV social norms research, addressing a critical gap.
Designed governance engagement strategy (e.g., IGP visits) to compensate for weak formal structures.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of psychosocial counsellors in 8 district police offices (exceeding target of 7), with pre/post-test data showing knowledge gains (avg. 22.61–35%).
Community Scorecard (CSC) process scaled to 657 participants (exceeding target of 580), with gender-disaggregated data collection.
Multi-year proposal design for direct FCDO grants to PIN, testing new funding modalities for GBV prevention.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Two UK visits for Nepal Police leadership conducted (2023/24), but PMS framework adoption and governance participation remain pending.
Not addressed: Activation of police-led task force in governance structures still outstanding despite lobbying efforts.
Addressed: Accelerated social norms work via PIN’s upfront research, mitigating lag identified in 2023 AR.
forward_recommendations: Secure formal police participation in NSC/IC by FY24/25, including IGP and RPDD DIG, with clear terms of reference for oversight.
Develop a phased approach to systemic reforms (e.g., PMS, QA systems) with incentives for Nepal Police, linking hardware support to software progress.
Clarify VfM pathways for justice committee capacity development, building on PIN’s GIPEA analysis.
Conduct a lessons-learned exercise on Bridging/Launching Project to inform future transition phases.
Strengthen partner coordination mechanisms, including shared theory of change for custody management and media components.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive mitigation of social norms lag via PIN’s research, but governance and police engagement risks were only partially addressed.
Risk of misaligned partner efforts was identified but not fully resolved (e.g., BBC MA and Nepal Police Spokesperson’s team).
Contingency planning for political transitions (e.g., new IGP) was effective in maintaining engagement but did not secure formal participation.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 657 community members (371 female, 286 male) participated in CSC sessions (target: 580).
1,882 community members (748 female, 1,134 male) participated in CSC action plan implementation (no target stated).
56 police personnel (38 female, 18 male) trained on gender-responsive investigation (target: 60).
Psychosocial counsellors deployed in 8 district police offices (target: 7).
policy_influence_achieved: Limited policy influence to date; Nepal Police showed interest in UK’s HMICFRS-inspired QA systems but no formal adoption.
MoHA engagement remains procedural; no evidence of systemic policy changes in GBV response or policing accountability.
capacity_building_results: Moderate capacity gains in community-police partnerships (CSC process) and GBV response (psychosocial counselling).
Limited progress in justice committee capacity development; PIN’s GIPEA analysis identified gaps but no institutionalized training pathways yet.
Nepal Police leadership demonstrated increased awareness of reform priorities (via UK visits) but limited operationalization.
unintended_consequences: Positive: CSC process exceeded female participation targets (371 vs. unspecified female target), suggesting strong community demand for gender-inclusive engagement.
Negative: Overemphasis on Output 1 (policing) created imbalances in programme delivery, with justice and governance outputs (Outputs 2–5) under-resourced.
scalability_evidence: CSC process demonstrated scalability across 3 provinces (Madhesh, Lumbini, Karnali) with adaptable gender-disaggregated approaches.
Psychosocial counselling model replicable in additional districts, but sustainability depends on Nepal Police’s long-term funding commitments.
GBV social norms work (via PIN) designed for multi-year scale-up but requires stronger police and justice system linkages.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance in Output 1 (policing) and potential for cross-cutting impact on GBV and governance with adapted delivery model.
Critical mass of relationships built with Nepal Police leadership, though formal governance participation remains pending.
Multi-year proposals from UNOPS and PIN provide a platform for coherent phase-two implementation if governance and VFM challenges are addressed.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model is partially sustainable: UNOPS’s policing components leverage existing MIPP relationships, but governance gaps and partner coordination issues persist.
Long-term sustainability depends on securing Nepal Police’s ownership of systemic reforms (e.g., PMS, QA systems) and MoHA’s commitment to justice committee capacity development.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium
planned_adaptations_future: Transition to multi-year phase with revised commercial approach (direct negotiation with UNOPS) and clear governance terms for police participation.
Rebalance output weightings to align with actual investments and address under-resourcing of justice/GBV components (Outputs 2–5).
Develop incentive structures for Nepal Police to prioritize software reforms (e.g., linking infrastructure support to progress on PMS adoption).
Strengthen monitoring of VfM pathways, particularly for justice committee capacity development and media components.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from direct delivery of specific services (e.g., COVID-19 vaccines) to system-wide support for institutional capacity and crisis preparedness. Removed COVID-19 vaccine policy commitment from IDA20 logframe due to declining demand, replaced with focus on health emergency preparedness. Added three new indicators (1.8, 1.10, 1.11) to monitor cross-cutting crisis preparedness.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IDA (World Bank) performed strongly in fragile/conflict-affected states (FCS/FCV), exceeding expectations in financing approvals (e.g., $11.8B in FY24 vs $20.6B milestone) and capacity-building (33% of FCS countries supported vs 26% milestone). Coordination with national/international stakeholders improved, but operationalization of crisis preparedness remains challenged by government prioritization of ex-post responses over ex-ante investments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-cutting crisis preparedness agenda improved multi-stakeholder coordination, though financial/technical capacity constraints in partner countries slowed operationalization. IDA’s Results Measurement System (RMS) effectively tracked long-term outcomes, but FCDO set additional milestones for FY24 to monitor progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to post-COVID context by repurposing vaccine-focused commitments toward broader health emergency preparedness. Leveraged IDA’s hybrid financial model to increase efficiency (e.g., longer-term debt issuance, adjusted capital buffers) and scale financing ($93B in IDA20 vs $52B in IDA17 with similar donor contributions).
adaptive_management_examples: Reprioritized from COVID-19 vaccines to health emergency preparedness based on declining demand.
Expanded crisis preparedness diagnostics piloted under IDA20, with recommendations to scale to more countries.
Adjusted financial model to release capital held against interest rate risk and private sector operations, enabling greater lending volumes.

main_implementation_challenges: Legacy impacts of COVID-19 on health, nutrition, and education in target countries persisted into IDA20, requiring recovery-focused interventions.
Governments in fragile contexts prioritized ex-post crisis responses over ex-ante preparedness investments, despite IDA’s emphasis on the latter.
Financial and technical capacity constraints in partner countries slowed operationalization of crisis preparedness plans.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic compressed IDA19 cycle into 2 years, accelerating IDA20 start by 1 year (July 2022) to support pandemic response.
Global inflation increased average IDA project supervision costs by ~20% over the past decade (to $246,000/project in FY24).
Rising instability and fragility worldwide heightened demand for IDA support in FCV contexts.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for crisis preparedness diagnostics and tools (e.g., One Health approaches, digital geotagging) to address complex, cross-sectoral risks (e.g., zoonotic diseases, climate-fragility nexus).
Increased debt sustainability challenges in IDA countries required adaptive financing instruments and transparency measures.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited government capacity in FCS/FCV countries to implement digital tools (e.g., geotagged data systems) and institutional reforms, despite IDA support.
Slow operationalization of crisis preparedness plans due to technical/financial gaps at country level.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 recovery delays materialized as ongoing health/nutrition/education deficits in IDA countries.
Fragility and conflict risks intensified in several IDA-eligible countries, increasing demand for FCV-focused interventions.

budget_execution_vs_plan: IDA20’s administrative expenses ratio improved to 66% (vs 70% in FY23 and 74% in FY22), staying well below the 100% benchmark (indicating full coverage of admin costs by revenue).
IDA commitments totalled $36B in FY24 ($12.1B as grants), on track to meet IDA20’s $93B replenishment target.
UK contribution of £1,414M (5.7% of total) reflected a 54% reduction from IDA19 due to ODA budget cuts, but remained the 3rd-largest donor after the US and Japan.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Administrative expenses as % of revenue declined to 66% (from 70% in FY23), indicating improved cost control. Average project supervision costs increased by ~20% in real terms over the past decade ($147K in FY13 to $246K in FY24), but deemed reasonable given global inflation.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: IDA’s leveraging model achieved a 4:1 ratio of lending to donor contributions ($4 lent per $1 donated). Financial innovations (e.g., longer-term debt issuance, adjusted capital buffers) enabled IDA20 to grow to $93B from $52B in IDA17 with similar donor inputs. MOPAN assessed IDA’s hybrid model as strong for scaling concessional funding.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: 28 of 36 milestones met or exceeded expectations. Policy priorities (e.g., climate, FCV) aligned with donor/recipient needs, with horizontal sector coverage allowing country-driven prioritization. Early achievement of several end-replenishment targets (e.g., FCS financing, One Health approaches).

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: IDA’s financial management was rated highly for transparency and risk-adjusted capital allocation. The shift to longer-term fixed-rate debt and right-sized buffers improved lending capacity without compromising sustainability.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Real cost increase of ~2% per annum over a decade for project supervision was judged reasonable. Leveraging model enabled IDA to maintain low administrative overhead (66% ratio) while expanding financing volumes.

key_delivery_lessons: Crisis preparedness requires sustained ex-ante investment and multi-stakeholder coordination; ex-post responses are less effective and more costly.
Digital tools (e.g., geotagged data systems) enhance project implementation in FCV contexts but require tailored capacity-building to overcome adoption barriers.
Flexible financial models (e.g., IDA’s hybrid leveraging) can scale impact but need adaptive risk management to address macroeconomic volatility (e.g., inflation, exchange rates).
successful_delivery_practices: IDA’s Results Measurement System (RMS) effectively tracked long-term outcomes while allowing FCDO to set annual milestones for accountability.
Cross-cutting themes (e.g., climate, FCV, gender) integrated into core financing improved coherence and impact, particularly in fragile states (e.g., 33% of FCS countries supported vs 26% target).
Policy commitments negotiated with recipient countries ensured alignment with national priorities, enhancing ownership and effectiveness.
management_adaptations_made: Repurposed COVID-19 vaccine commitments toward broader health emergency preparedness based on real-time demand assessment.
Increased impact weighting for Output 1 (from 10% to 25%) to reflect consolidated development results.
Piloted crisis preparedness diagnostics in IDA20, with plans to expand based on lessons learned.
innovations_attempted: One Health approaches to address zoonotic disease risks (16 countries supported in FY24 vs 13 milestone).
Digital open-source tools for geotagged data collection in FCV contexts (17 countries in FY24).
Financial innovations (e.g., longer-term debt, adjusted capital buffers) to maximize lending volumes.
previous_recommendations_progress: IDA19’s call for crisis preparedness was addressed in IDA20 through cross-cutting themes and new indicators (1.8, 1.10, 1.11).
Capacity-building in FCV states exceeded targets (e.g., 33% vs 26% for core government functions).
forward_recommendations: Expand use of crisis preparedness diagnostics to more IDA countries, with tailored support for operationalization.
Enhance deployment of the Bank’s new crisis toolkit at the point of crisis, ensuring holistic integration with national systems.
Monitor debt sustainability in IDA countries to mitigate risks to long-term financing impact.
Strengthen equity focus in results measurement, particularly for marginalized groups in FCV contexts.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was effective in anticipating COVID-19 recovery needs and adapting financial instruments (e.g., debt restructuring). However, operational risks in FCV contexts (e.g., capacity gaps) required ongoing adaptive management. The shift from vaccine support to preparedness demonstrated proactive risk response.

policy_influence_achieved: IDA20’s policy priorities (e.g., 35% climate financing, 20% FCV focus) were shaped by UK advocacy and adopted by donor/recipient countries.
Crisis preparedness and debt transparency commitments influenced national policies in FCV states (e.g., 33% of countries strengthened core government functions).
One Health approaches gained traction in 16 countries, supporting pandemic preparedness policies.
capacity_building_results: 17 FCS countries built capacity in digital geotagged data tools for project implementation.
33% of IDA FCS countries strengthened core government functions (vs 26% target), improving public service delivery and resilience.
Large-scale education assessments completed in 28 countries (vs 17-23 target), informing policy reforms.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Cross-cutting crisis preparedness improved coordination across sectors (e.g., health, climate, governance) but was not originally planned.
Negative: Reduced UK contribution (54% cut from IDA19) limited potential scale of interventions in some sectors.
scalability_evidence: IDA’s leveraging model (1:4 donor-to-lending ratio) demonstrates scalability, with $93B in IDA20 vs $52B in IDA17.
Digital tools and crisis diagnostics piloted in IDA20 are being considered for expansion to additional countries.
Policy commitments (e.g., climate, FCV) are replicable in future replenishments, as evidenced by early achievement of targets.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance in FY24 (Overall Output Score: A) with most milestones met or exceeded, particularly in FCV states (A+).
Alignment with UK priorities (e.g., climate, fragility) and demonstrated value for money (4:1 leveraging ratio).
IDA20’s financial innovations and crisis preparedness focus provide a foundation for sustained recovery in target countries.
Ongoing demand for IDA financing in FCV contexts (e.g., $11.8B approved in FY24 vs $20.6B milestone, with pipeline for FY25).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes – IDA’s hybrid financial model (donor contributions + capital markets) is assessed as strong and scalable. The shift to longer-term debt and adjusted buffers improves long-term sustainability. However, monitoring of debt sustainability in recipient countries is needed.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High – IDA20’s performance, alignment with UK objectives, and efficiency were highlighted as key strengths. The UK’s role as the 3rd-largest donor reflects continued satisfaction despite budget reductions.
planned_adaptations_future: Scale crisis preparedness diagnostics and tools to more countries, with tailored support for operationalization.
Enhance equity focus in results measurement, particularly for marginalized groups in FCV contexts.
Monitor and address debt sustainability risks in IDA countries to ensure long-term financing impact.
Expand use of digital tools (e.g., geotagged data) and institutional capacity-building in fragile states.

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK-South Africa Demographic Dividend Partnership Programme

output_1.title: Enhanced and robust generation and use of disaggregated demographic and socio-economic data to tackle drivers of the Demographic Dividend in South Africa

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Slower-than-expected mobilisation of suppliers and staff recruitment (4–6 months vs. planned 2 months) led to delays in Outcomes 1 and 2, though Outcome 3 progressed well. Adaptive management included re-framing towards greater focus on women’s rights and gender equality.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Mixed performance: one implementing partner caused dissatisfaction due to poor communication on recruitment delays (addressed in October 2022 meeting). Another partner exceeded targets under Outcome 3 (GBVF response), reaching 17,453 beneficiaries vs. 17,000 target.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: BHC Pretoria’s oversight was reactive rather than proactive; communication with two implementing partners was irregular, delaying identification of implementation issues. Structured meetings were recommended for future monitoring.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Limited coordination between programme components initially; recommendations included strengthening linkages to maximise impact. Regional coordination (e.g., shared concept notes across five countries) achieved economies of scale.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive processes used for service providers, ensuring technical and financial value. Consultant fees were negotiated down, and pro bono private-sector support maintained lean staffing for the GBVF Fund.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Lower than planned due to irregular communication; BHC team committed to more frequent, structured interactions post-review. Financial oversight was partially effective (one qualified audit opinion due to missing donor pledges).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by re-focusing on women’s rights and gender equality in response to rising GBV levels. Flexibility in regional delivery (e.g., adapting concept notes across countries) improved efficiency.
adaptive_management_examples: Re-framing programme towards women’s rights and gender equality due to increased GBV levels.
Combined stakeholder meetings to avoid duplication and drive efficiencies.
Single contract for DD assessments and policy briefs to leverage synergies.
Pilot projects in Eswatini and South Africa for economic justice/resilience (Output 3).

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in partner recruitment (4–6 months longer than planned) hindered progress on Outcomes 1 and 2.
Irregular communication between BHC and two implementing partners led to late detection of delays.
Limited progress on Outcome 2 (UK-SA gender equality collaborations) due to slow partner onboarding.
Qualified audit opinion for one partner due to missing formal donor pledges (R184,200/£90,000).
external_factors_impact: Increased levels of GBV and femicide in South Africa over the past two years, prompting a shift in programme focus.
COVID-19 not explicitly mentioned, but delays may reflect broader pandemic-related disruptions.
contextual_constraints_new: Underrepresentation of marginalised groups (e.g., LGBTQIA+, women with disabilities) in CBO support, identified as a gap for future funding rounds.
Need for stronger integration of disaggregated data for vulnerable groups in local planning.
partner_relationship_issues: Poor communication from one implementing partner on recruitment delays, resolved after October 2022 meeting.
Varied performance: strong delivery on Outcome 3 (GBVF) but slower progress on Outcomes 1 and 2.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Job profiling for public servant training (Output 1) was incomplete at review time.
Limited capacity among some municipalities to fully incorporate DD indicators into IDPs (only 10% achieved vs. target).
risk_materialization: Delivery delays (major risk) materialized due to recruitment issues, mitigated via closer monitoring.
Reputational risk (low likelihood, high impact) from potential fund misappropriation; mitigated via due diligence and pressing for outstanding financial statements.
Operational risk (moderate) of spend delays, addressed through pipeline planning.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Slower-than-planned disbursement due to implementation delays; June tranche rescheduled to December 2022. Partners expected to spend 2022 forecasts in full by year-end.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Good VFM achieved through: (1) competitive procurement, (2) economies of scale (e.g., shared contracts across five countries), (3) pro bono private-sector support, and (4) leveraging existing partnerships. Cost savings realized via combined stakeholder meetings and negotiated consultant fees.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Mixed: one partner submitted a qualified audit opinion due to missing donor pledges. BHC team lacked timely access to Annual Financial Statements for all partners, requiring follow-up in January 2023.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High efficiency in regional delivery (e.g., adapting concept notes across countries) and use of existing capacities. Staff costs minimized via co-funding synergies.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: pro bono support from private sector enabled lean staffing, but one cash receipt (£90,000) lacked a formal donor pledge, triggering audit qualification.

key_delivery_lessons: Regular, structured communication with partners is critical to detect delays early.
Flexibility in programme focus (e.g., shifting towards GBV response) can enhance relevance and impact.
Leveraging existing partnerships and regional synergies improves efficiency and cost-effectiveness.
successful_delivery_practices: Development of DD dashboards and checklists led to tangible uptake by municipalities (e.g., KZN, Eastern Cape).
Combined stakeholder meetings and shared contracts reduced duplication and costs.
Pilot projects for economic justice/resilience (Output 3) demonstrated quick wins in beneficiary reach (17,453 vs. 17,000 target).
management_adaptations_made: BHC committed to more frequent partner meetings to track mitigating actions.
Programme re-framed to prioritize women’s rights and gender equality in response to rising GBV.
Formal pledges now required for all GBVF Fund donations to prevent audit issues.
innovations_attempted: DD Indaba (Nov 2022) to validate dashboard methodology and training tools.
Use of regional media to raise awareness among GBV survivors about available support.
Single-contract approach for DD assessments and policy briefs to capture synergies.
forward_recommendations: Adjust Annual Review timing to align with partner reporting (end-December).
Strengthen linkages between programme components to maximize impact.
Improve visibility of programme work in South Africa, including government engagement.
Ensure future GBVF donations have formal pledges before fund deposits.
Prioritize inclusion of marginalised groups (e.g., LGBTQIA+, women with disabilities) in next funding round.
Set up regular meetings with underperforming partners to track corrective actions.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: while risks were identified (e.g., delivery delays, reputational risks), mitigation was reactive (e.g., closer monitoring only after delays occurred). Audit qualification highlighted gaps in financial controls.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.disaggregation: Data disaggregated by age/sex, but limited reach to marginalised groups (e.g., LGBTQIA+, women with disabilities).

policy_influence_achieved: DD indicators incorporated into Integrated Development Plans (IDPs) of KZN and Eastern Cape municipalities.
National DD Indaba (Nov 2022) validated dashboard methodology for national rollout.
Support to South Africa’s National Strategic Plan on GBVF (Pillars 2 and 3).
capacity_building_results: Capacity-building for 7 countries via National Transfer Accounts Training (Oct 2022).
Training tools for public servants developed (pending DD Indaba approval).
Job profiling initiated to identify officials for DD training.
unintended_consequences: Positive: DD dashboards sparked unplanned revisions to municipal IDPs in KZN/Eastern Cape.
Negative: Limited reach to marginalised groups in GBVF CBO support; underrepresentation in data disaggregation.
scalability_evidence: Dashboard methodology validated for national rollout across all South African municipalities.
Regional concept notes adapted for five countries, demonstrating replicability.
Pilot projects in Eswatini/South Africa (Output 3) provide models for economic justice interventions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme has established a strong foundation despite early delays, with notable progress on Outcome 3 (GBVF) and policy influence (e.g., DD indicators in municipal plans). Adaptive management (e.g., re-focus on women’s rights) aligns with evolving context.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Current model is efficient but requires stronger partner coordination and financial controls (e.g., formal donor pledges). Regional synergies improve scalability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium: BHC Pretoria acknowledged delays but recognized strong performance in GBVF response and policy uptake. Dissatisfaction with partner communication was addressed constructively.
planned_adaptations_future: Greater focus on women’s rights and gender equality in Theory of Change.
Enhanced visibility of programme work in South Africa, including government engagement.
Structured partner meetings to monitor underperforming activities.
Inclusion of marginalised groups in future GBVF funding rounds.
Alignment of Annual Review timing with partner reporting cycles.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Nepal in Business (NIB) Programme

output_1.title: Approval from the Government of Nepal

output_2.title: Procurement

output_3.title: Design

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted from direct FCDO delivery to a blended model using: 1) Commercial contracts for BSF/BERF (ITT released Feb 2024), 2) Technical assistance via Centres of Expertise (CoE) for SMEFF design, 3) Partnership with CASA for pilot interventions. Original business case envisioned faster procurement timelines (contracts now expected June 2024 vs planned Q1 2024).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Boston Consulting Group (BCG) delivered SMEFF design on schedule with high-quality outputs (e.g., DFI fund manager recommendation). CASA CoE demonstrated flexibility in adapting their market systems approach to NIB’s pilot requirements. Government of Nepal (GoN) engagement exceeded expectations with MoU signed Feb 2024 and joint public launch.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Insourced G7 Private Sector Development Advisor (CBS) hired Oct 2023 to bridge capacity gaps. BEK’s BIP Department provided £500K via CoE for design activities. Steering oversight from BII and BEK investment teams added during implementation. Original plan underestimated need for local contextual expertise (mitigated by hiring Nepali consultant for BCG team).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between BEK, BII, and CoE teams, though initial delays in ITT release (Feb 2024 vs planned Dec 2023) due to alignment challenges between FCDO procurement rules and Nepali market realities. BERF component yet to test inter-governmental coordination (federal/provincial/municipal).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: ITT for BSF/BERF released 28 Feb 2024 with bid moderation completed April 2024. Contract award delayed to June 2024 due to complex evaluation of blended finance proposals. SMEFF fund manager selection pending (IFC and FMO shortlisted). Procurement timelines extended by 3–6 months vs business case.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to: 1) BEK’s direct involvement in SMEFF design via BII advisory role, 2) Additional due diligence on DFI partners, 3) Monthly progress reviews with BCG/CASA. Original business case assumed lighter-touch oversight during design phase.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme utilized flexibility to: 1) Reallocate £500K from CoE for SMEFF design and CASA pilot, 2) Expand CASA’s scope beyond dairy/vegetables to high-growth sectors (meat processing, fish feed), 3) Adjust BSF pilot indicators to include enterprise growth metrics (sales, processing utilization).
adaptive_management_examples: Added local consultant to BCG team to navigate Nepali SME finance ecosystem after identifying knowledge gaps in international team.
CASA pilot adapted to focus on high-growth firms (vs value chains) and added sustainability indicators (wastage reduction, market share).
SMEFF design incorporated blended instruments (debt/equity/guarantees) based on BCG’s market assessment showing collateral gaps.
Policy reform advocacy added to BERF scope after identifying provisioning rates as barrier to agriculture SME lending.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed procurement timelines (ITT released 2 months late; contract awards pushed to Q2 2024).
Complexity of designing blended finance instruments for Nepali market (required 6+ months of BCG analysis).
Limited BEK internal capacity for programme oversight (mitigated by insourced advisor).
High provisioning requirements for non-collateralized loans (500x higher than India) creating disincentives for banks to lend to SMEs.
Difficulty sourcing domestic technical experts for niche SME capacity-building (e.g., medicinal plant processing).
external_factors_impact: Post-COVID economic slowdown in Nepal reduced private sector appetite for risk (affected SMEFF leverage targets).
Ukraine war’s global inflationary pressures increased input costs for Nepali SMEs (e.g., fuel, fertilizers).
Political transition risks from Nepal’s federalism implementation created uncertainty in business climate (e.g., overlapping provincial/municipal regulations).
Media scrutiny of UK-Nepal aid programmes required additional safeguarding due diligence.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated depth of collateral gaps in agriculture sector (banks require 500x higher provisioning than India).
Permeability of political-business elite networks requiring deeper political economy analysis to avoid capture.
Limited local capacity for ESG compliance in SMEs (e.g., child labor risks in supply chains).
Currency volatility (NPR depreciation) increasing costs of imported inputs for SMEs.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between FCDO procurement timelines and Nepali private sector’s decision-making speeds.
Challenges in negotiating fund manager terms with DFIs (IFC/FMO) due to differing risk appetites for Nepali SMEs.
CASA’s existing partnerships required renegotiation to focus on high-growth firms vs. value chains.
capacity_constraints_emerged: BEK lacked in-house blended finance expertise (addressed via BII advisory support).
Shortage of Nepali consultants with experience in both financial structuring and SME technical assistance.
Limited government capacity at provincial level to engage in BERF policy dialogues (requires targeted TA).
MELF team not yet operational (delaying baseline data collection).
risk_materialization: Macroeconomic instability (Likely/Major): Slower-than-projected growth due to COVID/Ukraine war impacts.
Federalism challenges (Likely/Major): Confusion over subnational roles delayed sector prioritization.
Safeguarding risks (Possible/Severe): Required enhanced due diligence on SME partners for ESG compliance.
Low government buy-in (Possible/Major): Mitigated via high-level MoU and joint launch, but subnational engagement remains weak.
Anti-competitive practices (Likely/Major): Cartels in agriculture sectors (e.g., dairy) limiting SME market access.

budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_explanation: Only insourced advisor costs (£20K) incurred. Design activities funded via £500K CoE voucher (not counted against NIB budget). Remaining £35.7M unspent as implementation begins FY 2024/25.

planned_indicators: Cost of consultants vs. market benchmarks
Unit cost of BDS per SME (to be benchmarked)
economy.issues_identified: Baseline data not yet available; CoE-funded design activities complicate cost tracking.

planned_indicators: Cost per job created in SMEs
Private finance leveraged per £ of FCDO grant
efficiency.issues_identified: Leverage targets at risk due to high provisioning requirements for SME lending.

effectiveness.issues_identified: TOC assumptions on job creation may need revision based on pilot data.

equity.issues_identified: Gender lens investing not yet operationalized in SMEFF design.

strengths: Transparent budget reallocations (e.g., CoE voucher utilization).
Strong BEK oversight of design phase expenditures.
Early engagement of BII for SMEFF financial structuring.
weaknesses: Delayed financial systems setup (MELF not operational).
No audited statements or narrative reports produced in Year 1.
Limited cost benchmarking data for Nepali market.

co_funding_materialization.planned: SMEFF designed to leverage 1:3 private capital (DFIs/local banks).
co_funding_materialization.actual: IFC and FMO expressed interest but no commitments yet. BII advisory support secured (non-financial).
co_funding_materialization.risks: High provisioning requirements may limit commercial bank participation.

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: NPR depreciation against GBP increased costs of imported technical assistance (e.g., BCG fees). Mitigated by using CoE voucher (GBP-denominated).

key_delivery_lessons: Local contextual expertise is critical for blended finance design (e.g., Nepali consultant enabled BCG’s market navigation).
Pilot phases should precede large-scale procurement to test assumptions (CASA pilot informed BSF design).
DFI partnerships require early alignment on risk-sharing models (SMEFF design took 6+ months).
Government buy-in at subnational level needs dedicated resources (current BERF scope may be insufficient).
successful_delivery_practices: Using CoE vouchers for design phase reduced upfront NIB budget drawdown.
Joint BEK-GoN public launch enhanced programme visibility and political ownership.
BCG’s multi-instrument approach (debt/equity/guarantees) addresses collateral gaps.
CASA’s focus on high-growth firms (vs. value chains) showed early traction in sales growth.
management_adaptations_made: Added BII advisory role to SMEFF governance structure.
Expanded MELF scope to include political economy analysis of sector cartels.
Increased oversight of DFI due diligence to mitigate safeguarding risks.
Revised BSF pilot indicators to track enterprise sustainability (e.g., wastage reduction).
innovations_attempted: Blended finance structure for SMEFF combining grant, debt, and guarantees.
Sector-agnostic BSF pilot (vs. traditional value chain approaches).
Integration of ESG standards into SME investment readiness criteria.
Use of RENT research collaboration to test adaptive management hypotheses.
forward_recommendations: Finalize MELF and baseline data collection in Q1 2024/25 to enable adaptive management.
Conduct political economy analysis of target sectors to mitigate elite capture risks.
Negotiate flexible provisioning requirements with Nepal Rastra Bank to improve SME lending.
Scale successful CASA pilot interventions (e.g., meat processing) via BSF in Year 2.
Develop gender-responsive financing products within SMEFF (e.g., collateral substitutes for women-led SMEs).
Strengthen subnational government engagement through dedicated BERF TA.

strengths: Proactive scenario analysis for macroeconomic risks (BEK-led).
Enhanced due diligence for safeguarding/ESG risks in SME selection.
BII’s involvement added financial structuring expertise.
gaps: Limited contingency planning for currency volatility impacts.
No formal risk register finalized (planned for inception phase).
Underestimation of federalism-related coordination risks.

direct.details: CASA pilot supported 4 SMEs in meat processing, fish feed, flour-based food, and medicinal plants.

evidence: GoN MoU signed (Feb 2024) demonstrates high-level buy-in.
BERF component designed to advocate for SME provisioning reforms (not yet implemented).
policy_influence_achieved.gaps: No policy changes achieved in Year 1; subnational engagement remains limited.

SMEs: CASA pilot SMEs reported 10–30% sales growth (e.g., meat processor expanded market share).
SMEs demonstrated improved ESG compliance (e.g., waste reduction in flour-based food producer).
institutions: BCG’s SMEFF design built capacity of BII/Nepal investment teams on blended finance.
BEK’s insourced advisor enhanced internal knowledge of private sector instruments.
capacity_building_results.gaps: No systematic capacity assessments conducted; MELF not yet operational.

positive: Media coverage of UK-GoN launch raised profile of SME support programmes in Nepal.
CASA pilot’s sector-agnostic approach attracted non-traditional SMEs (e.g., medicinal plants).
negative: Risk of elite capture in SME selection (mitigated via ESG due diligence).
Delayed procurement may have discouraged some potential SME applicants.

promising_practices: SMEFF’s DFI-led model replicable in other LDCs (e.g., Bangladesh, Rwanda).
BSF’s sector-agnostic BDS approach adaptable to other South Asian markets.
CASA’s enterprise growth indicators (sales, processing utilization) can standardize impact measurement.
constraints: Nepal-specific collateral challenges may limit scalability of financial products.
High transaction costs for small-scale blended finance in LDCs.

continuation_rationale: Achieved all Year 1 milestones (GoN approval, procurement, design).
Strong alignment with UK White Paper and GoN’s LDC graduation priorities.
Early evidence from CASA pilot demonstrates SME growth potential.
Blended finance structure (SMEFF) addresses critical market failure in SME access to finance.

strengths: DFI-led SMEFF model reduces long-term FCDO management burden.
BERF’s policy focus complements BSF’s firm-level interventions.
Flexible CoE funding mechanism enables adaptive design.
risks: Over-reliance on DFI partners for SMEFF mobilization.
Limited BEK capacity for oversight of three parallel facilities (BSF/BERF/SMEFF).
Subnational coordination challenges may persist.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize MELF and risk register in Q1 2024/25.
Launch BERF policy dialogues on SME provisioning reforms.
Scale CASA pilot successes via BSF in Year 2.
Negotiate SMEFF co-financing agreements with IFC/FMO.
Enhance gender and inclusion targets in SME selection criteria.
Develop exit strategy for low-performing partnerships (per MELF reviews).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Research for Health in Humanitarian Crises (R2HC) programme

output_1.title: Priority research needs identified in response to demand from humanitarian health practitioners and policy makers

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended from March 2025 to March 2026 with reduced budget (£14.5m → £13m). Added direct award mechanism for rapid research response (e.g., Mpox outbreak in DRC).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Elrha/R2HC exceeded expectations in commissioned reviews (5 completed vs. 3 planned) and stakeholder events (4 held vs. 5 planned). Grantees received strong support (100% developed stakeholder engagement strategies).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Steering Committees with technical experts/donors used for thematic reviews. Core Expert Group consulted for SRHR priorities. Governance aligned with FCDO’s ‘Shift the Power’ agenda.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Enhanced collaboration with Humanitarian Innovation Fund (HIF) for joint scoping papers (e.g., WASH/climate adaptations). Regional consultations involved >300 practitioners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Supplementary funding calls for existing grantees (£35k awarded in Dec 2023 for Afghanistan/Yemen/Bangladesh). New Accountable Grant Agreement (£999,949) signed with Johns Hopkins University in July 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: High oversight during grant extensions and closures. Monthly progress tracking for 24 grants extended beyond March 2025 (75% to close by Sept 2025).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: AGA extension enabled grant extensions to maximize impact. Adaptive funding for unforeseen crises (e.g., Mpox response). Supplementary grants for uptake activities.
adaptive_management_examples: Direct award mechanism for rapid Mpox research in Eastern DRC.
Extension of 24 grants to complete research/uptake in worsening crises.
Revised results framework to emphasize uptake over research production (post-2023 evaluation).

main_implementation_challenges: ODA budget uncertainties (2020–2021) caused delays and required AGA extension/rebudgeting.
Complexity of delivering research in active humanitarian crises (e.g., Afghanistan, Yemen, Cox’s Bazar).
Balancing rapid response needs with rigorous research standards.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted fieldwork and stakeholder engagements (mitigated via virtual events).
Political transitions (e.g., UK election July 2024) required alignment with new FCDO priorities (e.g., climate change, women/girls empowerment).
Currency fluctuations affected grant values in LMICs (not quantified).
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging climate-health crises required unplanned scoping (e.g., climate adaptations for WASH).
Increased demand for SRHR research in conflict settings (e.g., Eastern DRC).
Need for social/behavioral science integration in outbreak responses (e.g., Mpox).
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in co-funding commitments from potential donors (no new core funding secured beyond FCDO).
Capacity constraints among LMIC researchers required additional mentorship (addressed via peer-learning webinars).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited LMIC-led research capacity in climate-health and SRHR themes.
Grantees in protracted crises (e.g., Yemen) needed supplementary funding for completion.
risk_materialization: Budgetary risks materialized (e.g., £1.5m reduction from £14.5m to £13m).
Underspend risk identified; mitigation via revised forecasting and grant extensions.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: 92% execution (£13m spent vs. £14.5m planned). £500k reallocated for direct awards. Supplementary grants (£35k) addressed unforeseen needs.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM confirmed by 2023 Impact Evaluation: "good rate of achievement of different types of impact" from grants. Cost per publication (~£62k/publication) and citation metrics (225 cumulative) demonstrate efficiency.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong: 100% grantees developed stakeholder engagement strategies. Transparent reallocations (e.g., £999,949 to Johns Hopkins for climate/SRHR research).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded targets: 29 publications/year (vs. 20 planned); 19 new grey literature products (vs. 10 planned).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: NIHR/DHSC and Wellcome Trust continued as co-funders, but no new commitments secured beyond FCDO.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not quantified, but noted as a challenge for LMIC grantees.

key_delivery_lessons: Thematic prioritization (e.g., climate, SRHR) enhances funder engagement but requires sustained socialization.
Direct awards enable rapid response but need clear criteria to balance speed/rigor.
LMIC researcher capacity-building must be embedded in grant design.
successful_delivery_practices: Peer-learning webinars (9 held for Call 9 grantees) improved research quality.
Regional consultations (e.g., 300+ WASH practitioners) strengthened evidence uptake.
Stakeholder engagement strategies (100% compliance) boosted policy influence.
management_adaptations_made: Results framework revised to emphasize uptake (post-2023 evaluation).
Supplementary funding rounds introduced for crisis-affected grantees.
Extended grant timelines to align with FCDO’s AGA extension.
innovations_attempted: Direct award mechanism for unanticipated crises (e.g., Mpox).
Joint scoping with HIF (e.g., climate-adapted WASH).
Uptake/impact small grants to bridge research-policy gaps.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: Socialization of Food Security research (Global Health Practitioner Conference Oct 2024).
Ongoing: Regional partnerships for SRHR/NCDs (consultations underway).
Pending: Securing new core funding (no commitments yet).
forward_recommendations: Develop external engagement plan for research uptake by March 2025.
Synthesize impact case studies for non-specialist audiences by June 2025.
Update strategic engagement plan to secure post-FCDO funding by March 2025.
Agree evidence requirements for outcome/impact indicators with FCDO by March 2025.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive: Identified underspend risk early; mitigated via grant extensions and revised forecasting. Direct awards addressed emerging crises (e.g., Mpox).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: 100+ studies funded since 2013; 2023 evaluation confirmed uptake across LMIC/global stakeholders. Specific beneficiary numbers not quantified.
policy_influence_achieved: SRHR evidence note influenced FCDO programming.
Climate-health scoping papers informed humanitarian WASH adaptations.
NCD research priorities adopted by global health practitioners.
capacity_building_results: 13/13 grantees developed stakeholder engagement strategies.
Peer-learning webinars built LMIC researcher skills (e.g., research communications).
Regional consultations (e.g., SRHR) strengthened local ownership.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Direct awards created precedent for rapid FCDO-R2HC collaboration.
Negative: Budget reductions delayed some thematic calls (e.g., SRHR).
scalability_evidence: Joint HIF-R2HC approaches (e.g., climate-WASH) demonstrate scalability.
Thematic reviews (e.g., food security) attracted interest from other funders.

continuation_rationale: Fills unique niche in humanitarian health research funding (2023 evaluation).
Aligns with new UK government’s priorities (climate, women/girls, LMIC leadership).
Direct award mechanism proves value for rapid response (e.g., Mpox).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (dependent on securing post-FCDO funding; Elrha’s engagement ongoing).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (scored A in 2024; "meets important need" per evaluation).
planned_adaptations_future: Shift focus from research production to uptake/synthesis (2025).
Explore regional partnerships for SRHR/NCD thematic calls.
Integrate climate-health as cross-cutting priority.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme experienced a delayed start due to administrative and legal processes but successfully established foundational elements (staffing, data systems, inter-ministerial agreements). Shifted to a more collaborative, 'whole-of-government' approach to replace traditional siloed methods.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong performance in meeting/exceeding targets (e.g., PIOJ completed CRAT surveys, baseline assessments, and DELTA/GIS database workshops; MOESYI conducted data infrastructure assessments). Six coordination meetings were held (exceeding the target of three), indicating active engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance structure strengthened with the recruitment of key roles (Programme Manager, Finance Coordinator, GIS Expert) and establishment of Strategic Oversight and Operations Committees. Quarterly meeting schedules formalized to ensure ongoing coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-agency collaboration improved significantly, with six partner meetings convened (vs. target of three) and three Strategic Oversight Committee meetings. However, full integration of service delivery remains a work in progress, requiring standardized business processes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Achieved cost savings through strategic procurement (e.g., custom Case Management System developed for £60,000 vs. £500,000 for proprietary solutions; negotiated fixed-rate psychosocial service agreements at £40/session vs. market rate of £53). Flexible contracts (e.g., with BRAC) reduced retendering needs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensified with regular progress reporting (narrative and financial reports submitted on time) and establishment of formal committees (Strategic Oversight, Operations). Quarterly schedules implemented for sustained monitoring.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to delays by prioritizing foundational elements (e.g., data systems, staffing) and leveraging flexible contracts (e.g., PIOJ’s agreement with BRAC) to accommodate evolving research needs without retendering.
adaptive_management_examples: Shifted from proprietary to custom-built Case Management System (CMS) to achieve 88% cost savings while meeting functional requirements.
Adopted blended training models to exceed teacher training targets and reduce costs.
Used Ministry-owned venues for training to cut logistical expenses.
Flexible contract with BRAC allowed for continuity in research without retendering.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed start due to administrative and legal processes.
Need for stronger integration of cross-agency service delivery beyond individual collaborations.
Limited parental engagement in interventions, despite its critical role in reducing violence risk factors.
Legislative restrictions on data sharing across government agencies, hindering integrated service delivery.
external_factors_impact: High baseline violence levels in Jamaica (homicide rate of 40.1/100,000 in 2024, 3rd highest globally), exacerbating the urgency for effective interventions.
Socio-cultural norms contributing to persistent gender-based violence, particularly in low-income communities.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated complexity in aligning data-sharing practices with legal frameworks (e.g., statutory data protection requirements).
Capacity gaps in government agencies to fully utilize new data systems (e.g., DELTA/GIS) for evidence-based decision-making.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial siloed approaches among Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs) required concerted effort to transition to collaborative working models.
Varied levels of technical capacity among partners to implement data-driven interventions (e.g., MOESYI required additional laptops and training for data management).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Need for additional research personnel (e.g., PIOJ’s recruitment of Research Officer and Specialist to bolster data architecture).
Limited institutional capacity to sustain long-term data management and cross-agency coordination without continued support.
risk_materialization: Administrative delays in programme launch (mitigated by focusing on foundational elements).
Potential for fragmented service delivery due to insufficiently standardized business processes (partially addressed through governance strengthening).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track, with all financial reports submitted by deadlines. Cost savings achieved in multiple areas (e.g., CMS development, training logistics, psychosocial service agreements).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. Cost efficiencies realized through strategic procurement (e.g., 88% savings on CMS), negotiated service rates (£40 vs. £53 for psychosocial sessions), and use of existing resources (e.g., Ministry-owned training venues). Blended training models improved reach and reduced per-unit costs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Recruitment of dedicated Finance Coordinator improved oversight, reporting quality, and coordination. Financial progress reports met FCDO standards and deadlines.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Custom CMS solution cost £60,000 vs. £500,000 for proprietary alternatives (88% savings).
Psychosocial services secured at £40/session vs. market rate of £53 (25% savings).
Training conducted in Ministry-owned venues reduced logistical costs.
Bulk procurement of mathematics manipulatives from local supplier ensured timely delivery and cost control.

key_delivery_lessons: Cross-agency collaboration on individual initiatives is insufficient for true integrated service delivery; standardized business processes and governance frameworks are essential.
Data-sharing legislation can impede integration; proactive reviews of legal frameworks are needed to balance compliance with operational needs.
Parental engagement is critical but often overlooked; targeted strategies are required to involve parents in violence prevention interventions.
successful_delivery_practices: Recruitment of dedicated programme staff (e.g., Programme Manager, Finance Coordinator) significantly improved coordination and financial management.
Flexible contracts (e.g., with BRAC) enabled adaptive research procurement without retendering delays.
Blended training models increased teacher participation and reduced costs.
Case Management System (CMS) customization achieved substantial cost savings while meeting functional needs.
management_adaptations_made: Established quarterly meetings for Strategic Oversight and Operations Committees to formalize governance.
Prioritized foundational elements (data systems, staffing) during delayed start to ensure long-term programme viability.
Adopted a 'whole-of-government' approach to replace siloed methods, improving coordination across MDAs.
innovations_attempted: Development of a cross-government Social Intervention Information System (SIIS) prototype to enable case tracking and coordination.
Custom-built DELTA/GIS database to centralize community data for evidence-based policymaking.
Pilot of case conferences as structured knowledge-sharing platforms for frontline personnel.
forward_recommendations: Strengthen governance arrangements by documenting standardized business processes to drive integrated service delivery.
Implement formal case conferences grounded in the SIIS to enhance cross-sector collaboration and long-term tracking of at-risk youth.
Review and revise data-sharing legal frameworks to facilitate cross-government data access while ensuring compliance.
Expand parental engagement strategies to address gaps in current interventions.
Explore integration of community data into existing national repositories to better support policymaking.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Administrative delays were mitigated by focusing on foundational elements, but risks related to data-sharing legislation and service delivery fragmentation persist. Proactive adaptations (e.g., flexible contracts, cost-saving measures) demonstrated responsiveness.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Interventions commenced in 16 low-performing schools targeting vulnerable youth.
Baseline surveys completed in 2 Zones of Special Operations (ZOSO) communities (Norwood, Mount Salem).
Psychosocial support systems improved for students experiencing trauma, with educators trained to recognize mental distress.
policy_influence_achieved: Baseline data from ZOSO communities will inform Jamaica’s Citizen Security Plan and National Development Plan (Vision 2030).
DELTA/GIS database and SIIS prototype provide tools for evidence-based violence prevention strategies.
capacity_building_results: PIOJ’s research capacity strengthened with recruitment of Research Officer and Specialist.
MOESYI’s data management capabilities improved through infrastructure assessments and provision of laptops.
Training of educators in behavioural change tools and trauma awareness.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Custom CMS development created a replicable model for other government programmes.
Negative: Limited parental engagement may reduce long-term effectiveness of school-based interventions.
scalability_evidence: DELTA/GIS database and SIIS prototype designed for cross-government use, suggesting potential for national scalability.
Blended training models and cost-efficient procurement practices (e.g., bulk manipulatives) are transferable to other contexts.

continuation_rationale: Strong progress in foundational elements (data systems, governance, staffing) despite delayed start.
Demonstrated cost efficiencies and value for money (e.g., 88% savings on CMS, exceeded training targets).
Critical alignment with Government of Jamaica’s Citizen Security Plan and potential to inform national policymaking.
High risk of violence in Jamaica (3rd highest homicide rate globally) underscores the programme’s relevance.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
planned_adaptations_future: Formalize cross-ministerial governance frameworks to deepen service delivery integration.
Expand use of SIIS for long-term tracking of at-risk youth and case coordination.
Strengthen parental engagement components in school-based interventions.
Review data-sharing legislation to enable seamless cross-government collaboration.
Scale successful pilot initiatives (e.g., DELTA/GIS database, case conferences) to additional communities.

programme_metadata.programme_status: Active (emergency response delivered; multi-year programme in establishment phase)

output_1.title: Provision of emergency humanitarian assistance to vulnerable individuals

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted to integrated, multi-partner response (UNICEF, WFP, IOM, BRCiS, WHO, UNFPA, SCI) with emphasis on: 1) Joint organisational initiatives for packaged assistance; 2) Prioritisation of marginalised groups (women, children, disabled, clans in non-government areas); 3) Area-based coordination via Camp Coordination/Camp Management (CCCM) clusters. Crisis modifiers and early warning systems adopted from SHARP programme predecessor.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners generally met/exceeded targets (e.g., BRCiS at 99% for cash assistance, WHO at 110% for healthcare). Independent Review noted FCDO’s "programme power" effectively managed partner performance, though some underachievement occurred (e.g., WFP at 85% for food assistance due to currency fluctuations). Partners appreciated FCDO’s push on vulnerability prioritisation but required support to refine analysis of overlapping inequalities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO maintained a "strong team" for oversight, per Independent Review, with adaptive management to address famine risk. Governance included strategic donor partnerships (USAID, World Bank, Qatar, KSRelief) to compensate for budget reductions. Compliance workshops planned to harmonise reporting standards.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: System-wide push for prioritisation improved via: 1) Enhanced vulnerability analysis informing partner targeting; 2) Multi-donor coordination (e.g., US/UK for BRCiS, UK/Saudi for WFP); 3) Area-based approaches through CCCM clusters. Independent Review cited FCDO’s role in "addressing humanitarian needs in areas most in danger of famine."
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Rapid procurement enabled by pre-existing partnerships (e.g., UN Rapid Response Mechanism) and crisis modifiers. Some delays in currency exchange impacted WFP’s food assistance delivery (85% achievement).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: High oversight intensity due to famine risk, with Independent Review praising FCDO’s accountability in "complex environment." Balance sought between compliance demands and partner reporting burden.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility: 1) Reallocated funds to integrated response efforts; 2) Expanded cash assistance vertically/horizontally during drought; 3) Piloted anticipatory action via WFP’s Baxnaano linkage. Adaptive management included real-time vulnerability analysis adjustments.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocated £28m emergency funding within 9 months to avert famine, targeting newly displaced and hard-to-reach areas.
Shifted WFP cash transfers to higher-value disbursements ($120) for SAM-affected households, reducing recovery time.
Integrated Housing, Land, and Property (HLP) rights into humanitarian response via IOM’s CCCM cluster, reaching 5,200 individuals.
Established multi-donor funding extensions (e.g., QFFD, KSRelief) to sustain BRCiS and WFP programmes post-FCDO budget cuts.

main_implementation_challenges: Currency exchange fluctuations reduced purchasing power for food assistance (WFP underachievement).
Data scarcity on vulnerable populations hindered precise targeting; addressed via prioritised evidence generation.
Access constraints in hard-to-reach areas (HTRs) and non-government-controlled zones required adaptive delivery models.
Balancing FCDO’s compliance reporting requirements with partner capacity limitations.
external_factors_impact: Somalia’s longest-ever drought (2022–23) necessitated emergency famine-prevention focus, diverting from long-term resilience plans.
Global inflation and GBP depreciation affected procurement costs (e.g., food, fuel).
Political fragmentation in Somalia complicated coordination in non-government areas.
contextual_constraints_new: Overlapping vulnerabilities (displacement, disability, clan exclusion) required more nuanced analysis than initially planned.
Stigma around GBV reporting and disability inclusion emerged as barriers to service access, prompting OPD (Organisations of Persons with Disabilities) engagement.
Competition between humanitarian cash transfers and national safety nets (Baxnaano) created unintended disincentives for programme participation.
partner_relationship_issues: Some partners (e.g., WFP) faced initial resistance to integrating GESI (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) targets, later resolved via FCDO advocacy.
Reporting burdens strained smaller NGOs; mitigated via planned compliance workshops.
Co-financing partnerships (e.g., USAID, KSRelief) required alignment on monitoring standards.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited partner capacity for disability-inclusive data collection and HLP (Housing, Land, Property) rights integration.
Local NGOs needed support to implement crisis modifiers and early warning systems.
FCDO team required additional bandwidth to manage multi-donor coordination.
risk_materialization: Famine risk (Major) materialized as anticipated, prompting emergency response activation.
Currency risk impacted procurement (realized in WFP’s 85% achievement for food assistance).
Protection risks for marginalised clans and women/girls in HTRs were higher than projected, addressed via UNFPA/UNICEF partnerships.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £28m emergency funding fully disbursed (100%) within 9 months. Multi-year programme budget on track, with co-financing leveraging additional £Xm (exact figure not specified) from USAID, QFFD, and KSRelief.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated via: 1) Cost efficiency in cash transfers (e.g., $120 disbursements reduced SAM recovery time); 2) Co-financing partnerships stretched UK funds (e.g., BRCiS consortium); 3) Independent Review cited FCDO as a "smaller, but smarter" donor crowding in external resources. Area-based approaches (CCCM) reduced duplication.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong, per Independent Review: "FCDO maintained commitment to a strong team ensuring accountability for UK funds." Compliance workshops planned to standardise fraud/safeguarding reporting.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded in health/nutrition (196% achievement at lower per-unit costs) and WASH (100–107% achievement). Cash assistance demonstrated multiplier effects (e.g., debt settlement, food/health/education coverage).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Successful co-financing with: 1) USAID for BRCiS consortium; 2) Saudi Arabia (KSRelief) for WFP cash programmes; 3) Ongoing discussions with QFFD (Qatar) and World Bank for multi-year extensions.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Negative: GBP depreciation and Somali Shilling volatility reduced WFP’s food procurement capacity, contributing to 85% achievement vs. 100% target. Mitigated via flexible funding reallocation.

key_delivery_lessons: Integrated, multi-partner responses (e.g., UNICEF+WFP+IOM) maximise impact in complex crises.
Prioritising marginalised groups (women, disabled, excluded clans) requires dedicated vulnerability analysis tools.
Crisis modifiers and early warning systems (piloted in SHARP) are critical for shock responsiveness.
successful_delivery_practices: Area-based coordination via CCCM clusters improved service mapping and reduced gaps.
Strategic co-financing (e.g., US/UK for BRCiS) stretched resources and influenced wider donor engagement.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme had to refocus resources and adapt to new results targets due to ODA budget reductions. Delivery approach shifted to prioritize early mobilisation in select areas (e.g., Global Centre on Adaptation) while redesigning other components.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Global Centre on Adaptation (GCA) exceeded expectations in Output 1 (LLA awareness) and Output 2 (Nature-Based Solutions), demonstrating strong technical capacity and ability to leverage global networks. Local partners (e.g., Mongla municipality) engaged effectively in pilot initiatives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO’s Climate and Environment Team in Dhaka led implementation with cross-disciplinary inputs (climate, economic, governance advisers). Programme governance is being strengthened by June 2023, with a focus on finalizing logframes and Theory of Change.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Intensive stakeholder engagement was required to balance short-term budget adjustments with long-term ambitions. Coordination with GoB (e.g., Ministry of Environment) and multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank, ADB) was critical for influencing larger investments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: GCA utilized centrally managed services (HR, finance, procurement) from HQ and recruited local experts at lower costs than international consultants, improving efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Quarterly updates to the risk register and field visits (e.g., Mongla in December 2022) ensured active oversight. Partners maintained separate risk registers, aligned with FCDO’s due diligence requirements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by reallocating resources to high-potential areas (e.g., LLA pilots) and adapting to ODA reductions. The ability to "re-think types and scale of investments" was highlighted as a key strength.
adaptive_management_examples: Soft launch of the Global Hub on LLA at COP27 (November 2022) with 35 knowledge products, followed by a physical launch by Bangladesh’s Prime Minister in December 2022.
Formation of local/national advisory committees for Mongla’s climate-resilient town pilot, integrating UNDP’s climate resilience expertise.
Scaling up LLA through investment mobilization, pioneered by GCA, with high-level engagement opportunities identified for 2023.

main_implementation_challenges: ODA budget reductions forced programme redesign and reprioritization, delaying full mobilisation.
Balancing short-term budget phasing with long-term vision required intensive stakeholder engagement.
