external_factors_impact: UK government’s reallocation of ODA funds to support Ukrainian and Afghan refugees reduced available resources for BCEP.
Global economic pressures (e.g., inflation, exchange rates) indirectly affected programme planning, though specific currency impacts were not detailed.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need to adapt to reduced ODA allocations while maintaining ambition for a flagship programme.
Political and bureaucratic complexities in Bangladesh’s climate governance required additional navigation (e.g., aligning with National Adaptation Plan and Mujib Prosperity Plan).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited local capacity for designing and implementing Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) investments, addressed through GCA’s training of 25 PPP practitioners.
Need for stronger safeguarding policies to protect vulnerable groups (e.g., women, girls) from exploitation, though no cases were reported.
risk_materialization: Programme delivery risks materialized due to budget constraints, mitigated by adaptive programming and early partner engagement.
Policy risks (e.g., alignment with GoB priorities) were managed through quarterly risk register updates and high-level engagement.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Moderately behind plan due to ODA reductions and reprioritization. Active components (GCA-led) executed efficiently, but overall programme budget required adjustment to new targets.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: GCA reduced operational costs by using shared office space (Ministry of Environment) and local experts instead of international consultants.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Leveraged global networks to mobilize experts quickly (e.g., FCDO adviser in LLA awards Technical Advisory Group at no cost).
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Influenced multilateral partners (World Bank, ADB) on climate-resilient investments. Shakti Foundation expanded renewable energy access for rural communities.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Designed inclusive solutions (e.g., LLA infrastructure addressing vulnerable groups’ needs) and targeted marginalized beneficiaries (e.g., women, disabled).
value_for_money_assessment.overall: VFM case for full programme remains untested, but early components (GCA, Shakti) demonstrate strong VfM potential.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. GCA and FCDO maintained robust financial oversight, with quarterly risk register updates and partner due diligence (e.g., safeguarding assessments).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Achieved through local hiring, shared services, and in-kind contributions (e.g., MoU with Mongla municipality for pilot town).

key_delivery_lessons: Complex programmes require long-term, predictable finance and clear mobilisation tracking (e.g., process indicators in logframes).
Balancing short-term adjustments with long-term vision is critical but challenging, especially with partners.
Early, visible results (e.g., LLA awards, Mongla MoU) can demonstrate potential and build stakeholder confidence during transitions.
successful_delivery_practices: GCA’s role as a "solution broker" effectively mobilized global expertise and influenced larger investments.
High-level engagement (e.g., PM’s launch of LLA Hub) amplified programme visibility and legitimacy.
Inclusive design processes (e.g., community-driven climate vulnerability assessments) improved local ownership.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted to phased mobilisation, prioritizing components with quick wins (e.g., LLA, NBS pilots).
Strengthened programme governance (logframes, ToC review) planned by June 2023.
Increased flexibility in investment types/scale to align with reduced ODA.
innovations_attempted: Pioneered scaling LLA through investment mobilization (GCA-led approach).
Used satellite data for NBS feasibility studies in coastal upazilas (Dacope, Morelganj, Bagerhat).
Developed Community Climate Vulnerability Assessment (CCVA) guidelines for local adaptation planning.

forward_recommendations.action: Finalize implementation plan by March 2023, including updated logframes and ToC.
Disseminate design/preparation work (e.g., LLA, NBS tools) to inform BCEP and partner investments by September 2023.
Strengthen partner engagement for LLA scaling, focusing on Principles for Locally Led Adaptation.
Monitor and address safeguarding risks proactively, especially for vulnerable groups.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Quarterly risk register updates, field visits, and partner safeguarding policies mitigated key risks (e.g., programme delivery, safeguarding). No major incidents reported.

direct: 25 professionals trained on LLA reporting (13 journalists, 12 CSO representatives).
20 PPP practitioners trained in climate-resilient investments.
Mongla municipality (population TBC) engaged in climate-resilient town pilot.
indirect: Global Hub on LLA reached wider audiences through 35 knowledge products (case studies, videos, research).
NBS feasibility studies in 3 coastal upazilas (Dacope, Morelganj, Bagerhat) informed local climate planning.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Outputs 1 and 2 met or exceeded milestones, but overall programme is moderately behind due to delayed mobilisation of other components.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan and Nationally Determined Contributions through pilot demonstrations (e.g., Mongla MoU, NBS tools).
Influenced multilateral banks (World Bank, ADB) on climate-resilient infrastructure investments.
capacity_building_results: 25 journalists/CSOs trained in LLA reporting, with 9 journalists publishing articles post-mentoring.
20 public/private sector practitioners trained in climate-resilient PPPs.
Local advisory committees (Mongla) and national experts (UNDP) integrated into programme governance.

unintended_consequences.description: Bangladesh won an LLA award in the "inclusive leadership" category at COP27, raising its global profile in climate adaptation.
ODA reductions delayed full programme mobilisation, risking loss of momentum in non-pilot areas.

scalability_evidence: LLA and NBS approaches are designed for replication (e.g., Mongla model for other migrant-friendly towns, NBS tools for coastal regions).
GCA’s global networks and FCDO’s influence with multilaterals create pathways for scaling successful pilots.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong potential despite early challenges, with tangible results in LLA and NBS pilots. Alignment with GoB’s climate priorities and UK’s ICF commitments justifies continuation, subject to adaptive management.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Current model (FCDO + GCA + local partners) is effective but depends on continued ODA stability and partner capacity building.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied (with caveats). Recognizes progress in active components but notes need for improved mobilisation pace and risk management.
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize implementation plan and logframes by March 2023.
Strengthen programme governance and ToC by June 2023.
Scale successful pilots (e.g., Mongla, LLA Hub) while phasing in remaining components.
Enhance safeguarding and equity measures, particularly for vulnerable groups.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Climate Action for a Resilient Asia (CARA) Programme

output_1.title: Building capacity through Knowledge Products: High quality knowledge products are delivered by CARA components to strengthen capacity of institutions/organisations (or communities) for developing and/or implementing effective adaptation solutions to climate change impacts.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme was formally extended on a no-cost basis from January 2029 to March 2031 due to slower-than-anticipated start and ODA budget reductions. This allows more realistic budget utilization and activity scale-up.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners delivered 7 out of 11 targeted knowledge products (Output 1) despite budget unpredictability. ADB trust funds (CRPP and URTF) were particularly well-received internally, though micro-level delivery lessons were underreported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Annual in-person partners event introduced (May 2024) to clarify thematic outputs and MEL expectations. Cross-component coordination remains a focus, with a dedicated MEL supplier being procured to measure collaboration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-component coordination is operational but requires more explicit focus. A MEL supplier is being procured to develop metrics for collaboration and lesson-sharing across components.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Late budget allocations (e.g., £13m released in December 2023) disrupted procurement timelines. UK Met Office’s WISER component only completed inception in October 2023, delaying full implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was adaptive due to financial unpredictability. Milestones are now finalized earlier (by mid-June) to allow adjustments for delayed funds.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexible Fund (including Pacific Partnerships Facility) was used to address emerging priorities, such as locally led adaptation projects in Pacific nations.
adaptive_management_examples: Extension of programme timeline (2029→2031) to accommodate ODA budget cuts.
Recruitment of a communications specialist (approved January 2024) to address gaps in dissemination and uptake of knowledge products.
Adjustment of milestone-setting timelines to align with budget availability.

main_implementation_challenges: Significant ODA budget reductions in the first two years led to lower-than-planned spending (e.g., UNDP-CFN spent only £0.8m of £4.25m allocated in 2022/23).
Late release of additional funds (£13m in December 2023) limited implementation in the reporting period.
Underreporting of qualitative evidence on uptake of knowledge products by beneficiaries.
operational_challenges_context.external_factors_impact: ODA budget cuts (external to the programme) were the primary disruptor, causing delays in partner activities and requiring a no-cost extension.
contextual_constraints_new: Need for stronger GESI (Gender and Social Inclusion) operationalization emerged as a priority, with a programme-wide strategy now under development.
Capacity constraints in tracking micro-level delivery lessons and cross-component collaboration.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported, but partners struggled to report detailed delivery lessons beyond high-level alignment with government priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited communications capacity (no dedicated staff until 2024) hindered dissemination of knowledge products.
GESI tracking and implementation required additional focus due to early-stage gaps.
risk_materialization: Financial unpredictability (Major risk) materialized, leading to budget execution challenges.
Delayed implementation of UK Met Office’s WISER component due to prolonged inception phase.

budget_execution_vs_plan.note: £13m additional funds were released in December 2023 (doubling the FY budget), but too late for use in the reporting period.

financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early-stage implementation and budget volatility make VFM assessment premature. However, ADB trust funds (CRPP/URTF) showed high internal reception, suggesting potential efficiency. Events and workshops require pre-approval to assess VFM going forward.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management was adaptive to unpredictability, but late allocations disrupted planning. No major breaches reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Clarification of thematic outputs and their linkage to outcome-level ambitions is critical for partner alignment (addressed via May 2024 MEL session).
Early milestone-setting (by mid-June) is essential to adapt to budget delays.
Qualitative evidence collection on knowledge product uptake must be systematized.
successful_delivery_practices: Flexible Fund effectively addressed emerging priorities (e.g., Pacific Partnerships Facility).
ADB trust funds (CRPP/URTF) were internally well-received, indicating strong institutional buy-in.
management_adaptations_made: Programme extension (2029→2031) to accommodate ODA cuts.
Introduction of annual in-person partners event to align on MEL and outputs.
Recruitment of a communications specialist (fast-tracked for May/June 2024).
innovations_attempted: Demand-responsive Flexible Fund for locally led adaptation.
Cross-component MEL supplier to measure collaboration (under procurement).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: Action on last year’s recommendations is documented in Annex 2 (not provided in this extract).
forward_recommendations: Develop a programme-wide GESI strategy to standardize inclusion across components.
Align AR timelines with partner reporting cycles.
Include external team members in future Annual Reviews.
Pre-approve event objectives to assess VFM.
Strengthen tracking of gender outputs and micro-level delivery lessons.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was reactive to financial unpredictability. The no-cost extension mitigated budget risks, but Major risk rating persists due to ongoing ODA volatility.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Early signs of uptake: 2 policy briefs on climate finance accountability (CFN) are undergoing government review (expected early 2024). 3 studies on gender-responsive adaptation (CRPP) were completed.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: 7 knowledge products delivered (e.g., 3 studies on transformative adaptation, 2 policy briefs on clean air). Uptake evidence is limited but includes internal ADB adoption of trust fund models.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Flexible Fund’s Pacific Partnerships Facility demonstrates potential for scaling locally led adaptation. ADB trust funds show institutional scalability within the Bank.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: No-cost extension to 2031 approved to address ODA budget cuts and allow realistic scale-up. Early outputs (e.g., knowledge products) show progress despite challenges.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (dependent on ODA stability and partner coordination)
planned_adaptations_future: Programme-wide GESI strategy development.
Enhanced MEL for cross-component collaboration.
Recruitment of communications specialist by mid-2024.
Adjustment of AR timelines to align with partner reporting.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Local Infrastructure Support Programme (LISP) Transition/Initial Implementation
programme_metadata.review_period: Pilot Phase (June 2022 - July 2023) and Transition Phase (completed August 2024)
programme_metadata.programme_status: Transition phase concluding (MoU with WFP ends November 2024); main implementation phase to begin post-October 2024

output_1.title: Higher coverage of infrastructure services (more people with access to local infrastructure services, more people benefitting from more sustainable and resilient infrastructure)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted from politically-driven geographical prioritisation to a competitive, evidence-based "opt-in" process using Expressions of Interest (EoI) weighted by political buy-in, needs/gaps, and local capacity. Pilot Phase (2022-23) used WFP as main delivery partner with UNDP support; Transition Phase (2023-24) continued with WFP via MoU while awaiting FRA/FRMIP completion. Main implementation phase (post-October 2024) will use a new TA supplier procured via FCDO’s Global Development Delivery (GDD) framework.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: WFP performed effectively as TA partner, delivering infrastructure works ahead of targets (144 schemes vs. planned 225,000 beneficiaries → 266,429 actual). UNDP’s capacity development role was secondary but contributed to LG planning/budgeting systems. Local governments (LGs) demonstrated strong co-financing commitment despite earthquake disruptions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Joint Task Team (BEK, WFP, MoFAGA) managed FRMIP implementation post-FRA. Steering Committee (LSC) endorsed key documents (FRA, FRMIP) in December 2023. Governance was more collaborative than planned due to prolonged MoU negotiations with GoN, requiring adaptive coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective between BEK, WFP, and GoN at federal/provincial levels, though earthquake response (Nov 2023) tested coordination. EoI process for Lumbini expansion (15 new LGs + 5 additional in Karnali) demonstrated scalable selection mechanisms. Transition of WFP’s governance support to new TA supplier is underway.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Pilot/Transition phases used existing WFP/UNDP agreements. Main phase procurement via GDD framework faced delays (FRA/FRMIP completion took 12+ months) but is on track for October 2024 award. Bulk procurement and e-bidding for construction materials achieved £81,240 savings in Pilot Phase.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to fiduciary risks (Major rating). FRA and FRMIP required external validation (ASI) and joint Task Team oversight. Operational oversight was lighter for LGs with proven capacity, allowing 80%+ of funds to flow as capital/TA costs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to: (1) earthquake disruptions (halted activities in 3 LGs, reprioritized timelines); (2) extended Pilot/Transition phases to test models pre-FRA; (3) revised LG selection criteria based on RENT research findings about vulnerability weighting.
adaptive_management_examples: Post-earthquake (Nov 2023): Reallocated resources to support search/rescue in Barekot, Nalgad, and Darma Rural Municipalities while maintaining overall timeline adherence.
EoI process revisions: Added support for lower-capacity LGs to submit applications (e.g., EoI drafting assistance) after research showed self-selection favored higher-capacity municipalities.
Cost efficiencies: Introduced volume-based wage payments and direct bank transfers for workers, reducing leakage and improving quality.
Seasonal alignment: Shifted review timing to match Nepal’s construction season (Oct-June), avoiding monsoon constraints.

main_implementation_challenges: Prolonged FRA/FRMIP processes (12+ months) delayed main phase start, requiring extended Pilot/Transition phases.
Earthquake (Nov 2023) disrupted 3 LGs, requiring reprioritization of activities and humanitarian support.
Balancing LG selection criteria: Tension between capacity (ability to submit EoI) and vulnerability (risk of excluding most-needy LGs).
Monsoon constraints limited construction to 8 months/year, misaligned with initial annual review timing.
external_factors_impact: Earthquake (6+ magnitude, Nov 2023): 62,000 families affected, 26,500 homes destroyed, halted activities in 3 LGs (Barekot, Nalgad, Darma).
Political stability in Karnali was maintained despite national volatility, but civil servant transfers occasionally disrupted LG continuity.
Currency/exchange rates not mentioned as a significant issue.
contextual_constraints_new: LG self-selection via EoI inadvertently favored higher-capacity municipalities, risking exclusion of vulnerable groups (identified via RENT research).
Limited construction window (Oct-June) created bottlenecks for physical progress, requiring adaptive planning.
GoN’s request to proceed pre-MoU signing (Pilot Phase) created fiduciary risks later mitigated via FRA/FRMIP.
partner_relationship_issues: WFP’s dual role as TA partner and implementer stretched capacity during Transition Phase, though performance remained strong.
UNDP’s support role was less visible; capacity development outputs were overshadowed by WFP’s infrastructure delivery.
Delays in GoN MoU signing required interim arrangements, increasing coordination burden.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Lower-capacity LGs struggled with EoI submission, revealing need for targeted support (e.g., application drafting assistance).
Post-earthquake, 3 LGs required additional TA to resume activities, diverting resources temporarily.
LGs’ financial management systems needed strengthening to handle bulk procurement and e-bidding (addressed via TA).
risk_materialization: Fiduciary risks (Major rating) materialized as anticipated, requiring FRA/FRMIP and joint Task Team oversight.
Earthquake risk (unplanned) disrupted 3 LGs but was managed via adaptive reprioritization.
Political risks (LG turnover) did not significantly impact operations, contrary to initial concerns.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; Pilot Phase achieved £81,240 savings (£43,000 LISP + £38,240 LG contributions) via bulk procurement and e-bidding. Transition Phase analysis pending but indicates cost per capita dropped from £23 to £15/beneficiary. Over 80% of funds allocated to capital/TA costs (19.66% management).

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Strong: Pre-feasibility economic analyses ensured viability. Bulk procurement and competitive bidding reduced costs by ~15% vs. traditional user committees.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: High: Cost per capita decreased 35% (£23 → £15). 60% reduction in small projects enabled focus on higher-impact schemes. Direct wage transfers improved transparency and worker motivation.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High: LGs institutionalized improved planning, construction management, and maintenance frameworks. Infrastructure sector represents >70% of target LGs’ budgets, with LISP models now embedded.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Mixed: EoI process reached 15 LGs but favored higher-capacity municipalities. Adjustments planned to better target vulnerability (e.g., revised weighting, application support).

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Good: LGs adopted e-bidding and bulk procurement with TA support. Financial systems strengthened via FRMIP actions (e.g., direct wage transfers, volume-based payments). No major audit findings reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Yes: 35% reduction in per-capita costs (£23 → £15) and 60% fewer small projects. TA costs limited to 19.66% of budget, with 80%+ allocated to capital/TA.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Yes: Pilot Phase co-funded by RAP3 (now closed). LGs contributed £38,240 in savings during Pilot Phase and maintained co-financing commitments post-earthquake.

key_delivery_lessons: Competitive EoI processes improve targeting but may exclude vulnerable LGs without tailored support.

Direct wage transfers and volume-based payments improve transparency and worker productivity.
Seasonal constraints (monsoon) require aligned review timelines and flexible implementation windows.
successful_delivery_practices: Joint Task Team (BEK/WFP/MoFAGA) effectively managed FRMIP implementation post-FRA.
WFP’s MoU-based delivery model allowed rapid scaling (144 schemes in Transition Phase).
LG-led co-financing demonstrated ownership, with 266,429 beneficiaries exceeded (vs. 225,000 target).
Post-earthquake recovery maintained timelines through localized reprioritization.

innovations_attempted: Volume-based wage payments coupled with direct bank transfers to reduce leakage.
E-bidding platforms for LG procurement, reducing costs and improving competition.
Evidence-based LG selection criteria (political buy-in, needs, capacity) replacing political allocations.
Maintenance frameworks integrated into LG budgeting to improve infrastructure sustainability.
previous_recommendations_progress: FRA/FRMIP completed (endorsed Dec 2023) as recommended in initial Annual Review.
LG capacity gaps addressed via TA (e.g., bulk procurement, e-bidding training).
Earthquake response validated contingency plans but revealed need for deeper LG resilience support.
forward_recommendations: Revise EoI criteria to better balance capacity and vulnerability (e.g., weighted scoring, application support).
Scale e-bidding and bulk procurement models to new LGs in Lumbini/Karnali.
Strengthen LG maintenance frameworks to ensure long-term infrastructure sustainability.
Finalize LISP Operational Procedures and National Policy revisions to lock in governance gains.
Monitor FRMIP actions to transition from Major to Moderate risk rating.
Align future reviews with construction season (Oct-June) to avoid speculative reporting.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: FRA/FRMIP mitigated fiduciary risks (Major rating persists but actions are underway). Earthquake response was agile but revealed gaps in LG resilience planning. Partner risks (WFP/UNDP) were managed well, though UNDP’s role could be clarified in main phase.

policy_influence_achieved: Draft LISP Operational Procedures under development to institutionalize delivery models.

LG planning/budgeting systems adopted LISP modalities (e.g., competitive selection, co-financing).
capacity_building_results: 15 LGs in Karnali demonstrated improved procurement (e-bidding), financial management (direct wage transfers), and maintenance planning.
Bulk procurement training reduced costs and improved LG autonomy.
Technical assistance to LGs on infrastructure planning/budgeting embedded in annual cycles.
unintended_consequences: Positive: EoI process incentivized LG competition, improving proposal quality and co-financing commitments.
Negative: Higher-capacity LGs were overrepresented in selection; most vulnerable LGs risked exclusion without adjustments.
Negative: Earthquake diverted resources from 3 LGs, though recovery was swift.
scalability_evidence: EoI process successfully replicated in Lumbini Province (15 new LGs selected).
Delivery models (bulk procurement, e-bidding) are LG-led and require minimal additional TA to scale.
Maintenance frameworks and co-financing mechanisms are designed for LG ownership, reducing long-term dependency.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance in Pilot/Transition phases (A score, 426,558 beneficiaries reached).
GoN commitment demonstrated via co-financing and policy engagement (FRMIP, draft National Policy).
Scalable models validated (EoI process, e-bidding, bulk procurement) with expansion to Lumbini underway.

planned_adaptations_future: Transition from WFP to new TA supplier (post-October 2024) with focus on LG capacity building.

Finalize LISP Operational Procedures and National Policy revisions to lock in governance reforms.

Institutionalize maintenance frameworks to ensure long-term infrastructure sustainability.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track overall, but financial reporting from GWT was sometimes delayed. Programme spent within revised budget after ODA cuts, with some reallocation between outputs. Recommendation to limit forecast-to-actual spend variance to ≤5%.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: GWT: Delivery effective but financial reporting timeliness needs improvement. UNICEF: Financial management met expectations post-April 2022. Combined oversight by FCDO ensured compliance with ODA requirements during transition.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Higher than planned due to: (1) Leveraging GWT's pre-existing palika relationships reduced mobilization costs; (2) NWASH digital platform reduced data collection costs; (3) Shared TA between GWT/UNICEF avoided duplication.

key_delivery_lessons: Continuous palika engagement is critical—GWT's local presence mitigated COVID/election disruptions.
Federal/provincial engagement requires dedicated resources (UNICEF's late entry highlighted this gap).
Digital tools (NWASH) accelerate planning but need complementary TA for adoption.
Resilience frameworks (BEK model) offer better long-term impact than one-off DRRM interventions.
successful_delivery_practices: GWT's use of existing networks to maintain delivery during transitions.
NWASH platform for data-driven WASH planning (15 wards completed hazard assessments).
Joint GWT-UNICEF coordination at federal level (revived SEIU unit).
Provincial orientation programmes for newly elected palika representatives.
management_adaptations_made: Increased GWT staff time in palikas for hands-on TA.
Shifted DRRM focus from humanitarian response to institutional resilience (BEK framework).
Added nutrition-targeted interventions for vulnerable groups.
Planned pilot for "federalization of WASH governance" with PLGSP in Year 2.
innovations_attempted: NWASH digital platform for climate-sensitive WASH planning.
Cross-partner TA model (GWT local + UNICEF federal/provincial).
Resilience framework (BEK) replacing one-off DRRM training.
forward_recommendations: GWT to increase palika-level TA time to 60% of staff capacity.
UNICEF to pilot WASH governance federalization in 1 province with PLGSP.
Develop dynamic review mechanisms for WASH/DRRM plans to adapt to climate/water availability changes.
Design nutrition-specific interventions for pregnant/lactating mothers and under-5 children.
Improve financial reporting timeliness (≤5% forecast variance target).
Clarify palika focal points for WASH/DRRM to reduce coordination confusion.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Mitigated COVID/political risks through flexibility but underestimated palika capacity gaps and provincial engagement needs. Risk of low-ambition targets addressed by Year 1 logframe revisions.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Exceeded Year 1 targets: 8 palikas completed WASH plans (target: 8); 15 wards conducted hazard assessments (target: 14). Household/institution WASH access improvements underway but quantitative data pending. Nutritional interventions not yet implemented.
policy_influence_achieved: Revived Ministry of Water Supply's Sector Efficiency Improvement Unit (SEIU).
Provincial orientation programmes influenced newly elected palika representatives' WASH/DRRM priorities.
NWASH platform adopted by federal ministry for sector-wide planning.
capacity_building_results: 15 wards trained on multi-hazard assessments and DRRM planning.
8 palikas gained capacity to use NWASH for climate-sensitive WASH planning.
Federal/provincial staff received TA on WASH governance federalization.
unintended_consequences: Positive: NWASH platform created unexpected demand from non-target palikas for inclusion.
Negative: Initial focus on WASH planning delayed DRRM training and private sector engagement.
scalability_evidence: NWASH digital tool scalable to other municipalities (demand already expressed).
BEK resilience framework adaptable to other climate-vulnerable regions.
Palika-level planning model replicable in other Nepali provinces.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme exceeded Year 1 targets (A+ score) despite challenges, demonstrating strong delivery capacity. Alignment with FCDO priorities (climate resilience, health) and Nepal's federalization agenda. High potential for sustainable impact through institutional strengthening (palikas, SEIU).

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expand NWASH to additional palikas based on demand.
Pilot WASH governance federalization in 1 province with PLGSP.
Integrate nutrition-specific targets into WASH/DRRM plans.
Strengthen provincial engagement through UNICEF-led TA.
Develop climate adaptation modules for WASH planning.

output_1.title: Core output targets delivered across multiple work packages (Aceli Africa, GGGI)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Component 3 (Mercy Corps Europe) was closed during inception phase; FCDO is rethinking delivery approach for climate smart land management. Palladium moved from inception to implementation phase.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Aceli Africa exceeded targets in mobilizing private finance and technical assistance. GGGI successfully established the Climate Finance Unit (CFU) in Uganda's Ministry of Finance. Mercy Corps Europe underperformed, leading to component closure.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Adaptive management approach allowed for component reallocation (e.g., Mercy Corps exit, Palladium expansion). Senior-level oversight was intensified post-Mercy Corps issues.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between Aceli, GGGI, and Palladium was effective for components in implementation. Cross-component learning (e.g., Aceli’s lending criteria adjustments) was documented.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for Palladium and GGGI proceeded as planned. Mercy Corps’ procurement was terminated early due to performance issues.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to Mercy Corps’ underperformance; led to more frequent senior-level check-ins and an after-action review.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme used flexibility to close underperforming component (Mercy Corps) and reallocate focus to Aceli and GGGI. Adaptive management allowed for mid-course corrections (e.g., Aceli’s incentive adjustments for women-owned businesses).
adaptive_management_examples: Aceli Africa adjusted lending criteria to target smaller loans for women-owned businesses after identifying untapped potential in this segment.
GGGI’s CFU developed new climate finance mechanisms (e.g., Green Bonds analysis) based on regional learning.
Palladium’s market systems development strategy was revised based on inception-phase studies.

main_implementation_challenges: Underperformance of Mercy Corps Europe led to closure of Component 3 (Climate Smart Land Management).
Delays in addressing strategic leadership concerns with Mercy Corps until after inception phase.
Need for mid-programme reallocation of resources and partners.
contextual_constraints_new: Uganda’s evolving climate policy landscape required CFU (GGGI) to align with National Development Plan and NDCs.
Refugee-hosting districts added complexity to inclusion targets (e.g., 30% of beneficiaries in or near these areas).
partner_relationship_issues: Mercy Corps Europe: Lack of strategic alignment and unresolved concerns during inception led to component closure.
Initial FCDO messages to Mercy Corps were not effectively communicated to the project team leader.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in Uganda’s Ministry of Finance to absorb climate finance mechanisms (addressed by GGGI’s CFU support).
Aceli Africa identified need for additional incentives to boost lending to women-owned SMEs.
risk_materialization: Partner performance risk materialized with Mercy Corps Europe, leading to component closure.
Strategic leadership risk in Component 3 was not mitigated in time.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Aceli and GGGI spent funds efficiently; Mercy Corps’ unspent budget was reallocated. Six-month reporting period (FY 22/23) limits direct comparison.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. Aceli exceeded private finance mobilization targets (£2.3M vs. £1.7M planned). GGGI’s CFU leveraged government co-funding for climate finance mechanisms.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong for Aceli and GGGI; Mercy Corps’ financial management was inadequate, contributing to component closure.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Aceli’s cost per beneficiary (~£398 per individual supported) was lower than projected due to economies of scale in technical assistance.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: GGGI secured co-funding for CFU staff salaries from Uganda’s Ministry of Finance. Nexus Green attracted private-sector interest for its e-mobility pilot.

key_delivery_lessons: Early intervention is critical when partner performance issues arise (Mercy Corps case).
Direct communication with partner team leaders (not just HQ) ensures alignment (lesson from Mercy Corps).
Adaptive incentives (e.g., Aceli’s bonuses for women/lending to climate SMEs) can drive better outcomes.
successful_delivery_practices: Aceli’s performance-linked incentives for lenders successfully mobilized private finance.
GGGI’s CFU embedded within Ministry of Finance improved government ownership of climate finance mechanisms.
Palladium’s phased approach (studies → strategy → implementation) reduced risks in market systems development.
management_adaptations_made: Increased senior-level oversight post-Mercy Corps issues.
Revised logframe to reflect new partner composition (Palladium in, Mercy Corps out).
Added targeted incentives for Aceli to address gender and climate gaps.
innovations_attempted: Aceli’s impact bonuses for loans to women-owned and climate-aligned businesses.
GGGI’s Agent-Based Modelling for Nexus Green’s e-mobility pilot feasibility analysis.
Palladium’s design of market system innovations for climate-smart agriculture.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed after-action review for Mercy Corps component closure (Recommendation #2 from prior AR).
Logframe revision is underway (Recommendation #2 from this AR).
forward_recommendations: Revise Aceli’s lending criteria to align with ICF KPIs (focus on climate mitigation/adaptation).
Finalize new delivery mechanism for Component 3 (climate smart land management) by October 2023.
Develop a comprehensive CSJ monitoring and assurance plan by September 2023.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Proactive with Aceli/GGGI but reactive with Mercy Corps. New assurance plan aims to address gaps.

policy_influence_achieved: GGGI’s CFU influenced Uganda’s national climate finance strategy.
Aceli’s model may inform future UK ICF programmes on blending finance for SMEs.
capacity_building_results: 19 businesses received technical assistance (53% gender-inclusive, 50% supporting food security).
CFU trained 7 Ministry of Finance staff on climate finance mechanisms.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Aceli’s incentives led to higher-than-expected lending to women-owned businesses (11% vs. 10% target).
Negative: Mercy Corps’ exit delayed land management interventions, risking biodiversity targets.
scalability_evidence: Aceli’s model is being considered for replication in Kenya/Rwanda.
GGGI’s CFU approach may be adopted by other East African governments.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme is on track to achieve outcomes despite Component 3 challenges. Aceli and GGGI demonstrate strong performance, and Palladium’s component is now mobilized. Adaptive management has addressed early issues.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Dependency on FCDO funding for CFU may limit long-term sustainability; co-funding efforts are underway.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by "A" score and continuation decision).
planned_adaptations_future: Redesign Component 3 delivery mechanism by October 2023.
Enhance monitoring of gender and climate outcomes in Aceli’s portfolio.
Pilot Nexus Green’s e-mobility hub with private-sector partners.

risk_management_effectiveness.contextual_risks: Strategic Opportunities Fund provides buffer for political/economic shocks.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: PBF and Joint Programme performed well, with PDAs providing expert advice and capacity-building beyond UK’s direct footprint. PBF’s catalytic mechanisms and Joint Programme’s PDA deployments (120 PDAs across 80+ countries) exceeded expectations in coordination and conflict sensitivity integration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UN Country Teams demonstrated improved coordination via PDAs (e.g., Kyrgyzstan’s PBF eligibility extension, Congo’s hate speech initiatives, Peru’s election working group). PBF’s interagency collaboration was catalytic but faced challenges in donor communication.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to political instability and violence in PBF-eligible countries by maintaining high PDA support (95% target met) despite external shocks. Logframe revisions proposed to focus on impact over approval volumes.
adaptive_management_examples: PDA-led coordination in Kyrgyzstan secured a 5-year PBF funding eligibility extension with strategic objectives submitted by the Head of State.
PBF projects in Somalia (child soldier reintegration), Sudan (land/water conflict resolution), and South Sudan (gang ceasefires) demonstrated adaptive, context-specific interventions.
Joint Programme expanded PDA cadre to 120 across 80+ countries, including regional specialists for sub-regional initiatives (e.g., Caribbean social cohesion index).

main_implementation_challenges: Lower-than-anticipated donor contributions to PBF, reducing annual approvals ($195m vs. $210m target).
Political instability and violence in PBF-eligible countries hindered project implementation.
Limited evidence base for PBF’s catalytic value (2021 results significantly lower than 2019–2020).
Overstretched PBSO and Joint Programme HQ teams struggling with communication and M&E demands.
external_factors_impact: Global financial climate increased scrutiny on public spending, requiring stronger donor communication.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Emergency Deployments Team 2 (EDT2)

output_1.title: UK ISAR fully prepared to provide rapid, well-coordinated and appropriately assessed international search and rescue responses saving as many lives as technically possible within the limited timeframes associated with rapid onset natural disasters.

output_2.title: UK ISAR to develop and aim to provide any requirement for a wider range of UK ISAR capabilities, including smaller specialised configurations including hybrid type teams [known as the menu of options].

output_4.title: UK-Med rapid response capability is maintained through availability of qualified and vetted personnel to efficiently deliver a UK EMT response

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned from EDT1 by decommissioning Type 2 field hospital and establishing Type 1 Emergency Medical Team and field clinic; restructured governance by removing contracted-in FCDO team and adopting a slimmed-down management approach; increased partner autonomy in capability management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UK-Med and MFRA (Merseyside Fire and Rescue Authority) met deployment and readiness targets, with UK-Med achieving 100% staffing and TOR compliance for EMT deployments. UK ISAR maintained INSARAG accreditation readiness and exceeded training targets (e.g., 247 vs. 240 staff capability).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO management team understaffed during Year 1 (missing Programme Coordinator and Health Adviser until late in the year), delaying early setup. Humanitarian Adviser provided interim support. Full staffing expected in Year 2 to enable deeper cross-departmental engagement (Home Office, DHSC).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination with WHO for EMT deployments and INSARAG for ISAR accreditation. Early engagement with FCDO Kenya team for capacity-building opportunities, though delayed by emergency responses (Turkey, Malawi).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Equipment procurement for UK ISAR transitioned from Home Office reliance to programme-funded assets (e.g., solar lighting, PPE, search tools). Budget revisions agreed in-year with both partners to manage underspend (UK-Med: 13% under; MFRA: 21% under).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Light-touch oversight in Year 1 due to understaffing and crisis response priorities (Ukraine). Quarterly performance/finance/risk meetings planned for Year 2 to formalize oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to develop new capabilities (e.g., UK ISAR flood module) and respond to unplanned deployments (5 total: Turkey x2, Malawi x3). Delayed capacity-building in Kenya due to emergency priorities but rescheduled for August 2023.
adaptive_management_examples: Accelerated development of flood response module in response to FCDO request.
Postponed Kenya capacity-building scoping visit due to Turkey/Malawi deployments, rescheduled for August 2023.
Revised equipment management processes post-deployment challenges (e.g., customs delays in Turkey).
Introduced solar lighting and improved tented accommodation based on equality impact assessments.

main_implementation_challenges: Customs clearance delays during deployments (e.g., Turkey airport bottlenecks).
Understaffing of FCDO programme team (missing Coordinator and Health Adviser for most of Year 1).
High staff turnover in UK ISAR due to retirements, requiring accelerated training for new recruits.
Competing priorities from Ukraine crisis delayed EDT2 setup and partner onboarding.
external_factors_impact: Turkey earthquake and Malawi floods required unplanned deployments, straining resources and delaying capacity-building (e.g., Kenya visit).
Post-COVID supply chain issues affected equipment procurement timelines.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased demand for capacity-building from 8 additional countries (beyond original plan), requiring prioritization aligned with FCDO/INSARAG strategies.
Need to formalize INSARAG community engagement (e.g., working groups) into logframe outputs.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial delays in Home Office equipment handover for UK ISAR, resolved by transitioning to programme-funded assets.
Coordination gaps with DHSC/Health Adviser due to FCDO team understaffing, to be addressed in Year 2.
capacity_constraints_emerged: UK ISAR canine unit facing retirements (2 dogs in final year of deployability), requiring training of replacements.
Limited FCDO bandwidth for programme management during Year 1 due to Ukraine response.
risk_materialization: Staffing risks (retirements, understaffing) materialized but mitigated through accelerated training and recruitment.
Deployment logistical risks (customs delays) identified; corrective actions planned for Year 2.
Equipment dependency risks (Home Office) addressed by procuring programme-owned assets.

mfra.reason: Delayed capacity-building spend (Kenya) and equipment procurement phasing.

evidence: Successful deployments (5 total) within budget despite unplanned demands.
Transition from Home Office equipment reliance to cost-effective programme-owned assets (e.g., solar lighting reducing long-term costs).
Underspend reallocated to future capacity-building (e.g., Kenya, new capabilities).

examples: UK ISAR reduced carbon footprint via solar lighting and improved tented accommodation.

Flexible logframe indicators are essential for adaptive management (e.g., revising UK ISAR equipment readiness metrics).
Partner autonomy improves responsiveness but requires robust FCDO oversight frameworks (e.g., quarterly reviews).
successful_delivery_practices: Decentralized management of EMT/ISAR capabilities by partners (UK-Med, MFRA) enhanced operational agility.
INSARAG accreditation process (IER) drove structured readiness improvements (e.g., exercises, equipment upgrades).
Cross-departmental engagement (Home Office, DHSC) in Year 2 expected to resolve Year 1 coordination gaps.

Introduced impact equality assessments (e.g., improved tented accommodation).
Formalized capacity-building approval processes aligned with FCDO country priorities.
innovations_attempted: Developed UK ISAR flood response module (new capability).
Piloted hybrid ISAR team configurations ("menu of options").
Solar-powered lighting and individual tents to improve deployment conditions and sustainability.
previous_recommendations_progress: EDT1 lesson on equipment ownership addressed by procuring programme-controlled assets.
INSARAG engagement formalized via IER process and working group participation.
forward_recommendations: Revise Year 2 logframe to incorporate adaptive indicators (e.g., deployment speed metrics, partner capacity-building targets).

Logframe revision to reflect new capabilities (flood module) and capacity-building targets.

Post-IER (November 2023) expansion of capacity-building to Kenya and other prioritized countries.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Accelerating Action to End Child Marriage Phase II

output_1.title: Adolescent girls have increased knowledge, skills and support structures needed to advocate for themselves, improve their status and wellbeing and are making informed decisions regarding marriage, education, sexual and reproductive health

output_2.title: Families, communities, traditional and religious leaders, and other influencers are engaged in dialogue and consensus-building on alternatives to child marriage (including education), the rights of adolescent girls, and gender equality

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted focus to 12 core countries due to financial constraints, abandoning direct support to 'Rising Stars' countries. Increased emphasis on leveraging technical resources and global advocacy beyond the 12 focus countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Performance varied significantly by country. Some (e.g., Ethiopia, Niger, Uganda, Yemen, Zambia) exceeded targets for girl engagement, while others faced challenges due to: 1) Geopolitical instability (e.g., India's Foreign Contribution Regulation Act repeal disrupted community engagement), 2) Overestimated capacity (e.g., Burkina Faso, Ethiopia set unrealistic targets), 3) Political unrest (e.g., Bangladesh elections impacted implementation).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with UNFPA-UNICEF Global Programme was effective in aggregating results across 12 countries, but challenges remained in standardizing data collection and reporting processes. Regional advisers played a key role in technical support dissemination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Programme exceeded economy targets: 60% of goods/services procured via long-term agreements (vs 50% target), 99% of UNICEF services via competitive contracts (vs 95% target), and overhead costs reduced to 14% (vs 15% target).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by: 1) Adapting to geopolitical constraints (e.g., shifting from direct funding to technical support in non-core countries), 2) Allowing country-specific approaches to life skills/CSE delivery based on cultural taboos, 3) Reallocating funds post-COVID-19 disruptions.
adaptive_management_examples: In Bangladesh, successfully integrated married girls and disabled girls into CSE programs by adapting inclusion strategies.
In India, formed coalitions of faith-based/traditional leaders at district/state levels to sustain engagement despite regulatory challenges.
Revised target-setting methodologies after 2023 underperformance to make country-level goals more realistic.

main_implementation_challenges: Geopolitical instability (e.g., conflicts, elections, regulatory changes like India's FCRA repeal) disrupted community engagement in multiple countries.
Global 'polycrisis' (COVID-19 fallout, climate shocks, economic instability) threatened progress and required resource reallocation.
Inconsistent data collection systems across countries hindered aggregated outcome measurement.
Overambitious target-setting in some countries (e.g., Burkina Faso, Ethiopia) due to misjudged capacity or delayed funding.
Cultural taboos around CSE in certain contexts required alternative approaches (e.g., life-skills education as a proxy).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Caused activity disruptions and fund reallocations, slowing progress in 2020–2022.
Climate shocks: Exacerbated poverty and displacement, increasing child marriage risks in vulnerable regions.
Global rollback on gender equality: Created resistance to normative change in some conservative contexts.
Currency/exchange rate fluctuations: Not explicitly mentioned, but financial constraints suggest potential indirect impacts.
contextual_constraints_new: Emergence of 'Rising Stars' countries (high-burden areas beyond original 12) created demand for expanded support without additional funding.
Increased global instability (e.g., conflicts in Yemen, Sahel) limited access to certain programme areas.
Regulatory changes (e.g., India's FCRA) restricted NGO operations and community engagement.
partner_relationship_issues: Varied capacity among CSOs to deliver interventions, with some countries (e.g., Zambia) lagging in inclusive approaches compared to others (e.g., Bangladesh).
Delays in fund disbursement to partners affected timely implementation in some countries.
Challenges in sustaining contributions from traditional/religious leaders after initial engagement.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited human resources stretched across 12 countries, affecting depth of interventions.
Weak data disaggregation systems in some countries (e.g., Zambia) hindered monitoring of marginalized groups.
Reduced budgets in certain countries (e.g., Burkina Faso) constrained ability to meet engagement targets.
risk_materialization: Geopolitical risks (e.g., conflicts, regulatory changes) materialized, disrupting community-level activities.
Financial risks: Budget constraints led to prioritization of core countries over expanded reach.
Programmatic risks: Overestimated capacity in some countries resulted in unmet targets for social norm change indicators.

budget_execution_vs_plan.details: Budget implementation rate met/exceeded targets. However, financial constraints limited expansion to 'Rising Stars' countries and required reprioritization within the 12 core countries.

cost_savings_examples: Leveraged existing systems (e.g., India's school infrastructure) to deliver education to 2.4M+ adolescent girls at lower marginal cost.
Used global/regional advocacy to amplify impact beyond direct funding.
efficiency.challenges: Pace of change slower than intended due to stretched resources; long-term social norm transformation requires sustained funding beyond current levels.

effectiveness.catalytic_effect: Programme influence extended beyond direct reach, with 21M girls supported and 58M community members engaged since 2016.
effectiveness.cost_effectiveness_data: Needs strengthening to secure future funding in constrained environments.

strengths: Strong procurement practices (exceeded competitive contracting targets).
Effective reallocation of funds post-COVID-19 to prioritize core activities.
weaknesses: Delayed fund disbursement in some countries affected implementation timelines.
Limited flexibility to respond to exchange rate fluctuations or inflation in certain contexts.

examples: Delivered CSE/life-skills education at scale by integrating into existing school systems (e.g., India).
Achieved 58.2% recognition of child marriage abandonment benefits (vs 57.9% target) at relatively low per-beneficiary cost.
cost_efficiency_achieved.gaps: Long-term sustainability requires deeper systems-strengthening, which may increase upfront costs.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not explicitly mentioned; programme relied primarily on FCDO funding with technical support from UNFPA-UNICEF Global Programme.

key_delivery_lessons: Country-specific adaptation is critical: One-size-fits-all approaches fail (e.g., Bangladesh's success with marginalized groups vs. Zambia's struggles).
Data disaggregation is essential for equity but requires tailored support based on local capacity.
Realistic target-setting must account for geopolitical risks and partner capacity constraints.
Leveraging existing systems (e.g., schools, faith-based networks) improves cost-efficiency and sustainability.
successful_delivery_practices: Engaging traditional/religious leaders as agents of change (e.g., India's coalitions at district/state levels).
Combining life-skills education with CSE where direct sexuality education is taboo.
Using media platforms and vocational training to shift norms and build girls' agency.
management_adaptations_made: Revised target-setting methodologies post-2023 to align with country capacities.
Increased focus on technical assistance over direct funding to stretch resources.
Prioritized depth over breadth by concentrating on 12 core countries.
innovations_attempted: Pilot programmes to include married/disabled girls in CSE (e.g., Bangladesh).
Digital platforms for dialogue sessions in contexts with restricted physical access.
Partnerships with regional advisers to disseminate global goods (e.g., toolkits, evidence briefs).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Improved data disaggregation in some countries (e.g., Bangladesh) but remains inconsistent across the programme.
Outstanding: Addition of new outcome indicator on "confidence to resist social pressure" planned for next review.
forward_recommendations: Develop standardized reporting processes to enable cross-country result aggregation.
Strengthen cost-effectiveness data collection to attract additional funding.
Prioritize institutionalized systems-strengthening for sustainability (e.g., embedding CSE in national curricula).
Expand technical assistance to high-burden countries beyond the current 12, where feasible.
Enhance risk management for geopolitical and regulatory disruptions.

strengths: Proactive adaptation to COVID-19 and regulatory changes (e.g., India's FCRA).
Diversified delivery channels (schools, media, faith-based networks) mitigated single-point failures.
weaknesses: Underestimation of geopolitical risks in initial planning (e.g., conflicts in Yemen, Sahel).
Limited contingency funding for rapid response to emerging crises.

direct.girls_supported: 7,122,689 (2023) of 7,785,315 target (B rating) for life-skills/CSE interventions

beneficiaries_reached_actual.cumulative: 21 million girls supported and 58 million community members engaged since 2016 (via UNFPA-UNICEF Global Programme).

rationale_for_ratings.outcome: Progress is evident (e.g., 63.5% recognition of child marriage abandonment benefits in 2023 vs 44% in 2019) but uneven across countries. No region is on track to meet SDG 5.3 by 2030; pace of change is 20x slower than required.
rationale_for_ratings.evidence: Strong quantitative data on reach (e.g., participant numbers) but weaker on long-term normative change. Outcome measurement challenged by inconsistent external data sources.

examples: Strengthened laws/policies in multiple countries (e.g., increased sanctions for child marriage, improved SRH access).
Formation of coalitions (e.g., India's faith-based forums) to sustain advocacy.
policy_influence_achieved.gaps: Policy implementation remains uneven; some countries lack enforcement mechanisms.

capacity_building_results.girls: 78.7% of participants demonstrated comprehensive SRH knowledge (A++ rating); 65% reported increased self-efficacy to delay marriage (A+ rating).
capacity_building_results.partners: 455 partnerships established with national/regional actors, but CSO capacity varies significantly by country.
capacity_building_results.systems: Limited evidence of institutionalized systems change (e.g., CSE in national curricula) beyond pilot programmes.

positive: Increased demand for girls' education in some communities as a byproduct of dialogue sessions.
Emergence of girl-led advocacy groups in countries like Uganda and Zambia.
negative: Backlash from conservative groups in some contexts (e.g., resistance to CSE).
Potential stigmatization of married girls in programmes focused on 'at-risk' populations.

strengths: Model replicated across 12 diverse countries with adaptable frameworks.
Technical support extended to non-core countries via regional advisers.
barriers: High upfront costs for systems-strengthening limit rapid scaling.
Cultural/regulatory barriers require context-specific adaptations.

continuation_rationale: Programme remains aligned with FCDO priorities (SDG 5.3, gender equality, adolescent rights).
Demonstrated impact on normative change (e.g., 63.5% recognition of child marriage abandonment benefits) despite challenging context.
Catalytic role in global movement to end child marriage, with 21M girls reached since 2016.
Phase III (2023–2026) designed to address Phase II gaps (e.g., deeper systems-strengthening, targeted interventions).

strengths: Strong partnership with UNFPA-UNICEF ensures technical continuity.
Flexible, country-adaptive approach improves resilience.
risks: Dependence on donor funding limits long-term sustainability; institutionalization of interventions (e.g., CSE in schools) is incomplete.
Geopolitical and economic instability may further constrain progress.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (implied by continued funding and 'A' ratings, though explicit satisfaction statement missing)
planned_adaptations_future: Prioritize depth over breadth: Focus on institutionalizing interventions in core countries.
Strengthen cost-effectiveness data to attract co-funding.
Develop sustainability plans, including systems-strengthening and demand promotion.
Enhance risk management for geopolitical disruptions (e.g., contingency funds, adaptive delivery channels).
Improve outcome measurement by standardizing reporting processes across countries.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Humanitarian Enablers Programme (HEP)

output_1.title: H2H: Quality products and services result in an engaged and diverse H2H community whose collaboration adds value beyond their individual capabilities, responding to humanitarian crises to enable quality responses

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Original Business Case proposed a competitive Call for Proposals, but ODA budget reductions in 2022 led to direct award to H2H only. Financial improvements in 2023 allowed addition of ACAPS/INFORM and INSO, plus increased H2H grant. Programme now operates with 3 partners (H2H, ACAPS/INFORM, INSO) under Accountable Grants.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All three partners (H2H, ACAPS/INFORM, INSO) met or exceeded logframe targets. H2H demonstrated rapid crisis response (e.g., Libya, Sudan floods) and system-wide engagement (e.g., OCHA IM/Analysis Function review). INSO expanded operations to 17 high-risk contexts, while ACAPS/INFORM produced analysis for 150+ countries, directly informing FCDO and donor decisions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme uses Accountable Grants with partners, with FCDO maintaining oversight through regular reporting and follow-up meetings. Coordination includes liaison with FCDO’s regional programmes (e.g., Afghanistan, Sahel) where partners like INSO receive parallel funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between HEP and FCDO’s regional programmes (e.g., Syria, Somalia) for partners like INSO. HEP team facilitates information-sharing and alignment, though no formal pooled-fund mechanism exists yet (recommended for future).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Direct awards to H2H (2022) and subsequent additions of ACAPS/INFORM and INSO (2023) were justified by their proven track records under the predecessor Humanitarian Global Services (HGS) programme. No competitive tendering due to ODA constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to ODA budget volatility, requiring closer financial monitoring. Partners report satisfaction with FCDO’s engagement (e.g., H2H’s 70% member satisfaction with transparency/processes).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Financial headroom (£5.65m remaining) enabled rapid crisis responses (e.g., Pakistan floods, Türkiye/Syria earthquake in Year 1). In Year 2, all activations were funded through core HEP budget, indicating efficient use of flexibility.
adaptive_management_examples: Allocation of £500K ‘at-risk’ funds to H2H for Lebanon response (FY 24/25) after confirmation of availability.
Adjustment of H2H’s impact weighting (down to 60%) to accommodate new partners (ACAPS/INFORM, INSO).
Development of a membership strategy for H2H (finalised Sept 2024) based on CRM data showing 70% member satisfaction.
Planned mid-term evaluation (early 2025) to assess effectiveness of FCDO’s support to humanitarian enablers.

main_implementation_challenges: ODA budget reductions (2022) forced deviation from competitive Call for Proposals, limiting partner diversity initially.
Balancing rapid crisis response (e.g., H2H Fund activations) with long-term system-strengthening goals.
Ensuring equitable access to HEP services across global south/local organisations (identified as a gap in H2H’s growth strategy).
external_factors_impact: Geopolitical crises (e.g., Sudan conflict, Libya floods) increased demand for H2H/INSO services, testing partner capacity.
Climate-related disasters (e.g., Pakistan floods, Horn of Africa drought) required rapid reallocation of H2H Fund resources.
Post-COVID humanitarian funding constraints affected partner operations in some contexts (e.g., reduced INGO presence in fragile states).
contextual_constraints_new: Need for stronger MEAL frameworks to demonstrate impact (identified as a priority for Year 3).
Gaps in representation from global south organisations in H2H’s network (addressed in forthcoming growth strategy).
Delays in finalising Due Diligence Assessments for ACAPS (ongoing as of review date).
partner_relationship_issues: Initial tensions with H2H over financial management approach (resolved via agreement to treat H2H more like a pooled fund).
Coordination challenges between INSO’s HEP-funded activities and its parallel FCDO regional programmes (mitigated via HEP team liaison).
capacity_constraints_emerged: H2H’s CRM system (Salesforce) required upskilling for members to fully utilise engagement tracking.
ACAPS/INFORM faced demand surges for climate-risk analysis, requiring additional temporary staff.
INSO’s expansion to 17 contexts stretched monitoring capacity for SLT (Saving Lives Together) implementation.
risk_materialization: Moderate risk rating maintained due to: (1) ODA budget volatility, (2) high demand for partner services in unstable contexts, (3) delays in MEAL framework finalisation.
No critical risks materialized; existing mitigation measures (e.g., financial headroom, flexible grants) proved effective.

budget_execution_vs_plan.original_plan: £15m total (incl. £7.5m headroom). Competitive Call for Proposals envisioned.
budget_execution_vs_plan.actual_execution: £9.35m allocated to 3 partners (H2H: £6.35m; INSO: £1.4m; ACAPS/INFORM: £2m) as of 2024. £5.65m headroom remains for crisis responses.
budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_justification: ODA cuts (2022) reduced initial allocations; headroom used for Pakistan/Türkiye/Syria responses in Year 1. No headroom used in Year 2 (core budget sufficed).

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Partners selected based on proven track records (HGS programme history), avoiding procurement costs. Direct awards to H2H/INSO/ACAPS justified by their unique roles.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High: Partners’ services (e.g., H2H Fund activations, INSO security analysis, ACAPS risk monitoring) directly improved humanitarian response targeting, safety, and anticipation. Evidence includes case studies from 5 crises (Sudan, Libya, etc.) and donor uptake of INFORM data.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Moderate: Small programme size (£9.35m allocated) limits economies of scale, but partners leverage existing platforms (e.g., H2H’s 65-member network, ACAPS’ 150-country coverage).
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: Exceeds original VfM proposition by achieving all 3 ‘P’s (Prioritise, Protect, Prevent) despite reduced budget. Free-to-user model maximises reach (local/international orgs).

financial_management_quality.partner_level: Strong: H2H’s CRM system (Salesforce) improved transparency (70% member satisfaction). INSO/ACAPS met financial reporting deadlines.
financial_management_quality.fcdo_level: Effective oversight with quarterly reviews, but delays in Due Diligence for ACAPS noted. Recommendation to treat H2H as a pooled fund to streamline disbursements.

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High for sector: Partners’ global public goods (e.g., INFORM Risk Index, H2H Fund) reduce duplication in humanitarian data/analysis. Cost per beneficiary not quantified but indirect benefits evident (e.g., INSO training reached 17 contexts).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: H2H Fund leveraged 69% FCDO funds (£1.26m in 2023) with 31% from other donors. INSO/ACAPS attracted parallel FCDO regional funding (e.g., Sahel, Syria).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal: H2H Fund disbursements in CHF (£1.26m equivalent in 2023) managed via multi-currency accounts. No significant FX losses reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Direct awards to proven enablers (H2H/INSO/ACAPS) achieved faster mobilisation than competitive processes, but limited new entrants.
Flexible headroom (£7.5m) was critical for rapid crisis responses (e.g., Pakistan floods), but underused in Year 2 due to core budget sufficiency.
H2H’s pooled-fund model (recommended for adoption) demonstrated efficiency in channelling resources to niche service providers.
successful_delivery_practices: H2H’s case study comparisons (5 crises) provided actionable lessons for future activations (e.g., timeliness of data products in Sudan).
INSO’s SLT framework improved NGO security coordination in 17 contexts, with operational guidelines now being formalised.
ACAPS’ integration of climate risk data into INFORM tools enhanced crisis anticipation (e.g., Horn of Africa drought warnings).
management_adaptations_made: Impact weighting adjusted for H2H (down to 60%) to reflect expanded partner portfolio.
MEAL consultant hired to strengthen outcome monitoring (logframes under review Q3 2024).
Risk Appetite Statement to be drafted to clarify FCDO’s tolerance for innovative approaches (e.g., H2H’s experimental services).
innovations_attempted: H2H’s CRM system (Salesforce) improved member engagement tracking, enabling data-driven strategy development.
ACAPS’ ‘innovative component’ piloting new data visualisation tools to improve access negotiations in conflict zones.
INSO’s expansion into climate-security analysis (linking INFORM data with SLT frameworks).
previous_recommendations_progress: 2023 AR recommendation to diversify partners implemented via addition of ACAPS/INFORM and INSO.
Call for improved MEAL partially addressed (consultant hired; frameworks under revision).
Pooled-fund recommendation for H2H pending FCDO approval (planned for FY 24/25).
forward_recommendations: Finalise HEP’s overarching results framework (Q3 2024) to better capture systemic impact.
Conduct mid-term evaluation (early 2025) to assess progress toward Humanitarian Framework outcomes.
Develop H2H’s global south engagement strategy to address representation gaps.
Explore co-funding mechanisms to reduce reliance on FCDO headroom for crisis responses.

risk_management_effectiveness.planned_risks: Moderate risk rating justified by ODA volatility and high-demand contexts. Mitigation via headroom and flexible grants proved effective.
risk_management_effectiveness.unplanned_risks: No major unplanned risks materialized. Minor delays in Due Diligence (ACAPS) addressed via tracking system.
risk_management_effectiveness.adaptive_responses: Rapid reallocation of H2H Fund to Sudan/Libya crises demonstrated agility. Risk Appetite Statement to formalise adaptive approaches.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: H2H: 65 member organisations; INSO: 17 contexts (NGOs/UN agencies); ACAPS: 150+ countries (humanitarian actors).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Millions of crisis-affected people via improved aid targeting (e.g., H2H’s Sudan response reached 2.5m+ indirectly).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Exceeded: All partners met logframe targets; H2H Fund activated in 5 crises (vs planned 3).

policy_influence_achieved: H2H contributed to OCHA’s IM/Analysis Function review and Humanitarian Reform discussions.
INFORM data influenced FCDO/ECHO/BHA allocation decisions (e.g., climate-risk funding prioritisation).
INSO’s SLT framework adopted by NGOs in Syria/Somalia for security coordination.
capacity_building_results: H2H’s CRM training improved member organisations’ engagement (70% satisfaction).
INSO’s security training reached 1,200+ aid workers in 2023–24.
ACAPS’ data literacy workshops enhanced local NGOs’ use of risk analysis tools (e.g., in Horn of Africa).
unintended_consequences: Positive: H2H’s Sudan response unexpectedly improved local NGO coordination, now scaled to Libya.
Negative: Limited global south representation in H2H’s network (being addressed via growth strategy).
scalability_evidence: H2H Fund model replicated for Lebanon response (£500K allocation in FY 24/25).
INSO’s SLT framework being adapted for use in new contexts (e.g., Sahel).
ACAPS’ climate-risk tools integrated into UN’s Early Warnings for All initiative.

continuation_rationale: Consistent ‘A’ performance scores (2023–24) with high partner delivery and systemic impact.
Alignment with FCDO’s Humanitarian Framework priorities (Prioritise/Protect/Prevent) remains strong.
Financial headroom (£5.65m) enables further crisis responses and partner expansion.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High: Accountable Grants with proven partners (H2H/INSO/ACAPS) provide stability. Pooled-fund approach for H2H would enhance efficiency.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Adopt pooled-fund model for H2H to streamline crisis disbursements.
Expand H2H’s global south membership via targeted outreach (strategy in development).
Strengthen MEAL to capture long-term systemic impact (mid-term evaluation planned for 2025).
Explore co-funding with other donors to reduce FCDO headroom reliance.

funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: High (designed for agile, anticipatory, and under-the-radar crisis responses with no rigid geographic or thematic restrictions)
