funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Mixed (Pooled fund with **increased direct funding to LNNGOs**—emerging evidence shows 2023/24 shift toward LNNGO-led projects)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £18.38 million disbursed in 2023/24 (vs £19.79m in Year 1), reaching **1,950,946 people** (83% of Year 2 target) at **£9.42 per person** (11% cost increase vs baseline). Cumulative reach: 27.5M people across 80 countries since 2014
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: **70% of projects funded within 75 hours** (vs 72-hour target); 81% initiated within 7 days. **Guided spend limits introduced** (Oct 2023: monthly; Mar 2024: rota-specific) to manage disbursement capacity issues. **Anticipatory action increased to 22% of alerts** (vs 20-25% target)
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High (utilized for: 1) **geographic expansion** (44 countries in 2023/24 vs 54 in Year 1); 2) **LNNGO direct funding**; 3) **adaptive responses to COVID/conflict shocks**). **No formal budget revisions** but cost per person rose 11% (£8.45 → £9.42)

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: **Enhanced local governance**: Allocation Committees now include **>50% LNNGO representation** (up from baseline). **New MEAL team** provides real-time monitoring + learning dissemination. **No structural changes** to Save the Children UK’s fund manager role
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: **Increased**: 1) **Monthly guided spend limits** (since Oct 2023); 2) **Rota-specific spend guidance** (Mar 2024); 3) **Post-distribution surveys** for all projects. **No embedded FCDO advisors** but **more frequent Start Network reporting** to FCDO on localisation metrics
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: **Slower in complex contexts**: 36% of activations funded within 72 hours (vs 65-70% target) due to **risk mitigation prioritization**. **Anticipatory alerts (22%)** required additional validation. **No changes to collaborative model** but **strengthened LNNGO voting power** in committees

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: **Expanded LNNGO engagement**: 92% of projects involved LNNGOs in implementation (vs 79% in design). **Hub model scaled** (regional LNNGO clusters) to improve geographic coverage. **No partner removals** but **increased capacity-building** for LNNGOs
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Mixed: **LNNGOs (increased direct funding)**, INGOs (technical support), and **new women-led orgs** (tracked since 2023). **No private sector or multilateral partners** added

partner_roles_actual.LNNGOs: **Direct implementation (92% of projects)**, needs assessment (97% community involvement), and AAP leadership

consortium_actual.consortium_structure_actual: **Decentralized further**: **Regional LNNGO hubs expanded** (e.g., Africa, Asia) to improve local decision-making. **No changes to Save the Children UK’s fund manager role** but **increased LNNGO representation in governance**
consortium_actual.lead_partner_actual: Save the Children UK (unchanged) + **rotational LNNGO leadership in Allocation Committees** (now >50% LNNGO votes)
consortium_actual.consortium_governance_actual: **Stronger LNNGO influence**: 1) **Hubs formalized** for regional coordination; 2) **ICR sharing reviewed** to support LNNGO sustainability; 3) **AAP standards institutionalized** (97% community involvement in needs assessments)

substantive_changes_made: **Partner role shifts**: INGOs transitioned from co-implementation to **technical support/capacity-building** to prioritize LNNGO leadership
**Consortium governance**: LNNGO representation in Allocation Committees **increased to >50%**, with formalized regional hubs for decentralized decision-making
**Disbursement safeguards**: Introduced **guided spend limits** (monthly/rota-specific) to address 2023 capacity issues, balancing speed with financial sustainability
**Anticipatory action scaling**: Increased from 20% to **22% of alerts**, with new training for members on early warning systems (linked to FOREWARN network)

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: **No formal budget revision**, but **11% higher cost per person** (£8.45 → £9.42) due to inflation/complex contexts. **£18.38m disbursed in 2023/24** (vs £19.79m in Year 1)
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: **Geographic scope fluctuated**: 44 countries in 2023/24 (vs 54 in Year 1) but **cumulative reach expanded to 80 countries** since 2014. **No contraction**—focus shifted to **deeper LNNGO engagement** in existing locations
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: **Increased direct funding to LNNGOs** (evidence from 2023/24 projects) and **anticipatory action funding** (22% of alerts). **No shift away from pooled mechanism**

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: **Informal updates**: Assumptions on **LNNGO capacity** and **speed of response** adjusted based on 2023/24 learning (e.g., 36% 72-hour funding initiation vs 65-70% target), but **no formal ToC revision**

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: **No restructuring**, but **LNNGO governance power strengthened** via Allocation Committee representation (>50%) and hub expansion

programme_metadata.programme_title: Start Fund III - a global response mechanism for providing lifesaving humanitarian assistance through NGOs

output_1.title: Quality and timely crisis alerts are raised, which align with the Start Fund niche. Fund decision-making is collaborative and informed by humanitarian expertise and local knowledge.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Introduction of guided spend mechanisms (monthly and rota-specific) to manage disbursement capacity, implemented in October 2023 and March 2024 respectively. These were not part of the original business case but were introduced to address recurring issues of low disbursement capacity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated increased cautiousness in alert activation due to guided spend introductions, with 69% activation rate (82/118 alerts) compared to historical performance. Local and National NGOs (LNNGOs) showed high involvement in needs assessment (97%), design (79%), and implementation (92%) of responses, exceeding expectations for locally-led action.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Start Fund Allocation Committee and governance bodies operated as planned, with additional adaptive measures such as guided spend introductions to improve financial management. The MEAL (Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability, and Learning) team played an expanded role in upskilling partners and disseminating learning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination was effective within the Start Network, with pooled funding reducing duplicative competition. However, challenges remained in aligning global early warning systems (e.g., FOREWARN) with local responder needs, requiring better integration of risk analysis tools.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was efficient in crisis responses, with established suppliers offering discounts and local partners enabling access to hard-to-reach communities. Some delays occurred in complex contexts, balancing speed with risk mitigation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than planned due to the need to manage guided spend compliance and monitor LNNGO capacity. The MEAL team’s expanded role increased oversight but also supported partner performance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was used to introduce guided spend mechanisms and adapt to disbursement challenges. The fund also prioritized anticipatory action (22% of activated alerts) and locally-led responses, though geographic coverage of LNNGOs remained a constraint.
adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of monthly and rota-specific guided spend to address low disbursement capacity (October 2023 and March 2024).
Expansion of Hubs of LNNGOs and capacity-building initiatives to increase locally-led responses.
Review of Indirect Cost Recovery (ICR) sharing to improve financial sustainability for LNNGOs.
Adaptation of response pace in complex contexts to prioritize risk mitigation over speed.

main_implementation_challenges: Decline in the percentage of "under-the-radar" crisis alerts (45% in 2023/24 vs. 57% in 2022), linked to increased humanitarian needs and funding gaps leading to broader classification of alerts as "gap-filling."
Slower response times in complex operating contexts, with only 36% of activations initiating funding within 72 hours (though 70% within 75 hours).
Limited geographic coverage of LNNGO membership, constraining the fund’s ability to deliver locally-led responses in all regions.
Balancing speed of response with risk management, particularly in high-risk environments.
external_factors_impact: Global increase in humanitarian needs (300 million people affected by crises in 2024) exacerbated funding gaps for small-scale crises, aligning with the Start Fund’s niche but increasing pressure on resources.
Inflation and currency fluctuations (not explicitly detailed but implied in cost efficiency discussions).
Political and access constraints in some crisis contexts, slowing response implementation.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated cautiousness among members post-2023 due to disbursement capacity issues, leading to lower alert activation rates.
Need for greater integration of gender-sensitive and gender-transformative principles in alert cycles, identified as a gap during implementation.
Challenges in tracking and articulating the Start Fund’s broader systemic impact on the humanitarian sector, despite innovative delivery.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between international and local partners over Indirect Cost Recovery (ICR) sharing, with calls for standardized and mandatory ICR policies to improve LNNGO sustainability.
Variability in LNNGO capacity across regions, requiring tailored support to ensure effective participation in decision-making and response implementation.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity among some LNNGOs to lead responses in new geographic areas, hindering expansion of locally-led action.
Need for additional training and resources to enable anticipatory action, particularly in utilizing early warning systems and forecasting tools.
MEAL team capacity stretched due to increased oversight demands, though this was mitigated by support from Start Network’s Evidence and Learning team.
risk_materialization: Recurring low disbursement capacity at the end of 2023, prompting the introduction of guided spend mechanisms.
Slower-than-targeted response times in complex contexts, though this was a deliberate risk mitigation trade-off.
Funding gaps for small-scale crises became more pronounced, aligning with the Start Fund’s niche but increasing operational pressure.

budget_execution_vs_plan.disbursement_performance: £18,384,857.95 disbursed in 2023/24 (vs. £19,786,000 in 2022/23), reaching 1,950,946 people at a mean cost of £9.42 per person (up from £8.45 in 2022/23). Budget execution was constrained by guided spend introductions but aligned with risk management priorities.
budget_execution_vs_plan.underspend_overspend: No explicit underspend/overspend reported, but disbursement pace was managed through guided spend to avoid year-end capacity issues.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Pooled funding reduced donor reporting burdens and transaction costs. Most donors accepted Start Network/Save the Children UK reports as primary reporting, improving efficiency.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: 70% of projects received funding within 75 hours (vs. 72-hour target), and 81% initiated within 7 days. Anticipatory action improved efficiency by reducing long-term humanitarian costs.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High involvement of LNNGOs (92% in implementation) and affected communities (97% in needs assessment) improved response relevance. MEAL team monitoring ensured learning was disseminated for continuous improvement.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Direct funding to LNNGOs increased, aligning with localization commitments. Gender and age disaggregation showed balanced reach (52% female, 48% male; 41% children).
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: VFM exceeded projections due to innovative procurement (e.g., supplier discounts), local partner access to hard-to-reach areas, and reduced duplicative competition through pooled funding.

financial_management_quality.partner_compliance: Generally strong, with guided spend mechanisms introduced to address disbursement challenges. LNNGOs required additional support for ICR management.
financial_management_quality.transparency: High, with detailed financial reporting and audited accounts shared with donors. Start Network’s financial oversight was robust, though ICR policies required standardization.

cost_efficiency_achieved.per_person_cost: £9.42 per person reached in 2023/24 (up from £8.45 in 2022/23), attributed to higher proportions of anticipatory action and complex contexts.
cost_efficiency_achieved.administrative_costs: Pooled fund mechanism reduced administrative overheads. Indirect costs were managed through ICR sharing, though this required adaptation.
cost_efficiency_achieved.savings_realized: Savings achieved through established supplier discounts, local procurement, and reduced bidding burdens. Early warning systems improved efficiency by preventing crisis escalation.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized as planned, with £36,109,824.70 disbursed from multiple donors since the start of the business case (October 2022). No specific co-funding shortfalls reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Guided spend mechanisms effectively mitigated disbursement capacity risks but required careful communication to avoid over-caution among members.
Locally-led responses (92% implementation by LNNGOs) demonstrated higher relevance and efficiency, though geographic coverage gaps persisted.
Anticipatory action (22% of alerts) reduced long-term costs but needed stronger integration with early warning systems (e.g., FOREWARN).
Balancing speed and risk in complex contexts was critical; slower responses were justified by risk mitigation needs.
successful_delivery_practices: High community involvement in needs assessment (97%) and design (79%) improved response appropriateness.
Pooled funding reduced administrative burdens and enabled rapid disbursement (70% within 75 hours).
Capacity-building for LNNGOs (e.g., Hubs expansion) increased locally-led action, though further geographic scaling is needed.
MEAL team’s learning dissemination supported continuous improvement across responses.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced guided spend (monthly and rota-specific) to manage disbursement risks.
Expanded MEAL team oversight to monitor LNNGO performance and disseminate learning.
Prioritized gender-sensitive and anticipatory action training for members.
Reviewed ICR sharing policies to improve LNNGO financial sustainability.
innovations_attempted: Forecast-based financing (22% anticipatory alerts) to preempt crises.
Hubs of LNNGOs model to decentralize decision-making and improve local ownership.
Standardized supplier discounts and local procurement to reduce costs.
Integration of AAP (Accountability to Affected Populations) metrics into response design.
previous_recommendations_progress: Progressed on locally-led action (LNNGO involvement increased) but geographic gaps remain.
Improved anticipatory action (22% of alerts) though further integration with early warning systems is needed.
Enhanced AAP practices (97% community involvement in needs assessment) but gender-transformative principles require deeper integration.
ICR sharing policies under review to address LNNGO sustainability concerns.
forward_recommendations: Continue streamlining processes to improve response speed while maintaining risk management in complex contexts.
Expand LNNGO geographic coverage to increase locally-led responses, particularly in underrepresented regions.
Strengthen integration with global early warning systems (e.g., FOREWARN) to enhance anticipatory action.
Finalize and implement standardized ICR policies to improve LNNGO financial sustainability.
Develop quantitative/qualitative indicators to better evidence systemic impact and intervention quality.
Deepening gender-sensitive and transformative approaches throughout the alert cycle.

risk_management_effectiveness.proactive_risks: Guided spend mechanisms successfully addressed disbursement capacity risks. Anticipatory action mitigated crisis escalation risks.
risk_management_effectiveness.reactive_risks: Slower responses in complex contexts were a deliberate risk trade-off, demonstrating adaptive management.
risk_management_effectiveness.emerging_risks: Geographic gaps in LNNGO coverage and gender-transformative principles remain areas for improvement.
risk_management_effectiveness.overall_assessment: Risk management was effective, with adaptive measures (e.g., guided spend, MEAL oversight) balancing innovation with accountability. However, systemic risks (e.g., funding gaps for small-scale crises) persist.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.trend: Exceeded annual target by 36% (1,950,946 vs. 1,428,319), with cumulative reach of 27.5 million since inception.

policy_influence_achieved: Demonstrated the viability of locally-led, rapid-response funding mechanisms, influencing donor approaches to small-scale crises.
Contributed to sectoral commitments on localization (e.g., increased direct funding to LNNGOs).
Evidence from anticipatory action (22% of alerts) informed discussions on forecast-based financing in humanitarian systems.
capacity_building_results: Expanded LNNGO membership and Hubs improved local response capacity, with 92% of implementations led by LNNGOs.
Training on anticipatory action and early warning systems enhanced partner skills, though geographic coverage gaps remain.
MEAL team support upskilled partners in monitoring and learning, contributing to continuous improvement.

positive: Increased cautiousness among members (due to guided spend) improved financial sustainability but temporarily reduced alert activation rates.
High community involvement (97% in needs assessment) strengthened trust in local responders, with potential long-term benefits for humanitarian access.
negative: Guided spend introductions initially caused confusion, leading to a temporary dip in alert activations (69% vs. historical rates).
Focus on speed and localization in some contexts risked overlooking gender-transformative principles, requiring corrective action.

scalability_evidence: The Start Fund model has been replicated in other contexts (e.g., Start Ready for climate crises), demonstrating scalability.
Pooled funding and locally-led approaches are adaptable to different crises, though geographic LNNGO coverage limits immediate scalability.
Anticipatory action frameworks (e.g., FOREWARN integration) provide a template for other funds to adopt forecast-based financing.

continuation_rationale: The Start Fund remains highly relevant in addressing small-scale, underfunded crises, with demonstrated impact (27.5 million beneficiaries cumulatively).
Strong performance in locally-led responses (92% implementation by LNNGOs) and anticipatory action (22% of alerts) aligns with FCDO priorities.
Value for money is evident through efficient disbursement (70% within 75 hours) and cost-effective reach (£9.42 per person).
Adaptive management (e.g., guided spend, capacity-building) has successfully addressed operational challenges.

strengths: Pooled funding mechanism reduces donor burdens and enables rapid responses.
Locally-led model aligns with sectoral trends and improves relevance.
Strong MEAL and learning systems support continuous improvement.
risks: Dependence on LNNGO capacity and geographic coverage may limit scalability in some regions.
Sustaining anticipatory action requires ongoing investment in early warning systems.
Guided spend mechanisms need standardization to avoid over-caution in alert activations.
delivery_model_sustainability.overall: The delivery model is sustainable long-term with minor adaptations (e.g., ICR policies, LNNGO expansion).

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize and implement standardized ICR sharing policies to improve LNNGO financial sustainability.
Expand LNNGO Hubs to increase geographic coverage and locally-led responses.
Strengthen integration with global early warning systems (e.g., FOREWARN) to enhance anticipatory action.
Develop indicators to better evidence systemic impact and intervention quality for donors.
Deepening gender-transformative approaches in alert cycles and response design.
Explore opportunities to reduce per-person costs (currently £9.42) through further efficiencies in procurement and local partnerships.

output_1.title: FCDO, governments and other organisations have increased capacity and evidence to take action on nutrition across different sectors, including in policy and investments

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transition from EACDS2 contract (expiring Feb 2026) to GDD framework pending 2025 Spending Review outcome; potential short overlap period for handover. Original mid-term review postponed due to budget uncertainties.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: DAI-led consortium (with NutritionWorks, Options, Natural Resources Institute) exceeded expectations in TA delivery. delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme adapted to UK government election and ODA budget cuts by maintaining flexibility. Governance structures remained stable despite external shocks, with strong coordination between TA Facility, ATNi, and GNR components.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective cross-component coordination (TA Facility, ATNi, GNR) despite funding uncertainties. delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement under EACDS2 extended to Feb 2026 to avoid service gaps; transition to GDD framework delayed by Spending Review timelines. Initial procurement for TA Facility completed in Dec 2023 with rapid mobilisation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to ODA budget volatility and partner funding pauses. Adaptive management prioritised to mitigate risks from external factors (e.g., Ukraine/Gaza conflicts, global food crises).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged built-in flexibility to: 1) Extend contracts during funding pauses; 2) Reallocate resources to high-priority areas (e.g., Global Compact launch); 3) Adapt TA focus to emerging needs (e.g., climate-nutrition integration).

output_1.title: Disbursement of Humanitarian Cash Transfers to the most vulnerable Refugees in Jordan

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme expanded from £65m to £95m in May 2023 via a business case addendum, integrating four new humanitarian components (cash assistance via WFP/UNHCR and refugee economic inclusion research). Original social protection focus (Estidama++, Shamil TA) retained but now complemented by humanitarian cash transfers and technical deployments to UNHCR.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: WFP and UNHCR met cash transfer targets (219,976 refugees reached) despite funding shortfalls requiring reduced transfer values (JOD10 standard, JOD15 for most vulnerable). Shamil TA facility (led by Development Pathways) and ILO technical support became operational and exceeded inception milestones. Social Security Corporation (SSC) faced challenges with Estidama++ participant attrition and new social security cost structures.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO oversight includes quarterly programme board meetings, bi-weekly catch-ups, and narrative/financial reporting reviews. Governance adapted to include humanitarian partners (WFP/UNHCR) alongside original GoJ-focused structures. Coordination with British Embassy’s Humanitarian Inclusion Protection (HIP) team enhanced to align with broader UK objectives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between social protection (GoJ/SSC) and humanitarian components (WFP/UNHCR), though funding volatility for refugees created tensions. Programme boards and regular catch-ups facilitated adaptive management, e.g., adjusting cash transfer values in response to donor shortfalls.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Single £3.5m payment to WFP disbursed efficiently. Procurement for technical experts deployed to UNHCR progressed as planned. No major procurement delays reported, though currency exchange risks (JOD/GBP) monitored closely.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to integration of humanitarian components and need to manage risks from regional instability (e.g., Gaza crisis). FCDO increased engagement with UN agencies to ensure alignment with social protection goals.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to reallocate funds to humanitarian cash transfers and adjust transfer values (JOD10/JOD15 tiers) in response to refugee vulnerability assessments. Adaptive management used to address SSC’s legislative changes impacting Estidama++ costs.
adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of tiered cash transfer values (JOD10 standard, JOD15 for most vulnerable) to stretch limited funds further.
Rapid operationalization of Shamil TA facility and ILO support despite delayed inception.
Response to SSC’s January 2023 legislative changes by reassessing Estidama++ subsidy mechanisms.
Integration of refugee economic inclusion research to inform future policy adjustments.

main_implementation_challenges: Funding shortfalls for refugee cash assistance (WFP caseload reduced from 450,000 to 410,000 refugees due to donor cuts).
Estidama++ participant attrition and low transition rates to regular social security.
SSC’s legislative changes (January 2023) increased social security costs, impacting programme budget.
Regional instability (e.g., Gaza crisis) diverted humanitarian funding and increased refugee vulnerability.
Currency exchange fluctuations affecting programme costs in JOD.
external_factors_impact: Reduction in overall humanitarian donor financing for Syrian refugees in Jordan, limiting programme scope.
Macroeconomic pressures in Jordan (shrinking household incomes, high unemployment) exacerbating demand for social protection.
Gaza crisis creating competing priorities for UK aid and humanitarian partners.
Inflation and rising costs of social security/work permits affecting programme sustainability.
contextual_constraints_new: SSC’s abolition of tranche system for social security coverage (now 100% coverage only), increasing costs for self-employed workers.
New targeting model by WFP/UNHCR prioritizing households with severe food insecurity, reducing overall caseload but increasing per-beneficiary costs.
Debt levels among refugees increased by 25% (used for food/rent), signaling deeper vulnerability than anticipated.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between GoJ’s social protection priorities and humanitarian partners’ refugee-focused mandates.
Delays in SSC’s data-sharing for Estidama++ monitoring, hindering adaptive management.
UNHCR’s cash programme faced implementation lags due to funding uncertainty.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited SSC capacity to manage Estidama++ participant transitions to regular social security.
GoJ’s policy discussions on sustainable subsidy mechanisms slowed by bureaucratic processes.
FCDO’s need to balance oversight of expanded programme scope (8 components) with existing resources.
risk_materialization: Major: Funding shortfalls for refugee assistance (materialized as predicted in risk register).
Major: Regional instability (Gaza) diverting attention/resources (partially mitigated via adaptive management).
Moderate: SSC legislative changes increasing costs (mitigated through programme adjustments).
Minor: Delayed inception of Shamil TA facility (resolved by March 2024).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for social protection components (Estidama++, Shamil, ILO). Humanitarian components (WFP/UNHCR) faced under-spend risks due to donor funding volatility, but £3.5m disbursed as planned. Overall budget execution aligned with revised £95m ceiling post-addendum.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Preliminary analysis indicates good VfM, particularly for Estidama++ (10,416 participants enrolled, exceeding non-Jordanian refugee targets) and cash transfers (219,976 refugees reached). VfM framework under refinement to capture outcome-level impacts beyond outputs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong for FCDO-managed components (quarterly reviews, bi-weekly catch-ups). WFP/UNHCR financial reporting met standards, though funding gaps required adaptive disbursement strategies (e.g., tiered transfer values).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High for cash transfers (leveraged existing WFP/UNHCR systems). Estidama++ costs increased due to SSC legislative changes, but participant outreach exceeded targets. Technical assistance (Shamil/ILO) delivered within budget.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: No co-funding materialized beyond UK’s £95m commitment. Potential future co-funding for sustainable social security mechanisms under discussion with GoJ/donors.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: JOD/GBP fluctuations monitored but no significant adverse impacts reported. Programme budget in GBP provided buffer against exchange rate risks.

key_delivery_lessons: Integrating humanitarian and social protection components requires flexible funding mechanisms to respond to donor volatility.
Tiered cash transfer models (JOD10/JOD15) can optimize limited resources while targeting most vulnerable.
Early engagement with GoJ on legislative changes (e.g., SSC’s 100% coverage rule) is critical to mitigate cost impacts.
Demand-led technical assistance (Shamil) is effective but requires clear GoJ ownership for sustainability.
successful_delivery_practices: Quarterly programme boards + bi-weekly catch-ups enabled rapid adaptive management (e.g., adjusting cash transfer values).

forward_recommendations: Complete Estidama++ attrition analysis by September 2024 to inform subsidy mechanism design.
Develop sustainable social security contribution subsidy model with GoJ by 2025, led by ILO/FCDO.
Allocate 2025/26–2026/27 financial assistance budget strategically post-Estidama++ conclusion.

Advocate for sustained refugee cash assistance despite competing humanitarian priorities (e.g., Gaza).

Early results demonstrate effectiveness (Estidama++ enrollment, refugee cash assistance delivery).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: No major changes from original business case; budget support via quarterly disbursements maintained. Additional £550k required due to unanticipated shipping and medical/legal costs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: GPI managed budget with FCDO oversight, but faced challenges in health/legal spend control. PIO provided monthly expenditure reports and quarterly cost projections. Staffing gaps on Pitcairn and within FCDO team caused delays in milestone agreements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Managed via MoU between FCDO and GPI, with oversight from Pitcairn Administrator, Deputy Governor (NZ), and Governor’s Office. Interim programme manager led review due to staffing transitions.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: New shipping contract implemented (key cost driver). Fiduciary Risk Assessment (FRA) contractor selected via EACDS Framework; ToRs finalized slightly delayed but contract signed before June 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to budget overruns (medical/legal/shipping). Monthly expenditure reports and quarterly projections introduced to tighten financial control.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Budget flexibility used to cover unplanned costs (£550k uplift). Measures introduced to rationalize future spend, particularly in health and legal areas.
adaptive_management_examples: Additional funds allocated mid-year to cover shipping contract and medical costs.
Accelerated planning for FRA to address fiduciary risks.
Starlink terminal installation planned to improve telemedicine and reduce off-island medical referrals.
Review of logframe milestones post-first-year lessons to align with realistic delivery capacities.

main_implementation_challenges: Unanticipated cost overruns in shipping (new contract) and medical/legal expenditures, requiring mid-year budget adjustments.
Staff shortages on Pitcairn (e.g., Family and Community Advisor departure in February) and within FCDO team, delaying milestone agreements.
Delayed finalization of FRA Terms of Reference, though contract was later secured.
Exchange rate fluctuations (GBP-NZD) required close monitoring to ensure "reasonable assistance needs" were met.
external_factors_impact: Remoteness of Pitcairn Islands drove disproportionately high per-capita costs for essential services (e.g., shipping, medical evacuations).
No major external shocks (e.g., COVID-19, natural disasters) reported, but vulnerability to fuel price stability and vessel weather dependencies noted.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-expected shipping contract costs (lifeline for island access).
Increased off-island medical referrals and legal expenses beyond initial forecasts.
Limited local capacity to manage complex financial controls, necessitating FCDO oversight.
partner_relationship_issues: No major conflicts, but GPI’s financial management capacity required additional FCDO support (e.g., quarterly disbursements, expenditure reporting).
Delays in FRA preparation due to coordination between Pitcairn, NZ Governor’s Office, and FCDO.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GPI’s ability to attract/retain technical professionals (e.g., FCA position vacancy post-February).
Limited on-island administrative capacity to implement audited statement recommendations promptly.
FCDO team staffing gaps affected timely logframe reviews and milestone setting.
risk_materialization: Moderate fiduciary risks (stable trajectory) materialized in health/legal spend overruns.
Minor corruption risk (stable), with no evidence of misconduct but requiring ongoing FRA monitoring.
Assumption of "no more than one emergency medivac/year" tested but not breached; costs remained within revised budget.

budget_execution_vs_plan.actual_spend: Exceeded by £550k due to shipping/medical/legal costs; not fully utilized.
budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_explanation: Unforeseen shipping contract costs and higher medical referrals. Additional funds approved mid-year.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Costs high due to remoteness, but no evidence of waste. Quarterly disbursements introduced to improve control.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Budget support remains most efficient mechanism for Pitcairn’s needs, despite high per-capita costs.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Critical services (sea access, health, education) maintained; 100% achievement on key output indicators (e.g., diabetes check-ups, schooling).
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Funds targeted to essential services for all islanders, aligning with UK’s reasonable assistance obligations.
value_for_money_assessment.overall_vfm: Continues to represent VfM as the most cost-effective option for meeting Pitcairn’s obligations, though cost drivers (shipping, health) require ongoing management.

financial_management_quality.gioverning_body: GPI managed funds with FCDO oversight; monthly expenditure reports and quarterly projections introduced.
financial_management_quality.internal_controls: Audited statements and FRA processes in place, but implementation of recommendations lagged. New FRA planned for 2024/25 to strengthen controls.
financial_management_quality.transparency: Disbursements tracked via MoU; exchange rate monitoring ensured alignment with "reasonable needs" principle.

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High costs inherent to remoteness, but no evidence of inefficiency. Measures to rationalize health/legal spend planned for 2024/25 (e.g., telemedicine via Starlink).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: GPI revenues (£0.435m) contributed as planned. No additional co-funding materialized; opportunities to explore Darwin Plus/Essential Equipment funds flagged for future.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: GBP-NZD fluctuations monitored closely; no significant adverse impacts reported, but required active management to maintain service levels.

key_delivery_lessons: Quarterly disbursements and monthly reporting improved financial oversight but required additional FCDO capacity.
Remoteness-driven costs (e.g., shipping) must be factored into long-term budgeting with contingency buffers.
Local capacity constraints necessitate simplified milestones and qualitative targets (e.g., for public service provision).
successful_delivery_practices: Maintenance of 100% achievement on health/education indicators despite challenges.
Rapid contract finalization for FRA despite initial delays.
Collaborative milestone reviews with Pitcairn Administrator/Governor’s Office to align expectations.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced tighter financial controls (monthly reports, quarterly projections) post-budget overruns.
Planned recruitment of dedicated Programme Responsible Officer to address staffing gaps.
Accelerated FRA process to preempt fiduciary risks.
innovations_attempted: Starlink terminal installation to reduce medical referral costs via telemedicine.
Exploration of alternative funding streams (Darwin Plus, Essential Equipment).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on FRA recommendations; full implementation deferred to post-2024 FRA.
Health/legal spend rationalization measures initiated but not yet fully realized.
forward_recommendations: Review and simplify logframe milestones for 2024/25 to reflect realistic capacities.
Strengthen GPI’s budget management via FRA findings and targeted technical assistance.
Monitor impact of telemedicine/Starlink on reducing off-island medical costs.
Conduct annual shipping contract cost-benefit analysis to optimize sea access spend.
Explore co-funding opportunities with Darwin Plus/Essential Equipment programmes.

risk_management_effectiveness.identification: Key risks (fiduciary, shipping costs, health spend) identified and monitored quarterly.
risk_management_effectiveness.mitigation: Moderate success: budget uplifts addressed immediate risks, but structural issues (e.g., local capacity) persist.
risk_management_effectiveness.adaptability: Responsive to emerging risks (e.g., FRA acceleration, Starlink investment), but proactive measures (e.g., milestone simplification) needed.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 100% of residents received essential services (health, education, sea access).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.evidence: 100% diabetes check-ups, 100% school-age children educated off-island, 4 expatriate posts filled (police, doctor, teacher, FCA until Feb).

policy_influence_achieved.description: Programme aligns with UK’s Overseas Territories White Paper (2012), NSC Strategy (2019), and International Development Strategy (2022). No direct policy changes reported, but supports UK’s UN Charter obligations.
policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Medium (alignment documented but no new policies created).

capacity_building_results.description: Limited progress: FRA recommendations partially implemented; GPI’s financial management capacity remains dependent on FCDO oversight. Technical cooperation posts (e.g., FCA) filled but turnover risks persist.
capacity_building_results.evidence: Weak (no quantitative metrics; qualitative improvements noted).

positive: Starlink investment may improve telemedicine access beyond initial health goals.
Shipping subsidy indirectly supports tourism (island’s primary income source).
negative: Dependence on expatriate professionals may delay local capacity development.
Budget overruns risk reducing flexibility for future non-essential investments.

scalability_evidence.description: Model is highly context-specific (remote, small population); limited scalability to other territories. However, lessons on budget support for remote islands may inform similar programmes (e.g., Tristan da Cunha).
scalability_evidence.evidence: Weak (no documented scalability efforts).

continuation_rationale.justification: Programme is critical to meeting UK’s legal obligations to Pitcairn and ensuring essential services (health, education, sea access). No alternative mechanisms exist to deliver these outcomes cost-effectively.
continuation_rationale.evidence: High achievement on output indicators (A scores across all outputs), alignment with UK strategic priorities, and lack of viable exit strategy given Pitcairn’s remoteness.

programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (for maintaining essential services), but Medium for long-term self-sufficiency goals.

delivery_model_sustainability.adaptations_needed: Gradual reduction in budget support dependency via economic diversification (e.g., tourism, environmental funding) and capacity building.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (programme meets core objectives, though financial management requires strengthening).
planned_adaptations_future: Strengthen GPI’s financial controls via FRA recommendations (2024/25).
Explore co-funding with Darwin Plus/Essential Equipment to reduce FCDO burden.
Investigate telemedicine expansion to cut health referral costs.
Review shipping contract costs annually to optimize spend.
Recruit dedicated Programme Responsible Officer to improve oversight.

output_1.title: Research and learning are used to shape dialogue on addressing corruption and conflict, promoting collaboration and/or greater accountability.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Adopted adaptive, issue-based project approaches to navigate political constraints; shifted focus to shared incentives across service delivery sectors rather than direct political party engagement. partner_performance_reality.TIB: Moderately exceeded expectations in advocacy (54/38 targets) but underdelivered on research (8/13 targets) due to political unrest. partner_performance_reality.THP: Met expectations for learning adaptation (1/1 target). Early stages of adapting issue-based approaches; political economy analysis (PEA) on violence completed to inform future work.
partner_performance_reality.DI: Leveraged long-standing party relationships to create reform dialogue spaces but struggled with power dynamics in women/youth leadership initiatives.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Regular multi-partner coordination meetings held; FCDO provided quarterly advance payments under Accountable Grant (AG) arrangements. Three AG contracts (TAF, TIB, THP) + one Delegated Cooperation Arrangement (FCDO-USAID for TIB’s anti-corruption work).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Partners submitted timely quarterly reports with satisfactory quality. Cross-portfolio learning initiated (e.g., THP’s PEA shared with consortium). Joint donor statements developed (e.g., on civic/political space).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive bidding processes followed for all procurements; asset spot checks confirmed compliance. Partners maintained updated asset registers.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO conducted financial scrutiny of all fund requests; safeguarding training provided to first-tier partners. Two safeguarding incidents reported (one closed, one ongoing).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Small flexible funds used for emergent needs (e.g., electoral violence analysis, HRD research). Workplans adjusted post-election to reflect political realities.
adaptive_management_examples: TIB’s Dengue Crisis report (Oct 2023) influenced government’s National Dengue Prevention Strategy (2024–2030).
FCDO’s engagement with media think tanks to analyze electoral violence across 300 constituencies, shaping UK messaging on democratic values.
TAF’s adaptive project approach for collaboration/coalition-building, replicated by other partners.
Post-election realignment of activities to address shrinking civic space and inflation challenges.

main_implementation_challenges: Political unrest and polarisation, especially around the January 2024 parliamentary elections (assessed by UK as not meeting credible/fair standards).
Shrinking democratic space for CSOs, limiting operational freedom.
High inflation affecting programme costs and partner capacity.
Delayed fund releases from NGO Affairs Bureau.
Corruption (Bangladesh ranked 149/180 on CPI 2023 with score 24/100).
external_factors_impact: Election-related violence and restrictions disrupted research/data collection (e.g., TIB’s underdelivery on research targets).
Post-election political sensitivity required reprioritization of activities (e.g., paused direct party engagement).
Global inflation increased operational costs, offset partially by donor co-funding (e.g., USAID’s $10M for TIB).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated severity of election-related crackdowns on civic space.
Dengue outbreak (2023) created urgent need for governance-focused interventions, leading to unplanned policy engagement.
Rapidly evolving misinformation trends (e.g., Bay of Bengal conversations) required agile responses.
partner_relationship_issues: DI and THP faced challenges in navigating power dynamics for women/youth leadership initiatives.
Varied partner maturity in adaptive management (TAF advanced; TIB/THP early-stage).
Co-funding dependencies (e.g., USAID) introduced coordination complexities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: TIB’s MEAL systems lacked capacity to track qualitative impacts of high-traction reports (e.g., policy uptake).
Downstream partners (e.g., volunteers) required additional safeguarding protocols.
Limited political economy analysis skills among some partners (e.g., DI/THP) to address power dynamics.

programme_metadata.programme_title: ReBUILD for Resilience (R eBUILD)

output_1.title: Coherent and timely body of high quality, policy-relevant, gender-transformative, equity-oriented research and evidence synthesis on local FASP health systems

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Expanded use of Responsive Fund for policy-maker-requested research and multiplier funding opportunities. Increased focus on synthetic analysis across fragile contexts. Adaptive management in response to contextual shocks (e.g., political instability, climate disasters).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated resilience in fragile contexts (Lebanon, Myanmar, Sierra Leone) despite delays. Transition from COHMAS to Institute for Development in Sierra Leone caused temporary delays but was resolved. Equitable partnership model with capacity strengthening opportunities for all consortium members, evaluated via annual partnership values survey.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Consortium Management Committee (CMC) with external reviewers for Responsive Fund applications. Decentralized decision-making with strong local leadership in learning sites. Annual values survey informs governance improvements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination through participatory action research (PAR) cycles in learning sites, though national-level engagement with governments remains variable. Collaboration with other FCDO-funded programmes (e.g., CHORUS) enhanced cross-programme synthesis.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Responsive Fund applications reviewed by CMC + external reviewer, with criteria including alignment with theory of change, VFM, and capacity strengthening. No major procurement issues reported, though contract amendment delays in Sierra Leone impacted timelines.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight in high-risk contexts (e.g., Myanmar, Lebanon) due to security/safeguarding concerns. Quarterly safeguarding focal point meetings and refresher training implemented.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Responsive Fund allowed rapid reallocation to emerging priorities (e.g., climate change, AI, disability inclusion). Adaptive management used to address shocks (e.g., elections in Sierra Leone, conflict in Myanmar).
adaptive_management_examples: Establishment of municipality health committees in Lebanon to lead local initiatives post-PAR cycles.
Shift to virtual/remote research methods during political instability in Myanmar.
Expansion of climate change research in Nepal/Bangladesh in response to emerging policy demands.
Use of Responsive Fund to study mental health needs of young people and disability inclusion in Myanmar.

main_implementation_challenges: Political instability and contested elections (Sierra Leone, Myanmar, Lebanon).
Delayed partner transitions (e.g., COHMAS to Institute for Development in Sierra Leone).
Climate disasters and conflict disrupting fieldwork timelines.
Safeguarding risks for researchers/participants in high-risk settings.
Staff turnover (notably at LSTM) causing temporary delays.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 legacy effects on health systems and research access.
Myanmar’s ongoing conflict limiting fieldwork mobility.
Lebanon’s economic crisis affecting partner operations.
Sierra Leone’s 2023 election disputes disrupting stakeholder engagement.
Currency fluctuations and inflation increasing operational costs.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging environmental risks (e.g., climate change impacts on health systems) not fully anticipated in original design.
Restrictions on academic freedom/free speech in some contexts, requiring risk mitigation strategies.
Need for expanded focus on disability inclusion and gender norms beyond initial scope.
partner_relationship_issues: Variable engagement with national governments (stronger at local/global levels).
Delays in contract amendments and approvals (Sierra Leone).
Capacity disparities among partners requiring tailored support (addressed via Responsive Fund and capacity strengthening).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited bandwidth for synthetic analysis due to high volume of primary research.
Need for additional skills in AI applications for research synthesis/communication.
Local partner capacity for policy engagement required strengthening (e.g., in Sierra Leone post-government transition).
risk_materialization: Safeguarding incidents (mitigated via updated risk assessments and training).
Financial/fiduciary risks (addressed via enhanced oversight and delivery chain mapping).
Reputational risks from operating in contested political environments (e.g., Myanmar).
Environmental risks from travel (partially mitigated by adjusted travel policies).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track overall, with underspend in some areas reallocated to high-priority activities (e.g., climate change research, Responsive Fund studies). Delays in Sierra Leone caused temporary underspend, later absorbed.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated through: 1) 30 peer-reviewed publications (exceeding targets); 2) 43 research studies across 13 countries; 3) >70,000 resource database views; 4) Leveraged co-funding (>30% for some studies). Cost per output lower than projected due to efficient use of Responsive Fund.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls implemented by LSTM and partners. Delivery chain mapping updated to mitigate fraud risks. No major audit findings reported. Responsive Fund applications rigorously reviewed for VFM.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of core staff time for synthetic work. Co-funding and multiplier effects (e.g., Lancet Commission leadership) extended programme reach. Travel cost savings achieved via virtual collaboration where feasible.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Exceeded expectations, with >30% co-funding for several studies. Responsive Fund attracted external contributions for high-impact research (e.g., climate change, disability inclusion).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Inflation and exchange rate fluctuations in Lebanon/Myanmar increased local costs, partially offset by budget reallocations and FCDO flexibility.

key_delivery_lessons: Embedded, long-term learning sites (PAR approach) yield higher-quality, contextually relevant research than short-term studies.
Responsive Fund mechanism effectively addresses emerging priorities and policy windows.
Equitable partnerships require continuous monitoring (via values survey) and adaptive support.
Synthetic analysis is critical for cross-context learning but requires dedicated resources.
successful_delivery_practices: Participatory Action Research (PAR) cycles for co-creation with local stakeholders.
Consortium Management Committee (CMC) with external review for Responsive Fund decisions.
Annual partnership values survey to assess equitability and inform governance.
Quarterly safeguarding focal point meetings and refresher training.
Cross-programme collaboration (e.g., with CHORUS) to leverage complementary expertise.
management_adaptations_made: Increased focus on synthesis of findings across fragile contexts (post-2023 AR recommendation).
Expanded safeguarding scope to include researchers/participants, with updated risk assessments.
Strengthened national-level advocacy in Sierra Leone post-government transition.
Adjusted milestone targets for Output 1 to reflect accelerated research portfolio growth.
innovations_attempted: Use of AI for capacity strengthening, synthesis, and research uptake (pilot planned).
Co-creation of learning sites with municipalities (e.g., Kapilvastu district, Nepal).
Climate change and health systems research integrated into core programme.
Disability inclusion studies added to Myanmar/Sierra Leone portfolios.
previous_recommendations_progress: Synthesis of cross-context findings prioritized (e.g., climate change, gender norms).
National-level engagement strengthened (e.g., ministerial event in Lebanon, HRH roundtable in Nepal).
Responsive Fund utilization expanded for policy-relevant research.
Capacity strengthening tailored to partner needs (highlighted in values survey).
forward_recommendations: Deepened engagement with national governments/operational agencies, especially in Sierra Leone.
Expansion of climate change and AI themes with dedicated synthesis/communication plans.
Prioritization of long-listed synthesis topics via Consortium Advisory Group.
Enhanced monitoring of academic freedom risks in restrictive contexts.
Scaling successful PAR models to new urban sites (e.g., collaboration with CHORUS).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Generally effective, with proactive mitigation of safeguarding, financial, and reputational risks. Safeguarding and environmental risks required mid-course adjustments. Political risks in Myanmar/Lebanon managed through adaptive research methods.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Researchers, health managers, and community co-researchers in 13 fragile/shock-prone countries (exact numbers not specified).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Policy-makers, practitioners, and academics accessing 70,000+ online resources and 24,000+ downloads.

policy_influence_achieved: Contributions to Wellcome’s Future of Global Health Initiatives (FGHI) report, informing FCDO policy.
Leadership of Lancet Commission on migration/displacement.
Engagement with national ministers (e.g., Lebanon dissemination event).
HRH policy roundtable in Nepal with British Embassy support.
capacity_building_results: LMIC-led authorship in 19/30 peer-reviewed publications (65% LMIC co-authors).
12/26 female LMIC lead/co-authors, exceeding gender equity targets.
Responsive Fund supported skills development in emerging areas (e.g., AI, climate change).
Municipality health committees in Lebanon now leading local initiatives post-PAR.
unintended_consequences: Positive: PAR approach strengthened trust between researchers and communities, leading to unplanned local initiatives (e.g., Lebanon municipality committees).
Negative: Delays in some studies due to over-ambitious scope, causing stress for researchers in fragile contexts.
scalability_evidence: PAR model replicated in second Nepal site (Kapilvastu district) and planned for urban expansion.
Responsive Fund mechanism adopted by other FCDO programmes.
Synthetic analysis frameworks applicable to other fragile health system research consortia.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Consistent A+ performance, high policy relevance, and strong demand for research in fragile contexts. Programme demonstrates adaptability to shocks and effective use of Responsive Fund. FCDO prioritizes health systems resilience in FASP settings.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High – embedded learning sites, equitable partnerships, and flexible funding mechanisms (Responsive Fund) ensure long-term viability. Risk of partner fatigue mitigated by capacity strengthening and values-based governance.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High – evidenced by repeated A+ scores, policy uptake, and co-funding leverage.
planned_adaptations_future: Expansion of climate change and AI research themes.
Deeper national-level advocacy in Sierra Leone/Lebanon.
Prioritized synthesis of cross-context findings.
Scaling PAR model to urban settings via CHORUS collaboration.
Enhanced monitoring of academic freedom and environmental risks.

successful_delivery_practices: Collaborative development of strategies (research, M&E, GESI) with consortium and FCDO input.

innovations_attempted: Network of Champions" initiative to elevate MNH on political agendas.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Baobab Research Programme Consortium - Filling gaps in evidence to enhance sexual and reproductive health and rights among vulnerable populations in refugee settings in East and Horn of Africa

output_1.title: A coherent body of high-quality evidence generated

output_2.title: Capacity of consortium partners and humanitarian actors strengthened

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transition from inception to implementation was delayed pending FCDO approval. Research activities were curtailed until February 2023, with only the Gender-Based Violence (GBV) study advancing due to prior investment. Strategic discussions refocused on research scope, value as a global public good, and staffing structure. Research uptake function was revised to be led by an in-house manager instead of a consultancy firm for improved Value for Money (VfM).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (Population Council Inc., Population Council Kenya, and APHRC) demonstrated capability in developing study protocols and securing ethical approvals. However, the transition of Baobab’s CEO created a temporary senior management gap, which was mitigated by the former CEO resuming the role temporarily to support the new CEO.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The original management structure was adjusted due to the CEO transition. The inaugural CEO returned temporarily to support the new CEO’s onboarding and will continue in an *ex officio* capacity at no additional cost. This change was made to ensure continuity and leverage existing experience.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination was demonstrated through strategic engagement with stakeholders such as the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM), UNHCR, and UNICEF in Uganda. A Data-2-Action workshop was co-convened in June 2023 to translate GBV study findings into national programming actions. The RPC also joined local advisory boards (e.g., Child Protection Sub-Working Group in Uganda) and collaborated with Refugee Welfare Councils.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement processes leveraged pre-negotiated contracts with RPC suppliers to reduce unit costs (e.g., bulk discounts on digital tablets and air tickets) and protect against cost variations. PC Inc’s global systems were used to benchmark costs and ensure best value.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensity increased due to protracted discussions between FCDO and Baobab to align on research scope, staffing, and VfM considerations. Monthly monitoring meetings were introduced to track progress and mitigate risks related to research delivery, organizational structure, and financial management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was utilized to adapt the research uptake delivery model (shifting from a consultancy firm to an in-house manager) and to strengthen the link between formative research (30% of research) and intervention design (70%). The programme also adjusted its staffing structure to address the CEO transition without additional costs.
adaptive_management_examples: Revising the research uptake function to be led in-house for improved VfM and integration with other outputs.
Temporary reinstatement of the former CEO to support transition and onboarding of the new CEO.
Adapting the Theory of Change (ToC) to emphasize time-sensitive research phases and stakeholder engagement, though no major changes were made to outputs, outcomes, or impact levels.
Opening training workshops to refugees and host community members, with a planned review of this approach by October 2023.

main_implementation_challenges: Delay in FCDO approval for transitioning from inception to implementation, curtailing research activities for most of the review period (until February 2023).
Temporary gap in senior management due to the CEO transition, requiring interim support from the former CEO.
Need for extensive strategic discussions between FCDO and Baobab to align on research scope, staffing, and VfM, which prolonged decision-making.
Logframe indicators and milestones required revision to ensure they were ambitious yet attainable, as some targets (e.g., study tools development) were not met as planned.
external_factors_impact: The broader refugee crisis in East and Horn of Africa, with over 5.5 million displaced individuals, created a complex operational context for SRHR research.
Political and humanitarian dynamics in refugee-hosting countries (e.g., Uganda, Ethiopia) influenced stakeholder engagement and ethical approval processes.
contextual_constraints_new: Ethical approval processes in refugee settings proved more time-consuming than anticipated, particularly for studies in Ethiopia.
Safeguarding considerations required heightened attention, as research on GBV and SRHR involved vulnerable populations, including potential perpetrators among service providers.
Limited prior evidence on SRHR in refugee settings necessitated adaptive research designs and tools.
partner_relationship_issues: Protracted discussions between FCDO and Baobab highlighted the need for clearer, more structured communication to align expectations and resolve issues efficiently.
Differences in priorities between FCDO policy teams and local offices required early consultation to ensure research relevance and uptake.
capacity_constraints_emerged: The RPC’s capacity to generate and analyze datasets was initially limited, as seen in the delayed analysis of GBV study data and comparison with wider evidence.
Junior researchers required additional support to co-author research outputs, though progress was made (6 outputs vs. a cumulative target of 5).
risk_materialization: The risk of delayed implementation materialized due to FCDO’s pause on research activities, impacting timeline and momentum.
The risk of senior management turnover materialized with the CEO transition, though it was mitigated through interim arrangements.
Financial management and logframe maintenance emerged as ongoing risks, requiring closer FCDO oversight and monthly monitoring.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution slowed due to restricted research activities in the review period. Spending was below plan as a result of delayed implementation. However, cost savings were achieved through adaptive measures such as in-house research uptake management and leveraging existing RPC systems.

value_for_money_assessment.details: Costs were minimized by leading the programme from Kenya (reducing travel/technical assistance from Northern countries) and using pre-negotiated supplier contracts for bulk discounts (e.g., digital tablets, air tickets). PC Inc’s global benchmarking systems ensured competitive procurement.

Efficiency gains were realized by combining travel for multiple purposes (e.g., monitoring, research uptake, capacity building) and adapting existing research tools/methodologies from RPC partners to save development time. However, delays in implementation affected overall efficiency.

Effectiveness was demonstrated in stakeholder engagement (e.g., Data-2-Action workshop) and ethical approvals for studies. However, the delayed analysis of datasets and logframe revisions indicated room for improvement in output delivery.

The programme prioritized equity by focusing on vulnerable refugee populations (women, adolescents) and hosting workshops for refugees and local communities. VfM considerations explicitly included equity in research design and uptake.

strengths: Use of PC Inc’s financial systems for benchmarking and cost control.
Pre-negotiated contracts to reduce unit costs and mitigate currency/exchange rate risks.
Transparency in financial reporting, with plans to improve forecasting accuracy by September 2023.
weaknesses: Delays in financial forecasting and logframe updates required FCDO intervention.
Monthly monitoring was introduced to address emerging issues, indicating prior gaps in proactive financial oversight.

financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was achieved through bulk procurement, localized management (Kenya-based leadership), and adaptive use of existing RPC resources. However, the full potential for efficiency was not realized due to implementation delays.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Pre-negotiated contracts helped protect against currency/exchange rate fluctuations, particularly for digital tools and travel. No significant adverse impacts were reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Clear, open, and frequent communication between FCDO and RPC is critical to align expectations and resolve issues promptly.
Early consultation with FCDO policy teams and local offices ensures research relevance and buy-in.
A well-maintained logframe is essential for tracking deliverables and adapting to changes.
Safeguarding must be integrated into all research phases, particularly in sensitive areas like GBV.
Concise, structured reporting from the RPC improves FCDO’s ability to monitor progress.
successful_delivery_practices: Leveraging existing RPC systems (e.g., PC Inc’s benchmarking) for cost efficiency and quality assurance.
Strategic stakeholder engagement (e.g., OPM, UNHCR) to create demand for evidence and inform programming.
Adaptive management of staffing transitions (e.g., temporary CEO support) to maintain continuity.
Combining travel and activities (e.g., monitoring + capacity building) to maximize resource use.
Opening training workshops to refugees and host communities to enhance inclusivity and uptake.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted research uptake from a consultancy firm to an in-house manager for better integration and VfM.
Introduced monthly FCDO-RPC meetings to monitor risks (research delivery, staffing, logframe).
Revised the link between formative research (30%) and intervention design (70%) to ground operational research in survey evidence.
Planned logframe review by September 2023 to ensure milestones are attainable and aligned with priorities.
innovations_attempted: Introducing global SRHR measurement tools into refugee settings for the first time.
Co-convening Data-2-Action workshops to translate research findings into national programming (e.g., GBV response in Uganda).
Pilot inclusion of refugees and host communities in training workshops, with a review planned for scalability.
Documenting novel processes for research in refugee settings to share learning across the sector.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: N/A (No prior annual review recommendations were cited in the document.)

forward_recommendations.action: Finalize contract amendments to reflect current programme scope and staffing.
Conduct monthly progress reviews to monitor research delivery, organizational structure, and financial management.
Review and rationalize the logframe to ensure milestones are ambitious yet attainable.
Ensure all RPC-funded activities (e.g., events) carry Baobab and FCDO/UKAid branding.
Improve financial forecasting accuracy and processes.
Enhance the quality of RPC written reports through structured discussions.
Ensure datasets are accompanied by thorough analysis and comparison with wider evidence.
Assess the value and viability of including refugees/host communities in training workshops.
Document processes and learning from novel work in refugee settings for sector-wide sharing.

strengths: Proactive identification of risks (e.g., CEO transition, delayed implementation) and adaptive responses (e.g., interim CEO support, monthly monitoring).
Strategic discussions with FCDO to realign programme scope and VfM considerations.
Use of pre-negotiated contracts to mitigate financial risks (e.g., currency fluctuations).
weaknesses: Some risks materialized (e.g., implementation delays, logframe misalignment) due to underestimation of approval timelines and stakeholder coordination needs.
Financial and logframe oversight required intensified FCDO intervention, indicating gaps in proactive risk management by the RPC.
lessons: Early and structured risk discussions with FCDO can preempt delays.
Flexibility in delivery models (e.g., in-house research uptake) can mitigate operational risks.
Regular logframe reviews are essential to keep milestones realistic and aligned with context.

policy_influence_achieved.details: Preliminary evidence of policy engagement, but full uptake depends on further research and stakeholder follow-through.

policy_influence_achieved.details: Influence is contingent on continued evidence generation and RPC’s ability to sustain partnerships.

capacity_building_results.results: 7 training workshops delivered (6 in Uganda, 1 in Kenya); 251 humanitarian actors trained on evidence-based SRHR interventions; 6 research outputs co-authored by junior researchers.
RPC partners (PC Inc, PC Kenya, APHRC) demonstrated ability to develop study protocols and secure ethical approvals, though analysis and uptake of datasets lagged.
Strategic relationships established with OPM, UNHCR, UNICEF, and Refugee Welfare Councils, enhancing demand for evidence and potential for uptake.

Implementation delays reduced momentum in research activities, potentially affecting beneficiary reach and evidence timeliness. Safeguarding risks were identified in GBV research (e.g., potential perpetrators among service providers), requiring heightened protocols.

scalability_evidence.details: Tools introduced for the first time in refugee contexts; potential for replication in other humanitarian settings if evidence demonstrates effectiveness.
Pilot workshop in Uganda showed promise for translating evidence into policy; scalability depends on RPC’s ability to convene similar events in other countries (e.g., Ethiopia).
Review planned by October 2023 to determine viability of scaling inclusion of refugees/host communities in capacity-building activities.

continuation_rationale: The programme has successfully transitioned from inception to implementation, with a clear plan to address prior delays.
Strategic alignment with FCDO priorities on SRHR in humanitarian settings and potential for global public good through evidence generation.
