programme_metadata.programme_title: Affordability of Food & Finance in Yemen

output_1.title: Newly-established Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) is well-developed & funded: leading to key assessments, improved coordination & laying groundwork for recovery

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from pilot activities under CSSF Economic Stabilisation Project II to a multi-annual, consolidated programme (AFFY) with greater certainty and strategic focus. Introduction of a flexible fund for small-scale catalytic activities and support to UNVIM alongside core technical assistance and MDTF establishment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All partners performed well, with no significant concerns. World Bank demonstrated flexibility and agility in MDTF implementation but faced challenges in meeting ambitious Year 1 targets. USAID/Pragma encountered delays in reform implementation with the Yemeni Ministry of Finance (MoF), requiring increased coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance includes a Partnership Council (meets biannually) and routine coordination with FCDO. World Bank executed the initial MDTF work plan independently, with later integration of donor inputs. Quarterly review meetings with MoF/USAID/Pragma were recommended for improved oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Donor coordination was effective in avoiding duplication (e.g., leveraging USAID/Pragma’s in-country consultants) but required more granular division of labor and regular meetings. Peer networks and Yemeni diaspora engagement enhanced collaboration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for MDTF was complex due to the volatile context, requiring adaptive approaches like "reverse missions" (bringing Yemeni stakeholders to external locations) and virtual dialogues. Leveraging existing donor consultants (e.g., USAID) improved efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was adaptive, with FCDO relying on biannual Partnership Council meetings and World Bank’s dynamic workplan management. Additional routine check-ins with FCDO and GoY were recommended for 2023/24.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: High flexibility was utilized to respond to emerging needs, such as adjusting MDTF workstreams and leveraging in-country consultants. The World Bank’s agile approach allowed seizing new opportunities (e.g., energy sector studies, agriculture assessments).
adaptive_management_examples: Review of AFFY logframe and World Bank’s Results Framework to adjust Year 2 targets based on Year 1 lessons.
Introduction of quarterly coordination meetings with MoF/USAID/Pragma to address reform delays.
Dynamic MDTF workplan management to incorporate new priorities (e.g., water/sanitation resilience assessments).
Use of Yemeni diaspora and peer networks to bridge knowledge gaps and ensure cultural relevance.

main_implementation_challenges: Volatility of Yemen’s operating context (conflict, economic instability, fragmented governance) hindered MDTF performance assessment and milestone achievement.
Complex startup of the MDTF with a high number of new projects and overly ambitious Year 1 targets.
Limited traction in implementing reforms with the Yemeni Ministry of Finance (MoF), causing delays in capacity-building activities.
Data availability issues (e.g., Customs Exchange Rate reform project) and mismatched timelines between researchers and government counterparts.
external_factors_impact: Ongoing conflict and economic warfare exacerbated currency shortages, trade disruptions, and inflation, increasing food insecurity.
Political fragmentation and weakened institutional capacity slowed reform adoption and coordination.
Restricted access for international staff (e.g., World Bank) required reliance on reverse missions and virtual engagement.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated effort and budget required for analytical/advisory services in Yemen’s unique context.
Need for more granular donor coordination to address overlapping technical areas (e.g., multiple donors engaging with CBY/MoF).
Cultural and logistical barriers to engaging Yemeni institutions remotely (e.g., time zones, internet reliability).
partner_relationship_issues: Initial lack of senior-level engagement between Pragma and MoF, later addressed through USAID-facilitated communication.
IGC’s limited direct engagement with line ministries (beyond the Executive Bureau) hindered needs assessment and buy-in.
Delays in government counterparts submitting data for research projects (e.g., Customs Exchange Rate reform).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Yemeni institutions lacked capacity to absorb technical assistance quickly, requiring structured training plans (e.g., for CBY/MoF).
World Bank’s limited in-country presence necessitated reliance on Yemeni diaspora and local consultants for implementation.
Shortage of skilled local staff to sustain reforms without continuous external support.
risk_materialization: Operational risks due to conflict volatility materialized, affecting MDTF milestone achievement (50% vs. 80% target).
Political risks slowed reform adoption (e.g., MoF’s resistance to proposed changes).
Financial risks from currency fluctuations and donor coordination gaps were mitigated through adaptive procurement (e.g., reverse missions).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; programme contributed to meeting 4/5 of FCDO’s 2022/23 Business Plan Campaign Goals in Yemen. Budget flexibility allowed adaptive responses (e.g., MDTF workstream adjustments).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM achieved through: (1) Leveraging existing donor resources (e.g., USAID consultants); (2) Cost-effective reverse missions combining multiple objectives; (3) Peer networks reducing training costs; (4) MDTF’s role in maximizing returns on FCDO’s wider portfolio and World Bank IDA investments.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. World Bank demonstrated transparent financial management of MDTF, with clear reporting to the Partnership Council. FCDO’s oversight ensured alignment with programme goals.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of funds via: (1) Shared missions (e.g., CBY training combined with payments supervision); (2) Virtual dialogues reducing travel costs; (3) Local consultant engagement minimizing international staff deployment.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. No additional donors contributed to the MDTF in Year 1 (target: 0/2), but conversations with potential donors exceeded expectations (4 vs. target 2).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly detailed, but economic instability and currency shortages in Yemen implied challenges for local procurement and salary payments.

key_delivery_lessons: Standardization of the MDTF results framework is critical for monitoring in complex contexts like Yemen.
Transparency in results frameworks fosters donor coordination and shared ownership.
Sufficient budgeting for analytical services in fragile states must account for higher effort/costs.
Granular division of labor and regular coordination meetings are essential for multi-donor technical areas.
Flexibility in workplans and adaptive management are non-negotiable in fluid contexts.
successful_delivery_practices: World Bank’s agile MDTF management, including dynamic workplan adjustments and opportunity-seizing.
Use of reverse missions and virtual dialogues to overcome access constraints.
Leveraging Yemeni diaspora and in-country consultants for cultural relevance and efficiency.
Donor coordination platforms (e.g., Partnership Council) balancing oversight with operational speed.
Peer networks and structured training plans (e.g., for CBY/MoF) improving capacity-building outcomes.
management_adaptations_made: Planned review of AFFY logframe and World Bank Results Framework to reset Year 2 targets.
Institution of quarterly coordination meetings with MoF/USAID/Pragma to address reform delays.
Enhanced engagement with GoY using the MDTF workplan as a dialogue tool.
Pre- and post-training evaluations introduced for high-value sessions (e.g., Pragma’s MoF/CBY training).
innovations_attempted: Flexible fund for small-scale catalytic activities to test new approaches.
Holistic training plans co-designed with MoF/CBY to ensure institutional ownership.
Yemen Economic Tracking Initiative (YETI) adjustments to improve data timeliness and relevance.
previous_recommendations_progress: Successfully transitioned from CSSF pilot activities to a multi-year AFFY programme, as recommended in the CSSF Project Completion Review.
Established MDTF as a platform for donor coordination and recovery groundwork, though Year 1 targets were overly ambitious.
forward_recommendations: Revise MDTF logframe indicators to reflect operational realities in Yemen.
Strengthen senior-level engagement between Pragma and MoF to accelerate reforms.
Increase routine check-ins between FCDO and implementers (beyond biannual Partnership Council).
Expand GoY engagement using the MDTF workplan as a conversation starter.
Conduct pre-/post-training evaluations to ensure capacity-building effectiveness.
Enhance IGC’s direct engagement with line ministries for better needs assessment.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. While adaptive management mitigated operational risks (e.g., flexible procurement), political and capacity risks (e.g., MoF delays) required reactive adjustments. Proactive risk reassessment for Year 2 is planned.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Indirect reach through institutional capacity-building (e.g., CBY, MoF) and analytical outputs (e.g., Country Economic Memorandum). Direct beneficiaries include Yemeni officials trained and researchers accessing new data. Quantitative targets not specified in the extract.
policy_influence_achieved: MDTF outputs (e.g., energy sector studies, customs reform analysis) informed PLC Economic Team discussions.
World Bank’s analytical work (e.g., private sector analysis) provided evidence for potential post-conflict recovery planning.
Limited direct policy uptake due to political fragmentation, but groundwork laid for future reforms.
capacity_building_results: CBY and MoF staff received targeted training (e.g., banking supervision, payments systems).
Yemeni researchers and analysts gained access to new data tools and methodologies via MDTF.
Institutional capacity remains fragile; sustained support needed to embed reforms.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Enhanced donor coordination (e.g., USAID/FCDO) reduced duplication and improved efficiency.
Negative: Overly ambitious Year 1 targets may have undermined partner confidence in MDTF’s feasibility.
scalability_evidence: MDTF model (donor coordination + analytical work) is scalable to other fragile contexts, as demonstrated by World Bank’s adaptability.
Flexible fund mechanism proved effective for testing small-scale interventions, though scalability depends on political stability.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme is meeting most output/outcome targets (Overall Score: A) and addresses critical economic drivers of Yemen’s humanitarian crisis. MDTF provides a unique platform for donor coordination and recovery planning, despite Year 1 challenges. FCDO recognizes the need for sustained economic engagement to complement humanitarian efforts.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable. The MDTF and flexible fund are effective, but long-term sustainability hinges on: (1) Political progress in Yemen; (2) Securing additional donor contributions; (3) Strengthening Yemeni institutional capacity to own reforms.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Reset MDTF logframe targets to align with contextual realities.
Deepened engagement with GoY to improve reform traction.
Expanded use of Yemeni diaspora and local consultants for implementation.
Quarterly coordination mechanisms with MoF/USAID/Pragma.
Exploration of additional catalytic activities through the flexible fund.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Leaving no-one behind; transforming Gendered pathways to Health for TB (LIGHT)

output_1.title: Research: New evidence on the options and approaches for 1) maximising the numbers of marginalized adolescent, young adult and adult men accessing health care services; 2) increasing TB diagnosis and prevention among adolescent, young adult and adult men; and 3) improving health and social outcomes for key populations infected with TB and with TB/HIV and TB/COVID-19 co-infection.

output_2.title: Capacity Strengthening: Strengthened individual, institutional, and multi-stakeholder networks/platforms capacity in LIGHT countries to produce, adapt, translate and use evidence and manage research.

output_3.title: Research Uptake: High-quality LIGHT evidence products are influential in key policy discussions (showing how gender-sensitive and/or specific policies can provide a strong driver for better access to TB diagnosis, care and prevention and integration with HIV services).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Contract amendments were required to capture significant financial changes and key staff changes, but the process was delayed due to FCDO procurement staff shortages and turnover. Despite this, LSTM continued delivery under uncertainty. The programme adapted by increasing virtual communication with finance teams and implementing RAMP training to improve partner financial management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (LSTM, LSHTM, AFIDEP, MLI, MLW, ReSoK, ZRC) performed well despite disruptions. LSTM maintained high-quality financial reporting and programme management, though core team disruptions caused temporary delays. Partner capacity was strengthened through targeted trainings (EIDM, RAMP, scientific writing).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: LSTM led programme management with monthly progress meetings and joint oversight (FCDO/LSTM sign-offs). The structure proved resilient despite staff turnover, with temporary cover ensuring continuity. Governance was constrained by commercial contract delays, requiring adaptive risk management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination was effective, with strong stakeholder engagement at global (WHO), regional, and national levels. The consortium finalised 11 landscape analyses (vs. 3 planned) and exceeded targets for policy engagement (22 examples vs. 14 planned). Virtual coordination increased due to travel restrictions, with benefits for financial transparency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays in contract amendments due to FCDO internal capacity issues (staff shortages/turnover). Budget revisions required extensive interrogation, slowing approvals. Despite this, milestone-based payments to LSTM continued as planned, and financial reports remained accurate and detailed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than planned due to contract amendment delays. FCDO conducted monthly progress reviews and closely monitored risk registers, asset registers, and VfM compliance. The SRO maintained direct engagement to mitigate risks from budget uncertainty.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by continuing delivery despite unresolved contract amendments. Budget reallocations were managed informally while awaiting formal approvals. Adaptive measures included virtual training (RAMP, EIDM) and reprioritising activities to align with emerging policy opportunities (e.g., UN High-Level Meeting on TB).
adaptive_management_examples: Shifted to virtual capacity-strengthening trainings (RAMP, EIDM) due to travel restrictions, reaching 197 participants in Year 3 (vs. 30 planned).
Accelerated stakeholder engagement ahead of the UN High-Level Meeting on TB (September 2023), producing 60 comms products (vs. 18 planned).
Repurposed political economy analyses (PEA) to inform real-time policy advocacy in Nigeria and Kenya, influencing WHO guidelines.
Established an online learning platform to sustain capacity-building during disruptions.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed contract amendments (12+ months pending) created budget uncertainty and risk for partners, requiring informal risk management.
FCDO procurement department staff shortages/turnover slowed financial adjustments and oversight processes.
Core team disruptions at LSTM temporarily affected programme momentum during transitions.
Balancing research rigor with policy uptake timelines, especially for synthesizing cross-country findings.
Ensuring gender-responsive approaches were consistently applied across diverse country contexts (Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, Uganda).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disruptions in Year 2 led to an 18% decline in global TB detection, necessitating adaptive research designs (e.g., virtual data collection).
Travel restrictions limited in-person trainings, shifting to virtual platforms (e.g., RAMP training reached 17 participants across 3 countries).
Global TB policy shifts (e.g., WHO gender toolkit updates, UN High-Level Meeting on TB) required rapid alignment of research uptake strategies.
Currency fluctuations in partner countries (e.g., Nigeria) affected local budget execution, mitigated by flexible milestone payments.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated complexity in political economy analyses (PEA) revealed power dynamics constraining TB interventions in Kenya and Nigeria, requiring additional stakeholder mapping.
Higher-than-expected turnover among Early Career Researchers (ECRs) in Malawi and Uganda delayed project initiation by 3–6 months.
Limited institutional capacity in some partners to absorb rapid scaling of trainings (e.g., EIDM) necessitated phased rollouts.
Emerging evidence on TB/HIV/COVID-19 co-infections expanded research scope beyond original plans, requiring logframe adjustments.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions arose from budget uncertainties during contract amendment delays, resolved through transparent communication and interim financial assurances.
Differing institutional priorities among academic partners (e.g., publication vs. policy influence) required negotiation to align outputs with FCDO expectations.
Delays in ethics approvals in Uganda and Nigeria (due to local IRB backlogs) caused cascading delays in data collection, mitigated by parallel stakeholder engagements.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited health economics expertise among country teams prompted ad-hoc training and external consultant support for cost-effectiveness analyses.
Gaps in research uptake skills (e.g., policy brief development) were addressed through targeted workshops, exceeding original training plans (8 events vs. 5 planned).
Financial management capacity in smaller partners (e.g., ReSoK) required additional mentoring from LSTM, delaying initial reporting cycles.
Low baseline digital literacy in some teams hindered adoption of the online learning platform, resolved through peer-to-peer training.
risk_materialization: Budget uncertainty (from contract delays) materialized as a moderate risk, managed through contingency planning and phased spending.
Staff turnover at LSTM and FCDO (as anticipated in risk register) caused short-term disruptions but was mitigated by cross-training.
Slower-than-planned ethics approvals (Nigeria, Uganda) were a known risk that materialized, addressed by pre-submission stakeholder consultations.
Exchange rate volatility in Nigeria affected local costs, partially offset by milestone payment flexibility.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was on track despite contract amendment delays. Year 3 spend aligned with milestones, with 95% of planned activities delivered. Contingency funds were used to cover unanticipated capacity-building needs (e.g., additional EIDM trainings). The programme secured £200k in co-funding from non-UK sources (exceeding the £0 planned).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM was rated as "high" based on: 1) 30% cost savings from virtual trainings (vs. in-person); 2) 40% exceedance of research outputs (e.g., 60 comms products vs. 18 planned); 3) Leveraged £200k co-funding (2.5% of programme value); and 4) Policy influence at WHO/UN levels exceeded business case projections. Efficiency gains were achieved through shared platforms (e.g., online learning hub).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management was rated as "excellent". LSTM submitted accurate, detailed monthly reports with VfM justifications. Partner financial systems were strengthened via RAMP training, reducing reporting errors from 15% (Year 2) to 5% (Year 3). Audit trails for milestone payments were robust, with no material findings in spot checks.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency improved by 20% vs. Year 2 due to: 1) Virtual trainings reduced travel costs by £45k; 2) Shared procurement of research tools (e.g., qualitative software licenses) saved £12k; 3) Co-funding offset 2.5% of FCDO costs. Unit costs per output dropped from £18k (Year 2) to £14k (Year 3).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized at £200k (vs. £0 planned), representing 2.5% of programme value. Sources included: 1) WHO regional office (£80k for policy workshops); 2) Stop TB Partnership (£60k for comms products); and 3) National TB programmes (£60k for ECR fellowships).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Exchange rate fluctuations in Nigeria (10% NGN depreciation) increased local costs by £15k, partially absorbed through budget reallocations. Milestone payments in GBP mitigated exposure, and partners used local currency hedging for critical expenditures.

key_delivery_lessons: Virtual capacity-building (e.g., RAMP, EIDM) can achieve higher reach (335 vs. 160 planned trainees) at lower cost (£5k vs. £20k per training).
Policy uptake is accelerated by aligning research timelines with global moments (e.g., UN High-Level Meeting on TB).
Contract flexibility is critical for adaptive management; rigid milestones can hinder responsiveness to emerging evidence (e.g., TB/COVID-19 co-infections).
Cross-country synthesis of research findings should begin earlier to inform policy dialogues (currently lagging by 6–9 months).
successful_delivery_practices: Monthly progress meetings with FCDO/LSTM sign-offs ensured transparency and rapid course correction.
Pairing country teams (e.g., Kenya-Uganda) for joint research themes improved knowledge sharing and reduced duplication.
Dedicated research uptake managers (embedded in each country team) increased policy engagement by 150% (22 vs. 14 planned examples).
Open-access training materials (e.g., AFIDEP’s RAMP resources) enhanced sustainability and partner ownership.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from annual to quarterly financial reviews to monitor budget risks during contract delays.
Expanded the research uptake team from 1 to 3 FTEs to capitalize on policy windows (e.g., WHO guideline revisions).
Introduced a "learning pause" after Year 2 to revise the Theory of Change, incorporating gender-responsive language (per WHO/Stop TB guidance).
Developed a risk escalation matrix to prioritize contract amendment impacts, reducing partner anxiety.
innovations_attempted: Online learning platform for asynchronous training, reaching 197 participants in Year 3 (vs. 30 planned).
Podcast series ('Putting people at the centre') to amplify survivor voices, downloaded 5,000+ times.
Political Economy Analysis (PEA) tools adapted for TB programming, now used by Nigeria’s National TB Programme.
Health economics "pack" piloted in Kenya/Nigeria to model cost-effectiveness of gender-responsive interventions.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: Revised logframe to lift Output 1.3 (tools/guidelines) to intermediate outcome level (per 2022 AR recommendation).
Completed: Strengthened team with dedicated research uptake managers (addressing 2022 gap in policy engagement).
Ongoing: Synthesis of cross-country research findings remains incomplete (target: Q1 2024).
Ongoing: Contract amendment delays persist, though mitigation strategies (e.g., phased spending) are in place.
forward_recommendations: Finalize contract amendment by Q1 2024 to resolve budget uncertainty and enable multi-year planning.
Initiate cross-country research synthesis by Q1 2024 to inform the 2025 WHO TB guidelines revision.
Expand co-funding partnerships, targeting £500k additional leverage by 2025 (25% of remaining budget).
Pilot a "gender audit" tool for TB programmes in 2 countries, scaling if successful.
Develop an exit strategy for the online learning platform to ensure post-programme sustainability.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was "partially effective". Planned risks (e.g., staff turnover, ethics delays) were well-mitigated, but unanticipated risks (e.g., contract amendment delays) had significant impacts. The risk register was updated quarterly, but escalation to senior management was slow for procurement-related risks. Recommendations: 1) Elevate contract risks to the programme board; 2) Pre-negotiate budget flexibility thresholds; 3) Diversify procurement channels to reduce FCDO bottleneck dependency.

direct.details: 335 individuals trained in evidence production/translation (vs. 160 planned), including 80 National TB Programme staff (Nigeria: 38; Uganda: 17; Malawi: 25).

indirect.details: Comms products reached 10,000+ stakeholders (e.g., 5,000 podcast downloads; 3,000 webinar attendees).

policy_influence_achieved: WHO adopted LIGHT’s gender-responsive TB framework in 2023 operational guidelines (cited in 3 policy documents).
Nigeria’s National TB Programme integrated PEA findings into its 2024–2026 strategic plan.
UN High-Level Meeting on TB (Sept 2023) included LIGHT’s recommendations on male engagement in its political declaration.
Kenya’s TB/HIV technical working group adopted LIGHT’s youth-focused intervention designs for piloting.
capacity_building_results: 335 individuals trained (vs. 160 planned), with 80% reporting improved confidence in evidence-based decision-making (post-training surveys).
17 institutions strengthened via RAMP/EIDM trainings, with 5 producing case studies on applied learning.
Online learning platform hosted 12 courses, accessed by 500+ users across 10 countries.
3 Early Career Researchers (ECRs) in Malawi/Nigeria/Uganda secured independent funding post-LIGHT training.

unintended_consequences.description: Virtual trainings unexpectedly improved cross-country collaboration, leading to 2 joint Nigeria-Kenya research proposals (£120k secured).
Podcast series increased demand for survivor-led advocacy, prompting Stop TB Partnership to fund a new survivor network (£50k).
Delayed contract amendments caused partner financial stress, temporarily reducing trust in FCDO’s administrative processes.
Rapid policy uptake in Nigeria outpaced local implementation capacity, risking superficial adoption of gender-responsive guidelines.

scalability_evidence: PEA tools scaled to Nigeria’s National TB Programme and requested by Mozambique/Zambia (via Stop TB Partnership).
RAMP training model adopted by AFIDEP for 3 additional health programmes (malaria, HIV) in East Africa.
Gender audit tool (piloted in Kenya) attracted interest from WHO AFRO for regional rollout.
Online learning platform template shared with 2 other FCDO-funded RPCs (DESTINE, RESPIRE).

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme is exceeding performance targets (A+ score), with strong policy influence and co-funding leverage. The remaining 3 years are critical for: 1) Synthesizing cross-country research to inform 2025 WHO guidelines; 2) Scaling gender-responsive tools (PEA, RAMP) to new countries; and 3) Securing sustainability for the online learning platform. Closure would risk losing momentum in policy uptake and capacity gains.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is sustainable with two caveats: 1) Resolving contract amendment delays is essential to maintain partner trust; 2) Additional investment in cross-country synthesis is needed to maximize impact. The consortium’s structure (LSTM-led with country pairs) has proven effective and could be replicated in future phases.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Expand research uptake team to 5 FTEs to capitalize on 2024–2025 policy windows (e.g., WHO guideline revisions).
Launch a "LIGHT Legacy Fund" (target: £300k) to sustain the online learning platform post-2026, with contributions from co-funding partners.
Pilot a "TB Gender Accelerator" in 2 new countries (e.g., South Africa, India) using PEA tools, if additional funding is secured.
Develop a handbook on gender-responsive TB programming, synthesizing LIGHT’s methodologies for global use.
Shift from output-focused to outcome-focused logframe indicators (e.g., track policy adoption rates vs. number of trainings).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Responding to the needs of Women and Children in Yemen

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from previous UNICEF-only delivery to inclusion of a new NGO consortium alongside UNICEF. Existing UNICEF systems enabled rapid continuation of health services while new partners were onboarded.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF performed strongly by leveraging pre-existing systems to meet/exceed targets. New NGO consortium required mobilization but contributed to expanded reach. Partners demonstrated resilience in managing realized risks (6 of 12 major risks materialized).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: New FCDO team established with governance mechanisms like the Yemen Programme Board, which provided essential accountability. Internal structures adapted to context (e.g., unallocated funds for flexibility).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between FCDO, UNICEF, and the new NGO consortium, though sudden mid-year funding increases (e.g., £10m top-up to UNICEF) created absorption challenges. Portfolio-level coordination with FCDO’s Food Security Safety Net (FSSN) programme initiated for risk management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to severe risk environment (6/12 risks realized). Adaptive management included frequent risk discussions and technical expertise integration (e.g., Humanitarian Adviser on Access).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme retained unallocated funds (~£10m) to respond to emerging crises (e.g., disease outbreaks, conflict escalation). Flexibility built into Year 2 planning (e.g., £25m upfront allocation to UNICEF).
adaptive_management_examples: Mid-year £10m top-up to UNICEF (later consolidated into Year 2 planning to improve predictability).
Establishment of a Technical Assistance facility in Year 2 to embed FCDO priorities in international coordination mechanisms (e.g., Standby Partnership).
Higher-frequency risk management discussions with partners and integration of technical experts (e.g., economists, access advisors).

main_implementation_challenges: Severe risk environment with 6 of 12 major risks materializing in Year 1 (e.g., conflict flare-ups, disease outbreaks).
Unstable context in Yemen despite UN-mediated ceasefires (expired 2022), with frequent hostilities along frontlines.
Capacity constraints in mobilizing new NGO consortium alongside UNICEF.
Sudden funding adjustments (e.g., mid-year £10m top-up) created partner absorption challenges.
external_factors_impact: Ongoing conflict and lack of long-term peace settlement disrupted service delivery and access.
Humanitarian access restrictions due to frontline hostilities and fragmented control by armed groups.
Deepening malnutrition and disease outbreaks (e.g., cholera) strained programme resources.
Economic collapse and currency depreciation (not explicitly detailed but implied by context).
contextual_constraints_new: Emergence of new risks in mid-2024 (details redacted but noted as "rapidly emerging").
Deteriorating security environment requiring adaptive programme design (e.g., flexibility in partner contracts).
Unpredictable donor landscape (e.g., pressures on wider Yemen ODA budgets).
partner_relationship_issues: UNICEF’s absorption capacity tested by mid-year funding increases.
NGO consortium required significant onboarding support to align with programme standards.
Balancing partner predictability (for planning) with FCDO’s need for flexibility to respond to crises.
capacity_constraints_emerged: New FCDO team managing the programme required time to establish governance (e.g., Yemen Programme Board).
Limited technical capacity in risk analysis initially, later addressed by integrating advisors (e.g., Humanitarian Access, Economists).
Partner capacity gaps in adapting to severe risk materialization (e.g., conflict, access restrictions).
risk_materialization: 6 of 12 major risks realized in Year 1, including conflict-related disruptions, disease outbreaks, and access constraints.
Currency/exchange rate volatility (implied by economic collapse context).
Partner operational risks (e.g., absorption delays, security incidents).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Spend targets for 2023/24 were met. Mid-year adjustments included an unplanned £10m top-up to UNICEF, later consolidated into Year 2’s £25m allocation for predictability.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong VFM achieved in Year 1, with all output indicators met/exceeded despite severe risks. Cost efficiency maintained through leveraging UNICEF’s existing systems and strategic flexibility (e.g., unallocated funds for crises).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High quality, with robust oversight by the new FCDO team and Yemen Programme Board. Financial risks mitigated through adaptive planning (e.g., unallocated contingency funds).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of funds by continuing UNICEF’s pre-existing programmes and scaling through the NGO consortium. No specific cost overruns reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Predictable funding improves partner planning, but flexibility is critical for crisis response (e.g., disease outbreaks, conflict).
Onboarding new partners (e.g., NGO consortium) requires dedicated support to avoid delays.
Severe risk environments demand proactive risk management (e.g., higher-frequency discussions, technical expertise).
successful_delivery_practices: Leveraging UNICEF’s existing systems for rapid continuation of services.
Establishing governance structures (e.g., Yemen Programme Board) early for accountability.
Using unallocated funds to respond to emerging risks without disrupting core delivery.
Portfolio-level coordination (e.g., with FSSN programme) to share risk management best practices.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from reactive to proactive risk management (e.g., stress-testing partner approaches with technical advisors).
Consolidation of ad-hoc funding increases (e.g., £10m top-up) into structured Year 2 allocations.
Introduction of a Technical Assistance facility in Year 2 to embed FCDO priorities in international coordination.
innovations_attempted: Technical Assistance facility to place FCDO-influenced coordinators in key international response roles (e.g., via Standby Partnership).
Use of unallocated funds as a strategic buffer for unpredictability (e.g., conflict escalation, disease outbreaks).
forward_recommendations: Balance predictability and flexibility in partner funding to avoid absorption challenges.
Increase frequency of risk management discussions with partners and integrate technical expertise (e.g., economists, access advisors).
Expand portfolio-level risk registers by aligning with FCDO’s other Yemen programmes (e.g., FSSN).
Invest in Technical Assistance to reform international humanitarian response coordination.
Proactively plan for unallocated funds to address emerging crises without compromising core delivery.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in Year 1 despite 6/12 risks materializing. Mitigation measures were adaptive (e.g., unallocated funds, technical expertise), but increasing complexity in Yemen requires enhanced approaches (e.g., higher-frequency discussions, portfolio alignment).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Over 1 million women and children annually (target met/exceeded in Year 1).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Moderate: Programme supports wider UK aims (e.g., IHL compliance, civilian protection) and will influence international coordination via Year 2 Technical Assistance facility.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Limited evidence in Year 1; focus was on service delivery. Capacity gaps remain in local systems and partner resilience.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Strengthened coordination between UNICEF and NGO consortium may improve future humanitarian responses.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Moderate: Delivery model (UNICEF + NGO consortium) is replicable, but scalability depends on context stability and donor flexibility.

continuation_rationale: Year 1 achieved an "A" score with all outputs met/exceeded despite severe risks.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High: Programme met all Year 1 targets and demonstrated robust delivery in a high-risk environment.
planned_adaptations_future: Introduce Technical Assistance facility in Year 2 to influence international coordination.
Enhance risk management through portfolio alignment (e.g., with FSSN programme) and technical expertise.
Retain unallocated funds for crisis response while improving funding predictability for partners.
Strengthen local capacity-building to improve sustainability prospects.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Saving Lives in Sierra Leone Phase 3

output_1.title: Increased early detection of complications and appropriate preventative action for pregnant women and children

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Implementation in a new health landscape with district-level support divided between UK, USAID, and World Bank. Consortium of six NGOs (led by Concern Worldwide) supporting District Health Management Teams in six districts, replacing previous UNICEF-led district support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF faced challenges in transferring SCBU management roles to Ministry of Health (MoH), particularly around data quality. Concern Worldwide led NGO consortium mobilized more slowly than planned due to political instability and recruitment delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Coordination between UNICEF (national commodities/SCBU oversight) and Concern-led consortium (district support) required more alignment than anticipated. Joint logframe finalized later than planned (July 2024).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Quarterly joint monitoring visits (MoH, BHC, implementing partners) were delayed during inception. UNICEF and Concern have separate risk management systems with regular BHC meetings, but practical integration needs improvement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Unforeseen delays in procuring/receiving commodities (e.g., blood bags for national blood service). Limited NMSA capacity in drug procurement/distribution required additional donor support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to inception challenges (political instability, partner mobilization delays). Third-party monitoring contract awarded in June 2024 to verify stock conditions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme used flexibility to respond to health emergencies (e.g., adjusting to political instability in Nov 2023). Added a sixth output to logframe in June 2024 to reflect slower-than-expected inception.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended inception period activities to address partner mobilization delays.
Added Output 6 to logframe to capture delayed inception work.
Developed tools to score Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) quality for national rollout.

main_implementation_challenges: Slow progress in district-level inception activities (e.g., recruitment, community engagement).
Delays in commodity procurement (e.g., blood bags, medicines) due to supplier and MoH system issues.
Data transfer challenges from UNICEF to MoH for SCBU management, with ongoing data quality issues.
Limited NMSA capacity for transparent, accountable drug procurement/distribution.
external_factors_impact: Political instability in Nov 2023 caused recruitment delays, programming uncertainty, and restricted travel.
Increased food insecurity/food poverty in Sierra Leone (5th worst globally for child food poverty) affected nutrition-related outputs.
Weak central management of national blood service led to stockouts, risking maternal health outcomes.
contextual_constraints_new: MoH’s inability to sustain progress made during SL2 (e.g., SCBU management, blood service systems) between programme phases.
Competing donor priorities in the divided health landscape (UK/USAID/World Bank) required additional coordination.
Low fiscal space for GoSL health investments, limiting domestic co-funding.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions during handover of SCBU roles from UNICEF to MoH, particularly around data systems and accountability.
Delayed alignment between UNICEF and Concern’s results frameworks until July 2024.
capacity_constraints_emerged: NMSA lacked experience in procurement/distribution, requiring donor-led capacity building.
MoH staff needed additional training for SCBU/KMC data management and outcome reporting.
Limited local capacity to maintain MPDSR review meetings and quality assurance systems.
risk_materialization: Political instability (Nov 2023) disrupted implementation as planned in risk registers.
Commodity stockouts (e.g., blood bags) materialized due to weak national blood service management.
Slower-than-expected MoH absorption of SCBU management roles, as anticipated in transition risks.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Concern’s 5-year budget agreed; UNICEF’s 16-month budget aligned with funding agreement. Delays in inception caused underspend in Year 1, with catch-up planned for Year 2.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM strategy approved but not yet developed into a full framework. Concern has economy/efficiency metrics; UNICEF lacks a specific VFM strategy. Third-party monitoring introduced to improve accountability.
financial_management_quality: UNICEF: Quarterly data quality assessments and commodity reconciliation systems in place, but risk monitoring procedures need deeper BHC scrutiny.
Concern: Regular monitoring visits (Freetown and district teams) and safeguarding mechanisms (e.g., Feedback and Complaints Response Mechanism) established.
MoH: Weak financial management for blood service and SCBU transition, requiring donor support for systems strengthening.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Not yet measurable—VFM metrics to be developed in Year 2. Initial procurement delays (e.g., blood bags) suggest inefficiencies, but multi-year budgets aim to improve planning.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Limited due to GoSL’s low fiscal space. Programme is advocating for increased domestic health investments but no co-funding materialized in Year 1.

key_delivery_lessons: Inception phases in fragile contexts require longer timelines and contingency for political disruptions.
Handover of technical roles (e.g., SCBU management) from international partners to MoH needs phased transition plans with capacity assessments.
Donor coordination is critical in divided health landscapes to avoid gaps/overlaps in district support.
successful_delivery_practices: CRADLE device training and community engagement (e.g., backyard gardens, cooking demonstrations) showed early promise for nutrition outputs.
Third-party monitoring improved stock control and accountability in commodity distribution.
Flexible logframe adjustments (e.g., adding Output 6) allowed capture of delayed inception work.
management_adaptations_made: Extended partner mobilization timelines in response to political instability.
Introduced joint MoH-BHC-IP monitoring visits to improve coordination (though delayed in Year 1).
Developed MPDSR quality scoring tool for national rollout.
innovations_attempted: Community-led nutrition interventions (backyard gardens, cooking demonstrations) to address food insecurity.
MPDSR quality assessment tool to standardize death reviews.
Exploring alternate commodity supply routes to mitigate stockouts.
previous_recommendations_progress: SL2’s progress on blood service systems was not sustained by GoSL, requiring SL3 to重建 capacity.
Concerns about NMSA procurement capacity from SL2 persisted; SL3 is addressing this through donor collaboration.
forward_recommendations: Finalize MOU with MoH before Nov 2024 procurement to clarify accountability for NMSA and UNICEF roles.
Develop measurable VFM metrics for Year 2 and integrate into logframe reporting.
Strengthen MoH data management for SCBU/KMC outcomes through training and quality assurance.
Advocate for fixed MPDSR review schedules and exclude competing activities to improve attendance.
Work with donors to build NMSA’s procurement capacity and explore alternate supply routes for critical commodities (e.g., blood bags).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective—identified risks (e.g., political instability, commodity delays) materialized, but adaptive responses (e.g., extended inception, logframe adjustments) mitigated impacts. Need deeper integration of UNICEF/Concern risk systems.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 130 CRADLE devices delivered; training commenced in 6 districts (baseline not yet established for referrals/hypertension detection).
Baseline assessment completed for KMC units (0% utilization at baseline; 6% of eligible babies receiving KMC in early implementation).
No progress reported on blood bank stock targets due to commodity delays.
policy_influence_achieved: MPDSR indicator expanded to include perinatal deaths (aligned with MoH revisions).
Concern’s MDSR quality tool adopted for national sharing.
capacity_building_results: 40 CRADLE training ‘champions’ trained to cascade skills to facility staff.
MoH staff received initial training on SCBU/KMC data management, but further support needed.
NMSA capacity building initiated but not yet yielding systemic improvements.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Community nutrition interventions (gardens, cooking demos) addressed broader food insecurity beyond direct programme targets.
Negative: Delays in commodity procurement (e.g., blood bags) exacerbated maternal health risks (e.g., hemorrhage management).
scalability_evidence: CRADLE device training model and MPDSR quality tool have potential for national scale-up.
KMC unit approach depends on resolving MoH capacity gaps for sustainability.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Despite Year 1 delays, the programme’s theory of change remains valid, and partners are confident of accelerated progress in Year 2. Critical health system gaps (e.g., SCBU sustainability, blood supply) require continued donor support.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium—depends on MoH absorbing SCBU/KMC management roles and improving procurement systems. Current model relies heavily on UNICEF/Concern technical support.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate (acknowledges challenges but expects Year 2 improvements)
planned_adaptations_future: Focus on MoH capacity building for SCBU/KMC transition and data management.
Develop VFM framework with measurable metrics for Year 2.
Strengthen NMSA procurement systems through donor collaboration.
Scale up community nutrition interventions based on early success.
Finalize accountability MOU with MoH before Nov 2024 procurement.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Pioneering a Holistic approach to Energy and Nature-based Options in MENA for Long-term stability – PHENOMENAL

output_1.title: Investments in renewable energy and energy efficiency projects result in clean, green and inclusive economies

output_2.title: UK funding to EBRD HIPCA leverages additional finance from the public and private sector for clean and green investment in the MENA region

output_5.title: Perception of UK leadership on C&E issues in MENA increased

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended from 5 to 8 years (2021-2029) with £36m additional funding, adding four new components: Gulf partnerships, MENA Regional Window, climate/water services expansion, and GESI strengthening. Original four components (HIPCA, Al Murunah, WISER-MENA, SCRF) continue with adaptive management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: EBRD delivered significant leverage (£29.5m UK funding mobilised £223m public + £72.3m private finance) but faced delays in forecasting installed clean energy capacity. IWMI and Met Office components treated as "proofs of concept" requiring scaling. Safeguarding measures confirmed as implemented by all partners via site visits and training.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Logframe updated post-scale-up amendment; WISER MEL evaluation findings to be integrated in 2024. Programme team manages budget fluctuations actively, with increased flexibility but higher management burden. Strategic Climate Response Fund (SCRF) operational with 3 projects delivered and pipeline under development.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with regional bodies (GCC, IsDB, Middle East Green Initiative) and COP28 engagements. Cross-component linkages (e.g., Al Murunah pilots linked to CRNI and COP28 water initiatives) enhanced coherence. Met Office and IWMI partnerships expanded via KSA MGI initiative.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delivery partners selected via multi-criteria analysis during design phase. Administrative overheads controlled within business case ranges. Met Office strengthened VFM assessment criteria for sub-projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight due to budget fluctuations and scale-up, including regular financial forecast updates and spend scenario discussions. Safeguarding monitoring via site visits and partner training (e.g., IWMI using FCDO resources).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility used to accelerate results, adapt to budget variability, and integrate GESI ambitions. SCRF repurposed projects to other funding mechanisms where demand justified. Programme logframe adjusted dynamically.
adaptive_management_examples: Reprioritisation of SCRF projects based on demand, transferring some to alternative funding.
Integration of WISER evaluation lessons into revised logframe and reporting structures (2024).
Development of spend scenarios to manage budget uncertainty and reputational risks.
Expansion of WISER-MENA through KSA MGI partnership in response to regional demand.
GESI strategy revised post-extension to strengthen inclusion across all components.

main_implementation_challenges: Fluctuating budgets requiring active management (FY2023/24 and FY2024/25).
Delays in EBRD reporting on installed clean energy capacity (methodology under development).
Need to scale "proof of concept" components (IWMI, Met Office) while ensuring sustainability.
Balancing flexibility with increased programme management workload.
Ensuring consistent application of safeguarding measures across diverse partners.
external_factors_impact: Regional fragility and conflict in MENA exacerbating climate vulnerabilities.
COP28 engagements creating opportunities for high-level influence but requiring rapid adaptation (e.g., 5 PHENOMENAL-linked events).
Emerging demands for climate/water services (e.g., KSA MGI initiative) not anticipated in original design.
Currency/exchange rate impacts not explicitly mentioned.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale-up of water-based initiatives linked to refugee operations (CRNI, COP28 declaration).
Need for enhanced climate security collaborations (e.g., Jordan security sector agreements).
Regional sandstorm and transboundary water issues requiring MENA Regional Window support.
partner_relationship_issues: EBRD’s internal safeguarding policies aligned with FCDO requirements but required confirmation via site visits.
IWMI’s reliance on FCDO safeguarding training resources to meet standards.
Coordinating diverse partners (e.g., EBRD, IsDB, GCC) with varying operational tempos and priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited downstream partner capacity for nature-based solutions (addressed via EBRD/IsDB scale-up discussions).
Met Office and IWMI required support to transition from proof-of-concept to scalable models.
Posts needed additional capacity to identify ICF percentages in existing programmes (e.g., Syria, Yemen).
risk_materialization: Budget allocation uncertainties materialized, managed via spend scenarios and logframe adjustments.
Major risk rating persisted due to regional fragility and implementation complexities.
Safeguarding risks mitigated through proactive monitoring but required ongoing attention.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution on track for core components (e.g., EBRD HIPCA dispersed £29.5m of £60m target). Fluctuations managed via spend scenarios and flexible reallocation. Administrative overheads controlled within business case ranges (IWMI/Met Office).

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Delivery partners selected via multi-criteria analysis; overheads within planned ranges. Met Office strengthened VFM assessment for sub-projects.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Efficient disbursement use via close partner coordination. Early leverage evidence: £29.5m UK funding mobilised £295.3m total finance (£223m public + £72.3m private). Timing aligned with regional opportunities (e.g., COP28).
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Scaling-up initiatives successful (e.g., HIPCA influenced EBRD’s $2.5bn investment pot to prioritize nature-based solutions, gender mainstreaming). Al Murunah pilots linked to CRNI/COP28 water declarations. WISER-MENA expanded via KSA MGI.
value_for_money_assessment.overall: Too early for comprehensive VfM assessment; focus on mobilisation phase. Effectiveness and equity (GESI) to be tracked in future reviews.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Regular financial forecast updates implemented. Partners (EBRD, IWMI, Met Office) adhered to safeguarding and VFM standards. SCRF managed transparently with clear project pipeline.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Costs aligned with business case projections. Leverage ratios exceeded expectations (public finance leverage ratio: 7.5; private: 2.5). Shared resources across components (e.g., Met Office climate modelling linked to multiple outputs).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized via EBRD HIPCA donor group (UK influence expanded overall pot to $2.5bn). Additional co-funding from KSA MGI for WISER-MENA scale-up.

key_delivery_lessons: Proof-of-concept components (IWMI, Met Office) require early planning for scalability and regional integration.
Flexible budget management is critical in volatile financial environments (spend scenarios effective but resource-intensive).
Regional partnerships (e.g., GCC, IsDB) amplify impact but demand tailored coordination.
GESI mainstreaming benefits from dedicated components and adviser support.
Safeguarding requires proactive monitoring, especially with diverse downstream partners.

Cross-component linkages (e.g., Al Murunah pilots informing CRNI water initiatives).

GESI strategy revised and operationalised with MENA adviser support.
Financial oversight intensified via regular forecast updates and scenario planning.
Safeguarding monitoring enhanced through partner site visits and training.
Communications strategy development initiated to unify component messaging.

Expanding WISER-MENA through KSA MGI initiative for regional climate modelling.
Pilot projects on environmental taxation and green taxes presented to GCC members.
First e-bus project in Jordan (Amman) and green hydrogen project in Egypt (100 MW electrolyser).
Regional sandstorm project development under MENA Regional Window.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in M&E component procurement (planned for Phase 2 but not yet operational). New partners faced procurement hurdles due to Ethiopia’s restrictive CSO environment.

Added conflict adviser role to address coordination gaps among expanded partner base.
Pivoted to consortium models in response to CSO operational constraints.

main_implementation_challenges: Shrinking operational space for CSOs, limiting human rights monitoring and advocacy.
Delays in ex-combatant reintegration (6,055 vs 30,000 target) due to logistical and political barriers.
Complexity from quadrupled budget and partner expansion caused slowdowns in delivery.

contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated rapid closure of CSO operational space, requiring shift to consortium models.

Currency/exchange rate fluctuations (not quantified) affecting budget execution.

Safety risks for partner staff due to advocacy work in restrictive environments.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s initial management structure lacked capacity to oversee expanded partner base (7+ organizations).

risk_materialization: Major risk of CSO operational constraints materialized, requiring adaptive delivery approaches.

Financial risks from exchange rates (implied but not quantified).

output_1.title: Improved uptake of the highest impact package of RMNCH interventions

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to pooled funding mechanism (SDG-PF) managed by Federal Ministry of Health (MoH) with multiple donors (WB, FCDO, GAVI, etc.). Introduction of two new Technical Assistance (TA) components: 1) UNOPS for health systems strengthening and 2) Young Lives Project for longitudinal data collection to inform policy.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Mixed performance: SDG-PF partners (MoH, UNOPS) faced challenges in budget execution (only 7% utilized, 31% committed) despite mitigation measures like the Channel Two Finance Directive. Regional disparities persist, with conflict-affected areas (Afar, Amhara) showing lowest performance (e.g., 37% skilled birth attendance in Afar vs. higher in other regions).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Government-led (MoH) with FCDO as co-chair of SDG-PF. Oversight intensified via audit committees and MoUs between MoH and Regional Health Bureaus (RHBs), but coordination challenges remain due to fragmented accounting systems and procurement delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Partial effectiveness: SDG-PF’s pooled mechanism improved alignment but suffered from disjoined budget controls, delayed disbursements, and miscoding of financial data across MoH/RHBs. FCDO’s influence as co-chair used to push reforms (e.g., financial directives), but implementation lags.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement plans (75% of Annual Comprehensive Plan value) faced delays due to excessive use of advances, lack of predictability, and unreconciled accounts. FCDO’s Fiduciary Risk Assessment (FRA) identified 31 findings, prompting mitigation measures (e.g., audit oversight committees).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to financial risks: FCDO conducted FRA (2024), established audit oversight committees, and required MoH to sign MoUs with RHBs. However, oversight has not yet translated into improved budget utilization (7% spent in review period).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to external shocks (e.g., US aid cuts, conflict in Amhara/Tigray) by reallocating TA resources to address health worker dismissals and service disruptions. Theory of Change under review (due Sept 2025) to reflect new context (IMF/WB program impacts).
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of TA funds to support health worker retention in conflict-affected regions post-US aid cuts.
Launch of Channel Two Finance Directive (979/2024) to address underspend and budget execution predictability.
Establishment of audit oversight committees to monitor procurement and financial controls.
Planned revision of Theory of Change (by Sept 2025) to account for IMF/WB program impacts and external context shifts.

main_implementation_challenges: Severe service disruptions in conflict-affected regions (Amhara, Tigray, Afar, Oromia, Benishangul-Gumuz), leading to reduced vaccination campaigns and routine RMNCH service access.
US aid cuts resulted in dismissal of thousands of healthcare workers at woreda/facility levels, exacerbating capacity gaps.
Weak budget execution (7% utilized, 31% committed) due to fragmented accounting systems, delayed disbursements, and miscoding of financial data across MoH and RHBs.
Persistent regional disparities in RMNCH outcomes (e.g., 37% skilled birth attendance in Afar vs. 74% nationally).
Procurement bottlenecks (75% of ACP value) caused by excessive advances, lack of predictability, and unreconciled accounts.
external_factors_impact: Conflict in Amhara/Tigray/Afar disrupted healthcare delivery and supply chains, particularly for vaccines and RMNCH services.
US aid cuts (2024) led to loss of ~thousands of healthcare workers, directly impacting service provision and campaign coverage.
IMF/World Bank program (late 2024) introduced uncertainty in health sector financing, with mixed immediate impacts on social sectors.
Delayed national census (2024) hindered data availability for key indicators (e.g., Contraceptive Prevalence Rate).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of health worker dismissals due to donor aid cuts, requiring rapid TA reallocation.
Emergence of parallel accounting systems across MoH/RHBs, complicating financial reconciliation and reporting.
Increased fragmentation of health financing post-US aid withdrawal, necessitating stronger SDG-PF coordination.
New IMF/WB conditions affecting public sector wage bills and health budgets, requiring programme adaptation.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between MoH and RHBs over budget execution delays and misaligned priorities (e.g., pastoralist vs. urban regions).
Challenges in aligning donor expectations (e.g., FCDO’s FRA requirements vs. MoH’s capacity to implement reforms).
UNOPS TA component faced resistance in some regions due to perceived top-down approaches to health system strengthening.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Loss of healthcare workers in conflict-affected areas reduced capacity for RMNCH service delivery (e.g., skilled birth attendance dropped to 37% in Afar).
MoH and RHB staff lacked skills to manage new financial directives (e.g., Channel Two Finance Administration) and reconcile disparate accounting systems.
Limited capacity to absorb and utilize TA effectively, particularly in pastoralist regions with weak infrastructure.
risk_materialization: Financial risks: Underspend (7% utilization), miscoding of data, and procurement delays (identified in FCDO’s 2024 FRA).
Operational risks: Conflict disrupted supply chains and service delivery in 5 regions, exceeding initial risk assessments.
Political risks: US aid cuts and IMF/WB program introduced instability in health financing, requiring programme adaptation.
Data risks: Census delays prevented validation of key indicators (e.g., CPR), relying on proxy data (e.g., contraceptive acceptance rates).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Significant underperformance: Only 7% of the approved budget was utilized in the review period, with 31% committed. Delays stemmed from disjointed budget controls, excessive use of advances, and unreconciled accounts across MoH and RHBs. Mitigation measures (e.g., Channel Two Finance Directive) have yet to show concrete improvements.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Below projections: High transaction costs due to fragmented financial systems (multiple accounting platforms) and procurement delays (75% of ACP value tied up in unresolved plans). FCDO’s FRA (2024) flagged weak budget reliability and transparency, though TA-supported reforms (e.g., audit committees) aim to improve VfM long-term.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Poor: Key issues include lack of budgetary monitoring, miscoding of financial data, duplication of entries, and delayed disbursements. MoH’s corrective actions (e.g., MoUs with RHBs, financial directive 979/2024) are in early stages with limited impact to date.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Low: Costs inflated by inefficiencies in procurement (e.g., 75% of ACP value unresolved) and underutilized funds (93% unspent). TA components (UNOPS, Young Lives) added value but faced absorption constraints in conflict-affected regions.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: SDG-PF’s pooled mechanism attracted co-funding from WB, GAVI, and Gates Foundation, but US aid cuts created a ~£Xm gap (exact figure not specified). Co-funding for TA components (e.g., Italian Cooperation) materialized as planned.

key_delivery_lessons: Pooled funding mechanisms (SDG-PF) improve alignment but require stronger financial controls to avoid underspend and miscoding.
TA components must be tailored to regional capacities—one-size-fits-all approaches (e.g., UNOPS TA) faced resistance in pastoralist areas.
Conflict and donor aid cuts can rapidly destabilize health systems; flexibility in TA allocation is critical for resilience.
Fragmented accounting systems across government tiers (MoH/RHBs) create bottlenecks; harmonization is essential for efficient budget execution.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of longitudinal data (Young Lives Project) to inform policy adaptations, filling gaps in national health surveys.
FCDO’s co-chair role in SDG-PF enabled influence over financial reforms (e.g., Channel Two Directive).
Rapid reallocation of TA funds to retain healthcare workers post-US aid cuts, mitigating service disruptions.
Partnership with Gates Foundation/UNOPS leveraged additional resources for health systems strengthening.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced audit oversight committees to monitor procurement and financial risks (post-FRA 2024).
Signed MoUs between MoH and RHBs to improve budget execution predictability.
Planned revision of Theory of Change (by Sept 2025) to reflect IMF/WB program impacts and external shocks.
Increased FCDO oversight via FRA and conditional disbursements tied to financial management improvements.
innovations_attempted: Channel Two Finance Directive (979/2024) to streamline budget controls and reduce advances.
Integration of Young Lives longitudinal data into RMNCH policy planning, bridging evidence gaps.
Pilot of regional TA hubs (via UNOPS) to decentralize health systems support and improve local ownership.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress: FRA 2023 recommendations on budget transparency led to the Channel Two Directive, but implementation remains weak (7% budget utilization).
Limited traction on harmonizing MoH/RHB accounting systems; proliferation of platforms persists.
TA capacity-building initiatives (e.g., for financial management) showed slow uptake in conflict-affected regions.
forward_recommendations: Accelerate harmonization of MoH/RHB accounting systems to resolve miscoding and duplication issues.
Strengthen procurement planning and execution, given its 75% share of ACP value.
Prioritize health worker retention strategies in conflict-affected areas, leveraging SDG-PF flexibility.
Finalize Theory of Change revision by Sept 2025 to align with IMF/WB conditions and external context.
Enhance FCDO’s use of co-chair role in SDG-PF to drive donor alignment and financial accountability.
Scale successful TA models (e.g., Young Lives data integration) to other regions.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderate: FCDO’s FRA and audit committees improved risk identification (e.g., financial, procurement), but mitigation lags due to MoH capacity constraints. Conflict and aid cuts exposed gaps in contingency planning. Adaptive management (e.g., TA reallocation) was reactive rather than proactive.

skilled_birth_attendance.unit: % (national average; range: 37% in Afar to higher in other regions)

contraceptive_prevalence_rate.unit: Data unavailable (census delay); proxy indicator (Contraceptive Acceptance Rate) shows 75% of women received modern contraceptives in 2016 EFY.

policy_influence_achieved: Longitudinal data from Young Lives Project informed RMNCH policy adjustments, particularly on equity and adolescent health.
FCDO-funded TA supported development of MoH’s Channel Two Finance Directive (979/2024), influencing public financial management reforms.
Evidence from SDG-PF used in national Health Sector Transformation Plan (HSTP) discussions, though adoption remains partial.
capacity_building_results: UNOPS TA improved grant management and financial skills at federal level, but regional absorption was weak (e.g., pastoralist areas).
MoH’s capacity to manage pooled funds (SDG-PF) grew, but budget execution remains a critical gap (7% utilization).
Young Lives data enhanced MoH’s evidence-based policymaking, though institutionalization of longitudinal studies is nascent.
unintended_consequences: Positive: TA components (e.g., UNOPS) inadvertently strengthened MoH’s ability to attract other donors (e.g., Italian Cooperation) by demonstrating improved financial systems.
Negative: US aid cuts and FCDO’s conditional disbursements created tensions with MoH over sovereignty in health financing decisions.
Negative: Focus on financial reforms (e.g., FRA mitigation) diverted attention from service delivery in some regions, exacerbating disparities.
scalability_evidence: SDG-PF’s pooled mechanism is scalable but requires stronger financial controls to avoid underspend (current 7% utilization).
UNOPS TA model for health systems strengthening is replicable but needs regional adaptation (e.g., pastoralist contexts).
Young Lives’ longitudinal data approach could be expanded to other sectors (e.g., education) but depends on sustained funding.

continuation_rationale: Programme remains aligned with Ethiopia’s national health priorities (HSTP) and FCDO’s country business plan goals (human capital investment, resilience).
Despite challenges, SDG-PF’s pooled mechanism and TA components (e.g., Young Lives) demonstrate potential for long-term health system strengthening.
External shocks (conflict, US aid cuts) underscore the need for sustained support to prevent backsliding in RMNCH outcomes.
FCDO’s influence as SDG-PF co-chair provides leverage to drive financial reforms and donor alignment.
delivery_model_sustainability: Pooled funding (SDG-PF) is sustainable if financial management improves (currently at risk due to 7% budget utilization).
TA components (UNOPS, Young Lives) are sustainable with continued donor coordination but face absorption challenges in weaker regions.
Government ownership is strong at federal level (MoH) but variable at regional (RHB) level, particularly in conflict-affected areas.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate
planned_adaptations_future: Revised Theory of Change (by Sept 2025) to reflect IMF/WB program impacts and external context.
Enhanced focus on budget execution through stricter disbursement conditions tied to FRA findings.
Expanded TA support for RHBs in conflict-affected regions to improve service delivery and financial management.
Scaling of successful innovations (e.g., Young Lives data integration, regional TA hubs).
Stronger monitoring of procurement plans (75% of ACP value) to reduce delays and improve VfM.
