programme_metadata.programme_title: African Continental Free Trade Area Support Programme

output_1.title: ODI - Continental AfCFTA negotiations and implementation supported through high quality research, capacity building and evidence dissemination

output_2.title: ODI - Country AfCFTA negotiations and implementation supported through high quality research, capacity building and evidence dissemination

output_3.title: TMA - Continental AfCFTA negotiations and implementation on trade facilitation is supported through harmonizing policies and standards, operationalizing policies, installing digital solutions, and capacity building

output_4.title: TMA - Country and Regional Economic Community (REC) AfCFTA implementation on trade facilitation is supported through harmonising policies and standards, operationalising policies, installing digital solutions, and capacity building

output_5.title: Implementing partners deliver effectively, adapt to changing context, and work in partnership to support AfCFTA negotiations and implementation

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme has evolved to focus on three geographic levels: continental (AfCFTA Secretariat), regional (Lagos-Abidjan corridor), and national (Ghana, Nigeria, Benin, Togo, Cote D’Ivoire). Some budget reductions led to adjustments, such as reducing the number of Technical Advisers from 4 to 3.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ODI and TMA generally met expectations in terms of responsiveness and reporting, but there is room for improvement in reporting accuracy and coordination. TMA’s delivery on continental trade facilitation moderately did not meet expectations due to quality issues despite meeting quantity milestones.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme embedded a Senior Investment Expert within the AfCFTA Secretariat, which has been instrumental in driving negotiations and maintaining momentum. However, coordination between ODI, TMA, and the Secretariat requires improvement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between partners (ODI and TMA) was functional but not optimal. There were gaps in joint planning and delivery, particularly in aligning activities toward common outcomes. The review recommends improved collaboration and communication.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was adequate but could be strengthened with more proactive risk management and data-driven decision-making. The review highlights the need for improved contingency planning to avoid delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility in adapting to budget reductions (e.g., reducing Technical Advisers) and amending milestones (e.g., border assessments in Cote D’Ivoire). However, further adaptive management is needed to address planning and communication issues.
adaptive_management_examples: Amendment of border assessment milestones in response to delays, replacing physical assessments with desktop reviews for Seme-Krake and Benin-Togo borders.
Reduction of Technical Advisers from 4 to 3 due to budget constraints, while maintaining critical support to the AfCFTA Secretariat.
Embedding a Senior Investment Expert within the AfCFTA Secretariat to drive negotiations and high-level engagement.

main_implementation_challenges: Slow start and delays due to ODA budget reductions, which reduced the scope of work and impacted the timeline for achieving outcomes.
Planning and communication gaps between partners (ODI, TMA, and FCDO), leading to misaligned activities and missed opportunities for mitigation.
Quality issues in TMA’s delivery of trade facilitation outputs, where quantity milestones were met but quality assessments fell short.
Capacity constraints within the AfCFTA Secretariat and member states, affecting the pace of policy implementation and institutionalization.
external_factors_impact: ODA budget reductions disrupted initial planning and limited the programme’s ability to scale activities as originally envisioned.
Political and institutional dynamics within AfCFTA member states (e.g., delays in establishing National Trade Facilitation Committees) slowed progress.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated challenges in operationalizing digital solutions (e.g., internet infrastructure at border posts) and ensuring sustained use by local operators.
Limited budget lines for recurring costs (e.g., internet services) at border posts, risking blackouts and disrupted operations.
partner_relationship_issues: ODI and TMA worked independently at times, with insufficient joint planning or alignment of activities toward shared outcomes.
Feedback from the AfCFTA Secretariat indicated that while embedded experts (e.g., Senior Investment Expert) were valuable, broader coordination between partners could be improved.
capacity_constraints_emerged: The AfCFTA Secretariat and some member states lacked sufficient capacity to fully absorb and institutionalize programme outputs (e.g., trade policies, digital tools).
Delays in establishing permanent structures (e.g., Trade Working Groups in Nigeria and Benin) due to limited local ownership and budget constraints.
risk_materialization: Budget reductions materialized as a key risk, leading to reduced technical support (e.g., fewer Technical Advisers).
Staff absences and turnover disrupted continuity in some workstreams, highlighting the need for better contingency planning.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme spent £2.3 million in FY23/24, in line with adjusted plans following ODA reductions. Budget execution was constrained by earlier reductions, leading to reprioritization (e.g., fewer Technical Advisers).
value_for_money_assessment: Value for money was achieved in some areas (e.g., ODI’s high-quality research outputs and policy influence), but there were inefficiencies in TMA’s trade facilitation activities, where quality did not match quantity.

Opportunities for cost-sharing with other donors (e.g., for conferences) were underutilized, and some activities (e.g., NTFC Information Sharing Platform) lacked sustained uptake due to limited local capacity.
financial_management_quality: Financial management by ODI was satisfactory, with timely and accurate reporting. TMA’s financial management met basic requirements but required improvements in transparency and alignment with quality expectations.
Budget reductions were managed reactively rather than proactively, leading to last-minute adjustments (e.g., reducing Technical Advisers).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was demonstrated in ODI’s delivery of research and advocacy (e.g., leveraging existing events like WTO Public Forum for outreach).
TMA’s trade facilitation activities faced cost inefficiencies, particularly in digital solutions where uptake and sustainability were limited by local capacity and funding gaps.

key_delivery_lessons: Embedding experts within institutions (e.g., AfCFTA Secretariat) can significantly enhance influence and momentum, but requires clear terms of reference and alignment with institutional priorities.
Quality assessments must be prioritized alongside quantity milestones to avoid outputs that meet volume targets but fail to deliver impact.
Contingency planning is critical to mitigate risks such as staff absences, budget reductions, and delays in partner responsiveness.
successful_delivery_practices: ODI’s integration of research dissemination with high-profile events (e.g., WTO Public Forum, SOAS-ODI Conference) effectively amplified programme messages and engaged key stakeholders.
The Senior Investment Expert’s role in coordinating AfCFTA Protocol on Investment negotiations was highlighted as a best practice for embedding technical support.
Amending milestones in response to delays (e.g., replacing physical border assessments with desktop reviews) allowed the programme to maintain progress.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced a more structured approach to work planning for FY25/26, including outcome mapping to clarify pathways to impact.
Recommended improved coordination mechanisms between ODI, TMA, and the AfCFTA Secretariat to align activities and reporting.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of the Electronic Certificate of Origin (E-CO) system, though uptake was limited by private sector engagement and cost measurement gaps.
Development of an Information Sharing Platform for National Trade Facilitation Committees (NTFCs), though training and institutionalization remain works in progress.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on improving partner coordination, but gaps remain in joint planning and adaptive management.
Limited advancement in addressing quality issues in TMA’s trade facilitation outputs, though some corrective actions (e.g., desktop reviews) were implemented.
forward_recommendations: Substantially improve work planning for FY25/26 with clear outcome pathways, rigorous prioritization, and linked workstreams.
Enhance partner coordination through structured joint planning sessions and shared monitoring frameworks.
Strengthen adaptive management with data-driven decision-making, contingency planning, and proactive risk mitigation.
Measure external perceptions of the programme (e.g., via Secretariat feedback) to assess influence and reputation.
Explore cost-sharing opportunities with other donors to maximize value for money in conferences and advocacy.
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was reactive rather than proactive, with budget reductions and staffing issues impacting delivery. The review calls for a more structured, evidence-based approach to risk identification and mitigation.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: The programme engaged with the AfCFTA Secretariat, regional bodies (e.g., ECOWAS), and national governments in Ghana, Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and Cote D’Ivoire. Direct beneficiaries included technical advisers, trade officials, and private sector stakeholders involved in trade facilitation.
Quantitative targets for beneficiaries were not explicitly stated, but outputs (e.g., 9 policy studies, 9 advocacy events) suggest broad reach among policymakers and stakeholders.
policy_influence_achieved: Strong influence at the continental level, particularly through the Senior Investment Expert’s role in advancing the AfCFTA Protocol on Investment. The Secretariat’s feedback confirms that embedded support has shaped negotiation processes and high-level engagement.
National-level influence was mixed, with progress in some countries (e.g., Cote D’Ivoire’s trade facilitation strategy) but delays in others due to capacity constraints.
capacity_building_results: Capacity building for the AfCFTA Secretariat (e.g., NIC Advisors, Senior Investment Expert) was effective, with evidence of improved negotiation and coordination capacities.

At the national level, capacity building was uneven, with some countries (e.g., Central African Republic, Madagascar) benefiting from workshops, while others faced delays in institutionalizing support structures (e.g., NTFCs).
unintended_consequences: Positive: The programme’s focus on green trade (e.g., COP28 engagement, research on sustainable industrialization) unintentionally elevated the profile of climate considerations in AfCFTA discussions.
Negative: Limited local ownership of digital tools (e.g., Information Sharing Platform) risks low sustained use post-programme.
scalability_evidence: Approaches like embedding technical experts and leveraging high-profile events (e.g., WTO Public Forum) are scalable but require tailored adaptation to local contexts.
Trade facilitation models (e.g., E-CO system) show scalability potential but need stronger private sector engagement and cost-benefit evidence to encourage uptake.

continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated progress in key areas (e.g., continental policy influence, capacity building for the AfCFTA Secretariat) and shows potential to achieve its objectives with improved management and coordination.
FY25/26 is the final year of the current business case, necessitating a focus on consolidating outcomes and ensuring sustainability of interventions.
The review identifies correctable challenges (e.g., planning gaps, partner coordination) that do not warrant closure but require targeted adaptations.
delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model (ODI for policy, TMA for trade facilitation) is viable but requires stronger integration and local ownership to ensure long-term sustainability.
Embedded technical support (e.g., Senior Investment Expert) has proven effective and could be institutionalized within the AfCFTA Secretariat post-programme.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied with progress but expects improvements in coordination, adaptive management, and outcome focus for FY25/26.
planned_adaptations_future: Implement a more structured work planning process with clear outcome pathways and prioritization.
Strengthen partner coordination through joint planning mechanisms and shared monitoring tools.
Enhance adaptive management with proactive risk mitigation and contingency planning.
Focus on institutionalizing key outputs (e.g., NTFCs, digital tools) to ensure sustainability beyond the programme’s lifespan.
Explore options for scaling successful approaches (e.g., embedded experts, green trade integration) in future phases or related programmes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Building Peace and Stability in Iraq (BPSI) Programme

output_1.title: All components of the Building Peace and Stability Programme are mobilised in a timely manner and in line with the FCDO Programme Operating Framework.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme initially planned to mobilise an INGO-led consortium of Iraqi NGOs alongside IOM and a Third-Party Monitoring (TPM) component. Due to ODA budget uncertainty, only IOM was mobilised in FY 22/23. The consortium (led by IRC) and TPM were delayed until FY 23/24. The blended delivery model (multilateral + national NGOs) was not realised in Year 1 but is planned for Year 2.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IOM performed well in delivering the pilot phase (Nov 2022–Mar 2023), achieving key milestones. The IRC-led consortium was selected but not mobilised until June 2023 due to delays. Partners demonstrated flexibility in adapting to budget uncertainties and short-notice mobilisation requirements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Staffing gaps (e.g., loss of a UKBS Programme Manager) created oversight challenges. FCDO prioritised IOM delivery while awaiting clarity on ODA allocations, which impacted the rollout of other components. Coordination with UN agencies, donors, and government stakeholders was effective for advocacy socialisation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with IOM, UN agencies (IASC Framework), and Government of Iraq (GoI) was strong, particularly around Durable Solutions advocacy. However, the premature closure of Jeddah 5 camp (May 2023) by GoI scattered IDP communities, complicating assistance distribution and requiring adaptive coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for the IRC-led consortium was completed via a competitive call (Jan–Mar 2023), with 11 proposals received and IRC selected. Due diligence and accountable grant agreements were finalised by June 2023. IOM’s project was designed and mobilised under an MOU. Delays in TPM procurement were attributed to ODA uncertainty.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensive for IOM’s pilot phase, with regular quarterly reporting and partner meetings. However, staffing gaps and ODA pauses reduced oversight capacity for other components. FCDO relied on IOM’s existing systems for fiduciary and safeguarding risk management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: FCDO adapted by prioritising IOM’s delivery to meet political commitments (e.g., supporting returns from Al Hol, Syria) while delaying the consortium and TPM. The programme demonstrated flexibility in reallocating resources to address immediate needs (e.g., QIPs for infrastructure rehabilitation).
adaptive_management_examples: Shift from planned blended delivery (INGO consortium + IOM + TPM) to IOM-only in Year 1 due to ODA uncertainty.
Incorporation of lessons from IOM’s pilot phase (e.g., community gatekeepers for tension de-escalation) into Year 2 planning with IRC.
Revised logframe development to reflect results from IOM and IRC projects, pending ODA trajectory clarity.
Use of IOM’s complementary programming model to address barriers like civil documentation, housing, and security clearance, informed by real-time community feedback.

main_implementation_challenges: Uncertainty and pauses in ODA allocations (Aug 2022), delaying consortium mobilisation and TPM procurement.
Premature and forced closure of Jeddah 5 camp (May 2023) by GoI, dispersing IDPs and increasing protection risks.
Staffing gaps (e.g., UKBS Programme Manager departure) reducing programme oversight and management capacity.
Limited government capacity and political sensitivities around IDPs with perceived Daesh affiliations, stalling transition from humanitarian to development support.
Security constraints and opaque clearance processes hindering returns and reintegration.
external_factors_impact: Reduction in humanitarian funding globally, shifting donor focus to long-term development support in Iraq.
Media reporting on IDPs (including those with Daesh affiliations) was unexpectedly balanced, reducing reputational risks initially anticipated.
COVID-19 impacts not explicitly mentioned, but broader ODA pressures (e.g., HMG fiscal constraints) significantly disrupted planning.
contextual_constraints_new: GoI’s accelerated camp closure policy (e.g., Jeddah 5) created unanticipated dispersal of IDPs, complicating targeted assistance.
Lack of accurate data on IDP needs and barriers to return (e.g., home destruction, civil documentation gaps) emerged as a critical constraint.
Local government and community resistance to reintegrating IDPs, particularly women-headed households, due to stigma and security concerns.
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in consortium mobilisation strained relationships with shortlisted NGOs, risking loss of partner trust.
IOM’s pilot phase revealed tensions between national NGOs and local governments over resource allocation and prioritisation.
Potential reputational risks with partners if ODA reductions undermine UK commitments to Durable Solutions.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s reduced programme management capacity due to staffing gaps, impacting oversight of IOM and consortium mobilisation.
Limited capacity within GoI and local governments to absorb and reintegrate returning IDPs, exacerbating displacement protraction.
National NGOs (under IRC consortium) required additional support to meet FCDO’s compliance and reporting standards.
risk_materialization: Major fiduciary risks (fraud, corruption) were mitigated through due diligence but remained a high concern in Iraq’s context.
Safeguarding risks (e.g., diversion of funds to armed groups) were monitored but not materialised; media risks around Daesh-affiliated IDPs were lower than expected.
Operational risks from security restrictions and remote working persisted, requiring adaptive delivery models (e.g., IOM’s QIPs).

budget_execution_vs_plan.planned: Blended delivery through IOM, INGO consortium, and TPM.
budget_execution_vs_plan.actual: Only IOM was funded in Year 1 (£ allocation not specified). Consortium and TPM delayed to FY 23/24 due to ODA uncertainty. Budget reallocated to prioritise IOM’s pilot phase (Nov 2022–Mar 2023).
budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_rationale: ODA pauses (Aug 2022) forced reprioritisation to meet political commitments (e.g., Al Hol returns) with limited funds.

economy.planned: Cost-effective conflict prevention via local NGOs and multilateral partners.
economy.actual: IOM’s QIPs were more expensive than other peacebuilding activities but justified by their role in infrastructure rehabilitation and tension reduction. Economies of scale achieved through IOM’s existing systems.
economy.evidence: 18,300 direct and 1,300 indirect beneficiaries reached via QIPs; low start-up costs due to IOM’s established operations.

efficiency.planned: Efficient delivery through local partners with strong networks.
efficiency.actual: IOM’s pilot phase demonstrated efficient grassroots reach, but delays in consortium mobilisation reduced overall efficiency. National NGOs (once operational) expected to improve efficiency in Year 2.
efficiency.evidence: QIPs enhanced access to communities and local leaders, providing timely data for advocacy.

effectiveness.planned: Displaced populations rehabilitated and returned to Daesh-affected areas via government-civil society collaboration.
effectiveness.actual: Tangible progress at district level (e.g., IOM’s complementary programming) but limited national-level influence. Success dependent on evidence collection and influencing networks not yet fully developed.
effectiveness.evidence: Pilot phase addressed barriers like civil documentation and housing, but systemic change requires stronger GoI leadership.

equity.planned: Focus on poorest and most marginalised IDPs, including women-headed households.
equity.actual: IOM’s QIPs targeted marginalised groups, but reach was limited by camp closures and security constraints. Consortium in Year 2 aims to expand equity focus.
equity.evidence: Women-headed households prioritised in project design; 18,300+ beneficiaries included vulnerable IDPs.

strengths: Thorough pre-programme due diligence for IOM and IRC.
Regular quarterly reporting and partner meetings to monitor fiduciary risks.
IOM’s rigorous procurement and contracting processes maximised VFM.
weaknesses: Staffing gaps reduced FCDO’s capacity for financial oversight.
Delays in consortium mobilisation limited financial controls for that component in Year 1.
High corruption risk in Iraq required continuous mitigation efforts.

cost_efficiency_achieved.planned: Local NGOs to offer best value through lower overheads and sustainability.
cost_efficiency_achieved.actual: Not yet measurable (consortium operational from June 2023). IOM’s delivery was cost-efficient given economies of scale but higher per-unit costs for QIPs.
cost_efficiency_achieved.comparison: HART programme lessons suggest national NGOs will improve efficiency in Year 2.

key_delivery_lessons: ODA uncertainty severely disrupts programme mobilisation; contingency planning for budget pauses is critical.
Building relationships with flexible, reputable partners (e.g., IOM, IRC) enables rapid adaptation to funding changes.
Staffing stability is essential for oversight; gaps lead to delayed decision-making and partner management issues.
Pilot phases (e.g., IOM’s QIPs) provide valuable insights for scaling but require clear transition plans to full implementation.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted from Sudan due to conflict; expanded activities in Gulf Cooperation Council countries with additional £2m funding for FY 24/25 (£1m each to IOM/ILO).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IOM and ILO met/exceeded most milestones despite challenges. ILO built strong foundations for labour migration statistics; IOM delivered direct migrant support. Coordination between partners improved but still needs strengthening at regional/country levels.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: New governance structure launched in 2024 to improve coordination. FCDO oversight leveraged to enhance responsiveness to beneficiary needs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Regional Ministerial Forum on Migration (RMFM) emerged as a key coordination platform, though its long-term sustainability remains dependent on BRMM funding. Risk of duplication between IOM/ILO persists.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained active oversight, enabling adaptive management (e.g., reallocation of funds post-Sudan withdrawal, approval of additional £2m).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by reallocating resources after Sudan conflict, expanding scope to Gulf States, and approving additional funding for high-impact activities.
adaptive_management_examples: Withdrawal from Sudan in Year 2 due to conflict, with reallocation of activities to other EHOA countries.
Additional £2m funding approved for FY 24/25 to scale up successful interventions (e.g., entrepreneurship training, RMFM).
Early completion of some Outcome 3 milestones to accelerate policy ratification.

main_implementation_challenges: Conflict in Sudan forced cessation of activities in Year 2.
High ambition of Outcome 4 (migrant protection) requires long-term embedding of safeguards in national/regional frameworks.
Coordination gaps between IOM and ILO at regional/country levels risk duplication.
Sustainability of key interventions (e.g., RMFM, entrepreneurship training) unclear post-BRMM funding.
external_factors_impact: Conflict in Sudan disrupted implementation and required geographic reallocation.
Climate change increasingly drives migration decisions in vulnerable countries.
Gulf States’ labor market demands influence skills/protection priorities.
contextual_constraints_new: Rising climate-induced migration pressures in EHOA.
Gulf Cooperation Council countries’ evolving labor policies require adaptive negotiation strategies.
Post-pandemic economic recovery uneven across target countries, affecting labor migration opportunities.
partner_relationship_issues: IOM and ILO have strong individual relationships with governments but need deeper joint engagement, particularly with Gulf States.
Demand for entrepreneurship training outstrips supply, creating tensions with beneficiaries.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in South Sudan for labor force/migration surveys required targeted support.
National Statistical Offices (NSOs) in some countries lack resources to sustain data systems post-BRMM.
risk_materialization: Sudan conflict (political risk) materialized, requiring programme adaptation.
Major risk rating persisted due to complex regional dynamics (conflict, climate, governance).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; additional £2m approved for FY 24/25 to expand activities. Initial £20.5m budget includes £1.487m for Migration Multi-Partner Trust Fund (MMPTF).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High: Programme leveraged partnerships (ILO/IOM) to achieve system-level changes (e.g., labor migration data systems, policy frameworks) alongside direct beneficiary impacts. Independent review highlighted BRMM’s unique ‘mobility-skills-protection nexus’ as a VFM strength.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Implementing partners (ILO/IOM) demonstrated efficient use of funds, with most milestones met despite challenges. FCDO’s oversight ensured accountability.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient: Costs per beneficiary not specified, but programme achieved both direct impacts (e.g., training 80%+ trainees scoring ≥60% on post-tests) and systemic changes (e.g., labor migration statistics integration in national surveys).

key_delivery_lessons: Strong government relationships (ILO/IOM) enabled adaptive management but required deeper FCDO coordination to avoid duplication.
Regional platforms (e.g., RMFM) are critical for policy alignment but need sustainable funding models.
Direct beneficiary support (e.g., entrepreneurship training) has high demand and spillover effects, justifying potential expansion.
successful_delivery_practices: Phased approach to labor migration statistics (foundational work → capacity building → policy integration) proved effective.
Combining technical assistance (e.g., data tools) with advocacy (e.g., policy drafts) accelerated systemic change.
Flexible funding allowed scaling of high-impact activities (e.g., bespoke loan products for migrants).
management_adaptations_made: Launched new governance structure in 2024 to improve IOM/ILO coordination.
Reallocated resources post-Sudan conflict to maintain progress in other countries.
Increased impact weighting for Output 1.1 (from 5.3% to 10%) based on demonstrated results.
innovations_attempted: Bespoke loan products for migrants (in development) to support financial inclusion.
Regional Ministerial Forum on Migration (RMFM) as a diplomatic tool for Gulf States negotiations.
Integration of gender-sensitive labor migration statistics tools in national data systems.
previous_recommendations_progress: Improved IOM/ILO coordination (though gaps remain).
Advanced sustainability assessments for key interventions (ongoing).
forward_recommendations: Deepening IOM/ILO collaboration at country/regional levels to mitigate duplication.
Assessing long-term sustainability of entrepreneurship training and RMFM, including funding contingencies.
Strengthening engagement with Gulf States to embed migrant protections in Bilateral Labor Agreements.
Evaluating scalability of high-impact interventions (e.g., loan products, data tools).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Major risks (e.g., Sudan conflict) were managed through adaptive responses, but persistent ‘Major’ risk rating reflects unresolved regional instability. Proactive measures (e.g., additional funding, governance reforms) mitigated some operational risks.

policy_influence_achieved: Draft national policies finalized (e.g., labor migration governance frameworks).
Progress toward ratification of international labor conventions.
Gulf States negotiations advanced through RMFM platform.
capacity_building_results: National Statistical Offices (NSOs) in most target countries now integrate labor migration modules in surveys/censuses.
80%+ of trainees scored ≥60% on post-test evaluations for labor migration statistics.
South Sudan conducted its first labor force and migration survey with BRMM support.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Entrepreneurship training reduced migration pressure by improving local livelihoods (anecdotal evidence).
Positive: RMFM fostered unexpected regional alignment on migration issues.
scalability_evidence: Labor migration data tools adopted by multiple countries, suggesting regional scalability.
Entrepreneurship training model could be expanded with additional funding.
Bilateral Labor Agreement templates developed for Gulf States negotiations are replicable.

continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong progress toward outcomes despite complex context (conflict, climate, governance challenges).
Unique value in addressing interconnected migration-skills-protection challenges in EHOA.
High demand for interventions (e.g., entrepreneurship training) and potential for regional impact justification continuation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Current model is effective but depends on FCDO funding. Sustainability of key platforms (e.g., RMFM) and data systems requires long-term planning.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High: Programme scored ‘A’ for 2024, with praise for adaptive management and partner relationships.
planned_adaptations_future: Exploring funding contingencies for RMFM post-BRMM.
Scaling up entrepreneurship training and loan products based on demand/impact.
Deepening Gulf States engagement to embed migrant protections in bilateral agreements.
Strengthening monitoring of sustainability indicators.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme faced significant delays due to Government of Jordan (GoJ) approvals taking longer than anticipated. Workplans and targets were revised in-year to reflect this delay. Preparatory activities (e.g., consortium setup, staff mobilization, stakeholder consultations) were prioritized during the delay period.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: DRC (lead agency) and consortium partners (JRF, HI) focused on preparatory activities due to delays. No direct service delivery occurred during the review period, but partners demonstrated readiness through training, system establishment, and stakeholder engagement. Quarterly reports were submitted with minor delays in feedback response.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme leadership consists of a **Senior Responsible Owner (SRO)** and a **Programme Manager (also Programme Responsible Owner, PRO)**. Coordination mechanisms within the consortium were established, including regular meetings and joint planning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination was demonstrated during preparatory phases, including consortium mobilization, stakeholder consultations, and alignment with GoJ priorities. However, delays highlighted the need for closer donor involvement in government negotiations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: AGA signed with DRC in January 2022. Sub-grant agreements with partners (JRF, HI) were prepared but not fully executed due to delays. Procurement focused on staff contracts (retained due to Defence Orders) and preparatory activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO conducted **spot-check visits** in 2022 to assess financial systems, which were found to be robust. Regular monitoring was limited due to delayed implementation, but quarterly reports and ad-hoc risk reporting (e.g., exchange rate fluctuations) were reviewed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Budget was reprofiled to align with revised timelines (activities shifted to October 2022). Additional £1.5m was allocated to address priority needs identified by MoH and MoSD, increasing the budget from £11m to £12.54m.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised workplans and targets to account for GoJ approval delays.
Added new activities based on MoH/MoSD priorities, increasing budget.
Focused expenditures on preparatory work (e.g., training, stakeholder engagement) to mitigate idle costs.

main_implementation_challenges: **Delayed GoJ approvals** (longer negotiations than anticipated, requiring MoU signatures from MoPIC and line ministers).
**Exchange rate fluctuations** (11% GBP depreciation against USD in H1 2022, impacting delivery costs).
**Staff retention costs** due to Defence Orders preventing contract terminations during delays.
external_factors_impact: GoJ’s **Jordan Response Plan** and coordination channels were consulted, but final approvals required deeper donor engagement than expected.
Political expectation for **donor involvement in ministry-level negotiations** (not just technical teams).
contextual_constraints_new: Need for **MoU signatures from MoPIC** (not previously required for similar programmes).
Line ministry technical agreements were **insufficient to guarantee approval** without higher-level buy-in.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity to **start implementation** without GoJ approval, leading to focus on preparatory activities.
Exchange rate risks required additional financial management support from FCDO.
risk_materialization: **Moderate financial risk** (exchange rates, staff costs during delays).
**Delivery chain risks** (pending submission of risk map by DRC).

budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget increased from **£11m to £12.54m** to address MoH/MoSD priorities.
Expenditures focused on **staff costs and preparatory activities** (no direct service delivery in review period).
Budget lines reprofiled to October 2022 to align with GoJ approval timelines.
value_for_money_assessment: **Too early to assess VfM** due to delayed implementation.
Preparatory activities (e.g., training, stakeholder engagement) were prioritized to ensure readiness.
VfM metrics developed for future reviews but not yet applied.
financial_management_quality: DRC and partners have **solid financial systems** (confirmed via FCDO spot-checks).
Quarterly risk reporting and ad-hoc updates on exchange rate impacts.
Delivery chain risk map pending submission (deadline: December 2022).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Costs incurred for **staff retention and preparations** without output delivery.
Efforts to minimize costs (e.g., staff time spent on preparatory work).
currency_exchange_impacts: GBP depreciated by **11% against USD** (Jan–Jun 2022), increasing delivery costs.
FCDO provided guidance to DRC on managing exchange rate risks.

key_delivery_lessons: **Early government engagement is critical**: Involve MoPIC and line ministers (not just technical teams) in programme design to avoid approval delays.
**Donor visibility in negotiations**: GoJ expects direct donor participation in high-level discussions, not just delegate to implementers.
**Flexible budgeting**: Reprofiling and additional funds (e.g., £1.5m for MoH/MoSD priorities) helped adapt to delays.
successful_delivery_practices: Effective **consortium coordination** (DRC, JRF, HI) during preparatory phase.
Proactive **stakeholder consultations** (MoH, MoSD, MoPIC) to align priorities.
Use of **preparatory activities** (training, system setup) to mitigate idle costs.
management_adaptations_made: Revised logframe and workplans to reflect delays (target: February 2023).
Enhanced **financial oversight** (spot-checks, exchange rate monitoring).
Developed **delivery chain risk map** (pending submission).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Empowerment and Development for Girls Education (EDGE) Programme

output_1.title: Improved capacity of PEAS and PEAS network schools to deliver and scale up effective school management and safeguarding approaches

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme expanded with £4.17M costed amendment to construct two additional PEAS schools in Eastern and Southern Provinces. Logframe revised to streamline indicators, clarify alignment between PEAS and British Council components, and incentivize joint delivery through shared targets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: PEAS exceeded capacity-building targets (e.g., 400+ new boarding spaces, 350+ classroom places) but faced MoE delays in grant disbursements. British Council (BC) built trust with MoE but focused more on operational support than policy advocacy, limiting integration with PEAS’ evidence-based approaches.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Coordination between PEAS and BC improved via revised logframe but remains divergent in practice. PEAS leads school-level implementation; BC focuses on MoE capacity-building. Joint targets introduced but not yet fully operationalized.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Partial success: Joint logframe revisions and quarterly coordination meetings established, but components still operate semi-independently. BC’s policy influence was ad hoc (e.g., prompting MoE to commission a data gap report) rather than systematic.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: PEAS completed construction of 5 dormitories and 3 classroom blocks on schedule. BC’s procurement for policy events (e.g., 4 dissemination meetings) faced MoE delays in co-funding (e.g., per diems).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to MoE capacity constraints. PEAS provided contingency budgets for delayed teacher placements/grants. FCDO monthly finance reports used to monitor spend risks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to MoE’s delayed mock exams by using proxy indicators (e.g., 95% of school leaders reporting improved confidence in goal-setting). PEAS shifted to WhatsApp-based coaching to reduce travel costs.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised logframe to align PEAS/BC components and add joint targets.
Used WhatsApp for remote coaching to cut travel costs.
Advocated directly with MoE for grant-aided school status after initial delays.
PEAS led school selection assessments with District Education Offices to identify high-need government schools for TIEEZ expansion.

main_implementation_challenges: MoE capacity constraints caused delays in grant disbursements (66% of PEAS school costs covered vs. 80% target) and policy implementation (e.g., decentralization of disciplinary functions).
Divergent priorities between PEAS (school-level impact) and BC (MoE operational support) limited integrated outcomes.
Enrolment in PEAS schools slightly below capacity due to subject rotation requirements, affecting outcome indicator 1.4 (enrolment targets).
Politicized MoE processes (e.g., failure to produce annual statistics yearbook) required BC intervention to prompt action.
external_factors_impact: GRZ’s 2022 Free Secondary Education Policy increased enrolment pressure, straining government school resources and highlighting the need for PEAS’ capacity-building.
COVID-19 legacy effects (e.g., learning loss) likely contributed to lower-than-expected proficiency rates in G7/G9 (e.g., G7 English proficiency dropped from 67% to 63%).
Inflation and currency fluctuations (not explicitly quantified) implied in contingency budgeting for construction/materials.
contextual_constraints_new: MoE’s refusal to grant-aid PEAS schools until mid-year created financial sustainability risks.
Government teacher deployment delays required PEAS to cover supplementary costs.
Limited MoE data systems (e.g., lack of annual statistics yearbook) hindered evidence-based policy advocacy.
partner_relationship_issues: BC’s broad MoE support (e.g., Directorate operational improvements) was valued but not always aligned with PEAS’ specific policy advocacy goals (e.g., TIEEZ scale-up).
PEAS’ direct advocacy to MoE (e.g., for grant-aided status) proved more effective than BC-mediated approaches.
Some TIEEZ partner schools (e.g., in Kasama) showed lower gender parity in completion rates (F:75% vs. M:70%), suggesting variable partner engagement.
capacity_constraints_emerged: MoE’s slow progress on policy reforms (e.g., TSC disciplinary decentralization) due to financial/HR limitations.
PEAS schools required additional support to manage increased boarding capacity (e.g., safeguarding, staff training).
BC’s policy team lacked benchmarks to measure VFM for capacity-building activities.
risk_materialization: Moderate risk of MoE grant delays (materialized; 66% cost coverage vs. 80% target).
Risk of low policy uptake by MoE (partially materialized; 3 of 7 planned strategies drafted).
Risk of partner school disengagement (materialized in Kasama; lower girl completion rates).

budget_execution_vs_plan: Programme budget increased from £6.8M to £10.97M via £4.17M CDEL amendment for 2 additional schools. Budget execution on track, with contingency funds mitigating MoE grant delays.
PEAS spent efficiently on construction (5 dormitories, 3 classroom blocks) but faced unplanned costs due to MoE teacher deployment delays.
BC’s activities under-spent due to MoE’s slow co-funding (e.g., per diems for events).
value_for_money_assessment: PEAS component demonstrated strong VFM: cost per additional school place (~£2,460/student for 4,455 places) and improved learning outcomes (e.g., G9 English proficiency rose from 56% to 79%).
Efficiency gains: WhatsApp coaching reduced travel costs; prioritized boarding facilities to increase financial sustainability.
Effectiveness mixed: PEAS met output targets (e.g., 100% SIPs in network schools) but outcome 2 (MoE policy adoption) lagged (3/7 strategies drafted).
BC component VFM unclear due to lack of benchmarks; focus on operational support (e.g., venue costs) rather than measurable policy influence.
financial_management_quality: PEAS: High. Monthly FCDO finance reports monitored spend; contingency budgets addressed MoE delays. Transparent reporting on school-level cost coverage (66%).
BC: Adequate. Shared-cost principles applied (e.g., MoE contributed to event venues) but co-funding delays affected delivery.
MoE: Low. Chronic under-resourcing led to grant payment delays and underfunded PEAS schools.
cost_efficiency_achieved: PEAS: Achieved cost efficiencies via bulk construction (e.g., dormitories) and digital coaching. Cost per student place lower than government schools due to economies of scale.
BC: Limited evidence; policy-influencing costs not benchmarked against outcomes.
Programme-wide: 38,572 students reached at ~£284/student/year (£10.97M/4 years), but sustainability depends on MoE grant fulfillment.
co_funding_materialization: MoE partially materialized: Agreed to grant-aid PEAS schools mid-year but paid only 66% of school-level costs (target: 80%).
BC secured MoE in-kind contributions (e.g., venues) but cash co-funding (e.g., per diems) was inconsistent.
PEAS covered gaps via contingency funds, risking long-term financial sustainability.

key_delivery_lessons: Direct PEAS advocacy to MoE (e.g., for grant-aided status) was more effective than BC-mediated approaches.
Policy influence requires aligning with partners’ incentives (e.g., PEAS should lead TIEEZ scale-up advocacy, not BC).
Government capacity constraints necessitate flexible delivery (e.g., proxy indicators, digital tools).
Grant-aided models need early MoE buy-in to avoid financial sustainability risks.
successful_delivery_practices: PEAS’ construction of boarding facilities improved girl enrolment (e.g., 1,345 boarding places; 100% girl completion in some partner schools).
WhatsApp-based coaching reduced costs while maintaining support quality (95% of leaders reported improved confidence).
Joint logframe revisions clarified component alignment and introduced shared targets.
BC’s trust-building with MoE enabled interventions on politicized issues (e.g., data gap report).
management_adaptations_made: Streamlined logframe to reduce indicators and emphasize joint PEAS/BC targets.
Shifted from in-person to digital training (e.g., WhatsApp) to cut costs and improve reach.
Prioritized construction of income-generating assets (e.g., boarding facilities) to enhance school sustainability.
Adopted contingency budgets to mitigate MoE funding delays.
innovations_attempted: Cascading model: PEAS best practices shared with government schools via TIEEZ programme.
Development diplomacy: BC used EDGE resources to prompt MoE action on stalled initiatives (e.g., statistics yearbook).
Digital monitoring tools for school improvement plans (SIPs) to track progress remotely.
Co-funding mechanisms (e.g., MoE venue contributions) to stretch programme resources.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Improved PEAS/BC coordination via logframe revisions but integration remains incomplete.
MoE engagement strengthened (e.g., grant-aid agreement) but policy adoption still slow.
Gender parity improved in most partner schools (e.g., 100% girl completion in Southern/Luwingu) but lagged in Kasama (75% vs. 70% boys).
forward_recommendations: PEAS should lead direct advocacy for TIEEZ national scale-up, with BC providing targeted policy support.
Develop clear VFM benchmarks for BC’s capacity-building activities.
MoE should pre-commit to grant-aid timelines to avoid future delays.
Expand digital tools (e.g., WhatsApp) for low-cost monitoring and training.
Conduct a sustainability audit to assess PEAS schools’ financial viability post-EDGE.
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive: Contingency budgets and flexible indicators (e.g., proxy measures) mitigated MoE delays.
Reactive: Slow response to Kasama partner schools’ gender gaps; no preemptive measures for MoE capacity constraints.
Partially effective: Risks to policy adoption (outcome 2) were identified but not fully addressed due to BC’s operational focus.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.notes: Exceeds 2023 targets (33,612 total students) but enrolment in PEAS schools slightly below capacity due to subject rotation needs.

evidence: Learning outcomes improved (e.g., G9 English proficiency rose from 56% to 79%; girls outperformed boys in G7/G9).
But G7 proficiency declined (67% to 63%), suggesting COVID-19 learning loss persistence.
66% of PEAS school costs covered by sustainable income (target: 80%).
Only 3 of 7 MoE strategies/sub-sector documents developed (e.g., drafts for Secondary Education Directorate, TSC).
Limited evidence of MoE adopting PEAS/BC recommendations at scale.
BC’s policy influence was ad hoc (e.g., prompted data gap report) rather than systemic.

impact_evidence_strength.notes: Outcome 1 backed by quantitative data (e.g., proficiency rates, enrolment). Outcome 2 relies on anecdotal evidence (e.g., MoE feedback) and draft documents.

notes: PEAS schools: Likely sustainable if MoE fulfills grant-aid commitments (66% currently covered).
TIEEZ: Depends on MoE’s long-term adoption; no clear scale-up plan yet.
Policy reforms: MoE capacity constraints and slow progress (e.g., 3/7 strategies drafted) suggest low sustainability.

examples: MoE drafted 3 sub-sector strategies (e.g., Secondary Education Directorate) with EDGE input.
BC prompted MoE to commission a report on annual statistics yearbook gaps.
PEAS’ evidence on girl-focused interventions informed TSC’s safeguarding training resources.
But no large-scale policy adoption (e.g., TIEEZ model) yet.

evidence: 100% of PEAS schools have School Improvement Plans (SIPs).
95% of school leaders report improved goal-setting/tracking confidence.
Average World Management Survey score improved (primary: 3.9; secondary: 4.0).
TIEEZ schools showed variable progress (e.g., Kasama partner schools had lower girl completion rates: 75% vs. 100% in Southern/Luwingu).
50 partner secondary schools received capacity-building support.
Limited uptake of EDGE-generated evidence (e.g., only 4 dissemination events held).
MoE’s operational support improved but policy development lagged.

positive: PEAS schools’ excess capacity (e.g., 400+ boarding spaces) created flexibility for future enrolment growth.
BC’s trust-building with MoE enabled interventions on politicized issues (e.g., data gaps).
Digital tools (e.g., WhatsApp) improved monitoring reach in remote areas.
negative: MoE’s reliance on EDGE resources may reduce incentives for self-funded reforms.
Divergent PEAS/BC priorities delayed integrated outcomes (e.g., TIEEZ scale-up).
Some partner schools (e.g., Kasama) showed widening gender gaps in completion rates.

evidence: PEAS’ cascading model (TIEEZ) demonstrates potential for replication in other provinces.
MoE’s draft strategies (e.g., Secondary Education Directorate) reference EDGE approaches but lack implementation plans.
Cost per student (~£284/year) is competitive, but scalability depends on MoE’s financial commitment.
BC’s policy influence methods (e.g., trust-building) are transferable but not yet institutionalized.

continuation_rationale: PEAS component demonstrates strong output delivery (e.g., A scores, 38,572 students reached) and potential for impact if MoE adopts TIEEZ model.
BC’s MoE relationships provide a platform for future policy influence, though current approach needs refinement.
Alignment with GRZ’s Free Secondary Education Policy and BHC Lusaka country plan priorities.
Final year (2024–2025) critical for establishing 2 new PEAS schools and expanding TIEEZ to 60 schools.

delivery_model_sustainability.notes: PEAS’ school-level model is sustainable; BC’s capacity-building lacks long-term MoE ownership.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium
planned_adaptations_future: PEAS to lead direct advocacy for TIEEZ scale-up, with BC providing targeted support on high-opportunity policy areas.
Introduce VFM benchmarks for BC’s activities (e.g., cost per policy document influenced).
Develop a transition plan for MoE to assume full funding/responsibility for PEAS schools post-2025.
Expand digital monitoring tools to reduce oversight costs and improve data quality.
Conduct a lessons-learned exercise to inform potential Phase 2 design (e.g., deeper PEAS/BC integration).

output_1.title: GOK and business associations supported to strengthen anti-corruption and counter illicit finance practices

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme narrowed focus post-2022 ToC refresh to concentrate on anti-corruption and counter illicit finance. No-cost extension granted to October 2025 due to delays from June-July 2024 protests.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (BCCK, IEA, Mzalendo Trust, Hook Tangaza) delivered effectively despite challenges. LSK significantly strengthened its regulatory capacity. BHC staff vacancies caused some delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Close collaboration between BHC and implementing partners emerged as critical. BHC's high-level engagements (e.g., with LSK, BCCK) enhanced programme influence.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with GoK institutions (MITI, PPRA, EACC) improved, particularly around OGP and PPRI. Cross-BHC department collaboration maximized resources (e.g., joint work on BCCK-MITI MoU).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive bidding ensured economy; consultancy fees negotiated down (e.g., £6,000 savings with Hook Tangaza). Cost-saving measures like hosting PPRA launch at offices instead of hotels.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required due to political context (protests, FATF grey-listing). Adaptive management included real-time adjustments to partner support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: No-cost extension utilized to complete delayed activities. Programme adapted to protest-related disruptions by reprioritizing high-impact areas (e.g., OGP launch, LSK capacity-building).
adaptive_management_examples: Repurposed OGP launch as a platform to reinforce GoK-civil society collaboration post-protests.
Accelerated LSK’s regulatory tool development in response to Kenya’s FATF grey-listing (February 2024).
Shifted PPRI focus to embedding use by PPRA for high-risk procurement identification.

main_implementation_challenges: June-July 2024 nationwide protests against Finance Bill disrupted activities and distracted GoK partners.
BHC staff vacancies impacted delivery timelines.
OGP website data unavailability due to third-party hosting (Article 19).
Delayed GoK engagement in OGP multistakeholder forums initially hindered cluster actions.
external_factors_impact: Protests created both challenges (activity pauses) and opportunities (increased GoK willingness to tackle corruption).
Kenya’s addition to FATF ‘grey list’ (February 2024) accelerated demand for LSK’s regulatory reforms.
Post-2022 election context required ToC refresh to align with new political priorities.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of youth-led (‘Gen Z’) protests and their focus on corruption.
GoK’s economic mismanagement narratives increased public pressure but also created implementation distractions.
Limited prior engagement with Article 19 (OGP website host) caused data access issues.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial resistance from GoK officials to participate in OGP forums (later resolved via Mzalendo Trust’s influencing).
BHC-BCCK coordination gaps in early MoU implementation phases.
capacity_constraints_emerged: LSK’s initial lack of regulatory tools for AML/CFT supervision (addressed via KAP support).
CSO networks in counties (Bungoma, Kisumu, Mombasa) required additional capacity-building for PPRI use.
risk_materialization: Political instability (protests) materialized as a high-impact risk, leading to the no-cost extension.
Partner dependency risks exposed by BHC staff vacancies.
Data management risks realized with OGP website hosting issues.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; £379,666 spent during review period. No-cost extension allowed reallocation of unspent funds.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Achieved via competitive bidding and fee negotiations (e.g., £6,000 savings on Hook Tangaza contract). Partners selected cost-effective options (e.g., PPRA launch at offices).
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: 4/5 output expectations met. Resource maximization through cross-BHC coordination (e.g., joint BCCK-MITI MoU work).
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High multiplication of impact (e.g., Mzalendo Trust increased GoK OGP participation from 1 to 8 officials). PPRA adopted PPRI recommendations into procurement processes.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Gender and social inclusion integrated (e.g., Kisumu CSO network: 25/54 trained members were women; local community representation in advocacy).

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong; partners demonstrated transparent accounting and adaptive budgeting (e.g., reallocating funds post-protests).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeded targets in some areas (e.g., BO awareness raised at 60% lower cost than planned via targeted training).

key_delivery_lessons: Narrowing programme focus improved collaboration but limited systemic impact on corruption drivers.
BHC’s influencing role was critical to unlocking GoK engagement (e.g., OGP launch, LSK reforms).
Local political context (e.g., protests) can be leveraged as an opportunity for reform momentum.
successful_delivery_practices: Cross-partner coordination (e.g., BHC-BCCK-MITI) exceeded output expectations.
Embedding tools into GoK systems (e.g., PPRI in PPRA processes) ensured sustainability.
High-level launches (e.g., OGP NAP V by the President) amplified visibility and commitment.
management_adaptations_made: ToC refresh post-2022 elections to align with new context.
Increased BHC oversight during protests to mitigate delays.
Simplified monitoring frameworks to reduce reporting burden.
innovations_attempted: Used social media metrics (e.g., 1.1M OGP X impressions) to measure awareness-raising impact.
Piloted BO compliance tracking via BRS data requests (345 requests in 2024 vs. 300 in 2023).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Log frame complexity reduced but remains a challenge.
Pending: Measurement of behaviour change not yet operationalized.

forward_recommendations.action: Ensure tools/frameworks developed under KAP are utilized by GoK partners before closure.
Assess effectiveness of awareness-raising activities; consider pivoting if evidence of impact is weak.
Refresh KAP Log Frame to reduce complexity and improve measurability.
Transfer leadership of BCCK-MITI MoU reforms to DBT with KAP oversight.
Develop sustainability plan for LSK’s supervisory function via bilateral engagement.
Align OGP activities with HMG influencing objectives post-protests.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective; political risks (protests) were managed reactively via extension, but systemic corruption risks remained underaddressed.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 60 BCCK members trained on BO (100% of target); 8 GoK OGP representatives engaged (vs. 1 initially).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 1.1M social media impressions for OGP launch; 345 BO information requests by GoK entities (up from 300).

policy_influence_achieved: OGP NAP V launched by the President, with concrete milestones for BO and open contracting.
PPRA adopted PPRI recommendations into procurement risk assessments.
LSK’s AML/CFT guidance updated and regulatory tools developed for legal sector supervision.
capacity_building_results: LSK’s governance frameworks and regulatory capacity strengthened to meet FATF requirements.
CSO networks in 3 counties trained on PPRI use for procurement oversight.
BCCK positioned as a knowledge partner to GoK on business integrity reforms.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Protests increased GoK’s openness to anti-corruption reforms, enabling KAP to secure high-level commitments (e.g., OGP launch).
Negative: Protest-related delays reduced time for embedding some tools (e.g., PPRI in all target counties).
scalability_evidence: OGP model (multistakeholder forums) scalable to other African countries (evidenced by regional attendance at NAP V launch).
PPRI methodology adaptable for other procurement-risk contexts (PPRA already replicating in new counties).
LSK’s supervisory framework could be replicated for other high-risk professions (e.g., accountants).

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: No-cost extension to October 2025 approved to complete delayed activities and capitalize on post-protest reform momentum. Programme demonstrates strong policy influence (e.g., OGP, FATF compliance) and partner demand (e.g., LSK, PPRA).
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High for outputs; Medium for long-term behavioural change (systemic corruption drivers remain unaddressed).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium; current model relies heavily on BHC influencing and partner capacity. Sustainability plans needed for LSK’s supervisory role and CSO networks’ PPRI use.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (overall score of A, with 4/5 indicators met).
planned_adaptations_future: Focus on embedding tools (PPRI, BO frameworks) into GoK systems before closure.
Strengthen BHC-DBT coordination for BCCK-MITI MoU reforms.
Develop exit strategy for LSK’s AML/CFT supervision post-KAP.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Justice and Stability in the Sahel Programme

output_1.title: Improved conflict management capacity and collaboration among communities divided by conflict, and between them and institutions, to mitigate and resolve conflicts linked to land and natural resources

output_2.title: Strengthened resilience to climate shocks and stressors to reduce frequency and impact of resource and land-based conflict in the Sahel

output_3.title: Improved evidence base for more effective stabilisation programme design, delivery and coordinated action among key stakeholders

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners performed well, with JASS delivering tangible benefits through cash assistance, improved land access, and policy changes. Community engagement was strong, with positive feedback from beneficiaries and local partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme utilized a flexible and comprehensive approach, reinforcing existing community capacities and structures. The Steering Committee and Resilience Forum facilitated stakeholder engagement and learning dissemination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination was demonstrated through the Steering Committee and Resilience Forum, which brought together communities, stakeholders, and ministries to share experiences and build on programme learning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility in responding to community needs, adapting activities to reinforce existing capacities and structures.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: The programme adapted by incorporating stronger community engagement and responding to feedback from beneficiaries, including women and minority groups, to improve representation and empowerment.

operational_challenges_context.external_factors_impact: The Sahel region faces significant challenges from climate change, biodiversity loss, land and water scarcity, population growth, and social inequalities, which are core structural drivers of conflict.

financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: The programme delivered tangible benefits to vulnerable communities, including cash assistance, improved land access, and policy changes, demonstrating strong value for money. The programme is expected to leverage additional results through donor interest and adoption of successful practices.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: JASS Phase II aims to galvanize interest from other donors and donor networks in the Sahel to contribute funding or adopt successful practices, leveraging additional results and value for money.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.key_delivery_lessons: The programme’s strength lies in its flexible and comprehensive approach, with strong community engagement and reinforcement of existing capacities. Future phases should consider more stretching targets in the logical framework to capture stronger evidence of impact at individual, community, and wider levels.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.successful_delivery_practices: Participatory theatre performances, Model Husband’s initiative, community peace forums, and targeted peace initiatives were successful in building trust, representation, and respect for migration routes. These activities contributed to improved conflict management and gender inclusion.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.management_adaptations_made: The programme adapted by incorporating stronger targets on gender and learning, responding to community needs, and reinforcing existing capacities and structures.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.innovations_attempted: Innovative approaches included climate and gender-sensitive investments, participatory theatre, and the Model Husband’s initiative to address gender norms and women’s roles in agriculture.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: The programme responded well to recommendations from the previous Annual Review, delivering tangible benefits and improving community engagement.
forward_recommendations: Develop a clear exit strategy with three pillars: responsible engagement, clear communications with communities, and ensuring the functioning of community structures (COFOs).
Produce a consolidated evidence review summarizing significant evidence for advocacy and institutionalizing reforms.
Hold a learning workshop at the final Steering Committee to present key evidence and learning to wider stakeholders.
Assess the programme’s impact further for communities and strategic lessons for FCDO’s future programming.
Champion the programme as an example of integrated work at the nexus of humanitarian, development, peace, and climate, ensuring learning is captured and shared.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: The programme reached over 11,000 people through participatory theatre performances, trained 290 men through the Model Husband’s initiative, and engaged 6,061 participants in community peace forums. Women’s representation in COFOs and SCAP/RUs increased from 16% to 34%.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: The programme enabled policy changes in Mali and Niger by bridging the gap between formal and customary justice systems and restoring trust in the justice system among communities.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: The programme strengthened local peace infrastructure through community peace forums and GESI action plans, increasing women’s representation and empowering minority groups. The credibility of village chiefs was revitalized, and communities increasingly turned to COFOs and traditional leaders for conflict resolution.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: JASS Phase II aims to galvanize interest from other donors to adopt successful practices, indicating potential for scalability.

programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The delivery model, which emphasizes community engagement and reinforcement of existing capacities, appears sustainable. The programme’s flexible and comprehensive approach has been well-received by beneficiaries and partners.
planned_adaptations_future: Develop a clear exit strategy to ensure responsible programme closure.
Strengthen evidence collection to demonstrate impact at individual, community, and wider levels.
Set more stretching targets in the logical framework, particularly on gender and learning.
Capture and share learning from the programme’s integrated approach at the nexus of humanitarian, development, peace, and climate.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Demographic Transition in Iraq Programme (DTIP)

output_1.title: Improved national policies, and regulations on access to rights-based family planning with a focus on young people and vulnerable groups

output_2.title: Increased awareness of decision-makers, community leaders, influencers about family planning and reproductive rights, (including child marriage and its negative consequences) in the context of the demographic dividend

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNFPA has established strong relationships with Government Ministries and delivered tangible results (e.g., family planning costed action plan, behaviour change communication plan, national conference on Early Marriage).
