programme_metadata.programme_title: Data for Foundational Learning

output_1.title: Fund generation and coordination of comparable learning data using robust and internationally accepted assessments (Track)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme transitioned from mobilisation to active delivery in 2024/25. Two new major agreements were signed: (1) an Accountable Grant with NFER for global south leadership on learning assessments, and (2) an agreement with UNICEF to scale up tracking of learning globally. The ACER UK grant was extended and expanded to include capacity building and community of practice development.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (UIS, PAL Network, ACER UK, World Bank, NFER, UNICEF) have demonstrated strong performance in delivering activities, particularly in generating learning data and strengthening national assessment systems. Collaboration between partners (e.g., ACER UK and World Bank in Ghana) has been effective, though coordination challenges persist. The World Bank’s ALMA programme has complemented FCDO’s efforts by reaching geographies without FCDO presence.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme is managed directly by FCDO with a relatively small team. While management is described as "robust," the team’s capacity is stretched, limiting engagement with partners and country stakeholders. Governance includes regular coordination mechanisms (e.g., biannual partner meetings) and adaptive management practices.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination has been effective in some areas (e.g., ALMA and ACER UK collaboration in Ghana) but fragmented in others. The Global Coalition for Foundational Learning is leveraged for strategic alignment, though risks of inefficiency and duplication remain. Partners report satisfaction with FCDO’s support but highlight the need for clearer guidance (e.g., on SDG 4.1.1 reporting).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Partners have maintained cost discipline through competitive procurement (e.g., PAL Network’s transparent contracting) and efficiency measures (e.g., early workshop bookings, benchmarked costs by ACER UK). No major procurement issues were reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO’s oversight is described as robust but resource-constrained. The small team size limits proactive engagement, though partners appreciate the responsive support provided. Oversight includes monitoring of financial execution and alignment with the Theory of Change (ToC).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme has demonstrated flexibility by expanding scopes (e.g., ACER UK grant extension to include capacity building) and signing new agreements (NFER, UNICEF) to respond to emerging opportunities. Adaptive management is evident in adjustments to the logframe and ToC based on formative evaluation findings.
adaptive_management_examples: Extension and expansion of the ACER UK grant to include capacity building and community of practice development in response to country demand.
Signing of new agreements with NFER (for global south leadership) and UNICEF (for scaling up tracking) based on identified gaps.
Collaboration between ALMA and ACER UK in Ghana to address bottlenecks and leverage complementary strengths.
Postponement of logframe revisions pending the formative evaluation’s ToC updates, followed by planned comprehensive review post-March 2025.

main_implementation_challenges: Slow progress in some countries due to low prioritisation of foundational learning assessments by governments, leading to understaffed or undervalued national assessment units.
Fragmentation and coordination gaps among partners, risking inefficiencies in the learning assessment landscape.
Limited strategic focus on the "Use" pathway (data-driven policy/interventions) compared to "Track" and "Generate," potentially undermining long-term impact.
Insufficient integration of education in emergencies (EiE) contexts into programme activities and tools.
Delays in finalising guidance for SDG 4.1.1 reporting, leading to confusion among stakeholders.
external_factors_impact: Political and institutional barriers in partner countries hinder sustainable adoption of learning assessments (e.g., misalignment with national reporting structures).
High demand for technical assistance (TA) in countries without FCDO education advisers, partially addressed by ALMA’s complementary support via the World Bank.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging need to address learning data gaps in conflict-affected and protracted crisis contexts (EiEPC), which were not sufficiently anticipated in the original design.
Challenges in aligning AMPL (Assessment for Minimum Proficiency Levels) with national planning cycles, reducing its impact on education priorities.
partner_relationship_issues: While collaboration is generally strong (e.g., ACER UK/World Bank in Ghana), overlapping support in some countries (e.g., both ALMA and ACER UK in Ghana) requires careful coordination to avoid duplication.
Partners report satisfaction with FCDO’s management but highlight the need for clearer strategic direction on data use and EiE integration.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s small team size limits proactive engagement with partners and country stakeholders, risking slower progress on complex issues (e.g., logframe revisions).
National assessment units in partner countries often lack sufficient staffing or institutional value, slowing data generation and reporting.
risk_materialization: Risk of fragmentation in the learning assessment landscape (partially mitigated by coordination mechanisms like the Global Coalition for Foundational Learning).
Risk of limited policy uptake due to insufficient focus on the "Use" pathway (addressed in Recommendation 2 for 2025).
Risk of off-track SDG 4.1.1 reporting due to unclear methodologies (addressed in Recommendation 4 for May 2025).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme is largely on track financially, with no major underspending or overspending reported. Costs are driven by staff time, assessment tool development, workshops, and travel. Partners have maintained cost discipline through competitive procurement and efficiency measures (e.g., early bookings, benchmarked costs).

value_for_money_assessment.design_relevance: The programme design remains relevant to achieving SDG 4.1.1 objectives, with strong alignment between activities and intended outcomes. The formative evaluation confirms the programme’s potential for high value for money (VFM), though gaps in equity (e.g., EiE contexts) and coherence between partners were noted.
value_for_money_assessment.cost_efficiency: Efficiency is demonstrated through leveraged partnerships: World Bank funding unlocks additional resources and country relationships; PAL Network builds on past experience; ACER UK provides global standardisation expertise. The evaluation concludes that the programme is not overstretched given its resources, provided design and coordination issues are addressed.
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: The original business case proposition—that robust learning assessments are cost-effective relative to broader education system costs—remains valid. The programme continues to offer strong VFM, with early results indicating incremental progress toward outcomes. However, the business case underestimated challenges in coherence and political/institutional barriers to data use.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Partners have demonstrated strong financial management, including transparent procurement (PAL Network), cost benchmarking (ACER UK), and competitive contracting. FCDO’s oversight is described as robust, though the small team size limits depth of engagement.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficiency gains include: (1) Leveraging existing partner relationships (e.g., World Bank’s country portfolio via ALMA), (2) demand-driven TA reducing delays, (3) shared costs for workshops and tools (e.g., AMPL microsite updates). The evaluation notes no evidence of productivity risks despite the programme’s complexity.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding is materializing through partnerships: (1) World Bank’s ALMA programme leverages additional funds and country relationships, (2) UNICEF and NFER agreements expand reach without additional FCDO resources. No major co-funding shortfalls were reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Rapid, high-quality technical assistance (TA) is most effective when aligned with in-country FCDO education advisers or complementary partners (e.g., ALMA via World Bank).
Demand-driven delivery modalities (e.g., ACER UK’s extended scope, NFER’s global south leadership grant) enhance responsiveness and country ownership.
Fragmentation risks in the learning assessment landscape require proactive coordination (e.g., via the Global Coalition for Foundational Learning).
Political economy barriers to data use are often overlooked but critical for sustainable impact (addressed in Recommendation 7).
successful_delivery_practices: Collaborative TA delivery (e.g., ACER UK and World Bank in Ghana) to address bottlenecks through complementary strengths.
Leveraging existing platforms (e.g., ALMA’s use of World Bank country portfolios) to extend reach in geographies without FCDO presence.
Peer-to-peer learning opportunities (e.g., NFER’s East Africa Resource Centre grant for KNEC).
Transparency in procurement (PAL Network) and cost benchmarking (ACER UK) to ensure VFM.
management_adaptations_made: Postponement of logframe revisions pending the formative evaluation’s Theory of Change (ToC) updates (submitted January 2025), with a comprehensive review planned post-March 2025.
Expansion of ACER UK’s grant scope to include capacity building and community of practice development in response to country demand.
Inclusion of new partners (NFER, UNICEF) to address gaps in global south leadership and scaling up tracking.
innovations_attempted: NFER’s Accountable Grant for global south leadership on learning assessments, providing timely UK technical support to regional partners (e.g., KNEC in East Africa).
ALMA’s demand-driven TA model, which complements FCDO’s work in countries without FCDO education advisers.
Development of a community of practice among LICs/LMICs on learning assessments (via ACER UK’s expanded scope).

previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Postponed pending the formative evaluation’s ToC revision (submitted January 2025). Logframe review planned post-March 2025.

Map D4FL partners’ activities to explicitly plan for better national use of learning data and identify examples of globally comparable data being owned and used nationally.

strengths: Proactive identification of risks (e.g., fragmentation, limited "Use" pathway focus) and development of mitigation strategies (e.g., Recommendations 2 and 3).
Leveraging existing coordination mechanisms (e.g., Global Coalition for Foundational Learning) to address coherence gaps.
Responsive adaptations (e.g., expanding ACER UK’s scope to include capacity building) to emerging country demands.

Limited systematic application of political economy analysis to anticipate institutional barriers in partner countries.

World Bank (via ALMA) supports 2 more countries (Somalia, Tanzania).
track_output.gap: On track but behind the original target of 8 countries reporting. Expansion to 12+ countries by 2025 partially offsets the delay.

use_output.actual: Limited systematic evidence of data use for policy/interventions. Some countries (e.g., Kenya via KNEC) demonstrate leadership in embedding assessments into policy frameworks.
use_output.gap: Significant gap in demonstrating tangible "Use" outcomes due to limited strategic focus.

UIS collaboration with World Bank on AMPL implementation (e.g., Lebanon, Pakistan) strengthens alignment with global SDG 4.1.1 reporting.
PAL Network’s Common Assessment negotiations with 13 countries suggest potential for scaled-up adoption.
gaps: Limited evidence of data driving specific policy changes or instructional improvements at scale.
Political/institutional barriers in many countries slow the transition from data generation to use.

achievements: National capacity on learning assessments is being built in multiple countries (e.g., via ACER UK’s expanded scope, ALMA TA grants).
NFER’s grant to KNEC’s East Africa Resource Centre fosters peer-to-peer learning and regional leadership.
UIS and World Bank collaboration supports institutional strengthening (e.g., in Lebanon, Pakistan).

positive: ALMA’s reach into countries without FCDO presence (e.g., Djibouti, Mali) expands the programme’s geographic impact beyond original plans.
NFER’s global south leadership model (via KNEC) creates unexpected opportunities for regional ownership.
negative: Risk of fragmentation in the learning assessment landscape due to multiple partners working in the same countries (e.g., Ghana) without sufficient coordination.

funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium (predefined focal areas but with country-driven project selection within GEF’s strategic priorities)

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: GEF Council (32 members: 14 developed, 16 developing, 2 transition economies) with UK/FCDO as permanent member; Secretariat for coordination; World Bank as Trustee; Independent Evaluation Unit (IEO) for oversight
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: High (biannual Council meetings, IEO evaluations culminating in 2025 Overall Performance Study, Secretariat budget reporting)
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Consensus-based Council approvals for projects/programmes; country-driven project proposals reviewed by Secretariat and agencies

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Multiple partners (18 accredited agencies: MDBs like World Bank/AfDB, UN agencies like UNDP/UNEP/FAO, INGOs like WWF/Conservation International, and national development banks)
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral (MDBs/UN), International NGOs, National Development Banks
partner_selection_baseline.partner_roles_planned: Agencies develop/implement projects; Secretariat coordinates; World Bank manages Trust Fund; IEO evaluates; Council governs
partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Pre-accredited agencies with thematic/geographic specializations; countries select implementing agencies from accredited list

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (unchanged, but with expanded mandates: added Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF) and future BBNJ Agreement financing)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £330m UK contribution maintained; $5.33bn total GEF8 funding on track (50%+ of expected results achieved by mid-cycle); co-financing ratio improved to $8.5:$1 (vs $7 target)
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Accelerated project cycle (streamlined approvals to reduce time from proposal to disbursement); increased use of integrated programming (cross-sector/country); expanded private sector leverage mechanisms
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Medium-High (adaptive programming to accommodate new mandates like GBFF/BBNJ; underspend in GEF7 administrative budget repurposed for GEF8 expansions)

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: GEF Council structure unchanged; Secretariat expanded (15% FY25 budget increase for additional staff to manage new mandates); World Bank’s administrative support reduced (lower cost recovery rate negotiated)
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: High (enhanced: IEO’s 2025 Overall Performance Study added; new Risk Appetite Framework approved Feb 2024; conflict-sensitive programming guidance under development)
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Unchanged consensus-based Council approvals, but with faster project cycle times and increased delegation to Secretariat for operational decisions

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Multiple partners (unchanged 18 agencies), but with deliberate shift to reduce agency concentration: regional MDBs’ share increased from 5.6% (GEF7) to 7.3% (GEF8); UNDP’s share stable at ~30%
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (MDBs/UN), International NGOs, National Development Banks (no new types added)
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: Unchanged core roles, but agencies now required to demonstrate conflict-sensitive approaches in FCAS contexts (per Feb 2024 gap analysis)

substantive_changes_made: Expansion of GEF’s convention mandates to include GBFF (operational 2024) and future BBNJ Agreement financing (post-ratification)
Acceleration of project cycle times through Secretariat-led streamlining (reducing proposal-to-disbursement delays)
Increased administrative budget (+15% FY25) to support new mandates and expanded staffing

Enhanced conflict-sensitive programming guidance (FCAS gap analysis completed Feb 2024)
Shift in agency resource allocation: regional MDBs’ share increased from 5.6% to 7.3%

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: No change to UK’s £330m pledge, but administrative budget increased by 15% (FY25) to accommodate new mandates (GBFF/BBNJ) and staff expansion
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Scope expanded to include two new global environmental agreements (GBFF and BBNJ) without geographic contraction
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: No shift in primary modality (remains multilateral), but enhanced mechanisms for private sector leverage and integrated programming

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Implicit updates to assumptions about agency capacity in FCAS contexts (per Feb 2024 gap analysis) and private sector mobilization potential (ratio improved from 7:1 to 8.5:1)

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: Minor: Secretariat expansion and World Bank cost recovery renegotiation, but no Council/IEO structural changes
management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Enhanced: new Risk Appetite Framework and conflict-sensitive guidance added to existing oversight mechanisms
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: Operational decisions delegated more to Secretariat to accelerate project cycle, but Council approvals unchanged

delivery_adaptations.activity_only_adjustments: Streamlined project approval processes; increased use of integrated programming templates; enhanced gender monitoring indicators (though no change to core activities)

adaptation_triggers.learning_insights: Mid-cycle performance review (50%+ results achieved) and IEO evaluations triggered administrative/oversight enhancements
adaptation_triggers.strategic_opportunities: New global agreements (GBFF, BBNJ) created opportunities to expand GEF’s mandate

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High (proactive adjustments to accommodate new mandates while maintaining core delivery; evidence-based oversight enhancements)
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: High (repurposed GEF7 underspend for GEF8 expansions; adjusted administrative structures to support new roles)
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High (IEO evaluations and FCAS gap analysis directly informed governance/oversight adaptations)

fcas_context.fragility_level: Medium (GEF operates in 149 countries including FCAS, but Feb 2024 gap analysis identified need for enhanced conflict-sensitive guidance)
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Indirect (no active conflict disruption reported, but FCAS programming guidance strengthened)

market_conditions.cost_inflation_impacts: Moderate (5.6% salary increase and office expansion costs factored into FY25 budget)
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: Managed within administrative budget adjustments

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: High stability (no substantive changes to core delivery mechanisms; adaptations were enhancements within existing structure)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Comprehensive adaptation (minor but strategic adjustments across funding flexibility, governance oversight, and partner resource allocation to accommodate new mandates and improve efficiency)

programme_metadata.programme_title: Global Environment Facility 8th Replenishment Programme

output_1.title: Global environmental benefits to be delivered through approved GEF8 projects and programmes supported by UK

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: GEF8 introduced integrated programming across multiple countries/sectors (forests, food, cities, oceans, small islands, plastics) rather than single-sector focus. Increased emphasis on leveraging private sector support and encouraging innovative solutions through a new innovation window.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: 18 accredited agencies (MDBs, UN agencies, NGOs) delivered results exceeding expectations in most areas. UNDP's share remained stable (30.3% vs 30.4% in GEF7), while regional agencies' share increased slightly (7.3% vs 5.6%).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: GEF Council (32 members) and Secretariat maintained as planned. World Bank continues as Trustee. CEO re-elected for second term (2024-2028). New mandates (GBFF, BBNJ) added without structural changes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Secretariat improved complementarity with other climate funds (GCF, CIF) through planned Action Plan on Complementarity and Coherence. Streamlined project cycle reduced approval-to-disbursement time.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Independent Evaluation Unit (IEO) conducting planned evaluations culminating in 2025 Overall Performance Study (OPS) to inform GEF9 negotiations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to include new mandates (GBFF, BBNJ) mid-cycle. Administrative budget adjusted to accommodate expanded roles (e.g., additional staff, office space).
adaptive_management_examples: Increased UK's ICF scoring percentage from 70% to 80% based on 85% of GEF projects being climate-related (vs 83% in 2023).
Reduced World Bank cost recovery rates through renegotiation to manage administrative budget pressures.
Expanded office space and staffing (15% FY25 budget increase) to handle new mandates and increased disbursements.

main_implementation_challenges: Chemicals/waste reduction target (Indicator 1.9) substantially underperformed (3.5 vs 7.9 thousand metric tons).
Slower-than-planned restructuring caused FY24 administrative underspend (90% of budget used).
Negotiations with World Bank over cost recovery rates created budget uncertainty.
external_factors_impact: New mandates (GBFF, BBNJ) added mid-cycle required rapid adaptation of administrative and programming structures.
Global economic conditions affected co-financing mobilization (though $8.5:$1 ratio still exceeded $7:$1 target).
contextual_constraints_new: First expansion of GEF's convention responsibilities since 2013 (BBNJ mandate) required unplanned capacity building.
Increased demand for conflict-sensitive programming in FCAS countries identified via gap analysis (2024).
partner_relationship_issues: UNDP's dominant share (30.3%) persisted despite goal to reduce agency concentration.
Regional agencies' share increased only marginally (7.3% vs 5.6% target).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Secretariat required 15% budget increase for FY25 to handle expanded roles (new mandates, increased disbursements).
Staff turnover created temporary capacity gaps (FY24 underspend partly due to vacancies).
risk_materialization: Conflict-sensitive programming risks identified but mitigated via agency-level approaches (all agencies now have FCAS strategies).
Administrative cost pressures materialized but managed through World Bank renegotiation and GEF7 underspend drawdown.

FY2024.variance_reason: Staff turnover vacancies and slower restructuring pace.

FY2025.drivers: Additional staff for new mandates (GBFF, BBNJ), 5.6% salary increase, expanded office space.

value_for_money_assessment.original_proposition: Very good VfM per 2022 business case, with leverage ratio as key driver.

current_performance.efficiency_gains: Streamlined project cycle reduced approval-to-disbursement time.

value_for_money_assessment.comparative_advantage: Multilateral approach more effective for global systemic impact than bilateral interventions, per G20 review (Oct 2024).

financial_management_quality.budget_control: Underspend managed proactively (GEF7 surplus used to offset GEF8 cost pressures).
financial_management_quality.cost_recovery: World Bank agreed to reduce support levels to lower cost recovery rates.
financial_management_quality.transparency: Biannual Corporate Scorecard published with aggregated results.

cost_efficiency_achieved.administrative_costs: $27.5m FY24 spend (10% under budget) despite expanded scope.
cost_efficiency_achieved.programmatic_efficiency: Over 50% of GEF8 results achieved by midpoint for all but one indicator.

key_delivery_lessons: Integrated programming (cross-sector/country) more effective than single-sector approaches.
Multilateral funds can achieve higher leverage ratios than bilateral programmes for global challenges.
Mid-cycle adaptation to new mandates is feasible with flexible administrative budgets.
successful_delivery_practices: Biannual Corporate Scorecard provides transparent, data-driven performance tracking.
Conflict-sensitive programming gap analysis (2024) led to agency-level improvements.
Co-financing mobilization exceeded targets through proactive partner engagement.
management_adaptations_made: Increased ICF scoring percentage from 70% to 80% based on climate-related project data.
Renegotiated World Bank cost recovery rates to manage budget pressures.
Expanded Secretariat capacity (staff, office space) to handle new mandates.
innovations_attempted: New innovation window to encourage private sector solutions for environmental challenges.
Action Plan on Complementarity and Coherence with other climate funds (GCF, CIF) to harmonize procedures.
previous_recommendations_progress: GEF8 programming improvements (e.g., integrated approaches) implemented as recommended in GEF7 evaluations.
Enhanced gender monitoring framework (Indicator 2.5) met expectations per Council review.
forward_recommendations: Publish and implement Action Plan on Complementarity and Coherence at COP29.
Strengthen private sector engagement to further increase leverage ratios.
Monitor BBNJ mandate implementation closely given its untested nature.

proactive: Risk Appetite Statement approved (Feb 2024) with implementation actions.
Conflict-sensitive programming gaps addressed via agency-level strategies.
reactive: Administrative budget pressures mitigated through World Bank renegotiation and GEF7 surplus use.
Underperforming chemicals/waste indicator (1.9) flagged for corrective action.

policy_influence_achieved: Financial mechanism for Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBFF) and BBNJ Agreement.
Contributes to 6 major MEAs (UNFCCC, UNCBD, UNCCD, Stockholm Convention, Minamata Convention, BBNJ).
Influences UK ICF KPIs 1, 6, 11, 12, and 17.
capacity_building_results: 18 accredited agencies now have conflict-sensitive programming strategies for FCAS countries.
Secretariat expanded capacity to manage new mandates (GBFF, BBNJ).

positive: Higher-than-expected private sector mobilization ($106.6m vs £0 target).
Increased climate finance percentage (85% vs 83% in 2023) boosted UK ICF contributions.
negative: Chemicals/waste reduction underperformance (Indicator 1.9: 3.5 vs 7.9 thousand metric tons).

scalability_evidence: Integrated programming model (cross-sector/country) demonstrates scalability potential.
Leverage ratio (8.5:1) suggests replicable co-financing mobilization approach.
G20 review (Oct 2024) highlighted GEF's catalytic role in systemic change.

continuation_rationale: Over 50% of GEF8 results achieved by midpoint, with strong leverage ($8.5:$1 ratio).
Critical role in delivering UK ICF targets and supporting 6 major MEAs.
New mandates (GBFF, BBNJ) expand GEF's relevance to emerging global priorities.
G20 review (Oct 2024) affirmed GEF's catalytic role in climate/environment finance.

strengths: Stable governance structure (GEF Council, Secretariat, World Bank Trustee).
Proven ability to adapt to new mandates (GBFF, BBNJ) mid-cycle.
Strong co-financing mobilization ($24 billion) ensures programme scalability.
risks: Administrative cost pressures require ongoing management (FY25 budget +15%).
Partner concentration (UNDP 30.3% share) persists despite diversification goals.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Implement Action Plan on Complementarity and Coherence with other climate funds (COP29).
Monitor and address chemicals/waste indicator underperformance (1.9).
Prepare for GEF9 replenishment negotiations (starting 2025) with OPS2025 findings.
Further strengthen private sector engagement to increase leverage ratios.

funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Disbursements via MoU with UNDP and grant agreement with NDI, with structured milestones tied to election cycle
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium - Adaptive design intended but with predefined election-support components

governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly progress reviews with annual deep dives, aligned with election timeline
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Joint FCDO-UNDP/NDI steering committees for election phase, with adaptive decision-making post-2021

governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Decentralized for DDF (partner-led initiatives) vs centralized for ICAR (FCDO-advisor approvals); KIVU operates as semi-autonomous unit

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Multi-partner ecosystem: Diakonia (DDF hub) + ICAR (anti-corruption) + 20+ CSOs/media outlets (subgrantees) + KIVU (economic reforms)
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: INGO (Diakonia, ICAR), Local CSOs (JCTR, PAAGZ, TIZ, CTPD), Media (ZNBC, Mphangwe FM), Government (ACC, DEC, NPA, State House)
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: Diakonia: adaptive grant management; ICAR: technical mentoring; CSOs: local implementation; KIVU: economic policy reform; Media: public awareness
partner_names_actual: Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD)

consortium_actual.consortium_structure_actual: Informal network coordinated by FCDO, with Diakonia as de facto hub for governance work and ICAR for anti-corruption
consortium_actual.consortium_governance_actual: Ad-hoc coordination via FCDO’s programmatic reviews; no formal consortium agreements

substantive_changes_made: Shift from election-focused design (UNDP/NDI) to adaptive governance model (Diakonia DDF + ICAR)

Transition from structured milestones to Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA) methodology

funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope expanded (national radio campaigns, rural Ward Development Committees added); thematic scope expanded (economic reforms via KIVU)
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: Shift from multilateral (UNDP) to INGO-led (Diakonia) with direct CSO subgrants; addition of embedded advisory model (KIVU)

assumptions_updated: Assumption that election support would suffice for democratic strengthening revised to recognize need for long-term institutional work

management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: Shift from joint committees to decentralized (DDF) + centralized technical approvals (ICAR/KIVU)

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: Added rural areas (Ward Development Committees) and national media reach (radio programmes with 5M+ audience)

Expansion of radio programmes from 50 to 101 annually
Addition of Corruption Spotlight Series (not in original design but within adaptive framework)

learning_insights: Evidence that adaptive approaches yield better outcomes than linear designs

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High

adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Strong: Learning from KIVU fed into Prospero; DDF lessons informed FCDO’s civil society strategy

fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Low-level political tensions; no active conflict during implementation

programme_metadata.programme_title: Zambia Democratic Governance Programme

output_1.title: DDF facilitates dialogues with key actors to produce solutions to governance challenges identified in at least two DDF themes

output_2.title: DDF supports the implementation of agreed initiatives to address governance challenges

output_3.title: DDF uses learnings and best practices to influence governance policy and reforms

output_4.title: ICAR equips Zambia with appropriate competences and skills to effectively use their legal and enforcement instruments to recover stolen assets

output_5.title: ICAR supports Zambia to introduce suitable tools, procedures, instruments, policies or institutions to recover and manage stolen assets

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted to a more adaptive, iterative approach with smaller-scale testing and learning before scaling. Originally designed as a fixed set of interventions, now operates with flexibility to respond to emerging opportunities (e.g., KIVU’s evolution from State House support to economic policy reform).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (Diakonia, ICAR) exceeded expectations in engagement (e.g., 25 key stakeholders vs. 15 targeted) and initiative development (29 ideas vs. 15 planned). ICAR’s case-based mentoring built strong institutional relationships, though risk of over-reliance on individual relationships noted.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Current structure struggles to accommodate distinct evolution of components (e.g., KIVU’s economic reform work vs. DDF’s governance focus). Short-term fixes planned via programmatic review; longer-term governance restructuring may be needed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination within DDF workstreams (e.g., cross-thematic dialogues) but limited cross-programme learning (e.g., between DDF, ICAR, and KIVU). Diplomatic influencing feeds into programme focus, but formalized learning mechanisms (e.g., joint papers) are underutilized.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to adaptive model’s need for frequent approvals and adjustments. Administrative processes identified as a bottleneck (Recommendation #4 addresses streamlining).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Highly utilized: Programme pivoted to support economic reforms (KIVU), expanded anti-corruption mentoring (ICAR), and scaled community training (Diakonia). Adaptive funding allowed testing of 18 initiatives across 3 workstreams.
adaptive_management_examples: KIVU’s shift from State House strategy support to economic policy reform, delivering job-creating reforms aligned with Zambia’s 2024 National Budget.
ICAR’s expansion from ACC/DEC training to include National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) and multi-agency case support.
DDF’s iterative idea generation (29 ideas across 4 workstreams) and prioritization of 18 initiatives for funding.

main_implementation_challenges: Inefficiency of adaptive management at small scale (high management-to-delivery cost ratio).
Distinct evolution of programme components (e.g., KIVU’s economic work vs. DDF’s governance focus) straining governance structures.
Limited institutionalization of learning across partners/workstreams.
Risk of over-reliance on individual relationships (e.g., KIVU’s centre-of-government focus) rather than systemic capacity.
external_factors_impact: Closing civic space in Zambia constrained community engagement activities.
Political transitions (e.g., 2021 elections) required rapid adaptation of programme priorities.
Economic pressures (e.g., inflation, currency fluctuations) affected budget execution for local partners.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for deconfliction of ICAR’s training with other suppliers to avoid duplication.
Emerging risks in fraud and safeguarding requiring a dedicated risk assessment (Recommendation #5).
Decentralization reforms (e.g., Constituency Development Fund) created new entry points but also coordination challenges.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between adaptive flexibility and partners’ need for predictable funding streams.
ICAR’s deep engagement with ACC/DEC/NPA risked perceived ownership issues (e.g., "replacing" vs. "strengthening" capacity).
Diakonia’s small-scale community training limited reach in rural areas (addressed in Recommendation #1).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Local CSOs lacked capacity to absorb rapid scaling of initiatives (e.g., 18 new projects in one year).
Government counterparts (e.g., anti-corruption agencies) had limited bandwidth for multi-agency coordination despite ICAR’s support.
Programme management team stretched by administrative burdens of adaptive model (e.g., frequent re-approvals).
risk_materialization: Major risk of political interference in anti-corruption cases (mitigated via ICAR’s multi-agency approach).
Moderate risk of safeguarding incidents (prompted Recommendation #5 on risk assessment).
Minor risk of duplication in training (addressed via Recommendation #3).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track: Full £4.95M allocated across partners (Diakonia, ICAR, KIVU). Minor underspend in 2021/22 due to delayed partner onboarding; absorbed in subsequent years via adaptive reallocation.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High: Adaptive approach improved cost-efficiency by testing initiatives before scaling (e.g., radio programmes reached 5M+ at low marginal cost). However, management costs for small-scale adaptivity reduced VFM relative to larger programmes.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong: No major audit findings. Partners demonstrated transparent reporting (e.g., ICAR’s case-level expenditure tracking). Fraud risks proactively managed via upcoming assessment (Recommendation #5).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Mixed: Unit costs for community training and radio programmes were low, but overheads for adaptive management were higher than traditional models. Economic policy reforms (KIVU) leveraged existing government structures, reducing delivery costs.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: UNDP MOU (£500K) concluded; no new co-funding secured. Opportunities identified with Prospero programme for future collaboration.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal direct impact, but Zambian Kwacha depreciation increased local costs for partners (e.g., training venues, participant stipends).

key_delivery_lessons: Adaptive programmes at small scale (<£5M) incur disproportionate management costs; larger programmes may optimize VFM.
Political economy analysis must be iterative—static assessments at inception become outdated quickly (e.g., post-2021 election shifts).
Flexible funding mechanisms enable responsiveness but require streamlined approval processes to avoid delays.
successful_delivery_practices: ICAR’s case-based mentoring model built trust and institutional ownership in anti-corruption agencies.
DDF’s Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA) methodology generated 29 actionable ideas from stakeholders.
KIVU’s integration with Presidential Delivery Unit ensured economic reforms aligned with national priorities.
management_adaptations_made: Revised log-frame to remove expired partners and reweight outputs (e.g., Output 1 increased to 23%).
Introduced programmatic review (Recommendation #4) to address governance structure gaps.
Expanded ICAR’s scope to include NPA and multi-jurisdictional cases based on early successes.
innovations_attempted: Corruption Spotlight Series (radio programmes) to amplify anti-corruption messaging.
Ward Development Committee training pilots to decentralize governance engagement.
Cross-agency corruption task forces (ACC/DEC/NPA) with UK agency support for financial crime cases.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2022 recommendation to strengthen learning mechanisms partially addressed via diplomatic feedback loops but formalized papers pending (Recommendation #2).
2022 call for deeper economic policy integration achieved through KIVU’s expanded role.
2022 safeguarding concerns led to upcoming Fraud and Safeguarding Risk Assessment (Recommendation #5).
forward_recommendations: Scale community training in rural areas (Recommendation #1) with focus on Ward Development Committees.
Institutionalize learning via issue-based papers and advocacy plans (Recommendation #2).
De-conflict ICAR training to avoid duplication (Recommendation #3).
Streamline administrative processes (Recommendation #4) and conduct Fraud/Safeguarding Risk Assessment (Recommendation #5).
Explore integration with Prospero programme for economic governance synergies.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective: Proactive identification of risks (e.g., political interference, safeguarding) with mitigation plans. Adaptive model allowed rapid response to emerging risks (e.g., shifting KIVU’s focus post-election). However, risk of over-reliance on individual champions remains.

scalability_evidence: DDF’s PDIA methodology replicable for other governance programmes (e.g., potential application in Malawi).
ICAR’s mentoring model adaptable to other anti-corruption contexts (e.g., regional financial crime networks).
Community training pilots (Ward Development Committees) show potential for national rollout.

Adaptive learning justifies final-year investment to consolidate gains and address scalability challenges.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Current model effective but resource-intensive. Long-term sustainability hinges on institutionalizing adaptive practices (e.g., PDIA) within Zambian systems and securing co-funding (e.g., Prospero collaboration).

Develop exit strategy for ICAR’s mentoring to ensure institutional ownership.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tackling Serious and Organised Crime in Ghana Programme

output_1.title: Capability of state actors to detect, investigate, prosecute, recover, and manage proceeds/assets of crime linked to SOC has been strengthened.

output_2.title: National and Regional inter-agency partnership are strengthened to tackle IFF and SOC.

output_3.title: Public engagements and sensitisation for policy reforms are conducted to tackle IFF and SOC.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Original bespoke service provider model was abandoned due to ODA budget cuts. Initially delivered through Adam Smith International (ASI), then transitioned to GIZ (GOVID programme) from Jan 2022 to Sep 2023. Currently exploring supplier contract through FCDO framework arrangement as the most viable option for remaining two years.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: GIZ delivery was limited and concluded in Sep 2023. ACEP (with GACC and GII) delivered a short £144k election-focused project under Output 3, which performed well against targets but was insufficient as a standalone component. Previous ASI delivery reviewed in 2022 AR showed initial progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Faced a major recruitment gap for the lead advisory role, which was recently filled. Programme management was fragmented due to shifting delivery partners and lack of consistent oversight during transitions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Limited coordination during the reporting year due to GIZ exit and advisory gap. Some cross-institutional engagement occurred through the ACEP project (e.g., collaboration with EOCO and OSP), but overall coordination mechanisms were weak.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: ACEP project adhered to VfM principles, including leveraging existing media relationships to extend engagements to 14 media houses within the same budget. Previous procurement through GIZ was cost-effective due to shared overheads with GOVID programme.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was minimal during the GIZ transition and advisory gap. Recent appointment of a lead adviser is expected to improve oversight intensity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by pivoting to ACEP for Output 3 delivery and exploring new supplier contracts. However, lack of a stable delivery mechanism limited adaptive capacity.
adaptive_management_examples: Shift from GIZ to ACEP for Output 3 delivery to maintain some activity during transitions.
Exploration of three new delivery options (framework supplier, UK SOC unit collaboration, or technical assistance + CSO grants) to address implementation challenges.
Extension of media engagements from planned 7 to 14 platforms without additional budget through relationship leveraging.

main_implementation_challenges: Discontinuation of GIZ delivery mechanism in Sep 2023 created a major implementation gap.
Prolonged vacancy in the lead advisory role hindered strategic direction and partner coordination.
Fragmented delivery approach due to shifting partners (ASI → GIZ → ACEP) disrupted continuity.
Limited budget flexibility constrained ability to scale or sustain interventions.
external_factors_impact: Reductions in bilateral ODA budget forced abandonment of the original bespoke service provider model.
Political context of Ghana’s 2024 elections created both an opportunity (for Output 3) and a distraction from long-term institutional strengthening.
contextual_constraints_new: Transnational nature of SOC (e.g., Ghana-Nigeria cooperation) proved harder to operationalize than anticipated.
Civil society engagement required more sustained effort to translate awareness into policy reforms.
partner_relationship_issues: GIZ’s closure of GOVID programme misaligned with SOCG’s timeline, leaving no transition plan.
Delayed re-engagement with Government of Ghana partners (e.g., NCA, Home Office) weakened institutional buy-in.
capacity_constraints_emerged: State institutions (e.g., EOCO, OSP) showed limited absorptive capacity for technical assistance without continuous support.
CSOs required more handholding than expected to design and implement advocacy campaigns effectively.
risk_materialization: Risk of "Major" rating materialized in 2022–2023 due to delivery partner instability and advisory gaps.
Risk of fragmented delivery (identified in earlier reviews) fully materialized, leading to uneven progress across outputs.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Only £144k (4.1% of total programme value) was spent in the reporting year, all under Output 3.
Overall programme underspend due to halted GIZ activities and delayed procurement of new delivery mechanisms.
ACEP project remained within its micro-budget but could not compensate for stalled Outputs 1 and 2.
value_for_money_assessment: Individual ACEP project demonstrated good VfM (e.g., extended media reach without additional cost), but programme-level VfM is poor due to limited delivery scope.
Business Case VfM proposition remains untested; programme has not delivered enough to assess long-term cost-effectiveness.
Opportunity costs high: funds spent on Output 3 alone would have had greater impact if paired with Outputs 1 and 2.
financial_management_quality: ACEP adhered to sound procurement and financial management practices (e.g., competitive media rates, inclusive budgeting).
GIZ financial management during GOVID collaboration was efficient (low overheads), but closure disrupted continuity.
Lack of overarching financial tracking across outputs due to fragmented delivery.
cost_efficiency_achieved: ACEP project achieved cost efficiency by leveraging existing CSO networks and media relationships.
No data available on cost efficiency for Outputs 1 and 2 due to inactivity.

key_delivery_lessons: Delivery through existing programmes (e.g., GIZ GOVID) can reduce overheads but risks misalignment with programme goals if the host programme closes.
Over-reliance on a single delivery partner (or lack of backup options) creates vulnerability to external shocks (e.g., ODA cuts, partner exits).
Electoral cycles can catalyze short-term engagement (Output 3) but distract from long-term institutional reforms (Outputs 1 and 2).
successful_delivery_practices: ACEP’s use of local languages (English, Twi) and accessible media formats (jingles, animations) improved reach and inclusivity.
Leveraging existing media relationships to exceed planned engagements (14 vs. 7 platforms) without additional cost.
Inclusive design (e.g., disability-accessible website, targeted youth/women outreach) enhanced equity of benefits.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from GIZ to ACEP for Output 3 allowed minimal continuity during transitions.
Development of ToR for a framework supplier to consolidate future delivery under single management.
Recognition of need for programme extension (time/cost) to recover lost momentum.
innovations_attempted: Pilot integration of SOC awareness into electoral processes (e.g., PAC campaign linked to 2024 elections).
Cross-border cooperation attempts (Ghana-Nigeria) though not fully operationalized.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2022 AR recommendation to secure stable delivery partner not fully implemented; GIZ exit created further delays.
Need for log-frame/ToC updates (recommended in prior reviews) remains unaddressed; now slated for Nov 2024.
forward_recommendations: Secure a single supplier through FCDO framework to unify delivery of all three outputs (preferred option).
Pursue programme extension (time/cost) to allow full implementation of revised delivery strategy.
Update log-frame and ToC by Nov 2024 to align with new context and supplier engagements.
Re-engage GoG partners (NCA, Home Office, SOCNet) to rebuild institutional commitment.
Establish programme-wide VfM indicators to test Business Case propositions in next AR.
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk of delivery partner instability was identified but not mitigated proactively (e.g., no contingency plans for GIZ exit).
Recent adaptive responses (e.g., exploring framework supplier) show improved risk awareness but come late in the programme cycle.
Risk of limited impact due to output imbalance (Output 3 over-representation) now being addressed through delivery realignment.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Output 3: 38 journalists and 185 youth leaders sensitized on SOC/electoral integrity (exceeded targets of 40 journalists and 120 youth leaders).
Media reach extended to 14 platforms (vs. planned 7) through cost-efficient negotiations.
No data available for Outputs 1 and 2 due to inactivity.
policy_influence_achieved: Minimal direct policy influence; some indirect engagement with EOCO/OSP through ACEP project.
Public sensitisation laid groundwork for future advocacy but no documented policy uptake yet.
capacity_building_results: Output 3: Short-term capacity gains for journalists/youth leaders on SOC awareness, but no evidence of institutional capacity building (Outputs 1/2).
ACEP project’s inclusive approaches (e.g., disability-accessible materials) built some CSO capacity for future campaigns.
unintended_consequences: Positive: ACEP project’s electoral integrity focus unexpectedly strengthened CSO networks ahead of 2024 elections.
Negative: Fragmented delivery eroded trust with some state partners, complicating future engagement.
scalability_evidence: ACEP’s media engagement model (low-cost, high-reach) shows potential for scaling but requires stable funding.
No evidence of scalability for institutional strengthening (Outputs 1/2) due to lack of implementation.

continuation_rationale: Ongoing need to address SOC/IFF in Ghana aligns with UK priorities (cybercrime, illicit financial flows).
Gaps in donor support for SOC space persist, particularly for state capacity building and regional cooperation.
Recent appointment of lead adviser and planned delivery realignment (framework supplier) improve feasibility of recovery.
Programme’s original theory of change remains valid, but requires focused execution in remaining years.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Moderate (improved with proposed adaptations but constrained by time)
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Low (current fragmented model unsustainable; proposed framework supplier model aims to address this)
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Low (due to limited delivery to date, but recognition of external constraints and recent corrective actions)
planned_adaptations_future: Transition to a unified delivery supplier through FCDO framework by early 2025.
Seek programme extension (time/cost) to implement all three outputs comprehensively.
Update log-frame and ToC to reflect revised delivery plan and contextual changes.
Strengthen MEL systems to track progress across outputs and assess VfM at programme level.
Reinvigorate partnerships with GoG institutions (NCA, EOCO, OSP) and regional actors (Nigeria).

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK Support to Palestinian Refugees in the Near East 2022-2025

output_1.title: UNRWA delivers services which provide Palestinian refugees with protection, health, education, and livelihoods and meets their basic needs

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme had to cut funding for UNRWA’s OPTs Emergency Appeal in 2023 and continue funding cuts to UNRWA’s Regional Syria Emergency Appeal, requiring log frame modifications. UNRWA launched new Resource Mobilization and Outreach Strategy (ReMOS) 2023-25 to address funding gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNRWA maintained service delivery despite severe operational challenges (war in Gaza, West Bank operations, union strikes) but faced unprecedented demand and facility destruction. Achieved 99.2% vaccination coverage and 94.56% water supply connectivity in camps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UNRWA advanced reforms in gender equality, PSEAH, accountability to affected populations, and environmental sustainability. Established Women Advisory Forum, increased maternity leave, and implemented energy efficiency upgrades across all fields.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UNRWA served as primary coordinator for humanitarian operations in Gaza, managing cross-border aid movement, fuel distribution, and shelter for 1.777M IDPs. Coordinated with UN agencies and local partners despite severe access constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained oversight through regular engagement with UNRWA management on neutrality and service delivery, though operational constraints (war, strikes) limited some monitoring activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to rapid-onset crises (Gaza war, Ein Al-Hilweh conflict, Lebanon/Syria earthquake) by reallocating resources to emergency response, though UK funding reductions constrained flexibility.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of resources to Gaza emergency response post-October 2023, including food, shelter, and healthcare for 1.6M people.
Expansion of psychosocial support services in Jordan and West Bank to compensate for Gaza service suspensions.
Implementation of energy efficiency upgrades to reduce operational costs amid funding shortages.

main_implementation_challenges: War in Gaza (since October 2023) causing 149 UNRWA staff deaths, damage to 123 facilities, and displacement of 1.7M people into UNRWA shelters.
Israeli military operations in West Bank damaging UNRWA facilities and restricting movement.
Suspension of Palestinian worker permits (200,000 affected), exacerbating economic crisis.
Union strikes in West Bank disrupting service delivery.
Earthquake in Lebanon/Syria and Ein Al-Hilweh camp violence creating additional humanitarian needs.
external_factors_impact: UK ODA reductions (£1B in 2022-23, £1.5B in 2023-24) forced cuts to emergency appeals and core funding, contributing to UNRWA’s 2023 deficit.
COVID-19 recovery efforts competed with new crises, delaying educational catch-up programmes.
Regional political instability (Israel-Palestine conflict) created unprecedented demand for UNRWA services while destroying infrastructure.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of Gaza war’s impact on UNRWA operations (facility destruction, staff casualties).
Sudden onset of multiple simultaneous crises (earthquake, armed escalations, camp violence) stretching UNRWA’s capacity.
Israeli restrictions on aid access to Gaza and West Bank movement limitations.
capacity_constraints_emerged: UNRWA’s financial deficit limited ability to scale emergency response.
Data collection gaps due to service suspensions in Gaza (e.g., poverty line bridging indicator underreported).
Staff shortages and trauma among remaining personnel affecting service quality.
risk_materialization: Severe risk rating materialized due to war in Gaza and West Bank escalations.
Protection risks (GBV, child protection) increased with displacement and service interruptions.
Neutrality of education compromised by external conflicts (two indicators affected).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £19M disbursed in 2023 (50% of total £38M programme value). Original plan included funding for OPTs and Syria emergency appeals (£0 actually disbursed). Cost extension requested to accommodate 2024 needs (Gaza reconstruction, emergency appeals).
value_for_money_assessment: High VFM in core service delivery: 540,148 students educated (269,800 girls) and 2M+ health consultations at 99.2% vaccination coverage.
Emergency response provided critical aid to 1.6M in Gaza and 150,000 in West Bank despite funding constraints.
Energy efficiency upgrades generated cost savings and reduced emissions.
financial_management_quality: UNRWA maintained transparent financial reporting despite crisis conditions.
Audits confirmed proper use of funds, though deficit required reprogramming of activities.
Multi-year funding gaps created liquidity challenges for service continuity.
cost_efficiency_achieved: 96.30% educational survival rate (up from 95.78% in 2021/22) despite reduced per-student funding.
Psychosocial services reached 5,839 refugees (including 681 persons with disabilities) at minimal incremental cost.
Water infrastructure projects connected 76.38% of camp shelters to networks.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: No co-funding materialized for emergency appeals (OPTs or Syria). UNRWA relied on reprogrammed core budget funds.

key_delivery_lessons: Predictable multi-year funding is critical for UNRWA’s operational stability (2023 deficit linked to UK funding reductions).
Emergency appeals require pre-approved contingency funds to enable rapid response.
Neutrality mechanisms must be crisis-adaptive (external conflicts disrupted education targets).
successful_delivery_practices: Community outreach models (e.g., Women Advisory Forum) improved service accessibility.
