programme_metadata.programme_title: Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRIS) Programme

output_1.title: Resources mobilised, organisation structures and processes established and operationalised for delivery of interventions aligned to the mandate of IRIS

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme shifted focus to technical assistance in its first operational year, with delayed implementation of knowledge development, capacity building, and research pillars. The first call for proposals was launched at COP27 (Dec 2022), with 11 projects approved by Aug 2023, but administrative processes (e.g., due diligence, funding formalisation) took longer than planned, delaying project starts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) and the Multi-Partner Trust Fund (MPTF/IRAF) faced delays in operationalising performance monitoring and donor reporting frameworks. While structures were established (e.g., agreements between UK and IRAF), they were not yet functional due to slow project implementation. The IRIS Project Management Unit (PMU) successfully supported 5 applicants in proposal preparation, exceeding the target (5 vs. 3 expected).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The governance structure (Steering Committee, Trust Fund Management Committee) was functional but faced bottlenecks in decision-making (e.g., project approvals took 6+ months from EoI submission). The UK’s oversight was constrained by annual reporting cycles, limiting real-time monitoring. Interim reporting was proposed to address this.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between CDRI, IRAF, and SIDS was effective in selecting projects but struggled with post-approval administration (e.g., disbursement delays). The programme’s alignment with UK priorities (e.g., 2030 Roadmap, White Paper on International Development) was strong, but cross-HMG coordination (e.g., leveraging UK support at regional events) was underutilised.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The first call for proposals (COP27) was implemented as planned, with 11 projects approved out of 50 received (vs. a target of 30 received/10 approved). However, procurement for capacity-building processes was not yet developed. Due diligence for implementing partners took longer than expected, delaying disbursements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was lighter than planned due to reliance on annual reporting. The UK proposed interim reporting to increase visibility. The IRAF’s administrative capacity was stretched by parallel initiatives (e.g., potential urban resilience window), risking delays for IRIS.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted by prioritising technical assistance in Year 1 but deferred knowledge/capacity-building activities. Flexibility was used to support 5 applicants in proposal development (vs. original plan of 3).
adaptive_management_examples: Extended support to 5 applicants for proposal preparation (vs. target of 3) to improve quality of submissions.
Proposed interim reporting to address delays in annual oversight cycles.
Planned acceleration of project administration in Year 2 to mitigate underutilisation of funds.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in project implementation due to prolonged due diligence and funding formalisation (e.g., projects approved in Aug 2023 but not yet operational).
Underdeveloped processes for capacity-building and knowledge-sharing pillars, with focus skewed toward technical assistance.
Slow mobilisation of co-funding ($31M pledged vs. $50M target), risking underutilisation of UK’s £7.3M commitment.
Limited documentation of stakeholder consultations (e.g., SIDS feedback, regional events), reducing evidence for adaptive management.
external_factors_impact: Global economic pressures may have slowed donor commitments (e.g., Australia/EU pledges not yet fully disbursed).
High demand for resilient infrastructure in SIDS (13 countries in first cohort) outpaced administrative capacity, causing bottlenecks.
Geopolitical shifts (e.g., post-COVID recovery, climate finance priorities) increased competition for multilateral funding.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated administrative burdens in IRAF’s management of multiple funding windows (e.g., potential urban resilience window) diverted resources from IRIS.
SIDS’ varying absorptive capacities led to disparities in project readiness (e.g., some countries struggled with proposal development).
Currency fluctuations (USD/GBP) since COP26 announcement reduced the effective value of the £7.3M commitment.
partner_relationship_issues: CDRI’s dual role as implementer and IRAF manager created conflicts in prioritising IRIS vs. other IRAF initiatives.
Limited engagement with UK’s cross-HMG teams (e.g., missed opportunities at Latin American Climate Week 2023 to showcase IRIS).
Delays in operationalising donor reporting frameworks strained transparency with the UK.
capacity_constraints_emerged: IRAF’s Fund Management Unit lacked capacity to simultaneously manage IRIS and new funding windows, causing delays in project administration.
SIDS partners required more hands-on support for proposal development than anticipated (e.g., 5 of 11 approved projects needed PMU assistance).
UK’s programme team had limited bandwidth to monitor progress due to annual reporting cycles.
risk_materialization: Risk of underutilisation of funds due to slow disbursement (only 11 projects approved in Year 1 vs. 30 received).
Delayed operationalisation of performance monitoring (as projected in the business case).
Weaker-than-planned co-funding mobilisation ($31M vs. $50M target).

budget_execution_vs_plan.disbursement_status: Delayed; only 11 projects approved for funding in Year 1 (Aug 2023), with implementation not yet fully underway. Risk of underspending the £7.3M commitment due to slow pace.
budget_execution_vs_plan.co_funding_status: $31M pledged (vs. $50M target) from Australia (AUS $10M) and EU (EUR 5M), but disbursements lagging.

vfm_challenges: High transaction costs for small grants ($150K–$750K per project) relative to administrative overheads.
Delayed outcomes reduce cost-efficiency; benefits (e.g., resilient infrastructure pipeline) not yet quantifiable.
Opportunity costs from underutilised UK funds if disbursement pace does not improve.
vfm_opportunities: Potential for leveraging £7.3M to mobilise $50–60M in co-funding (if pace accelerates).
Economies of scale expected in Year 2 with streamlined project administration.

strengths: Transparent Multi-Partner Trust Fund (MPTF) structure with CDRI/IRAF oversight.
Established agreements for performance monitoring and donor reporting (though not yet operational).
weaknesses: Delays in operationalising financial controls (e.g., donor reporting frameworks).
Limited interim financial reporting reduced UK’s ability to track expenditures in real time.
Currency exchange risks (USD/GBP) not fully mitigated in funding agreements.

co_funding_materialization.details: $31M pledged (62% of $50M target) from Australia and EU, but disbursements pending. No private-sector co-funding secured yet.

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: The £7.3M commitment (announced as $10M at COP26) was based on 2021 exchange rates; subsequent GBP depreciation reduced the effective USD value of the UK’s contribution.

key_delivery_lessons: The proposal-to-disbursement timeline must be accelerated to avoid underutilisation of funds. Current pace risks leaving £7.3M unspent.
Balancing technical assistance with knowledge/capacity-building pillars is critical; Year 1 overemphasised the former.
Annual reporting is insufficient for adaptive management; interim reporting is needed for real-time oversight.
Stakeholder consultations (e.g., SIDS feedback) must be systematically documented to inform future calls for proposals.
successful_delivery_practices: IRIS PMU’s hands-on support for 5 applicants improved proposal quality and approval rates (11/50 EoIs approved).
Alignment with UK priorities (e.g., 2030 Roadmap, White Paper) strengthened programme justification.
Multi-donor MPTF structure (IRAF) provided a credible platform for co-funding mobilisation.
management_adaptations_made: Extended proposal support to 5 applicants (vs. planned 3) to enhance project pipeline quality.
Proposed interim reporting to address delays in annual oversight (not yet implemented).
Planned design of knowledge/capacity-building offer in Year 2 to rebalance programme pillars.
innovations_attempted: Demand-led research focus in first call for proposals (e.g., locally relevant technical knowledge for resilient infrastructure).
Regional multi-country projects (up to $750K) to foster collaboration among SIDS.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Project administration improved but still not streamlined; co-funding mobilisation lagging.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Increase the size of the next project cohort and convene donors to push for faster co-funding disbursements.
Strengthen communication strategy to highlight UK’s role in high-profile events (e.g., COP, regional climate weeks).
Develop and operationalise capacity-building processes in Year 2, integrating lessons from Year 1.
Review IRAF’s administrative capacity to ensure IRIS is not deprioritised relative to other funding windows.

strengths: Identified risks (e.g., underutilisation of funds, co-funding gaps) were accurately flagged in the business case.
Steering Committee approvals (11 projects) demonstrated risk-aware selection criteria.
weaknesses: Mitigation actions (e.g., accelerating disbursements) were slow to implement.
No contingency plans for IRAF capacity constraints or currency risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 11 projects approved across 13 SIDS (indirect reach: ~65M people in SIDS group, though direct beneficiaries not yet quantified).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.coverage_note: Projects are in early implementation; beneficiary data will be available post-2024.

evidence: Potential upstream influence on SIDS’ infrastructure standards (e.g., integration of resilience measures into national frameworks).
No quantifiable policy changes yet; early-stage technical assistance may inform future regulations.
policy_influence_achieved.pathways: Through CDRI’s convening power and knowledge-sharing networks (e.g., global partnerships for resilient infrastructure).

capacity_building_results.direct: 11 projects include capacity-building components (e.g., training for SIDS officials), but delivery not yet underway.
capacity_building_results.indirect: IRIS PMU’s proposal support strengthened 5 implementing entities’ ability to design resilient infrastructure projects.

positive: Increased visibility of SIDS’ infrastructure needs at COP27/COP28 (e.g., 50 EoIs received vs. 30 target).
Potential for IRIS to serve as a model for other climate-resilience facilities (e.g., IRAF’s urban resilience window).
negative: Risk of diverting IRAF’s attention from IRIS if new funding windows are prioritised.
Delayed projects may erode SIDS’ trust in the facility’s reliability.

scalability_evidence.potential: High (if administrative bottlenecks are resolved).
barriers: Slow disbursement pace limits demonstration of scalability.
Dependence on CDRI/IRAF’s capacity to manage growth.
scalability_evidence.examples: Regional multi-country projects (e.g., 3+ SIDS collaborations) show potential for replication.

continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with UK priorities (e.g., climate resilience, SIDS support, 2030 Roadmap).
Global significance: SIDS face existential climate threats, and IRIS addresses critical gaps in resilient infrastructure.
Potential for leveraging £7.3M to mobilise $50–60M in co-funding (if implementation accelerates).
First cohort of 11 projects (13 SIDS) demonstrates demand and relevance, despite delays.

strengths: Multi-donor MPTF structure (IRAF) provides long-term funding stability.
CDRI’s technical expertise and convening power add credibility.
risks: Administrative capacity constraints at IRAF/CDRI may limit scalability.
Dependence on co-funding materialisation ($31M pledged vs. $50M target).

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Moderate (acknowledges strategic value but concerned about implementation pace and VFM).
planned_adaptations_future: Streamline project administration to accelerate disbursements in Year 2.
Balance focus across all programme pillars (technical assistance, knowledge, capacity-building).
Enhance UK’s visibility through targeted communications (e.g., COP28, regional events).
Explore interim reporting mechanisms for real-time oversight.
Review IRAF’s capacity to ensure IRIS remains a priority.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (UNDP Pakistan as principal implementing partner)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £4.5 million over five years (2023–2029)
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Funds channeled through UNDP under a single multilateral agreement, with FCDO oversight and periodic disbursements tied to milestones in the inception phase (Jan–Jun 2024) and operational delivery (Jul 2024 onward).
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium - Original design allowed for reallocation across outputs but required FCDO approval for major shifts between budget lines or geographic areas.

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch FCDO oversight with UNDP as lead implementer; quarterly progress reviews and annual FCDO-led reviews. Embedded FCDO advisors *not* planned at design stage.
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly monitoring by FCDO, with UNDP providing detailed technical and financial reports. Annual independent reviews (e.g., this Annual Review).
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Joint FCDO-UNDP steering committee for strategic decisions; UNDP-led operational decision-making with FCDO approval for major adaptations (e.g., budget reallocations >10%, scope changes).

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single principal implementer (UNDP) with subcontracts to local consultants/NGOs for technical assistance. No consortium structure originally envisioned.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral (UNDP) + local/regional consultants and government counterparts (e.g., Planning Commission, line ministries).
partner_selection_baseline.partner_roles_planned: UNDP: overall implementation; FCDO: strategic oversight; Government of Pakistan: beneficiary and co-implementer (e.g., providing access to ministries, data, and policy forums).
partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award to UNDP based on existing FCDO-UNDP framework agreements; competitive selection for subcontracted technical experts.

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (UNDP Pakistan remains sole funding channel)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £4.5 million total budget unchanged, but *disbursement pace slowed* due to: (1) 6-month inception phase (Jan–Jun 2024) consuming ~20% of Year 1 budget; (2) delays in consultant recruitment affecting pilot implementation.
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Funds flowed as planned through UNDP, but *actual spending lagged* due to: (a) prolonged government counterpart approvals post-elections (Feb 2024); (b) UNDP procurement delays for technical experts. No shifts in modality, but *budget reallocations* occurred within outputs (e.g., more funds to climate change pilots due to traction).
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Medium - Flexibility *used* to reallocate ~15% of Year 1 budget across pilots (e.g., additional support to climate change NAP coordination), but no formal FCDO approval sought for shifts <10%.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Light-touch FCDO oversight *maintained*, but *intensified engagement* post-election (Feb 2024) due to political instability. UNDP remains lead, but FCDO now conducts *bi-monthly check-ins* (vs. quarterly planned) to navigate counterpart turnover.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned: *Bi-monthly* FCDO-UNDP calls (vs. quarterly) and ad-hoc meetings to address delays. Annual Review conducted as planned (Oct 2024).
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Steering committee *convened less frequently* (once in 2024 vs. planned bi-annually) due to political transitions. Operational decisions *delegated more to UNDP* to accelerate pilots, with FCDO ex-post approval for reallocations.

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Single implementer (UNDP) *expanded* to include *direct engagement* with 6+ line ministries (BISP, Economic Affairs Division, Climate Change, Power, Petroleum, Planning Commission) and statutory bodies (CCI, NEC, National Assembly). No formal consortium, but *de facto multi-stakeholder coordination* emerged.
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (UNDP) + Government (6 line ministries, CCI, NEC, National Assembly) + *new*: technical consultants for pilots (e.g., aid effectiveness dashboard, climate NAP).
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: UNDP: implementation lead; FCDO: strategic oversight; Government: *more active co-implementation* (e.g., BISP data-sharing pilot, NAP coordination). Parliament engagement *slower* than planned due to approval bottlenecks.

substantive_changes_made: Expanded *direct engagement* with line ministries beyond original plan (from 3–4 to 6+ ministries/statutory bodies in Year 1).
Shifted *pilot focus* toward high-traction areas (e.g., climate NAP coordination, social protection data-sharing) away from contentious issues (e.g., National Finance Commission reforms).
Increased *budget flexibility utilization* (~15% reallocation across outputs without formal FCDO approval, leveraging "medium" flexibility clause).
*Accelerated decision-making delegation* to UNDP for operational adjustments (e.g., pilot initiation) due to political delays.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: No change to total budget (£4.5m), but *disbursement delays* led to ~20% underspend in Year 1 (inception phase consumed more time/resources than planned).
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope *unchanged* (national/federal level), but *beneficiary scope expanded* via deeper engagement with additional ministries (e.g., Power, Petroleum).

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Core assumptions *challenged* by context: (1) Political instability post-elections (Feb 2024) slowed parliamentary engagement; (2) IMF fiscal constraints (2024) reduced government bandwidth for long-term reforms (e.g., National Finance Commission). *No formal ToC revision*, but programmatic focus *rebalanced* toward feasible pilots (e.g., climate NAP, aid dashboard).

management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Oversight *intensified* (bi-monthly check-ins vs. quarterly planned) but no structural changes.
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: *De facto* shift to more UNDP-led operational decisions with ex-post FCDO approval, but no formal restructuring.

activity_only_adjustments: Delayed baseline assessments (IGCI/IGPAAR indices) due to consultant recruitment lags.
Pilot timelines extended (e.g., social protection data-sharing pilot pushed to Q1 2025).
Reduced ambition on contentious reforms (e.g., National Finance Commission) in favor of shorter-term fiscal pact support.

contextual_shocks: Political transition (Feb 2024 elections) caused *counterpart turnover* and approval delays.
IMF program (2024) imposed fiscal constraints, reducing government capacity for long-term reforms.
Polarized post-election environment *stalled* progress on contentious issues (e.g., inter-governmental fiscal disputes).
performance_issues: UNDP procurement delays for technical consultants slowed pilot initiation.
Limited pool of qualified local experts *extended* recruitment timelines.
learning_insights: Early traction with climate change and social protection pilots *shifted focus* away from low-probability reforms (e.g., National Finance Commission).
Parliamentary engagement *deprioritized* due to high transaction costs (multi-level approvals).
strategic_opportunities: National Fiscal Pact (2024) aligned with NGP’s coordination goals, creating *new entry points* for federal-provincial dialogue support.
IMF-driven subsidy reforms (e.g., gas/fertilizer pricing) opened *technical assistance opportunities* for NGP (e.g., data analysis for Planning Commission).

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: Medium - Adaptations were *reactive* (e.g., responding to political delays) rather than proactive, but effectively leveraged flexibility to maintain momentum (e.g., pilot reallocations).
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: Medium - Baseline flexibility clause *used* for budget reallocations, but underutilized for strategic pivots (e.g., no formal ToC revision despite contextual shifts).
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Medium - Learning from inception phase (e.g., traction with climate pilots) *informed* activity adjustments, but limited documentation of adaptation rationale.

fcas_context.fragility_level: High - Pakistan faces chronic political instability, economic crises, and subnational conflicts (e.g., Balochistan, KP).
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Indirect - No active conflict in programme areas, but *political polarization* and institutional fragility (e.g., frequent counterpart turnover) disrupt implementation.

major_external_shocks.political_transitions: February 2024 elections led to *caretaker-to-elected government transition*, causing 3–6 month delays in counterpart engagement and approvals.
major_external_shocks.economic_shocks: IMF program (2024) imposed austerity measures, reducing fiscal space for governance reforms and prioritizing short-term stabilization over NGP’s long-term objectives (e.g., climate adaptation planning).
major_external_shocks.climate_disasters: 2024 floods in Punjab/Sindh *indirectly* affected programme by diverting government attention to relief efforts, though NGP’s climate work (e.g., NAP coordination) gained relevance.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: Commitment *fluctuated* post-elections: high-level support for NGP’s goals (e.g., fiscal coordination) but *reduced bandwidth* due to IMF conditions and political polarization.
policy_environment_changes: Shift from National Finance Commission reforms to *short-term National Fiscal Pact* (2024) to meet IMF requirements.
Subsidy reductions (gas/fertilizer) created *new demand* for NGP’s technical assistance on pricing reforms.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: Lower than expected - Frequent counterpart turnover and *limited absorptive capacity* in ministries (e.g., Planning Commission) slowed pilot implementation.

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Constrained - *Limited pool* of qualified local consultants (e.g., for baseline assessments) led to recruitment delays and higher-than-planned costs.
market_conditions.cost_inflation_impacts: Moderate - Pakistan’s inflation (2023–24) increased operational costs (e.g., consultant fees), but UNDP’s multilateral rates *mitigated* impact.
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: GBP-PKR depreciation (2023–24) *reduced real value* of £4.5m budget, but UNDP’s hedging minimized exposure.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Moderate - *One substantive change* (expanded partner engagement) with other mechanisms (funding, governance) stable. Adaptations were *incremental* rather than transformative.
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Partnership adaptation - Primary change was *broader and deeper* engagement with government partners (ministries, CCI, NEC) beyond original UNDP-centric design.
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate - Original design (single implementer + medium flexibility) *enabled* responsive adjustments, but underestimated political economy risks (e.g., counterpart turnover, IMF constraints).

programme_metadata.programme_title: National Governance Programme

output_1.title: Line ministries have the capacity to develop and implement plans in coordination with provinces to meet national targets and deliver a national coherent response

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme shifted focus from addressing highly contentious issues (e.g., National Finance Commission Award) to more tractable areas like the National Fiscal Pact, aligning with IMF conditions and political realities. Pilot interventions were prioritized in areas with higher potential for immediate traction (e.g., data exchange for social protection, aid effectiveness dashboard, climate change coordination).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNDP Pakistan (principal partner) was mobilized effectively but faced delays in recruitment and baseline assessments. Engagement with ministries (e.g., BISP, Economic Affairs Division, Ministry of Climate Change) exceeded targets for pilot initiatives, while parliamentary engagement progressed slower due to bureaucratic hurdles.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme established rapid engagement mechanisms with key ministries and statutory forums (e.g., Council of Common Interests, National Economic Council) but faced challenges in aligning institutional priorities across federal/provincial levels. The inception phase (Jan–Jun 2024) included extensive consultations to identify coordination gaps and pilot interventions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with provincial governments (e.g., Punjab) and federal ministries was initiated through pilot projects (e.g., social protection data exchange, climate adaptation planning). However, the complexity of multi-level coordination remained a persistent challenge, particularly in securing buy-in from parliamentary committees.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in recruiting consultants and mobilizing technical expertise hindered progress, attributed to stringent requirements and a limited pool of qualified candidates. Procurement timelines often misaligned with counterpart expectations, as approvals for technical assistance triggered recruitment processes late in the cycle.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified in pilot areas (e.g., BISP data exchange, Economic Affairs Division dashboard) but remained lighter in contentious policy domains (e.g., fiscal reforms). The programme adapted by focusing on "quick wins" while maintaining strategic engagement on long-term reforms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by rebalancing focus away from politically intractable issues (e.g., Net Hydel Profits) toward achievable goals (e.g., National Fiscal Pact, inter-governmental coordination indices). Pilot interventions were expanded from 2 to 3 based on early demand.
adaptive_management_examples: Shift from pursuing a National Finance Commission Award to supporting the National Fiscal Pact, aligning with IMF conditions and provincial fiscal realities.

Accelerated development of the Inter-Governmental Coordination Index (IGCI) and Inter-Governmental Planning and Anticipatory Action Readiness Score (IGPAAR) to benchmark progress despite baseline delays.
Expanded pilot support to include climate change coordination (National Adaptation Plan) and energy sector reforms (gas/fertilizer pricing) based on ministry demand.

main_implementation_challenges: Complexity of coordinating across federal/provincial governments and sectors, requiring significant alignment efforts and stakeholder buy-in.
Frequent changes in governmental counterparts, especially post-2024 elections, necessitating repeated re-engagement.
Delays in consultant recruitment and baseline assessments due to stringent requirements and limited candidate pools.
Slow progress in parliamentary engagement due to multi-level approval processes.
Political economy constraints limiting traction on contentious issues (e.g., fiscal reforms, hydel profits).
external_factors_impact: Post-election political instability (February 2024) and polarization hindered governance reforms and stakeholder continuity.
IMF program conditions (2024) prioritized short-term fiscal stabilization, reducing bandwidth for long-term structural reforms (e.g., climate adaptation, national planning).
Economic constraints forced the government to focus on immediate fiscal targets, delaying broader governance initiatives.
contextual_constraints_new: Emergence of the National Fiscal Pact as a shorter-term alternative to the National Finance Commission Award, requiring programme adaptation.
Heightened political sensitivity around inter-governmental fiscal relations, limiting progress on contentious issues.
Increased demand for technical assistance in energy and climate sectors due to IMF-driven subsidy reforms.
partner_relationship_issues: UNDP’s mobilization was timely, but recruitment bottlenecks affected delivery pace.
Ministries (e.g., BISP, Planning Commission) were responsive to pilot interventions, while parliamentary engagement lagged due to bureaucratic hurdles.
Provincial governments (e.g., Punjab) collaborated on social protection data exchange, but federal-provincial tensions persisted in fiscal domains.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited pool of qualified consultants for specialized roles (e.g., fiscal coordination, parliamentary oversight).
Ministries lacked baseline data on inter-governmental coordination, requiring programme support to develop indices (IGCI, IGPAAR).
High turnover of governmental counterparts disrupted continuity in technical assistance.
risk_materialization: Political instability and election-related transitions materialized as predicted, impacting stakeholder engagement.
Economic constraints (IMF conditions) reduced government capacity to prioritize long-term reforms, aligning with programme risk assessments.
Delays in baseline data collection affected early progress tracking but were mitigated through adaptive pilot initiatives.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme is in its early stages, with spending aligned to inception and pilot activities. No significant underspending or overspending was reported, but delays in consultant recruitment affected activity timelines. A multi-year financial forecast is planned by January 2025 to improve budget alignment.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indications suggest good VFM due to: (1) exceeding pilot targets (3 initiated vs. 2 planned); (2) leveraging existing BHC Islamabad priorities (climate, social protection); and (3) aligning with IMF-driven fiscal reforms. However, long-term VFM depends on sustaining coordination gains and policy uptake.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: UNDP’s financial management was deemed adequate, though recruitment delays impacted activity rollout. The programme’s shift to tractable pilots (e.g., data dashboards) demonstrated cost-conscious adaptation.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was achieved in pilot design (e.g., repurposing existing data systems for social protection) but challenged by high transaction costs in stakeholder coordination. The programme’s issues-based approach helped focus resources on high-impact areas.

key_delivery_lessons: Coordination complexity is both the programme’s core challenge and opportunity; early wins in pilot interventions build credibility for tackling larger reforms.
Political economy realities (e.g., IMF conditions, election cycles) must guide programme pacing and ambition—contentious issues require long-term engagement.
Recruitment delays can be mitigated by pre-emptive hiring for anticipated technical assistance needs, even before formal counterpart approvals.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid initiation of pilot interventions (e.g., BISP data exchange, aid effectiveness dashboard) demonstrated agility and built ministry trust.
Development of coordination indices (IGCI, IGPAAR) provided a structured framework for tracking progress despite baseline delays.
Engagement with statutory forums (CCI, NEC) and parliamentary committees, though slow, established critical entry points for future reforms.
management_adaptations_made: Rebalanced focus from contentious fiscal reforms to achievable coordination pilots (e.g., National Fiscal Pact support).
Accelerated pilot implementation to compensate for inception-phase delays, exceeding annual targets.
Strengthened alignment with BHC Islamabad priorities (climate, social protection) to enhance relevance and leverage existing resources.
innovations_attempted: Inter-Governmental Coordination Index (IGCI) and IGPAAR to quantify coordination improvements over time.
Digital dashboard for aid effectiveness (Economic Affairs Division) to enhance transparency and data-driven decision-making.
Cross-sectoral pilot interventions (e.g., linking social protection data with climate adaptation planning).
forward_recommendations: Prioritize areas with demonstrated traction (e.g., social protection data, climate coordination) while maintaining strategic engagement on long-term reforms.
Develop a multi-year financial forecast by January 2025 to improve budget predictability and alignment with programme phases.
Deepening collaboration with BHC Islamabad’s technical teams to ensure governance improvements directly support broader UK priorities.
Invest in pre-emptive recruitment pipelines to reduce delays in mobilizing technical expertise.
Monitor political economy shifts (e.g., IMF program reviews) to anticipate and adapt to changing reform windows.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective: political and economic risks were anticipated, but mitigation required adaptive rebalancing of outputs. The programme’s flexibility in shifting from intractable issues (e.g., NFC Award) to achievable goals (e.g., National Fiscal Pact) demonstrated responsive risk handling. However, recruitment risks were underestimated, requiring corrective action.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Early engagement reached key ministries (BISP, Economic Affairs, Climate Change, Planning Commission) and statutory forums (CCI, NEC). Pilot interventions directly benefited: (1) federal-provincial data exchange for social protection; (2) climate adaptation planning; and (3) economic reform dashboards. Parliamentary engagement is ongoing but slower.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Emerging evidence of influence in pilot domains (e.g., social protection data protocols, National Fiscal Pact alignment). Long-term policy uptake depends on sustained political commitment and institutionalization of coordination mechanisms (IGCI, IGPAAR).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Baseline assessments and pilot interventions (e.g., BISP data exchange, NAP coordination) began building capacity in inter-governmental planning. However, systemic capacity gains require longer-term engagement and scaling of successful pilots.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Pilot interventions (e.g., aid effectiveness dashboard) created demand for broader transparency tools across ministries.
Negative: Focus on tractable issues may divert attention from deeper structural reforms (e.g., fiscal decentralization) in the short term.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Pilot models (e.g., social protection data exchange, climate coordination) show potential for scaling, particularly if integrated into statutory forums (CCI, NEC) and aligned with IMF-driven fiscal reforms. The IGCI/IGPAAR indices could serve as scalable tools for benchmarking coordination nationally.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated early progress in pilot interventions and alignment with Pakistan’s evolving governance priorities (e.g., National Fiscal Pact, IMF reforms). Its focus on inter-governmental coordination remains critical for state effectiveness, and adaptive management has mitigated initial challenges. Continuation is justified to: (1) consolidate pilot gains; (2) institutionalize coordination indices; and (3) capitalize on political windows for reform.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is sustainable in the medium term, contingent on: (1) maintaining flexibility to adapt to political/economic shifts; (2) securing buy-in from new governmental counterparts; and (3) scaling successful pilots through statutory forums (CCI, NEC). Long-term sustainability requires deeper institutionalization of coordination mechanisms.
planned_adaptations_future: Expand successful pilots (e.g., data exchange, climate coordination) to additional ministries and provinces.
Strengthen parliamentary engagement through targeted support to standing committees aligned with programme priorities.
Develop a phased approach to contentious reforms (e.g., fiscal decentralization), leveraging short-term wins (National Fiscal Pact) to build momentum.
Enhance monitoring using IGCI/IGPAAR indices to demonstrate progress and inform adaptive management.
Deepening collaboration with BHC Islamabad to align governance improvements with UK strategic priorities (e.g., climate resilience, economic reform).

governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly reporting with annual deep dives; independent MEL (Component 5) for cross-cutting learning
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: FCDO retains strategic decision-making; operational decisions delegated to component suppliers/partners

activity_only_adjustments: Accelerated policy engagement (e.g., ADP chairmanship) to maintain momentum during procurement

programme_metadata.programme_title: Investments in Forests and Sustainable Land Use – Phase 2 (IFSLU2)

output_1.title: Demand-side measures: Enhanced markets for sustainably sourced products through public and private commitments to sustainable sourcing

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme transitioned from Phase 1 (£140m, 2015-24) to Phase 2 (£500m, 2023-34) with expanded scope and budget. Delivery now structured through five components (vs. previous phase's structure). Tender processes for major components (1, 3, 5) initiated in Year 1, with Component 2 using grant partnerships (IDH, Solidaridad, ISEAL) as interim delivery mechanism during procurement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Strategic partners (TFA, World Bank PROGREEN, WEF, CIFOR-ICRAF) performed as expected during transition phase, maintaining policy momentum (e.g., ADP chairmanship, Traders' Roadmap). Grant agreements signed with Solidaridad, IDH, and ISEAL for smallholder support, though full delivery contracts for Components 1/3 not yet operational.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Centralised programme management with component-specific oversight. Governance includes policy coordination (e.g., UK chairing ADP July–Dec 2024) and cross-component alignment mechanisms. Monitoring/evaluation (Component 5) not yet contracted (tender in 2025).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong policy coordination achieved through UK government leadership (e.g., ADP, FACT Dialogue secretariat). Operational coordination between components is nascent; plans to formalise collaboration mechanisms in Year 2 to avoid duplication (especially in Congo Basin).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for Components 1 (business incubation) and 3 (Congo Basin) in final stages (FY 2024/25 contract signing expected). Delays in procurement contributed to underspend and slower-than-planned mobilisation. Component 5 (MEL) tender delayed until 2025.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: High oversight during mobilisation phase due to transition risks. Policy engagement (e.g., ADP, TFA) received intensive oversight; operational delivery oversight will increase post-contract signing.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to extend Phase 1 partnerships (e.g., TFA, ADP) during Phase 2 mobilisation. Adaptive management used to sustain policy momentum despite procurement delays.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended UK chairmanship of ADP (July–Dec 2024) to bridge Phase 1/2 transition, refocusing from advocacy to implementation support.
Renewed TFA funding to maintain Traders' Roadmap progress (15 companies aligning to 1.5°C pathways).
Interim grant agreements with IDH/Solidaridad/ISEAL to prevent gaps in smallholder support.

main_implementation_challenges: Longer-than-expected transition from Phase 1 to Phase 2 (3.5 years from concept to implementation), causing momentum loss.
Procurement delays for major components (1/3) leading to underspend and deferred field activities.
Financial forecasting inaccuracies due to variable procurement timelines and bidder approaches to inception costs.
Risk of duplication in Congo Basin without formalised coordination mechanisms.
operational_challenges_context.external_factors_impact: No major external shocks reported; Phase 1’s success (£1.35bn private investment leveraged) created high expectations for Phase 2. Global policy environment (e.g., COP28, EU deforestation regulations) remains supportive.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated complexity in aligning new component contracts with existing partnerships (e.g., smallholder grants vs. future Component 1 services).
Emerging need for stronger cross-component coordination to avoid silos, particularly in Congo Basin.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: None reported; strategic partners (TFA, WEF, World Bank) engaged effectively during transition. Risk of partner fatigue if procurement delays persist.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited in-house capacity to manage parallel procurement processes for multiple components.
Gaps in monitoring/evaluation capacity until Component 5 contractor is onboarded (2025).
risk_materialization: Procurement timeline risks materialized, causing delays in contract awards and underspend.
Transition risks (loss of momentum) partially mitigated through policy engagement but affected operational readiness.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Significant underspend in Year 1 due to procurement delays. Initial forecasts overestimated inception costs; actual spend lower than planned. Budget execution expected to align with projections post-contract signing (FY 2024/25).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Phase 1 achieved high VFM (£11 private investment per £1 ODA; 8.6m hectares protected). Phase 2 targets similar or higher ratios but too early to assess. Early indicators suggest efficient use of mobilisation funds (e.g., leveraging existing partnerships).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls during mobilisation. Forecasting challenges identified (e.g., procurement variability) with plans to implement range-based forecasting. Grant management for Component 2 (smallholders) proceeded without issues.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Not yet measurable; mobilisation costs lower than forecast due to delayed procurement. Efficiency gains expected from scaled-up components (e.g., Component 1’s business incubation model).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: No co-funding reported in Year 1. Phase 1’s co-funding partnerships (e.g., private sector) provide a model for Phase 2, but actualisation pending contract awards.

key_delivery_lessons: Start planning for follow-on phases earlier to avoid gaps (e.g., Phase 2 design began 3.5 years pre-implementation but still faced delays).
Accelerate internal FCDO approval processes to compress design-to-procurement timelines.
Assume lower inception costs in forecasts to improve accuracy.
successful_delivery_practices: Policy engagement during mobilisation (e.g., ADP chairmanship) maintained momentum despite procurement delays.
Interim grant agreements prevented gaps in smallholder support.
Leveraging Phase 1 partnerships (e.g., TFA, PROGREEN) ensured continuity.
management_adaptations_made: Refocused ADP priorities from advocacy to implementation support to align with Phase 2 goals.
Adjusted financial forecasting methods to account for procurement variability.
innovations_attempted: Scaled-up business incubation model (Component 1) to drive private sector investment at ratio >1:11 (Phase 1 benchmark).
Integrated smallholder support (Component 2) with deforestation-free commodity chains (Component 1) for synergistic impact.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: Phase 1 recommendations (e.g., stronger MEL, private sector engagement) incorporated into Phase 2 design (e.g., Component 5 MEL contract, Component 1’s investment focus).
forward_recommendations: Rapidly mobilise Components 1/3 suppliers post-contract to recover lost time.
Formalise cross-component coordination (especially Congo Basin) to maximise impact.
Initiate Component 5 (MEL) tender in 2025 with emphasis on adaptive learning.
Improve financial forecasting using range-based scenarios.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderately effective. Transition risks were partially mitigated through policy engagement, but procurement risks materialized. Risk rating remains "Moderate" due to ongoing procurement and mobilisation challenges.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: No direct beneficiaries reached in Year 1 (mobilisation phase). Phase 1 reached 327,000 people (mainly smallholders); Phase 2 targets scaling this impact post-2025.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: Low (Year 1 focused on setup; outcomes expected from 2025 onward).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Weak (no implementation data yet; relying on Phase 1 evidence and mobilisation indicators).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium (strong Phase 1 foundation and policy alignment, but sustainability depends on private sector uptake post-2025).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: High (UK’s ADP chairmanship advanced deforestation-free trade policies; Traders’ Roadmap maintained momentum with 15 companies).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Not yet measurable; capacity-building activities (e.g., smallholder resilience, Congo Basin business development) will commence post-contract signing.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Medium (Phase 1’s £1:£11 leverage ratio demonstrates scalability potential, but Phase 2 models not yet tested).

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Phase 1’s proven impact (£1.35bn private investment, 8.6m hectares protected) and Phase 2’s strong mobilisation (policy leadership, partner engagement) justify continuation. Procurement delays are temporary; programme remains critical to FCDO’s climate/environment goals.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (with caveats: success hinges on rapid post-2025 implementation and private sector engagement).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (delivery model is scalable but requires effective coordination across components and sustained private sector buy-in).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High ("A" score for Year 1 mobilisation; alignment with ECED Goal 5 on deforestation).
planned_adaptations_future: Accelerate Component 1/3 implementation to recover timeline.
Strengthen MEL systems (Component 5) for real-time adaptive management.
Enhance cross-component coordination, particularly in Congo Basin.
Refine financial forecasting to reflect procurement realities.

programme_metadata.programme_title: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) Core Contribution 2021-2026

output_1.title: Improved performance on gender equality

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The UNCCD Secretariat successfully delivered COP15 in Abidjan (May 2022) with 7,000+ participants and 38 decisions adopted, including UK priorities on gender equality in land tenure. The Secretariat exceeded expectations in gender mainstreaming (88% of UN-SWAP indicators met/exceeded vs 74% UN average).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The Secretariat played a central role in strengthening synergies between the three Rio Conventions (UNCCD, UNFCCC, UNCBD) during 2022, particularly through aligned COP processes. External recognition noted progress in coherence between conventions on interlinked issues like land degradation, climate change, and biodiversity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: The programme SRO stretched capacity during COP15 negotiations across multiple tracks. Additional UK science/technology representation is recommended for COP16 to improve oversight and engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: Post-COP15, the Secretariat is updating its reporting system to improve accountability and monitoring of Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) commitments. The Global Land Outlook 2 report (April 2022) was launched to highlight challenges and solutions, reflecting adaptive response to emerging evidence.

main_implementation_challenges: Scale of global land degradation challenge remains vast and growing, with 40% of world’s land already degraded (Global Land Outlook 2, 2022).
Progress toward 2030 LDN targets remains off-track despite voluntary commitments covering 450M+ hectares of restoration.
Capacity constraints during COP15 negotiations required stretching SRO resources across multiple tracks.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging evidence from Global Land Outlook 2 (2022) indicates faster progress is needed to reverse land degradation and address increasing drought frequency/severity.
Need for greater coherence between Rio Conventions at national level to reduce burden on Parties servicing multiple frameworks.
operational_challenges_context.capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited UK science/technology representation during COP15 negotiations; additional resources recommended for COP16.

financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: The UK’s core contribution (£1.583M over 5 years) is judged to offer strong VFM, enabling the UK to drive the global agenda on land degradation through the UNCCD—the sole legally binding framework on this issue. The programme aligns with Integrated Review priorities (climate, biodiversity, food security) and leverages multilateral systems to achieve outcomes disproportionate to its cost (e.g., COP15 delivery, Global Land Outlook 2 report).

key_delivery_lessons: Strengthening synergies between Rio Conventions (UNCCD, UNFCCC, UNCBD) at national level can reduce burden on Parties and improve coherence. Joint implementation efforts should be prioritized ahead of COP16.
UNCCD’s gender mainstreaming progress (88% UN-SWAP indicators met/exceeded) demonstrates effective use of performance frameworks to drive institutional change.
successful_delivery_practices: UNCCD Secretariat’s support for COP15 (7,000+ participants, 38 decisions) was externally recognized as successful, particularly on gender and land tenure issues.
Launch of Global Land Outlook 2 report (April 2022) provided critical evidence base for policy and programming.
management_adaptations_made: Post-COP15, the Secretariat is updating its reporting system to improve LDN monitoring and accountability.
UK programme team to decide on appointing a science/technology representative for COP16 by April 2023 to address capacity gaps.
forward_recommendations: Enhance joint implementation between Rio Conventions at national level (e.g., aligned ministries, targets, reporting) to streamline efforts and reduce Party burden (by COP16).
Review and update UNCCD programme logframe and outcome indicators by August 2023 to reflect new reporting system data.
Appoint UK science/technology representative and finalize COP16 negotiating team by April 2023 to improve engagement with National Focal Points.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: COP15 decisions included UK priorities on gender equality in land tenure and synergy between Rio Conventions, with external recognition of progress (e.g., IISD summary). The Gender Action Plan roadmap and voluntary national reporting were adopted to accelerate implementation.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: The UNCCD Global Mechanism has a pipeline of 40 projects to support countries in accessing finance for DLDD, but scale remains insufficient to meet global challenges (40% of land degraded).

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme is on track to contribute to UNCCD Strategic Objectives (2018–2030), with early progress on outputs (e.g., gender equality, COP15 delivery) and alignment with UK priorities (climate, biodiversity, gender). The UNCCD remains the central global framework for addressing land degradation, and the UK’s core contribution leverages multilateral influence disproportionate to its cost.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model (core contribution to UNCCD Secretariat) is sustainable, but requires adaptive management to address capacity constraints (e.g., COP negotiations) and scale challenges (e.g., LDN target progress).
planned_adaptations_future: Strengthen national-level synergies between Rio Conventions to improve coherence and reduce Party burden.
Update programme logframe by August 2023 to reflect new UNCCD reporting system data.
Appoint UK science/technology representative for COP16 to enhance negotiation capacity.

output_4.title: Conclusion of the Demobilisation, Disarmament and Reintegration (DDR) of former RENAMO Combatants

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Component 1 (£4.4m) delayed due to procurement issues and ODA budget pauses; only Component 2 (£0.5m) reviewed during this period. UK funding contributed to UNOPS-managed basket fund for DDR activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNOPS and Peace Secretariat (PPS) performed adequately but faced challenges in political engagement and risk mitigation. Delays in demobilisation due to pension disputes were not proactively managed. PPS lacked contingency plans for known risks (e.g., rainy season timing).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UNOPS managed procurement, financial reporting, and donor coordination. Canadian High Commission played a coordinating role among donors. Quarterly donor meetings and reports were conducted as planned, but logframe lacked granular, gender-disaggregated milestones.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Donor coordination group met quarterly, but diplomatic engagement to resolve pension disputes was insufficient. UK lobbying at Head of Mission level eventually secured political commitments, but earlier intervention could have prevented delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for DDR activities (e.g., reinsertion kits, assembly centres) was managed by UNOPS. No major issues reported, but delays in demobilisation led to additional unplanned costs (e.g., extended basecamp operations).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO oversight was limited due to short review period (5 months) and reliance on UNOPS/PPS reporting. Quarterly risk reviews were conducted, but political risks (e.g., pension disputes) were not escalated promptly.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to delays by extending demobilisation timeline to May 2023. UK allocated additional £100k to address short-term funding gaps, but longer-term flexibility was constrained by ODA budget uncertainties.
adaptive_management_examples: Allocated additional £100k in FY 22/23 to support DDR closure despite initial funding constraints.
Leveraged UK diplomatic influence to secure presidential decree on pension payments, enabling final demobilisation.
Introduced 1st Secretary/Conflict Adviser joint role to improve cross-HMG coordination on political lobbying.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in final demobilisation of 421 ex-combatants due to disputes over pension provisions, extending timeline by 6 months.
Lack of contingency planning for known risks (e.g., rainy season, political disagreements).
Limited engagement with diplomatic community to preemptively address pension disputes.
Retrospective logframe reporting hindered real-time monitoring.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 restrictions complicated DDR processes and extended programme lifecycle.
Political tensions between Frelimo and Renamo over pension payments stalled progress.
Ongoing insurgency in Cabo Delgado created security concerns but did not directly disrupt DDR activities.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated complexity of pension negotiations required high-level political intervention (e.g., presidential decree).
Rainy season timing exacerbated logistical challenges for demobilisation.
Municipal election irregularities (October 2023) highlighted unresolved political inclusion issues under the Peace Accords.
partner_relationship_issues: PPS/UNOPS did not proactively share research (e.g., gender dynamics) with donors as planned.
Perceived impartiality of PPS was questioned due to heavy engagement with GoM and Renamo leaders.
Donor coordination group lacked mechanisms for early warning on political risks.
capacity_constraints_emerged: PPS had limited capacity to manage simultaneous political lobbying and operational DDR activities.
Short-term UK funding (£100k) constrained ability to address long-term reintegration needs.
Gender-sensitive M&E was implemented but not fully integrated into donor reporting.
risk_materialization: Pension disputes (high impact: 6-month delay).
Rainy season logistical challenges (moderate impact).

budget_execution_vs_plan: £100,000 (UK contribution) disbursed as planned to UNOPS-managed basket fund (total $11.7m).
Delays in demobilisation incurred additional unplanned costs (e.g., extended basecamp operations). Final costs pending next review.
Programme management costs at 3% of total (below World Bank’s 5% benchmark).
value_for_money_assessment: Economy: Low management costs (3%) and leveraged international donor commitments for 2024.
Efficiency: DDR process completed within 3 years despite COVID-19 and political setbacks. UK’s £100k influenced broader donor engagement.
Effectiveness: Demobilisation achieved (albeit delayed), with UK maintaining access to GoM and UN processes.

financial_management_quality: UNOPS provided timely quarterly reports and audited statements (last narrative report: March 2023; audited statement: June 2023).
Basket fund structure ensured transparency, but retrospective logframe limited real-time financial tracking.
No evidence of fund mismanagement, though risk register could have included more specific mitigation actions.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost per ex-combatant demobilised not explicitly stated, but programme deemed efficient relative to potential conflict costs.
Reinsertion support reached 90% (4,800/5,221) of ex-combatants, with no additional per-unit cost increases reported.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Majority of 2024 basket fund ($11.7m) secured via new international donor commitments, reducing UK’s proportional burden.

key_delivery_lessons: Early diplomatic engagement on political risks (e.g., pensions) could have prevented delays.
Quarterly milestones and gender-disaggregated data should be integrated into logframes.
Structured cross-HMG coordination (e.g., 1st Secretary/Conflict Adviser role) improves lobbying effectiveness.
successful_delivery_practices: UK’s modest funding leveraged significant UN and donor influence (e.g., UNSC events, PPS governance).
PPS’s gender-sensitive DDR training and equity-focused reintegration (50% women staff; 63% in senior roles).
High-level political commitment (Nyusi/Momade) ultimately resolved pension disputes.
management_adaptations_made: Added £100k to address short-term funding gaps.
Enhanced HoM-level lobbying to secure presidential decree on pensions.
Introduced joint 1st Secretary/Conflict Adviser role for better political coordination.
innovations_attempted: PPS’s use of high-level UN platforms (e.g., UNSC Presidency) to showcase Mozambique’s peacebuilding model.

previous_recommendations_progress.status: Partially addressed (£100k allocated, but no long-term extension).

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Include gender-disaggregated quarterly milestones.
Measure political engagement in logframe.
Share PPS research with donors.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Develop options for supporting the ‘next phase’ of Maputo Peace Accords (political inclusion, governance reforms).
Revise ToC/logframe if ODA reductions affect Outcome 1 ambition.
Enhance risk register with specific actions for fund mismanagement and reputational risks.
Integrate political engagement metrics into MEL systems.

scalability_evidence: DDR model (e.g., assembly centres, reinsertion kits) could be replicated in other post-conflict contexts.

continuation_rationale: Ongoing relevance of peacebuilding objectives in Cabo Delgado and central Mozambique.

UK’s modest funding leverages significant influence with GoM and international partners.
delivery_model_sustainability: Strengths: UNOPS-managed basket fund ensures donor coordination; PPS has strong gender equity policies.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied (with caveats)
planned_adaptations_future: Explore funding options for ‘next phase’ of Peace Accords (e.g., revised PPS governance).
Enhance MEL systems to include political engagement metrics and gender-disaggregated data.
Strengthen risk management with proactive diplomatic engagement on emerging issues.
Consider extending UK’s basket fund contribution if ODA permits, focusing on reintegration and reconciliation.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Mozambique Humanitarian Response Programme

output_1.title: Humanitarian assistance is prioritized for those most in need and affected by conflict and climate disasters

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme maintained flexibility to rapidly scale up during emergencies (e.g., Cyclone Freddy, cholera outbreak) through an internal risk facility. Additional £1.3m was allocated within 10 days for emergency response, demonstrating adaptive capacity beyond original plans.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (IOM, WFP, NRC, INSO, UNICEF) exceeded targets in most areas. WFP implemented vulnerability-based targeting (VBT) in 7/9 priority districts, though 2 districts were excluded due to local authority restrictions. IOM and NRC integrated Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) standards effectively. Rapid scale-up during Cyclone Freddy and cholera outbreak proved partners could handle dynamic crises.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Multi-year partnerships (4) with one short-term technical assistance component were maintained as planned. Coordination was strengthened through INSO’s security analysis and training, though decision-making on fund allocation during emergencies required rapid internal FCDO earmarking to avoid diverting resources from ongoing conflicts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective during emergencies (e.g., Cyclone Freddy response). INSO’s security assessments improved access in insecure areas. However, balancing disaster response with ongoing conflict needs required explicit FCDO guidance to prevent resource diversion.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was agile, enabling rapid allocation of £1.3m for Cyclone Freddy and cholera within 10 days. No major delays or issues reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Moderate oversight with a focus on flexibility. FCDO maintained close monitoring during scale-ups but allowed partners operational autonomy for rapid response.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Flexibility was critical for responding to unplanned emergencies (Cyclone Freddy, cholera). The Internal Risk Facility (IRF) was depleted after 18 months, limiting future flexibility for large-scale disasters.
adaptive_management_examples: Allocated £1.3m within 10 days for Cyclone Freddy and cholera response, exceeding original targets (e.g., 202,000 people reached vs. 150,000 planned).
WFP adjusted VBT implementation after 2 districts were blocked by local authorities, focusing on the remaining 7 districts.
IOM expanded mental health services to 30,758 people (vs. 5,900+10,000 planned) during Cyclone Freddy, though interventions were shorter-term for flood-displaced populations.
NRC shifted focus from new birth certificate issuance to supporting existing beneficiaries in accessing national IDs, based on ongoing discussions with FCDO.

main_implementation_challenges: Balancing emergency response (e.g., Cyclone Freddy) with ongoing conflict-related needs in the north, risking diversion of funds from protracted displacements.
Local authority restrictions blocked WFP’s VBT in 2/9 priority districts, reducing coverage of vulnerability-based targeting.
Depletion of the Internal Risk Facility (IRF) after 18 months, limiting capacity to respond to future large-scale disasters.
Ensuring durable solutions for returns without creating pull factors in insecure areas.
external_factors_impact: Cyclone Freddy (Feb 2023) displaced 124,000 people and affected over 1 million, requiring rapid scale-up.
Cholera outbreak in early 2023 necessitated a £370,000 unplanned allocation to UNICEF.
Ongoing conflict in northern Mozambique continued to displace populations, with over 1 million still dependent on humanitarian assistance.
Annual cyclone seasons regularly destroyed livelihoods and infrastructure, exacerbating humanitarian needs.
contextual_constraints_new: Local authorities in 2 districts refused to approve WFP’s vulnerability-based targeting, forcing adjustments to implementation plans.
Returns of displaced populations to areas of origin created challenges in balancing assistance without incentivizing premature returns.
Limited access to mental health services in local communities increased reliance on IOM’s interventions, which were originally designed for shorter-term displacement contexts.
partner_relationship_issues: No major partner relationship issues reported. Collaboration was effective during emergencies, though FCDO had to explicitly earmark funds to prevent conflicts between disaster response and ongoing programmes.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Partners had sufficient capacity to scale up during emergencies, but the IRF’s depletion constrained future flexibility.
Limited local capacity for disaster-risk reduction and climate mainstreaming outside of emergency response.
risk_materialization: Cyclone Freddy and cholera outbreak materialized as high-impact risks, requiring unplanned allocations.
Security risks in northern Mozambique persisted, affecting access and durable solutions for returns.
Fraud and safeguarding risks were mitigated through third-party monitoring recommendations, but not fully materialized.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was efficient, with all partners meeting targets. The programme absorbed an additional £1.3m for emergencies without disrupting core activities. However, the IRF was depleted faster than planned due to multiple crises.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High value for money achieved through: (1) Vulnerability-based targeting by WFP, ensuring assistance reached the most needy; (2) Rapid scale-up during Cyclone Freddy and cholera with minimal overhead; (3) Multiplier effects from strengthening humanitarian coordination (e.g., anticipatory action guidelines for the Government of Mozambique). Cost per beneficiary was optimized by exceeding targets (e.g., 202,000 reached vs. 150,000 planned).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial management by partners, with no reported fraud or major irregularities. The ability to allocate £1.3m within 10 days demonstrates robust systems. However, third-party monitoring was recommended to further reduce risks.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was high due to: (1) Exceeding beneficiary targets (e.g., 202,000 reached vs. 150,000); (2) Leveraging existing partner systems (e.g., WFP’s VBT, IOM’s mental health platforms); (3) Minimal overhead for emergency allocations. The focus on the "enabling environment" (e.g., anticipatory action guidelines) created long-term efficiencies.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexibility in funding and partner agreements is critical for responding to unplanned disasters, but must be balanced with clear earmarking to avoid diverting resources from ongoing crises.
Vulnerability-based targeting (VBT) improves aid effectiveness and value for money, but requires local authority buy-in to avoid implementation gaps.
Strengthening the enabling environment (e.g., anticipatory action, coordination platforms) has multiplier effects on the overall humanitarian response.
Rapid scale-up is possible with pre-positioned funds (e.g., IRF) and agile procurement, but such facilities can be depleted quickly in high-risk contexts.
successful_delivery_practices: Multi-year partnerships with IOM, WFP, NRC, and INSO enabled rapid scale-up during emergencies.
Integration of PSEA standards across all partners reduced safeguarding risks.
Mobile health clinics and legal services (e.g., NRC’s birth certificate support) improved access for remote populations.
WFP’s anticipatory action guidelines for the Government of Mozambique built national capacity for future disasters.
management_adaptations_made: FCDO introduced clearer earmarking of funds during emergencies to prevent diversion from conflict-related programmes.
Shifted focus from new birth certificate issuance to supporting existing beneficiaries in accessing national IDs (NRC).
Expanded mental health services during Cyclone Freddy, though adjusted for shorter-term displacement contexts (IOM).
innovations_attempted: WFP’s vulnerability-based targeting (VBT) replaced status-based assistance in 7 districts, improving aid equity.
IOM’s mental health interventions included PSEA messaging and gender-sensitive approaches, addressing gaps in local services.
NRC’s Skills Development Workshops on legal literacy empowered community advocates for sustainable rights awareness.
Use of the IRF for rapid emergency allocations (e.g., £1.3m in 10 days) demonstrated innovative financial agility.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Third-party monitoring was recommended in this review to improve safeguarding and targeting, but not yet implemented.
Durable solutions (e.g., returns programming) were identified as a gap and will be prioritized in the coming year.
Climate mainstreaming beyond emergency response (e.g., disaster-risk reduction in resettlement sites) remains underdeveloped.
forward_recommendations: FCDO should replenish the Internal Risk Facility (IRF) to restore flexibility for future disasters.
Conduct third-party monitoring to reduce fraud/safeguarding risks and improve targeting of vulnerable groups.
Engage more on durable solutions, including legal support for housing/land/property rights for returnees, while avoiding pull factors.
Explore localizing responses (e.g., shelter programmes) to reduce reliance on in-kind aid and empower local actors.
Mainstream climate-related priorities, such as disaster-risk reduction in resettlement sites, to address long-term vulnerability.
Balance support for returnees with those in protracted displacement, considering security constraints in northern Mozambique.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was effective in responding to materialized risks (e.g., Cyclone Freddy, cholera) through rapid allocations and adaptive programming. However, the depletion of the IRF highlights the need for better long-term risk financing. PSEA integration and vulnerability targeting mitigated operational risks, but third-party monitoring is needed to further strengthen safeguarding.

policy_influence_achieved: WFP’s vulnerability-based targeting (VBT) was adopted in 7/9 districts, influencing government approaches to aid distribution.
Anticipatory action guidelines developed with the Government of Mozambique will inform future disaster preparedness policies.
NRC’s legal documentation support aligned with national ID systems, improving access to services for displaced populations.
capacity_building_results: 13,200 individuals obtained legal identity post-NRC intervention, enabling access to education, health, and financial services.
IOM’s mental health services filled critical gaps in local systems, with 30,758 people supported (including trauma and violence survivors).
WFP’s multi-hazard action plan and anticipatory action team strengthened national capacity for forecast-based financing.
INSO’s security training improved NGO operational safety in insecure areas, though sustainability depends on continued funding.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Mobile legal clinics (NRC) empowered community advocates, creating sustainable local capacity for rights awareness.
Positive: Mental health interventions (IOM) reached host communities, reducing tensions between displaced and local populations.
Negative: Risk of becoming a pull factor for returns in insecure areas if assistance is not carefully managed.
Negative: Short-term mental health support for flood-displaced populations (vs. conflict-displaced) may have created disparities in service continuity.
scalability_evidence: WFP’s VBT model is scalable to other districts if local authority approval is secured.
IOM’s mental health and PSEA-integrated approaches could be expanded to other humanitarian contexts in Mozambique.
NRC’s legal documentation support is replicable but requires alignment with national ID systems.
The IRF model for rapid emergency response is scalable but depends on consistent replenishment.

continuation_rationale: Programme has demonstrated high impact in reaching 202,000 beneficiaries (exceeding targets) and strengthening humanitarian systems (e.g., VBT, anticipatory action).
Flexibility and rapid response capacity are critical in Mozambique’s high-risk context (conflict, cyclones, epidemics).
Partners have strong delivery records, but the depleted IRF and ongoing needs require continued support.
Opportunities exist to deepen work on durable solutions, climate mainstreaming, and localization.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Replenish the Internal Risk Facility (IRF) to restore emergency response capacity.
Increase focus on durable solutions, including legal support for returnees and housing/land/property rights.
Enhance climate mainstreaming through disaster-risk reduction in resettlement sites (e.g., via IOM).
Pilot localization initiatives to reduce in-kind aid dependency and empower local actors.
Implement third-party monitoring to improve targeting, safeguarding, and value for money.
Engage diplomatically to address local authority restrictions on VBT and other interventions.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Local procurement of materials reduced costs. Bulk purchasing and flexible partner work schedules improved efficiency. WFP’s agreement with Land Bank expected to reduce interbank transfer fees by 40%.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Implementing partners adapted work schedules, leveraged existing resources, and empowered field teams to respond to supply chain constraints. Flexible funding allowed redirection from water trucking to sustainable community water systems.
adaptive_management_examples: Redirection of funds from expensive water trucking to sustainable community water supply restoration in the Philippines.
Targeting adjustments to focus on households with children under 5 due to high stunting rates, despite excluding other vulnerable groups initially planned for support.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in response timelines for some interventions (e.g., Philippines typhoon response).
Targeting trade-offs: Focus on children under 5 excluded other vulnerable groups (e.g., elderly, single-parent households with older children).
Limited baseline data for preparedness component indicators (e.g., speed, proportionality).
contextual_constraints_new: Resource constraints led to prioritization of cash assistance for households with young children, requiring exclusion of other at-risk groups.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £2.833,979 disbursed in Year 1 (2024/25) across three crises (Vietnam, Philippines, Vanuatu). Allocations aligned with planned sectors (WASH, multi-sector, cash/logistics).

Local procurement and bulk purchasing enhance cost efficiency.

successful_delivery_practices: Rapid deployment of cash top-ups via government social protection programs (e.g., Philippines 4Ps).
Coordination with regional bodies (ASEAN AHA Centre, Partners in the Blue Pacific) strengthened preparedness.
Empowering field teams to address supply chain constraints improved responsiveness.
management_adaptations_made: Adjustments to targeting criteria to focus on children under 5 due to stunting risks.
Streamlined cash transfer processes (e.g., single instalment payments to reduce costs).
innovations_attempted: Exploration of anticipatory action frameworks (e.g., Philippines government bill).
Pilot of inclusion principles with Women-Led/Women’s Rights Organizations (WLOs/WROs).
forward_recommendations: Develop and update regional partner assessments to enhance response speed.
Complete Due Diligence Assessments (DDAs) within 3 months of agreements; streamline DDA processes where possible.

capacity_building_results: Enhanced regional partnership capacity (e.g., AHA Centre, DFAT bilateral mechanism).
