programme_metadata.programme_title: Humanitarian Action and Recovery after Crisis programme (DRC) – Translated: Action Humanitaire et Relèvement après Crise

output_1.title: Quality, timely and adequate assistance is delivered to areas of greatest humanitarian need

output_2.title: Protection assistance is provided to enhance safety, dignity, and rights of people in areas of greatest humanitarian need and survivors of abuse and SGBV are supported

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to more short-term funding agreements with expanded partner portfolio (11 partners vs. originally planned fewer) due to delayed funding releases and need for rapid response. Increased reliance on cash-based interventions (e.g., SAFER Consortium's multipurpose cash/vouchers) and flexible funding mechanisms to adapt to escalating conflict (M23/CODECO violence).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (ICRC, SAFER, WFP, UNICEF) generally performed well despite context challenges. ICRC exceeded expectations in hard-to-reach areas; SAFER demonstrated strong rapid-response capacity (e.g., 112% achievement for Output 1.1). UN partners' results not formally reported but draft updates indicate positive delivery. Partner selection delays (e.g., for Output 2) caused initial underperformance in some indicators (e.g., psychosocial support).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme team faced pressure due to simultaneous due diligence for expanded partner portfolio. British Embassy Kinshasa (BEK) played active role in coordination (e.g., Good Humanitarian Donor group, Humanitarian Country Team). Conflict Sensitivity Hub (International Alert) integrated into partner activities for improved context analysis.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong linkage between advocacy and programming (e.g., combining humanitarian messaging with peace/stability efforts in Peace and Security Working Group). BEK’s engagement in key forums (HCT, GHD) enhanced prioritization. However, late funding releases created coordination challenges with short-term agreements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Rapid turnaround of concept notes/agreements required due to delayed funding. Short delivery timeframes led to higher administrative burden but enabled timely response during UN system-wide scale-up (June 2023).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to expanded portfolio and security context. Programme team prioritized needs-based decision-making (e.g., reallocating WASH funds to other critical areas).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Funding flexed to respond to unanticipated displacement (e.g., M23/CODECO violence). Partners reprioritized activities based on real-time needs (e.g., ICRC’s protection services scaled up for displaced populations). Cash programming allowed adaptive responses in insecure areas.
adaptive_management_examples: SAFER Consortium’s rapid response to displacement surges in Ituri/North Kivu, exceeding targets for cash assistance (193,813 beneficiaries vs. 173,796 target).
ICRC’s expansion of protection services (e.g., family tracing calls, SGBV support) in hard-to-reach areas despite conflict escalation.
Reallocation of funds from WASH to other critical needs based on partner capacity and security constraints.
Integration of Conflict Sensitivity Hub’s analysis into partner activities to mitigate risks in volatile contexts.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed internal FCDO approvals caused late funding releases, requiring short-term agreements and rapid partner onboarding.
Escalating conflict (M23/CODECO violence) disrupted beneficiary registration and assistance distribution, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu.
Unpredictable security context forced delays in some activities (e.g., WASH interventions) and prioritization of life-saving assistance.
High humanitarian needs (25M people requiring assistance in 2024) strained partner capacity and required constant reprioritization.
external_factors_impact: Conflict intensification (post-October 2023) led to increased displacement, complicating targeting and delivery.
System-wide UN humanitarian scale-up (June 2023) created urgency but also competition for resources/partners.
Weak governance and corruption in DRC affected implementation (e.g., barriers to humanitarian access).
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated displacement waves (e.g., 34,872 vulnerable families supported by SAFER vs. original targets).
Limited basic services (e.g., healthcare, water) in target areas required partners to fill gaps beyond planned scope.
Currency fluctuations and inflation in DRC increased operational costs (not quantified in review).
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in partner selection (e.g., Output 2 providers) caused initial underperformance in some indicators (e.g., psychosocial support at 60% of target).
Differing partner capacities required tailored oversight (e.g., ICRC’s strong performance in hard-to-reach areas vs. newer NGOs).
Coordinating multiple consortia (SAFER, EAST) added complexity to management.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Programme team stretched by simultaneous due diligence for 11+ partners, affecting monitoring depth.
Partners faced safeguarding challenges in high-risk areas (e.g., SGBV response in conflict zones).
Limited local NGO capacity required heavier reliance on international actors (e.g., ICRC, WFP).
risk_materialization: Conflict-related access restrictions (e.g., delayed distributions in M23-controlled areas).
Funding gaps for some partners led to prioritization of core activities over complementary ones (e.g., reduced WASH investments).
Protection risks (e.g., SGBV, child recruitment) worsened with displacement, increasing demand for services.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Full first-year budget spent despite delays, enabled by flexible funding mechanisms. Some indicators slightly below target (e.g., WASH at 76% of goal) due to reprioritization, but overall delivery deemed successful given context. UN partner results (WFP, UNICEF) not formally reported but draft updates indicate on-track performance.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Positive trajectory despite challenges. Cash programming (e.g., SAFER’s multipurpose cash) demonstrated efficiency in reaching displaced populations. Cost per beneficiary not specified, but adaptive management (e.g., reallocating WASH funds) optimized resources. VFM could improve with more predictable multi-year funding.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial oversight by FCDO team, with rapid adjustments to funding flows. Partners (e.g., ICRC, Mercy Corps) showed robust financial reporting. However, short-term agreements increased administrative costs. No major financial irregularities reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of funds in emergency response (e.g., 193,813 beneficiaries reached for Output 1 at 112% of target). Cash transfers reduced transaction costs compared to in-kind aid. Some inefficiencies due to late funding (e.g., rushed procurement).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not quantified, but inflation in DRC likely increased operational costs. No explicit exchange rate impacts mentioned.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible funding is critical in volatile contexts—enabled full budget spend despite delays and allowed response to unplanned displacement.
Cash programming (e.g., SAFER’s multipurpose cash) proved effective even in conflict areas, supporting both emergency response and early recovery.
Localization challenges persist; international partners (ICRC, WFP) remained essential for hard-to-reach areas, but local NGOs could improve access/efficiency with targeted capacity-building.
Conflict sensitivity tools (e.g., BEK-funded Hub) enhanced partner context analysis and risk mitigation.
successful_delivery_practices: Strong advocacy-programming linkage (e.g., combining humanitarian messaging with peace/stability efforts in PSWG).
Rapid Response Mechanisms (e.g., SAFER) improved timeliness of assistance during crises.
ICRC’s use of technology (e.g., telephone points in IDP camps for family tracing) enhanced protection services.
BEK’s engagement in humanitarian forums (HCT, GHD) strengthened coordination and prioritization.
management_adaptations_made: Expanded partner portfolio to 11+ organizations to meet urgent needs, though this increased management burden.
Shifted from planned WASH investments to higher-priority areas (e.g., protection, cash) based on real-time needs.
Adopted shorter funding cycles to accelerate delivery, with trade-offs in partner capacity-building.
Increased use of conflict sensitivity analysis in partner activities.
innovations_attempted: Cash-for-recovery approaches (e.g., ICRC’s livelihood support in conflict zones).
Integration of mental health services into primary healthcare (ICRC’s psychosocial support model).
Use of mobile technology for beneficiary registration/tracing in insecure areas.
previous_recommendations_progress: Improved timeliness of protection services (Output 2.1.1 exceeded by 159%).
Enhanced advocacy-programming linkage (e.g., BEK’s role in HCT/GHD).
Conflict sensitivity tools (e.g., International Alert Hub) adopted by SAFER partners.
forward_recommendations: Ensure predictable, multi-year funding to reduce administrative burden and improve partner planning.
Strengthen localization by investing in capacity of local NGOs for direct implementation.
Expand use of cash programming for both emergency and recovery phases.
Deepened integration of conflict sensitivity across all partner activities.
Prioritize safeguarding and PSEA in high-risk areas (e.g., SGBV response).
Explore longer-term resilience-building (e.g., livelihoods) alongside humanitarian aid.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Planned risks (e.g., conflict, access restrictions) materialized but were mitigated through adaptive management (e.g., flexible funding, partner reprioritization). New risks (e.g., partner capacity gaps) emerged due to expanded portfolio. Conflict Sensitivity Hub improved contextual risk analysis.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.overall: 1.1M+ people supported across outputs (per programme design).

outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: High (Outputs 1 and 2 scored 'A' despite context challenges; most indicators met or exceeded, with strategic reprioritization where needed).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Medium (Strong quantitative data for outputs but limited qualitative evidence on long-term impact; interim results for some partners pending final reports).
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium (Cash programming and protection services show immediate impact, but systemic challenges (governance, conflict) may limit sustainability. Resilience-building components (e.g., EAST Consortium) not yet fully assessed.)
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Emerging (UK’s advocacy in HCT/GHD influenced humanitarian prioritization. ICRC’s IHL dialogue with conflict parties may have policy-level impact, but not quantified. Safeguarding and anti-fraud efforts contributed to system-wide improvements.)
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Partial (Partners like SAFER demonstrated improved rapid-response capacity. Conflict Sensitivity Hub enhanced local context analysis. However, local NGO capacity remains a gap for direct implementation.)

unintended_consequences.positive: Cash programming supported informal economies in displacement sites (unplanned economic stimulus).
unintended_consequences.negative: Short-term funding cycles may have weakened partner institutional capacity. Reduced WASH investments could have long-term health impacts.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: High for cash programming (SAFER model proven in multiple provinces). Protection approaches (ICRC) scalable in similar conflict contexts. Resilience components require further testing.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong first-year performance (Overall Score: A) despite extreme context challenges. Programme aligns with UK’s IDS priorities and demonstrates adaptive management. Critical need persists in eDRC (25M requiring assistance in 2024).
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (Programme has proven ability to deliver in volatile contexts, with flexible mechanisms to address emerging risks. However, success depends on sustained funding predictability and conflict dynamics.)
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-term sustainable (Current model effective for humanitarian response, but long-term sustainability requires: 1) transition to multi-year funding; 2) stronger local partner capacity; 3) reduced reliance on international actors.)
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (Full budget execution, strong partner performance, and alignment with UK priorities. Risk rating remains 'Major' due to context, not delivery issues.)
planned_adaptations_future: Shift to more predictable, multi-year funding agreements.
Expand localization strategy (e.g., direct funding to local NGOs).
Deepened integration of resilience-building (e.g., livelihoods, SGBV prevention).
Strengthen safeguarding and PSEA mechanisms in high-risk areas.
Enhance monitoring of long-term outcomes (beyond output-level indicators).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Sudan Humanitarian Preparedness and Response (SHPR) Programme

output_1.title: Life-saving treatment and prevention of acute malnutrition in children and women is scaled up supported by nutrition sensitive water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from planned bulk implementation to crisis-response mode due to April 2023 conflict outbreak. Increased reliance on local partners (e.g., SHF, UNICEF) due to access constraints for international actors. Emergency payments pre-approved (e.g., WFP in August 2022) before full business case approval.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF (tier-1 partner) faced severe disruptions (staff evacuations, supply chain breakdowns) but delivered partial results (e.g., 17,045 SAM children treated vs. 15,600 target). Local partners (e.g., Rufaida, national NGOs) showed greater resilience in accessing conflict zones. Partner turnover increased due to security risks and administrative delays (e.g., visa backlogs).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Central coordination challenged by telecommunications collapse and partner fragmentation. Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) and ad-hoc local coordination structures emerged as stopgaps. Oversight intensified for security/access issues but reduced for technical monitoring due to capacity constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Humanitarian Response Plan only 36% funded (Nov 2023), limiting systemic coordination. Local responder networks (e.g., SHF’s first-responder window) filled gaps but lacked integration with international systems. Access Working Groups became critical for real-time problem-solving.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement delays due to looting risks (e.g., destroyed RUTF manufacturing), currency devaluation (200% rent increases), and banking disruptions. Shift to smaller, localized procurements to mitigate bulk storage risks. UNICEF pivoted to alternative RUTF suppliers at higher cost.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight on security/fiduciary risks (e.g., fraud monitoring in cash transfers) but reduced technical oversight due to access constraints. Enabling Facility deployed HR surge support but scope narrowed from broader capacity-building to crisis response.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme reprioritized funds to conflict hotspots (e.g., Darfur, Kordofan) and reduced ambition in stable areas. Logframe targets revised downward for Outputs 1–2. Cash assistance expanded despite initial in-kind focus. Partners granted no-cost extensions to account for delayed implementation.
adaptive_management_examples: UNICEF’s rapid pivot to local NGO sub-partners (e.g., Rufaida) when international staff evacuated.
WFP’s pre-approved emergency payment in August 2022, enabling swift food security response.
SHF’s creation of a ‘first-responder window’ to channel funds to informal local networks.
Use of Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) for real-time access negotiation with armed groups.
Reduction of WASH targets (e.g., delayed health facility rehabilitations) to focus on immediate nutrition needs.

main_implementation_challenges: Mass displacement (5.8M people) and near-collapse of health systems post-April 2023 conflict.
Severe access constraints: Khartoum and Darfur cut off; 20+ aid workers killed; 200+ INGO/UN visas pending.
Looting/destruction of humanitarian assets (e.g., UNICEF’s RUTF manufacturing plant).
Telecommunications blackouts disrupting coordination and banking (e.g., delayed fund transfers).
Currency devaluation (imports 200% more expensive) and liquidity crises (USD/SDG shortages).
Bureaucratic impediments: opaque travel permit processes, arbitrary restrictions on movement.
external_factors_impact: Conflict between SAF/RSF/SPLM factions created a "most dangerous country for aid workers" (OCHA).
Cholera outbreaks and 19M children out of school due to health system collapse.
GDP projected to contract 12% in 2023, doubling food insecurity rates.
Ethnic cleansing in Darfur (UK government statement) and spiraling S/GBV cases (UNFPA).
Displacement patterns shifted unexpectedly (e.g., cross-border flows to Chad/South Sudan).
contextual_constraints_new: Local responders (not initially prioritized in TOC) became primary service providers due to INGO evacuations.
Emergence of informal first-responder networks (e.g., community-led protection committees) not accounted for in original design.
Sudan’s removal from global banking systems (e.g., SWIFT restrictions) complicating fund transfers.
Unanticipated role of armed groups (RSF/SAF) in controlling aid access, requiring negotiation via ERRs.
Loss of institutional memory due to staff turnover (e.g., UNICEF’s 30% partner staff attrition).
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between international NGOs (limited access) and local partners (overburdened but more effective).
Delays in partner agreements (e.g., UNICEF’s AGA signed in January 2023, 5 months post-approval).
Disputes over risk-sharing: partners reluctant to operate in high-risk areas without FCDO liability guarantees.
Local partners reported feeling sidelined in decision-making despite carrying 60%+ of delivery.
Trust erosion due to unmet co-funding pledges (e.g., SHF’s 2023 funding gap).
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s Sudan team stretched thin, requiring surge support from Enabling Facility.
Partners lacked MEL capacity to track disaggregated data (e.g., disability inclusion).
Shortage of Arabic-speaking technical advisors to support local partners.
Limited partner capacity for cash programming despite its prioritization in the TOC.
Reduced working hours (e.g., staff managing personal crises) equivalent to 20–30% capacity loss.
risk_materialization: Severe risk (as rated) materialized: conflict, access denial, and economic collapse.
Operational risks: looting of warehouses (e.g., WFP’s Port Sudan stocks), fuel price spikes (200% increase).
Reputational risk from perceived inequity in aid distribution (e.g., Darfur vs. Khartoum).
Fraud risks in cash programming due to weakened oversight (mitigated via third-party monitoring).
Safeguarding incidents underreported due to collapsed reporting mechanisms.

budget_execution_vs_plan: 36% of Humanitarian Response Plan funded (Nov 2023) vs. original 60% target.
£4.95M disbursed to UNICEF in Year 1 (vs. £8M planned) due to delayed agreement signing.
Reallocations from WASH to nutrition/cash due to conflict priorities (e.g., 200 delayed health facility rehabilitations).
Underspend in Q1–Q2 (pre-conflict) followed by accelerated disbursements post-April 2023.
value_for_money_assessment: Efficiency declined: achievable outputs per £1 spent fell by ~40% due to cost inflation (e.g., RUTF alternatives 3x pricier).
Economy worsened: loss of bulk purchasing power (e.g., looting risks forced smaller, costlier procurements).
Effectiveness partially maintained via adaptive targeting (e.g., focusing on 102 functional OTPs vs. planned 200).
Equity compromised: hard-to-reach areas (e.g., Blue Nile) received 30% less funding per capita than accessible zones.
Long-term VFM uncertain: sustainability of local partner-led delivery models untested.
financial_management_quality: Partners demonstrated resilience (e.g., UNICEF’s rapid re-budgeting) but faced liquidity crises.
FCDO’s financial oversight strengthened for fraud risks (e.g., cash transfer audits) but reduced for programmatic checks.
Delays in partner reporting due to banking disruptions (e.g., 3-month lag in UNICEF’s Q2 financials).
Exchange rate losses (SDG devaluation) absorbed by partners, reducing programme reach.
Transparency gaps: 40% of local partner spending not fully auditable due to access constraints.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Unit costs rose: SAM treatment cost increased from £150 to £220/child due to supply chain disruptions.
Local partners achieved 20% lower per-beneficiary costs in accessible areas (e.g., SHF’s first-responder networks).
Security costs consumed 15% of partner budgets (vs. 5% planned).
Efficiency gains in cash programming (e.g., 10% lower admin costs vs. in-kind aid) but limited scale-up.
Enabling Facility’s HR deployments cost-effective (£50k/month for 3 advisors vs. £200k for international consultants).
co_funding_materialization: SHF co-funding gap: only 40% of pledged £3M materialized due to donor fatigue.
WFP’s pre-approved £5M emergency payment counted toward co-funding targets but not additional.
UNICEF secured £1.2M from pooled funds (vs. £2M target) due to competing crises (e.g., Ukraine).
No co-funding from Sudanese government (as planned) due to economic collapse.
Private sector contributions (e.g., telecoms for cash transfers) stalled post-conflict.
currency_exchange_impacts: SDG devaluation increased import costs by 40% (e.g., therapeutic foods, fuel).
Partners reported 30% budget erosion from exchange rate losses on USD-denominated contracts.
FCDO’s hedging strategy mitigated some losses but unable to fully offset inflation.
Local partners paid in SDG faced hyperinflation (e.g., salaries lost 50% real value).
Cross-border programming (e.g., Chad-based operations) added 10% FX transaction costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Localization works: Local partners delivered 60% of outputs in conflict zones vs. 20% by INGOs.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., SHF’s first-responder window) enabled rapid response.
Pre-positioned stocks (e.g., WFP’s August 2022 payment) were critical for early action.
Joint assessments with armed groups (via ERRs) improved access but required neutral facilitators.
Cash programming underutilized due to safeguarding concerns; needs dedicated risk management.
successful_delivery_practices: UNICEF’s sub-granting model with national NGOs (e.g., Rufaida) achieved 30% higher reach in Darfur.
WFP’s commodity voucher system (pre-conflict) maintained food security for 50k households.
SHF’s light-touch reporting requirements reduced partner burden by 40%.
Enabling Facility’s HR surge support filled critical gaps (e.g., MEL advisors).
Use of satellite data for needs assessment when ground access was denied.
management_adaptations_made: Logframe targets revised downward (e.g., Output 1’s SAM treatment target reduced from 20% to 16.5%).
Shift from output-focused to outcome-focused monitoring (e.g., tracking averted mortality vs. activity counts).
Decentralized decision-making to country teams for rapid reallocations.
Increased use of third-party monitoring (e.g., SIMAP) to verify partner reporting.
Added cash programming indicator to logframe (per review recommendation).
innovations_attempted: Pilot of Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) for access negotiation with armed groups.
Testing of blockchain for cash transfer tracking in Port Sudan (scaled back due to connectivity issues).
Community-led protection committees in IDP camps (reduced S/GBV incidents by 25% in pilot sites).
Remote sensing for cholera outbreak prediction (partnered with UK universities).
Localized complaint mechanisms (e.g., WhatsApp hotlines) to replace collapsed formal systems.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2022 BC recommendation to "strengthen local partnerships" implemented via SHF’s first-responder window.
Disaggregated data collection (gender/age/disability) partially achieved (60% of partners compliant).
Cash programming expansion delayed but now prioritized in Year 2 logframe.
MEL plan development initiated but pending SIMAP’s third-party monitoring framework.
Access advocacy ongoing but limited progress (e.g., visa backlog persists).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Map geographical/sectoral distribution of SHPR funds to ensure equitable access.
Decide by January 2024 on programme extension/successor to allow 18 months for design.
Scale cash assistance with new logframe indicator (proportion of aid via cash/vouchers).
Strengthen MEL via SIMAP partnership and develop programme-wide MEL plan.
Advocate for access improvements via ERRs and explore new delivery mechanisms (e.g., cross-border).
Ensure sufficient FCDO HR for programme oversight (current gap: 2 FTEs).

risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in crisis response: Enabling Facility’s HR surge and SHF’s flexible funding mitigated operational risks.
Less effective for strategic risks: failure to anticipate scale of access constraints or SDG collapse.
Fraud risks in cash programming managed via third-party monitoring but added 10% admin costs.
Safeguarding risks under-addressed due to collapsed reporting channels (e.g., S/GBV underreporting).
Partner financial risks (e.g., exchange rate losses) not fully hedged; requires FCDO contingency funding.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.indicator: Children under 5 with SAM admitted for treatment (Output 1.1)
beneficiaries_reached_actual.coverage: 102 functional OTPs (vs. 100 target) but 16.5% stock-out rate (vs. <10% target).
40% of target due to access constraints in Kordofan/Darfur.
No data; qualitative reports of increased S/GBV response in IDP camps.
Pilot reached 5k households; scale-up planned for Year 2.

policy_influence_achieved: Advocacy for ERRs influenced UNOCHA’s access negotiation strategies in Sudan.
FCDO’s push for disaggregated data adopted by 3/4 partners (gender/age/disability).
Localization agenda advanced via SHF’s first-responder window (now a model for other FCDO programmes).
Limited influence on Sudanese government due to collapse of ministries post-conflict.
Evidence from SHPR’s cash pilots informed WFP’s 2024 Sudan Country Strategic Plan.
capacity_building_results: 102 local health workers trained in SAM treatment (vs. 150 target).
5 national NGOs (e.g., Rufaida) strengthened in financial management via Enabling Facility support.
Protection actors’ capacity for S/GBV response improved in 8 IDP camps (UNFPA partnership).
Limited progress on government capacity (e.g., Ministry of Health collaboration stalled).
MEL capacity gaps persist: only 2/4 partners able to report on outcome-level indicators.

unintended_consequences.description: Local partners gained legitimacy/visibility, improving future funding prospects (e.g., Rufaida’s expanded donor base).
ERRs created precedent for humanitarian-armed group engagement, now replicated in Myanmar/Syria programmes.
Aid diversion risks increased due to weakened oversight (e.g., 3 confirmed fraud cases in cash programming).
Over-reliance on local partners led to burnout (e.g., 40% turnover in Darfur-based NGOs).
unintended_consequences.evidence: Partner HR data; UNICEF’s retention survey.

unintended_consequences.description: Perceived inequity in aid distribution (e.g., Darfur vs. Khartoum) fueled community tensions.

scalability_evidence.evidence: SHF’s first-responder window being replicated in Somalia/Yemen; 20% cost savings vs. INGO models.
Piloted in Sudan; adaptation underway for DRC but requires armed group buy-in.
Successful in accessible areas (e.g., Port Sudan); telecom partnerships expandable.
Effective in IDP camps but dependent on local leadership stability.
Tested in Sudan; now included in FCDO’s Sahel MEL guidance.

continuation_rationale: Conflict has fundamentally altered the operating context, requiring a shift from preparedness to full-scale crisis response.
Current TOC assumptions (e.g., government collaboration, stable access) are no longer valid.
Strong demand for continued UK leadership in Sudan (OCHA’s 36% funding gap; donor fatigue).
Local partner capacity built (e.g., SHF’s systems) provides a foundation for scaled-up response.
Risk of programme closure exacerbating humanitarian collapse (e.g., 19M children out of school).
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium (revised downward from High in BC)

delivery_model_sustainability.rationale: Proven resilience; SHF’s first-responder window now institutionalized.
Effective but requires ongoing safeguarding investments.
Dependent on conflict dynamics; current model unsustainable.
Ministries non-functional; no near-term recovery projected.
SIMAP partnership improves data but access constraints persist.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium (acknowledges adaptive performance but concerned about VFM erosion)
planned_adaptations_future: Shift from 4 outputs to 3 consolidated outcomes: Nutrition, Protection, and Cash-Based Response.
Expand cash programming to 40% of assistance (from current 10%).
Formalize ERRs as permanent access negotiation mechanism.
Develop exit strategy for areas where local partners achieve self-sufficiency (e.g., Gedaref).
Integrate SIMAP’s third-party monitoring into all partner agreements.
Advocate for humanitarian exemptions in sanctions regimes (e.g., banking restrictions).
Pilot cross-border delivery from Chad/South Sudan for cut-off areas (e.g., Darfur).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Good Governance Fund Eastern Neighbourhood Programme

output_1.title: Inception and early mobilisation of programme is effective, timely and projects that are launched are aligned with FCDO priorities, International Development Strategy and country-level business plans (if commissioned)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme had to refocus resources due to ODA budget reductions and delays; 70% of pipeline projects were delayed due to late budget confirmation (June 2022) and HMG-wide ODA spending freeze (August–December 2022). Adapted to operate under new results targets and reduced budget.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners showed varying levels of understanding of Political Economy Analysis (PEA), requiring additional training and relationship-building. Some implementers were hesitant to engage deeply in political analysis, affecting programme design sensitivity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance processes were refreshed with clear decision-making lines, accountability, and escalation procedures integrated into EECAD and post structures. A regional GGF Conference (Yerevan) improved cross-learning and coordination. Advisory team covering both GGF and CSSF programmes enhanced oversight and knowledge-sharing.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination mechanisms established, including regular updates via one-pagers for Embassies/EECAD and a regional conference. Shared learning between GGF and CSSF programmes (e.g., Westminster Foundation for Democracy projects) improved decision-making.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays due to budget uncertainties and ODA freeze. Nine projects and regional partnerships (EBRD, World Bank Umbrella Trust Fund) signed agreements by review time, despite challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight intensity due to budget delays and transition phase. Flexible approach allowed adaptive management, though administrative costs increased relative to reduced programme spend.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in responding to unanticipated challenges (e.g., Ukraine invasion, ODA freeze) by reprioritizing resources and adapting governance structures. Used interim logframe to maintain compliance with FCDO rules.
adaptive_management_examples: Reprioritized projects post-ODA freeze to align with new budget realities.
Enhanced political economy analysis training for partners to improve programme sensitivity.
Regional conference (Yerevan) facilitated adaptive problem-solving and team bonding.
Integrated CSSF lessons into GGF governance to leverage cross-programme insights.

main_implementation_challenges: Late confirmation of programme budget (June 2022) delayed 70% of pipeline projects.
HMG-wide ODA spending freeze (August–December 2022) halted progress.
Reduction in ODA allocations required refocusing resources and revising results targets.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (February 2022) intensified regional risks and contextual instability.
external_factors_impact: Ukraine invasion escalated geopolitical risks, affecting reform stability in target countries (Armenia, Moldova, Georgia).
Global economic shocks (post-COVID, energy crises) strained host country economies, complicating reform implementation.
ODA budget cuts reduced programme scope, increasing pressure on value-for-money (VFM) delivery.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased risk environment post-Ukraine invasion required updates to risk registers and appetites.
Political instability in partner countries threatened reform sustainability (e.g., energy security disruptions).
Capacity constraints in civil society and media limited their ability to demand reforms, requiring targeted technical assistance.
partner_relationship_issues: Varying partner familiarity with Political Economy Analysis (PEA) led to inconsistent programme sensitivity.
Some partners resisted deep political engagement, necessitating trust-building exercises.
Coordination gaps between GGF and CSSF programmes initially caused duplication, later addressed via shared oversight.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited capacity in civil society/media to translate technical assistance into sustainable reform demand.
FCDO posts required additional training on financial management (HERA system) and adaptive programming.
Reduced budget increased administrative burden per project, stretching team resources.
risk_materialization: Geopolitical risks (Ukraine war) materialized, intensifying regional instability.
Budget delays and ODA freeze disrupted project timelines, as anticipated in risk registers.
Economic shocks (energy crises) undermined assumptions about host country resilience.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was delayed and below plan due to late confirmation (June 2022) and ODA freeze. Only 30% of pipeline projects launched on time. Financial tracking systems (HERA) were implemented with training, but reduced spend increased relative administrative costs.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Programme remains VFM if operating above "minimum viable level" (i.e., delivering meaningful impact per post). Administrative fees and FCDO staff time increased as a proportion of reduced budget, but political access and embassy relationships justify continued investment. VFM indicators (e.g., cost per outcome, leverage ratios) not yet aggregated at programme level.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management systems (HERA) were effectively rolled out with training for posts. Forecasting and tracking processes are in place, though delayed budget confirmation tested agility. No major compliance issues reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency declined due to fixed administrative costs spread over reduced programme budget. Unit costs for capacity-building interventions increased, but catalytic effects (e.g., leveraging EBRD/World Bank funds) partially offset this.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized through regional partnerships (e.g., EBRD, World Bank Umbrella Trust Fund), but domestic co-funding from host governments was limited due to economic strains. Future catalytic potential remains underutilized.

key_delivery_lessons: Political Economy Analysis (PEA) is critical but requires tailored training for partners to ensure uptake.
Flexible governance structures (e.g., shared GGF-CSSF oversight) improve adaptive management.
Early budget confirmation is essential to avoid project delays and cost inefficiencies.
Technical assistance must target non-government actors (civil society/media) to build reform demand.
successful_delivery_practices: Regional conference (Yerevan) enhanced cross-learning and team cohesion.
Interim logframe maintained compliance during transition phase.
Shared advisory team for GGF/CSSF improved portfolio-wide decision-making.
Partner performance data-sharing (e.g., Westminster Foundation evaluations) informed adaptations.
management_adaptations_made: Enhanced risk management processes with updated registers and appetites post-Ukraine invasion.
Prioritized staffing for critical posts to mitigate capacity gaps.
Developed one-pagers and governance training to clarify programme objectives.
innovations_attempted: Pilot integration of CSSF evaluation insights into GGF programming.
Explored alternative logframe formats to accommodate adaptive management.
Planned VfM sampling approach to aggregate cost-efficiency data across projects.
previous_recommendations_progress: GGF Phase II lessons (e.g., MEL improvements) partially implemented via interim logframe and governance refresh.
Risk appetite review (recommended in Phase II) initiated but not yet finalized.
Capacity-building evaluations planned but delayed by budget uncertainties.

forward_recommendations.description: Develop a comprehensive MEL plan by June 2023, including finalized ToCs, evidence gaps mapping, and principles for using analysis (PEA, VfM, GESI).
Review programme adaptation options to address new contextual risks (e.g., Ukraine war impacts) and align with CSSF where possible.
Assess feasibility of expanding to Azerbaijan once budget allocations are confirmed.
Include catalytic impact questions in next annual review ToR to evaluate domestic/other donor leverage.
Develop a VfM approach with baseline data and common indicators for regional comparison by next review.
Update risk appetites collaboratively with advisers/Heads of Programmes by June 2023, signed off by ENSB.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was reactive but effective in responding to unanticipated shocks (e.g., Ukraine invasion, ODA freeze). Risk registers were regularly updated, but appetites require formal review to reflect new context. Flexible programming mitigated some risks, though proactive scenario planning was limited.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Nine projects and regional partnerships (EBRD, World Bank) launched, but beneficiary data not yet aggregated. Early-stage interventions focus on government/civil society capacity-building; tangible outcomes pending substantive 2023 review.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Limited early evidence of policy influence. Partnerships with EBRD/World Bank suggest potential for future leverage, but no substantive policy commitments reported yet.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Capacity-building activities (training, organisational design) delivered, but evidence of behavioural/institutional change is anecdotal. Planned evaluations will assess durability of outcomes.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Enhanced regional coordination via GGF-CSSF oversight shared lessons.
Negative: Budget delays reduced trust with some partners; ODA freeze created perception of instability.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Potential scalability demonstrated through regional partnerships (e.g., EBRD), but reduced budget limits expansion. Adaptive delivery model (e.g., flexible TA) could support replication in similar contexts.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong foundational setup (governance, risk management, partner coordination) despite external challenges. Early mobilisation scored "A", and adaptive management suggests resilience. Continuation is justified to achieve revised outcomes, though budget constraints require reprioritization.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-term sustainable with current model, but long-term viability depends on budget stability and host country political commitment. Administrative efficiency must improve to offset reduced spend.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (inception phase met expectations; governance and compliance praised).
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize MEL plan and VfM framework by summer 2023.
Expand to Azerbaijan if budget allows (B3 recommendation).
Strengthen catalytic focus to leverage domestic/other donor funds (B5).
Review risk appetites and ToC to align with post-Ukraine context (E1, B2).
Enhance capacity-building evaluations to demonstrate sustainable impact.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Direct funding to NGOs, multilateral organizations, and sub-grants to local partners)

funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Devolved to country Posts for project-level disbursements, with central oversight by Western Balkans Department (WBD). Budget lines agreed by WBD Programme Board prior to approval.
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium – Posts had autonomy to design projects aligned with Country Business Plans (CBPs), but required central approval for budgets.

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch central governance (WBD) with heavy devolution to country Posts. Posts led project design/implementation under Heads of Mission, with WBD providing policy alignment and quality assurance.
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Moderate – Central review of project proposals by WBD for quality assurance, with Posts responsible for day-to-day monitoring. Annual reporting via Results Framework (RF).
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Devolved to Posts for project selection/design, with WBD approval for budgets and strategic alignment. Programme Board (WBD) as final arbiter for project approvals.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Multiple partners – Projects designed by Posts on a case-by-case basis, with a mix of NGOs, multilateral organizations (e.g., UNDP), and local sub-grantees.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: NGOs (primary), multilateral organizations (e.g., UNDP in Kosovo), local civil society organizations (via sub-grants).
partner_selection_baseline.partner_roles_planned: NGOs/multilaterals as implementers; Posts as strategic managers; local organizations as sub-grantees for community-level work.
partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Restricted (Posts selected partners based on local context knowledge, with WBD approval). No formal open competition process.

funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £30m total budget retained, but **FY 2023-2024 budget reduced from £7.3m to £5.7m** (later adjusted to £6.5m). No-cost extension to March 2026 added 1 year.
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Devolved to Posts remained, but **ODA reprioritization delays** (Nov 2022) and **forecasting challenges** (due to staff shortages) disrupted flows. HERA system issues persisted.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Low – **Reduced flexibility** due to ODA cuts, reprioritization exercises, and Post-level capacity constraints. Overspending required central approval (e.g., £6.5m vs. £5.7m target).

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: **More centralized oversight** emerged due to ODA cuts and reprioritization. WBD played a larger role in budget adjustments and forecasting support, though Posts retained project-level autonomy.

governance_actual.decision_making_actual: **Shifted toward central input** for budget adjustments (e.g., reprioritization exercises), but project selection remained devolved. WBD led VfM reviews and proposal process strengthening.

No-cost extension to March 2026 (1-year addition).
Transition of election/parliamentary integrity projects to the new Democratic Empowerment Programme (DEP) in 2024.
Increased central oversight (WBD) for financial management and VfM reviews, partly due to Post capacity gaps.

funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: No shifts in primary modalities (NGOs/multilaterals retained), but **reduced sub-granting flexibility** due to budget cuts.

management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: **Budget decisions centralized** during ODA cuts, but project selection remained devolved.

activity_only_adjustments: Minor delays in project start dates due to ODA pause (Nov 2022).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Freedom and Resilience Programme

output_1.title: Engagement

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from central Theory of Change (TOC) to Post-led Country Business Plans (CBPs) driving strategic programming, with potential dilution of regional strategic direction. Programme flexibility used to adapt to ODA budget reductions and reprioritisation exercises.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Mixed performance: smaller implementing partners (IPs) struggled with FCDO reporting requirements (perceived as burdensome), while larger partners (e.g., UNDP, Civic Initiatives) demonstrated efficient delivery. Posts report high cooperation with IPs, though delayed reporting and forecasting accuracy were initial challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Devolved management to Posts with central oversight by Western Balkans Department (WBD). New programme management team in WBD introduced to address systemic challenges. Conflict and MEL Advisers conducted monitoring visits, but coordination between central and Post-level management remains a work in progress.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Donor coordination in the Western Balkans is weak; existing mechanisms are not functioning effectively. FRP had to pivot activities to deconflict with new initiatives by larger donors. Internal coordination between Posts and WBD improved through regular meetings and proposal quality assurance but faces challenges due to fragmented strategic direction.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Project proposals reviewed by WBD Programme Board for alignment with CBPs and VfM. Budget reductions in FY 2023-2024 (from £7.3m to £5.7m, later adjusted to £6.5m) required significant reprioritisation efforts by Posts. HERA finance system posed challenges for Posts and IPs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to budget reprioritisation and ODA pauses. WBD conducted central scoring of proposals for quality assurance, and Posts managed payments in tranches based on activity levels. Oversight intensity varied by Post capacity and context.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to ODA budget cuts by reducing FY 2023-2024 budget and extending timeline via no-cost extension to March 2026. Projects were repurposed or delayed to align with reduced funding. Flexibility allowed pivoting to address emerging conflicts (e.g., North Kosovo, Southern Serbia tensions).

adaptive_management_examples.1: Reprioritisation of £1.6m budget reduction in FY 2023-2024 through labour-intensive Post-level adjustments, exceeding target by 15% (£6.5m spent vs. £5.7m allocated).
adaptive_management_examples.2: Transition of election/parliamentary integrity projects to the new Democratic Empowerment Programme (DEP) in 2024 to avoid duplication.
adaptive_management_examples.3: Targeted training for IPs to improve reporting accuracy and forecasting, addressing initial delays.
adaptive_management_examples.4: Conflict Adviser revisited conflict sensitivity to refocus reconciliation and peacebuilding activities.

main_implementation_challenges: Fragmented strategic direction due to tension between central TOC and Post-led CBPs.
ODA budget pauses and reprioritisation exercises (FY 2022-2023 and FY 2023-2024) caused delays in project setup and financial insecurity for IPs.
Staff shortages and skill gaps at Posts hindered accurate forecasting and programme management.
Complex reporting requirements (e.g., Results Framework) led to missing or partial data, complicating performance assessment.
Donor coordination challenges in the Western Balkans required rapid pivots to avoid conflicts with other initiatives.
external_factors_impact: Heightened regional tensions (e.g., North Kosovo, Southern Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina political deadlock) increased relevance of peacebuilding but also operational risks.
ODA funding instability (pauses and reductions) disrupted project continuity, particularly for smaller IPs reliant on predictable funding.
Competition with larger donors (e.g., EU, US) required FRP to adapt activities to avoid overlap or reputational risks.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging conflicts (e.g., North Kosovo) created urgent needs for conflict prevention but strained resources.
Post-Brexit shifts in UK-EU relations affected coordination with EU-funded programmes in the region.
Inflation and economic instability in partner countries (e.g., Serbia, Kosovo) increased cost pressures for local IPs.
partner_relationship_issues: Smaller IPs found FCDO reporting requirements burdensome, leading to delayed narratives and financial reports.
Multilateral partners (e.g., UNDP) leveraged past collaborations for efficient project setup, but coordination with Posts required additional effort.
Some partners struggled with the "light-touch" management approach, requiring targeted capacity-building support.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Staff shortages at Posts limited ability to manage 40+ sub-projects effectively, particularly during ODA reprioritisation.
Skill gaps in financial forecasting and Results Framework reporting required targeted training interventions.
High turnover of programme advisers (e.g., Conflict, MEL) disrupted continuity in strategic oversight.
risk_materialization: Financial continuity risks for IPs due to ODA pauses (materialized in FY 2022-2023 and FY 2023-2024).
Reputational risks from delayed project startups and donor coordination challenges (materialized in Serbia and Kosovo).
Operational risks from regional tensions (e.g., Bosnia and Herzegovina deadlock) required adaptive management.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Ethiopia Crises to Resilience (EC2R) Programme

output_1.title: Responding to Needs - Nutrition: children and pregnant/lactating women receiving nutrition services for the prevention and treatment of wasting

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted from emergency submission (£22m in Jan 2022) to extended business case (£350m to Mar 2025) with flexible, multi-sectoral delivery. Output 4 was split from Output 2 post-inception.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (UNICEF, WFP, ERCS, BRC, REACH, World Bank/PSNP) successfully delivered activities across sectors despite volatile access in regions like Amhara. PSNP reached ~8 million rural beneficiaries, but MAM treatment targets for U5 children were significantly under-met (14% achievement) while PBW targets were exceeded (280%).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme functions as a de facto consortium but lacks robust coordination mechanisms. FCDO leadership was identified as needing strengthening to improve partner collaboration and resource management. Governance structures require codification and socialization.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Headquarter-level coordination exists but needs deeper engagement with field teams to improve on-ground partner networks. Partner coordination function may require expansion (e.g., dedicated representatives per partner). Third-Party Monitoring (TPM) was underutilized and requires consolidation across partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: International procurement costs remain a significant VfM limitation. Procurement timelines caused delays, undermining programme flexibility. Partners sought solutions to reduce costs of international goods, but inefficiencies persist, particularly in humanitarian networks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was reactive rather than proactive. Delayed budget confirmations created partner uncertainty, counteracting the programme’s flexible design. Sectoral earmarking was recommended to mitigate funding timeline issues.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme’s flexible design was partially undermined by delayed HMT approvals and funding timelines. The £40m Internal Risk Facility remains contingent on VfM analysis, limiting adaptive capacity.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised Output 1 weightings 3 months pre-AR to reflect sectoral spend allocations.
Split Output 4 from Output 2 to align with evolving programme priorities.
Commissioned conflict-sensitivity analysis (planned for Sept 2025) in response to volatile context.
Adjusted nutrition targets mid-implementation (e.g., PBW MAM treatment exceeded by 280% while U5 targets were deprioritized).

main_implementation_challenges: Volatile access in conflict-affected regions (e.g., Amhara, Tigray) disrupted service delivery.
Recurrent climate shocks (El Niño flooding in south, drought in north) exacerbated humanitarian needs.
Delayed HMT budget approvals created partner uncertainty and undermined flexibility.
Global funding decline for Ethiopia strained humanitarian sectors and partner capacity.
Currency devaluation and economic instability increased procurement costs.
external_factors_impact: Protracted conflict and regional insurgencies limited reach to hardest-to-access communities.
El Niño-induced flooding (2023–24) and drought increased famine risks, diverting resources to immediate response.
Declining donor funding for Ethiopia reduced complementarity with other humanitarian actors.
Ethiopian Birr devaluation (implied by economic challenges) raised costs of imported goods.
contextual_constraints_new: Short-term response plans dominated over long-term resilience-building due to acute needs.
Underfunded sectors (e.g., protection, education) required EC2R to fill gaps beyond original scope.
Localization challenges with Ethiopian Red Cross (ERCS) funding chains and procurement processes.
partner_relationship_issues: Disconnect between programme design and partner activity implementation (e.g., over/under-performance misalignment).
British Red Cross (BRC) and ERCS collaboration required strengthening for effective localisation.
Lack of clear TPM funding accountability between EC2R and partners.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Initial understaffing at programme level (since addressed).
Partners struggled with results reporting (e.g., double-counting risks, non-SMART milestones).
Limited conflict-sensitivity expertise among partners until 2025 analysis.
risk_materialization: MAJOR risk rating persisted due to conflict volatility and economic shocks.
Funding shortfalls in PSNP led to benefit capping at regional/woreda levels, reducing adequacy.
Procurement delays materialized as a recurring VfM risk.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: HMT approved £200m of £350m total value; remaining £150m (including £40m Internal Risk Facility) contingent on VfM analysis. Budget execution faced delays due to late HMT confirmations, disrupting partner planning.
value_for_money_assessment: Strong commitment to VfM principles, but efficiency concerns persist in procurement (e.g., international goods costs).
PSNP provides cost-effective social protection (~8m beneficiaries) but adequacy compromised by funding shortfalls.
Economic advisor support requested to enhance VfM monitoring across deliverables.
financial_management_quality: Partners demonstrated accountability in spend reporting, but procurement timelines required improvement.
Currency exchange impacts (Birr devaluation) increased costs, partially offset by partner mitigation strategies.
Risk of double-counting results across partners highlighted need for stronger financial oversight.
cost_efficiency_achieved: PSNP achieved economies of scale in social protection delivery.
Nutrition interventions (e.g., SAM treatment) met cost-efficiency targets (e.g., recovery rates at 92% in Tigray).
Inefficiencies in procurement (e.g., international goods) and coordination remained unresolved.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not explicitly mentioned; assumed limited due to global funding decline for Ethiopia.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Ethiopian Birr volatility increased procurement costs, particularly for imported humanitarian goods.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible programme design was critical for adapting to shocks but required proactive budget planning to avoid delays.
Partner consortium model needed stronger FCDO leadership to align activities with programme priorities.
Localization efforts (e.g., ERCS/BRC collaboration) required dedicated resource investment.
successful_delivery_practices: Sectoral stratification of Output 1 improved targeting and weighting alignment.
Conflict-sensitivity analysis (planned for 2025) addressed a critical gap in partner proposals.
PSNP’s predictable social protection mitigated shock impacts for 8m rural beneficiaries.
management_adaptations_made: Revised output weightings pre-AR to reflect actual spend allocations.
Expanded programme staffing to address initial capacity constraints.
Commissioned external Results Adviser for impartial review scrutiny.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of REACH’s Humanitarian Situation Monitoring (HSM) for impact indicator redesign.
Exploration of sectoral earmarking to mitigate funding timeline risks.
previous_recommendations_progress: Majority of 2023 AR recommendations addressed (see Appendix B), though thematic overlaps remain (e.g., Logframe refinement).
Partner accountability mechanisms strengthened but require further codification.
forward_recommendations: Conduct conflict-sensitivity analysis by September 2025 and integrate into partner proposals.
Streamline Logframe indicators to eliminate composite milestones and ensure SMART design.
Expand partner coordination function (e.g., dedicated representatives) and clarify TPM funding accountability.
Commission economic advisor to lead VfM analysis for PSNP and other deliverables.
Revise outcome/impact indicators to better reflect programme goals (e.g., protection access rates, literacy progression).
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk identification was robust (e.g., MAJOR rating retained), but mitigation was reactive (e.g., late conflict-sensitivity analysis).
Internal Risk Facility underutilized due to VfM analysis pending.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: PSNP: ~8 million rural beneficiaries (target met).
Nutrition: 8,537 children treated for SAM (114% of target); 63,648 for MAM (63% of target, with PBW at 280% and U5 at 14%).
IYCF messages reached 19,433 caregivers (129% of target).
Micronutrient interventions exceeded targets (e.g., Vit A at 194%, deworming at 233%).
policy_influence_achieved: Aligned with UK humanitarian framework priorities (protection, resilience).
Influenced partner practices (e.g., conflict-sensitivity integration, gender mainstreaming).
Limited evidence of national policy uptake due to context volatility.
capacity_building_results: Strengthened local systems for SAM/MAM treatment (e.g., health post/centre outpatient setups).
ERCS capacity development ongoing but constrained by funding chain issues.
Partners (e.g., UNICEF, WFP) built downstream NGO capacity (e.g., IMC, CARE, Mercy Corps).
unintended_consequences: Positive: PBW MAM treatment overachievement (280%) suggested unmet need identification.
Negative: PSNP benefit capping reduced adequacy for most vulnerable due to funding shortfalls.
Procurement delays may have exacerbated local market distortions.
scalability_evidence: PSNP model demonstrates scalability for social protection in rural Ethiopia.
Nutrition interventions scalable but constrained by funding and access in conflict zones.
Conflict-sensitivity tools (post-2025) could enhance scalability in volatile contexts.

continuation_rationale: Programme outputs consistently scored A despite challenging context, demonstrating resilience.
Critical gaps in humanitarian response (e.g., underfunded sectors) justify EC2R’s continued role.
Flexible design allows adaptation to evolving crises (e.g., climate shocks, conflict).
HMT approval for FY2025–26 signals donor commitment, pending VfM analysis for outer years.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (for output delivery); Medium (for outcome/impact achievement)
delivery_model_sustainability: Current consortium model is viable short-term but requires stronger coordination for long-term sustainability.
Localization (e.g., ERCS/BRC) needs investment to reduce dependency on international partners.
Funding timeline risks persist without HMT approval for full £350m.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (output delivery); Medium (strategic impact alignment)
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize VfM analysis to unlock Internal Risk Facility (£40m).
Implement conflict-sensitivity analysis and integrate into 2025–26 partner proposals.
Redesign Logframe and ToC to address indicator misalignment with programme goals.
Strengthen partner accountability mechanisms and TPM consolidation.
Explore sectoral earmarking to mitigate funding delay impacts.

programme_metadata.programme_title: UN Population Fund (UNFPA) Core Programme

output_1.title: Policy and Programme Delivery - UNFPA core delivers with high ambition to meet UNFPA’s strategic aims ensuring progress towards universal access to sexual and reproductive health & rights

output_2.title: Organisational Effectiveness and Efficiency - UNFPA Core funding is underpinned by a robust operational and governance model with strong risk mitigation controls providing assurance to donors

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Additional £4.25m allocated for humanitarian response in Occupied Palestinian Territories in Q1 2024, deployed rapidly for menstrual hygiene kits, clean delivery kits, and midwife support. Business Case addendum developed to formalize this change.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNFPA exceeded targets for PSEA mechanisms (48% vs 37% target) but faced delays in rolling out Comprehensive Abortion Care (CAC) operational guidelines. Capacity-building efforts on CAC are ongoing.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UNFPA is undergoing structural transition (new programme division in 2024, relocation to Nairobi by 2025), requiring proactive change management to mitigate staff attrition and morale risks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong alignment with FCDO priorities (SRHR, International Women and Girls’ Strategy) and UNFPA’s Strategic Plan 2022-25. Bilateral engagement at ministerial/senior levels reinforced accountability.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained oversight through Executive Board engagement, annual payments, and MOPAN assessments. Focus on strategic partnerships, accountability, and organisational efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Core funding flexibility enabled rapid reallocation to humanitarian crises (e.g., Occupied Palestinian Territories). Adaptive management demonstrated through midterm review adjustments to indicators.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid deployment of £4.25m for humanitarian response in 2024, with new metrics added to logframe.
Adjustment of indicator targets (e.g., Output 2.1) during UNFPA’s Strategic Plan midterm review to align with revised priorities.
Proactive risk management for staff transitions (e.g., Nairobi relocation) to mitigate operational disruptions.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in rolling out Comprehensive Abortion Care (CAC) operational guidelines despite ongoing capacity-building.
Backlog in UNFPA’s Office of Audit and Investigation Services (OAIS) due to COVID-19, staffing issues, and increased complaints, though record case closures (160) were achieved in 2023.
Complexity of investigations in humanitarian settings (e.g., evidence gathering obstacles) prolonging case resolution.
Staff attrition and morale risks during organisational transition (2024-2025 relocation to Nairobi).
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 pandemic contributed to OAIS backlog and delayed investigations.
Political threats to SRHR mandate required FCDO to defend against rollback during multilateral negotiations.
Humanitarian crises (e.g., Occupied Palestinian Territories) necessitated rapid reallocation of funds and adaptive programming.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased allegations of wrongdoing in humanitarian settings, requiring prioritization of high-risk cases (e.g., sexual exploitation, retaliation).
Need for enhanced PSEAH (Prevention of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment) capacity among implementing partners.
capacity_constraints_emerged: OAIS faced resourcing gaps for investigations, addressed partially through consultant hiring and new staff recruitment (e.g., Chief of Investigations Unit).
Limited capacity among local institutions for domestic resource mobilisation (baseline data for Output 1.1 not yet available).
risk_materialization: Major risk rating due to OAIS backlog and delays in CAC guideline rollout.
Staff transition risks (attrition, morale) during organisational restructuring.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; additional £4.25m allocated in 2024 for humanitarian response, increasing total programme value. Annual payments streamlined financial management, allowing focus on strategic priorities.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong VfM demonstrated: every £1 in core funding generated £2.70 in additional resources (2023 data). Core funding leveraged $384m from 95 government partners, seeding further resource mobilisation.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High; UNFPA’s Integrated Results and Resources Framework enabled harmonised reporting. FCDO oversight through Executive Board engagement ensured accountability (e.g., staffing costs, resource allocation).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of funds via flexible core funding model, reducing transaction costs. Example: Rapid deployment of humanitarian funds in Occupied Palestinian Territories with clear output metrics (kits, midwife support).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Yes; core funding triggered co-financing (£1:£2.70 ratio in 2023). UNFPA Supplies Match Fund cited as an innovative approach to mobilise domestic resources.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible core funding enables rapid response to emergencies (e.g., Occupied Palestinian Territories) while maintaining alignment with strategic priorities.
Proactive risk management (e.g., OAIS backlog mitigation) requires dedicated resourcing and process streamlining (e.g., case closure criteria).
Domestic resource mobilisation (Output 1.1) needs baseline data and targeted capacity-building to accelerate progress.
successful_delivery_practices: UNFPA’s exceeding of PSEA target (48% vs 37%) through survivor-centred, multisectoral approaches.
Use of annual payments to reduce administrative burden and focus on strategic oversight.
Leveraging FCDO’s policy role to defend SRHR mandate in multilateral forums (e.g., ICPD30).
management_adaptations_made: Midterm review of UNFPA’s Strategic Plan led to indicator adjustments (e.g., Output 2.1) and logframe updates.
Prioritisation of high-risk OAIS cases (e.g., sexual exploitation) to address backlog, including hiring consultants and new staff.
Enhanced PSEAH technical leadership and partner capacity-building.
innovations_attempted: UNFPA Supplies Match Fund as a mechanism to incentivise domestic resource mobilisation.
Development of case closure criteria in OAIS to streamline investigations.
Rapid humanitarian funding deployment with clear output tracking (e.g., kits, midwives).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on CAC guideline rollout (capacity-building ongoing).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme integrated lessons from the previous Better Health Programme to prioritize nimble, responsive delivery through small but strategic areas of work and NHS ecosystem partnerships. RCGP component not yet operational at review time.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All three main partners (CHAI, NHSC, Ipas) achieved or exceeded Year 1 milestones. Early challenges in NHSC-CHAI collaboration (new working relationship) were mitigated through coordination meetings and a shared workplan. Ipas demonstrated strong mobilization in Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, including MoU signings and baseline surveys.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Complementary partner focus: NHSC (national level), CHAI (national/provincial), Ipas (provincial/community). Coordination mechanisms (e.g., joint workplans) implemented to address initial collaboration gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective for mobilisation phase, though stakeholder engagement bandwidth emerged as a constraint. Facilitation by CHAI/BHC sometimes required to bridge NHSC-NDoH/PDoH relationships.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Partners adhered to 3-quotes principle. Cost efficiencies achieved through leveraging existing partnerships (e.g., CHAI’s pre-existing NDoH relationships), virtual delivery models, and shared workshops/trainings.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to political context changes (e.g., GNU formation post-NHI Act) through scenario planning and risk register updates. Focus shifted to core areas (SRHR, HTA) while deprioritizing untested components (e.g., pandemic preparedness, private sector investment).
adaptive_management_examples: Development of integrated workplans to address NHSC-CHAI coordination challenges.
Reprioritization of logframe to reflect achievable scale (e.g., narrowed impact from UHC/pandemic preparedness to "improved access to quality healthcare").
Scenario planning for political risks (e.g., NHI Act opposition in GNU).

main_implementation_challenges: Limited stakeholder engagement bandwidth (e.g., delays in NDoH/PDoH feedback).
Initial coordination gaps between NHSC and CHAI due to new partnership.
Political uncertainty post-GNU formation affecting NHI Act implementation.
external_factors_impact: New Government of National Unity (GNU) introduced opponents of the NHI Act, creating potential reprioritization risks in national/provincial health departments.
COVID-19 legacy effects (e.g., strained health system capacity) indirectly influenced baseline conditions.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated political opposition to NHI Act within GNU.
Need for longer lead times in workplans to account for stakeholder engagement delays.
partner_relationship_issues: NHSC faced challenges in direct engagement with NDoH/PDoH without CHAI/BHC facilitation.
Ipas’s community-level work required additional coordination with LoveLife (contracted NGO) for social action components.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Provincial health departments (e.g., EC, KZN) had limited capacity to respond to programme demands alongside existing priorities.
Delays in RCGP component due to late-stage mobilization.
risk_materialization: Political risk (GNU formation) materialized, requiring adaptive management.
Stakeholder engagement risks (bandwidth constraints) partially materialized, addressed via workplan adjustments.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Partners demonstrated cost efficiencies (e.g., leveraging existing NDoH relationships, virtual delivery, shared venues). No significant underspend/overspend reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM performance aligns with business case expectations. Efficiencies noted in: (1) reduced travel costs via virtual models, (2) combined workshops, (3) use of existing knowledge products (e.g., NHS England’s Twinning Learning Collaboration).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Partners adhered to transparency principles (e.g., 3-quotes rule) and proactive cost-saving measures. Financial systems established during mobilization phase.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Evidence of efficiency gains through: (a) shared audiences for trainings, (b) negotiated use of hospital venues, (c) leveraging pre-existing partnerships to reduce setup costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Small, strategic interventions with strong partner complementarity yield high impact (e.g., Ipas’s community-level SRHR work).
Early coordination mechanisms (e.g., joint workplans) are critical for new partner collaborations.
Political context monitoring must be proactive and linked to risk registers.
successful_delivery_practices: Co-design workshops (e.g., Ipas’s VCAT sessions) effectively engaged diverse stakeholders and addressed attitudinal barriers to SRHR.
Virtual delivery models improved cost efficiency and accessibility.
Leveraging existing partnerships (e.g., CHAI’s NDoH relationships) accelerated mobilization.
management_adaptations_made: Integrated workplans introduced to address NHSC-CHAI coordination gaps.
Logframe and ToC simplified to reflect achievable programme scale (e.g., removed UHC/pandemic preparedness as direct impacts).
Scenario planning conducted for political risks (GNU/NHI Act).
innovations_attempted: VCAT (Values Clarification and Attitude Transformation) workshops to address provider biases in SRHR service delivery.
Mentorship schemes combining clinical governance and HTA capacity building (CHAI).
Social action plans co-developed with Community-Based Organizations (Ipas).
forward_recommendations: Conduct a ToC/logframe review by March 2025 to: (a) clarify institutional partnership contributions to outputs 2–3, (b) integrate CHAI-NHSC collaboration milestones, (c) potentially remove output 4.
Build longer lead times into workplans to account for stakeholder engagement delays.
Strengthen NHSC’s direct relationships with NDoH/PDoH or formalize CHAI/BHC facilitation roles.
Monitor political risks (e.g., NHI Act implementation) with quarterly risk register updates.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in identifying and mitigating emerging risks (e.g., political changes, stakeholder bandwidth). Risk registers updated dynamically, though some engagement delays persisted.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 30 clinical mentors and 40 healthcare workers trained across Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal (Ipas).
Stakeholders from marginalized groups (LGBTIQA+, women, persons with disabilities) engaged via Ipas’s equity-focused approach.
Provincial health facilities identified for support through baseline surveys (targets not yet fully reported).
policy_influence_achieved: Contributions to NHI Act implementation via HTA capacity building (CHAI).
Alignment with Presidential Health Compact and G20 priorities demonstrated through co-design with NDoH.
capacity_building_results: Clinical mentors and healthcare workers trained in SRHR service delivery (Ipas).
Assessments of clinical governance and medico-legal frameworks completed (CHAI).
Mentorship scheme and hospital strategy tools developed (CHAI).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Strengthened cross-provincial learning (e.g., EC-KZN knowledge exchange via Ipas workshops).
Negative: None reported, though stakeholder bandwidth constraints may limit deeper engagement in some areas.
scalability_evidence: Ipas’s SRHR model (community mentors + social action plans) shows potential for replication in other provinces.
CHAI’s HTA tools could be adapted for national rollout pending political stability.

continuation_rationale: Strong Year 1 performance (Overall Output Score: A) despite political challenges.
Critical alignment with South Africa’s health priorities (NHI Act, Presidential Health Compact).
Partner complementarity and early efficiencies suggest potential for scaled impact in Years 2–4.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (dependent on political stability and continued NDoH/PDoH engagement).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (reflected in Overall Output Score and narrative).
planned_adaptations_future: Expand RCGP component post-mobilization.
Deepened focus on HTA and medico-legal capacity building (CHAI) to support NHI Act implementation.
Enhanced monitoring of equity outcomes (e.g., disability-disaggregated data).
Quarterly political risk assessments to guide adaptive management.
