delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Centralised programme management with strong integration into FCDO Posts' strategies. New Programme Management Office (PMO) established to oversee learning, finance, and risk. Global Delivery Strategy completed in June 2024 to guide country strategies.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved coherence between components (country programmes, regional funds, expert deployments) through integrated delivery structure. Cross-regional learning facilitated by new GEDSI working group and MEL framework. Challenges remained in fully operationalising Theory of Change (TOC) across all funds.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of single DP experienced delays (high-value, complex process) pushing back implementation of new delivery model. Open calls for proposals under GRCF phased out in favor of targeted, demand-driven approaches. Average consultant fee rates generally at/below pre-agreed benchmarks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight through new KPIs for DP and robust MEL framework. PMO took on deeper financial forecasting responsibilities (previously handled by FCDO). More international travel post-COVID enabled better in-country monitoring.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme flexibly scaled up spend slightly above target (with approval) and adapted to ODA budget cuts by extending project timelines. Rapid establishment of 4 new country programmes (Brazil, India, Thailand, Vietnam) and 2 regional funds in response to evolving priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Replacement of GRCF with targeted regional funds based on evaluation findings about complementarities.
Integration of skill-shares into country programmes to improve synergies, reducing from three DPs to one.
Development of new MEL framework (October 2024) with stronger outcome indicators aligned to ICF metrics.
Creation of GEDSI working group and strategy to mainstream inclusion, informed by GRCF project lessons.
Adjustment to project timelines and budget phasing in response to department-wide ODA cuts.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed procurement of single DP (signed February 2024) pushed back transition to new delivery model.
Reduced MEL capacity (no MEL advisor/external provider in place for part of FY 2023-24) led to underreporting of training data.
Significant staff turnover in programme team (80% of country leads, 33% of central team) required onboarding during critical transition period.
Long causal chains for TA interventions made outcome measurement difficult within annual review cycles.
ODA budget cuts (FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24) forced reduction/extension of projects, delaying outcome achievement.
external_factors_impact: Post-COVID travel restrictions lifted, enabling more in-country engagement but requiring adjustment to pre-pandemic operating models.
Global economic pressures and ODA reductions (department-wide) constrained programme ambition and timeline.
Evolving political contexts in partner countries (e.g., Brazil, India) required adaptive engagement strategies.
Increased demand for climate finance technical assistance post-COP campaigns influenced programme priorities.
contextual_constraints_new: Underestimation of time required to operationalise new delivery model (single DP) and MEL system refresh.
Unanticipated complexity in integrating skill-shares/secondments into country programmes while maintaining flexibility.
Limited counterpart capacity in some countries to absorb technical assistance at the pace originally planned.
Data gaps in tracking long-term policy influence due to lack of baseline studies in early programme years.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial tensions during transition from three DPs to single DP, particularly around role clarity and handover processes.
Some implementing partners struggled with new reporting requirements under updated MEL framework.
Varied government engagement levels across countries, with some (e.g., Mexico, Colombia) more receptive than others (e.g., new country programmes).
capacity_constraints_emerged: MEL system underresourced during transition, leading to incomplete training data capture (e.g., 9,143 trainees recorded vs. 38,000-40,000 in prior years).
Limited in-house expertise on certain technical areas (e.g., climate finance instruments) required external consultant support.
High workload for programme team during procurement and onboarding of new DP, affecting strategic planning bandwidth.
Need for additional GEDSI expertise to operationalise new inclusion strategy across all components.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (risk identified in FY 2022-23) materialized, impacting timeline for new delivery model.
ODA budget cuts (macro-level risk) reduced programme scope and extended timelines for outcome achievement.
Partner government turnover in some countries (e.g., elections in India) slowed policy uptake of TA recommendations.
Major risk rating persisted due to combination of external ODA pressures and internal transition challenges.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Total spend slightly above target for FY 2023-24 (with prior approval) despite ODA cuts in prior years.
Budget reductions in FY 2022-23 and FY 2023-24 led to project extensions and delayed outcome achievement.
New delivery model (single DP) expected to improve cost efficiency through reduced transaction costs and larger calls for proposals.
Country programmes expanded from 6 to 10, requiring reallocation of funds across regions.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Good – Average consultant fees at/below benchmarks; leveraged networks to reduce duplication. Potential efficiencies from fewer, larger calls for proposals not yet fully realised.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Good – Strong output delivery (249 outputs) with 8/9 results exceeding milestones. Delays in procurement and MEL refresh affected operational efficiency.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Good at output level; mixed at outcome level due to long timeframes for policy influence. Independent evaluation needed to assess full results chain.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Mainstreamed GEDSI considerations but limited evidence of transformational change for marginalised groups. New GEDSI strategy and working group established to address gaps.

financial_management_quality: Robust oversight through new DP KPIs and PMO-led financial forecasting.
Transparency in grant processes (open, fair, competitive) maintained despite transition challenges.
Improved monitoring of project deliverables via increased in-country travel post-COVID.
No major audit findings reported; minor issues addressed through updated contractual arrangements.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost per output remained stable despite inflationary pressures, with economies of scale from expanded country programmes.
Reduction in overhead costs expected from single DP model (not yet quantified).
Leveraged £1.05m USD in co-financing for rural electrification in Mexico (7 states).
Travel costs increased post-COVID but judged necessary for effective delivery.
co_funding_materialization: Partial success: £1.05m USD leveraged in Mexico for rural electrification (against unspecified co-funding targets).
No comprehensive data on co-funding across all countries; new MEL framework includes indicators to track this going forward.
Some projects (e.g., ASEAN regional fund) designed to catalyse additional funding but results not yet evident.

key_delivery_lessons: Centralised programme management with strong Post integration enhances visibility and strategic alignment.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., regional funds) allow rapid response to emerging priorities (e.g., Amazon deforestation).
Demand-driven approaches (targeted calls vs. open proposals) improve relevance and uptake of TA.
Long timeframes for TA impact require realistic expectation-setting and extended MEL tracking post-project.
High staff turnover necessitates robust knowledge management systems and onboarding processes.
successful_delivery_practices: Integration of skill-shares into country programmes improved coherence and reduced transaction costs.
Use of local networks and UK public sector partnerships (e.g., for secondments) enhanced credibility and uptake.
Country-specific strategies with clear TOCs (e.g., Mexico mobility projects) demonstrated stronger outcome progress.
GEDSI mainstreaming through working groups and strategy development (though impact evidence is early-stage).
Proactive adaptation to ODA cuts by extending timelines and reprioritising high-impact activities.
management_adaptations_made: Transition from three DPs to single DP to reduce fragmentation and improve synergies.
New MEL framework (October 2024) with stronger outcome indicators and case study focus.
Establishment of PMO to centralise learning, finance, and risk management functions.
Development of "UK PACT Learning and Development Curriculum" for FCDO staff and partners.
Shift from open to targeted calls for proposals to align with government demand.
innovations_attempted: Expert Deployments model (replacing skill-shares) designed for greater flexibility and country alignment.
Regional funds (Amazon, ASEAN) to address cross-border climate challenges (e.g., deforestation).
GEDSI Strategy with dedicated working group to embed inclusion in climate action.
Use of task orders under new DP contract to commission learning pieces and adaptive interventions.
Pilot of outcome-level indicators aligned with ICF metrics to better track long-term impact.
previous_recommendations_progress: Global Delivery Strategy (Rec 1) completed in June 2024; country strategies refreshed in FY 2024-25.
MEL Framework (Rec 2) overhauled with new strategy signed off in October 2024; includes ICF-aligned indicators.
Structured learning approach (Rec 3) operationalised via PMO-led curriculum and task order process.
Team capacity-building (Rec 4) addressed through PMO presentations on finance/risk and "how UK PACT works" guide.
Financial forecasting (Rec 5) delegated to DP with robust KPIs; deep dives now DP responsibility.
All six FY 2022-23 recommendations fully or partially addressed, with new systems in place for sustainability.
forward_recommendations: Finalise operationalisation of new delivery model (single DP) and Expert Deployments by Q1 2025.
Strengthen application of TOC across all funds, with clearer linkages to climate mitigation outcomes.
Conduct independent evaluation to assess effectiveness across the full results chain (outputs to impact).
Develop systematic approach to track and demonstrate equitable impacts of GEDSI strategy.
Explore opportunities for larger, fewer calls for proposals to improve cost efficiency.
Establish baseline studies in new country programmes to enable robust outcome measurement.
Enhance knowledge management to capture lessons from staff turnover and country expansions.
risk_management_effectiveness: Major risks (procurement delays, ODA cuts) were identified early but mitigation was partially effective due to external constraints.
New DP contract includes KPIs to address delivery and financial risks, improving accountability.
GEDSI and MEL strategies introduced to mitigate programme coherence and impact measurement risks.
Risk rating remained "Major" due to persistent external pressures (ODA environment) and transition challenges.
Lessons from GRCF evaluation informed design of regional funds, reducing repetition of past risks.

New delivery model (single DP) and MEL framework position programme for improved outcome achievement.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Urban Climate Action Programme
programme_metadata.review_period: January 2024 - December 2024 (with CFF Phase 3 results from April 2021 - October 2024)

output_1.title: Programme cities have increased capacity and capability for developing and structuring low-carbon infrastructure projects and policies (CAI)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from traditional technical assistance (reports/workshops) toward direct financial and implementation-driven support based on evolving city needs. Increased focus on early-stage finance linkages and political engagement with mayors' teams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: C40 and GIZ both performed strongly, with C40 exceeding most milestones and GIZ-led CFF achieving all output indicators (with one neither moderately nor substantially exceeded). Synergies in 7 overlapping cities enhanced outcomes through coordinated knowledge exchange.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance structures established in 15 CAI cities (7 Africa, 5 LatAm, 3 SEA) to drive Climate Action Plan delivery. Adaptive management included targeted support for lagging cities (e.g., Dar es Salaam, Nairobi) and early engagement with investors in CFF Phase 4.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between CAI and CFF in 7 overlapping cities, with knowledge exchange and capacity-building synergies. CFF's multi-donor collaboration (Germany, USA, UK) informed Phase 4 extension.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: High oversight intensity for CFF project preparation (18 projects in 16 cities completed, except Johannesburg/Mbombela). CAI provided in-depth technical assistance for CAP implementation, including ICA integration and digital governance tools.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to city-specific challenges (e.g., bandwidth issues in Dar es Salaam/Nairobi) and shifting needs (e.g., prioritizing finance linkages over traditional technical assistance). Phase 4 designed to address finance mobilization gaps identified in Phase 3.
adaptive_management_examples: Targeted recovery support for Dar es Salaam and Nairobi after workplan delays
Early investor engagement in CFF Phase 4 (vs. last-mile in Phase 3)
Rebalancing CFF Phase 4 portfolio to include more secondary cities
Integration of Inclusive Climate Action (ICA) principles into governance structures across regions

main_implementation_challenges: Mobilizing finance for CFF projects despite strong technical preparation
Bandwidth constraints in cities like Dar es Salaam and Nairobi affecting workplan implementation
Political transitions disrupting continuity in city administrations
Skewed support toward C40 megacities (limited reach to secondary cities in Phase 3)

Currency/exchange rate risks (implied by finance mobilization challenges)

risk_materialization: Bandwidth-related delays in two African cities (mitigated through targeted support)
Finance mobilization challenges for CFF projects (persistent across phases)
Political transition risks (mitigated via early engagement/knowledge transfer in Year 4 plans)

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: CFF Phase 3 (£30.95M programme) completed 18 projects in 16 cities (except two late joiners). Four high-potential projects approved for further support. Phase 4 extension launched with UK/Germany funding.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong VFM demonstrated: CFF met all output indicators with one exception, and CAI achieved 6/7 output indicators. GHG reduction targets overachieved in Phase 3. Recommendation to recalibrate future targets for realism/ambition balance.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High quality: CFF's technical assistance received positive stakeholder feedback. Challenges in finance mobilization despite strong project preparation, prompting Phase 4 design changes (e.g., earlier investor engagement).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of resources: 87 workshops/trainings delivered (vs. 68 target) across regions. CAI's projected GHG reductions significant (final figures pending). CFF focused on project feasibility and upscaling successful initiatives.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Multi-donor collaboration successful (Germany, France, UK, USA in Phase 3; Germany/UK in Phase 4). Co-funding leveraged for CFF's extension and Phase 4 launch.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Reforming the United Nations System – Humanitarian (RUSH) Programme

output_1.title: Prevent – Payment by Results (PbR): Prevent and anticipate future shocks and build resilience in long-running crises by tackling the underlying drivers of humanitarian crises

output_5.title: PRIORITISE – NON PbR: Prioritise humanitarian assistance to people in greatest need

output_6.title: PROTECT - NON PBR: Protect the people most at risk, including from GBV

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The RUSH Programme shifted to a Payment by Results (PbR) framework, with 30% of funding (£32.4m annually) tied to joint targets aligned with UK reform priorities. This incentivized UN agencies (IOM, OCHA, UNHCR, UNICEF, WFP) to collaborate on anticipatory action, localisation, and protection outcomes. The model combines 70% unearmarked core funding with 30% results-based allocations, diverging from traditional input-based funding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UN agencies demonstrated strong collaboration under PbR incentives, with 93% of PbR indicators meeting/exceeding expectations vs. 80% for non-PbR. IOM expanded GBV specialist capacity; OCHA led humanitarian diplomacy in Syria, Gaza, and Ethiopia; UNHCR supported 19.3m people via 470 local partners. Performance was particularly strong in PSEA (3/5 agencies exceeded milestones) and localisation (all agencies met targets).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme operates through a central FCDO oversight mechanism with agency-specific accountability frameworks. Coordination occurs via joint target-setting under PbR, though the review notes a need for greater uniformity in indicators across agencies. The Anticipation Hub and other dialogue platforms facilitate cross-agency learning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination was demonstrated through: (1) Joint anticipatory action frameworks triggered in 10 countries (e.g., Bangladesh, Fiji, South Sudan), (2) Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) adoption in 82% of HRP countries, and (3) collaborative PSEA improvements (44% of IOM’s HRP countries now have full-time PSEA focal points, up from 8%). However, qualitative aspects of localisation partnerships require deeper assessment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintains periodic engagement with UN agencies to review logframe updates and milestone adjustments. The first Annual Review finalized the logframe, with plans for quarterly milestone reviews. Oversight focuses on PbR indicator performance, though the review recommends enhancing qualitative assessments of localisation and partnership quality.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme utilized flexibility to: (1) Adjust milestones mid-year for indicators significantly exceeded (e.g., anticipatory action coverage expanded from 5.5m to 6.8m people), (2) Incorporate new collective anticipatory action frameworks (e.g., El Niño responses in Madagascar/Zimbabwe), and (3) Revise localisation indicators to emphasize funding *quality* over percentage targets for 2024.
adaptive_management_examples: Expanded anticipatory action triggers from planned 5.5m to 6.8m people covered across 10 countries, including ad-hoc responses to El Niño in Madagascar/Zimbabwe.
Revised localisation metrics for 2024 to capture qualitative partnership aspects (e.g., OCHA’s 32% direct funding to national partners via CBPF, plus 8% indirect funding).
Adjusted PSEA targets after IOM exceeded its 8% baseline to reach 44% of HRP countries with full-time focal points.
Incorporated new IPC/Cadre Harmonisé food security analyses into 27/33 HRP countries (82% coverage), exceeding the 79% milestone.

main_implementation_challenges: Balancing PbR incentives with agency-specific KPIs led to varied ambition levels across indicators, requiring FCDO to harmonize targets.
Establishing baselines for new indicators (e.g., localisation quality metrics) delayed scoring for some 2023 milestones.

Coordinating anticipatory action across 5 UN agencies with distinct mandates (e.g., WFP’s food security focus vs. UNHCR’s protection role) required intensive dialogue platforms like the Anticipation Hub.
external_factors_impact: Global humanitarian funding gap (only 43% of $56.1bn needs met in 2023) increased pressure on RUSH’s £108m/year to demonstrate efficiency.
Climate shocks (e.g., tropical cyclones in Bangladesh/Fiji, floods in Somalia) necessitated rapid adaptation of anticipatory action frameworks mid-year.
Political access constraints (e.g., Syria, Gaza, Ethiopia) required OCHA-led humanitarian diplomacy to secure operational space for UN agencies.
contextual_constraints_new: Unprecedented scale of need (363.3m people requiring assistance in 2023) strained UN system capacity, particularly for protection services (e.g., GBV, PSEA).
Emergence of El Niño as a cross-regional threat (Madagascar, Zimbabwe) required unplanned anticipatory action coordination.
Localisation baselines revealed lower-than-expected starting points (e.g., IOM’s 6.1% funding to local actors; UNHCR’s 80% local partner proportion), necessitating revised trajectories.
partner_relationship_issues: Varied agency interpretations of "localisation" led to inconsistent reporting (e.g., OCHA’s 32% direct funding vs. UNHCR’s 85% local partner proportion).
Some UN agencies initially resisted PbR’s joint accountability mechanisms, though collaboration improved after early successes (e.g., joint anticipatory action in Somalia).
Capacity gaps among local/national partners (e.g., 57% of UNHCR’s funding went to 845 national NGOs, but quality of partnerships required deeper assessment).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited PSEA focal point coverage in high-risk contexts (e.g., IOM’s initial 8% baseline in HRP countries).
UNICEF’s 95% preparedness plan compliance masked variations in *quality* of local partner integration.
WFP and UNHCR’s joint targeting initiatives (e.g., Joint Assessment Framework) faced delays due to differing data systems.
risk_materialization: Major risk of "humanitarian access constraints" materialized in Syria, Gaza, and Ethiopia, requiring OCHA-led diplomacy.
Risk of "low localisation baselines" materialized, with initial metrics revealing lower-than-planned starting points (e.g., IOM’s 6.1% local funding transfer).
Risk of "indicator misalignment" partially materialized, as agency-specific KPIs led to varied ambition levels (e.g., PSEA vs. localisation targets).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme disbursed £108m annually as planned, with 70% as unearmarked core funding and 30% (£32.4m) tied to PbR targets. All agencies met financial reporting requirements, though the review notes a need to track *qualitative* outcomes of localisation spending (e.g., OCHA’s 32% direct funding to national partners via CBPF).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated through: (1) 84% of indicators met/exceeded expectations, with PbR indicators outperforming non-PbR (93% vs. 80%); (2) Anticipatory action cost efficiency (4.2m people assisted via 15 triggers at £21.6m PbR allocation, or ~£5/person); (3) Protection outcomes (19.3m people reached via UNHCR’s £32.4m PbR tranche). However, the review recommends deeper analysis of *long-term* cost savings from systemic reforms (e.g., reduced duplication via joint targeting).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial management observed, with all agencies submitting audited statements. Key strengths: (1) Transparent PbR tranche allocation tied to verified milestones; (2) Rapid reallocation to El Niño responses mid-year; (3) No significant findings from FCDO’s periodic financial reviews. Areas for improvement: Enhance tracking of co-funding leverage (e.g., UNHCR’s $1.37bn total partnerships vs. RUSH’s £32.4m PbR contribution).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency exceeded targets in anticipatory action (6.8m people covered vs. 5.5m planned) and PSEA (44% HRP country coverage vs. 8% baseline). However, localisation costs require further analysis—e.g., OCHA’s 32% direct funding to national partners via CBPF may reflect varying transaction costs across agencies.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial materialization: UNHCR reported $1.37bn in total partnership funding (including RUSH’s £32.4m PbR tranche), but the review does not quantify RUSH’s leverage ratio. FCDO recommends tracking co-funding more systematically in 2024.

key_delivery_lessons: PbR incentives effectively drove cross-agency collaboration (e.g., joint anticipatory action frameworks in 10 countries), but required clear milestone definitions to avoid varied interpretations.

Core funding flexibility enabled rapid responses to unplanned crises (e.g., El Niño in Madagascar/Zimbabwe), though baselines for new indicators (e.g., localisation quality) need earlier establishment.
UN agencies’ corporate frameworks (e.g., IPC for food security) provided robust monitoring tools but required adaptation to RUSH’s specific PbR indicators.
successful_delivery_practices: Anticipatory action triggers linked to climate hazards (e.g., tropical cyclones in Bangladesh, floods in Somalia) demonstrated scalability and cost efficiency (~£5/person assisted).
OCHA’s humanitarian diplomacy secured access in high-risk contexts (Syria, Gaza), enabling other agencies to operate.
UNHCR’s partnership model (85% local/national responders) showed how PbR can incentivize localisation without sacrificing accountability.
IOM’s GBV specialist expansion and PSEA focal points (44% coverage) proved effective in protection outcomes.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from percentage-based localisation targets to qualitative metrics (e.g., assessing *quality* of funding to local actors).
Incorporated IPC/Cadre Harmonisé analyses into 82% of HRPs, exceeding the 79% milestone.
Added ad-hoc anticipatory action triggers for El Niño after mid-year climate forecasts.
Revised PSEA milestones upward after IOM’s 44% coverage (vs. 8% baseline) demonstrated feasibility.
innovations_attempted: Joint Targeting Guidance between UNHCR and WFP, including a "Fundamentals of Targeting" training course for staff/partners.
Anticipation Hub as a cross-agency knowledge platform for anticipatory action learning (7 reports published in 2023).
Integration of climate risk data (e.g., tropical cyclone frameworks in Bangladesh/Fiji) into HRPs for the first time.
Pilot of indirect funding mechanisms via CBPF (8% of OCHA’s national partners accessed indirect funds).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: Not applicable—this is the first comprehensive Annual Review for RUSH.
forward_recommendations: Review and raise milestones for indicators exceeded by >20% (e.g., anticipatory action coverage, PSEA focal points).
Develop qualitative metrics for localisation (e.g., partnership quality, capacity transfer) to complement percentage targets.
Harmonize PbR indicators across agencies to reduce variability in ambition levels.
Expand joint targeting initiatives (e.g., UNHCR-WFP Joint Assessment Framework) to more contexts.
Systematically track co-funding leverage and long-term cost savings from systemic reforms.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective for operational risks (e.g., access constraints mitigated via OCHA diplomacy) but less so for strategic risks (e.g., localisation quality not fully captured by initial indicators). The PbR framework’s adaptive milestones allowed for course correction (e.g., El Niño responses), though some risks materialized due to baseline underestimates (e.g., PSEA focal point coverage).

anticipatory_action.notes: 4.2m assisted via 15 triggers; 2.6m covered by active frameworks.

protection_services.notes: UNHCR provided protection via 470 local partners in 29 countries.

actual.OCHA: 32% direct funding to national partners via CBPF (+8% indirect)

policy_influence_achieved: Anticipatory action integrated into HRPs for Ethiopia, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Somalia, with detailed flood planning in the latter two.
PSEA standards prioritized in 44% of IOM’s HRP countries (up from 8%), influencing UN-wide accountability frameworks.
Localisation targets adopted by Grand Bargain signatories, with RUSH’s 30% PbR tranche cited as a model for results-based funding.
capacity_building_results: IOM expanded GBV specialist roles across operations, with measurable increases in survivor support.
UNHCR’s 470 local partners (85% local/national) received capacity strengthening in protection service delivery.
OCHA’s CBPF direct funding mechanism (32% to national partners) built financial management capacity among local NGOs.
WFP and UNHCR’s joint targeting training reached 100+ staff, improving inter-agency coordination.

unintended_consequences.positive: PbR incentives inadvertently improved cross-agency data sharing (e.g., joint IPC analyses in 27/33 HRP countries).
unintended_consequences.negative: Focus on PbR indicators risked diverting attention from non-incentivized areas (e.g., 80% non-PbR indicators met vs. 93% PbR).

unintended_consequences.positive: Anticipatory action frameworks in Bangladesh/Fiji created templates adopted by non-RUSH agencies (e.g., Red Cross).
unintended_consequences.negative: Rapid scale-up of localisation (e.g., UNHCR’s 85% local partners) strained capacity of some national NGOs, requiring additional support.

scalability_evidence: Anticipatory action models (e.g., tropical cyclone frameworks) are being replicated in non-RUSH contexts (e.g., Caribbean hurricane preparedness).
PbR framework influenced other donors (e.g., EU, Germany) to adopt results-based funding for UN agencies.
Localisation metrics (e.g., CBPF direct funding) are being piloted by OCHA in additional pooled funds.
PSEA focal point model expanded from 8% to 44% coverage, demonstrating scalability across IOM’s global operations.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme is on track to achieve its outcomes, with 84% of 2023 indicators met/exceeded and strong PbR performance (93%). The RUSH model has demonstrated its ability to drive UN system reforms (e.g., anticipatory action, localisation, PSEA) at scale, aligning with FCDO’s humanitarian priorities. The first Annual Review confirmed the theory of change remains valid, though adjustments to indicators (e.g., localisation quality) are needed for sustained impact.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The PbR framework is sustainable long-term, given its success in incentivizing collaboration and efficiency. However, the review recommends: (1) Deepening qualitative assessments of localisation, (2) Expanding joint targeting initiatives, and (3) Systematically tracking co-funding leverage to ensure financial sustainability post-2027.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Raise milestones for high-performing indicators (e.g., anticipatory action, PSEA) to maintain ambition.
Introduce qualitative metrics for localisation (e.g., partnership quality, capacity transfer) in 2024.
Harmonize PbR indicators across agencies to reduce variability in target ambition.
Expand the Joint Assessment Framework (WFP-UNHCR) to additional agencies/contexts.
Develop a systematic approach to track co-funding and long-term cost savings from systemic reforms.
Incorporate climate risk analyses (e.g., El Niño) into HRPs proactively, not just reactively.

programme_metadata.programme_status: Transitioning to successor programme (Ukraine Economic Stabilisation Programme - UESP)

output_1.title: Support for core government functions

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Original business case extended 3 times via addendums to accommodate growing needs. Transitioned from emergency FREE programme to longer-term UESP (Ukraine Economic Stabilisation Programme) in March 2023, aligned with G7's 4-year IMF Extended Fund Facility arrangement. Delivery shifted from standalone emergency support to coordinated multi-year fiscal assistance framework.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (IBRD) performed as expected, with PEACE project disbursing $25.5 billion since 2022. UK relied entirely on World Bank's implementation and monitoring, with no direct involvement in output design. World Bank's reporting (ISR, Intermediate Results Indicators) formed the basis for UK's performance assessment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme management adapted to overlap with successor programme (UESP). Decision taken to combine FREE and UESP management cycles, with future reviews planned for April and consolidated risk monitoring. Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) led transition to UESP, announced by Prime Minister at 2023 Ukraine Recovery Conference.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination with G7 partners to provide "financing assurances" for Ukraine's IMF programme. UK's guarantees were part of a broader donor effort ($29.2 billion in 2022, $39.9 billion in 2023) representing ~1/3 of Ukraine's government expenditure. Coordination mechanisms evolved from emergency response to structured multi-year support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: No direct procurement by UK; funds channelled through World Bank's existing mechanisms (MDTF for grants, PEACE for guarantees). Guarantees were structured as tranches (e.g., $450m, $500m x3) to extend IBRD's lending capacity. Disbursements were timely, with two tranches ($200m and $298.8m) released in September and November 2023 under the fourth guarantee.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Light-touch oversight due to reliance on World Bank's systems. UK did not engage in detailed output design or monitoring, instead using World Bank's ISR reports and LCU analysis for performance assessment. Oversight focused on financial guarantees rather than operational delivery.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: High flexibility demonstrated through: (1) Three addendums to extend original business case; (2) Shift from grants ($74m) to guarantees ($1.95b); (3) Adaptation to Ukraine's evolving needs (e.g., pension costs, medical wages). Programme design allowed for rapid disbursement in response to fiscal shocks.
adaptive_management_examples: Transition from FREE to UESP to align with G7's long-term IMF-backed strategy.
Adjustment of guarantee tranches to match Ukraine's priority expenditures (e.g., 58% of fourth guarantee allocated to pensions/medical wages).
Integration of programme management cycles for FREE and UESP to streamline oversight.

main_implementation_challenges: Operating in an active warzone with high uncertainty and volatile fiscal needs.
Dependence on World Bank's implementation with limited UK control over output design.
Need to balance emergency response with long-term sustainability (e.g., debt repayment risks).
Coordinating with multiple donors (G7, IMF, EU) to avoid duplication and ensure complementarity.
external_factors_impact: Russia's full-scale invasion (February 2022) created a fiscal shock requiring $29.2b (2022) and $39.9b (2023) in donor assistance (~1/3 of Ukraine's government expenditure).
Prolonged war extended Ukraine's reliance on external support beyond initial emergency phase, necessitating shift to multi-year IMF programme.
Inflation and currency fluctuations (UAH depreciation) increased cost of public sector wages/pensions, requiring larger disbursements.
contextual_constraints_new: Ukraine's reduced access to international capital markets due to war risks.
Domestic revenue collapse (e.g., tax collection disruptions in conflict zones).
Need to prioritize military spending while maintaining civil servant salaries/social protection.
Uncertainty over post-war reconstruction financing and debt sustainability.
partner_relationship_issues: No significant issues reported; World Bank's PEACE project exceeded targets (e.g., 93% non-security staff paid on time, 99.4% pensions disbursed).
UK's role as guarantor limited direct engagement with GoU, relying on World Bank as intermediary.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoU's administrative capacity strained by war (e.g., maintaining payroll systems in conflict-affected regions).
World Bank's need to scale up monitoring for $25.5b PEACE disbursements across Ukraine.
UK's limited in-country presence required reliance on remote oversight and World Bank reporting.
risk_materialization: Major risk of economic collapse mitigated by donor coordination (G7 financing assurances).
Risk of public sector collapse addressed through timely salary/pension disbursements (e.g., 28.3% of Additional Financing 5 supported by UK guarantees).
Exchange rate volatility managed through IBRD's lending mechanisms.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Initial £74m grant fully disbursed via MDTF in March-April 2022.
$1.95b in guarantees facilitated $25.5b PEACE disbursements (UK's fourth guarantee alone supported $500m in 2023).
Disbursements aligned with GoU's priority expenditures: 59.8% ($298.8m) to pensions, 40.2% ($200m) to medical wages in latest tranche.
value_for_money_assessment: High VFM achieved through leverage: $1.95b UK guarantees enabled $25.5b World Bank lending (13:1 ratio).
Cost-effective compared to direct grants (e.g., $74m grant vs. $1.95b guarantees for similar fiscal impact).
PEACE's administrative costs absorbed by World Bank, reducing UK's overhead.
financial_management_quality: World Bank's financial management rated highly (timely disbursements, transparent reporting via ISR).
UK's financial oversight focused on guarantee drawdowns, with no reported irregularities.
Exchange rate risks mitigated by IBRD's currency hedging mechanisms.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Guarantee model reduced UK's upfront costs while amplifying impact (e.g., 28.3% of Additional Financing 5 funded by UK's $500m guarantee).
PEACE's reimbursement mechanism ensured funds reached intended beneficiaries (e.g., 99.4% pension payments on time).
co_funding_materialization: G7 donors provided complementary financing assurances, reducing UK's standalone exposure.
IMF's Extended Fund Facility ($39.9b in 2023) operated in parallel, creating a layered support structure.
currency_exchange_impacts: UAH depreciation increased local currency value of disbursements, partially offsetting inflationary pressures on wages/pensions.
IBRD's lending in USD provided stability amid UAH volatility.

key_delivery_lessons: Guarantee mechanisms are highly effective for scaling fiscal support in crisis contexts (13:1 leverage ratio achieved).
Reliance on IFIs (e.g., World Bank) enables rapid deployment but limits donor control over output design.
Emergency programmes require clear exit strategies (e.g., FREE's transition to UESP).
successful_delivery_practices: Use of tranched guarantees allowed phased disbursements aligned with GoU's cash flow needs.
Combining grant and guarantee instruments provided flexibility to respond to evolving crises.
Alignment with G7/IMF frameworks ensured coordination and reduced duplication.
management_adaptations_made: Consolidated programme management cycles for FREE and UESP to reduce administrative burden.
Shifted review timelines to April to align with Ukraine's fiscal year and loan tenors.
Enhanced risk monitoring to reflect prolonged war context (e.g., debt sustainability risks).
innovations_attempted: Pioneered use of guarantees to extend IBRD's lending capacity in active conflict zone.
Integrated fiscal support with signals of international backing to stabilize markets.
Explored linking fiscal assistance to technical support (e.g., public financial management) in UESP design.
previous_recommendations_progress: Implemented recommendation to transition from emergency (FREE) to structured (UESP) support.
Adopted combined management cycles for related programmes (FREE/UESP).
Strengthened coordination with G7 partners via IMF financing assurances.
forward_recommendations: Continue fiscal assistance as core UK strategy, given Ukraine's persistent financing gap.
Pursue Ukraine's self-sufficiency alongside fiscal support (e.g., domestic revenue mobilization).
Explore adding light conditionality to future guarantees to enhance development impact (e.g., PFM reforms).
Integrate technical assistance with fiscal support to build GoU capacity (e.g., tax administration).
Monitor debt sustainability risks as guarantees mature (first repayments due post-2026).
risk_management_effectiveness: Major risks (economic collapse, public sector failure) were mitigated through timely disbursements.
G7 financing assurances reduced systemic risks (e.g., IMF default contingencies).
Limited direct UK risk exposure due to World Bank's intermediary role and IBRD's preferred creditor status.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 28.3% of Additional Financing 5 ($1.77b) supported by UK's fourth guarantee, benefiting:

beneficiaries_reached_actual.pensions: $298.8m (59.8% of tranche) reaching ~11m pensioners (99.4% paid on time).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.medical_wages: $200m (40.2% of tranche) for healthcare workers in conflict-affected regions.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.public_sector: 93% of non-security staff salaries disbursed on time (e.g., teachers, administrators).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.social_protection: Social assistance payments maintained for vulnerable groups (e.g., IDPs).

beneficiaries_reached_actual: PEACE project reached 24m Ukrainians (58% of population) via essential services since 2022.
policy_influence_achieved: UK's guarantees influenced G7's shift to multi-year IMF-backed support (4-year Extended Fund Facility).
Signalled international confidence in Ukraine's fiscal management, stabilizing sovereign borrowing costs.
Contributed to IMF's decision to provide $39.9b in 2023, citing donor coordination as a key factor.
capacity_building_results: Indirect capacity support via sustained public sector operations (e.g., tax collection, payroll systems).
World Bank's LCU report noted improved GoU resilience in maintaining core functions despite war.
Limited direct UK capacity-building; potential for UESP to integrate technical assistance.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Stabilized UAH exchange rate by signalling long-term donor commitment.
Positive: Reduced brain drain by ensuring public sector wage continuity.
Negative: Risk of debt dependency if guarantees are not paired with economic reforms (addressed in UESP).
scalability_evidence: PEACE model demonstrated scalability from $74m grants to $25.5b disbursements via guarantees.
G7 adoption of similar guarantee structures for Ukraine suggests replicability.
Potential to apply model to other conflict-affected middle-income countries (e.g., Moldova).

continuation_rationale: FREE's emergency objectives achieved (prevented economic collapse, maintained public services).
Ukraine's needs evolved to require predictable, multi-year support (addressed by UESP).
G7/IMF framework provides more sustainable financing architecture for prolonged war.
delivery_model_sustainability: Short-term: High (UESP builds on FREE's mechanisms with stronger donor coordination).
Long-term: Medium (dependent on Ukraine's post-war recovery and debt management).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Transition all remaining FREE activities to UESP by 2025.
Integrate light conditionality in UESP to link fiscal support with reforms (e.g., anti-corruption, PFM).
Explore blending guarantees with technical assistance to enhance impact.
Monitor debt sustainability metrics as guarantee repayments commence post-2026.

output_1.title: Improved assurance processes and increased accountability

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: FCDO provides unearmarked resources to IFRC/BRC (vs. original business case’s potentially more earmarked approach), with £9m unearmarked funding in 2023 keeping UK as IFRC’s leading donor of Regular Resources. Emphasis on monitoring reforms (e.g., PSEAH, AAP) rather than direct programme implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IFRC: Mixed performance—87% of indicators met/exceeded (vs. 81% in 2022), but fewer indicators *exceeded* targets (e.g., financial transparency declined: 67/90 National Societies submitted audits vs. 73 in 2022). BRC: 100% of 15 indicators met/exceeded, with 33% substantially exceeded. IFRC’s influence over National Societies remains inconsistent, particularly in high-risk contexts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO remains a key member of IFRC’s Donor Advisory Group (DAG), using this platform to encourage reforms. IFRC’s Secretariat reduced spending on employee benefits, logistics, and consultancy, demonstrating cost discipline. Governance challenges persist in enforcing National Society compliance (e.g., statutory revisions, audits).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: IFRC’s coordination of 191 National Societies is strengthened by unearmarked funding, enabling rapid surge deployments (e.g., 36 CEA-focused staff in 2023 vs. 25 target) and DREF activations. However, regional disparities in accountability (e.g., Integrity Lines: 30/45 target) highlight coordination gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: IFRC procured CHF 230m+ in goods/services (40% via framework agreements), improving efficiency. BRC focused on capacity-building for National Societies in cash/voucher assistance (CVA) and anticipatory action (AA), reducing direct implementation costs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight on PSEAH and financial assurance due to underperformance (e.g., audits, Integrity Lines). FCDO increased engagement via DAG and targeted recommendations (e.g., Investment Framework for National Society Development).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme flexibility used to reallocate resources to high-priority areas (e.g., Morocco earthquake response, PSEA policy support). Adaptive management seen in revised CEA Global Strategy (2023–2025) and DREF AA pillar expansion.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised CEA Global Strategy to address accountability gaps in National Societies.
DREF Anticipatory Action (AA) pillar expansion to pre-position resources, reducing response costs.
Targeted support for 15 additional National Societies to implement PSEA policies in 2023.
Shift to monitoring progress in ‘priority contexts’ for National Society development, per FCDO-IFRC agreement.

main_implementation_challenges: Enforcing financial transparency: Only 67/90 National Societies submitted audited statements (down from 73 in 2022), citing cost barriers and low prioritisation.
Slow progress on Integrity Lines: 30/45 National Societies implemented hotlines/case management systems (missed for 2 consecutive years).
Inconsistent National Society compliance with PSEA policies (89/95 target) and statutory revisions (2024 pledge deemed overly ambitious).
Regional disparities in safeguarding and accountability mechanisms.
external_factors_impact: Global humanitarian crises (e.g., Morocco earthquake, Malawi floods) diverted resources but also demonstrated the value of anticipatory action (AA) and surge capacity.
Inflation/currency fluctuations (not explicitly quantified) may have affected procurement costs (CHF 230m spent in 2023).
Political instability in some National Society contexts hindered governance reforms.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-expected resistance from National Societies to standardised governance (e.g., statute revisions, audits).
Limited IFRC influence in high-risk contexts where humanitarian needs are acute but compliance is low.
Capacity constraints in National Societies to implement PSEA Action Plans (97 met target, but unclear if high-risk areas were prioritised).
partner_relationship_issues: IFRC’s ability to enforce standards on National Societies is limited by their autonomous status, requiring negotiation over mandates.
BRC’s direct delivery model contrasts with IFRC’s federated approach, creating tensions in accountability expectations.
Delays in clarifying which National Societies’ PSEA progress was driven by UNICEF partnerships vs. IFRC support.
capacity_constraints_emerged: National Societies lack resources for annual audits (cost cited as barrier) and PSEA implementation (e.g., 47 have policies, but only 30 have Integrity Lines).
IFRC Secretariat’s reduced spending on logistics/consultancy suggests internal capacity strains.
Slow uptake of CEA (Community Engagement and Accountability) mechanisms in some regions despite global strategy.
risk_materialization: Financial transparency risks materialized (audit submission decline).
PSEAH risks persisted due to slow policy adoption in high-risk National Societies.
Operational risks in surge deployments (e.g., Morocco earthquake) mitigated by pre-positioned DREF resources.

budget_execution_vs_plan.IFRC: Underspent on employee benefits, relief supplies, and consultancy (proportion of expenditure reduced). Procurement efficiency improved via framework agreements (40% of CHF 230m spend).
budget_execution_vs_plan.BRC: No significant deviations reported; 100% of financial indicators met/exceeded.
budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: On track, with cost savings in logistics and administration offsetting underperformance in National Society audits.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: IFRC reduced spending on non-programmatic costs (e.g., vehicles, storage). BRC leveraged volunteer networks (16m globally) to minimise deployment costs.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Cash/voucher assistance (CVA) increased to 47% of humanitarian aid (target: 50% by 2025), improving cost-efficiency. DREF Anticipatory Action reduced emergency response costs via pre-positioning.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: IFRC reached 46.8m people in protection/gender programming (vs. 31.5m target), but financial transparency lagged. BRC achieved all targets with 33% substantially exceeded.
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: Original VfM proposition focused on coordination costs and logistics; actual performance shows higher efficiency in procurement (framework agreements) but lower-than-planned influence over National Society governance.

financial_management_quality.IFRC: Mixed: Strong in procurement (CHF 146m quality-assured at field level) but weak in enforcing National Society audits. Secretariat demonstrated cost discipline.
financial_management_quality.BRC: Consistently high, with no reported issues.
financial_management_quality.overall: Adequate, with room for improvement in financial assurance mechanisms.

metrics: 47% of IFRC humanitarian aid delivered via cash assistance (up ~20% since 2021).
DREF AA interventions reduced emergency costs via early action.
Framework agreements covered 40% of procurement, expected to grow.
cost_efficiency_achieved.vs_plan: Exceeded in procurement efficiency; lagged in National Society financial compliance.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not explicitly mentioned; IFRC’s Regular Resources (unearmarked) relied on FCDO’s £9m leadership donation in 2023.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Procurement in CHF (CHF 230m spent) suggests exposure to GBP/CHF fluctuations, but no quantitative impact reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Unearmarked funding enhances IFRC’s flexibility but requires stronger accountability mechanisms to ensure National Society compliance.
National Society development progress is not fully captured by logframe indicators; contextual monitoring is needed.
PSEA and financial assurance reforms require tailored approaches for high-risk contexts (one-size-fits-all standards are ineffective).
Anticipatory Action (AA) and CVA demonstrate higher cost-efficiency than traditional response models.
successful_delivery_practices: DREF’s AA pillar: Pre-positioned resources reduced response costs and improved timeliness.
BRC’s training for National Societies in CVA preparedness enhanced local capacity.
IFRC’s CEA Global Strategy (2023–2025) provided a clear framework for accountability progress.
Framework agreements improved procurement speed and quality assurance.
management_adaptations_made: FCDO-IFRC agreement to monitor progress in ‘priority contexts’ for National Society development.
Revised PSEA targets to focus on high-risk areas (e.g., 15 additional National Societies in 2023).
Investment Framework for National Society Development to prioritise resource allocation.
Increased oversight on Integrity Lines and audits via DAG engagement.
innovations_attempted: Expansion of DREF AA protocols to new crises (e.g., Morocco earthquake).
Digital tools for PSEA reporting (Integrity Lines) in 30 National Societies.
CEA mechanisms integrated into 90 National Societies’ programmes (up from 85 in 2022).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on PSEA standards (47 policies implemented, but Integrity Lines lag).
Governance reforms (statute revisions) delayed; 2024 target deemed unrealistic.
Safeguarding Pledge for 2024 International Conference (40 signatories targeted).
forward_recommendations: Strengthen PSEA minimum standards with enforceable mechanisms for high-risk National Societies.
Leverage Investment Framework to prioritise resources in contexts with highest humanitarian need/risks.
Reassess National Society statute revision goals for feasibility; focus on incremental compliance.
Enhance transparency in reporting which National Societies meet standards (e.g., PSEA, audits) via disaggregated data.
Scale up anticipatory action (AA) and CVA to improve cost-efficiency further.

strengths: DREF’s AA pillar mitigated operational risks in rapid responses (e.g., Morocco).
PSEA Action Plans implemented in 97 National Societies (up from 66 in 2022).
FCDO’s DAG membership enabled proactive risk oversight.
weaknesses: Financial transparency risks persisted (audit submissions declined).
Slow progress on Integrity Lines (30/45 target) indicates gaps in safeguarding risk management.
Lack of common minimum standards for National Societies limits donor confidence.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.IFRC: 46.8 million reached in protection/gender programming (vs. 31.5m target).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.BRC: All targets met/exceeded (specific numbers not detailed).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.overall: Exceeded quantitative targets, but qualitative gaps remain in high-risk contexts.

policy_influence_achieved: IFRC’s Safeguarding Pledge to be presented at 2024 International Conference (target: 40 National Society signatories).
Advancement of AAP (Accountability to Affected Populations) and CEA standards across 90 National Societies.
DREF’s AA model influenced broader humanitarian sector practices in anticipatory financing.
capacity_building_results: 90 National Societies incorporated CEA mechanisms (up from 85 in 2022).
47 National Societies implemented PSEA policies (15 new in 2023); 97 have PSEA Action Plans.
BRC’s CVA training enhanced local response capabilities in multiple countries.
IFRC’s PER framework and CBF initiatives strengthened preparedness, though progress is uneven.

positive: Unearmarked funding allowed IFRC to respond flexibly to unanticipated crises (e.g., Morocco earthquake).
DREF’s AA interventions reduced long-term recovery costs in some contexts.
negative: Inconsistent enforcement of standards may erode trust in National Societies’ accountability.
Focus on high-profile crises (e.g., earthquakes) may divert attention from chronic underfunded contexts.

scalability_evidence: DREF’s AA pillar scaled to new crises (e.g., Equatorial Guinea, Dominican Republic) with measurable efficiency gains.
CVA delivery model (47% of IFRC aid) is replicable across other National Societies.
CEA Global Strategy provides a scalable framework for accountability, but requires tailored local adaptation.

continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with FCDO’s Humanitarian Framework priorities (early action, localisation, PSEAH).
Proven impact in protection/gender programming (46.8m reached) and anticipatory action.
BRC’s consistent high performance and IFRC’s progress in key areas (e.g., PSEA, CEA) justify continued investment.
Unearmarked funding model enables flexible responses to emerging crises.

strengths: IFRC’s federated structure and BRC’s technical expertise complement each other.
DREF’s AA and CVA models demonstrate cost-efficiency and scalability.
FCDO’s leadership in unearmarked funding enhances IFRC’s coordination role.
risks: Persistent gaps in National Society financial transparency and PSEA compliance.
Over-reliance on FCDO’s unearmarked funding may limit diversified donor base.
Governance reforms require long-term commitment beyond current AMP period.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (with caveats on National Society accountability)
planned_adaptations_future: Targeted support for high-priority National Societies via Investment Framework.
Stronger enforcement of PSEA and financial assurance standards in high-risk contexts.
Expanded use of anticipatory action and CVA to improve efficiency.
Disaggregated reporting on National Society progress to inform resource allocation.
Revised governance reform timelines to reflect contextual realities.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Nigeria Portfolio Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (PMEL) Programme

output_1.title: Timely, relevant and accessible outcome-level knowledge products produced to support HMG Nigeria learning

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The Data component was dropped as it became misleading with a false assumption of data generation as a discrete activity. The programme now operates through two unified components: Evidence and Learning, integrating data into both descriptive and evaluative analysis.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Oxford Policy Management Limited (OPML) performed well, consolidating its position and building relations with primary beneficiaries. The quality, delivery, and timeliness scored 5 out of 6 in contract KPIs. Feedback from beneficiaries (Programme and Block SROs) was largely positive regarding work products, issue understanding, and delivery approach.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: No changes to the Senior Responsible Officer (SRO), Programme Responsible Owner (PRO), Technical Adviser (Statistics Adviser), and Programme Manager roles. Bi-weekly meetings between FCDO and PMEL facilitated regular check-ins on activities, financials, stakeholder management, and emerging risks. The SRO and Statistics Adviser provided critical support in navigating internal organisational nuances.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: PMEL extended buy-in across teams, including senior leadership, through regular engagement mechanisms like the Delivery Board and Country Strategy Board. All blocks are now engaged, positioning PMEL to respond effectively to strategic pivots.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintained bi-weekly meetings with PMEL, ensuring consistent oversight. The oversight was described as strong, contributing to the programme’s successes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: PMEL demonstrated high agility in responding to knowledge product requests and aligning with HMG Nigeria’s evolving priorities. The programme adapted by merging data and evidence components into a unified approach.
adaptive_management_examples: Responded to internal organisational changes by refocusing efforts on areas of interest highlighted by the SRO and Statistics Adviser.
Adjusted the log frame to reflect the merged Evidence component, better integrating data into analysis.
Extended engagement in national multi-stakeholder networks and international learning fora beyond original plans.

main_implementation_challenges: Internal organisational changes within HMG Nigeria affected the completion of outcome case studies, though demand-led studies exceeded targets.
Low conversion rate from evidence products to lesson-learning sessions, risking limited circulation and use of reports.
Need for deliberate planning to link evidence to learning in a busy country office environment.
external_factors_impact: FCDO reforms in January 2025 realigned priorities toward economic growth and irregular migration, influencing programme trajectory.

US executive order freezing foreign aid for 90 days (January 2025) led to termination of contracts globally, indirectly affecting the development sector, including potential impacts on PMEL’s operating context.
contextual_constraints_new: Significant turnover expected among senior leadership and block leads in HMG Nigeria, requiring early engagement with successors to maintain buy-in.
Evolving FCDO global priorities (e.g., Growth, Security, Migration) necessitate continuous alignment of PMEL’s resources and focus.
risk_materialization: Organisational changes within HMG Nigeria disrupted the completion of planned outcome case studies, though mitigated by strong demand-led performance.

financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Strong value for money demonstrated through exceeding milestone targets (e.g., 11 demand-led studies delivered vs. 5 planned) while maintaining high quality (average score 3.6/4). The programme’s agility and responsiveness enhanced its cost-efficiency by aligning resources with HMG Nigeria’s evolving priorities.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management was strong, as reflected in the overall programme score of A+. Bi-weekly check-ins between FCDO and PMEL included financial oversight, ensuring transparency and accountability.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was high, supported by the programme’s ability to exceed output targets (e.g., demand-led studies) without additional resources, leveraging existing consultant pools effectively.

key_delivery_lessons: Agility and responsiveness to HMG Nigeria’s priorities were critical to success, enabled by regular insights from the SRO and Statistics Adviser.
Visibility, ease of contracting, and quality of service boosted PMEL’s reputation as a trusted provider of evidence and analysis.
Combining international and national expertise strengthened contextual relevance and delivery effectiveness.
Deliberate planning is required to improve the conversion of evidence products into learning sessions to avoid underutilisation of reports.
successful_delivery_practices: Bi-weekly check-ins with FCDO facilitated proactive management of activities, financials, and risks.
Leveraging both international and national consultants ensured a balance of global best practices and local contextual understanding.
High-profile exposure at Delivery Board and Country Strategy Board sessions enhanced PMEL’s credibility and uptake of its outputs.
management_adaptations_made: Revised the log frame to merge data and evidence into a unified Evidence component, reflecting the programme’s evolved approach.
Expanded engagement in national and international learning networks beyond the original scope.
innovations_attempted: Developed outcome case studies using contribution analysis to assess HMG Nigeria’s role in achieving outcomes, which informed high-level decisions and international events.
Pilot dissemination strategies (e.g., mini-workshops) to strengthen the evidence-to-policy pathway, though further formalisation is recommended.
forward_recommendations: Ensure alignment with the emerging Business and Country Plan to respond to FCDO’s evolving global priorities.
Proactively engage incoming senior leadership and block leads to maintain high levels of buy-in.
Build dissemination and outcome feedback into Terms of Reference for evidence products to strengthen learning pathways.
Formalise mechanisms to convert evidence products into lesson-learning sessions to maximise impact.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective risk management was demonstrated through adaptive responses to internal organisational changes (e.g., refocusing efforts when outcome case study targets were at risk) and proactive engagement with stakeholders to mitigate turnover risks.

policy_influence_achieved: Outcome case studies (e.g., PERL programme’s "Thinking and Working Politically" approach) informed high-level decisions and were presented at international events, indicating policy influence.
Demand-led studies (e.g., on PERL’s Value for Money) prompted follow-up analyses, demonstrating uptake of evidence in programming.
capacity_building_results: Enhanced capacity within HMG Nigeria to use evidence for adaptive strategies, as reflected in the programme’s contribution to learning resources and strategic discussions.
Strengthened multi-stakeholder engagement at national and international levels, broadening the application of learning.
unintended_consequences: Positive: PMEL’s reputation as a "useful" provider of evidence led to increased demand for its services, extending its influence beyond initial expectations.
Negative: Risk of reports remaining underutilised if dissemination and learning sessions are not formalised.
scalability_evidence: The programme’s adaptive management model and successful integration of international/national expertise suggest potential for scalability in similar contexts.
Lessons on linking evidence to learning could be applied to other FCDO programmes seeking to improve policy uptake.

continuation_rationale: The programme has exceeded performance expectations (A+ rating) and demonstrated strong alignment with FCDO’s evolving priorities.
High demand for PMEL’s services across HMG Nigeria, including senior leadership buy-in, justifies continuation.
The programme’s agility and adaptive management position it well to respond to future strategic shifts.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High; the unified Evidence and Learning components have proven effective, and the model is adaptable to changing contexts.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High; reflected in the A+ score, positive stakeholder feedback, and increased visibility at strategic boards.
planned_adaptations_future: Formalise dissemination strategies to improve evidence-to-learning conversion.
Strengthen engagement with new senior leadership to maintain alignment with FCDO priorities.
Further integrate learning into national and international networks to maximise impact.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme transferred from BEIS to FCDO in April 2022; implementation of a 6-month Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) to address blended finance delivery challenges; strengthened governance and management arrangements through revised Management Agreement signed March 2023.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IDB Group (IADB and IDB Invest) performance improved significantly following the PIP, particularly in blended finance delivery. By September 2022, FCDO approved $100m potential investment envelopes and IDB Invest Board approved four blended finance projects totaling $40m UKSIP financing.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Revised Management Arrangement signed (16 March 2023) formalized strengthened FCDO-IDB engagement, including regular (monthly/bi-monthly) coordination with UK embassies in target countries. FCDO now more actively involved in programme oversight and strategic direction.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved coordination between FCDO and IDB post-PIP, with structured dialogue and clear performance milestones. Embassy engagement enhanced to align programme activities with UK diplomatic priorities in-country.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight intensity post-PIP, with FCDO taking a more hands-on role in monitoring blended finance delivery and technical assistance progress. Regular performance reviews introduced as part of revised Management Arrangement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme flexibility utilized to implement the PIP and adapt management structures. Two-year no-cost extension (to December 2024) approved to allow completion of activities, reflecting adaptive response to delivery challenges.
adaptive_management_examples: Implementation of 6-month Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) to address blended finance bottlenecks, resulting in approval of $100m investment envelopes and $40m in blended finance projects.
Addition of Output 1.3 (engagement events with SIP partner governments) mid-year to reflect strengthened political engagement priorities.
Revised Management Arrangement (March 2023) incorporating lessons from PIP, including clearer roles for FCDO embassies and improved MEL processes.

main_implementation_challenges: Blended finance delivery delays prior to 2022, addressed through the PIP.
Coordination gaps between FCDO and IDB pre-2022, particularly around strategic alignment and embassy engagement.
Limited visibility of UKSIP’s technical assistance projects in public communications, reducing perceived UK impact in-country.
Need to better demonstrate transformational change and aggregate impact of interventions.
contextual_constraints_new: Transition from BEIS to FCDO management required adaptation of governance and reporting processes.
Rapid urbanization and industrial growth in target countries (Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Peru) created evolving demands for sustainable infrastructure solutions.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between FCDO and IDB on blended finance priorities, resolved through PIP.
Need for clearer communication between IDB and UK embassies on project milestones and external engagement opportunities.
risk_materialization: Blended finance delivery risks materialized pre-2022, prompting the PIP intervention.
Risk of limited UK visibility in partner countries due to dispersed project communications, partially mitigated by revised Management Arrangement.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; financial reflows from UKSIP investments have begun. Programme secured a two-year no-cost extension to December 2024 to ensure full delivery of results.
value_for_money_assessment: Improved VFM demonstrated through PIP-driven efficiencies in blended finance delivery (e.g., $40m approved in 2022 vs prior delays).
Potential for further VFM gains through strategic use of investment reflows to address climate financing gaps.
Need to better articulate aggregate transformational impact of UKSIP interventions to justify ICF spend.
financial_management_quality: Strengthened post-PIP, with clearer financial oversight by FCDO and improved reporting by IDB.
Revised Management Arrangement (March 2023) includes enhanced financial monitoring mechanisms.

key_delivery_lessons: Structured performance improvement plans (e.g., PIP) can effectively address delivery bottlenecks in complex multilateral programmes.
Regular, high-level dialogue between FCDO and implementing partners (IDB) is critical for aligning priorities and resolving blockages.
Proactive embassy engagement enhances programme visibility and supports UK diplomatic objectives in partner countries.
Flexibility in programme design (e.g., no-cost extensions, output adjustments) enables adaptive management in response to challenges.
successful_delivery_practices: Thematic investment envelopes ($100m approved in 2022) streamlined blended finance delivery.
Technical assistance projects with clear bankability outcomes (e.g., algorithms for energy grid connections in Colombia) demonstrated high impact.
Monthly/bi-monthly coordination with UK embassies improved in-country alignment and external communications.
management_adaptations_made: Revised Management Arrangement (March 2023) formalizing strengthened governance, MEL processes, and embassy engagement.
Introduction of Output 1.3 (engagement events) to track political dialogue and NDC ambition.
Earlier completion of Annual Reviews (e.g., 2022 AR completed by October 2023) to enable timely feedback.
innovations_attempted: Algorithm to optimize energy generation connection capacity in Colombia (Output 1.2), replicable in other markets.
Blended finance thematic envelopes to accelerate private sector investment in low-carbon infrastructure.
Integration of GESI (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) co-benefits into climate finance projects, with proportionate reporting requirements.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Strengthen FCDO-IDB engagement and update Management Arrangement.
Bring forward Annual Review completion date.
Finalize UKSIP evaluation plan.
Agree two-year no-cost extension.

forward_recommendations: Develop a strategy for using financial reflows to maximize climate impact in high-priority sectors/regions.
Enhance communications to host countries and markets to showcase UKSIP’s transformational change and ODA impact.
Strengthen coordination with other UK ICF programmes (e.g., UKPACT, UCAP) to improve synergies and avoid duplication.
Consolidate public information on UKSIP into a single, accessible platform to improve transparency.
Systematically integrate GESI co-benefits into project design and monitoring, while maintaining focus on climate finance mobilization.
risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management improved post-PIP, with proactive identification and mitigation of blended finance delivery risks.
Residual risks include need for clearer demonstration of aggregate impact and sustainability of market changes post-2024.
Revised Management Arrangement includes stronger risk reporting and escalation protocols.

examples: National Sustainable and Competitiveness Infrastructure Plan supported.
Infrastructure quality gaps assessed for transport, electricity, water, and sanitation sectors (Ministries of Environment and Economy).
Pre-feasibility studies for electric ferries (Santa Catarina, Florianópolis).
Infrastructure Investments Monitor adopted by Ministry of Finance.
Technical seminars on energy investment (Bank of Brazil).
Algorithm implemented to optimize energy generation connection capacity (Mining and Energy Planning Unit, Ministry of Mines).
6 engagement events on electric vehicle infrastructure and sustainable transport.
Study for Metrobus fleet replacement to reduce emissions (Mexico City Mobility Ministry).
Support for metrobus fare collection system tendering.

policy_influence_achieved: Adoption of sustainable infrastructure policies/regulations in all four countries (e.g., Peru’s National Infrastructure Plan, Colombia’s energy grid algorithms).
Methodologies for bankable low-carbon projects (Output 2) influencing private sector investment pipelines.
Increased NDC ambition through technical assistance (e.g., modal shift workshops in Brazil).
capacity_building_results: Public sector institutions (e.g., Ministries of Finance/Environment in Peru, Brazil) adopted UKSIP-supported tools for infrastructure planning.
Private sector capacity enhanced through 24 cumulative technical advisory engagements (Output 2.2) improving project bankability.
Knowledge-sharing events (e.g., 8+ workshops in Colombia/Brazil) built local expertise in sustainable transport and energy.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Strengthened UK diplomatic influence in target countries by linking climate policy dialogues with tangible technical assistance.
Negative: Limited visibility of UK’s role in early years due to dispersed project communications (being addressed through revised comms plan).
scalability_evidence: Colombia’s energy grid algorithm (Output 1.2) is replicable in other markets facing similar connection capacity challenges.
Blended finance thematic envelopes ($100m approved) demonstrate scalability of de-risking model for private investment.
Technical assistance methodologies (e.g., pre-feasibility studies for electric ferries) adaptable to other urban transport contexts.

continuation_rationale: Successful completion of PIP addressed critical delivery challenges, particularly in blended finance.
Strong 2022 performance (A+ score) and improved risk rating (Minor) justify continuation.
Two-year no-cost extension to December 2024 approved to ensure completion of active portfolio and achievement of outcomes.
Programme aligns with UK’s updated International Development Strategy (May 2022) priorities on climate finance and sustainable infrastructure.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model (FCDO-IDB partnership) is sustainable for extension period, with strengthened governance post-PIP.
Long-term sustainability depends on market uptake of blended finance instruments and host country ownership of policy reforms.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Strategic use of investment reflows to address climate financing gaps.
Enhanced coordination with other UK ICF programmes (e.g., UKPACT) to maximize impact.
Development of an evidenced narrative on UKSIP’s transformational change for external communications.
Systematic integration of GESI co-benefits into project design and monitoring.
