programme_metadata.programme_title: Global Health Security R&D Programme

output_1.title: Accelerated development by CEPI of new vaccines and platform technologies for diseases of epidemic and pandemic potential, ensuring equitable access for LMICs through an end-to-end approach

output_2.title: Progress made on development of accessible new products and innovations, including clinical trials and studies, and generation of new evidence and knowledge to inform policy and programmes

output_4.title: Global and UK epidemic research is co-ordinated and collaborative action facilitated, both during and between outbreaks, contributing to strengthened prevention, preparedness and response by LMICs

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The planned standalone Centre of Research for emerging infectious diseases was integrated into FCDO’s Science in Emergencies Centre of Expertise (SECE) to leverage synergies and reduce transaction costs. This shift was agreed with FCDO CSA during the review period.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: CEPI exceeded targets for preclinical activities and clinical trials (e.g., Chikungunya licensure achieved, Lassa and MERS Phase II progress). New partnerships were established with Institut Pasteur de Dakar and ISARIC, demonstrating strong collaboration. CEPI’s coordination of the Global Pandemic Preparedness Summit and launch of the Bio Funders Compact highlighted effective multi-stakeholder engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Cross-HMG coordination was strengthened through regular Strategic Response Funders Forum meetings (chaired by DHSC/FCDO) and UK international funder engagements. FCDO led the UK’s mpox and Marburg R&D responses, demonstrating adaptive governance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination was demonstrated through: 1) CEPI’s Global Pandemic Preparedness Summit (Brazil, July 2024), 2) Launch of the WHO viral families R&D prioritisation framework, 3) CEPI-ISARIC MOU for clinical trials, 4) FCDO’s leadership in xHMG funder groups, and 5) Rapid mobilization of R&D responses for mpox (DRC) and Marburg (Rwanda).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for new partnerships (e.g., Institut Pasteur de Dakar, ISARIC) was completed efficiently, with proposals agreed and strategic approaches drafted. A PDP call was launched in December 2023 and completed by December 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified through regular xHMG meetings, FCDO-led outbreak response coordination, and active tracking of CEPI’s portfolio (e.g., publications, LMIC/female authorship, project closures). CEPI’s Results Framework is being reformulated to include clearer "go/no-go" decision indicators by November 2025.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme’s built-in agility enabled rapid responses to Marburg and mpox outbreaks, including funding mobilization and coordination with DHSC/UKHSA. The shift of the Centre of Research into SECE demonstrated adaptive use of flexibility to optimize resources.
adaptive_management_examples: Integration of the Centre of Research into SECE to reduce costs and improve emergency response synergies.
Rapid mobilization of R&D funding for mpox (DRC) and Marburg (Rwanda) outbreaks, including multicountry studies led by Africa-based consortia (e.g., MpoxRec).
Adjustment of CEPI’s 2.0 strategy to prioritize late-stage trial progression and equitable access planning, with recommendations for 3.0 strategy development in 2025.
Launch of the Bio Funders Compact to incorporate biosecurity into R&D funding processes.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in early-stage clinical trials for Lassa fever and MERS (though progress was made in 2024 to catch up).
Need to strengthen LMIC-led research capacity to bring vaccine development and manufacturing closer to outbreak sites (highlighted in a Lancet comment).
Balancing ambitious R&D timelines (e.g., 100 Days Mission) with the complexities of equitable access planning and late-stage trial coordination.
external_factors_impact: Emergence of new outbreaks (Marburg in Rwanda, mpox in DRC) required rapid reallocation of resources and coordination efforts.

Climate change and environmental factors increasing the risk of diseases like Lassa fever, underscoring the urgency of vaccine development (e.g., modelling showed potential to save 3,300 lives over 10 years in West Africa).
Global geopolitical and economic pressures affecting supply chains and partnership dynamics (e.g., need for biosecurity safeguards in the Bio Funders Compact).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need to integrate biosecurity considerations into R&D funding (addressed via the Bio Funders Compact).
Higher-than-expected demand for LMIC-led research partnerships, leading to accelerated procurement (e.g., Institut Pasteur de Dakar, ISARIC).
Regulatory and logistical challenges in multicountry clinical trials (e.g., MpoxRec studies in DRC, Nigeria, Cameroon).
partner_relationship_issues: CEPI’s partnership with LMIC institutions required additional focus on equitable relationship management, particularly for capacity-building across the R&D spectrum (recommendation for 2025).
Coordination between CEPI, ISARIC, and other PDPs (e.g., Fiocruz in Brazil) needed strengthening to align priorities for the 100 Days Mission.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited LMIC capacity for late-stage vaccine manufacturing and clinical trial execution, necessitating targeted investments (e.g., CEPI’s 3.0 strategy focus).
Gaps in preclinical model development for priority pathogens (e.g., only 3 of 5 milestones met for enabling science programmes).
Need for additional training and resources to support LMIC-led research (e.g., Lassa fever epidemiology studies in Nigeria).
risk_materialization: Delays in clinical trials for Lassa fever and MERS (partially mitigated by 2024 progress).
Risk of inequitable access to vaccines/tools (addressed via CEPI’s 100% access plan compliance and ongoing strategy refinements).
Operational risks in outbreak responses (e.g., Marburg in Rwanda) were managed through rapid R&D mobilization and cross-HMG coordination.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Cumulative spend as of 2024 is £57,086,367 against a full-life budget of £175 million. CEPI’s portfolio management improved, with active tracking of publications, LMIC/female authorship, and project closures. No significant underspends or overspends reported.

evidence: Modelling showed that a Lassa fever vaccine could save 3,300 lives and avert $128 million in societal costs over 10 years in West Africa (Nature study).
Ebola vaccination modelling suggested prophylactic vaccination could prevent ~90% of an outbreak’s economic impact.
Systematic review found COVID-19 vaccination was cost-effective in mitigating transmission in many countries.
PDP model (used by CEPI) projected to save 40.7 million lives and 2.83 billion DALYs by 2040, with a return of $405 for every $1 invested (Global Health Impact evaluation).
value_for_money_assessment.assessment: High. The programme’s partnership approach and risk-pooling model demonstrate strong VfM, with evidence of significant health and economic returns.

evidence: Integration of the Centre of Research into SECE reduced transaction costs by avoiding a standalone structure.
CEPI’s active tracking of project closures and access plans improved resource allocation.
Leveraging existing platforms (e.g., ISARIC, PDPs) minimized duplication and maximized outputs (e.g., 5 studies underway, 21 publications in 2024).
value_for_money_assessment.assessment: High. Operational efficiencies were achieved through adaptive management and partnership synergies.

financial_management_quality.performance: CEPI now actively tracks publications (including LMIC/female authorship) and project closures, with plans to include these indicators in the Results Framework. Data provision to FCDO was timely and comprehensive.

No significant deviations from planned spending. CEPI’s reformulation of its Results Framework (due November 2025) will include clearer KPIs for "go/no-go" decisions and equitable access implementation.
CEPI provided data on access plans and publications but needs to improve narrative evidence for access plan implementation (recommendation for 2025).

cost_efficiency_achieved.efficiency: Costs were optimized through multicountry studies (e.g., MpoxRec in DRC/Nigeria/Cameroon) and leveraging existing platforms like ISARIC. The world’s first Marburg treatment trial and IMASOY plague trial were completed within budget.

Pooling resources with funders (Wellcome, BMGF, UKRI-MRC) reduced individual costs. For example, the ISARIC partnership through Oxford’s Pandemic Science Institute shared infrastructure and expertise.
Rapid mobilization for mpox and Marburg outbreaks demonstrated cost-efficient use of flexible funding, with coordinated responses avoiding duplication (e.g., FCDO-DHSC-UKHSA collaboration).

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialized. New partnerships (e.g., Institut Pasteur de Dakar, ISARIC) brought in co-funding from Wellcome and BMGF, but the full extent of planned co-funding is still being finalized (e.g., PDP call completed in December 2024).

key_delivery_lessons: LMIC-led research capacity must be prioritized to ensure sustainable and equitable R&D ecosystems. Current gaps risk delaying vaccine development and manufacturing near outbreak sites.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., rapid mobilization for mpox/Marburg) are critical for outbreak response but require pre-established partnerships and governance structures.
Cross-HMG coordination (e.g., xHMG Funders Forum) enhances VfM by aligning priorities and reducing duplication, but demands consistent high-level engagement.
Biosecurity considerations must be integrated into R&D funding early to mitigate risks of accidental or intentional misuse (addressed via the Bio Funders Compact).

successful_delivery_practices.practice: Integration of the Centre of Research into SECE
successful_delivery_practices.impact: Reduced transaction costs, improved emergency response synergies, and avoided duplication of efforts.
Enabled rapid progress on preclinical/clinical targets (e.g., Chikungunya licensure, Lassa/Nipah Phase II trials) and leveraged co-funding from Wellcome/BMGF.
Studies like MpoxRec (DRC/Nigeria/Cameroon) demonstrated cost efficiency and LMIC leadership in outbreak research.
The Global Pandemic Preparedness Summit (Brazil, 2024) reinvigorated momentum for the 100 Days Mission and launched the WHO viral families prioritisation framework.

management_adaptations_made.adaptation: Shift from standalone Centre of Research to SECE integration
management_adaptations_made.trigger: Recognized synergies with FCDO’s emergency response structures and cost savings.
Need for clearer KPIs on "go/no-go" decisions and equitable access (planned for November 2025).
Gaps identified in equitable relationship management and capacity building (recommendation for CEPI’s 3.0 strategy).

management_adaptations_made.adaptation: Inclusion of biosecurity in R&D funding
management_adaptations_made.trigger: Emerging risks of accidental/intentional misuse (addressed via the Bio Funders Compact).

innovations_attempted.description: Proof of concept completed for two pilot projects; antigen design started for 3 pathogens (poxviruses, arenaviruses, orthomyxoviridae). Aims to enable rapid response to Disease X.
Global initiative to incorporate biosecurity into bioscience research funding, safeguarding against misuse while accelerating R&D.
Co-developed at the Global Pandemic Preparedness Summit to guide R&D investments based on pathogen families rather than individual diseases.
MpoxRec consortium (Africa-led) and ISARIC’s dengue/Nipah studies demonstrated decentralized, collaborative research models.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Improve tracking of CEPI’s access plans and project closures
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Partially addressed. CEPI now tracks publications and closures but needs to enhance narrative evidence for access plan implementation (target: 2025).

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Strengthen LMIC partnerships
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Advanced. New partnerships established with Institut Pasteur de Dakar and ISARIC; CEPI’s 3.0 strategy will further prioritize equitable relationships.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Enhance cross-HMG coordination
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Fully addressed. Regular xHMG Funders Forum meetings and FCDO-led outbreak response coordination (e.g., mpox/Marburg) demonstrated improved collaboration.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: CEPI to prioritize late-stage trial progression in 2025
forward_recommendations.action: Strengthen relationships with multinational pharmaceutical corporations (MNCs) to advance candidates through Phase III and licensure.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Finalize nested logframe with clear KPIs
forward_recommendations.action: FCDO and CEPI to develop indicators for "go/no-go" decisions, down-selection of candidates, and equitable access by November 2025.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Clarify CEPI’s role in end-to-end vaccine development
forward_recommendations.action: Define "hand-offs" to other stakeholders (e.g., manufacturers, regulators) in the 3.0 strategy to ensure seamless progression from R&D to deployment.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Invest in LMIC R&D capacity
forward_recommendations.action: Prioritize capacity-building for vaccine development/manufacturing in LMICs, including training and infrastructure support (e.g., via Institut Pasteur de Dakar partnership).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Contribute to CEPI 3.0 strategy consultation
forward_recommendations.action: FCDO and DHSC to provide input on equitable access, biosecurity, and sustainability in 2025.

strengths: Rapid response to emerging outbreaks (mpox, Marburg) demonstrated effective risk mitigation through flexible funding and coordination.
Proactive adjustment of CEPI’s strategy to address delays in Lassa/MERS trials, with 2024 progress exceeding targets.
Integration of biosecurity risks via the Bio Funders Compact preempted potential misuse of R&D outputs.
weaknesses: Early-stage trial delays (Lassa, MERS) highlighted risks in ambitious timelines, though partially mitigated by 2024 catch-up efforts.
Equitable access risks persist; while 100% of CEPI-funded products have access plans, implementation narratives need strengthening (target: 2025).
Capacity constraints in LMICs remain a risk to sustainable R&D ecosystems, requiring long-term investment.
risk_management_effectiveness.overall_assessment: Effective. The programme demonstrated adaptive risk management, particularly in outbreak response and strategic adjustments. Ongoing risks (e.g., LMIC capacity, access implementation) are being addressed through 2025 recommendations.

direct: LMIC populations benefiting from CEPI’s vaccine pipeline (e.g., Chikungunya vaccine licensure in 2023, Lassa/MERS trials progressing).
Researchers and institutions in LMICs (e.g., Institut Pasteur de Dakar, ISARIC partners in Nigeria, DRC, Cameroon) involved in clinical trials and capacity-building.
Global health systems strengthened through WHO viral families prioritisation framework and 100 Days Mission coordination.
indirect: Potential 3,300 lives saved and $128 million in societal costs averted over 10 years via Lassa fever vaccine deployment (modelling evidence).
Up to 90% reduction in economic impact of Ebola outbreaks through prophylactic vaccination (modelling).
40.7 million lives projected to be saved by 2040 through PDP-model investments (Global Health Impact evaluation).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: Exceeded targets for preclinical activities (e.g., 4 viral families prioritized for vaccine libraries vs. original plan) and clinical trial progress (e.g., Chikungunya licensure achieved ahead of schedule). LMIC engagement targets were met or exceeded (e.g., 19% of CEPI publications with female lead authors, 4.8% with LMIC leads).

policy_influence_achieved.influence: Co-developed at the Global Pandemic Preparedness Summit (2024) to guide global R&D investments.
CEPI’s leadership in the G7 initiative accelerated progress toward reducing vaccine development timelines. The Brazil Summit (2024) reinvigorated global commitment.
Incorporated biosecurity into global R&D funding processes, setting a precedent for safeguarding life sciences research.
CEPI’s active participation shaped international agreements on equitable access and emergency vaccine supply (e.g., XVAX).

capacity_building_results.outcome: Proposal agreed (October 2024) to strengthen LMIC-led research on epidemic diseases, with focus on sustainable capacity.
Completed world’s largest Lassa fever study (ENABLE 1.0, Nigeria) and launched multicountry mpox studies, building LMIC clinical trial expertise.
Developed preclinical models for priority pathogens (e.g., Nipah, Lassa) and advanced international antibody standards, enhancing LMIC lab capabilities.
21 CEPI-supported publications in 2024, with 19% female lead authors and 4.8% LMIC leads, contributing to knowledge-sharing and workforce development.

unintended_consequences.description: The integration of the Centre of Research into SECE created unexpected synergies with FCDO’s broader emergency response mechanisms, improving cross-hazard coordination (e.g., climate, health, conflict).
unintended_consequences.evidence: Reduced transaction costs and enhanced multidisciplinary collaboration during Marburg/mpox responses.

unintended_consequences.description: CEPI’s focus on vaccine libraries for Disease X accelerated preclinical work on broad-spectrum platforms (e.g., mRNA-based mpox vaccine), which may have applications beyond the original scope.
unintended_consequences.evidence: Phase I/II trials initiated for mpox vaccine; antigen design started for 3 additional pathogen families.

unintended_consequences.description: Rapid mobilization for outbreaks (e.g., mpox, Marburg) occasionally diverted resources from long-term capacity-building initiatives, risking delays in sustainable LMIC research infrastructure.
unintended_consequences.evidence: Recommendation to balance outbreak response with capacity investments in CEPI’s 3.0 strategy.

scalability_evidence.scalability: High. mRNA and other platform technologies (e.g., mpox vaccine) are designed for rapid adaptation to new pathogens, enabling scalable responses to future outbreaks.
scalability_evidence.evidence: Successful preclinical proof-of-concept for 4 viral families; Phase I/II mpox trial demonstrates adaptability.

scalability_evidence.scalability: Medium-High. Models like ISARIC’s multicountry studies (mpox, dengue) and Institut Pasteur de Dakar collaboration can be replicated, but require sustained funding and capacity-building.
scalability_evidence.evidence: New partnerships in Senegal and Nigeria show potential for expansion to other LMICs.

scalability_evidence.scalability: High. The xHMG Funders Forum and PDP Funders Group provide scalable frameworks for aligning R&D investments across donors.
scalability_evidence.evidence: Successful coordination during mpox/Marburg responses and adoption of WHO viral families framework.

scalability_evidence.scalability: High. The compact’s biosecurity principles can be adopted by other funders to safeguard global R&D ecosystems.
scalability_evidence.evidence: Launched at the 2024 Global Health Security Conference with multi-stakeholder buy-in.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance against outputs (all scored A in 2024) and alignment with UK global health strategy priorities (e.g., 100 Days Mission, LMIC partnerships).
Demonstrated agility in responding to emerging outbreaks (mpox, Marburg) and adapting delivery models (e.g., SECE integration).
High VfM evidenced by cost-effectiveness modelling (e.g., Lassa vaccine could save 3,300 lives and $128M) and PDP model returns ($405 per $1 invested).
Critical role in strengthening global health security, particularly for LMICs, with scalable approaches (e.g., vaccine platforms, LMIC-led research).
Ongoing need to address capacity gaps in LMICs and advance late-stage trials, which require continued investment and coordination.

strengths: Partnership-based model (CEPI, ISARIC, Wellcome, BMGF) ensures shared risks and resources, enhancing long-term viability.
Flexible funding mechanisms enable rapid outbreak response while maintaining strategic R&D priorities.
Integration with FCDO’s SECE and cross-HMG structures embeds the programme within broader UK emergency response systems.
risks: Dependence on CEPI’s ability to transition candidates from late-stage trials to deployment (requires strengthened MNC partnerships).
Sustained LMIC capacity-building is essential but faces funding and logistical challenges.
Geopolitical or economic disruptions could impact co-funding and supply chains.
delivery_model_sustainability.assessment: High. The delivery model is sustainable with adaptive management, but long-term success hinges on addressing LMIC capacity and equitable access implementation.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High

planned_adaptations_future.adaptation: CEPI 3.0 strategy development
planned_adaptations_future.focus: Prioritize late-stage trial progression, equitable access implementation, and LMIC capacity-building. Clarify CEPI’s role in end-to-end vaccine development.

planned_adaptations_future.adaptation: Enhanced LMIC partnerships
planned_adaptations_future.focus: Expand collaborations like Institut Pasteur de Dakar and ISARIC to build sustainable research ecosystems in Africa and other regions.

planned_adaptations_future.adaptation: Results Framework reformulation
planned_adaptations_future.focus: Develop nested logframe with KPIs for "go/no-go" decisions, down-selection of candidates, and access plan implementation (target: November 2025).

planned_adaptations_future.adaptation: Biosecurity integration
planned_adaptations_future.focus: Incorporate Bio Funders Compact principles into all R&D funding streams to mitigate misuse risks.

planned_adaptations_future.adaptation: Policy engagement
planned_adaptations_future.focus: Strengthen contributions to the Pandemic Accord, 100 Days Mission, and WHO viral families framework to shape global health security priorities.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Programme to support Accountability and Inclusion (PARI)

output_1.title: Electoral institutions have improved capacity to implement elections and are more transparent and accountable

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Activities were restructured post-election to focus on gender/inclusion after lower-than-expected CENI engagement. PARI-TACS contract delayed by 10 months (started Dec 2024). New partnerships (e.g., JPC CENCO as direct implementer) introduced to meet localisation objectives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IFES faced lower CENI engagement than planned but successfully pivoted to gender/inclusion work. JPC CENCO exceeded targets (2.3M people reached). TCC supported 12 CSOs across 6 provinces. UN Women delivered two campaigns on women’s leadership. World Bank exceeded PFM reform targets in 6 provinces.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: BEK worked adaptively with partners to manage complex operating environment. Cross-project collaboration encouraged but not fully quantified.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: PARI-TACS contract procurement delayed by 10 months (signed Dec 2024). Other partner agreements (IFES, JPC CENCO, TCC, UN Women, World Bank) mobilised as planned by Q2 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme reallocated resources from CENI engagement to gender/inclusion activities. Indicators 1.1/1.2 adapted post-election. Theory of Change updated to reflect revised assumptions about CENI engagement.
adaptive_management_examples: IFES shifted from internal CENI assessments to external evaluations (e.g., Washington DC interviews) and organised a 140-participant forum on gender/inclusion.
BEK and IFES reprioritised activities toward Outcome Two (women’s political participation) after CENI engagement challenges.
JPC CENCO’s civic education adapted to local contexts (schools, universities, VCAT workshops) with 45% women/girls participation.
Activities in North/South Kivu paused due to security escalation (Jan 2025).

main_implementation_challenges: Lower-than-anticipated CENI engagement post-election, limiting reform adoption (only 1/37 IFES recommendations implemented).
10-month delay in PARI-TACS contract procurement (Dec 2024 start).
Security escalation in Eastern DRC (Jan 2025) forced pauses in North/South Kivu activities.
Need to adapt indicators post-election (e.g., shifting from election administration to gender/inclusion).
external_factors_impact: Post-election political context reduced CENI’s openness to external recommendations.
Security deterioration in Eastern DRC disrupted field activities in conflict-affected provinces.
contextual_constraints_new: CENI’s limited capacity/appetite for broader electoral reforms beyond gender/inclusion.
Delayed partner mobilisation (most projects started Autumn 2024) compressed implementation timeline.
partner_relationship_issues: IFES struggled with CENI’s resistance to external assessments but found traction on gender/inclusion.
First-time direct partnership with JPC CENCO required capacity-building support (safeguarding, financial reporting).
capacity_constraints_emerged: CENI’s technical capacity to implement recommendations was overestimated.
Provincial governments required additional World Bank support to develop PFM action plans.
risk_materialization: CENI engagement risk materialised (lower than planned).
Security risks in Eastern DRC disrupted operations.
Procurement delays (PARI-TACS) impacted timeline.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track; PARI-TACS contract (largest component) signed Dec 2024 with inception phase completed by April 2025. Other partner agreements (IFES, JPC CENCO, etc.) disbursed as planned.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High: Exceeded targets for impact stories (13 vs. 10) and beneficiary reach (e.g., JPC CENCO reached 2.3M people). She Leads curriculum (120 women) reported 91% skill application. Cost efficiency not quantified but implied through exceeded outputs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong: No major issues reported. BEK provided capacity-building to JPC CENCO on financial reporting/aid diversion. World Bank’s PFM support improved provincial financial management.

key_delivery_lessons: Localisation requires tailored capacity-building (e.g., JPC CENCO’s safeguarding training).
Electoral commission engagement is volatile; focus on thematic areas with demonstrated partner interest (e.g., gender/inclusion).
Flexible indicators are critical for post-election transitions.
successful_delivery_practices: Adaptive management (e.g., IFES’s pivot to gender/inclusion) maintained delivery despite CENI challenges.
Multi-channel civic education (JPC CENCO) effectively reached diverse audiences (2.3M people).
Microgrants (TCC) fostered CSO collaboration and local democratic engagement.
She Leads curriculum (IFES) achieved high beneficiary satisfaction (91% skill application).
management_adaptations_made: Reduced Output 1’s impact weighting from 25% to 10% post-election.
Shifted resources from CENI engagement to women’s political participation (Outcome Two).
Updated Theory of Change to reflect revised CENI engagement assumptions.
innovations_attempted: First She Leads curriculum in a francophone country (120 women trained).
Inter-generational dialogue campaigns (UN Women) linked women ministers with young leaders.
Positive masculinity campaign engaging 14 male Ministers.
DRC’s first Climate PEFA assessment (World Bank).
forward_recommendations: Prioritise activities with highest impact potential and encourage cross-project collaboration.
Diversify donor support to partners (per Due Diligence Assessment).
Assess sustainability of CENI gender/inclusion reforms beyond 2025.
Strengthen CSO networks (e.g., TCC’s 12-organisation network) for long-term advocacy.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Mitigated procurement delays (PARI-TACS) and security risks (pausing Kivu activities) but underestimated CENI’s resistance to reforms. Adaptive responses (e.g., shifting to gender/inclusion) preserved progress.

policy_influence_achieved: CENI adopted revised Gender, Inclusion and Elections 2025 Operational Plan (1/37 recommendations).
Provincial PFM action plans developed with World Bank support.
She Leads Network established for 2028 elections advocacy.
capacity_building_results: 120 women trained in She Leads curriculum (91% report daily skill use).
12 CSOs received TCC microgrants/capacity-building for democratic engagement.
JPC CENCO’s 45% women/girls participation in civic education.
World Bank’s PFM technical assistance improved provincial financial management.
unintended_consequences: Positive: She Leads Network created unplanned peer-support mechanisms.
Positive: Male Ministers engaged in positive masculinity campaign (14 participants).
Negative: Reduced CENI engagement limited broader electoral reform progress.
scalability_evidence: She Leads curriculum scalable to other francophone countries.
JPC CENCO’s civic education model adaptable to new provinces.
TCC’s CSO network model replicable for other democratic engagement programmes.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (Overall Score: A) despite challenges.
Critical to UK DRC Country Plan objectives (governance, democracy).
Post-election phase successfully mobilised with adaptive delivery.
High potential for sustained impact (e.g., She Leads Network, PFM reforms).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium: Localisation progress (e.g., JPC CENCO) but dependent on continued adaptive management and security stability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Update Theory of Change based on revised CENI engagement assumptions.
Expand CSO networks (TCC model) for broader advocacy.
Monitor sustainability of gender/inclusion reforms in CENI.
Assess scalability of She Leads curriculum to additional provinces.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Supporting Health Emergency Response in the Democratic Republic of Congo (SHER)

output_1.title: Through UNICEF, reduce the morbidity and mortality related to mpox and cholera in affected communities in targeted provinces (Sankuru, South Ubangi, South Kivu for mpox; North and South Kivu for cholera)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme activated earlier than originally planned (May 2024) due to mpox/cholera outbreaks. Expanded from initial 3 provinces (mpox) and 2 provinces (cholera) to include national digitisation of disease surveillance and WHO partnership for broader geographic coverage (South Kivu, North Kivu, Kinshasa).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNICEF exceeded milestones in surveillance (100% alerts investigated), mpox treatment centres (11 set up vs 10 targeted), and food support (103% of target). WHO partnership added mid-implementation to address gaps in national coordination. Both partners operated effectively in conflict-affected, hard-to-reach zones despite logistical challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO maintained oversight through British Embassy Kinshasa with direct engagement from HMA/DD for activation decisions. Coordination with GoDRC’s national response plans ensured alignment, though initial logframe was incomplete (lacking WHO components).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with GoDRC’s response architecture and other donors (e.g., WHO, UNICEF) through existing health system pillars (surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH). Challenges in Shabunda Health Zone due to accessibility constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Rapid procurement of £9m (£4.6m UNICEF, £4.4m WHO) within 4 months, aligned with GoDRC’s national plans. No major delays reported, though VfM framework was not pre-established (recommended for Year 2).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to outbreak urgency. Monthly progress reviews and adaptive management (e.g., extending UNICEF support to digitisation, adding WHO partnership).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged contingency design to pivot quickly: expanded geographic scope (5 provinces), added WHO as partner, and reallocated funds to address emerging mpox clade Ib. Initial business case triggers (HMA approval) enabled rapid activation.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended UNICEF support from 3 to 5 provinces and added national digitisation of surveillance.
Added WHO as implementing partner to cover Kinshasa and strengthen national coordination.
Adjusted food support targets upward (from 3,489 to 3,610 beneficiaries) based on higher-than-expected need.
Reprioritised CAC funding to focus on operational support for 59.5% of committees (1,115/1,872) due to cost overruns, while maintaining core activities.

main_implementation_challenges: Operating in conflict-affected, hard-to-reach zones (e.g., South Kivu, North Kivu) with limited infrastructure.
Higher-than-expected costs for community engagement (CAC operating support) led to partial coverage (59.5% vs 100% target).
Access constraints in Shabunda Health Zone prevented establishment of mpox treatment centres.
Rapidly evolving mpox outbreak (emergence of clade Ib with sexual transmission) required real-time adaptation of response strategies.
Coordinating with multiple actors (GoDRC, WHO, UNICEF, other donors) in a fragmented health system.
external_factors_impact: Ongoing conflict in Eastern DRC displaced populations, exacerbating cholera outbreaks and limiting health access.
Emergence of mpox clade Ib (novel sexual transmission) accelerated spread, requiring expanded geographic and demographic targeting.
Chronic underfunding of DRC’s health system constrained government-led response capacity.
Humanitarian crises (e.g., IDP movements) increased vulnerability to outbreaks in North/South Kivu.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of mpox clade Ib outbreak (40,000+ cases, 1,000+ deaths by Nov 2024) overwhelmed initial response plans.
Sexual transmission of mpox required additional RCCE strategies targeting at-risk groups.
Inflation and supply chain disruptions increased operational costs (e.g., CAC support, food aid).
partner_relationship_issues: Initial lack of a unified logframe for UNICEF/WHO components created reporting gaps (addressed in recommendations).
Delays in WHO partnership finalisation limited early coordination, though mitigated by UNICEF’s rapid deployment.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited GoDRC capacity to lead surveillance digitisation required UNICEF technical support.
Shortage of trained psychosocial workers for SGBV mitigation (only 43% of target reached).
Health zones like Shabunda lacked accessible infrastructure for treatment centres.
risk_materialization: Major: Conflict-related accessibility constraints (e.g., Shabunda HZ).
Major: Higher-than-planned outbreak severity (mpox clade Ib).
Moderate: Cost overruns for community engagement activities.
Moderate: Delayed policy uptake for PSEAH interventions (43% target achieved).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £9m disbursed (75% of £12m ceiling) in first 4 months, exceeding initial annual projections. Allocations: UNICEF (£4.6m), WHO (£4.4m). No underspend reported, though VfM analysis pending (framework to be developed in Year 2).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Not yet formally assessed (VfM framework recommended for next review). Preliminary indicators suggest cost-efficiency in treatment centre setup (11 vs 10 targeted) and food support (103% target at £0.03/beneficiary/day estimated). Challenges in RCCE cost-effectiveness due to inflation.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong: Rapid disbursement aligned with GoDRC plans; no fraud or major irregularities reported. Embassy Kinshasa maintained direct oversight. Audit trails for UNICEF/WHO transactions in place.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Mixed: Exceeded efficiency in some areas (e.g., mpox treatment centres at 110% physical target) but faced cost overruns in community engagement (CAC support covered 59.5% of target due to higher per-unit costs).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not applicable (programme designed as UK-only contingency fund).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly mentioned, though inflation in DRC likely affected local procurement costs (e.g., food aid, CAC stipends).

key_delivery_lessons: Contingency programmes must pre-negotiate flexible partnerships (e.g., WHO) to enable rapid scale-up.
Logframes should be comprehensive from outset to avoid mid-implementation gaps (e.g., missing WHO components).
Community engagement costs in conflict zones require buffer funding for inflation/access challenges.
Digitisation of surveillance systems (e.g., UNICEF’s work in North Kivu) should be prioritised early to improve outbreak tracking.
successful_delivery_practices: HMA-level activation triggers enabled timely response to mpox/cholera outbreaks.
UNICEF’s use of existing CAC networks accelerated community reach (59.5% covered despite cost constraints).
Modular treatment centre design allowed rapid deployment in 7 health zones.
Integration of PSEAH into RCCE activities (e.g., 5,800 children in awareness sessions) despite limited resources.
management_adaptations_made: Added WHO as partner to address national coordination gaps identified in first 2 months.
Reprioritised UNICEF funds to include surveillance digitisation based on GoDRC needs.
Adjusted food support targets upward in response to higher-than-expected mpox patient volumes.
Streamlined reporting between UNICEF/WHO to reduce duplication (post-recommendation).
innovations_attempted: Pilot of digital surveillance tools in North Kivu (UNICEF-led).
Targeted RCCE strategies for mpox clade Ib sexual transmission (e.g., influencer partnerships).
Mobile treatment units in inaccessible areas (e.g., Walungu, Kalehe).
previous_recommendations_progress: N/A (first annual review; no prior recommendations).
forward_recommendations: Develop a VfM framework for Year 2 to assess cost-effectiveness of response pillars.
Complete a unified logframe encompassing UNICEF/WHO activities before March 2025.
Conduct a regional lessons-learned exercise on mpox/cholera/Marburg responses (FCDO-led).
Explore longer-term health systems strengthening to mitigate future outbreaks (e.g., vaccination cold chains, lab capacity).
Pre-position buffer funds for community engagement to address inflation risks.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Major risks (conflict, outbreak scale) were anticipated but mitigation was reactive (e.g., adding WHO post-activation). Minor risks (e.g., CAC cost overruns) were not fully addressed in contingency planning. Risk of mpox endemicity now acknowledged as a programme limitation.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.mpox_surveillance: 1,422 suspected case alerts investigated (100% of target).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.mpox_treatment: 11 treatment centres established (110% of target) with 412 beds across 7 health zones.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.food_support: 3,610 mpox patients/dependents received aid (103% of target).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.RCCE: 59.5% of CACs (1,115/1,872) received operational support; broader awareness activities reached unspecified numbers via community dialogues/media.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.SGBV: 902 women/girls/boys reached with GBV/child protection info (43% of target); 5,800+ participated in awareness sessions.

policy_influence_achieved: FCDO’s public advocacy reinforced GoDRC-led response principles, though no specific policy changes documented.
Support for national mpox response plans (e.g., surveillance digitisation) may inform future GoDRC strategies.
capacity_building_results: 1,115 CAC members trained in mpox awareness/referrals (though operational support was partial).
Health workers in 11 treatment centres gained mpox case management experience.
Limited evidence of systemic capacity gains (e.g., no lab or cold chain improvements reported).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Expanded mpox treatment capacity (11 centres vs 10 planned) improved access in underserved zones (e.g., Walungu, Kalehe).
Negative: Partial CAC funding may have created inequities among communities; Shabunda HZ remained uncovered due to access constraints.
scalability_evidence: Treatment centre model replicable in other provinces (demonstrated in 7 health zones).
Digital surveillance tools (North Kivu) could be scaled nationally with additional funding.
RCCE strategies for mpox clade Ib adaptable to other viral haemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Marburg).
Limited scalability of food support due to cost constraints.

continuation_rationale: Programme is on track to meet output targets (e.g., 100% surveillance, 110% treatment centres) despite challenging context.
Critical role in supporting GoDRC’s mpox/cholera response, particularly in high-burden zones (e.g., South Kivu).
Flexible design allows adaptation to emerging threats (e.g., mpox clade Ib, future Marburg risks).
FCDO regional priorities align with health security goals in DRC (per HMA/DD approvals).
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium-High (for output delivery); Low (for containing mpox endemicity or addressing root causes of cholera).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Low. Programme relies on contingency funding and external partners (UNICEF/WHO). GoDRC’s limited health system capacity and ongoing conflict reduce long-term sustainability prospects.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (given performance in Year 1, though risk rating remains "Major" due to context).
planned_adaptations_future: Finalise VfM framework and unified logframe by March 2025.
Expand RCCE to address mpox sexual transmission risks (pending funding).
Explore partnerships for health systems strengthening (e.g., vaccination infrastructure).
Conduct mid-term review to assess progress toward national/regional health security outcomes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Core Funding to the United Nations Special Purpose Trust Fund (UN SPTF) for the Resident Coordinator (RC) System

output_1.title: Deliver well trained, experienced Resident Coordinators, who are deployed on time with fewer gaps between posts.

output_2.title: At country level, set clear guidance with benchmarks to UNCTs on value for money.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: DCO faced systemic recruitment challenges (62% completion vs 82% target for 120-day recruitment) due to host country approval delays and funding gaps. Training pauses and reduced candidate pipelines affected deployment timelines. Efficiency savings were achieved through common premises ($1.6m savings reported).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO engages via biannual DCO Programme Board meetings and regular dialogues. Recommendation made to strengthen governance through structured donor dialogues. DCO’s ‘business innovation group’ provided design support for LSSC pilots in 6 countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UN Country Teams (UNCTs) showed high consultation rates with development partners (89%) and civil society (89%) during Cooperation Framework design, but lower engagement with academia (51%) and youth (46%). Peer-to-peer learning mechanisms (e.g., RC retreat) were planned for Autumn 2023.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO conducts ongoing monitoring via Programme Board meetings and financial reporting (last audited statement: May 2023). Risk mitigation includes encouraging other Member States to increase SPTF contributions to address the $85m funding gap (2022).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: DCO adapted by fast-tracking RC recruitment and prioritizing diversity (e.g., Francophone/Arabic speakers). LSSC pilots were delayed but received design support. Common premises progress (30% vs 35% target) included government-provided rent-free facilities in 5 countries.
adaptive_management_examples: Fast-tracked RC recruitment system to reduce gaps, despite host country approval delays.
Paused RC training due to funding constraints but maintained 90% host country satisfaction with RC profiles (Indicator 1.1).
Shifted focus to common premises (30% achieved) and LSSC pilots (6 countries) to drive efficiencies, despite underachievement on LSSC approvals (0% vs 30% target).
Expanded selection pool to diversify RC nationalities (e.g., Francophone/Arabic speakers).

main_implementation_challenges: Systemic recruitment delays (62% completion vs 82% target) due to host country approval processes and DCO resource constraints.
Funding shortfall grew from $66m (2021) to $85m (2022), pausing training and reducing candidate pipelines.
No progress on Local Shared Services Centers (LSSCs) (0% vs 30% target) due to technical/operational barriers and funding gaps.
Backsliding on gender equality (42% vs 60% target) and poverty reduction (49% vs 75% target) in joint programmes.
external_factors_impact: Host governments’ delayed approvals for RC candidates disrupted deployment timelines.
Currency/exchange rate impacts not explicitly mentioned, but global inflation may have contributed to the $85m funding gap.
Geopolitical contexts (e.g., conflict zones) required specialized RC skillsets, exacerbating recruitment challenges.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated severity of DCO’s funding gap ($85m in 2022) led to paused training and reduced operational capacity.
Technical complexities in LSSC implementation (e.g., integrating IT/HR systems across UN agencies) were underestimated.
Lower-than-expected engagement with academia (51% vs 70% target) and youth (46% vs 60%) during Cooperation Framework design.
partner_relationship_issues: DCO’s limited capacity (due to funding gaps) strained its ability to meet FCDO’s oversight expectations (e.g., delayed LSSC progress).
Some UNCTs struggled to align joint programmes with gender/poverty targets, requiring additional FCDO monitoring.
capacity_constraints_emerged: DCO’s reduced training capacity for RCs due to funding shortfalls.
Limited bandwidth to process LSSC business cases (only 6 pilot designs evaluated by August 2023).
UNCTs in high-cost locations faced challenges transitioning to common premises (30% achieved vs 35% target).
risk_materialization: Severe risk of inadequate Member State funding to SPTF materialized, with the gap reaching $85m in 2022.
Recruitment delays (Indicator 1.2) and LSSC underperformance (Output 2.2) aligned with moderate risk ratings.
Gender equality and poverty reduction targets were not met, reflecting risks in outcome-level delivery.

budget_execution_vs_plan: DCO faced a $85m funding shortfall in 2022, leading to paused activities (e.g., RC training) and reduced operational capacity.
FCDO’s £15.6m contribution was executed as planned, but broader SPTF underfunding constrained delivery.
$1.6m in efficiencies achieved via common premises (e.g., government-provided rent-free facilities in 5 countries).
value_for_money_assessment: Overachievement at impact level (e.g., RC leadership effectiveness) and outcome-level savings (e.g., common premises) demonstrate partial VFM.
Delays in LSSCs and gender/poverty targets suggest VFM could be improved with better risk mitigation (e.g., donor coordination).
FCDO recommended holistic measurement of Outcome 3 to capture broader efficiency gains beyond Output 2.
financial_management_quality: DCO provided annual financial reporting via Operational Activities for Development Segment (last narrative report: May 2023).
Audited statements were submitted on time (May 2023), but funding gaps raised concerns about long-term sustainability.
FCDO’s Programme Board reviews included financial risk discussions, with mitigation actions agreed (e.g., encouraging other donors).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Common premises delivered $1.6m in savings (30% of UN premises vs 35% target).
LSSC pilots (6 countries) aimed to spur further efficiencies but faced implementation delays.
Efficiency gains were offset by recruitment costs (e.g., advertising RC positions 1 year in advance) and funding gap impacts.
co_funding_materialization: Planned co-funding from other Member States did not materialize sufficiently, exacerbating the $85m SPTF gap.
FCDO actively encouraged larger voluntary contributions but with limited success in Year 1.

key_delivery_lessons: RC selection reforms (e.g., profile matching, diversity efforts) successfully maintained 90% host country satisfaction (Indicator 1.1).
Funding gaps directly correlated with underperformance in recruitment (Indicator 1.2) and LSSCs (Output 2.2).
Common premises (30% achieved) demonstrated cost savings but required tailored approaches (e.g., government-provided facilities).
UNCT consultation rates varied by stakeholder group, highlighting need for targeted engagement strategies (e.g., youth/academia).
successful_delivery_practices: Peer-to-peer learning mechanisms (e.g., RC retreat) and DCO’s ‘business innovation group’ supported adaptive management.
Fast-tracked recruitment and advanced advertising (1 year prior) mitigated some deployment delays.
Strategic use of government-provided premises (e.g., Egypt, Fiji) reduced costs without compromising operations.
management_adaptations_made: DCO prioritized diversifying RC selection pool (e.g., Francophone/Arabic speakers) to address skill gaps in conflict zones.
FCDO increased oversight via biannual Programme Board meetings and structured risk reviews.
Output 1.1’s milestone was raised from 90% to 92% for Year 2 to sustain progress.
innovations_attempted: LSSC pilot designs in 6 countries (Brazil, Jordan, Kenya, Senegal, Tanzania, Vietnam) to test integrated service delivery models.
Removal of UN agency referral requirements for RC candidates to expand the selection pool.
Use of ‘reform checklists’ to track UNCT progress on strategic planning and stakeholder consultation.
previous_recommendations_progress: This was the first Annual Review; no prior recommendations existed. Baseline established for future tracking.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: DCO should strengthen governance via regular structured dialogues with top SPTF donors to address funding gaps.
Expand RC selection pool with updates on diversity efforts (e.g., language skills, regional representation).
Measure host government/UNCT ratings of RC effectiveness to holistically assess Outcome 3 progress.
Monitor UN’s commitment to common premises in 66 high-cost locations to ensure Output 2.1 progress.
Gather lessons from LSSC pilots (6 countries) to accelerate approvals and replication.
Set clear VFM benchmarks for UNCTs and track progress via peer learning (e.g., RC retreat).

risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive mitigation for severe funding risk (e.g., donor engagement) but limited success in Year 1.
Moderate risks (e.g., recruitment delays) were managed via adaptive measures (e.g., fast-tracking).
Recommendation to enhance governance could improve future risk responses (e.g., LSSC implementation).

policy_influence_achieved: RCs led UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks (UNSDCFs) in 162 countries, aligning UN activities with national/SDG priorities.
Common Country Analyses (CCAs) incorporated donor inputs (89% consultation rate with development partners).
Advocacy for UN Charter principles and human rights was cited as a key RC function, though specific policy uptake evidence was limited.
capacity_building_results: RC selection reforms improved perceived competence (90% host country satisfaction vs 78% baseline).
DCO’s ‘business innovation group’ supported LSSC pilot designs, building UNCT capacity for shared services.
Training pauses due to funding gaps created capacity risks for new RCs, particularly in conflict zones.

unintended_consequences.description: Common premises in Vietnam enabled ICT/HR integration across agencies, spurring unplanned operational efficiencies.
Funding gaps led to paused RC training, potentially reducing long-term capacity in high-need countries.
Focus on recruitment timelines (Indicator 1.2) may have diverted attention from gender/poverty outcomes (42% and 49% achievement).

scalability_evidence: LSSC pilots (6 countries) demonstrated potential for replication but faced barriers in approval processes.
Common premises model (30% adoption) showed scalability in rent-free government facilities (e.g., Egypt, Senegal).
RC selection reforms (e.g., diversity focus) could be scaled but require sustained funding for training.

continuation_rationale: Programme scored B overall with overachievement at impact level (RC leadership) despite funding challenges.
Critical to UK’s multilateral reform priorities (e.g., Foreign Secretary’s 2023 Chatham House speech).
DCO outlined plans to improve LSSC/recruitment progress, and FCDO mitigation actions address funding risks.
Value for money was demonstrated through efficiency savings ($1.6m) and strategic alignment with SDGs.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current model is partially sustainable but vulnerable to SPTF funding gaps (risk rated ‘severe’).
Long-term sustainability depends on donor coordination and DCO’s ability to scale common premises/LSSCs.
RC system’s reliance on host country approvals introduces ongoing operational risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Medium-High
planned_adaptations_future: Increase Output 1.1 milestone to 92% to sustain RC profile improvements.
Expand LSSC pilots with lessons from initial 6 countries to accelerate approvals.
Strengthen governance via structured donor dialogues to address funding gaps.
Monitor UN’s progress on common premises in 66 high-cost locations.
Introduce holistic measurements for Outcome 3 (e.g., host government/UNCT ratings of RC effectiveness).

programme_metadata.programme_title: The South Sudan Humanitarian and Resilience Programme (SSHARP)

output_1.title: Rapid emergency responses to new shocks are agile and conflict and gender sensitive

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Budget increased by 70% in-year due to Sudan crisis impact; mobilisation of 10 direct partners took 6 months (longer than typical). No fixed mobilisation deadline was set to avoid perverse incentives.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UN agencies performed strongly across the board. INGO performance was mixed: Emergency Rapid Response Mechanism (ERRM) exceeded milestone targets, while THRIVE missed all milestone targets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Complex mobilisation involving 7 Due Diligence Assessments (90 recommendations) and quality-focused contracting without rigid deadlines. BEJ maintained oversight flexibility.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UK's role as Chair of Humanitarian Donor Group (HDG) and seat on Humanitarian Country Team Plus (HCT+) enabled strategic coordination, though US policy changes disrupted system-wide planning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was delayed by 6-month mobilisation period but maintained quality standards. No evidence of procurement failures mentioned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to 90 DDA recommendations and in-year budget increase. BEJ prioritised quality over speed in partner selection and contracting.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to 70% budget increase and Sudan crisis impacts. BEJ retained authority for flexible resourcing decisions based on local conditions.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocated resources to address Sudan-induced displacement (1.1M new arrivals since April 2023).
Prioritised cholera response (imported from Sudan) and flooding emergencies (July–December 2024).
Shifted focus to "critical priorities" in Year 2 planning to avoid gap-filling in light of US funding cuts.

main_implementation_challenges: Delayed mobilisation (6 months) due to complex DDA process and partner selection.
US foreign assistance pause (January 2025) created funding uncertainty and partner operational disruptions (e.g., IOM global restructuring).
Sudan conflict spillover: 1.1M displaced persons, economic shocks (oil export disruptions), and cholera outbreaks.
Internal conflict in northern South Sudan (March 2025) caused displacement and reduced partner staffing.
external_factors_impact: US funding cuts (54.1% of 2024 humanitarian budget) forced NGOs to close operations and UN agencies to restructure.
Sudan war exacerbated South Sudan’s economic crisis (oil revenue loss) and humanitarian caseload.
Extreme flooding (July–December 2024) and cholera outbreaks strained response capacity.
Political instability in northern South Sudan disrupted implementation.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of US policy shift and its systemic impact on humanitarian architecture.
Sudan conflict’s prolonged economic/displacement effects on South Sudan (beyond initial assumptions).
Government revenue collapse due to oil export disruptions, limiting local capacity to absorb transitions.
partner_relationship_issues: Mixed INGO performance: THRIVE missed all milestones, while ERRM exceeded targets.
UN agencies outperformed INGOs, but coordination was strained by funding uncertainties.
Some partners reduced operations due to US funding cuts, requiring SSHARP to re-prioritise.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Local government capacity insufficient to absorb service transitions (e.g., health sector).
Reduced partner staffing in conflict-affected areas (northern South Sudan).
Limited bandwidth for resilience/livelihoods work due to overwhelming emergency needs.
risk_materialization: Assumption violation: US funding continuity (risk now realised).
Assumption under threat: Sudan war not causing internal conflict (signs of breakdown in northern South Sudan).
Humanitarian system functionality at risk due to donor coordination gaps.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Year 1 budget increased by 70% in-year (to ~£51m) due to Sudan crisis response. Mobilisation delays meant only partial year of implementation (6 months).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early to assess VFM; efficiency gains noted in ERRM’s rapid response mechanisms, but THRIVE’s underperformance raises concerns. BEJ scrutinising financial management tightly for Year 2.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong for UN partners; mixed for INGOs (e.g., THRIVE’s missed targets triggered action plans). 90 DDA recommendations indicate rigorous due diligence.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: ERRM demonstrated cost-efficiency in multisector responses (e.g., cash, WASH, protection bundles). No quantitative efficiency metrics provided.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible resourcing and local condition-informed decisions are critical in volatile contexts.
Quality-focused mobilisation (even if slower) prevents perverse incentives.
Donor coordination gaps (e.g., US policy shifts) can destabilise entire response systems.
successful_delivery_practices: ERRM’s rapid, multisector response model (exceeded cash/WASH/protection targets).
BEJ’s use of HDG/HCT+ platforms to steer collective prioritisation.
Layering resilience into emergency responses (e.g., flood-affected areas).
management_adaptations_made: Shifted Year 2 strategy to focus on "critical priorities" and transition opportunities.
Increased scrutiny of underperforming partners (e.g., THRIVE action plans).
Emphasised locally led action to reduce international substitution of services.
innovations_attempted: Mobile service provision in conflict/flood zones (e.g., Northern Bahr el Ghazal).
Integrated cholera/WASH responses with community engagement.
Pilot transitions from humanitarian health to government/World Bank-led programmes.
forward_recommendations: Accelerate transition from humanitarian to resilience/development mechanisms.
Strengthen diplomatic/policy leverage to urge government accountability.
Balance static/mobile service delivery models based on conflict dynamics.
Prioritise cash programming and community communication strategies.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Identified risks (US funding, Sudan spillover) materialised, but adaptive strategies (e.g., HDG coordination) mitigated some impacts. Need stronger contingency planning for systemic donor shifts.

policy_influence_achieved: UK’s HDG chairmanship shaped collective donor priorities (e.g., "humanitarian as exception" principle).
Advocacy for government accountability in health sector transitions (e.g., World Bank programme).
capacity_building_results: Limited evidence; resilience evaluation under procurement to establish baseline.
Local led-action emphasised but constrained by government capacity gaps.
unintended_consequences: Positive: ERRM’s rapid responses strengthened trust in affected communities.
Negative: Risk of creating dependency if resilience transitions are delayed.
scalability_evidence: ERRM model scalable for shock responses; resilience approaches require further testing.

continuation_rationale: Programme remains critical to address acute humanitarian needs (IPC baseline shows high caseload).
Adaptive design aligns with "humanitarian reset" priorities (donor coordination, transitions).
UK’s diplomatic role (HDG chair) provides unique leverage for system-wide impact.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium (high for humanitarian outputs; low for resilience/sustainability)
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Low (dependent on donor coordination and government capacity improvements)
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (for humanitarian delivery); Medium (for resilience progress)
planned_adaptations_future: Reprioritise Year 2 activities to focus on lifesaving core and transition-enabling investments.
Strengthen BEJ’s policy/diplomatic role to drive government accountability.
Explore efficiencies via locally led models and reduced service substitution.
Monitor US policy impacts and adjust coordination strategies accordingly.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Core Funding to UN Women of its 2022-2025 Strategic Plan

output_1.title: Public and private financing advance gender equality through gender responsive financing policies, strategies and instruments

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from joint business case with UNICEF, UNDP, and UNFPA to a standalone business case for UN Women in 2022. Core funding remains unearmarked, supporting UN Women’s Strategic Plan 2022-2025.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UN Women demonstrated strong alignment with UK priorities (International Development Strategy, Integrated Review Refresh, International Women and Girls Strategy) but requires improved transparency in resource allocation and coordination capacity at country level.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UK participates actively in UN Women’s Executive Board (non-member role) for oversight and governance. UN Women’s triple mandate (normative, operational, coordination) is leveraged effectively, though risk management and financial reporting need strengthening.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: UN Women enhanced cross-UN system coordination (e.g., IASC membership for humanitarian responses, PSEA interventions) but requires more consistent leadership in gender equality coordination at country level.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintains oversight through Executive Board engagement and continuous monitoring of UN Women’s performance. Financial reporting and risk management oversight identified as areas for increased intensity.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Core funding flexibility allows UN Women to allocate resources across strategic priorities, though reliance on earmarked voluntary funding risks financial instability and inefficient resource distribution.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: Adaptation to reduced UK core funding (from 0.7% to 0.5% GNI) while maintaining commitment to UN Women’s mandate. Shift to standalone business case to tailor monitoring and reporting to UN Women’s specific strategic plan.

main_implementation_challenges: Transparency gaps in UN Women’s resource allocation system.
Inconsistent capacity to lead and coordinate UN’s gender equality work at country level.
Lack of formal, systematic risk management practices, particularly in financial management.
Financial sustainability risks due to reliance on earmarked voluntary funding and excess reserves without clear strategic direction.
external_factors_impact: Reduction in UK ODA budget from 0.7% to 0.5% GNI (2020), requiring reprioritization of core funding allocations.
Global economic challenges and unanticipated costs affecting ODA spend coherence and value for money.
Increasing threats to UN Women’s mandate, necessitating stronger UK influence and support.
contextual_constraints_new: Delayed financial reporting due to core funding payment (2022) made in 2023, limiting real-time performance data.
Need for improved alignment with UN reform initiatives and other UN agencies to enhance field office effectiveness.
partner_relationship_issues: Concerns from donors (including FCDO) regarding UN Women’s excess reserves and lack of transparent spending plans.
Limited proactive communication to Member States on reform initiatives and programmatic decisions.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Insufficient capacity to systematically lead UN system coordination on gender equality at country level.
Gaps in implementing victim-survivor-centered policies for preventing sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA).
risk_materialization: Financial instability risk due to over-reliance on earmarked funding, as identified in the review.
Moderate programme risk rating persists due to unresolved transparency and coordination challenges.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Core funding payment for 2022 was executed in 2023, causing a lag in financial reporting alignment. Budget execution is on track but lacks transparency in allocation decisions.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Moderate. While UN Women delivers normative and operational results aligned with SDG 5, inefficiencies persist due to unclear resource allocation and excess reserves. FCDO recommends improved VFM through strategic reserve spending and transparency.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Requires strengthening. Key issues include: (1) Lack of systematic financial risk management; (2) Delayed reporting of 2022 funds; (3) Donor concerns over excess reserves without strategic utilization plans.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Not explicitly quantified. Efficiency is hindered by reliance on earmarked funding, which limits flexibility and may lead to suboptimal resource distribution.

key_delivery_lessons: Standalone business cases (vs. joint reviews) enable more tailored oversight but require robust risk management frameworks.
Core funding flexibility is critical for supporting UN Women’s mandate but must be balanced with financial sustainability planning.
UN Women’s triple mandate (normative, operational, coordination) is a strength but requires clearer prioritization and resource allocation.
successful_delivery_practices: Active UK engagement in UN Women’s Executive Board (non-member role) enhances oversight and influence.
UN Women’s leadership in cross-UN coordination (e.g., IASC, PSEA) demonstrates effective use of core funding for systemic impact.
High-level political advocacy and technical support to governments (e.g., Jordan, Mexico, Tanzania) successfully advanced gender-responsive financing frameworks.
management_adaptations_made: Transition to a UN Women-specific logical framework and theory of change in 2022, improving alignment with strategic plan.
Increased focus on preventing sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) through independent reviews and policy reforms.
innovations_attempted: Pilot initiatives to integrate gender equality targets into national investment/financing frameworks (7 countries in 2022).
Enhanced use of gender budget tracking systems (SDG Indicator 5.c.1) to improve public finance transparency.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partial progress on risk management (financial and operational risks remain unresolved).
Limited improvement in transparency of resource allocation and reserve spending plans.
forward_recommendations: Develop stronger risk management practices, particularly for financial reporting and reserve utilization.
Improve transparency in decision-making for programmatic and normative activities, including non-core contributions.
Enhance communication with Member States on reform initiatives (UN alignment, field office improvements).
Accelerate implementation of PSEA policies and victim-survivor-centered approaches.
Strategically allocate excess reserves with clear timelines and donor consultation.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Weak. While risks are identified (e.g., financial instability, coordination gaps), UN Women lacks a formal, systematic approach to mitigation. FCDO recommends urgent strengthening of risk management frameworks.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Indirect reach through UN Women’s global programmes (e.g., 105 countries supported for gender budget tracking systems; 7 countries incorporated gender equality targets in financing frameworks in 2022). Direct beneficiary data not specified.
policy_influence_achieved: Contributed to global norms and standards for gender equality (e.g., SDG 5.c.1 on gender budget tracking).
Influenced national policies in Jordan, Mexico, and Tanzania to integrate gender equality targets in financing frameworks.
Strengthened UN system accountability for gender equality through IASC and PSEA interventions.
capacity_building_results: Technical support provided to governments on gender-responsive financing methodologies.
Capacity development for UN Women field offices through reform initiatives (though effectiveness requires further evidence).
unintended_consequences: Positive: Enhanced UK influence in multilateral gender equality agenda despite reduced ODA budget.
Negative: Risk of financial instability due to earmarked funding reliance may undermine long-term programme sustainability.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Moderate. Approaches like gender budget tracking (SDG 5.c.1) and financing framework targets are scalable but require stronger UN Women coordination and donor support.

continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with UK strategic priorities (International Women and Girls Strategy, SDG 5).
