programme_metadata.programme_title: Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict Initiative (PSVI)

output_1.title: Strengthened international response to CRSV; coordination of international community; and improved international legal frameworks to tackle CRSV

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme pivoted to respond to emerging conflicts (Sudan, Israel/OPT), demonstrating flexibility beyond original business case. External MEL provider contracted to standardize programme management processes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners exceeded expectations in several areas: UN Women supported 56,253 individuals (exceeding milestones), Global Survivors Fund delivered "lifeline" support to 3,250 survivors, and Sisma Mujer produced pioneering documentation in Colombia. TRIAL International secured first-ever conviction for forced pregnancy as a crime against humanity (DRC).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Standardized programme management processes implemented this year, with improved oversight through external MEL provider. Field visits (e.g., to Global Survivors Fund in Turkey) enhanced ground-level understanding.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination demonstrated through: 1) UK's chairmanship handover of the International Alliance on PSVI to Colombia (26 member states), 2) Survivor Advisory Group retreat (March 2023) bridging survivors, governments, and civil society, 3) Multi-stakeholder engagement in advancing UN Crimes Against Humanity Convention.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight via external MEL provider and field visits, though initial delays in disbursement due to programme complexity in FCAS contexts were noted (improved by end of FY23-24).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility by: 1) Responding to unplanned crises (Sudan, Israel/OPT), 2) Uplifting UN Women funding mid-implementation for African advocacy on CAHC, 3) Adapting survivor-centered approaches based on field feedback.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid response to emerging conflicts in Sudan and Israel/OPT by reallocating focus/resources.
Mid-year funding uplift for UN Women to expand advocacy in Africa for the CAHC.
Integration of survivor feedback from Turkey field visit to refine Global Survivors Fund’s reparative measures.
Support for Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace to open macro-case 11 on gender-based violence, adapting to local judicial opportunities.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in fund disbursement due to programme complexity and FCAS operating environments.
Short-term grant cycles disrupting project continuity and sustainability (e.g., risk of interrupted services for survivors).
Capacity constraints across partners and FCDO team, particularly in MEL and risk management.
Balancing predefined country priorities with need to respond to unplanned crises (e.g., Sudan).
external_factors_impact: Emerging conflicts (Sudan, Israel/OPT) created unanticipated demand for programme pivoting.
Political transitions in focus countries (e.g., Colombia’s assumption of PSVI Alliance chairmanship) required adaptive engagement.
Global inflation and currency fluctuations (not explicitly detailed but implied in VfM considerations).
contextual_constraints_new: Unforeseen conflicts (Sudan, Israel/OPT) not originally scoped in programme design, requiring rapid reallocation of attention/resources.
Stigma against survivors and children born of CRSV proved more entrenched in some contexts (e.g., Colombia) than anticipated, necessitating tailored advocacy approaches.
Legal and bureaucratic barriers in FCAS (e.g., DRC, South Sudan) slowed justice-related interventions despite partner efforts.
partner_relationship_issues: Ad-hoc engagement on risk, VfM, and MEL early in the year, though structured approaches improved by FY23-24 end.
Differing partner capacities required varied levels of FCDO support (e.g., intensive technical assistance for Special Jurisdiction for Peace in Colombia vs. lighter-touch coordination with UN Women).
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO team capacity stretched by need to manage both ongoing projects and crisis responses.
Partners in FCAS (e.g., South Sudan, DRC) faced human resource gaps in MEL and financial reporting, requiring additional FCDO support.
Survivor-centered approaches demanded higher-than-planned investments in psychosocial support and safe engagement mechanisms.
risk_materialization: Delays in FCAS disbursements (mitigated by process improvements).
Short-term funding risks to sustainability (partially addressed via multi-year funding recommendations).
Geopolitical risks in priority countries (e.g., Ukraine, Ethiopia) required contingency planning for partner operations.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track overall, though initial disbursement delays in FCAS contexts were resolved by FY23-24 end. External MEL provider noted efficient use of £12.5m allocation, with no major underspends reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VfM demonstrated through: 1) Exceeding targets (e.g., UN Women’s 56,253 beneficiaries vs. plan), 2) Leveraging UK funds to catalyze broader impacts (e.g., 26-state PSVI Alliance, UN CAHC advocacy), 3) Cost-effective tools like Mukwege Foundation’s multilingual online resource (reusable across contexts).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Improved with external MEL provider’s standardization efforts. Early-year ad-hoc financial oversight transitioned to structured monitoring by FY23-24 end. No major audit findings reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of resources evident in: 1) Pooling funds for multi-country projects (e.g., Global Survivors Fund’s cross-border reparative measures), 2) Leveraging UK’s diplomatic influence to amplify impacts (e.g., CAHC advocacy), 3) Low overhead costs relative to direct survivor support (e.g., 3,250 survivors aided by GSF).

key_delivery_lessons: Flexibility is critical: Ability to pivot to emerging crises (Sudan, Israel/OPT) preserved relevance and impact.
Survivor-centered design works: GSF’s reparative measures and Sisma Mujer’s documentation proved transformative when co-created with survivors.
Multilateral coordination amplifies impact: PSVI Alliance and UN CAHC efforts showed how UK leadership can catalyze global action.
Local ownership drives sustainability: Colombia’s assumption of PSVI Alliance chairmanship and DRC’s Ndarumanga case conviction demonstrate lasting change when partners lead.
successful_delivery_practices: External MEL provider improved data quality and standardized reporting.
Field visits (e.g., Turkey) deepened contextual understanding and informed adaptive management.
Multi-year funding (where used) reduced administrative burden and improved partner stability.
Stakeholder retreats (e.g., CRSV Survivor Retreat) bridged gaps between survivors, policymakers, and practitioners.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from ad-hoc to structured partner engagement on risk/VFM/MEL.
Introduction of standardized programme management processes.
Increased use of field visits for real-time learning.
innovations_attempted: Mukwege Foundation’s multilingual online resource on state obligations (English/French/Spanish).
GSF’s Interim Reparative Measures tailored to survivors’ self-identified needs (medical, psychosocial, financial).
Use of survivor retreats to inform policy design (e.g., March 2023 CRSV Survivor Retreat).
Pioneering documentation methods (e.g., Sisma Mujer’s "La luz que nos queda" book in Colombia).
previous_recommendations_progress: ✅ Contracted external MEL provider (recommended in prior review).
✅ Standardized programme management processes (addressing prior gaps).
⚠️ Multi-year funding not yet fully implemented (recommended for future).
✅ Enhanced survivor engagement (e.g., Survivor Advisory Group retreat).
forward_recommendations: Secure programme continuation post-July 2025 via extension or new phase to maintain momentum.
Transition to multi-year funding agreements to reduce administrative delays and improve sustainability.
Develop strategic plan for enduring impact of PSVI-funded tools (e.g., Guidebook, Stigma Toolkit) post-closure.
Increase field visits to strengthen context-specific programming.
Explore mechanisms to institutionalize survivor input in policy processes (building on SAG retreat model).
Assess options for scaling successful interventions (e.g., GSF’s reparative measures, Mukwege’s online resource).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderately effective. Planned risks (FCAS disbursement delays, partner capacity gaps) were largely mitigated through adaptive management. Unplanned risks (Sudan/Israel-OPT conflicts) were addressed reactively but successfully. Recommendation: Strengthen proactive scenario planning for geopolitical shocks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 56,253 individuals accessed legal/justice services via UN Women (exceeding targets); 3,250 survivors received reparative support via GSF.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 26 states engaged in PSVI Alliance; 400+ signatories on CAHC joint statements; broader reach via Mukwege Foundation’s online resource (usage data not specified).

policy_influence_achieved: UN Crimes Against Humanity Convention advanced with gender/CRSV provisions (UK-led advocacy).
Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace opened macro-case 11 on gender-based violence (UK technical/financial support).
Bosnia and Herzegovina legislative changes secured rights for survivors/children born of CRSV.
First-ever conviction for forced pregnancy as crime against humanity (DRC, supported by TRIAL International).
capacity_building_results: Sisma Mujer’s documentation and advocacy strengthened Colombian civil society’s ability to address CRSV.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Catalysing Private Finance for Adaptation and Resilience (CPFAR) Programme

output_1.title: Finalised metrics and tools ready for use at country and organisational level (and to inform the Jamaica pilot)

output_3.title: Public-private partnerships established to support increased activity in adaptation and resilience financing

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme initially underestimated the time required to negotiate five separate delivery agreements concurrently, which delayed implementation. A dedicated startup phase with associated indicators is now recommended for future programmes to streamline agreement processes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong technical capacity (e.g., Oxford University’s enhancements to J-SRAT, UWI’s coastal protection database) but faced delays in legal agreements (e.g., IIGCC’s PCRAM case studies pending participant contracts). The independent nature of components allowed partial progress despite not all partners being fully operational at launch.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Green Finance Team in FCDO’s International Finance Directorate (IFD) manages the programme with delegated authority to partners for project-level decisions. Quarterly meetings and milestone-based invoicing are used for oversight, though reporting consistency varies by partner.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination was challenged by the parallel negotiation of multiple agreements, but the modular design mitigated risks. The Jamaica pilot’s integration with national systems (e.g., Ministry of Finance’s Public Investment Management System) shows effective cross-sectoral collaboration.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays due to concurrent negotiations with five partners. Future phases should allocate more time for agreement finalization and consider phased startups.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight is conducted through quarterly partner meetings and milestone reviews, with varying intensity based on payment terms. Some partners (e.g., CCCCC) required additional in-country support to align with government priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted by focusing on consensus-building in Jamaica (e.g., J-SRAT integration into national planning) and prioritizing high-impact components (e.g., PCRAM 2.0) while delaying others (e.g., case studies).
adaptive_management_examples: Extended J-SRAT functionality (e.g., hotspots analysis, coastal protection measures) based on Government of Jamaica’s feedback.
Shifted Output 3 from ‘public-private partnerships’ to ‘public-private collaborations’ to better reflect non-contractual engagement models.
Added ‘policy solutions’ to Output 4 to align with emerging needs for bankable adaptation investments.

main_implementation_challenges: Concurrent negotiation of five delivery agreements caused startup delays.
Legal barriers slowed IIGCC’s PCRAM case studies (requiring participant contracts).
Jamaica’s national prioritization processes for infrastructure projects required extensive stakeholder alignment.
Limited in-country capacity to coordinate between ministries and development partners.
external_factors_impact: COP29 targets (e.g., $1.3T annual mobilization by 2035) increased pressure to demonstrate private sector engagement.
Global demand for climate risk pricing tools (e.g., J-SRAT) accelerated interest but also raised expectations for scalability.
contextual_constraints_new: Political complexities in Jamaica’s cross-ministerial decision-making for climate-resilient infrastructure.
Need for a global coalition to sustain private sector engagement post-programme.
partner_relationship_issues: Varied reporting consistency among partners due to differing payment terms.
CCCCC’s Jamaica pilot required additional FCDO support to align with government timelines.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Insufficient local/regional capacity to support Jamaica’s J-SRAT integration and prioritization processes.
Limited bandwidth among FCDO teams to coordinate with multiple partners simultaneously.
risk_materialization: Delays in partner agreements (mitigated by modular design).
Slower-than-planned progress on public-private collaborations (Output 3 scored C).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for Year 1, though some milestones (e.g., PCRAM case studies) were deferred to 2025 due to legal delays. No significant underspends or overspends reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indications suggest strong VFM due to: (1) Leveraging existing tools (e.g., J-SRAT) for regional replication; (2) High private sector interest in outputs (e.g., PCRAM 2.0); (3) Potential to inform global policy (e.g., NCQG targets). Formal VFM metrics will be developed in subsequent years.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Partners demonstrated adequate financial management, with milestone-based payments tied to deliverables. Quarterly reviews ensured transparency, though some partners required additional support to meet reporting standards.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of resources in tool development (e.g., J-SRAT enhancements by UWI/Oxford) and capacity-building (e.g., 5 personnel trained in J-SRAT). Costs for global convening (e.g., CCRI Roundtable) were justified by multi-stakeholder engagement.

key_delivery_lessons: Underestimating the time for multi-partner agreements can delay implementation; future programmes should include a dedicated startup phase.
Modular design (independent components) reduces risk but requires robust coordination.
In-country capacity is critical for aligning with government systems (e.g., Jamaica’s J-SRAT integration).
Private sector engagement requires long-term coalitions beyond project lifecycles.
successful_delivery_practices: Delegated authority to partners for project-level decisions accelerated delivery (e.g., J-SRAT enhancements).
Quarterly milestone reviews maintained transparency and allowed adaptive management.
Pilot-focused approach (Jamaica) provided tangible examples for global scaling.
management_adaptations_made: Added ‘policy solutions’ to Output 4 to reflect evolving needs for bankable investments.
Shifted from ‘public-private partnerships’ to ‘collaborations’ to emphasize non-contractual engagement.
Prioritized consensus-building indicators (e.g., J-SRAT use in national planning).
innovations_attempted: J-SRAT’s integration with Jamaica’s Public Investment Management System to mainstream climate risk.
PCRAM 2.0’s investor-focused physical risk assessment methodology.
Cross-sectoral roundtables (e.g., CCRI Legacy Programme) to convene public/private stakeholders.
forward_recommendations: Establish a global coalition to sustain private sector engagement post-2026.
Increase in-country capacity (local/regional) to support Jamaica/Caribbean replication.
Develop measurable VFM indicators aligned with private sector KPIs (e.g., ICF).
Streamline management requirements for future phases (e.g., standardized reporting).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating startup delays through modular design but less so for Output 3 (public-private collaborations). Future risks should address sustainability of engagement mechanisms.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 5 personnel trained in J-SRAT use (3 in-person, 2 online).
13 attendees from 7 organizations at the CCRI Partners’ Roundtable.
Government of Jamaica’s Ministry of Finance using J-SRAT for project risk assessment.
policy_influence_achieved: J-SRAT integrated into Jamaica’s national planning systems.
PCRAM 2.0 methodology positioned to influence investor risk assessments globally.
Potential to inform NCQG’s $1T private sector mobilization targets.
capacity_building_results: Enhanced Government of Jamaica’s ability to assess climate risk in infrastructure projects.
UWI’s coastal protection database and Oxford’s J-SRAT upgrades built local analytical capacity.
unintended_consequences: Positive: J-SRAT’s broader adoption by Caribbean countries (via CCCCC roadmap).
Negative: Delays in prioritized project portfolio may postpone private sector crowding-in.
scalability_evidence: J-SRAT’s replication potential across CARICOM member states.
PCRAM 2.0’s applicability to other climate-vulnerable regions.
Public-private collaboration models (e.g., CCRI Roundtable) adaptable to other contexts.

continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with COP29/NCQG targets for private sector mobilization.
Demonstrated demand for tools (J-SRAT, PCRAM 2.0) and capacity-building.
Potential for regional scaling (Caribbean) and global policy influence.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (requires long-term coalition for private sector engagement)
planned_adaptations_future: Operationalize the Climate Finance Unit (CFU) in Jamaica to accelerate J-SRAT use.
Develop a prioritized portfolio of bankable resilience projects by March 2025.
Expand public-private collaborations beyond current partners (e.g., DFIs, regulators).
Refine indicators to better measure holistic success (e.g., private sector uptake).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Women and Girls Health: The Ending Preventable Deaths of Mothers, Babies and Children Support Programme

output_1.title: High quality Technical assistance provided to flagship countries

output_2.title: Flexible use of programme funding to respond and capitalise on identified additional opportunities for furthering global work towards ending preventable deaths, both centrally and in Posts

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme shifted to demand-led technical assistance model under Global Health Centre of Expertise, with embedded adviser roles in flagship countries. Enforced pause in recruitment due to UK Government's ODA spending reduction affected planned expansion (e.g., Bangladesh adviser role delayed). Transition from EACDS2 to GDD framework caused temporary delivery pause.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Technical assistance consultants consistently exceeded expectations (100% of 9 assignments met/exceeded objectives; 91% of consultancies fed into ongoing FCDO work). Government partners in flagship countries (e.g., Kenya, Somaliland, Nigeria) demonstrated strong engagement, with TA directly influencing policy documents (e.g., Climate Change and Health Vulnerability Assessments, Health Sector Coordination Frameworks).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Central coordination through FCDO's Global Health Centre of Expertise with decentralized delivery via embedded advisers (4 current roles in Ethiopia, Malawi, Nigeria, Somalia/Somaliland) and short-term TA consultants. Governance adapted to include multisectoral platforms (e.g., Health Development Partners groups in Nigeria).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Country dashboards enabled real-time monitoring and course correction. Coordinated TA assignments across 11 flagship countries, though Ethiopia's action plan remains incomplete. Cross-sectoral collaboration evident in Nigeria's Social Action Fund design (health, WASH, nutrition, economic security).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement via EACDS2 framework was effective (9 assignments completed), but transition to GDD framework caused delays. Flexible funding mechanisms allowed rapid response to emerging needs (e.g., climate adaptation TA in Kenya).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight due to ODA reductions and need to demonstrate impact. Quarterly check-ins and post-assignment follow-ups (3 completed) introduced to assess medium-term impact. Feedback surveys (avg. score 4.5/5) used for quality assurance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme pivoted to address emerging priorities (e.g., climate-health integration in Kenya, health financing in Nigeria). Flexible funds used for unplanned TA (e.g., HRH meetings in Nepal, Quality of Care strategy in DRC). Adapted to reduced ODA by focusing on catalytic interventions (e.g., leveraging £2.5m domestic co-funding in Nigeria).
adaptive_management_examples: Redesigned TA assignments in Kenya to include climate-health vulnerability assessments after identifying gaps in government capacity.
In Nigeria, adapted Social Action Fund design to include Ministerial inputs and pilot subnational implementation before national scale-up.
Somaliland: Supported drafting of Health Sector Coordination Framework to address donor duplication, though operationalization is pending.
Shifted from standalone TA to embedded adviser roles (e.g., Malawi's Programme Implementation Coordination Unit) for longer-term impact.

main_implementation_challenges: Transition delays from EACDS2 to GDD framework disrupted continuity of TA delivery.
UK Government's reduction in ODA spend enforced recruitment pauses (e.g., Bangladesh adviser role) and required reprioritization.
Ethiopia's action plan remains incomplete due to contextual challenges, affecting regional progress tracking.
Limited capacity in fragile contexts (e.g., Somalia/Somaliland, South Sudan) slowed institutionalization of TA outputs (e.g., Health Sector Coordination Framework).
external_factors_impact: ODA budget cuts reduced programme ambit and forced focus on fewer, higher-impact interventions.
Political transitions in flagship countries (e.g., Nigeria's new administration) required re-engagement with ministries.
Climate change exacerbated health vulnerabilities (e.g., Kenya's droughts), necessitating unplanned TA on climate adaptation.
Global inflation and currency fluctuations (e.g., Nigerian naira devaluation) affected value of domestic co-funding (₦2.5bn allocation).
contextual_constraints_new: Post-0.3% ODA announcement, country action plans became misaligned with reduced funding realities, requiring updates.
Increased demand for health financing TA (e.g., Nigeria's Child Nutrition Fund) outstripped available flexible funds.
Fragile contexts (e.g., DRC, South Sudan) required more intensive TA to achieve basic milestones (e.g., Quality of Care strategy validation).
Gender and equity provisions (e.g., informed consent for C-sections in Somaliland) faced cultural resistance despite government support.
partner_relationship_issues: Ministry of Health leadership changes in Kenya and Nigeria caused delays in TA sign-offs (e.g., 6-month lag for Climate Change and Health Vulnerability Assessment).
In Somalia/Somaliland, donor coordination challenges persisted despite the Health Sector Coordination Framework draft.
Some TA assignments required creative delivery approaches due to "hurdles with leadership" (per consultant feedback).
Limited engagement from non-flagship countries (e.g., Yemen, Syria) due to crisis priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Flagship countries lacked capacity to operationalize TA outputs (e.g., Somaliland's Health Sector Coordination Framework remains pending validation).
Shortage of skilled HRH in Nepal and DRC hindered implementation of TA recommendations (e.g., midwifery skills training).
FCDO posts struggled to absorb TA lessons into ongoing work without dedicated knowledge management systems.
Reduced programme staffing (due to ODA cuts) limited ability to monitor post-TA follow-ups.
risk_materialization: Political risk: Delays in government validation of strategies (e.g., DRC's Quality of Care plan).
Financial risk: Currency devaluation in Nigeria reduced real value of domestic co-funding.
Operational risk: Transition to GDD framework caused temporary delivery pause.
Reputational risk: High demand for TA outstripped supply, risking partner dissatisfaction.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend due to delayed GDD transition and ODA cuts, but flexible funds allowed reallocation to high-priority TA (e.g., climate-health in Kenya). Budget execution improved in Q4 2024/25 after adaptive measures (e.g., reduced Bangladesh adviser scope).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated through catalytic effects: £2.5m Nigerian government co-funding leveraged against £1.6m UK investment in Child Nutrition Fund. TA assignments achieved 90%+ satisfaction with avg. cost of £150k/assignment. Demand-led model reduced duplication (e.g., Somaliland's Health Sector Coordination Framework).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls with no audit findings. Quarterly financial reviews introduced to track TA spend against action plans. Currency risk mitigated via local currency accounts in Nigeria and Kenya.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost per TA assignment decreased by 12% YoY due to bulk procurement under EACDS2. Embedded advisers (£80k/year) proved more cost-effective than short-term TA (£200k/assignment) for sustained engagement.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Exceeded targets: Nigerian government contributed ₦2.5bn ($1.6m) + $2.2m from 11 states for nutrition commodities, against planned £1m leverage. Somaliland and Kenya governments provided in-kind support (e.g., office space, staff time).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Nigerian naira devaluation reduced real value of domestic co-funding by ~20%. Mitigated by front-loading USD-denominated TA contracts and negotiating local currency payments for advisers.

key_delivery_lessons: Demand-led TA model proved effective but requires clearer prioritization criteria to manage oversubscription.
Embedded advisers (vs. short-term TA) achieved higher government buy-in and sustainability (e.g., Nigeria's Social Action Fund).
Country dashboards enabled data-driven decision-making but need integration with FCDO's central M&E systems.
Flexible funds were critical for responding to unplanned needs (e.g., climate TA) but require clearer allocation rules.
successful_delivery_practices: Multisectoral TA assignments (e.g., Nigeria's Social Action Fund combining health, WASH, nutrition) achieved broader impact.
Post-assignment follow-ups (e.g., Malawi's health coordination improvements) provided evidence for medium-term impact.
Government co-chairing of platforms (e.g., Nigeria's Health Development Partners group) increased ownership.
Use of local consultants (e.g., DRC's Quality of Care strategy) improved contextual relevance.
management_adaptations_made: Introduced quarterly check-ins to monitor TA progress and adapt to government delays.
Revised TOR development to explicitly address engagement with marginalized groups.
Established mechanism to track diplomatic engagement instances within TA assignments.
Expanded M&E instruments to capture flexible funding usage beyond Strategic Flexible Fund.
innovations_attempted: Piloted climate-health integration TA in Kenya, linking vulnerability assessments to health planning.
Tested "TA bundles" (e.g., Malawi's coordination unit design + metrics development) for synergistic impact.
Developed digital dashboards for real-time tracking of mortality trends and TA alignment with action plans.
Experimented with subnational TA delivery (e.g., Nigeria's pilot states for Social Action Fund).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Country Action Plans reviewed but not fully updated post-ODA cuts. Climate TA remained limited (only 1 assignment in Kenya).
Completed: Improved tracking of TA assignments via dashboards, enabling country-level narratives.
Ongoing: Bottleneck analysis integrated into HWCN stocktakes but requires stronger linkage to business planning.
forward_recommendations: Update Country Action Plans to reflect post-ODA funding realities and align with new country business plans.
Increase focus on health financing and climate TA to match FCDO priorities, allocating 30% of flexible funds to these areas.
Strengthen knowledge management by documenting diplomatic engagement instances and equity impacts in all assignments.
Develop a "light touch" mechanism to map TA across countries and compare with action plan needs.
Conduct a lessons-learned review on transition from EACDS2 to GDD to inform future framework shifts.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderately effective. Proactive mitigation of political risks (e.g., engaging new Nigerian administration early) and financial risks (currency hedging). However, operational risks (e.g., GDD transition delays) were underestimated. Risk register requires updates to reflect ODA reduction impacts.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Technical assistance reached government ministries in 11 flagship countries (e.g., 10/11 action plans completed; 9 TA assignments in 6 countries). Indirect beneficiaries include populations covered by influenced policies (e.g., Nigeria's Social Action Fund targets 11 states).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.vs_targets: On track for government engagement (10/11 action plans completed) but behind on population-level mortality reductions (data not yet available; dashboards developed for 2026 tracking).

policy_influence_achieved: Kenya: Climate Change and Health Vulnerability Assessment and HNAP workplan integrated into ministry planning.
Somaliland: Health Sector Coordination Framework drafted (pending validation) to reduce donor duplication.
Nigeria: Social Action Fund design adopted by federal government with ₦2.5bn allocation; Child Nutrition Fund leveraged $4.1m in domestic/state funding.
DRC: Quality of Care strategy revised to prioritize maternal/child health, awaiting validation.
capacity_building_results: 100% of TA assignments (9/9) met capacity-building objectives (e.g., Malawi's health coordination improvements, Nepal's HRH fact sheet updates).
Embedded advisers built institutional capacity (e.g., Somalia's MoHD engagement on coordination frameworks).
Limited evidence of sustained capacity in fragile contexts (e.g., South Sudan) due to high staff turnover.

positive: TA on climate-health in Kenya catalysed cross-ministerial collaboration on adaptation planning.
Nigeria's Child Nutrition Fund leveraged unexpected state-level co-funding ($2.2m).
Somaliland's Health Sector Coordination Framework draft spurred donor alignment discussions.
negative: ODA cuts reduced programme ambit, limiting reach to non-flagship crisis countries (e.g., Yemen).
Delays in Ethiopia's action plan created regional disparity in progress tracking.
High demand for TA led to prioritization challenges, risking equity (e.g., marginalized groups in DRC).

scalability_evidence: Nigeria's Social Action Fund model designed for national scale-up post-pilot.
Kenya's climate-health TA approach replicable in other climate-vulnerable flagship countries (e.g., Malawi).
Somaliland's Health Sector Coordination Framework template adaptable for other fragile contexts.
Demand-led TA model proven scalable across 11 countries, with potential for expansion to non-flagship nations.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong demand (100% TA satisfaction), catalytic impact (e.g., £4.1m leveraged in Nigeria), and alignment with FCDO priorities (HWCN approach, climate-health). Adaptive management has mitigated ODA cuts, and the GDD transition positions the programme for scaled delivery. Country dashboards and action plans provide clear pathways to SDG targets.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes, with adaptations. The demand-led TA model is sustainable if flexible funds are secured. Embedded advisers enhance long-term impact, but reduced ODA requires prioritization of flagship countries. Transition to GDD framework resolves procurement risks.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Reallocate 30% of flexible funds to health financing and climate TA to match FCDO priorities.
Update Country Action Plans by Q1 2026 to reflect post-ODA funding and new business plans.
Expand dashboard functionality to track equity impacts and diplomatic engagement.
Pilot subnational TA delivery in 2–3 additional countries (e.g., Bangladesh, Pakistan).
Strengthen knowledge management to capture and disseminate TA lessons across FCDO networks.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Improving Essential Equipment for Aided Overseas Territories Programme
programme_metadata.review_period: December 2022 – December 2023 (with programme extension to 31 March 2024)

output_1.title: Improved ability to respond to sea rescue and firefighting emergencies and including roads maintenance

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme end date extended from September 2023 to March 2024 due to procurement and shipping delays. Flexible approach adopted to accommodate irregular shipping schedules and operational readiness (e.g., training, infrastructure preparation for large equipment like CT scanners).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Overseas Territory (OT) governments (Montserrat, St Helena, Tristan da Cunha) performed well in prioritizing needs and coordinating procurements. Delays were primarily due to external factors (shipping, supplier lead times) rather than partner underperformance. Montserrat and St Helena met expectations (score: A), while Tristan da Cunha faced shipping-related delays (score: B).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Cross-OT coordination was effective but lacked clearly defined FCDO internal roles (e.g., no dedicated leads for logframe monitoring or maintenance planning). Decision-making was decentralized across OTs, leading to some inconsistencies in risk management and timeline optimism.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with OT governments was strong, with joint prioritization of equipment needs. However, internal FCDO coordination across the Overseas Territories Directorate (OTPD) was ad hoc, with limited cross-OT learning or standardized maintenance planning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: 99% of items procured by review date, but 51% physically delivered due to shipping constraints. Procurement was timely, but lead times for specialized equipment (e.g., CT scanners, fire tenders) and shipping delays (e.g., Tristan da Cunha’s fire equipment delayed to January 2024) impacted delivery.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was lighter than planned due to FCDO’s reliance on OT governments for implementation. No major compliance issues reported, but maintenance planning and training schedules were under-monitored initially.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to extend timeline (September 2023 → March 2024) and reallocate minor funds to address urgent needs (e.g., Montserrat’s power outage crisis). Flexibility in procurement (e.g., refurbished fire tender for Montserrat) helped meet regulatory requirements cost-effectively.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended programme end date to accommodate shipping delays and operational readiness (e.g., training, infrastructure prep for CT scanners).
Reprioritized deliveries during Montserrat’s power outage crisis (August 2023), demonstrating agile response to emergent needs.
Used refurbished equipment (e.g., fire tender for Montserrat’s airport) to meet compliance standards within budget.

main_implementation_challenges: Irregular shipping schedules causing delays (e.g., Tristan da Cunha’s fire equipment delayed from September 2023 to January 2024).
Supplier lead times for specialized equipment (e.g., CT scanners, oxygen generators) longer than anticipated.
Infrastructure readiness delays (e.g., Montserrat’s hospital not yet complete to house CT scanner).
Training schedules lagging due to equipment arrival delays and OT capacity constraints.
external_factors_impact: Shipping disruptions (global and regional) affected 49% of equipment deliveries, particularly for bulkier items (e.g., 33 fire equipment items for Tristan da Cunha).
Montserrat’s power outage crisis (August 2023) diverted attention and resources, highlighting vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure.
COVID-19 legacy effects on supply chains (not explicitly stated but implied in shipping delays).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated aging infrastructure issues (e.g., Montserrat’s power plant failures) created urgent, unplanned needs.
Limited local capacity for equipment maintenance in smaller territories (e.g., Tristan da Cunha), risking long-term sustainability.
Regulatory compliance challenges (e.g., airport safety equipment needing ASSI certification) added complexity to procurements.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported. OT governments were collaborative, but their limited administrative capacity occasionally slowed processes (e.g., customs clearance, training coordination).
capacity_constraints_emerged: OTs lacked dedicated asset management systems for maintenance planning, requiring FCDO support to develop schedules.
Training backlogs due to delayed equipment arrivals and OT staff availability (e.g., Montserrat’s mammography machine training pending until 2024).
FCDO’s internal capacity constraints post-merger (e.g., incorrect AMP data, lack of maintenance planning leads).
risk_materialization: Shipping delays (high risk in business case) materialized, affecting 49% of deliveries.
Infrastructure dependencies (e.g., hospital construction for CT scanner installation) caused delays.
Maintenance planning risks emerged as a gap, requiring post-hoc mitigation.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track: 99% of £5 million allocated funds committed to procurements. Minor underspend likely due to delayed deliveries (e.g., Tristan da Cunha’s fire equipment), but no cost overruns reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Good VfM achieved through: (1) competitive procurement (e.g., refurbished fire tender); (2) reduced long-term costs (e.g., mammography machine eliminating overseas referrals); (3) agile responses to crises (e.g., power outage support). However, maintenance planning gaps risk long-term VfM if unaddressed.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Generally strong, but FCDO internal systems (e.g., Aid Management Platform) caused data inaccuracies post-merger. OT governments managed funds transparently, with no fraud or misprocurement reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High: Equipment procurements met or undercut market rates (e.g., fire tender for Montserrat’s airport). Operational efficiencies gained (e.g., St Helena’s road maintenance equipment reducing long-term costs).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not applicable (100% FCDO-funded).

key_delivery_lessons: Underestimated shipping and supplier lead times—future programmes should buffer timelines by 20–30%.
Maintenance planning must be integrated from design phase, not retrofitted.
Cross-OT coordination requires dedicated FCDO leads (e.g., for logframes, risk management).
OT capacity constraints necessitate simpler training schedules and localized technical support.
successful_delivery_practices: Flexible procurement (e.g., refurbished equipment) balanced cost and compliance.
OT-government partnerships effectively prioritized needs (e.g., CT scanner for Montserrat).
Agile crisis response (e.g., Montserrat power outage) demonstrated programme adaptability.
management_adaptations_made: Extended programme timeline to March 2024 to accommodate delays.
Added maintenance planning as a formal deliverable for future phases.
Initiated cross-OTPD learning sessions to share lessons (e.g., shipping workarounds).
innovations_attempted: Used refurbished fire tender to meet ASSI standards at lower cost.
Piloted modular training approaches (e.g., virtual sessions for Tristan da Cunha) to address capacity gaps.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Maintenance planning was identified as a gap in prior reviews but only mitigated reactively in this phase.
forward_recommendations: Develop a centralized OT equipment maintenance fund and asset management system.
Assign dedicated FCDO leads for cross-OT coordination, risk management, and logframe monitoring.
Explore non-ODA funding options for critical infrastructure to reduce dependency.
Conduct a lessons-learned workshop with OT governments to standardize procurement and training approaches.
Integrate climate/resilience criteria into equipment selection (e.g., backup power for medical devices).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective: Identified risks (e.g., shipping delays) materialized, but mitigation was reactive (e.g., timeline extensions). Proactive risk management (e.g., contingency contracts for shipping) was lacking.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.Montserrat: CT scanner, oxygen generator, mammography kit (pending commissioning), fire tender (operational). Direct beneficiaries: ~5,000 residents; indirect: reduced off-island medical referrals.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.St Helena: Haematology/Biochemistry analyzers (operational), airport fire safety equipment (operational), sea rescue engines (installed). Direct beneficiaries: ~4,500 residents; indirect: improved airline safety compliance.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.Tristan da Cunha: ECG, pulse oximeter, endoscopy equipment (operational), fire equipment (delayed). Direct beneficiaries: ~250 residents; indirect: reduced medical evacuation needs.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium (high for equipment in use; low for Tristan da Cunha due to maintenance capacity gaps)
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Limited but emerging: Programme influenced OT government priorities (e.g., Montserrat’s health equipment included in long-term planning). ASSI compliance at airports sets regulatory precedents.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Mixed: Operational training delivered (e.g., St Helena’s sea rescue staff), but maintenance capacity remains weak in smaller OTs. FCDO’s internal capacity for cross-OT coordination improved through adaptive management.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Equipment arrivals catalysed OT government investments in complementary infrastructure (e.g., Montserrat’s hospital prep for CT scanner).
Negative: Shipping delays eroded trust in timely deliveries, risking future engagement.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: High potential for replication in other OTs or small island states with similar needs. Model of flexible, demand-driven equipment funding is transferable, but requires stronger maintenance planning.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong demand (OTs remain dependent on UK ODA for critical equipment) and effective delivery (99% procurement rate, high VfM). Extension will address remaining deliveries (e.g., CT scanners) and embed maintenance systems. FCDO views it as a valuable agile mechanism for OT support.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High (if maintenance and training gaps are addressed)
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-term sustainable with adjustments: Requires (1) dedicated maintenance funding; (2) clearer FCDO-OT roles; (3) exploration of non-ODA funding for recurring needs.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (programme seen as a success despite delays, with strong OT government buy-in)
planned_adaptations_future: Extend to March 2024 to complete deliveries and training.
Incorporate maintenance planning into future phases with earmarked funds.
Pilot a cross-OT equipment asset register to improve coordination.
Explore blending ODA with OT government co-funding for sustainability.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Amplifying Movements, Organisations and Activism to End Violence and Support Gender Equality in Sierra Leone (MOVE)

output_1.title: WROs and women's / girls' groups are resourced to operate to tackle SGBV and its drivers, through grant making by redistributing resources to WRO and girls’ activism in flexible and appropriate ways

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme adopted a fully participatory grant-making (PGM) process led by a survivor-led, intergenerational panel (11 women from 8 districts), which replaced traditional donor-driven priority-setting. The British High Commission (BHC) ceded decision-making authority to this panel, aligning with the programme's feminist principles but requiring significant upfront investment in panel formation and capacity-building.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The implementing partner, Purposeful, performed effectively in operationalizing the PGM process, including: 1) Proactively adjusting panel composition to ensure intergenerational representation when initial selections lacked age diversity; 2) Co-creating grant criteria and processes with panel members; 3) Exceeding grantee targets (19 selected vs. 15 planned, with 16% unregistered groups). Grantees reported that flexible, multi-year funding enabled sustained operations and responsiveness to emerging needs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance shifted from traditional donor-led structures to a model where the grant-making panel (comprising activists and survivors) holds primary decision-making authority. The BHC maintains oversight through an Accountable Grant Arrangement (AGA) but defers to panel decisions. Purposeful acts as a "skilled intermediary" facilitating the process while reducing administrative burdens on grantees.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between BHC, Purposeful, and the grant-making panel was effective during the inception phase. The panel's January 2024 workshop successfully aligned stakeholders on participatory processes. However, the model requires ongoing dialogue to balance UK compliance requirements with flexible, non-extractive engagement practices.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The PGM process was implemented as planned, with a two-week open call for panel members followed by co-creation of funding criteria. Procurement of grantees was completed by April 2024, with grants disbursed at the start of FY 2024/25. The process prioritized grassroots organizations typically excluded from traditional funding mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was lighter than traditional programmes, focusing on supporting the panel's autonomy while ensuring compliance. The BHC monitored through milestone reviews (e.g., panel formation by January 2024, grantee selection by April 2024) rather than prescriptive interventions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated high flexibility by: 1) Adjusting panel composition mid-process to ensure representation; 2) Allowing grantees to use funds for core operations and emergent needs; 3) Accepting unregistered groups (16% of grantees). Grantees reported that flexible funding improved their ability to sustain work and respond to community needs.
adaptive_management_examples: Proactively expanded the grant-making panel's age range after initial selections lacked intergenerational diversity, adding older activists to balance the group.
Published a blog in July 2024 to share learning on participatory grant-making, demonstrating transparency and adaptive knowledge management.
Reduced burdensome reporting requirements for grantees, assessing compliance needs against the scale of funding and local context.

main_implementation_challenges: Designing and operationalizing a participatory grant-making process within a bilateral donor framework, requiring shifts in traditional power dynamics and compliance practices.
Balancing UK compliance requirements with the programme's commitment to flexible, non-extractive funding for grassroots organizations.
Ensuring meaningful inclusion of marginalized groups (e.g., women with disabilities, unregistered organizations) in grant-making while maintaining accountability.
external_factors_impact: Entrenched societal norms in Sierra Leone, where 60% of women experience physical violence, 83% undergo FGM/C, and two-thirds of girls report sexual violence, creating a high-risk environment for activists.
Low help-seeking behavior (only 40% of SGBV survivors seek assistance) and high social acceptance of VAWG, which undermines prevention efforts.
Nascent national response systems for SGBV, with limited support services and institutional resilience, placing greater burden on grassroots responders.
Emerging regional/global backlash against women's rights, risking regression on gender equality gains.
contextual_constraints_new: Frontline partners faced unanticipated backlash from communities, including pressure to cease operations and personal safety threats, which were not fully accounted for in risk planning.
The depth of trauma and personal investment among grantees (e.g., survivors leading SGBV response) required additional psychosocial support and adaptive management approaches.
High turnover and burnout among grassroots activists due to the emotionally demanding nature of SGBV response work.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between traditional donor accountability expectations and the programme's feminist principles of trust-based, flexible funding.
Challenges in establishing equitable partnerships where grantees (many of whom are survivors) feel valued and respected, given historical extractive donor practices.
Differences in risk tolerance between BHC (bound by UK aid regulations) and grantees operating in high-risk, fluid contexts.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Grantees (particularly unregistered groups) required more intensive capacity-building than anticipated to manage multi-year funds and comply with basic reporting requirements.
The grant-making panel, while expert in activism, needed training on collective decision-making, ethical considerations, and participatory processes.
Purposeful's role as intermediary demanded higher-than-expected resources to bridge between donor compliance needs and grantee flexibility.
risk_materialization: Community backlash against SGBV responders materialized as a significant risk, with partners reporting pressure to stop work and safety concerns.
The risk of "regression on the rights agenda" noted in the review began to emerge, consistent with global trends of closing civic space for women's rights organizations.
Operational risks related to working with unregistered groups (16% of grantees) required adaptive management to ensure accountability without imposing excessive burdens.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme is on track financially, with the participatory grant-making process completed within the six-month inception period. First tranche of grants (covering 19 grantees) was disbursed at the start of FY 2024/25, aligning with planned timelines. No significant underspend or overspend reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indicators suggest strong VFM due to: 1) Exceeding grantee targets (19 vs. 15) without additional cost; 2) Leveraging Purposeful's existing infrastructure to reduce overheads; 3) Directing 100% of grant funds to frontline responders, minimizing administrative leakage. The programme's alignment with FCDO's International Women and Girls Strategy enhances strategic VFM.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by Purposeful was assessed as effective, with transparent processes for: 1) Panel member stipends; 2) Grantee disbursements; 3) Monitoring of fund usage. The AGA framework provided adequate safeguards while allowing flexibility. No audit findings or financial irregularities reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was demonstrated through: 1) Participatory design reducing costly external consultations; 2) Multi-year grants lowering transaction costs for grantees; 3) Focus on core funding, which reduced grantees' need for multiple small grants. The programme's unit cost per grantee (~£44,737 over 3.5 years) is competitive for SGBV interventions in the region.

key_delivery_lessons: Participatory grant-making is resource-intensive during inception but builds trust and ownership, leading to stronger implementation. The six-month design phase was critical for success.
Flexible, multi-year funding enables grantees to focus on impact rather than survival, but requires donors to tolerate higher perceived risk and adapt monitoring approaches.
Working with unregistered groups is feasible with proportionate due diligence, but demands creative solutions for financial accountability (e.g., fiscal sponsors).
Trauma-informed approaches are essential when funding survivor-led organizations, as personal investment in the work affects both resilience and vulnerability.
successful_delivery_practices: Co-creation of grant criteria with the panel ensured buy-in and relevance to local contexts, resulting in 19 high-quality grantees.
Proactive adjustment of panel composition to include older activists demonstrated commitment to intergenerational equity.
Reducing burdensome reporting requirements (e.g., simplifying narrative reports) improved grantee satisfaction without compromising accountability.
Publicly sharing learning (e.g., blog on PGM) enhanced transparency and contributed to sector-wide knowledge.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from prescriptive oversight to milestone-based monitoring, focusing on panel decision-making processes rather than outputs.
Increased support for grantee capacity-building, particularly for unregistered groups, to manage funds and comply with basic requirements.
Established regular check-ins between BHC, Purposeful, and the panel to address emerging challenges (e.g., backlash against grantees).
Adjusted financial disbursement schedules to align with grantees' cash flow needs, reducing liquidity pressures.
innovations_attempted: Survivor-led grant-making panel with full decision-making authority, a rarity in bilateral aid programmes.
Use of flexible, core funding for SGBV response, allowing grantees to allocate resources to emergent needs (e.g., safety measures for activists facing backlash).
Trauma-informed grant management practices, including psychosocial support referrals for grantees.
Non-extractive engagement model, where grantee objectives drive interactions rather than donor agendas.
forward_recommendations: Continue open dialogue between BHC and Purposeful to refine proportionate, flexible assurance mechanisms that meet UK compliance needs without overburdening grantees.
Share learning on participatory grant-making within FCDO communities of practice to inform similar programmes.
Develop a trauma-informed support system for grantees, including access to psychosocial resources and peer networks.
Monitor the emerging risk of rights regression and civic space closure, adapting programme strategies to protect grantees and sustain gains.
Explore opportunities to influence national SGBV response systems by documenting and amplifying grantees' local successes.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was partially effective. While planned risks (e.g., community backlash) were identified, the programme demonstrated adaptive capacity in responding to them (e.g., adjusting panel composition, providing grantee support). However, the emerging global trend of rights regression was not fully anticipated in initial risk registers. The participatory model itself served as a risk mitigation strategy by embedding local ownership.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Early indicators suggest potential for policy influence through: 1) Grantees' advocacy work connecting local and global campaigns; 2) The programme's alignment with Sierra Leone's national SGBV strategies; 3) Purposeful's role in amplifying grassroots voices. However, concrete policy changes are not yet measurable in this first year.
capacity_building_results: Grantees reported improved ability to sustain operations and respond to community needs due to flexible, multi-year funding.
The grant-making panel developed skills in collective decision-making, ethical grant-making, and participatory processes.
Unregistered groups gained experience in managing institutional funds, though additional support is needed for long-term sustainability.

unintended_consequences.description: Grantees experienced increased legitimacy and visibility within their communities due to association with the programme, enhancing their ability to advocate for change.
Some grantees faced heightened backlash and safety risks as a result of their increased profile and funding, requiring unplanned security measures.
The programme's feminist approach inspired other donors in Sierra Leone to explore more flexible, participatory funding models.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: The participatory grant-making model demonstrates scalability potential, as evidenced by: 1) Strong demand (over 100 panel applicants); 2) Successful adaptation to local contexts (e.g., intergenerational representation); 3) Interest from other donors in replicating the approach. However, scalability depends on donors' willingness to cede control and tolerate higher perceived risks.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme should continue based on: 1) Strong first-year performance (Overall Output Score: A); 2) Alignment with FCDO's International Women and Girls Strategy; 3) Early progress in addressing entrenched SGBV challenges in Sierra Leone; 4) High demand and positive feedback from grantees; 5) Potential for scalable impact through the participatory model. The review notes that outcomes/impacts are not yet demonstrable (as expected in Year 1) but that the foundation for success has been laid.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is assessed as sustainable in the medium term, given: 1) Strong partnership between BHC and Purposeful; 2) Grantee ownership fostered through participatory processes; 3) Flexible funding that adapts to context. Long-term sustainability depends on addressing emerging risks (e.g., rights regression) and securing continued political support for feminist funding approaches.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Enhance support for grantees facing backlash, including safety planning and psychosocial resources.
Strengthen monitoring of policy influence pathways to capture grantees' advocacy impacts.
Explore opportunities to document and scale successful grantee practices (e.g., community-based SGBV response models).
Adjust risk management strategies to address the emerging threat of civic space closure.
Deepening the trauma-informed approach across all programme components.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Knowledge for Development and Diplomacy (K4DD) Programme

output_1.title: K4DD outputs are produced to quantity, quality, and timeliness standards (Helpdesk: Rapid Evidence Reviews and Emerging Issues Reports)

output_2.title: Learning is enhanced through effective engagement with the Expert Challenge Sessions, Evidence and Policy Clinics, and Learning Products

output_3.title: Wider learning and use of evidence is enhanced through effective uptake and use of K4DD products

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme was designed to operate with both ODA and non-ODA funding, but has only received ODA funding in FY 2024/25, restricting its scope to development-focused activities only. The full launch was delayed until end-September 2024 due to funding uncertainties and the UK General Election.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The IDS-led consortium (including University of Birmingham, Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, University of Manchester, RUSI, and ACU) was formalized by April 2024 and is operating at full capacity. Partners are fulfilling commissions through both a core standing team and an ad-hoc global pool of researchers. Informal feedback on consortium performance has been positive, particularly regarding the responsiveness of the Helpdesk and the quality of pilot learning events.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: IDS and FCDO established operational ways of working, including a formalized consortium structure and a monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) approach. An Advisory Group was created to oversee programme governance. The management structure has proven effective in scaling up Helpdesk output (140+ reports delivered) but faced challenges in coordinating the Learning Service due to lower initial demand.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between FCDO and the consortium has been effective for the Helpdesk (exceeding quantity, timeliness, and quality targets) but less so for the Learning Service, where scheduling conflicts and FCDO staff turnover have delayed events. The delayed programme launch also reduced coordination opportunities for promotional and demand-generation activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Commissions are fulfilled either through the core consortium team or via ad-hoc consultancy contracts with a global pool of researchers. This flexible procurement model has enabled the programme to meet high demand for Rapid Evidence Reviews while maintaining quality standards (91% top-rated feedback). No procurement-related challenges were explicitly noted beyond the funding constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has been more intensive than originally planned due to the need to manage rapid scaling of the Helpdesk and address the lack of non-ODA funding. The Advisory Group and FCDO have played active roles in reviewing progress, particularly for pilot events like the Evidence and Policy Clinics.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by: 1) Accommodating unplanned requests for regular Evidence Summaries (e.g., monthly Humanitarian Evidence Discourse Summary), 2) Adjusting the Learning Service targets due to delayed launch and lower demand, and 3) Securing funding to test AI tools for improving efficiency in report production (Sept 2024–March 2025).
adaptive_management_examples: Reduced Year 1 target for Expert Challenge Sessions due to delayed launch and lower demand, with a revised process for managing Learning Service requests.
Introduction of regular Evidence Summaries (e.g., MPOX Health Evidence Summary) despite these not being part of the formal offer, in response to FCDO needs.
Planned evaluation of AI tools to address potential future demand surges, with testing funded and scheduled for Sept 2024–March 2025.
Updated guidance for Evidence and Policy Clinics to reflect the longer-than-anticipated time required for delivery, with adjusted customer expectations.

main_implementation_challenges: Lack of non-ODA funding in FY 2024/25, restricting the programme to ODA-eligible activities only and limiting accessibility for FCDO staff requiring non-development-focused evidence.
Delayed full launch (until end-September 2024) due to funding uncertainties and the UK General Election, which reduced demand generation and promotional activities.
Lower-than-expected publication permissions for Helpdesk outputs, limiting external visibility and uptake.
Scheduling challenges for Learning Service events (Expert Challenge Sessions and Evidence and Policy Clinics) due to FCDO staff turnover and busy calendars.
Low survey response rates (16%) for Helpdesk feedback, complicating impact assessment and quality monitoring.
external_factors_impact: The UK General Election created uncertainty around non-ODA funding allocations, directly limiting programme scope and delaying communications.
High FCDO staff turnover and calendar constraints reduced participation in Learning Service events, slowing progress on longer-term engagement activities like Evidence and Policy Clinics.
contextual_constraints_new: The need for both ODA and non-ODA funding was underestimated in the business case; the absence of non-ODA funds has created a structural constraint on programme delivery.

Demand for the Helpdesk exceeded initial projections (140 RERs delivered vs. 120 targeted), while demand for the Learning Service was lower than anticipated, revealing a mismatch in user engagement across different outputs.
Publication restrictions on Helpdesk outputs (lower-than-expected permissions) were not fully anticipated, limiting the programme’s ability to achieve its goal of wider external uptake.
capacity_constraints_emerged: The consortium’s capacity to manage surges in Helpdesk demand post-launch (Sept 2024) is a growing concern, though initial demand-management approaches (e.g., redirecting out-of-scope requests) have been implemented.
The time required to deliver Evidence and Policy Clinics was underestimated, requiring adjustments to guidance and customer expectations.
risk_materialization: The risk of insufficient non-ODA funding materialized, restricting programme activities to ODA-eligible topics only.
The risk of delayed demand generation due to external factors (General Election, funding uncertainty) materialized, particularly affecting the Learning Service.
The risk of low survey response rates materialized (16%), limiting the programme’s ability to systematically track impact and user satisfaction.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme is executing its £5 million budget as planned for ODA-funded activities, but the absence of non-ODA funding in FY 2024/25 has created a significant gap. This has narrowed the scope of deliverables and required reprioritization of resources toward ODA-eligible outputs only. No over- or under-spending was reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: The programme demonstrates strong value for money in its Helpdesk output, exceeding targets for quantity (140 RERs delivered vs. 120 targeted), timeliness (100% on-time delivery vs. 70% target), and quality (91% top-rated vs. 60% target). However, the lack of non-ODA funding has reduced the programme’s ability to fully deliver on its original value-for-money proposition, which included both development and diplomacy-focused activities. The cost efficiency of the Helpdesk (£35,714 per RER at target volume) is high, but this is offset by underutilization of the Learning Service.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by the IDS-led consortium has been effective, with no reported issues in budget execution or reporting. The accountable grant mechanism has allowed for flexible resource allocation, such as securing additional funding for AI tool testing. However, the inability to access non-ODA funds has required reactive adjustments to financial planning.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The Helpdesk has achieved higher-than-planned cost efficiency due to exceeding output targets (140 RERs delivered vs. 120 planned) without proportional cost increases. The Learning Service has lower cost efficiency due to delayed demand, but this is expected to improve post-launch (Sept 2024).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: No co-funding materialized during the review period. The programme was designed to leverage both ODA and non-ODA funds, but only ODA funding was allocated in FY 2024/25.

key_delivery_lessons: The Helpdesk’s demand-driven model is highly effective but requires robust demand-management processes to handle potential surges post-launch (Sept 2024). Initial approaches (e.g., redirecting out-of-scope requests) should be regularly reviewed.
The Learning Service requires more proactive demand generation and awareness-raising within FCDO, as its value proposition is less immediately apparent than the Helpdesk’s.
Publication permissions for Helpdesk outputs are a critical bottleneck for achieving wider external impact; options to improve permissions (e.g., clearer guidelines, incentives) should be explored.
The time and resource requirements for Evidence and Policy Clinics were underestimated; future planning should account for longer lead times and more intensive facilitation needs.
successful_delivery_practices: The flexible consortium model (core team + ad-hoc global pool) has enabled rapid scaling of Helpdesk output while maintaining quality.
Pilot events (e.g., the first Evidence and Policy Clinic on Public Financial Management) received positive informal feedback, validating the Learning Service’s approach.
Regular Evidence Summaries (e.g., Humanitarian Evidence Discourse Summary) were introduced successfully in response to unplanned FCDO needs, demonstrating adaptability.
The monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) framework was established early and has provided a strong basis for tracking progress, despite low survey response rates.
management_adaptations_made: Reduced the Year 1 target for Expert Challenge Sessions from 3.5 to 1 completed (with 3 in progress) due to delayed launch and lower demand.
Secured funding to test AI tools for improving the efficiency of Rapid Evidence Reviews and Emerging Issues Reports (Sept 2024–March 2025).
Updated guidance for Evidence and Policy Clinics to reflect longer delivery timelines and manage customer expectations.
Implemented initial demand-management approaches for the Helpdesk (e.g., minimizing ‘double unit’ requests) in anticipation of post-launch surges.
innovations_attempted: Introduction of unplanned regular Evidence Summaries (e.g., bi-weekly MPOX Health Evidence Summary) to address emerging FCDO priorities.
Planned evaluation of AI tools to automate or assist in producing Rapid Evidence Reviews, Emerging Issues Reports, and Evidence Summaries, aiming to improve efficiency and scalability.
Pilot Evidence and Policy Clinics as a longer-term, multi-event learning format, with lessons fed into subsequent iterations.
forward_recommendations: Prioritize securing non-ODA funding for FY 2025/26 to restore the programme’s full scope (development and diplomacy-focused activities).
Strengthen demand generation for the Learning Service through targeted FCDO engagement, leveraging positive feedback from pilot events.
Review and enhance the publication permissions process to increase the proportion of Helpdesk outputs available externally, aligning with the programme’s wider impact goals.
Monitor and refine demand-management approaches for the Helpdesk post-launch (Sept 2024), including potential use of AI tools to improve efficiency.
Improve survey response rates for Helpdesk feedback by testing incentives, shorter surveys, or targeted follow-ups, and develop outcome/impact evaluation methods to strengthen MEL.
Update the Evidence and Policy Clinic guidance and customer communications to reflect the longer time requirements identified during piloting.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management has been partially effective. Planned risks around funding (non-ODA) and demand generation materialized, but the programme adapted by reprioritizing ODA-eligible activities and delaying non-critical components. The Advisory Group and FCDO oversight have helped mitigate operational risks (e.g., Helpdesk quality and timeliness), but strategic risks (e.g., limited external uptake due to publication restrictions) require further attention.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: FCDO staff across departments (exact numbers not specified); 142 Helpdesk reports delivered to users, with 23 feedback responses (16% response rate).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Wider development and diplomacy communities via public-facing website (uptake data not available due to delayed launch and publication restrictions).

policy_influence_achieved: Several Helpdesk reports have fed into high-priority FCDO strategies and policies, including thinking on local leadership and development partnerships (specific examples annexed in the review).
The pilot Evidence and Policy Clinic on Public Financial Management received positive feedback from FCDO policy customers, suggesting potential for longer-term policy influence.
capacity_building_results: FCDO staff have gained improved access to timely, high-quality evidence through the Helpdesk, with 91% of surveyed reports rated in the top two quality grades.

The Learning Service (Expert Challenge Sessions and Evidence and Policy Clinics) has begun to strengthen FCDO teams’ capabilities in evidence-informed analysis, though scale remains limited due to delayed demand.
Consortium partners (e.g., IDS, University of Birmingham) have developed new processes for rapid evidence synthesis and facilitated learning, enhancing their institutional capacity.
unintended_consequences: Positive: The programme’s flexibility in accommodating unplanned Evidence Summaries (e.g., MPOX Health Evidence Summary) has addressed emerging FCDO priorities not originally scoped in the business case.

Negative: The lack of non-ODA funding has unintentionally created a perception among some FCDO staff that K4DD is only for development-focused work, potentially limiting its use for diplomacy-related evidence needs.
scalability_evidence: The Helpdesk’s demand-driven model has demonstrated scalability, with output exceeding targets (140 RERs delivered vs. 120 planned) without proportional cost increases. The consortium’s flexible resourcing (core team + ad-hoc global pool) supports further scaling.
The Learning Service’s scalability is less evident due to lower initial demand, but the pilot Evidence and Policy Clinics suggest potential for replication if demand increases post-launch.
Planned AI tool evaluations (Sept 2024–March 2025) could enhance scalability by reducing the time/cost per output.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated strong performance in its first year, particularly through the Helpdesk (exceeding quantity, timeliness, and quality targets) and positive feedback on pilot Learning Service events. It aligns with FCDO’s evidence needs and complements other services. However, its full potential remains unrealized due to funding constraints (lack of non-ODA funds) and delayed demand generation. Addressing these issues—particularly securing non-ODA funding and scaling up the Learning Service—would unlock greater impact.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is sustainable in the short to medium term for ODA-funded activities, but its long-term sustainability depends on: 1) Securing non-ODA funding to restore the full scope of work, 2) Successfully managing post-launch demand surges for both the Helpdesk and Learning Service, and 3) Improving external uptake through resolved publication permissions and targeted communications.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Test and integrate AI tools to improve the efficiency of Rapid Evidence Reviews and other outputs (Sept 2024–March 2025).
Strengthen demand-generation strategies for the Learning Service, including targeted engagement with FCDO teams and promotion of pilot event successes.
Review and update processes for managing Helpdesk demand post-launch, including potential triage mechanisms or expanded resourcing.
Explore options to increase publication permissions for Helpdesk outputs, aligning with the programme’s goal of wider external impact.
Advocate for non-ODA funding allocation in FY 2025/26 to enable full delivery of the programme’s original scope (development and diplomacy).
Enhance MEL systems to capture longer-term outcomes and impact, addressing current gaps in survey response rates and external uptake data.
