programme_metadata.programme_title: Open Societies Enabling Fund (OSEF)

output_1.title: Innovative measures, campaigns, studies, and guidelines are implemented by select media to create counter narrative and ensure respectful reporting on human rights for particular minorities

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme initially managed in-house due to low value and post-COVID re-engagement needs. Two Business Case amendments expanded scope, budget (from £600,000 to £4.8M), and duration (to 2030), adding a funded staff member and shifting to a more holistic democratic governance approach. Only 4 of 6 planned projects were implemented due to due diligence delays and election context.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong technical expertise in human rights and media but had lower-than-expected administrative capacity for international donor project management, requiring significant programme team support for quality control (e.g., campaign materials, proposals).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: In-house management with direct engagement of CSOs, supplemented by a newly recruited Human Rights Programme Assistant (per first Business Case amendment). Coordination with FCDO’s Centre for Expertise on Democratic Governance influenced the second amendment’s expanded scope.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Direct engagement with national/local CSOs successfully reconnected post-COVID partnerships but revealed capacity gaps. Coordination with election monitoring bodies (KPU, BAWASLU) and diplomatic channels (e.g., Women in Power Empowering Women reception) was effective but ad-hoc.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Six projects identified via bidding process, but protracted due diligence and election context limited implementation to four projects. Grant amendments (e.g., October 2024) added funding for *Pilkada* monitoring and Papua-focused activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to partners’ administrative capacity gaps, requiring hands-on programme team involvement in proposal development, output quality control, and adaptive support (e.g., WhatsApp mentoring groups).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by: 1) Adding election transparency projects via Business Case amendments; 2) Adjusting training content (e.g., PUSAD Paramadina’s participant selection); 3) Expanding geographic focus (e.g., Papua election monitoring); 4) Extending timeline to 2030.
adaptive_management_examples: Added intensive WhatsApp mentoring for human rights defenders when issues escalated (Output 1.1.c).
Included high-level networking events (e.g., Women MPs engagement by KAPAL Perempuan) not originally planned.
Shifted from 6 to 4 projects due to context changes, reallocating funds to election monitoring.
Expanded *Pilkada* and Papua focus mid-implementation based on emerging needs.

main_implementation_challenges: Post-COVID re-engagement with CSOs required rebuilding relationships and identifying new partners in a restricted civic space.
Election period (Feb–Nov 2024) created a dynamic, unpredictable context for project implementation.
Protracted due diligence processes delayed project start-ups, reducing the number of projects implemented.
Partners’ limited administrative capacity for donor reporting/financial management increased programme team workload.
Original theory of change was overly broad, complicating progress tracking.
external_factors_impact: Indonesia’s 2024 national/regional elections created both opportunities (e.g., election monitoring relevance) and risks (e.g., political sensitivity, delayed partner engagement).
Post-COVID recovery limited CSO operational capacity and required relationship rebuilding.
New Criminal Code (effective 2026) added urgency to human rights advocacy but also uncertainty about enforcement.
contextual_constraints_new: Shrinking civic space and increased vulnerability of human rights defenders exceeded initial assessments.
Local political dynamics (e.g., Papua’s election context) required unplanned adaptations like in-depth regional monitoring.
Inflation/currency fluctuations (not quantified) may have affected budget execution.
partner_relationship_issues: Some CSOs struggled with donor compliance (e.g., financial reporting, procurement documentation).
Delays in partner onboarding due to due diligence backlogs and election-related disruptions.
Divergent expectations between partners’ grassroots approaches and FCDO’s results-focused requirements.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Programme team underestimated the administrative support needed for CSO partners, leading to the recruitment of a dedicated Human Rights Programme Assistant.
Limited CSO capacity for monitoring/evaluation and adaptive management (e.g., adjusting activities mid-implementation).
Need for external implementer identified to provide future capacity building to partners (per second Business Case amendment).
risk_materialization: Election-related political sensitivity materialized, requiring careful messaging and diplomatic coordination.
CSO administrative weaknesses risked output quality, mitigated by programme team interventions.
Delayed project starts due to due diligence risks were partially offset by flexible budget reallocation.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Initial £600,000 budget increased to £4.8M via amendments, with annual £750,000 allocation post-2024. Projects delivered within approved budgets, though administrative costs were higher than anticipated due to partner capacity gaps.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. Achieved core outputs (e.g., election monitoring recommendations, media campaigns) within budget, with unplanned but high-value additions (e.g., policy recommendations for electoral reform, Papua-specific analysis). CSO-led monitoring enhanced public trust in democratic processes, aligning with Business Case goals.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Adequate but resource-intensive. Partners required significant programme team support for financial compliance (e.g., receipt documentation, audit trails). No major fraud or misappropriation reported, but administrative burdens slowed disbursements.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient for outputs delivered, though transaction costs were higher due to in-house management and partner hand-holding. Cost per beneficiary not quantified in the review.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not mentioned; assumed fully FCDO-funded post-amendments.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly quantified, but programme budget increases may reflect inflationary pressures.

key_delivery_lessons: CSO technical expertise ≠ donor management capacity; future programmes should budget for capacity-building support.
In-house management is viable for small-scale programmes but unsustainable at larger scales (per second amendment).
Election periods offer high-impact opportunities but require flexible timelines and risk mitigation.
Direct CSO engagement post-COVID was valuable for relationship-building but resource-intensive.
successful_delivery_practices: Adaptive mentoring (e.g., WhatsApp groups) improved support for at-risk human rights defenders.
High-level networking (e.g., Women MPs event) amplified policy influence beyond original scope.
Rapid Business Case amendments allowed responsive expansion (e.g., *Pilkada* monitoring).
Partner-led election monitoring (NETGRIT) generated actionable policy recommendations.
management_adaptations_made: Recruited Human Rights Programme Assistant to address administrative gaps.
Shifted from 6 to 4 projects to focus resources on higher-impact activities.
Added election integrity workshops and diplomatic follow-up (e.g., KPU/BAWASLU engagement).
Expanded geographic focus (Papua) based on monitoring findings.
innovations_attempted: Crowd-sourced election monitoring via NETGRIT’s *JagaSuara* app.
Community mediation training for interfaith leaders in conflict-prone areas (e.g., Bukittinggi).
Feminist journalism training for regional reporters to improve election coverage diversity.
previous_recommendations_progress: First Business Case amendment addressed administrative capacity gaps by funding a dedicated staff member.
Second amendment responded to calls for a longer-term, governance-focused approach (per Centre for Expertise advice).
Election monitoring recommendations were shared with KPU/BAWASLU, though systemic uptake remains pending.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Convene a workshop to develop a comprehensive election reform agenda using *Pemilu*/*Pilkada* monitoring lessons.
Appoint an external implementer to provide CSO capacity building on project management and donor compliance.
Refine the theory of change to focus on democratic governance, with clearer logframe criteria for future projects.
Leverage election monitoring findings for diplomatic engagement on death penalty and civic space issues.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Anticipated risks (e.g., election sensitivity, CSO capacity) materialized but were mitigated through adaptive management (e.g., amendments, staff recruitment). Unplanned risks (e.g., Papua’s election complexities) required reactive adjustments. Future risk management should include contingency funds for partner capacity-building.

policy_influence_achieved: Election monitoring reports shared with KPU/BAWASLU, with recommendations for transparency improvements.
Women MPs engagement laid groundwork for 2024–2029 parliamentary caucus on gender equality.
Media training contributed to more inclusive election coverage (evidenced by collaborative journalistic pieces).
capacity_building_results: 90 community leaders certified in mediation/peacebuilding (PUSAD Paramadina).
45 journalists trained in inclusive election reporting (KONDE Media).
Human rights defenders received adaptive mentoring, improving resilience during election period.

unintended_consequences.description: Election monitoring app (*JagaSuara*) gained unexpected traction, with volunteers beyond NETGRIT’s network contributing data.
Delayed project starts reduced CSO trust in FCDO’s disbursement timelines, risking future engagement.

scalability_evidence: Election monitoring model (crowd-sourced + CSO analysis) is replicable for future Indonesian elections.
Media training curriculum can be adapted for other ASEAN contexts (per UK-Indonesia Partnership Roadmap).
Community mediation approach has potential for national scale-up via Inter-Religious Harmony Forums.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with UK-Indonesia Partnership Roadmap and FCDO’s democratic governance priorities. Early outputs (e.g., election monitoring, media campaigns) demonstrate impact, and expanded scope (to 2030) allows for deeper systemic change. CSO partnerships, though resource-intensive, are critical for credible human rights advocacy in Indonesia’s constrained civic space.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Current in-house model is unsustainable at scale; transition to external implementer (planned for 2025) will be critical. CSO capacity-building is essential for long-term viability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by budget increases and scope expansion via amendments).
planned_adaptations_future: Appoint an external implementer to manage partner capacity-building and compliance.
Refocus theory of change on democratic governance with clearer logframe metrics.
Expand diplomatic leverage of programme findings (e.g., election reform, death penalty).
Increase coordination with FCDO’s Centre for Expertise on Democratic Governance.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Development Influencing And Learning in Nepal (DIAL Nepal)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme deployed a flexible, small-projects model (up to £250,000 per project) aligned with the "small projects PROF guide" to ensure proportionate management. This allowed for agile responses to subnational opportunities, diverging from BEK’s original portfolio constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners in the ‘Lumbini Provincial Planning Commission’ project delivered high-quality outputs (e.g., a technically sound periodic plan and legal framework for provincial statistics), exceeding expectations in relationship-building. The ‘Dialogue Driven Partnership’ (DDP) project demonstrated strong convening power through its ‘Horizons’ event series and ‘Partners Roundtable,’ fostering inclusive policy dialogues and integrated working.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: An empowered governance structure with a Delivery Board was established, using tools like reporting templates, spot checks, field visits, and wash-out meetings. This ensured alignment with BEK’s strategic objectives and ODA compliance, while maintaining proportionate oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with the FCDO Nepal Portfolio Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (PMEL) function enabled cross-portfolio learning and adaptive management. The DDP project consolidated portfolio approaches within FCDO, promoting unified development partnerships.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Proposals were reviewed by the Monthly Delivery Board with input from thematic leads, commercial advisors, and group heads to ensure compliance with the PROF guide and ODA requirements. No major procurement issues were reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was proportionate, combining ex-ante approvals (Delivery Board) with ex-post tools (spot checks, field visits). This balanced flexibility with accountability, particularly for small, high-impact projects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme leveraged its flexible design to respond to short-term influencing opportunities, such as supporting the Lumbini Provincial Planning Commission and convening dialogues on emerging policy topics. This adaptability was a core strength.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid support to the Lumbini Provincial Planning Commission to deliver a periodic plan, capitalizing on a window of opportunity for evidence-based policy influence.
Adjustment of DDP’s ‘Horizons’ event series to address emerging strategic topics, shifting participant attitudes toward inclusive policy dialogues.
Integration of GESI (Gender Equality and Social Inclusion) dimensions into project concept notes based on real-time learning.

main_implementation_challenges: Maintaining momentum in relationship-building with subnational stakeholders amid limited BEK resources for provincial engagement.
Balancing the higher risk appetite (accepting that not all interventions would succeed) with the need for robust mitigation measures.
contextual_constraints_new: The need for continuous engagement to sustain relationships built through DIAL projects, requiring dedicated resources (e.g., ‘provincial engagement lead’ roles).
Political and institutional fragmentation at the subnational level, necessitating tailored approaches for each province.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited BEK capacity to allocate dedicated provincial engagement leads, risking erosion of hard-won relationships without sustained effort.
Dependence on external partners (e.g., Lumbini Government) to operationalize outputs like the periodic plan, requiring ongoing BEK support.
risk_materialization: The risk of insufficient follow-through on policy dialogues (e.g., DDP events) without structured post-event engagement (e.g., technical/policy briefs).
Potential reputational risk if small projects failed to deliver, mitigated by the programme’s explicit acceptance of higher risk for higher reward.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. The programme’s £2m budget is being executed as planned, with two projects (Lumbini Provincial Planning Commission and Dialogue Driven Partnership) demonstrating efficient use of funds. No over/under-spending was reported.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. The programme’s flexible, small-projects model (£250k/project cap) enabled cost-efficient delivery of high-impact outputs (e.g., Lumbini’s periodic plan) and strategic relationships, aligning with BEK’s influencing objectives.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Financial oversight was proportionate, with clear approval processes (Delivery Board) and compliance checks (ODA, PROF guide). Spot checks and field visits confirmed adherence to budget allocations.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: The programme achieved cost efficiency by leveraging existing BEK structures and focusing on high-value, low-cost interventions (e.g., dialogue events, technical assistance).

key_delivery_lessons: Small, flexible projects can deliver outsized influence when aligned with strategic objectives and backed by robust governance (e.g., Delivery Board).
Subnational engagement requires dedicated resources (e.g., provincial leads) to sustain relationships and capitalize on policy windows.
Policy dialogues must be followed by structured outputs (e.g., technical briefs) to maximize impact and learning.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of the ‘small projects PROF guide’ to ensure proportionate management structures.
Integration of GESI dimensions into project design, enhancing inclusivity and relevance.
Coordination with PMEL to embed learning across BEK’s portfolio, fostering adaptive management.
management_adaptations_made: Allocation of ‘provincial engagement lead’ responsibilities to group heads to maintain relationship momentum.
Enhanced post-event follow-up (e.g., policy briefs) to deepen the impact of dialogue initiatives like DDP’s ‘Horizons’ series.
innovations_attempted: The ‘Dialogue Driven Partnership’ model, combining horizon-scanning events with partners’ roundtables to foster systemic change.
Rapid-response funding for subnational opportunities (e.g., Lumbini’s periodic plan), demonstrating agility in policy influencing.
forward_recommendations: Continue DIAL as a vehicle for subnational influencing and learning, with a focus on operationalizing outputs (e.g., Lumbini’s periodic plan).
Strengthen BEK’s provincial engagement capacity by formalizing ‘provincial leads’ to sustain relationships.
Maximize the use of DDP dialogue content to produce actionable policy briefs and engage wider stakeholders.
Explore scaling successful approaches (e.g., Provincial Planning Commission support) to other provinces.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. The programme’s risk appetite was balanced with mitigation measures (e.g., robust project selection, proportionate oversight). Risks related to partner performance and political access were actively managed through adaptive engagement strategies.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Key stakeholders in Lumbini Province (government officials, planning commission members) and participants in DDP dialogues (policy influencers, development partners).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Broader provincial populations benefiting from evidence-based planning (e.g., Lumbini’s periodic plan) and inclusive policy dialogues.

policy_influence_achieved: Lumbini Provincial Planning Commission adopted a UK-supported periodic plan, setting the province’s strategic direction.
DDP dialogues shifted attitudes toward inclusive policy-making, with BEK recognized as a "modern development partner."
Strengthened UK-Nepal relationships at subnational levels, enhancing BEK’s access and influence.
capacity_building_results: Lumbini Government’s capacity to manage provincial statistics and evidence-based planning was institutionalized through legal frameworks.
BEK’s adaptive influencing capacity was strengthened via DIAL’s learning integration and coordination with PMEL.
unintended_consequences: Positive: DIAL’s agile model became a catalyst for broader BEK portfolio cohesion, fostering integrated diplomacy-development approaches.
Negative: None reported, though the programme’s small scale limits its ability to address systemic constraints alone.
scalability_evidence: The Provincial Planning Commission model (Lumbini) is replicable in other provinces, with BEK’s new portfolio prioritizing similar interventions.
DDP’s dialogue-driven approach can be scaled to other policy domains, as demonstrated by its consolidation within FCDO’s portfolio.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: DIAL has proven instrumental in achieving BEK’s influencing objectives, delivering high-impact outputs (e.g., Lumbini’s plan) and strengthening subnational relationships. Its flexible, learning-focused model aligns with FCDO’s priorities for adaptive, locally led development.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes. The small-projects model is cost-efficient and scalable, with strong governance (Delivery Board) and integration into BEK’s ways of working.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Formalize provincial engagement leads to sustain relationships.
Expand support to other Provincial Planning Commissions based on Lumbini’s success.
Deepen coordination with PMEL to embed adaptive influencing lessons across BEK’s portfolio.
Explore co-funding opportunities to leverage DIAL’s results for larger programmes.

programme_metadata.programme_title: ASEAN-UK Supporting the Advancement of Girls Education (ASEAN-UK SAGE) Programme

output_1.title: Policy dialogues, informed by rigorous and robust evidence on issues pertaining to the situated context

output_3.title: Women in STEM Scholarships and pilots to improve girls’ employment prospects through digital and STEM skills

output_4.title: Technical assistance services (to support AMS implement RED and pilot project-type interventions)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme shifted from including 'papers' as part of Output 1 (policy dialogues) to focusing exclusively on dialogues/conferences to ensure clearer messaging to policymakers. The distinction between dialogues and digital reports/tools was formalized in October 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Delivery partners (British Council, SEAMEO, ACER, EdTech Hub) and 11 ASEAN Member States (AMS) faced challenges in clarifying governance roles, responsibilities, and coordination mechanisms. The complexity of managing a multilateral programme with bilateral components in ODA-eligible countries created operational ambiguities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The governance structure proved more complex than planned, with unclear roles for coordination, accountability, and decision-making among FCDO, British Council, and partners. A consolidated joint workplan and budget for FY 2025/6 was delayed, highlighting gaps in alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination mechanisms were partially effective but required strengthening. Protocols for research collaboration, FCDO approvals, and a unified communications strategy were identified as critical gaps. The programme struggled to balance regional ASEAN focus with bilateral activities in 11 countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than initially planned due to the need to clarify roles and align partners. FCDO and British Council had to intervene frequently to resolve ambiguities in governance and workplan consolidation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility in adapting Output 1 (removing 'papers' to focus on dialogues) and reallocating technical assistance (e.g., 72 services delivered vs. 60 planned). However, flexibility was constrained by delays in workplan approvals and unclear decision-making processes.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised Output 1 in October 2024 to exclude 'papers' and focus on policy dialogues for clearer messaging to policymakers.
Increased technical assistance delivery (72 services vs. 60 planned) to support SEA-PLM and SEAMEO capacity building.
Postponed Lao PDR pilots due to uncertainty about future programming, prioritizing value for money (VFM) and sustainability.

main_implementation_challenges: Unclear governance structure and roles among FCDO, British Council, and 11 AMS, leading to delays in workplan consolidation and budget finalization.
Difficulty balancing the programme’s regional ASEAN focus with bilateral activities in ODA-eligible countries, creating operational ambiguities.
Lack of protocols for research collaboration, FCDO approvals, and communications, hindering coordinated influencing efforts.
Delayed development of a unified Theory of Change (ToC) and logframe, complicating outcome-level measurement and adaptive management.
external_factors_impact: UK ODA reductions to 0.3% necessitated a reconsideration of programme design and future options beyond 2025/6, adding pressure to demonstrate value for money (VFM).
Regional disparities in ASEAN Member States (AMS) required tailored approaches, increasing complexity in delivering uniform technical assistance and policy dialogues.
contextual_constraints_new: Emerging evidence on the Out-of-School Children and Youth (OOSCY) situation in the region (via 2024 research) revealed unanticipated scale and nuances, requiring revisions to Outcome 2 of the ToC.
Political and institutional dynamics within ASEAN and individual AMS occasionally slowed decision-making, particularly for cross-border initiatives like SEA-PLM.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions arose from ambiguous roles between delivery partners (British Council, SEAMEO, ACER, EdTech Hub) and AMS, leading to overlaps in technical assistance and research activities.
Delays in finalizing joint workplans and budgets (e.g., FY 2025/6) strained partnerships, as partners lacked clarity on resource allocation and priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: SEAMEO’s capacity to measure results and support AMS was initially weaker than expected, requiring additional technical assistance from the programme.
Limited capacity among some AMS to absorb and scale up evidence-based interventions (e.g., structured pedagogy, TaRL) without sustained support.
risk_materialization: Moderate risks related to governance ambiguity and partner coordination materialized, as evidenced by delayed workplans and unclear accountability.
Financial risks associated with ODA reductions and currency fluctuations (not explicitly detailed) were mitigated through adaptive budgeting but remained a concern.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution was largely on track, though delays in workplan finalization (FY 2025/6) created temporary misalignments. The programme delivered 72 technical assistance services against a target of 60, indicating efficient resource utilization in some areas.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: VFM was deemed acceptable but required improvement. A refresh of VFM indicators was mandated by September 2025 to ensure alignment with reduced ODA levels (0.3%) and maximize taxpayer value. The programme’s regional approach and leverage of multilateral partnerships (e.g., SEAMEO) enhanced cost efficiency.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management by implementers (British Council, partners) was satisfactory, though oversight was intensified to address governance ambiguities. No major financial irregularities were reported, but delays in workplan approvals posed challenges for timely disbursements.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was achieved in technical assistance (20% over-delivery) and policy dialogues (e.g., leveraging existing events like Education World Forum 2024). However, efficiency was offset by higher-than-planned coordination costs due to governance complexities.

key_delivery_lessons: Multilateral programmes in middle-income contexts require **explicit governance frameworks** upfront to clarify roles among diverse partners (FCDO, British Council, AMS, delivery partners).
**Regional programmes with bilateral components** need clear guidelines on what activities are permissible in non-ODA-eligible countries to avoid operational ambiguities.
**Policy dialogues must be strategically targeted** to ensure they reach decision-makers with actionable evidence, rather than treating all events equally.
successful_delivery_practices: Leveraging existing high-profile events (e.g., Education World Forum, ASEAN Education Ministers’ Meeting) to amplify policy dialogues and technical assistance.
Flexible reallocation of technical assistance resources (e.g., 72 services delivered vs. 60 planned) to respond to AMS demands.
Collaboration with SEAMEO and EdTech Hub to produce and disseminate region-wide research (e.g., OOSCY studies) at key forums like SEAMEO High Officials Meetings.
management_adaptations_made: Removed 'papers' from Output 1 to focus on high-impact policy dialogues, clarifying the programme’s influencing strategy.
Increased oversight on workplan consolidation and budget finalization to address delays (target: June 2025 for FY 2025/6).
Mandated a review of the Theory of Change (ToC) and logframe by September 2025 to strengthen outcome-level indicators and regional integration.
innovations_attempted: Pilot projects to improve girls’ employment prospects through digital/STEM skills (though Lao PDR pilots were postponed due to sustainability concerns).
Development of a Women in STEM Scholarships alumni strategy to maximize long-term value for money (VFM) and policy influence.
Use of EdTech Hub’s expertise to support AMS in adopting data-driven approaches to education challenges (e.g., SEA-PLM, AI in education).
previous_recommendations_progress: The recommendation to develop an **options paper on the future of the Women in STEM Scholarships** was not completed; now prioritized for September 2025.
An **alumni strategy for scholarship recipients** was delayed but is now included in the 2025/6 workplan.
No progress was reported on revising the logframe for Output 3 (pilots) to clarify milestones for 'implemented' vs. 'validated' activities.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Establish clear roles and responsibilities for coordination, accountability, and decision-making among FCDO, British Council, and partners.
Finalize a consolidated joint workplan and budget for FY 2025/6 to avoid delays.
Develop a clearer vision for how SAGE will influence and strengthen institutions through its four output areas, including deeper engagement with multilaterals.
forward_recommendations.responsible: British Council and partners with FCDO

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Create protocols for research collaboration and a communications strategy to maximize policy influencing.
forward_recommendations.responsible: British Council in collaboration with all partners

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Clarify the balance between regional ASEAN focus and bilateral activities in ODA-eligible countries.
forward_recommendations.responsible: FCDO with British Council and partners

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Review and revise the Theory of Change (ToC), logframe, and MEL processes to ensure outputs lead to outcomes.
forward_recommendations.responsible: British Council in collaboration with all partners

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Consider all options for programming beyond 2025/6 in light of ODA reductions to 0.3%.
Finalize the value for money (VFM) indicator refresh to ensure taxpayer value.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management was **partially effective**. While financial and delivery risks were mitigated through adaptive management (e.g., postponing Lao PDR pilots), governance and coordination risks materialized due to unclear roles. The programme’s response to ODA reductions was proactive but requires stronger contingency planning.

direct.policy_dialogues: 2 high-level dialogues delivered (e.g., Education World Forum 2024, SEAMEO High Officials Meeting) reaching Ministers of Education and senior officials from 11 AMS.
direct.technical_assistance: 72 services provided to AMS (vs. 60 planned), supporting SEA-PLM and SEAMEO capacity building.
direct.women_in_stem: 11 scholarships awarded in 2024 (including recipients from Timor-Leste and Cambodia).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Research on Out-of-School Children and Youth (OOSCY) disseminated across 11 countries, informing regional policies (e.g., ASEAN Education Ministers’ Meeting).

policy_influence_achieved: SEA-PLM regional learning assessment gained traction among 7 AMS, with technical assistance supporting its adoption.
Evidence from OOSCY research influenced discussions at the 13th ASEAN Education Ministers’ Meeting on inclusive education.
UK’s focus on basic education (a unique offering among ASEAN Dialogue Partners) strengthened political buy-in from ASEC and AMS.
capacity_building_results: SEAMEO’s capacity to measure results and support AMS improved through targeted technical assistance.
AMS officials reported increased ability to use evidence (e.g., SEA-PLM data) for education planning, though scaling remains uneven.
Women in STEM scholars began acting as role models, with an alumni strategy under development to formalize their influence.

unintended_consequences.description: The programme’s regional approach unexpectedly strengthened collaboration among AMS on shared challenges (e.g., OOSCY), fostering peer learning.
Delays in governance clarification and workplan approvals created frustration among partners, risking long-term engagement.

scalability_evidence: The SEA-PLM assessment and structured pedagogy interventions (e.g., Teaching at the Right Level) demonstrated potential for scale-up, with AMS expressing interest in expanding pilots.
Policy dialogues at events like the Education World Forum provided a scalable model for influencing multiple countries simultaneously.
Limited evidence on the scalability of Women in STEM Scholarships due to unresolved questions about long-term funding and alumni engagement.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme is deemed **strategically vital** for UK engagement in Southeast Asia, particularly as a flagship initiative under the ASEAN-UK Plan of Action (2022–2026). Its focus on basic education—a unique offering among ASEAN Dialogue Partners—has secured strong political support from ASEC and AMS. While governance and VFM challenges exist, the programme’s regional influence and alignment with ASEAN’s Socio-Cultural Community Blueprint 2025 justify continuation, subject to adaptations.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: The current delivery model is **partially sustainable**. Strengths include its multilateral approach, leverage of partners like SEAMEO, and flexibility to adapt to AMS needs. However, sustainability risks stem from unclear governance, ODA reductions, and the need for stronger outcome-level measurement. Long-term sustainability depends on resolving these issues and securing co-funding or ASEAN ownership.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied (with reservations)
planned_adaptations_future: Revising the Theory of Change (ToC) and logframe by September 2025 to clarify how outputs lead to outcomes and strengthen regional integration.
Developing a communications strategy to better articulate policy wins and enhance influencing at the outcome level.
Exploring options for programming beyond 2025/6, including potential reductions in scope or deeper focus on high-impact pillars (e.g., foundational learning).
Finalizing protocols for research collaboration and FCDO approvals to streamline decision-making.
Assessing the feasibility of transitioning certain activities (e.g., SEA-PLM support) to ASEAN or multilateral ownership to improve sustainability.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Growth Research Platform (GRP)

output_1.title: Development of high-quality, policy-relevant research and analysis undertaken in collaboration with policymakers and practitioners which provides new insights on investment, firms, productivity, structural transformation, and economics of conflict

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Integration of existing programmes (PEDL, STEG) with new elements (ReCIPE, PRW) under unified GRP structure. ReCIPE and PRW are in inception phases with tailored delivery approaches.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: PEDL and STEG partners maintained high performance (both scored "A" in recent reviews). ReCIPE successfully hosted its first annual conference with participation from World Bank, OECD, and FCDO. PRW delivered 3 studies directly informing FCDO guidelines.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Centralized coordination under GRP with thematic leadership (e.g., ReCIPE’s 9 research themes led by academic experts). VoxDev operates as a cross-cutting dissemination platform.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Synergies emerging between research areas (e.g., ReCIPE’s conflict focus complementing PEDL/STEG’s economic growth work). PRW acts as a responsive mechanism for FCDO policy teams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Competitive procurement for research grants (e.g., ReCIPE’s pathfinding papers commissioned from theme leaders). PRW projects procured via CEPR’s existing frameworks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Light-touch oversight for PEDL/STEG (leveraging their recent "A" scores). Higher engagement with ReCIPE/PRW during inception (e.g., monitoring conference outputs, PRW study reviews by FCDO’s Quality Assurance Unit).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Adaptive inception phases for ReCIPE/PRW (e.g., ReCIPE’s conference adjusted to incorporate policy panel after initial academic focus). PRW responded to FCDO’s urgent evidence needs (e.g., SME cost-effectiveness review).
adaptive_management_examples: ReCIPE’s conference expanded to include OECD/FCDO policy panel beyond academic presentations.
PRW’s rapid evidence reviews (e.g., macro-fiscal study) tailored to FCDO’s immediate priorities.
VoxDev shifted dissemination strategies in response to declining social media reach (e.g., increased blog production, exploration of Bluesky/YouTube).

main_implementation_challenges: Inception-phase delays: ReCIPE’s pathfinding papers likely to miss March 2025 deadline; PRW still establishing responsive mechanisms.
Dissemination tracking: Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Perplexity) obscures user engagement metrics for VoxDev outputs.
Social media limitations: Platforms like X (Twitter) actively discourage external link clicks, reducing outreach effectiveness.
external_factors_impact: AI disruption: Untrackable interactions via AI summaries/chatbots (e.g., Google AI, ChatGPT) reduce visibility of GRP’s policy influence.
Geopolitical context: ReCIPE’s conflict research gains urgency amid global fragility trends (e.g., OECD/FCDO engagement at Paris conference).
contextual_constraints_new: Indirect AI-mediated access to GRP outputs complicates impact attribution.
Need for new dissemination platforms (e.g., Bluesky, YouTube) to counter declining traditional social media efficacy.
capacity_constraints_emerged: ReCIPE’s pathfinding paper delays highlight capacity bottlenecks among theme leaders.
VoxDev’s team requires upskilling to manage AI-driven dissemination tracking and multimedia content production.
risk_materialization: Dissemination risks: Reduced trackability of evidence use due to AI intermediation (as flagged in lessons section).
Inception delays: ReCIPE’s pathfinding papers behind schedule, though mitigated by conference outputs.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Synergies between PEDL/STEG/ReCIPE/PRW driving efficiencies (e.g., shared VoxDev platform, joint conferences).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. Research aligned with FCDO priorities (e.g., growth, conflict prevention) and procured competitively. PRW’s responsive studies demonstrate cost-effective policy influence.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. CEPR’s existing systems (used for PEDL/STEG) extended to ReCIPE/PRW. No reported issues in financial reporting or audit compliance.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Improved via platform integration (e.g., shared dissemination costs through VoxDev). PRW’s rapid studies leverage existing CEPR infrastructure.

key_delivery_lessons: Inception phases require flexible milestones (e.g., ReCIPE’s conference outputs compensated for delayed pathfinding papers).
Responsive mechanisms (e.g., PRW) must balance speed with quality assurance (e.g., FCDO QA Unit reviews).
Dissemination strategies need continuous adaptation to digital ecosystem changes (e.g., AI, social media algorithms).
successful_delivery_practices: Thematic conferences (e.g., ReCIPE’s Paris event) effectively bridge research and policy communities.
VoxDev blogs repurposing existing content (7 of top 50 pages in 2024) demonstrate high engagement.
PRW’s direct linkage to FCDO committees (e.g., Investment and Delivery Committee) ensures policy uptake.
management_adaptations_made: Increased VoxDev blog production (target: weekly by end-2025) to counter social media decline.
Exploration of AI-specific tracking tools (e.g., VoxDev LLM) to monitor indirect evidence use.
ReCIPE’s synthesis paper added to address cross-cutting themes beyond individual pathfinding papers.
innovations_attempted: VoxDev’s country-specific blog reflections localizing global research findings.
Potential VoxDev LLM to enable direct interrogation of research outputs via AI.
ReCIPE’s typology framework for conflict contexts (integrating pathfinding paper insights).
previous_recommendations_progress: Enhanced dissemination: VoxDev blogs and multimedia (YouTube) partially address prior calls for broader outreach.
Policy engagement: PRW’s FCDO studies fulfill recommendations for stronger policy linkages.
forward_recommendations: Develop AI-resistant impact tracking metrics (e.g., direct policymaker feedback loops).
Expand VoxDev’s multimedia presence (e.g., podcast series, video abstracts) to diversify dissemination.
Formalize ReCIPE’s conflict typology framework as a tool for FCDO’s fragile states strategies.
Conduct a mid-term review of PRW’s responsiveness to ensure alignment with evolving FCDO priorities.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Proactive adaptation to AI/dissemination risks (e.g., exploring Bluesky, LLM), but reactive to inception delays (e.g., ReCIPE papers).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: ReCIPE conference (100+ researchers/policymakers); PRW studies (FCDO teams across private sector/PFM domains).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: VoxDev users (including AI-mediated access; exact numbers untrackable).

policy_influence_achieved: PRW’s SME cost-effectiveness review adopted by FCDO’s Investment and Delivery Committee.
ReCIPE’s conflict research agenda informed by OECD/FCDO dialogue at Paris conference.
VoxDevLits cited in FCDO programme designs (per anecdotal feedback).
capacity_building_results: ReCIPE’s pathfinding papers will include southern researcher contributions (per ToC Condition E).
VoxDev’s country-specific blogs authored by local researchers (e.g., reflections on VoxDevLits).
unintended_consequences: Positive: AI-driven dissemination (e.g., ChatGPT) expands indirect reach beyond traditional audiences.
Negative: Loss of user data due to AI intermediation hinders targeted follow-ups.
scalability_evidence: PRW’s responsive model replicable for other FCDO priority areas (e.g., climate, health).
ReCIPE’s conflict typology framework adaptable to new fragile contexts.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong first-year performance (Overall Score: A) with successful integration of existing/new elements. ReCIPE/PRW show potential for high policy impact despite inception challenges. Alignment with FCDO’s Growth & Development priorities remains robust.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. Platform synergies (e.g., VoxDev, joint conferences) and CEPR’s established systems ensure long-term viability.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by "A" score and PRW’s adoption by FCDO committees).
planned_adaptations_future: Full GRP review in June/July 2025 to assess integrated performance post-inception.
Enhanced tracking of AI-mediated dissemination impacts.
Expansion of PRW’s geographic/policy coverage based on demand signals.
Formalization of ReCIPE’s conflict typology for FCDO use.

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK voluntary membership contribution to the International Solar Alliance (ISA) in 2023 and 2024

output_1.title: Policy & Capacity Building: Enabling policy environment and capacities for solar energy deployment and clean energy transition

output_2.title: Analytics & Advocacy: Provide analytics and advocate for informed and coordinated action to catalyse solar access and transition in all member countries

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: ISA delivered nine programmes across 55 Member Countries, including 21 demonstration projects (e.g., solarisation of healthcare centres in Burkina Faso). Collaborated with 33 global partners (UNEP, EU, UNIDO). UK’s contribution leveraged additional funding (e.g., France’s voluntary contribution).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: ISA coordinated with multilateral partners (UNEP, EU, UNIDO) and national governments (e.g., Uganda’s solar energy roadmap). Public recognition of UK’s role in ISA Assembly and regional conferences.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: ISA adapted by restructuring demonstration projects and spreading recruitments to reduce 2024 budget from USD 27.38M to USD 24.18M. Focus shifted to resource mobilisation (e.g., Multi-Donor Trust Fund).
adaptive_management_examples: Budget restructuring (2024) to align with recruitment timelines and project priorities.
Launch of targeted initiatives like the SolarX Startup Challenge (30 winners in 2024, expanding to LAC region in 2025).
Development of ‘Solar Data Portals’ (2024) to improve data-driven decision-making.

main_implementation_challenges: Resource mobilisation remains a critical challenge despite UK/France contributions (ISA relies heavily on Indian Government funding).
Need to balance core operational costs with expanding programme delivery in 55+ countries.
external_factors_impact: Political transitions in UK and India (2024) required reaffirmation of climate commitments but aligned with programme goals (e.g., UK’s ‘clean energy superpower’ agenda).
G20’s 2023 tripling renewable energy target increased pressure on ISA to scale solar deployment in LDCs/SIDS.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated need for virtual governance processes (e.g., electronic voting at Assembly meetings) to improve efficiency.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited staff onboarding in 2024 due to recruitment delays, requiring budget adjustments.
risk_materialization: Minor risk of over-reliance on Indian Government funding partially mitigated by UK/France contributions.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: ISA’s 2024 budget reduced from USD 27.38M to USD 24.18M due to restructuring. UK’s £82,000/year (USD 50,000) contribution fully disbursed as planned. Indian Government committed USD 13M over 3 years, improving financial sustainability.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High: UK’s contribution leveraged additional funding (France) and supported core operations with measurable outputs (e.g., 7.65 GW solar capacity aggregated, 103 pro-solar policy endorsements). Recommendations include reducing merchandise costs and adopting virtual events.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. ISA demonstrated ability to adjust budgets dynamically (e.g., 2024 restructuring) and secure co-funding. Transparent reporting on programme expenditures (e.g., demonstration projects, analytics tools).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient: 103 countries benefited from policy/advocacy support with minimal UK funding. Cost per beneficiary low (e.g., 1,291 participants in solar training programmes).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialized: France followed UK’s lead with a voluntary contribution (2024). Ongoing efforts to expand Multi-Donor Trust Fund.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Exchange rate fluctuations noted (USD 50,000 = £82,000 at current rates), but no significant adverse impacts reported.

key_delivery_lessons: Small, targeted contributions can catalyse broader funding (e.g., UK’s £82K leveraged France’s contribution).
Multilateral platforms (ISA) amplify UK influence in climate diplomacy (e.g., strengthened UK-India partnership).
Flexible budgeting (e.g., 2024 restructuring) enables responsiveness to operational constraints.
successful_delivery_practices: Collaboration with global partners (UNEP, EU) to deliver demonstration projects (e.g., Burkina Faso healthcare centres).
Data-driven advocacy tools (e.g., ‘Ease of Doing Solar’ reports, Solar Data Portals) enhanced policy uptake.
Startup challenges (SolarX) effectively engaged entrepreneurs in Africa/India, with 50+ winners supported.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted focus to resource mobilisation (Multi-Donor Trust Fund) in response to funding gaps.
Expanded virtual governance (e.g., electronic Assembly voting) to improve efficiency.
innovations_attempted: SolarX Startup Challenge (scalable solar business models in Africa/India/LAC).
Solar Data Portals (2024) to standardise data access for member countries.
Regulatory roadmaps (e.g., Uganda’s solar integration plan) tailored to country contexts.
forward_recommendations: Continue sharing UK’s due diligence approach with other embassies to encourage further contributions.
Explore UK support for ISA’s analytics/advocacy work (e.g., research collaborations).
Recommend ISA adopt virtual events and limit merchandise for cost savings.
Prioritise governance discussions in 2025 regional committees.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective: Minor risks (e.g., funding reliance) were proactively addressed through budget restructuring and donor diversification. No major risks materialized.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 1,291 participants in training programmes; 5 countries supported via analytics tools (vs. 3 in 2023).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 103 countries endorsed pro-solar policies; 19 countries with 7.65 GW aggregated solar capacity.

policy_influence_achieved: ISA’s ‘Ease of Doing Solar’ report influenced member country regulations (e.g., Uganda’s solar roadmap).
G20’s 2023 renewable energy tripling target aligned with ISA’s mission, amplifying UK’s policy impact.
UK’s contribution cited as catalyst for France’s funding and strengthened UK-India climate partnership.
capacity_building_results: 21 demonstration projects showcased scalable solar solutions (e.g., Burkina Faso healthcare solarisation).
SolarX Startup Challenge supported 50+ entrepreneurs (30% women) in Africa/India.
Regulatory workshops in Uganda improved local capacity for solar project implementation.

positive: UK’s contribution enhanced diplomatic ties with India, leading to high-level engagements (e.g., UK High Commissioner meeting with Indian Energy Minister).
ISA’s visibility increased, attracting new members (6 countries ratified post-UK funding).

scalability_evidence: SolarX Startup Challenge expanding to LAC region (COP30 2025).
Demonstration projects (e.g., solar mini-grids) replicated in multiple countries.
Policy tools (e.g., Solar Data Portals) designed for adoption by all 103 member countries.

continuation_rationale: Small UK contribution (£122K) leveraged significant outcomes: additional funding (France), policy influence (103 countries), and diplomatic benefits (UK-India partnership).
Strong alignment with UK priorities: clean energy transition, Global South engagement, and climate mitigation (1.5°C goal).
ISA’s operational effectiveness demonstrated (7.65 GW capacity, 21 projects, high-risk management).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-High (dependent on diversifying funding beyond Indian Government/UK contributions).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Increase focus on resource mobilisation (Multi-Donor Trust Fund).
Expand analytics/advocacy support (e.g., Solar Data Portals, research collaborations).
Explore virtual governance to reduce costs and improve inclusivity.

output_1.title: Anticipatory action - Threats, risks and upcoming emergencies are identified and mitigated

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: FAO performed in line with or better than expectations on indicators fully under their control but worse on wider reach indicators due to lower-than-anticipated funding. IPC exceeded expectations on data coverage and crisis response activation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO maintains a well-maintained institutional relationship with FAO/IPC and monitors performance through donor forums, but detailed oversight is limited by partial 2024 reporting.

main_implementation_challenges: Lower-than-anticipated overall funding for anticipatory action, reducing reach (e.g., Output 1.1 missed target of 2.2M people due to donor funding constraints).
Global funding crunch reshaping humanitarian response environment, with reduced ODA from key donors (e.g., US).
Humanitarian reform processes (e.g., UN80) creating uncertainty in operational priorities.
external_factors_impact: Reductions in US and other donor funding disrupted assumptions about SFERA’s resource availability (now <$300K for emerging crises).
Policy environment instability affecting anticipatory action (AA) and resilience programming.
contextual_constraints_new: DIEM (Data in Emergencies Monitoring) likely to operate in fewer countries due to donor cuts, reducing data availability for IPC analyses.
Conflict-driven crises (e.g., Sudan, Gaza, Myanmar) straining IPC’s capacity to monitor sudden-onset emergencies.
risk_materialization: Major risk rating unchanged since Business Case approval, with challenges in access/oversight due to remote/conflict-affected operating environments.
Funding shortages materialized as a key risk, limiting programme scale (e.g., Output 2.1 reached only 43M of 70M target).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Partial 2024 data suggests under-execution against reach targets (e.g., Output 1.1, 2.1) due to broader donor funding constraints, but FAO/IPC met or exceeded technical milestones (e.g., Output 1.2, 1.3, 4.1–4.4).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early evidence suggests VfM is being demonstrated (e.g., FAO’s anticipatory actions in Honduras/Niger, IPC’s 100% activation rate for sudden-onset crises), but comprehensive assessment deferred to updated 2025 review.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: SFERA’s co-funding assumptions no longer hold; programme now operates with <$300K for emerging crises vs. planned levels.

key_delivery_lessons: Anticipatory action (Output 1) can exceed technical milestones (e.g., 42 country offices supported vs. 30 target) even with funding constraints, but reach is limited by donor coordination gaps.
IPC’s data systems (Output 4) are highly effective in crisis response (100% activation rate) but vulnerable to donor cuts affecting DIEM’s geographic coverage.
successful_delivery_practices: FAO’s use of anticipatory cash transfers (e.g., Honduras hurricane response) and livestock feed distribution (Niger bushfires) demonstrates effective local adaptation.
IPC’s globally led analyses (e.g., Gaza, Myanmar) provide critical real-time data despite access challenges.
management_adaptations_made: FCDO will revise FAO’s logframe in the updated 2025 review to better reflect performance and funding realities.
Risk appetite aligned with FCDO’s Humanitarian Directorate, with regular reviews to address emerging challenges (e.g., funding crunch).
innovations_attempted: IPC’s new Events Visualization in Emergencies (EVE) tool for crisis monitoring (36 countries in 2024).
FAO’s integration of climate-adaptive farming techniques into anticipatory action packages.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Assess programme viability under FCDO’s new UN core funding Business Case (late 2025).
Capture International Climate Finance (ICF) indicators more explicitly in reporting.
Evaluate SFERA/OER’s work given 2025 funding environment changes.
Address data gaps in IPC’s analysis pipeline and prioritize high-risk areas.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Risk management is active (regular reviews, alignment with HFRD) but constrained by external funding volatility and high-risk operating environments (conflict/remote areas).

Output_1.1.notes: Missed due to donor funding shortages.

Output_4.1.target: 60% of food crisis countries covered by IPC/CH
Output_4.1.notes: Exceeded target; 80% coverage for major crises.

policy_influence_achieved: FAO’s anticipatory action protocols (e.g., Central America hurricanes, Niger bushfires) influenced local/regional disaster risk reduction strategies (77 DRR plans developed).
IPC’s data used in Global Report on Food Crises (2024) and by Food Security Clusters (e.g., Sudan, Gaza).
capacity_building_results: 42 FAO country offices (vs. 30 target) now capable of designing anticipatory action strategies.
28 countries engaged in FAO’s anticipatory action protocols (vs. 24 target).
Cameroon: 12 communal Disaster Risk Management plans implemented.

unintended_consequences.description: Reduced DIEM coverage due to donor cuts may weaken early warning systems in non-prioritized countries.
IPC’s crisis activation in conflict zones (e.g., Myanmar restricted publications) provided otherwise unavailable food security data.

scalability_evidence: FAO’s anticipatory action model (e.g., cash transfers, livestock feed) is replicable but constrained by funding.
IPC’s globally led analysis approach (5 non-TWG analyses in 2024) demonstrates scalability for rapid-onset crises.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: Satisfied with technical performance (Outputs 1/4 scores: A/A+) but concerned about reach and funding sustainability.
planned_adaptations_future: Reassess milestones for FAO/IPC to balance ambition with funding realities.
Explore integration with FCDO’s new UN core funding mechanism.
Prioritize high-risk countries in IPC’s data collection to mitigate donor cuts.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Switched from a planned 2-phase evaluation (£500k + £100k) to a single-phase evaluation (£600k) due to feedback during early market engagement (EME) that the original budget was insufficient. Procurement was conducted via FCDO’s Global Evaluation and Monitoring Framework Agreement (GEMFA) instead of an open tender.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Oxford Policy Management (OPM) performed as expected: delivered the inception report on time (March 2025), addressed feedback from EQUALS and the FCDO Management Group satisfactorily, and received an "excellent" rating from EQUALS for the inception report.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: An FCDO Management Group was established, including the Senior Responsible Owner (SRO), Programme Responsible Officer (PRO), RED’s Evaluation Advisor, and a Government Social Research member. This structure was not pre-detailed in the document but is now operational.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between OPM, EQUALS (quality assurance), and the FCDO Management Group was effective, as evidenced by the timely delivery and high-quality inception report.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement via GEMFA was successful, with "excellent" feedback on the Terms of Reference (ToR) from EQUALS. OPM was selected through a competitive bidding round in late 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was robust, with EQUALS conducting an independent quality assurance review of the inception report and the FCDO Management Group providing additional feedback. The hybrid payment mechanism (output-based milestones + quarterly expenses) is functioning as planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by adjusting the evaluation design (single-phase instead of two-phase) and budget (increased to £600k) in response to market feedback during EME.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.adaptive_management_examples: Responded to EME feedback by revising the evaluation approach and budget to ensure feasibility and quality. Adjusted procurement strategy to use GEMFA based on supplier interest.

operational_challenges_context.main_implementation_challenges: Initial budget (£500k) was deemed insufficient by potential suppliers during early market engagement, requiring a revision to £600k and a shift to a single-phase evaluation.
operational_challenges_context.risk_materialization: No significant risks materialized; the programme remains low-risk as per EQUALS’ assessment and the satisfactory inception phase.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget increased from the originally planned £500k (Phase 1) + £100k (Phase 2) to £600k for a single-phase evaluation due to supplier feedback. The revised budget is being executed as planned, with a hybrid payment model (milestone-based + quarterly expenses) working effectively.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indications suggest good value for money, given the "excellent" EQUALS rating for the inception report and the potential for high-quality evidence generation. Final VFM assessment will depend on the full evaluation outcomes.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High; the hybrid payment mechanism is functioning well, and financial oversight by the FCDO Management Group is robust.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.key_delivery_lessons: Early market engagement (EME) was critical in identifying budget and design flaws, leading to a more feasible evaluation approach. Using GEMFA for procurement streamlined the process and ensured supplier quality.

output_1.title: Establishment of the regional climate and health research hubs to commission research into building climate-resilient primary healthcare systems

output_2.title: Establishment of a Climate and Health Centre for Impact and Learning

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Pillars 2 and 3 paused due to UK ODA budget reduction from 0.5% to 0.3% of GNI; Pillar 1 mobilized via new partnership with Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC) to co-fund the Advancing Research for Climate and Health (ARCH) programme.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: IDRC successfully managed the competitive selection process for five regional research hubs (Colombia, Malaysia, Lebanon, Ghana, Kenya) with FCDO oversight. All hubs were mobilized by October 2024 with workplans developed, though the Asia hub faced delays due to Malaysian Government clearance requirements.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO established a part-time Climate and Health Adviser role (filled February 2025) and drafted a logframe for Pillar 1. Full programme logframe development is pending mobilization of Pillars 2 and 3 and the ODA prioritization process outcome.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between FCDO and IDRC, including joint selection of hubs and alignment on ARCH project management. However, misalignment between ARCH’s annual reporting cycle and FCDO’s annual review period created monitoring challenges.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: MOU with IDRC signed in July 2024 (two months behind target) due to delays in business case approval. Competitive process for hub selection was robust, with 152 expressions of interest and 29 full proposals reviewed by an external committee.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Light FCDO resourcing leveraged IDRC’s grant management systems and technical expertise, reducing administrative overheads. IDRC managed risk, finances, and hub performance directly, with FCDO providing strategic oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to ODA budget cuts by pausing Pillars 2 and 3 while proceeding with Pillar 1. Delayed the Year 2 annual review by three months (to August 2026) to align with ARCH reporting timelines.
adaptive_management_examples: Negotiated co-funding partnership with IDRC to leverage additional CAD10 million (£1 FCDO : £1.60 total investment ratio).
Delayed global partner meeting from 2024 to June 2025 due to Malaysian Government clearance delays for the Asia hub.
Drafted a call for proposals for Pillars 2 and 3 but paused procurement pending ODA prioritization decisions.

main_implementation_challenges: UK Government’s reduction of ODA spending from 0.5% to 0.3% of GNI, pausing Pillars 2 and 3.
Delays in business case approval (approved 24th April 2024) slowed MOU signing with IDRC to July 2024.
Staffing changes and temporary gaps in the FCDO Health Research Team contributed to mobilization delays.
Malaysian Government clearance requirements delayed the Asia hub agreement signing to February 2025.
Misalignment between ARCH annual reporting (June) and FCDO annual review (May) cycles.
external_factors_impact: ODA budget cuts directly halted progress on Pillars 2 and 3, requiring a business case review and potential logframe revisions.
Global economic shifts and research funding landscape changes may affect long-term assumptions in the Theory of Change (e.g., decision-maker engagement with evidence).
contextual_constraints_new: Nascent field of climate-health research with limited existing collaboration between climate and health researchers, requiring additional effort to build a global research community.
Need for stronger LMIC research leadership and local community engagement to ensure contextually relevant solutions.
partner_relationship_issues: No major issues reported; IDRC’s management of hubs and funds was described as effective, with robust grant systems and technical support.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s light resourcing model relied heavily on IDRC’s capacity, which performed well but created dependency.
Limited in-house FCDO expertise in the climate-health nexus required external technical support from IDRC.
risk_materialization: ODA budget reduction (high impact: paused Pillars 2 and 3).
Delays in Malaysian Government clearances (moderate impact: delayed Asia hub mobilization and global partner meeting).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: FCDO’s Humanitarian Department split into two new departments: Humanitarian Partnerships and Policy Department (HPPD) and Humanitarian Crisis Response Department (HCRD), both under the Humanitarian, Food Security and Resilience Directorate. delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners delivered effectively on projects (e.g., Wilton Park’s AI conference was "highly effective"), but capacity constraints emerged due to the high volume of projects (11 in FY 2024-25). Smaller projects (e.g., £15,010 for WHO EMT Secretariat) stretched oversight resources despite successful outcomes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Cross-departmental fund management (HPPD and HCRD) enabled agility but created capacity bottlenecks. Programme team and policy leads struggled with dual roles (project management + core duties), leading to delays in project agreements and oversight gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Convening power was a key strength (e.g., AI conference brought together NGOs, governments, academia, and private sector), but coordination within FCDO was challenged by the high number of projects and limited dedicated programme management resources.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in moving from project approval to agreement completion impacted timelines, shifting expectations for both FCDO and partners. Smaller projects faced disproportionate administrative burdens relative to their funding levels.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was more intensive than planned due to the volume of projects, with PRoF (Programme Operating Framework) requirements creating a fixed burden regardless of project size. This led to recommendations to limit future projects to ≤10 and introduce a £100k minimum threshold.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The fund’s agile design allowed rapid response to emerging priorities (e.g., AI in humanitarian action, climate finance), but flexibility was constrained by capacity limits. Adaptive management included reprioritizing convening activities over piloting due to proposal trends.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Majority of partners (APNOR, WRC, IDSF, MMPTF) delivered on time and within budget, with several exceeding expectations in reach and influence. APNOR faced initial fund-transfer challenges due to local fiscal regulations and RLO capacity constraints but resolved them by Year 1 end. WRC overachieved targets (e.g., 9 advocacy grants instead of 8) due to unanticipated opportunities (e.g., Syria’s political opening). Steering Committee engagement with MMPTF was highlighted for broadening donor base.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was sufficient to ensure on-time, on-budget delivery but revealed gaps in indicator clarity and partner reporting alignment. Recommendations include more in-person monitoring visits and earlier planning for activities like Meaningful Refugee Participation (MRP) training.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by capitalizing on unplanned opportunities (e.g., Syria’s political changes for WRC grants) and adapting to delays (e.g., RPFF postponement).
