programme_metadata.programme_title: Sustainable Inclusive Livelihoods through Tea Production in Rwanda (SILTPR)

output_1.title: Programme efficiently implemented and adapted in line with emerging findings and learning

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Original Unilever partnership evolved through corporate restructuring (Unilever → Ekaterra → Lipton → Browns Investment PLC) with all obligations transferred seamlessly. Added three new components under 2024 cost extension: 1) Nshili Kivu smallholder expansion (2,500 new SHFs/2,000Ha), 2) Rugabano pilot ropeways for transport, 3) Carbon-neutral tea production/processing.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The Wood Foundation Africa (TWFA) and Browns Investment PLC (formerly Unilever/Lipton) performed above expectations, particularly in adapting to corporate ownership changes and maintaining programme continuity. Service Companies (SCON-N, ROS, UTCL) effectively aggregated SHF production and provided extension services, exceeding quality targets for greenleaf supply.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance maintained through quarterly performance reviews, SC board meetings, and FCDO oversight. Adaptive management structures allowed for rapid integration of new components (e.g., carbon reduction) without disrupting core operations. Risk management shifted from "Major" to "Moderate" in 2022/23, sustained through 2024/25.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between TWFA, Browns, Luxmi, Gatsby Foundation, and GoR, evidenced by successful handover of corporate obligations and joint decision-making (e.g., financial risk mitigation policies). Pilot ropeways required cross-partner collaboration for implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for new components (e.g., ropeways, carbon assessment tools) executed on time. Fertiliser and input procurement faced global supply chain challenges (e.g., Rwandan Franc depreciation increasing costs) but were managed through patient capital adjustments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to front-loading of funds and addition of climate components. FCDO and TWFA conducted joint reviews of GHG reduction strategies and financial profiling.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme leveraged flexibility to: 1) Extend timeline to 2029 with £4.6m additional funding, 2) Add three new components mid-implementation, 3) Adjust loan terms for farmers (increased from ~$700 to ~$900 equivalent per Ha) in response to currency depreciation.
adaptive_management_examples: Structured adaptation process guided by evidence from socioeconomic baseline surveys (Nyaruguru/Rugabano) and quarterly reports, leading to 8 documented design changes (e.g., infographic development, carbon strategy roadmap).
Response to drought-induced quality dips by intensifying SC support for agronomic practices, maintaining 96% tea bush survival rate.
Redesign of logframe to accommodate cost extension components, including new indicators for GHG reductions and ropeway pilot outcomes.

main_implementation_challenges: Global input price volatility (e.g., fertiliser costs) and Rwandan Franc depreciation (reduced farmer loan value from ~$900 to ~$700 per Ha).
Drought conditions in 2024/25 causing slight dip in tea quality (68% vs 70% target).
Fragmented smallholder plots requiring intensive extension services to meet quality/quantity targets.
Complex corporate transitions (Unilever → Browns) requiring contractual renegotiations without programme disruption.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 (historical): Disrupted early supply chains but mitigated through patient capital adjustments.
Climate change: Drought reduced tea quality; addressed via adaptive agronomic support.
Global economic pressures: Input cost increases managed through SC bulk procurement and loan term adjustments.
Currency fluctuations: Rwandan Franc depreciation offset by increasing loan amounts in local currency (RWF 1m → ~$900 equivalent).
contextual_constraints_new: Need for decarbonisation in tea processing (new climate policy requirements).
Higher-than-anticipated transport costs for greenleaf, prompting ropeway pilot innovation.
Limited access to patient capital for new SHFs in expansion areas (Nshili Kivu).
partner_relationship_issues: Corporate ownership changes (Unilever → Browns) required careful contract renegotiation but were handled smoothly with no programme interruption.
Initial scepticism from Luxmi (new partner) about Rwandan tea quality addressed through demonstration of SHF supply consistency.
capacity_constraints_emerged: SC capacity stretched by 176% increase in seasonal workers (70,902 vs 40,321 target), requiring additional training.
Need for specialised carbon assessment skills to meet new Net Zero components, addressed via external consultants.
GoR regulatory delays in approving new factory expansions (e.g., Kibeho launch rescheduled to Sept 2025).
risk_materialization: Business model risk (untested at outset) reduced as tea harvests proved viable (risk rating downgraded from Major to Moderate in 2022/23).
Drought risk materialised in 2024/25, impacting quality but not quantity (mitigated via agronomic support).
Currency risk materialised (Franc depreciation) but managed through local-currency loan adjustments.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track with 120% achievement in greenleaf production (5.88m kg vs 4.9m target). Front-loaded funding required reprofiling of results expectations for 2025–2029. Additional £4.6m allocated for new components (ropeways, carbon reduction, NKTF expansion) fully absorbed.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VfM confirmed: programme delivers economic (120% greenleaf production, 176% seasonal employment) and climate (GHG reduction roadmap) outcomes. Cost per kg of greenleaf produced declined by 15% since 2020 due to economies of scale in SC operations.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Funds disbursed via farmers’ bank accounts (enhancing financial inclusion), with zero-interest loans tied to milestones (land prep/planting). Quarterly audits and FCDO reviews found no material irregularities. Currency risk managed via dynamic loan adjustments.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Exceeds plan: cost per Ha of tea established reduced from $1,200 to $950 due to SC bulk input procurement and shared extension services. Ropeway pilot expected to reduce transport costs by 30%.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially materialised. Browns Investment PLC and Luxmi contributed to factory upgrades (Kibeho, Nshili Kivu) but co-funding for carbon components remains pending.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Rwandan Franc depreciation reduced dollar-equivalent value of farmer loans from ~$900 to ~$700 per Ha. Mitigated by increasing loan amounts in RWF terms (now RWF 1m/Ha, up from RWF 800k).

key_delivery_lessons: Service Company (SC) model effectively de-risks private investment by guaranteeing quality/quantity of greenleaf supply.
Patient capital (zero-interest loans) critical for tea establishment phase (3-year maturity aligns with first harvest).
Adaptive management frameworks (quarterly reviews + evidence-based design changes) enable mid-course corrections (e.g., 8 adaptations in 2024/25).
Climate components require upfront capacity building (e.g., GHG baseline assessments before Net Zero strategies).
successful_delivery_practices: Infographic-based progress reporting improved stakeholder communication (Annex C).
Front-line extension workers (via SCs) achieved 96% tea bush survival rate through hands-on training.
Corporate transition management (Unilever → Browns) preserved programme continuity via clear obligation transfers.
Ropeway pilot design incorporated farmer feedback to reduce post-harvest losses.
management_adaptations_made: Added climate indicators (R10, R11, R20) to ToC and logframe post-cost extension.
Increased oversight of GHG reduction studies following moderate risk rating on climate components.
Revised farmer loan terms to offset currency depreciation impacts.
Expanded SC workforce to handle 176% seasonal employment surge.
innovations_attempted: Pilot ropeways for greenleaf transport (expected 30% cost reduction).
Carbon-neutral tea processing roadmap (first in Rwanda).
Digital monitoring tools for real-time quality tracking at collection points.
Public-private partnership for Nshili Kivu expansion (2,500 new SHFs).
previous_recommendations_progress: 2023 recommendation to "explore scaling" led to NKTF expansion component (2,000Ha).
2022 VfM suggestion to bulk-procure inputs implemented, reducing costs by 15%.
2021 call for stronger climate integration addressed via Net Zero factory roadmaps.
forward_recommendations: Finalise co-funding agreements for carbon components with Browns/Luxmi.
Scale ropeway model to additional factories if pilot succeeds.
Develop patient capital facility for new SHFs in expansion areas.
Launch Kibeho factory (Sept 2025) with high-profile UK-Rwanda trade linkages.
Conduct mid-term evaluation of GHG reduction strategies by 2026.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Highly effective. SCs built financial inclusion via bank account linkages for loan disbursements.
GHG assessment capacity developed in 3 factories (Nshili Kivu, Shagasha, Mulindi).

Ropeway pilot designed for easy replication in other hilly tea regions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High. SILTPR cited as "flagship" programme in BHC Kigali portfolio, delivering on both economic and climate goals. A++ performance rating reflects exceptional adaptation and results.

Expand NKTF model to additional 5,000 SHFs if patient capital secured.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Direct/Grant/Contract - £18M via Govt of Nepal systems as financial aid, £32M via contracts with UNDP, suppliers, and partners)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £50M total budget (NCCSP: £24M, Renewable Energy: £18M, Clean Bricks: £4.5M, PIF: £1.75M, MEL: £1.75M)
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Direct financial aid to Govt of Nepal (NCCSP), contracts with UNDP (NCCSP bridging phase), commercial suppliers (Renewable Energy), and specialized partners (PIF, MEL, ICIMOD). Original plan assumed continuation of Phase 1 (2011-2016) fund flow mechanisms for NCCSP.

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch for PIF/MEL; intensive oversight for NCCSP financial aid (fiduciary risk management via existing Govt systems). Centralized DFID management with component leads for each area (NCCSP, Renewable Energy, etc.).
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly reporting for contracts; annual audits for financial aid to Govt of Nepal. MEL unit designed for cross-portfolio learning but not originally tasked with real-time adaptive management.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: DFID-led with Govt of Nepal consultation. Pre-federalism structure assumed Ministry-level coordination for NCCSP financial aid.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Multiple partners with clear component divisions: UNDP (NCCSP bridging), Govt of Nepal (NCCSP financial aid), commercial suppliers (Renewable Energy), ICIMOD (Clean Bricks), Oxford Policy Management (PIF), MEL contractor.
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral (UNDP), Government (Govt of Nepal), Private (commercial suppliers for Renewable Energy), Research (ICIMOD), NGO/Think Tank (Oxford Policy Management for PIF).

partner_roles_planned.Govt of Nepal: Direct financial aid recipient for NCCSP (£18M); policy counterpart for PIF

funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £2.2M spent by Year 2 (vs £10.8M planned). Budget reallocations between components; one-year extension to March 2023 approved. NCCSP delivery slowed (£1.2M spent vs £5.5M planned).

OJEU procurements delayed for NCCSP TA and Renewable Energy suppliers. MEL and PIF contracts finalized but with phased implementation.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High - Substantive reallocations due to federalism (e.g., NCCSP redesign for local government budgets), procurement delays, and enhanced due diligence (e.g., Clean Bricks pause).

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Intensified oversight: New "joint partner meetings" introduced to coordinate UNDP, NCCSP TA supplier, MEL, and PIF. Political economy analysis (via PIF) now informs adaptive management. MEL unit expanded to track GESI, unit costs, and supplier performance in real-time.
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Monthly coordination for NCCSP redesign; quarterly joint partner meetings. MEL unit now conducts "process learning" for adaptive feedback. Enhanced due diligence for Clean Bricks and NCCSP financial aid.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Shift to collaborative decision-making with Govt of Nepal at *local* level (mayors/palikas) for NCCSP. PIF’s political economy analysis now central to intervention pathways. DFID retains final approval but with greater delegation to component leads.

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Multiple partners retained but with *role expansions*: UNDP (extended bridging + capacity building for 14 palikas), new NCCSP TA supplier (replacing UNDP long-term), delayed Renewable Energy supplier. ICIMOD role formalized with safeguarding compliance requirements.
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (UNDP extended), Government (Govt of Nepal at *local* level via palikas), Private (commercial suppliers pending), Research (ICIMOD with stricter oversight), NGO/Think Tank (Oxford Policy Management for PIF).

partner_roles_actual.UNDP: Extended to 14 palikas for Climate Resilient Development Planning; capacity building for local governments; piloting climate finance integration tools.
partner_roles_actual.Govt of Nepal: Role shifted from central ministry to *local palikas* (14 selected for NCCSP pilots). Financial aid paused until new mechanisms designed.
partner_roles_actual.Commercial Suppliers: Renewable Energy supplier delayed; Clean Bricks (ICIMOD) paused for due diligence then restarted with safeguarding measures.
partner_roles_actual.Oxford Policy Management: PIF implementation commenced with political economy analysis shaping intervention pathways.
partner_roles_actual.MEL Contractor: Expanded to GESI audits, unit cost tracking, and cross-portfolio performance monitoring.

partner_names_actual: Government of Nepal (Ministry of Forestry and Environment, 14 palikas)

substantive_changes_made: NCCSP fund flow mechanisms *redesigned* for federalism: Shift from central Govt to local palikas (mayors) with new climate finance integration tools.
Pausing of £18M financial aid to Govt of Nepal pending new fiduciary controls for local government systems.
Extension of UNDP’s role from bridging phase to full capacity-building for 14 palikas (Climate Resilient Development Planning).
Enhanced due diligence processes (e.g., Clean Bricks pause and safeguarding reforms).
Introduction of joint partner meetings and real-time MEL "process learning" for adaptive management.
One-year programme extension (to March 2023) to accommodate delays and redesign.
Theory of Change revision planned to reflect federalism opportunities and output adjustments.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Budget *scale unchanged* but *tempo slowed*: £2.2M spent by Year 2 (vs £10.8M planned). Reallocations between components (e.g., NCCSP underspend).

funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: Shift from direct financial aid to *contract-heavy* delivery (UNDP extension, new TA supplier). Local government fund flows replaced central Govt mechanisms.

theory_of_change_revisions.pathway_changes: Added federalism as a *new opportunity*: Local palikas (mayors) as entry points for climate finance integration. Emphasis on capacity-building for local governments to manage funds (vs original central ministry focus).
theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Original assumption of stable Govt of Nepal systems *invalidated* by federalism. New assumptions: Local government capacity limits require phased scaling; political economy analysis needed for policy influence.

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: Yes: Joint partner meetings introduced; MEL unit repurposed for adaptive management; PIF’s political economy analysis now central to decision-making.
management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Yes: Monthly coordination for NCCSP redesign; real-time MEL feedback loops; enhanced due diligence for financial aid.
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: Yes: Shift from central ministry to local palikas for NCCSP; PIF’s intervention pathways now guide programme adjustments.

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: No locations *removed*, but NCCSP delivery *paused* during redesign. 14 palikas selected for pilots (subset of original scope).
geographic_scope_changes.geographic_focus_shifted: Yes: From central Govt to *local* palikas (mayors) as primary counterparts for NCCSP.

activity_only_adjustments: Minor delays in Renewable Energy supplier procurement (not yet substantive).
GESI integration reviews (planned as part of original MEL scope).

contextual_shocks: Nepal’s *federalisation* (2017): Required complete redesign of NCCSP fund flows and governance.
Enhanced due diligence requirements (FCDO-wide): Triggered Clean Bricks pause.
performance_issues: OJEU procurement delays for NCCSP TA and Renewable Energy suppliers (12+ months).
Slower-than-planned NCCSP delivery due to paused financial aid.
learning_insights: Political economy analysis (via PIF) revealed opportunities to integrate climate finance into local government budgets.
MEL’s process learning identified need for capacity-building at palika level.
strategic_opportunities: Federalism as an opportunity: Local palikas (mayors) as new entry points for climate resilience planning.
Potential synergies with DFID Nepal’s disaster resilience portfolio (recommended for future exploration).

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High - Proactive use of political economy analysis (PIF) and MEL process learning to redesign NCCSP. Joint partner meetings improved coordination.
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: High - Baseline medium flexibility *fully utilized*: Budget reallocations, fund flow redesign, programme extension, and partner role adjustments.
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High - MEL’s GESI reviews and PIF’s political economy analysis directly informed NCCSP redesign and Theory of Change updates.

fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Low - No active conflict during implementation, but residual tensions from civil war (1996-2006) and federalism disputes.

major_external_shocks.political_transitions: Nepal’s *federalisation* (2017): Creation of 753 local governments (palikas) replaced centralised systems, requiring programme redesign.
major_external_shocks.climate_disasters: Floods/landslides (2017-2018) affected NCCSP target areas, but no major programme disruptions reported.

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: High commitment at local level (palikas) post-federalisation, but *capacity gaps* delayed NCCSP financial aid. Central ministry roles diminished.
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: Federalism required new Local Adaptation Plan of Action (LAPA) framework revisions (led by PIF).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Climate Smart Development for Nepal

output_1.title: Poor people and SMEs are better able to cope with current climate related shocks (floods, landslides and droughts) and prepare for future change

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme re-designed to align with Nepal's federalisation process; new tool developed for integrating climate resilience into local government budgets; piloting in 14 local governments before scaling up. main_implementation_challenges: Procurement delays for NCCSP TA and Renewable Energy suppliers (OJEU process).
Pause in financial aid to NCCSP during redesign of fund flow mechanisms for federalism.
Enhanced due diligence requirements for clean bricks initiative.
Slow spending due to re-shaping delivery models (only £2.2M spent vs £10.8M planned by Year 2).
operational_challenges_context.external_factors_impact: Nepal’s federalisation process required significant programme redesign, including new fund flow mechanisms and alignment with local government structures. Political economy shifts necessitated adaptive management (e.g., engaging newly elected mayors).

New local government spending units lacked capacity to manage financial aid as envisioned in the Business Case.
Need to pilot approaches before scaling due to untested federal systems.
operational_challenges_context.partner_relationship_issues: Coordination challenges among multiple suppliers (UNDP, TA, MEL, PIF) required proactive management; recommendations made for joint partner meetings.

DFID and suppliers needed time to understand fiduciary risks in new federal system.
MEL unit identified gaps in GESI integration across components.
risk_materialization: Procurement delays (NCCSP TA, Renewable Energy supplier).
Fiduciary risks in new government systems (prompted pause in financial aid).
Slower-than-planned spending due to federalisation adjustments.

budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_reason: Procurement delays (NCCSP TA, Renewable Energy) and reshaping NCCSP delivery model for federalism. Only 20% of planned spend executed.

value_for_money_assessment.progress_vs_bc_assumptions: BC assumptions (e.g., £2.52 benefit per £1 cost for adaptation) still valid, but no funds spent yet on adaptation investments. Scaling up required to realize benefits.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency_achieved: Unit costs tracked by MEL; supplier performance monitored, but efficiency data limited due to early implementation phase.
value_for_money_assessment.equity_considerations: MEL reviewed GESI integration in clean bricks, MEL, and PIF components; progress made but improvements needed.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: MEL unit operationalized to track unit costs, supplier performance, and equity. GESI review identified gaps in financial allocations and M&E systems.

key_delivery_lessons: Federalisation requires flexible delivery models and piloting before scaling (e.g., NCCSP’s 14-palika pilot).
Political economy analysis is critical for adapting to context changes (e.g., PIF’s intervention pathways).
Coordination mechanisms must be formalized early for multi-supplier programmes.
successful_delivery_practices: Redesigning NCCSP to align with federal Nepal, including tools for climate finance integration.
PIF’s early relationship-building with Government of Nepal.
MEL’s framework for tracking economy, efficiency, effectiveness, and equity.
management_adaptations_made: Paused financial aid to NCCSP to manage fiduciary risks during transition.
Extended programme end date by one year (to March 2023) to accommodate delays.
Commissioned GESI review to improve inclusion in policies and M&E systems.
innovations_attempted: New tool for integrating climate resilience into local government budgets.
Piloting Climate Resilient Development Planning in 14 palikas.
PIF’s ‘intervention pathways’ to influence climate policies/institutions.
forward_recommendations: Accelerate onboarding of new NCCSP and Renewable Energy suppliers to build on bridging phase work.
Use PIF to deepen political economy analysis in climate resilience and energy sectors.
Establish regular joint partner meetings to improve supplier collaboration.
Formalize GESI integration strategy across all components.
Revise Theory of Change and log frame to reflect federalism opportunities.
Develop new energy strategy using DFID’s ‘Whole Systems Approach’.
Reduce programme complexity by combining energy work with other DFID Nepal programmes.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive risk management (e.g., pausing financial aid to mitigate fiduciary risks; enhanced due diligence for clean bricks). However, procurement delays and federalisation risks materialized, requiring adaptive responses.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.mel: M&E framework in place; research studies completed.

UNDP hosted workshops to design capacity-building approaches for NCCSP.
PIF provided strategic support to Government of Nepal on climate finance systems.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: Potential for scaling NCCSP’s Climate Resilient Development Planning after pilot in 14 palikas; clean bricks initiative could expand if safeguarding measures are met.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates adaptive management and potential for impact despite delays. Federalisation alignment positions NCCSP as a model for future programmes. One-year extension granted to achieve results.

planned_adaptations_future: Scale up NCCSP delivery after pilot phase.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Building Sustainable Anti-Corruption Action in Tanzania (BSAAT)

output_1.title: Financial aid improves the capacity and coordination of government authorities to tackle corruption

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from private sector and social norms components to greater focus on Judiciary and Serious Organised Crime (SOC). EU co-financing (36% of funds) introduced via Contribution Agreement. Potential cancellation of Financial Aid component due to election irregularities, requiring alternative delivery model design.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Government of Tanzania partnership remained strong (publicly praised at Anti-Corruption Day), but top-level engagement dropped post-election. Beneficiary institutions (BIs) maintained focus on targets despite disruptions. EU partnership effective but requires formalized leadership structure.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Complex delivery model validated by results, but high transaction costs limit FCDO team's advisory capacity. Proposed BSAAT Advisory Board (EU/UK co-chaired) to improve integration. UNDP being considered as managing agent for SOC components.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong integration between output workstreams (e.g., prosecutions/Slynn Foundation, fiduciary risk/FA) demonstrated value. Theme-based logframe recommended to enhance coordination. EU/UK Contribution Agreement requires amendment for new logframe and component changes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in procuring private sector implementing partner led to workstream pause. SOC component in mobilization phase with UNDP designing implementation. KPMG provided technical support on fiduciary risk.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FA Steering Committee focused on effectiveness, but remote oversight during COVID reduced relationship quality. Political exposure and fund disbursement delays exposed vulnerabilities in FA delivery model.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to context by reallocating resources from private sector/social norms to SOC/Judiciary. Alternative delivery models explored for Output 1 due to potential FA cancellation.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of resources to SOC/Judiciary components in response to implementation challenges in private sector.
Design of alternative delivery model for Output 1 (Financial Aid) following election-related aid pause.
Introduction of VfM tracking for FA indicators and focus on outcome-level case studies.
Proposal for BSAAT Advisory Board to formalize EU/UK coordination.

main_implementation_challenges: COVID-19 disruptions (travel restrictions, remote engagement costs, delayed judicial processes).
Tanzania’s 2020 election irregularities led to UK aid pause and proposed cancellation of Financial Aid component.
Political economy shifts post-election reduced top-level government engagement.
High programme management transaction costs limiting core advisory work.
Delays in fund disbursement and political exposure in FA delivery model.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Derailed judicial engagement, travel-dependent activities (e.g., Slynn Foundation’s sentencing guidelines work), and increased remote management costs.
2020 Elections: Irregularities prompted UK aid freeze, exposing reputational risks tied to State House leadership of FA component.
EU Co-financing: Contribution Agreement introduced additional governance layers (36% of funds).
Human Rights Concerns: UK reservations about election credibility and violations increased contextual risk.
contextual_constraints_new: Reduced top-level government engagement post-election despite technical cooperation remaining strong.
Heightened reputational risk due to association with government departments linked to election irregularities.
SOC component required mobilization phase, delaying impact.
Private sector component dropped from logframe (July 2020), challenging original Theory of Change.
partner_relationship_issues: State House leadership of FA component became politically sensitive post-election.
Remote relationship management during COVID weakened counterpart ownership and sustainability.
EU partnership effective but lacks formalized leadership structure (proposed Advisory Board to address this).
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO team capacity stretched by high transaction costs, limiting strategic advisory work.
Judicial engagement constrained by COVID-related travel bans (e.g., delayed Sentencing Guidelines work).
Beneficiary institutions welcomed KPMG’s fiduciary risk support, indicating gaps in internal capacity.
SOC component required external design support (UNDP) due to limited in-house expertise.
risk_materialization: Political Risk: Election irregularities and UK aid freeze materialized, threatening FA component.
COVID-19 Risk: Disrupted travel-dependent activities (e.g., judicial training, MLA coordination).
Reputational Risk: Association with election-linked government departments increased exposure.
Delivery Model Risk: Vulnerabilities in FA component (political exposure, fund delays) confirmed.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for 80% of programme outputs (3/5 outputs met expectations). FA component faces cancellation due to political risks, requiring budget reallocation. EU funds (36%) disbursed via Contribution Agreement, but delays noted in FA fund flows.

value_for_money_assessment.performance: Moderate. FA component delivered strong results (60% of 40 output indicators met/exceeded), but COVID reduced efficiency of travel-dependent activities. SOC component in mobilization phase limits VfM demonstration.
Challenged. Remote engagement increased transaction costs (e.g., heavy coordination burdens). High programme management costs limited advisory capacity.
Emerging focus. FA data disaggregation and SOC safeguarding efforts planned to address "Leave No One Behind" agenda.
Mixed. Small investments across institutions proved cost-effective for systemic influence, but FA fund delays and political risks reduced cost certainty.

financial_management_quality: Strong tracking of FA VfM indicators introduced for first time.
KPMG’s technical support on fiduciary risk welcomed by beneficiary institutions.
Delays in FA fund disbursement exposed liquidity risks for implementing partners.
EU Contribution Agreement governance added complexity but ensured transparency.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Small, targeted investments (e.g., conflict-of-interest systems, public expenditure tracking) delivered outsized results (e.g., 132% of audit red flag targets met). However, remote coordination and political contingencies increased overheads.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: EU contributed 36% of funds as planned via Contribution Agreement, but private sector co-funding dropped after component cancellation.

key_delivery_lessons: FA component resilient to remote delivery (dedicated focal points in BIs maintained progress).
Travel-dependent activities (e.g., judicial engagement, MLA coordination) faltered under COVID.
Small, dispersed investments across institutions effective for systemic influence.
Political risks in FA delivery model (State House reliance) cannot be fully mitigated.
successful_delivery_practices: Conflict-of-interest systems (e.g., Online Declaration System installed in 9 offices).
Public expenditure tracking (PETS) exceeded targets (132% of audit red flags detected).
Expert audit testimony in court (17 cases) strengthened prosecutions.
SOC counterpart relationships influenced child protection safeguarding.
management_adaptations_made: Resource reallocation from private sector/social norms to SOC/Judiciary.
Introduction of VfM tracking for FA indicators and outcome-level case studies.
Proposal for BSAAT Advisory Board to formalize EU/UK coordination.
Exploration of UNDP as managing agent for SOC components.
innovations_attempted: Theme-based logframe to integrate output workstreams.
Alternative delivery model design for Output 1 (post-FA cancellation).
Disaggregated FA data to measure equity impacts.
Slynn Foundation’s Sentencing Guidelines (delayed by COVID but pivotal for judicial engagement).
previous_recommendations_progress: Logframe revised (July 2020) to drop private sector component and align with SOC focus.
FA Steering Committee enhanced effectiveness tracking, but outcome-level mapping pending.
EU Contribution Agreement amendments proposed but not yet finalized.
forward_recommendations: Design alternative delivery model for Output 1 in partnership with EU/Government of Tanzania.
Fast-track UNDP’s managing agent role for SOC components post-design phase.
Establish BSAAT Advisory Board (EU/UK co-chaired) to improve integration.
Amend EU/UK Contribution Agreement to reflect component changes and potential programme extension.
Prioritize asset seizure outcomes to test deterrence theory (convictions alone insufficient).
Develop SOC safeguarding programmes to address vulnerable persons (VFM equity measure).

risk_management_effectiveness.effectiveness: Partial. Mitigation strategies (remote delivery) kept FA component on track but increased costs and reduced sustainability.
Limited. FA component vulnerabilities exposed; alternative models now required.
Moderate. High transaction costs identified; Advisory Board proposed to streamline governance.
Insufficient. Private sector component drop challenged collective action theory; ToC revision recommended.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 9 ES offices received Online Declaration System; 58 persons trained on GRIS; 37 ES staff trained on conflict-of-interest systems. 1,026 Suspicious Transaction Reports processed; 507 Public Expenditure Tracking Surveys conducted.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Media coverage of CAG findings (65 articles); 329 PETS projects with at-risk monies identified (TZS 103,901,914.80).

policy_influence_achieved: Conflict of Interest system operationalized (Finance Act amendment passed).
Beneficial Ownership legislation enacted (July 2020).
Mutual Legal Assistance (MLA) SOPs drafted (though not finalized).
Sentencing Guidelines advanced (delayed by COVID).
Public praise from Government of Tanzania at Anti-Corruption Day indicates alignment with national priorities.
capacity_building_results: 58 personnel trained on GRIS software.
37 ES staff trained on Online Declaration System.
17 auditors provided expert testimony in court (strengthening prosecutions).
KPMG’s fiduciary risk support welcomed by beneficiary institutions.
SOC counterpart relationships established for child protection safeguarding.

unintended_consequences.description: SOC component’s focus on child protection/safeguarding emerged as an unplanned priority with strong counterpart engagement.
UK aid pause post-election disrupted FA component, risking loss of momentum in conflict-of-interest and beneficial ownership reforms.
Remote delivery reduced sustainability of judicial engagement (e.g., Sentencing Guidelines delays).

scalability_evidence: Small-investment approach (e.g., public expenditure tracking, audit red flags) demonstrated scalability across multiple institutions.
Conflict-of-interest and beneficial ownership systems designed for national rollout.
SOC safeguarding models replicable in other East African contexts (per UNDP design work).
Limited evidence on deterrence impact (asset seizure outcomes not yet tested).

continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with Government of Tanzania’s anti-corruption priorities (publicly praised at Anti-Corruption Day).
FA component delivered results but faces cancellation; alternative model required to sustain Output 1.
SOC and judicial components show promise but need time to mature (currently in mobilization/early implementation).
EU co-financing (36%) provides leverage for continued partnership, but governance structures need formalization.
COVID and election disruptions were external shocks; core delivery model (small investments across institutions) remains valid.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: Medium-High (conditional on delivery model adaptation and political risk mitigation)

delivery_model_sustainability.sustainability: Medium. EU funds secure (36%) but FA component cancellation requires reallocation. High transaction costs need reduction.
Medium. Government alignment strong at technical level but top-level engagement dropped post-election.
High. Capacity built in conflict-of-interest, beneficial ownership, and audit systems.
Medium. Advisory Board and UNDP managing agent could improve coordination but add complexity.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (with caveats on political risk management and VfM efficiency)
planned_adaptations_future: Design alternative delivery model for Output 1 (post-FA cancellation) in partnership with EU/Government of Tanzania.
Finalize EU/UK Contribution Agreement amendments for new logframe and potential extension.
Establish BSAAT Advisory Board (EU/UK co-chaired) to streamline governance.
Accelerate SOC component implementation via UNDP managing agent.
Test deterrence theory through asset seizure outcomes (beyond convictions).
Develop equity-focused VfM measures (disaggregated data, vulnerable person case studies).
Revise Theory of Change to reflect dropped private sector component and SOC emphasis.

programme_metadata.programme_title: UK - Ghana Partnership for Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) Programme

output_1.title: T1 Investment Acceleration: Enhanced capability, opportunity and motivation of new and existing investors through the programme to invest in key sectors in Ghana

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Budget cuts in 2021/22 reduced commercial contract from £16.7M to £12M, leading to a leaner two-member in-country management team. Programme shifted focus to three sectors (automotive, pharmaceuticals, textiles/garments) instead of the planned five, with new scoping in agricultural processing and light manufacturing due to GoG requests.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Palladium International Limited (Supplier) faced challenges due to budget cuts, affecting partner engagement strategy. GoG stakeholders (Vice President’s office, MoTI, MoT, GIPC) praised JET’s strategic policy advice and investment facilitation, but fiscal constraints limited GoG’s ability to implement reforms (e.g., Cabinet approval delays for industrial policies).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Reduced to a two-member in-country team post-budget cuts, with reliance on short-term advisors and grants to compensate for capacity gaps. Oversight by FCDO Ghana and Palladium HQ required strengthening, particularly in risk management, MEL, and quality assurance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: JET acted as a trusted coordinator between GoG, investors, and SMEs, particularly in automotive (EV policy alignment) and pharmaceutical sectors. However, coordination was hindered by GoG’s fiscal constraints and political transitions (e.g., upcoming 2024 elections).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Long recruitment timeframes and budget cuts delayed procurement of specialist advisors. Grants and strategic partnerships (e.g., with DFIs) were underutilized but identified as critical for Year 4–5 delivery.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was weaker than planned due to reduced management capacity. Remedial actions included hiring new staff (August 2024) for risk/financial management and MEL, and commissioning a political economy analysis to guide engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by scaling back T&G sector work due to budget cuts and reprioritizing automotive/pharmaceuticals. Flexibility in sector scoping (e.g., agricultural processing) responded to GoG requests but stretched limited resources.

adaptive_management_examples.1: Shifted from five to three primary sectors (automotive, pharmaceuticals, T&G) with exploratory work in new sectors (agricultural processing).
adaptive_management_examples.2: Developed EV regulatory standards to align with Ghana Automotive Policy, demonstrating policy coherence.
adaptive_management_examples.3: Established MOU-stage investment for solar-powered electric vehicles (2024), adapting to investor interest in green transitions.
adaptive_management_examples.4: Reduced in-country team size to maximize frontline delivery funds, compensating with short-term advisors.

main_implementation_challenges: Budget cuts (2021/22) reduced contract value from £16.7M to £12M, limiting delivery capacity and partner engagement.
GoG fiscal constraints delayed Cabinet approval of industrial policies (e.g., auto components, pharmaceuticals, garments sectors), stalling incentive-based investments.
Macroeconomic trends (e.g., inflation, currency depreciation) dampened private sector expansion and FDI attraction.
Long recruitment lead times for specialist roles (e.g., transaction advisors, MEL experts) created capacity gaps.
Political transitions (2024 elections) introduced uncertainty around policy continuity and stakeholder priorities.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 (implied): While not explicitly stated, budget cuts and economic downturns post-2020 likely exacerbated FDI attraction challenges.
Global economic slowdown reduced investor appetite for high-value manufacturing in Ghana.
Ghana’s cedi depreciation and inflation (50% higher costs vs. 2021/22) increased operational expenses for SMEs and investors.
GoG’s limited fiscal space for incentives (e.g., tax reliefs) reduced attractiveness of greenfield investments.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated GoG requests to expand into agricultural processing/light manufacturing diverted resources from core sectors.
SMEs’ limited capacity to meet investor due diligence requirements (e.g., ESG standards) emerged as a barrier to deal closure.
Outdated sector analyses undermined JET’s ability to identify Ghana’s ‘right to win’ investment opportunities.
Gender and Social Inclusion (GESI) risks were under-addressed in early phases, requiring late-stage capacity building.
partner_relationship_issues: GIPC and MoTI praised JET’s technical support but struggled to operationalize policies due to fiscal constraints.
Private sector partners (e.g., automotive investors) reported high likelihood of deal closure (e.g., EV MOU) but cited GoG delays as a risk.
Consortium partners’ roles were underutilized; Year 4–5 strategy aims to formalize their support for delivery.
capacity_constraints_emerged: In-country team reduced to two members post-budget cuts, overstretching remaining staff.
Lack of transaction advisors delayed deal progression (e.g., only 2 of 5 investment leads deemed ‘high likelihood’ by 2024).
Limited MEL and GESI expertise hindered adaptive management and risk mitigation.
Supplier’s technical capacity for SME support and sector analysis required external reinforcement.
risk_materialization: Budget cuts (2021/22) materialized as a major risk, reducing contract value by £4.7M.
GoG’s inability to grant fiscal incentives (due to macroeconomic crises) stalled policy implementation.
Investor leads in T&G sector were deprioritized due to resource constraints, limiting diversification.
Political risk (election uncertainty) delayed policy reforms critical for sectoral growth.

budget_execution_vs_plan.execution_rate: Budget cuts led to underspending in early years, but Year 4–5 uplifts aim to restore capacity. 50% higher operational costs in 2023/24 vs. 2021/22 due to inflation.
budget_execution_vs_plan.unspent_funds_reallocation: Funds reallocated from management overheads to frontline delivery (e.g., SME support, investor facilitation).

value_for_money_assessment.planned_vfm: Business case projected cost-efficient policy reforms and FDI attraction to drive manufacturing growth.
value_for_money_assessment.actual_vfm: Mixed: Output targets (e.g., investment leads) were met/exceeded, but outcome-level results (jobs, investments realized) lagged. VFM weakened by budget cuts reducing leverage over GoG/SMEs.
vfm_drivers: High attribution of investment leads (£97.4M identified in 2023/24) to JET’s facilitation.
Policy outputs (e.g., EV standards) achieved with limited funds, demonstrating efficiency.
However, low conversion of leads to actual investments (£0 realized vs. £7.5M target) questioned long-term VFM.
vfm_improvement_needs: Stronger MEL to track investment-to-job creation pathways.
Transaction advisors to accelerate deal closure.
Updated sector analyses to target high-potential opportunities.

financial_management_quality.supplier_performance: Palladium’s financial management was adequate but required strengthening in risk oversight and reporting quality. Audit findings (implied) led to August 2024 recruitment of financial/risk specialists.
financial_management_quality.fcdo_oversight: FCDO Ghana’s oversight was reactive; recommendations included short-term MEL support and external strategic advice.
financial_management_quality.grant_management: Modest grant component underutilized; Year 4–5 strategy prioritizes grants for SME support and DFI partnerships.
financial_management_quality.currency_impacts: Ghanaian cedi depreciation increased local costs, reducing purchasing power for programme funds.

cost_efficiency_achieved.planned: Business case assumed efficient policy reforms would catalyze private investment with minimal public funds.
cost_efficiency_achieved.actual: Cost-efficient in output delivery (e.g., £97.4M leads identified with reduced budget) but inefficient in outcome conversion (e.g., 432 jobs vs. 2,250 target).
efficiency_gaps: High transaction costs for investor facilitation without commensurate deal closures.
Delayed policy implementation increased opportunity costs for SMEs.

co_funding_materialization.planned: Business case anticipated GoG and private sector co-funding for incentives and SME matching funds.
co_funding_materialization.actual: Limited materialization due to GoG fiscal constraints. No evidence of private sector co-funding in 2023/24.
co_funding_materialization.barriers: GoG’s macroeconomic crisis (debt restructuring, IMF programme) restricted fiscal space for co-funding.

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Cedi depreciation (implied by 50% cost increase vs. 2021/22) eroded programme purchasing power, requiring budget reallocations to maintain activities.

key_delivery_lessons: Output-level success (e.g., investment leads) does not guarantee outcome achievement (e.g., jobs/investments realized).
GoG’s fiscal constraints are the primary bottleneck for policy implementation; JET must align expectations with political-economic realities.
Short-term advisors and grants can compensate for capacity gaps but require proactive planning.
Sector diversification (e.g., agricultural processing) should be balanced against core sector depth.
successful_delivery_practices: JET’s role as a neutral broker between GoG, investors, and SMEs built trust and facilitated dialogue (e.g., EV policy coherence).
Adaptive sector prioritization (e.g., scaling back T&G to focus on automotive/pharmaceuticals) preserved resources for high-potential areas.
Investor facilitation approaches (e.g., desk research, missions, GoG linkages) were effective in lead generation.
High-level GoG engagement (Vice President’s office, MoTI) ensured policy relevance.
management_adaptations_made: Reduced in-country team to maximize frontline funds, with August 2024 recruitment to address gaps in risk/MEL.
Commissioned political economy analysis to inform 2024 election engagement strategy.
Planned Year 4–5 strategy refresh (October 2024) to realign ToC and logframe with contextual changes.
Established investment committee and transaction advisor roles to accelerate deal progression.
innovations_attempted: EV regulatory standards development to align with global green transitions.
Solar-powered electric vehicle investment facilitation (MOU stage).
Pilot SME support models (e.g., firm-level vs. sector-wide approaches) to identify scalable practices.
Stories of Change documentation to capture qualitative impacts (though quality needed improvement).
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: Supplier recruited risk/financial management staff (August 2024) but MEL and GESI capacity gaps persist.
ToC update initiated but not finalized; targeted for November 2024 completion.
Logframe review pending ToC refresh; indicators remain misaligned with outcome ambitions.
Stakeholder engagement strengthened (e.g., high-level forum planned for October 2024) but election uncertainty remains a risk.

forward_recommendations.action: Update ToC by November 2024 to reflect economic/political context and increased Year 4–5 budget.
Revise logframe indicators/targets to align with realistic outcome pathways (e.g., adjust job/investment targets).
Establish investment committee and hire transaction advisors to progress £97.4M investment leads to closure.
Refresh SME support approach using international best practices (e.g., DFI partnerships, grant instruments).
Update sector analyses to identify Ghana’s ‘right to win’ investments and inform intervention prioritization.
Strengthen GESI and ESG integration in risk register and SME support (e.g., due diligence, capacity building).
Conclude Year 4–5 staff recruitments and finalize consortium partner agreements to boost delivery capacity.

risk_management_effectiveness.planned_approach: Business case identified risks (e.g., GoG fiscal constraints, investor appetite) but underestimated macroeconomic volatility.
actual_practice: Reactive: Risks like budget cuts and cedi depreciation were managed post-materialization rather than mitigated proactively.
Risk register lacked GESI/ESG-specific risks until late stages.
Supplier’s risk oversight improved post-August 2024 recruitments but remains dependent on FCDO guidance.
gaps: No contingency plans for GoG’s prolonged fiscal constraints.
Limited scenario planning for election-related policy disruptions.
Underestimation of SMEs’ capacity gaps in meeting investor ESG requirements.
improvements_needed: Integrate macroeconomic scenario analysis into risk management.
Develop investor due diligence tools to address ESG/GESI risks.
Formalize political economy analysis updates pre/post-elections.

investments_realized.notes: £97.4M in leads identified (exceeding cumulative target) but no investments materialized in 2023/24.

policy_beneficiaries.description: GoG institutions (MoTI, GIPC, Vice President’s office) received technical support for EV standards and automotive policy coherence.
policy_beneficiaries.reach: High-level engagement but limited Cabinet-level policy adoption.

smes_supported.description: Investment plans, investor linkages, and regulatory advice provided to SMEs in automotive/pharmaceuticals.
smes_supported.reach: Number not specified; five investment leads included SME partnerships.

programme_metadata.programme_value_gbp: £33m (£30m from Prosperity Fund and £3m from Commonwealth Summit 2018-20 Fund)

output_1.title: Centre for Disaster Protection - staffed and operational

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme established two co-located components: the directly-implemented Centre for Disaster Protection (Centre) and the World Bank Disaster Protection Programme (DPP). Both are based in London, with the Centre led by a Director and leadership team, supported by Oxford Policy Management as Managing Agent. The World Bank DPP operates through a Single Donor Trust Fund (SDTF) with 5 staff, including the Bank’s Practice Manager for Crisis and Disaster Risk Finance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partnerships with the World Bank and Government Actuary’s Department (GAD) are working well. A new partnership with the Met Office was agreed in principle, and others are under discussion. The Managing Agent (Oxford Policy Management) was rated as 'Exceeding Expectations' in its first annual supplier scorecard review.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Centre’s leadership team (Director, Director of Operations, Heads of Country Programmes, Multilateral Programmes, and incoming Head of Research, Evidence, and Innovation) is in place. Governance structures, including the Advisory Board and Expert Advisory Group, are operational and meet regularly. The Centre developed a 5-year strategic vision, approved by the Advisory Board in September 2019.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: The co-location of the Centre and World Bank DPP in London has facilitated joint working and networking with multilaterals, HMG, and industry. The Centre and DPP collaborate on technical assistance, regional solutions (e.g., South East Asian Disaster Risk Insurance Facility), and global public goods (data, models, knowledge).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Operating policies (e.g., procurement, conflict of interest) were agreed upon. The Managing Agent’s contract was extended to ensure continuity for staff and additional programme funds.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: The Advisory Board and Expert Advisory Group provide oversight, meeting every 6 months. The Centre’s leadership team offers strong direction, including through the 5-year strategic vision.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme adapted by establishing a new workstream on crisis risk finance in response to international demand for analysis and advice. The Centre also refreshed its Theory of Change (ToC), Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) framework, and Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) policies to align with its new strategy.
adaptive_management_examples: Development of a new crisis risk finance workstream to meet international demand.
Refresh of the Centre’s ToC, M&E framework, and GESI policies to reflect the 5-year strategy.
Reallocation of unneeded funds from the Multidonor Trust Fund (MDTF) back to the Centre’s budget after the MDTF transitioned into the larger Global Risk Financing Facility (GRIF).
Extension of the Managing Agent’s contract to ensure continuity and accommodate additional funds.

main_implementation_challenges: Establishing the Centre’s structures, functions, and international credentials in its early phases.
Balancing demand for technical assistance with the need to develop global public goods and innovative solutions.
Ensuring complementarity between the Centre and World Bank DPP’s technical assistance to countries.
operational_challenges_context.capacity_constraints_emerged: The need to recruit and onboard qualified staff quickly to scale up activities, including the delayed arrival of the Head of Research, Evidence, and Innovation (planned for December 2019).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme’s initial £1.5m contribution to the World Bank’s Multidonor Trust Fund (MDTF) was fully committed, and projects progressed well. Unneeded funds were reallocated back to the Centre’s budget after the MDTF transitioned into the Global Risk Financing Facility (GRIF), funded by a larger DFID programme.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early findings from the Prosperity Fund Evaluation and Learning Team were positive. Recommendations included finalizing the Theory of Change (ToC), M&E framework, and 5-year strategy to better reflect the programme’s expansion in Disaster Risk Finance (DRF) coverage and its impact (e.g., country capacity, GESI, speed of payouts, resilience). The Centre is also updating success indicators to capture secondary benefits and development impact more effectively.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: The Managing Agent (Oxford Policy Management) was rated as 'Exceeding Expectations' in its first annual supplier scorecard review, indicating strong financial management. Operating policies (e.g., procurement, conflict of interest) were formalized.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: The MDTF (co-financed with Germany) transitioned into the larger Global Risk Financing Facility (GRIF), which is now funded by a separate DFID programme. This allowed the reallocation of unspent funds back to the Centre.

key_delivery_lessons: Co-location of the Centre and World Bank DPP in London enhanced collaboration and networking with multilaterals, HMG, and industry.
Early investment in governance structures (Advisory Board, Expert Advisory Group) and operating policies (procurement, conflict of interest) provided a strong foundation for implementation.
Flexibility in reallocating funds (e.g., from MDTF to Centre budget) allowed the programme to adapt to changing circumstances.
successful_delivery_practices: Recruitment of experienced staff from the City of London, UK Government, and industry strengthened the Centre’s technical capacity.
Development of a 5-year strategic vision provided clear direction and helped establish the Centre’s niche in disaster risk finance.
Partnerships with the World Bank, GAD, and Met Office leveraged complementary expertise and expanded the programme’s reach.
management_adaptations_made: Transition from setup phase to delivery phase, including the development of new workstreams (e.g., crisis risk finance) in response to demand.
Refresh of the ToC, M&E framework, and GESI strategy to align with the 5-year vision and improve impact measurement.
Evolution of governance arrangements as the Centre moves toward a longer-term structure.
innovations_attempted: Establishment of Innovation Labs to generate and incubate new solutions for disaster risk finance.
Pilot of a training programme on risk-based approaches for 90 insurance supervisors (via the Access to Insurance Initiative).
Exploration of regional solutions, such as the South East Asian Disaster Risk Insurance Facility (SEADRIF) and new drought models for African Risk Capacity (ARC).
previous_recommendations_progress: The first annual evaluation (2019) found that the Centre had made considerable progress in establishing its structures and scaling up activities. Recommendations from the evaluation—such as finalizing the ToC, M&E framework, and governance—are being actioned.

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Finalize and align the Theory of Change (ToC), M&E framework (including value for money), and GESI strategy within the new 5-year strategy. Update success indicators to better reflect DRF coverage and impact (e.g., country capacity, GESI, speed of payouts, resilience).
Develop a country/client mapping to identify where the Centre and DPP are working, potential targets, and areas of highest added value.
Confirm and implement a medium-term structure for the Centre.
Evolve and update governance arrangements for the Centre.
forward_recommendations.lead: Centre and DFID (with Managing Agent support)

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Refresh engagement with the private sector and civil society, and quantify secondary benefits indicators.
Develop new and existing partnerships to increase the Centre’s scope and impact (e.g., with Insurance Development Forum, Commonwealth Secretariat, NERC, regional organizations).
Incoming Head of Research and Evidence (R&E) to develop an R&E strategy and workplan for the Centre.
Grow the Centre’s R&E partnerships and portfolio, focusing on demand-driven applied innovation and learning.
Ensure the Centre and DPP have the skills/experience to work effectively in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS).
Expand and improve training offers, ensuring they respond to demand and include follow-up to apply new skills.
Ensure complementarity in technical assistance between the Centre and DPP, with strong links to delivery and GESI principles.
Incorporate deep-dive recommendations and sovereign-level technical assistance into the domestic market development workstream of the SDTF.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: The programme’s risk rating remained 'Moderate' for both 2018 and 2019, indicating that risks were managed effectively during this period. The Advisory Board and Expert Advisory Group provide regular oversight, and adaptive management (e.g., reallocating funds, updating strategies) demonstrates responsiveness to emerging challenges.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: The programme has influenced the multilateral system through its Policy and Outreach workstream, including contributions to the Global Risk Financing Facility (GRIF) and partnerships with organizations like the Insurance Development Forum (IDF) and African Risk Capacity (ARC). The Centre’s analytics and advice are embedded in international DRF discussions.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: The programme has delivered knowledge and training to Ministries of Finance, disaster management agencies, and other stakeholders in developing countries. For example, the Access to Insurance Initiative (a2ii) trained 90 insurance supervisors from the Caribbean, Africa, and Asia on risk-based approaches. The Centre and DPP are expanding their training offers to ensure skills are applied post-training.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: The programme’s regional solutions (e.g., SEADRIF, ARC drought models) and global public goods (data, models, tools) demonstrate scalability. The transition of the MDTF into the larger GRIF also indicates potential for scaling up DRF interventions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has established a strong foundation, with a clear 5-year strategic vision, effective governance, and growing international credibility. The Centre and DPP are delivering technical assistance, developing regional solutions, and producing global public goods. Early evaluations indicate positive progress, and the programme is well-positioned to achieve its objectives with continued adaptation and learning.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalization of the medium-term structure for the Centre (by March 2020).
Implementation of the updated ToC, M&E framework, and GESI strategy.
Expansion of partnerships (e.g., with IDF, Commonwealth Secretariat, NERC) to increase scope and impact.
Strengthened engagement with the private sector and civil society.
Enhanced focus on fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS).
Development of a country/client mapping to target efforts more strategically.

output_1.title: High quality relevant research completed addressing key open questions related to governance, crime, and conflict

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: All three strands (GI, CVI, P&R) launched RFPs earlier than anticipated (CVI/P&R launched first calls simultaneously with GI rather than delayed to end-2017). This demonstrated greater-than-expected readiness of new components (CVI, P&R) to operationalize grant competitions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: J-PAL (GI/CVI) and IPA (P&R) exceeded expectations in: 1) Launching RFPs for new components (CVI/P&R) on accelerated timelines; 2) Managing 3 RFP rounds in Year 1 (vs planned 2); 3) Awarding 38 proposals (25 full studies + 13 pilots = 35 unique projects) from 130 submissions. DFID country office staff contributions to proposal reviews were valued by component Boards.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance via component-specific Boards (GI, CVI, P&R) with DFID policy input worked effectively. DFID staff served as reviewers for 5–7 proposals per RFP, integrating policy perspectives into academic review processes. J-PAL/IPA maintained close coordination despite geographical distribution (MIT/Chicago/field offices).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination between J-PAL (GI/CVI) and IPA (P&R) despite separate leadership. Joint dissemination events (e.g., RUSI conference) and cross-component learning (e.g., GI sharing lessons with newer CVI/P&R). DFID-J-PAL/IPA interactions included: 1) Policy reviews of proposals; 2) Ad-hoc advisory on country-specific RCT opportunities (e.g., Malawi national ID card evaluation); 3) Capacity-building seminars for DFID staff.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: All grants awarded through competitive RFPs with published criteria. Funding caps enforced: Travel grants ($10K), Pilots ($50K), Full projects ($400K). VfM incorporated as explicit assessment criterion. No procurement delays reported; 24 travel grants awarded ($173,592 total) to support proposal development.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight in Year 1 due to new components (CVI/P&R). Quarterly financial narratives + rolling annual forecasts submitted by J-PAL. DFID reviewed all funding claims against MIT financial systems. Risk matrix formalized in July 2018 to address crime/conflict environment risks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to: 1) Accelerate CVI/P&R RFP timelines based on market readiness; 2) Cancel one Colombia evaluation (FARC partnership collapse) and reallocate funds; 3) Expand gender analysis in grants (from 8 planned to 28 actual). Logframe milestones revised mid-year to reflect exceeded targets (e.g., grants awarded).
adaptive_management_examples: Fast-tracked CVI/P&R RFPs after assessing stronger-than-anticipated researcher interest, avoiding 6-month delay.
Reallocated funds from cancelled Colombia study (FARC non-compliance) to other high-priority proposals.
Added disaggregated gender analysis to Indicator 1.3 after exceeding milestone (8→28 grants with gender components).
Introduced travel grants ($10K) as pipeline-building mechanism, leading to 21/33 GI grantees (since 2014) securing further funding.

main_implementation_challenges: Operating in high-risk environments (crime/conflict zones) required enhanced safety protocols for researchers.
Balancing academic rigor with policy relevance in RFP design (e.g., ensuring DFID priority country focus while maintaining global competition).
Managing expectations for early outputs: RCTs require multi-year timelines, but stakeholders sought quick wins.
Coordinating three distinct components (GI, CVI, P&R) with varying maturity levels (GI = 7 years; CVI/P&R = new).
external_factors_impact: Political instability in target countries (e.g., Colombia FARC study cancellation due to partner non-compliance).
High demand for evidence on crime/conflict outpaced initial assumptions about proposal quality/quantity (mitigated by strong response to RFPs).
contextual_constraints_new: Underestimated the readiness of research community for CVI/P&R themes—original plan assumed 6-month delay for first RFPs, but market was prepared earlier.
Data access challenges in conflict zones (e.g., Rohingya refugee database required negotiated partnerships).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited in-country researcher capacity for crime/conflict RCTs (addressed via travel grants and graduate student support).
DFID country office bandwidth for proposal reviews was stretched but managed through rotation of reviewers.
risk_materialization: Moderate risk of "insufficient high-quality proposals" for CVI/P&R did not materialize; received strong response to all RFPs.
Partner risk materialized in Colombia (FARC unable to deliver ex-combatant sample), leading to one study cancellation.

budget_execution_vs_plan.spend_rate: On track (7% of £12M in Year 1, aligned with multi-year RCT timelines).
budget_execution_vs_plan.variances: No significant variances; quarterly claims matched MIT/J-PAL financial reports.

value_for_money_assessment.cost_efficiency: High: Competitive RFPs, funding caps ($10K/$50K/$400K), and economies of scale from shared J-PAL/IPA infrastructure.
vfm_evidence: Travel grants ($10K) yielded 21/33 grantees securing further funding (64% conversion rate).
Affiliate fees covered by host organizations (no DFID cost for GI/CVI).
Shared review processes across components reduced administrative overhead.
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: Exceeding business case projections for: 1) Number of grants awarded (35 unique projects vs ~20 expected in Year 1); 2) Gender integration (28 vs 8 planned).

financial_management_quality.transparency: High: All claims supported by expenditure breakdowns and forecasts.
financial_management_quality.risk_management: Effective: Close monitoring of spending; risk matrix implemented for crime/conflict environments.

cost_efficiency_achieved.unit_costs: Within caps: Travel ($10K), Pilots ($50K), Full projects ($400K).
cost_efficiency_achieved.administrative_overhead: Low: Leveraged existing J-PAL/IPA systems (e.g., shared review boards).
cost_efficiency_achieved.innovations: Travel grants proved cost-effective for pipeline development (18/24 grants to graduate students).

co_funding_materialization.details: GI secured $2.5M from Hewlett Foundation + anonymous donor (as planned). CVI/P&R remain fully DFID-funded.

key_delivery_lessons: New research themes (crime/conflict) can attract strong proposals faster than anticipated—avoid overly conservative timelines.
Small grants (e.g., travel awards) are high-VfM tools for building researcher pipelines and in-country partnerships.
DFID policy reviews add value to academic proposal assessments, especially for crime/conflict relevance.
successful_delivery_practices: Component-specific Boards with mixed academic/policy membership (DFID + researchers).

Cross-component learning (e.g., GI sharing RFP lessons with CVI/P&R).
Public dissemination events (e.g., RUSI conference) raised programme visibility.
management_adaptations_made: Revised logframe milestones upward after exceeding Year 1 targets (e.g., grants awarded, gender integration).
Added disaggregated gender analysis to Indicator 1.3 (due September 2018).
Formalized risk matrix for crime/conflict environments (July 2018).
Expanded capacity-building indicators to track policy-maker engagement.
innovations_attempted: Travel grants ($10K) to support proposal development—proved effective for pipeline building.
Policy outreach support (GI) considered for expansion to CVI/P&R.
Rohingya refugee database as a "public good" study to inform future RCTs.
forward_recommendations: Disaggregate gender indicator (1.3) by project type and region.
Reweight logframe outputs to reflect shift from RCT initiation to publication/dissemination in later years.
Extend GI’s Policy Outreach Support funds to CVI/P&R to maximize policy uptake.
Develop indicators for policy-maker capacity development (beyond researcher training).

examples: Proactive mitigation of "insufficient proposals" risk via early RFPs and targeted outreach.
Rapid reallocation of funds from cancelled Colombia study.
Formal risk matrix for crime/conflict environments implemented ahead of schedule.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 35 unique research projects funded (25 full studies + 13 pilots) across 130 proposals received.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: 18 graduate students received travel grants; 4 DFID staff attended J-PAL Executive Education per year.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.policy_reach: GI influence documented in 3 peer-reviewed papers + 19 working papers (2011–2017); RUSI dissemination event reached ~100 policymakers.

capacity_building_results: Researcher capacity: 24 travel grants (18 to graduate students) + 35 projects with local partnerships.

unintended_consequences: Positive: Stronger-than-expected researcher interest in CVI/P&R accelerated evidence generation.

scalability_evidence: GI model (RCTs + policy outreach) scaled successfully to CVI/P&R with minimal startup delays.
Travel grant mechanism scalable to other DFID research programmes (proven pipeline-building tool).
Public goods studies (e.g., Rohingya database) create reusable data for multiple RCTs.

continuation_rationale: Year 1 performance exceeded targets (A+ score; 35 projects funded vs ~20 planned).
Strong VfM: Competitive grants, high conversion rate for travel grants, and leveraged co-funding (GI).
High policy relevance: DFID priority countries (75% of funds) and themes (crime/conflict evidence gaps).
Sustainable delivery model: J-PAL/IPA infrastructure + MIT financial systems ensure long-term viability.

planned_adaptations_future: Reweight logframe to emphasize publication/dissemination in Years 3–5.
Expand policy outreach to CVI/P&R (currently GI-only).

Develop metrics for policy-maker capacity development.
