programme_metadata.programme_title: Building Resilience and Adapting to Climate Change (BRACC) programme

output_1.title: Intensified and diversified agricultural production and improved nutrition for targeted vulnerable communities

output_3.title: Vulnerable households and communities in targeted areas have reduced exposure to drought and floods

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme underwent major changes in FY2021-2022, consolidating to three key components: 1) Climate-resilient livelihoods (UN-led PROSPER consortium), 2) Scalable safety net 'crises modifier' (PROSPER), and 3) Natural resource management (Modern Cooking for Healthy Forests with USAID co-financing). Original INGO consortium outputs were removed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners (WFP, FAO, UNDP, UNICEF, RCO) performed well despite challenges, using budget flexibility and adapting activities (e.g., providing extra inputs for winter cropping). UN consortium effectively delivered integrated interventions, though funding delays affected timeliness. FAO faced procurement delays for irrigation systems.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: UN-led consortium (PROSPER) acted as convening mechanism with WFP as lead agency. Governance was adaptive, with FCDO providing budget assurances mid-2022 to mitigate funding uncertainties. Coordination with USAID for natural resource management component was effective.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination within PROSPER consortium, though early-year funding uncertainties created planning challenges. FCDO’s early announcement of lean season response funding catalysed donor alignment. Collaboration with governance programmes (e.g., justice reforms) enhanced forestry sector impacts.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays due to forex limitations (fuel shortages) and global supply chain issues (e.g., fertiliser prices). FAO’s irrigation equipment procurement was delayed, affecting 36 of 50 planned hectares. Partners used flexibility to source inputs locally when possible.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to macroeconomic challenges. FCDO increased engagement to manage partner expectations on funding timelines and cost increases. Oversight focused on adaptive budget management and risk mitigation (e.g., allowing cash transfers instead of inputs).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Partners utilized budget flexibility to reallocate funds (e.g., winter cropping inputs) and adapt activities (e.g., shifting from in-kind inputs to cash transfers). FCDO approved cost adjustments to address inflation and forex shortages.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocated funds to provide extra agricultural inputs during winter cropping season to offset global supply delays.
Shifted from in-kind input distribution to cash transfers for some activities to address procurement challenges.
Adjusted extension services delivery through 2,404 trained Community-Based Facilitators (CBFs) to reach 70,000 farmers, exceeding targets.
Revised logframe to reflect reduced intensity of nutrition interventions due to rising poverty/food insecurity.
Accelerated lean season response funding announcements to catalyse donor coordination.

main_implementation_challenges: Macroeconomic instability: Global economic challenges led to increased food/fertiliser prices and fuel shortages, disrupting input procurement.
Funding uncertainties: Delays in FCDO budget allocations (confirmed only mid-2022) hindered partner planning and activity timelines.
Inflation and forex limitations: Rapid inflation and currency constraints affected partners’ ability to procure inputs, leading to activity delays.
Supply chain disruptions: Global shortages (e.g., fertiliser) and local fuel shortages impacted delivery of agricultural inputs.
Reduced programme intensity: Budget reductions limited the scope of nutrition interventions, requiring logframe revisions.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 (implied): While not explicitly stated, global supply chain disruptions (e.g., fertiliser shortages) suggest pandemic-related impacts.
Global economic crisis: Rising commodity prices (food, fuel, fertiliser) strained household resilience and programme budgets.
Climate shocks: Recurrent weather-related stresses in Malawi increased demand for programme interventions (e.g., lean season response).
Political/economic instability in Malawi: Contributed to forex shortages and delayed government approvals for programme activities.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated rise in poverty/food insecurity: Eroded household incomes, reducing the programme’s ability to achieve original nutrition outcomes.
Legal/regulatory gaps in forestry sector: Required additional FCDO support to strengthen enforcement (e.g., 72% increase in convictions for forestry crimes).
Urban charcoal demand: Proved more resistant to change than anticipated, requiring adjusted strategies in the Modern Cooking for Healthy Forests component.
Partner capacity limits: Some PROSPER partners struggled with rapid inflation and funding uncertainty, proposing shifts to cash-based interventions.
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in budget confirmation strained trust initially, but were mitigated by FCDO’s mid-2022 assurances and flexible cost adjustments.
FAO’s procurement delays for irrigation systems created tensions, though partners collaborated to find interim solutions (e.g., solar pumps).
Differing partner approaches to cash vs. in-kind transfers required negotiation to align with programme goals.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited government capacity to absorb programme support (e.g., extension services) required increased reliance on Community-Based Facilitators (CBFs).
Reduced FCDO hub capacity (early closure) hindered Value for Money (VFM) reporting and data consolidation.
Partners’ financial management systems were stressed by inflation, requiring additional FCDO oversight.
risk_materialization: Macroeconomic risks (inflation, forex shortages) materialized, affecting procurement and activity costs.
Supply chain risks (global fertiliser shortages) disrupted input distribution plans.
Political risks: Delays in government approvals for forestry sector reforms slowed progress.
Climate risks: Increased frequency of shocks heightened demand for safety net interventions.
Partner performance risks: Some partners struggled with adaptive management, requiring additional support.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Overall budget execution was on track despite delays, with most milestones achieved by year-end. Funding uncertainties caused mid-year adjustments, but partners used flexibility to realign activities.
Original programme value (£90.5m) was maintained, though allocations were revised annually based on need (e.g., lean season response).
Budget reductions led to revised output weightings (e.g., Output 1 increased from 25% to 30% impact weighting).
value_for_money_assessment: VFM reporting was hindered by the early closure of the BRACC Hub, limiting quantitative assessments. Qualitative evidence suggests strong VFM in:
- Integrated interventions (e.g., linking food-for-assets to VSL groups) improved household incomes sustainably.
- Forestry sector reforms achieved a 72% increase in convictions for illegal activities, demonstrating cost-effective enforcement.
- Lean season response catalysed additional donor funding, leveraging FCDO’s investment.
Challenges: Reduced intensity of nutrition interventions due to budget constraints may affect long-term VFM.
financial_management_quality: Partners demonstrated strong financial management by adapting to funding delays and inflation (e.g., reallocating budgets, using local procurement).
UN consortium (PROSPER) maintained transparent reporting, though some partners required additional support to manage cost increases.
FCDO’s financial oversight was intensified to address risks from macroeconomic instability, including closer scrutiny of cash transfer proposals.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiencies were realised through:
- Community-Based Facilitators (CBFs) reaching 70,000 farmers at lower cost than traditional extension services.
- Village Savings and Loans (VSL) groups reducing reliance on external financial services (25,867 beneficiaries vs. 20,000 target).
- Co-financing with USAID for the Modern Cooking for Healthy Forests programme shared costs for natural resource management.
Inefficiencies: Procurement delays (e.g., FAO’s irrigation systems) and inflation increased some activity costs.
co_funding_materialization: USAID co-financing for the Modern Cooking for Healthy Forests programme materialised as planned, supporting forestry sector interventions.
FCDO’s early lean season response funding leveraged additional donor contributions, though specific co-funding amounts were not detailed.
currency_exchange_impacts: Forex limitations caused fuel shortages and delayed input procurement, requiring partners to use local currency reserves or adjust activity timelines.
Exchange rate fluctuations increased costs for imported goods (e.g., agricultural inputs), partially offset by local procurement strategies.

key_delivery_lessons: Integrated packages of interventions (e.g., linking food-for-assets to VSL groups) are more effective at building resilience than standalone activities.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., annual allocations based on need) allow for adaptive responses to shocks but require early confirmation to avoid delays.
Community-based models (CBFs, VSL groups) achieve higher outreach and sustainability than top-down approaches.
Early donor coordination (e.g., lean season response announcements) amplifies impact and leverages additional resources.
Legal/regulatory reforms (e.g., forestry sector) require sustained advocacy and media engagement to drive systemic change.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of Farmer Field Schools (FFS) and CBFs to scale Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) adoption (74.6% of households implementing ≥4 practices).
Adaptive procurement strategies (e.g., local input sourcing, winter cropping inputs) to mitigate global supply chain disruptions.
Strategic media engagement to raise awareness of forestry crimes, increasing convictions by 72%.
Cash transfer mechanisms as a flexible alternative to in-kind inputs during procurement delays.
Cross-programme collaboration (e.g., with FCDO governance teams) to strengthen sectoral reforms.
management_adaptations_made: Revised logframe to reflect reduced nutrition intervention intensity due to rising poverty.
Increased oversight of partner financial management to address inflation risks.
Shifted from input-based to cash-based interventions where procurement was unfeasible.
Accelerated exit planning for PROSPER programme’s final year (2023).
Enhanced coordination with USAID to align natural resource management activities.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of crop insurance payouts (USD 320,232 to 13,584 households) to mitigate climate shock impacts.
Integration of nutrition messaging into agricultural extension and watershed activities.
Use of media advocacy to complement legal reforms in the forestry sector.
Testing of solar-powered irrigation systems (21 hectares) as a climate-resilient technology.
Development of a harmonised grievance redress mechanism (HGRM) for beneficiary feedback.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: UN continued support to VSL groups and linkages to CUMO village agents in overlap areas.
Partially completed: Insurance activities remain under Output 2 (not moved to Output 3 as recommended), but cash transfers were excluded from global figures.
Ongoing: Logframe revision to reflect programming shifts (e.g., reduced nutrition focus) is in progress for 2023.
forward_recommendations: Finalise exit plans for PROSPER programme by February 2023, ensuring sustainability of VSL groups and CBF networks.
Update the logframe to align with reduced intervention intensity and revised nutrition targets.
Explore media advocacy as a tool for systemic reform in forestry and other sectors.
Conduct a final evaluation to identify the most effective intervention combinations for different household categories.
Strengthen FCDO’s catalytic role in social protection by continuing early lean season response announcements.
Address VFM reporting gaps caused by the BRACC Hub’s closure by identifying proportional indicators for the final year.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective: Proactive management of macroeconomic risks (e.g., flexible budgets, local procurement) mitigated major disruptions.
Partially effective: Supply chain risks (e.g., fertiliser shortages) were addressed reactively, causing delays.
Lessons: Earlier contingency planning for global commodity price fluctuations could have reduced procurement delays.
Success: Legal reforms in the forestry sector (72% increase in convictions) demonstrate effective risk mitigation through systemic changes.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 300,000 poor and vulnerable households (1.7 million people) targeted; actual reach not fully quantified but exceeded in some areas:
- 74.6% of households adopted ≥4 Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) practices (vs. 50% target).
- 25,867 beneficiaries accessed financial services (vs. 20,000 target) through VSL groups.
- 13,584 households received crop insurance payouts (USD 320,232).
- 2,404 Community-Based Facilitators (CBFs) trained, supporting 70,000 farmers.
policy_influence_achieved: Strengthened legal/regulatory framework in the forestry sector, with a 72% increase in convictions for illegal activities.
Collaboration with FCDO governance programmes influenced justice sector reforms (e.g., training for law enforcement).
Media advocacy raised public awareness of forestry crimes, contributing to policy dialogue.
Early lean season response funding shaped donor coordination and humanitarian funding strategies.
capacity_building_results: 2,404 CBFs trained to deliver extension services, reaching 70,000 farmers (exceeding expectations).
70,000 farmers received improved extension support through Farmer Field Schools (FFS).
VSL groups (862 total) built financial literacy and savings capacity among 25,867 beneficiaries.
Government capacity in disaster risk management was strengthened through PROSPER’s crises modifier component.
Forestry sector law enforcement capacity improved, as evidenced by increased convictions.
unintended_consequences: Positive: VSL groups created unintended social cohesion and empowerment, particularly among women (GESI impacts).
Positive: Media engagement on forestry crimes sparked broader public debate on environmental governance.
Negative: Reduced nutrition intervention intensity may have exacerbated food insecurity for the most vulnerable households.
Negative: Delays in irrigation system procurement limited climate adaptation benefits for some farmers.
scalability_evidence: Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) practices (adopted by 74.6% of households) demonstrate scalability through FFS/CBF models.
VSL groups (862 established) show potential for replication in other regions, with 25,867 beneficiaries reached.
Crises modifier approach (scalable safety nets) was adopted by other donors, indicating demand for expansion.
Forestry sector reforms (e.g., legal frameworks) provide a model for other countries facing deforestation challenges.
Limitations: Nutrition intervention scalability is constrained by budget reductions and rising food insecurity.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (Overall Output Score: A) despite challenges, with high likelihood of achieving core resilience outcomes.
Demand for programme interventions remains high due to recurrent climate shocks and food insecurity in Malawi.
Successful adaptive management (e.g., flexible funding, integrated interventions) demonstrates programme agility.
Co-financing with USAID and donor coordination (e.g., lean season response) indicate sustained partner commitment.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Climate-Compatible Growth Programme

output_1.title: PARTNERSHIPS: National & regional partnerships built and maintained to co-create research agendas, build capacity and drive evidence uptake

output_2.title: RESEARCH: Additions of: evidence, insight, frameworks, methods, data, tools and their application (collectively referred to as 'knowledge products')

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Management model adjustments agreed between FCDO and CCG by mid-July 2022 to address under-resourcing. New structure prioritizes full resourcing of management team (including Programme Manager, Project Manager, and International Partnerships lead roles). Advisory Group of senior academics to be established by October 2022 for independent oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: University Partnership (Loughborough, UCL, Oxford, Cambridge, Imperial, Open University, KTH Royal Institute) performed well in research outputs and international engagement (e.g., co-chairing SuM4All, Green Grids Initiative, Energy Transition Council). However, capacity constraints emerged due to vacancies in key management roles (e.g., Deputy Programme Director absence, Programme Manager departures).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Under-resourced compared to Business Case (Annex 3), with gaps in Programme Manager (x2 vacancies), International Partnerships lead, and Deputy Programme Director roles. Recruitment underway for full-time Programme Manager and part-time Project Manager as of June 2022. Safeguarding processes implemented (training for partners, due diligence checks).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination with FCDO Posts in-country (Vietnam, Laos, Kenya, Zambia) and international partners (e.g., World Bank, ADB, IEA, IRENA). Challenges in integrating workstreams funded outside the University Partnership (e.g., World Bank/ADB projects) to maximize synergies. Collaboration with UK PACT in Kenya underway but requires broader agreement to avoid duplication.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight planned via: (1) Independent review of CCG by external organization (contracted by September 2022, completed by December 2022); (2) Strategic Advisory Group established by October 2022; (3) Quarterly Logframe target agreements tied to budget approvals.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to expand from 4 to 6 partner countries in FY22/23. Research agenda adjusted to align with UK International Development Strategy (May 2022) and Clean Green Initiative priorities. Capacity-building approach refined to focus on long-term institutional embedding (previously relied on independent consultants).
adaptive_management_examples: Response to management capacity gaps: Recruitment drive for Programme/Project Managers and restructuring of management roles by July 2022.
Alignment with post-COP26 priorities: New partnerships with Energy Transition Council, Green Grids Initiative, and Sum4All to reflect global climate commitments.
Capacity-building shift: Transition from consultant-led to institution-focused training (e.g., courses for LMIC government officials, embedding tools in national planning processes).

main_implementation_challenges: Management capacity constraints due to unexpected departures (2 Programme Managers) and prolonged vacancies (International Partnerships lead, Deputy Programme Director).
Budget uncertainty delaying recruitment and planning for FY23/24 and FY24/25.
Balancing core research with expanding country partnerships (from 4 to 6 countries in FY22/23) while maintaining quality.
Integrating externally funded workstreams (e.g., World Bank/ADB projects) with University Partnership activities to avoid fragmentation.
external_factors_impact: Post-COVID recovery prioritized in partner countries, affecting engagement timelines (e.g., delayed in-person workshops).
Global energy crisis (2022) increased demand for CCG’s evidence on clean energy transitions but also raised expectations for rapid policy support.
COP26 commitments (e.g., Just Energy Transition Partnerships) created opportunities for new partnerships but required agile alignment of research agendas.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated demand for technical assistance from partner countries (e.g., Vietnam, Kenya) on energy transition planning, stretching capacity.
Currency fluctuations in some partner countries (e.g., Zambia) affecting local implementation costs.
Political transitions in partner countries (e.g., Kenya elections in 2022) temporarily slowed policy engagement.
partner_relationship_issues: Delays in formalizing MoUs with new partner countries (expansion to 6 countries) due to administrative hurdles.
Differing expectations between academic partners (focused on rigorous research) and FCDO Posts (seeking rapid policy-relevant outputs).
Challenges in ensuring equitable authorship in knowledge products (e.g., 23% LMIC authorship in peer-reviewed papers vs. 40% target).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited bandwidth in partner country institutions to absorb CCG’s tools/data, requiring more hands-on support than planned.
University Consortium’s reliance on short-term consultants for capacity-building (rather than institutional embedding) initially hindered sustainability.
Safeguarding training rollout delayed for downstream partners due to resource constraints (addressed by August 2022).
risk_materialization: Management capacity risks (as identified in Business Case) materialized due to staff turnover and health-related absences.
Risk of fragmented delivery mitigated via mid-2022 management restructuring and independent review.
Budget uncertainty risk partially addressed by FCDO’s commitment to confirm FY23/24–24/25 funding by July 2022.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for FY22/23, but delays in confirming FY23/24–24/25 budgets created short-term planning challenges. Recruitment freezes lifted post-July 2022 budget confirmation. No over/under-spend reported in review period.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM in research outputs (e.g., 91 open-source tools, 122 non-peer-reviewed knowledge products) and international partnerships (leveraging £1bn Ayrton Fund alignment). Lower VFM in capacity-building due to initial over-reliance on consultants; improvements planned via institutional embedding approach by end-2022.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls within University Partnership (e.g., Loughborough’s safeguarding due diligence, FCDO-compliant procurement). Independent review (Dec 2022) to assess financial systems robustness.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of ICF funds for core research (e.g., 1 peer-reviewed paper, 122 non-peer-reviewed products in review period). Costs for country operations higher than planned due to expanded scope (6 countries) and currency impacts (e.g., Zambia).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding from international partners (e.g., World Bank, ADB) materialized for specific workstreams (e.g., climate-compatible urban productivity). No evidence of unmet co-funding commitments in review period.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minor impacts reported in Zambia and Kenya, increasing local implementation costs. Mitigated via budget reallocations within country programmes.

key_delivery_lessons: University-led consortia require dedicated programme management capacity (beyond academic roles) to handle FCDO compliance, partner coordination, and adaptive management.
Early confirmation of multi-year budgets is critical for research programmes to retain staff and plan long-term partnerships.
Capacity-building is most effective when embedded in institutions (vs. consultant-led), but requires upfront investment in relationship-building.
successful_delivery_practices: Co-chairing global initiatives (e.g., SuM4All, Green Grids Initiative) amplified CCG’s influence and aligned research with partner country priorities.
Open-source tools (91 developed) and data-sharing platforms improved uptake by governments and multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank, UNDP).
Country-specific co-creation events (125 participants) ensured research relevance and local ownership.
management_adaptations_made: Restructured management team to separate academic leadership (e.g., Programme Director) from operational roles (e.g., Programme/Project Managers).
Introduced quarterly Logframe target-setting linked to budget approvals to improve accountability.
Established Advisory Group (by Oct 2022) for independent challenge on strategic direction.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of ‘Rapid Response Facility’ with Energy Transition Council to provide just-in-time technical assistance to countries.
Integration of behavioural economics into energy transition modelling (e.g., identifying skills gaps for green jobs).
Cross-sectoral analytics combining energy, transport, and labour market data to inform national development strategies.
previous_recommendations_progress: Safeguarding: Video training for international partners finalized by August 2022 (addressing Inception Phase recommendation).
Management capacity: Partial progress—recruitment underway for Programme/Project Managers but structural risks remain until fully resourced.
Partner country expansion: On track (4 to 6 countries in FY22/23) but MoU delays persist.
forward_recommendations: FCDO to confirm FY23/24–24/25 budgets by July 2022 to enable staffing and partnership planning.
CCG to finalize institutional capacity-building strategy by December 2022, reducing reliance on consultants.
Independent review (Dec 2022) to assess delivery model sustainability and propose adjustments for Phase 2.
Strengthen LMIC authorship in knowledge products (target: >40% LMIC authors in peer-reviewed papers).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Planned risks (e.g., management capacity) materialized but were mitigated through restructuring. Emerging risks (e.g., currency fluctuations, political transitions) required reactive adjustments. Independent review to formalize risk register updates.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 125 participants in co-creation events; 112 knowledge uptake activities; training for LMIC government officials (numbers not specified).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Evidence uptake by multilateral partners (e.g., World Bank, ADB) and global initiatives (e.g., Sum4All, Green Grids Initiative) reaching millions through policy influence.

policy_influence_achieved: CCG’s principles embedded in Energy Transition Council’s ‘Code of Conduct’ for energy planning (endorsed by 18 organizations).
Contributions to Vietnam’s and Kenya’s national energy strategies via scenario modelling and stakeholder workshops.
Tools adopted by World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Platform (ESMAP) for country-level support.
capacity_building_results: 112 capacity-building activities delivered (though participant feedback data missing for this year).
Open-source tools (91) and datasets adopted by partner country institutions (e.g., ministries of energy in Zambia, Laos).
Training for LMIC officials on strategic energy planning (alignment with Paris Agreement goals).
unintended_consequences: Positive: CCG’s cross-sectoral approach (energy + transport) influenced broader climate-compatible urban planning in partner cities (e.g., Hanoi, Nairobi).
Negative: Initial focus on rapid knowledge product delivery led to lower LMIC authorship (23% vs. 40% target), risking perceptions of ‘Northern-led’ research.
scalability_evidence: Methods tested in 4 countries (Vietnam, Laos, Kenya, Zambia) deemed replicable; expansion to 6 countries in FY22/23.
Open-source tools (e.g., modelling software) designed for adaptation to new contexts (e.g., ADB’s use in Southeast Asia).
Policy frameworks (e.g., ‘Code of Conduct’ for energy planning) adopted by multilateral organizations for global rollout.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong performance (Overall Output Score: A) and alignment with FCDO priorities (Clean Green Initiative, International Development Strategy). High demand from partner countries for CCG’s evidence and tools. Independent review (Dec 2022) to inform Phase 2 adjustments.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (contingent on addressing management capacity gaps and securing multi-year budgets). University Partnership model effective for research but requires stronger operational support for delivery at scale.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by "A" score and expansion to 6 countries). Concerns remain about management resilience and LMIC authorship targets.
planned_adaptations_future: Restructured management team (full implementation by Q4 2022) with clear FTE allocations.
Institutional capacity-building strategy to replace consultant-led approaches by end-2022.
Deeper integration with UK PACT and other Ayrton Fund programmes to leverage synergies.
Advisory Group to provide strategic oversight and challenge from October 2022.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Revenue Mobilisation, Investment and Trade Programme (REMIT)

output_1.title: Federal Board of Revenue’s (FBR’s) Strategic Plans (for Inland Revenue and Custom) implemented. Tax base is broadened by reducing the complexity of the tax system and by tackling of international tax evasion. Improved federal and provincial coordination.

output_2.title: FCDO supports the work of the Government of Pakistan to prioritise export sectors. Once established, support functions are provided which lower tariff and non-tariff measures as part of a national export strategy.

output_3.title: Improved macroeconomic governance and operations.

output_4.title: Improved Business Environment.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Initial focus shifted to mobilising technical assistance (TA) instruments and forming partnerships due to COVID-19. World Bank Trust Fund (Pakistan @100) became operational in January 2020; International Trade Centre (ITC) commenced inception in May 2020. HMRC support on international tax cooperation delayed due to FBR leadership changes and COVID-19 disruptions. Commercial supplier procurement underway, expected operational Q1 2021.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank Trust Fund and ITC performed well in partnership establishment. HMRC support faced delays due to FBR’s internal instability (frequent leadership changes) and limited engagement during COVID-19 lockdowns. Local policy think tank engaged via emergency grant for COVID-19 response (exporter needs/food supply chain).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with IMF, World Bank, and other donors (ADB, EU, US) identified as critical but challenging. Political economy constraints required adaptive engagement, particularly for "mega buy" reforms like GST harmonisation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Commercial supplier procurement process ongoing; delays attributed to FCDO procedures. Emergency accountable grant to local think tank demonstrated procurement flexibility for COVID-19 response.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted milestones to account for COVID-19 economic fallout. Emergency grant mechanism used for urgent technical assistance. Theory of Change remained valid but timeframes adjusted for contextual challenges.
adaptive_management_examples: Re-evaluation of macroeconomic indicators post-COVID-19 (led by SRO, due March 2021).
Political economy analysis session planned with partners (World Bank, ITC, local experts) to assess reform feasibility (due January 2021).
Mapping of policy "mega buys" (e.g., GST harmonisation) to prioritise high-impact interventions (due April 2021).
High-level UK engagements planned to support GST harmonisation at federal/provincial levels (due February 2021).

main_implementation_challenges: Frequent leadership changes within FBR causing delays in strategic plan approvals and HMRC support agreements.
COVID-19 disruptions: lockdowns limited partner engagement, slowed compliance activities (e.g., Post Clearance Audit), and delayed milestones like IRS Strategic Plan approval.
Economic contraction (-0.4% GDP in 2020) and IMF programme pause (shift from $6B EFF to $1.4B Rapid Financing Instrument) altered reform context.
Complex political economy of reforms, requiring navigation of vested interests and public acceptance.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Lockdowns, locust swarms, and supply chain disruptions necessitated emergency grants and milestone adjustments.
IMF programme shift: Ambition of reform milestones reduced; economic contraction (first since 1952) affected revenue mobilisation targets.
Global transparency standards: OECD’s evolving AEOI requirements demanded continuous adaptation (e.g., remote HMRC support during COVID-19).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated severity of COVID-19’s economic impact (e.g., tax-to-GDP ratio pressures, export declines).
Provincial-federal tensions in GST harmonisation, requiring high-level UK diplomatic engagement.
Limited capacity for remote technical assistance in areas requiring in-person collaboration (e.g., tax audits).
partner_relationship_issues: FBR leadership instability led to repeated delays in approvals and engagement (e.g., HMRC scoping report response pending since November 2019).
World Bank/ITC partnerships progressed smoothly, but coordination with IMF and ADB required stronger alignment on reform priorities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FBR’s limited bandwidth for simultaneous strategic planning and COVID-19 crisis response.
Delayed commercial supplier onboarding reduced implementation capacity for Output 1 activities.
Provincial governments’ varying readiness for GST harmonisation reforms.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 pandemic (Major risk, materialized).
FBR leadership turnover (Moderate risk, materialized).
Economic contraction exceeding projections (Major risk, materialized).
IMF programme restructuring (Moderate risk, materialized).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for Year 1. £39M programme value unchanged; emergency grant disbursed for COVID-19 response. Commercial supplier procurement delays may affect Year 2 expenditure plans.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High potential VFM identified in "mega buy" reforms (e.g., GST harmonisation could generate $6B/year in additional revenue). World Bank Trust Fund’s early successes (e.g., GST harmonisation agreement, tariff reduction evidence) demonstrate cost-efficiency. Challenges in quantifying VFM due to early-stage implementation and COVID-19 disruptions.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls evident in emergency grant disbursement and World Bank/ITC partnerships. Delays in commercial supplier procurement suggest need for streamlined processes.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Efficient use of existing partnerships (e.g., leveraging World Bank’s pre-COVID relationships). Emergency grant mechanism provided rapid response without significant overhead.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible milestone-setting is critical in volatile contexts (e.g., COVID-19, political instability).
Pre-existing partner relationships (e.g., World Bank) enable faster adaptation than new procurements.
High-level diplomatic engagement is essential for politically sensitive reforms (e.g., GST harmonisation).
Remote technical assistance has limitations in areas requiring institutional trust (e.g., tax transparency).
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid deployment of emergency grants for contextual shocks (COVID-19/locust swarms).
Cross-donor coordination (e.g., aligning with IMF/World Bank priorities) amplified influence.
Leveraging OECD peer review processes to maintain transparency standards despite disruptions.
Targeted capacity-building for FBR on AEOI and risk-based audits, despite leadership changes.
management_adaptations_made: Adjusted Theory of Change timeframes to reflect COVID-19 economic realities.
Prioritised "mega buy" reforms (e.g., GST harmonisation) for maximal impact.
Increased focus on political economy analysis to navigate vested interests.
Enhanced monitoring of partner costs and delivery instruments.
innovations_attempted: Emergency accountable grants for agile crisis response.
Remote HMRC support for OECD transparency commitments during lockdowns.
Mapping of policy "mega buys" to concentrate resources on high-impact interventions.

forward_recommendations.action: Re-evaluate macroeconomic indicators to reflect post-COVID-19 trajectory (due March 2021, led by SRO).
Conduct political economy analysis with partners to identify feasible reform pathways (due January 2021, led by Governance Adviser).
Develop roadmaps for policy "mega buys" (e.g., GST harmonisation) and integrate into commercial supplier’s inception (due April 2021, led by Economic Adviser).
Intensify high-level UK engagements to support GST harmonisation at federal/provincial levels (due February 2021, led by Governance Adviser).
Strengthen donor coordination (IMF, World Bank, ADB, EU) to align technical assistance and policy advocacy.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Anticipated risks (e.g., FBR capacity, political economy) materialized but were mitigated through adaptive management (e.g., emergency grants, milestone adjustments). Unanticipated risks (e.g., COVID-19 severity) required reactive measures. Proactive risk mapping for "mega buys" recommended.

policy_influence_achieved: In-principle agreement on GST harmonisation (potential $6B/year revenue impact).
Evidence generated to support lowering import tariffs for manufacturing inputs.
FBR’s progress on OECD transparency standards (AEOI peer review completed).
Customs strategic plan finalised; IRS plan delayed but underway.
capacity_building_results: FBR’s risk-based audit capacity strengthened (legal changes legislated via Finance Bill 2020–21).
Post Clearance Audit (PCA) compliance gap analysis initiated, though COVID-19 slowed sector-specific plans.
HMRC support on international tax cooperation delayed but OECD commitments remain on track.

unintended_consequences.description: COVID-19 delays in tax base broadening may exacerbate revenue shortfalls in short term.
Emergency grant to local think tank strengthened relationships with non-traditional partners (e.g., food supply chain experts).

scalability_evidence: GST harmonisation model could be replicated for other federal-provincial tax reforms.
World Bank Trust Fund’s multi-donor approach demonstrates scalability potential for technical assistance.
AEOI tools and risk-based audit methods adaptable to other South Asian contexts.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates strong potential to achieve transformational economic impact (e.g., GST harmonisation, export growth) despite COVID-19 setbacks. Early successes (World Bank partnerships, OECD compliance) justify continuation, but challenges require adaptive management and donor coordination.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium. Current model relies heavily on FBR stability and donor alignment; risks remain from political economy constraints and capacity gaps.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High ("A" score reflects broad alignment with expectations, though risks are "Major").
planned_adaptations_future: Refocus on "mega buy" reforms with clear roadmaps and high-level UK support.
Enhance political economy analysis to anticipate and mitigate resistance.
Accelerate commercial supplier onboarding to address capacity constraints.
Strengthen monitoring of cross-output synergies (e.g., tax reforms + export strategies).
Deepen coordination with IMF/World Bank to align technical assistance with macroeconomic priorities.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Regional Economic Development for Investment in Trade (REDIT) Programme

output_3.title: Design an effective valuation improvement approach

output_4.title: Undertake Enhancement of the Integrated Customs Management System (ICMS)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transition from TMA Kenya Country Programme (KCP) Strategy 2 (2017-2023) to KCP Strategy 3 (2024-2030), emphasizing six interrelated portfolios: trade/investment environment, product quality/standards, digital infrastructure, physical infrastructure, green/sustainable trade, and inclusion of women/youth/PWD.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: TradeMark Africa (TMA) expanded donor base (UK 5%, EU 46%, Denmark 43%, Finland 2%, Netherlands 4%) with cumulative UK funding of £50M. Improved engagement post-appointment of new REDIT Programme Officer (PRO) and Programme Manager in 2023, addressing prior coordination gaps.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: TMA’s KCP strategy developed collaboratively with FCDO and approved by TMA’s board (where FCDO is represented). Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) from APEX Department (Nairobi-based) enhanced coordination between bilaterally and centrally managed aspects.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Improved transparency and objectivity in stakeholder engagement, particularly with Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) and private sector (e.g., KIFWA, KAM). Expanded stakeholder consultations (2,288 vs. targeted 200) for customs valuation design.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO increased proactive management post-2023 leadership changes, with regular consultative forums in Mombasa/Nairobi. TMA secured additional core funds to cover unplanned stakeholder engagement costs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to include additional stakeholders (clearing agents, consolidators) in customs valuation design, approved by FCDO for broader ownership. Prioritized Customs Valuation Enhancement (CVE) project as a "low-investment, high-return" initiative during budget constraints.
adaptive_management_examples: Expanded stakeholder consultations beyond initial targets (200 → 2,288) to ensure valuation methodologies were widely accepted.
Secured TMA core funds to cover unbudgeted costs for inclusive stakeholder engagement.
Reprioritized budget to focus on CVE project during 2022/23 funding pause.

main_implementation_challenges: Budget constraints in 2022/23 led to temporary funding pause (resumed in July 2023 with £560,000).
High demand for stakeholder inclusion in customs valuation design required unplanned budget allocations.
Transition between TMA’s KCP Strategy 2 and 3 required realignment of programme priorities.
external_factors_impact: Kenya’s GDP growth (5.6% in 2023) driven by services (finance, trade, tourism) with manufacturing lagging, influencing trade policy focus on value chains (rice, coffee, textiles, etc.).
Global shift toward sustainability standards (e.g., AfCFTA) necessitated alignment of programme goals with green trade practices.
Delayed review of Kenya’s Integrated National Export Development and Promotion Strategy created policy uncertainty.
contextual_constraints_new: Need to integrate digital trade systems (e.g., AI for customs monitoring) to align with AfCFTA and UK-Kenya Economic Partnership Agreement.
Increased competition for trade corridor investments requiring regional coordination beyond Kenya.
partner_relationship_issues: Leadership transitions at REDIT (PRO/Programme Manager exit in 2023) temporarily disrupted stakeholder confidence.
Initial resistance from clearing agents/traders to participate in valuation design due to perceived costs (later resolved via TMA core funding).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited HMRC engagement in digital trade system integration despite strategic importance for UK-Kenya trade.
Gaps in TMA’s capacity to monitor AI/technology adoption in customs processes.
risk_materialization: Funding pause in 2022/23 (mitigated by reprioritization to CVE project).
Stakeholder expansion risks (e.g., managing diverse expectations from 2,288 participants).

budget_execution_vs_plan: Funding paused in 2022/23 due to UK fiscal pressures; resumed with £560,000 (July 2023–June 2024).
Cumulative UK funding via REDIT: £50M (vs. £84.1M programme value).
TMA’s KCP Strategy 3 budget realigned to prioritize high-impact areas (e.g., customs valuation, digital infrastructure).
value_for_money_assessment: CVE project identified as "low-investment, high-return" with prioritized funding.
Stakeholder engagement costs exceeded plans but justified by broader ownership of valuation reforms (2,288 participants vs. 200 targeted).
No explicit VFM metrics provided; emphasis on qualitative outcomes (e.g., reduced trade barriers).
financial_management_quality: TMA secured additional core funds to cover unplanned stakeholder engagement costs.
FCDO’s proactive oversight post-2023 improved budget transparency (e.g., reprioritization to CVE).
No reported audit findings or financial irregularities.
co_funding_materialization: TMA’s KCP Strategy 3 leveraged multi-donor funding (UK 5%, EU 46%, Denmark 43%, etc.), reducing reliance on REDIT funds.
Co-funding enabled expansion of activities (e.g., digital infrastructure) beyond REDIT’s original scope.

key_delivery_lessons: Effective partnership management is critical; leadership transitions (e.g., REDIT PRO/Programme Manager in 2023) can disrupt implementation if not managed proactively.
Flexible budget allocation (e.g., TMA core funds for stakeholder engagement) enables adaptive delivery.
Regional trade programmes require integrated strategies to address cross-border disparities (e.g., policy alignment across East Africa).
successful_delivery_practices: Consultative forums (Mombasa/Nairobi) with diverse stakeholders (e.g., KRA, KIFWA, KAM) ensured buy-in for customs valuation reforms.
Prioritization of high-impact, low-cost projects (e.g., CVE) during budget constraints.
Designation of Nairobi-based SRO improved coordination between bilateral (REDIT) and central (CMP) programme aspects.
management_adaptations_made: Increased FCDO oversight post-2023 to address prior coordination gaps.
Expanded stakeholder engagement scope (2,288 participants) to enhance reform ownership.
Reprioritized funding to CVE project during fiscal pressures.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of enhanced customs valuation module with dispute resolution logic and multi-source pricing data.
Exploration of AI for customs monitoring (recommended for further study via East Africa Research Hub Fund).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Conduct a study on value for money of digital trade systems (e.g., AI for customs) via East Africa Research Hub Fund.
Develop a flexible regional trade strategy aligning UK priorities with East African trade policies (e.g., AfCFTA, UK-Kenya EPA).
Enhance HMG internal coordination for regional trade initiatives, including HMRC’s role in digital system integration.

risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive mitigation of funding pause via reprioritization (CVE project).
Stakeholder expansion risks managed through TMA core funding.
No evidence of systematic risk assessment updates in response to external factors (e.g., AfCFTA, sustainability standards).

policy_influence_achieved: Customs valuation module enhancements aligned with Kenya’s Integrated National Export Development Strategy (under review).
Support for AfCFTA implementation through non-tariff barrier reduction and digital trade systems.
Influence on green trade policies via TMA’s KCP Strategy 3 (2024–2030).
capacity_building_results: 2,288 stakeholders (traders, customs officials, clearing agents) engaged in customs valuation design.
Kenya Revenue Authority’s capacity strengthened via ICMS enhancements (dispute resolution, data integration).
Private sector advocacy supported (e.g., KAM, KIFWA) for trade competitiveness.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Expanded stakeholder engagement (beyond initial targets) increased reform ownership but required unplanned budget allocations.
Negative: Potential delays in digital system integration due to limited HMRC engagement.
scalability_evidence: Customs valuation module designed for replication across East African trade corridors (e.g., Single Customs Territory framework).
Digital trade innovations (e.g., AI for customs) scalable if pilot studies (recommended) demonstrate VFM.
TMA’s multi-donor model (KCP Strategy 3) provides a template for regional programme expansion.

continuation_rationale: Consistent "A" performance ratings (2018–2023, excluding 2022/23 pause) with stable risk profile (Moderate).
Alignment with UK-Kenya Economic Partnership Agreement and emerging UK-Africa strategy.
TMA’s KCP Strategy 3 (2024–2030) provides a robust framework for regional trade expansion.
delivery_model_sustainability: TMA’s multi-donor funding model (UK 5% of KCP budget) reduces dependency on REDIT funds.
FCDO’s representation on TMA’s board ensures strategic oversight.
Risk of sustainability gaps in digital trade systems without HMRC engagement.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Integration of digital trade systems (AI, data-sharing frameworks) pending VFM study results.
Expanded focus on green/sustainable trade to align with global standards (e.g., AfCFTA).
Strengthened regional coordination to address cross-border trade disparities.
