programme_metadata.programme_title: Kenya Integrated Refugee and Host Community Programme (PAMOJA)

output_1.title: Enhanced relationship with government and other relevant policy stakeholders on refugee policy that supports social and economic integration of refugees and host communities

output_3.title: Enhanced access to livelihood opportunities including increased delivery of services by the private sector for refugees and host community (data to be disaggregated to include people with disabilities and other special needs groups)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme extended to March 2025 (from original Nov 2023 end date) to accommodate refugee policy shifts (Kenya Refugee Act 2021) and increased arrivals. Pivoted to support GoK's Shirika Plan for refugee integration, including promotion of Kakuma/Dadaab camps to municipalities and alignment with national socio-economic development programmes (KISEDP, GISEDP).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNHCR and IFC (via KKCF) performed satisfactorily, with 12 downstream partners contributing to delivery. UNHCR led humanitarian assistance and policy engagement, while IFC focused on private sector solutions. Partners demonstrated flexibility in adapting to GoK's policy shifts (e.g., Shirika Plan). Zero-tolerance safeguarding policies were effectively implemented with no reported incidents.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance adapted to include closer coordination with GoK entities (e.g., Directorate of Refugee Services, Turkana County Government) and refugee-led organisations. Weekly UN Country Team Meetings opened to international stakeholders to improve coordination. FCDO provided proactive risk monitoring (e.g., El Niño preparedness).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective during crises (e.g., El Niño floods response). UK-led coordination improved multi-stakeholder engagement, including refugees, host communities, private sector, and donors. Challenges remained in full alignment with GoK's decentralised implementation of the Shirika Plan due to resource constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: No major issues reported. Cash transfer mechanisms (e.g., for health, shelter, WASH) were highlighted as cost-effective and transparent. Procurement adapted to include local partners and refugee-led organisations per localisation recommendations.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to dynamic context (e.g., refugee influxes, policy changes). FCDO increased monitoring of risks related to GoK's policy implementation and climate impacts. Safeguarding oversight remained rigorous with automated feedback mechanisms (KASI kiosks).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility: (1) Extended timeline to align with GoK's refugee policy transition; (2) Reallocated resources to respond to El Niño floods and increased arrivals; (3) Adjusted milestones to reflect budget amendments and Shirika Plan priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Pivoted from encampment-focused delivery to integration support (e.g., municipal status for camps, NHIF expansion to Kakuma).
Scaled up cash transfers as a cost-effective, dignity-preserving assistance modality.
Commissioned technical assistance to support Shirika Plan finalisation and implementation.
Increased engagement with refugee-led organisations (RLOs) and local partners to address contextual nuances.

main_implementation_challenges: Unanticipated refugee influxes (13,042 new arrivals in Dadaab, 1,308 in Kakuma in Q3 2023) straining resources amid reduced humanitarian funding.
GoK's slow rollout of the Shirika Plan due to resource constraints and stakeholder buy-in challenges, despite political commitment.
El Niño floods displaced ~27,000 individuals in Dadaab and 589 in Kakuma, requiring emergency response pivots.
Balancing immediate humanitarian needs with long-term resilience-building under the new refugee policy framework.
external_factors_impact: Kenya Refugee Act 2021: Shift from encampment to integration created both opportunities (e.g., municipal status for camps) and implementation challenges (e.g., regulatory gaps).
Climate change: Droughts and floods increased refugee vulnerability and host community resilience pressures.
Regional conflicts (Somalia, South Sudan) drove new displacements, exceeding planned capacity.
Global funding cuts to refugee responses limited programme scalability.
contextual_constraints_new: Need for refugee identification documents (addressed via GoK Gazette Notice 143, Sept 2023) initially delayed service access.
Limited private sector engagement in Turkana/Garissa counties constrained livelihood opportunities.
Host community tensions over resource sharing in areas with high refugee-to-host ratios (e.g., Kalobeyei).
Delayed finalisation of Shirika Plan implementation frameworks created planning uncertainties.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between UNHCR's humanitarian mandate and IFC's private sector focus required mediation.
Downstream partners varied in capacity to adapt to policy shifts (e.g., local NGOs vs. international agencies).
Refugee-led organisations (RLOs) required additional support to meet fiduciary and reporting standards.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GoK's limited technical capacity to operationalise the Shirika Plan at county level.
Shortage of skilled labour in Turkana/Garissa for private sector initiatives (e.g., KKCF projects).
FCDO team bandwidth stretched by increased coordination demands during crises (e.g., El Niño).
Gaps in partner capacity to deliver Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) mainstreaming.
risk_materialization: Risk 1 (GoK deprioritising refugee policy): Partially materialised—commitment exists but implementation lags due to resources.
Risk 2 (Climate change impacts): Fully materialised—El Niño floods disrupted services and increased needs.
Safeguarding risks: Mitigated via proactive measures (no incidents reported).
Financial risks: Managed through budget reallocations and no-cost extension.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track despite challenges. No-cost extension to March 2025 allowed reallocation of £55.2M budget to address increased needs (e.g., refugee influxes, El Niño response). Budget amendments aligned with revised milestones and Shirika Plan priorities.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated through: (1) Cost-effective cash transfers (cheaper than in-kind aid, with multiplier effects); (2) Leveraging KKCF's multi-donor fund to attract private sector co-investment; (3) Shared services (e.g., NHIF expansion) reducing per-beneficiary costs. VFM exceeded business case projections due to adaptive modalities.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Partners (UNHCR/IFC) maintained transparent financial reporting and zero-tolerance for safeguarding breaches. FCDO's proactive risk management (e.g., El Niño preparedness) prevented major fiscal losses. Audit findings (if any) were not reported as significant.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Higher than planned: (1) Cash transfers reduced delivery costs by ~20% vs. in-kind aid; (2) Municipal status for camps lowered administrative overheads; (3) Co-location of services (e.g., health, education) improved economies of scale.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. KKCF attracted private sector co-funding but fell short of targets due to investor risk aversion in Turkana/Garissa. GoK's financial contributions to Shirika Plan were limited by fiscal constraints.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal direct impact reported. Kenyan Shilling stability mitigated exchange rate risks, though inflation (e.g., post-COVID, fuel prices) increased operational costs for partners.

key_delivery_lessons: Policy-aligned programming is critical: PAMOJA's success hinged on adapting to GoK's Refugee Act 2021 and Shirika Plan, demonstrating the value of flexibility in humanitarian-development nexus programmes.
Localisation works: Refugee-led organisations (RLOs) and local partners provided context-specific insights but required tailored capacity support.
Cash transfers outperform in-kind aid: Evidence showed higher efficiency, dignity, and economic multiplier effects, validating UK's advocacy for this modality.
Climate resilience must be proactive: Early warning systems and preparedness (e.g., El Niño response) saved lives and reduced costs compared to reactive measures.
successful_delivery_practices: Multi-stakeholder coordination: Weekly UN Country Team Meetings improved information-sharing and reduced duplication.
Automated feedback mechanisms (KASI kiosks) enhanced accountability and safeguarding without overburdening staff.
Pivoting to municipal governance models for camps improved service delivery and host-refugee integration.
Disaggregated data collection (e.g., by disability, gender) strengthened inclusivity and targeting.
management_adaptations_made: Restructured programme to align with Shirika Plan, including new outputs on policy implementation support.
Increased oversight of GESI mainstreaming after identifying gaps in partner delivery.
Adopted a 'no regrets' approach to climate risks (e.g., pre-positioning El Niño response supplies).
Streamlined reporting to focus on resilience indicators over traditional humanitarian metrics.
innovations_attempted: Kakuma Kalobeyei Challenge Fund (KKCF): Multi-donor trust fund to incentivise private sector engagement in refugee contexts.
Refugee identification documents: Advocacy led to GoK's Gazette Notice 143, enabling service access.
Cash-for-work programmes linked to municipal services (e.g., waste management) to build livelihoods and infrastructure.
Digital feedback tools (KASI) for real-time beneficiary input.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2022 recommendation to strengthen GESI: Partially addressed via disaggregated data collection but requires deeper partner capacity building.
2022 call for private sector engagement: Progressed through KKCF but limited by investor risk appetite.
2021 advice on policy influence: Successfully achieved via Shirika Plan advocacy (e.g., GoK's Global Refugee Forum pledges).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Restructure PAMOJA to fully align with Shirika Plan by April 2024, focusing on refugee management documents and socio-economic development programmes (KISEDP/GISEDP).
Provide technical assistance to GoK for Shirika Plan implementation, including evidence generation for policy dialogue on refugee movement and livelihoods.
Prioritise basic needs for refugees amid funding cuts, using UK's influencing role to advocate for increased donor support and prevent service gaps.
Deepened localisation: Expand partnerships with refugee-led organisations (RLOs) and local NGOs, including women-led groups, to enhance inclusion and contextual relevance.
Review and update output indicators to reflect resilience-building and developmental outcomes, deprioritising less impactful activities.

learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Highly effective in mitigation (e.g., El Niño preparedness) but challenged by external risks (e.g., GoK's implementation capacity). Proactive measures (e.g., weekly risk reviews, early warnings) reduced impact of materialised risks. Safeguarding and financial risks were well-managed with no major incidents.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.refugees: ~450,000 (target met, with additional 13,042 new arrivals in 2023)
notable_achievements: 40,000 refugees + 1,000 host community members accessed NHIF-expanded health services in Kakuma/Kalobeyei.
350 jobs (100 for women) supported via private sector initiatives by Dec 2024 (target on track).
6 workshops held on Shirika Plan consultations, influencing national policy.

policy_influence_achieved: GoK's endorsement of Shirika Plan and pledges at Global Refugee Forum (Dec 2023) directly linked to PAMOJA's advocacy.
Gazette Notice 143 (Sept 2023) recognising refugee IDs enabled service access, aligning with PAMOJA's policy goals.
Municipal status for Kakuma/Dadaab camps institutionalised integration approaches.
capacity_building_results: Turkana County Government capacity strengthened to manage NHIF expansion and municipal services.
12 downstream partners trained on GESI mainstreaming and adaptive management.
Refugee-led organisations (RLOs) gained representation in Shirika Plan consultations.

positive: Refugee economic activities (e.g., cash-for-work) inadvertently boosted local markets in host communities.
Policy advocacy spurred broader donor engagement with Shirika Plan (e.g., EU, World Bank).
negative: Host community tensions in Kalobeyei due to perceived resource competition.
Delayed Shirika Plan implementation created temporary service gaps for new arrivals.

scalability_evidence: KKCF model (private sector trust fund) replicable in other refugee contexts (e.g., Uganda, Ethiopia).
Cash transfer modalities adopted by other donors in Kenya based on PAMOJA's evidence.
Municipal governance approach for camps scalable to other protracted displacement settings.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates high relevance to GoK's refugee policy shift (Shirika Plan) and FCDO's humanitarian-development nexus goals. Strong performance (consistent 'A' scores) and adaptive management justify extension to March 2025 to consolidate gains, respond to increased needs, and support policy implementation.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium-High. Current model (UNHCR/IFC partnership with local actors) is viable but requires: (1) GoK's sustained commitment to Shirika Plan; (2) Continued donor funding for humanitarian needs; (3) Strengthened private sector engagement.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High. Programme aligned with FCDO's Kenya Humanitarian Framework 2022-2025 and delivered policy influence, VFM, and adaptive responses to crises.
planned_adaptations_future: Full alignment with Shirika Plan by April 2024, including revised logframe and indicators.
Increased focus on resilience-building (e.g., climate-adaptive livelihoods, local governance).
Expansion of cash transfer programmes and refugee-led service delivery.
Technical assistance to GoK for Shirika Plan implementation, with emphasis on gender-inclusive economic opportunities.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Direct UK funding + World Bank Multi-Donor Trust Fund (MDTF) contribution)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £94.55M (Phase 3) for 100,000 households in 4 counties (Turkana, Marsabit, Mandera, Wajir) with shock-responsive scale-up to 270,000 additional households (Group 2)
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLIs) via Kenya’s National Treasury (NT) to incentivise GoK results; direct cash transfers to beneficiary bank accounts (Equity Bank). Emergency payments triggered by Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) during droughts.
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium (shock-responsive mechanism built in, but core budget tied to DLIs and GoK fiscal processes)

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch FCDO oversight with World Bank as primary implementing partner; National Drought Management Authority (NDMA) as GoK lead. Programme Management Unit (PMU) planned for capacity-building.
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly joint reviews (FCDO/WB/GoK) with annual audits. DLIs provide real-time performance monitoring.
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: GoK-led (NDMA) with FCDO/WB approval for major adaptations. DLIs create automatic disbursement triggers for results.

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single implementing framework (KSEIP) with World Bank as lead partner; GoK (NDMA) as operational lead. UNICEF originally planned for NICHE component (nutrition).
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral (World Bank), Government (GoK/NDMA), Commercial (Payment Service Provider - Equity Bank).

partner_roles_planned.World Bank: Fiducial agent for MDTF; DLI management; technical assistance to GoK.
partner_roles_planned.GoK/NDMA: Programme implementation; beneficiary targeting; PSP contracting.
partner_roles_planned.Equity Bank: Payment Service Provider (PSP) for cash transfer disbursements.
partner_roles_planned.UNICEF: NICHE component implementation (nutrition + health education).

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: World Bank: Pre-existing partnership; GoK: Mandated by NSNP structure; Equity Bank: Competitive bidding (retained from Phase 2); UNICEF: Direct selection for NICHE.

consortium_baseline.lead_partner_planned: World Bank (fiscal agent) with GoK/NDMA as operational lead.

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Mixed (FCDO grant to WB MDTF + direct FCDO funding for NICHE). WB remains primary channel, but FCDO now directly funds NICHE (originally WB-IDA/UNICEF).
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £94.55M core budget + £20M supplementary GoK funding secured. Expanded to 4 new counties (Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu, Tana River) with 32,000 additional households. NICHE pilot extended to non-HSNP counties (Kitui, Kilifi, West Pokot).
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: DLIs retained but delayed by GoK budget processes. Emergency payments (Group 2) funded by EU (not GoK) in 2019. Direct FCDO funding for NICHE after GoK rejected UNICEF implementation.
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: Low in practice. GoK budget shortfalls (KES 2.7bn/£20M) required supplementary approvals; delays in NT disbursements affected Group 2 payments. FCDO repurposed HSNP Phase 3 funds for NICHE expansion.

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Intensified oversight due to GoK transition risks. PMU established within NDMA; stronger NDMA leadership observed (DLI-driven accountability). FCDO/WB joint missions increased to bi-annual (May/Oct 2019).
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Monthly engagement on budget delays; ad-hoc crisis management for NT disbursement issues. DLIs remain but supplemented by direct FCDO/WB lobbying for supplementary budgets.
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: GoK (NDMA) retains operational lead, but FCDO/WB intervene on fiscal risks (e.g., supplementary budget advocacy). NICHE delivery shifted to FCDO direct management after GoK-UNICEF dispute.

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Multi-partner with shifts: WB remains lead; UNICEF removed from NICHE; FCDO directly manages NICHE. Equity Bank retained as PSP.
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (WB), Government (GoK/NDMA), Commercial (Equity Bank), NGO (none - UNICEF exited).

partner_roles_actual.World Bank: MDTF management; DLI enforcement; technical assistance (unchanged).
partner_roles_actual.FCDO: Direct NICHE funding/management (new role); joint WB advocacy for GoK budget releases.

substantive_changes_made: Shift from WB-IDA/UNICEF to direct FCDO funding/management of NICHE component due to GoK objections to UN agency implementation.
Expansion of NICHE pilot to non-HSNP counties (Kitui, Kilifi, West Pokot) using repurposed HSNP Phase 3 funds.
Increased FCDO/WB advocacy role to secure GoK supplementary budgets (KES 2.7bn) for Group 1 payments.
Emergency payments (Group 2) funded by EU instead of GoK in 2019 due to budget delays.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Budget increased by ~£20M via GoK supplementary approvals (though delayed). NICHE expansion drew £X from HSNP Phase 3 (exact figure not specified).
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope expanded to 4 new counties (32,000 households) + NICHE extended to 3 non-HSNP counties.
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: Direct FCDO funding introduced for NICHE (replacing WB-IDA/UNICEF). Emergency payments shifted to EU funding temporarily.

theory_of_change_revisions.assumptions_updated: Assumption that GoK would fund NICHE via WB-IDA/UNICEF proved invalid; assumption that NT would ringfence social protection budgets was not met.

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: PMU established within NDMA; intensified FCDO/WB oversight on budget risks.
management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Increased from quarterly to bi-annual joint missions + ad-hoc fiscal advocacy.
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: FCDO/WB took more active role in GoK budget negotiations (e.g., supplementary budget lobbying).

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: Added: Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu, Tana River (32,000 households); NICHE expanded to Kitui, Kilifi, West Pokot.

delivery_adaptations.activity_only_adjustments: Minor delays in Group 2 emergency payments (July→September, August→October) due to NT cash flow issues.

adaptation_triggers.contextual_shocks: GoK fiscal consolidation (Big 4 agenda) caused budget delays; political resistance to UNICEF implementation of NICHE.
adaptation_triggers.performance_issues: NT disbursement delays risked beneficiary payment timeliness (Group 2).
adaptation_triggers.learning_insights: Recognised need for stronger NDMA capacity (PMU establishment).
adaptation_triggers.strategic_opportunities: KSEIP framework enabled HSNP expansion to 4 new counties; NICHE pilot leveraged HSNP Phase 3 funds.

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High (proactive FCDO/WB engagement to secure supplementary budgets; rapid NICHE restructuring).
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: Medium (shock-responsive mechanism used, but budget flexibility constrained by GoK fiscal processes).
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High (PMU established based on NDMA capacity gaps; NICHE adapted to GoK preferences).

fcas_context.fragility_level: High (drought-prone ASAL regions: Turkana, Marsabit, Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu, Tana River).
fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Chronic inter-communal violence and resource-based conflicts in ASAL counties.

major_external_shocks.political_transitions: GoK fiscal consolidation under new NT Cabinet Secretary (2019); resistance to UNICEF-led NICHE implementation.
major_external_shocks.economic_shocks: GoK revenue underperformance; currency pressure (KES depreciation).
major_external_shocks.climate_disasters: Recurrent droughts triggering Group 2 emergency payments (e.g., 2019 VCI-based scale-up).

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: GoK commitment to social protection remained strong (Vision 2030/NSNP), but fiscal prioritisation shifted to Big 4 agenda, delaying HSNP disbursements.
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: Social protection funding remained in development (not recurrent) budget, increasing vulnerability to cuts.
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: NDMA capacity improved with PMU but still reliant on FCDO/WB for budget advocacy; NT disbursement delays persisted.

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Limited PSP options; Equity Bank retained as sole provider. No market issues reported.
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: KES depreciation (e.g., KES 5,400 = £41 at Dec 2019 vs. higher in earlier phases) affected cash transfer value.

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Moderate (2 substantive changes: funding modality + partners; governance intensified but not restructured).
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Comprehensive adaptation (funding + governance + partnership changes, though consortium stable).
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate (DLI/shock-responsive mechanisms worked, but GoK fiscal risks underestimated; UNICEF role proved unfeasible).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Hunger Safety Net Programme Phase III

output_1.title: Maintained timeliness and predictability of payments to HSNP households for both regular and emergency payments

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Transitioned operations to the World Bank under KSEIP (Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Programme), embedding HSNP within a broader £200m WB programme using Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLIs) to incentivise results. Expanded HSNP to four additional drought-affected counties (Garissa, Isiolo, Samburu, Tana River) with ~32,000 new households.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank partnership is working well, supporting integration of HSNP into the wider National Safety Net Programme (NSNP) and improving coordination among GoK departments. NDMA (National Drought Management Authority) successfully managed recruitment of a Programme Management Unit (PMU) and contracting of a Payment Service Provider (Equity Bank).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: NDMA, with WB/DFID support, established a PMU to lead HSNP implementation and build capacity for eventual full GoK ownership. A draft transition plan is being developed for March 2020 to outline NDMA’s takeover of key functions.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Joint WB/DFID engagement (e.g., JRIS missions) improved coordination between NDMA and other GoK departments (e.g., National Treasury). DLIs incentivised cross-programme collaboration under NSNP.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Equity Bank was successfully contracted as the Payment Service Provider (PSP) for Phase 3, continuing from Phase 2. No major procurement issues reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight by DFID/WB due to transition risks, including joint review missions (May/October 2019) and Internal Audit Department assessments. Responsibility for delivery shifted to GoK via DLIs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to GoK budget delays by advancing payments using underspend from FY 18/19. NICHE component was repurposed from WB IDA loan to DFID grant due to GoK constraints on UN agency funding.
adaptive_management_examples: Advanced payments to beneficiaries using FY 18/19 underspend to mitigate GoK budget delays.
Repurposed NICHE funding from WB IDA loan to DFID grant to align with GoK preferences.
Engaged intensively with National Treasury to secure supplementary budget approval (KES 2.7bn) for HSNP shortfall.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in National Treasury (NT) disbursements to NDMA, affecting timely payments to Group 2 (emergency) households (e.g., July payments made in September).
GoK budget shortfalls (KES 2.7bn/£20m) requiring supplementary budget negotiations.
Transition risks as GoK assumes ownership, including safeguarding and fund disbursement delays.
Social protection budgets remained in the development (not recurrent) budget, limiting ringfencing.
external_factors_impact: GoK fiscal consolidation due to underperforming revenues and prioritisation of the President’s "Big 4" policy agenda, leading to budget cuts.
Household-level risks identified in DFID’s September 2019 Country and Programme Level Assurance Review.
contextual_constraints_new: GoK resistance to funding government programmes through UN agencies (e.g., UNICEF for NICHE), requiring repurposing of funds.
Need to align county selection for NICHE with GoK priorities (e.g., inclusion of non-HSNP counties like Kitui, Kilifi, West Pokot).
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between NDMA (MoD&ASALs) and State Department of Social Protection (ML&SP) under NSNP, though DLIs improved coordination.
Challenges in GoK’s capacity to manage transition, requiring intensive DFID/WB support.
capacity_constraints_emerged: NDMA’s limited capacity to fully assume HSNP management without PMU support (transition plan underway).
National Treasury’s cash flow problems delayed disbursements, affecting emergency payments.
risk_materialization: Delays in NT disbursements (as anticipated in risk registers).
Household-level safeguarding risks identified in Internal Audit review.
Funding shortfalls for Group 1 households, addressed via supplementary budget.

budget_execution_vs_plan: GoK’s approved FY19/20 budget initially underfunded HSNP by KES 2.7bn (£20m), requiring supplementary budget approval in December 2019.
Emergency payments to Group 2 households were delayed (July paid in September, August in October) due to NT cash flow issues.
DFID/WB lobbied successfully for supplementary budget inclusion, but disbursements remained tied to development (not recurrent) budget.
value_for_money_assessment: DLIs under KSEIP improved VfM by linking disbursements to results, incentivising GoK efficiency.
Cost per beneficiary remained stable (e.g., regular transfers at KES 5,400/£41 every two months).
Shock-responsive mechanism (Group 2) demonstrated cost efficiency compared to traditional food aid.
financial_management_quality: NDMA managed funds effectively with WB/DFID oversight, though NT delays created liquidity challenges.
Equity Bank (PSP) performed reliably in disbursing CTs to beneficiary accounts.
Supplementary budget process highlighted need for better GoK budget planning.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Regular CTs reached ~100,000 households (600,000 people) at £41/household/2 months.
Emergency scale-up (Group 2) added 270,000 households at KES 2,700/£20.40 per one-time payment.
Administrative costs reduced via integrated NSNP systems (e.g., shared targeting with other CT programmes).
co_funding_materialization: GoK funded 100% of regular CTs for Group 1 in FY19/20 (post-supplementary budget).
EU funds were used for emergency payments (Group 2) instead of GoK funds as planned.
DFID’s £74.4m contribution to WB’s MDTF leveraged additional WB/GoK co-financing.

key_delivery_lessons: DLIs effectively incentivised GoK performance but required intensive donor coordination (WB/DFID).
Transition to GoK ownership increased delivery risks (e.g., NT disbursement delays).
Flexible funding (e.g., underspend reuse) mitigated short-term budget gaps.
successful_delivery_practices: Joint WB/DFID review missions (JRIS) improved real-time problem-solving.
PMU model successfully built NDMA capacity while ensuring continuity.
Shock-responsive triggers (e.g., Vegetation Condition Index) enabled timely emergency scale-up.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted NICHE funding from WB IDA loan to DFID grant to align with GoK preferences.
Intensified engagement with NT to ringfence social protection budgets (ongoing).
Developed transition plan for NDMA to assume full HSNP management by 2024.
innovations_attempted: Integration of HSNP into KSEIP’s DLI framework to strengthen GoK accountability.
Pilot of NICHE (Nutrition Improvement through Cash and Health) in Marsabit/Turkana.
Exploration of graduation/economic inclusion components within KSEIP.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: NT disbursement delays persist despite supplementary budget approval.
Completed: PMU recruitment and PSP contracting.
Ongoing: Transition plan finalisation and NICHE county selection.
forward_recommendations: Ringfence social protection budgets in GoK’s recurrent (not development) expenditure (Action: WB/DFID/NDMA to engage NT by Year 2).
Finalise graduation/economic inclusion component delivery model by February 2020 (Action: SRO to lead discussions).
Amend Business Case to reflect NICHE expansion to non-HSNP counties (Kitui, Kilifi, West Pokot).
Conduct risk reassessment to address transition and safeguarding risks (Action: DFID/WB/GoK).
risk_management_effectiveness: Proactive: Joint risk identification via JRIS missions and Internal Audit reviews.
Reactive: Supplementary budget secured to address funding shortfall, but delays impacted beneficiaries.
Gaps: Household-level risks (e.g., safeguarding) require stronger mitigation.

HSNP’s shock-responsive mechanism remains vital for drought-prone ASAL regions.

DLIs and integrated NSNP systems improve sustainability prospects.

Expand NICHE to non-HSNP counties (Kitui, Kilifi, West Pokot) via Business Case amendment.
Strengthen NDMA’s capacity for full HSNP management by 2024.
Advocate for social protection budgets to be moved to GoK’s recurrent expenditure.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Reducing Insecurity and Violent Extremism in Northern and Coastal Regions of Kenya (REINVENT) programme

output_1.title: Accountable and effective police (and other security agencies) addressing community security, violent extremism and election security

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adapted to 0.5% ODA budget reduction through collaborative prioritization with FCDO, Supply Partner (SP), and programme partners. Adaptive management enabled quick scaling of activities to remain responsive to evolving priorities and complex political context (e.g., COVID-19, elections).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong collaboration, particularly in co-funding (e.g., MoD/BATUK covered 2/3 of POLICARE centre construction costs, NPS provided land, FCDO/REINVENT covered remaining costs). Joint accountability mechanisms (e.g., NPS Service Delivery Index) secured high-level buy-in from police leadership (IG, DIGs, Regional Commanders).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme leveraged existing governance structures (e.g., Kenya-UK North East Advisory Group) and integrated diplomatic engagement (e.g., High Commissioner’s public endorsements) to amplify impact. Multi-agency coordination (e.g., with IPOA, IAU, National Crime Research Centre) strengthened accountability and evidence-based decision-making.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination with FCDO’s Sub-National team and British High Commission (BHC) enabled access to county/regional/national stakeholders. Violence hotspot mapping and Ministerial briefings informed by REINVENT data were discussed at Heads of Mission (HoMs) level, demonstrating cross-donor alignment (US, World Bank, EU).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement adapted to budget reductions and context shifts (e.g., COVID-19, elections) through flexible workstream strategies and log frame adjustments. Supply Partner (Tetra Tech) maintained robust safeguarding procedures and business continuity planning.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight intensified in high-risk areas (e.g., election security, GBV response) with monthly safeguarding risk assessments shared with FCDO. High-level engagement (e.g., IG, DIGs) ensured ownership of reforms (e.g., NPS Service Delivery Index).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme utilized adaptive management to pivot activities (e.g., digital platforms for election security SOPs, hate speech monitoring tools) and respond to emerging priorities (e.g., criminal gangs, GBV spikes during COVID-19). Budget flexibility allowed reallocation to critical areas like election security and POLICARE centres.
adaptive_management_examples: Development and rollout of the **NPS Service Delivery Index** (baseline conducted in 47 counties, endorsed by police leadership, with targets set for 1,200 stations).
Rapid deployment of **digital tools** (e.g., SSOs mobile app for election security SOPs, adapted for Android/iOS).
Scaling up **GBV response** (e.g., SGBV Situation Room in Mombasa, toll-free helpline promoted by High Commissioner, leading to increased calls).
**Multi-agency election security strategies** localized in 3 target counties (Kwale, Nakuru, Isiolo) following national manual approval.
**Policare Centre** co-funding model (MoD/BATUK, FCDO, NPS) ensuring timely delivery and joint accountability.

main_implementation_challenges: Budget reductions due to UK ODA cuts (0.5% GNI) requiring reprioritization of activities.
COVID-19 pandemic disruptions (Delta variant surge in 2021, containment measures, socio-economic impacts, increased VAWG/GBV cases).
Political instability and election-related violence risks ahead of August 2022 general elections.
Complex security context (Al Shabaab threats, criminal gangs, historical election violence).
Capacity constraints in partner institutions (e.g., IAU, IPOA) to investigate and conclude police misconduct cases.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Stretched health systems, economic downturn, increased domestic violence, and protests (e.g., May 2021). Forced remote working and hygiene protocols to limit transmission.
Political: Upcoming elections evoked class/economic marginalization tensions, risking violence recurrence. High Commissioner’s diplomacy (e.g., GBV Situation Room publicity) mitigated some risks.
Economic: National debt and poverty spikes due to COVID-19 exacerbated insecurity and VAWG.
Regional: Kenya’s role as a stability anchor in East Africa increased UK exposure to transnational threats (e.g., Al Shabaab).
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated surge in **criminal gang activity** in Coastal regions, requiring evidence-based responses.
**Election security gaps** in localizing national strategies (e.g., delays in Kwale, Nakuru, Isiolo rollout).
**Hate speech proliferation** ahead of elections, necessitating integration into violence monitoring tools.
**Safeguarding risks** during remote working (mitigated via monthly risk assessments and partner training).
partner_relationship_issues: Slow adoption of reforms by mid-level police officers despite high-level buy-in (e.g., NPS Service Delivery Index).
Delays in IAU/IPOA case investigations due to capacity limits, though technical support (e.g., training 60 IAU officers) improved conclusions.
Co-funding dependencies (e.g., POLICARE centre) required intensive coordination to align partner contributions.
capacity_constraints_emerged: IAU and IPOA lacked capacity to process rising misconduct cases (addressed via REINVENT technical support and training).
Limited NPS data management skills for the **Service Delivery Index** (baseline required validation by senior leadership).
Partner institutions (e.g., National Crime Research Centre) needed evidence-based briefings to act on criminal gangs/GBV.
risk_materialization: COVID-19 disruptions (health, economic, safeguarding) materialized as high-risk, mitigated via adaptive delivery (e.g., remote working, VFM adjustments).
Election violence risks partially materialized (e.g., criminal gang activity), addressed through violence monitoring and multi-agency coordination.
Budget reduction risks were managed via collaborative reprioritization with FCDO/SP.
Safeguarding risks (e.g., VAWG during COVID-19) were proactively managed via monthly assessments and partner training.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Budget execution adapted to 0.5% ODA reduction through collaborative reprioritization. Year 3 log frame and theory of change revised to align with reduced budget (£20M total). Adaptive management enabled quick reallocation to critical areas (e.g., election security, GBV response).

evidence: High-level commitment secured for police reforms and GBV prevention, aligning with UK-Kenya Security Compact.
VFM data plan with 17 indicators categorized under **4Es** (Equity, Effectiveness, Efficiency, Economy).
Cost-effectiveness measured at outcome level (mid-line evaluation) and will be reassessed at programme end.
Illustrative VFM per output summarized in Section C of the review.
Examples of evidence-based choices: POLICARE centre co-funding, NPS Service Delivery Index, and GBV hotspot mapping.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Robust financial management demonstrated through: (1) Monthly safeguarding risk assessments shared with FCDO; (2) Supply Partner’s standalone safeguarding register and procedures; (3) Business continuity planning to mitigate COVID-19 disruptions; (4) Transparent co-funding arrangements (e.g., POLICARE centre).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency maintained via: (1) Adaptive scaling of activities (e.g., digital tools for election SOPs reduced training costs); (2) Leveraging partnerships (e.g., MoD/BATUK co-funding); (3) Repurposing existing platforms (e.g., SSOs mobile app for election security).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialized successfully in key areas: (1) **Policare Centre**: MoD (via BATUK) covered 2/3 of construction costs, FCDO/REINVENT covered 1/3; (2) **NPS Service Delivery Index**: NPS provided in-kind support (land, leadership endorsement).

key_delivery_lessons: **Broad partnerships enhance efficiency**: Co-funding (e.g., POLICARE centre) secured greater commitment and timely delivery.
**Top-level buy-in is critical**: Senior NPS leadership endorsement (IG, DIGs) was pivotal for reform ownership (e.g., Service Delivery Index).
**Diplomacy-development integration amplifies impact**: High Commissioner’s publicity of GBV helpline increased calls; REINVENT evidence informed HoMs discussions.
**Adaptive management works**: Quick scaling of activities (e.g., digital tools, election strategies) ensured responsiveness to COVID-19/elections.
**Localization requires flexibility**: National election security manual needed tailored rollout in 3 counties (Kwale, Nakuru, Isiolo).
successful_delivery_practices: Multi-stakeholder co-funding models (e.g., POLICARE centre).
High-level endorsement strategies (e.g., NPS leadership for Service Delivery Index).
Digital adaptation (e.g., SSOs app for election SOPs).
Evidence-based advocacy (e.g., violence hotspot mapping for HoMs).
Safeguarding procedures (monthly risk assessments, partner training).
management_adaptations_made: Revised Year 3 log frame and theory of change to align with reduced budget.
Enhanced coordination with BHC/FCDO Sub-National team for stakeholder access.
Strengthened VFM measurement via ITAD diagnostic framework and 4Es categorization.
Expanded violence monitoring to include hate speech ahead of elections.
innovations_attempted: NPS **Service Delivery Index**: First comprehensive baseline for 47 counties, endorsed for nationwide rollout.
**Policare Centres**: Co-funded, multi-agency hubs for community security.
**Digital SOPs**: Mobile app for election security protocols (Android/iOS).
**GBV Situation Room**: Toll-free helpline with High Commissioner’s endorsement.
**Violence hotspot mapping**: Data-driven tool for HoMs and security institutions.
previous_recommendations_progress: 2020 AR recommendation to **strengthen police accountability** advanced via IAU/IPOA annual reports and 60 IAU officers trained.
Call to **localize election security strategies** partially met (3 counties targeted; national manual approved).
Need for **top-level NPS buy-in** achieved (IG/DIGs endorsed Service Delivery Index).

Public confidence-building measures (e.g., accountability fora in 12+ police stations).

output_1.title: Global Questions - Analytical products generated by research institutions. Products are generated by research institutions and partners (including in affected countries and regions) that are high quality and relevant to policy makers, for policy dialogue with both origin and host countries and to the development and humanitarian community.

output_2.title: Operational Learning - Impact Evaluations implemented by WBG-UNHCR-DFID teams. Better knowledge and understanding of the impact of selected Programme s on refugees, IDPs and host communities.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The inception phase was successfully completed with the preparation of DFID mandatory documents, identification of priorities, and development of the budget and work-plan. The implementation phase began with the launch of impact evaluations, preparation of analytical studies, and initiation of the Global Questions activities, Ph.D.-Post Doc Fellowship Programme, and data collection workshops. The programme is on track to deliver robust new evidence for policy-making.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: The World Bank experienced recruitment delays, which were temporarily addressed through short-term recruitment. This did not critically impact the first year but requires immediate attention to ensure uptake and ultimate impact. UNHCR and DFID collaboration is progressing as planned, with regular coordination mechanisms being established.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: DFID and the World Bank agreed to review governance arrangements post-inception to ensure clear timelines and processes for all activities, including grant awards. Regular monthly meetings between the World Bank team and DFID SRO, and quarterly Advisory Committee meetings, are now planned.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination mechanisms are being formalized, including stakeholder consultation workshops for the Global Questions initiative. The Advisory Committee is actively involved in strategic decisions, such as widening the multi-stakeholder partnership and addressing gender-focused research.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: The preparation of Terms of Reference (ToR) for global tenders is underway, with tenders expected to launch in Spring 2018. Contracts for the four Global Questions areas are targeted to be awarded by October 2018. Delays in initial fund disbursement led to a revised payment schedule, signed in October 2017.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight has intensified post-inception, with regular catch-up meetings between DFID and the World Bank to monitor progress, expenditure, and Value for Money (VFM) indicators. The World Bank has also started resourcing additional staff to support the Trust Fund Manager, improving efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility in addressing recruitment delays through short-term measures. Adaptive management was also evident in revising governance arrangements and payment schedules to accommodate initial delays.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised payment schedule to address delays in fund disbursement, signed in October 2017.
Short-term recruitment by the World Bank to mitigate staffing gaps during inception.
Planned review of governance arrangements to improve timelines and processes for grant awards and partner coordination.

main_implementation_challenges: Recruitment delays in the World Bank team, temporarily addressed through short-term hires but requiring long-term resolution.

financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Value for Money (VFM) performance remains on track, aligning with the original business case proposition. successful_delivery_practices: The inception phase successfully established foundational documents (log frame, Theory of Change, Risk Register) and priorities, enabling a smooth transition to implementation.

programme_metadata.programme_title: FCDO-Medical Research Council Concordat 2018 - 2023 Programme
programme_metadata.programme_status: Extended (costed extension approved in 2024, now ending 2028)

output_1.title: High-quality, peer-reviewed research that can change policy or practice in priority areas

output_2.title: New evidence effectively communicated, shared and disseminated

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme received two extensions (2023 no-cost extension to 2025, followed by 2024 costed extension to 2028) due to COVID-19 disruptions and slower-than-anticipated spend. Original 9-year timeline (2018-2027) now extended to 10 years (2018-2028). Delivery model leverages MRC's existing systems for peer review and grant management, with FCDO providing strategic oversight and diplomatic reach for policy influence.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: MRC has exceeded expectations in research output quality (e.g., 3.68 Relative Citation Ratio) and policy influence (e.g., WHO approval of oral HIV tests for children). Partnership benefits from decades of collaboration, with MRC demonstrating strong adaptive capacity (e.g., rapid response to Mpox outbreak in 2024). Quarterly meetings ensure alignment, though some reporting integration gaps remain.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Unchanged from original plan: MRC retains operational management with FCDO oversight. Quarterly joint meetings address programme matters ad-hoc. No formal asset register; funds transferred directly to research institutions as ring-fenced project budgets.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination between MRC and FCDO, with FCDO using its diplomatic networks to amplify research uptake. Example: MRC's Gambia unit coordinated Phase 1/2 trials for microarray patch vaccines, while FCDO facilitated policy dialogues for adoption. Some delays in aligning reporting systems (e.g., ResearchFish tool underutilized).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Single annual transaction (paid in arrears) minimizes administrative burden. Procurement leverages MRC's existing UKRI-compliant systems, with no major issues reported. Cost efficiency maintained through shared infrastructure (e.g., peer review panels).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO conducts risk monitoring every 6 months (or more frequently if risks emerge). MRC's internal risk management includes expert panels from relevant work areas. Oversight intensity matches original plan, with no escalations reported.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated high flexibility: repurposed funds for COVID-19 research (2020–2021) and Mpox response (2024). Adaptive management enabled rapid support for time-sensitive trials (e.g., R21/Matrix-M malaria vaccine). Extensions allowed reallocation of unspent funds to high-priority areas.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid funding reallocation for COVID-19 research (2020), including studies on vaccine duration effectiveness (published in *The Lancet* with RCR 92.94).
2024 response to Mpox outbreak using existing funding mechanisms.
Adjustment of portfolio milestones post-extension to reflect delayed spend and new priorities (e.g., malaria vaccine implementation research).
Support for negative/nil result reporting to improve shared learning (new focus in 2024).

main_implementation_challenges: Slower-than-anticipated spend rate (led to two extensions).
COVID-19 disruptions (2020–2021) delayed fieldwork and reduced output velocity.
Complexity of tracking long-term policy impact from research outputs.
Underutilization of reporting tools (e.g., ResearchFish) for portfolio-wide progress monitoring.
Need to balance flexibility with accountability in extended timeline.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19: Paused fieldwork, shifted priorities to pandemic response, and reduced 2020–2021 output volume (though citation impact remained high).
2025 Spending Review uncertainty paused negotiations for a new 6-year strategic partnership, leading to a shorter 3-year extension.
Global health crises (e.g., Mpox 2024) required rapid reprioritization of funds.
Exchange rate fluctuations (not quantified) may have affected LMIC-based research costs.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased competition for LMIC research talent post-COVID, affecting capacity in some partner institutions.
Emerging regulatory barriers in certain countries for clinical trials (e.g., data-sharing restrictions).
Need to demonstrate impact in a tighter fiscal environment (FCDO budget pressures).
partner_relationship_issues: Minor gaps in reporting alignment (e.g., MRC's internal systems not fully synchronized with FCDO's monitoring needs).
Delays in MRC notifying FCDO of upcoming funding calls, limiting amplification opportunities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: LMIC-based researchers faced heightened workloads due to pandemic response demands.
Limited administrative capacity at some African partner institutions to manage increased reporting requirements post-extension.
MRC's peer review panels experienced higher volumes of applications for crisis-related research.
risk_materialization: Slower spend rate (mitigated via extensions).
COVID-19 operational disruptions (mitigated via flexible funding reallocation).
Risk of reduced policy influence due to delayed extensions (mitigated via continued FCDO diplomatic support).
No major fiduciary or reputational risks materialized; existing risk management systems deemed effective.

budget_execution_vs_plan.execution_rate: 59% of revised allocation spent; slower than original timeline but aligned with extended schedule.
budget_execution_vs_plan.variance_explanation: Delays due to COVID-19 and cautious spend rates in early years. Extensions realigned budget with actual delivery pace.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: High: Leverages MRC's existing UKRI systems to minimize administrative costs (e.g., single annual transaction, no asset register). 87% of MRC's 2023–24 expenditure went to research/innovation.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: High: Unit costs reduced via shared peer review panels and cross-Research Council learning. Value-for-money reviews conducted pre-approval for all grants.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High: Research outputs exceed citation benchmarks (RCR 3.68 vs. target >2.0), with demonstrated policy impact (e.g., WHO malaria vaccine recommendation).
value_for_money_assessment.comparison_to_business_case: Outperforms original VfM proposition due to higher-than-expected citation impact and policy influence per pound spent. Costed extension maintains efficiency by avoiding programme restart costs.
value_for_money_assessment.co_funding_leveraged: Yes: Contributions to EDCTP and other multi-donor platforms (e.g., malaria vaccine trials).

financial_management_quality.mr_cystems: Strong: UKRI-compliant audit and management procedures. Risks monitored quarterly with FCDO.
financial_management_quality.fcdo_oversight: Effective: Six-monthly risk reviews, with ad-hoc checks for emerging hazards. No major fiduciary issues identified.
financial_management_quality.transparency: High: Timely reporting on portfolio costs and progress, though some delays in aligning MRC's internal systems with FCDO's monitoring tools.
financial_management_quality.cost_control: Robust: Budgets scrutinized pre-approval; savings identified where costs deemed inappropriate. No evidence of overspend.

cost_efficiency_achieved.administrative_costs: Minimized via MRC's existing infrastructure (e.g., no separate asset management).
cost_efficiency_achieved.research_unit_costs: Tracked per study; examples include measles-rubella vaccine trial (MAP) achieving equivalent immune response at lower delivery cost.
cost_efficiency_achieved.comparative_advantage: MRC's economies of scale reduce per-project management costs vs. standalone FCDO-funded research.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially: Leveraged EDCTP and other multi-donor funds for specific trials (e.g., R21 malaria vaccine), but no quantitative data provided on co-funding volumes.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not quantified in review, but acknowledged as a potential risk for LMIC-based research costs.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible funding mechanisms enable rapid response to emergencies (e.g., COVID-19, Mpox) without compromising long-term goals.
Longstanding partnerships (e.g., FCDO-MRC) reduce delivery risks and improve adaptive capacity.
Policy influence requires sustained diplomatic engagement alongside research dissemination (e.g., WHO approval of oral HIV tests).
Negative/nil result reporting should be systematically incorporated to avoid publication bias.
successful_delivery_practices: MRC's use of existing UKRI systems for peer review and grant management minimizes overhead.
Quarterly FCDO-MRC meetings ensure strategic alignment without micromanagement.
Narrative case studies (e.g., Zimbabwe HIV testing) effectively demonstrate policy impact.
Open-access publishing (95% of 2023 outputs) maximizes research uptake.
management_adaptations_made: Added focus on tracking long-term impact via narrative case studies (2023–2024).
Increased IP protection efforts (2 patents filed in 2023: TB diagnostic method and protein combination).
Pilot of ResearchFish tool for portfolio monitoring (though adoption remains partial).
Stronger integration of LMIC-led research (40% of 2023 authors vs. 30% target).
innovations_attempted: Microarray patch (MAP) vaccine delivery for measles/rubella (Phase 1/2 trial completed; Phase 3 planned).
Youth Friendship Bench mental health intervention scaled to 65,500 adolescents in Zimbabwe (2023).
Use of Relative Citation Ratio (RCR) to quantify research influence beyond publication counts.
Rapid-response funding calls for emerging outbreaks (e.g., Mpox 2024).
previous_recommendations_progress: Improved reporting of policy outcomes via narrative case studies (6 produced in 2023 vs. 1 expected).
Enhanced IP management (2 patents in 2023 vs. none previously).
Partial progress on integrating reporting systems (ResearchFish adoption ongoing).
Limited advancement on co-funding tracking (no quantitative data provided).

forward_recommendations.action: Reevaluate Concordat approach for extended years (2024–2028), including new milestones and risk assessment.
Develop a 3-year strategic partnership framework to replace paused 6-year plan, focusing on key FCDO priorities.
Improve reporting practices, including case studies on nil/negative results and better use of ResearchFish.
Provide timely notice of MRC funding calls to FCDO for amplification via networks.
Complete internal assessment of future boards/schemes (e.g., African Research Leadership) with early FCDO input.

risk_management_effectiveness.systems: MRC's risk management processes (quarterly expert reviews + FCDO oversight) deemed effective. No major risks materialized without mitigation.
risk_management_effectiveness.adaptations: Added focus on currency/exchange rate risks and LMIC capacity constraints post-COVID.
risk_management_effectiveness.gaps: Limited quantitative tracking of co-funding materialization and exchange rate impacts.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 65,500 adolescents received mental health therapy via Youth Friendship Bench (Zimbabwe, 2023).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: WHO malaria vaccine recommendation (R21/Matrix-M) expected to benefit millions in LMICs post-2024 rollout.

policy_influence_achieved.example: WHO approval of oral HIV tests for children under 12 (Zimbabwe study).
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Incorporated into Zimbabwe's national HIV testing programme; PEPFAR updated guidance.

policy_influence_achieved.example: WHO recommendation of R21/Matrix-M malaria vaccine (2024).
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Rollout began in 2024; FCDO funding implementation research to support adoption.

policy_influence_achieved.example: Microarray patch (MAP) vaccine delivery for measles/rubella.
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Phase 3 trial planned; potential to revolutionize vaccine delivery in remote areas.

policy_influence_achieved.example: Youth Friendship Bench mental health intervention.
policy_influence_achieved.uptake: Scaled nationally in Zimbabwe; expansion to regional countries underway.

capacity_building_results.evidence: 40% of 2023 publications LMIC-led (vs. 30% target); increasing RCR parity between LMIC/HIC authors.
MRC Gambia and Uganda units led high-impact trials (e.g., MAP vaccine study).
6 narrative case studies in 2023 demonstrated LMIC government uptake of research (e.g., Zanzibar malaria surveillance).

unintended_consequences.description: COVID-19 research pivot (2020–2021) produced highly cited studies (e.g., *Lancet* paper with RCR 92.94), strengthening MRC's reputation and attracting additional funding.
Delayed extensions (2023–2024) created uncertainty for researchers, risking talent attrition in LMIC partners.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Scaled to 65,500 adolescents in Zimbabwe (2023); being adopted in neighboring countries.
Phase 1/2 trial success (Gambia) enables progression to Phase 3; potential for global adoption if Phase 3 succeeds.
Zimbabwe model influenced WHO/PEPFAR guidelines; replicable in other high-burden settings.

continuation_rationale.justification: Programme demonstrates high performance (consistent 'A' scores), strong policy impact (e.g., WHO malaria vaccine recommendation), and cost efficiency. Extensions mitigate COVID-19 disruptions and allow completion of high-potential trials (e.g., MAP vaccines).
evidence: Sustained research quality (RCR 3.68 vs. target >2.0).
Policy influence (6 case studies in 2023).
Flexibility to address emerging crises (e.g., Mpox 2024).
Low administrative costs (87% of funds to research).

strengths: Proven partnership (decades of FCDO-MRC collaboration).
MRC's robust peer review and risk management systems.
Flexible funding mechanisms adaptable to crises.
risks: Dependence on FCDO's long-term funding commitments (post-2028 uncertainty).
LMIC partner capacity constraints may limit scalability in some regions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (consistent 'A' ratings, strong VfM, and alignment with FCDO strategic priorities).
planned_adaptations_future: Develop a 3-year strategic partnership framework by December 2025 to replace the paused 6-year plan.
Refocus portfolio on FCDO's key priorities (e.g., malaria, mental health, vaccine delivery).
Enhance reporting on long-term impact and nil/negative results.
Explore co-funding opportunities to diversify funding sources post-2028.
Strengthen LMIC-led research capacity via targeted schemes (e.g., African Research Leadership).

funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High (utilized to pivot to Ukraine, reprioritize strands, and fund open-source tech)

governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: **Monthly check-ins** for high-priority projects (e.g., Ukraine tracker) + ad-hoc reviews for emerging crises
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: **Decentralized operational decisions** to programme leads for rapid response, with SRO/PRO sign-off for strategic shifts (e.g., strand pausing)

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Multiple partners retained but **new open-source actors added** (e.g., Centre for Information Resilience) and **HEROs/Palladium role expanded** for deployable expertise
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Original types + **new open-source investigation orgs**; reduced academic engagement (due to Research strand pause)
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: **Shift to real-time data/analysis**: Partners like Crisis Group and open-source orgs prioritized for live conflict tracking (e.g., Ukraine, Sahel)

substantive_changes_made: **Strand consolidation**: Paused ‘Research and Evidence’ strand (originally 50% of focus) to concentrate on ‘Risk Assessment, Early Warning and Monitoring’ due to SCF halt and ODA cuts.
**Ukraine pivot**: Rapid reallocation of funds to open-source analysis and real-time tracking (e.g., Ukraine Invasion Tracker).
**Open-source expansion**: Added partnerships with open-source investigation orgs (e.g., Centre for Information Resilience) for real-time conflict data.
**HEROs programme scaling**: Increased reliance on Palladium’s HEROs for deployable civilian expertise (e.g., Bosnia DCE).
**Logframe revision**: Milestones for Research strand reduced to zero (Nov 2022); Global Conflict Risk Assessment targets adjusted from 4 to 3.

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Increased by £5.52m (68% growth) via 3-year extension (March 2022), but **ODA cuts reduced operational flexibility** in FY 2022/23.
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: **Geographic focus narrowed** to high-priority FCAS (Ukraine, Sahel, Bosnia) while **thematic scope contracted** (Research strand paused).
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: **Shift from academic research to operational risk analysis**: Reduced grants to universities; increased contracts for real-time data providers.

pathway_changes: Removed Research and Evidence pathway (linked to paused SCF).
Strengthened **policy uptake pathways** for risk assessments (e.g., direct feed into OCSM’s Global Conflict Risk Assessment).
Added **crisis response mechanisms** (e.g., Ukraine rapid-analysis model).
assumptions_updated: Assumption that SCF would drive demand for research **invalidated** (SCF paused).
**New assumption**: Open-source data and deployable expertise are critical for real-time conflict response.

management_restructuring.governance_restructured: **Tighter operational oversight** added for HEROs/Palladium deliveries (lesson from Bosnia DCE delays).
management_restructuring.oversight_changed: Increased from quarterly to **monthly for high-priority projects** (e.g., Ukraine tracker).
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: **Delegated authority to programme leads** for rapid reallocation, with SRO/PRO approval for strategic changes (e.g., strand pausing).

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: **Added**: Ukraine (post-invasion); **Removed**: No locations dropped, but **reduced engagement in non-priority FCAS**.
geographic_scope_changes.geographic_focus_shifted: From **global thematic research** to **targeted FCAS hotspots** (Ukraine, Sahel, Bosnia).
geographic_scope_changes.country_changes: No countries removed; **Ukraine added as urgent priority**.

contextual_shocks: **Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (Feb 2022)**: Triggered rapid reallocation to open-source analysis and risk tracking.
**ODA budget cuts (FY 2022/23)**: Forced pause of Research strand and reprioritization.
**HMG Strategic Conflict Framework (SCF) pause**: Removed original justification for Research strand.
performance_issues: **HEROs/Palladium delivery delays** (e.g., Bosnia DCE) led to tighter oversight.
learning_insights: Open-source data proved more **policy-relevant** than academic research for real-time decision-making.
**Flexible funding** enabled rapid Ukraine response, validating the model.
strategic_opportunities: OCSM’s establishment (2021 Integrated Review) created demand for **operational risk tools** (e.g., Global Conflict Risk Assessment).

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: High (baseline flexibility enabled Ukraine pivot and strand consolidation).
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: High (lessons from Bosnia DCE and open-source partnerships directly informed governance tweaks).

fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Active conflict in **Ukraine (2022–23)**, Sahel (ongoing jihadist violence), Bosnia (political instability).

**HMG Strategic Conflict Framework (SCF) pause**: Removed a key programme pillar.

major_external_shocks.conflict_escalation: **Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (Feb 2022)**: Dominated programme reprioritization.

political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: Shift from **long-term research** (SCF-linked) to **immediate risk analysis** (OCSM-driven).
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: **FCDO’s reduced ODA capacity** limited ability to absorb academic research; **OCSM’s operational focus** aligned better with GSRA’s pivot.

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: **Open-source investigation orgs** (e.g., Centre for Information Resilience) emerged as critical suppliers; **academic partners reduced** due to strand pause.
