programme_metadata.programme_title: Fiscal Transparency and Accountability Initiative (FTAI)

output_1.title: More effective and transparent government audit through peer to peer support

output_2.title: Embedding transparency in Ukraine's reconstruction process

output_3.title: Promoting open contracting globally

output_4.title: Promoting budget transparency including by increasing the capacity of CSOs

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: FCDO approved a time and cost extension in April 2024, adding two years and £6.5 million to the programme to: (a) mitigate initial delays, and (b) allocate £3.8 million to the DREAM platform in Ukraine and £2.7 million for emerging priorities like climate finance and debt transparency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: All three partners (OCP, IBP, NAO) performed at or above expectations. NAO exceeded targets by establishing partnerships with five SAIs (vs. planned three), OCP made steady progress with DREAM in Ukraine, and IBP met log-frame indicators in focus countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme operates under FCDO’s Centre of Expertise for Public Finance, with three pillars: Peer-to-Peer Support, Evidence into Action, and the Public Finance Resource Centre. No significant deviations from planned governance were noted.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination among partners was effective but could be improved. The review recommends formalizing collaboration strategies and standardizing reporting templates to enhance synergy.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was executed as planned, with grants allocated to OCP (£3.3m for DREAM), IBP (£2.35m for global campaigns), and NAO (£1.45m for SAI capacity building). No procurement issues were flagged.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was consistent with plans, though the review noted a need for more formalized monitoring of outcome/impact indicators (e.g., case studies in standard formats).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated flexibility by reallocating resources to address delays (e.g., Ukraine war impacts) and emerging priorities (e.g., DREAM’s expanded role in Public Investment Management).
adaptive_management_examples: In Ukraine, OCP adapted DREAM’s use from transparency reporting to project selection, aligning with broader infrastructure investment goals.
In Kenya, NAO adjusted training workshops to better contextualize proposals for local political/constitutional setups based on partner feedback.
Allocated £2.7m from the extension to new priorities like climate finance and debt transparency.

main_implementation_challenges: Initial delays required a time/cost extension to mitigate impacts.
Lack of standardized case studies for monitoring outcome/impact indicators.
External factors (e.g., Ukraine war) disrupted legislative progress but also created opportunities for strategic relationship-building.
external_factors_impact: The war in Ukraine delayed some legislative reforms but accelerated the adoption of DREAM for reconstruction transparency.
Political transitions in focus countries (e.g., Tanzania) required adaptive engagement strategies.
Global economic pressures (e.g., debt crises) highlighted the need for expanded focus on sovereign debt transparency.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated demand for DREAM’s use beyond reconstruction (e.g., Public Investment Management) required scaling up technical support.
Civil society constraints in some countries limited participation in budget processes despite government openness (e.g., Rwanda).
Currency fluctuations and inflation in Ukraine affected project costs, though DREAM’s donor support mitigated risks.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited local capacity to fully utilize transparent fiscal data (e.g., Rwanda’s OAG needed support to implement participatory audits).
NAO’s rapid expansion of SAI partnerships (5 vs. planned 3) stretched resources for tailored support.
risk_materialization: Delays in Ukraine’s legislative reforms due to war (mitigated by focusing on DREAM implementation).
Underestimation of demand for DREAM’s broader applications, requiring additional funding.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. The £6.5m extension was fully allocated: £3.8m to DREAM and £2.7m to new priorities. Original grants to OCP, IBP, and NAO were executed as planned.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High. The programme exceeded output targets (e.g., NAO’s 5 SAI partnerships vs. 3 planned) and demonstrated cost efficiency (e.g., DREAM’s expansion to £5bn in tracked projects with minimal additional cost).
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Partners submitted progress reports on time, and FCDO’s oversight ensured compliance. No financial irregularities were reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Above planned levels. For example, DREAM’s scalability reduced per-project monitoring costs, and NAO’s in-country visits optimized training delivery (57 days across 8 visits).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partially. While no co-funding shortfalls were noted, the extension’s £6.5m covered gaps caused by external factors (e.g., Ukraine war).
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Minimal direct impact, though Ukraine’s economic instability increased the relative value of DREAM’s transparency tools for donors.

key_delivery_lessons: Peer-to-peer models (e.g., NAO’s SAI collaborations) are highly effective but require contextualization to local governance structures.
Digital platforms (e.g., DREAM) can exceed transparency goals if designed for scalability and multi-stakeholder use.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., the £2.7m reallocation) enable responsive adaptation to emerging priorities.
successful_delivery_practices: NAO’s short in-country visits combined with remote support optimized capacity-building efficiency.
OCP’s collaborative approach with Ukraine’s government ensured DREAM’s rapid adoption and donor buy-in.
IBP’s use of the Open Budget Survey (OBS) provided measurable benchmarks for transparency progress.
management_adaptations_made: Added two years to the programme to address delays and expand scope.
Prioritized standardization of reporting (e.g., case study templates) to improve outcome monitoring.
Formalized collaboration strategies among partners to reduce duplication.
innovations_attempted: DREAM’s expansion from a transparency tool to a project selection platform in Ukraine.
NAO’s introduction of participatory audit methodologies in Rwanda’s OAG.
Use of OCDS (Open Contracting Data Standard) in Rwanda’s e-GP procurement system to enhance data usability.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed: While the theory of change remains unchanged, the review reiterates the need to update inputs/outputs to reflect new pathways (e.g., climate finance).
Not yet implemented: Standardized case study formats and outcome indicator tracking are still pending.
forward_recommendations: Update the theory of change to clarify ambition and pathways for emerging priorities (e.g., climate finance, debt transparency).
Review and revise the results framework/logframe within two months, including milestones and final targets.
Allocate the remaining £2.7m to high-impact areas like climate finance and responsible infrastructure.
Improve partner collaboration through formalized strategies and shared learning platforms.
Develop a process for systematically generating evidence on fiscal transparency impacts.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Moderately effective. Planned risks (e.g., Ukraine war delays) were mitigated through adaptive management, but unanticipated demands (e.g., DREAM’s scalability) required reactive adjustments. The review recommends proactive scenario planning for similar future risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: Five SAIs (Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania) received NAO capacity-building; DREAM tracked £5bn in Ukraine reconstruction projects; IBP’s OBS covered 125 countries (with focus on Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania).
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Civil society organizations in focus countries gained tools to demand fiscal transparency; Ukrainian citizens and donors accessed DREAM for monitoring.

policy_influence_achieved: Rwanda’s OAG adopted participatory audits and OCDS in procurement systems.
Tanzania’s government collaborated with civil society to improve budget transparency (second-highest OBS improvement).
Ukraine’s DREAM platform influenced Public Investment Management reforms.
capacity_building_results: NAO trained SAI staff in performance audits, IT auditing, and risk assessment (e.g., Kenya’s OAG improved annual report transparency).
OCP’s support enabled Rwanda’s RPPA to integrate OCDS into e-GP systems, enhancing procurement data usability.
IBP’s OBS data helped civil society in focus countries advocate for budget reforms.
unintended_consequences: Positive: DREAM’s adoption for broader public investment management in Ukraine exceeded original scope.
Negative: Rapid SAI partnership expansion stretched NAO’s capacity for deep contextualization in some countries.
scalability_evidence: DREAM’s success in Ukraine demonstrates potential for replication in other post-conflict/reconstruction contexts.
NAO’s peer-to-peer model is scalable to additional SAIs with tailored adjustments.
OCDS integration in Rwanda’s procurement system can be adapted by other countries.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme demonstrates strong performance (Overall Output Score: A), high value for money, and alignment with FCDO’s public finance priorities. The extension addresses initial delays and expands focus to emerging areas (climate finance, debt transparency).
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Yes, with adaptations. The peer-to-peer and digital platform models are proven, but require continued partner coordination and standardized monitoring.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Update the theory of change and results framework to reflect new priorities.
Strengthen outcome/impact monitoring through standardized case studies.
Allocate remaining £2.7m to climate finance, debt transparency, or responsible infrastructure.
Enhance partner collaboration and evidence-generation mechanisms.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Mixed (Grant/Contract to consortium of Institute for Fiscal Studies and ODI Global)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £15m full-life budget (2023-2030) across 6 partner countries (Ethiopia, Ghana, Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria)
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Direct funding to lead consortium (IFS/ODI) with sub-contracts for country-level delivery; annual tranches based on milestones
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium - Built-in flexibility for country-specific adaptations but within fixed annual envelopes

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch central governance with country-level embedded advisors; joint IFS/ODI programme management unit (PMU) in London
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly progress reviews with FCDO; annual independent reviews; country-level MEL frameworks
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Consortium-led decision-making with FCDO approval for major adaptations; country teams empowered for operational decisions

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Consortium model (IFS + ODI Global) as core implementers with direct partnerships with 6 country Finance Ministries/TPUs
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Research institutes (IFS/ODI) + Government (TPUs in Finance Ministries) + Revenue Authorities

partner_roles_planned.IFS: Technical lead on microsimulation modeling and tax policy analysis
partner_roles_planned.ODI: Capacity building and policy advocacy support
partner_roles_planned.TPUs: Primary beneficiaries and co-implementers of policy reforms

partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award to IFS/ODI consortium based on Phase I/II performance; government partners pre-selected via FCDO country offices

consortium_baseline.lead_partner_planned: Joint leadership (no single designated lead; IFS/ODI co-lead)
consortium_baseline.consortium_governance_planned: Joint Steering Committee (IFS/ODI/FCDO); shared PMU; consensus-based decision-making

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Mixed (Grant/Contract to consortium) with increased multilateral coordination (World Bank/IMF)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £15m maintained but with reprioritized country allocations (Kenya/Nigeria delayed rollout; Uganda/Rwanda expanded)
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Flexible tranches with accelerated disbursements for high-performing countries (e.g., Uganda data lab); delayed disbursements for Kenya/Nigeria
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High - Significant reallocation between countries and activities (e.g., data initiatives scaled up, classroom training reduced)

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Enhanced central governance with new Senior Project Manager (joint IFS/ODI); increased FCDO integration via country offices
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Monthly check-ins for high-priority countries (Uganda/Rwanda); ad-hoc technical reviews for emerging issues (e.g., Ethiopia GDP methodology)
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: More decentralized to country teams for operational decisions; FCDO approval retained for budget reallocations >10%

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Expanded to include UNU-WIDER (Uganda data lab) and increased World Bank/IMF coordination; core consortium (IFS/ODI) retained
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Original partners + UNU-WIDER (research) + World Bank/IMF (policy coordination)

partner_roles_actual.IFS: Technical lead (unchanged) + increased cross-country knowledge sharing (e.g., Ethiopia-Uganda GDP methodology)
partner_roles_actual.ODI: Capacity building (reduced classroom training; increased on-job mentoring) + new Sustainability Checklist tool
partner_roles_actual.TPUs: Expanded role in data governance (e.g., Rwanda’s shared folders system)
partner_roles_actual.Revenue Authorities: Active data collaborators (e.g., Uganda’s VAT database co-creation)

partner_names_actual: Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) - Uganda

consortium_actual.consortium_structure_actual: Core IFS/ODI consortium retained but with operational partnerships (e.g., UNU-WIDER); no formal consortium expansion
consortium_actual.lead_partner_actual: Joint leadership maintained; new Senior Project Manager as de facto operational lead
consortium_actual.consortium_governance_actual: Original governance retained but with added Sustainability Working Group and Skills Development Working Group

funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope contracted (Kenya/Nigeria delayed); technical scope expanded (data management tools, sustainability planning)
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: Increased coordination with multilateral partners (World Bank/IMF) for policy alignment; no shift in core funding modality

geographic_scope_changes.country_changes: No countries removed; two countries (Kenya/Nigeria) had implementation paused

Postponement of Data for Tax Policy Analysis note publication

t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Adequate - Core design (consortium model, embedded advisors) proved resilient, but underestimated capacity-building complexity and country-specific shocks

programme_metadata.programme_title: Tax Analysis in Developing Countries, Phase III

output_1.title: Taxpayer micro-level data is made available to support improved modelling and analyses of national tax policies

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Target for Output 1.1 (data mapping in new countries) was revised downward from 2 countries to 0 due to delays in Kenya and Nigeria beyond TaxDev's control. Programme leveraged existing partnerships (e.g., UNU-WIDER in Uganda) and introduced new tools like the Sustainability Checklist to improve long-term data management.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong demand for hands-on tax policy analysis support, which exceeded expectations but created time constraints for capacity-building activities. Uganda and Rwanda showed exceptional progress in data management, while Ethiopia faced persistent macroeconomic challenges limiting revenue gains despite strong advisory support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: A new Senior Project Manager (jointly funded by IFS/ODI) was introduced in London to identify cross-country efficiencies. Skills Development Working Group was established to standardize training materials. Coordination with IMF/World Bank was strengthened for aligned engagements in partner countries.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination was demonstrated through shared methodologies (e.g., tax-to-GDP estimation between Ethiopia and Uganda) and joint events (e.g., Annual Public Finance Conference with World Bank). However, integration with wider FCDO country portfolios remains inconsistent, particularly in Ethiopia where macroeconomic challenges persisted.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was adaptive, with increased focus on sustainability tools (e.g., Sustainability Checklist) and transition planning. Previous recommendations on data protection policies and systematic resource-building remained unaddressed as of 2025.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by reprioritizing advisor time toward high-demand policy analysis (e.g., VAT progressivity research in Uganda) while deprioritizing data mapping in new countries due to external delays. Adaptive use of existing partnerships (e.g., UNU-WIDER in Uganda) to amplify impact.
adaptive_management_examples: Introduction of the Sustainability Checklist to guide support decisions for Tax Policy Units (TPUs).
Replication of the Uganda data lab model (UNU-WIDER/URA partnership) considered for other countries.
Shift from planned data mapping in Kenya/Nigeria to deepening support in core countries due to delays.
New Skills Development Working Group to standardize training materials across countries.

main_implementation_challenges: Mismatch between programme timeline/incentives and the complexity of sustainable capacity-building in TPUs.
High demand for policy analysis support left limited time for capacity-building activities.
Macroeconomic challenges in partner countries (e.g., falling tax-to-GDP ratio in Ethiopia despite strong advisory support).
Delayed programme rollout in Kenya and Nigeria due to factors beyond TaxDev's control.
external_factors_impact: UK ODA cuts and reprioritization reduced predictability of funding, though TaxDev III remained a "patient, dedicated" programme.
Macroeconomic instability in partner countries (e.g., Ethiopia) limited revenue gains despite technical improvements.
COVID-19 impacts not explicitly mentioned, but broader PFM challenges persisted.
contextual_constraints_new: TPUs' organizational culture, HR policies, and pay structures emerged as critical but unaddressed barriers to sustainable capacity-building.
Limited awareness among TPU staff about the programme's 2030 end date, raising transition risks.
Need for broader PFM reforms to complement tax policy improvements (e.g., Ethiopia case).
partner_relationship_issues: Strong demand for research support created tension with capacity-building goals, as advisors prioritized immediate analysis over long-term training.
Varied progress across countries: Uganda/Rwanda excelled in data management, while Ethiopia struggled with macroeconomic headwinds.
FCDO country teams' engagement with TaxDev advisors was inconsistent, limiting integration with wider UK support.
capacity_constraints_emerged: TPUs lacked institutional structures (e.g., data-sharing protocols, analytical skills retention) to sustain gains post-2030.
Advisors' time constraints due to high demand for policy analysis reduced focus on systemic capacity-building.
Limited progress on previous recommendations (e.g., data protection policies, standardized training resources).
risk_materialization: Delayed rollout in Kenya/Nigeria (operational risk).
Macroeconomic risks in Ethiopia materialized, offsetting technical improvements in tax policy.
Sustainability risks due to TPUs' reliance on TaxDev support without embedded institutional changes.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Staff costs remained within budget in 2025. Programme identified cost-sharing opportunities (e.g., joint conferences with World Bank) to optimize spend. Travel costs were carefully managed based on value-for-money assessments by partner governments.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Strong. Salaries, travel, and research dissemination were main cost drivers, with market rates for tax expertise and judicious travel spending.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Strong. Cross-country sharing of tools/templates (e.g., tax-to-GDP methodologies between Ethiopia/Uganda) and expert time maximized outputs. New Senior Project Manager role introduced to identify further efficiencies.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Strong. Evidence of increased use of data/evidence in tax policymaking (e.g., Output 4 demand), but sustainability of impact remains a question. New tools (Sustainability Checklist, Skills Development Working Group) introduced to address this.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Moderate. Some progress in integrating equity considerations (e.g., VAT progressivity research in Uganda), but broader equity impacts not systematically measured.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. Costs were transparent and aligned with delivery needs. Collaborative funding models (e.g., joint IFS/ODI Senior Project Manager) improved coordination. No significant financial management issues reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High. Efficiency gains through: (1) Shared methodologies/tools across countries, (2) Leveraging existing partnerships (e.g., UNU-WIDER in Uganda), (3) Strategic use of international travel based on partner feedback.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. Cost-sharing achieved for specific events (e.g., Annual Public Finance Conference with World Bank), but broader co-funding (e.g., from partner governments) not systematically tracked.

key_delivery_lessons: Sustainable capacity-building requires addressing systemic issues (HR policies, organizational culture) beyond technical training.
Demand-driven support (e.g., policy analysis) can crowd out long-term capacity goals if not actively managed.
Cross-country learning (e.g., Uganda/Rwanda data management models) accelerates progress but requires intentional knowledge-sharing mechanisms.
Programme persistence over time yields gradual gains (e.g., tax expenditure reporting improvements), but macroeconomic context can limit visible impacts.
successful_delivery_practices: Use of embedded advisors to build trust and tailor support to TPU needs.
Introduction of practical tools (Sustainability Checklist, Skills Development Working Group) to institutionalize learning.
Leveraging existing partnerships (e.g., UNU-WIDER/URA in Uganda) to amplify data access and analytical capacity.
Strategic collaboration with multilateral partners (IMF/World Bank) to align engagements and reduce duplication.
management_adaptations_made: Shift from data mapping targets to deepening support in core countries due to external delays.
Prioritization of sustainability planning (e.g., Sustainability Checklist) in response to repeated review recommendations.
Creation of cross-cutting roles (Senior Project Manager) to identify efficiencies and standardize processes.
Increased focus on transition planning for 2030 programme end, though TPU awareness remains low.
innovations_attempted: Sustainability Checklist to guide support decisions and transition planning.
Skills Development Working Group to create standardized training materials.
Replication of Uganda's data lab model (UNU-WIDER/URA partnership) explored for other countries.
Collaborative research on equity impacts (e.g., VAT progressivity in Uganda).

unaddressed: Finalization and publication of the "Data for Tax Policy Analysis" note.
Development of special data protection protocols for embedded staff.
partially_addressed: Capacity-building deepened through new working groups, but systemic challenges (HR, culture) remain unaddressed.
Integration with wider FCDO country portfolios improved in some cases (e.g., Ghana) but remains inconsistent.

forward_recommendations: Develop a transition plan for 2030 programme end, including TPU awareness-raising and institutionalization of tools/processes.
Pilot new capacity-building approaches in Kenya/Nigeria to address systemic barriers (e.g., HR policies, organizational culture).
Strengthen FCDO country team engagement to integrate TaxDev with broader PFM support (e.g., World Bank/IMF collaborations).
Complete pending recommendations on data protection policies and systematic resource-building.
Expand equity-focused research (e.g., tax progressivity) and integrate findings into policy dialogues.

strengths: Proactive adaptation to external delays (e.g., Kenya/Nigeria) by reprioritizing resources.
Introduction of tools (Sustainability Checklist) to mitigate transition risks.
Diversified partnerships (e.g., IMF/World Bank) to share risks and align support.
weaknesses: Repeated failure to address data protection risks despite prior recommendations.
Limited contingency planning for macroeconomic shocks (e.g., Ethiopia's falling tax-to-GDP ratio).
Late focus on transition planning for 2030 programme end.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 6 partner countries' Tax Policy Units (TPUs) received support, with notable progress in Uganda, Rwanda, and Ghana on data management and analytical capacity.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Policymakers in partner countries demonstrated increased demand for evidence-based tax policy tools, though broader revenue impacts were limited by macroeconomic factors (e.g., Ethiopia).

evidence: Increased use of data/evidence in tax policymaking processes (e.g., VAT analysis in Uganda, customs data in Ghana).
TPU advisors reported gradual gains in tax expenditure reporting and policy costing.
Demand for TaxDev research from policymakers signals growing influence.
limitations: Macroeconomic challenges (e.g., Ethiopia) limited translation of policy improvements into revenue gains.
Policy influence varied by country; stronger in Uganda/Rwanda, weaker where PFM reforms lagged.

achievements: Improved data access/management in Uganda (URA data lab), Rwanda (structured RRA processes), and Ghana (customs data).
TPU staff demonstrated increased ability to clean/analyze administrative datasets (e.g., beer excise data in Rwanda).
New Sustainability Checklist and Skills Development Working Group introduced to institutionalize capacity.
gaps: Limited progress on systemic issues (HR policies, pay structures) critical for long-term retention of skills.
Capacity gains remained concentrated in core countries; Kenya/Nigeria lagged due to delayed rollout.

positive: Stronger cross-country collaboration (e.g., methodology-sharing between Ethiopia/Uganda).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Budget reduced from £25M to £14.4M (£8.4M WB, £6M ACTED) due to UK ODA cuts; Kazakhstan added as new country; some original activities dropped. New e-commerce output (1.6) added in response to government demand.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank (Pillar 1) performed well overall (A scores) but faced government-led administrative reforms in Uzbekistan that slowed progress. ACTED (Pillar 2) struggled in Uzbekistan (C score) due to lack of strategic direction, though performed well in Tajikistan/Kyrgyzstan (A scores). Both partners showed strong adaptability to context changes (e.g., WB's response to political/economic shifts, ACTED's 100% activity delivery rate).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance structure developed post-2022 review but not yet finalized. SRO handover from Bishkek-based to new structure in progress. Coordination between pillars identified as weak point, with collaboration outcomes unmet.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Donor-government coordination platform for regional development established but requires stronger coherence between FCDO and WB visions. Regular WB-government stakeholder meetings introduced for work program adjustments. Pillar collaboration outcomes (2 cases required) remained unmet due to weak inter-pillar linkage mechanisms.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight needed for ACTED's Pillar 2 in Uzbekistan due to underperformance (C score). WB's Pillar 1 required less intensive oversight due to consistent A scores, though adaptive management was noted (e.g., e-commerce inception mission).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: High flexibility demonstrated: (1) WB adapted to political/economic changes (e.g., DSGE training expansion, Sanarip Aymak scaling); (2) ACTED adjusted work plans to meet 100% delivery; (3) New e-commerce output added mid-implementation in response to Kyrgyz government request. Budget reallocations made to prioritize strategic coherence post-ODA cuts.
adaptive_management_examples: WB's addition of e-commerce output (1.6) after Kyrgyz government request, including 4 new activities (SME onboarding, policy/regulatory support).
ACTED's 100% delivery rate despite context challenges, with embedded adaptation planning in work plans.
WB's response to Uzbekistan's administrative reforms by maintaining Pillar 1 A score through adjusted timelines.
Methodology pilots for Sanarip Aymak expanded from 2 to 4 LSGs based on initial results (5-9% increases in registrations/certificates).
Gender mainstreaming integrated into regional development via hands-on LSG training and inclusive socio-economic methodologies.

main_implementation_challenges: Uzbekistan's government-led administrative reforms caused personnel turnover, slowing Pillar 1 progress.
ACTED's Pillar 2 underperformance in Uzbekistan (C score) due to weak strategic direction and organizational issues.
Kyrgyzstan's Pillar 2 activities lacked clear pathways to outcomes/impact despite A score.
Coordination between Pillar 1 (WB) and Pillar 2 (ACTED) remained weak, with collaboration outcomes unmet.
Budget reductions (from £25M to £14.4M) required reprioritization and dropped activities, increasing delivery pressure.
external_factors_impact: Uzbekistan: Administrative reforms created personnel instability, delaying policy engagement.
Kyrgyzstan: Stable operating environment (no political crises) facilitated smooth implementation.
Tajikistan: Absence of external shocks and clear development needs enabled strong performance (A scores).
Regional: Post-COVID economic fluctuations required adaptive responses (e.g., DSGE model updates for inflation/remittance data).

Media/civil society sustainability challenges in Uzbekistan (no CSOs met outcome 4's "sustainable business plan" bar).
partner_relationship_issues: WB-FCDO alignment gaps identified, particularly in Kazakhstan where WB's large scale contrasted with need for local NGO engagement (e.g., gender training).
ACTED's underperformance in Uzbekistan strained trust; required stronger FCDO oversight.
Delayed finalization of governance structures post-SRO handover created temporary coordination gaps.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Kyrgyz LSGs: Initial 79.7% passport registration (vs. 80% target) revealed data usage capacity gaps, addressed via hands-on training (5-9% improvement in system metrics).

risk_materialization: Budget reduction risk materialized: £10.6M cut led to dropped activities and reprioritization pressure.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: Original £25M budget reduced to £14.4M (£8.4M WB, £6M ACTED) due to UK ODA cuts. Despite reductions, 100% of planned activities delivered to high standard (per WB/ACTED reports). E-commerce output added without additional funding, reallocating existing resources.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated: (1) WB's L2Kgz toolkit provided unique high-frequency data (e.g., public views on reforms) not available elsewhere; (2) Sanarip Aymak training led to 5-65% improvements in system usage metrics (e.g., 65.15% increase in certificates issued); (3) DSGE training equipped 14 policymakers with macroeconomic modeling skills. However, Kazakhstan extension requires flexible results framework to maintain VFM given short timeline.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial management by both partners: (1) WB met 100% activity delivery with adapted work plans; (2) ACTED achieved full milestone completion despite budget cuts. Action plan developed for National Bank of Kyrgyzstan (not in logframe) shows proactive cost control. No major audit findings reported.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency exceeded expectations in some areas: (1) Sanarip Aymak training covered 100% of LSGs with minimal additional cost, yielding 79.7% passport registration (near target); (2) E-commerce output leveraged existing WB capacity without new funding. However, Uzbekistan's Pillar 2 inefficiencies (C score) indicate room for improvement in ACTED's resource allocation.

key_delivery_lessons: Demand-driven approach is critical: Government buy-in (e.g., Kyrgyz e-commerce request) ensures higher impact than top-down designs.
Flexible output specifications enable adaptability: WB's ability to adjust milestones (e.g., 1.2-1.4) and add new outputs (1.6) was key to maintaining A scores.
Local partner scale matters: In Kazakhstan, WB's large-scale operations struggled to engage downstream NGOs, suggesting need for hybrid delivery models.
Clear scope agreements prevent misalignment: Lessons from Kazakhstan highlight need for upfront WB-government-FCDO alignment on outputs/timelines.
Hands-on training > theoretical capacity building: Sanarip Aymak's 5-65% metric improvements came from practical LSG training, not just tool development.
successful_delivery_practices: WB's adaptive work planning: Embedded adaptation mechanisms in annual plans to respond to political/economic changes (e.g., Uzbekistan reforms).
ACTED's milestone tracking: 100% activity delivery rate achieved through rigorous progress monitoring.
Pilot-based scaling: Sanarip Aymak methodologies piloted in 2 rayons/4 LSGs before wider rollout, ensuring relevance.
Gender mainstreaming integration: WB's gender assessment informed Country Partnership Framework and was embedded in LSG training/capacity building.
Stakeholder co-design: E-commerce output developed via Kyrgyz government collaboration, ensuring ownership.
management_adaptations_made: Governance structure overhaul post-2022 review to address SRO handover gaps (finalization pending).
Added regular WB-government stakeholder meetings to adjust work programs dynamically.
Revised output milestones (e.g., 1.2-1.4) to be more specific and measurable.
Developed action plan for National Bank of Kyrgyzstan (outside logframe) to address emerging financial stability needs.
Planned hire of Astana-based projects officer to address Kazakhstan oversight gap.
innovations_attempted: Sanarip Aymak system: Digital platform for LSG socio-economic planning, leading to 79.7% passport registration and 65% increase in certificates issued.
DSGE model training: Equipped 14 Kyrgyz policymakers with advanced macroeconomic modeling skills for inflation/remittance analysis.
E-commerce output (1.6): New activities to onboard SMEs on B2B platforms and develop regulatory frameworks, added mid-implementation.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Introduced a new ‘buy-in’ process for teams to access Evaluation Technical Assistance (ETA) when budget constraints prevented direct funding (~£300k of ETA work bought in by teams).

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Differentiated fee rates by expertise level (principal/expert) with capped QA days to control costs. Output-based payments with 20% retained until KPI evidence (e.g., user feedback) is submitted. Competitive tender process ensured VfM.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned: Added quarterly KPI validation (user feedback surveys, quality checks on 24% of QAs) and financial scrutiny (expert-level confirmation on invoices).

adaptive_management_examples: Developed MIS dashboards in response to demand for portfolio-wide evaluation data, demonstrated at PDC 2023 with high interest.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Transformative Economic Policy Programme

output_1.title: High quality technical assistance on trade and investment policies and capability development delivered to the Bangladesh government (by UNDP)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted from indirect to direct funding for think tanks; closed bilateral IGC partnership; launched new technical assistance component with Deloitte for banking sector reform; increased flexibility in response to political transition.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: UNDP faced persistent recruitment delays and capacity constraints, limiting responsiveness to reform agenda. Think tanks demonstrated high effectiveness in policy influence during reform window. Deloitte's technical assistance for banking sector was timely and impactful.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Programme maintained strong flexibility with strategic reserves, enabling rapid pivoting. Governance included senior engagement with interim government officials (e.g., central bank governor, BIDA head).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Close collaboration with interim government and inclusion of partners in government commissions enhanced coordination. UNDP's slow processes created bottlenecks in trade/investment policy support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: High-cost commercial partner (Deloitte) used for banking sector TA due to specialized expertise (£2,500/day fee rate, above FCDO ceiling). UNDP's procurement of external studies was discontinued due to poor value for money.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight of UNDP due to delivery delays; direct engagement with interim government replaced some planned indirect mechanisms. Strategic fund component allowed flexible oversight of think tanks.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Strategic reserves and flexible design enabled launch of new banking reform component post-political transition. Programme restructured delivery models (e.g., direct think tank funding) to align with reform priorities.
adaptive_management_examples: Launched Deloitte-led technical assistance for Bangladesh Bank in response to banking crisis (Summer 2024).
Reprioritized support to interim government's reform agenda, including think tank involvement in government commissions.
Discontinued low-value UNDP-commissioned studies; shifted to high-impact data tools like Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI).
Closed bilateral IGC partnership to reallocate resources to higher-priority areas.

main_implementation_challenges: Persistent UNDP recruitment delays and understaffing (e.g., BIDA's Research and Analytics Unit not fully functional).
Slow UNDP internal processes limiting responsiveness to interim government's reform timeline.
Difficulty in retaining skilled personnel for trade/investment policy components.
High fee rates for specialized consultants (e.g., £2,500/day for banking sector experts) stretching budget.
external_factors_impact: Political transition in 2024 (fall of previous government, interim government reforms) created both opportunities (reform openness) and challenges (instability).
Economic turbulence (banking sector crisis, LDC graduation pressures) increased demand for rapid programme adaptation.
IMF programme alignment required adjustments to policy support priorities.
contextual_constraints_new: Interim government's ambitious but unstable reform agenda required rapid programme realignment.
Unexpected need for banking sector stabilization (Summer 2024 crisis) diverted resources.
LDC graduation timeline (2026) accelerated demands for trade policy and investment reforms.
partner_relationship_issues: UNDP's delivery capacity constraints led to tensions over unmet expectations (e.g., BIDA RAU, Ministry of Commerce trade negotiators pool).
Think tanks' direct funding model improved alignment but required closer management to avoid mission creep.
Commercial partners (e.g., Deloitte) delivered high-quality TA but at premium costs, raising VfM concerns.
capacity_constraints_emerged: BIDA and Ministry of Commerce lacked internal capacity to absorb TA effectively (e.g., RAU understaffed, trade negotiators pool unformed).
UNDP's project management weaknesses exposed by recruitment delays and phase discontinuities.
Local think tanks required additional support to sustain policy influence post-programme.
risk_materialization: Political instability risk materialized with 2024 government transition, requiring programme pivot.
Banking sector instability risk materialized (Summer 2024), prompting emergency TA intervention.
Partner delivery risks (UNDP) persisted, though mitigated by flexible funding reallocation.

budget_execution_vs_plan: Overall budget execution aligned with increased ambition in 2024/25, though UNDP components underperformed.
Strategic fund component fully utilized for high-impact interventions (e.g., banking reform, think tank commissions).
Cost overruns in commercial TA (Deloitte) offset by savings from discontinued UNDP studies.
value_for_money_assessment: High VfM demonstrated in think tank support (low-cost, high policy influence during reform window).
PMI data tool (£1m total cost) provided unique, high-value economic indicator adopted by central bank.
UNDP-commissioned studies delivered poor VfM (low quality, unused by policymakers) and were discontinued.
Commercial TA (Deloitte) justified by critical need and expertise, despite premium costs.
financial_management_quality: Strong financial controls for strategic fund component, enabling rapid reallocation to emerging priorities.
UNDP faced challenges in financial planning due to recruitment delays and phase mismanagement.
Think tanks managed funds efficiently, with incentives for judicious spending.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Think tank delivery model highly cost-efficient (low overhead, high leverage of local expertise).
PMI tool achieved economies of scale as a public good used by multiple stakeholders.
UNDP's TA delivery inefficiencies (e.g., underutilized RAU) reduced cost-effectiveness in trade/investment components.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible programming is critical in volatile contexts (e.g., political transitions, economic crises).
Direct funding to local partners (think tanks) enhances agility and policy influence compared to multilateral intermediaries.
High-cost commercial expertise is justified for niche, high-stakes interventions (e.g., banking sector stabilization).
Data tools (e.g., PMI) can bridge evidence gaps and gain rapid policy uptake if designed for local relevance.
successful_delivery_practices: Strategic use of reserves to launch time-sensitive components (e.g., Deloitte TA for Bangladesh Bank).
Inclusion of think tank staff in government commissions leveraged programme investments for systemic influence.
Rapid pivot to interim government priorities demonstrated adaptive management strength.
Discontinuation of low-value activities (UNDP studies) freed resources for higher-impact work.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from indirect to direct think tank funding to improve alignment and accountability.
Closed underperforming components (e.g., bilateral IGC partnership) to focus on core priorities.
Increased oversight of UNDP delivery through dedicated project leads and alternative models (e.g., external project management firms).
Reprioritized TA to address immediate crises (banking sector) while maintaining long-term capacity building.
innovations_attempted: Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI): First forward-looking economic indicator in Bangladesh, adopted by central bank for monetary policy.
Flexible funding for think tanks to second staff to government commissions without compensation.
Hybrid delivery model combining commercial TA (Deloitte), multilateral support (UNDP), and local partners (think tanks).
Digital Business Identification (DBID) platform transferred to Ministry of Commerce for sustainable use.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed UNDP delivery delays through increased oversight but persistent issues remain.
Successfully implemented recommendations to leverage reform windows (e.g., interim government engagement).
Strategic fund component used effectively for adaptive programming as recommended in prior reviews.
forward_recommendations: Scope a successor programme by 2026 to sustain reforms post-TEPP, incorporating lessons on delivery models and partner capabilities.
Urgent action to resolve UNDP delivery constraints (e.g., appoint dedicated project lead, explore alternative providers like UNCTAD).
Maximize the interim government's reform window with high-impact, time-sensitive interventions (e.g., LDC graduation support).
Develop transition plans for think tanks to ensure sustained policy influence beyond programme lifecycle.
Conduct a VfM review of commercial TA costs to balance expertise needs with cost control.
risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in responding to materialized risks (e.g., political transition, banking crisis) through flexible design.
Proactive mitigation of partner risks (e.g., shifting from UNDP to direct think tank funding where feasible).
Strategic reserves proved essential for unplanned high-impact interventions.
Ongoing challenges in managing UNDP's structural delivery risks despite mitigations.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Interim government officials (central bank, BIDA, Ministry of Commerce) directly supported through TA.
Four local think tanks received capacity-building, with staff embedded in government reform commissions.
Policymakers and private sector analysts using PMI data for economic decision-making (monthly reach since Dec 2023).
Bangladesh Bank and commercial banks benefited from stabilization TA during 2024 crisis.
policy_influence_achieved: PMI adopted by central bank for monetary policy decisions.
Think tank staff contributed to interim government's economic reform commissions and task forces.
BIDA and Ministry of Commerce reforms advanced through targeted TA (e.g., investment summit, trade negotiators pool).
Banking sector stabilization measures influenced by Deloitte TA, preventing systemic crisis.
capacity_building_results: BIDA's Research and Analytics Unit established (though understaffed), providing foundation for evidence-based policymaking.
Think tanks developed mid-tier talent now engaged in government reform processes.
Ministry of Commerce initiated trade negotiators pool (though not yet fully operational).
Central bank staff trained on crisis response through Deloitte TA.
unintended_consequences: Positive: PMI became a trusted economic indicator beyond initial scope, used by private sector for investment decisions.
Positive: Think tanks' involvement in government commissions elevated their long-term credibility and influence.
Negative: UNDP's delivery delays created frustration among government partners, risking trust in multilateral TA.
scalability_evidence: PMI model scalable to other sectors/regions in Bangladesh given its policy uptake and low cost.
Think tank capacity-building approach replicable for other policy domains (e.g., climate, health).
Banking sector TA model (Deloitte) could be adapted for other financial stability challenges in similar contexts.
Digital tools (e.g., DBID platform) transferable to other government agencies for service delivery.

continuation_rationale: Strong alignment with UK's Growth Mission and Bangladesh Country Plan, especially post-LDC graduation.
Proven ability to deliver high-impact results in volatile contexts (e.g., banking crisis response, PMI adoption).
Interim government's reform agenda presents a unique window for economic policy influence.
Think tanks and data tools (PMI) provide sustainable platforms for continued engagement.
delivery_model_sustainability: Current hybrid model (commercial + local partners) is effective but requires adjustments to UNDP's role.
Direct think tank funding and strategic reserves should be retained for flexibility.
Long-term sustainability depends on government ownership of reforms (e.g., PMI, BIDA RAU).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Reduce reliance on UNDP by exploring alternative partners (e.g., UNCTAD, World Bank) for trade/investment TA.
Expand PMI to cover additional sectors (e.g., services, agriculture) to deepen economic insights.
Develop a transition plan for think tanks to secure independent funding post-2028.
Incorporate LDC graduation support as a cross-cutting priority in future phases.
Conduct a lessons-learned exercise to inform successor programme design by 2026.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Investing in Nature, Forests and Land Use (Inafolu) Programme

output_1.title: Investment

output_2.title: Enabling environment

output_3.title: Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL)

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from planned direct investment in GoI financial agencies to partnership-based approach (GGGI, KADIN, UN-REDD) due to stalled dialogue. Added new partnerships (KADIN for private sector engagement, UN-REDD for provincial carbon schemes) to complement GGGI’s work. Adaptive programming used to respond to political delays (e.g., presidential election).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: GGGI faced delays in inception phase due to GoI engagement challenges (election-related slowdowns), requiring extension of inception phase. TAF (Output 2B) performed as expected, with strong subnational engagement. KADIN and UN-REDD partnerships added to address gaps in private sector and carbon finance mobilization.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Biweekly catch-ups with GGGI (Output 1) and quarterly reporting from all partners. MEL component still in procurement, limiting programme-level results tracking. Governance structures with GoI partially established (MoUs signed, but workplans pending).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Cross-output coordination emerging (e.g., links between Output 1’s UN-REDD carbon schemes and Output 2’s Ecological Fiscal Transfers). Challenges in aligning new partnerships (KADIN, UN-REDD) with GGGI’s work; coherence efforts planned for Nov 2024.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Output 3 (MEL) procurement ongoing. Output 2A (Spatial Planning) procurement not started due to unresolved concept with GoI. Accountable Grants signed for KADIN (Apr 2024) and TAF (Sep 2023) within planned timelines.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to GGGI’s inception delays and political context. Monthly progress bulletins and ad-hoc check-ins supplement formal reporting. MEL contractor (once procured) expected to strengthen oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme used flexibility to: (1) Add KADIN/UN-REDD partnerships to Output 1; (2) Extend GGGI’s inception phase; (3) Develop IKN-focused activities under Output 2B. CDEL/RDEL balance shifted from majority-CDEL to even split, requiring adaptive budget management.
adaptive_management_examples: Added KADIN partnership to leverage private sector networks after GGGI’s GoI engagement delays.
Explored UN-REDD’s provincial carbon scheme to diversify investment mobilization pathways.
Developed IKN-focused activities under Output 2B to respond to GoI’s request for Nusantara Capital City support.
Extended GGGI’s inception phase to accommodate election-related delays.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in GoI engagement (presidential election in Feb 2024 stalled MoU finalization and workplan approvals).
GGGI’s limited capacity during inception phase (recruitment of investment officers ongoing).
Unresolved concept for Output 2A (Spatial Planning) with GoI, halting procurement.
CDEL compliance challenges (risk of perverse incentives for community-based interventions like FPIC).
Shift in CDEL/RDEL balance from majority-CDEL to 50/50, requiring reprioritization.
external_factors_impact: Indonesia’s February 2024 presidential election paused GoI engagement for ~6 months, delaying Output 1’s inception.
New administration (taking office Oct 2024) creates uncertainty for policy alignment and partner strategies.
Legislative reforms (e.g., multi-use forestry licenses) enabled new partnerships (e.g., KADIN’s Regenerative Forest Business Hub).
Global carbon market fluctuations may affect Output 1’s investment mobilization targets.
contextual_constraints_new: GoI’s request for IKN (Nusantara Capital City) support required unplanned adaptation of Output 2B.
Subnational authorities’ varying capacity to implement FoLU policies (e.g., Riau Province’s carbon scheme readiness).
Limited MEL capacity delayed programme-level results framework development (expected July 2025).
partner_relationship_issues: GGGI’s slow progress in formalizing GoI agreements raised concerns about delivery pace.
TAF’s strong subnational trust contrasts with GGGI’s national-level focus, requiring better coordination.
KADIN’s private-sector approach complements but risks duplicating GGGI’s efforts without clear division of labor.
capacity_constraints_emerged: GGGI lacked dedicated investment officers until mid-2024 recruitment drive.
FCDO’s limited in-house FoLU technical expertise required reliance on partners for adaptive management.
MEL contractor’s absence hindered real-time learning and theory-of-change refinement.
risk_materialization: Political risk: Election delays materialized, affecting GoI engagement (mitigated via inception phase extension).
Partner capacity risk: GGGI’s understaffing for investment mobilization (mitigated via recruitment and KADIN partnership).
CDEL compliance risk: Emerged as a constraint for community-focused interventions (ongoing mitigation).
Policy alignment risk: New administration’s priorities (post-Oct 2024) may require programme adjustments.

budget_execution_vs_plan.overall: Underspend due to delayed implementation (Output 1 inception extension, Output 2A procurement pause).
budget_execution_vs_plan.output_2: £10.63M allocated to TAF (Setapak 4); spend on track. Output 2A (£0 spent; procurement pending).
budget_execution_vs_plan.output_3: Procurement ongoing; no spend to date.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Local resourcing achieved (all staff except GGGI Team Leader are local). NPAC rates within benchmarks (GGGI: 13%; TAF: 13.4%).
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Limited by inception delays; efficiency gains expected post-2024 with full implementation. Quarterly reporting and biweekly GGGI check-ins enable adaptive resource use.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: Too early to assess outcome-level VfM. Early signs of equity focus (indigenous/women/youth groups targeted in Output 2B).
value_for_money_assessment.transformational_potential: High if investment mobilization (Output 1) and policy reforms (Output 2) align; risks remain due to GoI engagement delays.

financial_management_quality.gggi: Sound but slowed by GoI approval processes. Budget revisions pending post-election.
financial_management_quality.taf: Strong; transparent reporting and subnational partner management.
financial_management_quality.fcdo: Proactive in reallocating underspend to new partnerships (KADIN/UN-REDD).

cost_efficiency_achieved.planned: NPAC rates on target; local hiring reduced costs.
cost_efficiency_achieved.unplanned: Inception phase extension added ~£500K to Output 1’s pre-implementation costs.
cost_efficiency_achieved.opportunities: Co-funding potential with UN-REDD/Riau Province carbon scheme (under exploration).

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not explicitly mentioned; assumed managed within NPAC contingencies.

key_delivery_lessons: Adaptive programming is critical in politically volatile contexts (e.g., election delays).
Diversified partnerships (GGGI + KADIN + UN-REDD) can mitigate single-partner risks.
CDEL compliance requires early planning to avoid perverse incentives for community engagement.
Subnational trust (TAF’s CSO networks) can compensate for national-level delays (GGGI/GoI).
successful_delivery_practices: Biweekly GGGI check-ins enabled rapid response to delays.
TAF’s subnational CSO partnerships facilitated early Output 2B progress.
Flexible grant mechanisms (Accountable Grants) allowed quick onboarding of KADIN/UN-REDD.
MEL Adviser’s process-based outputs provided interim learning despite framework delays.
management_adaptations_made: Extended GGGI’s inception phase to accommodate GoI delays.
Added KADIN/UN-REDD to Output 1 to diversify investment pathways.
Developed IKN-focused activities under Output 2B to align with GoI priorities.
Shifted CDEL/RDEL balance management to maintain flexibility.
innovations_attempted: UN-REDD’s provincial results-based carbon scheme (Riau Province).
KADIN’s Regenerative Forest Business Hub (private-sector policy alignment).
IKN-focused forest management activities (Output 2B adaptation).
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: N/A (first Annual Review; no prior recommendations).

forward_recommendations.recommendation: Extend programme timeline or reduce budget to align with delayed implementation.
Finalize MEL Hub contract to develop programme-level results framework.
GGGI to prioritize investment officer recruitment and public/private finance mobilization.
Clarify Output 2A (Spatial Planning) concept with GoI to initiate procurement.
Enhance coordination between GGGI, KADIN, and UN-REDD to avoid duplication.
Develop CDEL-for-nature guidelines to balance compliance with community engagement.

weaknesses: Underestimated election-related delays (6-month pause in GoI engagement).

Increased oversight of GGGI’s recruitment plans.
Prioritized MEL Hub procurement to improve risk monitoring.

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from in-person to phone surveys (Call 4 and Call 5) due to COVID-19, enabling real-time data collection on pandemic impacts. Planned hybrid approach (phone + fieldwork) for Round 7 to balance cost and effectiveness.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Oxford University and country teams (Ethiopia, India, Peru, Vietnam) delivered effectively despite COVID-19 challenges. New leadership (Director Catherine Porter) improved strategic direction, financial management, and stakeholder engagement. Loss of qualitative research lead (Gina Crivello) disrupted team capacity temporarily.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Centralized coordination by Oxford University with decentralized country teams. New Programme Manager appointment strengthened oversight. Advisory Board engagement increased for strategic alignment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong South-South and in-country networks facilitated dissemination. Challenges in donor coordination due to shifting priorities (e.g., Ukraine war, economic downturn). Internal silos persisted among partners despite multisectoral approach.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Oxford’s rigid procurement processes ensured cost savings (e.g., preferred supplier discounts, digital publications). Technology upgrades (virtual meetings, webinars) improved efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Increased oversight under new leadership, addressing prior issues (poor forecasting, limited outreach). Regular Advisory Board consultations planned for Round 7 design.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Adapted survey methods (phone surveys) and fundraising strategies (£2.5m target for Round 7) in response to budget constraints. Pilot innovations (GPS data collection, climate data matching) integrated into core activities.
adaptive_management_examples: Rapid deployment of COVID-19 phone surveys (Call 4/5) to capture real-time pandemic impacts.
Development of Stata module "ttestex" and technical notes to support external researchers.
Pilot of remote data tracking/transmission to reduce costs and improve mobility tracking (e.g., internally displaced populations).
Revised fundraising break clause negotiations with FCDO to secure Round 7 funding.

main_implementation_challenges: Securing additional funding for Round 7 (£2.5m target) amid donor priority shifts (COVID-19, Ukraine war, economic downturn).
Managing smaller budget while maintaining data quality and policy influence.
Staff absences due to COVID-19 and sudden loss of qualitative research lead (Gina Crivello).
Balancing in-person fieldwork costs with phone survey limitations post-pandemic.
external_factors_impact: COVID-19 disrupted in-person data collection, requiring shift to phone surveys (Call 4/5).
Ukraine war and economic instability reduced donor appetite for long-term research funding.
Climate change impacts (e.g., India climate data matching) revealed new vulnerabilities in education/skills development.
contextual_constraints_new: Increased mobility of study populations (internal migration/displacement) complicating tracking.
Data protection laws limiting open-access data sharing in some countries.
Competing national priorities (e.g., India’s child marriage law reforms) requiring rapid evidence turnaround.
partner_relationship_issues: Silos among implementing partners hindered multisectoral coordination.
Delays in co-funding materialization (e.g., Old Dart Foundation for Peru activities in 21/22).
Varied capacity across country teams to adapt to new technologies (e.g., remote data transmission).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Reduced qualitative research capacity after loss of lead researcher.
Limited bandwidth for fundraising due to core team focusing on survey delivery.
Need for upskilling in data matching (e.g., GPS/climate data integration) and dissemination strategies.
risk_materialization: Funding shortfalls for Round 7 (partially mitigated by fundraising efforts).
COVID-19-related data collection delays (addressed via phone surveys).
Policy uptake risks (e.g., India’s marriage law reform required sustained advocacy).

budget_execution_vs_plan: Underspend in FY 21/22 due to phone surveys replacing costlier fieldwork.
£2.5m fundraising target set for Round 7 to supplement FCDO funding.
Cost savings from digital dissemination (social media, virtual events) and preferred supplier discounts.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Strong: Oxford’s procurement processes and bulk discounts reduced operational costs. Phone surveys saved ~30% vs. fieldwork.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: High: Open-access data enabled third-party research (14,331 cumulative downloads; 2,942 new downloads in 2022). South-South networks amplified reach.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High: Policy influence (e.g., India’s child marriage law) and 75 citations (62 peer-reviewed) demonstrate impact. Target of 4 policy impact stories/year proposed.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Moderate: Data accessibility constrained by anonymity requirements. Country-specific dissemination addressed local needs (e.g., media coverage in Ethiopia, Peru).
value_for_money_assessment.environment: Not assessed in detail; digital-first approach reduced travel emissions.

financial_management_quality: Improved under new leadership (better forecasting, transparent reporting).
Break clause revisions requested to align fundraising with FCDO VfM requirements.
No major audit findings reported; compliance with Oxford’s financial controls.
cost_efficiency_achieved: Phone surveys reduced per-survey costs by ~30% while maintaining response rates (attrition: -0.7% in Call 5).
Data matching pilots (e.g., GPS/climate) leveraged existing datasets at minimal cost.
Virtual events (COP26, IAAH) cut travel costs while expanding global reach.

South-South networks are critical for contextualizing global findings (e.g., climate-education links in India).

programme_metadata.programme_title: Community-Led, Responsive, and Effective Urban Health Systems – CHORUS Programme
programme_metadata.review_period: Third full year of implementation (Year 4 of programme)

output_1.title: Research co-produced and effectively disseminated to research users

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme expanded Innovation Fund (IF) calls (17 projects funded from 31 applications) to support early/mid-career LMIC researchers while addressing core research pillars. Second-round IF projects initiated with desk reviews during ethical approval processes to expedite progress. Co-design approach required more time/resources than originally planned, particularly in complex urban contexts with multiple stakeholders.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners exceeded expectations in policy influence (5 instances of policy/programme decision-making impact), research uptake (58 products vs. 32 target), and stakeholder engagement (52 workshops vs. 25 target). Bangladesh partner (ARK) adapted the "Simple App" for diabetes/hypertension training, now recommended by government. Nepal’s Pokhara Metropolitan City used CHORUS needs assessments for annual planning. Some delays in journal article production (7 published vs. higher targets) attributed to capacity constraints among early-career researchers leading publications.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: University of Leeds provides oversight via a Committee monitoring financial systems and capacity building. Action Learning Groups (ALGs) maintained for mentorship but challenged by researchers’ workloads during data collection. Mid-point capacity assessment survey initiated to optimize resource allocation. Leadership functions increasingly distributed to LMIC partners (planned to expand further).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination evidenced by cross-country collaboration (e.g., joint projects with ReBUILD for Resilience), South-South partnerships (writing workshops, peer-learning), and knowledge exchange (bilateral IF projects, cross-partner mentorship). Stakeholder engagement combined with other projects to minimize costs and maximize reach. Challenges in maintaining ALGs due to competing priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Moderate oversight with proactive risk mitigation. FCDO-CHORUS relationship described as "close" to ensure alignment with priorities. Oversight Committee at University of Leeds strengthened financial processes. Safeguarding training made mandatory and delivered in-person to address risks from expanded research activities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted by: 1) Scaling down Project 2 ambitions to meet timelines; 2) Recruiting separate teams for Project 2s to unlock capacity; 3) Securing additional funding from University of Leeds to address staffing gaps and support joint projects; 4) Moving significant costs from Year 4 to Year 5 due to delays. Innovation Fund flexibility allowed rapid response to emerging research needs (e.g., 17 projects funded targeting early-career researchers).
adaptive_management_examples: Scaled down Project 2 ambitions to accelerate progress and recruited dedicated teams for Project 2 implementation.
Secured additional funding from University of Leeds to address capacity issues and fund collaboration with ReBUILD for Resilience (R4R).
Adjusted publication strategy to support early-career researchers, accepting longer timelines for higher-quality outputs (7 published, 36 in pipeline).
Conducted desk reviews for second-round IF projects during ethical approval waits to expedite progress.
Aligned Year 4 partner meeting in Utrecht with a European conference to reduce travel costs.
Developed a mid-point capacity assessment survey to rebalance workloads and optimize impact.

main_implementation_challenges: Co-design process in urban contexts demanded more time/resources than anticipated due to complex stakeholder dynamics (e.g., power imbalances, competing priorities).
Balancing Innovation Fund demands (capacity strengthening for early-career researchers) with central team capacity, requiring additional funding.
Delays in journal article production (target of 10 not met; 7 published) due to early-career researchers leading publications.
Staff turnover and safeguarding risks as research activities expanded, mitigated via mandatory training and rapid backfilling.
Policy maker turnover in Nigeria and Bangladesh required frequent engagement to maintain advocacy.
external_factors_impact: Risk of civil unrest/natural disasters (e.g., Dengue outbreaks, extreme weather in Bangladesh) caused minor delays, mitigated via updated risk register.
COVID-19 legacy effects (not explicitly stated but implied in delays and safeguarding protocols).
Currency/exchange rate impacts not mentioned.
contextual_constraints_new: Urban health research complexity underestimated: informal provider networks, multi-sectoral collaboration, and slum population engagement required tailored approaches per country.
Higher-than-expected demand for mentorship/support from early-career researchers via Innovation Funds and publication processes.
Ethical approval processes for Project 2s caused delays, addressed via preliminary desk reviews.
partner_relationship_issues: Minor risks from partners not fully understanding FCDO priorities, mitigated via close FCDO-CHORUS collaboration.
Staff churn in some partners led to temporary delays, addressed via rapid backfilling and empowerment of early-career researchers.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Early-career researchers leading publications slowed output (7 articles vs. higher targets) but strengthened capacity long-term.
Innovation Fund demand outstripped central team capacity, requiring additional funding to maintain support quality.
Action Learning Groups (ALGs) struggled to maintain engagement during peak data collection periods.
risk_materialization: Moderate safeguarding risks materialized as research expanded, managed via mandatory training and reporting measures.
Staff turnover risks materialized but mitigated via quick replacements and early-career researcher empowerment.
Policy maker turnover in Nigeria/Bangladesh materialized; frequent engagement maintained advocacy.
Financial risks from underspend in outer years and approaching programme deadline noted but not yet materialized.

budget_execution_vs_plan: 65% of Year 4 budget allocated to LMIC partners (target: increase in Year 5).
Significant costs moved from Year 4 to Year 5 due to delays and additional University of Leeds funding for staff capacity/joint projects.
Direct research and staff costs remained highest drivers; overheads, travel, and training aligned with forecasts.
No major underspend/overspend issues reported; variance management targeted at ≤10%.
value_for_money_assessment: Delivered against outputs while maintaining VfM, with focus on economy, efficiency, and effectiveness.

Cost-saving measures included: 1) Aligning partner meeting with European conference to reduce travel costs; 2) Combining stakeholder engagements with other projects; 3) Using in-house expertise/resources (e.g., securing additional University of Leeds funding).
Efficiency gains via collaboration with ReBUILD for Resilience (R4R) for joint gender/equity reviews and shared dissemination of IF project findings.
Equity achievements: 74% of intervention populations in informal settlements/slums; 86% of pipeline articles led by LMIC researchers (67% early-career, 50% female).
financial_management_quality: Moderate risk level maintained via University of Leeds Oversight Committee monitoring financial systems and capacity building.
Strengthened processes reduced risk of irregularities, though underspend in outer years poses future risk.
Transparency in budget reallocations (e.g., moving costs to Year 5) and proactive risk mitigation (e.g., safeguarding training).
cost_efficiency_achieved: Economies of scale through shared resources (e.g., joint projects with R4R, combined stakeholder engagements).
LMIC partner leadership increased (planned to expand further), reducing reliance on UK-based costs.
In-house capacity building (e.g., writing workshops) reduced external consultancy needs.
co_funding_materialization: Additional funding secured from University of Leeds to address capacity gaps and support joint projects.

key_delivery_lessons: Co-design in urban contexts yields high policy relevance but requires more time/resources to navigate stakeholder complexities (e.g., power dynamics, priorities).
Innovation Funds effectively upskill early-career researchers but create central team capacity demands, necessitating additional funding.
Publication strategies must balance quality (early-career leadership) with timeliness (7 articles published vs. higher targets).
Action Learning Groups (ALGs) are valuable but vulnerable to workload pressures during data collection phases.
Flexibility in project ambitions (e.g., scaling down Project 2 scope) can accelerate progress without compromising outcomes.
successful_delivery_practices: Cross-country collaboration (e.g., joint R4R projects, South-South writing workshops) amplified impact and efficiency.
Mandatory safeguarding training and in-person delivery mitigated risks from expanded research activities.
Aligning events with existing conferences (e.g., Utrecht partner meeting) reduced costs while maintaining engagement.
Preliminary desk reviews during ethical approval waits expedited IF project progress.
Empowering early-career researchers to lead publications strengthened capacity despite slower output.
management_adaptations_made: Recruited separate teams for Project 2s to unlock capacity and meet timelines.
Secured additional funding to support Innovation Funds without diverting central team resources.
Implemented mid-point capacity assessment survey to rebalance workloads.
Adjusted forecasting practices to meet 10% variance targets and deadlines.
Distributed leadership functions more evenly across LMIC partners.
innovations_attempted: Innovation Fund (IF) mechanism to support early-career researchers while addressing core research pillars (17 projects funded).
Gender and equity reviews integrated into all projects, with 86% of pipeline articles led by LMIC researchers (67% early-career, 50% female).
Joint projects with ReBUILD for Resilience (R4R) to share learning on urban slum healthcare.
Development of the "Simple App" in Bangladesh for diabetes/hypertension training, now government-recommended.
Use of Action Learning Groups (ALGs) for mentorship, though challenged by workloads.

risk_management_effectiveness: Effective mitigation of safeguarding risks via mandatory training and reporting measures.

Frequent engagement with new policymakers in Nigeria/Bangladesh maintained advocacy despite turnover.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: 74% of intervention populations reside in informal settlements/urban slums (100% in Nigeria/Ghana; targeted facilities in Nepal/Bangladesh).

Indirect reach via policy influence: Bangladesh government adopted "Simple App" for primary healthcare training; Nepal’s Pokhara Metropolitan City integrated CHORUS needs assessments into annual planning.
17 Innovation Fund projects funded, targeting early-career LMIC researchers and urban poor communities.
policy_influence_achieved: Bangladesh: Government recommendations now include CHORUS-adapted "Simple App" for diabetes/hypertension training.
Nepal: Pokhara Metropolitan City used CHORUS needs assessments to design annual plan/budget.
Ghana: CHORUS data informed revisions to community health planning policies/manuals.
Five instances of policy/programme decision-making influence documented in Year 4.

scalability_evidence: Approaches demonstrated scalability via: 1) Policy adoption in Bangladesh/Nepal; 2) Cross-country collaboration (e.g., R4R joint projects); 3) Innovation Fund model replicable for other research consortia.
Urban Health Data Hub (planned for Nepal) and "Simple App" (Bangladesh) designed for broader adaptation.
Lessons from multi-sectoral collaboration and slum engagement applicable to similar urban health programmes.

continuation_rationale: Programme scored A+ in Year 4, exceeding most output milestones (e.g., policy influence, research uptake, capacity strengthening).
Significant progress in implementing Project 1s across all countries and initiating Project 2s, with clear pathways to completion.
Strong evidence of policy influence (e.g., Bangladesh app adoption, Nepal budget integration) and capacity building (86% LMIC-led publications).
High likelihood of achieving long-term objectives (SDG 3, 6, 11) despite challenges in demonstrating quantitative impact within programme timeline.
Effective adaptive management (e.g., securing additional funding, adjusting Project 2 scope) ensures resilience.
