programme_metadata.programme_title: Small Island Developing States Capacity and Resilience Programme (SIDAR)

output_1.title: Governance: SIDAR decision-making is informed by effective programme governance structures

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme expanded from £40m to £54.5m with extended end date (March 2028) due to in-year funding opportunity. Flexible, pragmatic approach adopted to address high costs of doing business in SIDS (e.g., adjusted management fees for Pacific institutions like SPREP).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners like UNDESA (for SIDS4), GGGI (Pacific advisers), and SPREP delivered key interventions, though some delays occurred in hiring technical staff and project start-ups. Regional boards (Caribbean, Pacific) engaged actively, but attendance metrics occasionally fell short (e.g., October 2024 board missed 75% attendance threshold).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: SIDS Steering Group functions as a communication forum but requires improvements to focus on practical value over governance metrics. Regional boards (Caribbean, Pacific) operate routinely, with SIDS Hub Central Team attending most meetings. Quarterly ASIDS ODA Board provides additional assurance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Strong coordination for SIDS4 conference (logistical and strategic support), including preparatory meetings and side events. Cross-regional collaboration seen in OECD coordination events (e.g., Bangkok February 2024) and AOSIS Task Force Secretariat funding. Community of Practice events facilitated South-South exchanges (e.g., GCF accreditation support).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Delays in due diligence and hiring key personnel (e.g., AIS region) impacted project start-ups. Flexible contracting approaches used to embed Pacific Islander advisers (6/7 positions filled). Some procurement challenges persisted due to high operational costs in SIDS (e.g., internet connectivity, office space).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight required for SIDS4 due to its strategic priority, diverting resources from other improvements. Limited M&E capacity within the team led to reliance on ad-hoc compliance checks. Third-party monitoring considered for future phases.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to support SIDS4 as a priority, reallocating staff and funds. Flexible funding used for OECD analysis papers (e.g., ODA graduation process) and regional workshops (e.g., 8 national climate training workshops in the Caribbean). Pragmatic adjustments made to management fees for Pacific partners.
adaptive_management_examples: Reallocation of resources to prioritize SIDS4 conference support, including UNDESA-funded preparatory meetings.
Embedding Pacific Islander advisers (via GGGI) in 7 countries to address local capacity gaps, with 11 climate finance proposals and 7 technical studies supported.
Adjusting procurement thresholds for SPREP to account for high operational costs in Pacific SIDS.
Funding OECD-AOSIS Task Force Secretariat and launching a "Partnership of Action" document at SIDS4.

main_implementation_challenges: Staffing pressures and resource diversion to SIDS4 limited progress on programme improvements (e.g., delayed logframe overhaul, VFM metrics).
Delays in project start-ups due to due diligence, hiring, and agreement signing (especially in AIS region).
High costs of doing business in SIDS (e.g., data, technical expertise, connectivity) strained budgets and required flexible fee adjustments.
Limited M&E capacity within the team, risking compliance and results tracking.
external_factors_impact: SIDS4 conference (May 2024) became a dominant priority, absorbing significant staff time and funds but yielding high visibility (e.g., UK Ministerial engagements, Partnership of Action launch).
Global economic pressures (e.g., debt sustainability in SIDS) influenced programme focus on financial resilience (e.g., OECD working papers on ODA graduation).
Climate crisis urgency amplified demand for SIDAR’s capacity-building support, particularly in accessing climate finance.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated complexity in hiring local technical staff (e.g., due diligence hurdles in AIS region).
Currency/exchange rate volatility and inflation in some SIDS increased operational costs (e.g., office space, consultant fees).
Competition for limited local expertise in climate finance and safeguards required creative solutions (e.g., regional helpdesks, South-South exchanges).
partner_relationship_issues: Occasional attendance shortfalls in regional boards (e.g., October 2024 Caribbean Board missed quorum but was deemed non-critical).
Differing priorities between SIDS governments and regional bodies (e.g., SPREP) required negotiation on safeguarding policies and GCF accreditation.
Delays in co-funding commitments from some partners (e.g., Canadian support for SIDS4 side events materialized late).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Programme management team stretched by growth to 21 component lines, risking compliance standards.
M&E capacity gap identified; original Business Case provision for M&E support not yet implemented.
Regional disparities in capacity (e.g., AIS region lagged until lead adviser was hired in 2024).
risk_materialization: Risk of under-spend due to delayed project start-ups (mitigated via no-cost extensions and reallocation to SIDS4).
Risk of governance indicators being misaligned with strategic impact (e.g., Steering Group metrics focused on process over outcomes).
Risk of partner dependency (e.g., reliance on GGGI for Pacific advisers created bottlenecks in hiring).

budget_execution_vs_plan.summary: Budget execution improved in 2024 with full utilization of £14.5m uplift, but delays in project start-ups (e.g., AIS region) risked under-spend. No-cost extensions planned for some components to align with March 2028 end date.
budget_execution_vs_plan.variance: Additional £14.5m (36% increase) allocated in 2024, fully committed for FY24/25. Original £40m baseline extended to £54.5m.

value_for_money_assessment.summary: VFM rationale holds: small SIDAR investments leverage larger climate finance (e.g., GGGI-supported proposals, SPREP’s GCF accreditation). Cost efficiency achieved by prioritizing local hires (e.g., Pacific Islander advisers) over international consultants.
evidence: 11 climate finance proposals and 7 technical studies supported via GGGI (early-stage but promising leverage).
OECD analysis papers (e.g., ODA graduation) influenced global discussions at cost of ~£50k per paper (high strategic return).
Caribbean regional helpdesk strengthened with 8 national workshops at ~£20k per workshop.
value_for_money_assessment.challenges: High operational costs in SIDS (e.g., SPREP’s safeguarding policy support required fee adjustments). Limited competition for services increases prices (e.g., data, technical expertise).

financial_management_quality.summary: Financial management deemed effective but strained by rapid scaling. Flexible approaches (e.g., adjusted fee thresholds) maintained equity while ensuring compliance.
strengths: Transparent reporting to SIDS Board and ASIDS ODA Board.
Proactive adjustments to procurement processes (e.g., SPREP negotiations).
Successful absorption of £14.5m uplift without major disruptions.
weaknesses: Delayed financial close-outs for some components due to hiring lags.
Limited ex-ante cost-benefit analysis for new initiatives (e.g., SIDS Future Forum).

cost_efficiency_achieved.summary: Cost efficiency demonstrated in staffing (local hires) and regional coordination (e.g., shared helpdesks). However, SIDS-specific cost drivers (e.g., connectivity, office space) reduced marginal efficiency gains.
metrics: ~30% lower costs for Pacific advisers (local hires) vs. international consultants.
£1.2m spent on SIDS4 support leveraged £5m+ in partner contributions (e.g., UNDESA, AOSIS).
Caribbean workshops cost ~£160k total, reaching 8 countries (£20k/country).

co_funding_materialization.summary: Partial materialization: Canadian co-funding for SIDS4 side events secured late. AOSIS and OECD partnerships delivered in-kind contributions (e.g., Task Force Secretariat).
co_funding_materialization.gaps: Some planned co-funding from SIDS governments did not materialize due to fiscal constraints (e.g., debt crises).

financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Exchange rate volatility in some SIDS (e.g., Pacific currencies) increased local costs by ~5-10% for certain activities, requiring budget reallocations.

key_delivery_lessons: Flexible, demand-driven approaches (e.g., embedded advisers) yield higher traction than rigid frameworks.
Regional bodies (e.g., SPREP, 5Cs) are effective conduits for technical assistance but require tailored support (e.g., safeguarding policies).
High-visibility events (e.g., SIDS4) can catalyze progress but divert resources from long-term capacity building.
Local ownership (e.g., Pacific Islander advisers) enhances sustainability but requires upfront investment in hiring processes.
successful_delivery_practices: Embedded technical advisers (GGGI model) accelerated climate finance proposal development (11 proposals in 6 months).
South-South exchanges (e.g., GCF accreditation CoP) fostered peer learning at low cost (~£15k/event).
Strategic publications (e.g., OECD ODA graduation paper) amplified SIDS voices in global forums (e.g., Financing for Development Conference).
Regional helpdesks (Caribbean) provided scalable technical support (8 workshops, 5Cs platform).
management_adaptations_made: Reallocated resources to prioritize SIDS4, accepting delays in other areas.
Adjusted procurement thresholds for Pacific partners to reflect contextual costs.
Initiated discussions on third-party monitoring to address M&E capacity gaps.
Extended programme by 1 year (to 2028) to accommodate delayed start-ups.
innovations_attempted: Partnership of Action document (launched at SIDS4) to formalize donor-SIDS collaboration.
Resilient Islands podcast series (9 episodes, 1101 listeners) for knowledge dissemination.
Debt sustainability working papers presented at World Bank/IMF Spring Meetings (April 2024).
Blue Economy Forum side events to integrate climate and ocean finance agendas.

partial: Programme extension (1 year) implemented as recommended in 2023 AR.
Delivery chain mapping and VFM metrics developed but not fully operationalized due to SIDS4 priorities.
limited: Comms plan and equity approach (Social Development Adviser) not advanced due to staffing pressures.
Logframe overhaul deferred; current version remains internally focused.

forward_recommendations: Finalize pipeline for FY25/26 to ensure full budget utilization, including multi-year commitments where possible.
Overhaul logframe to focus on external outcomes (e.g., climate finance accessed, policy influence) and align with ICF indicators.
Address M&E capacity gap via FCDO support or third-party contract, including potential for wider compliance monitoring.
Assess strategic impact of activities (e.g., OECD papers vs. regional workshops) to prioritize high-traction interventions.
Strengthen AIS region delivery with dedicated resources and clearer FCDO post engagement.
Develop a risk-based approach to procurement to balance flexibility with compliance.

strengths: Proactive adjustments to mitigate under-spend (e.g., no-cost extensions).
Flexible fee structures for Pacific partners reduced financial risks.
SIDS4 contingency planning ensured successful delivery despite resource constraints.
weaknesses: Governance risks (e.g., Steering Group attendance) not fully addressed by current metrics.
Limited ex-ante risk assessment for new components (e.g., SIDS Future Forum).
M&E gaps hindered real-time risk tracking (e.g., partner performance).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.summary: Direct beneficiaries include 7 Pacific SIDS (via GGGI advisers), 8 Caribbean countries (via workshops), and global audiences (e.g., SIDS4 participants, OECD DAC). Indirect reach includes SIDS populations benefiting from improved climate finance access.
quantitative: 11 climate finance proposals developed (potential to unlock £100m+ in funding).
SIDS4 conference support enabled participation by 30+ SIDS delegations.
1101 unique listeners to Resilient Islands podcast; 1448 downloads.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.gaps: AIS region engagement limited; beneficiary data for policy influence (e.g., OECD papers) not quantified.

policy_influence_achieved.example: OECD ODA graduation paper informed discussions at 4th International Conference on Financing for Development.
Partnership of Action document launched at SIDS4 with UK Ministerial endorsement.
SPREP safeguarding policies strengthened with UK support, influencing GCF accreditation standards.

capacity_building_results.outcome: 11 climate finance proposals, 7 technical studies, 8 institutional strategies developed.
8 national workshops on climate safeguards; helpdesk platform expanded.
SIDS representatives engaged in capacity-building dialogues with donors.
GCF accreditation knowledge shared across 15+ entities.

unintended_consequences.description: SIDS4 visibility raised UK’s profile as a SIDS champion, leading to additional partner engagements (e.g., Canadian co-funding).
Resource diversion to SIDS4 delayed other capacity-building initiatives (e.g., AIS region start-ups, logframe revisions).
Local adviser model (Pacific) created demand for similar approaches in other regions (e.g., Caribbean expressions of interest).

scalability_evidence.evidence: Replicated in 7 Pacific SIDS; interest from Caribbean and AIS regions.
Caribbean platform expanded to include South-South exchanges; SPREP exploring similar model.
ODA graduation analysis adopted by DAC for broader SIDS discussions.

continuation_rationale: Programme demonstrates high strategic value in advancing UK’s SIDS and climate priorities (e.g., SIDS4 leadership, GCF access).
Strong demand for capacity-building support (e.g., 21 component lines, partner requests for extensions).
VFM rationale validated by early leverage results (e.g., climate finance proposals, policy influence).
Extended funding (to £54.5m) and timeline (to 2028) reflect FCDO’s sustained commitment.

strengths: Regional partnerships (e.g., SPREP, 5Cs) provide scalable platforms for technical assistance.
Local adviser model (Pacific) enhances sustainability and ownership.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., adjusted fees) adapt to SIDS contexts.
risks: Dependence on key partners (e.g., GGGI, UNDESA) may limit long-term autonomy.
M&E capacity gaps could undermine results tracking and accountability.
High operational costs in SIDS may challenge cost efficiency at scale.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Finalize FY25/26 pipeline with multi-year commitments to improve planning stability.
Overhaul logframe to emphasize external outcomes and align with ICF indicators.
Address M&E capacity gap via FCDO support or third-party contract.
Strengthen AIS region delivery with dedicated adviser and FCDO post engagement.
Develop risk-based procurement approach to balance flexibility and compliance.
Explore co-funding mechanisms to reduce fiscal pressure on SIDS governments.
Expand successful models (e.g., embedded advisers, helpdesks) to other regions.

funding_modality_baseline.primary_modality: Multilateral (£80m contribution to $1bn World Bank Trust Fund for Sudan Family Support Programme - SFSP)
funding_modality_baseline.delivery_scale_planned: £80m UK contribution to $1bn multi-donor Trust Fund; designed to i) close Sudan’s funding gap for IMF programme agreement and ii) provide cash transfers to mitigate economic shocks from reforms
funding_modality_baseline.planned_disbursement_approach: Funds channeled through World Bank Trust Fund to implement cash transfers and economic stabilization activities, with IMF/WB/AfDB coordination
funding_modality_baseline.budget_flexibility_planned: Medium (designed for multi-year economic reform support with some contingency for shocks, but tied to IMF/WB policy frameworks)

governance_baseline.management_structure_planned: Light-touch FCDO oversight with World Bank as primary implementing partner; quarterly donor coordination meetings
governance_baseline.oversight_intensity_planned: Quarterly monitoring via Trust Fund governance structures; annual FCDO programme reviews
governance_baseline.decision_making_planned: Consensus-based donor decisions within Trust Fund framework; World Bank operational autonomy for implementation

partner_selection_baseline.partnership_approach_planned: Single multilateral implementer (World Bank) with IMF/AfDB as coordinating partners
partner_selection_baseline.partner_types_planned: Multilateral (World Bank Trust Fund), International Financial Institutions (IMF, AfDB)
partner_selection_baseline.partner_roles_planned: World Bank: Trust Fund manager and implementer; IMF: macroeconomic reform oversight; AfDB: complementary financing
partner_selection_baseline.selection_method_planned: Direct award to World Bank Trust Fund (pre-existing multilateral mechanism)

funding_modality_actual.primary_modality_actual: Multilateral (World Bank Trust Fund) with expanded UN agency implementation (UNICEF, WFP, Mercy Corps)
funding_modality_actual.delivery_scale_actual: £80m UK contribution repurposed across three phases: 1) 2020/21: £8m to SFSP; 2) 2022/23: £18m to emergency cash/food transfers; 3) 2024/25: £29m to "Sudan Somoud" community resilience programme (total £55m disbursed to date)
funding_modality_actual.disbursement_approach_actual: Phase 1: World Bank Trust Fund → halted post-coup; Phase 2: Emergency cash/food via UN agencies; Phase 3: Community resilience via World Bank contracting UNICEF/WFP/Mercy Corps directly (STARS mechanism)
funding_modality_actual.budget_flexibility_actual: High (multiple repurposings: from economic reform → emergency relief → community resilience; timeline extended by 3 years)

governance_actual.management_structure_actual: Intensified FCDO oversight post-coup; monthly donor coordination; World Bank operational role reduced in Phase 2; direct NGO contracting in Phase 3
governance_actual.oversight_intensity_actual: Monthly monitoring during emergency phase; enhanced due diligence for NGO contracts; geo-enabled WB monitoring systems introduced
governance_actual.decision_making_actual: Donor consensus required for each repurposing (May 2022, Dec 2023); FCDO ministerial approvals for business case addenda

partners_actual.partnership_approach_actual: Multi-partner: World Bank (Trust Fund manager) + UNICEF/WFP/Mercy Corps (implementers) + local NGOs/SMEs
partners_actual.partner_types_actual: Multilateral (World Bank), UN Agencies (UNICEF, WFP), INGOs (Mercy Corps), Local NGOs, Farmer Cooperatives, SMEs
partners_actual.partner_roles_actual: World Bank: fiscal agent and strategic oversight; UNICEF: basic services delivery; WFP: food security/agricultural inputs; Mercy Corps: community resilience; Local actors: service provision and governance (CDCs)

consortium_actual.consortium_structure_actual: De facto consortium formed in Phase 3: World Bank as fiscal agent with UNICEF/WFP/Mercy Corps as parallel implementers under shared results framework
consortium_actual.lead_partner_actual: World Bank (fiscal) with UNICEF (operational lead for basic services)
consortium_actual.consortium_governance_actual: Donor Steering Committee (monthly); World Bank contract management for NGOs; CDC-led community governance

substantive_changes_made: Repurposing from economic reform (SFSP) to emergency cash/food transfers (May 2022) due to coup
Shift from World Bank-led implementation to UN agency delivery post-coup
Redesign to community resilience focus ("Sudan Somoud") with 3-year extension (Dec 2023)
Introduction of direct NGO contracting by World Bank via STARS mechanism
Expansion from national economic reforms to subnational basic services/food security
Addition of Community Development Committees (CDCs) as governance structures
Integration of private sector (SMEs, farmer cooperatives) into delivery model

funding_scale_changes.budget_increased_decreased: Budget scale unchanged (£80m total), but allocation shifted: £18m to emergency phase, £29m to resilience phase (from original £8m to SFSP)
funding_scale_changes.scope_expanded_contracted: Geographic scope contracted (from national to Northern/River Nile/Kassala states) but beneficiary focus expanded (from reform mitigation to IDP/host communities)
funding_scale_changes.modality_shifts: Shift from: 1) WB Trust Fund → UN agencies (emergency phase); 2) Cash transfers → in-kind food/services; 3) Central government → community/NGO delivery

pathway_changes: Original: Economic reform → macro stability → debt relief → growth
Revised: Community resilience → basic services → social cohesion → climate adaptation (with long-term govt reintegration as aspirational)
Added intermediate outcomes: CDC functionality, SME/cooperative viability, GBV service integration
assumptions_updated: Assumption of rapid return to civilian government dropped
Banking system collapse required shift from cash to in-kind transfers
Added assumption: "Community-led structures can substitute for state service delivery in FCAS context"

management_restructuring.oversight_changed: From quarterly to monthly donor coordination; added WB geo-monitoring and NGO contract oversight
management_restructuring.decision_making_reformed: Donor consensus now required for all major pivots (previously WB had operational autonomy)

geographic_scope_changes.locations_added_removed: Removed: National-level IMF/WB reforms; Added: Northern, River Nile, Kassala states (high-IDP areas)
geographic_scope_changes.geographic_focus_shifted: From urban/peripheral (reform focus) to urban/peri-urban with IDP inflows (resilience focus)

activity_only_adjustments: Minor delays in procurement (4 weeks) due to governance clearances
Revised SME eligibility criteria to increase uptake
Adjustments to agricultural input distribution models (private sector engagement)

contextual_shocks: October 2021 military coup (halted SFSP)
Collapse of Sudanese banking system (disabled cash transfers)
Ongoing conflict (shifted from reform to humanitarian/resilience)
Mass IDP movements (changed geographic targeting)
performance_issues: World Bank OP7.30 policy blocked original SFSP implementation
Delays in disbursement conditions (PIM/ESF approvals)
Coordination problems in UN agency contracting chains
learning_insights: Effectiveness of CDC-led service prioritization
Private sector (SMEs/coops) as viable service providers in FCAS
Need for flexible NGO contracting mechanisms (STARS)
strategic_opportunities: Donor consensus on repurposing unspent funds (May 2022)
World Bank’s expanded local presence and geo-monitoring capacity
EU/CRW additional funding mobilization ($110m potential)

adaptation_quality_assessment.adaptive_management_quality: High
adaptation_quality_assessment.flexibility_utilization: Baseline medium flexibility fully utilized; additional flexibility secured via business case addenda
adaptation_quality_assessment.learning_integration: Strong (e.g., CDC model adopted from pilot evidence; SME eligibility revisions based on uptake data)

fcas_context.conflict_exposure: Active conflict throughout implementation (post-2021 coup)

major_external_shocks.political_transitions: October 2021 military coup (overthrew civilian-led transition); no return to civilian governance as of 2025
economic_shocks: Collapse of Sudanese pound (inflation >300% at peak)
major_external_shocks.climate_disasters: Droughts exacerbating food insecurity (triggered agricultural support pivot)
major_external_shocks.conflict_escalation: Ongoing armed conflict between SAF/RSF (since April 2023) disrupted supply chains and service delivery

political_economy_factors.government_commitment_shifts: From civilian-led reform partnership (2020) to de facto military regime (2021–present); no functional MoF for fiscal coordination
political_economy_factors.policy_environment_changes: World Bank OP7.30 policy activation (blocked sovereign engagements post-coup)
political_economy_factors.institutional_capacity_reality: Ministries non-functional; CDCs became primary governance structures; UN agencies filled service delivery gaps

market_conditions.supplier_market_reality: Severe supply chain disruptions; reliance on UN/WFP procurement networks; local NGO capacity limited outside Khartum
market_conditions.cost_inflation_impacts: Programme costs increased ~40% due to currency devaluation and import restrictions
market_conditions.exchange_rate_impacts: SDG depreciation eroded local currency value of disbursements (mitigated via in-kind procurement)

t0_t1_summary_comparison.overall_stability_assessment: Low (all 4 delivery mechanisms substantively changed)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.adaptation_pathway: Comprehensive adaptation (funding + governance + partners + consortium + ToC)
t0_t1_summary_comparison.baseline_design_quality: Poor (original design assumed stable civilian transition and functional state institutions; lacked FCAS-contingency plans)

programme_metadata.programme_title: Sudan Economic Impact and Reform Programme (SEIR)

output_1.title: Community Led Basic Service Delivery

output_2.title: Improving Food Security

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme was redesigned in 2023 to shift from cash transfers/food support to community resilience and basic service delivery. Phase II extended by three years with focus on transferring to Government of Sudan if conditions permit. Delivery now channels through UNICEF and WFP with direct NGO contracting by World Bank.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: World Bank faced delays due to policy OP7.30 post-coup (2021), but later adapted by repurposing funds to emergency cash/food transfers (2022) and community resilience (2023). UNICEF/WFP showed operational flexibility but coordination challenges extended procurement timelines by ~4 weeks. Local partners (CDCs) performed well in service prioritization despite capacity constraints.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Shifted from centralized Trust Fund management to decentralized implementation via UN agencies and NGOs, with Community Development Committees (CDCs) playing a stronger oversight role. World Bank’s direct NGO contracting (via STARS) reduced overhead layers.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination between World Bank, UNICEF, WFP, and Mercy Corps improved post-2023 redesign but suffered from "long delivery chain" inefficiencies. Donor consensus mechanisms worked for major pivots (e.g., 2022 emergency repurposing) but slowed decision-making.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement faced delays due to: 1) Disbursement conditions tied to Project Implementation Manual (PIM) and Environmental/Social Framework (ESF) approvals (resolved Nov 2024); 2) Banking system collapse post-conflict; 3) Governance clearance bottlenecks. Adaptive measures (e.g., private-sector agricultural input distribution) mitigated some delays.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned due to Severe risk rating. World Bank increased local presence and geo-enabled monitoring, but donor access to real-time data remained limited. FCDO conducted more frequent check-ins post-2021 coup.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: High flexibility utilized for: 1) 2022 repurposing of $100m to emergency cash/food transfers; 2) 2023 shift to community resilience; 3) Extension of timeline by 3 years. Business case addendums approved at ministerial level for both pivots.
adaptive_management_examples: Repurposed $100m from stalled SFSP to emergency cash/food transfers in 2022, reaching 2.4m people pre-conflict.
Redesigned programme in 2023 to focus on community resilience (Somoud project) after banking system collapse made cash transfers unviable.
Revised SME matching grant eligibility criteria mid-implementation, increasing applications from 0 to 300 (225 underwent due diligence).
Switched to private-sector channels for agricultural input distribution to bypass procurement delays.

main_implementation_challenges: Post-coup (Oct 2021) suspension of World Bank’s SFSP due to OP7.30 policy on de facto governments.
Collapse of Sudan’s banking system during conflict, blocking cash transfer mechanisms.
Disbursement conditions (PIM/ESF approvals) delayed implementation until Nov 2024.
Procurement coordination issues between UN agencies, NGOs, and World Bank (4-week delays).
Assumption of rapid return to civilian-led government proved incorrect, requiring programme redesign.
external_factors_impact: 2021 military coup halted IMF/WB programmes and triggered donor policy restrictions (e.g., WB OP7.30).
Ongoing conflict (post-April 2023) destroyed banking infrastructure, limiting financial transactions.
Humanitarian crisis diverted focus from economic reforms to emergency food/security needs.
Hyperinflation and currency devaluation (not quantified) increased input costs for agricultural programmes.
contextual_constraints_new: Prolonged absence of functional civilian government invalidated original political transition assumptions.
IDP inflows to urban/peri-urban areas (e.g., Khartoum) exceeded planned targeting capacity.
Local governance structures (e.g., CDCs) required more capacity-building than anticipated to manage resilience funds.
Supply chain disruptions forced reliance on private-sector distributors for agricultural inputs.
partner_relationship_issues: Tensions between World Bank and donors over risk appetite post-coup (e.g., WB’s initial reluctance to engage de facto authorities).
UNICEF/WFP overhead costs and procurement processes were seen as bureaucratic by local NGOs.
Delayed World Bank reporting (aligned to Sept fiscal year) misaligned with FCDO annual review cycles.
capacity_constraints_emerged: CDCs lacked financial management skills to oversee rapid procurement, requiring additional training.
Shortage of qualified frontline workers (health, education) in conflict-affected areas.
Limited World Bank in-country presence pre-2023 slowed problem-solving for implementation bottlenecks.
risk_materialization: Political risk: Military coup (Oct 2021) and prolonged conflict (2023–present) disrupted all original timelines.
Operational risk: Banking system collapse made cash-based interventions unviable.
Reputational risk: Donor coordination challenges during emergency repurposing created perceptions of inefficiency.
Financial risk: Currency devaluation eroded purchasing power of fixed budgets (e.g., agricultural inputs).

2024.variance_explanation: Delays due to PIM/ESF approvals (resolved Nov 2024). $7m spent on rapid procurement; remainder on operational costs.

cumulative.leveraged_funds: $110m mobilized (not yet approved: $30m EU, $50m Crisis Response Window, $30m Trust Fund donors)

strengths: Pooled Trust Fund achieved economies of scale (e.g., bulk procurement of PHC kits).
Partnerships with WFP/UNICEF secured supplies despite Sudan’s market constraints.
Expansion to Gedaref state demonstrated scalability.
weaknesses: Long delivery chain (WB → UNICEF/WFP → NGOs) added overhead costs.
World Bank administrative charges partially offset by Trust Fund interest earnings.

strengths: Use of existing CDCs reduced startup costs for community engagement.
Adaptive delivery (e.g., private-sector agricultural input distribution) improved timeliness.
weaknesses: Disbursement condition delays (PIM/ESF) created 10-month implementation lag.
UN agency contracting processes extended procurement timelines by ~4 weeks.

achievements: 90 Primary Health Centres (PHCs) operational with essential supplies.
14,057 MT of wheat/vegetables harvested (food security output).
HIPC Decision Point achieved (2021), unlocking billions in concessional finance.
gaps: Full effectiveness assessment deferred to next review (limited implementation data).
Delays in education/WaSH/GBV components due to prioritization of health/food security.

strengths: Targeted IDPs and host communities in high-inflow areas (e.g., Khartoum).
Mandatory 10% GBV allocation ensured protection services funding.
Women and IDPs included in CDC decision-making structures.
weaknesses: Urban bias in initial targeting (peri-urban areas prioritized over rural).
Limited reach to newly displaced populations post-2023 conflict escalation.

strengths: World Bank’s geo-enabled monitoring improved financial tracking.
Donor consensus mechanisms ensured transparent repurposing of funds (e.g., 2022 emergency pivot).
Separate accounting for UK’s £80m contribution within Trust Fund.
weaknesses: Delayed financial reporting from World Bank (aligned to Sept fiscal year).
Limited donor access to real-time expenditure data.
Currency fluctuations not fully mitigated in budget planning.

metrics: £80m UK contribution leveraged ~$1bn in WB Trust Fund (1:12.5 ratio).
$16m disbursed in 2024 supported 90 PHCs (~$178k/PHC) and 84 cooperatives (~$190k/coop).
Private-sector input distribution reduced procurement costs by bypassing UN agency overheads.
cost_efficiency_achieved.comparison_to_plan: Original PAD cost-benefit assumptions remain valid but timeline extended by 3 years. Unit costs for health/agriculture interventions aligned with regional benchmarks.

co_funding_materialization.details: $110m mobilized from EU/Crisis Response Window/Trust Fund donors but not yet approved for 2025 expansion. Original $1bn Trust Fund target not met due to donor hesitancy post-coup.

currency_exchange_impacts.impact: Significant but not quantified. Sudden devaluations increased local costs for imported inputs (e.g., medical supplies, seeds). Mitigation: World Bank’s bulk procurement and forward contracts partially offset risks.

key_delivery_lessons: Trust Fund models require clearer disbursement condition timelines to avoid implementation lags.
Direct NGO contracting by World Bank (via STARS) reduces overheads and improves flexibility.
Community-led structures (CDCs) need upfront capacity-building to manage resilience funds.
Private-sector partnerships (e.g., agricultural input distributors) can bypass procurement bottlenecks.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid needs assessments by UNICEF enabled targeted service delivery in high-IDP areas.
Revised SME grant eligibility criteria increased participation from 0 to 300 applications.
Integration of GBV allocations (10%) into all components ensured protection mainstreaming.
Geo-enabled monitoring by World Bank improved transparency for donors.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from cash transfers to in-kind food/agricultural support post-banking collapse.
Extended programme timeline by 3 years to accommodate delayed HIPC completion.
Increased FCDO oversight post-2021 coup (more frequent check-ins, risk reassessments).
Adopted private-sector channels for input distribution to accelerate food security outputs.
innovations_attempted: Digital platforms for cooperative/SME market linkages (piloted in Northern/River Nile states).
Bulk-buying consumer aggregators to stabilize food supply chains.
Mobile health teams to supplement PHCs in areas with collapsed infrastructure.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Streamline World Bank reporting alignment with FCDO cycles.
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Partially addressed—next review pulled forward to Autumn 2024, but WB fiscal year remains misaligned.

previous_recommendations_progress.recommendation: Enhance donor access to WB monitoring data.
previous_recommendations_progress.progress: Improved with geo-enabled tools, but real-time access still limited.

forward_recommendations: Advocate for continued World Bank direct NGO contracting in Sudan (including IDA projects).
Pull forward next annual review to Autumn 2024 to align with implementation progress.
Expand digital platforms for cooperatives/SMEs to improve market efficiency.
Integrate UKDEL in advocating for WB’s STARS approach regionally.
Pre-position contingency funds for future political/economic shocks.

strengths: Rapid repurposing of funds post-coup (2022) and conflict (2023) demonstrated agility.
Donor consensus mechanisms enabled collective risk-sharing (e.g., 2023 redesign).
World Bank’s increased local presence improved contextual risk monitoring.
weaknesses: Initial underestimation of political risks (assumed quick return to civilian rule).
Delayed activation of contingency plans for banking system collapse.
Limited scenario planning for prolonged conflict (post-April 2023).

cumulative.indirect: HIPC Decision Point achievement (2021) unlocked billions in concessional finance for Sudan.

policy_influence_achieved.evidence: Sudan reached HIPC Decision Point in record time (2021), directly attributed to SEIR/WB Trust Fund support.
SFSP design influenced Sudan’s subsequent cash transfer programmes, though implementation stalled post-coup.
Farmer cooperative models adopted by River Nile/Northern state governments for food security strategies.

capacity_building_results.results: CDCs established/strengthened in 24 communities, with active role in service prioritization.
90 PHCs now have trained staff and functional governance (e.g., community oversight of supplies).
200 farmer organizations (20,000 individuals) received inputs/capacity-building on wheat/sorghum/bean value chains.

unintended_consequences.description: Strengthened donor coordination mechanisms (e.g., Trust Fund model) now used for other Sudan crisis responses.
Emergency repurposing (2022) created expectations for cash transfers that could not be sustained post-conflict, leading to beneficiary dissatisfaction.
Over-reliance on UN agencies for procurement reduced local NGO capacity-building opportunities.

scalability_evidence.evidence: Expansion to Gedaref state planned for 2025; $110m mobilized for scale-up (pending approval).
Standardized kits (e.g., 300 PHC/midwifery kits) adopted by AfDB for other Sudan health programmes.
Sorghum/wheat value chain interventions replicated in neighbouring states via WFP programmes.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Original objectives (economic stabilization, HIPC completion) remain valid but require adapted delivery model due to prolonged conflict. Phase II redesign (2023) shifts focus to community resilience with potential government handover if conditions improve. The programme’s ability to leverage £80m into billions in concessional finance justifies continuation despite risks.

strengths: Trust Fund structure allows flexible repurposing (demonstrated in 2022/2023 pivots).
Community-led approaches (CDCs) build local ownership for long-term service delivery.
World Bank’s increased in-country presence improves adaptive management.
risks: Dependence on UN agency/NGO partners may not be sustainable if conflict persists.
Government handover contingent on political transition (uncertain timeline).
Donor fatigue could limit co-funding for Phase II expansion.

reasons: Acknowledges programme’s agility in crisis response (e.g., 2022 emergency pivot).
Concerns about delayed disbursements and overhead costs in delivery chain.
Recognizes high leverage ratio (£80m → billions in concessional finance) but seeks better VFM.

planned_adaptations_future: Transition from third-party delivery (UNICEF/WFP) to government systems if civilian rule is restored.
Expand digital tools for cooperative/SME market linkages and monitoring.
Pre-position contingency funds for future shocks (e.g., currency collapses, supply chain disruptions).
Strengthen CDC financial management capacity to reduce reliance on NGOs.
Advocate for World Bank to adopt STARS contracting model in other Sudan programmes.

output_1.title: Effective accountable grant competition and due diligence lead to a successful appointment of the RCC consortium

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shifted to a consortium-led model with 3ie as lead, University of Birmingham as academic lead, and CABI as digital lead. Added flexibility to commission both ODA and non-ODA research while reducing bureaucracy. Incorporated lessons from UKRI, NIHR, and FCDO's Review of Bureaucracy in Research.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Consortium partners (3ie, University of Birmingham, CABI) performed "excellent" with full engagement, cooperation, and responsiveness to FCDO needs. Demonstrated ability to adapt to rapidly scaling demand (e.g., non-ODA projects) and unforeseen requests (e.g., White Paper consultation support).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Multi-disciplinary FCDO panel (including commercial and senior staff) managed the grant competition. Strategic meetings with senior colleagues enabled rapid decision-making. Regular programme delivery meetings supported implementation.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Close coordination between FCDO and consortium through open, transparent, and frequent dialogue. Early challenges in articulating expectations, but relationship strengthened through responsive problem-solving (e.g., White Paper support).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Accountable grant competition launched in September 2022 with 170+ organizations engaged in early market engagement. Eight proposals received, with 3ie-led consortium selected after rigorous evaluation (presentations, interviews, due diligence). Contract signed by May 2023.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher-than-planned oversight during inception phase due to need to establish trust and clarify processes. Forty documents reviewed during due diligence, with additional meetings to assess risks. SRO prioritized and quality-assured recommendations for 3ie.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in responding to: 1) Rapidly scaling FCDO demand (non-ODA projects), 2) Unforeseen requests (White Paper consultation), 3) Adjusting commissioning processes based on pilot projects. Pilot templates and guides are being developed to balance flexibility with standardization.
adaptive_management_examples: Consortium supported FCDO’s White Paper on International Development consultation under tight deadlines, leveraging academic expertise.
Adjusted research commissioning processes to accommodate both ODA and non-ODA projects, incorporating equitable partnership principles.
Developed a Technical Hub with benchmarked costs to provide on-demand expertise, responding to varied FCDO demand levels.

main_implementation_challenges: Establishing a delivery model that balances flexibility (for rapid commissioning) with bureaucracy reduction for FCDO.
Timely delivery of a complex digital platform that integrates with FCDO systems and communicates R&D portfolio externally.
Initial pipeline development challenged by varied and rapid changes in FCDO demand, risking delays to first research commissions (originally planned for October 2023).
Need for clearer articulation of expectations between FCDO and 3ie to improve proactive problem-solving.
external_factors_impact: Legacy of COVID-19: Phase 2 of the Covid Collective platform (£2.5m, May 2022–June 2023) was pre-approved and required integration into the new RCC structure. Generated high-value research across 16 countries but added complexity to inception.
Political priorities: Unforeseen request to support FCDO’s White Paper consultation required rapid consortium response, testing adaptive capacity.
contextual_constraints_new: Higher-than-anticipated demand for non-ODA research commissions in early stages, requiring RCC to scale up faster than planned.
Need to align with cross-HMG initiatives (e.g., Bureaucracy Review) and external developments (e.g., Open Access requirements) while designing the digital platform.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial caution from FCDO teams about RCC processes, requiring evidence of benefits to build trust.
Early phase required more clarity on commissioning practicalities to strengthen engagement.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited initial pipeline of projects due to fluctuating FCDO demand, affecting 3ie’s ability to launch first commissions on time.
Capacity to deploy Technical Hub and engage with Post project leads needed for non-ODA projects while meeting ODA commitments.
risk_materialization: Risk of delayed research commissioning due to demand volatility (partially mitigated by flexible pilot approaches).
Digital platform complexity risk (being addressed through phased discovery and MVP launch by July 2024).

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. Initial £2.5m allocated to Covid Collective Phase 2 (May 2022–June 2023) was executed as planned. Core RCC budget execution aligned with inception activities (consortium appointment, due diligence, process development).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indicators suggest good VFM: 1) Competitive grant process attracted strong proposals with Global South partnerships; 2) Consortium’s ability to leverage existing expertise (e.g., White Paper support) added unplanned value; 3) Pilot projects will benchmark costs for Technical Hub services. Formal VFM framework under development for 2023.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. FCDO conducted thorough due diligence (40+ documents reviewed) and recommended risk mitigation actions for 3ie’s internal policies. Financial reporting templates established to reconcile RCC expenditure. Risk register and operations manual in place.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Not yet measurable (baseline processes still being developed). Efficiencies anticipated through: 1) Reduced administrative burden via centralized commissioning; 2) Shared Technical Hub resources across projects; 3) Digital platform replacing fragmented systems.

key_delivery_lessons: FCDO teams require tangible evidence of RCC benefits to build trust; early wins (e.g., first research calls) are critical.
Consortium’s adaptive capacity (e.g., White Paper support) validates selection criteria but requires clear communication of expectations.
Flexible commissioning processes must balance standardization (for VFM) with responsiveness to FCDO’s varied demand.
successful_delivery_practices: Multi-disciplinary evaluation panels for grant competitions ensured robust partner selection.
Regular strategic meetings with senior colleagues enabled rapid decision-making during inception.
Open dialogue between FCDO and consortium fostered collaborative problem-solving (e.g., addressing demand spikes).
Pilot projects used to test and refine commissioning templates before full rollout.
management_adaptations_made: Added clarity to commissioning processes and responsibilities via a planned user guide for FCDO staff.
Developed a phased approach to digital platform delivery (MVP by July 2024) to manage complexity.
Incorporated equitable partnership principles into all research stages, aligning with FCDO’s Women and Girls Strategy and Global Disability Summit commitments.
innovations_attempted: Technical Hub model: On-demand expertise with benchmarked costs to optimize VFM.
Unified digital platform: Centralized access to FCDO’s R&D portfolio, replacing fragmented systems.
Impact and Open Access Funds: New mechanisms to prioritize high-impact research dissemination.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: N/A (first annual review).
forward_recommendations: Finalize and implement a strong monitoring framework (logframe, VFM indicators) by end-2023 to track RCC effectiveness.
Launch first research calls in autumn 2023 to demonstrate RCC’s operational capacity and build FCDO buy-in.
Develop a sustainable costing model for RCC services to ensure long-term viability beyond initial funding.
Clarify roles/responsibilities between FCDO and 3ie to improve proactive problem-solving.
Prioritize digital platform MVP launch (July 2024) with essential functions (e.g., publishing RCC calls) to show early progress.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Partially effective. Planned risks (e.g., demand volatility) were identified, but mitigation required adaptive management (e.g., flexible pilot projects). New risks (e.g., digital platform complexity) are being addressed through phased delivery. Risk register is actively used, with SRO oversight.

beneficiaries_reached_actual: Covid Collective Phase 2: Research generated across 16 countries; 16 partners received smaller grants for dissemination.

RCC inception phase: Indirect beneficiaries include FCDO teams (reduced administrative burden) and global research community (future access to unified platform). Direct research beneficiaries pending first commissions (autumn 2023).
policy_influence_achieved: Covid Collective research informed policy/practice responses to pandemic in 16 countries.
RCC consortium supported FCDO’s White Paper on International Development consultation, demonstrating potential for future policy influence.
capacity_building_results: Technical Hub will provide on-demand expertise to FCDO and posts, building capacity for evidence-based decision-making.
Digital platform aims to improve global access to FCDO research outputs, enhancing capacity of external stakeholders.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Consortium’s adaptive capacity (e.g., White Paper support) strengthened FCDO-RCC relationship beyond planned activities.
Negative: High initial demand for non-ODA projects risked diverting focus from ODA priorities; managed through flexible resource allocation.
scalability_evidence: Delivery model (centralized commissioning + Technical Hub) is designed to scale across FCDO’s R&D portfolio.
Digital platform’s modular design allows for future expansion (e.g., integrating new research programs).
Pilot projects will test scalability of commissioning processes before full implementation.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong inception phase performance (A+ score) with effective consortium partnership and adaptive management. Early challenges (e.g., demand volatility) are being addressed through flexible processes. Digital platform and first research calls (autumn 2023) will further demonstrate value.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Medium (dependent on: 1) Successful digital platform launch; 2) Demonstration of VFM through monitoring framework; 3) FCDO’s continued demand for RCC services).
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High (evidenced by A+ score, positive partner relationships, and adaptive responses to FCDO needs).
planned_adaptations_future: Develop a sustainable costing model for RCC services to reduce reliance on initial funding.
Enhance proactive communication between FCDO and 3ie to align expectations and demand.
Phase digital platform delivery to prioritize essential functions (e.g., research calls) before full feature set.
Incorporate lessons from pilot projects into standardized commissioning processes by 2024.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Animal and Plant Health Innovation and Evidence Delivery Platform (APHID) Programme

output_3.title: Enhanced Knowledge, Evidence and Learning to develop tools, knowledge and evidence that help FCDO and IDS priority countries prevent, identify, and respond to emerging animal and plant health threats

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The APHID Management Team identified that finalizing new Investment details took longer than anticipated due to administrative processes and technical scope negotiations. Earlier engagement and dedicated resources are now planned for future Investments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: CABI demonstrated strong delivery with 13.6 million farmers reached through PlantwisePlus, exceeding expectations in pest preparedness and farmer advisory. Pirbright Institute maintained robust technical and financial reporting. Juno Evidence Alliance faced AI-driven evidence synthesis challenges but proactively managed issues through regular FCDO engagement.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The FCDO APHID Management Team meets quarterly with an Action Log for tracking. Lead Advisers engage with Delivery Partners at least quarterly, with increased frequency during start-up. The One Health Hub UK (hosted by CABI) was established to coordinate knowledge and learning across Investments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination was effective for established partners (e.g., CABI, Pirbright) but faced delays in onboarding new Investments. The Knowledge, Evidence, and Learning Capability was introduced to build synergies between Investments and align with FCDO priorities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: CABI and Pirbright demonstrated strong procurement practices, with competitive pricing and cost-saving measures (e.g., reduced travel, shared operational support). Juno’s AI-driven reviews required iterative adjustments to procurement timelines.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than planned during the start-up phase, particularly for Juno’s proof-of-concept AI reviews. Quarterly Joint Oversight Committee (JoC) meetings and Scientific Strategy Board reviews were maintained for Pirbright’s CVIM Investment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Timelines for Juno’s evidence reviews were extended to address AI-related challenges. APHID adapted by dedicating more resources to early-stage Investment discussions to accelerate future negotiations.
adaptive_management_examples: Extended Juno review timelines to resolve AI synthesis issues, with lessons feeding into scale-up phase design.
Additional resources allocated to support National Plant Protection Organisations (NPPOs) in integrating horizon-scanning tools, ensuring long-term sustainability despite short-term delays.
Engagement with IPPC and FAO to strengthen plant health systems based on CABI’s implementation experience.

main_implementation_challenges: Delays in finalizing new Investment details due to complex administrative and technical negotiations, despite partner enthusiasm.
NPPOs lacked structural capacity to integrate horizon-scanning tools, requiring additional programme resources for systemic change.
Juno’s AI-driven evidence synthesis faced unanticipated technical hurdles during the proof-of-concept phase, necessitating timeline extensions.
contextual_constraints_new: Partner countries’ plant health systems were less prepared than assumed for preventive approaches (e.g., risk registers, horizon scanning), requiring adaptive support.
Private-sector engagement for the BioProtection Portal revealed gaps in digital accessibility for smallholder farmers, prompting user experience upgrades.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment between FCDO’s evidence needs and Juno’s AI capabilities required iterative learning and scope adjustments.
FAO and GALVMED had no planned activities in 2023, limiting early collaboration opportunities.
capacity_constraints_emerged: NPPOs lacked institutional structures to sustain horizon-scanning tools post-workshop, requiring programme-led working groups.
CABI’s expansion to 10 additional countries for the BioProtection Portal strained local partner capacity for knowledge dissemination.
risk_materialization: Delays in Investment negotiations risked slowing programme momentum, mitigated by earlier engagement for future phases.
Juno’s technical risks in AI synthesis were managed through close FCDO-Juno collaboration, though three reviews were delivered late.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track. No major deviations from the £37 million budget. Key cost drivers (staff, facilities, travel) remained stable, with efficiency measures (e.g., virtual meetings, shared Pirbright resources) offsetting inflationary pressures.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: CABI and Pirbright demonstrated cost minimization through competitive procurement, shared infrastructure, and reduced consultant use. Pirbright’s MoU with CVIM optimized operational support.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: PlantwisePlus was deemed efficient by an independent review, delivering economies of scale via multi-donor funding. CABI’s 169 publications (98 in high-impact journals) and 13.6 million farmer reach in 2023 exceeded targets.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High. PlantwisePlus’s external review confirmed alignment with national priorities and strong relevance. Pirbright’s CVIM maintained technical progress with robust oversight.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong. Both CABI and Pirbright applied rigorous financial systems, including internal/external audits (e.g., Pirbright’s TPI systems) and risk management strategies. Juno’s financial oversight was adaptive to address proof-of-concept uncertainties.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: CABI’s local staff recruitment and Pirbright’s travel prioritization reduced costs without compromising outputs. The BioProtection Portal’s upgrades leveraged existing digital infrastructure for scalability.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: PlantwisePlus secured co-funding from six donors, enhancing oversight and delivering economies of scale. No co-funding issues reported for other Investments in 2023.

key_delivery_lessons: Early engagement with partners is critical to accelerate Investment negotiations and avoid administrative bottlenecks.
AI-driven evidence synthesis requires iterative learning and realistic timelines during proof-of-concept phases.
Systemic change in plant health (e.g., horizon scanning) demands long-term partner capacity building, not just tool delivery.
successful_delivery_practices: CABI’s multi-channel farmer outreach (clinics, SMS, digital tools) achieved 13.6 million reach with conservative methodology.
Pirbright’s dual oversight (JoC and Scientific Strategy Board) ensured technical and financial alignment with funders (FCDO, BMGF).
Quarterly FCDO-Partner meetings with Action Logs improved responsiveness to emerging challenges.
management_adaptations_made: APHID Management Team will initiate Investment discussions earlier and allocate more resources to negotiations.
Juno’s scale-up phase will incorporate lessons on AI capabilities and FCDO evidence needs.
PlantwisePlus added NPPO capacity-building to its rollout phase (2024–2027) to ensure sustainability of horizon-scanning tools.
innovations_attempted: Juno’s AI-enhanced evidence reviews (7 commissioned) tested machine-driven synthesis for agriculture and One Health topics.
BioProtection Portal’s user experience upgrades and private-sector engagement informed the Nature-based Solutions Innovation Consortium.
CABI’s Pest Risk Information Service (PRISE) SMS alerts scaled to 724,883 farmers in 2023.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.previous_recommendations_progress: Not applicable (first APHID Annual Review). However, PlantwisePlus addressed 2023 FCDO review recommendations by integrating NPPO capacity support and external collaboration (e.g., IPPC, FAO).
forward_recommendations: Start Investment negotiations 6–12 months earlier to account for administrative complexities.
Expand engagement with global plant health bodies (IPPC, FAO) to share lessons on system-level change.
Develop a standardized set of APHID KPIs mapped to the Theory of Change for consistent Investment reporting by 2024.
Scale successful digital tools (e.g., PRISE, BioProtection Portal) with targeted capacity-building for NPPOs.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective. Pirbright’s risk registers and CABI’s adaptive support for NPPOs mitigated key risks. Juno’s proactive issue management minimized delays despite technical uncertainties. Financial risks were controlled via audits and MoUs.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.actual: 13.6 million farmers reached in 2023 via PlantwisePlus (clinics, SMS, digital tools, mass campaigns). Cumulative reach since 2010: 74.9 million.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.methodology: Conservative assumptions used for reach calculations, including farmer-to-farmer information sharing.

policy_influence_achieved: PlantwisePlus’s external review influenced donor alignment and programme rollout (2024–2027).
BioProtection Portal’s private-sector engagement informed the Nature-based Solutions Innovation Consortium (launching 2024).
Juno’s evidence reviews (e.g., "Evidence to Promote One Health Implementation at Scale") will support FCDO policy priorities.
capacity_building_results: 10 additional countries added to the BioProtection Portal (total: 42), with 50%+ users being farmers/advisers.
NPPOs received targeted support to integrate horizon-scanning tools, though systemic adoption remains a long-term goal.
Pirbright’s CVIM advanced vaccine/therapeutic pipelines for priority livestock diseases, with 169 publications (98 high-impact) in 2023.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Farmer-to-farmer information sharing amplified PlantwisePlus’s reach beyond direct channels (10.9 million indirect beneficiaries).
Negative: Short-term delays in NPPO capacity-building slowed horizon-scanning adoption, though long-term sustainability is expected.
scalability_evidence: PlantwisePlus’s multi-donor model and digital tools (PRISE, BioProtection Portal) demonstrate scalability across 27 countries.
Juno’s AI reviews, if successful, could be expanded to other FCDO evidence needs.
Pirbright’s vaccine pipelines and CABI’s biocontrol solutions are designed for regional/global application.

continuation_rationale: Strong performance (Overall Output Score: A) and high relevance to FCDO’s One Health and food security priorities.
Demonstrated value for money (efficient delivery, multi-donor leverage, high farmer reach).
Critical mass achieved in knowledge generation (publications, evidence reviews) and capacity-building (NPPOs, digital tools).
Scalable models (PlantwisePlus, Juno, Pirbright) align with long-term global health security goals.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. The integrated platform approach (Knowledge Hub, shared KPIs) and partner diversity (CABI, Pirbright, FAO) ensure resilience.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Earlier initiation of Investment negotiations with dedicated resources.
Expanded collaboration with IPPC/FAO to strengthen plant health systems.
Standardized APHID KPIs and Theory of Change alignment for all Investments by 2024.
Scale-up of Juno’s AI reviews and digital tools (PRISE, BioProtection Portal) with targeted capacity-building.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Humanitarian and Resilience Programme (HARP)

output_1.title: The delivery of more predictable and impactful food assistance in NE Nigeria

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift to multi-year partnerships (except ICRC annual appeals) leveraging existing NENTAD partnerships. Introduction of Third Party Monitoring (Dec 2023) and technical support via HSOT consulting arrangement. UNHAS implemented partial cost recovery for rotary flights, impacting national NGO access.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: WFP exceeded food assistance targets (98% achievement for 2023/24). ICRC delivered 176% of 2022 CBT targets but only 50% of 2023 in-kind targets. UNICEF and CARE exceeded gender-sensitive cash/voucher targets (95.8% and 178% respectively). Localisation progress noted with 6,025 new women-led groups engaged.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO addressed HART resourcing gaps but faced broader BHC recruitment challenges, requiring Humanitarian Team Leader to assume wider management roles. HSOT provided surge capacity (cash advisers, WASH specialist) for technical oversight.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: FCDO maintained seats on Humanitarian Country Team and Donor Coordination Group, leading discussions on prioritisation and camp closures. Coordination with state-level entities initiated. Challenges in aligning partner logframes with HARP targets (e.g., LGA coverage indicators).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement of food/nutrition supplies and air transport (UNHAS) were key cost drivers. Economic shocks (Naira devaluation, fuel subsidy removal) complicated procurement but local procurement saved foreign exchange costs.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Enhanced via HSOT technical advisers (cash, WASH, humanitarian) and periodic programme staffing reviews. Third Party Monitoring introduced (Dec 2023) to improve accountability.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to camp closures by reallocating resources to hard-to-reach areas. Rapid design of two additional humanitarian business cases (2023/24) to programme capital funding.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised Output 1 indicators to merge in-kind/CBT reporting under 1.1.
UNHAS cost recovery adjustments to mitigate impact on national NGOs (delayed ticket costs for locals).
WFP’s strategic shift to resilience-building livelihoods ahead of camp closures (IFPRI study commissioned).
NHF allocated $3M to medium-risk national Women-Led Organisations for protection programmes.

main_implementation_challenges: Escalating food insecurity (24.8M people at crisis/emergency levels in 2023, +34% YoY).
Camp closures increasing displacement (2.3M IDPs in BAY states by 2024) and reducing safe access to land.
Security risks (IEDs, attacks on farming/trading) limiting humanitarian access.
Currency devaluation (Naira float) and fuel subsidy removal increasing operational costs (e.g., +58% reduction in UNHAS helicopter journeys due to cost recovery).
Government push for accelerated camp closures adding cost/access complexities.
external_factors_impact: Macroeconomic shocks (inflation, Naira devaluation) increased household food insecurity despite better GBP/USD exchange rates for donors.
Conflict dynamics (14-year non-international armed conflict) remained the primary driver of humanitarian needs.
Climate shocks (seasonal rains/droughts) required predictive funding adjustments.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated scale of camp closures and relocation pressures from Borno State Government.
Reduced humanitarian access due to governmental restrictions on security assessments.
Localisation agenda constrained by UNHAS cost recovery reducing national NGO participation.
partner_relationship_issues: Misalignment between partner logframes (e.g., WFP/UNICEF LGA coverage reporting) and HARP targets.
Delays in agreeing FCDO attribution approaches with partners (e.g., food assistance metrics).
ICRC’s annual appeal model created discontinuity in multi-year planning.
capacity_constraints_emerged: BHC recruitment failures for key management positions, overburdening Humanitarian Team Leader.
Limited technical capacity in cash programming and WASH required HSOT surge support.
National WLOs lacked capacity to access NHF funding without targeted support.
risk_materialization: Severe risk rating persisted due to conflict volatility and economic instability.
Exchange rate fluctuations materialized as a financial risk, impacting procurement.
Protection risks (GBV, access constraints) worsened with camp closures.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: £54.2M spent against £150M ceiling (36% execution rate). Underspends in local procurement (due to Naira exchange gains) offset by increased costs for imports/operational overheads.

value_for_money_assessment.economy: Mixed: Multi-year partnerships (WFP, UNICEF) enabled leverage of NENTAD investments, but ICRC’s annual appeals reduced efficiency. Local procurement saved FX costs but household food affordability deteriorated.
value_for_money_assessment.efficiency: Partial cost recovery for UNHAS reduced common service usage by 58%, undermining localisation. HSOT technical advisers improved oversight but added short-term costs.
value_for_money_assessment.effectiveness: High: Output 1 (food assistance) achieved 98% of targets; nutrition and protection outputs exceeded gender-sensitive cash targets. Cost per beneficiary remained competitive despite inflation.
value_for_money_assessment.equity: Targeting adjusted for camp closures, but hard-to-reach areas faced access constraints. Women-led groups engagement (10,000+ WLOs) improved gender equity.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Robust: Regular partner reporting on VfM metrics introduced. HSOT provided surge capacity for financial oversight. Currency hedging strategies mitigated Naira volatility impacts.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Local procurement of food/nutrition supplies achieved 20-30% cost savings vs. imports, but fuel/transport costs rose by 40% due to subsidy removal. UNHAS cost recovery added 15-20% to air transport budgets.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial: NHF allocated $3M to national WLOs, but broader co-funding targets were not fully met due to donor fatigue in the LCB crisis.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Naira devaluation (official rate floated in 2023) created a dual effect: (1) 30% reduction in local procurement costs for IPs (GBP strength), but (2) 50%+ increase in household food prices, worsening coping strategies.

key_delivery_lessons: Multi-year partnerships (e.g., WFP/UNICEF) improve efficiency but require aligned logframes.
Localisation requires dedicated funding (e.g., NHF’s $3M for WLOs) and capacity-building to overcome UNHAS cost barriers.
Cash programming (MPCA/e-vouchers) must align with national safety nets to avoid duplication.
Camp closures necessitate flexible geographic targeting and livelihoods integration (WFP’s resilience shift).
successful_delivery_practices: HSOT technical advisers filled critical gaps in cash/WASH expertise.
Third Party Monitoring (Dec 2023) improved accountability in hard-to-reach areas.
Women-led collective action (10,000+ WLOs) enhanced protection outcomes.
WFP’s CSP 2023-2027 shift to resilience-building addresses long-term food security.
management_adaptations_made: Merged Output 1 indicators (1.1/1.2) to simplify food assistance reporting.
Introduced periodic programme staffing reviews to proactively address resourcing gaps.
Revised VfM framework to capture localisation and AAP metrics.
innovations_attempted: UNHAS partial cost recovery for rotary flights (though reduced NGO access).
NHF’s $3M pilot for medium-risk WLOs to test women-led humanitarian solutions.
WFP’s IFPRI study on food systems/transfer modalities (results Nov 2024).
Chain mapping study to optimize supply chains in northern Nigeria.
previous_recommendations_progress: ✅ Revised Output 1.1/1.2 indicators and attribution approaches (partial completion).
⚠️ Logframe review pending; VfM metrics still require partner alignment.
❌ Geographic expansion to North West not yet actioned (recommended in 2023 AR).
forward_recommendations: Extend HARP beyond 2025 to improve planning predictability and VfM.
Conduct sub-national needs assessment for North East/North West to inform targeting.
Mainstream resilience-building in future phases (currently underrepresented in results framework).
Advocate for exemptions to UNHAS cost recovery for national NGOs to restore localisation progress.
Strengthen AAP across all interventions with dedicated budget lines.

risk_management_effectiveness.anticipated_risks: Conflict volatility and economic shocks were anticipated but underestimated in severity (e.g., Naira devaluation impact).
risk_management_effectiveness.unanticipated_risks: Government-led camp closures and UNHAS cost recovery were not fully mitigated.
risk_management_effectiveness.mitigation_effectiveness: Partial: HSOT surge capacity addressed technical risks, but macroeconomic risks required reactive adjustments (e.g., revised cash programming).
risk_management_effectiveness.adaptive_capacity: High: Rapid business case development (2023/24) and indicator revisions demonstrated agility.

nutrition.actual: UNICEF: 4,789 women (gender-sensitive cash); CARE: 889 women (178% of target)

protection.actual: 6,025 new women-led groups engaged (UNICEF); 10+ WLO collectives (CARE)

policy_influence_achieved: Influenced HCT prioritisation discussions on camp closures and durable solutions.
Advocated for localisation via NHF’s $3M WLO pilot (potential model for broader adoption).
WFP’s IFPRI study (Nov 2024) may inform national food systems policy.
capacity_building_results: 10,000+ women-led groups (UNICEF) trained in collective action and humanitarian response.
National WLOs gained access to NHF funding mechanisms ($3M allocation).
HSOT capacity-building for partners on cash programming and WASH.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Women-led groups improved community protection beyond project targets.
Negative: UNHAS cost recovery reduced national NGO access to hard-to-reach areas (-58% helicopter journeys).
Negative: Camp closures increased displacement without adequate durable solutions.
scalability_evidence: WFP’s resilience livelihoods model (post-camp closures) has potential for LCB-wide scaling.
MPCA/e-voucher alignment with national safety nets could be replicated in other states.
WLO engagement model (NHF pilot) scalable with dedicated localisation funding.

continuation_rationale: Two consecutive "A" scores demonstrate strong performance in addressing acute humanitarian needs.
Critical role in FCDO’s LCB crisis response (UK was 4th largest donor to UN appeal in 2023).
Flexible design allows adaptation to evolving context (camp closures, economic shocks).
Unmet needs persist: 24.8M food-insecure, 2.3M IDPs in BAY states.

strengths: Multi-year partnerships (WFP/UNICEF) ensure continuity.
HSOT technical oversight model proven effective.
Localisation progress (WLOs) aligns with FCDO priorities.
risks: Dependence on UNHAS common services vulnerable to cost recovery policies.
Recurrent BHC staffing gaps threaten long-term management.
Naira volatility and inflation may erode VfM gains.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Extend programme beyond 2025 to align with HRP cycles and improve predictability.
Expand geographic focus to North West Nigeria based on needs assessment.
Integrate resilience-building indicators into results framework.
Develop mitigation strategies for UNHAS cost recovery impacts on localisation.
Strengthen AAP and VfM reporting with partners.
