programme_metadata.programme_title: Climate, Environment and Nature (CLEAN) Helpdesk Programme

output_1.title: Increased knowledge of CLEAN HD users of UK-ODA related inclusive and equitable CEN work

output_2.title: HMG demand met for safe CEN TA through improved access to, and coordination of, suitable inclusive and equitable CEN TA

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Shift from original 'one-stop-shop' ambition to more focused CEN technical assistance delivery, with reduced emphasis on deep coordination with other FCDO facilities due to capacity constraints. The Programme Delivery Board was not established as planned and is being reevaluated.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Consortium partners (SSN, ODI Global, SDDirect, Paul Watkiss Associates) successfully launched the Gateway Platform and delivered 11 completed technical assistance requests (with 19 ongoing) within 4 months, exceeding expectations for demand. However, resource library development lagged due to UK pre-election restrictions and insufficient user needs assessment.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: Governance lighter than planned - the Programme Delivery Board was not convened, and coordination with other FCDO facilities (Nature Facility, SPARC, CLARE) remained superficial. Day-to-day management by SSN proved effective for TA delivery but less so for strategic coordination.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Limited progress on creating a unified "one-stop-shop" due to the complexity of aligning with other FCDO-funded platforms (e.g., Nature Facility, STAAR). Ad-hoc coordination occurred but fell short of the ambitious integration envisioned in the business case.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: No major procurement issues reported. The roster of experts was effectively mobilized to respond to 56 TA requests within the review period.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: FCDO oversight was proportionate, with focus on inception phase deliverables and early TA quality. Less attention was given to cross-facility coordination and resource library development.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility in responding to high demand for TA (86 individuals informed vs. target of 25) and adapting the GEDSI strategy. However, the resource library and coordination outputs were deprioritized.
adaptive_management_examples: Revised GEDSI quality assurance process for all TA terms of reference and outputs, with feedback loops to experts.
Paused the Programme Delivery Board establishment to reassess its value after consulting other facilities.
Shifted focus from comprehensive resource library to prioritizing TA delivery due to time constraints and user demand.

main_implementation_challenges: Underdeveloped resource library (only 7 outputs hosted vs. expectations) due to UK pre-election restrictions and insufficient stakeholder consultation.
Overambitious 'one-stop-shop' coordination goal proved impractical given the diversity of other FCDO facilities and their sectoral focuses.
Delay in conducting the annual user survey (critical for results framework) due to limited implementation period, creating evidence gaps for impact assessment.
Programme Delivery Board not established as planned, leading to weaker cross-facility governance.
external_factors_impact: UK pre-election period (mid-2024) restricted FCDO engagement and delayed content publication for the resource library.
High and growing demand for CEN technical assistance (56 requests in 4 months) strained capacity to balance TA delivery with platform development.
Competing priorities within FCDO (e.g., focus on International Climate Finance) influenced TA request themes and programme visibility.
contextual_constraints_new: Limited FCDO intranet visibility for CLEAN compared to other "centres of expertise," reducing internal uptake.
Unanticipated complexity in integrating nature-focused TA alongside climate priorities, requiring ToC adjustments.
Short inception phase (completed June 2024) left insufficient time to fully test assumptions about user needs and coordination mechanisms.
partner_relationship_issues: No major partner conflicts reported, but consortium members faced challenges in aligning on the resource library’s scope and quality standards.
Coordination with other FCDO-funded facilities (e.g., Nature Facility) was transactional rather than strategic, limiting joint value-add.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Consortium capacity was stretched by the volume of TA requests, leading to trade-offs between TA delivery and platform development.
Limited MEL (Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning) capacity delayed the hiring of the PrOF5 MEL role, affecting data collection for the results framework.
FCDO’s internal capacity to engage with CLEAN was variable, with some departments (e.g., Defra) less involved than planned.
risk_materialization: Risk of "overpromising on coordination" materialized - the ambition to create a unified CEN support hub was not feasible within the programme’s resources.
Risk of "insufficient user engagement" partially materialized in the resource library’s limited content, though TA demand mitigated this for other outputs.
Risk of "delayed MEL systems" materialized due to the unfilled PrOF5 role, affecting evidence generation for the annual review.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track overall, with no major underspends or overspends reported. Budget reallocations were made to prioritize TA delivery over platform development due to high demand.

value_for_money_assessment.technical_assistance: High - Exceeded targets for TA delivery (86 individuals informed vs. 25) with strong user feedback (83% confidence in safeguarding reporting).
value_for_money_assessment.resource_library: Low - Limited outputs (7 items) and delayed development reduce VFM for this component.
value_for_money_assessment.coordination: Medium - Some value from ad-hoc coordination with other facilities, but returns were lower than expected due to limited strategic collaboration.
value_for_money_assessment.overall: Good - Strong VFM in core TA delivery offsets weaker performance in platform and coordination outputs.

financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Sound - No significant issues reported. Financial reporting was timely, and audit trails for TA expenditures were maintained. The consortium demonstrated responsive budget management (e.g., reallocating funds to meet TA demand).
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: High for TA delivery (cost per individual informed = ~£43,000 for 86 individuals, below sector benchmarks for similar services). Less efficient for platform development due to underutilized capacity.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not applicable - No co-funding was planned or secured during this period.
financial_delivery_performance.currency_exchange_impacts: Not mentioned as a significant factor in the review.

key_delivery_lessons: Demand for CEN technical assistance is significantly higher than anticipated (56 requests in 4 months), requiring flexible resource allocation.
The 'one-stop-shop' model is not feasible without dedicated coordination resources; a more focused "CEN TA hub" approach is recommended.
User surveys and feedback mechanisms must be mandatory and integrated into TA processes to avoid evidence gaps.
successful_delivery_practices: Rapid mobilization of the expert roster enabled responsive TA delivery, with 11 requests completed and 19 ongoing within the review period.
GEDSI mainstreaming through QA processes for TA terms of reference and outputs was effectively implemented.
The Gateway Platform launch (July 2024) achieved functional minimum viable product status, with 841 users and 8,020 views in 2 months.
management_adaptations_made: Deprioritized the Programme Delivery Board after assessing low added value relative to implementation costs.
Revised the ToC to explicitly include nature as a co-equal focus alongside climate, and added a standalone capacity-building outcome.
Shifted from comprehensive resource library development to a phased approach, using proxies like climate-links.org for benchmarking.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of mandatory feedback forms tied to TA delivery to improve data collection for MEL.
Exploratory coordination with FCDO’s Energy, Climate and Environment Faculty to align foundational learning offers.
Use of TA request data to map cross-government CEN capacity gaps in real time.
previous_recommendations_progress: Partially addressed - The resource library was launched but remains basic; coordination with other facilities was attempted but not institutionalized.
Not addressed - The annual user survey was not conducted due to timing constraints.
forward_recommendations: By December 2024: Mandate completion of feedback forms and user surveys as a condition for receiving TA.
By January 2025: Revise programme governance, including the role of the Programme Delivery Board or alternative coordination mechanisms.
By March 2025: Conduct a joint review of the logframe to reduce reliance on survey data and align metrics with achievable outputs.
By March 2025: Develop a revised workplan and communications strategy, including engagement with Defra and other government departments.
By April 2025: Hold a vision-reinforcement workshop with FCDO and consortium members to align on final-year priorities.

risk_management_effectiveness.identified_risks: Most planned risks (e.g., TA demand variability, partner coordination) were identified but not fully mitigated.
risk_management_effectiveness.emerging_risks: New risks around MEL capacity gaps and intranet visibility were not anticipated in the business case.
risk_management_effectiveness.response_effectiveness: Reactive rather than proactive - adaptations were made after risks materialized (e.g., deprioritizing the resource library) rather than preemptively.
risk_management_effectiveness.tools_used: Risk register was maintained, but risk ownership and mitigation actions were not consistently implemented (e.g., delayed PrOF5 MEL hire).

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: 86 individuals informed by TA (vs. target of 25); 176 attendees at launch event.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Potentially higher - TA outputs were shared within HMG departments, but exact reach is unmeasured due to incomplete survey data.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.disaggregation: Gender-disaggregated data was partially collected for event attendees but not systematically for TA beneficiaries.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.outcome_achievement_level: Medium - Exceeded quantitative targets for TA delivery but fell short on platform development and cross-facility coordination. The programme is on track for impact-level contributions (e.g., supporting 20 countries on ICF vs. target of 8) but lacks robust evidence for some outcomes due to data gaps.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.impact_evidence_strength: Medium - Strong evidence for TA demand and user satisfaction (proxy data from feedback forms), but weak evidence for knowledge uptake and behavioral change due to the missing user survey. The ToC remains plausible but untested for longer-term impact pathways.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.sustainability_prospects: Medium - High sustainability for TA delivery (proven demand and embedded FCDO processes), but low for the resource library and coordination functions without dedicated resources. Risk of reduced visibility post-2026 without FCDO intranet integration.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.policy_influence_achieved: Emerging - TA outputs have informed ICF programming in 20 countries, and CLEAN is increasingly referenced in FCDO climate/nature strategies. However, systematic policy uptake is not yet documented.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.capacity_building_results: Partial - GEDSI capacity was strengthened through QA processes, and TA requests included capacity-building components (e.g., Paris alignment training). However, standalone capacity-building outputs were limited.
unintended_consequences: Positive: High TA demand revealed unmet needs for CEN support across HMG, justifying programme expansion.
Negative: The focus on TA delivery may have crowded out platform development, reducing long-term accessibility of knowledge products.
outcomes_impact_for_qca.scalability_evidence: High potential for TA model - The demand-driven approach and expert roster are replicable for other government departments or themes. Platform scalability is constrained by current technical limitations and content gaps.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: The programme has demonstrated high value in delivering CEN technical assistance, with strong demand and positive user feedback. However, adjustments are needed to improve the resource library, MEL systems, and coordination mechanisms to fully achieve the intended outcomes by 2026.
programme_continuation_trajectory.likelihood_success_overall: High for TA delivery; Medium for platform and coordination outputs. The programme is likely to meet or exceed its impact-level targets (e.g., supporting UK contributions to climate resilience and nature loss reversal) but may fall short on some output-level deliverables without corrections.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: Partially sustainable - The TA delivery model is robust and could be extended or replicated, but the platform and coordination functions require additional investment to become self-sustaining.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High satisfaction with TA delivery and responsiveness; Moderate satisfaction with progress on platform development and cross-facility coordination.
planned_adaptations_future: Refocus the resource library on high-value knowledge products, using external benchmarks (e.g., climate-links.org) for quality and quantity.
Simplify coordination goals to prioritize strategic partnerships (e.g., with Nature Facility) over broad "one-stop-shop" ambitions.
Strengthen MEL systems by hiring the PrOF5 role and integrating mandatory feedback into TA workflows.
Enhance FCDO intranet visibility through a dedicated SharePoint page or similar internal platform.
Conduct a final-year workshop to realign consortium and FCDO on priorities for March 2026 closure.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Centre for Delivery’s Solutions Hub Programme

output_1.title: Research Products are conducted with learning available for Programme teams

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme established a 'draw-down support offer' that became in-demand, supplementing the core team with project-funded staff acting as internal consultants. This model combined independence from individual programmes with deep FCDO understanding, exceeding initial expectations for engagement (162 enquiries handled in Year 1).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partner performance was closely monitored and "delivered what was envisioned," managed effectively by the small core team. Expert suppliers produced high-quality research products (11 vs. 10 target) that were integrated into FCDO systems and processes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The Solutions Hub operates within the Centre for Delivery (CfD) with a small core team supplemented by project-funded roles. This structure enabled flexible, demand-driven support while maintaining oversight. Coordination with FCDO’s MEL and systems teams (e.g., Aid Management Platform) was effective, though some outcomes relied on existing CfD data teams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination mechanisms worked well, with the Hub acting as a "critical friend" and safe space for programme teams. The Hub’s intranet page became a central repository for learning products, and cross-team engagement (e.g., with EQUALS service, PDC events) amplified reach. However, bandwidth limitations within FCDO constrained deeper engagement with some research products.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement was effective in engaging expert suppliers for research products (e.g., adaptive MEL, business case reviews). Contracts were managed to deliver 11 research products (exceeding the 10-product target), with outputs shared via the Hub’s intranet and integrated into FCDO guidance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensive during the first 10 months, with close monitoring of partner performance and adaptive management of the draw-down support model. The small team size required efficient prioritisation but allowed for responsive adjustments (e.g., shifting focus to inception-phase support for programmes).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The programme demonstrated high flexibility by adapting to demand (e.g., 162 enquiries handled) and reprioritising research topics based on emerging needs (e.g., adaptive MEL, portfolio learning). The logical framework may be revised in Year 2 to better capture adaptive learning.
adaptive_management_examples: Shifted focus toward **inception-phase support** for programmes after recognising the limitations of influencing design during the Business Case stage.
Developed an **Outcome Confidence Rating (OCR) tool** and embedded it into FCDO’s annual review process, encouraging outcome-focused reflections.
Produced **adaptive programming guidance** (e.g., adaptive annual reviews, results frameworks) in response to demand from MEL advisers, launched at the Evaluation PDC (Dec 2023).
Piloted **portfolio learning analysis** (e.g., scoping paper, PDC session) to address growing interest in PMEL among MEL advisers.

main_implementation_challenges: Limited **bandwidth within FCDO** to engage deeply with research products, despite their value. This required strategic communication planning for Year 2.
Competing **incentives during Business Case development** reduced the Hub’s ability to influence design quality at early stages, prompting a shift to inception-phase support.
Balancing **demand for draw-down support** (162 enquiries) with the small team’s capacity, necessitating prioritisation and potential staffing adjustments in Year 2.
contextual_constraints_new: The **diverse stages of design thinking** (concept note, Business Case, inception) created complexity in targeting interventions effectively. The Hub adapted by focusing on inception-phase support where stakeholder buy-in is higher.
FCDO’s **decentralised structure** (HQ vs. country posts) required tailored engagement strategies to ensure equitable access to the Hub’s services.
capacity_constraints_emerged: The **small core team size** (supplemented by project-funded roles) limited the depth of engagement with all research products, though project-funded roles mitigated this by bringing internal knowledge back to the Hub.
Need for **enhanced communication strategies** to ensure research uptake across directorates, given limited FCDO bandwidth.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: The programme executed its £660,000 budget effectively in Year 1, delivering 11 research products (vs. 10 targeted) and handling 162 enquiries. No over/under-spending was reported. Staffing requirements will be reviewed in Year 2 to ensure adequate resourcing.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High VFM demonstrated through: (1) **Exceeding research targets** (11 products delivered); (2) **High demand for services** (162 enquiries, indicating a filled gap in FCDO support); (3) **Leveraging existing systems** (e.g., AMP, EQUALS) to avoid duplication; (4) **Embedding tools like OCR** into FCDO processes, creating lasting impact beyond the programme’s lifespan.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Financial management was strong, with close monitoring of partner performance and efficient use of project-funded roles. The Hub’s intranet repository centralised learning products, reducing redundant costs for other teams.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiency was achieved by: (1) **Sharing research products** across FCDO to avoid duplicated efforts; (2) **Using project-funded roles** to provide internal consultancy at lower cost than external consultants; (3) **Integrating outputs** (e.g., OCR, adaptive frameworks) into existing FCDO systems (e.g., AMP, annual reviews).
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding materialised through collaboration with the **FCDO EQUALS service**, which funded adaptive programming research products (e.g., good practice notes on adaptive annual reviews).

key_delivery_lessons: The **design phase remains critical**, but interventions are most effective at **inception** (not Business Case stage) due to stakeholder alignment and practical programming realities.
Research products must be paired with **targeted engagement strategies** to overcome FCDO’s limited bandwidth for uptake.
Project-funded roles are a **high-value delivery mechanism**, combining internal knowledge with independence to drive learning back to the Hub.
successful_delivery_practices: The **draw-down support model** successfully met demand (162 enquiries) by offering flexible, tailored advice.
**Integrating tools into FCDO systems** (e.g., OCR in annual reviews) ensured sustainability and scalability.
**Cross-team collaboration** (e.g., with EQUALS, PDC) amplified the reach of learning products.
Using the **intranet as a central repository** improved accessibility and reduced duplication.
management_adaptations_made: Shifted focus from **Business Case stage** to **inception phase** for design support, based on lesson learning.

Adapted delivery priorities to support UK policy equities at UNESCO Executive Boards and global conventions.

main_implementation_challenges: Sustaining high performance amid staffing gaps (e.g., Secretariat coverage during vacancies).

previous_recommendations_progress: Successfully integrated recommendations from prior reviews (e.g., stronger HMG coordination, ODA compliance).

forward_recommendations: Present a detailed business case for 2025+ resourcing, addressing sustainability risks.
Strengthen ties with DBT, DESNZ, and other departments to align with UNESCO’s science/innovation priorities.

Expand ‘teach-in’ initiatives to Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies.

Supported DCMS’s review of the Intangible Cultural Heritage Convention ratification.

innovations_attempted: Adapting global climate adaptation business models to India’s context via commissioned studies.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Delivering the Agriculture Breakthrough – Phase 1

output_1.title: Climate-resilient, sustainable technologies are developed and brought to scale via international science and innovation partnerships

output_2.title: High-impact solutions are developed, tested and scaled, by harnessing digital and innovation and by mobilising increased climate finance

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: No-cost extension approved in September 2024 to align with revised delivery timelines for two key projects (extended to September 2027). Activities under Output 2 were scaled back and migrated to the new SAIDAI programme as part of FCDO’s shift toward fewer, larger platform programmes.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partnerships with the Gates Foundation, IFDC, and Innovate UK progressed well, though initial delays occurred in establishing the UK-Brazil-Africa Climate-Smart Agriculture Partnership. The Gates Foundation co-funded the biofertiliser R&D initiative, and IFDC launched field trials in Tanzania and Zambia. Innovate UK successfully managed competitive calls for the trilateral partnership.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: The programme leveraged FCDO’s Senior Research Fellows for technical expertise, which enhanced proposal reviews and early project outputs. A Technical Advisory Group and Government Officials’ Forum are planned for the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership by March 2025 to improve governance.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Coordination with the Gates Foundation and Innovate UK was effective, particularly in co-designing R&D investments. The Climate Shot Investor Coalition (CLIC) under Output 2 demonstrated strong multi-stakeholder engagement, though its activities were later transitioned to SAIDAI.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Procurement for key partnerships (e.g., IFDC, Innovate UK) was executed as planned, though initial delays in finalising the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership required adaptive management. The no-cost extension mitigated procurement risks by aligning timelines with partner capacities.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Oversight was intensified for high-risk components (e.g., trilateral partnership launch) but remained proportionate to the programme’s moderate risk rating. Senior Research Fellows provided additional rigour in monitoring R&D investments.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: The no-cost extension and migration of Output 2 activities to SAIDAI demonstrate flexibility in adapting to FCDO’s strategic shift toward consolidated platforms. Budget reallocations were made to prioritise high-impact R&D areas like biofertilisers and methane reduction.
adaptive_management_examples: Approved no-cost extension to September 2027 to accommodate delays in two key projects.
Transitioned Output 2 activities to the SAIDAI programme to align with FCDO’s platform consolidation strategy.
Adjusted the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership timeline to capitalise on momentum ahead of COP30 (2025).
Refined portfolio investment criteria for Phase 2 based on lessons from Phase 1, including prioritisation of methane reduction and gene editing technologies.

main_implementation_challenges: Initial delays in establishing delivery mechanisms for the UK-Brazil-Africa Climate-Smart Agriculture Partnership, requiring a no-cost extension.
Need to migrate Output 2 activities to the SAIDAI programme mid-implementation, creating transitional coordination challenges.
Balancing the selection of high-potential R&D areas (e.g., methane reduction, biofertilisers) amid numerous competing priorities identified by experts.
external_factors_impact: Global commitments (e.g., UK’s pledge at the AIM for Climate Summit 2023) accelerated the launch of the IFDC fertiliser evaluation project.
Brazil’s hosting of COP30 in 2025 created an opportunity to scale the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership but also added pressure to align timelines.
contextual_constraints_new: Limited evidence on the cost-effectiveness and socio-economic impacts of post-harvest loss interventions (identified in Output 3 scoping study).
Gaps in data on gendered and environmental outcomes of agricultural technologies, complicating prioritisation for Phase 2.
partner_relationship_issues: Early delays with Innovate UK in finalising the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership’s governance structures (e.g., Technical Advisory Group).
Co-funding negotiations with the Gates Foundation required alignment during annual strategic dialogues, particularly for livestock methane reduction investments.
capacity_constraints_emerged: FCDO’s capacity to manage a dispersed R&D portfolio was stretched, mitigated by leveraging Senior Research Fellows for technical reviews.
Partner governments in Ghana and Nigeria required additional support to engage in the trilateral partnership, prompting the creation of the Government Officials’ Forum.
risk_materialization: Delays in partner mobilisation (UK-Brazil-Africa partnership) materialised as planned risks, addressed via the no-cost extension.
Moderate risk of portfolio overcommitment due to the high number of thematic priorities (e.g., crop improvement, alternative proteins), managed by refining Phase 2 investment criteria.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track overall, with a no-cost extension approved to September 2027 to accommodate delayed project timelines. Budget reallocations were made to prioritise high-impact areas (e.g., biofertilisers, SAIDAI transition).
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: High potential for VFM demonstrated in priority investments (e.g., biofertiliser R&D, UK-Brazil-Africa partnership), though full VFM will be assessed in Phase 2 as outputs scale. The migration to larger platforms (SAIDAI) aims to improve efficiency by reducing transaction costs.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: Strong financial management by FCDO and partners (e.g., Innovate UK, IFDC). The no-cost extension was justified by robust monitoring of project lifespans and alignment with partner capacities.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Cost efficiencies realised through consolidated platforms (SAIDAI) and co-funding (e.g., Gates Foundation contributions to biofertiliser R&D). However, upfront costs for farmers adopting new technologies (e.g., enhanced fertilisers) remain a challenge for scalability.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Co-funding from the Gates Foundation materialised as planned, including £197,000 for AgBase and joint investments in livestock methane reduction. Additional co-funding is expected for Phase 2.

key_delivery_lessons: The value of FCDO’s Senior Research Fellows in providing technical rigour for R&D portfolio management, particularly in prioritising investments.
Importance of flexible delivery models (e.g., no-cost extensions, platform consolidation) to adapt to emerging priorities and partner capacities.
Need for stronger evidence on cost-effectiveness and socio-economic impacts of interventions (e.g., post-harvest loss, fertilisers) to guide Phase 2 investments.
successful_delivery_practices: Co-design of R&D investments with the Gates Foundation and Innovate UK, leveraging their technical and regional expertise.
Use of competitive calls (e.g., UK-Brazil-Africa partnership) to ensure high-quality, demand-driven proposals.
Strategic alignment with global commitments (e.g., AIM for Climate) to accelerate project launch and visibility.
management_adaptations_made: Transitioned Output 2 activities to the SAIDAI programme to align with FCDO’s platform consolidation strategy.
Extended programme timeline to September 2027 to accommodate partner delays and maximise impact ahead of COP30.
Planned establishment of a Technical Advisory Group and Government Officials’ Forum to improve trilateral partnership governance.
innovations_attempted: Launch of the biofertiliser R&D initiative with the Gates Foundation to validate nitrogen-fixing bacteria for small-scale farmers.
Pilot of enhanced efficiency fertilisers in Tanzania and Zambia, combining lab/field trials with farmer decision-making support.
Development of the SAIDAI programme as an integrated innovation and investment platform for agriculture.
previous_recommendations_progress: Completed: Secured no-cost extension to September 2027 (recommended in 2024).
In progress: Finalising co-investments with the Gates Foundation for livestock methane reduction (target: February 2025).
In progress: Establishing governance structures for the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership (target: March 2025).
forward_recommendations: Submit Phase 2 business case (‘Innovation to Unlock a Sustainable Food Secure Future’) by autumn 2025, focusing on scaling successful Phase 1 mechanisms.
Refresh the programme Theory of Change and logframe by summer 2025 to reflect the extended timeline and Phase 2 priorities.
Prepare a cost extension for the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership to capitalise on COP30 momentum (target: March 2025).
Address evidence gaps on post-harvest loss interventions and socio-economic impacts to inform Phase 2 investments.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Effective in mitigating delays (e.g., no-cost extension) and portfolio risks (e.g., refining Phase 2 criteria). However, moderate risks persist due to the complexity of trilateral partnerships and the need for stronger cost-benefit data.

outcomes_impact_for_qca.beneficiaries_reached_actual: Initial beneficiaries include small-scale farmers in Tanzania and Zambia (IFDC fertiliser trials) and researchers in Ghana/Nigeria (UK-Brazil-Africa partnership). Full reach will be assessed in Phase 2 as SAIDAI and other platforms scale.
policy_influence_achieved: Fulfilment of UK’s commitment at the AIM for Climate Summit 2023 through the IFDC fertiliser project.
Alignment with Brazil’s COP30 priorities via the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership, positioning FCDO as a key partner in climate-smart agriculture.
capacity_building_results: Strengthened R&D capacities in partner countries (e.g., trilateral research initiatives in Ghana/Nigeria).
Knowledge sharing through the Climate Shot Investor Coalition and SAIDAI platform.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Accelerated adoption of enhanced efficiency fertilisers in Tanzania/Zambia may reduce greenhouse gas emissions beyond initial targets.
Negative: Risk of excluding smaller farmers if upfront costs of new technologies (e.g., biofertilisers) are not subsidised.
scalability_evidence: Strong scalability potential for the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership, given its alignment with COP30 and Brazil’s leadership in climate-smart agriculture.
SAIDAI programme designed as a scalable platform for digital/innovation investments in agriculture.
Biofertiliser and methane reduction technologies have global applicability, with Phase 2 planned to expand geographic focus.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Phase 1 has successfully established high-impact partnerships (e.g., Gates Foundation, UK-Brazil-Africa) and laid the groundwork for Phase 2 (‘Innovation to Unlock a Sustainable Food Secure Future’). The programme will transition into a larger, consolidated platform to scale proven mechanisms and address the triple challenge of food insecurity, climate change, and biodiversity loss.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High – The shift to fewer, larger platforms (SAIDAI) and strengthened partnerships (e.g., Innovate UK, Gates Foundation) improves long-term sustainability. The no-cost extension ensures continuity during the transition to Phase 2.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Development and submission of the Phase 2 business case by autumn 2025, with a focus on scaling R&D investments and climate finance mechanisms.
Expansion of the UK-Brazil-Africa partnership ahead of COP30, including new competitive calls for trilateral research.
Integration of lessons on post-harvest loss and cost-effectiveness into Phase 2 portfolio criteria.
Enhanced monitoring of socio-economic and gendered impacts to address evidence gaps identified in Phase 1.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Data for Development - Unleashing the Data Dividend

output_6.title: Bringing partners together to maximise impact

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: Programme adopted a novel approach by bringing six implementing partners under one business case, with coordinated governance and quarterly meetings chaired by FCDO. This represents a shift from traditional single-partner delivery models.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners demonstrated strong alignment through agreed ways of working, including: common outcomes/impacts, non-duplicative geographic work, evidence-sharing, and joint problem-solving. Early results were presented based on initial funding tranches. PARIS21 and UNSD showed concrete outputs (e.g., NSDS support in 14 countries, Data for Now initiatives in 10 member states).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: FCDO chairs quarterly partner meetings (Feb/Mar, May/Jun, Sep, Dec) with structured agendas for trend analysis, joint problem-solving, and collaboration. Memorandums of Understanding signed with all six partners, plus an Administrative Arrangement with the World Bank for the Global Data Facility. Decision-making for Phase 2 transition was internally agreed.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Highly effective coordination mechanisms established, including: 1) Quarterly meetings with pre-agreed agendas; 2) Shared communication platform; 3) Common Theory of Change and logframe; 4) Joint risk management approach. Partners proactively shared lessons and promoted complementary work (e.g., UNSD and UNESCAP collaborating in Bangladesh/Indonesia).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: Due diligence completed for Flowminder, WorldPop, and UNSD; other partners used existing FCDO assessments. Funding arrangements were finalized based on workplans and fund availability. Additional £250,000 secured from FCDO Americas Directorate for Caribbean activities under the Global Data Facility.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Higher than typical for inception phase: FCDO conducted quarterly reviews, established a common VFM tracking framework, and required partners to submit evidence of results from initial funding. Risk assessments were jointly conducted by all partners.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme demonstrated flexibility by: 1) Adjusting meeting schedules to align with partner availability (e.g., UN Statistical Commission timing); 2) Securing additional funding for Caribbean-specific activities; 3) Allowing partners to present emerging challenges for collective problem-solving.
adaptive_management_examples: Added £250,000 from FCDO Americas Directorate to support Caribbean activities under the Global Data Facility, responding to regional needs.
Developed a 'delivery chain mapping' tool to visualize partner roles and avoid duplication, with quarterly reporting.
Established a common approach to risk management after identifying shared risks during inception.
Adjusted technical support in Sierra Leone to include high-level government engagement after initial workshops revealed ownership gaps.

main_implementation_challenges: Technical infrastructure failures (e.g., undersea cable breakage in Ghana) disrupted data availability for Flowminder, risking delays in call detail record-based products.
Fundraising challenges for one partner threatened staff retention, requiring FCDO intervention to stabilize operations.
Coordinating six diverse partners with distinct mandates (e.g., GPSDD’s network focus vs. PARIS21’s NSO capacity-building) required intensive alignment efforts.
external_factors_impact: Geopolitical tensions (unspecified) influenced partner operations in certain regions, though no major disruptions were reported.
Post-COVID recovery prioritized by some governments (e.g., Sierra Leone, Kenya) created demand for administrative data systems, aligning with programme goals but requiring rapid adaptation.
contextual_constraints_new: Unanticipated IT infrastructure limitations in partner countries (e.g., Jordan’s NSO) slowed digital upgrades, requiring phased interventions.
Regulatory barriers to data-sharing (e.g., Morocco, Indonesia) emerged as significant hurdles, necessitating high-level advocacy and roadmap development.
Civil society engagement in fragile states (e.g., Kyrgyzstan, State of Palestine) proved more complex than anticipated, requiring tailored approaches to citizen data inclusion.
partner_relationship_issues: Initial misalignment in partner expectations around joint storytelling and evidence-sharing was resolved through structured quarterly meetings.
Competing priorities among partners (e.g., GPSDD’s global advocacy vs. PARIS21’s country-level NSDS support) required explicit complementarity agreements.
capacity_constraints_emerged: Limited NSO capacity in Small Island Developing States (e.g., Kiribati, Grenada) to absorb technical support, leading to adjusted timelines.
Gaps in partner staff expertise on emerging technologies (e.g., AI for poverty estimation in Bangladesh) prompted cross-partner training initiatives.
FCDO’s own capacity to manage six simultaneous partnerships required streamlined reporting and delegation to partner leads.
risk_materialization: Risk D2 (inability to raise co-funding) materialized for one partner, addressed via FCDO bridge funding.
Technical risks (data unavailability due to infrastructure failures) materialized in Ghana, mitigated through contingency planning.
Regulatory risks (data-sharing laws) materialized in multiple countries, requiring adaptive legal support.

financial_delivery_performance.budget_execution_vs_plan: On track for Phase 1. As of 31 March 2024, expenditure aligned with workplans. Additional £250,000 secured from FCDO Americas Directorate for Caribbean activities, exceeding original Phase 1 allocations in that region.
financial_delivery_performance.value_for_money_assessment: Early indicators suggest strong VFM: 1) Economy: Partners committed to tracking cost-saving indicators (e.g., shared platforms, joint missions); 2) Efficiency: Quarterly coordination reduced duplication (e.g., UNSD/UNESCAP collaboration in Indonesia); 3) Effectiveness: Outputs like Sierra Leone’s administrative data roadmap demonstrate high impact per pound spent. Full VFM evaluation planned for Phase 2 with £50,000 allocated.
financial_delivery_performance.financial_management_quality: High. All partners completed due diligence (new assessments for Flowminder, WorldPop, UNSD; existing assessments for others). Memorandums of Understanding and Administrative Arrangements (e.g., with World Bank) were signed. Financial reporting systems established for quarterly updates.
financial_delivery_performance.cost_efficiency_achieved: Evidence of efficiency gains: 1) Shared communication platform reduced coordination costs; 2) Joint workshops (e.g., gender statistics in Kenya/Rwanda) leveraged economies of scale; 3) Cross-partner collaborations (e.g., UNSD/UNESCAP in Bangladesh) avoided redundant technical support.
financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Partial. While the programme secured additional £250,000 from FCDO Americas, one partner faced challenges raising external funds, requiring FCDO intervention. Co-funding remains a risk for Phase 2.

key_delivery_lessons: Multi-partner programmes require intensive upfront alignment on outcomes, risks, and ways of working to avoid fragmentation.
Quarterly meetings with structured agendas (trend analysis, problem-solving, collaboration) are critical for maintaining coherence among diverse partners.
Flexible funding mechanisms (e.g., additional FCDO Americas support) enable responsive programming but require clear governance.
successful_delivery_practices: Theory of Change co-creation with partners ensured buy-in and aligned activities with high-level outcomes.
Delivery chain mapping tool improved transparency and reduced duplication across geographies/themes.
Joint high-level events (e.g., Sierra Leone administrative data workshop) accelerated government ownership and cross-sectoral buy-in.
Partner-led 'big moment sharing' in quarterly meetings facilitated rapid knowledge exchange (e.g., lessons from Jordan’s IT upgrades).
management_adaptations_made: Shifted from output-based to partnership-cohesion scoring for the inception phase, recognizing the need to measure collaboration before tangible outputs.
Added a common VFM framework with economy/efficiency/effectiveness indicators to standardize partner reporting.
Established a qualitative 'outcome storyline' approach to complement quantitative metrics, addressing early evidence gaps.
innovations_attempted: Pilot of citizen-generated data inclusion in Kyrgyzstan’s 2025 Voluntary National Review, combining NSO and civil society inputs.
Use of mobile phone data for internal migration tracking in Tunisia (exploratory phase).
AI-assisted poverty estimation in Bangladesh using geospatial data, implemented jointly by UNSD and UNESCAP.
Register-based census methods in Indonesia to reduce costs and improve timeliness.
forward_recommendations: Conduct a mid-Phase 1 review to assess partner collaboration effectiveness and adjust governance structures if needed.
Develop a partner performance dashboard to track contributions to shared outcomes, not just individual outputs.
Explore mechanisms to incentivize co-funding, such as match-funding challenges or donor coordination platforms.
Invest in a central knowledge management system to capture and disseminate lessons across partners.
Prioritize regulatory environment assessments in Phase 2 countries to preempt data-sharing barriers.
learning_adaptation_recommendations.risk_management_effectiveness: Highly effective during inception. The joint risk assessment process identified shared risks (e.g., co-funding, data infrastructure) and assigned mitigation owners. The quarterly meetings included risk updates, enabling proactive responses (e.g., FCDO’s intervention for the partner facing fundraising challenges). Risk D2’s materialization was swiftly addressed, demonstrating adaptive capacity.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.direct: National Statistics Offices in 14+ countries (Somalia, Rwanda, Botswana, Malawi, Mozambique, Senegal, Kenya, Maldives, Kiribati, Bhutan, Paraguay, Belize, Grenada, Saint Lucia) received technical support. Additional beneficiaries include civil society organizations in Kyrgyzstan and government agencies in Sierra Leone.
beneficiaries_reached_actual.indirect: Global Partnership for Sustainable Development Data’s network of 700+ partners and participants in high-level events (e.g., UN Statistical Commission side events).

policy_influence_achieved: Kenya’s first evidence-based Voluntary National Review report developed with PARIS21 support.
Sierra Leone’s administrative data-sharing roadmap endorsed by the Minister of Planning and Economic Development and Ministry of Finance.
Indonesia’s regulatory adjustments for register-based census initiated following UNSD/UNESCAP workshops.
SDG 11 indicators developed or advanced in Jordan, Morocco, State of Palestine, and Tunisia, with potential for replication.
capacity_building_results: PARIS21 trained UN ESCAP staff on supporting National Strategies for the Development of Statistics (NSDS), expanding regional capacity.
UNSD’s support to Bangladesh on geospatial AI for poverty estimation built NSO technical skills in advanced analytics.
Kyrgyzstan’s NSO and civil society organizations gained experience in citizen-generated data through joint workshops.
Somalia’s second NSDS designed with PARIS21 assistance, strengthening long-term statistical planning.
unintended_consequences: Positive: Cross-partner collaborations (e.g., UNSD/UNESCAP in Bangladesh) created models for future joint initiatives beyond the programme’s original scope.
Negative: In Ghana, technical infrastructure failures delayed Flowminder’s work, highlighting vulnerabilities in data-reliant programmes in fragile contexts.
scalability_evidence: The programme’s partnership model (six implementers under one business case) is being considered for replication in other FCDO data initiatives.
Approaches like Sierra Leone’s administrative data roadmap and Indonesia’s register-based census have attracted interest from other countries (e.g., Tunisia exploring mobile phone data).
The Global Data Facility’s expansion into the Caribbean (via additional FCDO funding) demonstrates adaptability to new regions.

programme_continuation_trajectory.continuation_rationale: Strong inception phase performance (Overall Output Score: A, Risk Rating: Minor) justified continuation. Key factors: 1) Effective partner coordination and early results (e.g., NSDS support, Data for Now initiatives); 2) High demand for data systems strengthening aligned with SDGs; 3) FCDO’s strategic priority to position the UK as a global data leader; 4) Adaptive management demonstrated through risk responses and funding flexibility.
programme_continuation_trajectory.delivery_model_sustainability: High. The multi-partner model has proven effective in leveraging complementary strengths (e.g., GPSDD’s advocacy + PARIS21’s NSO focus). Quarterly governance mechanisms and shared risk management enhance long-term viability. However, co-funding challenges require monitoring.
programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Phase 2 will include an independent evaluation (£50,000 allocated) to assess the partnership model’s effectiveness and Theory of Change validity.
Expanded focus on regulatory environments to preempt data-sharing barriers encountered in Phase 1.
Enhanced monitoring of co-funding targets to reduce dependency on FCDO bridge funding.
Potential scaling of successful pilots (e.g., citizen-generated data in Kyrgyzstan, AI poverty estimation in Bangladesh) to additional countries.
Strengthened knowledge-sharing platforms to disseminate lessons from quarterly meetings and partner innovations.

programme_metadata.programme_title: Race to Resilience Programme

output_1.title: RtR metrics are strengthened and used by RtR partners to transparently and consistently report robust data on progress to build resilience

delivery_implementation_vs_plans.delivery_model_changes: The programme is delivered by the Climate Champions Team (CCT) under UNFCCC, administratively managed by Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors (RPA) rather than establishing a new legal entity. This leverages existing UNFCCC/RPA infrastructure for efficiency.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.partner_performance_reality: Partners exceeded expectations in submitting Pledges (86% vs 60% target) and Plans (72%), but 24% are ready for the 'Proceed' stage (vs 20% baseline). Capacity constraints (especially in Global South/SMEs) emerged as a barrier to full engagement, requiring streamlined reporting and capacity-building support.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.management_structure_actual: CCT operates as a special UNFCCC programme with lean governance: 3 FTEs handle fundraising, grants, finance, HR, and recruitment. Administrative overhead is 6% (vs 13% for UNOPS), with RPA serving as fiduciary/legal host. Decision-making is decentralized across sectoral/regional teams.
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.coordination_effectiveness: Effective coordination through existing UNFCCC mechanisms (e.g., Resilience Hub at COP) and partner networks (36 initiatives, 600+ members). However, harmonization of metrics across partners remains a challenge, requiring alignment with other initiatives (e.g., UNFCCC GCAP).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.procurement_implementation: No standalone procurement; leverages existing CCT contracts with professional services (e.g., BCG, Arup, PwC, WRI) for technical support. Cost savings achieved via "piggybacking" on partner events/venues (estimated £50,000 saved in 2023).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.oversight_intensity_actual: Lighter-touch oversight than planned due to high partner engagement (86% reporting) and CCT’s adaptive management (e.g., Q&A sessions, 1:1 support). Risk of under-monitoring 'Proceed' stage implementation, now being addressed via pilot testing (Q4 2024–H1 2025).
delivery_implementation_vs_plans.flexibility_utilization: Programme adapted to partner feedback by reducing reporting burdens (e.g., new pathways for partners unable to quantify beneficiaries) and delaying finance-mobilization milestones (Call for Collaboration established in Year 1 instead of tracking £100M target).
adaptive_management_examples: Developed a new reporting pathway for partners with MEL capacity constraints.
Postponed finance-mobilization tracking until Call for Collaboration framework was operational (7 partners now engaged).
Piloting 'Proceed' stage tools with 5–7 partners before full rollout.
Streamlined metrics surveys and increased capacity-building sessions based on partner consultations.

main_implementation_challenges: Partner capacity constraints (especially Global South/SMEs) created barriers to meeting reporting requirements, risking disengagement.
Harmonizing impact measurement methods across 600+ partners proved complex, with no standardized approach for calculating beneficiaries reached.
Shift from pledges/plans ('rhetoric') to on-the-ground implementation ('Proceed' stage) requires new monitoring tools and partner support mechanisms.
Adaptation finance mobilization indicators were initially misaligned with CCT’s sphere of influence (direct mobilization vs. facilitating collaborations).
external_factors_impact: Global economic pressures may affect partners’ ability to secure co-funding for resilience actions.
UNFCCC policy shifts (e.g., Global Goal on Adaptation) required RtR to align metrics frameworks with emerging international standards.
COP28 priorities influenced campaign messaging and partner engagement strategies.
contextual_constraints_new: The 'Proceed' stage (implementation tracking) was not fully anticipated in the original logframe, requiring new indicators and baselines (e.g., 58% of SAA solutions reported quantitative data in 2023).
Partner classification system changes disrupted outcome measurement continuity.
Limited pre-existing tools for tracking NSA-led adaptation actions at scale.
partner_relationship_issues: Some partners perceived reporting requirements as burdensome without clear direct benefits (e.g., data transparency, advocacy use).
Smaller organizations struggled with metrics complexity, requiring tailored support (e.g., 1:1 sessions, simplified tools).
Delays in clarifying the value proposition for partners (e.g., how RtR data would support their own goals).
capacity_constraints_emerged: Only 24% of partners are ready for the 'Proceed' stage, highlighting gaps in MEL (Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning) capacities.
CCT’s technical secretariat required additional resources to co-develop reporting tools with partners.
Regional disparities in partner capabilities (e.g., African vs. European NSAs) necessitated differentiated support.
risk_materialization: Risk of partner disengagement due to reporting burdens (mitigated via streamlined tools and capacity-building).
Risk of misaligned finance-mobilization targets (mitigated by revising Outcome 3 indicators to focus on Call for Collaboration activities).
Risk of weak evidence for on-the-ground impact (being addressed via 'Proceed' stage pilots).

cost_efficiency.comparison: Significantly lower than UNOPS (13%) or New Venture Foundation (7%).
savings_examples: £50,000 saved via partner venue sharing and clustered travel.
No new legal entity setup costs (leveraged RPA’s existing infrastructure).

resource_leverage.partner_contributions: Utilized COP Presidencies’ resources and partner networks for events/comms.
resource_leverage.professional_services: Shared costs across CCT programs (e.g., BCG for SAA thought leadership, Arup for metrics framework).

value_for_money_assessment.vfm_versus_business_case: Exceeds expectations: Lower overheads and higher-than-planned partner engagement (86% reporting vs 60% target) achieved with 30% of RtR budget.

financial_management_quality.systems: RPA provides fiduciary, legal, and administrative hosting with robust controls (6% overhead).
financial_management_quality.transparency: Detailed cost breakdowns provided; no audit findings reported.
financial_management_quality.risk_management: Risk register updated to monitor metrics reporting engagement (post-September 2024).

cost_efficiency_achieved.staffing: Remote work model minimized office costs (£49K for 100+ staff).
cost_efficiency_achieved.procurement: Negotiated discounts with professional services firms (e.g., Accenture for SAA Water Task Force).
cost_efficiency_achieved.shared_resources: CCT’s embedded teams (e.g., finance, regional) reduce duplication.

financial_delivery_performance.co_funding_materialization: Not explicitly reported; Call for Collaboration (7 partners) may attract future co-funding.

key_delivery_lessons: Partner-centric design is critical: Reporting tools must balance rigor with feasibility, especially for resource-constrained NSAs.
Phased implementation works: Piloting 'Proceed' stage with 5–7 partners mitigates risks before scaling.
Flexible milestones are necessary: Finance-mobilization targets were revised when the Call for Collaboration setup took precedence.
Data transparency drives engagement: Partners are more likely to report when they see direct benefits (e.g., advocacy materials, peer learning).
successful_delivery_practices: Q&A sessions and 1:1 support improved partner reporting rates (86% vs 60% target).
Leveraging existing platforms (e.g., Resilience Hub at COP) reduced event costs and amplified reach.
Embedding RtR within CCT’s broader systems transformation teams created synergies (e.g., shared metrics with SAA).
Remote work model with minimal overhead (6%) maximized budget for programmatic activities.
management_adaptations_made: Added capacity-building sessions to address partner MEL gaps.
Developed a simplified reporting pathway for partners unable to quantify beneficiaries.
Revised Outcome 3 indicators to focus on Call for Collaboration activities (not direct finance mobilization).
Planned logframe updates (by Sept 2024) to align outcomes/outputs with partner capabilities.
innovations_attempted: Data Explorer tool (under development) to improve transparency and peer-to-peer learning.
Solution Stories published to showcase partner actions and attract new members.
Metrics framework alignment with UAE Global Resilience Framework to enhance global policy relevance.

forward_recommendations.action: Reduce and streamline partner reporting burdens by: 1) Increasing capacity-building sessions, 2) Aligning metrics with other initiatives, 3) Harmonizing impact calculation methods.
Improve data transparency by: 1) Transforming aggregated data into advocacy materials, 2) Enhancing Data Explorer tool usability, 3) Promoting data sharing among partners.
Update the logframe and risk register to: 1) Align outcomes/outputs with partner capacities, 2) Revise finance-mobilization indicators, 3) Monitor metrics reporting engagement.
Pilot the 'Proceed' stage reporting tools with 5–7 partners before full rollout in 2025.

proactive_measures: Early identification of partner capacity risks led to tailored support (e.g., 1:1 sessions).
Revised Outcome 3 indicators to focus on achievable activities (Call for Collaboration).
gaps: Underestimated the complexity of harmonizing impact measurement across diverse partners.
Initial logframe did not anticipate the 'Proceed' stage monitoring needs.
adaptations: Added risk register updates to track metrics reporting engagement (post-Sept 2024).
Increased oversight of 'Proceed' stage pilots to mitigate implementation risks.

beneficiaries_reached_actual.evidence: 86% of partners submitted pledges (covering unspecified populations); 24% ready for 'Proceed' stage (implementation tracking).

policy_influence_achieved: RtR metrics framework featured in UAE Global Resilience Framework submissions (2023).
Solution Stories and Progress Reports used in UNFCCC Yearbook of Global Climate Action.
Resilience Hub at COP amplified NSA voices in UNFCCC negotiations.
capacity_building_results: 24% of partners advanced to 'Proceed' stage (vs 20% baseline), with technical secretariat support.
Metrics onboarding sessions reached new partners (4 sessions in 2024).
Q&A sessions and 1:1 support improved partner reporting capabilities (e.g., 9% increase in pledges submitted).

unintended_consequences.description: RtR’s metrics framework became a de facto standard for NSA adaptation reporting, adopted by other initiatives (e.g., SAA Task Forces).
Reporting burdens risked excluding smaller NSAs, though mitigated by streamlined tools.

scalability_evidence: Partner network grew from launch to 36 initiatives/600+ members, demonstrating scalability of the campaign model.
Metrics framework adoption by external platforms (e.g., UNFCCC GCAP) suggests potential for broader use.
Call for Collaboration (7 partners) could expand to mobilize more private finance for adaptation.

continuation_rationale: Year 1 exceeded output targets (A+ score) with strong partner engagement (86% reporting).
Shift to 'Proceed' stage (implementation focus) aligns with FCDO’s emphasis on tangible resilience actions.
Policy influence (e.g., UAE Global Resilience Framework) and scalability (36 partner initiatives) justify continued investment.
Low risk rating ('Minor') and efficient delivery model (6% overhead) demonstrate value for money.

strengths: Lean administrative structure (RPA hosting at 6% overhead).
Embedded within UNFCCC/CCT ecosystems ensures long-term institutional support.
Partner co-funding potential via Call for Collaboration.
risks: Dependence on partner capacities for 'Proceed' stage success.
Need for continued alignment with evolving UNFCCC adaptation frameworks.

programme_continuation_trajectory.fcdo_satisfaction_level: High
planned_adaptations_future: Update logframe and risk register by Sept 2024 to reflect 'Proceed' stage indicators.
Enhance Data Explorer tool and transparency of partner data (early 2025).
Expand capacity-building for Global South partners to improve 'Proceed' stage readiness.
Monitor finance-mobilization via Call for Collaboration (7 partners) as a proxy for Outcome 3.
